The nine periods and their boundaries

Every date in Greek history before about 500 BC is a convention agreed by modern scholars, and most of the period names are modern too. "Minoan" was coined by Arthur Evans after 1900, "Mycenaean" came into use after Schliemann's excavations of 1876, "Hellenistic" was Droysen's invention of 1836, and "Dark Age" is a label that many archaeologists now avoid. The boundaries below are the ones used in most current handbooks; where a boundary is genuinely contested, the table says so.

PeriodConventional rangeDefining marker
Early Bronze Age (Early Minoan / Early Helladic)c. 3100–2000 BCMetal-using villages; Cycladic figurines; no palaces yet
Minoan palatial Cretec. 1950–1450 BCFirst palaces c. 1950; Neopalatial peak c. 1700–1450; Linear A
Mycenaeanc. 1600–1100 BCShaft Graves c. 1600; mainland palaces c. 1400–1200; Linear B Greek
Bronze Age collapsec. 1200–1150 BCPalaces burn; writing lost; population falls
Early Iron Age ("Dark Age")c. 1100–800 BCProtogeometric and Geometric pottery; iron; small communities
Archaicc. 800 (or 776) – 480 BCAlphabet, Homer, polis, colonisation, tyrants, lawgivers
Classical480–323 BCFrom the Persian invasion to the death of Alexander
Hellenistic323–31/30 BCSuccessor kingdoms; ends with Actium and the fall of Ptolemaic Egypt
Roman Greece146 BC (or 27 BC) – AD 330Sack of Corinth; province of Achaea; ends with the founding of Constantinople
Late AntiqueAD 330–529Christian empire; pagan schools close; Justinian's edict

Two boundaries deserve a note. The Archaic period has no agreed start: some books begin it at 800 with the alphabet, others at the traditional first Olympiad in 776, others at 750 with the first colonies. And "Roman Greece" has two possible beginnings, because Rome destroyed Corinth and took effective control in 146 BC but did not organise the province of Achaea until Augustus in 27 BC.

Where sources disagree. The term "Dark Age" comes from Anthony Snodgrass's 1971 book and reflects the loss of writing, monumental building and figurative art between c. 1100 and 800. Since the discovery of the Lefkandi "heroön" on Euboea (c. 950 BC, with gold, Near Eastern imports and horse burials), many scholars argue the darkness was uneven and prefer the neutral "Early Iron Age". Both terms remain in use.

The anchor dates: a list to copy out

Fifteen dates. The first two are approximate; everything from 776 is a traditional or recorded date. The year 594/3 is written that way because the Athenian year began in midsummer and straddles two of ours.

DateEventWhy it matters
c. 1450 BCMycenaean Greeks take over KnossosGreek-speakers inherit Minoan palace culture; Linear B begins recording Greek.
c. 1200 BCDestruction of the Mycenaean palacesWriting, kingship and long-distance trade vanish for three centuries; the world Homer half-remembers ends here.
776 BCFirst Olympiad (traditional)The Greeks' own year zero; later historians counted everything from it.
c. 750–700 BCAlphabet in use; Homer's poems take shape; colonisation beginsGreek literacy, literature and the Mediterranean-wide Greek world all start in one generation.
594/3 BCSolon archon at AthensDebt cancellation and a written constitution: the first step toward Athenian democracy.
508/7 BCCleisthenes reforms AthensThe ten tribes and the Council of 500 create the machinery of democracy.
490 BCMarathonAthens alone defeats a Persian expeditionary force and acquires a founding myth.
480 BCThermopylae and SalamisXerxes' invasion is turned back at sea; Plataea in 479 finishes the land war.
431 BCPeloponnesian War beginsAthens against Sparta for twenty-seven years; Thucydides' subject.
404 BCAthens surrendersThe Athenian empire ends; Sparta's hegemony begins and quickly fails.
399 BCExecution of SocratesThe democracy's most famous act of intolerance; Plato's life's work begins.
338 BCChaeroneaPhilip II of Macedon defeats Athens and Thebes; the independent polis is finished as a great power.
323 BCDeath of Alexander at BabylonHis generals carve up the empire; the Hellenistic kingdoms are born.
146 BCRome destroys CorinthMainland Greece passes under permanent Roman control.
31 BCActiumOctavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra; the last Greek kingdom falls the next year.
AD 529Justinian bans pagan teachingThe Platonic school at Athens stops; the conventional end of ancient Greek thought.

Bronze Age: Crete and the mainland

Minoan Crete is the first literate, urban civilisation on European soil. Evans divided its pottery into Early, Middle and Late Minoan (EM, MM, LM), each with subdivisions; Nikolaos Platon later proposed an alternative scheme based on the palaces (Prepalatial, Protopalatial, Neopalatial, Postpalatial). Both systems are still in use, and the relationship between them is approximate. The first palaces at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia rise around 1950 BC; after a destruction around 1700 they are rebuilt larger, and the Neopalatial period (c. 1700–1450) is the age of the frescoes, the bull-leaping, Linear A, and the Theran town at Akrotiri buried by the volcano. Around 1450 almost every Cretan site except Knossos is destroyed, and Knossos itself begins producing documents in Linear B, which Michael Ventris showed in 1952 to be Greek. The simplest explanation is a mainland takeover.

The mainland Mycenaeans first appear as a wealthy warrior elite in the Shaft Graves at Mycenae (c. 1600 BC), whose gold masks Schliemann wrongly attributed to Agamemnon. Palaces follow at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes and elsewhere around 1400. The Linear B tablets are bureaucratic inventories, not literature, but they give us the king (wanax), the gods (Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Dionysus, Athena all appear) and the Pylos coast-watchers of the final year. Hittite letters refer to a kingdom of Ahhiyawa, which most scholars take to be Achaea, a Mycenaean power active in western Anatolia.

Where sources disagree. Whether Ahhiyawa is Mycenaean Greece is argued from the Tawagalawa Letter and related Hittite texts. The identification is accepted by most Hittitologists and Aegean prehistorians but remains an inference; no Mycenaean text names a kingdom at all.

Collapse and the Early Iron Age

Between about 1225 (Thebes) and 1180 (Pylos) the palaces burn. Mycenae and Tiryns fall around 1200, are partly reoccupied, and decline. Linear B stops. Settlement numbers across the Peloponnese fall by something like two thirds over the next century. The pottery phase LH IIIC (c. 1190–1050) is a long, uneven afterglow, with some sites (Tiryns, Lefkandi, Perati) thriving briefly, and then Submycenaean and Protogeometric wares mark the Early Iron Age proper.

The Greeks remembered this as migration. Thucydides 1.12 says that after Troy the Boeotians settled Boeotia in the sixtieth year and the Dorians took the Peloponnese in the eightieth; Herodotus 1.56 traces the Dorians through Pindus and Doris. The "Dorian invasion" dominated nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century explanations and is now almost universally dropped as a cause, because there is no archaeological signature of a new population. What replaced it is discussed below.

Recovery is visible from about 950 (Lefkandi), accelerates after 900 (Geometric pottery, the Athenian Kerameikos), and by 800–750 the Greeks are trading with Phoenicians at Al Mina and on Euboea, adopting the Phoenician alphabet, founding Pithekoussai on Ischia (c. 770) and Cumae, and then Naxos, Syracuse (734/3) and the rest. Thucydides 6.3–5 gives foundation dates for the Sicilian colonies counted backwards from their later history; they are the earliest Greek dates with any claim to precision.

Archaic and Classical

The Archaic centuries build every institution the Classical world inherits. Hesiod, writing around 700, mentions competing at funeral games for Amphidamas of Chalcis (Works and Days 654–659), which ties him to the Lelantine War, the first war Greeks remembered. Lawgivers (Zaleucus at Locri, Draco at Athens c. 621, Solon in 594/3), tyrants (Cypselus at Corinth c. 657, Peisistratus at Athens 546–527), hoplite warfare, temples in stone, and the Panhellenic sanctuaries at Olympia, Delphi, Isthmia and Nemea all belong here. Sparta's peculiar constitution forms in the seventh and sixth centuries; the Athenian democracy is created in 508/7.

The Classical period is bracketed by Persia and Macedon. Herodotus is the source for 490–479; Thucydides for 431–411; Xenophon's Hellenica carries the story to 362. Within it: the Athenian empire and Pericles (Parthenon begun 447), the plague of 430, Sicily 415–413, the oligarchic coups of 411 and 404, the Theban ascendancy after Leuctra (371), and Philip's victory at Chaeronea in 338. Alexander crosses to Asia in 334, wins at Granicus, Issus (333) and Gaugamela (331), reaches the Indus and dies at Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323; the date is fixed by a Babylonian astronomical diary, which makes it the most securely dated event in Greek history before the Roman period.

Hellenistic to Late Antique

From 323 the story is dynastic. The Wars of the Successors end at Ipsus (301) and Corupedium (281), leaving three major kingdoms: Antigonid Macedon, Seleucid Asia and Ptolemaic Egypt. Greek becomes the common language from the Adriatic to Afghanistan; Alexandria, with its Library, replaces Athens as the intellectual capital. Rome arrives through the Macedonian Wars (Cynoscephalae 197, Pydna 168) and destroys Corinth in 146, the same year it destroys Carthage. Athens is sacked by Sulla in 86 BC after backing Mithridates. Actium (31) and the deaths of Antony and Cleopatra (30) remove the last Greek monarchy.

Under Rome, Greece is a cultural province: Hadrian completes the Olympieion at Athens (AD 131/2), Pausanias writes his guidebook around 150–180, and the Second Sophistic revives Attic prose. The Herulian sack of Athens in AD 267 is the first serious blow. Constantine founds Constantinople in 330, Theodosius I bans pagan cult in 391–392 (the Olympic games are usually said to end around 393, though the last firmly attested victor is earlier), Alaric raids Greece in 396, and in 529 Justinian's law forbidding pagans to teach (Codex Justinianus 1.11.10) is applied at Athens, where the chronicler John Malalas records a ban on the teaching of philosophy. Damascius and Simplicius, the last heads of the Platonic school, travelled to the Persian court; Agathias, Histories 2.30–31, tells the story.

Where sources disagree. Whether anything was "closed" in 529 is argued between Cameron and Watts in module 7.4. Treat "the closing of the Academy" as a convenient endpoint, not a documented event on one day.

How the Greeks themselves dated things

No Greek state had an era. Each city named the year after its chief magistrate: at Athens the eponymous archon, at Sparta the senior ephor, at Argos the priestess of Hera. Because these lists ran independently and the civic years began at different seasons, a Panhellenic event had to be dated by several at once. Thucydides 2.2 does exactly that for the outbreak of the war: the forty-eighth year of Chrysis's priesthood at Argos, Aenesias ephor at Sparta, Pythodorus archon at Athens, in the spring. He then abandons magistrate dating and counts "by summers and winters", explaining at 5.20 that magistrate years are unreliable because an event can fall anywhere within one.

The Olympiad system was the solution. Hippias of Elis compiled a list of Olympic victors around 400 BC; Plutarch, Numa 1.4, notes that it rested on no firm authority. Timaeus of Tauromenium (c. 350–260 BC) was the first historian to date systematically by Olympiads, and Eratosthenes of Cyrene (c. 276–194) made the system the backbone of his Chronographiai, counting from the first Olympiad in what we call 776 BC. An Olympiad is a four-year span, so "the third year of the 75th Olympiad" is 478/7. Diodorus Siculus in the first century BC gives each year by Olympiad, Athenian archon and Roman consul together, which is why his history is so easy to synchronise.

For the deep past the Greeks had only genealogy, and they counted roughly three generations to a century (Herodotus 2.142). Eratosthenes fixed the fall of Troy at 1184/3 BC by counting backwards from the first Olympiad through the Return of the Heraclidae and the Ionian migration; the figure is preserved by Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis 1.21, and Censorinus, De die natali 21. It became canonical, but it was never the only answer: the Parian Marble (an inscribed chronicle of 264/3 BC) gives 1209/8, Herodotus 2.145 implies about 1250, Ephorus gave 1135 and Duris of Samos 1334. Apollodorus of Athens turned Eratosthenes's scheme into verse in the second century BC, and that is largely how it reached the Roman and Christian chronographers.

Where sources disagree. The date 776 is itself under pressure. Mallwitz's reading of the Olympia stratigraphy and Christesen's of the victor lists, both pushing the real start towards 700, are set out in module 5.1. The Greeks' zero point may be two or three generations too early.

The three big chronological debates

When did Thera erupt?

The eruption buried Akrotiri in the Late Minoan IA phase. Archaeologists working from Egyptian synchronisms (Minoan pottery in dated Egyptian contexts, Theran pumice at Tell el-Dab'a) placed it around 1530–1500 BC. Radiocarbon, including an olive branch buried in the tephra (Friedrich and others, 2006) and large sequences of short-lived samples analysed by Sturt Manning, points to 1620–1600. Recent refinements to the calibration curve (Pearson and others, 2018 onwards) narrow the gap and make a date around 1560–1540 possible, but the dispute has not closed. It matters because the whole Aegean Late Bronze Age sequence has to shift by up to a century depending on the answer.

Where sources disagree. Scientific dating favours the "high" chronology (c. 1600); Egyptian-based archaeology favours the "low" (c. 1500). Manning and Höflmayer have each moved toward the middle; Bietak has not. Say "c. 1600–1500, contested".

Why did the palaces fall around 1200?

Ancient explanation: migration, the Dorians. Modern candidates: raiders from the sea (the "Sea Peoples" whom Ramesses III fought in his eighth year, c. 1177, recorded at Medinet Habu); earthquake (Amos Nur's "earthquake storm" hypothesis); drought (pollen and isotope data from Cyprus and Syria, Kaniewski and Drake); internal revolt; and Colin Renfrew's "systems collapse", in which an over-specialised palace economy fails when any one input is interrupted. Eric Cline's synthesis (1177 B.C., 2014) argues for a cascade of several. There is no consensus beyond the view that no single cause is adequate, and that the destructions were spread over forty years rather than a single event.

When was Homer written down?

Milman Parry showed in the 1930s that the poems are products of oral formulaic composition, so "written down" and "composed" may be different moments. The Greeks themselves disagreed: Herodotus 2.53 puts Homer "four hundred years before my time", roughly 850; the Peisistratid recension story (Cicero, De oratore 3.137; pseudo-Plato, Hipparchus 228b) has Athens producing an official text in the sixth century. Modern positions: Richard Janko's linguistic statistics put the Iliad around 750–725; M. L. West argued on internal evidence for a seventh-century Iliad (c. 680–640) and a later Odyssey; Gregory Nagy's evolutionary model has no single moment, with the text crystallising only in the Panathenaic performances of the sixth century and fixed by Alexandrian editors. The earliest Greek alphabetic inscriptions in hexameter, the Dipylon oinochoe (c. 740) and Nestor's cup from Pithekoussai (c. 730), show that the metre and the writing system coexisted by the late eighth century, which is a floor, not a date.

Where sources disagree. Eighth century (Janko), seventh (West) or a sixth-century crystallisation (Nagy): the range is two hundred years, and the question is partly about what "the text of Homer" means.

A mental map for memorising

Hold the whole span as five blocks of roughly equal weight, each with one date and one image.

GREEK CHRONOLOGY: FIVE BLOCKS
|
+-- BRONZE  (c. 2000-1200 BC)     image: bull-leapers and gold masks
|     1450  Greeks at Knossos
|     1200  palaces burn
|
+-- IRON / ARCHAIC (1200-480)      image: alphabet and hoplite
|     776   first Olympiad
|     750   Homer, colonies
|     594   Solon        508  Cleisthenes
|
+-- CLASSICAL (480-323)            image: Parthenon
|     490   Marathon     480  Salamis
|     431   war begins   404  Athens falls   399  Socrates
|     338   Chaeronea    323  Alexander dies
|
+-- HELLENISTIC (323-31)           image: Alexandria's library
|     146   Corinth destroyed
|     31    Actium
|
+-- ROMAN / LATE ANTIQUE (31 BC - AD 529)   image: Hadrian's arch
      AD 267 Heruli sack Athens
      AD 330 Constantinople
      AD 529 Justinian's edict

Two rhythms help. The Classical period is almost exactly the span between two Persian-related events, 480 and 323, and its middle is the war of 431–404. And the two "falls of Greece", 338 (to Macedon) and 146 (to Rome), are separated by 192 years, close to the 195 years that separate 1200 and the end of the Early Iron Age at 1000 if you want a symmetry to hang the two dark passages on. The symmetry is a mnemonic, not a fact.

Self-test

  1. Which script records the earliest Greek, and roughly when does it first appear at Knossos?
    Answer

    Linear B, deciphered by Ventris in 1952; it appears at Knossos after the Mycenaean takeover around 1450 BC.

  2. Give the conventional date range of the Classical period and the two events that define its limits.
    Answer

    480–323 BC: Xerxes' invasion (Thermopylae and Salamis) to the death of Alexander at Babylon.

  3. Why is the Athenian date for Solon's archonship written 594/3 rather than 594?
    Answer

    The Attic civic year began in midsummer, so each archon year overlaps two Julian years.

  4. Who first used Olympiads systematically as a dating framework, and who made the system canonical?
    Answer

    Timaeus of Tauromenium first; Eratosthenes of Cyrene in his Chronographiai.

  5. What date did Eratosthenes give for the fall of Troy, and name one source that preserves it.
    Answer

    1184/3 BC; preserved by Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis 1.21 (also Censorinus, De die natali 21).

  6. How does Thucydides date the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War at 2.2?
    Answer

    By three magistrates at once: the 48th year of Chrysis as priestess of Hera at Argos, Aenesias as ephor at Sparta, Pythodorus as archon at Athens.

  7. State the "high" and "low" dates for the Thera eruption and which kind of evidence supports each.
    Answer

    High, c. 1620–1600 BC, from radiocarbon (the olive branch, Manning's sequences); low, c. 1530–1500, from Egyptian synchronisms and pottery.

  8. Name three modern explanations for the collapse around 1200 BC other than the Dorian invasion.
    Answer

    Any three of: Sea Peoples raids, earthquakes, drought, internal revolt, systems collapse (Renfrew), or Cline's multi-cause cascade.

  9. Which event is the most securely dated in Greek history before the Roman period, and why?
    Answer

    Alexander's death on 10/11 June 323 BC, fixed by a Babylonian astronomical diary.

  10. What did Justinian actually do in AD 529, and what is the scholarly caveat?
    Answer

    He forbade pagans to teach (Codex Justinianus 1.11.10), applied at Athens according to Malalas; Alan Cameron argued there was no single formal "closing" of the Academy, so 529 is a conventional endpoint.

Carry forward

  1. Before about 500 BC every Greek date is a modern reconstruction or an ancient back-calculation; treat "776" and "1184" as traditions to be weighed, not facts to be trusted.
  2. The Bronze Age collapse of c. 1200 is the hinge of the whole story: Homer, the myths of the Heraclidae and the sense of a lost heroic age all look back across it.
  3. The Greeks dated by magistrates and Olympiads, and reconciling those lists is how Thucydides, Eratosthenes and Diodorus built chronology; every later date you meet rests on that scaffolding.

Give me an in-depth report that builds a memorisable timeline of ancient Greek history from the Early Bronze Age to the closing of the Academy in AD 529. Crete before the Greeks: the shape of the period

Bronze Age Crete is organised by two chronologies, both still in use: Arthur Evans's ceramic phases (Early, Middle, Late Minoan) and Nikolaos Platon's palatial phases. Absolute dates remain approximate.

Platon phaseEvans phaseApproximate dates BCWhat happens
PrepalatialEM I – MM IAc. 3100–1900Village societies; tholos tombs of the Mesara; Myrtos; first seals and metalwork
ProtopalatialMM IB – MM IIc. 1900–1700First palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia; Kamares ware; Hieroglyphic and early Linear A; peak sanctuaries flourish; earthquake destruction c. 1700
NeopalatialMM III – LM IBc. 1700–1450Rebuilt palaces, Zakros founded; frescoes, villas, Linear A archives; Thera erupts in LM IA; island-wide destructions at the end of LM IB
Final PalatialLM II – LM IIIA2c. 1450–1300Knossos alone survives as a palace; Linear B in Greek; warrior graves; final destruction of the palace
PostpalatialLM IIIB – LM IIICc. 1300–1050Decentralised Crete; refuge settlements such as Karphi

"Minoan" is a modern label taken from the mythical king Minos, popularised by Evans though used earlier by Karl Hoeck, whose Kreta (1823–29) headed its second volume "Das Minoische Kreta" (1828). We do not know what the islanders called themselves. Egyptian texts refer to Keftiu, probably Crete, and Odyssey 19.172–7 lists Eteocretans ("true Cretans") among the island's later peoples, which may preserve a memory that a pre-Greek population survived.

The palaces, and what a "palace" was

Four large court-centred complexes dominate the picture. Knossos, near Heraklion, is the largest at roughly 13,000 square metres of ground floor, excavated by Evans from 1900. Phaistos, overlooking the Mesara plain, was dug by the Italian mission under Halbherr and Pernier; its Protopalatial phase is unusually well preserved because the Neopalatial builders shifted the plan rather than building directly on top. Malia, on the north coast, retains much of its Protopalatial character and has a town around it studied more fully than most. Zakros, at the far east end, was found by Platon in 1961 and is the only palace never looted after its LM IB destruction, so its storerooms, workshops and treasury were recovered intact, including the rock-crystal rhyton.

What the four share is a plan: a long central court aligned roughly north–south; a west court with raised walkways and stone-lined pits (kouloures) of disputed purpose; long magazines holding storage jars (pithoi); sunken rooms Evans called "lustral basins"; dark "pillar crypts"; stepped "theatral areas"; light-wells and pier-and-door partitions. There are no obvious throne rooms before LM II, no fortification walls, and no temple as a separate building type.

Function is contested. Evans saw royal residences, the seat of a "Priest-King". Colin Renfrew, in The Emergence of Civilisation (1972), reframed them as hubs of a redistributive economy: surplus flowed in, was recorded by scribes and flowed out as rations and craft goods. Since the 1990s Jan Driessen, Ilse Schoep and others have argued that the central court was the point of the design, that the buildings were made for gatherings and ritual, and that "palace" smuggles in a monarchy for which there is no direct evidence. Driessen prefers "court compound". The honest position is that these complexes combined storage, administration, craft production and ceremony, and that we cannot say who, or what kind of body, sat at the top.

Where sources disagree. Evans's "Priest-King" rests on a composite fresco and the Minos myth, not on any text or burial. Renfrew's model underestimates private exchange; Driessen's explains the courts but struggles with the scale of storage. "Heterarchy" and faction models now compete with the older palace-state model; there is no consensus on Minoan political organisation.

Linear A and why it is unread

Three scripts were used on Bronze Age Crete. Cretan Hieroglyphic appears on seals and a few tablets from MM I to MM II. Linear A runs from about MM II to LM IB (c. 1800–1450) and is the administrative script of the Neopalatial period. Linear B, which adapted Linear A to write Greek, replaced it at Knossos after 1450.

Linear A survives on roughly 1,400 documents, mostly small clay tablets, roundels and nodules, totalling only about 7,400 signs. The largest archive, around 150 tablets, comes from the villa at Hagia Triada. Non-administrative texts are rarer but important: a recurring sequence conventionally read (j)a-sa-sa-ra-me appears on stone libation tables from peak sanctuaries and caves, and is generally taken as a religious formula or divine name. Because Linear B borrowed most of its signs, approximate phonetic values can be assigned to perhaps three-quarters of Linear A. The word ku-ro at the foot of lists can be shown by arithmetic to mean "total", and ki-ro probably "deficit". That is close to the limit of secure meaning.

The script is unread for structural reasons. The corpus is small and repetitive. There is no bilingual text. The documents are lists, not sentences, so grammar barely shows. And the language is unknown: no later Cretan language can be shown to descend from it, and the Eteocretan inscriptions of the first millennium (Praisos, Dreros) are too few and too late to help. Proposals have identified it as Luwian (Leonard Palmer), as Semitic (Cyrus Gordon, Jan Best), as a form of early Greek or Indo-European (Gareth Owens), and as an isolate. None produces readings that work across the corpus.

Where sources disagree. Whether Linear A sign values can be carried over from Linear B is itself disputed; John Younger accepts it as a working tool, sceptics note that Linear B may have reassigned values. Treat every published "translation" of Linear A as a hypothesis.

Religion as reconstructed from images and places

Minoan religion must be rebuilt from frescoes, seals and rings, figurines, cult vessels and the places where they were deposited. There are no readable texts and no temples in the Greek sense. The central institution of the Protopalatial period was the peak sanctuary: open-air sites on summits such as Juktas above Knossos, Petsophas above Palaikastro, Kophinas and Atsipades, where worshippers left clay figurines of men, women, animals and detached human limbs, the last presumably for healing. Alan Peatfield's survey showed that many were abandoned or absorbed into palace control in the Neopalatial period. Caves were the second category: Psychro on Lasithi (later the Dictaean Cave), Kamares, and Arkalochori, where a hoard of bronze and precious-metal double axes was found.

Four symbols recur. The bull dominates: bull-leaping on seals and on the Knossos "Taureador" frescoes (which most now date to LM II–IIIA, after the Mycenaean takeover), stone bull's-head rhyta from Knossos and Zakros, and the sacrifice scene on the Hagia Triada sarcophagus. The double axe (Greek labrys) appears as a votive, on pottery and incised on pillars, often with the "horns of consecration" that crown buildings and altars; Evans read it as the goddess's emblem, but it may simply mark sacrifice. The snake goddess is known from two faience figurines from the Temple Repositories at Knossos (c. 1600), both heavily restored: the smaller figure's head, and the cat on it, are modern. Whether they show a goddess, a priestess or a votary is open. The labyrinth is not a Minoan image at all; it is a Greek word and story, discussed below, though Linear B tablet KN Gg 702 records offerings to da-pu2-ri-to-jo po-ti-ni-ja, "the Lady of the Labyrinth", at Knossos around 1375 BC.

Gold rings add epiphany scenes: a small figure descending from the sky, worshippers shaking a tree or embracing a boulder. Nanno Marinatos reads these as a coherent theology centred on a goddess and her consort; Martin Nilsson insisted on a plurality of deities. Evans's single Mother Goddess has been largely abandoned, but the sources cannot settle how many gods there were.

Where sources disagree. At Anemospilia on Juktas, Yannis and Efi Sakellarakis excavated a small building destroyed by earthquake c. 1700 with a young man bound on a platform and a bronze blade on his body, which they read as human sacrifice interrupted by the quake. Peter Warren's "Room of the Children's Bones" at Knossos (LM IB) produced cut-marked juvenile bones he interpreted as ritual cannibalism. Both readings remain controversial and sit awkwardly with the gentle Minoans of Evans's imagination.

The Thera eruption and its dating problem

Some time in LM IA the volcano of Thera (Santorini) erupted, burying the town of Akrotiri, excavated by Spyridon Marinatos from 1967, under pumice and ash. Akrotiri is culturally Minoanised, with frescoes, lustral basins and Linear A, and its destruction gives a fixed horizon across the Aegean.

The date is one of the sharpest disputes in Aegean archaeology. Radiocarbon, above all on an olive branch buried alive in the pumice (Friedrich et al. 2006) and on short-lived seeds from Akrotiri, points to c. 1620–1600 BC. The conventional chronology, built on Egyptian synchronisms for LM IA and LM IB pottery and on Theran pumice at Tell el-Dab'a in Egypt, puts it around 1530–1500. The gap is a century. Work since 2018 on fluctuations in atmospheric radiocarbon (Pearson et al.) shows the scientific date could fall in the later sixteenth century, which narrows but does not close the gap.

What is no longer believed is Marinatos's 1939 thesis that the eruption destroyed Minoan civilisation. The palaces were burnt at the end of LM IB, two or three generations after the ash fell. Driessen and Macdonald in The Troubled Island (1997) argue that LM IB Crete shows signs of a society under stress, but the link between volcano and collapse is indirect at best.

Where sources disagree. The "high" (c. 1620–1600) and "low" (c. 1530–1500) chronologies for Thera remain unreconciled. Adopting the high date stretches LM IA and LM IB and alters every synchronism with Egypt. Most handbooks now give a range rather than a date.

The Mycenaean takeover

At the end of LM IB, c. 1450, almost every major site on Crete was destroyed by fire: Phaistos, Malia, Zakros, Hagia Triada, Gournia, Mochlos, Palaikastro and the villas. Knossos was damaged but continued, and in LM II it acquires mainland Greek features: "warrior graves" with swords and boar's-tusk helmets; mainland pottery shapes; a throne room whose final form, with griffin frescoes, most now date to LM II–IIIA; and above all administration in Linear B, which writes Greek. The Knossos archive records a kingdom controlling central and western Crete, with place names such as Phaistos, Amnisos and Kydonia, roughly 100,000 sheep, and a ruler styled wanax.

Whether this was a conquest is debated. The old view was an invasion from the Argolid. Driessen and Macdonald argue that Crete was already weakened and that the LM IB fires may be partly internal. Others reply that a Greek-writing bureaucracy at exactly one surviving centre is hard to explain without new rulers from outside. The date of the Knossos tablets was itself a famous quarrel: Evans dated the palace's final destruction to c. 1400; Leonard Palmer argued in the 1960s that the tablets belonged to c. 1200 like those at Pylos; John Boardman defended Evans's stratigraphy. The current view places most tablets in LM IIIA2, c. 1375–1350.

Where sources disagree. Evans, Palmer and Boardman could not agree on when Knossos fell within a range of two centuries, and the excavation records of 1900–1904 were never good enough to settle it. The LM IIIA2 compromise is widely held but not universal.

Arthur Evans and the making of "Minoan"

Evans began excavating the Kephala hill at Knossos, where Minos Kalokairinos had already dug in 1878, in March 1900, and published The Palace of Minos in four volumes (1921–35). His achievements are real: he recognised a pre-Greek civilisation, distinguished the three scripts, built the relative chronology still in use, and recorded a vast site before it decayed.

Much of what visitors see, however, is his. In the 1920s he rebuilt large parts of the palace in reinforced concrete, with the architects Christian Doll and Piet de Jong, inventing upper storeys, columns and staircases. The frescoes were restored by Émile Gilliéron father and son from fragments that were sometimes very small: the "Prince of the Lilies" combines pieces that may belong to two or three figures; the "Saffron Gatherer" was restored as a boy and later shown to be a monkey. Several "Minoan" ivory goddesses in museums outside Greece are now suspected forgeries from the Gilliérons' circle. Beyond objects, Evans supplied a story: a peaceful, goddess-worshipping thalassocracy, a "Pax Minoica" ruled by a Priest-King. That picture drew on Frazer and on the Minos legend, and fitted a post-1918 longing for a civilisation without war.

The critique is now mature: J. A. MacGillivray's Minotaur (2000), the essays edited by Yannis Hamilakis as Labyrinth Revisited (2002) and Cathy Gere's Knossos and the Prophets of Modernism (2009) trace how far the Minoans are a modernist artefact. On the specific point of peace, swords from Malia and Arkalochori and fortifications at sites such as Petras make the "unarmed Minoans" hard to sustain; Barry Molloy argues that violence was simply underrepresented in the art Evans privileged. The chronology, the scripts and the architecture are Evans's permanent contribution; the Priest-King, the Mother Goddess and the restored frescoes are early twentieth-century interpretations.

The myths later Greeks attached to Crete

Minos is in Homer already a king of Knossos who "reigned in nine-year periods" and was the confidant of Zeus (Odyssey 19.178–9), the son of Zeus and grandfather of the Cretan leader Idomeneus (Iliad 13.450–3), and a judge of the dead (Odyssey 11.568–71). Thucydides 1.4 makes him the first ruler to build a navy, colonise the Cyclades and suppress piracy; Herodotus 3.122 pointedly refuses to count him among human rulers, and at 7.170–1 reports that he died at Camicus in Sicily pursuing Daedalus. Plato's Laws opens by crediting Minos with Crete's laws; Athenian tragedy made him a tyrant exacting tribute of youths.

Europa, daughter of Phoenix in Iliad 14.321–2 and of Agenor in Apollodorus, Library 3.1.1, was carried from Tyre to Crete by Zeus as a bull and bore Minos, Rhadamanthys and Sarpedon (Moschus, Europa; Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.833–75). Pasiphae, Minos's wife, conceived a passion for a bull Poseidon sent when Minos failed to sacrifice it; Daedalus built her a wooden cow and the child was the Minotaur, properly named Asterios (Apollodorus 3.1.3–4; Euripides' lost Cretans). Daedalus appears in Homer only as the maker of a dancing-floor for Ariadne at Knossos (Iliad 18.590–2); his labyrinth, his flight with Icarus and the boy's fall come from Apollodorus, Epitome 1.12–15, Diodorus 4.76–9 and Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.183–235. Theseus and the Minotaur is fullest in Plutarch, Theseus 15–19, who also records Philochorus's rationalising version in which the labyrinth was a prison and "Taurus" a Cretan general; Odyssey 11.321–5 has an older version in which Artemis kills Ariadne on Dia. Talos, the bronze man who circled Crete three times a day and died when Medea opened the vein in his ankle, is in Apollonius, Argonautica 4.1638–88 and Apollodorus 1.9.26. The birth of Zeus is Cretan from Hesiod onwards: Rhea bears him at Lyktos and hides him in a cave on Mount Aigaion (Theogony 477–84); later writers divide the honour between Dicte (Apollodorus 1.1.6) and Ida (Diodorus 5.70), with the Kouretes clashing their shields to drown his cries. Callimachus, Hymn to Zeus 8–9, mocks the Cretans as liars for showing a tomb of Zeus.

What, if anything, do they preserve?

The myths are Greek, reshaped between the eighth and first centuries BC, and most of their detail serves Greek concerns: Athenian politics in the Theseus story, Hellenistic learning in Callimachus, Roman taste in Ovid. But a cautious case for residue can be made on four points.

  1. Knossos was remembered as the great centre. Homer's "great city Knossos", Minos's seat, matches the fact that Knossos outlasted every other palace and was the capital of the Linear B kingdom. Mycenaean Greeks ruled there for two centuries and could carry the memory forward, as Nilsson argued in The Mycenaean Origin of Greek Mythology (1932).
  2. Specific cult sites are continuous. Linear B tablet KN Fp 1 records offerings to di-ka-ta-jo di-we, "Dictaean Zeus"; KN Gg 705 records offerings to Eleuthia at Amnisos, and Odyssey 19.188 places the cave of Eileithyia at Amnisos; the "Lady of the Labyrinth" has been noted. The Idaean and Psychro caves show cult from Minoan through Roman times. Here the chain from Bronze Age to Homer is documented.
  3. The bull and the craftsman. The island whose art is saturated with bulls became the island of the bull-god, the bull-lover and the bull-man; the island with the most elaborate architecture in the Aegean became the home of the archetypal engineer. This is probably later reinterpretation of visible ruins and images, but of real things.
  4. Thalassocracy. Minoan material at Kythera, Thera, Melos, Kea, Rhodes and Miletus shows real overseas presence behind Thucydides' sea-empire, though whether it was political control, trade or settlement cannot be decided from pottery.

Against these, the central figures resist. "Minos" may be a title rather than a name (Evans's suggestion, unprovable), or a Greek invention to give the island a founder. The labyrinth is probably not derived from labrys, as Maximilian Mayer proposed in 1892; both words are pre-Greek and the link is folk etymology. No Minoan image shows a bull-headed man. The sober conclusion is that Greek myth preserves the importance of Knossos, a few cult names, and an impression of bulls and ingenious buildings, and invents nearly everything else.

Where sources disagree. Ancient writers themselves split: Thucydides and Plato treat Minos as a historical lawgiver and admiral; Herodotus removes him from human history; Philochorus and Plutarch rationalise the Minotaur into a man. Among moderns, Nilsson's view that the myths carry Mycenaean memory is accepted in outline, but how much of the Cretan cycle is pre-Greek rather than Mycenaean or Archaic remains uncertain.

Self-test

  1. Name the two chronological schemes used for Bronze Age Crete and who proposed each.
    Answer

    Evans's tripartite ceramic scheme (Early, Middle, Late Minoan) and Platon's palatial scheme (Prepalatial, Protopalatial, Neopalatial, Postpalatial).

  2. Which palace was never looted after its destruction, and who excavated it?
    Answer

    Zakros, excavated by Nikolaos Platon from 1961.

  3. Give two architectural features common to all four palaces.
    Answer

    Any two of: a north–south central court, a west court with raised walkways, long magazines with pithoi, lustral basins, pillar crypts, light-wells and pier-and-door partitions, no fortification walls.

  4. Why does Jan Driessen prefer the term "court compound" to "palace"?
    Answer

    Because the central court appears to be the organising purpose of the design, suggesting gathering and ritual, and "palace" presupposes a monarch for whom there is no direct evidence.

  5. State three reasons Linear A remains undeciphered.
    Answer

    A small corpus (c. 1,400 documents, c. 7,400 signs); no bilingual text; texts are lists rather than sentences; the underlying language is unknown and has no proven descendant.

  6. What do the two dating methods say about the Thera eruption, and roughly how far apart are they?
    Answer

    Radiocarbon (olive branch, seeds) gives c. 1620–1600 BC; Egyptian-based archaeological synchronisms give c. 1530–1500 BC; a gap of about a century, narrowed but not closed by recent radiocarbon recalibration.

  7. What changed at Knossos in LM II that points to Mycenaean rule?
    Answer

    Warrior graves with mainland weapons, the final form of the throne room, mainland pottery shapes, and administration in Linear B, which writes Greek.

  8. Name two elements of the Knossos visitors see today that are Evans's rather than Minoan.
    Answer

    Any two of: the reinforced-concrete reconstructions of upper storeys and staircases; the Gilliéron fresco restorations such as the Prince of the Lilies; the restored heads and cat of the snake goddess figurines.

  9. Which Linear B tablet names a "Lady of the Labyrinth", and why does it matter?
    Answer

    KN Gg 702 from Knossos, c. 1375 BC. It shows the word "labyrinth" in use at Knossos as a cult name roughly six centuries before Homer, a documented link between Bronze Age Crete and the later myth.

  10. In Homer, what is Daedalus said to have made, and where?
    Answer

    A dancing-floor for Ariadne in "broad Knossos" (Iliad 18.590–2); the labyrinth and the flight with Icarus are later additions.

Carry forward

  1. Minoan Crete is a non-Greek civilisation whose language is unread; after c. 1450 BC Knossos was ruled by Greek-speaking Mycenaeans using Linear B, and this two-century Mycenaean Crete is the bridge through which anything Cretan reached later Greek myth.
  2. Much of the popular "Minoan" image, the Priest-King, the peaceful Mother Goddess civilisation, the restored frescoes and concrete palace, is Arthur Evans's early twentieth-century interpretation; separate his permanent contributions (chronology, scripts, the site) from his reconstructions.
  3. Greek myths about Crete preserve the importance of Knossos, a handful of cult names and places (Dictaean Zeus, Eileithyia at Amnisos, the Lady of the Labyrinth) and the island's bull imagery, but invent almost all narrative detail; use them as evidence for Archaic and Classical Greek thinking about the past, not as records of Minoan history.

GREECE · UNIT 1 · The Bronze Age and the long dark · 1.2 · 2,746 words

Mycenaean Greece

Schliemann and the shaft graves

Heinrich Schliemann came to Mycenae in 1876 fresh from Troy, carrying a literal reading of Pausanias (2.16.6), who says the graves of Agamemnon and his companions lay inside the walls. Everyone else had assumed the tholos tombs outside the citadel were meant. Schliemann dug just inside the Lion Gate and found a circular enclosure of upright slabs, Grave Circle A, with five shaft graves (a sixth was cleared by the Greek ephor Stamatakis in 1877): nineteen bodies with gold death-masks, diadems, inlaid daggers, silver and gold vessels, Baltic amber and ostrich-egg rhyta. The telegram "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon" is probably a later embellishment, but it captures the claim.

The claim was wrong by three or four centuries. The shaft graves date to Late Helladic I–IIA, roughly 1600–1450 BC, well before any plausible Trojan War horizon. An earlier circle, Grave Circle B (c. 1650–1550 BC), was excavated by Papadimitriou and Mylonas in 1951–54 outside the later walls. Together they show a warrior elite emerging from the modest Middle Helladic world and suddenly rich in exotic goods, Minoan craftsmanship and weapons. Why is still argued: mercenary service in Egypt against the Hyksos, control of metal routes to the north and west, or competitive display among chiefdoms consolidating into states. Circle A was deliberately re-enclosed when the citadel wall was extended around 1250 BC, so the thirteenth-century rulers already treated these graves as ancestral monuments.

Where sources disagree. Schliemann's reliability (Calder and Traill against Easton on the Troy treasure, module 10.10; the Mask of Agamemnon, module 10.2) bears on the findspots, not on the Mycenaean dates. Absolute dating also hangs on the Thera eruption: radiocarbon favours c. 1620–1600 BC, Egyptian synchronisms c. 1530–1500 BC. The gap is not closed.

The palace centres and citadel architecture

By the fourteenth century the mainland was organised around a handful of palatial states, each controlling a hinterland of perhaps 2,000 square kilometres. The core building is the megaron: columned porch, vestibule, and a main hall with a great circular hearth ringed by four columns, a throne against the right-hand wall, and painted floors and walls. This is the room Homer's heroes feast in.

  • Mycenae sits on a hill between two ravines in the Argolid. Its Cyclopean walls were built in three stages; the Lion Gate with its relieving triangle belongs to the second, c. 1250 BC. The final extension (c. 1200) enclosed an underground cistern, a sign of siege anxiety. Nine tholos tombs lie outside; the Treasury of Atreus (c. 1250) has a corbelled dome 13.5 m high, unmatched until the Pantheon.
  • Tiryns, near the Argive shore, has walls up to 8 m thick with corbelled galleries, and the best preserved megaron plan, with a boar-hunt fresco.
  • Pylos in Messenia, excavated by Carl Blegen from 1939, is unwalled and burned in a single fire that baked its 1,100 tablets. Blegen dated the fire c. 1200; pottery re-study (Mountjoy) puts it at the LH IIIB–IIIC transition, c. 1180. In 2015 Davis and Stocker found the undisturbed Griffin Warrior grave of c. 1450, with the Pylos Combat Agate.
  • Thebes lies under the modern town on the Kadmeia. Tablets recovered since 1964, especially the Pelopidou Street archive of 1993–95, show a palace controlling much of Boeotia, perhaps including the fortress of Gla and the drained Copais basin.
  • Knossos was Minoan, but after the destructions of c. 1450 it was run by Greek-speakers keeping Linear B archives, the only Mycenaean administration on Crete of this scale.
Where sources disagree. The Knossos tablets' date was the Palmer–Boardman controversy of the 1960s: Leonard Palmer argued Evans had mis-stratified them and they belonged c. 1200, contemporary with Pylos; John Boardman defended c. 1400. Consensus now puts most in LM IIIA2, c. 1375–1350, with the Room of the Chariot Tablets earlier, though Hallager and Niemeier have kept a later date for part of the archive.

Linear B and its decipherment

Arthur Evans found the first tablets at Knossos in 1900, named the script Linear B to distinguish it from the earlier, still undeciphered Linear A, believed it recorded a non-Greek language, and sat on most of the material until his death in 1941. Alice Kober showed in the 1940s that the language was inflected and worked out which signs shared consonants or vowels without knowing what either was. Michael Ventris, an architect, built on Kober's grids, tested the hypothesis that place-names such as Amnisos and Knossos were spelt syllabically, and found the result read as archaic Greek. He announced it on the BBC on 1 July 1952, then published with John Chadwick, "Evidence for Greek Dialect in the Mycenaean Archives", Journal of Hellenic Studies 73 (1953). Confirmation came when Blegen read the new Pylos tablet Ta 641: ti-ri-po-de stood beside a drawing of a tripod, and qe-to-ro-we ("four-eared") beside a four-handled jar. Ventris died in a car crash in 1956, weeks before Documents in Mycenaean Greek appeared.

The script has about 87 syllabic signs plus ideograms and numerals, and fits Greek badly: no voiced/unvoiced distinction, no final consonants. The tablets are not literature but single-year accounts on unbaked clay, surviving only where fire baked them.

What the tablets reveal

  • The wanax (wa-na-ka) stands at the top, with a temenos (estate) three times anyone else's (Pylos Er 312), his own "royal" craftsmen, and a role in cult. Whether each palace had its own wanax or one at Mycenae stood over all is unknown; Homer's anax andrōn Agamemnon preserves the word.
  • The lawagetas (ra-wa-ke-ta, "leader of the people") is second, with a temenos one-third the size. Older scholarship made him a war-leader; the tablets never show him commanding anything, and the title vanishes from later Greek.
  • Below them: telestai (landholders with obligations), hequetai ("followers", with chariots and distinctive cloaks), a qa-si-re-u (basileus) who is merely a local headman, often of bronzesmiths, and the damos, the village community, which holds land collectively and in one case (Pylos Ep 704) disputes a priestess's claim.
  • Slaves (do-e-ro, do-e-ra) are common; many are "slaves of the god" who nevertheless hold land. The Pylos Aa/Ab/Ad series lists some 750 women with children, rationed in wheat and figs, many labelled by origin on the Anatolian coast and islands: Milesian, Knidian, Lemnian, "women of Asia". One group is ra-wi-ja-ja, "captives". These look like the war-booty women of the Iliad.
  • Textiles were the chief industry. Knossos counted some 100,000 sheep, set wool targets per flock and tracked cloth through workshops; Pylos ran flax. A planned, quota-driven economy on the Near Eastern model, though less total than once thought.
  • Chariots: the Knossos Sc series issues chariots, corslets and horses to named men; Sd/Se/Sf inventory chariot bodies with and without wheels; Pylos Sa lists wheels. Knossos could field well over a hundred.
  • Defence: the Pylos "o-ka" tablets (An 657 and related) post coast-watchers under named officers, and Jn 829 collects "temple bronze" for spear-points. Whether this is the emergency before the destruction is debated.

Gods attested by name

The surest attestations are: Zeus (di-we, dative), Hera (e-ra), Poseidon (po-se-da-o, the dominant god at Pylos, which fits his later Messenian and Arcadian cults), Hermes (e-ma-a2), Artemis (a-te-mi-to, genitive, at Pylos) and Eileithyia (e-re-u-ti-ja, receiving honey at Amnisos, exactly as Odyssey 19.188 remembers). Ares appears both as a-re and as Enyalios; Paiawon is the later Apolline epithet Paean; Dionysus (di-wo-nu-so) occurs at Pylos and Khania, overturning the old idea that he was a late import. "Potnia" (Mistress) is the most frequent divine title, often qualified: a-ta-na po-ti-ni-ja at Knossos is probably "Mistress of Athana", and may or may not be Athena. There are female doublets, Diwia and Posidaeia, who later disappear. Apollo and Aphrodite are absent; Demeter is uncertain.

Where sources disagree. Pylos Tn 316, written hastily shortly before the fire, lists gold vessels and human beings (po-re-na) brought to Potnia, Zeus, Hera, Hermes and others. Chadwick and Palaima read the people as cult attendants or dedicated servants; others, following earlier suggestions, see human sacrifice in extremity. The tablet does not settle it. Likewise di-wo-nu-so was long treated as a personal name, not the god, until the Khania tablet paired it with Zeus in a context of offerings.

Religion and burial

Mycenaean religion left no clear temples before the thirteenth century. The exception is the Cult Centre at Mycenae: small shrines below the palace with a fresco of goddesses, and a "Temple" holding grotesque terracotta figures over half a metre tall, coiled clay snakes and a dais. Comparable shrines stand at Phylakopi on Melos and at Methana. Elsewhere the evidence is small "Phi", "Psi" and "Tau" figurines in houses and tombs, and processions and libations on palace walls. Iconography borrows heavily from Crete: double axes, horns of consecration, griffins flanking the throne at Pylos and Knossos. The tablets add offerings of oil, honey, wine and animals at monthly festivals, and a priesthood of both sexes holding land and slaves. What is missing is myth. No tablet names a hero; the Linear B men called a-ki-re-u (Achilleus) and e-ko-to (Hektor) are ordinary people, the latter a "slave of the god".

Burial changed. The shaft graves were a brief Argolid phenomenon. From the late sixteenth century the mainland adopted the tholos, a corbelled dome under a mound entered by a dromos, first in Messenia and then for ruling families everywhere, and the rock-cut chamber tomb for the broader elite. Both were reopened over generations, earlier skeletons swept aside, which shows the grave goods mattered at the funeral rather than for eternity. Inhumation was the rule; cremation, Homer's universal rite, is rare until the twelfth century. There is no cult at tombs in the palatial period; the hero-cult offerings at Mycenaean tombs belong to the eighth century, when Greeks rediscovered them.

Ahhiyawa, Wilusa and a historical Troy

The Hittite archives at Hattusa contain about 28 texts naming a western power called Ahhiyawa (earlier Ahhiya), collected in Beckman, Bryce and Cline, The Ahhiyawa Texts (2011). Emil Forrer proposed in 1924 that the name is Achaia; Ferdinand Sommer's objections held the field for decades, but the equation is now generally accepted. The key documents:

  • The Indictment of Madduwatta (fifteenth century): a man of Ahhiya, Attarissiya, raids Anatolia and Cyprus with chariots. Forrer saw Atreus; almost nobody follows him.
  • The Annals of Tudhaliya I/II list among the rebel lands of Assuwa both Wilusiya and Taruisa, matching Greek (W)ilios and Troia, Homer's two names for one city.
  • The Alaksandu Treaty (Muwatalli II, c. 1280) binds a king of Wilusa named Alaksandu, phonetically Alexandros, Paris's other name. Among the oath-gods is a damaged [A]ppaliunas, which some read as Apollo, Troy's protector in the Iliad.
  • The Manapa-Tarhunta Letter reports a freebooter, Piyamaradu, attacking Wilusa and Lazpa (Lesbos).
  • The Tawagalawa Letter (Hattusili III, c. 1250) addresses the king of Ahhiyawa as "Great King" and "my brother", the rank of Egypt and Babylon, complains that Piyamaradu operates from Ahhiyawan Millawanda (Miletus), and calls "the matter of Wilusa over which we were at enmity" settled. Tawagalawa, the king's brother, is plausibly Etewoklewes, Eteokles.
  • The Shaushgamuwa Treaty (Tudhaliya IV, c. 1220) lists the Great Kings and then erases Ahhiyawa, suggesting its standing had collapsed.

The implication is modest but real: a Greek-speaking kingdom treated as an equal by the Hittite king, holding Miletus, active on the Anatolian coast, and at some point in the thirteenth century in dispute with the Hittites over Wilusa. It does not supply a siege or a ten-year expedition.

Where sources disagree. Mycenae is the default capital of Ahhiyawa; Joachim Latacz argued for Thebes on the strength of its tablets and Near Eastern seals; earlier scholars favoured Rhodes. At Hisarlık, Troy VI fell c. 1300 to what Blegen judged an earthquake, Troy VIIa to fire c. 1180 with arrowheads and unburied bodies; which, if either, is "Homer's Troy" is open. The Korfmann–Kolb quarrel over the Lower Town is set out in module 10.10; here it is enough that a ditch and settlement outside the citadel are now accepted.

Trade with Egypt and the Levant

Egyptian records know the Aegean as Keftiu (Crete), whose envoys carry Minoan-style vessels in the Theban tombs of Senenmut and Rekhmire, and Tanaja (Danaoi?), whose towns appear on a statue base of Amenhotep III at Kom el-Hetan (c. 1380): the names have been read as Mycenae, Nauplion, Kythera, Messenia and Thebes alongside Knossos, Amnisos and Phaistos, like the itinerary of a diplomatic voyage. Faience plaques stamped with Amenhotep III's name have been found at Mycenae. In return, LH IIIA2 pottery turns up at Amarna, at Ugarit, Tell Abu Hawam and Beth Shan, and across Cyprus, where local imitations followed.

The Uluburun shipwreck off Kaş (c. 1320) shows the mechanism: ten tonnes of Cypriot copper ingots and a tonne of tin, glass ingots, Canaanite jars of terebinth resin, ebony, ivory, Baltic amber, a gold scarab of Nefertiti and, among the personal possessions, Mycenaean swords and seals, probably those of two Mycenaean envoys travelling west on a Levantine ship. The Kadmeia at Thebes yielded Kassite Babylonian lapis lazuli cylinder seals, and Linear B records men called a3-ku-pi-ti-jo (Egyptian) and ku-pi-ri-jo (Cypriot). The exchange was asymmetric: Mycenaeans needed copper and tin, which they lacked entirely, and exported perfumed oil in stirrup jars, textiles, slaves and perhaps mercenaries. Whether this was royal gift-exchange, private enterprise or both is unresolved; the tablets never mention foreign trade.

How much Homer remembers

The Iliad and Odyssey took their shape in the eighth century, four hundred years after the palaces burned, in a society of small chiefdoms and iron tools. The question is what survived the gap in the oral tradition.

Genuine Bronze Age memories:

  • The boar's-tusk helmet Meriones lends Odysseus (Iliad 10.261–65), leather with rows of sliced tusk, is exactly the helmet from the shaft graves, Dendra and the Pylos and Thera frescoes, obsolete by the twelfth century. No poet after 1100 could have seen one.
  • Nestor's cup (Iliad 11.632–37), heavy, gold-studded, four-handled with two doves at each handle, resembles the gold cup from Shaft Grave IV with two dove-topped handles. The match is inexact, but the type is Bronze Age.
  • Bronze weaponry throughout; silver-studded swords; the tower shield of Ajax and the body-covering shield that strikes Hector's ankles and neck (Iliad 6.117), a sixteenth-century form.
  • The title anax, the god-list, Eileithyia's cave at Amnisos, and the Catalogue of Ships (Iliad 2.494–759), whose geography ignores Ionia and names places such as Pylos, Dorion and Eutresis that mattered in the Bronze Age and not later.
  • Names: Achilleus, Hektor and Alexandra all occur in Linear B, so the onomastic stock is old.

Iron Age reality or invention:

  • Universal cremation; iron as a familiar metal; paired throwing spears rather than the single thrusting spear; chariots used as battlefield taxis by men who dismount to fight, because the poets no longer knew how chariotry worked.
  • Basileus as "king", Phoenician traders, a temple of Athena at Troy, the hero's house with a hearth-room rather than a palace with archive and workshops, and a politics of assemblies and quarrelsome peers rather than the wanax's scribal bureaucracy. Nothing in Homer suggests writing or taxation.
  • Agamemnon's Mycenae is a petty kingship; the real Mycenae counted sheep by the tens of thousands.
Where sources disagree. Moses Finley (The World of Odysseus, 1954) held that Homer's society is essentially the tenth and ninth centuries with a Bronze Age veneer. Anthony Snodgrass called it an amalgam matching no single period. Susan Sherratt (1990) proposed layers that entered the tradition at different dates and froze. Latacz treats the Catalogue and the Hittite texts as evidence of a real coalition war; most Anglophone scholars think that exceeds the evidence. The honest answer is that Homer remembers objects, names, places and a few institutions, and invents or updates almost everything about how people lived and fought.

Self-test

  1. Which ancient author led Schliemann to dig inside the walls of Mycenae, and what did he find?
    Answer

    Pausanias 2.16.6, who placed the royal graves inside the walls. Schliemann found Grave Circle A with its gold-rich shaft graves of c. 1600–1450 BC.

  2. Why can the shaft-grave burials not be Agamemnon and his companions?
    Answer

    They date to Late Helladic I–IIA, three to four centuries before any Trojan War horizon of c. 1250–1180 BC.

  3. Describe the megaron.
    Answer

    Porch, vestibule and main hall with a large central hearth ringed by four columns, a throne on the right wall and painted decoration; the core of every Mycenaean palace.

  4. Who, besides Ventris, made the decipherment of Linear B possible, and what did Pylos Ta 641 prove?
    Answer

    Alice Kober's grids of inflected sign groups and John Chadwick's philological collaboration. Ta 641 showed the word ti-ri-po-de beside a drawn tripod, confirming the readings were Greek.

  5. Rank the wanax, the lawagetas and the basileus as the tablets show them.
    Answer

    The wanax is supreme with the largest estate; the lawagetas second with one-third of that; the qa-si-re-u is a mere local headman, often over bronzesmiths.

  6. Name five Olympian gods attested by name in Linear B and two who are absent.
    Answer

    Attested: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Hermes, Artemis (also Ares, Dionysus, Eileithyia). Absent: Apollo (unless Paiawon counts) and Aphrodite.

  7. What did the Pylos palace mainly produce and administer?
    Answer

    Textiles and flax, with women workers rationed and counted; also bronze, chariots, land tenure and offerings to the gods.

  8. What is the Tawagalawa Letter and what does it say about Wilusa?
    Answer

    A letter of Hattusili III (c. 1250) to the king of Ahhiyawa, addressed as Great King and brother, mentioning Piyamaradu's raids from Miletus and a past dispute "over Wilusa" now settled.

  9. What does the Uluburun wreck tell us about Mycenaean trade?
    Answer

    Bulk copper and tin, glass, resin and luxury goods moved westward on a Levantine ship c. 1320, apparently with Mycenaean passengers; the Aegean imported metals and exotica and exported oil, cloth and people.

  10. Give one object Homer remembers accurately from the Bronze Age and one practice he gets from his own time.
    Answer

    The boar's-tusk helmet (Iliad 10.261–65) is genuinely Mycenaean; universal cremation is an Iron Age practice.

Carry forward

  1. The Mycenaean world was a literate, bureaucratic palace economy ruled by a wanax, and it ended c. 1200–1180 BC; everything in later Greece, including Homer, grew up after a four-century gap in which writing, palaces and kingship were lost.
  2. Most of the Olympian pantheon, Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Hermes, Artemis, Ares, Dionysus, was already worshipped by name in the Bronze Age, so Greek religion has a continuous spine even where myth and cult practice changed.
  3. Hittite texts prove an Achaean great power active on the Anatolian coast and in dispute over Wilusa/Ilios; they make a Trojan war plausible as a type of event without confirming the one Homer tells, and that distinction governs how to read every later "historical" use of myth.

GREECE · UNIT 1 · The Bronze Age and the long dark · 1.3 · 2,848 words

The collapse of 1200 and the Dark Age

What collapsed, and whenExplanations, and how scholars weigh them nowThe Dark Age in the groundMovements of people: Ionia and the HeracleidaeHow the heroic age became a golden ageSelf-testCarry forward

What collapsed, and when

Between about 1225 and 1150 BC the interlocking palace economies of the eastern Mediterranean failed one after another. The Mycenaean world went first and most completely. The palace at Thebes burned in LH IIIB1, probably in the later thirteenth century. Mycenae suffered a destruction around 1250 and a far heavier one at the end of LH IIIB, about 1190–1180, alongside Tiryns and Midea. The palace at Pylos burned at roughly the same moment, so hot that its unbaked Linear B tablets were fired and preserved: the last administrative year of a Mycenaean state, frozen. Nothing like the palaces was rebuilt. Writing vanished with them, because Linear B was a palace instrument for recording rations, flocks, bronze and labour, and when the bureaucracies died the script had no other users. Greece was illiterate for some four centuries, until an alphabet adapted from Phoenician appears on the Dipylon oinochoe (c. 740) and Nestor's cup from Pithekoussai (c. 730).

The same decades saw Hattusa abandoned under its last king, Suppiluliuma II; Ugarit destroyed, its final letters never sent; Emar on the Euphrates sacked; Troy VIIa burnt; and Hazor, Lachish and Megiddo levelled over a longer spread of dates. Egypt fought off two assaults by coalitions of "peoples of the sea", under Merneptah (c. 1208) and Ramesses III (c. 1177), survived, and then slid into the weak Third Intermediate Period. Assyria contracted but did not fall; Cyprus and the Phoenician coast recovered quickly; Carchemish carried a Hittite dynasty into the Iron Age.
