The elder generation: children of Cronus

Zeus

Birth. Cronus swallows each child Rhea bears; she gives birth to Zeus in Crete, hides him in a cave, and hands Cronus a swaddled stone (Theogony 453–506).

Domains and epithets. Sky, weather, kingship, and above all the binding of social relationships. Xenios protects the guest–host bond, which is why the Cyclops episode is a crime against Zeus (Odyssey 9.270–271); Horkios witnesses oaths; Polieus presides over the city. Meilichios, "the gentle one", was worshipped as a huge snake with holocaust offerings at the Athenian Diasia (Thucydides 1.126.6): Zeus had a chthonic face too.

Cult. Olympia, with the Games and Pheidias' seated statue (Pausanias 5.11); Dodona, the oak oracle (Iliad 16.233–235); Nemea; the Cretan caves.

Art. Mature, bearded, enthroned or striding with the thunderbolt; eagle, sceptre, oak.

Defining myths. The Titanomachy and the swallowing of Metis to forestall a successor (Theogony 617–720, 886–900); the Prometheus–Pandora cycle, which fixes the human condition (Theogony 521–616; Works and Days 42–105); the mortal unions (Europa, Danaë, Semele, Alcmene) that found royal lines and feed Hera's grievance.

Where sources disagree. Hesiod makes Zeus the youngest child of Cronus (Theogony 478). Homer's Poseidon resents Zeus as a brother "born earlier" (Iliad 15.166), and at 13.355 Zeus is explicitly the elder. Homer gives no birth story at all; his Zeus has always ruled.

Hera

Birth. Daughter of Cronus and Rhea (Theogony 454).

Domains and epithets. Legitimate marriage, sovereignty, the Argolid. Teleia, "the fulfilled", is Hera as wife; Argeia ties her to her favourite city (Iliad 4.51–52); Her hostility to Zeus's children by other women is not mere jealousy: it is the goddess of lawful marriage defending the institution she embodies.

Cult. The Argive Heraion (Pausanias 2.17); Samos, whose temple Herodotus calls the largest he knew (3.60); Olympia, where girls raced at the Heraia (Pausanias 5.16.2).

Art. Matronly, veiled, high polos crown, sceptre; pomegranate or cuckoo.

Defining myths. The persecution of Heracles; the seduction of Zeus in Iliad 14 with Aphrodite's borrowed girdle; her punishments, hung from heaven with anvils at her feet (Iliad 15.18–24) and bound in Hephaestus' throne until Dionysus brought him back drunk (Pausanias 1.20.3). Hera is the only Olympian Zeus must repeatedly coerce, which is itself a statement about her rank.

Poseidon

Birth. Son of Cronus and Rhea (Theogony 453–457).

Domains and epithets. The sea, but equally the earthquake (Ennosigaios, "earth-shaker"; Asphaleios, "the steadier") and the horse (Hippios).

Cult. Isthmia; Sounion; Mycale; Pylos, where he already receives offerings in the Linear B tablets.

Art. Indistinguishable from Zeus except for the trident; dolphin, horse, bull.

Defining myths. The division of the cosmos by lot, which he insists makes him Zeus's equal in honour (Iliad 15.187–193); the contest with Athena for Attica, salt spring against olive (Herodotus 8.55; Apollodorus 3.14.1); the pursuit of Odysseus for blinding Polyphemus (Odyssey 1.68–75).

Demeter

Birth. Daughter of Cronus and Rhea (Theogony 454).

Domains and epithets. Cultivated grain and the settled order it brings. Thesmophoros, "law-bringer", names her autumn women's festival. Arcadia knew a darker goddess: Erinys at Thelpusa and Melaina, the Black Demeter, horse-headed in a cave at Phigalia (Pausanias 8.42.1–4).

Cult. Eleusis and the Mysteries, open to anyone Greek-speaking and unpolluted by homicide; the Thesmophoria, kept by married women in almost every city.

Art. Veiled, with wheat ears, poppies, torch, sceptre; the pig is her victim.

Defining myths. The rape of Persephone, Demeter's wandering, her nursing of Demophoön at Eleusis and the famine that forces Zeus to compromise (Homeric Hymn 2); the gift of agriculture to Triptolemus, absent from the Hymn but central to Athenian claims (Apollodorus 1.5.2).

Where sources disagree. The Hymn says Zeus gave Persephone away "without Demeter's knowledge" (2.3); Hesiod compresses the story into two lines without comment (Theogony 912–914). Whether the Hymn describes actual Eleusinian ritual or a poet's reconstruction is uncertain.

Children of Zeus: Athena, Apollo, Artemis

Athena

Birth. Zeus swallows the pregnant Metis and bears Athena from his head (Theogony 886–900, 924–926). Homeric Hymn 28 has her leap out fully armed; Pindar adds Hephaestus' axe (Olympian 7.35–38). In the Iliad Ares sneers that Zeus "yourself bore this mad, destructive daughter" (5.875–880), so Homer knows the motif but never narrates it.

Domains and epithets. Intelligent craft in every form: weaving (Ergane), shipbuilding, horse-taming, and the disciplined side of war (Promachos) against Ares' frenzy. Polias is the guardian of the Acropolis and the oldest cult; Parthenos is the title of the great temple; Pallas and Tritogeneia were already obscure to the Greeks.

Cult. Athens: the Panathenaia and its peplos, the Plynteria washing of the olive-wood image, the Arrhephoria, the Chalkeia shared with Hephaestus.

Art. Helmet, spear, shield with gorgoneion, snake-fringed aegis, owl, olive.

Defining myths. The contest for Attica; the birth of Erichthonius from Hephaestus' spilled seed and her fostering of the Athenian line (Apollodorus 3.14.6); her partnership with Odysseus and Heracles, standing beside the hero rather than fighting for him.

Apollo

Birth. Leto, refused by every land, is accepted by barren Delos and labours nine days because Hera detains Eileithyia (Homeric Hymn 3.25–126). Hesiod gives only the parentage (Theogony 918–920).

Domains and epithets. Prophecy, music, purification and healing, and the plague that is healing's reverse. Pythios and Delios name the two sanctuaries; Delphinios guards harbours and the admission of young men to citizenship; Lykeios is the wolf god or the light god, depending on which ancient etymology one trusts; Smintheus, the mouse god, opens the Iliad (1.39). Phoebus, "bright", is not evidence of a sun god; that identification is late fifth-century.

Cult. Delphi, oracle and Pythian Games; Delos and the Ionian festival (Hymn 3.146–164); Didyma and Claros; the Athenian Thargelia with its scapegoats.

Art. Beardless, long-haired youth; bow or lyre; laurel; tripod and omphalos.

Defining myths. The killing of the dragon and the founding of the oracle (Hymn 3.300–374); the plague on the Greek camp (Iliad 1); the slaughter of Niobe's children (Iliad 24.602–617).

Where sources disagree. The Hymn's dragon is female and nameless; the male Python is later. Aeschylus has Delphi pass peacefully from Gaia to Themis to Phoebe to Apollo (Eumenides 1–19); Euripides has Apollo seize it by violence (Iphigenia among the Taurians 1234–1283). Even the lyre is contested: in Homeric Hymn 4 Hermes invents it and trades it to Apollo.

Artemis

Birth. Twin of Apollo by Leto (Theogony 918–920).

Domains and epithets. The margins: wild animals and the hunt (Agrotera; Potnia Theron, "mistress of animals", Iliad 21.470), the dangerous transitions of girls into wives and wives into mothers (Lochia, Kourotrophos), and the sudden death of women, which Homer lays at her arrows. Orthia at Sparta, Brauronia in Attica, Ephesia in Asia.

Cult. Brauron, where Athenian girls "played the bear" before marriage; Ephesus and its many-breasted statue; Sparta, with the flogging of youths at Orthia's altar (Pausanias 3.16.7–11).

Art. Short chiton, bow and quiver, deer or hound; the crescent is Hellenistic and Roman.

Defining myths. Actaeon, torn by his hounds (Callimachus, Hymn 5.107–118; Apollodorus 3.4.4, with varying motive); Iphigenia and the substituted hind (Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis 1581–1595). In the Iliad Hera boxes her ears and calls her "a lion to women" (21.479–496), a Homeric demotion of a goddess who elsewhere terrifies.

Children of Zeus: Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes

Ares

Birth. Son of Zeus and Hera (Theogony 921–923).

Domains and epithets. Not war as institution but the frenzy within it. His Homeric epithets are abusive: brotoloigos, "ruin of mortals", miaiphonos, "blood-stained". Zeus calls him "the most hateful to me of all the gods" (Iliad 5.890).

Cult. Thin. Sparta sacrificed puppies to Enyalios (Pausanias 3.14.9); the Areopagus took his name from his trial for killing Halirrhothius (Apollodorus 3.14.2).

Art. Armed warrior, hard to tell from a mortal hoplite without inscription.

Defining myths. Wounded by Diomedes with Athena's help (Iliad 5.855–909); bound thirteen months in a bronze jar by Otus and Ephialtes (Iliad 5.385–391); caught in Hephaestus' net with Aphrodite (Odyssey 8.266–366).

Where sources disagree. The Homeric Hymn to Ares (8) praises a planetary, philosophical Ares who grants restraint. Most scholars think it a late addition, possibly by the fifth-century AD Neoplatonist Proclus; a minority defends an earlier date. Read it as evidence for late antique religion, not Homer's world.

Aphrodite

Birth. Two incompatible accounts. Hesiod: she grows from the foam around the severed genitals of Uranus and steps ashore on Cyprus (Theogony 188–206). Homer: daughter of Zeus and Dione, who comforts her on Olympus (Iliad 5.370–417). Plato's Pausanias turns the doublet into a heavenly Ourania and a vulgar Pandemos (Symposium 180d–e); in real Athenian cult Pandemos meant "of all the people" and was respectable.

Domains and epithets. Sexual desire and its persuasion, but also gardens, the sea (Euploia, Pontia) and, at Sparta and Corinth, an armed Areia. Kypris and Kythereia fix her islands.

Cult. Paphos, where Homer already sends her (Odyssey 8.362–363); Cythera; Acrocorinth; Athens, with Pandemos below the Acropolis.

Art. Clothed and dignified until Praxiteles (c. 350 BC); dove, swan, mirror, apple, myrtle, and the child Eros, who in Hesiod is a primordial power that merely attends her (Theogony 120, 201).

Defining myths. The Judgement of Paris; the seduction of Anchises and the conception of Aeneas (Homeric Hymn 5); the destruction of Hippolytus for refusing her (Euripides, Hippolytus 1–57).

Hephaestus

Birth. Hesiod has Hera bear him alone, "in strife with her husband", as an answer to Zeus's solo birth of Athena (Theogony 927–929). Homer makes him son of Zeus and Hera (Iliad 1.578). Apollodorus reports both (1.3.5).

Domains and epithets. Fire as technology, metalwork, and craft that borders on magic. Klytotechnes, "famed craftsman"; Amphigyeeis and Kyllopodion, "lame", "crook-footed", the only disabled Olympian.

Cult. Lemnos, where the Sintians received him after his fall (Iliad 1.590–594); Athens, the one mainland city that honoured him seriously, with the Hephaisteion above the Agora, the Chalkeia, and a torch-race reorganised in 421/0 BC.

Art. Bearded workman in exomis and pilos, hammer and tongs.

Defining myths. The making of Pandora (Works and Days 60–82) and of Achilles' shield (Iliad 18.468–617); the net that traps Aphrodite with Ares (Odyssey 8); the Return, led drunk by Dionysus to free Hera from the throne, a favourite of vase painters from the François Vase on.

Where sources disagree. Homer gives two incompatible falls. In Iliad 1.590–594 Zeus hurls Hephaestus by the foot for defending Hera, and he lands on Lemnos. In Iliad 18.395–405 Hera throws him down because he was born lame, and Thetis and Eurynome hide him for nine years. Ancient critics noticed; modern ones treat them as two traditions the poet declined to reconcile.

Hermes

Birth. Born to the nymph Maia in a cave on Mount Cyllene (Theogony 938–939). Homeric Hymn 4 gives the one-day career: born at dawn, he invents the lyre from a tortoise by midday, steals Apollo's cattle at evening, drives them backwards to hide the tracks, and is back in his cradle by morning, lying with a straight face to his elder brother.

Domains and epithets. Every kind of crossing: boundaries, roads, herds, markets, messages, luck, trickery, athletics, the passage of souls. Psychopompos conducts the dead (Odyssey 24.1–14); Argeiphontes, traditionally "Argus-slayer", may originally mean "shining"; Dolios, "the tricky", openly worshipped at Pellene.

Cult. Arcadia; the herms at every Attic crossroads and door, whose mutilation in 415 BC was treated as a plot against the state (Thucydides 6.27).

Art. Archaic: bearded traveller with winged boots, petasos, kerykeion, ram. Classical: beardless athletic youth. The herm, a bearded head on a square pillar with erect phallus, is the commonest image.

Defining myths. The cattle theft and the exchange of lyre for herd; the guiding of Priam through the Greek camp (Iliad 24.334–467); the slaying of Argus to free Io (Apollodorus 2.1.3).

Dionysus

Birth. Son of Zeus and the mortal Semele of Thebes (Theogony 940–942; Iliad 14.323–325). Hera tricks Semele into asking Zeus to appear in his true form; the lightning kills her, and Zeus sews the foetus into his thigh and bears him at term (Euripides, Bacchae 1–42, 88–104; Apollodorus 3.4.3). The double birth is why he is "twice-born".

Domains and epithets. Wine and release (Lyaios, "the loosener"), ecstatic possession, the mask and the theatre, vegetation (Dendrites), and a dark complement: Omestes, "raw-eater", to whom Plutarch says Themistocles sacrificed three Persian prisoners before Salamis (Themistocles 13.2–3). Bromios, "the roarer"; Eleuthereus, from the border village whose image came to Athens and gave the City Dionysia its god.

Cult. Athens above all: the City Dionysia with its tragic and comic competitions, the Lenaia, the Rural Dionysia with phallic processions, and the Anthesteria, at which new wine was opened and the archon's wife was married to the god. Delphi, where he was said to be buried beside the tripod (Plutarch, Isis and Osiris 365a).

Art. Archaic: bearded, ivy-crowned, long-robed, with kantharos and thyrsus; from the late fifth century a soft beardless youth. Panther, leopard skin, satyrs and maenads; the mask on a pillar in women's rites.

Defining myths. Pentheus, who refuses the god and is dismembered by his own mother (Bacchae); the pirates turned to dolphins when vines sprout from the mast (Homeric Hymn 7); the marriage to Ariadne.

Where sources disagree. Herodotus thought Dionysus one of the youngest gods and his rites an import from Egypt (2.49, 2.145–146), and for a century scholars treated him as a late arrival from Thrace or Phrygia, reading the "resistance myths" as memories of his coming. The Linear B tablets from Pylos and Khania, which name di-wo-nu-so around 1200 BC, overturned that. The resistance myths are now generally read as a pattern internal to his worship, the god who arrives as a stranger each year, not as history.

What an Olympian is

An Olympian is a god who belongs to Zeus's household on the mountain and shares in his order. The category is defined by three contrasts.

Against the Titans. The Titans are the previous government. The Theogony is a succession myth: Uranus is castrated by Cronus, Cronus deposed by Zeus, and Zeus alone ends the cycle by swallowing Metis so that no son can surpass him. What they lack is a stable distribution of honours. Zeus's innovation is to apportion timai, spheres of honour, to each god and make the apportionment stick. Olympians hold such portions under Zeus; Titans do not. Homer's Poseidon makes exactly this point when he insists that the cosmos was divided by lot into three and Zeus should keep to his share (Iliad 15.187–199).

Against the chthonic gods. Olympians receive sacrifice upwards: the throat cut with head raised, thigh bones burnt on a high altar, smoke rising, worshippers eating the meat. Chthonic powers, the dead, Hades, the Erinyes, receive sacrifice downwards, into a pit or low hearth, often as a holocaust no one eats, often at night. This is a working distinction, not a wall. Zeus Meilichios took holocausts as a snake; Demeter at Phigalia was horse-headed in a cave; Hermes conducted souls; Dionysus had a tomb at Delphi. Olympians live above and come down; chthonic gods live below and must be reached down to. Modern scholars debate how sharp the Greeks felt this line to be; the current view is that it was real in ritual but constantly crossed.

Against the heroes. Heroes are dead mortals who retain power around their graves. Heracles is the exception who crosses the boundary, feasting with the gods while his shade stays in Hades, as the Odyssey awkwardly admits (11.601–604). Hero cult is local and tied to a tomb; Olympian cult is translocal and shared by all Greeks, which is what Herodotus means when he says Homer and Hesiod "made a theogony for the Greeks" and gave the gods their titles, honours and skills (2.53). An Olympian is thus also a Panhellenic god, whose Delphic, Delian, Olympian or Eleusinian festivals were open to any Greek. That is why the list of twelve is a Panhellenic product even though no two cities agreed on its membership.

The category is not a matter of birth. Aphrodite, on Hesiod's account, is older than Zeus; Dionysus has a mortal mother; Hephaestus may have no father. What makes them Olympians is that they take their seats at the one table and their portions from the one distribution.

Self-test

  1. Which ancient structure gives the earliest firm evidence for a cult of "the Twelve Gods" at Athens, and who dedicated it?
    Answer

    The Altar of the Twelve Gods in the Agora, dedicated by the younger Peisistratus around 522 BC (Thucydides 6.54.6–7).

  2. Give the two incompatible accounts of Aphrodite's birth and the authors who transmit each.
    Answer

    Hesiod, Theogony 188–206: she grows from the foam around Uranus' severed genitals. Homer, Iliad 5.370: she is the daughter of Zeus and Dione.

  3. How do Homer and Hesiod disagree about Zeus's birth order among the children of Cronus?
    Answer

    Hesiod makes Zeus the youngest (Theogony 478); Homer's Poseidon calls him the elder brother (Iliad 13.355, 15.166).

  4. What does the epithet Zeus Xenios protect, and which Odyssean episode hinges on it?
    Answer

    The guest–host relationship. Odysseus invokes Zeus as avenger of suppliants and strangers against Polyphemus (Odyssey 9.270–271).

  5. Name Hephaestus' two falls from heaven as told within the Iliad itself.
    Answer

    Zeus throws him to Lemnos for defending Hera (1.590–594); Hera throws him down for his lameness and Thetis and Eurynome shelter him (18.395–405).

  6. Why is Dionysus no longer regarded as a late foreign import into Greek religion?
    Answer

    Linear B tablets from Pylos and Khania record his name (di-wo-nu-so) around 1200 BC, centuries before Herodotus' or the Thracian-origin theory's dates.

  7. What is the difference between Olympian and chthonic sacrifice in ritual practice?
    Answer

    Olympian: upwards, on a raised altar, thigh bones burnt and meat eaten. Chthonic: downwards into a pit or low hearth, often a whole-burnt offering eaten by no one, often at night.

  8. Which three versions of how Apollo acquired Delphi do the Homeric Hymn, Aeschylus and Euripides give?
    Answer

    Hymn 3: he kills the she-dragon. Aeschylus, Eumenides 1–19: peaceful succession from Gaia, Themis and Phoebe. Euripides, Iphigenia among the Taurians 1234–1283: violent seizure.

  9. Which Olympian did Zeus call "the most hateful to me of all the gods", and where?
    Answer

    Ares, Iliad 5.890, after Ares is wounded by Diomedes.

  10. Why does Hestia have almost no mythology, and what does Plato say about her in the Phaedrus?
    Answer

    She is the hearth and cannot act away from it; Plato says she alone stays in the house of the gods while the others ride out (247a).

Carry forward

  1. "The twelve Olympians" is a civic and artistic convention with shifting membership, not a doctrine; always ask which city's twelve a source is using.
  2. Homer, Hesiod and the Hymns are independent and often incompatible witnesses; an Olympian's "biography" is a set of competing local traditions, and the epithets preserve the local layers the poets flattened.
  3. An Olympian is defined by sharing in Zeus's distribution of honours and by Panhellenic, upward-facing cult, not by parentage; Titans, chthonic powers and heroes each lack one or more of these.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the twelve Olympian gods, one structured profile each: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, and Dionysus (and explain the Hestia/Dionysus substitution and why "twelve" is a convention). For each: birth myth, domains, the most important epithets and what they reveal (Zeus Xenios, Athena Polias, Apollo Pythios, etc.), main cult centres and festivals, attributes in art, the two or three defining myths, and the places where Homer, Hesiod and the Homeric Hymns disagree. Finish with a section on what an Olympian is as a category: what makes these gods different from the Titans, the chthonic gods and the heroes. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 2 · Mythology I: the cosmos and the gods · 2.3 · 2,932 words

The underworld and the chthonic gods

Hades the god and Hades the placeThe abduction of Persephone and the Homeric Hymn to DemeterThe geography of the underworldFrom Homer to VirgilThe famous punishedThe katabasis traditionHecate, the Erinyes, Thanatos and HypnosOlympian and chthonic in ritualSelf-testCarry forward

Hades the god and Hades the place

In Homer "Hades" is nearly always a person. The dead go "to the house of Hades"; using the god's name for his realm is a later shorthand. Greeks heard the name as "the Unseen" (a-ides), an etymology Plato toys with in Cratylus 403a; modern linguists reject it, and the origin is uncertain.

His position is fixed in Iliad 15.187–193: the three sons of Cronus drew lots, and Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades "the murky darkness", with earth and Olympus held in common. Hesiod, Theogony 453–506, gives the brothers' birth, and at 767–774 the "echoing halls of the strong god" guarded by the hound. Hades is Zeus's near double: Homer calls him Zeus Katachthonios, "Zeus of the Underworld" (Iliad 9.457), and his epithets Pylartes "gate-fastener" (Iliad 8.367) and Polydegmon "receiver of many" (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 17) describe a jailer, not a judge. Agamemnon calls him "unyielding and inexorable, and therefore most hateful of gods to mortals" (Iliad 9.158–159). He has little mythology beyond the abduction of Persephone and the moments when heroes force his doors; Heracles wounds him with an arrow "at Pylos among the dead" (Iliad 5.395–404).

Cult reflects this remoteness. Pausanias 6.25.2 knew only one true temple of Hades, at Elis, opened once a year. Elsewhere he was approached under euphemisms: Plouton, "the Wealthy One", which from the fifth century (Sophocles, Antigone 1200) softens him into giver of the harvest; Klymenos at Hermione (Pausanias 2.35.9); Eubouleus in Eleusinian and Orphic texts. The place itself has no stable location in Homer. Odysseus sails to it across Oceanus (Odyssey 10.508–515, 11.13–22); yet Patroclus's ghost goes beneath the earth "like smoke" (Iliad 23.100), and Hades fears Poseidon's earthquake will split the ground above him (Iliad 20.61–65).

Where sources disagree. Whether Homer's Hades lies beyond the western Ocean or below the earth has troubled readers since the Alexandrian critics. Most modern scholars (Sourvinou-Inwood, "Reading" Greek Death, 1995) treat the two as alternative traditional images rather than parts of one map.

The abduction of Persephone and the Homeric Hymn to Demeter

Hesiod disposes of the story in two lines: Zeus gave Persephone to Hades, who "snatched her from her mother" (Theogony 912–914). The full narrative is the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, 495 hexameters usually dated between about 650 and 550 BC and preserved in a single Moscow manuscript found in 1777.

The narrative

Persephone is gathering flowers on the Nysian plain when the earth opens at a narcissus Zeus has grown as a lure; Hades carries her off in his chariot (1–20). Only Hecate and Helios hear her cry. Demeter searches nine days with torches, refusing food; on the tenth Hecate joins her and Helios names the thief, adding that Hades is "no unworthy son-in-law" (62–89). Demeter leaves Olympus disguised as an old woman. At Eleusis she sits by the Maiden Well, is found by the daughters of King Celeus, and becomes nurse to the infant Demophoön (98–183). She refuses wine and asks for the kykeon, barley meal in water with pennyroyal (206–211); the servant Iambe makes her laugh (202–205). Each night she lays the child in the fire to make him immortal, until Metaneira spies and shrieks; Demeter reveals herself and orders a temple built above the Kallichoron spring (231–274). Then she withholds the harvest for a year, until Zeus relents (305–313). Hades releases Persephone but "secretly gave her a honey-sweet pomegranate seed to eat" (371–374). Because she has eaten below she must return: one third of the year with Hades, two thirds with her mother (398–403, 445–447). Demeter restores the grain, teaches her rites to Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus and Celeus (473–479), and the hymn closes on the initiate's reward:

Blessed is he among men on earth who has seen these things.

The uninitiated "never has a share in such things once dead, down in the mouldering gloom" (480–482).

Where sources disagree. The hymn tells the pomegranate twice: the narrator says Hades gave it "secretly" (372), but Persephone tells her mother he "forced me against my will" (411–413). On the division of the year the hymn says one third below; Ovid (Metamorphoses 5.564–567; Fasti 4.613–614) says half. The abduction site also moves: Nysa in the hymn, Enna in Sicily for Diodorus 5.3–4 and Ovid, Eleusis itself in the local version in Pausanias 1.38.5.

Eleusis

Almost every element of the Mysteries has its aition in the hymn: the Kallichoron, where initiates danced; the kykeon drunk after fasting; the ritual obscenity of the procession, echoing Iambe; the torchlight; the ancestors of the priestly clans, the Eumolpidae and Kerykes. Demophoön has been read as the shadow of the child initiated "from the hearth", a known Eleusinian office. The hymn omits Athens, one argument for dating it before Athenian control of the sanctuary (Richardson, 1974). Clinton (Myth and Cult, 1992) argues instead that the hymn reflects the Thesmophoria more than the Mysteries, whose own myth centred on Demeter's gift of grain.

The seasons

The hymn ties Persephone's return to spring, "when the earth blooms with every kind of fragrant spring flower" (401–403). But in Greece grain is sown in October and harvested in May and June; the dead season is the parched summer. Nilsson (1940) therefore argued that Persephone's months below are those the seed-corn spends in underground storage jars from harvest to sowing. The hymn's text resists this, since it names spring, and Demeter's famine is a withholding of germination, not a winter. Most recent commentators (Foley, 1994) read the hymn less as seasonal allegory than as a story about marriage, loss and mortality, to which seasonal meaning was later attached.

The geography of the underworld

Circe's sailing directions (Odyssey 10.508–515) are the first map: walk from Ocean's shore to where "into Acheron flow Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus, which is a branch of Styx". Hesiod adds the house of Styx (Theogony 775–806) and the chasm of Tartarus (720–819). Plato systematises four rivers in Phaedo 112e–113c. Virgil assembles everything.

NameMeaningEarliest attestationRole
Styx"Hateful"Iliad 8.369; Hesiod, Theogony 383–403, 775–806Boundary and oath of the gods; a perjured god lies breathless a year and is exiled nine
AcheronFolk-linked to achos, "grief"Odyssey 10.513Main river; also a real river in Thesprotia with an oracle of the dead (Herodotus 5.92η)
Cocytus"Wailing"Odyssey 10.514Tributary of Styx
Pyriphlegethon"Fire-blazing"Odyssey 10.513River of fire; rings Tartarus in Aeneid 6.550–551
Lethe"Forgetting"Aristophanes, Frogs 186; Plato, Republic 621aAbsent from Homer and Hesiod; a plain in Plato, a river drunk before rebirth in Aeneid 6.713–715

Charon and Cerberus

Charon is absent from Homer and Hesiod. He first appears in the lost epic Minyas, quoted by Pausanias 10.28.2, and is a stock figure by the fifth century: Euripides, Alcestis 252–257; Aristophanes, Frogs 180–270, where he charges two obols. Virgil's filthy, fire-eyed ferryman (Aeneid 6.298–304) is the one Dante inherited. Cerberus is in Homer only as "the hound of Hades" (Iliad 8.368). Hesiod names him, gives him fifty heads and explains his job: he fawns on those who enter and devours any who try to leave (Theogony 310–312, 769–774). Three heads become standard in sixth-century art.

The judges

In Homer only Minos sits "holding a golden sceptre, giving judgements to the dead" (Odyssey 11.568–571); the dead come to him as litigants, and he settles disputes rather than weighing souls. Rhadamanthys in Homer lives in Elysium (Odyssey 4.564). The tribunal of three is Plato's: in Gorgias 523e–524a Rhadamanthys judges the dead of Asia, Aeacus those of Europe, Minos hears appeals. Virgil keeps Minos shaking the urn of lots (Aeneid 6.432) and makes Rhadamanthys inquisitor of Tartarus (6.566–569).

Where sources disagree. Whether Homer's Minos judges the dead at all is contested: Sourvinou-Inwood reads him as continuing his earthly kingship, and sees the moralised afterlife as a sixth- to fifth-century development. Aeacus is a judge in Plato, but the doorkeeper of Hades in the manuscripts of Aristophanes' Frogs and in Lucian, Dialogues of the Dead 20.

Tartarus, the asphodel meadow, Elysium

Tartarus in Homer is a prison for gods, "as far beneath Hades as heaven is above earth" (Iliad 8.13–16, 478–481). Hesiod makes it a primordial being (Theogony 119) and a chasm so deep that a bronze anvil falls nine days to reach it (720–725). It holds the Titans; no mortal is punished there. The ordinary dead occupy the asphodel meadow (Odyssey 11.539, 573; 24.13). Elysium in Homer is not in the underworld at all: Menelaus will be sent alive to "the Elysian plain at the ends of the earth", where Rhadamanthys lives (Odyssey 4.561–569). Hesiod's Isles of the Blessed house the heroes of the fourth race (Works and Days 167–173). Pindar, Olympian 2.56–80, gives the earliest full statement of posthumous judgement, the good passing to the Isle of the Blessed.

Where sources disagree. Reece (2007) has argued that the "asphodel meadow" is a misdivided "ashy meadow" (spodos), refitted by folk etymology to the plant; the matter is open.

From Homer to Virgil

Homer's underworld is flat and undifferentiated. The dead are witless shadows who need blood to speak (Odyssey 11.23–50, 147–149); three sinners are punished and one man judges, but the ordinary dead are neither rewarded nor penalised. Between Homer and Virgil the picture is moralised and mapped. Hesiod and the Hymn to Demeter introduce a blessed fate for the few. The Orphic gold tablets, from Hipponion (c. 400 BC) onward, give the initiate a route: avoid the spring by the white cypress and drink from the Lake of Memory. Aristophanes, Frogs 145–158, shows a popular version, with a slough of mud for perjurers and parricides and myrtle groves for initiates. Plato builds the eschatological myths of Gorgias 523a–527a, Phaedo 107d–115a and Republic 614b–621d: judgement at a meadow where roads fork, Tartarus for the incurable, purgation and rebirth for the rest, and a plain of Lethe where souls drink and forget.

Virgil, Aeneid 6, fuses these layers into the itinerary that became the Western default. The vestibule holds personified Grief, Disease, Old Age, Fear, Hunger, Death and Sleep (273–281). Acheron, Cocytus and Styx are one tangled flood (295–297). Charon refuses the unburied, who wait a hundred years (325–330). Beyond Cerberus, drugged with a honeyed cake (417–423), lie the infants, the falsely condemned under Minos, the suicides and the Fields of Mourning (426–476). The road forks (540–543): left to Tartarus, ringed by Phlegethon, where Tisiphone guards the gate and Rhadamanthys interrogates (548–627); right to Elysium, now underground with its own sun (637–678). Anchises explains that souls are purged for a thousand years, drink Lethe and return to bodies (713–751). None of this is Homeric; it is Platonic, Orphic-Pythagorean and Stoic.

Where sources disagree. Virgil's Theseus, "sitting and destined to sit for ever" in Tartarus (6.617–618), contradicts the Greek tradition that Heracles freed him (Apollodorus 2.5.12). Virgil is also at odds with himself: Elysium is both final home and a waiting-room before rebirth.

The famous punished

Odysseus sees three sinners together (Odyssey 11.576–600). What they share is offence against the gods in person, which is why they are the exception to Homer's indifferent afterlife.

SinnerPunishmentOffence and source
TityosStretched over nine plethra while two vultures tear his liver (Odyssey 11.576–581)Attempted rape of Leto (Apollodorus 1.4.1; Pindar, Pythian 4.90)
TantalusStands in receding water under fruit the wind snatches away (Odyssey 11.582–592); or crouches beneath a hanging rock (Pindar, Olympian 1.55–64; Euripides, Orestes 4–10)Stole nectar and ambrosia (Pindar); served his son Pelops to the gods, a version Pindar rejects
SisyphusRolls a stone uphill that always falls back (Odyssey 11.593–600)Betrayed Zeus's abduction of Aegina; chained Thanatos so no one died (Pherecydes, FGrH 3 F 119)
IxionBound to an ever-turning wheel (Pindar, Pythian 2.21–48)First kin-murderer, then attempted Hera at Zeus's table; Zeus substituted the cloud Nephele
The DanaidsPour water for ever into a leaking vessel (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.462–463; Horace, Odes 3.11.21–32; Hyginus, Fabulae 168)Murdered their husbands, the sons of Aegyptus, on the wedding night (Apollodorus 2.1.5)
Where sources disagree. Homer never names the offences of Tantalus and Sisyphus; the explanations are later and multiple. Ixion's wheel in Pindar spins through the air, and only Virgil (Aeneid 6.601) settles him in Tartarus. The Danaids' water-carrying is not attested before the Roman period: in Plato, Gorgias 493a–c, and in Polygnotus' painting at Delphi (Pausanias 10.31.9–11) the leaking jar belongs to the uninitiated in general.

The katabasis tradition

Odysseus. Odyssey 11 is strictly a nekyia, a summoning of the dead at a pit on Ocean's shore; yet from 11.568 Odysseus sees Minos, Tityos and Heracles as though inside. Analysts since Wilamowitz have treated 11.565–627 as an interpolation; unitarians reply that Homer moves the camera without caring.

Heracles. The twelfth labour is already in Iliad 8.367–369. Apollodorus 2.5.12 gives the full form: initiated first at Eleusis, he descends at Taenarum, frees Theseus, fails to free Pirithous, and drags Cerberus up with Persephone's consent. Bacchylides 5.56–175 has him meet Meleager's ghost and ask for Deianira in marriage, with terrible irony. The Eleusinian initiation (also Euripides, Heracles 610–619) recasts the labour as an initiate's rehearsal of death.

Orpheus. The earliest allusion is Euripides, Alcestis 357–362, where Admetus wishes he had Orpheus' voice to bring Alcestis back; the wish implies success. Plato, Symposium 179d, says the gods showed Orpheus only a phantom and sent him away for cowardice. The named Eurydice and the backward look first appear together in Virgil, Georgics 4.453–527, followed by Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.1–85.

Theseus and Pirithous. The friends descend to carry off Persephone for Pirithous; Hades seats them on the Chair of Forgetfulness, where they grow fast to the rock (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23–24; Pausanias 10.29.9). Heracles frees Theseus; when he reaches for Pirithous the earth quakes. Odyssey 11.631 names the pair, but Hereas of Megara (in Plutarch, Theseus 20.2) charged that Pisistratus inserted the line to flatter Athens.

Where sources disagree. Bowra (1952) argued that Orpheus' failure is Virgil's invention; Heath (1994) and most since reply that Plato's Symposium and the Attic relief of Orpheus, Eurydice and Hermes (c. 410 BC) show a failed return a century before Virgil, though not the backward glance. Hermesianax (fr. 7 Powell) calls the wife Agriope; the name Eurydice is not secure before the first century BC.

Hecate, the Erinyes, Thanatos and Hypnos

Hecate. Hesiod's hymn (Theogony 411–452) makes her daughter of Perses and Asteria, honoured by Zeus above all, with nothing chthonic about her; West (1966) defends the passage as Hesiod's own. In the Hymn to Demeter she hears the cry, carries a torch in the search, and ends as Persephone's attendant (24–25, 52–62, 438–440). By the fifth century she is goddess of crossroads, ghosts and sorcery: Medea's mistress (Euripides, Medea 395–397), recipient of monthly suppers at crossroads (Aristophanes, Plutus 594–597), invoked with howling dogs in Theocritus, Idyll 2.

The Erinyes. In Homer they avenge wrongs against parents and oaths (Iliad 9.454, 571; 19.259–260). Hesiod makes them daughters of Gaia from the blood of Uranus (Theogony 185); Aeschylus makes them daughters of Night, black-robed, dripping from the eyes (Eumenides 46–56, 321–322), and settles them in Athens as the Semnai Theai. Three in Euripides (Orestes 408), they are named Allecto, Tisiphone and Megaera in Virgil and Apollodorus 1.1.4. Demeter was worshipped as Demeter Erinys at Thelpusa (Pausanias 8.25.4–7), a hint that the fury was once an earth-goddess.

Thanatos and Hypnos. Night bore Death and Sleep fatherless (Theogony 211–212); Sleep is gentle, Death has "a heart of iron, pitiless as bronze" (758–766). In Iliad 16.671–683 the twins carry Sarpedon's body to Lycia, the scene on the Euphronios krater. Only Euripides puts Death on stage, black-robed and armed with a sword, wrestled into submission by Heracles (Alcestis 24–76, 843–849). Sisyphus's binding of Thanatos, so that no one could die until Ares freed him, is Pherecydes'.

Olympian and chthonic in ritual

Greek ritual expresses the distinction between upper and lower powers through orientation. To the Olympians one sacrificed (thuein) on a raised altar (bomos) a white victim, head pulled back so the throat faced the sky; the meat was shared, the god receiving thigh-bones and fat in smoke. To the powers below one sacrificed into a pit (bothros) or on a low hearth (eschara) a black victim with head pressed down so the blood ran into the earth, often at night, the victim burnt whole, the celebrant turned away. Homer knows the code: in the oath of Iliad 3.103–104 a white lamb is brought for Helios and a black one for Earth; for the dead Odysseus digs a pit, promises Tiresias an all-black ram and lets the blood run into the trench (Odyssey 11.23–36), turning his face away as Circe instructed (10.527–529). The verb for offerings to heroes and the dead was enagizein; Herodotus 2.44 notes that some Greeks sacrifice to Heracles as an immortal and others make offerings to him as a hero. Zeus Meilichios received pigs burnt entire (Xenophon, Anabasis 7.8.4–5).

Where sources disagree. How systematic this dichotomy was is the central modern argument. Rohde, Harrison and Nilsson built on it a two-tier religion of sky-gods and earth-powers. Schlesier (1991–92) attacked the dichotomy as a nineteenth-century construct; Scullion (1994) defended a modified version; Ekroth (2002) showed from inscriptions and bone deposits that heroes, and often underworld gods, received ordinary thysia with a shared meal, holocausts being rare. Burkert's compromise, that the categories mark two poles of a spectrum, is now the usual position.

Self-test

  1. Which passage fixes Hades' share of the cosmos, and how was it allotted?
    Answer

    Iliad 15.187–193: the three sons of Cronus drew lots. Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the darkness; earth and Olympus were common.

  2. Which two deities hear Persephone's cry in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter?
    Answer

    Hecate, in her cave, and Helios. Hecate later joins the search and Helios names Hades as the abductor.

  3. What fraction of the year does Persephone spend below according to the hymn, and who gives a different figure?
    Answer

    One third (398–403, 445–447). Ovid gives half the year in Metamorphoses 5 and Fasti 4.

  4. Why does Nilsson's seed-corn interpretation sit awkwardly with the hymn's own text?
    Answer

    Nilsson placed Persephone's absence in summer, when seed-corn is stored underground, with her ascent at autumn sowing. The hymn says she returns when the earth blooms in spring (401–403).

  5. Is Charon in Homer? Where does he first appear?
    Answer

    No. He first appears in the lost epic Minyas, quoted by Pausanias 10.28.2, and is a fixture by the fifth century (Euripides, Aristophanes).

  6. What is Minos doing in Odyssey 11, and who turned him into one of three judges?
    Answer

    He is giving judgements to the dead who bring disputes to him, continuing his kingship, not weighing lives. Plato, Gorgias 523e–524a, makes him, Rhadamanthys and Aeacus a tribunal.

  7. Where is Elysium in Homer, and where in Virgil?
    Answer

    In Odyssey 4.561–569 it is a plain at the ends of the earth, reached alive by Menelaus. In Aeneid 6 it is underground, the right-hand branch of the fork beyond Charon and Cerberus.

  8. What is wrong with saying "the Danaids carry water in leaking jars in the Greek underworld"?
    Answer

    The image is Roman (Ovid, Horace, Hyginus). In Plato's Gorgias and Polygnotus' Delphic painting the leaking jar punishes the uninitiated in general, not the daughters of Danaus.

  9. What is the earliest text to say that Orpheus failed, and when is the name Eurydice first secure?
    Answer

    Plato, Symposium 179d, where the gods show him only a phantom. The name Eurydice is not secure before the first century BC; Hermesianax calls her Agriope.

  10. List four ritual markers that separate a chthonic from an Olympian sacrifice.
    Answer

    Low pit or hearth rather than raised altar; black rather than white victim; head pressed down so blood enters the earth rather than throat to the sky; victim burnt whole rather than shared and eaten. Night-time and the averted face are further markers.

Carry forward

  1. Homer's underworld is not moral. Reward, punishment and judgement for ordinary mortals enter between the sixth and fourth centuries through Eleusis, Orphic and Pythagorean teaching and Plato, and Virgil fixes the result; read every later afterlife against that sequence.
  2. The Persephone myth is first a cult myth of Eleusis and a story about marriage and loss; the seasonal allegory is secondary and does not fit the Greek farming year cleanly. Keep the hymn's own promise, a better lot after death for the initiate, in view for the modules on mystery cult and Plato.
  3. The Olympian and chthonic distinction is a real grammar of ritual gesture, not two religions. Treat it as a spectrum with heroes and figures such as Zeus Meilichios and Hecate in the middle, and expect it to recur in hero cult, oath-ritual and tragedy.
