GREECE · UNIT 3 · Mythology II: the heroes · 3.2 · 3,500 words

Heracles

Birth: Alcmene, Amphitryon and the hatred of HeraYouth, Thebes and the killing of the childrenThe Twelve LaboursThe parergaOmphale, Troy and OechaliaDeianira, Nessus and the robeThe pyre on Oeta, the apotheosis and HebeThe politics: Heracleidae, Sparta, Macedon and AthensSelf-testCarry forward

Birth: Alcmene, Amphitryon and the hatred of Hera

Heracles is a Perseid on both sides. Alcmene was the daughter of Electryon of Mycenae, son of Perseus; Amphitryon, her husband, was the son of Alcaeus, another son of Perseus. When Amphitryon killed Electryon, by accident in Apollodorus (Library 2.4.6), he was driven from the Argolid and took Alcmene to Thebes. She refused him until he had avenged her brothers, killed by the Taphians. While he was away Zeus came to her in Amphitryon's shape and, Apollodorus says, made the one night three times its length (2.4.8). Amphitryon returned the next day and lay with her too; the twins were Heracles, by Zeus, and Iphicles, a night younger, by the mortal husband. Hesiod's Shield of Heracles 1–56 tells the same story and already says Zeus intended the child as a defender of gods and men.

Hera's hatred begins before the birth. In Iliad 19.95–133 Zeus boasts that a man of his blood will be born that day to rule all his neighbours; Hera makes him swear it, holds back the birth goddesses from Alcmene and hurries on the labour of Sthenelus' wife, so that Eurystheus arrives in the seventh month and the oath falls to him. The child was first called Alcides; Apollodorus (2.4.12) says the Pythia renamed him Heracles, while Diodorus (4.10.1) explains the name as glory won through Hera's persecution. The infant suckled by an unwitting Hera, whose spilt milk became the Milky Way, is Hellenistic (Diodorus 4.9.6; the Catasterisms).

The serpents are the first labour in miniature. Pindar, Nemean 1.33–72, is the fullest early telling: Hera sends two snakes into the nursery, the infant strangles one in each hand, Amphitryon rushes in with drawn sword, and Teiresias prophesies the beasts he will kill, the war against the Giants and his final rest with Hebe. Theocritus, Idyll 24 makes him ten months old, Apollodorus (2.4.8) eight.

Where sources disagree. Apollodorus also records, from Pherecydes of Athens, that Amphitryon himself put the serpents in the cradle to learn which twin was his: Iphicles fled, Heracles stood his ground. The Hera version became canonical, but the Pherecydes version is older than most surviving texts and removes the goddess entirely.

Youth, Thebes and the killing of the children

Apollodorus (2.4.9) lists the teachers: Amphitryon for the chariot, Autolycus for wrestling, Eurytus for archery, Castor for fighting in armour, Linus for the lyre. Heracles killed Linus with a blow of the lyre and was acquitted under a law of Rhadamanthys permitting the return of a blow. Sent to the cattle-farms, at eighteen he killed the lion of Cithaeron while staying with Thespius, who gave him his fifty daughters. Returning, he mutilated the heralds of Erginus of Orchomenus who were collecting tribute from Thebes, then killed Erginus in the war that followed, losing Amphitryon in the fighting. Creon gave him his daughter Megara.

The madness is where the biography forks. In Apollodorus (2.4.12) and Diodorus (4.11.1–2) Hera drives him mad soon after the marriage; he throws his children into the fire, is purified by Thespius and goes to Delphi, where the Pythia tells him to serve Eurystheus for twelve years and perform ten labours, after which he will be immortal. The madness causes the labours. Euripides reverses the order. In Heracles (c. 416 BC) the hero returns from Cerberus to find Lycus about to kill Megara and the children; he saves them, and only then do Iris and Lyssa descend at Hera's command (822–873). He kills Megara and the three boys thinking them Eurystheus' family, is stopped from killing Amphitryon by Athena's thrown stone, and wakes to be talked out of suicide by Theseus, whom he has just freed from Hades. The point is deliberate: madness strikes a man who has finished the civilising work and has nothing left to earn, and the rescue is by human friendship, not divine favour.

Where sources disagree. Madness before the labours makes them expiation; madness after (Euripides) makes them irrelevant to it. Most scholars treat the Euripidean placement as his own invention; Wilamowitz argued he preserved an older sequence. The children number three in Euripides and Apollodorus, five in Pherecydes, eight in Pindar, Isthmian 4.63–64. Megara is killed in Euripides but given to Iolaus in Apollodorus 2.6.1.

The Twelve Labours

The canonical order is Apollodorus, Library 2.5.1–12; Diodorus 4.11–26 has the same twelve with the hind and boar, and the birds and stables, swapped, and Cerberus before the apples. The earliest complete set is not a text but the twelve metopes of the temple of Zeus at Olympia (c. 460 BC), where the Augean stables come last, a local compliment. The two lost epics that fixed the saga, Peisander of Camirus' and Panyassis' Heracleia, survive only in fragments. Apollodorus explains the number: the Pythia ordered ten, but Eurystheus disallowed the Hydra, because Iolaus helped, and the stables, because Heracles had demanded wages, so two more were added (2.5.11).

No.LabourLocationTaskWhat it is about
1Nemean lionNemea, ArgolidStrangle an invulnerable lion; flay it with its own clawsAcquiring his emblem; strength before technique
2Lernaean HydraLerna, ArgolidMany-headed snake reared by Hera (Hesiod, Theogony 313–318); Iolaus cauterises the necks; arrows dipped in the venomIntelligence and help against a Hera-bred monster; the poison that will kill him
3Ceryneian hindArcadia, chased to the Hyperboreans (Pindar, Olympian 3.26–32)Capture alive a golden-horned hind of ArtemisRestraint; the first task where killing is forbidden
4Erymanthian boarMt Erymanthus, ArcadiaNet the boar in snow; the centaur fight at Pholus' cave, Chiron woundedCollateral damage: violence spills onto the innocent
5Augean stablesElisClear the dung in a day by diverting the Alpheus and PeneusEngineering as heroism; the broken bargain leads to the Elean war and the Olympic Games (Pindar, Olympian 10.24–59)
6Stymphalian birdsLake Stymphalus, ArcadiaScare the birds with Athena's bronze rattle and shoot themClearing land for cultivation
7Cretan bullCreteCapture Poseidon's bull alive; released, it ends at MarathonFirst labour outside the Peloponnese; a thread handed to Theseus
8Mares of DiomedesBistonian ThraceTake the man-eating mares; Abderus devoured, Abdera founded over his graveTaming the barbarian north
9Belt of HippolyteThemiscyra on the ThermodonFetch the Amazon queen's war-belt; Hera in Amazon shape provokes a fight; Hesione at Troy on the way backHera turns a gift into a killing; the Trojan debt he later collects
10Cattle of GeryonErytheia, beyond GadesKill three-bodied Geryon (Hesiod, Theogony 287–294); drive the cattle home through Italy, Sicily and ScythiaThe journey to the sunset; first assault on death's frontier; the Pillars
11Apples of the HesperidesThe garden at the world's endFetch Hera's wedding apples guarded by Ladon; Atlas and the skyImmortality as the object; the apples return to Athena because a mortal may not keep them
12CerberusHades, entered at TaenarumBring up the dog; Eleusinian initiation first; Theseus freedThe conquest of death, after which the labours stop

The pattern is visible once the table is laid out. The first six labours clear the Peloponnese of beasts: the hero as culture-bringer, the alexikakos who makes the land habitable. Labours seven to nine push to the edges of the Greek world. The last three are not about monsters but about the boundary of mortality: the west where the sun goes down, the garden holding the fruit of eternal life, and the house of Hades. Burkert read Geryon's cattle as a death-journey older than the heroic frame, a raid on the herds of the dead; whatever one makes of that, the ordering already makes the labours a descent and return, which is why the apotheosis follows so naturally. Hera reared the Hydra, gave the apples at her wedding and appears among the Amazons: the labours are her war against him by proxy.

Where sources disagree. Pausanias 2.37.4 says the Hydra had one head until Peisander gave it many. The apples: Apollodorus 2.5.11 reports both that Heracles sent Atlas and held up the sky, and (from Pherecydes) that he killed the serpent himself; Euripides, Heracles 394–399 and Sophocles, Women of Trachis 1099–1100 follow the second. The Cretan bull is either Europa's or the Minotaur's father; Apollodorus gives both. Heracles comes up from Hades at Troezen in Apollodorus, Taenarum or Heraclea Pontica elsewhere.

The parerga

The side-deeds stitch Heracles into every other saga. The Argonauts. He joined the Argo but did not reach Colchis. Apollonius (Argonautica 1.1207–1357) leaves him in Mysia searching for Hylas, snatched by a nymph; Herodotus 7.193 has him put ashore at Aphetae to fetch water. Apollodorus 1.9.19 collects the variants: Herodorus says he never sailed, being enslaved to Omphale at the time; Demaratus says he reached Colchis. The reason for the ejection is structural: a crew that includes Heracles has no need of Jason.

Prometheus. Hesiod, Theogony 526–534 already has Heracles kill the eagle with Zeus' consent, to increase his son's glory. Apollodorus 2.5.11 sets it on the Caucasus during the apple quest and adds the unbinding; Prometheus in return told him to send Atlas for the apples, and Chiron, incurably wounded in the boar episode, gave up his immortality so that Prometheus might be freed (2.5.4). Antaeus. A Libyan son of Earth who forced strangers to wrestle and roofed Poseidon's temple with their skulls (Pindar, Isthmian 4.52–55); Heracles, finding that he drew strength from the ground, lifted him and broke him in the air (Apollodorus 2.5.11). Busiris. An Egyptian king who sacrificed a foreigner each year to end a drought; Heracles let himself be led to the altar and killed Busiris, his son and the herald (Apollodorus 2.5.11; Diodorus 4.27.2–3). The Pillars. On the Geryon journey he set up two pillars at the straits as the mark of how far he had gone. Pindar makes them the limit of human achievement, beyond which not even the wise can pass (Olympian 3.43–45; Nemean 3.21–23); Diodorus 4.18.5 reports both that he narrowed the strait to keep out sea-monsters and that he cut it open.

Where sources disagree. Herodotus 2.45 rejects the Busiris story outright: the Egyptians abhor human sacrifice, and the tale of Heracles slaughtering thousands at the altar is simple-minded. He also insists there are two Heracleses, an old Egyptian god and a Greek man, a problem he cannot resolve (2.43–44).

Add the Gigantomachy, where the oracle required a mortal ally (Pindar, Nemean 1.67–69; Apollodorus 1.6.1–2), and the help given to the Dorian king Aegimius against the Lapiths in return for a third of his land, which Apollodorus 2.7.7 and Diodorus 4.37.3–4 record as the origin of the Dorian claim through Hyllus.

Omphale, Troy and Oechalia

After the labours Heracles won Iole at Oechalia in an archery contest and was refused her by Eurytus, his old teacher. When Iphitus, the one son who had taken his side, came to Tiryns searching for stolen cattle, Heracles in a second fit of madness threw him from the walls (Apollodorus 2.6.1–2). The Odyssey treats this as plain crime: he killed a guest in his own house with no regard for the gods or the table (21.22–30), and Iphitus' bow, passed to Odysseus, is the weapon of the suitors' slaughter. Sophocles, Women of Trachis 270–273 makes it an ambush. Disease followed, the Pythia refused to answer, and Heracles carried off the tripod and fought Apollo until Zeus parted them with a thunderbolt. The oracle then came: he must be sold into slavery and the price paid to Eurytus as blood-money. Hermes sold him to Omphale, queen of Lydia: three years in Apollodorus (2.6.3), one in Sophocles (Trach. 248–253). In Lydia he caught the Cercopes, killed Syleus, and fathered the son from whom Herodotus 1.7 derives the Lydian Heraclid dynasty. The exchange of clothes, Heracles in Omphale's gowns, is Hellenistic and Roman (Ovid, Heroides 9; Lucian, Dialogues of the Gods 13); the fifth century had him working, not spinning.

Troy. Laomedon had cheated him of the immortal horses promised for saving Hesione. Heracles sailed with eighteen ships in Apollodorus 2.6.4, six in Iliad 5.638–642, where Tlepolemus taunts Sarpedon that his father took Troy with a fraction of the present force. Laomedon and all his sons died except Podarces, ransomed by Hesione's veil and so renamed Priam, the bought one. Hera's storm then drove Heracles to Cos (Iliad 14.249–256). Peloponnesian campaigns followed: Augeas killed and the Olympic Games founded; Pylos taken from Neleus (Iliad 11.690–693); Hippocoon of Sparta destroyed and Tyndareus restored (Apollodorus 2.7.3), the first link between Heracles and the Spartan throne.

Oechalia. Years later, settled at Trachis after killing Eunomus, he marched on Oechalia, killed Eurytus and his sons and took Iole (Apollodorus 2.7.7). Sophocles sets Oechalia in Euboea (Trach. 74, 237); Homer's catalogue puts it in Thessaly (Iliad 2.730); Pausanias 4.2.2–3 admits nobody could agree.

Deianira, Nessus and the robe

Deianira, daughter of Oeneus of Calydon, had been courted by the river-god Achelous; Heracles wrestled him for her, and her account of that terror opens Sophocles' play (Trach. 9–27). Crossing the Evenus, Heracles entrusted her to the centaur ferryman Nessus, who tried to rape her midstream; Heracles shot him from the bank with a Hydra-poisoned arrow. Dying, Nessus told her to keep the blood from his wound as a charm that would hold Heracles' love. Apollodorus 2.7.6 specifies seed mixed with blood; Sophocles, more decorous, has only the clotted blood round the arrow (572–577). The poison of the second labour has been waiting for decades.

Sophocles' tragedy is the version that matters. Heracles has been away fifteen months; Lichas brings home captives from Oechalia, among them a silent girl. Deianira learns she is Iole and that she is to share the house. She does not rage; she reasons that love is a disease no one chooses, then reaches for the charm, anoints a robe and sends it to Heracles, who is sacrificing to Zeus at Cape Cenaeum. The wisp of wool she used, left in the sun, crumbles and foams (695–704); she knows. Hyllus arrives to describe the robe eating into his father's flesh and Lichas hurled onto the rocks, and curses his mother. Deianira kills herself with a sword on the marriage bed (930–931). Heracles is carried in raving; when he learns it was Nessus' blood he understands the old oracle that he would die by nothing living, and becomes calm. He orders Hyllus to carry him to Oeta and burn him, and to marry Iole. The play's last line reads the whole catastrophe as the will of Zeus.

Where sources disagree. Deianira dies by the sword in Sophocles but hangs herself in Apollodorus 2.7.7 and Diodorus 4.38.3. Modern critics divide on whose play it is: for some she is the true subject and the title names the women who witness her; for others Heracles' late entrance is the point. The date is unknown, with guesses from the 450s to the 420s.

The pyre on Oeta, the apotheosis and Hebe

The pyre on Oeta above Trachis is a real place: excavation on the summit found an ash altar with Geometric and Archaic offerings and later inscriptions to Heracles, a cult older than any literary account. In Apollodorus 2.7.7 nobody will light the pyre until Poeas does so and receives the bow; Sophocles, Philoctetes 801–803 gives it to Philoctetes; Diodorus 4.38.4–5 to Iolaus. All agree that a cloud carried him up with thunder, and Diodorus adds (4.39.1) that no bones were found. Heracles was reconciled with Hera, who in Diodorus 4.39.2 adopted him by a ritual rebirth, and married Hebe, Youth, by whom he had Alexiares and Anicetus (Apollodorus 2.7.7).

The apotheosis is old. Hesiod, Theogony 950–955 says Heracles, his grievous labours completed, made Hebe his wife on Olympus and lives untroubled and unaging among the immortals. Pindar closes Nemean 1 with Teiresias prophesying the same, and in Nemean 3.22 calls him heros theos, hero-god, the only figure of Greek myth who is fully both. Herodotus 2.44 approves of the Greeks who keep two cults, sacrificing to one Heracles as an Olympian and offering to the other as a dead hero.

Where sources disagree. Homer is the awkward witness. In Iliad 18.117–119 Achilles says not even Heracles escaped death, but was overcome by fate and Hera's anger. In Odyssey 11.601–627 Odysseus meets his shade in Hades, "but he himself feasts with the immortal gods". Ancient critics already flagged lines 602–604 as an insertion, attributed by some to Onomacritus under the Peisistratids. Whether the split-Heracles compromise is Homeric or sixth-century Athenian remains disputed.

The politics: Heracleidae, Sparta, Macedon and Athens

Heracles left no city. He was born at Thebes, belonged by blood to Argos, served at Tiryns, died in Thessaly, and his children were refugees. That is precisely what made him usable: an ancestor without a homeland gave every claimant the same thing, a right that pre-dated the current occupants.

The Heracleidae. After his death Eurystheus pursued the children. They fled to Athens, where Demophon took them in; Eurystheus marched on Attica, Macaria gave her life for the victory, and Eurystheus was killed (Euripides, Children of Heracles; Apollodorus 2.8.1). Hyllus then tried to re-enter the Peloponnese, misread an oracle, and was killed at the Isthmus by Echemus of Tegea (Herodotus 9.26). The great-grandsons, Temenus, Cresphontes and Aristodemus, returned with the Dorians, crossed from Naupactus and drew lots: Argos to Temenus, Messenia to Cresphontes, Sparta to the twin sons of the dead Aristodemus, Procles and Eurysthenes, founders of the two royal houses (Apollodorus 2.8.2–5; Diodorus 4.57–58; Pausanias 3.1.5–6). This is the Greeks' own explanation of what we call the Dorian migration; Thucydides 1.12.3 dates it eighty years after Troy and calls it the Dorians with the Heracleidae. The two names are not interchangeable: the Dorians are the people, the Heracleidae their kings, and the link between them is Aegimius' adoption of Hyllus, from whom one of the three Dorian tribes, the Hylleis, took its name.

Sparta. This explains an otherwise strange fact: the two kings were not, in their own view, Dorians. Barred from the Athenian Acropolis as a Dorian, Cleomenes answered, "I am no Dorian but an Achaean" (Herodotus 5.72). Herodotus gives Leonidas' pedigree back to Heracles in twenty generations (7.204) and Leotychides' in 8.131. Tyrtaeus (fr. 2 West), in the seventh century, already sings that Zeus gave this city to the Heracleidae. The ideology is one of restoration: Heracles had held the Peloponnese by right as Zeus' son and been cheated by Eurystheus; his descendants took back their own. It also gave Sparta a title to the whole peninsula, on which Spartan foreign policy drew for three centuries, and the story of Heracles restoring Tyndareus meant the hero had already decided once who ruled Sparta.

Macedon. The Argead kings traced themselves to Temenus of Argos and so to Heracles. Herodotus 8.137–139 tells how Perdiccas came from Argos to Macedonia, and how Alexander I, challenged at Olympia as a barbarian, proved his Argive descent and was admitted to the stadium (5.22). Heracles in the lion-scalp on nearly every silver tetradrachm of Alexander the Great made the ancestor visible across the empire. Alexander besieged Tyre for seven months when refused the right to sacrifice to Heracles-Melqart (Arrian 2.15.7–16.8), stormed Aornos because Heracles was said to have failed there (Arrian 4.28.1–4), and named a son Heracles. The Ptolemies then claimed the same ancestor through Alexander (Theocritus, Idyll 17.26–27). For a Macedonian king Heracles did three things: proved Greekness to Greeks who doubted it, justified rule by conquest, and offered a precedent for a mortal becoming a god.

Athens. Athens claimed no descent but kept him anyway, and in the sixth century he appears on Attic vases more often than any other figure, far more than Theseus. The ties were specific. Heracles was the first foreigner initiated at Eleusis, and the Lesser Mysteries at Agrae were said to have been founded for his purification (Apollodorus 2.5.12; Diodorus 4.14.3). He freed Theseus from Hades, and in Euripides' Heracles 1322–1337 Theseus repays him with Athenian land and cult; Plutarch, Theseus 35.2–3 says Theseus dedicated to Heracles all his own sanctuaries but four. The Athenians sheltered his children, and cited that service at Plataea (Herodotus 9.27). At Marathon the army camped in his precinct, and after the battle in his precinct at Cynosarges (Herodotus 6.108, 6.116). For a democracy he offered a hero who belonged to no one's aristocracy, who worked and suffered, and who had been Athens' guest.

Where sources disagree. John Boardman argued (1972–1989) that the Peisistratids adopted Heracles as personal propaganda, with his introduction to Olympus mirroring Peisistratus' return to Athens in a chariot beside a woman dressed as Athena (Herodotus 1.60), and that the fall in Heracles scenes and rise of Theseus after 510 marks the democracy's rebranding. R. M. Cook and others replied that Heracles was popular everywhere in sixth-century art and that painters followed buyers, not tyrants. The shift to Theseus after 510 is real; its cause is uncertain.

Self-test

  1. Why was Eurystheus, and not Heracles, born to rule Mycenae, according to Homer?
    Answer

    In Iliad 19.95–133 Zeus swore that a Perseid born that day would rule; Hera delayed Alcmene's labour and hastened Eurystheus' birth in the seventh month, so the oath fell to him.

  2. In Apollodorus, does the madness come before or after the labours, and what difference does it make?
    Answer

    Before: the killing of the children leads to Delphi and the sentence of service to Eurystheus, so the labours are expiation. Euripides puts it after, so the labours earn nothing and the madness is pure divine malice.

  3. Why twelve labours when the Pythia ordered ten?
    Answer

    Eurystheus disallowed the Hydra (Iolaus helped) and the Augean stables (Heracles demanded wages), so two more were set (Apollodorus 2.5.11).

  4. Which three labours are about mortality rather than monsters, and why?
    Answer

    Geryon's cattle (the far west, the sunset), the apples of the Hesperides (the fruit of immortality) and Cerberus (Hades itself). Each takes him to a boundary of death and back, preparing the apotheosis.

  5. Give two incompatible ancient accounts of why Heracles did not reach Colchis with the Argonauts.
    Answer

    Apollonius: left in Mysia searching for Hylas. Herodotus 7.193: put ashore at Aphetae to fetch water. Herodorus: he never sailed, being enslaved to Omphale at the time.

  6. What was the Hydra's connection to Heracles' death?
    Answer

    He dipped his arrows in its venom; the arrow that killed Nessus carried it, Nessus' poisoned blood became Deianira's love-charm, and the robe anointed with it burned Heracles alive.

  7. How does Deianira die in Sophocles, and how in Apollodorus?
    Answer

    Sophocles, Women of Trachis 930–931: by the sword, on the marriage bed. Apollodorus 2.7.7 and Diodorus: she hangs herself.

  8. What does Herodotus 2.44 say about the Greek worship of Heracles?
    Answer

    That the Greeks who keep two cults act rightly: sacrificing to one Heracles as an immortal Olympian and offering to the other as a hero, that is, a dead man.

  9. Why could Cleomenes of Sparta say "I am no Dorian but an Achaean"?
    Answer

    The Spartan kings descended from Heracles through the Heracleidae, not from the Dorian people they led; the Dorians were the followers whom Aegimius' adoption of Hyllus had bound to the Heraclid line.

  10. Name three concrete Athenian ties to Heracles despite the absence of any claim of descent.
    Answer

    Any three of: initiation at Eleusis and the founding of the Lesser Mysteries; the shelter given to the Heracleidae; Theseus' dedication of his shrines to Heracles (Plutarch, Theseus 35); the Athenian camp in his Marathon precinct (Herodotus 6.108); the Cynosarges gymnasium; his rescue of Theseus from Hades.

Carry forward

  1. Heracles is the only Greek figure who is both hero and god, heros theos, and the Greeks knew the contradiction: the split between the Olympian bridegroom of Hebe and the shade in Hades (Odyssey 11) is the model for every later argument about whether a man can become divine, from Alexander to the Hellenistic kings.
  2. The labours read as a sequence: clearing the Peloponnese, pushing to the edges of the Greek world, then three assaults on the frontier of death. Keep that shape; the colonising Heracles of the western Greeks and the Heracles of Stoic moral philosophy both grow from it.
  3. Descent from Heracles is a political instrument, not a tribal fact. The Heracleidae are kings, the Dorians a people, and the "return" legitimates rule as restoration rather than conquest; Sparta, Macedon and the Ptolemies all drew on it, while Athens shows that a city could own the hero through cult and hospitality without owning his blood.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Heracles, the complete life. Cover: birth (Alcmene, Amphitryon, Hera's hatred, the serpents), youth, the madness and the killing of his children; the Twelve Labours in the canonical order with the location, the monster or task, and what each labour is "about"; the parerga (side adventures: the Argonauts, Prometheus, Antaeus, Busiris, the Pillars); the servitude to Omphale, the sack of Troy and Oechalia; Deianira, Nessus and the poisoned robe; the pyre on Oeta and the apotheosis; his marriage to Hebe. Then the politics: why Dorian Sparta and the Macedonian kings claimed descent from him, the Heracleidae, and why Athens kept him too. Sources: Apollodorus, Diodorus, Euripides' Heracles, Sophocles' Women of Trachis, Pindar. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 3 · Mythology II: the heroes · 3.3 · 3,238 words

Theseus and Athens

Sources: a hero assembled lateTroezen, the rock and the roadAthens: Medea, the Pallantidae and the bullCrete: tribute, Labyrinth, Naxos, the black sailThe king's deeds: Amazons, Centaurs, Helen, HadesPhaedra, Hippolytus and ScyrosThe synoikismos and the democratic TheseusMaking a rival to HeraclesSelf-testCarry forward

Sources: a hero assembled late

No archaic poem about Theseus survives whole. Homer knows him in passing: Nestor lists him among the men of old (Iliad 1.265, a line ancient critics already suspected as an Athenian insertion), Odysseus names "Theseus and Pirithous" in the underworld (Odyssey 11.631), and the Nekyia records Ariadne's death on Dia (11.321–325). A lost epic Theseis existed by the end of the sixth century (Aristotle, Poetics 1451a). Everything coherent is fifth-century or later: Bacchylides' dithyrambs 17 and 18, the tragedians, the Atthidographers Hellanicus, Cleidemus and Philochorus, read only in quotation, Diodorus 4.59–63, Apollodorus (Library 3.15.6–16.2; Epitome 1.1–24), Pausanias, and above all Plutarch's Life of Theseus, c. AD 100, paired with Romulus. Plutarch warns that beyond Theseus lie only "marvels and tragedy" (1.3); he knows he is handling a biography built by Athenians for Athenian purposes. The question throughout is less what Theseus did than when Athens decided he had done it.

Troezen, the rock and the road

Birth and the tokens

Aegeus, king of Athens and childless, received at Delphi an oracle he could not read. At Troezen the wise king Pittheus understood it, got Aegeus drunk and put him to bed with his daughter Aethra (Plutarch 3; Apollodorus 3.15.6–7). Before leaving, Aegeus hid a sword and sandals under a great rock: a son who could lift it was to come secretly to Athens with the tokens, since Aegeus feared the fifty sons of his brother Pallas. Troezen added that the same night Aethra, prompted by Athena, waded to the islet of Sphairia and was taken by Poseidon (Pausanias 2.33.1). The double paternity is deliberate: Bacchylides (17.33–36) and the tragedians treat Poseidon as the real father, making Theseus the equal of Heracles, son of Zeus, while Aegeus supplies the throne.

At sixteen Theseus lifted the rock and refused the safe sea crossing. Plutarch (6–7) gives the motive: raised on the fame of Heracles, his kinsman through Pittheus, he chose the brigand-infested Isthmus road so as to arrive in Athens with deeds behind him. The emulation of Heracles is built in from the first step.

The six labours of the road

OpponentPlaceMethod and outcome
Periphetes "Corynetes"EpidaurusClub-wielder killed with his own club; Theseus kept it, as Heracles kept the lion-skin
Sinis "Pityocamptes"Isthmus of CorinthBent pines to tear travellers apart; killed the same way. Theseus took his daughter Perigune
Phaea, the Crommyonian sowCrommyonKilled; some made Phaea a murderous woman nicknamed "sow"
ScironScironian cliffs, MegaridForced travellers to wash his feet, kicked them to a giant turtle; thrown off his own cliff
CercyonEleusisWrestled travellers to death; lifted and dashed down. Credited as the origin of scientific wrestling
Procrustes (Damastes, Polypemon)Erineus, by the CephisusFitted guests to his bed by stretching or hacking; fitted to it himself

Sources: Plutarch 8–11; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.1–4; Bacchylides 18.16–30. Each labour sits on the real road, a map of Attica's frontier dressed as a mythic clearing of the land.

Where sources disagree. Bacchylides 18, the earliest list, names Sinis, the sow, Sciron, Cercyon and Procoptes: five, not six. Periphetes is absent from the earliest cycle cups and enters art only around 500 BC; Jenifer Neils argued he was added to give Theseus a club to match Heracles' weapon. Megara denied that Sciron was a bandit at all and made him a just war-leader (Plutarch 10.2–3). Procrustes' name and parentage shift from source to source.

Athens: Medea, the Pallantidae and the bull

Aegeus had taken in Medea, exiled from Corinth, who promised him children by her drugs. She recognised the stranger and persuaded the old king to poison him at a banquet. Theseus drew his sword to carve the meat; Aegeus saw it, dashed the cup away and acknowledged his son (Plutarch 12; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.5–6; Euripides' lost Aegeus dramatised the scene). The Pallantidae, cheated of the succession, rose in arms, were betrayed by their herald Leos and destroyed (Plutarch 13).

The Marathonian bull was Theseus' first deed as acknowledged prince: he dragged it alive through the city and sacrificed it to Apollo Delphinius (Plutarch 14). Pausanias 1.27.10 makes it the Cretan bull Heracles had let loose in the Peloponnese, so that Theseus literally finished a labour of Heracles. The old woman Hecale who sheltered him on the way, and the Hecalesia he founded for her, gave Callimachus his Hecale.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch has recognition, Pallantidae, bull; Apollodorus (Epitome 1.5) has Medea send Theseus against the bull first, hoping it would kill him. Whether the Marathonian bull is an Attic doublet of the Cretan bull or an independent local legend is uncertain, as is whether it predates Athens' fifth-century investment in Marathon.

Crete: tribute, Labyrinth, Naxos, the black sail

Androgeos, son of Minos, had been killed in Attica (Apollodorus 3.15.7; Plutarch 15). Minos made war, plague followed, and the oracle told Athens to grant what Minos asked: seven youths and seven maidens, every nine years, for the Labyrinth and the Minotaur. The third tribute fell due after Theseus' arrival. He volunteered, or was chosen by lot, or, in Hellanicus (Plutarch 17.3), Minos came in person and picked him. He promised Aegeus to change the black sail for a white one if he lived (scarlet, said Simonides, Plutarch 17.5).

Ariadne loved him at sight and gave him the thread Daedalus devised; he killed the Minotaur, led the fourteen out, stove in the Cretan ships and sailed with her (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.7–9; Plutarch 19). Bacchylides 17 adds a scene found nowhere else in literature: on the voyage out Minos molests the maiden Eriboea; Theseus defies him; Minos, to prove his descent from Zeus, calls down lightning and throws his ring into the sea for the son of Poseidon to fetch; Theseus dives, is received by the Nereids and Amphitrite, who gives him a purple cloak and a wreath, and reappears dry beside the ship. The Onesimos cup in the Louvre (G 104, c. 500–490) paints the same scene with Athena watching. Plutarch (19) also reports the rationalisations of Philochorus and Cleidemus: the Labyrinth a prison, "Taurus" a brutal general beaten in Minos' funeral games. On the return the ships touched at Delos, where Theseus danced the geranos, the crane dance imitating the Labyrinth's turns (Plutarch 21; Callimachus, Hymn to Delos 307–315); the François Vase (c. 570) already shows it.

Where sources disagree. Ariadne's fate is the most fractured part of the legend. Odyssey 11.321–325: Artemis killed her on Dia on Dionysus' testimony. Hesiod fr. 298 (in Plutarch 20): Theseus left her for Aigle. Theogony 947–949: she is Dionysus' immortal bride. Paeon of Amathus (Plutarch 20): she died in childbirth on Cyprus. Catullus 64 and Ovid, Heroides 10 fix the image of the woman abandoned on Naxos. Plutarch concludes that the stories "do not agree". Most modern scholars take Ariadne to be an older Aegean goddess absorbed into a hero's story, which is why she cannot be made to die in only one way.

Theseus forgot the sail. Aegeus, watching from the Acropolis (Pausanias 1.22.5) or Cape Sunium, saw black and threw himself down; the sea took his name. Theseus landed at Phalerum on the seventh of Pyanepsion, and the autumn festivals, the Pyanepsia's boiled beans, the Oschophoria's vine-branches and boys dressed as girls, the Cybernesia for his helmsmen, were all explained as commemorating that homecoming (Plutarch 22–23). This is aetiology running backwards: existing rites given a hero to explain them.

The king's deeds: Amazons, Centaurs, Helen, Hades

Theseus the king is a looser assemblage than the boy on the road, and these stories were attached later.

The Amazons. Theseus sailed to the Black Sea, with Heracles or alone, and carried off the Amazon Antiope. The Amazons invaded Attica to recover her, camped on the Areopagus and were beaten inside the city; Antiope fell fighting beside Theseus, or was killed by him when she opposed his marriage to Phaedra (Plutarch 26–28; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.16–17). Aeschylus, Eumenides 685–690, knows the Amazon camp in 458, and Herodotus 9.27 has the Athenians at Plataea cite the victory among the deeds that earn them the place of honour. The Attic Amazonomachy was the Persian invasion given a heroic prototype; it was painted on the Theseion and the Stoa Poikile and carved on the shield of Athena Parthenos.

The Centauromachy. Pirithous of Thessaly drove off Theseus' cattle from Marathon to test him; the two admired each other and swore friendship. At Pirithous' wedding to Hippodameia the drunken Centaur Eurytion assaulted the bride (Odyssey 21.295–304 knows the crime without Theseus), and Theseus and the Lapiths slaughtered the Centaurs (Plutarch 30; Ovid, Metamorphoses 12). It joined the Amazonomachy on the Theseion and the Parthenon metopes as Athens' picture of order against barbarism.

Helen. Theseus and Pirithous, both widowed, swore to marry daughters of Zeus. They took Helen from Sparta as a child; the lot gave her to Theseus, who hid her at Aphidna with his mother Aethra. While he was away the Dioscuri took Aphidna with help from Decelea (Herodotus 9.73), recovered Helen, installed Menestheus in Athens and carried off Aethra as Helen's slave, which is why she stands beside Helen on the walls of Troy (Iliad 3.144). Plutarch (31) notes that Hellanicus made Theseus fifty and Helen a child, and that Attic writers tried to clean it up: he was keeping her for Idas and Lynceus, or Tyndareus had entrusted her to him.

Hades. Pirithous chose Persephone. Hades received the pair with a feigned welcome and fixed them to a seat of forgetfulness. Heracles, come for Cerberus, tore Theseus free but had to leave Pirithous (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.12; Epitome 1.23–24; Euripides, Heracles 619, where Theseus repays the debt with asylum). Plutarch (31, 35) prefers Philochorus' euhemerised version: "Hades" was Aidoneus, king of the Molossians, with a wife Persephone, a daughter Core and a dog Cerberus. Either way the pairing is the point: each hero now needs the other.

Where sources disagree. The Amazon is Antiope in nearly every Attic author and on the Eretria pediment (c. 510–500); Hippolyte appears in Cleidemus and later writers. Whether Theseus sailed with Heracles or alone split the Atthidographers (Plutarch 26.1–2). The Helen abduction was already in Alcman and Stesichorus, so Athens inherited an embarrassment rather than inventing it; Isocrates (Helen 18–20) reframes it as proof of Theseus' good taste.

Phaedra, Hippolytus and Scyros

Theseus married Phaedra, Ariadne's sister. Hippolytus, his son by the Amazon, was raised at Troezen. Phaedra conceived a passion for him; rejected, she hanged herself and left a tablet accusing him; Theseus cursed him with one of Poseidon's wishes, and a bull from the sea panicked his horses on the Troezenian shore. Artemis revealed the truth too late (Euripides, Hippolytus, 428 BC; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.18–19; Pausanias 2.32.1–4 for the Troezenian cult, where girls cut a lock of hair before marriage). Euripides' first Hippolytus, in which Phaedra propositioned him openly, was so badly received that the surviving play rewrote her as a woman fighting her desire. Theseus here is the tragic father, and that is how the theatre most often used him: the decent king who receives Oedipus (Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus) and the mothers of the Seven (Euripides, Suppliant Women).

The end is bleak. Menestheus, an Erechtheid, used Theseus' absence and the nobles' resentment to turn the people against him. Theseus came back from Hades to a hostile city, cursed it at Gargettus, sent his sons to Euboea and sailed to Scyros, where he held land. King Lycomedes, fearing him or bribed by Menestheus, led him up a height to show him his estates and pushed him off (Plutarch 35; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.24; Pausanias 1.17.6). Menestheus led the Athenians to Troy (Iliad 2.552). No one in Athens, Plutarch says, gave Theseus a thought, until Marathon.

The synoikismos and the democratic Theseus

Thucydides 2.15.1–2 is the earliest full statement. Under Cecrops and his successors Attica was a set of towns with their own councils that sometimes fought one another; Theseus, "a man of power as well as intelligence", dissolved the local councils and created one council-chamber and one prytaneion in Athens, and the Athenians still kept the Synoikia in his memory. Plutarch (24–25) expands: Theseus went from deme to deme persuading, offered the powerful a kingship without a king (he would be war-leader and guardian of the laws only), named the city, founded the Panathenaea, divided the people into Eupatridae, Geomoroi and Demiourgoi, struck ox-stamped coins, set up the Isthmian pillar reading "This is not the Peloponnese but Ionia", and founded the Isthmian Games for Poseidon in imitation of Heracles' Olympic Games for Zeus.

Fifth-century Athens turned this into a founding of democracy. Euripides, Suppliant Women 403–408, has Theseus tell the Theban herald that Athens is not ruled by one man: the people rule by yearly turns. Isocrates (Helen 35–37) says he handed the city to the people and kept only the dangers for himself. Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians 41.2 lists Theseus' settlement as the first "inclining a little from kingship" towards the people. The claim became so standard that Pausanias (1.3.3), seeing Theseus painted with Demokratia and Demos in the Stoa of Zeus, protested that it was simply untrue: kings ruled Athens for generations after Theseus, down to Codrus.

Where sources disagree. Pausanias' objection is the ancient form of the modern consensus. A political unification of Attica did happen, but attaching it to Theseus is Athenian ideology and the democratic colouring belongs to the fifth and fourth centuries. The date of the real unification is uncertain: some archaeologists put it in the Mycenaean palace period, most in the late Dark Age or eighth century, and Robin Osborne has argued that the demes kept such distinct identities that "unification" is the wrong word. Plutarch's ox-stamped coins are anachronistic by several centuries.

Making a rival to Heracles

Heracles belonged to everyone: Argive by birth, Theban by upbringing, Dorian through the Heraclid kings of Sparta, Argos and Messenia. He was also Athens' favourite hero for most of the sixth century: on Attic black-figure pottery between about 570 and 510 he outnumbers every other figure, and John Boardman argued from 1972 onward that the Peisistratids cultivated him deliberately, his introduction to Olympus by Athena mirroring the tyrant's own return under the goddess's protection. Theseus had been in Attic art since the seventh century, but almost only as the Minotaur's killer: a Troezenian with an Athenian father, not yet the city's own.

The vase evidence

Around 510–500 BC this changes abruptly. The "cycle cups", red-figure kylikes with a sequence of Theseus' deeds round the outside and the Minotaur in the tondo, appear in Attic workshops; the fully developed type is the Codrus Painter's cup in London (British Museum E 84, c. 440–430). The road labours, the bull, the carrying-off of Antiope (Myson's amphora, Louvre G 197) and the Amphitrite scene all enter the repertoire within a generation. Theseus takes over Heracles' iconography: the club, the wrestling hold, the bull. On the Athenian Treasury at Delphi (c. 500, or after 490; the date is contested) the metopes split evenly, Heracles on one side, Theseus on the other, now equals. The Hephaisteion in the Agora (c. 450) repeats the pairing.

Where sources disagree. Who sponsored the change? Boardman and H. A. Shapiro tied it to the fall of the tyrants in 510 and Cleisthenes' reforms: Theseus as the democratic answer to the Peisistratid Heracles. Neils put the earliest cycle cups in the 520s, under Hippias, which would make Theseus a Peisistratid project too. Henry Walker and Sophie Mills doubt that painters followed anyone's brief and see a broader appetite for a native hero as Athens became conscious of itself as an Ionian power facing Dorian Sparta. The Theseis, undated but late sixth-century on most views, fits any reading. The firm point is the images: before c. 520 a Minotaur-slayer, after c. 500 a complete heroic career.

Marathon and Bacchylides

Many Athenians at Marathon in 490, Plutarch says (35.5), believed they saw Theseus' phantom in armour charging the Persians ahead of them. The Stoa Poikile painting of the battle (Pausanias 1.15.3) showed Theseus rising from the earth beside Athena and Heracles, a careful equality, since the army had camped in Heracles' sanctuary at Marathon (Herodotus 6.108). Bacchylides' two dithyrambs belong to the following decades, probably the 480s or 470s. Ode 18 is a dialogue between Aegeus and a chorus about a stranger approaching the city with five brigands dead behind him: Theseus as Athens wanted him, arriving to save it. Ode 17 was sung by Ceans at Delos but is Athenian in content: Theseus son of Poseidon, defender of Athenian children against a Cretan tyrant, crowned under the sea and leading Ionian youths in Delian dances. It is hard not to connect a hymn performed at Delos with the Delian League founded there in 478/7, though the ode's exact date is unknown.

Cimon and the bones

In 476/5, the archonship of Phaedon, Delphi told the Athenians to bring home Theseus' bones and keep them with honour (Plutarch, Theseus 36.1). Cimon took Scyros and expelled its Dolopian pirates (Thucydides 1.98.2, who says nothing about bones) and, according to Plutarch (Cimon 8.5–7), saw an eagle tearing at a mound, dug, and found a coffin with a body of great size, a bronze spear and a sword. The city received them with processions and sacrifices "as if Theseus himself were returning", and buried them in the middle of the city, in a precinct that became a refuge for runaway slaves and the poor, "since Theseus too had been a protector of the weak" (Theseus 36.2). The Theseia on the eighth of Pyanepsion, and the eighth of every month sacred to him as to Poseidon, were fixed then.

The logic is plain. Cimon, son of Marathon's victor, was the leading man of the 470s and needed a civic rather than a clan hero. A hero whose bones lay under the city, who had beaten Amazons from the east, who was Poseidon's son and had saved Ionian children from an island tyrant, who had unified Attica by persuasion and given the people a share in rule, was the ideal patron of a maritime, Ionian, newly imperial Athens. The translation copied what Sparta had done with Orestes' bones at Tegea (Herodotus 1.67–68): Athens now had a hero cult in the Dorian manner, aimed at outranking the Heraclids' ancestor.

Where sources disagree. Thucydides dates the Scyros campaign only relatively; Plutarch's archon gives 476/5, but some scholars (Podlecki among them) argue for 475/4 or later, and whether the oracle preceded or followed the conquest is uncertain. The Theseion itself has never been found. Pausanias (1.17.2–3) saw it east of the Agora with Micon's paintings of the Amazonomachy, the Centauromachy and the ring episode; the marble temple above the Agora that older maps call the "Theseion" is the Hephaisteion.

Plutarch

Plutarch's Life is the end product. He pairs Theseus with Romulus because both founded a city out of scattered peoples, both carried off women, both died in exile. He is candid about the process: the proverb "another Heracles" (29.3) existed because the imitation was deliberate, and the cult began only after Marathon and the bones. His sources are the Atthidographers, whose fragments survive largely because he quoted them. The Life is therefore both the best evidence for the manufactured Theseus and itself a late layer of the manufacture.

Self-test

  1. Which two fathers are claimed for Theseus, and what does each contribute to his story?
    Answer

    Aegeus, king of Athens, who gives him the Attic throne, and Poseidon, who makes him a god's son on a par with Heracles (Plutarch 3, 6; Bacchylides 17; Pausanias 2.33.1).

  2. Name the six opponents on the road from Troezen to Athens, in order.
    Answer

    Periphetes at Epidaurus, Sinis at the Isthmus, the Crommyonian sow Phaea, Sciron on the Megarian cliffs, Cercyon at Eleusis, Procrustes at Erineus.

  3. Why is Bacchylides 18 important for the labours?
    Answer

    It is the earliest surviving list, and it names only five opponents, omitting Periphetes, which suggests the club-bearer was a later addition designed to give Theseus a Heraclean weapon.

  4. How does Aegeus recognise Theseus, and what role does Medea play?
    Answer

    Medea persuades Aegeus to poison the stranger; Theseus draws his sword to carve the meat, Aegeus recognises the token and knocks the cup away (Plutarch 12; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.5–6).

  5. What scene does Bacchylides 17 add to the Cretan voyage that appears in no other literary source?
    Answer

    Minos throws his ring into the sea to test Theseus' claim to be Poseidon's son; Theseus dives, is received by Amphitrite and the Nereids, and returns crowned and dry.

  6. Give three different ancient accounts of what happened to Ariadne.
    Answer

    Killed by Artemis on Dia on Dionysus' word (Odyssey 11); abandoned for Aigle (Hesiod fr. 298); made Dionysus' immortal wife (Theogony 947–949); died in childbirth on Cyprus (Paeon of Amathus in Plutarch 20). Any three.

  7. Which episode in Theseus' legend did Athens inherit rather than invent, and how did Athenian writers handle it?
    Answer

    The abduction of the child Helen, already in Alcman and Stesichorus. Athenian writers softened it: he was holding her for Idas and Lynceus, or Tyndareus entrusted her to him, or (Isocrates) it showed his good taste.

  8. What exactly does Thucydides 2.15 credit Theseus with, and what does he not say?
    Answer

    He dissolved the local councils of the Attic towns and created one council and prytaneion in Athens, the synoikismos commemorated by the Synoikia. He says nothing about democracy; that colouring comes from Euripides, Isocrates and Aristotle.

  9. What happened in 476/5, who did it, and what did Athens gain?
    Answer

    Cimon took Scyros, found a giant skeleton with bronze weapons and brought it to Athens as Theseus' bones on Delphi's instruction; they were buried in the Theseion in the city centre, which became a refuge for slaves and the poor, and gave Athens a civic hero cult modelled on Sparta's recovery of Orestes.

  10. What is the main disagreement among modern scholars about the Theseus cycle cups?
    Answer

    Whether their appearance around 510 reflects the new Cleisthenic democracy replacing a Peisistratid Heracles (Boardman, Shapiro), a slightly earlier Peisistratid initiative (Neils), or no political programme at all (Walker, Mills).

Carry forward

  1. Theseus is Heracles rebuilt for Athens: the club, the bull, the descent to Hades, the son-of-a-god parentage are all borrowed, and the pairing of the two heroes on the Athenian Treasury and the Hephaisteion is the visible form of a political claim about Ionian Athens against Dorian Sparta.
  2. The legend has datable layers: a Minotaur-slayer in archaic art, a full heroic career from c. 510–500, a Marathon epiphany, a state cult after 476/5, a democratic founder in the tragedians and orators. Later modules on Athenian self-image, the Delian League and the tragedians will assume this layering.
  3. Hero cult is a political instrument. Bone translations (Orestes to Sparta, Theseus to Athens), the attachment of existing festivals to a founder, and the retrojection of present institutions onto a mythical king are patterns that recur across the Greek world; Theseus is the clearest case of all three at once.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Theseus. Cover: birth at Troezen, the sword and sandals, the six labours on the road to Athens, Medea at Aegeus' court, the Marathonian bull, the Cretan tribute, Ariadne, the Labyrinth and the Minotaur, Naxos, the black sail and Aegeus' death; the later deeds (the Amazons and Hippolyta, the Centauromachy at Pirithous' wedding, the abduction of Helen, the descent to Hades, Phaedra and Hippolytus, death on Scyros); and the "synoikismos" and his invention as the founder of Athenian democracy. Then the crucial part: how and why Athens manufactured Theseus as a rival to Dorian Heracles in the 6th to 5th centuries (Cimon bringing the bones back from Scyros in 476, the Theseion, the vase evidence, Bacchylides, Plutarch's Life). Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 3 · Mythology II: the heroes · 3.4 · 2,850 words

Jason, the Argonauts and Medea

Pelias and the one-sandalled manThe Fleece: Athamas, Ino, Phrixus and HelleThe ship and the crewThe voyage outColchisThe return routesIolcus: the death of PeliasCorinth: Glauce and the childrenAfter Corinth: Athens and the MedesSelf-testCarry forward

Pelias and the one-sandalled man

The Argo is the oldest ship in Greek literature. Homer calls her "Argo, known to all" and has Circe say that only she ever passed the Planctae, "because Hera loved Jason" (Odyssey 12.69–72); the Iliad knows Jason's son Euneus ruling Lemnos (7.467–469); Hesiod has Jason take Medea from Aeetes after "the painful tasks the overbearing king Pelias laid on him" (Theogony 992–1002). The frame is archaic. The connected narratives are later: Pindar's Pythian 4 (462 BC), Apollonius of Rhodes' Argonautica (mid third century BC), the summary in Apollodorus, Library 1.9.16–28, and the unfinished Latin epic of Valerius Flaccus (c. AD 70–90).

Pelias, son of Poseidon and Tyro, held Iolcus in Thessaly, having displaced his half-brother Aeson, Jason's father. An oracle warned him of a man from the hills wearing one sandal. In Pindar the stranger arrives at the market with two spears, a leopard skin and uncut hair, reared by Chiron on Pelion after his parents smuggled him out as a baby (Pythian 4.71–120). Apollonius compresses: Jason lost a sandal fording the swollen Anaurus and arrived at Pelias' sacrifice to Poseidon (Argonautica 1.5–17). Apollodorus adds a trap: Pelias asked Jason what he would do with a man destined to kill him, and Jason, prompted by Hera, said he would send him for the Golden Fleece; Hera wanted Medea brought to Greece to destroy Pelias, who had neglected her honours (Library 1.9.16). Pindar's Pelias pleads piety: Phrixus' ghost demands his soul and the fleece be brought home (Pythian 4.156–167).

Where sources disagree. Jason's mother is Alcimede in Apollonius (1.47, 1.233) and Pherecydes, but Polymede in Apollodorus (1.9.16) and Polymele elsewhere. Whether Jason volunteers the quest (Apollodorus, Valerius Flaccus 1.22–90) or has it imposed under a veneer of piety (Pindar) changes the moral balance of the whole epic; Apollonius leaves the mechanism almost unstated.

The Fleece: Athamas, Ino, Phrixus and Helle

The fleece came from Boeotian Orchomenus. Athamas, son of Aeolus, married the cloud-nymph Nephele and had Phrixus and Helle; he then took Ino, daughter of Cadmus, who hated her stepchildren. Ino had the women parch the seed-corn; when the crop failed and Athamas sent to Delphi, she bribed the messengers to report that Phrixus must be sacrificed to Zeus. At the altar Nephele (or Zeus through Hermes) sent a golden-fleeced ram; the children mounted it and flew east. Helle fell into the strait that took her name; Phrixus reached Aia in Colchis, where Aeetes, son of Helios, married him to his daughter Chalciope and hung the fleece of the sacrificed ram on an oak in the grove of Ares under a sleepless serpent (Apollodorus 1.9.1; Apollonius 2.1140–1156, 4.123–182).

Herodotus gives the story a living cult: at Alus in Achaea Phthiotis the eldest Athamantid, if caught entering the town hall, was sacrificed to Zeus Laphystius (7.197).

Where sources disagree. Whether the ram spoke (Hesiodic fragments in the scholia) is contested; Apollonius (2.1144–1147) says only that Hermes made the fleece golden. Why the fleece matters is also unstable: in Pindar it is Phrixus' soul that must be fetched; in Apollonius Pelias simply wants Jason dead; rationalisers (Diodorus 4.47, after Dionysius Scytobrachion) made the "ram" a tutor called Crius. No early source explains the fleece's power; it is uncertain whether it ever had one.

The ship and the crew

Argus built the ship at Pagasae under Athena's direction, with a speaking beam from the oak at Dodona in her keel (Apollonius 1.18–19, 4.580–591). Apollonius opens with a catalogue of some fifty-five men (1.23–233), modelled on the Iliadic Catalogue of Ships, and the roster is where the myth does its political work. It assembles the generation before Troy: Peleus and Telamon, fathers of Achilles and Ajax; Oileus, father of the lesser Ajax; Laertes in Apollodorus' list; Menoetius, father of Patroclus; Admetus; Augeas of Elis. The Dioscuri bring Sparta aboard; Meleager and the Thestiads bring Aetolia; Idas and Lynceus come from Messenia, the seers Idmon and Mopsus, the flying Boreads Zetes and Calais, Euphemus of Taenarum who runs on water, Periclymenus the shape-changer, and Tiphys the helmsman.

The list matters for three reasons. First, it is a pan-Hellenic charter: every region claims a bench, and local traditions kept adding names, which is why Apollodorus and Hyginus differ from Apollonius. Second, particular names serve particular patrons. Pindar's shorter list (Pythian 4.171–183) singles out Euphemus because Arcesilas of Cyrene descended from him; the clod of Libyan earth Triton gives Euphemus is the charter of Cyrene's foundation (4.13–56; Apollonius 4.1731–1764). Third, the roster signals the heroism being tested: the strength of Heracles and the song of Orpheus both come aboard, and Heracles is set aside before Colchis.

Orpheus, first in Apollonius' catalogue, keeps the rowing time, calms a quarrel with a cosmogonic song (1.494–515) and sings down the Sirens (4.891–919). Heracles is elected leader by acclamation and defers to Jason (1.341–349). Peleus is the steady counsellor of Book 4; Telamon the hot-tempered accuser when Heracles is left behind.

Where sources disagree. Atalanta is an Argonaut in Apollodorus (1.9.16) and Diodorus (4.41), but Apollonius excludes her: Jason feared quarrels over love among the men (1.769–773). Heracles' departure is told four ways: left in Mysia searching for Hylas (Apollonius 1.1207–1362); left at Aphetae in Thessaly (Herodotus 7.193); never embarked, because Argo declared she could not bear his weight (Pherecydes, in Apollodorus 1.9.19); walked to Colchis after losing Hylas (Theocritus, Idyll 13.73–75). Valerius Flaccus diverts him to free Prometheus (5.154–176). His strength makes Jason redundant, so each poet finds a way to remove him.

The voyage out

Lemnos

The Lemnian women had murdered their husbands, who had taken Thracian concubines after Aphrodite cursed the women with a foul smell. Hypsipyle, who had spared her father Thoas, received the Argonauts; they lingered until Heracles shamed them back to sea (Apollonius 1.609–909). Euneus, Jason's son by Hypsipyle, is Homeric, making Lemnos the oldest attested episode. In Pindar the stop is on the way home (Pythian 4.251–254).

Cyzicus

King Cyzicus of the Doliones welcomed them; Heracles killed the six-armed Earthborn who attacked the ship. Driven back by a night storm, the Argonauts fought the Doliones in the dark without recognising them and Jason killed Cyzicus; his wife Cleite hanged herself (1.936–1077). The episode sets the epic's note of blundering guilt.

Hylas

In Mysia Heracles snapped an oar and went to cut another; his squire Hylas, sent for water, was pulled into the spring by its nymph. Heracles raged through the woods; at dawn the others sailed without him. Telamon accused Jason of plotting it, until the sea-god Glaucus announced that Heracles was fated for other labours (1.1153–1362). Valerius Flaccus gives the loss most of Books 3 and 4.

Amycus

Amycus, king of the Bebryces, forced strangers to box him; Polydeuces killed him with a blow behind the ear (2.1–97). Theocritus, Idyll 22, lets him live after swearing to stop.

Phineus and the Harpies

On the Thynian coast the blind seer Phineus, wasted by the Harpies who snatched his food, begged the Boreads for help. Zetes and Calais chased them to the Floating Islands, where Iris swore the Harpies would trouble him no more; the islands became the Strophades, "turning". Phineus then prophesied the route as far as Colchis, withholding the end (2.178–530).

Where sources disagree. Apollonius says Zeus blinded Phineus for revealing the divine will too fully (2.181–184). A Hesiodic fragment has him choose long life over sight. Apollodorus (1.9.21, 3.15.3) and Sophocles' lost Phineus plays make it punishment for blinding his own sons at the instigation of their stepmother Idaea. Whether the Harpies died or were spared also varied.

The Clashing Rocks

At the Bosporus the Clashing Rocks (Symplegades) crushed whatever passed. On Phineus' advice Euphemus released a dove; it lost only its tail feathers, and the crew rowed through on the backwash as Athena shoved the ship with one hand, losing only the stern ornament. The rocks then rooted for ever (2.549–610). Homer's Planctae (Odyssey 12.59–72) are a different hazard; Apollonius keeps both, placing the Planctae on the homeward route.

Beyond the Bosporus Apollonius adds the Mariandyni, where Idmon dies of a boar's tusk and Tiphys of illness (2.815–898); the Amazons; the island of Ares, where the shipwrecked sons of Phrixus join them (2.1093–1230); and the Caucasus, where they hear Prometheus scream under the eagle (2.1246–1259).

Colchis

Book 3 of Apollonius moves to Olympus: Hera and Athena ask Aphrodite to have Eros make Medea, Aeetes' younger daughter and priestess of Hecate, fall in love with Jason (3.6–166). Aeetes, warned by prophecy of his own children's treachery, sets a task he himself performs: yoke the bronze-footed, fire-breathing bulls of Hephaestus, plough the plain of Ares, sow the dragon's teeth of Cadmus, and kill the armed men who spring up (3.401–421). Medea's sleepless soliloquies (3.616–824) made her, not Jason, the centre of the poem.

At the temple of Hecate Medea gives Jason the Promethean drug, grown from the Titan's blood, that makes him invulnerable for a day (3.844–866, 3.1013–1062). He yokes the bulls, ploughs, and throws a boulder among the Earthborn so that they kill each other (3.1278–1407). Aeetes plots to burn the ship; Medea flees at night, sings the serpent to sleep with a juniper sprig dipped in her drug, and Jason lifts down the fleece (4.123–182). Valerius Flaccus follows this outline but gives Medea a far longer resistance to Venus and inserts, in Book 6, a Colchian civil war against Aeetes' brother Perses in which Jason fights for Aeetes before being cheated.

Apsyrtus

Aeetes sends his son Apsyrtus in pursuit. In Apollonius the Colchians catch the Argonauts at the Brygean islands near the Danube mouth; the Argonauts are ready to surrender Medea for arbitration, and she, furious, extracts a promise from Jason. She lures Apsyrtus to a parley in a temple of Artemis, where Jason cuts him down and performs a murderer's rites, licking and spitting the blood (4.410–481). The Colchians give up, and Zeus decrees purification by Circe.

Where sources disagree. Apollodorus (1.9.24) and Pherecydes make Apsyrtus a small child whom Medea dismembers aboard, scattering the pieces so that Aeetes stops to gather them; they were buried at Tomi, "cuttings". Euripides has Jason say Medea "killed her brother at the hearth" (Medea 1334), placing the murder in Colchis, as in Sophocles' lost Colchian Women. Apollonius moves the deed far from home and gives Jason the blow, sparing Medea the pollution and deepening Jason's.

The return routes

SourceRoute
Hesiod (fr. 241, via scholia on Apollonius 4.259) and Pindar, Pythian 4.25–27, 251–262Up the Phasis into the encircling Ocean; the Red Sea; Argo carried twelve days across Libya to Lake Tritonis; Lemnos; home
Hecataeus (same scholia)Phasis to Ocean, then Nile to the Mediterranean
Herodorus of HeracleaBack exactly the way they came, through the Bosporus
Apollonius, Argonautica 4Up the Ister (Danube), down a branch to the Adriatic; up the Eridanus (Po) and down the Rhodanus (Rhone) to the Tyrrhenian Sea; Circe; Sirens; Scylla and Charybdis; Drepane; storm to Libya; Lake Tritonis; Crete; Anaphe; Aegina; Pagasae
Diodorus 4.56 (citing Timaeus)Up the Tanais (Don), overland to the northern Ocean, round to Gades and into the Mediterranean

Apollonius' Book 4 carries the moral weight. Circe purifies the couple but drives them from her house (4.659–752). Hera summons Thetis to steer them past the Planctae, reminding her that Medea will one day be Achilles' wife in Elysium (4.783–832), a detail already in Ibycus and Simonides. Orpheus outsings the Sirens (4.891–921). At Drepane (Corcyra) a second Colchian fleet demands Medea; Queen Arete rules that a married woman cannot be returned, so Jason and Medea consummate the marriage hastily in the cave of Macris on the fleece (4.1098–1169): a wedding by necessity. A storm flings the ship into the Libyan Syrtis; the crew carry Argo twelve days to Lake Tritonis, lose Canthus and Mopsus, and are guided out by Triton, who gives Euphemus the clod (4.1228–1764). On Crete Medea kills the bronze giant Talos with the evil eye (4.1638–1693). The poem ends abruptly at Pagasae.

Iolcus: the death of Pelias

Apollodorus supplies the homecoming Apollonius omits (1.9.27). Pelias, assuming the Argonauts dead, had forced Aeson to drink bull's blood and had murdered Jason's infant brother Promachus. Jason handed over the fleece and waited. Medea went to Pelias' daughters and demonstrated rejuvenation by cutting up an old ram, boiling it with herbs, and drawing out a lamb. Persuaded, the daughters cut their father in pieces and boiled him; Medea had no intention of restoring him. Euripides dramatised the scene in his lost first production, the Peliades (455 BC). Pelias' son Acastus held funeral games (shown on the Chest of Cypselus, Pausanias 5.17.9–11) and expelled Jason and Medea. Diodorus (4.52) exempts Alcestis, who alone refused.

Where sources disagree. The Nostoi (fr. 6) said Medea boiled Aeson and made him young again; Simonides and Pherecydes said she rejuvenated Jason; Ovid gives the Aeson version (Metamorphoses 7.159–293). The cauldron is double-edged: healing for kin, butchery for an enemy. Nothing in Hesiod or Pindar hints at revenge on Pelias; the plot may be a sixth-century development.

Corinth: Glauce and the children

Euripides' Medea (431 BC, third prize) overwrote all other versions. Jason and Medea have lived some years in Corinth with two sons when Jason marries the daughter of King Creon; she is unnamed in the play, Glauce in Apollodorus (1.9.28) and Pausanias, Creusa in Seneca and Hyginus. Creon orders Medea into exile. She secures a day's grace, obtains from the passing Aegeus of Athens an oath of asylum (Medea 663–758), feigns reconciliation, and sends her sons to the bride with a poisoned robe and diadem; the girl burns, and Creon dies clinging to her (1136–1230). Medea kills the boys inside the house, appears above the roof in the chariot of Helios with the bodies, denies Jason their burial, and announces a cult for them at the sanctuary of Hera Akraia (1378–1383) before leaving for Athens.

That cult is the clue to the older Corinth. Eumelus' Corinthiaca, as reported by Pausanias (2.3.10–11), made Aeetes the first king of Corinth; the Corinthians later summoned Medea from Iolcus as rightful queen, and Jason reigned through her. Medea hid each newborn in Hera's temple, believing the goddess would make them immortal; when they died she was exposed, Jason left, and Medea handed Corinth to Sisyphus. The children die by a failed deification, the Demeter-and-Demophon pattern, not by murder. The scholia to Medea 264 preserve two more versions: Creophylus said Medea poisoned Creon and fled, leaving the children at Hera's altar, where Creon's kin killed them and blamed her; Parmeniscus said the Corinthian women, resenting a foreign sorceress as queen, killed her fourteen children in the temple, and a plague followed until Delphi ordered an annual expiation in which seven boys and seven girls served a year in the sanctuary with shorn hair and black clothes. Pausanias (2.3.6–7) saw the children's tomb and a statue of Deima, Terror. The scholiast also repeats the gossip that the Corinthians paid Euripides five talents to shift the guilt to Medea.

Where sources disagree. Whether Euripides invented deliberate child-murder is the central dispute. The ancient hypothesis says he borrowed it from Neophron of Sicyon; most modern scholars (following Page's 1938 edition) treat Neophron's fragments as a later reworking, though a minority revive Neophron's priority. What is clear is that the Akraia rite predates the play, and that every pre-Euripidean strand has the children killed by others or by a botched rite. The dragon-drawn chariot is also later: Euripides mentions only a chariot.

After Corinth: Athens and the Medes

In Athens Medea married Aegeus and bore him Medus (Apollodorus 1.9.28; Hesiod, Theogony 1001, already names a Medeius, son of Jason and Medea, reared by Chiron). When Theseus arrived unrecognised from Troezen, Medea persuaded Aegeus to poison him at a feast; Aegeus recognised the sword and dashed the cup aside, and Medea was driven out (Plutarch, Theseus 12; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.5–6; Euripides' lost Aegeus). Two destinations follow. In one she returns to Colchis with Medus, finds Aeetes deposed by his brother Perses, and restores him (Apollodorus 1.9.28; Diodorus 4.56). In the other she passes into the Iranian interior, where Medus names Media. Herodotus (7.62) says the Medes "were once called Arians, but when the Colchian Medea came to them from Athens they changed their name". It is Greek folk-etymology projected onto a real people, but it shows that by the fifth century an Athenian audience watching Medea flee to Aegeus knew where she would end up.

Her last home is the Isles of the Blest as Achilles' consort (Apollonius 4.811–815); the grand-daughter of Helios never dies in any source. Jason hanged himself (Neophron) or was crushed asleep beneath the rotting stern of the Argo at the Isthmus (Staphylus). The ship became a constellation.

Where sources disagree. Medea's son is Medus by Aegeus in Apollodorus and Diodorus, but Medeius by Jason in Hesiod. Whether the Medes were named from Medea or Medus splits Herodotus from the mythographers. Modern scholars treat the Athenian episode as fifth-century Attic appropriation, giving Athens a share in a Panhellenic heroine and a foil for Theseus; Euripides' Aegeus scene is its earliest trace.

Self-test

  1. What sign marked the man who would kill Pelias, and how did Jason acquire it in Apollonius?
    Answer

    A single sandal. In Argonautica 1.5–17 Jason lost the other crossing the flooded river Anaurus on his way to Pelias' sacrifice to Poseidon.

  2. How does Pindar's Pelias justify sending Jason to Colchis?
    Answer

    He claims the ghost of Phrixus has demanded that his soul and the fleece be brought home, and that he is too old to go himself (Pythian 4.156–167).

  3. Who engineered the near-sacrifice of Phrixus, and what did Herodotus find at Alus?
    Answer

    Ino, Athamas' second wife, by parching the seed-corn and bribing the Delphic messengers. Herodotus 7.197 reports a cult of Zeus Laphystius at Alus in which the eldest Athamantid was barred from the town hall and liable to sacrifice.

  4. Give the four distinct accounts of how Heracles left the expedition.
    Answer

    Left in Mysia searching for Hylas (Apollonius); left at Aphetae in Thessaly (Herodotus 7.193); never embarked because Argo refused his weight (Pherecydes); walked to Colchis after Hylas (Theocritus 13). Valerius Flaccus adds the freeing of Prometheus.

  5. Why does Apollonius exclude Atalanta?
    Answer

    Jason feared quarrels over love among the crew (Argonautica 1.769–773). Apollodorus and Diodorus include her.

  6. What is the oldest attested episode of the voyage, and where?
    Answer

    The stay on Lemnos: Homer knows Euneus, son of Jason and Hypsipyle, as king of Lemnos (Iliad 7.467–469), and the Odyssey (12.69–72) knows the Argo passing the Planctae.

  7. What were Aeetes' tasks?
    Answer

    Yoke the bronze-footed fire-breathing bulls of Hephaestus, plough the plain of Ares, sow the dragon's teeth of Cadmus, and kill the armed Earthborn who sprang up (Argonautica 3.401–421).

  8. How does the killing of Apsyrtus differ between Apollonius and Apollodorus?
    Answer

    In Apollonius Apsyrtus is an adult pursuer ambushed by Jason in a temple of Artemis near the Danube mouth; in Apollodorus he is a child taken aboard, dismembered by Medea and scattered so Aeetes would stop to gather the pieces. Euripides places the murder in Colchis.

  9. In Eumelus' Corinthiaca, how do Medea's children die?
    Answer

    She hides each newborn in the temple of Hera Akraia expecting immortality; they die. There is no murder (Pausanias 2.3.10–11).

  10. Which two different fathers are given for Medea's son who gave his name to the Medes?
    Answer

    Jason (Medeius, Hesiod Theogony 1001) and Aegeus (Medus, Apollodorus 1.9.28; Diodorus 4.56). Herodotus 7.62 derives the Medes' name from Medea herself.

Carry forward

  1. The Argonaut roster is a political charter: it assembles the fathers of the Trojan War generation and gives every Greek region a bench, which is why cities kept adding names and why Pindar singles out Euphemus for Cyrene.
  2. Medea the deliberate child-killer is Euripides' creation of 431 BC, laid over a Corinthian cult of Hera Akraia whose older stories blamed the Corinthians or a failed rite; always ask which Medea a source means.
  3. Greek mythic geography is poetic, not cartographic: the five incompatible return routes show poets rerouting the Argo through whatever edges of the known world their own century was exploring.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the voyage of the Argo and the Medea story. Cover: Pelias and the one-sandalled man, the Golden Fleece back-story (Phrixus and Helle, Athamas and Ino); the crew and why the list matters (Heracles, Orpheus, the Dioscuri, Peleus, Telamon, Meleager, Atalanta in some versions); the voyage outward (Lemnos, Cyzicus, Hylas, Amycus, Phineus and the Harpies, the Clashing Rocks); Colchis, Aeetes, the tasks, Medea's help and the killing of Apsyrtus; the return route variants; Pelias' death by Medea's trick; Corinth, Glauce and the child-murder as told by Euripides, and the older versions where Medea does not kill her children; Medea's later life in Athens and the Medes. Sources: Apollonius of Rhodes, Pindar Pythian 4, Euripides, Apollodorus, Valerius Flaccus. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
