The Theban cycle: Cadmus to Antigone

The founding: Cadmus, Europa and the Sown MenThe daughters: Semele, Pentheus, ActaeonThe second founding: Amphion, Zethus and NiobeLaius and Chrysippus: two origins for the curseOedipusEteocles, Polynices and the SevenAntigone and CreonThe Epigoni, the sack and the necklaceThe lost epics and the three tragediansSelf-testCarry forward

The founding: Cadmus, Europa and the Sown Men

The Theban saga begins outside Greece. Europa, a princess of Tyre, is carried off by Zeus in the form of a bull to Crete, where she bears Minos, Rhadamanthys and Sarpedon (Hesiod, Catalogue of Women fr. 140–141 M-W; Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.833–875; Apollodorus, Library 3.1.1). Her brother Cadmus is sent to find her with orders not to return without her. He never does; the search is what moves a Phoenician house into Boeotia.

Where sources disagree. Europa's father is Agenor in Apollodorus and most later writers, but Homer (Iliad 14.321–322) and Hesiod make her the daughter of Phoenix. Later genealogists reconciled the two by making Phoenix a son of Agenor. Herodotus (1.2) treats the abduction as a historical Cretan raid.

Delphi tells Cadmus to abandon the search, follow a cow and found a city where she lies down (Pausanias 9.12.1–2; Apollodorus 3.4.1). She halts at the site of Thebes. Companions sent for water to the spring of Ares are killed by the dragon guarding it; Cadmus kills the dragon and, on Athena's instruction, sows its teeth. Armed men, the Spartoi, spring up and fight until five survive: Echion, Oudaios, Chthonios, Hyperenor and Pelorus (Apollodorus 3.4.1; Euripides, Phoenician Women 657–675, 931–944; Ovid, Met. 3.1–130). They are the Theban aristocracy: Echion will marry Agave and father Pentheus; Creon's line will be reckoned Spartan-born. Because the dragon was sacred to Ares, Cadmus serves the god for a "great year" and is then given Harmonia, daughter of Ares and Aphrodite, with the gods attending the wedding (Hesiod, Theogony 937, 975–978; Apollodorus 3.4.2).

Among the gifts is a necklace made by Hephaestus; Apollodorus (3.4.2) adds a variant in which Zeus had given it to Europa and Cadmus passed it on. Statius (Thebaid 2.265–305) makes it a thing forged in malice. It will bribe Eriphyle, kill Alcmaeon and end in the Delphic treasury. Herodotus (5.58–59) credits Cadmus with bringing letters to Greece and claims to have seen "Cadmeian" script on tripods in the Theban Ismenion. The children are Semele, Agave, Autonoe, Ino and Polydorus. In old age Cadmus and Harmonia go to Illyria and are turned into serpents (Euripides, Bacchae 1330–1339; Ovid, Met. 4.563–603).

Cadmus ── Harmonia
├── Semele ── Zeus ── Dionysus
├── Agave ── Echion (Spartos) ── Pentheus
├── Autonoe ── Aristaeus ── Actaeon
├── Ino ── Athamas ── Learchus, Melicertes
└── Polydorus ── Nycteis
    └── Labdacus
        └── Laius ── Jocasta
            └── Oedipus ── Jocasta
                ├── Eteocles ── Laodamas
                ├── Polynices ── Argeia ── Thersander
                ├── Antigone
                └── Ismene

Rival line: Nycteus ── Antiope ── Zeus ── Amphion (── Niobe), Zethus

The daughters: Semele, Pentheus, Actaeon

Three of Cadmus's daughters lose a son, and the deaths are the foundation myths of Dionysiac Thebes. Semele, loved by Zeus, is tricked by Hera into asking him to come as he comes to his wife; the thunderbolt kills her, and Zeus sews the unborn child into his thigh until term (Hesiod, Theogony 940–942; Euripides, Bacchae 1–42, 88–104; Ovid, Met. 3.253–315). Her sisters said she had lied about a divine lover, and that slander is the reason Dionysus comes to Thebes (Bacchae 26–31).

Where sources disagree. Homeric Hymn 1 (1–9) explicitly rejects Thebes as the birthplace in favour of Nysa. Diodorus (3.62–64) distinguishes an older Dionysus from the Theban one. Tragedy made the Theban version canonical.

Pentheus, son of Agave and Echion, rules while the aged Cadmus stands aside. In Euripides's Bacchae (405 BC) he denies the god, imprisons the stranger, is lured into maenad dress to spy on the women of Cithaeron, is perched in a fir and torn apart by his mother and aunts, who take him for a lion; Agave carries the head home and Cadmus leads her into recognition (1216–1300). Aeschylus wrote a lost Pentheus; Theocritus (Idyll 26) and Ovid (Met. 3.511–733) retell it. Apollodorus (3.5.5) says Labdacus later died "in the same way" for the same impiety, giving the resistance to Dionysus a dynastic pattern.

Actaeon, son of Autonoe, is eaten by his own hounds. In the version that became standard he sees Artemis bathing and is turned into a stag (Callimachus, Hymn 5.107–118; Ovid, Met. 3.138–252), but that is not the oldest motive.

Where sources disagree. Apollodorus (3.4.4) says Acusilaus blamed Zeus's anger at Actaeon's courting of Semele and calls the bathing story merely "the more common". Stesichorus (in Pausanias 9.2.3) had Artemis wrap him in a deerskin to stop him marrying Semele. Euripides (Bacchae 337–340) has him boast of outhunting the goddess. The voyeur motif owes its prominence to Hellenistic poetry.

The second founding: Amphion, Zethus and Niobe

Polydorus dies while Labdacus is a child; Nycteus and then his brother Lycus rule as regents. Nycteus's daughter Antiope is impregnated by Zeus and bears twins on Cithaeron who are exposed and raised by a herdsman. Lycus and his wife Dirce keep Antiope a slave until she escapes and finds her sons, who kill Lycus and tie Dirce to a bull; the spring where she dies carries her name (Apollodorus 3.5.5; Pausanias 9.5.5–9; Hyginus, Fabulae 7–8; Euripides's lost Antiope). The brothers wall the city, Zethus carrying stones, Amphion moving them with the lyre Hermes gave him.

Where sources disagree. Homer makes the twins the founders: Antiope's sons "first founded the seat of seven-gated Thebes" (Odyssey 11.260–265), which cannot be squared with Cadmus. Pausanias (9.5.6) gave Cadmus the acropolis and the twins the lower town. Modern scholars see two independent foundation legends spliced, with the Labdacids written out of the city for exactly the interval the twins rule.

Amphion marries Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, who boasts herself more worthy of worship than Leto; Apollo and Artemis kill the children in a day. Homer is the first witness (Iliad 24.602–617): six sons and six daughters lie nine days unburied, and Niobe is turned to stone on Sipylus. Aeschylus and Sophocles each wrote a lost Niobe; Ovid gives the fullest version (Met. 6.146–312). Apollodorus (3.5.6) records the disagreement over numbers himself: Homer six and six, Hesiod ten and ten, Herodorus two and three, his own source seven and seven, with one daughter, Chloris, surviving to marry Neleus. Amphion dies by Apollo's arrows (Hyginus 9) or his own hand (Ovid 6.271); Zethus dies of grief (Pausanias 9.5.9). The throne reverts to Laius, who had been sheltered in exile by Pelops.

Laius and Chrysippus: two origins for the curse

The curse on the house has two rival explanations, and the choice determines the moral shape of everything that follows. The first is Pelopid: as Pelops's guest, Laius falls in love with his son Chrysippus and abducts him in his chariot; the boy dies, by suicide or killed by his half-brothers Atreus and Thyestes, and Pelops curses Laius never to have a son, or to die by him if he does (Hyginus 85; Apollodorus 3.5.5; schol. Euripides, Phoenician Women 1760, citing "Peisander", where Hera sends the Sphinx to punish Thebes for not avenging the crime). Euripides wrote a lost Chrysippus, and Plato (Laws 836c) and Athenaeus (13.602f) treat Laius as the inventor of pederasty.

The second is Apolline. In Aeschylus, Seven against Thebes 742–757, Apollo "thrice" told Laius at Delphi that he would save the city only by dying childless, and Laius, "mastered by folly", begot Oedipus anyway. No Pelops is needed; the fault is disobedience.

Where sources disagree. Whether Chrysippus is pre-Euripidean is contested. Lloyd-Jones argued that Aeschylus's lost Laius (467 BC) used the abduction and that the "ancient transgression" of Seven 742 refers to it; Hutchinson and most recent commentators find no trace of Chrysippus before Euripides. Sophocles's Oedipus Tyrannus is silent on both: the oracle to Laius there (711–714) is a prediction, not a prohibition.

Oedipus

The epic Oedipus is not the tragic one. In the Odyssey (11.271–280) his mother, called Epicaste, married him in ignorance; the gods made it known "at once"; she hanged herself and he went on ruling Thebes "in woes". The Iliad (23.679–680) knows funeral games for Oedipus at Thebes, so he died there. Hesiod (Works and Days 162–163) knows a war at Thebes "for the flocks of Oedipus". Nothing about blinding or exile. The lost Oedipodea (6,600 lines, attributed to Cinaethon) focused on the Sphinx and the marriage; its one secure fragment says the Sphinx killed Haemon, son of Creon, "most beautiful" of the Thebans, and Pausanias (9.5.10–11) reports that in it the four children were born of a second wife, Euryganeia. Pherecydes gave Oedipus three wives in sequence.

Where sources disagree. Epic denied that Eteocles, Polynices, Antigone and Ismene were children of incest. The incestuous brood is secure first in Aeschylus (Seven 752–757, the "field" that bore a "bloody root") and dominates Sophocles and Euripides. Whether Aeschylus invented it is uncertain.

The tragic plot is Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus (c. 429 BC), with Apollodorus 3.5.7–9 filling gaps. Laius has the infant's ankles pierced and pinned (OT 718, 1034) and exposed on Cithaeron; the Theban herdsman passes him to a Corinthian shepherd, and the childless Polybus and Merope raise him. Taunted as a bastard, he goes to Delphi and hears he will kill his father and marry his mother. Avoiding Corinth, he meets Laius where three roads meet in Phocis (OT 733–734; Pausanias 10.5.3–4 saw the graves at the Cleft Way) and kills him and all but one attendant in a quarrel over the road. The Sphinx, offspring of Echidna (Hesiod, Theogony 326–327, where she is "Phix"), kills Thebans who fail her riddle of the creature with one voice and two, three and four feet; Oedipus answers "man" and she leaps from the rock (Apollodorus 3.5.8). Creon has offered throne and widow to the liberator.

Sophocles then builds the discovery as an investigation of his own design: plague, Tiresias's refusal and accusation (316–462), Jocasta's attempt to discredit oracles that only tightens the net (707–770), the Corinthian messenger revealing the adoption, the herdsman forced to speak. Jocasta hangs herself; Oedipus blinds himself with her brooches (1268–1279). He asks for exile; the play ends with Creon undecided. In Oedipus at Colonus (401 BC) the blind man, led by Antigone, reaches the grove of the Eumenides at the poet's own deme. Creon tries to seize him; Polynices begs a blessing and receives the curse that the brothers will die by each other's hands (1370–1396); summoned by thunder, Oedipus goes into the grove, and only Theseus knows the grave that will protect Athens against Thebes (1518–1534).

Where sources disagree. Homer implies burial at Thebes. Lysimachus (schol. OC 91) placed the grave at Eteonos in Boeotia after Thebes refused the body. Pausanias (1.28.7) saw a tomb on the Areopagus and was told the bones came from Thebes. Colonus is an Athenian claim, probably Sophocles's own shaping of a local cult.

Eteocles, Polynices and the Seven

The sons' quarrel has its own curse. The Thebais (fr. 2–3 West) told how Polynices set before his blind father the silver table and gold cup of Cadmus which Laius had used, and Oedipus cursed the sons to divide their inheritance "with the sword"; and how they later sent him the haunch of the sacrifice instead of the shoulder, and he prayed they die at each other's hands. Euripides (Phoen. 63–68) simplifies: the sons locked their father away, and he cursed them. They agree to rule in alternate years; Eteocles refuses to yield; Polynices goes to Argos (Apollodorus 3.6.1). A Stesichorus fragment (P. Lille 76) shows a sixth-century version in which the queen, still alive, proposes that one son keep the kingdom and the other take the flocks and gold, after Tiresias has foretold the fratricide.

At Argos Polynices and Tydeus, exiled from Calydon, brawl at Adrastus's door; he recalls an oracle to yoke his daughters to a boar and a lion, recognises the beasts on their shields, and marries Argeia to Polynices and Deipyle to Tydeus (Euripides, Suppliants 131–150). The seer Amphiaraus, married to Adrastus's sister Eriphyle, foresees that every leader but Adrastus will die and refuses to go; bound by oath to let Eriphyle settle disputes with Adrastus, he is undone when Polynices bribes her with Harmonia's necklace. He goes, charging his sons Alcmaeon and Amphilochus to kill their mother and march on Thebes (Apollodorus 3.6.2; Pindar, Nemean 9.13–27; Odyssey 15.244–247 already knows he died "because of a woman's gifts"). At Nemea the infant Opheltes dies while his nurse Hypsipyle shows the army water; Amphiaraus renames him Archemorus, "beginner of doom", and the Nemean games are founded (Bacchylides 9.10–24; Euripides, Hypsipyle). Tydeus goes ahead as envoy and kills all but one of the fifty Thebans sent to ambush him (Iliad 4.382–398).

Where sources disagree. The list of Seven is unstable. Aeschylus (Seven 375–652), Sophocles (OC 1313–1325) and Euripides's Suppliants put Eteoclus at a gate and keep Adrastus out of the seven; Phoenician Women (1104–1140) includes Adrastus and omits Eteoclus. Apollodorus (3.6.3) notes that "some" exclude Tydeus and Polynices as non-Argives and count Eteoclus and Mecisteus.

EteoclusArgosNeistanKilled by Leades (Apollodorus); fills Adrastus's place in the tragic lists

In Euripides, Tiresias declares that only the death of a pure-born Spartos can save the city, and Creon's son Menoeceus kills himself on the walls against his father's wish (Phoen. 911–1018); no earlier source knows this, and it is probably Euripides's invention on the model of Macaria in his Children of Heracles. The assault fails at every gate; the brothers meet in single combat and kill each other, and in Euripides Jocasta stabs herself over the bodies (1427–1459).

Antigone and Creon

Creon takes power and, in Sophocles's Antigone (c. 442 BC), decrees that Polynices lie unburied on pain of death. Antigone buries him and, caught, defends the unwritten laws of the gods against the city's decree (450–470). Ismene refuses to help and is later refused a share of the guilt. Haemon, Antigone's betrothed, argues with his father and fails; she is walled into a rock tomb. Tiresias warns Creon of pollution; he relents too late, finds Antigone hanged and Haemon dead by his own sword, and his wife Eurydice kills herself cursing him (1192–1316).

Where sources disagree. This ending is Sophoclean, not traditional. In Euripides's lost Antigone (per the ancient hypothesis to Sophocles's play) she is married to Haemon and bears a son, Maeon. In Phoenician Women 1627–1766 she refuses Haemon and goes into exile with her father. Euripides's Suppliants and the Athenian funeral orations (Herodotus 9.27.3; Lysias 2.7–10) say Theseus recovered the Argive dead and buried them at Eleusis; Pindar (Olympian 6.15) and Pausanias (9.18.3) have seven pyres at Thebes. The Antigone scene at the end of Aeschylus's Seven (1005–1078) is regarded by most editors as a fourth-century addition made under Sophocles's influence.

The Epigoni, the sack and the necklace

Ten years later the sons of the Seven return. Apollodorus (3.7.2) names Alcmaeon and Amphilochus, Aegialeus son of Adrastus, Diomedes son of Tydeus, Promachus son of Parthenopaeus, Sthenelus son of Capaneus, Thersander son of Polynices and Euryalus son of Mecisteus. Delphi promises victory if Alcmaeon leads; he agrees only after Eriphyle, bribed a second time by Thersander with Harmonia's robe, presses him (3.7.5). At Glisas the Theban king Laodamas, son of Eteocles, kills Aegialeus and falls to Alcmaeon. Tiresias advises the Thebans to parley while they slip away by night, and dies on the road drinking from the spring Tilphussa (Apollodorus 3.7.3; Pausanias 9.33.1). The Epigoni sack the empty city, send Tiresias's daughter Manto to Delphi as first-fruits, and install Thersander. Adrastus dies of grief at Megara. Sthenelus's boast in the Iliad (4.405–410), "we took the seat of seven-gated Thebes", is the oldest allusion.

Where sources disagree. Herodotus (5.61) and Pausanias (9.5.13) have Laodamas survive and lead the Thebans to Illyria. Herodotus (4.32) doubted Homer wrote the Epigoni, which was also credited to Antimachus of Teos.

Alcmaeon kills Eriphyle as ordered and is driven mad by her Erinys. Purified by Phegeus at Psophis, he marries Phegeus's daughter Arsinoe (Alphesiboea in Pausanias 8.24.8) and gives her the necklace and robe. The land withers; Delphi sends him to ground that did not exist when his mother cursed him, the new silt at the mouth of the Achelous, where he marries the river's daughter Callirhoe. She demands the heirlooms; Alcmaeon tells Phegeus he must dedicate them at Delphi to be cured, a servant betrays the lie, and Phegeus's sons ambush and kill him (Apollodorus 3.7.5–6; Pausanias 8.24.8–10). Callirhoe prays that her infant sons Acarnan and Amphoterus grow up in a day; they kill Phegeus and his sons and dedicate necklace and robe at Delphi. Ephorus (in Athenaeus 6.232d–e) closes the circuit: in the Third Sacred War the Phocian Phayllus plundered the necklace for his mistress, who went mad, and whose son burnt the house down. Four generations after Harmonia's wedding the necklace was still destroying its owners.

The lost epics and the three tragedians

Three Theban epics circulated under Homer's name or those of shadowy early poets. The Oedipodea (6,600 lines) covered the Sphinx and the marriage; the Thebais (7,000 lines), opening "Sing, goddess, of thirsty Argos", the first war, and Pausanias (9.9.5) ranks it just after the Iliad and Odyssey; the Epigoni (7,000 lines), opening "Now, Muses, let us begin on the younger men", the second; an Alcmaeonis followed. About two dozen lines survive from all of them. They establish that the epic Oedipus kept his throne and remarried, that the curse on the sons was provoked by concrete dishonour (the cup, the haunch), and that Adrastus's horse, Tydeus's cannibalism and Amphiaraus's descent were fixed before tragedy.

Aeschylus, Seven against Thebes (467 BC), third play of a connected trilogy (Laius, Oedipus, Seven, with the satyr-play Sphinx), compresses the war into one day inside the walls. Polynices never appears. The centrepiece is the Scout's description of each Argive champion's shield, answered by Eteocles's assignment of a defender (375–676), until the seventh gate pairs him with his brother and he chooses to go. Aeschylus's shaping is structural: an Erinys working through three generations, Eteocles as sympathetic defender rather than usurper, and the Delphic prohibition rather than Chrysippus as root fault. The original ending was almost certainly the lament over the two corpses.

Sophocles wrote his three Theban plays across forty years and never as a trilogy; they contradict one another. In Antigone Ismene says Oedipus died "hated and infamous" (49–52); in Colonus he dies a blessed hero of Attica. Creon is humane in Oedipus Tyrannus, a tyrant in Antigone, a thug in Colonus. Sophocles's lasting contributions are the self-blinding with the brooches, the plague and investigative structure, the Corinthian upbringing, the exile and the Athenian death. The Tyrannus is also the play that made incestuous parentage the centre of the story rather than a variant.

Euripides, Phoenician Women (c. 409 BC), is deliberately encyclopaedic. Jocasta is alive and speaks the prologue; blind Oedipus is shut inside the palace; Antigone views the Argive army from the roof in a scene modelled on the Iliad's view from the walls (88–201); the brothers meet under truce and fail to agree (446–637), Eteocles declaring he would go to the stars for Tyranny; Menoeceus dies for the city; Jocasta dies over her sons; Creon issues the edict and the exile order; Antigone chooses her father over Haemon. The chorus is Phoenician, kin of Cadmus, which lets the play open on the whole Tyrian prehistory. The ancient hypothesis already called it "overfull", and the authenticity of much of the exodos after 1582 is disputed: Fraenkel excised heavily, Mastronarde retains most.

Where sources disagree. How much of the canonical Oedipus is Sophoclean invention is uncertain. Some argue the self-blinding and exile were already in Aeschylus's lost Oedipus, reading the "twin pains" of Seven 782–783 as the eyes; others find that phrase too ambiguous to carry the weight. Nothing before 467 BC shows Oedipus blind.

Self-test

  1. Why does Cadmus come to Boeotia, and what does Delphi tell him to do instead?
    Answer

    He is searching for his abducted sister Europa under orders not to return without her. Delphi tells him to abandon the search, follow a cow and found a city where she lies down (Pausanias 9.12.1–2; Apollodorus 3.4.1).

  2. Who are the Spartoi, and which later figures descend from them?
    Answer

    The armed men who sprang from the sown dragon's teeth; five survived. Echion fathered Pentheus by Agave, and Creon's line, including Menoeceus and Haemon, was counted Spartan-born, which is why Tiresias demands a Spartos in Phoenician Women.

  3. Trace the necklace of Harmonia from its making to its last recorded owner.
    Answer

    Made by Hephaestus; given by Cadmus (or Zeus via Europa) to Harmonia; used by Polynices to bribe Eriphyle; given by Alcmaeon to Arsinoe; reclaimed by deceit for Callirhoe; dedicated at Delphi by Acarnan and Amphoterus; plundered by the Phocian Phayllus for his mistress, who went mad (Ephorus in Athenaeus 6.232d–e).

  4. Give three different motives for Actaeon's death and a source for each.
    Answer

    He courted Semele and angered Zeus (Acusilaus in Apollodorus 3.4.4; cf. Stesichorus in Pausanias 9.2.3); he boasted of outhunting Artemis (Euripides, Bacchae 337–340); he saw Artemis bathing (Callimachus, Hymn 5; Ovid, Met. 3).

  5. How does Homer's account of Amphion and Zethus conflict with the Cadmus story, and how did Pausanias reconcile them?
    Answer

    Odyssey 11.260–265 calls the twins the first founders and wallers of Thebes. Pausanias 9.5.6 assigned Cadmus the acropolis (Cadmeia) and the twins the lower city.

  6. State the two rival explanations for the curse on Laius's house and name a source for each.
    Answer

    Pelops's curse after Laius abducted Chrysippus (Euripides's lost Chrysippus; schol. Phoen. 1760; Hyginus 85); Laius's disobedience of Apollo's thrice-repeated command to die childless (Aeschylus, Seven 742–757).

  7. In what three ways does the epic Oedipus differ from the Sophoclean one?
    Answer

    He keeps ruling Thebes and dies there (funeral games, Iliad 23.679); he is not said to be blinded; his four children are by a second wife, Euryganeia, not by his mother (Oedipodea, via Pausanias 9.5.10–11).

  8. Which champion does Aeschylus place at each gate, and whom does he omit who appears in Phoenician Women?
    Answer

    Tydeus (Proetid), Capaneus (Electran), Eteoclus (Neistan), Hippomedon (Onca), Parthenopaeus (Northern), Amphiaraus (Homoloid), Polynices (Seventh). He omits Adrastus, whom Euripides includes in place of Eteoclus.

  9. Why does Athena withhold immortality from Tydeus, and how does Amphiaraus die?
    Answer

    Tydeus, dying, split open Melanippus's head and ate his brains, and Athena recoiled (Apollodorus 3.6.8; Thebais fr. 9). Amphiaraus, fleeing Periclymenus by the Ismenus, was swallowed alive with his chariot when Zeus split the earth (Pindar, Nemean 9.24–27).

  10. Give three points on which Sophocles's three Theban plays are inconsistent.
    Answer

    Oedipus dies disgraced (Antigone 49–52) but blessed at Colonus; Creon is reasonable in Oedipus Tyrannus, tyrannical in Antigone, violent in Colonus; Antigone opens with both brothers dead, while Colonus shows Polynices alive and being cursed. They were written over forty years and never planned as a trilogy.

Carry forward

  1. Epic and tragedy are different layers: the epic Oedipus rules on, remarries and dies at home; the blinding, exile, incestuous children and Athenian death are fifth-century shaping, much of it Sophoclean. Always ask which layer a detail belongs to.
  2. A house curse needs a mechanism, and the mechanism is an object or a vow: Harmonia's necklace, Cadmus's cup, the oath to Eriphyle, the Delphic prohibition. Follow the object and you follow the curse; the same pattern governs the Pelopids and the Trojan cycle.
  3. Thebes is the city Athenian drama uses to think about itself from outside: autochthony gone wrong (the Spartoi), tyranny against law (Creon and Antigone), state against family. Theseus's role in Colonus and Suppliants shows Theban myth being rewritten as Athenian political claim; read every later "Athenian" ending with that in mind.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Theban saga across five generations. Cover: Cadmus, Europa, the dragon's teeth and the Spartoi, Harmonia and the necklace; Semele and the birth of Dionysus; Pentheus and the Bacchae; Actaeon; Amphion and Zethus, Niobe; Laius, Chrysippus and the origin of the curse; Oedipus (the exposure, Corinth, the oracle, the crossroads, the Sphinx, Jocasta, the discovery, the blinding, Colonus); Eteocles and Polynices, the Seven against Thebes by name with their fates, Amphiaraus; Antigone and Creon; the Epigoni and the sack of Thebes; and Alcmaeon and the necklace. Treat the lost epics (Oedipodea, Thebais, Epigoni) and show how Aeschylus' Seven, Sophocles' three Theban plays and Euripides' Phoenician Women each reshape the material. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 3 · Mythology II: the heroes · 3.6 · 2,944 words

The other heroes: Bellerophon, Meleager, Atalanta, Pelops, Tantalus

What a secondary saga isBellerophonThe Calydonian boar huntAtalanta's race and HippomenesThe house of TantalusCephalus and ProcrisProcne, Philomela and TereusIo, Danaus and the DanaidsCecrops, Erichthonius and Athenian autochthonySelf-testCarry forward

What a secondary saga is

The great cycles absorbed whole epic poems. The sagas here survive as digressions inside other works, as lost tragedies known from fragments, as paragraphs in Apollodorus' Library, and as episodes Ovid reworked. That mode of survival matters. Each story was carried by a city or region with a stake in it, and the version we read usually served that stake: Corinth's Bellerophon, Olympia's Pelops, Argos' Io, Athens' Cephalus, Procne and Erichthonius. Read them as local charters stitched into the Panhellenic fabric.

Bellerophon

The oldest account is a speech. In Iliad 6.152–205 Glaucus the Lycian tells Diomedes that his grandfather Bellerophon, from Corinthian Ephyra, was desired by Anteia, wife of King Proetus of Argos. Refused, she accused him of attempted rape. Proetus would not kill a guest, so he sent him to his father-in-law in Lycia with a folded tablet bearing "many baneful signs" (6.168–169) that told the recipient to kill the bearer. He survived the Chimaera, the Solymi, the Amazons and an ambush, and won the king's daughter and half the kingdom. Yet Homer ends darkly: Bellerophon "became hated by all the gods" and wandered alone on the Aleian plain (6.200–202).

Homer never mentions Pegasus. The winged horse enters with Hesiod, Theogony 319–325, where the Chimaera is killed by "Pegasus and noble Bellerophon"; the horse's birth from Medusa's neck is at 280–286. The Corinthian form is Pindar's, Olympian 13.60–92: Athena appears in a dream by her altar, hands Bellerophon a golden bridle and tells him to sacrifice to his father Poseidon. The fall, in Isthmian 7.44–47, is the attempt to ride Pegasus to heaven; Zeus threw him, and Pegasus went on to carry the thunderbolt. Euripides' lost Stheneboea and Bellerophon dramatised the queen and the crippled hero; Apollodorus 2.3.1–2 gives the compact version.

Where sources disagree. Homer calls Proetus' wife Anteia; tragedy and Apollodorus call her Stheneboea. Homer makes Bellerophon son of Glaucus; Hesiod's Catalogue (fr. 43a) and Pindar make Poseidon his father. Whether Homer's "baneful signs" are writing is disputed: they are the only possible reference to a written message in the poems. The fall is hubris in Pindar, a gadfly sent by Zeus in the scholiasts, and absent from Homer, where the hero simply loses divine favour.

The interest is Corinthian and Lycian. Corinth stamped Pegasus on its coinage from the sixth century, located the horse's capture at the Peirene spring, and received Pindar's ode. The Lycian frame in Homer gives a Trojan ally a Greek pedigree.

The Calydonian boar hunt

In Iliad 9.529–599 Phoenix urges Achilles with the example of Meleager. Oeneus of Calydon in Aetolia forgot Artemis at the harvest sacrifice; she sent a boar that wrecked his orchards. Meleager killed it with many hunters, but Artemis stirred war between the Aetolians and the Curetes of Pleuron over the head and hide. His mother Althaea, whose brother he had killed, cursed him; he withdrew in anger until his wife Cleopatra persuaded him to fight, and got none of the promised gifts. There is no brand, no Atalanta, no death on stage: Homer's point is the cost of resentment held too long.

The brand appears in the fifth century. Phrynichus' Pleuroniae alluded to it, and Bacchylides 5.93–154 gives it in full: Meleager's ghost tells Heracles that when he killed his uncles over the hide, Althaea burned the log on which the Fates had made his life depend, and he felt his strength ebb in the field. Apollodorus 1.8.2–3 is the synthesis: the Fates' prophecy at his birth, the catalogue of hunters, Atalanta drawing first blood, Meleager killing the boar and giving her the hide, his uncles Plexippus and Toxeus taking it from her because a woman had no right to it, Meleager killing them, Althaea burning the brand and hanging herself. Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.260–546, dramatises Althaea's wavering. Pausanias 10.31.3–4 records that Hesiod's Catalogue had Meleager killed by Apollo.

Where sources disagree. Homer's Meleager seems to die by the curse working through Apollo; Bacchylides and Apollodorus make the brand the mechanism, and scholars argue whether the brand is an archaic folk-motif Homer suppressed to preserve his parallel with Achilles, or a later invention. Apollodorus 1.8.2 reports that some denied Atalanta was at the hunt at all. Her parentage splits: daughter of Iasus of Arcadia, or of Schoeneus of Boeotia (Hesiod, Ovid); Apollodorus 3.9.2 records both.

The saga served Aetolia, otherwise marginal to the heroic map: it made Oeneus' house host of a Panhellenic gathering a generation before the Argonauts and Troy, and gave Diomedes (Tydeus' son, Oeneus' grandson) a glorious ancestry. The Arcadians claimed Atalanta: Pausanias saw the boar's tusks at Tegea in the temple of Athena Alea, whose pediment showed the hunt (8.45.6–7, 8.46.1).

Atalanta's race and Hippomenes

Atalanta refused marriage and set a test: a suitor must outrun her, and losers died. In the Boeotian version, Hesiod's Catalogue (frr. 72–76) followed by Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.560–707, she is Schoeneus' daughter and the winner is Hippomenes, who drops three golden apples from Aphrodite; Atalanta stoops for each and loses. In the Arcadian version, Apollodorus 3.9.2, she is Iasus' daughter, exposed at birth and suckled by a bear, and the suitor is Melanion. Both agree on the end: the couple made love in a sacred precinct and were turned into lions, which ancient lore held could not mate with each other. Her son Parthenopaeus, one of the Seven against Thebes (Aeschylus, Seven 526–549), links into the next cycle.

Where sources disagree. The winner (Hippomenes or Melanion), the father (Schoeneus or Iasus), the apples' source, and whether the suitor ran ahead with Atalanta armed in pursuit (the Hesiodic scheme) or side by side. Whether the huntress of Calydon and the runner were originally one heroine is uncertain; Apollodorus clearly felt the two needed reconciling.

The house of Tantalus

This saga must be held in full, because the Oresteia and the Trojan War presuppose it.

Zeus + Pluto (a nymph)
  └─ TANTALUS (Sipylus, Lydia)
       ├─ Niobe
       └─ PELOPS + Hippodamia (daughter of Oenomaus of Pisa)
            ├─ ATREUS + Aerope ─── Agamemnon, Menelaus
            ├─ THYESTES ──┬── sons killed and served at the feast
            │             └── (by his daughter Pelopia) AEGISTHUS
            ├─ Pittheus ─── Aethra ─── Theseus
            ├─ Nicippe + Sthenelus ─── Eurystheus
            └─ Chrysippus (by a nymph; killed by his half-brothers)

Tantalus. Son of Zeus, king at Sipylus in Lydia, admitted to the gods' table. His crime is told three ways: he served his son Pelops to the gods to test them (Apollodorus, Epitome 2.3; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.403–411); he stole nectar and ambrosia for mortals (Pindar, Olympian 1.60–64); he repeated the gods' secrets (Euripides, Orestes 10). In Odyssey 11.582–592 water recedes from his lips and fruit lifts away; in Pindar a stone hangs over his head.

Pelops and the shoulder. The gods detected the dish; only Demeter, grieving for Persephone, ate a shoulder. Clotho restored the boy in a cauldron and Demeter replaced the shoulder with ivory. Pindar knows this and rejects it: at Olympian 1.25–53 he calls Pelops "ivory-shouldered" yet refuses to call the gods gluttons, blames an envious neighbour, and has Poseidon carry the boy to Olympus as Zeus did Ganymede. Pausanias 5.13.4–6 says the shoulder-blade was later taken to Troy and lost at sea.

Hippodamia and the chariot race. Oenomaus of Pisa, warned he would die at a son-in-law's hands, raced every suitor to the Isthmus and speared the losers. Pelops prayed to Poseidon for a golden chariot and winged horses (Olympian 1.71–88) and in Pindar wins cleanly. In Apollodorus, Epitome 2.4–8, and Pausanias 6.20.17, he or Hippodamia bribes the charioteer Myrtilus, son of Hermes, who fits wax linchpins; Oenomaus is dragged to death. Myrtilus had been promised a night with Hippodamia; when he claimed it, Pelops threw him into the sea off Geraestus, and as he fell he cursed the race of Pelops. At Olympia the Taraxippus that frightened horses was said to be his ghost (Pausanias 6.20.15–19).

Atreus and Thyestes. Exiled from Pisa after killing Chrysippus, the brothers came to Mycenae, where an oracle had told the people to choose a Pelopid king. Atreus kept a golden lamb he had vowed to Artemis; his wife Aerope, Thyestes' lover, gave it to Thyestes, who proposed that the lamb's owner should rule. Zeus had Atreus counter-propose that the sun reverse its course, and it did (Euripides, Electra 699–746, where the chorus doubts it). Atreus then recalled Thyestes under pretence of reconciliation and served him his own sons, showing him the hands and feet afterwards. Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1583–1602, has Aegisthus tell it.

Aegisthus' birth. An oracle told Thyestes that only a son begotten on his own daughter could avenge him. He raped Pelopia at Sicyon by night, unrecognised; she took his sword. Atreus married her; the child was exposed, suckled by a goat (aix, hence the name) and raised as Atreus' own. Sent to kill the captured Thyestes, Aegisthus was recognised by the sword, learned the truth and killed Atreus (Apollodorus, Epitome 2.14; Hyginus, Fabulae 87–88).

Where sources disagree. Pindar's rejection of the feast is the first explicit case of a Greek poet correcting a myth on moral grounds; most scholars take the feast as traditional and Pindar's abduction as the revision. Whether Pelops cheated divides Pindar from the mythographers; the east pediment of the temple of Zeus at Olympia (Pausanias 5.10.6–7) showed the moment before the race and left it open. Hesiod's Catalogue fr. 194 and Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1569 and 1602, insert a Pleisthenes between Atreus and Agamemnon. How often the brothers exchanged the throne, and whether Aerope was drowned or banished, vary with every source.

The stake was Olympia's. The Pelopion stood inside the Altis, with black-ram sacrifices to Pelops as a hero (Pausanias 5.13.1–3), and the race against Oenomaus competed with Heracles as the foundation legend of the games. The Lydian origin gave the Peloponnese its name and an eastern pedigree. Above all the saga gave tragedy an inherited curse, Myrtilus' and Thyestes' both, that made the deaths of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra seem fated.

Cephalus and Procris

Procris, daughter of Erechtheus of Athens, married Cephalus of Thoricus. Odysseus sees her in Hades (Odyssey 11.321) without a story. The narrative comes from the Athenian genealogist Pherecydes (FGrH 3 F 34): Cephalus, returning disguised after a long absence, tested his wife and seduced her with gold. Apollodorus 3.15.1 and Antoninus Liberalis 41 continue: shamed, Procris fled to Minos in Crete, cured him of Pasiphae's curse, and was rewarded with the hound Laelaps and a spear that never missed. Returning disguised as a boy, she beat Cephalus at the hunt and offered the gifts for his favours; when he agreed, she revealed herself and they were reconciled. Then, hunting with the spear, Cephalus threw at a rustle in the undergrowth and killed Procris, who had followed suspecting a lover. Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.690–865, makes the suspicion arise from Cephalus calling on the breeze, aura, which an eavesdropper took for a name. Tried on the Areopagus, Cephalus was exiled and later gave his name to Cephallenia (Strabo 10.2.14).

Where sources disagree. The order and motivation of the mutual tests differ in every source; Ovid drops the Minos episode and the sale for gold to keep Procris sympathetic. Whether the Cephalus loved by Eos is Procris' husband or a separate son of Hermes and Herse was already disputed in antiquity.

The interest is Attic. Thoricus' deme calendar lists offerings to Cephalus and Procris; the Areopagus trial made the story a precedent for jurisdiction over involuntary homicide; Cephallenia's claim shows the saga travelling west with colonists.

Procne, Philomela and Tereus

Pandion of Athens, at war with Labdacus of Thebes, won the alliance of Tereus the Thracian and gave him his daughter Procne (Apollodorus 3.14.8). She bore Itys. Years later she asked to see her sister Philomela; Tereus fetched her, raped her on the way, cut out her tongue and hid her, telling Procne she was dead. Philomela wove the story into a robe. Procne found her and in revenge killed Itys and served him to Tereus. He pursued the sisters with an axe; all three became birds: Procne the nightingale, Philomela the swallow, Tereus the crested hoopoe. The canonical shape is Sophocles' lost Tereus, known from fragments and a papyrus hypothesis, and Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.412–674. An older relative exists: in Odyssey 19.518–523 the nightingale is Pandareus' daughter who killed her son Itylus by mistake. Hesiod, Works and Days 568, already calls the swallow "daughter of Pandion".

Where sources disagree. Thucydides 2.29.3 denies that Tereus was a Thracian king: he lived at Daulis in Phocis, where "the women did the deed about Itys", and poets call the nightingale Daulian. Pausanias 10.4.8–9 agrees; the Megarians showed Tereus' tomb at Megara (Pausanias 1.41.8–9). Greek sources make Procne the nightingale and Philomela the swallow; Latin poets reversed the pair, which is why English "Philomel" means the nightingale. Aeschylus, Suppliants 60–62, and Hyginus 45 make Tereus a hawk.

The interest was Athenian in two senses. The alliance with Tereus mirrors fifth-century courtship of Thracian kings, notably Sitalces, whose connection Thucydides is anxious to dissociate from the barbaric Tereus. And the tale made Pandion's daughters a warning about giving Athenian women to foreign husbands, an anxiety that also shapes Euripides' Ion.

Io, Danaus and the Danaids

Io, priestess of Hera at Argos and daughter of the river Inachus, was loved by Zeus and turned into a cow. Hermes killed her guard Argus, and Hera's gadfly drove Io across the world. Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 561–886, stages her arrival in the Caucasus and Prometheus' prophecy: in Egypt Zeus will restore her by a touch, she will bear Epaphus, and in the thirteenth generation her line will produce Heracles. Suppliants 291–324 retells it from the Danaids' side. Apollodorus 2.1.3–5 runs the genealogy: Epaphus begets Libya; Libya and Poseidon beget Agenor (father of Cadmus and Europa) and Belus; Belus begets Aegyptus and Danaus, with fifty sons and fifty daughters. Fearing his nephews, Danaus built the first ship, sailed to Argos and claimed the kingdom as Io's descendant; a wolf killing a bull at the walls decided the Argives for him (Pausanias 2.19.3–4). His daughters found the springs of Lerna (Pausanias 2.37.1). When Aegyptus' sons came demanding marriage, Danaus consented and gave each daughter a dagger; all killed their husbands but Hypermnestra, who spared Lynceus. From them descend Abas, Acrisius, Danae, Perseus, and so Heracles.

Where sources disagree. Io's father is Inachus in Aeschylus, Iasus in Hesiod and Acusilaus, Peiren in others (Apollodorus 2.1.3). Aeschylus has Hera transform her (Suppliants 299); Apollodorus has Zeus do it to hide her. Herodotus 1.1–2 reports a rationalised version in which Phoenician traders carried her off, and at 2.41 identifies her with Isis. The Danaids' punishment in Hades, filling leaking jars, is not attested before the Hellenistic period (pseudo-Plato, Axiochus 371e); classical Argos knew them as founders of springs and of the Thesmophoria (Herodotus 2.171), not as sinners.

The saga is Argive throughout. Hera's great sanctuary lay between Argos and Mycenae, and Io as her priestess binds the goddess to the royal line; Danaus' arrival explains the Homeric name Danaoi and claims the first ship and the Lernaean springs; Epaphus and Libya gave Argos kinship with Egypt and Phoenicia, which Herodotus took seriously enough to trace the Spartan kings to Egypt via Perseus (6.53–54).

Cecrops, Erichthonius and Athenian autochthony

Athens claimed its people had never migrated but were born from Attic soil. Cecrops was the first king, "autochthonous, with a body compounded of man and serpent" (Apollodorus 3.14.1). Under him Athena and Poseidon contested Attica: Poseidon's trident made a salt spring, Athena planted the olive, with Cecrops as witness, and the gods judged for Athena (Herodotus 8.55, who saw both in the Erechtheum; Pausanias 1.26.5). Herodotus 8.44 lists the stages of the Athenian name: Cranai, Cecropidae, Athenians under Erechtheus, Ionians.

Erichthonius is the autochthon proper. Hephaestus tried to rape Athena; his semen fell on her thigh; she wiped it with wool (erion) and threw it to the earth (chthon), which bore the child. Athena put the infant in a chest with a snake and gave it to Cecrops' daughters Pandrosus, Herse and Aglaurus with orders not to look. Two did, saw the serpent-child, went mad and leapt from the Acropolis. Athena raised the boy; as king he set up the olive-wood image of Athena Polias and founded the Panathenaea; his son was Pandion. Sources: Euripides, Ion 20–26, 265–274; Apollodorus 3.14.6; Pausanias 1.18.2 and 1.24.7. In Euripides' lost Erechtheus (fr. 360) Praxithea boasts that the Athenians "are not immigrants brought in from elsewhere".

Where sources disagree. Homer, Iliad 2.546–551, knows only Erechtheus, "whom Athena reared and the grain-giving earth bore"; Erichthonius does not appear before the fifth century, and most scholars hold the two were originally one figure, split so that the earth-born child could become grandfather of the warrior king. Pausanias 1.18.2 names only Aglaurus and Herse as the disobedient sisters; Pandrosus, with her own precinct beside the Erechtheum, is usually exonerated. The political reading, that autochthony underwrote both democratic equality and exclusion of foreigners (Loraux, Rosivach), dominates modern scholarship; Thucydides 1.2.5 gives it a rational form: Attica's poor soil deterred invaders, so the population never changed.

The interest is Athens' self-image and its monuments. The Erechtheum housed Athena Polias, the olive, Poseidon's sea and Cecrops' tomb; the Arrhephoroi, girls who carried a covered basket by night from the Acropolis (Pausanias 1.27.3), re-enacted the chest and the sisters. The funeral orations (Lysias 2.17; Plato, Menexenus 237b–c; Isocrates, Panegyricus 24–25) made autochthony the first item in praise of the city: alone among Greeks, the Athenians had driven no one out and held their land by birth.

Self-test

  1. What does Homer's Bellerophon carry to Lycia, and why does it matter for the history of writing?
    Answer

    A folded tablet with "many baneful signs" (Iliad 6.168–169) ordering the bearer's death. It is the only possible reference to a written message in Homer, and scholars dispute whether the signs are script.

  2. Which hero does Phoenix use Meleager to warn, and what elements of the later saga are missing from his telling?
    Answer

    Achilles (Iliad 9). Homer has no fatal brand and no Atalanta; Meleager is undone by his mother's curse and his own withdrawal from battle.

  3. Name the two versions of Atalanta's parentage and the two names of the suitor who won her race.
    Answer

    Daughter of Iasus of Arcadia (suitor Melanion) or of Schoeneus of Boeotia (suitor Hippomenes).

  4. How does Pindar alter the story of Pelops in Olympian 1, and why?
    Answer

    He denies that Tantalus served Pelops to the gods, blaming the tale on slander, and substitutes Poseidon's abduction of the boy to Olympus; he will not attribute gluttony to the gods. Tantalus' crime becomes theft of nectar and ambrosia.

  5. Who is Myrtilus and what is his lasting effect on the family?
    Answer

    Oenomaus' charioteer, son of Hermes, who sabotaged the chariot with wax linchpins. Pelops threw him into the sea, and as he fell he cursed the Pelopids; the curse is one explanation for the crimes of Atreus and Thyestes and their descendants.

  6. Explain the derivation of Aegisthus' name and the circumstances of his birth.
    Answer

    From aix, goat: exposed as an infant and suckled by a goat. Thyestes begot him by raping his daughter Pelopia, following an oracle that only such a son could avenge the feast.

  7. What two gifts did Procris bring back from Crete, and how did one of them kill her?
    Answer

    The hound Laelaps and a spear that never missed, rewards from Minos. Cephalus, hunting, threw the spear at a rustle in the bushes and killed Procris, who had followed him suspecting a lover.

  8. Where does Thucydides locate Tereus, and why does he insist on it?
    Answer

    At Daulis in Phocis, not Thrace (2.29.3). He wants to deny any link between the mythical Tereus and Teres, father of Athens' Thracian ally Sitalces.

  9. Trace the line from Io to Perseus.
    Answer

    Io and Zeus beget Epaphus; Epaphus begets Libya; Libya and Poseidon beget Belus; Belus begets Danaus; Danaus' daughter Hypermnestra and Lynceus beget Abas, then Acrisius, Danae and Perseus.

  10. What etymology did Athenians give for Erichthonius, and how was his birth re-enacted in cult?
    Answer

    From erion (wool) and chthon (earth): Athena wiped Hephaestus' semen with wool and threw it to the ground. The Arrhephoroi carried a covered basket by night from the Acropolis, re-enacting the chest entrusted to Cecrops' daughters.

Carry forward

  1. Myth was local property before it was Panhellenic. Each saga here is a city's charter (Corinth, Olympia, Argos, Athens), and the surviving version served the stronger interest; counter-claims from Daulis, Megara, Arcadia or Boeotia show the competition in action.
  2. The house of Tantalus supplies the inherited curse that the Trojan generation and the Oresteia presuppose: Tantalus' feast, Myrtilus' curse, Thyestes' feast and Aegisthus' birth are the backstory to Agamemnon's murder and Orestes' revenge.
  3. Genealogy is argument. Io's line makes Argos the parent of Perseus, Heracles, Cadmus and Europa and kin to Egypt; Erichthonius makes Athenians born of their own soil. When a later module presents a hero's pedigree, ask which city gained from it.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the secondary heroic sagas. Cover: Bellerophon (Proetus' wife, the letter, the Chimaera, Pegasus, the fall); the Calydonian boar hunt (Oeneus, Artemis, Meleager, Atalanta, the brand and Althaea); Atalanta's race and Hippomenes; the house of Tantalus in full (Tantalus' crime, Pelops and the shoulder, Hippodamia and the chariot race, Myrtilus' curse, Atreus and Thyestes and the feast, Aegisthus' birth) as the set-up for the Trojan generation; Cephalus and Procris; Procne, Philomela and Tereus; Io and the line that leads to Danaus and the Danaids; Erichthonius, Cecrops and the Athenian autochthony myths. For each, give the sources and the regional interest it served. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

Love, hubris and metamorphosis

Ovid's method and agendaLove that fails: Orpheus and EurydiceLove and the image: Narcissus and Echo, PygmalionApollo's loves: Daphne and HyacinthusAphrodite's loves: Adonis and PsycheHubris and the gods' justiceFalling and burning: Phaethon and IcarusZeus's loves and their victims: Callisto, Leda, GanymedeShape, sex and hospitality: Tiresias, Lycaon, Baucis and PhilemonWhat survives mainly through Ovid, and how Roman that makes itSelf-testCarry forward

Ovid's method and agenda

The Metamorphoses is a Latin hexameter poem in fifteen books, finished around AD 8, the year Augustus exiled its author to Tomis. Its proem (1.1–4) promises a carmen perpetuum, a continuous song from the creation of the world to Ovid's own day, and some 250 stories are chained together by transitions of place, kinship, theme or verbal sleight, ending with the apotheosis of Julius Caesar (15.745–870). The form is epic; the sensibility is the love elegist's. Ovid narrates violence with a declaimer's detachment, gives his gods the manners of Roman aristocrats, and treats transformation as diagnosis: a body is made to show what the person already was. Lycaon becomes the wolf he behaved like (1.237–239); Niobe, who could not stop weeping, becomes a rock that weeps.

His sources were overwhelmingly Hellenistic and overwhelmingly lost. Nicander's Heteroioumena, Boios's Ornithogonia, Parthenius's Metamorphoses and Callimachus's Aetia supplied catalogues of change-tales; Antoninus Liberalis, who summarised Nicander and Boios in the second century AD, is our best control for what that tradition looked like without Ovid. Behind them stand Euripides, Hesiod's Catalogue of Women, and, for Orpheus, Virgil's Georgics. Ovid also uses embedded narrators: Book 10's Pygmalion, Hyacinthus, Ganymede and Adonis are all sung by Orpheus, a grieving man who has sworn off women, and his choice of subjects is characterisation, not neutral report.

Where sources disagree. Whether the poem is Augustan, anti-Augustan or indifferent is the longest quarrel in Ovidian scholarship. Brooks Otis (1966) read a poet failing to be serious; Karl Galinsky (1975) one who preferred play to politics. Since the 1990s Philip Hardie and Denis Feeney have stressed how the Lycaon council scene (1.163–252), which compares the gods' alarm to Rome's at a plot against "Augustus", invites a parallel between Jupiter's arbitrary power and the princeps's. Leo Curran (1978) and Amy Richlin (1992) asked whether Ovid's sympathy for the poem's roughly fifty rape victims is real or aesthetic. None of this is settled.

Love that fails: Orpheus and Eurydice

The version everyone knows is Virgil's. In Georgics 4.453–527 Orpheus descends, charms Hades, and loses Eurydice by looking back on the threshold; Ovid retells it in Metamorphoses 10.1–85 with a lighter touch and finishes it in 11.1–66 with his death at the hands of Thracian women. The backward glance and the double death are first attested in Virgil, around 29 BC.

The Greek evidence tells a different story. Euripides, Alcestis 357–362 (438 BC), has Admetus wish he had Orpheus's voice so that he too could sing his wife back, which only makes sense if Orpheus succeeded. Isocrates, Busiris 8, lists raising the dead among his deeds. Hermesianax (fr. 7 Powell) calls the wife Agriope and has him recover her; the name Eurydice first appears in the Lament for Bion 123–124, around 100 BC, again implying success. The one classical dissent is Plato, Symposium 179d: the gods showed Orpheus only a phantom and sent him away, because a mere cithara player lacked the courage to die for love as Alcestis did. Pausanias 9.30.6 rationalises: Orpheus thought he saw her ghost at the oracle of the dead and killed himself when it did not follow.

Where sources disagree. C. M. Bowra (1952) argued the failure version was a Hellenistic invention which Virgil perfected; others take Plato's phantom as evidence it was current in the fourth century. Apollodorus, Library 1.3.2, gives the looking-back condition in Greek, but writes after Virgil. Which version is older is uncertain; that the tragic Orpheus is the Roman one is not.

Love and the image: Narcissus and Echo, Pygmalion

Narcissus (Met. 3.339–510) was believed an Ovidian creation until 2004, when a papyrus of Parthenius (P.Oxy. 4711) showed a Greek telling about fifty years older in which the boy falls for his reflection and kills himself. Conon, Narrations 24, has him spurn a male lover, Ameinias, who kills himself and curses him; Pausanias 9.31.7–9 reports a rationalised version in which Narcissus gazed at his reflection to recall a dead twin sister. Ovid's innovations are the slow wasting-away instead of suicide, Tiresias's framing prophecy, and above all Echo. She is Greek (Longus, Daphnis and Chloe 3.23, has her torn apart at Pan's instigation), but her punishment by Juno, her reduction to repeating last words, and her pairing with Narcissus have no known source before Ovid. The match is too neat to be accidental: the boy who can only love himself meets the girl who can only say what she has heard.

Pygmalion (Met. 10.243–297) is the clearest case of Ovid transforming a Greek story beyond recognition. Philostephanus of Cyrene (third century BC), known from Clement, Protrepticus 4.57, told of a Cypriot king who fell in love with an ivory cult statue of Aphrodite and took it to bed; Christian writers cite it as a scandal of idolatry. Ovid makes him an artist, the statue his own work, and Venus the answerer of his prayer rather than its object, so the story becomes about art rather than fetish. The statue is never named in Ovid; "Galatea" is an eighteenth-century addition popularised by Rousseau.

Apollo's loves: Daphne and Hyacinthus

Daphne (Met. 1.452–567) is the poem's first love story and sets the pattern of pursuit, prayer and transformation. Ovid motivates Apollo's passion by Cupid's arrow, shot in revenge for mockery; this is his. Parthenius, Erotika Pathemata 15, makes Daphne a Laconian huntress courted by the youth Leucippus, who disguises himself as a girl to join her band; Apollo, jealous, inspires the girls to bathe, Leucippus is exposed and killed, and Daphne, fleeing Apollo, becomes the laurel. Pausanias 8.20.2–4 tells the same tale in Arcadia with Daphne as daughter of the river Ladon. Ovid moves her to Thessaly as daughter of Peneus, cuts Leucippus, and ends with the laurel on the oak-wreathed doors of Augustus's house (1.562–563), a pointedly Roman close.

Hyacinthus (Met. 10.162–219) is a Spartan cult figure older than any love story: the Hyacinthia at Amyclae appear in Euripides, Helen 1469–1475, and the -nth- in his name is pre-Greek, which led Nilsson and Burkert to see a pre-Dorian vegetation god absorbed by Apollo. Apollodorus 1.3.3 and 3.10.3 make him beloved of Thamyris and then of Apollo, who kills him accidentally with a discus. The jealous Zephyrus who deflects the discus appears in Palaephatus 46 and Lucian, Dialogues of the Gods 14, not in Ovid, who keeps the death an accident and has Apollo inscribe the flower with AI AI. Pausanias 3.19.3–5 saw Hyacinthus carried to heaven on the altar at Amyclae, a hint of resurrection the poets dropped.

Aphrodite's loves: Adonis and Psyche

Adonis is one of the few myths here with early, rich Greek evidence. Sappho fr. 140a (c. 600 BC) is a ritual lament: "Delicate Adonis is dying, Cytherea; what shall we do?" Panyassis (in Apollodorus 3.14.4) gives the incest of Smyrna with her father, the birth from the myrrh tree, and a quarrel between Aphrodite and Persephone over the infant settled by Zeus dividing the year. Aristophanes, Lysistrata 387–398, and Theocritus, Idyll 15, show the women's Adonia; Bion's Lament is the Hellenistic pathetic treatment. Ovid, Met. 10.503–739, tells Myrrha's incest at length, then the boar, the anemone and Venus's grief, inserting the Atalanta race. He omits Persephone and the shared year, converting a seasonal cult myth into elegiac romance.

Where sources disagree. Frazer read Adonis as a dying-and-rising vegetation god kin to Tammuz. Marcel Detienne (1972) argued the reverse: the Adonia's quick-sprouting, quick-withering gardens celebrate sterile seduction, the opposite of Demeter's grain. Whether any Greek source before late antiquity has Adonis actually return to life is doubtful.

Eros and Psyche is Latin, late, and embedded: Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4.28–6.24, second century AD, told by an old woman to a kidnapped bride. The skeleton is a folk-type (the lost supernatural husband), and Hellenistic art shows Eros and Psyche embracing from the fourth century BC, but no Greek literary version survives, and the Greek Onos that shares Apuleius's donkey plot lacks Psyche entirely. Whether Apuleius invented the tale, adapted a lost Greek original, or dressed folklore in Platonic allegory is uncertain. It is the most influential ancient fairy tale and it is not, in any recoverable sense, a Greek myth.

Hubris and the gods' justice

Arachne (Met. 6.1–145) has no Greek narrative source. Virgil, Georgics 4.246, calls the spider "hated by Minerva", so a story existed, and a scholion on Nicander preserves an Attic tale of Arachne and her brother Phalanx punished for incest. The contest, the tapestries and the transformation as we know them are Ovid's. Arachne's tapestry depicts the rapes of the gods (6.103–128) while Minerva's depicts their majesty, and Arachne's is better; the goddess tears it and beats her, and the metamorphosis is a reprieve from suicide, not justice.

Marsyas is old. Herodotus 7.26 saw the satyr's skin hanging at Celaenae; Plato, Symposium 215b–c, has Alcibiades liken Socrates to him. Apollodorus 1.4.2 and Diodorus 3.59 give the contest with Apollo and the flaying. Ovid, Met. 6.382–400, skips the contest and spends nineteen lines on the skinning.

Niobe is Homeric. Achilles tells Priam (Iliad 24.602–617) that Niobe lost six sons and six daughters for comparing herself to Leto and now stands as rock on Sipylus, still weeping. Hesiod fr. 183 M-W gave her ten and ten; Aeschylus's Niobe had a long-silent heroine mocked in Frogs 911–920. Ovid, Met. 6.146–312, gives seven and seven, as does Apollodorus 3.5.6. Pausanias 1.21.3 climbed Sipylus and reports the rock looks like a weeping woman only from a distance.

Salmoneus of Elis drove a chariot dragging bronze cauldrons and threw torches, claiming to be Zeus; the real bolt killed him and his city (Apollodorus 1.9.7; Virgil, Aeneid 6.585–594). Capaneus, scaling the wall of Thebes, swore not even Zeus's fire would stop him and was struck from the ladder (Aeschylus, Seven Against Thebes 423–446; Apollodorus 3.6.7). Midas is the comic variant: a historical Phrygian king (Assyrian Mita, eighth century BC) whose dedications Herodotus 1.14 saw at Delphi. The golden touch is a proverb in Aristotle, Politics 1257b, but is told fully only in Ovid, Met. 11.85–145; the asses' ears are in Aristophanes, Plutus 287, and Ovid adds the barber and the whispering reeds (11.146–193).

What the pattern teaches is not that the gods are just but that they are jealous of a boundary. Niobe's children are innocent; Arachne's work is superior; Marsyas's crime is a music lesson. The offence is the refusal of the gap between mortal and immortal, and the punishment asserts the gap by force. Pindar's "do not seek to become Zeus" (Isthmian 5.14) is the sober version; Ovid's is to make Minerva lose the contest and win anyway.

Falling and burning: Phaethon and Icarus

Phaethon's fullest surviving telling is Ovid, Met. 1.750–2.400: the quest to prove paternity, the Sun's palace, the runaway chariot, the scorched earth, the thunderbolt, the Heliades turned to poplars weeping amber. Euripides wrote a Phaethon (c. 420 BC) of which substantial fragments survive; Plato, Timaeus 22c, has an Egyptian priest cite the fall as a memory of a real conflagration; Apollonius, Argonautica 4.597–611, has the Argonauts pass the smoking body in the Eridanus.

Icarus is told twice by Ovid, in Ars Amatoria 2.21–96 and Met. 8.183–235, with the ploughman and shepherd gaping at the flyers as if at gods. Greek literary attestation is thin before Apollodorus, Epitome 1.12–13, though vase painters knew a winged Icarus by the sixth century BC. Diodorus 4.77 rationalises: they fled Crete by ship and Icarus drowned landing carelessly; Pausanias 9.11.4–5 says Daedalus invented sails. Both myths concern a son's grasp at a father's power, and both end in water.

Zeus's loves and their victims: Callisto, Leda, Ganymede

Callisto (Met. 2.401–530) is an Arcadian nymph of Diana's band whom Jupiter rapes disguised as Diana; exposed at the bath, she is expelled, bears Arcas, and is turned into a bear by Juno; years later Jupiter stops Arcas from spearing his mother and sets both in the sky, where Juno persuades Ocean never to let them bathe. Apollodorus 3.8.2 lists Greek variants: Hesiod, Eumelus, Asius and Pherecydes each gave her a different father; Zeus took the form of Artemis or Apollo; Zeus or Hera made her a bear; Artemis shot her. Ovid's placing of the whole punishment in Juno's hands and his pity for the mute bear are his emphases.

Leda is a story Ovid barely tells (one line in Arachne's tapestry, 6.109), so its fame is not his doing. Homer knows Leda as mother of Castor and Polydeuces (Odyssey 11.298–304) and Helen as daughter of Zeus, but never joins them with a swan. The Cypria makes Nemesis Helen's mother; Apollodorus 3.10.7 reconciles the two by having a shepherd bring Nemesis's egg to Leda. Euripides, Helen 17–21, has Helen report the swan "if the story is true"; Pausanias 3.16.1 saw the egg hung in a Spartan temple.

Ganymede is Homeric and not overtly erotic there. Iliad 20.231–235 says the gods carried him off to be Zeus's cupbearer for his beauty; Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 202–217 records the horses given to Tros in compensation. Theognis 1345–1348 makes the desire explicit and uses it to justify pederasty; Plato, Laws 636c–d, says the Cretans invented the tale to excuse theirs. The eagle is a fourth-century addition, famous from Leochares's bronze (Pliny, Natural History 34.79); Ovid, Met. 10.155–161, gives Orpheus seven lines on it.

Shape, sex and hospitality: Tiresias, Lycaon, Baucis and Philemon

Tiresias has two transformation stories, and Ovid chooses one. In Met. 3.316–338 he strikes two mating snakes, becomes a woman for seven years, returns to manhood by striking them again, is asked whether men or women get more pleasure from sex, agrees with Jupiter that women do, and is blinded by Juno, Jupiter compensating with prophecy. This is Hesiod's Melampodia (fr. 275 M-W, via Apollodorus 3.6.7), where the ratio is one part of pleasure to the man and nine to the woman. The rival version is Callimachus, Hymn 5.57–136: young Tiresias stumbles on Athena bathing with his mother Chariclo, is blinded by the sight, and receives prophecy in consolation. Ovid takes the sex-change because it poses the question of pleasure immediately before Narcissus and Pentheus, both stories about looking.

Lycaon in Ovid (Met. 1.163–252) tests Jupiter by serving him human flesh; Jupiter destroys the house and Lycaon runs howling into the fields as a wolf, the first human metamorphosis in the poem and the trigger for the flood. The Greek Lycaon is a cult founder. Pausanias 8.2.1–7 makes him founder of the games of Zeus Lycaeus who sacrificed an infant on the altar and became a wolf, and Pausanias, unusually, believes it. Apollodorus 3.8.1 blames his fifty sons, who mixed a child's entrails into Zeus's meal. Plato, Republic 565d–e, uses the Lycaean rite as his image for the making of a tyrant. The ash altar on Mount Lykaion has been excavated; the 2016 find of an adolescent burial in it is suggestive and nothing more.

Baucis and Philemon (Met. 8.611–724) has no Greek source at all. An old Phrygian couple host disguised Jupiter and Mercury; the wine jug refills; the gods drown the inhospitable neighbours and turn the pair, at death, into an oak and a linden intertwined. The pattern is the theoxeny of Odyssey 17.485–487 and Callimachus's Hecale, in which an old woman hosts Theseus; Acts 14:11–12, where Lycaonians take Paul and Barnabas for Zeus and Hermes, suggests the Anatolian setting carried real belief. Whether Ovid drew on a lost Hellenistic tale or composed it himself is uncertain.

What survives mainly through Ovid, and how Roman that makes it

StoryEarliest Greek evidenceWhat is Ovid's
Orpheus and EurydiceEuripides, Alcestis; Plato, SymposiumBackward glance (Virgil first); the tone
NarcissusParthenius (P.Oxy. 4711); CononEcho's pairing; wasting death
PygmalionPhilostephanus (via Clement)Sculptor; statue comes to life
DaphneParthenius 15; PausaniasCupid's arrow; Augustan laurel
ArachneNone narrative (Virgil's hint)Everything
Baucis and PhilemonNoneEverything
PhaethonEuripides fragmentsFullest surviving telling
Midas's golden touchAristotle's proverbFull narrative; barber and reeds
Eros and PsycheNone (Apuleius, Latin)Not Ovid; Roman in text
Niobe, Marsyas, Ganymede, Leda, Tiresias, Adonis, LycaonHomer, Hesiod, Herodotus, SapphoSelection and colouring only

Three stories (Arachne, Baucis and Philemon, the living statue of Pygmalion) and one that is not Ovid's (Psyche) have no recoverable Greek telling. Several more (Daphne's motive, Echo, Narcissus's slow death, Phaethon's full arc, Midas's gold) are Greek in outline and Ovidian in everything a reader remembers. How Roman does that make them? In naming, entirely. In tone, considerably: the declamatory speeches, the Augustan laurel, the gods as a senate. In substance, less than it looks, because the loss of Nicander, Boios and Parthenius means absence of a Greek source is usually absence of evidence. The 2004 Narcissus papyrus demoted Ovid's most celebrated invention to adaptation in an afternoon; Arachne or Baucis could go the same way. The honest position is that this group of myths reached Europe through a Roman poet who improved almost everything he touched and told us nothing about what he had changed.

Self-test

  1. Which fifth-century Greek text implies that Orpheus successfully brought his wife back from Hades?
    Answer

    Euripides, Alcestis 357–362: Admetus wishes he had Orpheus's voice to recover his wife, which presupposes Orpheus succeeded.

  2. What did the 2004 publication of P.Oxy. 4711 change about Narcissus?
    Answer

    It showed Parthenius had told the reflection story roughly fifty years before Ovid, so Narcissus is no longer an Ovidian invention; Echo's pairing with him still is.

  3. How did Philostephanus's Pygmalion differ from Ovid's?
    Answer

    He was a Cypriot king in love with an ivory cult statue of Aphrodite; Ovid made him a sculptor whose own statue Venus brings to life.

  4. Who is Leucippus and why does Ovid omit him?
    Answer

    In Parthenius 15 and Pausanias 8.20 he is Daphne's mortal suitor, disguised as a girl and exposed through Apollo's jealousy. Ovid cuts him so Apollo's desire is unrivalled and Cupid's arrow supplies the motive.

  5. How many children does Niobe lose in Homer, Hesiod and Ovid?
    Answer

    Twelve in Iliad 24; twenty in Hesiod fr. 183; fourteen in Ovid and Apollodorus.

  6. Which two transformation stories are told of Tiresias, and whose are they?
    Answer

    The snake-striking sex change from Hesiod's Melampodia, used by Ovid; and the blinding for seeing Athena bathe, from Callimachus, Hymn 5.

  7. What is the earliest literary evidence for the golden touch and for the asses' ears of Midas?
    Answer

    The golden touch is a proverb in Aristotle, Politics 1257b; the asses' ears appear in Aristophanes, Plutus 287. The full narratives are Ovid's.

  8. Where does the Eros and Psyche story come from, and is it Greek?
    Answer

    Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4.28–6.24, Latin, second century AD. No Greek literary version survives; the Greek Onos that shares the donkey plot lacks Psyche.

  9. Name two stories in this module with no known Greek narrative source before Ovid.
    Answer

    Arachne (only Virgil's hint) and Baucis and Philemon (none at all). Echo's pairing with Narcissus is a third candidate.

  10. What does Ovid make the Lycaon episode do structurally, and what political reading does it invite?
    Answer

    It is the first human metamorphosis and the cause of the flood; Ovid compares the gods' alarm to Rome's at a plot against Augustus, inviting a parallel between Jupiter's power and the princeps's.

Carry forward

  1. Absence of a Greek source is usually absence of evidence: Nicander, Boios and Parthenius are lost, and Narcissus has already moved from Ovid's column to Greece's.
  2. Metamorphosis in Ovid is diagnosis, not reward or punishment: the body is made to show what the person already was, and the gods who impose it are jealous of a boundary, not just.
  3. Embedded narrators matter: Orpheus's Book 10 and Arachne's tapestry are characterised speech, and reading them as Ovid's own view flattens the poem.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Greek myths of transformation, love and divine punishment, with a clear account of which survive mainly through Ovid and how Roman that makes them. Cover: Orpheus and Eurydice (and the older versions where he fails differently); Narcissus and Echo; Pygmalion; Apollo and Daphne; Apollo and Hyacinthus; Adonis and Aphrodite; Eros and Psyche (Apuleius, so late and Latin); Arachne; Marsyas; Midas; Phaethon; Icarus; Callisto; Leda; Ganymede; Tiresias' two transformations; Baucis and Philemon; Niobe; Lycaon; the hubris pattern (Arachne, Marsyas, Niobe, Salmoneus, Capaneus) and what it teaches about the gods.
