GREECE · UNIT 4 · Mythology III: the Trojan cycle · 4.1 · 3,684 words

Causes of the war and the gathering at Aulis

The lost poems and what Proclus preservedTroy before PriamThe house of PriamThe wedding on Pelion and the Judgement of ParisHelen: birth, suitors, oathThe abduction, and the Helen who never wentMustering the GreeksAulis again, Tenedos, the landing, and nine yearsSelf-testCarry forward

The lost poems and what Proclus preserved

Almost everything that happens before the Iliad opens was told in poems that no longer exist. The Iliad covers some fifty days of the tenth year and assumes its audience knows the rest. The rest was supplied by the Epic Cycle, hexameter poems of probably the seventh and sixth centuries BC, later arranged into a sequence running from the marriage of Earth and Sky to the death of Odysseus. The Trojan section comprised six:

PoemBooksAttributed toSpan
Cypria11Stasinus of Cyprus (or Hegesias; some said Homer)Zeus's plan to the eve of the Iliad
Aethiopis5Arctinus of MiletusPenthesilea, Memnon, death of Achilles
Little Iliad4Lesches of MytileneArms of Achilles to the Horse entering Troy
Sack of Ilion2Arctinus of MiletusThe night Troy fell
Returns5Agias of TroezenHomecomings, death of Agamemnon
Telegony2Eugammon of CyreneOdysseus after the Odyssey

What survives is a few dozen quoted lines, scattered testimonia, and the prose summaries in Proclus' Chrestomathy, preserved in Photius, Library cod. 239 and in the Venetus A manuscript of the Iliad. Proclus' page on the Cypria is the backbone of every modern account of the war's causes. It is also a summary of a poem as edited to dovetail with Homer, so episodes that originally overlapped the Iliad may have been trimmed. The standard editions are M. L. West, Greek Epic Fragments (2003) and The Epic Cycle (2013).

Where sources disagree. The Suda makes this Proclus the fifth-century Neoplatonist; most scholars since Wilamowitz prefer a second-century AD grammarian. The Cypria's authorship was contested in antiquity: Herodotus 2.117 denies it to Homer because the Cypria had Paris reach Troy from Sparta in three days, whereas Iliad 6.289–292 sends him via Sidon. Proclus' summary includes the Sidon detour, so either Herodotus knew a different text or the summary has been harmonised with Homer.

One fragment matters for everything that follows. The scholia to Iliad 1.5 quote the poem's opening (fr. 1 West): Earth, weighed down by the countless tribes of men, appealed to Zeus, who resolved to lighten her by means of the Trojan War, planning it with Themis. The war is a divine design, and Helen, Paris and the apple are its instruments. Hesiod, Catalogue of Women fr. 204.95–119 M–W has a related version: after Helen's marriage Zeus plans strife to bring the race of heroes to an end.

Troy before Priam

Aeneas gives the Trojan pedigree at Iliad 20.215–241, the longest in Homer; Apollodorus, Library 3.12.1–3 expands it. Dardanus, son of Zeus and the Pleiad Electra, founded Dardania on the slopes of Ida before Ilios existed on the plain; Apollodorus brings him from Samothrace after a flood to marry Bateia, daughter of the local king Teucer, whence the poets' name Teucrians. His son Erichthonius owned three thousand mares, on which Boreas as a stallion fathered twelve foals that ran over standing corn without breaking it. Erichthonius' son Tros named the people and had three sons: Ilus, Assaracus and Ganymedes.

Zeus + Electra
  └─ Dardanus (+ Bateia, d. of Teucer)
       └─ Erichthonius
            └─ Tros
                 ├─ Ilus ── founds Ilion
                 │    └─ Laomedon
                 │         ├─ Tithonus (+ Eos) ── Memnon
                 │         ├─ Priam (born Podarces) (+ Hecuba)
                 │         ├─ Lampus, Clytius, Hicetaon
                 │         ├─ Hesione (+ Telamon) ── Teucer
                 │         └─ Astyoche (+ Telephus) ── Eurypylus
                 ├─ Assaracus
                 │    └─ Capys
                 │         └─ Anchises (+ Aphrodite) ── Aeneas
                 └─ Ganymedes (taken by Zeus)

Ganymedes became Zeus's cup-bearer, and Zeus paid Tros with the immortal horses Laomedon later owned (Iliad 5.265–267). Ilus won a spotted cow as a wrestling prize in Phrygia and was told to found a city where she lay down; she lay down on the hill of Ate, and the Palladium fell from heaven as confirmation (Apollodorus 3.12.3). Hence two lines: Ilus–Laomedon–Priam ruling the city, and Assaracus–Capys–Anchises–Aeneas in Dardania, which Poseidon at Iliad 20.302–308 prophesies will outlive the city.

Laomedon is the pivot because he cheats everyone. Apollo and Poseidon built the walls for him and were refused their wages (Iliad 21.441–457). Poseidon sent a sea-monster; an oracle demanded Laomedon's daughter Hesione. Heracles killed the monster for the promised horses of Zeus, was cheated too, and came back with six ships (Iliad 5.638–651), sacked the city and killed Laomedon and all his sons but one. Hesione, given to Telamon, ransomed her brother Podarces with her veil, hence Priam, as if from priamai, I buy (Apollodorus 2.6.4). The etymology is folk, but the point stands: Troy had fallen once already within its king's lifetime.

Where sources disagree. Dardanus' origin shifts with politics: Arcadian or Samothracian in Homer's tradition and Apollodorus, an emigrant from Italian Corythus in Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1.61 and Virgil, Aeneid 3.167–168, so that Aeneas is going home. Laomedon's wife is Strymo in Apollodorus, Placia or Leucippe elsewhere; Homer never names her.

The house of Priam

Priam had fifty sons, nineteen by Hecuba (Iliad 24.495–497), and twelve married daughters (6.248). Hecuba is daughter of Dymas the Phrygian in Homer (16.718), of Cisseus in Euripides (Hecuba 3), of the river Sangarius in a view Apollodorus 3.12.5 records. The children who matter for the war:

ChildMotherRoleChief sources
HectorHecubaEldest; commander; kills Protesilaus in the CypriaIliad
Paris (Alexander)HecubaExposed on Ida; herdsman; judge of the goddessesPindar, Paean 8a; Apollodorus 3.12.5
CassandraHecubaDisbelieved prophetessAeschylus, Agamemnon 1202–1212
HelenusHecubaSeer; prophesies before Paris sailsProclus
DeiphobusHecubaMarries Helen after Paris diesLittle Iliad; Odyssey 8.517
TroilusHecuba (or Apollo)Killed by Achilles in the early yearsIliad 24.257; Apollodorus Epit. 3.32
PolyxenaHecubaSacrificed at Achilles' tombSack of Ilion; Euripides, Hecuba
PolydorusLaothoe (Homer) / Hecuba (Euripides)Youngest; killed by Achilles or PolymestorIliad 20.407–418; Euripides, Hecuba
LycaonLaothoeSold on Lemnos, later killed by AchillesIliad 21.34–135
Creusa, LaodiceHecubaWives of Aeneas and HelicaonApollodorus 3.12.5; Iliad 3.122

The Paris birth-legend is the one the war needs. Hecuba dreamt she bore a torch that set the city ablaze; the seer Aesacus read it; the infant was exposed on Ida, suckled by a bear, raised by the herdsman Agelaus, and earned the name Alexander, defender of men, by driving off cattle-thieves (Apollodorus 3.12.5). He lived with the nymph Oenone until the goddesses came. His recognition at Priam's funeral games is the plot of Euripides' lost Alexandros (415 BC) and Hyginus, Fabulae 91. Homer knows none of this, though the herding is implied at Iliad 24.29, where the goddesses come to Paris' farmyard.

The wedding on Pelion and the Judgement of Paris

Zeus and Poseidon pursued the Nereid Thetis until Themis revealed that her son would be greater than his father (Pindar, Isthmian 8.26–48; Apollodorus 3.13.5 credits Prometheus). So she was married down to a mortal, Peleus of Phthia, who caught her on the shore at Sepias as she changed shapes. Homer knows the wedding as a feast of all the gods, Apollo playing the lyre (Iliad 24.59–63), and knows Thetis went unwillingly (18.432–434). The gifts were Chiron's ash spear and Poseidon's horses Xanthus and Balius (16.140–144, 16.866–867).

Proclus says only that at the wedding Eris provoked a quarrel about beauty among Athena, Hera and Aphrodite, and that Zeus had Hermes lead them to Alexander on Ida. Paris, "excited by the prospect of marriage with Helen", chose Aphrodite. The bribes are spelled out by Helen herself at Euripides, Trojan Women 924–931: Athena offered conquest of Greece, Hera kingship over Asia and Europe, Aphrodite Helen. Apollodorus, Epitome 3.2 is the earliest surviving text to make the quarrel's object an apple thrown by Eris; Lucian, Dialogues of the Gods 20 gives the inscription "to the fairest". The Judgement is on the Chigi vase (c. 640 BC) with Alexandros labelled, so it is at least as old as the Cycle.

Where sources disagree. The apple is absent from Homer, from Proclus and from every quoted fragment of the Cypria; whether the poem had it is uncertain. Homer's one allusion to the Judgement, Iliad 24.25–30, was athetised by Aristarchus as foreign to Homer; Reinhardt's 1938 essay argued the reverse, that the whole Iliad presupposes it. Whether Eris was uninvited (Apollodorus; Hyginus 92) or merely present and quarrelsome (Proclus) is also open.

The consequences were immediate. Aphrodite told Paris to build ships; Helenus and Cassandra prophesied; Aphrodite ordered Aeneas to sail with him. Hera and Athena became Troy's enemies, which is the fixed condition of the Iliad.

Helen: birth, suitors, oath

Helen is Zeus's daughter throughout Homer (Iliad 3.199), and Leda is mother of Castor and Polydeuces by Tyndareus (Odyssey 11.298–300). There is no swan in Homer. The Cypria (fr. 10 West, in Athenaeus 8.334b–d) made her daughter of Zeus and Nemesis, who fled him in animal shapes until he caught her as a goose; Apollodorus 3.10.7 adds the egg found by a shepherd and given to Leda to hatch. Euripides, Helen 17–21 brings the swan to Leda herself, with Helen's own "if the story is true". Hesiod fr. 24 M–W gave her an Oceanid mother. Of her twin brothers Polydeuces is Zeus's and Castor mortal; in the Cypria they die fighting Idas and Lynceus during Paris' visit to Sparta and share immortality on alternate days (Proclus; Pindar, Nemean 10.55–90). At Iliad 3.236–244 Helen scans the plain for them, not knowing.

Before the suitors came Theseus. Alcman (fr. 21), Hellanicus and Stesichorus knew that Theseus and Peirithous carried off the child Helen to Aphidna and that the Dioscuri recovered her, taking Theseus' mother Aethra as her servant; Aethra is still with Helen at Iliad 3.144. Stesichorus and Euphorion, cited by Pausanias 2.22.6, made Iphigenia Helen's daughter by Theseus, given to Clytemnestra to raise.

The wooing is the climax of Hesiod's Catalogue (frr. 196–204 M–W): a roll of suitors with their gifts; Menelaus bid through Agamemnon and offered most; Odysseus sent nothing, knowing Menelaus would win; Achilles was still a boy with Chiron (fr. 204.87–92). The oath is in Apollodorus 3.10.9: Tyndareus, fearing the losers would turn on the winner, took Odysseus' advice to make all suitors swear to defend whoever was chosen, and in return Odysseus got help in winning Penelope. Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis 49–71 has the oath sworn over a burnt sacrifice and Helen allowed to choose. Their one child was Hermione (Odyssey 4.12–14).

Where sources disagree. Thucydides 1.9 rejects the oath as the reason the Greeks followed Agamemnon, preferring his superior power and fleet. Homer never mentions the oath: his Greeks fight for Menelaus' honour and for plunder. The Hesiodic fragment that preserves it (204.78–85) is damaged exactly where its wording would be.

The abduction, and the Helen who never went

Proclus gives the Cypria's sequence. Paris was entertained by the Dioscuri and then by Menelaus in Sparta and gave Helen gifts. Menelaus sailed to Crete (for his grandfather Catreus' funeral, Apollodorus, Epitome 3.3), telling Helen to look after the guests. Aphrodite brought them together; they loaded most of the household property and sailed by night; Hera's storm drove them to Sidon, which Paris captured; at Troy they celebrated the marriage. Homer keeps the pieces: Paris left "with his wife and much property" (Iliad 13.626–627); they first lay together on the islet of Cranae (3.443–445); Sidonian women came on that voyage (6.289–292); Paris later offers to return the property but not Helen (7.362–364). Iris told Menelaus, who went to Agamemnon and then to Nestor, and Nestor delayed proceedings with four digressions.

Herodotus heard another story from the priests at Memphis (2.113–120). Paris was blown to Egypt; King Proteus kept Helen and the goods and expelled him; the Greeks besieged Troy for ten years disbelieving the Trojans' truthful denial; Menelaus collected Helen on his way home. Herodotus adds his own argument: Priam would never have let his city burn to keep Paris' mistress.

The poetic form is older. Stesichorus (fr. 192 PMG, at Plato, Phaedrus 243a) recanted a poem that had blamed Helen:

That story is not true; you did not go in the well-benched ships.

The ancients said Helen blinded him for slander and restored his sight when he retracted (Isocrates, Helen 64; Pausanias 3.19.11–13). The device was an eidolon, a phantom of cloud that went to Troy while the woman stayed in Egypt. Euripides staged it in Helen (412 BC): Hera, cheated at the Judgement, made the image; Hermes carried Helen to Proteus; Menelaus washes up with the phantom, which dissolves into air. At Electra 1280–1283 Zeus sends the phantom "so that strife and slaughter might come upon mortals": the Cypria's depopulation plan in a new key.

Where sources disagree. Whether Stesichorus wrote one Palinode or two is argued from a papyrus commentary (P.Oxy. 2506) that seems to mention two recantations. Whether Helen went willingly is the oldest dispute of all: Homer's Helen blames herself and Aphrodite by turns (Iliad 3.173–176, 3.399–412); Gorgias' Encomium acquits her under every heading; Herodotus' priests assume force. The Cypria, as summarised, makes Aphrodite the agent and says nothing of Helen's will.

Mustering the Greeks

Agamemnon and Menelaus went round the kings invoking the oath. Odysseus, warned by an oracle (Hyginus 95) that he would return after twenty years alone and destitute, feigned madness. In the Cypria and Apollodorus, Epitome 3.7, Palamedes exposed him by snatching the infant Telemachus and drawing his sword; Odysseus dropped the act. The ox and horse yoked together and the salt sown in the furrows are late (Hyginus 95; Lucian, On the Dance 46). The episode founded the enmity that killed Palamedes: by the Cypria (fr. 27 West, via Pausanias 10.31.2) Odysseus and Diomedes drowned him while fishing; in Euripides' lost Palamedes, Hyginus 105 and Apollodorus, Epitome 3.8 he was framed with a forged letter and buried gold, and stoned.

Achilles' recruitment has incompatible shapes. Homer's is plain: Nestor and Odysseus came to Phthia, and Achilles and Patroclus were sent off openly with their fathers' advice (Iliad 11.765–790; 9.252–259). The Cyclic version puts Achilles on Scyros only after the first abortive expedition, when a storm drove him there and he married Lycomedes' daughter Deidameia (Proclus; cf. Iliad 19.326, Neoptolemus growing up on Scyros). The version everyone remembers is later still: Calchas foretold that Troy would not fall without Achilles; Thetis hid him, aged nine, among Lycomedes' daughters under the name Pyrrha; Odysseus laid weapons among women's gifts and sounded a trumpet, and the boy seized the arms (Apollodorus 3.13.8; Hyginus 96; Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.162–170; Statius, Achilleid). Pausanias 1.22.6 saw Polygnotus' painting of Achilles among the maidens in the Propylaea, so the disguise was known by the mid-fifth century.

Where sources disagree. The Scyros stories cannot be reconciled: Homer has Achilles conquer Scyros as a warrior (9.668), the Cypria has him land there grown and blown off course, the later tradition hides him there as a child. Apollodorus, Epitome 3.16 makes him fifteen when he sailed; the Iliad's Achilles, with a son old enough to fight by the tenth year, must be older. The chronology was never made consistent.

The host gathered at Aulis. Homer's Catalogue of Ships (Iliad 2.494–759) totals some 1,186 vessels; Thucydides 1.10 rounds to 1,200; Apollodorus (Epitome 3.11–14) gives 1,013. A serpent devoured a sparrow and her eight chicks at the altar and was turned to stone; Calchas read nine years of war and the city taken in the tenth (Iliad 2.299–332).

Telephus and the false start

The Cypria has the fleet sail, miss Troy and sack Teuthrania in Mysia believing it was Troy. The king, Telephus, son of Heracles and Auge, killed Thersander son of Polyneices and drove them to the ships until Dionysus tripped him in a vine and Achilles wounded his thigh (Pindar, Isthmian 8.49–50; Apollodorus, Epitome 3.17). A storm scattered the returning fleet; this is when Achilles reached Scyros. Telephus' wound would not heal; Apollo's oracle said the wounder would heal it. He came to Argos in rags and, in Euripides' Telephus (438 BC, parodied in Aristophanes' Acharnians), seized the infant Orestes as hostage until he was heard. Achilles cured him with rust from the spear (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.20; Hyginus 101), and Telephus, married to Priam's sister Astyoche, agreed to guide the fleet but not to fight. His son Eurypylus would come to Troy's aid in the last year (Odyssey 11.519–521).

Where sources disagree. Apollodorus (Epitome 3.18) separates the Mysian fiasco from the second muster by eight years, so that the whole affair lasts twenty, matching Helen at Iliad 24.765–766, "this is now the twentieth year". The Iliad elsewhere counts nine years of war (2.134, 2.295). Most scholars treat the twenty-year scheme as a later harmonisation of Helen's loose phrase; Proclus gives no interval.

Aulis again, Tenedos, the landing, and nine years

Iphigenia

At the second gathering Agamemnon shot a deer and boasted that Artemis herself could not have done better. She sent storms; Calchas declared only Agamemnon's daughter would appease her; Iphigenia was fetched on the pretext of marriage to Achilles. So far Proclus. He continues: Artemis snatched her away, set a deer on the altar, carried her to the Taurians and made her immortal. Hesiod, Catalogue fr. 23a M–W agrees under another name, Iphimede made immortal as Artemis Einodia, that is Hecate; Stesichorus' Oresteia likewise made her Hecate. Euripides built two plays on the rescue: Iphigenia among the Taurians (c. 414), where she is Artemis' priestess until Orestes arrives, and Iphigenia at Aulis (405), where a messenger reports the deer on the altar. In the Taurians (20–24) the offence differs: Agamemnon had vowed Artemis the fairest thing the year produced, which turned out to be his daughter. Apollodorus, Epitome 3.21 records the boast and a third cause, Atreus' undelivered golden lamb.

Against the rescue stands the sacrifice. Aeschylus, Agamemnon 184–247 has contrary winds from the Strymon rotting ships and men, Agamemnon putting on "the yoke of necessity", and the girl lifted over the altar like a goat, gagged so she cannot curse the house; then the chorus stops: what followed it did not see. Pindar, Pythian 11.22–23 has her "slaughtered at the Euripus"; Sophocles' and Euripides' Electra plays assume she died; Lucretius 1.84–101 makes her death the exemplum of religious crime. Homer knows neither version: at Iliad 9.144–145 Agamemnon offers Achilles any of three living daughters, Chrysothemis, Laodice and Iphianassa.

Where sources disagree. Whether Iphianassa is Iphigenia under another name (so the scholiasts) or a different sister (Sophocles, Electra 157 names both) is undecided. The deer ending of Iphigenia at Aulis (1532–1629) is widely held to be a later addition, its final lines certainly Byzantine; the substitution is thus secure for the Cypria and Hesiod but not for Euripides' last play. And the causes of Artemis' anger are three incompatible stories, none adopted by Aeschylus, whose portent is eagles devouring a pregnant hare (Agamemnon 114–138).

Tenedos and Lemnos

At Tenedos Achilles killed its king Tennes despite Thetis' warning that Tennes' killer would die by Apollo's hand (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.26). At a feast Philoctetes was bitten by a water-snake and, because of the stench of the wound, was left on Lemnos (Proclus). Homer agrees on the island and the snake and adds that the Argives "would soon remember" him (Iliad 2.721–725). Sophocles' Philoctetes (409 BC) puts the bite at the shrine of the nymph Chryse (1326–1328) and makes Odysseus the abandoner (5–11). Achilles also quarrelled with Agamemnon at Tenedos over a late invitation to the feast, the first rehearsal of the Iliad's opening.

Where sources disagree. Sophocles' Lemnos is uninhabited, dramatically essential and historically absurd: in Homer it has a king, Euneus son of Jason, who buys Lycaon from Patroclus (Iliad 21.40–41, 23.746–747). Hyginus 102 replaces the snake with one of Heracles' poisoned arrows falling on Philoctetes' foot as punishment for revealing the site of Heracles' pyre.

Protesilaus and the landing

An oracle said the first man ashore would be the first to die, and Thetis warned Achilles (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.29). Protesilaus of Phylace leapt first and was killed; his brother Podarces took his forty ships (Iliad 2.695–710). Homer leaves his killer "a Dardanian man" and lingers on the wife tearing her cheeks and the house left half-built; the Cypria named Hector. Achilles killed Cycnus, son of Poseidon, whom Ovid (Metamorphoses 12.72–145) later made invulnerable, and routed the Trojans. The Greeks sent Menelaus and Odysseus into the city to demand Helen and the property; Antenor protected them, Antimachus urged the Trojans to kill Menelaus, and the demand was refused (Iliad 3.205–224, 11.138–142). Protesilaus' widow Laodamia and his three hours' leave from the dead are the matter of Euripides' lost Protesilaus and Hyginus 103–104; his tomb at Elaeus was a working cult site when Xerxes' governor plundered it (Herodotus 7.33, 9.116–120).

The first nine years

Proclus compresses nine years into a paragraph. The Greeks besieged the city and ravaged the countryside and neighbouring towns. Achilles asked to see Helen, and Aphrodite and Thetis arranged a meeting, found nowhere else. When the army wanted to go home Achilles held it. He raided Aeneas' cattle on Ida (Iliad 20.89–96), sacked Lyrnessus, Pedasus and twenty-three cities in all by his own count (9.328–329), and killed Troilus, whom Apollodorus (Epitome 3.32) has ambushed in the sanctuary of Thymbraean Apollo, a scene Attic pots show at a fountain-house. Patroclus sold Lycaon on Lemnos. From the spoils Achilles received Briseis of Lyrnessus and Agamemnon Chryseis of Thebe (Iliad 1.366–369, 2.690–693), the fuel of the Iliad's quarrel. Palamedes died. And Zeus, Proclus ends, planned to relieve the Trojans by detaching Achilles from the alliance; there followed a catalogue of Trojan allies. The Cypria closes exactly where Iliad 1 opens.

Thucydides 1.11 rationalised the nine years: the Greeks lacked supplies, farmed the Chersonese and raided for food, and never brought full strength against the walls. That is a man who had watched sieges, not a poet; but it shows that by the fifth century the long delay had itself become a problem the story had to explain.

Self-test

  1. Who preserved the summaries of the Epic Cycle, and in what two places do they survive?
    Answer

    Proclus, in the Chrestomathy; in Photius, Library cod. 239 and in the Venetus A manuscript of the Iliad. His identity (Neoplatonist or second-century grammarian) is disputed.

  2. According to Cypria fr. 1, why did Zeus bring about the Trojan War?
    Answer

    To relieve Earth, weighed down by the multitude of men; he planned it with Themis.

  3. Trace the line from Zeus to Priam in Homer's genealogy.
    Answer

    Zeus and Electra, Dardanus, Erichthonius, Tros, Ilus, Laomedon, Priam (Iliad 20.215–241). Aeneas descends from Tros through Assaracus, Capys and Anchises.

  4. Why was Podarces renamed Priam, and who ransomed him?
    Answer

    Heracles sacked Troy after Laomedon cheated him; Hesione ransomed her brother with her veil, and the name was explained from priamai, I buy (Apollodorus 2.6.4).

  5. Which three goddesses did Paris judge, and what did each offer according to Euripides?
    Answer

    Hera, Athena and Aphrodite; Hera offered rule over Asia and Europe, Athena conquest of Greece, Aphrodite Helen (Trojan Women 924–931).

  6. What is Helen's parentage in the Cypria, and how does it differ from Euripides' Helen?
    Answer

    In the Cypria she is daughter of Zeus and Nemesis, caught as a goose, with Leda hatching the egg; in Euripides Zeus came to Leda herself as a swan.

  7. What was the oath of Tyndareus, who proposed it, and which historian rejected it as the cause of the expedition?
    Answer

    All suitors swore to defend whichever man Helen married; Odysseus proposed it in exchange for help winning Penelope (Apollodorus 3.10.9); Thucydides 1.9 said Agamemnon's power, not the oath, assembled the fleet.

  8. What is the eidolon of Helen, and which three authors transmit the Egyptian story?
    Answer

    A phantom of cloud that went to Troy while the real Helen stayed in Egypt: Stesichorus' Palinode, Herodotus 2.113–120 (Helen in Egypt, without the phantom) and Euripides' Helen.

  9. How does Aeschylus' account of Iphigenia at Aulis differ from the Cypria's?
    Answer

    Aeschylus (Agamemnon 184–247) has her gagged and sacrificed, with contrary winds as the cause and no rescue; the Cypria has Artemis substitute a deer and carry her to the Taurians, immortal, after Agamemnon's boast over a deer.

  10. Who killed Protesilaus, and why was Philoctetes left on Lemnos?
    Answer

    Homer says only "a Dardanian man"; the Cypria and Apollodorus name Hector. Philoctetes was bitten by a water-snake at Tenedos (or at Chryse's shrine, in Sophocles) and abandoned because of the stench of the wound.

Carry forward

  1. The war is a divine plan before it is a human quarrel: Zeus's decision to depopulate the earth (Cypria fr. 1; Hesiod fr. 204) underlies the Judgement, the oath and Helen's flight, and the "will of Zeus" in the Iliad's fifth line inherits it.
  2. Knowledge of the pre-Iliadic story rests on summaries of lost poems read through fifth-century tragedy and Roman-era handbooks; nearly every episode has an early (Cyclic) and a late (Apollodorus, Hyginus) form, and the familiar version is usually the late one.
  3. Troy had already been sacked once, by Heracles, for Laomedon's broken faith; the Trojan War is a second reckoning, and Aeneas' Dardanian line is marked from the start as the one that will survive it.

GREECE · UNIT 4 · Mythology III: the Trojan cycle · 4.2 · 3,280 words

The Iliad

What the Iliad isBook by bookStructureThe characters and what they carryThe gods, fate and ZeusThemesOral style and the Parry–Lord theoryThe Homeric Question and the current viewWhat the poem leaves outSelf-testCarry forward

What the Iliad is

The Iliad is a poem of roughly 15,700 hexameter lines, divided since Hellenistic times into 24 books, telling about fifty days in the tenth year of the siege of Troy. Its subject is announced in the first word, mēnis, the wrath of Achilles: how it began, what it cost, and how it ended not in victory but in a shared meal with the father of the man he killed. Aristotle (Poetics 23) singled out this restraint as the mark of Homer's superiority over the poets of the Epic Cycle, who tried to narrate the whole war.

Book by book

BookSummary
1Agamemnon refuses the priest Chryses' ransom for his daughter; Apollo sends plague. Forced to return Chryseis, Agamemnon seizes Achilles' prize Briseis. Achilles withdraws from the war and has his mother Thetis extract from Zeus a nod that the Greeks will suffer for it.
2Zeus sends a deceiving Dream promising Agamemnon victory. Agamemnon tests the army by proposing retreat and they bolt for the ships until Odysseus restores order. The Catalogue of Ships and the Trojan Catalogue close the book.
3A truce is sworn for a duel between Paris and Menelaus. From the wall Helen identifies the Greek leaders for Priam (the Teichoskopia). Menelaus is winning when Aphrodite snatches Paris away and deposits him in Helen's bedroom.
4The gods debate; Zeus concedes Troy's eventual fall and Athena incites Pandarus to shoot Menelaus, breaking the truce. Agamemnon reviews the contingents and general battle begins.
5The aristeia of Diomedes, whose sight Athena clears so that he can distinguish gods; he wounds Aphrodite and, with Athena beside him in the chariot, Ares himself. Aeneas is rescued by Aphrodite and Apollo.
6Glaucus and Diomedes discover inherited guest-friendship and refuse to fight. Hector goes into Troy, meets Hecuba, scolds Paris, and takes leave of Andromache and the infant Astyanax at the Scaean Gate, the poem's most tender domestic scene.
7Hector challenges any Greek; Ajax wins the lot and fights him to a draw ended by nightfall. The dead are buried and the Greeks build a wall and trench round the ships.
8Zeus forbids divine interference, weighs the two sides' fates and thunders the Greeks back behind their wall. The Trojans camp on the plain, their watchfires compared to stars.
9Agamemnon, in despair, is persuaded by Nestor to send Odysseus, Phoenix and Ajax to Achilles with lavish gifts. Achilles refuses, reveals the choice between a short glorious life and a long obscure one, hears Phoenix's parable of Meleager, and yields only to Ajax's bluntness: he will fight when Hector reaches his own ships.
10The Doloneia: Diomedes and Odysseus go out by night, capture and kill the Trojan spy Dolon, then slaughter the Thracian king Rhesus and steal his horses. Already in antiquity suspected of being a later insertion.
11Agamemnon's aristeia, until he, Diomedes, Odysseus and the healer Machaon are all wounded. Achilles sends Patroclus to Nestor, who urges him to fight in Achilles' armour if Achilles will not.
12The Trojans assault the Greek wall on foot. Sarpedon delivers his speech on why princes must fight in front, and Hector smashes a gate with a boulder.
13Poseidon secretly aids the Greeks behind Zeus's back; Idomeneus has his aristeia; the fighting is a grinding stalemate at the ships.
14Hera seduces Zeus on Ida with Aphrodite's charm and the help of Sleep, freeing Poseidon to rally the Greeks. Ajax fells Hector with a stone.
15Zeus wakes, recalls Poseidon, has Apollo revive Hector and lays out the whole plan to come: Patroclus will die, Hector will die, Troy will fall. The Trojans reach the ships and Ajax alone holds them off with a pike.
16Patroclus begs to fight; Achilles lends his armour with orders to drive the Trojans from the ships and no further. Patroclus kills Sarpedon, ignores his orders, and is struck by Apollo, speared by Euphorbus and killed by Hector, to whom he prophesies death.
17Day-long struggle over Patroclus' corpse. Hector puts on Achilles' armour; Menelaus and Ajax finally carry the body off while Antilochus runs to tell Achilles.
18Achilles learns of the death and his cry reaches Thetis in the sea; he accepts that killing Hector means his own death. Unarmed, wreathed in Athena's fire, he routs the Trojans by his shout alone. Hephaestus forges the new armour and the Shield.
19Public reconciliation: Agamemnon blames Atē and returns Briseis and the gifts; Achilles refuses food. His horse Xanthus speaks, foretelling his death.
20Zeus releases the gods into battle. Achilles fights Aeneas, who is saved by Poseidon, and would kill Hector but for Apollo's mist.
21Slaughter at the river: Achilles kills the suppliant Lycaon, telling him that even Patroclus had to die. The river Scamander rises against him and is burned back by Hephaestus; the gods brawl; Apollo decoys Achilles while the Trojans flee inside.
22Hector alone stays outside despite his parents' pleas, runs three laps round the walls, and turns when Athena, disguised as his brother Deiphobus, deceives him. Achilles kills him, refuses his dying plea for burial and drags the body behind his chariot while Priam, Hecuba and Andromache lament.
23Patroclus' ghost asks for burial. Achilles sacrifices twelve Trojan youths on the pyre and then presides, with sudden courtesy, over funeral games.
24Achilles drags Hector's corpse for twelve days until the gods intervene. Hermes escorts Priam by night to the Greek camp; the old king kisses the hands that killed his son, and the two weep together. Achilles returns the body, grants a truce, and the poem ends with Hector's funeral.

Structure

The poem narrates about 51 days but spends almost all its length on four. Nine days of plague and twelve of the gods' absence pass in Book 1; the first day of battle fills Books 2–7; the second, Book 8; the night of the Embassy and the Doloneia, Books 9–10; the third and longest day, Books 11–18; the fourth, Books 19–22. Then come the funeral of Patroclus, twelve days of outrage to Hector's corpse, and the eleven-day truce. A ten-year war is made present through four days that contain it.

Where sources disagree. Handbooks speak of "three great days of battle" (Books 2–7, 11–18, 19–22), treating the short second day in Book 8 as a bridge; others count four. The crowded first day, with two duels and a broken truce, led Analyst critics since Lachmann to see it as a stitching-together of once separate episodes.

Cedric Whitman (Homer and the Heroic Tradition, 1958) argued that the poem is built as a ring, like the concentric bands of Geometric vase painting. Book 1 and Book 24 mirror each other: an old father (Chryses, Priam) comes to ransom a child from an Achaean who at first refuses; twelve-day intervals frame each; Thetis travels between Achilles and Zeus in both; the quarrel of gods in 1 answers the council of gods in 24. Books 2 and 23 both catalogue the Greek host, at arms and at play. Hector's duel with Ajax (7) answers his duel with Achilles (22). Not every pairing persuades, but the outer frame is undeniable.

Within the ring the plot turns on a few load-bearing scenes. The Embassy (Book 9) is where the heroic exchange of honour for service is tested and found wanting; after it Achilles' isolation is chosen, not imposed. The death of Patroclus (Book 16) is the hinge: everything before it is the consequence of the wrath against Agamemnon, everything after it the consequence of grief for Patroclus, and the wrath is transferred from Greek to Trojan. Zeus himself summarises the chain at 15.59–71. The Shield (18.478–608) halts the narrative to show the whole world of cities, harvest, dance and lawsuit that the battle has excluded; Achilles carries a cosmos into a fight he knows to be his last. The duel (Book 22) is the long-delayed climax, staged so that the reader sees it from the Trojan wall. The ransom (Book 24) replays Book 1 redeemed: a supplicating father is received rather than driven off.

The characters and what they carry

CharacterWhat the poem makes of them
AchillesThe absolute hero and the problem of absolutes. His choice of short life and lasting fame (9.410–416) is made consciously; his grief exposes the hollowness of the honour system he was raised in. He alone articulates the shared condition of mortals to an enemy (21.106–113, 24.525–533).
AgamemnonAuthority without the stature to justify it. He commands by rank, not merit, and treats honour as property to be confiscated. His admission that Zeus sent Atē upon him (19.86–138) is an apology that still refuses blame.
HectorDefender of a city, husband and son, driven by shame before his people (aidōs, 6.441–446; 22.99–110). He is not Achilles' equal and knows it; his tragedy is overreach after one day's success, against Polydamas' counsel (18.249–313).
PriamKingship in old age, fatherhood reduced to supplication. In Book 24 he does what no hero does: walks unarmed into the enemy camp and asks for pity.
HelenCause and conscience. She weaves the war into cloth (3.125–128), reproaches herself without pause, and is the last to speak over Hector (24.761–775). The poem never says plainly whether she went willingly.
AndromacheWhat war costs those who do not fight. Her plea in Book 6, premonition in 22 and lament in 24 trace a widow's story in three scenes; her forecast of Astyanax's fate (24.734–738) points outside the poem.
DiomedesThe model younger warrior: devastating in Book 5, yet he knows how far a mortal may go against a god (6.129–141), and speaks sense in Book 9 when Achilles has refused.
AjaxDefence, endurance, plain speech. He never has an aristeia of slaughter; his glory is holding the line (15.674–746) and his short speech to Achilles (9.624–642) is the one that moves him.
OdysseusPersuasion, craft and loyalty to the collective. He saves the army in Book 2, leads the Embassy, and quietly omits Agamemnon's demand that Achilles submit (9.158–161).
NestorThe authority of memory. His counsel sets both the Embassy and the fatal plan for Patroclus in motion (11.794–803).
PatroclusGentleness (enēeiē, 17.670) inside a warrior; Achilles' surrogate in armour and in death, and the one person he values above his own honour.
ParisDesire and irresponsibility, the archer who fights from a distance, yet not simply a coward: Hector concedes his courage (6.521–523).
Where sources disagree. The nature of Achilles' bond with Patroclus is nowhere stated. Aeschylus in the lost Myrmidons and Phaedrus in Plato's Symposium (180a) took it as erotic; Xenophon (Symposium 8.31) denied it. Modern readers divide the same way, and the text supports either reading without settling it.

The gods, fate and Zeus

The gods are a quarrelling aristocratic household whose interventions are constant and partisan. Athena and Hera hate Troy; Apollo, Aphrodite and Ares defend it; Zeus loves Hector and Sarpedon but has decided the war's outcome. Divine action takes three forms: direct combat (5.855–861; the theomachy of Book 21), rescue in mist or disguise, and the inward prompting of an impulse the human experiences as his own.

Fate (moira, aisa) sits beside this and never quite coincides with it. Zeus weighs destinies in golden scales (8.69–74; 22.209–213), which suggests he reads fate rather than decrees it. When Sarpedon is about to die, Zeus wonders aloud whether to save him; Hera does not say he cannot but that the other gods will not approve, and he desists (16.431–461). The same happens with Hector (22.167–185). The phrase "beyond fate" (hyper moron, 20.30, 21.517) names a possibility that must be prevented, so fate can in principle be broken.

Where sources disagree. One line of scholarship, following Wilamowitz and the Dios boulē ("plan of Zeus") of 1.5, treats fate as simply the will of Zeus seen from below. Another holds that moira is an older, impersonal order that Zeus administers but does not author, as in Hesiod's Moirai. A third, influential since the oral-poetry turn, reads fate as the tradition itself: what "must" happen is what the audience already knows happened. The Sarpedon scene is the crux and supports all three.

For the humans the result is double motivation: Patroclus dies because he disobeyed and because Apollo struck him. The poem does not treat these as rival explanations; a god's intervention doubles the weight of the human act.

Themes

Mēnis

The first word. Elsewhere in Homer the noun is reserved for gods; Leonard Muellner (The Anger of Achilles, 1996) argued it names a sanction against violated order, not personal temper. It is what Agamemnon provokes by overturning the rules of distribution, and what Achilles must formally renounce (19.67–68, 19.74–75) before the poem can proceed to its second movement.

Timē and kleos

Timē is honour made visible in prizes, seats and shares of meat; kleos is fame in song, the only immortality a hero can have. Achilles accepts the bargain of kleos aphthiton (9.413) but in the same speech rejects the exchange of goods for honour: no gifts can equal a life, because a life once breathed out cannot be recovered (9.401–409). Sarpedon's speech (12.310–328) gives the system's positive case.

Mortality

Glaucus compares generations to leaves (6.146–149); Apollo tells Poseidon that mortals are not worth a god's quarrel (21.462–466); Achilles tells Lycaon that Patroclus died, and so will he (21.106–113). The gods' immunity is the foil that makes human courage legible.

Pity

Eleos and the related aidōs are what Achilles loses after Book 16. He kills suppliants, mutilates Hector, sacrifices prisoners; Apollo accuses him of having destroyed pity itself (24.44). Priam's appeal, "pity me, remembering your own father" (24.503–504), restores it, and the two men's shared weeping is the resolution the wrath plot never offered.

The heroic code and its breakdown

The code says that honour is quantifiable, that a king's distribution is just, and that death is worth fame. Book 1 breaks the second premise, Book 9 the first, and Books 18–22 show a hero fighting for grief rather than honour: a force beyond the code's limits, compared to fire, a lion, a star. Book 24 does not restore the code; it finds something outside it.

Oral style and the Parry–Lord theory

The Iliad repeats itself at every level. About a third of its lines recur in whole or in part; heroes bear fixed epithets; arming, sacrifice and launching a ship follow set sequences, the "type-scenes" catalogued by Walter Arend (1933). Milman Parry, in his Paris theses of 1928 and his Harvard papers of 1930–32, showed that the epithet system is both extensive and economical: for a given hero in a given metrical slot there is almost always exactly one epithet, which is why Achilles is "swift-footed" when sitting still. No poet with a pen would build such a system; it is the toolkit of singers composing in performance.

Parry and Albert Lord tested this against living oral epic in Yugoslavia in 1933–35, recording singers who produced poems of thousands of lines without writing. Lord's The Singer of Tales (1960) generalised the results: oral poets do not memorise texts but recompose them from formulae and themes, and every performance is a new version.

Where sources disagree. How the oral poem became the written one is unresolved. Lord proposed a "dictated text", one performance taken down by a scribe. Gregory Nagy proposes instead a long "evolutionary" crystallisation through repeated performance, with no decisive moment of writing before the Athenian recension. Martin West (The Making of the Iliad, 2011) argues for a single literate poet composing over decades, expanding his own text. Critics also note that the Yugoslav songs are nowhere near the Iliad in scale, which some take as proof that writing was involved and others as proof only that Homer was better.

The Homeric Question and the current view

Ancient scholars already argued about the text. The chōrizontes ("separators") assigned the two epics to different poets; Zenodotus and Aristarchus at Alexandria athetised lines they thought spurious, and Aristarchus' judgements survive in the scholia.

The modern Question opens with Friedrich August Wolf's Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795), which argued that the poems were transmitted orally and shaped by later editors. Nineteenth-century Analysts (Lachmann, Kirchhoff, Wilamowitz) tried to dissect an original core from accretions, pointing to inconsistencies such as the dual verb forms in Book 9 (9.182–198), which seem to assume two ambassadors rather than three. Unitarians, culminating in Wolfgang Schadewaldt's Iliasstudien (1938), replied that the design of the whole is too coherent for a committee. Parry's work changed the terms: inconsistencies are what oral composition produces, and coherence is what a great singer produces.

Neoanalysis (Kakridis, Kullmann) added that the poet drew on specific earlier stories: the death of Patroclus and the fight over his body appear modelled on the death of Antilochus and Achilles' own death in the tradition later written down in the Aethiopis, which explains why the Iliad keeps forecasting Achilles' death in scenes it does not need.

On date and place, most scholars put the poem in Ionia or the eastern Aegean, in the second half of the eighth century BC, with the Odyssey somewhat later. The language is Ionic with an Aeolic layer, and the tradition preserves Bronze Age fossils: a boar's-tusk helmet (10.261–265), a Catalogue of Ships naming places abandoned after the Mycenaean collapse. The Greek alphabet was in use for hexameters by about 740–730 (the Dipylon jug, Nestor's cup). Hittite texts name a city Wilusa, generally equated with (W)Ilios, and Hisarlık shows a city (Troy VI/VIIa) destroyed around 1300 and again around 1180.

Where sources disagree. Richard Janko's statistical study of the language (1982) supports a date around 750–725. West and Walter Burkert argue for the seventh century, Burkert because the reference to Egyptian Thebes (9.381–384) would suit the period after 663. Nagy declines to assign a date at all. Whether the Trojan War happened is a separate question, argued between Korfmann and Kolb and treated in module 10.10. The evidence shows that Troy existed and was destroyed, not by whom.

What the poem leaves out

The Iliad assumes a listener who knows the story and declines to tell most of it. The causes of the war are glanced at only: the Judgement of Paris in one passage (24.25–30), Helen's abduction only through her own regret. There is no Iphigenia at Aulis (Agamemnon's daughters are three others, 9.144–145), no Palamedes, and Achilles has no invulnerable body: Asteropaeus draws his blood (21.166–167) and there is no heel.

At the other end the omissions are more deliberate still. The death of Achilles is foretold by Thetis (18.95–96), by Xanthus (19.416–417) and by the dying Hector (22.358–360), who names Paris and Apollo, but the poem ends with him alive. The Wooden Horse appears only in the Odyssey (4.271–289, 8.492–520) and the Cyclic Little Iliad and Sack of Ilion, known through Proclus' summaries. The fall of Troy is certain, stated by Zeus (15.69–71), by Hector (6.447–449) and by Agamemnon (4.164–165), but it is never shown. Priam's vision of his own body eaten by dogs at his door (22.66–76) lets the audience supply the ending the poet withholds.

The effect is that the Iliad is about the war without being the story of the war. By stopping at Hector's funeral the poet makes the burial of an enemy, not the capture of a city, the act the whole poem has been moving towards. This is what Aristotle meant by praising Homer for taking one part and using the rest as episodes: the omissions are the design.

Self-test

  1. What is the first word of the Iliad, and why does its normal usage matter?
    Answer

    Mēnis, wrath. In Homer the word is otherwise applied to gods, so giving it to Achilles marks his anger as something more than a human temper, a sanction against violated order (Muellner).

  2. Roughly how many days does the poem cover, and how many of them are days of battle?
    Answer

    About 51 days; four days of fighting (Books 2–7, 8, 11–18, 19–22), of which three are usually called the great battle days.

  3. Name three correspondences between Book 1 and Book 24 that support the ring-composition reading.
    Answer

    An old father (Chryses, Priam) comes to ransom a child; a twelve-day interval frames each book; Thetis travels between Achilles and Zeus in both; a divine quarrel in 1 is answered by a divine council in 24.

  4. Why is the death of Patroclus called the hinge of the poem?
    Answer

    Before it, the plot is driven by Achilles' wrath at Agamemnon; after it, by grief and the transferred wrath against Hector. Zeus states the whole causal chain in 15.59–71.

  5. What does Achilles reject in Book 9, and what does he accept?
    Answer

    He rejects the exchange of gifts for honour, because no goods equal a life (9.401–409), but he accepts and states the choice of a short life with imperishable fame (9.410–416).

  6. What does the Sarpedon episode in Book 16 show about Zeus and fate?
    Answer

    Zeus considers saving Sarpedon against his fate and desists because Hera warns of the other gods' disapproval, not because it is impossible, so fate is a norm Zeus upholds rather than an absolute limit.

  7. What did Milman Parry demonstrate about Homeric epithets, and why does it imply oral composition?
    Answer

    That the epithet system is extensive and economical: for each hero and metrical slot there is usually one epithet. Such a system serves a singer composing in performance, not a writer choosing words for sense.

  8. Which book was already suspected in antiquity of being a later addition, and what is its name?
    Answer

    Book 10, the Doloneia, the night raid of Diomedes and Odysseus.

  9. Give the mainstream date and place of the poem's composition, and one argument for a later date.
    Answer

    Ionia or the eastern Aegean, second half of the eighth century BC. Burkert argued for after 663 because 9.381–384 praises the wealth of Egyptian Thebes, which would suit that period.

  10. Name three major Trojan War events the Iliad does not narrate, and one passage where each is foreshadowed.
    Answer

    The death of Achilles (Hector's prophecy, 22.358–360); the Wooden Horse (not in the Iliad at all; Odyssey 8.492–520); the fall of Troy (Zeus, 15.69–71; Hector, 6.447–449).

Carry forward

  1. The Iliad is built on omission and compression: four days stand for ten years, and the audience supplies the fall of Troy the poet refuses to show. Later Greek literature, from the Epic Cycle to tragedy, works inside the space Homer left.
  2. Honour (timē) and fame (kleos) are an economy of exchange, and Achilles is the first figure to find that economy inadequate to a human life. Every later Greek hero, from Ajax to Antigone, is measured against that refusal.
  3. The poem is the end product of a long oral tradition, fixed in writing around the late eighth or seventh century; its formulae, type-scenes and inconsistencies are evidence of how it was made, and the Homeric Question is really the question of how an oral art became a text.

GREECE · UNIT 4 · Mythology III: the Trojan cycle · 4.3 · 3,179 words

The fall of Troy: the lost Epic Cycle

Three lost poems and how we read them

The Iliad ends with Hector's funeral; the Odyssey begins ten years later. The gap was filled by three archaic hexameter poems later grouped into the Epic Cycle: the Aethiopis in five books, attributed to Arctinus of Miletus; the Little Iliad in four, attributed to Lesches of Mytilene; and the Iliou Persis ("Sack of Ilion") in two, again given to Arctinus. None survives. We have roughly a page of plot summary for each, a few dozen quoted lines in all, and a vast penumbra of retellings.

The summaries come from the Chrestomathy of a certain Proclus, described by Photius (Bibliotheca cod. 239) and preserved for the Trojan poems in manuscripts of the Iliad, above all the tenth-century Venetus A. Proclus gives author, book count and a bare narrative, trimmed so that the poems run on from one another without overlap. Fragments quoted elsewhere show that the Little Iliad originally narrated the sack as well, with details that contradict the Iliou Persis. Proclus' text is a harmonised storyline, not a faithful abstract of each poem.

Where sources disagree. Proclus' identity is unsettled: some take him for the fifth-century Neoplatonist; most editors (Severyns, Davies, West) prefer the second-century grammarian Eutychius Proclus. The poems' dates are equally uncertain. Ancient chronographers placed Arctinus in the eighth century; West dates the surviving forms of all three to the seventh or sixth.

The other witnesses are of four kinds. Quoted fragments and testimonia in scholia, Pausanias and Tzetzes, collected by Bernabé, Davies and West (Loeb Greek Epic Fragments, 2003). Vase painting from the seventh century on, often older than any surviving text of an episode: the Mykonos relief pithos (c. 670 BC) already shows the Wooden Horse with warriors visible through portholes and, below, the killing of women and children. Fifth-century tragedy, which mined the poems systematically: Aristotle, Poetics 1459b, lists ten plays drawn from the Little Iliad alone, including Judgement of the Arms, Philoctetes, Neoptolemus, Sinon, Sack of Troy and Trojan Women. And late continuous narratives: Virgil's Aeneid 2, told from the Trojan side; Quintus of Smyrna's Posthomerica (probably third century AD), fourteen books covering exactly the ground of the three poems; Tryphiodorus' Sack of Troy; and the mythographers Apollodorus (Epitome 5) and Hyginus.

Where sources disagree. Whether Quintus read the cyclic poems or worked from summaries, scholia and the tragedians is disputed. His sequence matches Proclus closely; but he never contradicts the mythographic consensus where fragments show the archaic poems did, which suggests they were already lost to him.

The Aethiopis: Penthesilea and Memnon

Proclus opens with the arrival of Penthesilea, daughter of Ares, "Thracian by birth", with her Amazons. Later sources (Apollodorus, Epitome 5.1; Quintus 1.18–32) explain she sought purification after accidentally killing her sister Hippolyta. She fights with distinction; Achilles kills her; the Trojans bury her. Thersites, the railer of Iliad 2, mocks Achilles for his "alleged love" for the dead Amazon, and Achilles kills him. A quarrel follows; Achilles sails to Lesbos, sacrifices to Apollo, Artemis and Leto, and is purified by Odysseus. The love motif is thus already in the poem as rumour. Art made it the centre: Exekias' amphora in London (c. 530 BC) shows Achilles' spear in the throat of a fallen Penthesilea who looks up at him; the Penthesilea Painter's cup in Munich (c. 460 BC) makes that exchanged look the whole subject; Quintus 1.657–674 and Propertius 3.11.13–16 say outright that she conquered her conqueror once the helmet came off. Note the structure: the killing of Thersites is a stain, and Odysseus removes it, foreshadowing his inheritance of Achilles' arms.

Memnon, son of Eos and Tithonus, king of the Ethiopians (Hesiod, Theogony 984–985), arrives in armour made by Hephaestus. He kills Antilochus, Nestor's son, who had thrown himself between his father and the enemy (Pindar, Pythian 6.28–42; cf. Odyssey 4.187–188). Achilles kills Memnon; Eos obtains immortality for her son from Zeus. The episode deliberately doubles the Iliad: a friend's death drives Achilles to kill an enemy champion mourned by a divine mother, and the victor's own death is the price.

The weighing of souls (psychostasia) is the best-known element of the Memnon story and is absent from Proclus. Its model is Iliad 22.209–213, where Zeus weighs the death-fates of Achilles and Hector. Aeschylus wrote a Psychostasia in which Zeus weighed the souls of Achilles and Memnon with Thetis and Eos pleading on either side (Plutarch, Moralia 17a; Pollux 4.130). Attic vases of c. 520–470 BC show Hermes holding a balance with two small winged figures in the pans while the mothers watch.

Where sources disagree. Whether the Aethiopis contained a weighing is unknown; Proclus omits much. Some scholars think the vases reflect the epic, others Aeschylus, others a free-floating motif with Egyptian antecedents. Homer weighs keres, death-fates; the vases and Aeschylus weigh souls, and the pleading mothers add a courtroom logic foreign to the Iliad.

The death and funeral of Achilles

Achilles routs the Trojans, bursts into the city, and is killed "by Paris and Apollo". The double agency is Homeric: dying Hector foretells it at Iliad 22.359–360, and Xanthus the horse had said he would fall "to a god and a man" (19.416–417). Pindar, Paean 6, has Apollo take Paris' likeness; Hyginus, Fabulae 107, keeps the disguise and puts the wound in the ankle. In the Aethiopis a battle rages over the body: Ajax carries it to the ships while Odysseus holds off the Trojans, the composition on the handles of the François Vase (c. 570 BC). This partnership is the seed of the later quarrel.

The heel is late. The earliest evidence for an arrow in the lower leg is a Chalcidian amphora of c. 540 BC (lost, known from drawings); Apollodorus, Epitome 5.3, also says the ankle. But nothing archaic or classical makes it his only vulnerable point; Asteropaeus wounds his arm at Iliad 21.166–167. Invulnerability appears first in Statius, Achilleid 1.133–134 and 1.269–270, where Thetis dipped the infant in the Styx; that she held him by the heel is spelled out only by Servius on Aeneid 6.57. Apollodorus, Library 3.13.6, knows an older-looking story: Thetis laid the baby in the fire by night to burn away his mortality and Peleus interrupted her.

Where sources disagree. A different death circulates late: Achilles lured to the sanctuary of Thymbraean Apollo by a promise of marriage to Polyxena and ambushed by Paris and Deiphobus (Dictys 4.11; Dares 34; Hyginus 110). It has no archaic authority but became the standard medieval version.

The funeral in the Aethiopis: Thetis arrives with the Muses and Nereids and laments; then she snatches her son from the pyre and carries him to the White Island (Leuke) in the Black Sea; the Achaeans heap a mound and hold games. Odyssey 24.36–94 gives seventeen days of mourning, the Muses singing antiphonally, the bones placed with those of Patroclus in a golden amphora, the mound on the headland above the Hellespont, and games with prizes from Thetis.

Where sources disagree. The two accounts cannot both be right about where Achilles ended. In Odyssey 11.467–540 his shade is in Hades and resents it; in the Aethiopis he is translated bodily to Leuke, where he received historical cult; Pindar, Olympian 2.79–80, sends him to the Isle of the Blest. Monro observed that the Odyssey never narrates an event told in the Cycle; whether this means Homer knew and avoided the poems, or that the poems were composed to fill his gaps, remains the central question of Cycle scholarship (Burgess 2001 argues the tradition is older than Homer; West 2013 that the poems as we have them are later).

The Judgement of the Arms and the madness of Ajax

The Aethiopis ends and the Little Iliad begins with the quarrel of Ajax and Odysseus over the arms. In the Little Iliad, on Nestor's advice, spies listened under the Trojan walls and overheard two girls: one said Ajax was the braver because he carried the body; the other, prompted by Athena, replied that any woman can carry a load but would not stand and fight (fr. 2 West, in the scholia to Aristophanes, Knights 1056). Homer differs: at Odyssey 11.543–567 "the sons of the Trojans and Pallas Athena" judged, and Ajax's shade will not speak to Odysseus even in Hades. Pindar makes it a secret ballot corrupted by eloquence (Nemean 7.20–27, 8.23–34).

Ajax, driven mad, slaughters the Achaean herds and kills himself at dawn. Exekias' amphora in Boulogne (c. 540 BC) shows him alone, fixing the sword hilt in the earth. Sophocles' Ajax (probably 440s) is the fullest treatment: Athena displays the deluded hero to Odysseus; Ajax recovers and delivers the deception speech (646–692); alone on stage he plants the sword Hector gave him (Iliad 7.303–305) and falls on it (815–865), apparently in view of the audience. The second half is the fight over burial, which Odysseus, the enemy, secures against the Atreidae. That has epic backing: Little Iliad fr. 3 West says that because of Agamemnon's anger Ajax was laid in a coffin, not cremated, the only hero at Troy denied the pyre. Ovid adds the hyacinth lettered AI AI (Metamorphoses 13.394–398).

The Little Iliad: Philoctetes, Paris, Neoptolemus, the Palladium

With Achilles and Ajax dead the war can only be ended by oracle. Odysseus captures the Trojan seer Helenus, who reveals the conditions. Diomedes fetches Philoctetes from Lemnos, where he had been abandoned with his festering snake-bite; Machaon heals him; he kills Paris with the bow of Heracles. Menelaus mutilates the corpse; the Trojans bury it. Deiphobus marries Helen, which the Odyssey presupposes when Menelaus and Odysseus go to "the house of Deiphobus" on the night of the sack (8.517–520).

Where sources disagree. The Little Iliad has Diomedes alone fetch Philoctetes. Aeschylus made it Odysseus; Euripides (431 BC) Odysseus and Diomedes; Sophocles (409 BC) Odysseus and Neoptolemus, which puts Neoptolemus at Troy before Philoctetes, reversing Proclus' order (Dio Chrysostom, Oration 52 compares the plays). Paris' death also grows: Apollodorus, Library 3.12.6, Quintus 10.259–489 and Ovid, Heroides 5 have the wounded Paris carried to the nymph Oenone, who refuses to heal him and then kills herself. None of this is in Proclus.

Odysseus brings Neoptolemus from Scyros, gives him his father's arms, and Achilles' ghost appears to him. Eurypylus, son of Telephus, arrives with a Mysian army bought by Priam's gifts and is killed by Neoptolemus (Odyssey 11.519–521). Epeius, by Athena's design, builds the Wooden Horse. Odysseus disfigures himself, enters Troy as a beggar, is recognised by Helen and plans the capture with her (cf. Odyssey 4.242–264). Then Odysseus and Diomedes steal the Palladium, the image of Athena on which Troy's safety depended. The leaders enter the horse; the rest burn the camp and sail to Tenedos; the Trojans breach their own wall to bring the horse in.

The Palladium's afterlife is long. Later Greek versions make the theft a test: Diomedes carried the image, Odysseus tried to kill him from behind, Diomedes saw the sword's shadow in the moonlight and drove him back at sword-point, the "Diomedean compulsion" of the proverb collectors (Conon, Narratives 34). Argos and Athens both claimed the real image. Rome claimed most: Aeneas brought it, and it lay in the temple of Vesta as the pledge of empire (Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1.68–69; Ovid, Fasti 6.421–436). Virgil's Sinon makes the theft the Greeks' sacrilege against Athena (Aeneid 2.162–170).

The Wooden Horse: Laocoön, Sinon, Cassandra

The Iliou Persis opens with the Trojans debating the horse: throw it from the cliff, burn it, or dedicate it to Athena. The third view prevails and they feast. Then "two serpents appear and destroy Laocoön and one of his two sons"; Aeneas and his people, alarmed by the portent, withdraw to Mount Ida. Sinon, who had entered the city under false pretences, raises the fire signal; the fleet returns, the men climb out, and the slaughter begins. In Arctinus the serpents strike after the decision is made. They do not warn; they punish.

Virgil reverses the function. In Aeneid 2.13–249 Laocoön alone sees through the gift, hurls a spear into the horse's flank (2.50–53), and is destroyed with both sons by serpents swimming from Tenedos (2.199–233) while the horse still stands outside the walls; the Trojans read the death as punishment for the spear and drag the horse in. Between the two scenes stands Sinon's speech (2.57–198), the pretended deserter who claims to have escaped sacrifice at Odysseus' hands. Sophocles wrote both a Laocoön and a Sinon; Dionysius 1.48 cites the Laocoön for Aeneas' withdrawal to Ida, so Sophocles followed Arctinus there.

Where sources disagree. Arctinus: one son dies, and no offence is stated. Servius on Aeneid 2.201 reports that in Bacchylides and Euphorion the serpents came for a prior fault, Laocoön having lain with his wife before Apollo's image; Hyginus 135 makes him a priest of Apollo who married against the god's will. Virgil: two sons, and the moral ambiguity is the point. The Vatican marble group (Pliny, Natural History 36.37) shows both sons, as in Virgil; whether it depends on Virgil or both on a Hellenistic model is unresolved.

Cassandra is the unheeded prophet. The Iliad knows her only as Priam's most beautiful daughter (13.365–366); her prophetic gift and Apollo's curse that she would never be believed appear first in Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1202–1212. Virgil has her open her lips in vain "by the god's command" (2.246–247); Quintus 12.525–585 gives her a full speech and has the Trojans drive her off with stones; Lycophron's Alexandra is one enormous riddling prophecy in her mouth. In Proclus she appears only at her violation.

The sack

Proclus' sequence is terse. Neoptolemus kills Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios in his own courtyard. Menelaus finds Helen, kills Deiphobus, and leads her to the ships. Ajax son of Oileus drags Cassandra away by force, pulling down the image of Athena she clings to; the Greeks mean to stone him, he escapes to Athena's altar, and the goddess's anger falls on the fleet. Odysseus kills Astyanax; Neoptolemus takes Andromache; the spoils are divided. Demophon and Acamas find their grandmother Aethra among Helen's servants. The Greeks burn the city and slaughter Polyxena at Achilles' tomb.

Priam and Astyanax

Priam had foreseen his death at Iliad 22.60–71. The altar scene is in Pindar, Paean 6.112–117, and Euripides, Trojan Women 16–17, and reaches its height in Aeneid 2.506–558: Pyrrhus kills Polites before his father's eyes, drags Priam by the hair through his son's blood, and leaves "a huge trunk on the shore, a nameless body". The Little Iliad told it otherwise: Neoptolemus dragged Priam from the altar and killed him at the door of his house (fr. 25 West, from Pausanias 10.27.2, who notes the discrepancy because Polygnotus' painting at Delphi followed Lesches). Attic vases of c. 500–470 BC, above all the Kleophrades Painter's hydria in Naples, merge two deaths: Priam sits on the altar with the bleeding body of Astyanax in his lap as Neoptolemus strikes.

Where sources disagree. Astyanax's killer is a clean split. The Iliou Persis names Odysseus. The Little Iliad (fr. 29 West, in Tzetzes) has Neoptolemus seize the child from his nurse and hurl him from the tower. Andromache already fears a Greek will throw him from the wall at Iliad 24.734–738. Euripides, Trojan Women 709–739, keeps both: the army votes on Odysseus' motion and Talthybius carries out the sentence; the body returns on Hector's shield (1123–1250).

Cassandra, Polyxena, Helen and the women

Cassandra's violation becomes a sexual assault only gradually. Alcaeus fr. 298 (c. 600 BC) already treats Ajax's crime as the cause of Athena's wrath against the Greeks; Proclus says he "dragged her away by force"; Apollodorus, Epitome 5.22, Lycophron, Alexandra 348–364, and Quintus 13.420–429 make the rape explicit, Quintus adding that the statue turned its eyes to the roof. Locris was believed to have sent maidens to serve Athena at Troy for a thousand years in expiation (Lycophron 1141–1173). Cassandra falls to Agamemnon (Odyssey 11.421–423) and dies with him.

Polyxena's sacrifice closes the Iliou Persis. Ibycus (fr. 307) is the earliest poet named for it, and a Tyrrhenian amphora in London (c. 570–560 BC) shows three warriors holding her horizontal while Neoptolemus cuts her throat over the mound. Euripides' Hecuba (c. 424 BC) makes the demand come from Achilles' ghost and has Talthybius describe how she refused to be held and knelt to the blade (518–582). A fragment of the Cypria (fr. 34 West) knew a different end: Polyxena wounded by Odysseus and Diomedes during the sack and buried by Neoptolemus.

Euripides' Trojan Women (415 BC) is built on the division. Talthybius announces the lots: Cassandra to Agamemnon, Polyxena to "serve at Achilles' tomb" (a euphemism Hecuba does not yet understand), Andromache to Neoptolemus, Hecuba to Odysseus. Helen alone is argued over (860–1059) and, as the audience knows from Homer, never punished; Little Iliad fr. 28 West already had Menelaus catch sight of her breasts and drop the sword. Hecuba's end varies: Hecuba 1259–1273 prophesies her transformation into a dog and burial at Cynossema; Apollodorus, Epitome 5.23, gives her to Odysseus or to Helenus.

Where sources disagree. Whether Trojan Women comments on the Athenian destruction of Melos in winter 416/5 is an old controversy. The play was in preparation before the massacre, and many scholars now read it as a general meditation on victors and victims rather than topical protest; the question is not closed.

Aeneas and the Roman claim

The Greek tradition gives Aeneas survival but no destiny. Poseidon at Iliad 20.302–308 says he is fated to escape so that the line of Dardanus shall not die and his descendants will rule the Trojans. In the Iliou Persis he reads the Laocoön portent and leaves for Ida; the Little Iliad, in Tzetzes' fragment, has Neoptolemus take him captive. Attic black-figure vases found in Etruria (c. 520–470 BC) show him carrying Anchises out of the city, so the escape was popular in Italy well before Roman literature. Hellanicus of Lesbos (fifth century BC), reported by Dionysius 1.45–48 and 1.72, is the first Greek to bring him to Italy and found Rome. Rome then annexed the sequence: Naevius and Ennius told it in Latin; the Julii descended themselves from his son Iulus; Virgil built Aeneid 2 around Aeneas' own narrative, with Hector's ghost, the loss of Creusa and the escape with Anchises and Ascanius, and sent Troy's gods and the Palladium to the Tiber.

Where sources disagree. The Tabula Iliaca Capitolina (Augustan) shows Aeneas departing "for Hesperia" and claims to follow Stesichorus' Iliou Persis; most scholars doubt that a sixth-century poet sent him west and read the label as Augustan flattery. A hostile tradition also existed: Menecrates of Xanthus (in Dionysius 1.48) said Aeneas betrayed Troy; Livy 1.1 preserves the softer form, that he and Antenor were spared for having urged peace; Dares and Dictys make them open the gates. The Roman claim was asserted against as well as from the Greek material.

Self-test

  1. Name the three poems of the Epic Cycle that cover the end of the war, their attributed authors and book counts.
    Answer

    Aethiopis, Arctinus of Miletus, five books; Little Iliad, Lesches of Mytilene, four books; Iliou Persis, Arctinus, two books.

  2. Through what text do we know their plots, and what is the main distortion of that text?
    Answer

    The summaries in Proclus' Chrestomathy, preserved by Photius (Bibliotheca cod. 239) and in Iliad manuscripts. They were trimmed to remove overlap, so the Little Iliad's own account of the sack is omitted.

  3. Why does Achilles need purification in the Aethiopis, and who purifies him?
    Answer

    He killed Thersites for mocking his supposed love for the dead Penthesilea; Odysseus purifies him on Lesbos after sacrifices to Apollo, Artemis and Leto.

  4. What is the Homeric model for the weighing of souls, and what does Aeschylus change?
    Answer

    Iliad 22.209–213, where Zeus weighs the death-fates of Achilles and Hector. Aeschylus' Psychostasia weighs the souls of Achilles and Memnon, with Thetis and Eos pleading.

  5. Which is the earliest source to make Achilles invulnerable except at the heel?
    Answer

    Statius, Achilleid 1.133–134 (dipping in the Styx), with the heel spelled out in Servius on Aeneid 6.57. Archaic art shows an ankle wound but no invulnerability.

  6. How does the Little Iliad decide the Judgement of the Arms?
    Answer

    Spies overhear two Trojan girls; one says Ajax was braver for carrying the body, the other, prompted by Athena, that even a woman can carry but would not fight. Odysseus wins.

  7. What is unusual about Ajax's burial in the epic and in Sophocles?
    Answer

    He is buried in a coffin, not cremated, because of Agamemnon's anger (Little Iliad fr. 3 West); in Sophocles his enemy Odysseus secures the burial against the Atreidae.

  8. How does the function of the Laocoön episode differ between Arctinus and Virgil?
    Answer

    In Arctinus the serpents strike after the horse is inside and the decision made: a punishment, prompting Aeneas to leave. In Virgil Laocoön attacks the horse outside the walls and his death persuades the Trojans to bring it in.

  9. Who kills Astyanax in each of the two poems, and how does Euripides handle the discrepancy?
    Answer

    Odysseus in the Iliou Persis; Neoptolemus in the Little Iliad. In Trojan Women the army votes on Odysseus' motion and Talthybius executes it.

  10. What is the earliest evidence that Aeneas' escape was known in Italy?
    Answer

    Attic black-figure vases found in Etruria, c. 520–470 BC, showing Aeneas carrying Anchises; the literary link to Rome begins with Hellanicus in the fifth century.

Carry forward

  1. Proclus' summaries are a harmonised storyline, not the poems. Where a quoted fragment contradicts the summary (Priam's death, Astyanax, Aeneas' capture), the fragment shows what the poem actually said.
  2. Vase painting is often the oldest witness to an episode and must be weighed against the texts, not read as illustration of them; the Mykonos pithos, the Chalcidian amphora and Exekias predate every surviving literary version of what they show.
  3. Famous details are frequently late accretions: the heel, the explicit rape of Cassandra, Oenone, Laocoön's two sons, Aeneas' voyage west. Ask for each episode what the archaic poems, Homer, the tragedians and the Roman poets contribute, because the Odyssey and the Nostoi depend on which version of the sack and of Athena's anger one accepts.
