The Returns and the Odyssey

The Nostoi: a lost epic and its witnessesThe returns, hero by heroThe Odyssey: structure, and why it starts in the middleBook by bookThe wanderings in orderRecognition, the suitors and the bowThemesAgainst the Iliad, and the question of one poetSelf-testCarry forward

The Nostoi: a lost epic and its witnesses

The Nostoi ("Returns") was a five-book epic of the Trojan Cycle attributed to Agias (Hagias) of Troezen. It bridged the Iliou Persis and the Odyssey, and it is lost. What survives is the plot summary in Proclus' Chrestomathy, a few fragments, and the parallel digest in Apollodorus, Epitome 6. Proclus' outline: Athena sets Agamemnon and Menelaus quarrelling over when to sail; Diomedes and Nestor leave first and arrive safely; Menelaus follows and is blown to Egypt with five ships; Calchas and others go overland to Colophon, where Calchas dies after losing a prophecy contest to Mopsus (Strabo 14.1.27); Agamemnon sails late, sees Achilles' ghost, survives the storm off the Capherean rocks in which Locrian Ajax drowns, and is murdered on arrival by Aegisthus and Clytemnestra; Neoptolemus, warned by Thetis, goes home by land; Orestes' revenge closes the poem, and Menelaus reaches Sparta last of all.

The Odyssey is the oldest witness to several of these returns. Nestor's narrative (Odyssey 3.130–312) and Proteus' report to Menelaus (4.499–569) are miniature Nostoi embedded in Homer, older than the Cyclic poem by at least a generation.

Where sources disagree. Proclus names Agias; Eustathius and the Suda mention a Colophonian poet, and some fragments were assigned to Eumelus of Corinth. Whether Proclus summarises the archaic poem or a later redaction is uncertain; M. L. West (Loeb Greek Epic Fragments, 2003) treats the attribution as conventional.

The returns, hero by hero

Menelaus in Egypt

Nestor tells it first (Odyssey 3.276–312): Menelaus lost his helmsman Phrontis off Sunium and stopped to bury him; a storm off Cape Malea sent part of the fleet to Crete and five ships to Egypt. He stayed eight years (4.82–89), gathering wealth in Cyprus, Phoenicia, Ethiopia and Libya. Becalmed on Pharos, he was helped by Eidothea to ambush her father Proteus, who told him to sacrifice in Egypt and revealed the deaths of Ajax and Agamemnon and Odysseus' captivity with Calypso (4.351–570). Proteus also promised him Elysium rather than Hades, as Zeus' son-in-law (4.561–569). He reached Sparta on the day Orestes held the funeral feast for Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (3.311).

Herodotus heard another story from the priests at Memphis (Histories 2.113–120): Paris was blown to Egypt, king Proteus confiscated Helen, the Greeks fought ten years for a woman never in Troy, and Menelaus, collecting her afterwards, sacrificed two Egyptian children for a wind and fled. Herodotus argues Homer knew this version (citing Odyssey 4.227–230) but rejected it as unsuited to epic. Stesichorus' Palinode (fr. 192 PMG, via Plato, Phaedrus 243a) had already denied Helen went to Troy, and Euripides' Helen (412 BC) built a play on the Egyptian Helen and the phantom at Troy.

Where sources disagree. Homer's Proteus is a shape-shifting sea-god; Herodotus' is a mortal king at Memphis. Whether the Egyptian version is local tradition or Greek rationalising reflected back by Herodotus' informants is disputed; Alan Lloyd's commentary leans to the latter.

Nestor

The one uncomplicated return (Odyssey 3.130–183). After the Atreidae quarrelled, half the army left with Menelaus; at Tenedos Odysseus turned back to Agamemnon, while Nestor and Diomedes pressed on, took the open-sea route from Lesbos to Geraestus, and Nestor reached Pylos "nor did a wind fail" (3.182–183). Proclus and Apollodorus (Epitome 6.1) agree. In Book 3 Nestor's piety becomes the standard against which every other return is measured.

Diomedes

Homer knows only that he came home (3.180–181). Later tradition made Argos unliveable: Nauplius, avenging Palamedes, corrupted the chiefs' wives, and Aegialeia took Cometes as lover (Apollodorus, Epitome 6.9); Mimnermus (fr. 22 West) blamed Aphrodite, avenging her wound in Iliad 5. Diomedes went to Italy, was received by Daunus and founded Argyripa (Arpi) in Apulia. Lycophron (Alexandra 592–632) and Virgil (Aeneid 11.243–295) tell of his companions turned into birds on the Diomedean islands (Strabo 6.3.9); in Virgil the Latin embassy finds a chastened Diomedes who refuses to fight Aeneas again. Pindar (Nemean 10.7) says Athena made him a god.

Idomeneus

Nestor says Idomeneus lost no man on the way home (3.191–192). Two later traditions undo this. In Apollodorus (Epitome 6.9–10) his foster son Leucus seduces and kills queen Meda, seizes ten cities and expels the returning king. Servius (on Aeneid 3.121) has Idomeneus vow in a storm to sacrifice the first living thing he meets, which is his own son; plague follows and the Cretans drive him out. Virgil settles him in the Sallentine plain of Calabria (Aeneid 3.121–122, 400–401).

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (5.79.4) says Idomeneus and Meriones died in Crete and were honoured with a tomb at Knossos, contradicting the exile. The child-sacrifice vow appears only in Servius and later mythographers; its antiquity is uncertain.

Ajax son of Oileus and the shipwreck

Locrian Ajax had dragged Cassandra from Athena's statue during the sack (Proclus, Iliou Persis), and the goddess's anger followed the fleet; in Euripides' Trojan Women (77–94) she and Poseidon agree the storm in advance. Homer's version (Odyssey 4.499–511) is pointed: Poseidon drove Ajax onto the rocks of Gyrae but saved him, and he "would have escaped his doom, hated though he was by Athena", had he not boasted he had survived against the gods' will; Poseidon split the rock and he drowned. The Nostoi set the wreck at the Capherean rocks of Euboea, where Apollodorus (Epitome 6.7–11) adds Nauplius lighting false beacons. Lycophron (Alexandra 1141–1173) links the crime to the historical Locrian tribute of maidens to Athena at Troy.

Neoptolemus

Odysseus tells Achilles in Hades that his son returned unharmed (11.505–537), and Book 4 opens with his wedding to Hermione. The Nostoi gave the route: warned by Thetis, he went overland through Thrace, met Odysseus at Maroneia, buried Phoenix, and reached the Molossians in Epirus, where Peleus recognised him. Apollodorus (Epitome 6.12–14) adds Andromache and their son Molossus, ancestor of the Epirote kings (Strabo 7.7.8); Virgil's Buthrotum (Aeneid 3.294–336) is this settlement. His death at Delphi is contested. Pindar, Paean 6.98–120, says Apollo killed him in the sanctuary for slaughtering Priam at an altar; in Nemean 7.34–47, apparently answering Aeginetan offence, Pindar makes it a quarrel over sacrificial meats and him the honoured hero of Delphic rites. Euripides' Andromache (1085–1165) has Orestes engineer the murder. Pausanias (10.24.6) saw his tomb.

Teucer

Telamon banished Ajax's half-brother from Salamis for failing to bring Ajax home or avenge him (Sophocles' lost Teucer; Pacuvius). He founded Salamis in Cyprus, stated as fact by Pindar (Nemean 4.46), used by Isocrates to flatter Evagoras (Evagoras 18), and turned by Horace into "nil desperandum Teucro duce" (Odes 1.7.21–32). Euripides opens Helen (68–163) with Teucer in Egypt on his way to Cyprus; Virgil has him visit Belus in Sidon (Aeneid 1.619–626). Justin (44.3.2–3) takes him on to Spain, a late foundation legend of no archaic authority.

Philoctetes in Italy

Homer has him home safe (Odyssey 3.190) and the only archer who outshot Odysseus at Troy (8.219–220). Later writers drive him from Thessalian Meliboea by revolt and settle him in southern Italy: Lycophron (Alexandra 911–929) names Crimissa, Petelia and Macalla, with his tomb by the Crathis; Strabo (6.1.3) credits him with Petelia, Crimissa and Chone near Croton; the pseudo-Aristotelian Mirabilia (107) says he dedicated Heracles' bow in the temple of Apollo Alaeus at Macalla. Virgil's "little Petelia, propped on Philoctetes' wall" (Aeneid 3.402) sits among the Italian Greek cities. With Diomedes in Apulia and Idomeneus in Calabria, the Nostoi gave Magna Graecia heroic founders and gave Rome's poets a map of displaced Greeks to set against Aeneas.

The Odyssey: structure, and why it starts in the middle

Three movements. The Telemachy (Books 1–4) opens on Olympus and in Ithaca and sends Telemachus to Pylos and Sparta, where the returns of Nestor and Menelaus are told and Odysseus is spoken of but absent. The Phaeacian narration (Books 5–12) brings Odysseus from Ogygia to Scheria, where in Books 9–12 (the Apologoi) he tells his wanderings in the first person. The return and vengeance (Books 13–24) runs from Eumaeus' hut to the palace, the bow, the slaughter, and the reunions with Penelope and Laertes. The scholia report that Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus set the poem's telos at 23.296, where Odysseus and Penelope go to bed.

The poem begins in the tenth year, with Odysseus seven years on Calypso's island, and lets him narrate the earlier adventures himself. Horace coined the phrase: Homer "hurries the hearer into the midst of things", in medias res (Ars Poetica 148–149). Aristotle (Poetics 1451a) praised the Odyssey for making one action, not one life. The gains are large. The fabulous material is put in Odysseus' mouth, so the poet does not vouch for it and his reliability becomes part of his character. Telemachus grows up while his father is offstage. The weight falls on homecoming, not adventure. And the opening council, where Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for suffering they bring on themselves (1.32–43), frames the whole poem as a moral demonstration.

Where sources disagree. Analysts (Kirchhoff, Wilamowitz, Denys Page, The Homeric Odyssey, 1955) found Book 24's language, second Nekyia and Laertes scene late. Unitarians (Heubeck in the Oxford commentary; Stephanie West) answer that the plot needs the suitors' families dealt with and that the three-generation reunion is its goal. Current consensus leans to keeping Book 24, but it is not settled.

Book by book

BookSummary
1Proem. Divine council; Zeus on Aegisthus and human responsibility. Athena as Mentes finds the suitors feasting and tells Telemachus to call an assembly and seek news. Penelope stops Phemius' song of the returns.
2First Ithacan assembly in twenty years. Antinous blames Penelope and exposes the shroud trick. Halitherses reads the omen of two eagles. Athena as Mentor finds a ship; Eurycleia keeps the secret.
3Pylos. Nestor tells of the quarrel of the Atreidae, his return, Menelaus' delay and Orestes' revenge. Athena leaves as an eagle; Telemachus drives to Sparta with Peisistratus.
4Sparta. Helen recognises Telemachus by his likeness; tales of Odysseus at Troy; Menelaus narrates Proteus and the deaths of Ajax and Agamemnon. In Ithaca the suitors plan an ambush; Penelope learns of the voyage.
5Hermes sent to Calypso; she protests, then helps build the raft. Poseidon's storm; Ino's veil; after two days in the sea Odysseus lands on Scheria and sleeps under an olive.
6Nausicaa at the river. Odysseus emerges, likens her to Artemis and the Delian palm, prays for homophrosyne in marriage. She clothes him and directs him to the palace.
7Athena guides him through the city; Alcinous' palace and garden. He clasps Arete's knees; Alcinous promises passage. He tells only of Calypso, not his name.
8Games; Euryalus taunts, Odysseus throws the discus. Demodocus sings Ares and Aphrodite, then the wooden horse. Odysseus weeps "like a woman over her fallen husband"; Alcinous asks his name.
9"I am Odysseus son of Laertes." Cicones; storm off Malea; Lotus-eaters; Polyphemus: Maron's wine, Nobody, the blinding, the ram, the boast and the Cyclops' curse.
10Aeolus' bag of winds, opened in sight of Ithaca; refused a second time. Laestrygonians destroy eleven ships. Circe turns the scouts to swine; Hermes gives moly; a year's stay; she sends him to Hades.
11Nekyia. Elpenor; Tiresias on Thrinacia, the suitors, the inland journey with an oar and a gentle death; Anticleia; catalogue of heroines; Agamemnon, Achilles, silent Ajax; the sinners; Heracles' phantom.
12Circe's warnings. Sirens; Scylla chosen over Charybdis, six men lost; Thrinacia and Helios' cattle; Zeus' bolt sinks the ship; Odysseus on the keel through Charybdis to Ogygia.
13Departure with gifts; landed asleep at Phorcys' harbour. Poseidon petrifies the Phaeacian ship. Athena as a shepherd lifts the mist; Odysseus lies to her; she disguises him as a beggar.
14Eumaeus hosts the beggar with exemplary xenia and will not believe Odysseus lives. Odysseus spins a Cretan life and the tale of the cloak at Troy.
15Telemachus leaves Sparta, takes on the seer Theoclymenus, evades the ambush and goes to Eumaeus, who tells how Phoenicians kidnapped him as a child.
16Athena restores Odysseus; father and son recognise each other and plan. The suitors learn the ambush failed; Antinous proposes murder, Amphinomus delays; Penelope confronts Antinous.
17Theoclymenus prophesies Odysseus is present. Odysseus walks to town; Melanthius kicks him; the dog Argos recognises him and dies. Antinous throws a footstool; Penelope asks for the beggar.
18Odysseus beats the beggar Irus and warns Amphinomus in vain. Athena beautifies Penelope, who extracts gifts from the suitors. Melantho abuses him; Eurymachus throws a stool.
19The arms removed. Odysseus and Penelope talk; the brooch. Eurycleia finds the scar (the boar-hunt digression). Penelope's dream of geese and eagle; gates of horn and ivory; she announces the bow contest.
20Sleepless Odysseus reassured by Athena; Zeus thunders at a servant's curse. Philoetius arrives loyal. Ctesippus throws an ox-hoof; Theoclymenus sees the hall dripping blood and leaves.
21The bow of Iphitus. Telemachus nearly strings it; all suitors fail. Odysseus reveals himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius by the scar, strings the bow like a lyre and shoots through the axes; Zeus thunders.
22Antinous shot at his cup. Odysseus names himself. Eurymachus, Amphinomus, Leodes die; Melanthius caught fetching arms; Athena's aegis. Phemius and Medon spared. The maids hanged; the hall purified.
23Penelope stays sceptical. The test of the bed built round the olive trunk; recognition. Athena holds back dawn. Odysseus recounts his wanderings and Tiresias' last journey.
24Hermes leads the suitors to Hades; Agamemnon and Achilles converse; Amphimedon gives the suitors' version. Odysseus tests Laertes, proves himself by scar and orchard trees. Eupeithes raises the families; Laertes kills him; Athena imposes peace.

The wanderings in order

The Apologoi run from Troy to Ogygia as variations on hospitality, appetite and restraint. The Cicones at Ismarus (9.39–61) are an ordinary raid gone wrong because the crew will not leave the beach. A storm off Malea (9.80–81) pushes the fleet out of the known world. The Lotus-eaters (9.82–104) are the gentlest danger: whoever eats forgets his nostos. Polyphemus (9.105–566) is the inverted host who eats his guests; Odysseus beats him with wine, a stake and the name "Nobody" (Outis, punning on me tis, "no one", and metis, "cunning", 9.405–414), then undoes the victory by shouting his real name (9.502–505), giving the Cyclops something to curse. Poseidon's hostility dates from that boast. Aeolus (10.1–79) gives perfect hospitality and the winds in a bag; the crew's suspicion opens it in sight of Ithaca, and Aeolus refuses a man the gods evidently hate. The Laestrygonians (10.80–132) sink eleven of twelve ships. Circe (10.133–574) turns men to pigs; Hermes' moly and a drawn sword win Odysseus a year's comfort the crew must break for him. The Nekyia (Book 11) is Circe's errand: Tiresias gives the terms of return (11.100–137) and the dead set Odysseus' choice of life beside Achilles' regret (11.488–491). He passes the Sirens bound to the mast (12.165–200), chooses Scylla over Charybdis and loses six men (12.201–259), and is forced to land on Thrinacia, where the starving crew kill Helios' cattle (12.260–402). Zeus' bolt sinks the last ship; Odysseus alone survives a second Charybdis and drifts to Calypso (12.403–453), where seven years pass and immortality is offered and declined (5.203–224). Only then comes Phaeacia, the halfway house between fairyland and Ithaca, with its ideal palace and magic ships (Books 6–8, 13).

Where sources disagree. Strabo (1.2.9–19) took the geography seriously; Eratosthenes said you would find Odysseus' route when you found the cobbler who sewed the bag of winds. Sicily for the Cyclopes and Laestrygonians was conventional by Thucydides (6.2.1); most modern scholars treat the wanderings as deliberately off the map.

Recognition, the suitors and the bow

Aristotle (Poetics 1459b) called the Odyssey "complex" because anagnorisis runs through it. The scenes are graded. Telemachus (16.172–219) must be told and shown a transformation; the dog Argos (17.290–327) knows by scent and dies. Eurycleia (19.386–507) finds the boar's-tusk scar, and the poet suspends the moment for seventy lines to tell how Odysseus got it on Parnassus; Auerbach's "Odysseus' Scar" (Mimesis, ch. 1) made this the type-case of Homer's fully lit narrative. Eumaeus and Philoetius (21.188–225) are shown the scar deliberately. Penelope (23.85–230) refuses every proof and sets her own test: she orders the bed moved, and Odysseus' protest that he built it round a living olive trunk is the one secret no impostor could know. Laertes (24.315–348) is tested almost cruelly before the scar and the list of trees convince him.

Where sources disagree. Philip Harsh (1950) argued Penelope recognises Odysseus in Book 19 and sets the contest knowing who will win; Amory and Winkler developed an "intuitive" recognition. Most commentators (Heubeck, Russo) keep her ignorant until the bed test and read the contest as a surrender she cannot explain. The text is deliberately opaque.

The suitors number 108 (16.245–253). Antinous is violent and unrepentant, Eurymachus smooth and dishonest, Amphinomus decent enough that Odysseus warns him and Athena still refuses him escape (18.125–157). The bow (21.11–41) was a guest-gift from Iphitus, later murdered by Heracles, and never went to Troy; it belongs to the house. The contest is to string it and shoot through twelve axes. Telemachus nearly strings it and is checked by his father's glance (21.128–129); every suitor fails. Odysseus turns it over "as a man skilled in the lyre stretches a string", plucks it so it sings like a swallow, and shoots through the axes as Zeus thunders (21.404–423). Book 22 opens with Antinous killed at his wine-cup, the inversion of the feast he has stolen, and ends with the maids hanged and the hall fumigated.

Themes

Nostos. The first word is andra, but the organising noun is return. The other returns in Books 3, 4 and 11 define Odysseus' by contrast: Nestor's effortless, Menelaus' rich but late, Agamemnon's fatal, Achilles' never. Nostos is not arrival but restoration of a position: husband, father, son, king.

Xenia. Good hosts (Nestor, Menelaus, Alcinous, Eumaeus) ask the stranger's name only after feeding him; bad hosts eat the guest (Polyphemus, Laestrygonians) or eat the host out of house (the suitors). The disguises make the second half a theoxeny, and the poem says so: "the gods go about cities in the likeness of strangers" (17.485–487).

Metis. Odysseus' intelligence is practical and verbal: the pun, the Cretan lies, the bow. It is set against bie, force, which belongs to the Cyclops and to Achilles; Athena loves him for it (13.291–299). Penelope shares it (the shroud, the gifts, the bed), and the poem calls their marriage homophrosyne (6.181–185).

Identity. Odysseus is polytropos, and he gives his name with full weight only three times: to the Cyclops (disastrously), to the Phaeacians (9.19–20), and to the suitors (22.35). Each disguise shed is a stage in becoming himself; he refuses Calypso's immortality because it would be a life without a name.

The oikos. The household is the unit the poem defends: stores, servants, bed, land. The slaughter is not revenge but repair of an oikos the suitors are consuming (bioton katedousin, "they eat up the livelihood", 1.160 and often). Laertes in his orchard, Eumaeus with his pigs, Penelope at her loom and Telemachus coming of age are parts of one institution.

Against the Iliad, and the question of one poet

The Iliad is tragic: its subject is anger, its horizon death, and its hero chooses glory over return. The Odyssey is comic in the old sense: its subject is survival, its horizon home, and its hero chooses return over immortality and hears glory recanted by Achilles' ghost (11.488–491). The gods differ. In the Iliad they quarrel, deceive each other and fight on the field; justice is not their business. In the Odyssey Zeus opens the poem insisting men suffer by their own fault (1.32–43), Poseidon's hostility is provoked and bounded, and the plot is largely a partnership between Athena and one mortal. The Odyssey moralises: the suitors are warned, Eumaeus rewarded. The world differs too: the Iliad is aristocratic and martial on one plain; the Odyssey has swineherds, beggars, Phoenician traders, a farm dog and the kitchen, and it travels. Pseudo-Longinus (On the Sublime 9.11–15) read this as biography, the Odyssey as "the work of old age", a setting sun lapsing into fable. Aristotle (Poetics 1459b) put it structurally: the Iliad simple and pathetic, the Odyssey complex and ethical.

Authorship was contested in antiquity. The chorizontes ("separators"), Xenon and Hellanicus, assigned the poems to different poets on grounds of language and inconsistency; Aristarchus answered them, and the single Homer prevailed, composing the Iliad young and the Odyssey old. The modern debate begins with Wolf's Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795); Milman Parry's demonstration in the 1930s that both poems are built from oral formulaic diction changed its terms, since shared technique makes shared authorship unprovable by style alone.

Where sources disagree. Janko's linguistic statistics (Homer, Hesiod and the Hymns, 1982) put the Odyssey slightly later but within a generation, compatible with one poet. M. L. West (The Making of the Odyssey, 2014) argues for a different seventh-century poet with the Iliad before him. Nagy's evolutionary model dissolves the question: both texts crystallised over centuries of performance. Monro's Law, that the Odyssey never repeats an Iliad episode, is accepted by all and explained differently: one poet's design, or a successor's deference. Unresolved.

Self-test

  1. Who is the traditional author of the Nostoi, and how do we know its plot?
    Answer

    Agias (Hagias) of Troezen. The poem is lost; we have Proclus' summary in the Chrestomathy, a few fragments, and the parallel in Apollodorus, Epitome 6.

  2. Where does Homer's Menelaus learn the fate of Agamemnon and Ajax, and from whom?
    Answer

    On Pharos off Egypt, from the sea-god Proteus, ambushed with Eidothea's help (Odyssey 4.351–570).

  3. How does Herodotus' Egyptian version of Helen differ from Homer's?
    Answer

    In Histories 2.113–120 Helen never reaches Troy; king Proteus of Memphis keeps her, and Menelaus collects her after the war, then sacrifices two Egyptian children and flees.

  4. Why does Locrian Ajax drown, according to Proteus in Odyssey 4?
    Answer

    Poseidon saved him from the wreck at Gyrae, but Ajax boasted he had escaped against the gods' will; Poseidon split the rock and he drowned. Athena's anger over Cassandra lay behind the storm.

  5. Give Pindar's two incompatible accounts of Neoptolemus' death.
    Answer

    Paean 6: Apollo killed him at Delphi for slaughtering Priam at an altar. Nemean 7: he died in a quarrel over sacrificial meats and became the presiding hero of Delphi.

  6. Which Italian cities did tradition assign to Philoctetes, and what did he dedicate there?
    Answer

    Petelia, Crimissa, Chone and Macalla near Croton (Lycophron, Strabo); Heracles' bow and arrows in the temple of Apollo Alaeus (pseudo-Aristotle, Mirabilia 107).

  7. Name the three movements of the Odyssey and their books.
    Answer

    Telemachy, 1–4; Phaeacian narration (with the Apologoi, 9–12), 5–12; return and vengeance, 13–24.

  8. What is the pun in Odysseus' false name, and where does it pay off?
    Answer

    Outis, "Nobody", echoes me tis, "no one", and metis, "cunning". It pays off at 9.405–414 when the other Cyclopes hear that "no one" is hurting Polyphemus and leave.

  9. What is Penelope's test, and why can only Odysseus pass it?
    Answer

    She orders the bed moved out of the chamber (23.177–230). Odysseus built it round a living olive trunk, so it cannot be moved, and only the two of them know.

  10. Who were the chorizontes, and what is Monro's Law?
    Answer

    Hellenistic critics (Xenon, Hellanicus) who held the two epics had different authors. Monro's Law observes that the Odyssey never retells an Iliad episode; both sides accept it and explain it differently.

Carry forward

  1. The Nostoi are a system of contrasts, not a list: Nestor, Menelaus, Agamemnon and Achilles are placed round Odysseus so that his return defines the right way home. Later modules on Agamemnon and Orestes, and on Aeneas, build on this frame.
  2. The displaced heroes (Diomedes, Idomeneus, Philoctetes, Teucer) are the mythic charter of Greek settlement in Italy and Cyprus, and the material Virgil reworks for Aeneas. Keep the geography in mind for Magna Graecia and Roman transmission.
  3. The Odyssey is a poem about metis, xenia and the oikos, and its gods are more moral than the Iliad's. Zeus' speech on human responsibility is the hinge for later modules on Hesiod, Solon and tragedy.

Give me an in-depth report in two parts. Part one: the Nostoi, the returns of the other heroes: Menelaus in Egypt, Nestor, Diomedes, Idomeneus, Ajax son of Oileus and the shipwreck, Neoptolemus, Teucer, Philoctetes in Italy. Part two: Homer's Odyssey: a book-by-book summary of all 24 books; the structure (the Telemachy, the Phaeacian narration, the return and vengeance) and why the poem starts in the middle; every episode of the wanderings in order (Cicones, Lotus-eaters, Polyphemus, Aeolus, Laestrygonians, Circe, the Nekyia, Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, Helios' cattle, Calypso, Phaeacia); the recognition scenes; the suitors and the bow; the themes (nostos, xenia, metis, identity, the oikos); the differences in tone, theology and world from the Iliad and the ancient and modern views on whether the same poet wrote both. The house of Atreus after Troy

The killing of Agamemnon and CassandraElectra, the exile of Orestes, and the matricideThe Erinyes, Delphi and the trial at AthensThe later wanderings: Iphigenia, Hermione, NeoptolemusAeschylus' Oresteia: from vendetta to lawSophocles' ElectraEuripides: Electra, Orestes and the Iphigenia playsAthens' myth about its own courtsSelf-testCarry forward

The killing of Agamemnon and Cassandra

Agamemnon came home from Troy with three debts hanging over him. He had cut his daughter's throat at Aulis so the fleet could sail; he brought back Priam's daughter Cassandra as a concubine; and his wife had meanwhile taken his cousin Aegisthus, son of Thyestes, whose children Atreus had served to him at table. Every version of what happened next mixes these three motives differently, and the mixture tells you what the story is for.

The oldest account is Homer's, told in pieces. Zeus opens the Odyssey (1.29–43) complaining that Aegisthus took Agamemnon's wife and killed him despite a warning from Hermes. Nestor (Od. 3.254–312) describes the seduction: Clytemnestra at first resisted "for her mind was good", until Aegisthus removed the bard set to guard her. Proteus (Od. 4.512–537) supplies an ambush: a paid watchman, twenty men hidden, a feast, Agamemnon slaughtered "like an ox at the manger". Agamemnon's ghost (Od. 11.405–434) adds that he heard the cry of Cassandra, "whom treacherous Clytemnestra killed beside me", and that his wife would not close his eyes. In Homer, then, Aegisthus is the killer and Clytemnestra the accomplice who kills Cassandra; the venue is a banquet, not a bath; Iphigenia is never mentioned.

Between Homer and Aeschylus the woman moves to the centre. Stesichorus' Oresteia (fr. 210–219 PMG) survives in scraps: Clytemnestra's dream of a snake with a bloodied head, the nurse who saves the child, Apollo's gift of a bow to Orestes against the Erinyes. Pindar, Pythian 11.17–37, makes Clytemnestra kill both victims and asks what Homer never asked: was it Iphigenia's slaughter that stung her, or "nightly beddings" with a lover? Aeschylus' Agamemnon (458 BC) answers "both, and more": Clytemnestra alone kills, in the bath, netting her husband in a robe and striking three times (Ag. 1372–1398), then kills Cassandra, and claims the deed as justice for Iphigenia and as the work of the house's old alastor. Aegisthus arrives only afterwards to boast.

Where sources disagree. Who actually struck? Homer gives the blow to Aegisthus; Pindar and Aeschylus to Clytemnestra; Sophocles (El. 97–99) and Euripides (El. 86–87) have them act together. The weapon is also contested. Aeschylus' Agamemnon speaks of the sword (1528) but Clytemnestra calls for "a man-killing axe" at Choephori 889, and vase-painters show an axe; Fraenkel argued for a sword in the murder itself, Davies (1987) for an axe. Sophocles' Electra is explicit that it was an axe (El. 99). The question matters because the axe is a sacrificial tool, and the sacrificial colouring of the killing is central to Aeschylus.

Electra, the exile of Orestes, and the matricide

Homer knows no Electra. The Iliad names Agamemnon's daughters as Chrysothemis, Laodice and Iphianassa (9.144–145), and Aelian (Varia Historia 4.26) records that the lyric poet Xanthus renamed Laodice "Electra", the unmarried one. She is a sixth-century invention who grows: minor for Aeschylus, the whole play for Sophocles and Euripides. In the Odyssey Orestes simply returns "from Athens" in the eighth year and kills Aegisthus (3.306–310); Zenodotus read Phocis. The lyric poets supply the rescue: a nurse, Arsinoe in Pindar (Pyth. 11.17), Laodameia in Stesichorus, Cilissa in Aeschylus (Cho. 734–765), smuggles the boy to Strophius of Phocis, where he grows up with Pylades.

The matricide is already in Homer if you read 3.309–310 closely: Orestes holds a funeral feast for "his hateful mother and the coward Aegisthus", so she is dead the same day, though Homer will not say who killed her. The Hesiodic Catalogue of Women (fr. 23a Merkelbach–West) is blunt: Orestes "killed his mother". From Stesichorus onward Apollo commands the act, and Aeschylus makes the oracle's threats central (Cho. 269–296): if Orestes fails, his father's Erinyes will bring leprosy, madness and exclusion from every altar. Aeschylus gives the canonical scenes. Electra matches a lock of hair on the tomb to her own, then footprints, then a piece of weaving (Cho. 164–234). Orestes enters the palace as a Phocian stranger bearing news of his own death; Aegisthus dies first, then Clytemnestra, who bares her breast and pleads with the son she nursed (Cho. 896–898), while Pylades speaks his only three lines to recall Apollo's oracles. The moment the deed is done Orestes sees what the chorus cannot: women in black, wreathed in snakes (Cho. 1048–1062).

Where sources disagree. Where does the house of Atreus live? Homer has Agamemnon rule Mycenae; Aeschylus moves the action to Argos, probably because Athens had just made an alliance with Argos (and the Eumenides advertises it, 762–774); Stesichorus and Simonides, according to the scholia on Euripides' Orestes, placed the palace in Lacedaemon, and Sparta later claimed Orestes' bones (Herodotus 1.67–68). The mythic geography is political, not antiquarian.

The Erinyes, Delphi and the trial at Athens

What happens to a matricide? Stesichorus' answer was a bow from Apollo to drive the Erinyes off: self-help, not law. Aeschylus' Eumenides converts the pursuit into a legal process. Orestes is purified at Delphi with pig's blood (Eum. 280–283) and sent to embrace the ancient image of Athena at Athens, where the Erinyes catch him. Athena refuses to judge alone a case too great for one person and summons "the best of my citizens" to form a homicide court for all time (Eum. 470–489, 681–710). Apollo testifies for the defence; the Erinyes prosecute; the vote is equal and Orestes is acquitted (752–753). Athena then does what Homeric gods never do: she persuades. The Erinyes accept a cult beneath the hill and a share in the city's prosperity, becoming the Semnai Theai, escorted to their new home in torchlight.

The hill is the Areopagus, and the council that met there was Athens' homicide court. In 462/1 BC, three years before the play, Ephialtes stripped it of its wider political powers (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 25) and left it the trials for deliberate killing. Aeschylus gives this reduced body a divine charter and the loftiest praise, as a court "untouched by gain, reverent, swift to anger" (Eum. 704–706). Others told the aetiology differently. Euripides, Iphigenia among the Taurians 940–986, has Orestes tried at the Areopagus but also explains the Choes festival by his visit: Athenians would neither refuse hospitality nor share a table with a polluted man, so each drank from his own pitcher. Pausanias (1.28.5) and Demosthenes (23.66) record an older tradition that the hill was named from the trial of Ares for killing Halirrhothius. Apollodorus (Epitome 6.25) names Orestes' accusers variously as Tyndareus, Erigone (daughter of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra) or Perilaus; in Hyginus (Fabulae 122) Erigone hangs herself at the acquittal.

Where sources disagree. Two cruxes. First, Athena's vote. At Eum. 734–741 she says she will add her pebble to Orestes' side and that an equal count acquits. Either the human jurors split evenly and she breaks the tie (so her vote decides), or they are one short for Orestes and her pebble creates the tie that acquits (so the play founds the Athenian rule that an equal vote favours the defendant, attested at Antiphon 5.51 and Aristotle, Problems 29.13). Gagarin (1975), Hester (1981) and Sommerstein (1989) favour the tie-creating reading; the staging cannot be recovered. Second, politics. Dover (1957) and Dodds (1960) read the trilogy as a conservative plea for restraint after Ephialtes' reforms and his murder; Podlecki (1966) and Macleod (1982) see Aeschylus endorsing the democratic settlement while warning against civil strife. Athena's words cut both ways: "neither anarchy nor despotism" (Eum. 696). The disagreement is genuine and unlikely to be settled.

The later wanderings: Iphigenia, Hermione, Neoptolemus

Iphigenia among the Taurians

The Cypria, as summarised by Proclus, already had Artemis snatch Iphigenia from the altar at Aulis, substitute a deer, and make her immortal among the Taurians; Herodotus (4.103) reports that the Tauri of the Crimea sacrificed shipwrecked strangers to a goddess they called Iphigenia. Euripides' Iphigenia among the Taurians (c. 414 BC) ties these threads to Orestes. Acquitted at Athens but still hunted by Erinyes who refused the verdict (IT 970–978), he is sent by Apollo to steal the Tauric image of Artemis. He and Pylades are captured and brought to the priestess who sacrifices Greeks; she is Iphigenia, and the letter she asks Pylades to carry to Argos triggers the recognition. They escape Thoas by a feigned purification at sea, and Athena directs the image to Halae Araphenides in Attica, where a token drop of blood from a man's throat replaces human sacrifice, and installs Iphigenia as priestess at Brauron (IT 1446–1467). Both were real Attic cults. Sparta claimed the Tauric image as its own Artemis Orthia (Pausanias 3.16.7–11); Megara showed Iphigenia's tomb (Pausanias 1.43.1).

Where sources disagree. Did Euripides invent Orestes' voyage to the Taurians? No earlier source connects Orestes with the Crimea or with Iphigenia's return, and the Brauron and Halae aetiologies look like an Athenian appropriation of a Peloponnesian heroine. Most scholars treat the plot as Euripidean invention built on Herodotus' notice; a minority posit a lost epic or local Attic tradition. Uncertain, but the Athenian motive is clear: the cult of Iphigenia at Brauron predates the play, and the play explains why it is there.

Hermione and the death of Neoptolemus at Delphi

In the Odyssey (4.3–9) Menelaus gives Hermione to Achilles' son Neoptolemus, fulfilling a promise made at Troy. Tragedy inserts a prior claim: Tyndareus had betrothed Hermione to Orestes before the war. Pindar twice tells how Neoptolemus died at Delphi: in Nemean 7.34–47 in a quarrel over sacrificial meat; in Paean 6.117–120 at Apollo's own hand, in revenge for Priam. Euripides' Andromache (c. 425 BC) gives the murder to Orestes, who incites the Delphians and carries Hermione off (Andr. 993–1008, 1085–1165). Apollodorus (Epit. 6.14) names the killer Machaereus. Euripides' Orestes (408 BC) ends with Apollo arranging the marriage and announcing Neoptolemus' death as still to come (Or. 1653–1659). Thereafter Orestes rules Argos and, through Hermione, Sparta; his son Tisamenus leads the Achaeans against the returning Heraclids. He dies of a snakebite in Arcadia (Apollodorus, Epit. 6.28), and the Spartans later carry his giant bones from Tegea (Herodotus 1.67–68).

Aeschylus' Oresteia: from vendetta to law

The Oresteia (458 BC) is the only complete trilogy we possess, and its argument is cumulative. Agamemnon shows a world where justice is retaliation and every act of justice is also a crime: the war punishes Helen but costs Iphigenia; Clytemnestra's killing avenges her daughter and Thyestes' children, and is also adultery and husband-murder. Imagery of nets, hunting and sacrifice binds killer and killed, and Cassandra, who sees the whole chain from Thyestes' feast to her own death, cannot be believed. Choephori narrows the frame to the family and asks whether a son can be commanded to do a thing that damns him; he can, and the Erinyes come anyway. Eumenides widens it to the city. The movement is from house to polis, from blood-right to a jury, from the Erinyes as hunters to the Erinyes as guardians of civic fear. Athena's founding speech is the thesis: fear must not be expelled from the city, but housed in an institution rather than loose in the bloodline.

Aeschylus also makes gender carry the weight. The Erinyes argue that a wife's killing of a husband is not kin-murder; Apollo retorts that the mother is merely the nurse of the father's seed (Eum. 657–666); Athena, motherless, votes for the male. Zeitlin (1978) read the trilogy as "the dynamics of misogyny", founding law on the subordination of the female; others reply that the Erinyes end honoured, not defeated, and that the point is integration rather than suppression.

Sophocles' Electra

Sophocles' Electra (date unknown; usually placed 420–410) takes the middle play of Aeschylus and removes its frame. There is no Delphic prologue, no Erinys, no madness, no trial. The oracle Orestes consulted asked only how to kill, not whether (El. 32–37). The play is about Electra: grief as a way of life, isolation, a sister Chrysothemis who has made terms with the usurpers, two set-piece confrontations with Clytemnestra. The old tutor delivers a brilliant false report of Orestes' death in a chariot crash at the Pythian games (El. 680–763), so that Electra receives the urn she believes holds his ashes before he reveals himself (1098–1231). Clytemnestra is killed first, offstage, while Electra shouts "strike twice, if you have the strength" (1415), and the play ends with Aegisthus led in to die where Agamemnon fell. There is no divine epilogue.

Where sources disagree. Is this a clean revenge or an indictment? Jebb, Bowra and recently March (2001) read the play as Sophocles restoring the Homeric view that Orestes' act was simply right, the ending as triumph. Sheppard (1927), Kells (1973) and Winnington-Ingram (1980) point to the ominous silence about the Erinyes, Electra's near-derangement in the final scenes, and the ambiguous last words of the chorus, and read an irony Sophocles leaves unspoken. The relative dating of Sophocles' and Euripides' Electra plays is also unresolved: the once-standard 413 date for Euripides, based on the Dioscuri's reference to Sicily (El. 1347–1348), was undermined by Zuntz on metrical grounds, who argued for c. 420, so either poet may be answering the other.

Euripides: Electra, Orestes and the Iphigenia plays

Euripides lowers the social register and raises the moral temperature. In his Electra Aegisthus has married Electra to a poor but decent farmer so that her children cannot threaten him; a hut replaces the palace. The recognition parodies Aeschylus: Electra scoffs that hair, a footprint and weaving could prove anything (El. 524–544), and an old man identifies Orestes by a scar. Aegisthus is killed while hospitably sacrificing to the Nymphs; Clytemnestra is lured by the lie that Electra has given birth. The killers are instantly broken by remorse, and the Dioscuri deliver the judgment Aeschylus withheld: "she has justice, but you have not acted justly" (El. 1244); Phoebus is wise, "but his oracle was not". Orestes must go to Athens for trial, Electra marries Pylades, and the siblings part for ever.

Orestes (408 BC) picks up six days after the matricide. Orestes lies on a sickbed, intermittently mad; the Argive assembly is to vote on stoning the pair; Menelaus promises help and gives none. Tyndareus makes the play's most striking speech (Or. 491–525): Orestes should have prosecuted his mother and driven her out, because law exists precisely so that blood need not answer blood. Condemned, Orestes, Pylades and Electra plot to murder Helen and hold Hermione hostage, and are about to burn the palace when Apollo announces that Helen is a star and Orestes will be acquitted at Athens, marry Hermione and rule Argos. Iphigenia at Aulis (405 BC, posthumous) returns to the source of the chain, with Agamemnon writing and unwriting the letter that summons his daughter, and Iphigenia choosing to die for Greece.

Where sources disagree. Verrall and the rationalist school read Euripides' Apollo as a fraud exposed, and the epilogues as deliberately unconvincing. Later critics (Zuntz, Burnett, Kovacs) see tragic irony without atheism: the gods are real and their commands bind, which is exactly what makes them intolerable. The ending of the Orestes is the test case, and there is no consensus. The authenticity of the final scene of Iphigenia at Aulis is also doubted on linguistic grounds.

Athens' myth about its own courts

Athens had five homicide courts: the Areopagus for deliberate killing, the Palladion for involuntary killing, the Delphinion for killing admitted but claimed as lawful, Phreatto for exiles accused of a second killing, and the Prytaneion for killings by unknown hands or objects. Orestes attached himself to this system because his case fitted it: a killing admitted, commanded by a god, done to avenge a father, and therefore a dispute about justification. The Choes story shows a second use of the myth, turning a ritual oddity at the Anthesteria into a memory of hospitality to the polluted. The cult of the Semnai Theai in a cave at the foot of the Areopagus, where acquitted defendants sacrificed, sealed the identification of court and myth.

The payload is larger than any single court. Fifth-century Athens told itself that it was the city where other cities' crises were resolved: Oedipus dies at Colonus, the Heraclids find refuge, Orestes is judged. The Orestes story made that self-image specifically about law. Aeschylus claims that Athens invented trial by jury, with a goddess presiding, as the replacement for vendetta; the tie-vote rule, the jurors' oath and the Areopagus' primacy all receive divine warrant. Tyndareus' speech in Euripides shows the same assumption from the other side: an Argive elder lectures Orestes on a legal culture that is recognisably Athenian. Whether or not Aeschylus meant to defend Ephialtes, Athenians afterwards could not think about homicide law without seeing a matricide standing by Athena's statue. The myth did what foundation myths do: it made a recent, contested, human institution look older than the gods who sanctioned it.

Self-test

  1. In the Odyssey, who kills Agamemnon, who kills Cassandra, and where does the killing take place?
    Answer

    Aegisthus kills Agamemnon in an ambush at a feast (Od. 4.512–537, 11.405–434); Clytemnestra kills Cassandra beside him (11.421–423). There is no bath and no mention of Iphigenia.

  2. Which source first asks whether Iphigenia or adultery motivated Clytemnestra, and roughly when?
    Answer

    Pindar, Pythian 11.22–25, in the 470s or 450s BC, before Aeschylus' trilogy of 458.

  3. Why is Electra absent from Homer, and who named her?
    Answer

    Homer's daughters of Agamemnon are Chrysothemis, Laodice and Iphianassa (Il. 9.144–145). According to Aelian, the lyric poet Xanthus renamed Laodice "Electra" because she was unmarried.

  4. What three tokens does Aeschylus' Electra use to recognise Orestes, and how does Euripides treat them?
    Answer

    A lock of hair, footprints and a piece of weaving (Cho. 164–234). Euripides' Electra dismisses all three as absurd (El. 524–544); Orestes is recognised by a scar instead.

  5. What political event immediately preceded the Oresteia, and how does the Eumenides relate to it?
    Answer

    Ephialtes' reforms of 462/1 BC stripped the Areopagus of its political powers, leaving it homicide jurisdiction. Aeschylus gives this homicide court a divine foundation by Athena; whether he thereby endorses or regrets the reform is disputed.

  6. State the two readings of Athena's vote in the Eumenides.
    Answer

    Either the jurors tie and Athena's vote breaks it for Orestes, or the jurors are one short and her pebble creates the tie, which under the Athenian rule acquits (Antiphon 5.51). The second founds the tie-acquittal rule; the text (734–741) allows both.

  7. How does Euripides' Iphigenia among the Taurians account for the Attic cults at Halae and Brauron?
    Answer

    Athena orders Orestes to install the stolen Tauric image of Artemis at Halae Araphenides, with a token blood-letting replacing human sacrifice, and makes Iphigenia priestess at Brauron (IT 1446–1467).

  8. Give two incompatible versions of how Neoptolemus died at Delphi.
    Answer

    Pindar, Nemean 7: killed in a quarrel over sacrificial meat; Paean 6: killed by Apollo avenging Priam; Euripides, Andromache: murdered by Delphians incited by Orestes; Apollodorus names the killer Machaereus.

  9. What structural change does Sophocles make to the order of the killings, and what is its effect?
    Answer

    Clytemnestra is killed first, Aegisthus last, so the play ends not with the Erinyes but with Aegisthus led in to die where Agamemnon died, and no divine epilogue follows. Whether this is triumph or unspoken irony is disputed.

  10. What is Tyndareus' argument in Euripides' Orestes, and why does it matter for the myth's Athenian meaning?
    Answer

    Orestes should have used the law to prosecute and exile his mother instead of killing her, since law exists to end the chain of blood for blood (Or. 491–525). It shows the Athenian assumption that legal process, not vendetta, is the default even in the heroic age.

Carry forward

  1. The Orestes story is the Greek test case for justified killing: the same act is both commanded and polluting, and every version from Homer onward shifts blame among Aegisthus, Clytemnestra, Apollo and Orestes to make a different point. Watch for the same pattern of "justice that is also crime" in the Theban and Heraclid material.
  2. Aeschylus turns a vendetta into a court case and uses the trilogy to charter the Areopagus; Athens thereafter read its homicide courts, its Anthesteria rituals and its asylum-city self-image through this myth. Expect the technique of mythic aetiology for recent institutions to recur in Athenian tragedy and local history.
  3. Sophocles and Euripides work by subtraction and relocation: removing the divine frame (Sophocles), or lowering the social setting and letting a god condemn his own oracle (Euripides). The three Electras are the clearest demonstration in surviving literature of how tragedians argued with one another through the same plot.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the aftermath of Troy in the house of Atreus. Cover: the murder of Agamemnon and Cassandra by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (and the older Homeric version where Aegisthus is the main killer); Electra and the exile of Orestes; the matricide; the pursuit by the Erinyes; the trial at Athens and the founding of the Areopagus; Iphigenia among the Taurians; Orestes and Hermione, the death of Neoptolemus at Delphi. Then compare the three tragic treatments in detail: Aeschylus' Oresteia as a trilogy about the move from vendetta to law; Sophocles' Electra; Euripides' Electra, Orestes and Iphigenia plays. Explain what each playwright changes and why, and how this story became Athens' myth about its own legal system. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 5 · The Archaic age, 800 to 480 BC · 5.1 · 2,900 words

The eighth-century renaissance

What "renaissance" means hereThe alphabet: borrowing and earliest evidenceEuboeans abroad: Al Mina and PithekoussaiHomer fixed in writing, and the Peisistratid questionHesiod: a person with a biographyPanhellenic sanctuariesThe first temples and the Geometric styleHero cult at Mycenaean tombsThe population surgeSelf-testCarry forward

What "renaissance" means here

The label comes from a 1981 Athens symposium published as The Greek Renaissance of the Eighth Century B.C. (ed. Robin Hägg, 1983), and Anthony Snodgrass gave it analytical shape in Archaic Greece (1980) as a "structural revolution". The claim is not that Greece recovered what Mycenae had lost; the eighth century produced things the palaces never had: an alphabet with vowels, the polis, Panhellenic festivals, monumental temples built by communities rather than kings, written poetry and a conscious relationship with a heroic past. Almost every strand below has its first secure archaeological horizon between roughly 800 and 700 BC, and almost every strand is also contested in its date or cause. Keep the two facts together.

The alphabet: borrowing and earliest evidence

Herodotus 5.58 says the Phoenicians who came with Cadmus brought letters to Boeotia and that the Ionians still called them phoinikeia grammata. The letter names (alpha, beta, gamma) are meaningless in Greek and transparent in Semitic (aleph "ox", beth "house"), the letter order is Phoenician, and the earliest Greek letter-forms match Phoenician forms of the ninth and early eighth centuries. The Greek contribution was to reassign the Phoenician consonant signs the language did not need (aleph, he, yod, ayin, waw) to vowels, making the script fully phonetic for the first time anywhere.

The earliest inscriptions cluster around 770–720 BC and are already literary in ambition:

  • The Dipylon oinochoe (Athens, c. 740–730), a wine jug scratched with a hexameter and a garbled second line: a prize for "whoever of all the dancers now dances most nimbly". It uses the Attic local script.
  • Nestor's cup (Pithekoussai, Ischia, c. 740–720), a Rhodian kotyle from a child's cremation, inscribed in Euboean letters with one iambic-like line and two hexameters:
    Nestor's cup I am, good to drink from.
    The joke, that whoever drinks will be seized by desire for Aphrodite, presupposes an audience that knows an epic Nestor with a famous cup (compare Iliad 11.632–637).
  • Scraps from Lefkandi, Eretria, Methone and the Osteria dell'Osa jar in Latium (c. 775, five letters, reading disputed) push the date of first use back towards 800.

Within two generations the script had split into local varieties (Kirchhoff's "red", "blue" and "green" groups), which implies either very rapid diffusion from one point or several near-simultaneous adaptations.

Where sources disagree. Joseph Naveh (1973) argued from letter-forms that the borrowing happened c. 1100 and that three centuries of writing on perishable material are simply lost; most epigraphists (Jeffery, Johnston) hold to c. 800 or a little before, because the alphabet shows no trace of the changes Phoenician script underwent between 1100 and 800. The place is equally open: Euboea, Cyprus, Crete, Rhodes and the Syrian coast all have advocates. Barry Powell (Homer and the Origin of the Greek Alphabet, 1991) proposed that one Euboean adapter devised the vowels specifically to record hexameter poetry; the earliest texts being verse fits his thesis, but most scholars think commercial and ownership uses simply do not survive.

Euboeans abroad: Al Mina and Pithekoussai

Euboea, with Lefkandi (the rich Toumba "heroön" burial of c. 950 BC), Eretria and Chalcis, was the Greek region least affected by the post-palatial collapse and the first to re-enter long-distance exchange. Euboean pendent-semicircle skyphoi turn up on Cyprus, at Tyre and along the Levantine coast from the ninth century.

Al Mina, at the mouth of the Orontes in north Syria, was excavated by Leonard Woolley in 1936–37. Its lowest levels (c. 800–700) contain large quantities of Euboean and Cycladic pottery alongside Cypriot and Levantine wares. John Boardman treated it as a Greek trading station, perhaps the point where Greeks learned the alphabet and the Near Eastern motifs that flood into Orientalising art. Others (Graham, Waldbaum, Luke) read it as a native port that Greek traders visited and where some Greek pottery was consumed by locals; there are no Greek burials, no Greek cult and no Greek graffiti securely of that date.

Pithekoussai on Ischia is different: an actual settlement. Strabo 5.4.9 says Eretrians and Chalcidians founded it and prospered from the fertility of the soil and from gold-working until internal quarrels and volcanic activity drove them out; Livy 8.22.5–6 says the Chalcidians moved from Pithecusae to Cumae on the mainland. Giorgio Buchner's excavations from 1952 revealed the San Montano cemetery (over a thousand graves), the Mazzola metalworking quarter with iron slag and crucibles, and imports from Corinth, Rhodes, Phoenicia, Egypt and Etruria. Nestor's cup came from grave 168. A Late Geometric krater from the site carries the earliest Greek shipwreck scene. Foundation c. 770 makes it the oldest Greek settlement in the west, and its mixed material culture (Semitic graffiti, Levantine amphorae) suggests Phoenicians lived alongside Greeks.

Where sources disagree. Was Pithekoussai a colony (apoikia) or a trading post (emporion)? Buchner and Ridgway stressed its metal trade with Etruria; Strabo's emphasis on agriculture, the size of the cemetery and the family burials point to a permanent community. The Euboean primacy itself is sometimes questioned: the Lelantine War tradition (Thucydides 1.15.3; Herodotus 5.99) has Chalcis and Eretria destroy each other's strength around 700, which would explain why Corinth, not Euboea, dominates the seventh century.

Homer fixed in writing, and the Peisistratid question

The Iliad and Odyssey are oral-formulaic in technique (Parry, Lord) but reached us as written texts. Three questions follow: when, where, and how much Athens had to do with it.

Ancient dating was guesswork. Herodotus 2.53 puts Homer and Hesiod "four hundred years before my time", about 850; the Contest of Homer and Hesiod makes them contemporaries and rivals. Modern estimates diverge. Richard Janko (Homer, Hesiod and the Hymns, 1982) used the statistical frequency of archaic linguistic features to place the Iliad c. 750–725 and the Odyssey a generation later; Martin West (The Making of the Iliad, 2011) argued for a poet working c. 680–640 who composed with writing over years. Gregory Nagy's evolutionary model denies any single fixing: the poems crystallised gradually through Panhellenic performance, reaching a stable text only in the Hellenistic period.

The Athenian strand rests on late sources. Cicero, De oratore 3.137, says Peisistratus "is said to have first arranged the books of Homer, previously confused, as we now have them"; Pausanias 7.26.13 and Aelian, Varia Historia 13.14 agree. The pseudo-Platonic Hipparchus 228b credits Peisistratus' son Hipparchus with bringing the poems to Athens and compelling the rhapsodes at the Panathenaia to perform them in sequence; Diogenes Laertius 1.57 attributes the same relay rule to Solon. Josephus, Against Apion 1.12, claims Homer left nothing in writing and that the songs were later stitched together from memory. A scholiast on Pindar, Nemean 2.1, says Cynaethus of Chios, of the Homeridae, interpolated many verses and first recited Homer at Syracuse in 504/501.

Where sources disagree. Friedrich Wolf (1795) took the Peisistratid recension as the moment the text was created; Minna Skafte Jensen (1980) revived a strong version, dating the written poems to sixth-century Athens. Most Homerists now accept a weaker form: the texts existed earlier in Ionia (the dialect is Ionic, the Atticisms thin and superficial), but Athens was the "Panathenaic bottleneck" through which the vulgate passed, which is why nearly all medieval manuscripts descend from an Attic exemplar. Whether an eighth-century poet wrote, dictated, or never touched writing remains uncertain, and the Nestor's cup joke is the only external evidence that epic Nestor was known to Greeks in the 720s.

Hesiod: a person with a biography

Hesiod is the first Greek who tells us his name, his father's history and his grievances. In Works and Days 633–640 his father left Aeolian Cyme in Asia Minor fleeing poverty and settled at Ascra under Helicon in Boeotia, "bad in winter, hard in summer, never good". In Theogony 22–34 the Muses met him pasturing lambs on Helicon and gave him a laurel staff. In Works and Days 650–662 he crossed to Chalcis for the funeral games of Amphidamas and won a tripod with a song; Plutarch, Moralia 153f, says Amphidamas died fighting Eretria, which would tie Hesiod to the Lelantine War c. 700. The poem is addressed to his brother Perses, who bribed "gift-devouring kings" to win more than his share of their inheritance (27–41, 38–39, 263–264).

The world of Works and Days is a village of independent farmers under local basileis who judge in the agora. The farm has oxen, a few slaves (dmoes), a hired man and woman taken on seasonally, a ploughman ideally forty years old (441). Time is read from the stars: plough when the Pleiades set (383–384), reap when they rise; sail only in the fifty days after the solstice (663–694). Hesiod recommends one son to keep the estate whole (376–380), a glimpse of land pressure. His theology is moral: Zeus watches the crooked judgement, and the just city flourishes while the unjust starves (225–247). The five races of men (109–201) place the heroes who fought at Thebes and Troy as a separate race before our iron age.

Where sources disagree. West (1966) dated the Theogony c. 730–700 and made Hesiod older than Homer; Janko's linguistic statistics put both Hesiodic poems after the Odyssey, c. 700–650. Attempts to date the star calendar astronomically give results spread over two centuries. Some (Lamberton, Nagy) treat "Hesiod" as a traditional persona like "Homer"; the specificity of Ascra, Perses and Amphidamas persuades most that a real poet stands behind at least Works and Days. Pausanias 9.31.4 reports that the Boeotians of Helicon accepted only Works and Days as genuine.

Panhellenic sanctuaries

Catherine Morgan (Athletes and Oracles, 1990) showed that Olympia and Delphi grew from local cult places into inter-regional meeting grounds during the eighth century, with bronze dedications (tripods, figurines) multiplying sharply after c. 800. François de Polignac (1984) argued that extra-urban sanctuaries defined the territory of emerging poleis; the Panhellenic ones did the same for the Greek world as a whole.

The 776 date comes from the victor list compiled by Hippias of Elis around 400 BC, naming Coroebus of Elis as first stadion winner (preserved via Eusebius' Chronicle). Plutarch, Numa 1.4, already doubted its reliability. Pausanias 5.8.5 records a tradition that the games had lapsed and were refounded by Iphitus of Elis with Lycurgus of Sparta, whose names stood on a bronze discus at Olympia (5.20.1; Plutarch, Lycurgus 1.1, citing Aristotle).

Why festivals mattered: Greeks had no shared state, king or capital, and Iliad 2.684 still uses "Hellenes" for Achilles' Thessalians only (Thucydides 1.3 noticed this). What they had was shared gods and shared competition. Herodotus 8.144 later defines Greekness as common blood, language, "shrines of the gods and sacrifices", and customs; the eighth century is when the third item acquired places. The sacred truce (ekecheiria) let men from warring cities meet; the games ranked them by a common standard; the oracle gave colonists (Thera to Cyrene, Herodotus 4.150–159) a neutral authority. Hesiod's Panhellenes (Works and Days 528) is the first appearance of the word.

Where sources disagree. Alfred Mallwitz (1988) argued from the stratigraphy of the stadium and wells that organised games cannot predate c. 700, making 776 a back-calculation. Paul Christesen (Olympic Victor Lists, 2007) treats Hippias' early entries as reconstruction. Morgan accepts that cult activity intensified around 776 even if the formal festival is later. The Olympia and Delphi evidence is good; Isthmia and Nemea are eighth-century only in the loosest sense.

The first temples and the Geometric style

Mycenaean religion had no freestanding temple. The eighth century invented the type: a long hall housing a cult image, oriented to an altar outside, built by a community. The earliest are mudbrick on stone socles with wooden posts, not stone buildings; the all-stone Doric temple belongs to the seventh century (Isthmia, c. 690–650; Corinth's old temple; Thermon). Key eighth-century examples:

  • Samos, Heraion, Hekatompedon I (c. 800): a hundred-foot hall with a central row of posts; Hekatompedon II (c. 670) added the first peristyle.
  • Eretria, Apollo Daphnephoros: an apsidal hut of c. 800 (the "Daphnephoreion"), then a hekatompedon c. 750.
  • Dreros, Crete (c. 750–700): small temple with a central hearth and three hammered bronze statuettes of Apollo, Leto and Artemis, the earliest surviving Greek cult images.
  • Terracotta temple models from Perachora and the Argive Heraion (c. 750–700) show steep thatched or tiled roofs over apsidal and rectangular plans.

The painted pottery of the period gives it its name. After Protogeometric (c. 1050–900), Attic workshops built decoration from compass-drawn circles, meanders and zigzags; around 760 the Dipylon Master reintroduced the human figure on monumental funerary vases. The Dipylon amphora (Athens NM 804) shows the prothesis, the laying-out of the dead woman, with mourners in silhouette with triangular torsos. Late Geometric kraters add chariot processions, sea battles and the occasional mythical candidate (the conjoined "Siamese twins" read as the Aktorione-Molione of Iliad 11.709). Nicolas Coldstream's Geometric Greece (1977) remains the handbook; Snodgrass (Homer and the Artists, 1998) argued that very few Geometric scenes illustrate Homer specifically, and most are generic heroic imagery.

Hero cult at Mycenaean tombs

From about 750 BC Greeks began leaving offerings at Bronze Age tombs that had stood unvisited for four centuries: the tholos at Menidi in Attica, chamber tombs at Mycenae and Prosymna in the Argolid, tholoi in Messenia, the Thorikos tombs. The deposits are Late Geometric cups, kraters and figurines, often broken deliberately. At about the same time cults of named heroes appear with built shrines: Agamemnon at Mycenae, Menelaus and Helen at Therapne near Sparta (both c. 700), Pelops at Olympia, Odysseus at Polis Bay on Ithaca, and the warrior burials at Eretria's West Gate (c. 720–680) over which a triangular heroön was later raised.

The phenomenon has three principal explanations.

  1. Coldstream (JHS 96, 1976) argued that the newly circulating Homeric epics taught Greeks that the great tombs belonged to heroes, and veneration followed. Hector's own tomb is imagined as a landmark (Iliad 7.86–91).
  2. Snodgrass (1982, 1988) reversed the causation: a growing population of farmers moving onto new land encountered old tombs and claimed the dead as ancestors, legitimating possession. The epics reflect the same interest rather than creating it.
  3. Carla Antonaccio (An Archaeology of Ancestors, 1995) separated "tomb cult" (episodic, anonymous, tied to local groups) from "hero cult" proper (named figures, continuous, often polis-sponsored) and denied that the former needs epic at all. James Whitley (JHS 108, 1988) noted the regional contrast: dispersed rural cults in Attica, state-focused ones in the Argolid.

For myth the implications are large. Hesiod's scheme makes the heroes a distinct race, "demigods", who lived before us (Works and Days 156–173). Homer calls them "men of former times" and gives them strength no living man has. The eighth century is when Greeks decided that the ruins around them belonged to that race and that its members could still be reached by sacrifice: myth became local history, anchored to visible places, and cities began to compete for ownership of particular heroes.

Where sources disagree. The chronological hinge is whether offerings precede or follow the likely diffusion of epic. If Janko's early Homer is right, Coldstream's sequence works; if West's seventh-century Homer is right, tomb cult comes first and epic cannot be its cause. The Lefkandi Toumba burial (c. 950) with its later tumulus shows that honouring extraordinary dead predates both.

The population surge

Snodgrass (Archaic Greece, 1980) counted datable Attic graves and found a roughly sevenfold rise across the eighth century, implying growth rates near 4 per cent a year; he proposed a demographic explosion driving colonisation, land hunger, hero cult and the polis itself. The colonising dates support a surge in the second half of the century: Cumae c. 750, Naxos 734, Syracuse 733, Leontini and Catane 729, Megara Hyblaea 728, Sybaris c. 720, Taras 706 (Thucydides 6.3–5 for Sicily). Odyssey 9.116–141, the empty island off the Cyclopes with soil that "would bear all things in season", reads like a colonist's survey. Hesiod's advice to raise one son and Theran tradition of drought-driven emigration (Herodotus 4.151) point the same way.

Where sources disagree. Ian Morris (Burial and Ancient Society, 1987) argued that the grave count measures burial visibility, not population: before c. 750 only an elite received formal burial, and afterwards the practice extended to all adults, so the "explosion" is partly social. John Camp (1979) read a cluster of abandoned Agora wells around 700 as a drought and famine, suggesting the surge overshot. Settlement surveys in the Argolid, Boeotia and Euboea nonetheless show real increases in site numbers. The consensus is growth, sustained and significant, but at rates far below Snodgrass's figure; 1 per cent a year compounded over a century would still double the population and strain a village economy of the kind Hesiod describes.

Self-test

  1. What did Greek adapters do with Phoenician signs such as aleph and he, and why did it matter?
    Answer

    They reassigned consonant signs Greek did not need to write vowels, making the first fully phonetic alphabet; Phoenician had written consonants only.

  2. Where was Nestor's cup found, what script is it in, and what does its joke presuppose?
    Answer

    Grave 168 at Pithekoussai on Ischia, c. 740–720, in Euboean letters; it presupposes an audience familiar with an epic Nestor and his famous cup.

  3. Which ancient author says Eretrians and Chalcidians founded Pithekoussai, and what is the main modern dispute about Al Mina?
    Answer

    Strabo 5.4.9. The dispute is whether Al Mina was a Greek trading post (Boardman) or a Levantine port that merely consumed Greek pottery.

  4. Name the Latin source for the Peisistratid recension and state the weak form of the hypothesis most scholars now accept.
    Answer

    Cicero, De oratore 3.137. Weak form: the poems existed earlier in Ionia but passed through sixth-century Athenian Panathenaic performance, which shaped the surviving vulgate.

  5. Give two biographical facts Hesiod states about himself and the passages that contain them.
    Answer

    His father migrated from Aeolian Cyme to Ascra (Works and Days 633–640); he won a tripod at the funeral games of Amphidamas at Chalcis (650–662). Also the Muses on Helicon (Theogony 22–34) and the dispute with Perses (27–41).

  6. Where does the 776 date come from, and who doubted it in antiquity and in modern scholarship?
    Answer

    Hippias of Elis's victor list, naming Coroebus; Plutarch (Numa 1.4) doubted it, as do Mallwitz (games not before c. 700) and Christesen.

  7. According to Herodotus 8.144, what four things made someone Greek?
    Answer

    Common blood, common language, shared shrines and sacrifices, and shared customs.

  8. Were the first Greek temples built of stone? Give one eighth-century example and its construction.
    Answer

    No; they were mudbrick on stone socles with wooden posts. Samos Hekatompedon I (c. 800) or the Eretria hekatompedon (c. 750). Stone Doric temples begin in the seventh century at Isthmia.

  9. Contrast Coldstream's and Snodgrass's explanations of eighth-century offerings at Mycenaean tombs.
    Answer

    Coldstream: Homeric epic inspired veneration of tombs as heroic. Snodgrass: expanding farming populations claimed old tombs as ancestral to legitimate land; epic reflects the same interest rather than causing it.

  10. What was Ian Morris's objection to Snodgrass's sevenfold population increase?
    Answer

    Grave counts track who received formal burial, not how many people lived; after c. 750 burial extended from an elite to all adults, so much of the rise is a change in practice.

Carry forward

  1. The eighth century created, rather than restored: alphabet with vowels, polis, temple, Panhellenic festival and written epic all have their first horizon here, and Euboea is the hinge between the Near East and the West.
  2. The Homeric and Hesiodic texts are datable only within a window of roughly 750–650, and Athens shaped their transmission in the sixth century; every later module that cites Homer rests on this uncertainty.
  3. Hero cult at Bronze Age tombs is the moment myth became local history: Greeks fixed the heroic age as a separate race, attached it to visible places, and cities began to own heroes. That link between landscape, cult and story governs everything from Sparta's Menelaion to Athenian tragedy.

Give me an in-depth report on the Greek "renaissance" of the eighth century BC. Cover: the adoption of the Phoenician alphabet and its earliest evidence (Nestor's cup, the Dipylon jug); the Euboeans, Al Mina and Pithekoussai; the fixing of the Homeric poems in writing and the Peisistratid recension question; Hesiod as a datable person and the world of Works and Days; the rise of the Panhellenic sanctuaries (Olympia and the 776 date, Delphi, Delos, Isthmia, Nemea) and why shared festivals mattered to a people with no shared state; the first stone temples and the Geometric style; hero cult at Mycenaean tombs beginning in this century and what it means for myth; and the population surge.
