GREECE · UNIT 5 · The Archaic age, 800 to 480 BC · 5.2 · 2,711 words

The polis and colonisation

What a polis wasAristotle's definitionOikos, phratry, tribe and demeCitizens, metics and slaves in outlineHow a colony was foundedThe main waves and sitesWhy they wentColonisation and Greek identitySelf-testCarry forward

What a polis was

The word polis is usually translated "city-state", and the translation misleads in both halves. A polis was not primarily a built-up place and not quite a state. It was a community of citizens (politai) who together owned a territory (chora) with a settlement at its centre, governed themselves through shared laws and offices, and worshipped shared gods. Thucydides puts it in the mouth of Nicias to the beaten Athenians in Sicily:

men are the city, not walls or empty ships.
(Thucydides 7.77.7).

The physical polis nonetheless had recognisable parts. The acropolis, the fortified height, was the oldest element and often the Bronze Age core; in the Archaic period it generally shed its palace function and became the seat of the principal cult, as at Athens. The agora, the open gathering place, was the real innovation: a space that belonged to no one household and where the assembly met, justice was done and trade happened. Homer already knows it. The Phaeacian city in the Odyssey has walls, harbours, temples and an agora paved with set stones (Homer, Odyssey 6.262–272), and the shield of Achilles shows elders judging a blood-price case in the agora (Iliad 18.497–508).

Laws were the third element. The earliest surviving polis law is from Dreros in Crete, inscribed around 650–600 BC, limiting the chief magistrate (kosmos) to one term in ten years and binding the whole citizen body to the rule. Named lawgivers (Zaleucus of Locri, Charondas of Catana, Draco and Solon) mark the period, and two of the earliest are from western colonies. Cults completed the structure: a polis had a tutelary deity, civic festivals, and a sacred calendar, and the great stone temples that begin around 700 (Isthmia, Samos, Corinth) are the first monumental architecture of the Greek world since the Bronze Age.

A polis differed from a mere city in that the people remained the polis wherever they were. When the Phocaeans sailed away from Persian rule in 545 the polis went with them (Herodotus 1.164–165); when the Athenians evacuated Attica in 480 the polis was on the ships at Salamis. A city is a place; a polis is a membership. Most were tiny: Mogens Hansen's Copenhagen Polis Centre catalogued 1,035 poleis, most with territories under 100 square kilometres.

Where sources disagree. When did the polis emerge? Ehrenberg argued for a sudden crystallisation around 800–700; Snodgrass tied it to the eighth-century population surge, Morris to a change in who received formal burial (the argument is in module 5.1). The current consensus is a long process, 900–600, with no single birth moment.

Aristotle's definition

Aristotle's Politics opens by deriving the polis genetically. Man and woman form the household (oikos); households form the village (kome); villages form the polis, which is the first community that is self-sufficient (autarkes) and which exists "for the sake of living well" (Politics 1252b27–1253a1). Hence the famous dictum that man is by nature a politikon zoon, a polis-dwelling animal, and that whoever lives outside a polis is either a beast or a god (1253a2–29). In Book 3 he defines the polis by the citizen rather than the territory: a citizen is one who shares in judgement and office (1275a22–23), and the polis is a sufficient multitude of such citizens (1275b20–21). The polis is not its walls: one could wall in the Peloponnese without making it a polis (1276a26–30).

Two cautions. Aristotle writes in the 330s, and his definition is normative and Athens-shaped. His household-village-polis sequence is logical, not historical, though it maps well onto the synoecism of villages archaeologists see in the 8th century.

Oikos, phratry, tribe and deme

Beneath the polis sat older units. The oikos was the household: the kin group, its land, livestock, dependants and slaves, under a male head. Hesiod's advice to acquire a house, a woman and a plough-ox first (Works and Days 405) shows the oikos as the unit of survival.

The phratry ("brotherhood") was a group of oikoi claiming common descent and sharing cults, especially of Zeus Phratrios and Athena Phratria. In Athens phratry membership was the practical proof of legitimate birth and hence citizenship. Homer's Nestor advises Agamemnon to marshal the army by tribes and phratries (Iliad 2.362–363), the earliest literary attestation of both.

The tribe (phyle) was the largest kin unit. Ionian poleis, Athens included, had four (Geleontes, Hopletes, Argadeis, Aigikoreis); Dorian poleis had three (Hylleis, Dymanes, Pamphyloi), and Tyrtaeus names them fighting as units at Sparta (Tyrtaeus fr. 19 West).

The deme was a village or ward, a territorial not a kin unit. Its moment came in 508/7, when Cleisthenes reorganised Athens into ten new tribes built from 139 demes drawn from three regions, deliberately cutting across the old kin loyalties (Herodotus 5.66–69; Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 21). The reform lies just after our period but is where the process was heading: the polis overriding the clan.

Where sources disagree. The older view (Fustel de Coulanges, and still in many textbooks) treated phratry and tribe as primordial clan structures the polis gradually dissolved. Denis Roussel (1976) and Félix Bourriot argued the reverse: the genos and phratry as we see them are products of the polis, formalised to regulate citizenship, not survivals from a tribal past.

Citizens, metics and slaves in outline

Citizenship in the Archaic polis normally required descent from a citizen father, legitimate birth and, often, a property or hoplite qualification for full participation. Solon in 594/3 graded Athenians into four property classes with different access to office (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 7). Women transmitted citizen status but held no political rights.

Resident foreigners, metoikoi, were a product of the polis becoming attractive. Metics paid a tax, needed a citizen sponsor, could not own land, and served in the army. Slavery was ubiquitous and took two forms. Chattel slaves, bought and foreign, concentrated in households and workshops; Theopompus claimed Chios was the first Greek polis to buy barbarian slaves (FGrH 115 F122). Dependent populations such as the Spartan helots and Thessalian penestai were conquered peoples bound to the land. Solon's abolition of debt-bondage for Athenians (Constitution of the Athenians 6) marks the moment when the line between citizen and slave hardened: a citizen could no longer become one.

How a colony was founded

The Greek term was apoikia, "a home away", and the standard mechanics, as reconstructed from Herodotus, Thucydides and inscriptions, ran as follows. The mother-city (metropolis) decided, or a faction within it was pushed, to send out settlers. An oikistes (founder) was appointed, almost always an aristocrat, with near-absolute authority over the voyage and the first settlement; he laid out the site, divided the land into lots (kleroi), founded the cults, and on death was buried in the agora and worshipped as a hero.

Delphi's role was to sanction. Herodotus's account of Cyrene has the Theraeans consult Apollo repeatedly, ignore the first instruction, suffer seven years of drought, and finally comply (Herodotus 4.150–159). The oracle's authorisation gave the venture legitimacy and the oikist his mandate. Whether Delphi directed settlement or ratified choices already made is unresolvable; many foundation oracles were composed after the fact. Thucydides records that at Naxos in Sicily, the first Greek colony there, the settlers raised an altar to Apollo Archegetes ("Founder-Leader") on which all later sacred envoys from Sicily sacrificed before sailing to Greece (Thucydides 6.3.1).

Mother-city ties were real but loose. The colony took fire from the metropolis's hearth, its cults and calendar, its dialect and alphabet, and often its constitution. It was nonetheless an independent polis from day one. The 4th-century Cyrene foundation decree (SEG 9.3, Meiggs and Lewis 5), which claims to transcribe the original 7th-century Theran oath, specifies that one son per household was to be sent on pain of death, that settlers would retain Theran citizenship if the venture failed within five years, and curses those who broke the agreement. Corinth was unusual in trying to hold its colonies close (Thucydides 1.24–55).

Where sources disagree. Robin Osborne (1998) attacked the whole state-sponsored model as a 5th-century retrojection: the 8th-century ventures, he argued, were private, piecemeal and mixed, and only later did poleis invent oikists and foundation dates to own them. Malkin and others accept a messier reality but note that oikist cults are archaeologically early. Thucydides' Sicilian dates (6.3–5), probably from Antiochus of Syracuse, remain the backbone of the chronology, and the pottery broadly supports them.

The main waves and sites

The first move was Euboean. Chalcis and Eretria, trading at Al Mina in Syria from around 800, planted Pithecusae on Ischia in the Bay of Naples by about 770, a mixed emporium with metalworking and Phoenician and Etruscan finds. Cumae on the mainland opposite followed around 750 (Strabo 5.4.4; Livy 8.22.5–6), the first true Greek polis in Italy, and the one from which the Etruscans and ultimately the Romans took their alphabet.

Sicily and Italy. From 734 the Chalcidians and Corinthians divided eastern Sicily: Naxos, Leontini and Catana to Chalcis, Syracuse to Corinth (Thucydides 6.3–4). Syracuse became the greatest Greek city of the west and reduced the native Sicels to a serf class, the Kyllyrioi. On the Italian toe and instep, Achaean settlers from the northern Peloponnese founded Sybaris and Croton, both on rich coastal plains; Sybaris became a byword for luxury before Croton destroyed it in 510 (Herodotus 5.44–45). Taras (Tarentum) was Sparta's only colony, founded, the tradition says, by the Partheniai, sons born of irregular unions during the First Messenian War and denied full citizenship (Strabo 6.3.2, citing Antiochus and Ephorus). The story is a stasis story, and that is its point.

The Black Sea. Megara and Miletus led here. Megara founded Chalcedon around 685 and Byzantium opposite around 660; Herodotus has Megabazus call the Chalcedonians blind for missing the better site (Herodotus 4.144). Pliny credits Miletus with ninety Black Sea colonies (Natural History 5.112), an exaggeration, but Sinope, Olbia at the Bug-Dnieper mouth and Panticapaeum in the Crimea were real, trading grain, fish, slaves and metals for wine, oil and pottery. Herodotus describes the Scythian king Scyles, who kept a Greek house at Olbia and was killed for it (Herodotus 4.78–80).

Cyrene. Herodotus gives Theran and Cyrenaean versions (4.150–158): drought, the stammering oikist Battus, a failed first settlement on the island of Platea, then the mainland. Cyrene was ruled by Battiad kings for eight generations and grew rich on horses, grain and silphium.

Massalia. The Phocaeans founded Marseille around 600, beating the Carthaginians at sea to do it (Thucydides 1.13.6). Justin preserves the legend of the Gallic princess Gyptis choosing the Greek Protis as husband (Justin 43.3.8–12), a myth of consensual settlement. Massalia pushed wine, writing and coinage up the Rhône and founded Emporion in Spain.

Naucratis. This was not a colony but an emporion, a licensed trading port in the Nile Delta. Herodotus says Amasis (570–526) granted it to the Greeks, with a shared sanctuary, the Hellenion, funded by nine Ionian, Dorian and Aeolian cities, plus separate temples of Aegina, Samos and Miletus (Herodotus 2.178–179). Archaeology shows Greek presence from about 620, under Psammetichus I, so Amasis probably regularised what already existed.

Why they went

Three motives are given by the sources and all three were usually in play. The first was land. Stenochoria, "narrowness of land", is the term Greeks used, and the Cyrene story opens with drought and the Taras story with men who had none. Plato lists famine, overpopulation and civil strife as the standard causes of colonisation (Laws 708b, 740e). Archilochus, a settler on Thasos, complained that the island stood "like the backbone of an ass, crowned with wild wood" (Archilochus fr. 21 West), the voice of a man who went for land and found rock.

The second was trade. Al Mina and Pithecusae were emporia before they were poleis, placed for metals rather than fields; Massalia, Naucratis and the Black Sea sites were commercial in placement if not always in motive. The third was stasis, internal conflict. The Partheniai of Taras and the Phocaeans fleeing Persia are explicit cases; Theognis of Megara is full of the bitterness of displaced aristocrats. A colony exported the losers of a civil quarrel.

Where sources disagree. Older scholarship split colonies into "agrarian" and "commercial" types; Graham's Colony and Mother City (1964) stressed land hunger, Boardman's The Greeks Overseas the commercial side. The present view is that the dichotomy is false: land was the goal, but sites were chosen by people who already knew the sea lanes. Population pressure is easier to assert than to prove.

Colonisation and Greek identity

In 750 there was no word for "Greek" in the sense Herodotus would later use. Homer speaks of Achaeans, Argives and Danaans; Hellenes in the Iliad are one small people in Thessaly (Iliad 2.684). By 500 the term covered everyone from Massalia to the Crimea, and the catalyst was distance. Confronted with Sicels, Scythians and Etruscans, settlers discovered what they shared with the Megarian in the next bay: language, gods, the agora, the symposium. Herodotus's eventual definition of Greekness as common blood, language, shrines and sacrifices, and customs (Herodotus 8.144.2) is the end-point of a process that colonisation set going. The Panhellenic sanctuaries are the institutional expression: Olympia (traditionally from 776), Delphi, the Hellenion at Naucratis, the altar of Apollo Archegetes. Jonathan Hall argues that Hellenicity was first aggregative, built from linking genealogies, and only became oppositional after the Persian Wars.

Myth travelled with the settlers and was replanted. Odysseus's wanderings were pinned to the west: Scylla and Charybdis at the Straits of Messina, the Cyclopes in Sicily, Circe at Monte Circeo, the Phaeacians at Corcyra. Heracles was made to drive Geryon's cattle through Italy and Sicily, giving every city a founding visit from the hero. The Black Sea became the Argonauts' sea; Eumelus of Corinth's Corinthiaca gave Corinth a claim on Medea; Olbia worshipped Achilles as Pontarches on the island of Leuce (Arrian, Periplus 21–23); the Crimea became Iphigenia's Tauris. Cyrene received a nymph of that name, carried off by Apollo from Thessaly (Pindar, Pythian 9.5–70). Carol Dougherty has shown that foundation narratives follow a pattern (crisis, oracle, marriage or murder, new city) that made each colony's story legible to every other Greek.

Relations with the other seafarers were mixed. The Phoenicians were in the west first, at Carthage (traditionally 814), Motya in western Sicily, Gadir and Sardinia; Thucydides says they held headlands round Sicily and withdrew westwards when the Greeks arrived in numbers (Thucydides 6.2.6). Greeks took the alphabet from them and shared Pithecusae and Naucratis with them, but by the 6th century competed. The Etruscans were the Greeks' best customers for pottery and learned writing, the symposium and hoplite arms from Cumae; yet around 540–535 an Etruscan-Carthaginian fleet met the Phocaeans of Alalia in Corsica, and the Greeks, though victorious, had to abandon the island (Herodotus 1.166–167). By 550 the frontier had hardened into spheres: Greeks in eastern Sicily, southern Italy, the Black Sea and Provence; Phoenicians in the far west; Etruscans in the Tyrrhenian.

Where sources disagree. Was the Greek-native encounter colonial in the modern sense? The old model of Hellenisation, Greeks civilising passive natives, has given way to Malkin's "middle ground" and attention to intermarriage (the Gyptis story, mixed burials at Pithecusae). Critics reply that Syracuse enslaved the Sicels; violence was real. The archaeology supports both, in different places.

Self-test

  1. In what sense is "city-state" a misleading translation of polis?
    Answer

    A polis was a community of citizens, not a place: "men are the city" (Thucydides 7.77.7). It could move with its people, as the Phocaeans and the Athenians at Salamis showed, and most were far too small to be called states.

  2. How does Aristotle define a citizen, and where?
    Answer

    One who shares in judgement and office (Politics 1275a22–23); the polis is a sufficient body of such people.

  3. What is the earliest surviving polis law, and what does it do?
    Answer

    The Dreros law from Crete, c. 650–600 BC, forbidding the chief magistrate (kosmos) from holding office again within ten years.

  4. Distinguish phratry, tribe and deme.
    Answer

    Phratry: a kin-based brotherhood controlling proof of legitimate birth. Tribe (phyle): the largest kin unit, four in Ionian and three in Dorian cities. Deme: a territorial village or ward, made the basis of Athenian citizenship by Cleisthenes in 508/7.

  5. What were the duties of an oikistes?
    Answer

    Lead the expedition, choose and lay out the site, divide land into lots, found the cults; after death he was buried in the agora and received heroic cult.

  6. Which document preserves the terms of the Cyrene foundation, and what did it stipulate?
    Answer

    The 4th-century Cyrene foundation decree (SEG 9.3), claiming to quote the 7th-century Theran oath: one son per household must go; settlers could return with citizenship if the colony failed within five years; curses on breakers of the oath.

  7. Name the mother-cities of Syracuse, Taras, Byzantium, Olbia and Massalia.
    Answer

    Corinth, Sparta, Megara, Miletus, Phocaea.

  8. Why is Naucratis not a colony in the usual sense?
    Answer

    It was an emporion, a trading port in Egypt under Pharaonic control, shared by nine Greek cities with a common Hellenion; the Greeks had no territory or independent polis there (Herodotus 2.178–179).

  9. What does the Taras foundation story reveal about motives for colonisation?
    Answer

    The Partheniai were Spartans of irregular birth denied full citizenship: colonisation as a safety valve for stasis, exporting the losers of an internal dispute.

  10. What happened at Alalia, and why does it matter?
    Answer

    Around 540–535 an Etruscan-Carthaginian fleet fought the Phocaean settlers of Corsica (Herodotus 1.166); the Greeks won but had to leave. It marks the hardening of the western Mediterranean into Greek, Phoenician and Etruscan spheres.

Carry forward

  1. The polis is a body of citizens sharing laws, land and cults, not a walled town; every later argument about democracy, tyranny and citizenship in this course is an argument about who belongs to that body.
  2. Colonies were independent poleis from birth, authorised by Delphi and led by an oikist, and they doubled the Greek world between 750 and 550; the west and the Black Sea are where lawgivers, philosophers and tyrants will keep appearing.
  3. "Greekness" was forged at the edges: contact with Sicels, Scythians, Phoenicians and Etruscans produced the shared identity that Olympia, Delphi and Herodotus would later define, and myth was redrawn onto the new map to make it Greek.

Hoplites, lawgivers and tyrants

The hoplite panoply and the phalanxThe "hoplite revolution" and the Lelantine WarLawgivers and the first written codesThe age of tyrantsWhat "tyrannos" meant then, and laterWhy tyranny arose and how it endedThe Seven SagesCoinage from LydiaSelf-testCarry forward

The hoplite panoply and the phalanx

The hoplite took his name from his hopla, his arms, and the kit defined the man. Its centrepiece was the aspis: a round wooden shield about 90 cm across, bronze-faced, held by a central arm-band (porpax) and a hand-grip at the rim (antilabe). That double grip is the diagnostic feature. Worn on the forearm, the shield projects to the bearer's left and covers the exposed side of his neighbour, which only makes sense in a line. With it went a bronze helmet (the face-enclosing "Corinthian" type is classic), a bell cuirass, greaves, a thrusting spear of some 2 to 2.5 m with iron head and bronze butt-spike, and a short sword. The full kit weighed 20 to 30 kg and was costly: the hoplite was a man of property.

The archaeology dates the pieces. A warrior grave at Argos of about 720 BC held a bell cuirass and helmet; the double-grip shield appears around 700 to 675 BC. The earliest clear picture of massed ranks is the Protocorinthian Chigi olpe of about 650 to 640 BC. Tyrtaeus of Sparta, in the mid-seventh century, describes men standing "foot by foot, shield pressed on shield" (fr. 11 West); the Iliad mostly shows duels, but 13.130–133 has "shield on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man". The classical phalanx was a close-ordered block, usually eight deep, that advanced in step and broke the enemy by push and spear. Whether this already fits the seventh century, or is a fifth-century form read backwards, is the heart of the next debate.

The "hoplite revolution" and the Lelantine War

Aristotle supplied the thesis. At Politics 4.1297b16–28 he says the first constitutions after the kingships were cavalry-based, since infantry was "useless without organisation"; as cities grew and "those with heavy arms grew stronger, more people came to share in the constitution". From this the modern "hoplite revolution" was built: a new class of middling farmers, indispensable in the phalanx, demanded political weight and broke the aristocratic monopoly, often by backing a tyrant. Antony Andrewes' The Greek Tyrants (1956) gave it classic form, noting that Nicolaus of Damascus makes Cypselus of Corinth polemarch before his coup.

Where sources disagree. Anthony Snodgrass (1965) showed that the panoply was adopted piecemeal over fifty years, which fits evolution rather than revolution. Hans van Wees (Greek Warfare: Myths and Realities, 2004) and Peter Krentz argue that archaic fighting stayed open and fluid, with archers and light-armed men in the line (so Tyrtaeus fr. 11.35–38), and that the rigid phalanx is classical. Victor Davis Hanson and Donald Kagan defend the orthodox view; the exchange is in Kagan and Viggiano, Men of Bronze (2013). The political half has fared worst: no archaic source shows hoplites acting as a class, and most tyrants are better explained as winners of aristocratic feuds. Aristotle's schema is a fourth-century theory, not a record.

The Lelantine War is the test case for early warfare. Chalcis and Eretria fought over the plain between them, conventionally around 700 BC. Thucydides 1.15.3 calls it the one pre-Persian war in which "the rest of Hellas" divided into alliances; Herodotus 5.99 explains that Samos had helped Chalcis and Miletus Eretria, so that in 499 Eretria repaid the debt. Hesiod won a tripod at the funeral games of Amphidamas at Chalcis (Works and Days 654–659), and later tradition made Amphidamas a casualty. Strabo 10.1.12 reports a stele at Amarynthus recording a pact to ban missiles, and Archilochus fr. 3 West speaks of fighting "not with bows or slings" but with swords, "the war-work of the spear-famed lords of Euboea". Chalcis seems to have won.

Where sources disagree. All of this is reconstruction from scraps. Victor Parker (1997) and others argue that the "great war with alliances" is a construct Thucydides built from a long local feud and scattered colonial rivalries, and that the missile ban, if real, belongs to aristocratic self-image rather than the phalanx. The date is uncertain within half a century.

Lawgivers and the first written codes

Writing law down was political: it took the law out of the memory of aristocratic judges. Tradition names three archaic lawgivers of very different solidity.

Zaleucus of Locri in southern Italy, placed around 660 BC, was reputedly the first Greek to write a code; Ephorus (in Strabo 6.1.8) credits him with fixing penalties in advance rather than leaving them to the judge. Aristotle names him with Charondas of Catana (Politics 2.1274a22–31); Timaeus denied he had existed at all (Cicero, De Legibus 2.15).

Draco of Athens is solid in one respect: his homicide law was republished on stone in 409/8 BC and partly survives (IG I³ 104), distinguishing intentional from unintentional killing. His date is 621/0 (Athenian Constitution 4.1). Aristotle says his laws had "nothing distinctive except severity" (Politics 2.1274b15–18); Plutarch, Solon 17, preserves Demades' joke that they were written in blood. Solon repealed all but the homicide law.

Where sources disagree. Athenian Constitution 4 describes a full "constitution of Draco" with a hoplite franchise and a council of 401. Most scholars, P. J. Rhodes among them, regard the chapter as a late fifth- or fourth-century insertion, perhaps oligarchic propaganda of 411. Draco the law-writer is real; Draco the constitution-maker probably is not.

Lycurgus of Sparta is the limiting case. Plutarch opens his Life admitting that nothing about him is undisputed, including his existence. Herodotus 1.65–66 has him receive the constitution from Delphi or from Crete; Thucydides 1.18.1 dates Spartan good order to more than four centuries before 404; Aristotle makes him guardian of King Charillus (Politics 2.1271b25). Tyrtaeus' Eunomia (fr. 4 West) and the "Great Rhetra" in Plutarch, Lycurgus 6, show institutions being fixed in the seventh century but name no lawgiver. "Lycurgus" is best read as the name Sparta gave a long process so it could be called a single, god-given act.

What actually survives in stone is Cretan. The earliest Greek law inscription, from Dreros (c. 650–600 BC), forbids the kosmos, the chief magistrate, to hold office again for ten years. The Great Code of Gortyn, about 450 BC, is later than our period but the only extensive Greek code we have: some 600 lines in twelve boustrophedon columns on a public wall, regulating rape and adultery (fines graded by status), divorce and property division, the heiress and whom she must marry, adoption, debt and the position of the serf-like woikeus. Earlier Gortynian fragments reach into the seventh century. Both confirm that the first written laws were less about crime than about limiting magistrates and settling property.

Pheidon of Argos

Aristotle calls Pheidon a king who turned kingship into tyranny (Politics 5.1310b26). Ephorus (Strabo 8.3.33) makes him tenth from Temenus, says he recovered the whole "lot of Temenus", and credits him with the "Pheidonian" measures and even silver coinage. Herodotus 6.127 calls him the most arrogant of Greeks for expelling the Elean judges and running the Olympic games himself.

Where sources disagree. Pausanias 6.22.2 puts his Olympiad in 748; many emend to 668, beside the Argive victory over Sparta at Hysiae (669). Herodotus makes his son a suitor around 575, a century later. The coinage claim is anachronistic, since no Greek coined before the mid-sixth century. His date is unknown within 150 years.

Cypselus and Periander of Corinth

Herodotus tells the Cypselid story through the Corinthian Socles, warning Sparta against restoring Hippias (5.92). The Bacchiad clan ruled as a closed oligarchy; an oracle foretold that the child of the lame Bacchiad Labda, married out of the clan, would destroy them, and his mother hid the baby from ten assassins in a chest (kypsele). Cypselus overthrew the Bacchiads and ruled about thirty years; Aristotle classes him as a tyrant who rose by popular leadership and notes he kept no bodyguard (5.1310b29, 1315b27–28). Corinth under the Cypselids founded Ambracia, Leucas and Potidaea.

Periander is Herodotus' type of the tyrant turned monster. Thrasybulus of Miletus answered his request for advice by lopping every ear of corn that stood above the rest (5.92ζ). He killed his wife Melissa and burned the clothes of Corinth's women to warm her ghost (5.92η); he quarrelled with his son Lycophron and sent 300 Corcyraean boys to Lydia for castration (3.48–53). Yet the same man appears in lists of the Seven Sages, is credited with the diolkos across the Isthmus, and ruled forty years. Aristotle counts the dynasty at seventy-three and a half years (5.1315b22–29).

Cleisthenes of Sicyon

The Orthagorids lasted a century, the longest tyranny Aristotle knew, because they treated subjects moderately and largely obeyed the laws (Politics 5.1315b12–21). Cleisthenes fought Argos, banned rhapsodes for Homer's praise of Argives, and tried to oust the Argive hero Adrastus by importing his enemy Melanippus from Thebes (Herodotus 5.67). He renamed the Dorian tribes Hyatai, Oneatai and Choireatai, "pig-men, ass-men and swine-men", and his own Archelaoi, "rulers of the people" (5.68). The contest for his daughter Agariste, ending with Hippocleides dancing on a table (6.126–130), gave her to the Alcmaeonid Megacles; their grandson was the Athenian reformer Cleisthenes. Herodotus reads the tribe names as anti-Dorian contempt; some moderns think the insulting versions are hostile Argive distortions and the "anti-Dorian policy" a modern construct.

Pittacus of Mytilene

After the fall of the Penthilid kings and the tyrants Melanchrus and Myrsilus, Mytilene chose Pittacus as aisymnetes, which Aristotle defines as "an elective tyranny" (Politics 3.1285a30–b1). The exiled poet Alcaeus raged that the city had "set up base-born Pittacus as tyrant" (fr. 348). Pittacus had killed the Athenian Phrynon in single combat in the war over Sigeum (Strabo 13.1.38), ruled ten years, then laid down office (Diogenes Laertius 1.75). Aristotle preserves one law: double penalties for offences committed drunk (Politics 2.1274b18–23). He shows that "tyrant" could cover an elected emergency magistrate.

Polycrates of Samos

Polycrates seized Samos with his brothers about 538, killed one and exiled the other, and ruled a navy of a hundred penteconters (Herodotus 3.39). He plundered friend and foe alike; Amasis of Egypt renounced his friendship when a ring Polycrates threw into the sea came back in a fish (3.40–43). Sparta and Corinth besieged Samos on behalf of exiles and failed (3.54–56); Thucydides 1.13.6 records his dedication of Rheneia to Delian Apollo. He kept Anacreon and Ibycus at court, and the tunnel of Eupalinus, the mole and the Heraion that Herodotus admires (3.60) belong at least partly to his reign. In 522 the satrap Oroetes lured him to the mainland and crucified him (3.120–125).

The Peisistratids of Athens

Peisistratus took power three times. In 561/0, leading the "men beyond the hills" against the plain and coast factions, he wounded himself, was voted a bodyguard of club-bearers and seized the Acropolis (Herodotus 1.59; Athenian Constitution 14). Expelled, he returned by marrying Megacles' daughter and driving in beside a tall woman dressed as Athena (1.60); expelled again, he spent some ten years raising money in Thrace and allies in Eretria, and won at Pallene around 546 (1.61–64). He ruled until his death in 527/6.

The Athenian sources are strikingly kind. Herodotus says he governed "according to the existing laws" (1.59.6); Athenian Constitution 16 calls his rule an age of Cronus, with a tithe, loans to farmers and travelling rural judges. Thucydides insists the family "practised virtue and intelligence", exacted only a twentieth, adorned the city and fought its wars, interfering only to keep one of themselves in office (6.54). Hippias succeeded as eldest. In 514 Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed Hipparchus at the Panathenaea over a love affair (6.54–59); Thucydides' point, against Athenian belief, is that Hipparchus was never tyrant and the murder made Hippias harsher. The exiled Alcmaeonids worked on Delphi to push Sparta, and in 510 Cleomenes expelled Hippias (Herodotus 5.62–65), who ended by guiding the Persians to Marathon.

Where sources disagree. Athenian Constitution 15.4 has Peisistratus disarm the Athenians after Pallene; Thucydides 6.56–58 has Hippias do it after the murder. The chronology of the three attempts differs between Herodotus and Athenian Constitution 14–15, whose figures Rhodes finds internally inconsistent. Thucydides also corrects Herodotus 5.55 and popular memory that the lovers "freed Athens".

What "tyrannos" meant then, and later

Tyrannos is probably a Lydian loanword, and it enters Greek with the Lydian king Gyges: its first attestation is Archilochus fr. 19 West, where the speaker does not care for Gyges' gold "nor desire great tyranny". In the seventh and sixth centuries it meant a sole ruler whose power was not hereditary kingship, without implying how he ruled. Herodotus uses tyrannos and basileus almost interchangeably; Sophocles could title a play Oedipus Tyrannos about a king his audience pitied; Pittacus the elected magistrate and Periander the murderer are both "tyrants". Solon refuses tyranny in his verse (fr. 32–33 West), so the office could be declined, but not yet simply abominated.

The pejorative sense hardened in democratic Athens after 510, when Harmodius and Aristogeiton received cult and statues and Hippias became a traitor at Marathon. By the fourth century the philosophers had a theory. Plato's Republic 8–9 makes the tyrant the final degeneration of soul and city. Aristotle defines tyranny as deviant kingship, rule for the ruler's benefit over unwilling subjects (Politics 3.1279b, 4.1295a), and lists its methods: cut down the outstanding, forbid clubs and common meals, keep the people poor and busy, use spies, make wars (5.1313a34–1314a29). English inherits this sense. Reading it back into Cypselus or Cleisthenes of Sicyon is the standard error.

Why tyranny arose and how it ended

Thucydides 1.13.1 gives the oldest explanation: as Hellas grew stronger and "the acquisition of wealth became more of an object", revenues grew and tyrannies were set up. Aristotle sorts tyrants by origin (Politics 5.1310b): kings who overstepped (Pheidon), holders of high office in Ionia and Sicily, and demagogues who were also generals, such as Peisistratus and Theagenes of Megara. The modern hoplite theory has largely yielded to a view of the tyrant as the aristocrat who won: Cypselus against the Bacchiads, Peisistratus against rival factions, Polycrates against his brothers. Lydia offered a model of splendid monarchy next door. The one economic case with evidence is Athens, where Solon's poems describe debt-bondage a generation before Peisistratus.

Tyrannies ended for three reasons. First, succession: Aristotle observes that most barely outlived the founder, the sons being raised in luxury and arrogance, and he names the three longest, the Orthagorids at a hundred years, the Cypselids at seventy-three and a half and the Peisistratids at thirty-five (5.1315b). Second, Sparta: Thucydides 1.18.1 says most tyrannies were put down by Sparta, and later lists (Plutarch, On the Malice of Herodotus 21; the Rylands papyrus) credit her with Corinth, Sicyon and Athens. Third, Persia, which after 546 made the Ionian tyrants its clients. Thucydides' verdict (1.17), that tyrants cared only for their own safety and achieved nothing except against neighbours, sits awkwardly with the Athenian building and festival evidence.

The Seven Sages

The earliest list is Plato's (Protagoras 343a): Thales of Miletus, Pittacus of Mytilene, Bias of Priene, Solon of Athens, Cleobulus of Lindos, Myson of Chen and Chilon of Sparta. Diogenes Laertius 1.40–42 records substitutes, Periander, Anacharsis, Epimenides and others, and that Demetrius of Phalerum dated their recognition to the archonship of Damasias, 582/1. Their wisdom was gnomic: "know thyself", "nothing in excess", Pittacus' "know the moment". Stories gathered around them: the golden tripod passed from sage to sage until it reached Delphi (Plutarch, Solon 4), and Solon's visit to Croesus (Herodotus 1.29–33), which Plutarch admits cannot fit the dates but refuses to give up (Solon 27).

The group overlaps tellingly with lawgivers and tyrants: Solon, Pittacus, Periander, Chilon the Spartan ephor. Dicaearchus already called them "shrewd men with a turn for legislation" rather than sages (Diogenes Laertius 1.40); Richard Martin reads them as performers of wisdom, a political role rather than a school. The list canonises the archaic ideal of the wise statesman.

Coinage from Lydia

Herodotus 1.94 says the Lydians were the first to strike gold and silver coin and the first retailers; Xenophanes (fr. 4, in Pollux 9.83) agreed, though Pollux also records rival claimants including Pheidon. The earliest coins are electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, stamped with a lion's head or other badge; the key deposit is the foundation fill of the Artemision at Ephesus, now dated by most around 600 BC. One early piece reads "I am the badge of Phanes". Croesus replaced electrum with separate gold and silver about 550. Greek cities followed: Aegina's silver "turtles" from about 550, Corinth's Pegasi, Athens' Wappenmünzen and, from about 515, the owls. Before coins, value was reckoned in cattle and in iron spits, from which obol and drachma, a "handful" of six spits, take their names.

Where sources disagree. Aristotle (Politics 1.1257a31–41) explains coinage as a convenience of trade. Numismatists have doubted it: Robert Cook (1958) proposed payment of mercenaries, Colin Kraay (1964) state payments and taxes, since early issues are too large for retail; Henry Kim (2001) countered with tiny early fractions. The Artemision date, and so the birth of coinage, has moved between about 640 and 560 and is not settled.

Self-test

  1. What feature of the aspis ties the hoplite to a formation rather than to individual combat?
    Answer

    The double grip (porpax and antilabe) fixes the shield on the forearm so that its left half overhangs and protects the neighbour, which only works in a line.

  2. Which object is the earliest clear depiction of a phalanx, and roughly when?
    Answer

    The Protocorinthian Chigi vase, about 650 to 640 BC.

  3. Which passage of Aristotle underlies the "hoplite revolution" thesis?
    Answer

    Politics 4.1297b16–28, on constitutions passing from cavalry to the heavy-armed as cities grew.

  4. Why does Thucydides single out the Lelantine War?
    Answer

    It was, he says, the only pre-Persian war in which the rest of Greece took sides in alliances (1.15.3).

  5. Which of Draco's laws survives, and how?
    Answer

    His homicide law, republished on stone in 409/8 BC (IG I³ 104).

  6. What is the earliest surviving Greek law inscription and what does it regulate?
    Answer

    The Dreros law, Crete, c. 650–600 BC, forbidding the kosmos to hold office again within ten years.

  7. What did Aristotle call Pittacus' position and why does it matter?
    Answer

    An aisymnetes, "an elective tyranny" (Politics 3.1285a), showing the word tyrant could cover a legitimately chosen ruler.

  8. What error about the Peisistratids does Thucydides correct in 6.54–59?
    Answer

    That Hipparchus was tyrant when murdered; Hippias was the eldest and ruler, and the murder made the tyranny harsher rather than ending it.

  9. Name the three longest tyrannies in Aristotle's reckoning.
    Answer

    The Orthagorids of Sicyon (100 years), the Cypselids of Corinth (73½) and the Peisistratids of Athens (35).

  10. What is the earliest attestation of the word tyrannos, and whose name is it linked with?
    Answer

    Archilochus fr. 19 West, in the mouth of a speaker rejecting the gold and "great tyranny" of Gyges of Lydia.

Carry forward

  1. Archaic "tyrant" is a neutral word for an unconstitutional sole ruler, usually an aristocrat who won a factional fight; the moral sense is a construction of democratic Athens and fourth-century philosophy, and must not be read back.
  2. Aristotle's Politics and Athenian Constitution are theories built on thin tradition, not records: the hoplite revolution, the constitution of Draco and the typology of tyrants are fourth-century schemata to be tested, not assumed.
  3. Written law and coinage were both instruments for taking power out of aristocratic hands and fixing it in public, impersonal form; this is the ground on which Solon, Cleisthenes and the Athenian democracy will build.

Sparta

Messenia and the helots

Sparta's peculiarity begins with a land grab. Between roughly 735 and 715 the Spartans crossed Taygetus and took the Messenian plain, the richest farmland in the Peloponnese; a revolt in the mid-seventh century took a generation to crush. The only contemporary witness is the poet Tyrtaeus, who says the first war lasted "nineteen years" under "our fathers' fathers" until the enemy abandoned Ithome (fr. 5 West), and describes the defeated as "like asses worn down by great burdens", handing over half of all the land produced (frs. 6–7 West). Everything else, Aristomenes included, comes from Pausanias, Description of Greece book 4, written in the second century AD from Messenian traditions formed after liberation in 369.

The conquered became helots, a status the ancients themselves found hard to classify: Pollux (Onomasticon 3.83) puts them "between free men and slaves", Strabo (8.5.4) calls them state slaves. Bound to the land, they owed a fixed share to an individual Spartiate, lived in their own villages and were freed only by the state; Messenian helots, unlike Laconian ones, remained a conquered people. Thucydides says "most Spartan institutions have always been designed with a view to security against the helots" (4.80), recording in the same passage that about two thousand helots who claimed to have fought best were garlanded as free and then made to disappear. The treaty of 421 bound Athens to help Sparta "if the slaves revolt" (Thucydides 5.23). Each year the ephors declared war on the helots so that killing them carried no pollution (Plutarch, Lycurgus 28, citing Aristotle). The earthquake of 465/4 triggered the great revolt on Ithome (Thucydides 1.101–103).

Where sources disagree. Critias (fr. 37 DK) said that in Sparta "the slaves are most slaves and the free most free", and Jean Ducat's Les Hilotes (1990) treats helotage as a coherent system of institutionalised contempt. Nino Luraghi (The Ancient Messenians, 2008) argues that a "Messenian" ethnic identity was largely constructed after 369 and that the eighth-century conquest narrative is a retrojection. Whether Messenians existed as a people before liberation is genuinely uncertain.

Lycurgus and the Great Rhetra

Herodotus (1.65–66) says the Spartans were the worst-governed Greeks until Lycurgus gave them laws; Delphi hailed him as "god or man, I do not know which". Plutarch opens his Life admitting that "nothing whatsoever can be said about the lawgiver Lycurgus that is not disputed" (Lycurgus 1). Xenophon (Constitution of the Lacedaemonians 10.8) makes him contemporary with the Heraclids, Aristotle with the first Olympiad. Lycurgus had a hero-cult and sanctuary (Herodotus 1.66; Plutarch, Lycurgus 31). A lawgiver with a shrine and a biography of pure anecdote is almost certainly a culture hero credited after the fact with an evolved system; "Lycurgan" is a label, not a date.

The institutions were real. Two hereditary kings, Agiad and Eurypontid, descended from the twin sons of Aristodemus (Herodotus 6.52), were priests of Zeus Lacedaemon and Zeus Uranius and generals (Herodotus 6.56–59; Xenophon, Constitution 15); after 506 only one king could lead an army (Herodotus 5.75). The gerousia was twenty-eight men over sixty elected for life, plus the kings; it prepared business and tried capital cases. The apella, all Spartiates, voted by shouting without right of amendment; Thucydides 1.87 shows the ephor Sthenelaidas pretending he could not hear the result and forcing a division. The five ephors, elected annually, summoned the assembly, exchanged monthly oaths with the kings and could fine or imprison any magistrate (Xenophon, Constitution 8, 15); Aristotle thought them "like tyrants", poor men open to bribes (Politics 1270b).

The Great Rhetra (Plutarch, Lycurgus 6) is the earliest Greek constitutional text we have in roughly its own words: a dedication to Zeus Syllanios and Athena Syllania; the people "tribed into tribes and obed into obes"; a gerousia of thirty including the kings (archagetai); assemblies "season by season between Babyka and Knakion"; the elders to introduce and set aside business, the people to have the power of decision. A rider, attributed to kings Theopompus and Polydorus, lets elders and kings dissolve the assembly "if the people speak crookedly". Tyrtaeus' Eunomia (fr. 4 West) versifies the same scheme, anchoring it in the seventh century.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch (Lycurgus 7) and Aristotle (Politics 1313a) say Theopompus added the ephorate about 130 years after Lycurgus; Herodotus (1.65) credits Lycurgus with it. Forrest and Cartledge accept a seventh-century core for the Rhetra; others treat the whole text as a fourth-century or later reconstruction, and the clause giving the people power rests on Wade-Gery's emendation, not a manuscript reading.

The agoge, the syssitia and the krypteia

Xenophon, Constitution 2–4, and Plutarch, Lycurgus 16–18, five centuries apart, agree on a shape. A newborn boy was inspected by the tribal elders and, if weak, exposed at the Apothetae (Plutarch only). At seven he joined the agelai ("herds") under the paidonomos and his whip-bearers. Boys went barefoot, had one cloak a year, slept on reeds, were kept hungry, encouraged to steal and whipped if caught (Xenophon, Constitution 2.1–9; Plutarch, Lycurgus 17–18, with the stolen fox). Youths of about twenty, eirenes, commanded the younger; the age-grade vocabulary (rhobidas, pais, melleiren, eiren) survives only in Roman-era inscriptions. Both authors treat pederastic attachments as normal and educational, Xenophon (2.12–14) implausibly denying any sexual element. At twenty a youth stood for a mess; at thirty he was a full citizen. Those who failed became hypomeiones, "inferiors" (Xenophon, Hellenica 3.3.6). The word agoge is not attested for the system before the Hellenistic period.

The syssitia (Spartan pheiditia; Alcman fr. 98 and Aristotle know the older andreia) were groups of about fifteen who dined together every evening for life; admission needed a unanimous vote by bread pellets (Plutarch, Lycurgus 12). Each member contributed monthly a medimnos of barley, eight choes of wine, five minae of cheese, two and a half of figs and a little money. Aristotle saw the flaw: a man who could not pay lost his citizenship, so the egalitarian mess became a wealth filter (Politics 1271a). The messes were also the army's basic unit (Herodotus 1.65; Xenophon, Constitution 5).

The krypteia is described in two incompatible ways. Plato (Laws 633b–c) makes it an endurance test, young men roaming barefoot in winter without servants. Plutarch, quoting Aristotle (Lycurgus 28), makes it a death squad: youths with daggers hiding by day and killing helots on the roads by night.

Where sources disagree. Jeanmaire (1913) read the krypteia as an initiatory rite of passage; others see a secret police. Nigel Kennell (The Gymnasium of Virtue, 1995) argued that much of Plutarch's agoge, including the whipping contest at Artemis Orthia that Roman tourists watched from a purpose-built theatre (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 2.34), is a third-century and Roman reconstruction; Jean Ducat (Spartan Education, 2006) finds more of a Classical core. Infant exposure rests on Plutarch alone.

Spartan women and property

Xenophon (Constitution 1.3–9) says Lycurgus prescribed physical training for girls to produce strong children and allowed an elderly husband to bring in a younger man to father children, or a man to borrow another's wife with consent. Plutarch (Lycurgus 14–15) adds processions, choral mockery of bachelors, naked exercise and a wedding in which the bride's head was shaved and she was dressed as a man before the groom came to her in the dark and returned to his mess. Girls married late, about eighteen, and Cynisca, sister of Agesilaus, won the Olympic chariot race in 396 and 392 (Pausanias 3.8.1).

Property is the key. The 9,000 equal, inalienable kleroi of Plutarch (Lycurgus 8, 16) are contradicted by Aristotle, who says land was unevenly held, women controlled nearly two-fifths of it through heiresses (patrouchoi) and large dowries, and this was ruining the state (Politics 1270a). Stephen Hodkinson (Property and Wealth in Classical Sparta, 2000) showed that partible inheritance including daughters, combined with marriage between wealthy houses, produces exactly this concentration. Aristotle also calls the women licentious and useless when Thebes invaded in 370/69 (Politics 1269b).

Where sources disagree. The equal-lots scheme is now widely seen as a third-century ideal projected back. Sarah Pomeroy (Spartan Women, 2002) accepts real female economic power; sceptics note the entire picture is drawn by male non-Spartans with an argument to make, and whether wife-sharing was an institution or occasional elite practice is uncertain.

The Peloponnesian League

"The Lacedaemonians and their allies" is the ancient name; the League is a modern term. It began in the sixth century when Sparta, having failed to helotise Tegea, instead bound her by treaty after bringing home the bones of Orestes (Herodotus 1.66–68); a clause preserved by Aristotle (fr. 592 Rose, in Plutarch, Greek Questions 5) required Tegea to expel Messenians. Allies paid no tribute and kept autonomy, but swore to have the same friends and enemies and to follow Sparta's lead; Sparta's method was to install congenial oligarchies (Thucydides 1.19). Each ally had one vote in a congress whose majority bound all, though Sparta first decided in her own assembly whether to put the question (Thucydides 1.87, 1.119–125). Corinth's refusal in 506 to attack Athens and her defeat of the proposal to restore Hippias (Herodotus 5.75, 5.91–93) are the first sign that allies could say no, and probably mark the congress's birth. The standard escape clause, "unless gods or heroes prevent", appears in the Argive treaty of 418 (Thucydides 5.30). The League dissolved after Leuctra in 371, when Epaminondas freed Messenia.

Where sources disagree. Larsen argued for a formal constitution with a congress from the late sixth century; de Ste Croix (The Origins of the Peloponnesian War, 1972) and Cartledge stress bilateral oaths, with the congress appearing only when a historian needs to explain a Spartan defeat.

Religion, festivals and the divine ancestors

Sparta's festivals repeatedly shaped her wars. The Hyacinthia at Amyclae, in early summer, honoured Apollo and the dead youth Hyacinthus, whose tomb lay beneath Apollo's colossal archaic statue (Pausanias 3.19.2–3); mourning gave way to choruses, chariot races, girls in wicker carts and a feast at which citizens entertained helots and foreigners (Polycrates in Athenaeus 4.139d–f). The Spartans delayed marching to Plataea for it (Herodotus 9.7), the Amyclaeans went home for it even on campaign (Xenophon, Hellenica 4.5.11). The Gymnopaedia, in midsummer, was choral dancing in the agora in full heat (Pausanias 3.11.9; Plato, Laws 633c); Demaratus was humiliated there (Herodotus 6.67), and when news of Leuctra arrived during the men's chorus the ephors let the dance finish (Xenophon, Hellenica 6.4.16). The Carneia, in late summer, honoured Apollo Carneius, ram-god of the Dorian migration: Demetrius of Scepsis (Athenaeus 4.141e–f) describes nine tents each housing nine men dining under command as in a camp, and the staphylodromoi who chased a garlanded runner for good luck. Its truce is why only Leonidas' advance guard reached Thermopylae (Herodotus 7.206), and the Argives twice manipulated their calendar around it (Thucydides 5.54, 5.75–76). Add Artemis Orthia at Limnae, with its thousands of lead votives and grotesque masks, and the Menelaion at Therapne, where Helen and Menelaus received cult (Herodotus 6.61).

The kings claimed Heracles. Herodotus traces Leonidas through Aristodemus to Hyllus and Heracles (7.204); Tyrtaeus sings that "Zeus himself gave this city to the Heraclidae" (fr. 2 West), making the Dorian conquest a recovery of the hero's inheritance. The Dioscuri, Laconian twins buried at Therapne (Pindar, Nemean 10.55–59), doubled the dual kingship; after 506 one Tyndarid, represented by the dokana of two beams and crossbars, went to war with the one king while the other stayed home (Herodotus 5.75; Plutarch, On Brotherly Love 478a). Sparta also annexed the pre-Dorian past: Menelaus and Helen, the bones of Orestes and later of Tisamenus (Pausanias 7.1.8), and Cleomenes' retort on the Athenian acropolis, "I am no Dorian but an Achaean" (Herodotus 5.72).

Where sources disagree. Pausanias ties the Gymnopaedia to Apollo; lexicographers tie it to the dead of Thyrea (Herodotus 1.82). The sixth-century "Achaean policy" of claiming pre-Dorian heroes to legitimise rule (Leahy, Boedeker, Malkin) is a modern inference, not a Spartan statement.

Tyrtaeus and Alcman: the only Spartan voices

Nearly everything written about Sparta was written by outsiders; the exceptions are two seventh-century poets. Tyrtaeus wrote elegiacs for the Messenian war: historical pieces (frs. 2, 4–7 West) and exhortations that became the canon of hoplite ethics: "it is a fine thing for a brave man to die, fallen in the front ranks" (fr. 10.1–2); the warrior who "plants his feet and stands fast, biting his lip" (fr. 11); excellence as courage above wealth, beauty or athletic victory (fr. 12). Spartans sang him on campaign at the king's tent (Lycurgus, Against Leocrates 106–107; Philochorus in Athenaeus 14.630f). Athenian tradition made him an Athenian, even a lame schoolmaster sent by Delphi (Plato, Laws 629a; Pausanias 4.15.6).

Alcman, a generation later, is the Sparta nobody expects. The Louvre Partheneion (fr. 1 PMGF, a papyrus found at Saqqara in 1855) is a girls' choral song naming the leaders Hagesichora and Agido, comparing them to racehorses, invoking Aotis, and teasing itself about its singing; fr. 3 praises Astymeloisa with "limb-loosening desire". Elsewhere he writes of sleeping mountains (fr. 89), of the old man who wishes to be a sea-bird (fr. 26), of porridge and honey cakes (fr. 17). This is a Sparta of luxury, humour and cosmopolitan taste, matching the sixth-century Laconian pottery and bronzes exported to Samos and Etruria. Austerity came later, if it ever fully came.

Where sources disagree. Ancient scholars already argued whether Alcman was Lydian from Sardis or Spartan from Messoa (Suda; Palatine Anthology 7.18, 7.709). Calame (1977) reads the Partheneion as initiatory ritual, others as a festival of Orthia or Helen; the occasion is unknown. On Tyrtaeus, Snodgrass saw a developed phalanx; van Wees and Krentz read fr. 11's mixed fighting as a looser order.

Oliganthropia

Demaratus tells Xerxes Sparta has about 8,000 men (Herodotus 7.234). At Leuctra about 1,200 served and 400 died in an afternoon (Xenophon, Hellenica 6.4.15). Aristotle says the land could support 1,500 cavalry and 30,000 hoplites but there were "not even a thousand" (Politics 1270a); Plutarch gives 700 for the 240s, about 100 with land (Agis 5). Aristotle's name for the disease is oliganthropia, and he blamed the property system. Earthquake, war and late marriage contributed, but the mechanism was social: men fell below the mess contribution and became hypomeiones, like Cinadon, whose conspiracy of 399 drew on helots, neodamodeis, inferiors and perioikoi who "would gladly eat the Spartiates raw" (Xenophon, Hellenica 3.3.4–11). Plutarch (Agis 5) blames a law of the ephor Epitadeus permitting gifts and bequests of land; the gold that flooded in after 404 (Plutarch, Lysander 17) did the rest.

Where sources disagree. Hodkinson doubts Epitadeus existed, since partible inheritance already explains the concentration; others accept a fourth-century change. Whether the Spartiate body shrank chiefly by downward mobility or by real population loss remains debated.

The Spartan mirage

François Ollier coined le mirage spartiate (1933–43) for the gap between Sparta and what others made of her. The admirers were Athenian from the start: Critias; Plato, whose Republic and Laws lean on the model; and Xenophon, who served under Agesilaus, put his sons through Spartan training as trophimoi (Plutarch, Agesilaus 20) and wrote the Constitution and the encomiastic Agesilaus. Yet Constitution 14 says bluntly that Spartans of his day no longer obey Lycurgus, hoard money and prefer governing abroad: the ideal is already a lost past. Plutarch drew on Aristotle, Dicaearchus, Phylarchus and the Stoic Sphaerus, adviser to Cleomenes III, whose revolution of the 220s revived "Lycurgan" institutions and partly invented them. Polybius (6.45–50) passed the model to Rome; Rousseau, Prussia, the Third Reich and the film 300 each found what they wanted.

Modern correction runs in three directions. Chronology: Finley's "sixth-century revolution" and the archaeology of Orthia and Laconian pottery show an Archaic Sparta that was wealthy and open, with austerity arriving late. Property: Hodkinson's demonstration that Sparta was a highly unequal society of landowners from the start, and that the homoioi, "the similars", shared a lifestyle, not wealth. Texts: Kennell's and Ducat's redating of the agoge and Luraghi's dismantling of the Messenian narrative show how far Hellenistic and Roman Sparta rebuilt itself for philosophers and tourists. Most of what we "know" about Sparta is what someone wanted her to be.

Where sources disagree. Xenophon is read by some (Humble, Lipka) as a quietly critical observer and by others as a committed Laconiser, and the original position of chapter 14 is disputed. Mogens Hansen (2009) argued Sparta was a normal polis; Hodkinson replied that in land tenure, helotage and the perioikoi it was structurally unlike any other.

Self-test

  1. What is the one contemporary source for the Messenian Wars, and what does it say the helots owed their masters?
    Answer

    Tyrtaeus (frs. 5–7 West): the war lasted nineteen years and the conquered paid half of all produce, "like asses worn down by great burdens".

  2. According to Thucydides 4.80, what governing principle lay behind most Spartan institutions?
    Answer

    Security against the helots; the same passage records the garlanding and disappearance of about 2,000 helots.

  3. Name the four organs of the Spartan constitution and the body of thirty named in the Great Rhetra.
    Answer

    Two kings, the gerousia (28 elders plus the kings), five ephors, and the apella; the Rhetra's gerousia of thirty includes the kings as archagetai.

  4. Give two reasons to doubt that Lycurgus was a historical person.
    Answer

    He received hero-cult; his dates vary by centuries between authors; Plutarch admits nothing about him is undisputed; Herodotus already knew rival accounts of the laws' origin.

  5. What were the monthly contributions to a Spartan mess, and why did Aristotle think the messes undermined equality?
    Answer

    A medimnos of barley, eight choes of wine, five minae of cheese, two and a half of figs, and some money; a man who could not pay lost citizenship, so the mess filtered by wealth (Politics 1271a).

  6. How do Plato and Plutarch (citing Aristotle) differ on the krypteia?
    Answer

    Plato (Laws 633b–c) describes a winter endurance test; Plutarch (Lycurgus 28) describes youths with daggers hiding by day and killing helots by night.

  7. What fraction of Spartan land did Aristotle say women controlled, and by what mechanism?
    Answer

    Nearly two-fifths, through heiresses (patrouchoi) and large dowries under partible inheritance (Politics 1270a).

  8. Which festival explains why only Leonidas' advance guard reached Thermopylae, and which explains the delay before Plataea?
    Answer

    The Carneia (Herodotus 7.206) and the Hyacinthia (Herodotus 9.7).

  9. Why did one of the Dioscuri accompany the Spartan army after 506?
    Answer

    Because a new law allowed only one king on campaign, so one Tyndarid (represented by the dokana) went with him and the other stayed with the king at home (Herodotus 5.75).

  10. Trace Spartiate numbers from 480 to the 240s with the sources.
    Answer

    About 8,000 (Herodotus 7.234); about 1,200 at Leuctra with 400 dead (Xenophon, Hellenica 6.4.15); "not even a thousand" (Aristotle, Politics 1270a); 700, about 100 with land (Plutarch, Agis 5).

Carry forward

  1. Sparta is a conquest state: helotage explains the agoge, the messes, the krypteia, the League and the final collapse. Read every Spartan institution as an answer to the Messenian problem.
  2. "Lycurgan" is a label for an evolved system, and much of what Plutarch describes was reconstructed in the third century and under Rome. Date the source before trusting the detail: Tyrtaeus, Alcman, Herodotus and Thucydides outrank Xenophon, who outranks Plutarch.
  3. Equality was a lifestyle ideology over a landowning oligarchy. Property, inherited through women as well as men, concentrated in few hands and produced oliganthropia; this thread connects Archaic Sparta to Leuctra, to Agis and Cleomenes, and to the Roman Sparta the admirers visited.

Cover: the conquest of Messenia and the helots; the Lycurgan "constitution" (two kings, gerousia, ephors, apella, the Great Rhetra) and why Lycurgus probably never existed; the agoge in detail, the syssitia, the krypteia; Spartan women and property; the Peloponnesian League; the "Spartan mirage": how Xenophon, Plutarch and later admirers idealised Sparta and how modern scholarship corrects it; Spartan religion and festivals (Hyacinthia, Gymnopaedia, Carneia); demographic decline; Sparta's self-image through Heracles and the Dioscuri; and Tyrtaeus and Alcman as the only Spartan voices.
