Athens from Solon to Cleisthenes

Draco's code (621/0)The crisis of debt bondageSolon's reforms (594/3)The regional factionsPeisistratus: three attempts and his ruleHippias, Hipparchus and the tyrannicidesSparta, Isagoras and the reforms of CleisthenesThe earliest meaning of "demokratia"Self-testCarry forward

Draco's code (621/0)

Seventh-century Athens was run by the Eupatridai through nine annual archons chosen by birth and wealth and through the Areopagus, a council of ex-archons for life (Athenaion Politeia 3). Around 632 Cylon, an Olympic victor, seized the Acropolis; his supporters were lured out of sanctuary and killed, and the blood guilt fell on the Alcmaeonid archon Megacles (Herodotus 5.71; Thucydides 1.126). That curse would be invoked against Alcmaeonids for a century and a half. Draco legislated a decade later, in the archonship of Aristaechmus (Athenaion Politeia 4.1). What survives securely is his homicide law, republished on stone in 409/8 (IG I³ 104). It distinguishes intentional from unintentional killing, gives jurisdiction to the basileis and the fifty-one ephetai, lays out which kinsmen may pardon, and protects a man who kills a thief or adulterer caught in the act. Its importance is procedural: killing moved from vendetta into a written public process that aristocratic judges could no longer make up case by case.

The rest is reputation: Demades' quip that Draco wrote in blood, with death for idleness and for stealing vegetables (Plutarch, Solon 17); Aristotle's verdict that nothing was notable but the severity (Politics 1274b). Solon repealed everything except the homicide law (Athenaion Politeia 7.1), which is why only that law survived to be reinscribed.

Where sources disagree. Athenaion Politeia 4 describes a full "constitution of Draco": citizenship for all who bore arms, a council of 401 by lot, fines reckoned in minae. Rhodes, Hignett and Wallace treat the chapter as a late fifth- or fourth-century oligarchic fiction inserted into the text; it assumes coinage Athens did not yet have and mirrors the programme of the 411 oligarchs. Treat Draco as a lawgiver, not a constitution-maker.

The crisis of debt bondage

Athenaion Politeia 2 and Plutarch (Solon 13) describe Attica a generation later: the many enslaved to the few; the poor farming the land of the rich as pelatai and hektemoroi ("sixth-parters"); every loan secured on the borrower's person, so that defaulters and their families were sold, some abroad. Solon's own verses confirm Athenians sold into slavery and men fleeing debt (fr. 36 West). The horoi he says he uprooted were markers recording the obligation on the land or the man who worked it. Behind this lay population pressure on poor soil, bad harvests that forced smallholders to borrow seed from richer neighbours, and a law that gave creditors the debtor's body; there was no coinage, and obligations were in produce.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch says the hektemoroi paid a sixth of their produce; some moderns read the name as meaning they kept a sixth, a servile tenancy. Wider still: were they free smallholders who had mortgaged ancestral plots (Woodhouse, Finley) or a hereditary dependent class whose status Solon abolished without touching land ownership (Rhodes, Gallant)? Solon fr. 34 says he refused to give good and bad an equal share of the land, so there was no redistribution. The economics remain uncertain.

Solon's reforms (594/3)

Solon, a Eupatrid of moderate means and a poet known for a Salamis elegy, was elected archon and mediator for 594/3 (Plutarch, Solon 14.3; Athenaion Politeia 5.2). Athenaion Politeia 12 lets him speak: he stood "like a wolf among many dogs" (fr. 37), holding a shield over both parties.

The seisachtheia

The "shaking-off of burdens" cancelled existing debts and banned for the future all loans secured on the person (Athenaion Politeia 6.1; Plutarch, Solon 15). Solon bought back Athenians sold abroad, some of whom "no longer spoke the Attic tongue" (fr. 36), and freed those enslaved at home. Both sources report, and Athenaion Politeia rejects, the charge that his friends borrowed heavily knowing cancellation was coming.

The four property classes

Wealth, measured in annual produce, replaced birth as the qualification for office (Athenaion Politeia 7.3–4; Plutarch, Solon 18):

ClassQualificationAccess
Pentakosiomedimnoi500 measuresAll offices; treasurers of Athena from this class only
Hippeis300 measuresArchonship and major offices
Zeugitai200 measuresLesser offices; the hoplite class
Thetesbelow 200Assembly and lawcourts only

Athenaion Politeia 7.4 cites an Acropolis dedication by Anthemion son of Diphilus recording his rise from thete to hippeus. The classes may be older military categories; Solon tied political rights to them.

The Council of 400

Solon is said to have created a council of 400, a hundred from each of the four Ionian tribes, to prepare business for the assembly, leaving the Areopagus as guardian of the laws (Athenaion Politeia 8.4; Plutarch, Solon 19, who calls the two councils the ship's twin anchors).

Where sources disagree. Hignett argued the Council of 400 never existed and was invented to give the oligarchs of 411 a precedent. Rhodes and most recent work accept it, noting the "Boule" that resists Cleomenes in Herodotus 5.72 before a Cleisthenic council can have met. Separately, Athenaion Politeia's intervals between Solon and Peisistratus do not fit 594/3, and Hammond and Sealey have moved the legislation to 592/1 or later.

The Heliaia and the right of appeal

Athenaion Politeia 9.1 names Solon's three most "democratic" measures: the ban on loans on the person; the right of any citizen who wished (ho boulomenos) to prosecute on behalf of a wronged party; and ephesis, appeal from a magistrate's verdict to the dikasterion, the people sitting as a court. Plutarch (Solon 18.2–3) adds that the thetes' admission to the courts seemed trivial and proved decisive. Whether the Heliaia was the assembly sitting judicially (Hansen) or a separate sworn body is debated.

Other laws and his poetry

The laws were inscribed on wooden axones. Solon forbade the export of produce except olive oil (Plutarch, Solon 24), regulated wills and funerals, and is credited by Athenaion Politeia 10 with reforming weights, measures and coinage, though Athens struck no coins before the mid sixth century. Herodotus 1.29 says the Athenians swore to keep the laws ten years; Plutarch and Athenaion Politeia say a hundred. His meeting with Croesus (Herodotus 1.30–33) is chronologically impossible.

His poetry is the only contemporary voice in the whole period. Fr. 4 preaches that dysnomia brings countless ills and eunomia sets all in order; fr. 36 is his defence before the "black earth, mother of the Olympian gods", blaming the leaders' greed, not the gods. Fr. 5 states his principle:

I gave the people as much privilege as suffices.
Herodotus barely treats Solon as a reformer; the detail depends on Athenaion Politeia and Plutarch, writing over two centuries later and already shaping Solon into the father of democracy.

The regional factions

Solon pleased nobody fully. Athenaion Politeia 13 records two years with no archon (probably 590/89 and 586/5), then Damasias, who clung to the archonship for two years and two months until forced out, and a compromise board of ten archons: five Eupatrids, three farmers, two craftsmen. Herodotus 1.59 and Athenaion Politeia 13.4 then describe three regional factions: the Plain under Lycurgus son of Aristolaides, oligarchic and landed; the Coast under Megacles son of Alcmaeon, "moderate"; and the men beyond the hills (Herodotus' hyperakrioi, Athenaion Politeia's diakrioi) under Peisistratus, including the poorest and those "of impure descent" who feared a review of the citizen roll. The reality was three aristocratic networks, each rooted in a district.

Peisistratus: three attempts and his rule

Peisistratus, of a family claiming Neleid descent and based at Brauron, won fame against Megara by capturing Nisaea. Herodotus 1.59–64 and Athenaion Politeia 14–17 tell the story.

  1. First attempt (c. 561/0). He wounded himself and his mules, drove into the Agora claiming an ambush, and on Aristion's motion was voted a bodyguard of club-bearers, with which he seized the Acropolis. He ruled without disturbing the offices until Megacles and Lycurgus combined to expel him, in the sixth year (Athenaion Politeia 14.3).
  2. Second attempt. Megacles, losing to Lycurgus, offered Peisistratus his daughter and restoration. A tall woman, Phye of Paeania, was dressed as Athena and driven into the city with heralds announcing the goddess was bringing Peisistratus home; Herodotus (1.60) calls it by far the silliest trick ever played on people reputed the cleverest in Greece. Peisistratus refused to have children by the Alcmaeonid bride, Megacles turned, and Peisistratus left Attica.
  3. Third attempt (c. 546). Ten years of exile: Rhaecelus on the Thermaic Gulf, silver from Mount Pangaeum, money and men from Thebes, Eretria, Lygdamis of Naxos and Argos. Landing at Marathon, he caught the Athenians at Pallene after their midday meal and routed them (Herodotus 1.62–63), then lodged hostage sons of his opponents with Lygdamis, whom he made tyrant of Naxos.
Where sources disagree. Athenaion Politeia 17.1 gives thirty-three years from first coup to death, nineteen in power; Aristotle, Politics 1315b, gives seventeen in power. Herodotus' exile lengths and the archon-dated intervals cannot all be reconciled; 561/0, 546/5 and 527/6 are conventions.

Herodotus says Peisistratus governed by the existing laws and governed well; Athenaion Politeia 16 calls his rule "the age of Cronus" and credits loans to small farmers, travelling deme judges, and a policy of keeping the people busy in the countryside. Thucydides 6.54.6 adds that a Peisistratid always held one of the offices. Athenaion Politeia 16.4 has him take a tithe on produce; Thucydides 6.54.5 says a twentieth, perhaps a reduction under the sons.

The Panathenaia, Homer and the buildings

The Great Panathenaia, every fourth year with athletic and musical contests, was reorganised in 566/5 under the archon Hippocleides (Pherecydes, FGrH 3 F 2), before the first coup; the tyrants enlarged it. Plato's Hipparchus (228b–c) says Hipparchus made the rhapsodes recite Homer at the festival in relay, each taking up where the last stopped, and brought Anacreon and Simonides to Athens.

Where sources disagree. Cicero (De oratore 3.137), Pausanias 7.26.13 and the scholia credit Peisistratus with first assembling the books of Homer, the "Peisistratean recension". No source before the Hellenistic period mentions it; Davison and West treat it as a late construction, Merkelbach defended a core, and Nagy's model gives the Panathenaic rule a real part in fixing the text without any editor. The performance is attested; the edition is not.

The buildings are attested in stone. Peisistratus the Younger, the tyrant's grandson, as archon in 522/1 dedicated the Altar of the Twelve Gods in the Agora and the altar of Pythian Apollo, whose inscribed base survives (Thucydides 6.54.6–7). The dynasty began the colossal Olympieion, which Aristotle (Politics 1313b) lists among tyrants' devices for keeping subjects busy; the Enneakrounos fountain-house (Pausanias 1.14.1), the first telesterion at Eleusis and work at Brauron belong to them. Hipparchus set herms along the roads inscribed with maxims such as "walk thinking just thoughts" (Plato, Hipparchus 228d–229b).

Hippias, Hipparchus and the tyrannicides

Peisistratus died in 527/6 and his eldest son Hippias ruled, with Hipparchus as patron of poets and Thessalus, son of an Argive wife, as a hot-headed third. Thucydides (1.20, 6.54–59) insists on Hippias' rule against the popular belief that Hipparchus was tyrant when killed.

In 514, at the Great Panathenaia, Harmodius and Aristogeiton, Gephyraeans, killed Hipparchus by the Leocoreion as he marshalled the procession (Herodotus 5.55–56; Thucydides 6.56–57). Thucydides' motive is a love quarrel: Hipparchus courted Harmodius, Aristogeiton's beloved, was rebuffed, and had Harmodius' sister publicly barred from carrying a basket in the procession. The plotters meant to kill Hippias too, panicked when they saw an accomplice chatting with him, and struck only Hipparchus. Harmodius died on the spot, Aristogeiton under torture. Herodotus 5.55 and Thucydides 6.59 agree the tyranny then grew harsher: executions, disarmament of the citizens (Athenaion Politeia 18.4), and a marriage alliance with Lampsacus for its influence with Darius.

Where sources disagree. Athenaion Politeia 18 makes Thessalus, not Hipparchus, the rejected lover who insulted Harmodius, and adds that Aristogeiton under torture named Hippias' own friends so that the tyrant killed his supporters. Thucydides wrote his digression precisely because most Athenians had the facts wrong. Which brother gave the insult is unrecoverable.

The legend was built after 510. Antenor's bronze pair, the first statues of mortals in the Agora, was carried off by Xerxes and replaced by Kritios and Nesiotes in 477/6; the descendants received meals in the Prytaneion and tax exemption (Demosthenes 20.18); drinking songs sang that they "killed the tyrant and made Athens isonomous" (PMG 893–896). Herodotus 6.123 protests that the pair only enraged the surviving Peisistratids and that the Alcmaeonids were the real liberators. Two families and a city were competing for credit, and the tyrannicides won because they were dead, Athenian and unembarrassing, whereas the truth involved Sparta and a cursed aristocratic house.

Sparta, Isagoras and the reforms of Cleisthenes

The exiled Alcmaeonids failed by force at Leipsydrion (Athenaion Politeia 19.3), then rebuilt the Delphic temple and, Herodotus says (5.62–63), bribed the Pythia to tell every Spartan enquirer to free Athens. Sparta's first expedition, by sea under Anchimolius, was destroyed at Phalerum by Thessalian cavalry; the second, under King Cleomenes, besieged the Peisistratids on the Acropolis, captured their children being smuggled out, and forced Hippias to leave for Sigeum within five days (Herodotus 5.64–65; Athenaion Politeia 19.5–6), in 511/10.

Two aristocrats then fought for the city: Isagoras son of Teisander, archon for 508/7, and Cleisthenes the Alcmaeonid, grandson of the tyrant of Sicyon. Herodotus 5.66 says Cleisthenes, losing in the contest of aristocratic clubs, "took the demos into his faction" and set about reforming the tribes. Isagoras summoned Cleomenes, who demanded expulsion of the "accursed"; Cleisthenes withdrew, seven hundred households were driven out, and Cleomenes tried to dissolve the Council and install three hundred of Isagoras' friends. The Council refused, the people rose, and the Spartans and Isagoras were besieged on the Acropolis and let out under truce on the third day; their Athenian allies were executed (Herodotus 5.70–73; Athenaion Politeia 20). Cleisthenes was recalled; Cleomenes' revenge invasion of 506 collapsed at Eleusis when the Corinthians went home (Herodotus 5.74–77).

Where sources disagree. Herodotus puts the reforms before Cleomenes' intervention; Athenaion Politeia 20–21 puts them after, in Isagoras' archonship. The "Boule" that defied Cleomenes may therefore be the Solonian 400 (Rhodes) or the new 500 (Wade-Gery). Herodotus 5.73 also records an Athenian embassy to Sardis offering alliance to Persia, which the democratic tradition preferred to forget.

The reforms

Athenaion Politeia 21 gives the structure. Ten new tribes replaced the four Ionian tribes; the Pythia chose their eponymous heroes from a list of a hundred. Attica's villages became about 139 demes, each with a demarch, a register and an assembly. Membership was hereditary, so a man kept his deme wherever he moved, and citizens were to be named by deme rather than father so that the newly enrolled could not be exposed. Demes were grouped into thirty trittyes, ten each from city, coast and inland, and every tribe drew one trittys from each region by lot. The Council of 500 took fifty from each tribe; phratries, clans and priesthoods were left alone. Ten tribal regiments followed, and from 501/0 ten generals, one per tribe, and the bouleutic oath (Athenaion Politeia 22.2). Athenaion Politeia 22.1 adds ostracism: the assembly voted yearly whether to hold one, a quorum of six thousand scratched names on sherds, and the man named most often left for ten years without losing his property.

Where sources disagree. Ostracism was first used in 487, against the Peisistratid connection Hipparchus son of Charmus, and Athenaion Politeia strains to explain the twenty-year gap. Androtion (FGrH 324 F 6) seems to date the law to just before 487; Rhodes thinks Harpocration misreports him, others take Androtion literally. On motives, D. M. Lewis showed that trittys boundaries sometimes cut across rival clans' cult centres while keeping Alcmaeonid strongholds together, a gerrymander; Andrewes saw rational administration. Both may be true.

The problem solved is the one this module has traced: regional aristocratic power. Plain, Coast and Hill had each been a geographical bloc of dependants; once every tribe had to contain city, coast and inland demes, no district could become a faction. The deme register also settled the status of men of doubtful descent whom a review in 510 had threatened. Herodotus compares the renaming to Cleisthenes of Sicyon's, done from contempt; Athenaion Politeia says the aim was "to mix up the people so that more should share in the state". The second is the better explanation.

The earliest meaning of "demokratia"

The word does not occur in the sixth century. Herodotus 6.131 says Cleisthenes "set up the tribes and the democracy", but that is fifth-century usage. The drinking songs of the 500s praise the tyrannicides for making Athens isonomos; isonomia, equal share in the law, is the term Otanes uses for popular rule in Herodotus 3.80 and Aristagoras at Miletus (5.37); isegoria, equal right to speak, is Herodotus' own word for what made Athens strong after 510 (5.78). Aeschylus, Suppliants 604 (463), has "the people's ruling hand" as a periphrasis; Herodotus 6.43 applies demokratia to the regimes Mardonius set up in Ionia in 492; and an Athenian named Demokrates was born about 470. The compound belongs to the 470s or 460s.

Kratos is power or victory, not mere rule: Sealey argues the word was coined by opponents to mean the mob's grip, Hansen holds it neutral from the start. And demos meant both the whole citizen body and the common people against the few, carrying both senses at once. What Cleisthenes made was not called democracy by its makers; it was a reorganisation of the citizen body that gave the whole demos machinery to act. Herodotus' generation named it and credited Cleisthenes; the fourth century, uneasy with the radical version, moved the founding back to Solon (Athenaion Politeia 9; Mossé). Both attributions are retrospective.

Self-test

  1. What is the only law of Draco known to have survived Solon's repeal, and how do we know its text?
    Answer

    The homicide law. It was reinscribed on stone in 409/8 (IG I³ 104), and Athenaion Politeia 7.1 and Plutarch, Solon 17 say Solon kept only the homicide laws.

  2. Why do most scholars reject Athenaion Politeia 4, the "constitution of Draco"?
    Answer

    It presupposes coinage Athens did not yet have, matches the oligarchic programme of 411 (a council of about 400, citizenship for those bearing arms) and is unknown to Aristotle's Politics; it is regarded as a late insertion.

  3. Name Solon's three "most democratic" measures according to Athenaion Politeia 9.
    Answer

    The ban on loans secured on the person; the right of any volunteer (ho boulomenos) to prosecute on behalf of a wronged party; and ephesis, appeal to the people's court (dikasterion or Heliaia).

  4. List Solon's four property classes with their qualifications.
    Answer

    Pentakosiomedimnoi (500 measures), hippeis (300), zeugitai (200), thetes (below 200; assembly and courts only).

  5. Who led the three regional factions after Solon, and which groups did Athenaion Politeia place in the Hill party?
    Answer

    Lycurgus son of Aristolaides (Plain), Megacles son of Alcmaeon (Coast), Peisistratus (Hill). The Hill party included the poorest and those of doubtful descent who feared a review of the citizen roll.

  6. Describe the trick by which Peisistratus returned the second time, and Herodotus' verdict on it.
    Answer

    A tall woman, Phye, was dressed as Athena and driven in a chariot into Athens with heralds proclaiming the goddess was restoring Peisistratus. Herodotus 1.60 called it by far the silliest trick ever played on people reputed the cleverest in Greece.

  7. What does the "Peisistratean recension" claim, and what is its evidential status?
    Answer

    That Peisistratus first collected and arranged the books of Homer (Cicero, De oratore 3.137; Pausanias 7.26.13). No source before the Hellenistic period mentions it; most scholars regard it as a later construction, though the Panathenaic recitation rule (Plato, Hipparchus 228b) is genuine.

  8. On what two points does Thucydides correct the popular Athenian story of the tyrannicides?
    Answer

    That Hippias, not Hipparchus, was the ruling tyrant in 514; and that the murder arose from a love quarrel and panic, not a planned liberation, after which the tyranny grew harsher. Herodotus 6.123 adds that the Alcmaeonids, not the pair, actually freed Athens.

  9. What were the trittyes, and what political problem did they address?
    Answer

    Thirty groups of demes, ten each from city, coast and inland; each tribe took one from each region by lot. This broke up the regional blocs that had sustained the factions of Plain, Coast and Hill.

  10. Why is the Cleisthenic date of ostracism disputed?
    Answer

    Athenaion Politeia 22.1 credits the law to Cleisthenes, but it was first used in 487, twenty years later; Androtion seems to date the law to just before 487, and scholars disagree over whether Harpocration's report of Androtion is accurate.

Carry forward

  1. Athenian constitutional history is reconstructed from writers two to four centuries later (Athenaion Politeia, Plutarch) who projected the needs of their own day back onto Draco, Solon and Cleisthenes; only Solon's verses are contemporary. Always ask who is remembering and why.
  2. The Cleisthenic tribes, trittyes, demes and Council of 500 are the skeleton of every later Athenian institution: the army, the generals, the courts, the Council's prytanies and the citizen's very name all run through them.
  3. Rival memories of the liberation of 510 (tyrannicides, Alcmaeonids, Sparta) show how a city invents its founding story; the same contest over credit, and over the words isonomia and demokratia, continues into the fifth century.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Athens from Draco to the reforms of Cleisthenes, c. 620 to 500 BC. Cover: Draco's code; the crisis of debt bondage; Solon's reforms in detail (the seisachtheia, the four property classes, the Council of 400, the Heliaia, the right of appeal) and his own poetry; the regional factions; Peisistratus' three attempts at tyranny and his rule, including the Panathenaia, the Homeric recension and the building programme; Hippias and Hipparchus, the tyrannicides and the invention of that myth; the Spartan intervention and Isagoras; Cleisthenes' reforms (the ten tribes, the demes, the trittyes, the Council of 500, ostracism) and what problem they solved; and the earliest meaning of "demokratia". Use Herodotus, the Athenaion Politeia and Plutarch's Solon. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 5 · The Archaic age, 800 to 480 BC · 5.6 · 3,024 words

Lyric poets and the first philosophers

The lyric age and its genresThe symposium as settingThe poets, in orderWhat is new compared with epicWhy philosophy began in IoniaThe Milesians and PythagorasFrom the critique of the gods to the denial of changeEmpedocles, Anaxagoras, DemocritusSelf-testCarry forward

The lyric age and its genres

Between roughly 700 and 450 BC the Greek world produced two things it had not produced before: short poems in which a named individual speaks about the present, and prose arguments about what the world is made of. Both arose on the same Aegean coasts and were carried by the same institutions. The Greeks did not call the first group "lyric" in our sense. For Alexandrian scholars lyrikos meant song to the lyre, and their canon of nine (Alcman, Alcaeus, Sappho, Stesichorus, Ibycus, Anacreon, Simonides, Pindar, Bacchylides) excluded Archilochus, Tyrtaeus, Solon and Theognis, whose metres were recited or sung to the pipe.

Five genres matter. Elegy uses the elegiac couplet, was accompanied by the aulos, and ranges from battlefield exhortation (Tyrtaeus) to political reflection (Solon) and erotic complaint (Mimnermus). Iambus is defined less by its iambic and trochaic metres than by occasion and tone: abuse, obscenity, mock-narrative. Its home was Paros and the cult of Demeter, where ritual insult was licensed. Monody is solo song to the lyre in short stanzas, perfected on Lesbos by Sappho and Alcaeus in Aeolic dialect. Choral lyric was composed for a trained chorus that sang and danced at public festivals; its idiom is Doric-coloured and its scale larger, with myth and prayer woven round the occasion. Epinician, the victory ode for an athlete at the four great games, emerges last, in the late sixth century, as choral lyric commissioned by the very rich.

Where sources disagree. M. L. West (Studies in Greek Elegy and Iambus, 1974) argued that iambos names a genre of performance context, not a metre, since Archilochus used elegiacs for abuse too. Others keep the metrical definition. Whether Sappho's songs were solo pieces for a circle of girls or choral pieces for public occasions is also contested; André Lardinois has argued for a larger choral share than the traditional "monodic Sappho" allows.

The symposium as setting

Most of this poetry was first heard at the symposium, the after-dinner drinking party of aristocratic men. Seven to fifteen guests reclined in the andron, wine was mixed with water in a krater under a symposiarch, and the evening moved through libations, songs passed round with a myrtle branch, kottabos, flute-girls and talk. Xenophanes fr. 1 describes the clean floor, garlands and incense, and the rule that one should drink only as much as lets one walk home unaided. Alcaeus fr. 346 opens

Let us drink. Why wait for the lamps? There is a finger of daylight left.
Theognis addresses fellow drinkers; Anacreon's whole persona is sympotic; the Attic skolia, including the Harmodius song, were sympotic rounds.

The setting explains the poems' brevity, their address to a named companion, their audience of equals, their factional politics and their erotic code. It also explains preservation: songs that pleased were resung for generations, which is why the Theognidean corpus accreted. Oswyn Murray's Sympotica (1990) is the standard collection.

Archilochus is dated by his mention of a total eclipse (fr. 122), almost certainly that of 648. He fought as a mercenary on Thasos, threw away his shield and said so (fr. 5), preferred a short bow-legged captain to a tall preening one (fr. 114), and feuded with Lycambes, who had broken off a marriage to his daughter Neobule; the Cologne epode (fr. 196a) narrates the seduction of her younger sister. Tyrtaeus wrote for Spartans in the Second Messenian War: fr. 10 and 12 reshape Homeric vocabulary into an ethic of dying in the front rank for the city. Alcman's Louvre Partheneion (fr. 1), sung by a chorus of girls, praises their leaders Hagesichora and Agido with sunrise and racehorse imagery.

Sappho composed nine books, of which one complete poem (fr. 1, the prayer to Aphrodite, preserved by Dionysius of Halicarnassus) and a few near-complete ones survive, swelled by papyri published in 2004 and 2014. Fr. 16 argues that the most beautiful thing is whatever one loves, taking Helen as proof; fr. 31, quoted in On the Sublime 10, inventories the body's collapse at the sight of a beloved girl. Alcaeus, her contemporary in Mytilene, fought the tyrants Melanchrus and Myrsilus and then his former ally Pittacus; fr. 332 exults over Myrsilus' death, fr. 129 curses Pittacus from exile, and fr. 6 gives the first ship-of-state allegory.

Mimnermus is the poet of youth's brevity: we are like leaves in spring (fr. 2). Solon answered him, wishing for eighty years rather than sixty (fr. 20), and used verse for politics: fr. 4 analyses Athenian dysnomia, fr. 13 asks the Muses for honest wealth, and fr. 36, in iambic trimeters, calls the black Earth to witness that he pulled up her boundary stones. Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 5–12, quotes him as evidence. Theognis addresses the boy Cyrnus with aristocratic advice about trusting no one; the 1,400 surviving lines are an anthology grown around a sixth-century core.

Anacreon served Polycrates of Samos and then the Pisistratids, singing of Eros throwing a purple ball (fr. 358) and a Thracian filly who needs a rider (fr. 417). Simonides is the first professional across genres: epinicians, laments (the Danae fragment, fr. 543), Persian War epigrams and the recovered Plataea elegy (fr. 11 West). Pindar's forty-five epinicians survive complete because schools read them: Olympian 1 for Hieron of Syracuse (476) retells and corrects the Tantalus myth; Pythian 1 (470) describes Etna's eruption. Bacchylides, Simonides' nephew, was almost lost until a papyrus reached the British Museum in 1896; Ode 5 celebrates the same Hieron victory as Olympian 1.

Where sources disagree. Theognis' date is uncertain: the Suda places him c. 540, but internal allusions have been used for dates from the 630s to the 480s, and West treats the corpus as stratified. The Thermopylae couplet "Go tell the Spartans" is ascribed to Simonides only by late sources; Herodotus 7.228 names him only for the epigram to the seer Megistias.

What is new compared with epic

Four things. First, the present: epic narrates a heroic past in a timeless formulaic dialect; lyric speaks of this war, this party, this girl, in local dialect. Second, the speaking I: Homer never names himself; Archilochus, Sappho and Alcaeus speak in their own names about their own feelings, and Sappho fr. 31 is the first sustained description of an inner physiological state in Western literature. Third, revaluation: Archilochus' lost shield, Sappho's preference of the beloved to cavalry, Xenophanes' claim (fr. 2) that a wise man is worth more to a city than an Olympic victor, Tyrtaeus' transfer of arete from the champion to the hoplite line, all bend Homeric values to the polis and the person. Fourth, form: dozens of metres instead of one, strophic music instead of recitation, a scale in lines rather than books.

Where sources disagree. Bruno Snell (The Discovery of the Mind, 1946) read this as the birth of individual self-consciousness. Kenneth Dover and West replied that the lyric "I" is often a performed persona: Lycambes and Neobule may be stock iambic figures, and sympotic song lends its singer a borrowed voice. Gregory Nagy adds that reperformance detaches the "I" from any one historical speaker. The truth is probably in between, and differs poet by poet.

Why philosophy began in Ionia

Miletus around 600 was the richest Greek city: colonies across the Black Sea, Lydia next door, a trading post at Naucratis in Egypt, overland routes from Mesopotamia. Babylonian eclipse records and Egyptian land-measurement were available to anyone who asked, and Herodotus says Thales did (2.109; 1.74 for his prediction of the 585 eclipse). But borrowed data does not explain the leap to asking what everything is, and three further conditions are usually cited. Ionia had no priestly class with a monopoly on cosmology; Hesiod's Theogony already offered a systematic account, and the Milesians dropped the gods from the system. The polis gave public argument prestige: G. E. R. Lloyd (Magic, Reason and Experience, 1979) argued that open debate in assembly and lawcourt bred a culture in which rival accounts competed before an audience, and Jean-Pierre Vernant linked Anaximander's cosmos, with the earth held at the centre by symmetry, to the ideal of isonomia. Alphabetic writing let a short prose book travel and be criticised by name: Heraclitus attacks Hesiod, Pythagoras, Xenophanes and Hecataeus in one fragment (B40).

Where sources disagree. How much is Near Eastern inheritance is still argued: Walter Burkert and M. L. West (Early Greek Philosophy and the Orient, 1971) stress Iranian and Babylonian parallels; others hold that the move to an impersonal, argued cosmology has no clear eastern precedent. The eclipse prediction is doubted by most historians of astronomy, since no method then available could fix a solar eclipse's visibility at a given place.

The Milesians and Pythagoras

The Milesians are known through Aristotle (Metaphysics A 3, 983b–984a), Theophrastus' lost Physical Opinions and later compilers such as Simplicius and Diogenes Laertius, cited by Diels–Kranz (DK) numbers. "Presocratic" is a modern label; Democritus outlived Socrates.

Thales (fl. 585): everything comes from water, the earth floats on water, and the magnet shows that soul-like power pervades matter: "all things are full of gods" (Aristotle, On the Soul 405a, 411a). No writing of his survived even in antiquity. Anaximander (c. 610–546): the source is the apeiron, the boundless, which is no named stuff; from it opposites separate out and pay each other penalty for injustice "according to the assessment of time" (B1, via Simplicius). The drum-shaped earth stays put because it is equidistant from everything and has no reason to move (Aristotle, On the Heavens 295b), the first argument from sufficient reason. Anaximenes (fl. 546): the source is air, which becomes fire by rarefaction and wind, cloud, water, earth and stone by condensation. This is the first mechanism: a process by which one stuff becomes the appearances of many.

Pythagoras (c. 570–495) left Samos for Croton about 530 and founded a community with rules of secrecy, diet and conduct. He wrote nothing. Two doctrines are securely his: transmigration of souls, mocked already by Xenophanes (B7), who has him recognise a dead friend's voice in a beaten puppy; and the belief that number and ratio underlie reality, which Aristotle attributes to "the so-called Pythagoreans" (Metaphysics 985b–986a) and connects to the discovery that musical concords are whole-number ratios.

Where sources disagree. Aristotle imposes his own category of material cause on Thales; whether Thales meant that things originated from water or still are water is unknowable. On Pythagoras, Burkert's Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (1972) argued that the historical man was a religious wonder-worker and the mathematics was credited to him by Platonists; Leonid Zhmud has defended a genuinely mathematical Pythagoras. The theorem's attribution rests on sources a thousand years later.

From the critique of the gods to the denial of change

Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570–475), a wandering poet, turned Ionian inquiry on religion. Homer and Hesiod attributed theft, adultery and deceit to the gods (B11); Ethiopians make their gods snub-nosed and black, Thracians blue-eyed and red-haired (B16); if oxen and horses had hands they would draw gods like oxen and horses (B15). Against this he set one god, greatest among gods and men, unlike mortals in body or thought, who sees, hears and thinks as a whole and shakes everything by thought without moving (B23–26). He observed sea-shells inland (Hippolytus, Refutation 1.14) and inferred that the earth had once been mud. B34 is the first statement of epistemic humility: no man has seen the clear truth about the gods, and one who spoke it would not know.

Heraclitus of Ephesus (fl. c. 500) wrote aphorisms designed to be hard. The logos, the account according to which all things happen, is common to all, yet men live as if they had private understanding (B1, B2). Opposites are one: the road up and down (B60), sea water purest and foulest (B61). Everything is in exchange like goods for gold (B90), and the exchange is fire, "kindling in measures and going out in measures" (B30). Strife is justice (B80); war is father of all (B53). The river fragment B12 says that on those who step into the same rivers different waters flow, a statement about identity through change rather than its denial. He despised polymathy without understanding (B40) and held the soul deep beyond finding (B45).

Where sources disagree. Plato (Cratylus 402a) made Heraclitus the philosopher of universal flux, and the slogan panta rhei and the "cannot step twice" version (B91, via Plutarch) are probably Platonic sharpenings. G. S. Kirk and Miroslav Marcovich argued that the genuine fragments emphasise measure and stability within change; Karl Popper and Jonathan Barnes defended the radical reading. Whether Xenophanes was a monotheist or merely posited a supreme god among lesser ones (B23 says "among gods and men") is also unresolved; Aristotle complained that he "made nothing clear" (Metaphysics 986b).

Parmenides of Elea (born c. 515) wrote a hexameter poem in which a goddess instructs the poet after a chariot ride to the gates of Night and Day. The Way of Truth (B2, B8, preserved by Simplicius) argues from one decision: either it is, or it is not; "it is not" cannot be thought or said, since one cannot think nothing (B3). Therefore what-is is ungenerated (from what could it have come?), imperishable, continuous, unmoving, complete, like a well-rounded ball. Coming-to-be, perishing and change are names mortals have laid down (B8.38–41). The Way of Opinion that follows gives a cosmology of Light and Night which the goddess calls deceptive; it contains the first correct statement that the moon shines with borrowed light (B14–15). Zeno of Elea (c. 490–430), his pupil, defended this by reducing plurality and motion to absurdity. Aristotle (Physics 239b) preserves the four motion paradoxes: the Dichotomy (to cross a stadium one must first cross half, then half the remainder, without end), the Achilles, the Arrow (at each instant it occupies a space equal to itself, so is at rest) and the Moving Rows. Simplicius preserves the plurality arguments: if things are many they are both infinitely small and infinitely large (B1–2).

Where sources disagree. G. E. L. Owen and Barnes read Parmenides as a strict numerical monist (only one thing exists); Patricia Curd's "predicational monism" holds that each real thing must be one and unchanging, which makes the pluralists his heirs rather than opponents. The status of the Doxa, best-possible physics or demonstration of error, is also open. Aristotle's answer to Zeno, that a line is only potentially infinitely divisible, has not satisfied everyone.

Empedocles, Anaxagoras, Democritus

After Parmenides, a physicist had to explain change without letting anything come from nothing. Three answers followed.

ThinkerUnchanging realsSource of changeKey fragments
Empedoclesfour roots: earth, water, air, fireLove and Strife, in a cosmic cycleB6, B17, B115, B117
Anaxagorasinfinitely many seeds, "everything in everything"Mind (Nous) starts a rotationB11, B12, B17
Leucippus and Democritusatoms and voidcollision and entanglement by necessityB9, B125, B118

Empedocles of Acragas (c. 492–432) kept Parmenides' ban on generation by making four eternal "roots" (B6) mix and separate under Love and Strife, which alternately dominate in a cycle (B17). In the stage of separating Strife, limbs wander alone, "faces without necks" (B57), and only viable combinations survive. Perception works by effluences fitting pores (B89). He also wrote as a fallen god, exiled thirty thousand seasons for bloodshed (B115), who has been "boy and girl, bush, bird and silent fish" (B117), and forbade eating flesh as kin-murder (B137). The tale that he died leaping into Etna (Diogenes Laertius 8.69) is legend.

Anaxagoras of Clazomenae (c. 500–428) moved to Athens, taught Pericles, and was prosecuted for impiety for saying the sun is a fiery stone larger than the Peloponnese (Plutarch, Pericles 32). His core claim: nothing comes to be or perishes, but things are mixed and separated (B17); in everything there is a portion of everything (B11), so hair can grow from food; and the original mass was set spinning by Mind, "unlimited, self-ruling and mixed with nothing" (B12). Socrates in Plato's Phaedo (97b–98c) records his disappointment that Anaxagoras introduced Mind and then explained everything mechanically.

Democritus of Abdera (c. 460–370), building on the shadowy Leucippus, answered Parmenides and Zeno at once: reality is uncuttable bodies (atoma) moving in void, differing only in shape, arrangement and position, as A and N, AN and NA, N and Z differ (Aristotle, Metaphysics 985b). Atoms collide, rebound and tangle into infinite worlds by necessity. Sensible qualities are not in things: "by convention sweet, by convention bitter; in reality atoms and void" (B9), to which the senses reply, "wretched mind, you take your evidence from us and then throw us down" (B125). He would rather find one causal explanation than gain the kingdom of Persia (B118).

Where sources disagree. The Strasbourg papyrus of Empedocles (published 1999) has reopened whether On Nature and Purifications were two poems or one; Catherine Osborne and Brad Inwood argue for one. Anaxagoras' trial is placed anywhere from the 450s to 431 and is doubted outright by Jaap Mansfeld. Epicurus denied that Leucippus ever existed (Diogenes Laertius 10.13). Whether Democritus' atoms were physically or conceptually indivisible, and so whether he had really answered Zeno, is argued by David Furley and others.

Self-test

  1. Which lyric poets did the Alexandrian canon of nine exclude, and why?
    Answer

    Archilochus, Tyrtaeus, Mimnermus, Solon and Theognis, because elegy and iambus were recited or sung to the pipe, not sung to the lyre, so were not lyrikos in the strict ancient sense.

  2. How is Archilochus dated, and to what year?
    Answer

    By his reference to a total solar eclipse in fr. 122 West, almost certainly that of 648 BC.

  3. What is the argument of Sappho fr. 16?
    Answer

    That the most beautiful thing on earth is whatever one loves, proved by Helen's choice of Paris over her family, and applied to the absent Anactoria, whom the speaker prefers to Lydian chariots and infantry.

  4. In which fragment and metre does Solon defend his reforms, and whom does he call as witness?
    Answer

    Fr. 36 West, in iambic trimeters; he calls the black Earth, from whom he pulled up the boundary stones, as witness before the court of Time.

  5. Name the four conditions usually cited for the birth of philosophy in Ionia.
    Answer

    Contact with Egyptian and Babylonian knowledge through trade; the absence of a priestly monopoly on cosmology; the polis culture of open public argument (Lloyd, Vernant); and alphabetic literacy enabling short prose books to circulate and be criticised by name.

  6. What is Anaximander's argument for why the earth stays where it is?
    Answer

    It is equidistant from everything at the extremes and so has no more reason to move in one direction than another (Aristotle, On the Heavens 295b), the first argument from sufficient reason.

  7. What did Xenophanes infer from sea-shells found inland?
    Answer

    That land and sea had once been mixed and the earth had been mud, so that the earth undergoes long cycles of change (Hippolytus, Refutation 1.14).

  8. Why do Kirk and Marcovich doubt that Heraclitus taught universal flux?
    Answer

    Because the genuine fragments (B12, B30, B90) stress measure, exchange and identity through change, while the slogan panta rhei and the "cannot step twice" formulation come from Plato (Cratylus 402a) and Plutarch rather than from Heraclitus' own words.

  9. State Parmenides' central inference in two steps.
    Answer

    "It is not" cannot be thought or said, since nothing cannot be thought (B2, B3); therefore what-is cannot have come from or pass into what-is-not, and so is ungenerated, imperishable, unmoving and complete (B8).

  10. How does Democritus explain the difference between things made of the same atoms?
    Answer

    By shape, arrangement and position of atoms, which Aristotle illustrates with letters: A differs from N in shape, AN from NA in order, N from Z in position (Metaphysics 985b).

Carry forward

  1. Archaic lyric and Ionian philosophy are products of the same world: the polis, the symposium and the Aegean trade routes gave a named individual the standing to speak in the present tense and to argue in public, which is why Xenophanes is both a sympotic poet and a critic of Homer's gods.
  2. Parmenides is the hinge of Greek thought. Every later physics (Empedocles, Anaxagoras, the atomists) is an attempt to allow change while obeying his ban on coming-to-be from nothing, and Plato's Forms and Aristotle's analysis of change both start from him.
  3. Almost everything here survives in fragments quoted by later writers with their own agendas, Aristotle and Plato above all; always ask who is quoting, why, and what frame they have imposed before treating a Presocratic "doctrine" or a lyric "confession" as the author's own.

GREECE · UNIT 6 · The Classical age, 480 to 323 BC · 6.1 · 2,765 words

The Persian Wars

The empire that came west: Cyrus, Cambyses, DariusThe Ionian Revolt and the burning of Sardis, 499–494The first expedition and Marathon, 490The interwar decade: Themistocles, Laurion, ostracismXerxes' invasion: canal, bridges, Thermopylae, Artemisium, 480The evacuation of Athens and SalamisPlataea, Mycale and the Serpent Column, 479Herodotus: method, sources, biases, trustThe war and Greek identity; the Athenian claimSelf-testCarry forward

The empire that came west: Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius

Herodotus opens with Cyrus (Book 1) because his whole work asks how a people the Greeks had scarcely heard of in 560 BC came to stand in Attica in 490. Cyrus overthrew the Median king Astyages (c. 550), defeated Croesus of Lydia and took Sardis (c. 546; Herodotus 1.84–86), and with Lydia inherited the Greek cities of the Ionian coast, which Croesus had made tributary. Babylon fell in 539 (1.188–191).

Cambyses (530–522) added Egypt (Book 3). Herodotus' portrait of him as a madman who stabbed the Apis bull is probably Egyptian priestly polemic; Egyptian evidence shows a conventional king.

Darius (522–486) came to the throne through the murder of a man who was either a usurping Magus or, as the more sceptical reading of his own Behistun inscription suggests, the real brother of Cambyses. Herodotus 3.70–88 tells of the seven conspirators; Behistun gives Darius' version. He organised satrapies with fixed tribute (3.89–97) and pushed west: a Scythian expedition across the Danube (Book 4), then Thrace and Macedon. By 500 the Ionian Greeks were the empire's westernmost subjects.

Where sources disagree. Herodotus (3.80–82) has the conspirators debate monarchy, oligarchy and democracy, and insists the debate happened though "some Greeks do not believe" it. Most scholars treat it as fifth-century Greek material, not Persian tradition.

The Ionian Revolt and the burning of Sardis, 499–494

The revolt began not from a surge of liberty but from the private trouble of Aristagoras, tyrant of Miletus, who had promised Artaphernes, satrap at Sardis, an easy conquest of Naxos and failed (Herodotus 5.30–35). Facing ruin, he raised Ionia, abolished the tyrannies, and went begging for help. Sparta refused (5.49–51). Athens sent twenty ships, Eretria five.

In 498 the Ionians and Athenians marched up from Ephesus and took Sardis. A soldier set fire to a reed-roofed house, the flames spread, and the temple of Cybebe burned with the city (5.100–102). The Greeks were beaten near Ephesus and the Athenians went home. Herodotus' set-piece is Darius hearing the news, shooting an arrow into the sky, praying to be allowed to punish the Athenians, and ordering a servant to say to him three times at every dinner, "Master, remember the Athenians" (5.105).

The revolt was ground down; the decisive battle was at sea off Lade in 494, where the Samian contingent deserted (6.7–17); Miletus was stormed, its men killed, its women and children deported to the Persian Gulf (6.18–20). Herodotus calls the Athenian ships the "beginning of evils" for Greeks and barbarians (5.97).

Where sources disagree. Herodotus treats the revolt as Aristagoras' opportunism; modern historians, following hints at 5.28 and the fact that the Ionians abolished tyranny everywhere, see economic pressure from Persian control of Black Sea trade and resentment of satrap-backed tyrants. Herodotus' contempt for Ionians (1.143) probably colours his reading.

The first expedition and Marathon, 490

Darius' first attempt, under his son-in-law Mardonius in 492, took Thasos and Macedon but lost its fleet in a storm off Mount Athos (6.43–45). In 490 Datis and Artaphernes sailed straight across the Aegean instead, with Hippias, the aged exiled tyrant of Athens, aboard. They burned Eretria (6.101) and Hippias guided them to the plain of Marathon (6.102).

The Athenians marched out under the polemarch Callimachus and ten generals including Miltiades. Before leaving they sent the runner Philippides to Sparta; he arrived the next day (6.105–106). The Spartans said they would come, but not before the full moon ended the Carneia festival. The Plataeans came in full force. The generals were split five to five; Miltiades won Callimachus' casting vote (6.109) and attacked on his own day of command.

Herodotus' battle is brief (6.111–117). The Athenians thinned their centre to match the Persian line and stacked the wings. They advanced "at a run" across roughly eight stades. The centre gave way to the Persians and Sacae; the wings won, turned inward and routed the enemy to the ships, where Callimachus died. Herodotus counts 6,400 Persian dead and 192 Athenian. The fleet rounded Sunium to attempt Athens, found the army already back, and went home. Two thousand Spartans arrived after the full moon, viewed the dead and praised the Athenians (6.120).

Miltiades' triumph lasted a year. He failed at Paros, was prosecuted by Xanthippus, fined fifty talents, and died of a wound (6.132–136).

Where sources disagree. The run from Marathon to Athens with the news and the runner's dying word is not in Herodotus. It first appears in Plutarch (On the Glory of Athens 347c), who names the runner Thersippus or Eucles, and in Lucian (On a Slip of the Tongue 3), who calls him Philippides and so fuses two stories. The modern marathon rests on Lucian. Herodotus' "run" is the whole phalanx charging. The Persian cavalry's absence from his battle is unexplained.

The interwar decade: Themistocles, Laurion, ostracism

Darius died in 486; Xerxes spent his first years on an Egyptian revolt, and Athens used the pause. Themistocles, archon in 493/2, had already begun fortifying Piraeus in preference to the open beach at Phalerum (Thucydides 1.93). In 483/2 a rich new vein of silver was struck at Maroneia in the Laurion mines. Themistocles persuaded the assembly to build two hundred warships with the surplus rather than distribute ten drachmas a head, ostensibly for the war with Aegina (7.144); Herodotus calls it the decision that saved Greece. Aristotle (Constitution of the Athenians 22.7) gives a different mechanism: a hundred talents lent to a hundred rich citizens, each to build a trireme. The figures do not reconcile; the policy is not in doubt.

Ostracism, the device Cleisthenes created and Athens first used in 487, removed the opposition. Each year the assembly could vote to hold one; the man named on most potsherds left for ten years, keeping his property. The first victim, Hipparchus son of Charmus, was a Pisistratid kinsman; Megacles the Alcmaeonid followed in 486, Xanthippus in 484, and Aristides, Themistocles' chief rival, in 482 (Aristotle, Constitution 22). Friends of tyranny and Persia went first, then opponents of the sea policy. Plutarch (Aristides 7) has an illiterate voter ask Aristides to write "Aristides" on his sherd. A deposit of 190 ostraka naming Themistocles, found on the Acropolis north slope, was written by about fourteen hands: ballots prepared for distribution. Ostracism was organised politics.

The exiles were recalled before Xerxes arrived.

Xerxes' invasion: canal, bridges, Thermopylae, Artemisium, 480

Book 7 opens with a council in which Mardonius urges war, Artabanus warns against it, and a dream twice compels Xerxes (7.8–18). Herodotus is explicit that the gods wanted him to go. A canal was cut through the isthmus behind Mount Athos (7.22–24); its line has been confirmed by coring. Two bridges of ships were thrown across the Hellespont at Abydos after a first pair broke in a storm and Xerxes had the sea whipped and the engineers beheaded (7.33–36). His army totals, 1,700,000 infantry and over five million souls (7.60, 7.184–186), are impossible; modern estimates run from 80,000 to 250,000. His 1,207 triremes are at least arguable.

The Greek response was a league sworn at the Isthmus in 481 under Spartan command; Argos, Crete and Syracuse stayed out, and Thessaly and most of Boeotia went over once a first position at Tempe was abandoned (7.173). The chosen line was Thermopylae on land and Artemisium at sea, mutually dependent.

Leonidas held the pass with about 7,000 men, including 300 Spartans chosen from those with living sons, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans (7.202–205). For two days the Persians, Immortals included, failed to break the hoplites in the narrows. Then Ephialtes of Malis showed them the Anopaea path over the mountain; the Phocians guarding it fled (7.213–218). Leonidas dismissed most of the allies and died with the Spartans and Thespians; the Thebans surrendered. Herodotus records Dieneces' "we shall fight in the shade" (7.226), the epitaphs (7.228), and Aristodemus, the survivor who redeemed himself at Plataea (7.229–231).

At Artemisium the Greek fleet of 271 ships under the Spartan Eurybiades fought three indecisive days against a Persian fleet already mauled by storms (8.1–18); Themistocles used a Euboean bribe of thirty talents to keep Eurybiades and the Corinthians in place (8.4–5). On news of Thermopylae the fleet withdrew to Salamis.

Where sources disagree. Herodotus (7.220) says Leonidas dismissed the allies deliberately to win glory for Sparta and fulfil a Delphic oracle, but admits another version in which the allies simply left. Diodorus (11.9–10) adds a night attack on the Persian camp. Whether Leonidas was a sacrifice, a rearguard, or a man awaiting reinforcement remains open.

The evacuation of Athens and Salamis

Delphi, consulted twice, finally promised that "the wooden wall alone shall not fall" and said Salamis would destroy "the children of women" (7.141). Themistocles argued that the wooden wall meant the ships and that the children destroyed would be Persian (7.143). The city was evacuated to Salamis, Aegina and Troezen (8.41); a few held the Acropolis behind a wooden barricade until the Persians scaled the north face, killed them and burned the temples (8.51–53). The "Decree of Themistocles" found at Troezen in 1959 purports to record the order; it is a fourth-century text and its authenticity is disputed.

The Greek fleet, 378 ships (8.48), lay in the strait between Salamis and Attica. The Peloponnesians wanted to retreat to the Isthmus. Themistocles threatened to take the Athenians to Italy (8.62), then sent his slave Sicinnus by night to tell Xerxes the Greeks were about to flee (8.75). Aristides arrived from Aegina to report the exits closed (8.79). In the narrows Persian numbers became a liability; the Phoenicians broke first; Artemisia of Halicarnassus, Herodotus' compatriot, escaped by ramming a Persian ally (8.87–88); Xerxes watched from the shore.

Aeschylus' Persians, produced in 472, is the only surviving eyewitness account; its messenger speech agrees with Herodotus on the night message and dawn attack but counts 310 Greek ships. Xerxes withdrew to Asia, leaving Mardonius and the army in Thessaly (8.113–120).

Plataea, Mycale and the Serpent Column, 479

Over winter Mardonius sent Alexander of Macedon to detach Athens with an offer of autonomy. The Athenian reply, as Herodotus writes it, is a founding text: as long as the sun holds its course they will not come to terms with Xerxes, and they will not betray "the Greek thing", shared blood, shared tongue, shared sanctuaries and sacrifices, shared ways of life (8.143–144). Mardonius burned Athens a second time.

Sparta, after dawdling behind its Isthmus wall, marched under the regent Pausanias with 5,000 Spartiates; Herodotus' allied hoplite total is 38,700 (9.28–30). The armies faced each other across the Asopus for more than ten days. Persian horse fouled the Greek spring and cut supply lines; a night withdrawal went wrong and left the Spartans and Tegeans isolated. Mardonius attacked them, and the decisive fight was Spartan hoplites against Persian infantry behind a wall of wicker shields. Mardonius fell (9.63); the Persians broke and were slaughtered in their stockade. Pausanias refused the suggestion to impale Mardonius' corpse in revenge for Leonidas, saying such deeds were fit for barbarians (9.78–79).

On the same day, Herodotus claims, the Greek fleet under Leotychidas landed at Mycale in Ionia and destroyed the beached Persian fleet (9.100–101). The Ionians changed sides again. The Histories end with the Athenians besieging Sestos on the Hellespont in winter 479/8 (9.114–121).

From a tenth of the Plataea spoils the Greeks dedicated a gold tripod at Delphi, set on a bronze column of three intertwined serpents (9.81). Pausanias had it inscribed with a couplet naming himself; the Spartans erased it and the allies replaced it with the names of the thirty-one cities who fought, Lacedaemonians first, Athenians second (Thucydides 1.132; the names survive). The gold was melted by the Phocians in the Third Sacred War (Pausanias 10.13.9). Constantine moved the bronze column to his hippodrome in Istanbul, where it still stands, headless: the one monument of the war that can be seen and read today.

Where sources disagree. Simonides' Plataea elegy (P.Oxy. 3965, published 1992) gives Pausanias and the Spartans full Homeric credit; Herodotus is cool towards Pausanias and generous to Athens; Plutarch (Aristides 19) says he belittles the allies. The Spartan and Athenian shares of Plataea were contested within a generation.

Herodotus: method, sources, biases, trust

Herodotus of Halicarnassus was born around 484, a subject of Persia, and lived into the 420s. He wrote fifty years after the events, from oral tradition. His sources, where he names them, are the traditions of cities and great families (the long defence of the Alcmaeonids against the charge of signalling with a shield at Marathon, 6.121–131, shows a family source at work), Delphi, Persian logioi (1.1) and monuments he saw himself. His rule is at 7.152: he must report what is said, not believe all of it.

His biases are visible. He is pro-Athenian: 7.139, where he says Athens saved Greece and braces for the unpopularity of saying so, is the spine of the work. He follows Athenian slander of Corinth (8.94, which he notes other Greeks deny), is ambivalent about Themistocles, is hostile to Ionians and Thebans, inflates Persian numbers, and loves dreams and oracles. He also names Persian commanders correctly, knows Persian customs, and respects Persian courage as later Greek writers do not.

Why did the Greeks win? He gives several answers at once. Freedom made men fight: Demaratus tells Xerxes the Spartans are free but have a master, law, which they fear more than Persians fear the king (7.104), and Herodotus himself says Athens grew strong once its tyrants fell because free men work for themselves (5.78). Divine jealousy punishes excess: Artabanus warns that the god strikes down the tall (7.10). Themistocles says publicly that gods and heroes, not men, did the deed (8.109). Modern explanations add hoplite armour against lighter Persian infantry, Persian dependence on a fleet to feed an oversized army, and the Greek choice of narrow ground at every battle.

How far to trust him? Thucydides (1.20–22) implies he wrote to please; Plutarch wrote On the Malice of Herodotus. Detlev Fehling (1971) argued that Herodotus invented his source citations; Pritchett and most scholars rejected this, and archaeology has vindicated details such as the Athos canal and the Serpent Column names. The reasonable position: his sequence and the shape of the war are reliable; speeches, numbers, motives and Persian court scenes are literary; where he reports a dispute, the dispute is real.

Where sources disagree. For 480–479 the alternatives to Herodotus are thin. Aeschylus is a play; Simonides is fragmentary; Diodorus Book 11 depends on the fourth-century Ephorus and contradicts Herodotus on numbers; Ctesias, a Greek doctor at the Persian court around 400, survives only in epitome and is trusted by no one. Herodotus is the mainstream because he is the only full one.

The war and Greek identity; the Athenian claim

Before 480 the word barbaros meant a speaker of babble, no more. After it, the Persian became the barbarian: the despot's slave, whipped into battle (7.223), luxurious and servile, against the free hoplite who fights for his own. Aeschylus' Persians first builds the contrast fully; Edith Hall's Inventing the Barbarian (1989) traces how tragedy fixed it within a generation. Herodotus is subtler than his successors, but the polarity runs through Books 7 to 9, and 8.144 is the earliest surviving definition of Hellenic identity by blood, language, religion and custom.

The war gave the Greeks shared monuments: the Marathon mound, the Thermopylae epitaphs, the Serpent Column, the Stoa Poikile with Marathon painted beside the Trojan War, the burnt Acropolis temples left unrepaired for a generation. Plataea founded a cult of Zeus the Liberator and the Eleutheria festival. The "Oath of Plataea", preserved in Lycurgus (Against Leocrates 80–81), Diodorus 11.29 and a fourth-century stele from Acharnae, was already called a forgery by Theopompus.

Athens turned the war into title. The argument is laid out by the Athenian envoys at Sparta in Thucydides (1.73–75): we fought alone at Marathon, we gave the fleet, the general and the resolve at Salamis, and so we deserved the empire we took. The Delian League of 478/7, formed after Pausanias disgraced himself and the Ionians asked Athens to lead (Thucydides 1.95–96), was formally a war alliance against Persia; it became the Athenian empire, and every funeral oration recited Marathon and Salamis as its warrant. Herodotus, writing while that empire fought Sparta, knew what his 7.139 would be used for and said it anyway. The Persian Wars are the point at which the Greeks began to describe themselves to themselves, and the Athenians were the loudest voice in the description.

Self-test

  1. What private failure of Aristagoras of Miletus triggered the Ionian Revolt, according to Herodotus?
    Answer

    His failed expedition against Naxos, promised to the satrap Artaphernes and funded by Persia; facing ruin, he raised Ionia in revolt (Herodotus 5.30–35).

  2. What did Darius order a servant to say to him at dinner after Sardis was burned?
    Answer

    "Master, remember the Athenians", three times at every meal (Herodotus 5.105).

  3. Why were the Spartans absent from Marathon, and when did they arrive?
    Answer

    They were observing the Carneia festival and would not march before the full moon; 2,000 arrived after the battle, having marched from Sparta in three days (Herodotus 6.106, 6.120).

  4. Does Herodotus report a runner carrying news from Marathon to Athens?
    Answer

    No. He reports Philippides running to Sparta before the battle. The run to Athens appears first in Plutarch and Lucian; Herodotus' "run" is the phalanx charging.

  5. How did Themistocles get the Athenians to build a fleet, in Herodotus' version?
    Answer

    He persuaded them to spend the Laurion silver surplus on 200 ships instead of a ten-drachma distribution, nominally for the war with Aegina (Herodotus 7.144). Aristotle gives a different mechanism of 100 talents lent to 100 rich men.

  6. Who was ostracised in 482, and why does that matter?
    Answer

    Aristides, Themistocles' main rival; his removal cleared the way for the naval policy. He was recalled before Salamis and commanded at Plataea.

  7. Name two engineering works Xerxes undertook for the invasion.
    Answer

    The canal through the Athos isthmus (Herodotus 7.22–24) and the twin ship-bridges over the Hellespont at Abydos (7.33–36).

  8. What was the "wooden wall" in the Delphic oracle, and how did Themistocles interpret it?
    Answer

    The oracle said the wooden wall alone would not fall; Themistocles argued it meant the ships, not the Acropolis palisade, and that Salamis would destroy Persian, not Greek, "children of women" (Herodotus 7.141–143).

  9. What happened to the inscription Pausanias put on the Serpent Column?
    Answer

    The Spartans erased his self-glorifying couplet and the allies replaced it with the names of the thirty-one cities that fought (Thucydides 1.132); the column stands in Istanbul.

  10. State Herodotus' rule for handling what he is told, and the passage where he states it.
    Answer

    He is obliged to report what is said but not to believe all of it, and this applies to his whole work (Herodotus 7.152).

Carry forward

  1. Herodotus is a single oral-tradition historian writing fifty years on: trust his sequence and his honestly reported disputes, not his numbers, speeches or Persian court scenes.
  2. The war created the Greek-barbarian polarity and the freedom-versus-slavery frame; the Athenian definition of Greekness at Herodotus 8.144 is where Hellenic identity is first stated.
  3. Athens converted Marathon and Salamis into a claim to lead; the Delian League and the Athenian empire of the next module rest on that claim, and Sparta's resentment of it is the road to the Peloponnesian War.
