The Athenian empire and the radical democracy

The fifty years and their sourcesFrom league to empireCimon, Ephialtes and the AreopagusPericles and the reforms of the 450sHow the radical democracy workedThe building programme and who paidThe First Peloponnesian War, c. 460–446The criticsWas it democratic?Self-testCarry forward

The fifty years and their sources

The Pentecontaetia is Thucydides' name for the roughly fifty years between the Persian retreat after Plataea and Mycale (479) and the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War (431). His account (Thucydides 1.89–118) is a compressed, undated digression explaining how Athens became powerful enough to frighten Sparta into war, and it is almost the only continuous narrative we have. The rest is patchwork: Plutarch's Lives of Aristides, Cimon and Pericles, written five centuries later from lost sources; Diodorus Siculus 11–12, who dates by archon year but often wrongly; the Athenaion Politeia attributed to Aristotle (23–28) for constitutional change; Old Comedy; and the stones, above all the Athenian Tribute Lists and building accounts.

Where sources disagree. Thucydides gives almost no absolute dates, so the chronology is reconstructed from Diodorus' archon years, Plutarch's asides and epigraphy. Scholars still argue whether the Egyptian expedition fell in 460–454 or 459–453 and whether the First Peloponnesian War began in 461 or 460. Treat dates below as approximate to a year or two unless an inscription fixes them.

From league to empire

Founding, 478/7

After the Spartan regent Pausanias disgraced himself at Byzantium the allies asked Athens to take over, and Sparta let the leadership go (Thucydides 1.95). Aristides assessed the first contributions and the allies swore oaths, sinking iron ingots to mark their permanence (Athenaion Politeia 23.5; Plutarch, Aristides 25). The treasury was placed on Delos and the synod met there. Members contributed ships or money (phoros); Thucydides 1.96 gives the first assessment as 460 talents, a figure many think too high for the early League. Ten Athenian Hellenotamiai handled the money from the start.

The slide to compulsion

Thucydides says the allies brought much of it on themselves: they preferred to pay rather than serve, so their fleets dwindled while Athens' grew (1.99). Naxos tried to leave around 470–468 and was besieged and "enslaved contrary to the established rule" (1.98.4), Thucydides' phrase for losing autonomy. Thasos revolted in 465–463 over its mainland mines; after a siege of over two years it surrendered walls, ships and mines (1.100–101). Sparta had secretly promised Thasos an invasion of Attica and was stopped only by the great earthquake and helot revolt. Cimon's victory at the Eurymedon (c. 467) and the destruction of an Athenian fleet in Egypt (c. 460–454) bracket this stage: one showed the League's purpose fulfilled, the other the cost of continuing it.

454 and after

In 454/3 the treasury moved from Delos to Athens, on a Samian proposal according to Plutarch (Pericles 12), and most historians connect it with the Egyptian disaster. From that year one-sixtieth of each city's tribute was dedicated to Athena and inscribed on stone; these quota lists are our best evidence for membership and payment. The synod is never heard of again. Other instruments multiplied: garrisons and Athenian officials; transfer of serious lawsuits to Athenian courts; imposed democracies, as at Erythrae (c. 453); and cleruchies, settlements of Athenian citizens on confiscated allied land that gave poorer Athenians a farm and the empire a garrison. They were planted on Naxos, Andros, Lemnos, the Chersonese and at Brea in Thrace; the Brea decree (IG I3 46) restricts settlers to the two lowest property classes.

The Peace of Callias with Persia, around 449, would have removed the League's reason for existing. Diodorus 12.4 and fourth-century orators affirm it; Thucydides never mentions it and Theopompus called it a forgery. The quota list for 449/8 is missing, which some read as a suspension of tribute while Athens debated what came next.

Samos, 440–439

Samos, one of the few remaining ship-contributing allies, revolted after Athens intervened in its quarrel with Miletus and imposed a democracy. Pericles commanded a nine-month siege (Thucydides 1.115–117); Sparta's allies debated intervention and, on Corinth's insistence, voted against (1.40). Samos lost fleet and walls and paid an indemnity. The empire could no longer be broken from inside.

Where sources disagree. Russell Meiggs (The Athenian Empire, 1972) traced a steady hardening of control from the 450s in the language of decrees. G. E. M. de Ste. Croix argued that the allied demos in most cities preferred Athenian rule to their own oligarchs, citing Thucydides 8.48 and Samian loyalty in 412–404. Others point to how fast allies revolted whenever Athens weakened. Both readings work because loyalty was divided along class lines within each city.

Cimon, Ephialtes and the Areopagus

Through the 470s and 460s the leading Athenian was Cimon, son of Miltiades: aristocratic, pro-Spartan, repeatedly elected general, victor at Eion, Scyros and the Eurymedon. His policy was the League as crusade against Persia and friendship with Sparta; his spoils funded public walks and open dinners (Plutarch, Cimon 10). His rivals were Themistocles, ostracised in the late 470s, and then Ephialtes son of Sophonides, about whom we know little.

The Areopagus, the council of ex-archons, had emerged from the Persian Wars with great prestige and, the Athenaion Politeia (23.1) believed, a general "guardianship of the laws". In 462/1 Ephialtes, with Pericles as junior associate, prosecuted individual Areopagites and then transferred most of the council's powers to the Council of 500, the Assembly and the popular courts, leaving it homicide trials and some religious functions (Athenaion Politeia 25; Plutarch, Cimon 15). The timing was political: Cimon had taken 4,000 hoplites to help Sparta against the rebels on Ithome, and the Spartans sent them home alone of all the allies (Thucydides 1.102). The insult destroyed his position; he opposed the reforms on his return and was ostracised in 461. Ephialtes was murdered soon after.

Where sources disagree. What the Areopagus lost in 462 is uncertain; Aristotle's text speaks only of "additional powers". Reconstructions range from the audit and vetting of magistrates to hearing eisangeliai for offences against the state. Hignett doubted the Areopagus ever held a formal guardianship and thought fourth-century tradition inflated the reform. Aeschylus' Eumenides (458), which stages the Areopagus' foundation as a homicide court, is read as comment on the reform, but whether approving or cautionary is disputed.

Pericles and the reforms of the 450s

Pericles son of Xanthippus inherited Ephialtes' faction and was the most influential Athenian from about 460 until his death in 429, elected general fifteen years running from 443. Thucydides' "in name a democracy, in fact rule by the first man" (2.65.9) is a flourish: Pericles held no office beyond the annual generalship and in 430 was fined and deposed.

Three reforms carry his name. Pay for jurors, two obols a day, introduced according to the Athenaion Politeia (27.3–4) to compete with Cimon's private generosity; it was the first state pay for civic service and opened the courts to men who could not afford a lost day's wages. The citizenship law of 451/0, requiring an Athenian father and mother (Athenaion Politeia 26.4; Plutarch, Pericles 37); its motive is debated between protecting the value of citizenship now that it carried pay and land, curbing aristocratic foreign marriages, and Aristotle's bare "because of the number of citizens". It lapsed during the war, when Pericles himself sought an exemption for his son by Aspasia, and was re-enacted in 403. And the opening of the archonship by lot to the zeugitai, the third property class, from 457 (Athenaion Politeia 26.2). His remaining rival, Thucydides son of Melesias, attacked the use of allied money on buildings and was ostracised in 443 (Plutarch, Pericles 11–14).

How the radical democracy worked

  • The Assembly (ekklesia): all adult male citizens, meeting on the Pnyx, perhaps 6,000 of a citizen body of 30,000–40,000 at a time. It decided war, peace, finance and legislation and elected generals; any citizen could speak.
  • The Council of 500 (boule): fifty from each of the ten Cleisthenic tribes, chosen by lot from citizens over thirty for one year, at most twice in a lifetime. It prepared the Assembly's agenda (every motion needed a probouleuma), supervised magistrates and finance and ran the navy; each tribal fifty presided for a tenth of the year.
  • The law courts (dikasteria): 6,000 sworn jurors a year, chosen by lot from volunteers over thirty, sitting in panels of 201, 501 or more. No judges, no advocates; litigants spoke for themselves against a water clock and the panel voted without deliberation. The courts heard private suits, public prosecutions, the audit of every outgoing magistrate and allied cases.
  • The lot: almost all of some 700 annual magistracies were filled by lot, on the principle that any citizen was competent and that election favoured the rich. Only offices needing expertise, chiefly the ten strategoi and the financial boards, were elected and repeatable.
  • The generals: one per tribe, elected annually, commanding by land and sea and, being re-electable, the only continuous leadership the system allowed. Pericles' tenure shows what this permitted; Arginusae in 406 shows the risk.
  • Liturgies: the richest 1,200 or so citizens and metics funded public services in rotation from their own pockets: a festival chorus (choregia) or, most expensively, a warship for a year (trierarchy). They were the main direct levy on wealth and a route to esteem.
  • Ostracism: each year the Assembly voted whether to hold one; if so, every citizen could scratch a name on a sherd, and provided 6,000 voted the man with most was exiled for ten years without loss of property. Used against Themistocles, Cimon and Thucydides son of Melesias.
  • The graphe paranomon: prosecution of a decree's proposer for proposing something contrary to law. First attested in 415 but generally thought to have replaced the Areopagus' guardianship after 462. Conviction annulled the decree and fined the proposer; it made the courts, not the Assembly, the final arbiter.

The system's core was lot, rotation, pay and accountability: every officeholder was vetted before office, could be deposed during it and was audited after it. Its weakness was that a persuasive speaker could move the Assembly fast, with nothing to slow it beyond the Council's agenda control and the threat of later prosecution.

Where sources disagree. Whether fifth-century Athens distinguished laws (nomoi) from decrees (psephismata), as the fourth century did, is unclear; if not, the graphe paranomon before 403 may have meant something looser. Mogens Hansen's standard reconstruction relies on fourth-century evidence and he concedes that the fifth-century Assembly may have been both more powerful and less regulated. The number of meetings a year and the date of Assembly pay are uncertain.

The building programme and who paid

The Acropolis had lain in ruins since 480; a tradition held that the Greeks had sworn at Plataea not to rebuild destroyed temples. The programme began in 447 with the Parthenon, Ictinus and Callicrates as architects and Phidias overseeing the sculpture; it was dedicated at the Panathenaea of 438 and the sculpture finished by 432. Mnesicles' Propylaea followed from 437 and was left incomplete when war came. The building accounts (IG I3 436–451) survive in part; Plutarch (Pericles 12–13) gives the only narrative.

Plutarch frames the programme as a controversy: Thucydides son of Melesias charged that Athens was adorning herself like a courtesan with money extorted from the allies for a war against Persia; Pericles replied that the allies paid for protection, received it, and had no claim on the surplus, and that the works spread wealth to every trade. Whether tribute actually paid for the Parthenon is less certain than Plutarch implies. The accounts show payments from the treasurers of Athena, the Hellenotamiai and the sale of spoils, and a transfer of a 5,000-talent reserve to Athena around 449 is usually inferred. Lisa Kallet-Marx and others argue that tribute's direct share was smaller than tradition holds and that Athens' own revenues, Laurium silver, harbour dues, court fees and public leases, covered much of it. The total cost is unknown; figures such as 470 talents for the building are modern estimates from incomplete accounts.

Where sources disagree. The Oath of Plataea is accepted by some as explaining the thirty-year delay and rejected by others, including Theopompus in antiquity, as a fourth-century fabrication. The Callias decrees, crucial for how League money reached Athena, are dated to 434/3 by tradition and to the late 440s by others. The Parthenon's function is itself debated: with no attested altar or priestess, some treat it as a treasury and votive monument rather than a cult temple.

The First Peloponnesian War, c. 460–446

The breach of 462 was followed by Athenian alliances with Argos and Thessaly and by the settlement of the Messenian rebels at Naupactus after Ithome fell (Thucydides 1.102–103). Megara, at war with Corinth, left the Peloponnesian League for Athens around 460, giving Athens the Isthmus roads and the port of Pegae; Corinth became Athens' bitterest enemy. The war was fought with Sparta's allies more than with Sparta. Athens beat Corinth at sea and at Megara (Myronides, 458), took Aegina into the League as a tributary (457) and finished its own Long Walls. Sparta marched into Boeotia and won at Tanagra (457); sixty-two days later Myronides crushed the Boeotians at Oenophyta and Athens dominated Boeotia and Phocis for a decade. The Erechtheid casualty list (IG I3 1147), with dead in Cyprus, Egypt, Phoenicia, Halieis, Aegina and Megara in one year, shows the scale of commitment.

Cimon, recalled, negotiated a five-year truce in 451 and died on Cyprus around 450. By the mid-440s overextension told. The Boeotian exiles beat Tolmides at Coronea in 447 and Athens evacuated Boeotia. In 446 Euboea revolted; Megara defected and killed its garrison; the Spartan king Pleistoanax invaded Attica and withdrew without fighting, for which he was exiled at home (Thucydides 1.113–114; Plutarch, Pericles 22–23, who says Pericles bribed him). Pericles reduced Euboea and planted a cleruchy at Histiaea. The Thirty Years' Peace of 446/5 gave up Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen and Achaea; each side kept its allies, neutrals might join either, and disputes were to go to arbitration (Thucydides 1.115.1). Athens lost its land empire and kept its sea empire. Thucydides' speakers in 432–431 refer back to this war constantly; it is why Megara and Corinth mattered so much in 431.

The critics

Criticism began in the democracy's lifetime; Thucydides' Cleon calls the demos "spectators of words" (3.38). The most sustained fifth-century critique is the Constitution of the Athenians preserved among Xenophon's works but not his; its unknown author, the "Old Oligarch", probably wrote in the 420s. His argument is a backhanded tribute: the system is bad because it gives power to the poor over the good, but every feature of it, pay, the lot, the courts' grip on the allies, the licence of slaves and metics, the naval empire, is perfectly designed to keep the poor in power, and he sees no way of changing it short of destroying it (Pseudo-Xenophon 1.1–9, 3.1–9).

Plato's hostility runs deeper. In the Gorgias (515e) Socrates says Pericles made the Athenians lazy, cowardly, talkative and greedy by introducing pay. In Republic 557a–564a democracy is the regime of licence, where the lot gives office to the unqualified and excess of freedom breeds tyranny; the ship whose sailors brawl over the helm (488a–489a) is the Assembly. Plato's objection is epistemic: government is a craft, and crafts belong to those who know. Aristotle classed Periclean Athens as the extreme democracy in which the demos rather than law is sovereign (Politics 1292a), yet conceded that the many judging together may judge better than the few (1281a–b).

Where sources disagree. Thucydides' own verdict is divided: the Funeral Oration (2.35–46) is the finest surviving defence of Athenian freedom, and 2.65 blames Pericles' successors rather than the system; yet the Mytilenean and Sicilian debates show an Assembly swayed by anger and greed, and 8.97 praises the moderate regime of 411 as the best government of his lifetime. Whether he was a critic of democracy or of demagogues remains open.

Was it democratic?

The modern debate turns on who was excluded. Women of citizen family counted for descent after 451 but had no political existence: no Assembly, no juries, no outright property, no voice in court except through a male kyrios. Metics, perhaps 10,000–20,000 adult males, paid a monthly tax, served in the army and performed liturgies, but could not vote, own land or marry citizens. Slaves are hardest to count, with estimates from 60,000 to 150,000 for Attica. On the widest estimates those with political rights were perhaps a tenth of the population and a third of adult males.

One school, from the Old Oligarch to Moses Finley (Democracy Ancient and Modern, 1973) and Josiah Ober (Mass and Elite in Democratic Athens, 1989), accepts the exclusions and insists that among the included the democracy was real and unprecedented: direct participation, lot, pay, the sovereignty of the Assembly over wealth and birth, ordinary citizens forcing the elite to speak their language. Ellen Meiksins Wood stressed that the achievement was the equality of the working peasant with the aristocrat, and that slavery, though real, was not the basis of citizen leisure since most citizens worked. Against this, others point out that tribute and slave labour made pay and public building possible, so that the democracy of the citizens was financed by the subjection of others, and feminist historians since the 1970s have argued that the 451 law made the exclusion of women constitutive: citizen mothers became necessary and received nothing.

The honest position is that "democracy" in Athens meant what the word says, power of the demos, and that the demos was a hereditary, male, free minority. Within it, the direct power exercised by ordinary men has no parallel before or since. Outside it, the regime looked like any other Greek city, and in its empire rather worse.

Self-test

  1. What is the main ancient source for the Pentecontaetia, and what is its chief limitation?
    Answer

    Thucydides 1.89–118, a digression explaining the growth of Athenian power. It is compressed, selective and almost undated, so the chronology must be reconstructed from Diodorus, Plutarch and inscriptions.

  2. Where was the League treasury first kept, when was it moved, and what evidence does the move produce?
    Answer

    On Delos. Moved to Athens in 454/3. From then one-sixtieth of each city's tribute was dedicated to Athena and inscribed, producing the Athenian Tribute Lists.

  3. Name the three major allied revolts of the period with approximate dates.
    Answer

    Naxos c. 470–468, Thasos 465–463, Samos 440–439. Euboea (446) and Byzantium (440) were lesser or concurrent revolts.

  4. What was a cleruchy and who went?
    Answer

    A settlement of Athenian citizens on confiscated allied land, giving the settlers a farm and Athens a garrison. The Brea decree restricts settlers to the two lowest property classes.

  5. Why did Cimon fall from power in 462/1?
    Answer

    He led 4,000 hoplites to help Sparta against the helot revolt at Ithome and the Spartans dismissed them alone of all allies. The humiliation discredited his pro-Spartan policy, Ephialtes carried the Areopagus reforms in his absence, and Cimon was ostracised on his return.

  6. What did the Areopagus retain after 462?
    Answer

    Homicide trials and certain religious functions. Its "additional" powers, probably the audit and vetting of magistrates and a general guardianship of the laws, went to the Council, Assembly and courts.

  7. What did the citizenship law of 451/0 require, and what happened to it?
    Answer

    Both parents had to be Athenian. It lapsed during the Peloponnesian War (Pericles obtained an exemption for his son by Aspasia) and was re-enacted in 403.

  8. Which offices were elected rather than filled by lot, and why?
    Answer

    The ten generals and the main financial boards, because they required expertise. They could be held repeatedly, which made the generalship the only route to continuous leadership.

  9. What were the terms of the Thirty Years' Peace of 446/5?
    Answer

    Athens gave up Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen and Achaea; each side kept its existing allies; neutrals could join either; disputes were to go to arbitration. Athens kept its sea empire and lost its land empire.

  10. What is the core of Plato's objection to Athenian democracy, as distinct from the Old Oligarch's?
    Answer

    Plato's objection is epistemic: government is a craft requiring knowledge, and the lot and Assembly hand it to the ignorant (Republic 488–489, Protagoras 319). The Old Oligarch's is one of class: the system gives power to the poor over the good, and does so with irritating efficiency.

Carry forward

  1. Empire and democracy grew together and funded each other: tribute, cleruchies and court fees paid for the jury pay and buildings that made the radical democracy work, and the demos that voted at home was the body that rowed the fleet holding the allies down. Keep this coupling in mind for the Peloponnesian War and the coups of 411 and 404.
  2. The First Peloponnesian War and the Thirty Years' Peace are the back-story of 431: Corinth's grievance, Megara's double defection, Sparta's fear of Athenian land power and the arbitration clause all return in Thucydides book 1.
  3. The constitutional machinery (lot, rotation, pay, the courts as final arbiter, the graphe paranomon) is what later modules will see tested under stress, from the Mytilenean debate to Arginusae and the trial of Socrates; and the exclusion of women, metics and slaves is the measure every later critic, ancient and modern, applies to the achievement.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Athens in the Pentecontaetia, 479 to 431 BC. Cover: the Delian League's founding and conversion into an empire (the tribute, the move of the treasury in 454, cleruchies, the revolts of Naxos, Thasos and Samos); Cimon and Ephialtes and the stripping of the Areopagus in 462; Pericles' position and the reforms (pay for jurors, the citizenship law of 451); how the radical democracy actually worked: the Assembly, the Council of 500, the law courts, the lot, the generals, liturgies, ostracism, the graphe paranomon; the building programme (Parthenon, Propylaea) and who paid; the First Peloponnesian War; and the critics (the "Old Oligarch", Plato) and modern debates about whether it was really democratic, given slaves, women and metics. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

The Peloponnesian War

Causes: the truest cause and the stated grievances

Thucydides distinguishes two kinds of explanation. The grievances openly argued about, the aitiai, were Corcyra, Potidaea and the Megarian Decree. Behind them lay the alēthestatē prophasis, the truest cause, "least spoken of openly": the growth of Athenian power and the fear it produced in Sparta (Thucydides 1.23.6; restated at 1.88 and 1.118.2). The Pentecontaetia (1.89–118) exists to make that claim visible.

The grievances are told with care. Epidamnus, a Corcyraean colony with a Corinthian founder, appealed to Corinth; Corcyra sought alliance with Athens; Athens granted a defensive alliance only, and at Sybota in 433 its ships fought Corinthians (1.24–55). Potidaea, a Corinthian colony paying tribute to Athens, was ordered to pull down its seaward wall and expel its Corinthian magistrates; it revolted and Athens besieged it (1.56–65). The Megarian Decree, excluding Megarians from Attic markets and imperial harbours, is mentioned almost in passing (1.67.4, 1.139.1–2), though Sparta made its repeal the final condition for peace and Pericles refused to yield to an ultimatum dressed as a small request (1.140–144).

At Sparta the Corinthians urge war (1.68–71), Archidamus counsels delay (1.80–85), and the ephor Sthenelaidas carries the vote (1.86).

Where sources disagree. Aristophanes (Acharnians 515–539; Peace 605–611) makes the Megarian Decree and Pericles' personal position the cause, as many Athenians evidently believed. De Ste. Croix (The Origins of the Peloponnesian War, 1972) accepts Thucydides' verdict and blames Spartan aggression; Kagan (The Outbreak of the Peloponnesian War, 1969) argues the war was avoidable and that Thucydides overstates structural causation; Badian (From Plataea to Potidaea, 1993) reads Thucydides as a partisan concealing Athenian provocation. The weight of the Megarian Decree remains uncertain.

The Archidamian War: Pericles' strategy, the Funeral Oration, the plague

The war began in spring 431 with a Theban night attack on Plataea (2.2–6), followed by the first invasion of Attica. Pericles' strategy (1.140–144, 2.13) was deliberately unheroic: abandon the countryside, bring the population inside the walls, refuse pitched battle against superior Peloponnesian hoplites, use the fleet to raid the Peloponnese and keep tribute flowing, and make no new conquests while the war lasted. His verdict at 2.65 is that the plan would have worked had Pericles' successors kept to it.

The Funeral Oration for the dead of the first year (2.35–46) is an idealised portrait of what the city claimed to be: equal laws, public honour by merit (2.37), citizens who are "lovers of the city" (2.43.1), the whole earth the tomb of famous men (2.43.3). It is followed, by evident design, with the plague of 430 (2.47–54), described clinically from Thucydides' own illness, refusing to speculate on causes and recording instead the collapse of law and piety when the pious and impious died alike. The toll he gives later is 4,400 hoplites and 300 cavalry (3.87). Pericles, deposed and fined, defended the empire as a tyranny now unsafe to lay down (2.60–64), was re-elected, and died in 429.

Where sources disagree. Delbrück classed Periclean strategy as exhaustion that could not produce victory; Kagan argues it assumed a Spartan readiness to tire that never appeared, and that Athens had no plan for ending the war. The plague's identity is contested: Papagrigorakis and colleagues (2006) reported typhoid DNA from a Kerameikos mass grave, but the method has been challenged, and smallpox, measles and an extinct pathogen all have defenders.

Mytilene and the Mytilenean Debate

In 428 Mytilene, one of the few allies still contributing ships rather than tribute, revolted and appealed to Sparta (3.2–6). Spartan help came too late; starving, and with the demos refusing to fight once armed, Mytilene surrendered in 427 (3.27–28). The assembly voted to execute all adult males and enslave the rest, then regretted it and reconvened.

In the paired speeches (3.37–48) Cleon, "the most violent of the citizens" (3.36.6), argues that democracy cannot rule an empire, that pity and fine speaking are the vices of empire, and that exemplary terror is justice. Diodotus, otherwise unknown, answers from interest rather than mercy: the death penalty does not deter because hope and desire drive men to risk everything (3.45), and killing the demos along with the oligarchs will teach every subject city that revolt has no exit. Diodotus wins narrowly; a second trireme, its crew eating as they row, overtakes the first as Paches reads the original decree (3.49). Thucydides then records that the Mytileneans Paches had sent to Athens as chief culprits, "a little more than a thousand", were executed (3.50).

The same summer the Plataeans were executed after a sham Spartan trial (3.52–68), and the Corcyraean civil war produced the analysis of stasis at 3.82–83.

Where sources disagree. The "more than a thousand" at 3.50.1 has troubled editors, since Paches had sent only ringleaders; some propose corruption (thirty for a thousand), though the manuscripts agree. Whether Diodotus is a real speaker or a construct for the argument Thucydides wanted heard is uncertain.

Pylos and Sphacteria, Cleon and Brasidas, Amphipolis

In 425 Demosthenes fortified Pylos on the Messenian coast (4.2–6). The Spartans, alarmed at a base in helot country, landed 420 hoplites on the island of Sphacteria; the Athenian fleet then defeated the Peloponnesian ships and cut the island off (4.8–23). Sparta offered peace to recover the men; Cleon had the assembly demand more (4.17–22). When the blockade dragged on and Cleon attacked the generals, Nicias offered him the command; trapped by his own rhetoric, Cleon accepted and promised to bring the Spartans back within twenty days, "a mad promise" that came true (4.27–28). Demosthenes' light-armed troops wore the hoplites down, and 292 survivors, about 120 of them Spartiates, surrendered: the first time Spartans had done so, a shock to Greece (4.29–41). Athens held them as hostages against invasion.

Fortune then turned. In the north Brasidas, the one Spartan in Thucydides with initiative and charm, marched through Thessaly and in winter 424/3 took Amphipolis, the colony on the Strymon guarding timber and the Hellespont route (4.78–88, 102–108). Thucydides himself, commanding at Thasos, arrived too late and held only Eion; he says at 5.26 that he was exiled for twenty years after Amphipolis. In 422 Cleon led an expedition to recover the city; caught in a disordered withdrawal, his army was routed and he was killed fleeing, while Brasidas died of his wounds in victory and was buried in the agora as the city's second founder (5.6–11).

Where sources disagree. Thucydides' hostility to Cleon is unmistakable, and Woodhead ("Thucydides' Portrait of Cleon", 1960) argued it distorts the record: Pylos and the raised tribute of 425 both served Athens, and the ancient life by Marcellinus claims Cleon secured Thucydides' exile. Whether Thucydides was negligent at Amphipolis cannot be settled from his own brief account.

The Peace of Nicias and the rise of Alcibiades

With Cleon and Brasidas, the two men Thucydides says most wanted war, dead (5.16), Nicias and King Pleistoanax negotiated a fifty-year peace in spring 421 (5.18–19) and an Athenian-Spartan alliance (5.23). Thucydides insists this was a suspect truce, not peace, and counts the war as one twenty-seven-year whole (5.26). Sparta could not deliver Amphipolis; Athens kept Pylos; Corinth, Boeotia, Megara and Elis rejected the treaty; Argos became the centre of a rival alliance (5.27–48).

Into this stepped Alcibiades, Pericles' ward, young and personally offended that Sparta had negotiated through Nicias (5.43). He built an alliance of Athens, Argos, Mantinea and Elis in 420, tricking the Spartan envoys into denying their own full powers before the assembly (5.44–46). The confrontation came at Mantinea in 418, the largest hoplite battle of the war, where King Agis won decisively and restored Spartan prestige (5.64–74). His extravagance made the Athenians suspect him of aiming at tyranny, a suspicion that, Thucydides says, "not long after brought the city down" (6.15).

The Melian Dialogue

In 416 Athens attacked Melos, a Dorian island outside the empire (5.84–116). Before the siege the Athenian envoys and Melian councillors talk in private, and Thucydides casts it as dialogue rather than paired speeches. The Athenians refuse to discuss justice, which applies only between equals in power, while "the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must" (5.89); their rule follows a law of nature the Melians themselves would obey (5.105). The Melians answer with hope, the gods and Spartan kinship; the Athenians dismiss all three (5.103–105). Melos resisted, was betrayed and taken; the men were killed, the women and children enslaved, and 500 colonists planted (5.116.4).

The placement is deliberate: the Dialogue closes Book 5 and Sicily opens Book 6, so the logic of power without limit expounded at Melos is tested at Syracuse. Thucydides offers no comment of his own.

Where sources disagree. No one supposes Thucydides had a transcript of a closed meeting; the Dialogue is treated as his own composition. De Romilly (Thucydides and Athenian Imperialism, 1947) reads it as the climax of a critique of imperial reasoning; others as a realistic record of how such negotiations went. Xenophon (Hellenica 2.2.3) shows Athenians in 405 remembered Melos as a crime they now feared to pay for.

The Sicilian Expedition

In 415 Segesta appealed to Athens against Selinus and Syracuse with promises of money that proved fraudulent (6.6, 6.46). Nicias argued against the venture and tried to deter the assembly by demanding an enormous force; the Athenians voted him everything (6.9–14, 6.20–26). Alcibiades argued that empire cannot stand still (6.16–18). The command was shared between Nicias, Alcibiades and Lamachus.

Before sailing, the Herms were mutilated in a single night, and informers added charges that Alcibiades had parodied the Mysteries (6.27–29). The fleet left anyway: 134 triremes and about 5,100 hoplites (6.43). In Sicily the generals disagreed (6.47–49); then the Salaminia arrived to recall him, he slipped away at Thurii, and at Sparta advised sending a commander to Syracuse and fortifying Decelea (6.53, 6.61, 6.88–93).

In 414 the Athenians seized Epipolae and began a wall of circumvallation; Lamachus was killed, and the city was near surrender when the Spartan Gylippus arrived, slipped past the blockade, and built a counter-wall that cut the Athenian line (6.96–103, 7.1–7). Nicias, ill, asked to be relieved or massively reinforced; the assembly sent Demosthenes and Eurymedon with 73 ships and some 5,000 hoplites (7.8–16, 7.42). Demosthenes' night assault on Epipolae collapsed in confusion as Dorians on both sides sang the same paean (7.43–45). He urged immediate withdrawal; Nicias refused, fearing the assembly (7.47–49). When he agreed, a lunar eclipse on 27 August 413 led the soothsayers to prescribe a delay of thrice nine days (7.50). The Syracusans closed the Great Harbour and destroyed the fleet in a battle narrated as watched from the shore like a theatre (7.69–71). The army retreated overland; Demosthenes' division surrendered, Nicias' was cut down at the Assinarus (7.75–85). Both generals were executed, the prisoners penned in the quarries, and Thucydides calls it "the greatest action of this war", a total destruction from which "few out of many returned home" (7.86–87).

Where sources disagree. Thucydides judges at 2.65.11 that the fault lay less with the expedition than with those at home who failed to support it, which sits uneasily with 6.1 and Nicias' warnings; Kagan thinks the venture unwinnable, Lazenby that it was lost by command decisions in 414. Plutarch (Nicias 19–28), using the Syracusan historians Philistus and Timaeus, has Nicias and Demosthenes take their own lives; Diodorus 13.19 gives a long Syracusan debate on their fate.

The Decelean War and the oligarchic coup of 411

Athens did not collapse. Sparta fortified Decelea in 413, Attica was occupied all year, slaves deserted, and Athens replaced tribute with a five-per-cent harbour tax (7.19, 7.27–28). Ionia revolted, and Sparta built a fleet with Persian money under three treaties with Tissaphernes that conceded the King's right to the cities of Asia (8.18, 8.37, 8.58). Alcibiades, now distrusted at Sparta, crossed to Tissaphernes and played each side against the other while negotiating his return (8.45–56).

That return was to come through a change of constitution. Officers at Samos led by Peisander and Phrynichus were told Alcibiades could bring Persian support if democracy were abolished (8.47–54). In 411 the assembly at Colonus was induced to appoint Four Hundred to govern on behalf of Five Thousand who were never listed (8.63–70); Thucydides shows how a small conspiracy paralyses a city by making each man suspect his neighbour (8.66). The fleet at Samos refused to follow, made Thrasybulus and Thrasyllus its leaders and recalled Alcibiades, whose one indisputable service was to stop it sailing against Athens (8.73–82, 8.86). At Athens the extremists began fortifying Eetioneia to admit a Spartan fleet; Theramenes broke with them, Phrynichus was assassinated, and when Euboea revolted the Four Hundred fell (8.89–96). Power passed to the Five Thousand, those who could furnish arms, under which, Thucydides says, "the Athenians appear to have been better governed than ever in my time" (8.97.2). The History breaks off in autumn 411 after Cynossema (8.104–109).

Where sources disagree. Aristotle's Constitution of the Athenians 29–33 preserves constitutional documents for 411 that cannot be fully reconciled with Thucydides, and scholars dispute whether the Five Thousand ever functioned or whether democracy simply returned by stages in 410. Thucydides' praise of the interim regime is read both as moderate-oligarchic sympathy and as a verdict on performance alone.

Arginusae, Aegospotami, the siege and the Thirty

Xenophon's Hellenica begins where Thucydides stops. Alcibiades and Thrasybulus destroyed the Peloponnesian fleet at Cyzicus in 410; Xenophon preserves the dispatch, "Ships gone; Mindarus dead; men starving; don't know what to do" (1.1.23). Alcibiades returned home in 407 (1.4.8–20), but after Lysander, funded by Cyrus the Younger, beat his deputy at Notium in 406 he withdrew to Thrace (1.5.11–17).

In 406 Callicratidas blockaded Conon at Mytilene; Athens melted temple dedications, enrolled slaves as rowers, and at the Arginusae islands won its last great victory, losing 25 ships to the enemy's 70 (1.6.24–38). A storm prevented rescue of the crews from the wrecks, and at Athens the generals were deposed; six returned. Theramenes, one of the trierarchs assigned to the rescue, blamed them; Euryptolemus argued for separate trials under the law, but the assembly condemned all six by a single vote, against the decree of Cannonus, and executed them, Pericles the younger among them. The Athenians later repented and prosecuted Callixenus, the proposer (1.7). Plato (Apology 32b) and Xenophon (Memorabilia 1.1.18) say Socrates, presiding, refused to put the motion.

In 405 Lysander took Lampsacus; the Athenian fleet of 180 ships beached opposite at Aegospotami, an open shore. For four days Lysander refused battle while the crews scattered for food; on the fifth he struck the empty ships and took almost the whole fleet. Conon escaped with eight ships; Lysander executed the Athenian prisoners, some 3,000 according to Plutarch (Lysander 13), after Xenophon's account of the capture (2.1.20–32). "That night no one slept" in Athens (2.2.3). After months of blockade Theramenes negotiated, and in spring 404 Athens accepted terms: Long Walls and Piraeus fortifications demolished, the fleet cut to twelve ships, exiles recalled, Athens to follow Sparta's lead. The walls came down to flute music, the Peloponnesians believing "this day was the beginning of freedom for Greece" (2.2.10–23).

Under Lysander's pressure thirty men were appointed to draft laws; they ruled instead, with a Spartan garrison on the Acropolis and a reign of judicial murder that Aristotle sets at not fewer than 1,500 dead (Constitution of the Athenians 35.4). When Theramenes objected to killing rich men for their property, Critias struck his name off the list of Three Thousand and had him dragged from the altar to drink hemlock (2.3.11–56). Thrasybulus seized Phyle with seventy men in winter 404/3, grew to a thousand, took the Piraeus, and killed Critias at Munychia (2.4.2–19). Lysander moved to crush the democrats, but King Pausanias, jealous of him, brokered reconciliation instead. In autumn 403 the democracy was restored under an amnesty forbidding anyone except the Thirty, the Ten and the Eleven to "remember past wrongs" (2.4.28–43).

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (13.101–103), following Ephorus, orders the Arginusae accusations differently and makes the generals strike first against Theramenes. On Aegospotami, Diodorus 13.105–106 has Philocles sail out with thirty ships and be caught in disorder, not a simple surprise on the beach; Plutarch (Lysander 11) follows Xenophon. On the Thirty, Constitution of the Athenians 34–35 says the peace terms required the "ancestral constitution" and that Theramenes brokered the appointment, which Xenophon omits and Lysias 12.71–76 uses against him. Xenophon's chronology of 404/3 is unreliable in detail.

Thucydides as historian

Thucydides states his method at 1.20–22. He distrusts tradition and poets, checks reports against one another, and writes for use, not a prize composition for one hearing but "a possession for all time" (1.22.4), because what happened will, human nature being constant, happen again in similar form. For events he claims autopsy or cross-examined testimony, admitting that eyewitnesses differ through partiality and memory. For speeches he claims to keep "as closely as possible to the general sense of what was actually said" while making speakers say what the situation seemed to demand (1.22.1). Herodotus is never named, but 1.20.3 corrects him and the whole opening answers him.

The speeches carry the analysis, placed in antithetical pairs whose arguments recur across the work. Three propositions hold it together: states are driven by fear, honour and interest (1.76.2); the strong rule wherever they can (5.105); and under plague, siege and civil war the restraints of law and language give way "as long as human nature remains the same" (3.82.2). This does not make him an amoralist: his Athens is undone less by Sparta than by its own excess and by factional ambition after Pericles (2.65).

His composition is itself a problem. He says he began writing at the outbreak, but 5.26 shows he knew the end. Ullrich's thesis of 1846, that an Archidamian War history was later reworked, began the "Thucydidean question"; most now read the work as composed and revised over decades, accepting that Book 8 and much of Book 5 are unfinished, with documents not yet turned into narrative and no speeches.

He matters partly through reception: Hobbes translated him in 1629 as the most politic of historians, and international relations theory adopted the Melian Dialogue as a founding text of realism, usually without its context; the "Thucydides trap" is a modern coinage. More durably, he set a standard of evidence and causation the discipline still measures itself by, he refused consolation, and he showed that a narrative can argue. He is also a difficult witness: exiled, aristocratic, admiring of Pericles, hostile to Cleon. Reading him well means reading him against himself.

Where sources disagree. Cornford (Thucydides Mythistoricus, 1907) saw a tragedian shaping events into hubris and nemesis; Hunter (Thucydides the Artful Reporter, 1973) argued the narrative was built to fit conclusions already drawn; Connor (Thucydides, 1984) and Rood (Thucydides: Narrative and Explanation, 1998) treat the shaping as the method itself. Loraux's "Thucydides is not a colleague" (1980) warns against reading him as a modern positivist. The reliability of the speeches remains the most contested question in the field.

Self-test

  1. What does Thucydides identify as the "truest cause" of the war, and where does he say it?
    Answer

    The growth of Athenian power and the fear this caused in Sparta; stated at 1.23.6 and restated at 1.88 and 1.118.2, with the Pentecontaetia (1.89–118) as the supporting narrative.

  2. Name the three stated grievances and the Athenian action in each.
    Answer

    Corcyra: a defensive alliance and ships that fought Corinth at Sybota (433). Potidaea: an ultimatum to demolish walls and expel Corinthian magistrates, then a siege. Megara: the Megarian Decree excluding Megarians from Attic markets and imperial harbours, whose repeal Pericles refused.

  3. What were the main elements of Pericles' war strategy, and what did Thucydides say at 2.65 about why it failed?
    Answer

    Abandon Attica, stay behind the walls, refuse land battle, use the fleet and reserve to outlast Sparta, and make no new conquests. Thucydides says his successors did the opposite, pursuing private ambition and gain, above all in Sicily.

  4. Who opposed Cleon in the Mytilenean Debate, and on what grounds did he argue against the massacre?
    Answer

    Diodotus (3.42–48). He argued from Athenian interest, not pity: the death penalty does not deter because hope and desire drive men to risk; killing the demos would deprive Athens of the party inside every city that might open its gates.

  5. Why was the surrender on Sphacteria in 425 so shocking to Greece?
    Answer

    Some 292 Lacedaemonian hoplites, about 120 of them Spartiates, surrendered rather than die (4.38–40), contradicting the Thermopylae image of Spartans who never yield; Athens then held them as hostages against invasion.

  6. Where and when did both Cleon and Brasidas die, and what was the consequence?
    Answer

    At Amphipolis in 422 (5.6–11). With the two chief proponents of war gone, Nicias and Pleistoanax negotiated the Peace of Nicias in 421 (5.16–19).

  7. Give the central proposition of the Athenians in the Melian Dialogue and the fate of Melos.
    Answer

    Justice applies only between equals in power; the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must (5.89), by a law of nature (5.105). Melos was besieged, betrayed and taken; the men were killed, women and children enslaved, and 500 Athenian colonists settled (5.116).

  8. List three decisions or events that turned the Sicilian Expedition from near-success into catastrophe.
    Answer

    Any three of: the recall of Alcibiades; Gylippus' arrival and counter-wall in 414; the failed night attack on Epipolae; Nicias' refusal to withdraw when Demosthenes urged it; the lunar eclipse delay of 27 August 413; the defeat in the Great Harbour and the retreat to the Assinarus.

  9. What was legally wrong with the Arginusae trial, and who recorded that Socrates objected?
    Answer

    The six generals were tried and condemned collectively by a single vote, contrary to the decree of Cannonus requiring individual trials; Euryptolemus argued against it (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.7). Plato (Apology 32b) and Xenophon (Memorabilia 1.1.18) record that Socrates, as a presiding prytanis, refused to put the motion.

  10. What terms did Athens accept in 404, and how did the democracy return in 403?
    Answer

    Demolition of the Long Walls and Piraeus fortifications, a fleet of twelve ships, recall of exiles, and following Spartan leadership (Xenophon, Hellenica 2.2.20). Thrasybulus' democrats from Phyle took the Piraeus and killed Critias at Munychia; King Pausanias, outflanking Lysander, brokered a reconciliation and amnesty (2.4).

Carry forward

  1. Thucydides separates stated grievances from structural cause, and the whole History is built to argue that distinction; later Greek historians, and modern readers, inherit both the method and its blind spots.
  2. The war's turning points were political as much as military: the plague and Pericles' death, the rejection of Spartan peace in 425, the recall of Alcibiades, and the Arginusae trial each show the Athenian assembly destroying its own instruments.
  3. The Melian principle, that the strong rule where they can, is tested at Syracuse and answered at Aegospotami; the fourth century begins with Sparta holding the hegemony Athens lost, Persia paying for it, and the Athenian amnesty of 403 as the model for ending civil war.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Peloponnesian War, 431 to 404 BC, following Thucydides and then Xenophon's Hellenica for the end. Cover: the causes as Thucydides frames them (the truest cause versus the stated grievances: Corcyra, Potidaea, the Megarian Decree); the Archidamian War, Pericles' strategy, the Funeral Oration and the plague; Mytilene and the Mytilenean Debate; Pylos and Sphacteria, Cleon and Brasidas, Amphipolis; the Peace of Nicias; Alcibiades; the Melian Dialogue; the Sicilian Expedition in detail and its catastrophe; the Decelean War, the oligarchic coup of 411, Arginusae and the trial of the generals; Aegospotami, the siege, the surrender, the Thirty Tyrants and the restoration of 403. Then Thucydides as historian: his method, his speeches, his view of human nature and power, and why he still matters. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 6 · The Classical age, 480 to 323 BC · 6.4 · 4,670 words

Tragedy and comedy

Two festivals: the City Dionysia and the LenaeaTheatre, masks, chorus and the three actorsOrigins: dithyramb, Thespis and the goatAeschylusSophoclesEuripidesAristotle's Poetics: plot, hamartia, catharsisOld Comedy and AristophanesMenander, New Comedy, and six plays to read firstSelf-testCarry forward

Two festivals: the City Dionysia and the Lenaea

Attic drama was competitive worship, staged twice a year for Dionysus and financed as a public duty. The City Dionysia fell in Elaphebolion (late March), when the seas reopened and allies and foreigners filled the city; the Lenaea in Gamelion (January/February), when the audience was Athenian only, as Dicaeopolis says when he claims he may abuse the city because "no strangers are present" (Aristophanes, Acharnians 502–8). Comedy entered the Lenaea around 440, tragedy about 432, and the Lenaea stayed comedy's home: Acharnians, Knights, Wasps and Frogs were Lenaean.

The Dionysia began with the statue of Dionysus Eleuthereus brought back by torchlight from the Eleutherae road, and a proagon at which each poet presented his unmasked actors. Then the pompe, with sacrificial bulls, phalloi carried by the allies and the choregoi in finery. Before the plays the city displayed itself: the allies' tribute was carried through the orchestra, war orphans paraded in new armour, benefactors were crowned (Isocrates, On the Peace 82; Aeschines, Against Ctesiphon 41–8).

The eponymous archon chose three tragic poets months ahead ("granting a chorus") and assigned each a choregos, a rich citizen who paid for the chorus's training, costume and upkeep; Lysias 21.1–5 prices a tragic chorus at thirty minae. The state paid poet and, from 449, actors. Programme: twenty dithyrambic choruses, five comedies (three in wartime, probably), and three days of tragedy, one poet per day with a tetralogy of three tragedies and a satyr play. Aeschylus preferred connected tetralogies (the Oresteia plus the lost satyr play Proteus); Sophocles and Euripides usually did not. Judging was built against bribery: names from each tribe were sealed in urns, one judge drawn from each at the festival, and of their ten tablets only five were counted (Lysias 4.3). Plutarch, Cimon 8, records the archon in 468 making Cimon's generals judge, and Sophocles beating Aeschylus. The inscribed results, through Aristotle's lost Didascaliae and the hypotheses prefixed to our texts, give us most of our dates.

Where sources disagree. Simon Goldhill ("The Great Dionysia and civic ideology", 1987) read the pre-play ceremonies as a civic frame that tragedy then questioned, making the genre democratic to its core. Jasper Griffin (CQ 1998) replied that the plays concern mythical kings and families and the reading is a projection; Scott Scullion ("Nothing to do with Dionysus", 2002) doubted the Dionysiac setting shaped the plays at all.

Theatre, masks, chorus and the three actors

The stone Theatre of Dionysus on the Acropolis's south slope is Lycurgan (330s) and later. The fifth-century theatre had wooden benches (theatron), an orchestra not yet the circle of Epidaurus, and from at least 458 a wooden skene whose central door served as palace, tent or cave, flanked by two side entrances (eisodoi). Two machines matter: the ekkyklema, a platform rolled out to show an interior tableau (the bodies in Agamemnon 1372ff), and the mechane, a crane for gods, which Trygaeus on his dung beetle begs the operator to handle carefully (Peace 174–6). Plato's "more than thirty thousand" spectators (Symposium 175e) is a boast; the Lycurgan theatre held perhaps fifteen thousand, and Eric Csapo argues the fifth-century cavea nearer six thousand.

All performers were masked, in full-head pieces of stiffened linen, cork or wood, naturalistic beside the later towering onkos; Pollux's twenty-eight tragic masks (Onomasticon 4.133–54) are Hellenistic. Masks let three men play twelve roles and men play women, and fixed the face, so that voice, posture and text carried meaning. The chorus numbered twelve under Aeschylus, fifteen from Sophocles (Life of Sophocles 4), twenty-four in comedy; the dancers were citizen amateurs, and the poet was their didaskalos, "teacher". The three-actor rule is Aristotle's: Aeschylus added the second actor and "gave the lead to speech", Sophocles the third and scene painting (Poetics 1449a15–18). No surviving tragedy needs more than three speakers at once; the doublings are interpretative (one actor may have played both Clytemnestra and Cassandra). From 449 protagonists had their own prize.

Origins: dithyramb, Thespis and the goat

Aristotle derives tragedy "from those who led off the dithyramb", comedy from the leaders of phallic songs, and says tragedy grew out of something "satyr-like" before acquiring dignity (Poetics 1449a9–21). Herodotus 1.23 credits the dithyramb's shaping to Arion at Corinth; the Suda adds that Arion "invented the tragic mode". Herodotus 5.67 mentions "tragic choruses" for the hero Adrastus at Sicyon, transferred to Dionysus by the tyrant Cleisthenes. The Peloponnesians claimed both genres (1448a29–b2).

The Athenian story centres on Thespis of Icaria. The Marmor Parium places his first tragic victory between 538 and 528, under Pisistratus. Tradition gives him the first actor stepping out to "answer" the chorus (hypokrites), masks of white lead and then linen, and a wagon-stage (Horace, Ars Poetica 275–7); Plutarch has Solon rebuke him for "telling such lies" (Solon 29.6). Nothing genuine survives. Of his successors, Pratinas of Phlius is credited with the satyr play, and Phrynichus was fined for making the theatre weep with his Capture of Miletus (Herodotus 6.21). Tragoidia is "goat-song": a goat prize, a goat sacrifice (Walter Burkert, 1966) or singers dressed as goats; nobody knows which.

Where sources disagree. Gerald Else (The Origin and Early Form of Greek Tragedy, 1965) rejected the dithyramb and the ritual model, arguing that Thespis and Aeschylus invented a literary form from epic and Solonian elegy. Most scholars keep a choral-Dionysiac background, but the Cambridge ritualists' dying-god drama is dead and Winkler's ephebe thesis unproven. Between Thespis and Persians lie sixty years we cannot see.

Aeschylus

Born at Eleusis c. 525/4, Aeschylus fought at Marathon (his epitaph, in the ancient Life and Pausanias 1.14.5, names Marathon and not poetry) and probably Salamis; first victory 484, thirteen in all; death at Gela 456/5. Of seventy to ninety plays, seven survive, the oldest drama we possess. His signature is the connected trilogy, in which a curse or divine purpose unfolds across generations and justice itself changes shape. His choruses are vast and theologically searching; his stagecraft, as Oliver Taplin showed (The Stagecraft of Aeschylus, 1977), works through entrances, exits and silences: Cassandra's muteness, the crimson cloth, the Furies' torchlit exit. Aristophanes's Aeschylus in Frogs is the maker of towering diction who taught Athenians to fight (1019–27).

He goes knowingly under Oedipus's curse; both die. The Antigone ending is probably a later addition.

Where sources disagree. Antiquity never doubted Prometheus Bound. Mark Griffith (The Authenticity of Prometheus Bound, 1977) showed its metre, vocabulary, chorus-handling and stagecraft differ from the other six; M. L. West (Studies in Aeschylus, 1990) proposed the son Euphorion, c. 440–430. Lloyd-Jones and Podlecki defend it. Call it "attributed to Aeschylus".

Sophocles

Sophocles (c. 496–406/5), of Colonus, was the most successful dramatist Athens had and a public man: Hellenotamias in 443/2, general with Pericles against Samos in 441/0, one of the probouloi after Sicily in 413, and after death honoured as the hero Dexion. Some 123 plays, eighteen Dionysia victories, never third (Life). He beat Aeschylus at his first attempt in 468 and in 406 brought his chorus on in mourning for Euripides. Reported innovations: the third actor, scene painting, the chorus raised to fifteen, a treatise On the Chorus (Suda), and the self-contained play in place of the trilogy. His seven plots hinge on a single, isolated will meeting a limit, whose refusal is at once catastrophe and distinction; he is the master of peripeteia and late recognition, and the Poetics is in effect a theory of Oedipus Tyrannus. He is also the most steadily religious of the three: oracles come true, gods are present and opaque.

Haemon fails to move his father; Tiresias warns; Creon relents too late: Antigone has hanged herself, Haemon dies on her body, Eurydice follows.
Oedipus Tyrannus (Theban)c. 429–425; second prizePlague-stricken Thebes; Oedipus vows to find Laius's killer. Tiresias, Jocasta, a Corinthian messenger and the old herdsman each supply a piece until he learns he killed his father and married his mother. Jocasta hangs herself; he blinds himself and asks for exile.

Theseus grants asylum; Creon seizes his daughters and is foiled; Polynices begs blessing and is cursed. Thunder calls; Oedipus walks off unled and vanishes, becoming Athens's protecting hero.

Shamed, he delivers a deceptive calm speech and dies on Hector's sword mid-play. Teucer defends the body against the Atreidae; his enemy Odysseus secures its burial.
Philoctetes (Trojan)409, first prizeTroy needs the marooned Philoctetes and Heracles's bow. Odysseus sends young Neoptolemus to deceive him; the boy wins trust, takes the bow, cannot bear the lie and returns it. Heracles appears and orders both to Troy. No woman on stage.
Electra (Argive)c. 420–410; order relative to Euripides's play unknownElectra lives in open hatred in Clytemnestra's house. The tutor reports Orestes's fictitious chariot death; Electra mourns over an urn until her brother reveals himself. Clytemnestra is killed inside; Aegisthus is driven in to die. No Furies follow.
Women of Trachis (Heracles)Uncertain; 450s to 420sHeracles's captives arrive, among them his new concubine Iole. Deianira sends him a robe anointed with Nessus's "love charm", which eats him alive; she kills herself in silence. Heracles recognises the oracle and orders Hyllus to marry Iole and burn him on Oeta.

Euripides

Euripides (c. 485/480–406) was by tradition born on Salamis, knew Anaxagoras, Protagoras and Socrates, won only four times in life, and died at the court of Archelaus of Macedon. He was the most performed dramatist of later antiquity, which is why nineteen plays survive: seven from the same school selection as the other two sevens, and the "alphabetic" ten (Helen to Hippolytus, with Cyclops) from a chance-preserved volume of a complete edition. He is the great disturber. A prologue monologue lays out the backstory; a god on the crane often imposes an ending the action has not earned; between come formal debates, monody in the new music, slaves and women at the centre, heroes in rags. Aristophanes spent three comedies on him for teaching the people "to chatter" (Frogs 954–8). Aristotle calls him "the most tragic of the poets" while faulting his plots (Poetics 1453a29).

Where sources disagree. The Macedonian exile rests on late sources; Scott Scullion ("Euripides and Macedon", CQ 2003) argued it is spun from the plays. Rhesus, transmitted as his, was doubted by an ancient hypothesis; most moderns place it in the fourth century, though Ritchie (1964) defended it.
PlayDateSummary
Medea (Argonautic; Corinth)431, third prizeJason abandons Medea for Creon's daughter. Granted a day's grace and sanctuary from Aegeus, she sends the bride a poisoned robe that kills her and Creon, kills her two sons after debating with herself, and appears above the house in the Sun's chariot.
Hippolytus (Attic; Theseus)428, first prize; a revised versionAphrodite makes Phaedra love her chaste stepson. The nurse betrays the secret; Hippolytus swears silence; Phaedra hangs herself leaving a tablet accusing him. Theseus curses his son, who is dragged by his horses. Artemis reveals the truth; father and dying son reconcile.
Alcestis (Thessalian; Admetus)438, second prize, in the satyr-play slotAlcestis dies on stage in place of her husband, who promises never to remarry. Heracles, hosted by a lying Admetus, learns the truth, wrestles Death at the tomb and returns with a veiled woman Admetus must accept. Tragicomic, hence "pro-satyric".
Children of Heracles (Heracles; Attic)c. 430Iolaus and Heracles's children seek refuge at Marathon from Eurystheus; Demophon protects them; an oracle demands a maiden, and Macaria volunteers. Iolaus is rejuvenated in battle; captured Eurystheus prophesies his grave will guard Attica against Argive descendants, meaning Sparta.
Andromache (Trojan aftermath)c. 425; perhaps not first staged at AthensNeoptolemus's concubine Andromache is threatened by his barren wife Hermione and Menelaus, who use her child as bait; old Peleus rescues them. Orestes carries Hermione off and has Neoptolemus murdered at Delphi. Thetis consoles Peleus. Fiercely anti-Spartan.
Hecuba (Trojan aftermath)c. 424Polyxena is demanded for Achilles's tomb and dies nobly despite Hecuba's plea to Odysseus. Then Polydorus's body washes up: his Thracian host Polymestor killed him for gold. Hecuba blinds Polymestor and kills his sons; he foretells her transformation into a dog.
Suppliant Women (Theban; Attic)c. 423Mothers of the Argive seven beg at Eleusis for Theseus to recover their sons' bodies from Thebes. Urged by his mother Aethra, he defeats Thebes and buries the dead; Evadne leaps onto Capaneus's pyre. Athena imposes an Argive oath of alliance with Athens.
Electra (Argive)c. 420–413Electra is married to a decent poor farmer. Orestes, recognised from a scar, kills Aegisthus at a sacrifice; Electra lures Clytemnestra with a feigned childbirth and they kill her, then collapse in remorse. The Dioscuri tidy up and criticise Apollo.
Heracles (Heracles; Thebes)c. 416Heracles returns from Hades in time to kill the usurper Lycus. Then Iris and Madness descend; he slaughters wife and children. Waking bound to a pillar he wants death; Theseus persuades him to live in Athens. He calls the gods' crimes poets' lies.
Trojan Women (Trojan aftermath)415, second prize, with the lost Alexandros and PalamedesTroy burns; Hecuba watches the allotments: Cassandra to Agamemnon, Andromache to Neoptolemus. Astyanax is thrown from the walls. Helen pleads against Hecuba before Menelaus. Hecuba buries the child on Hector's shield. Staged months after Athens destroyed Melos.
Iphigenia among the Taurians (Argive aftermath)c. 414Saved from Aulis by Artemis, Iphigenia is her priestess among the Taurians, sacrificing Greeks. Orestes comes to steal the image; a letter brings recognition. They trick King Thoas with a sham purification and escape; Athena founds the cults at Brauron and Halae.
Ion (Attic foundation)c. 413Temple boy Ion is Apollo's son by Creusa, who exposed him. The oracle gives him to Xuthus; Creusa tries to poison him; he hunts her to the altar; the Pythia produces the exposure cradle and mother and son recognise each other. Athena, not Apollo, explains.
Helen (Trojan aftermath)412The Helen at Troy was a phantom; the real one sat chaste in Egypt. Shipwrecked Menelaus finds her; the phantom dissolves. They fake his death and escape in the ship meant for his sea-burial; the Dioscuri stop King Theoclymenus. Romance about names and bodies.
Phoenician Women (Theban)c. 409Jocasta, alive, fails to reconcile Eteocles and Polynices; Tiresias demands Menoeceus's death and the boy gives it; the brothers die in single combat and Jocasta over them; Creon exiles blind Oedipus, and Antigone goes with him. The ending is expanded by later hands.
Orestes (Argive)408Six days after the matricide, Argos votes to stone Orestes and Electra; Menelaus temporises, Tyndareus denounces. The pair and Pylades plot to kill Helen and hold Hermione hostage; with the palace about to burn Apollo appears and assigns everyone marriages. Near-nihilist.
Bacchae (Theban; Dionysus)405, posthumous, first prizeDionysus returns to Thebes; Pentheus denies and arrests him. Escaped, the god dresses the unmanned king as a maenad to spy; the bacchants led by his mother Agave tear him apart. She returns with his head as a lion's; Cadmus restores her to sanity.
Iphigenia at Aulis (Trojan)405, posthumousAgamemnon has lured Iphigenia to Aulis with a false marriage to Achilles. He wavers; Clytemnestra discovers the truth; Achilles offers protection; the army demands blood. Iphigenia chooses to die for Greece. Unfinished at Euripides's death; both ends are suspect.
Rhesus (Trojan; authorship disputed)Transmitted as Euripides; probably fourth centuryIliad 10 from the Trojan side: Hector receives the Thracian ally Rhesus; Odysseus and Diomedes, guided by Athena, kill him; his mother the Muse laments. A night play of sentries and passwords, with no prologue and no tragic centre.

The satyr play and Cyclops

The fourth play of a tetralogy was a satyr play: shorter, in tragic metre, with a chorus of satyrs led by their father Silenus in horse-tails and phalloi, treating a heroic myth as burlesque with stock motifs of captivity, monster, marvellous invention and cowardly bragging. Horace (Ars Poetica 220–50) calls it relief for an audience "drunk and lawless". Papyri preserve much of Aeschylus's Net-Haulers and Sophocles's Trackers. Euripides's Cyclops is the only complete one; date uncertain, perhaps 408 with Orestes (Seaford), perhaps the 420s. Silenus and the satyrs are Polyphemus's slaves on Etna. Odysseus trades wine for food, is betrayed by Silenus, watches two men eaten, gets the Cyclops drunk and blinds him with the heated stake while the satyrs cheer and invent excuses not to help. Odyssey 9 as farce, an hour after Agave's severed head.

Aristotle's Poetics: plot, hamartia, catharsis

The Poetics (c. 335) is lecture notes, incomplete (the book on comedy is lost), by a reader of plays seventy years after our last tragedy. Tragedy is "an imitation of an action that is serious, complete and of magnitude ... through pity and fear accomplishing the katharsis of such emotions" (1449b24–8). Of its six parts, plot is "the soul" (1450a38), spectacle "least artistic". The best plot is complex, with peripeteia and anagnorisis coinciding as in Oedipus (1452a22–33); its hero is "between the extremes" and falls "not through vice but through some hamartia" (1453a7–17).

Hamartia is not "tragic flaw". In the Nicomachean Ethics (1135b) hamartema is a mistake made in ignorance of a particular: Oedipus did not know the man at the crossroads. Bremer (Hamartia, 1969) and Stinton (1975) dispute whether it shades into culpable error; Stinton's "range of meanings" is the consensus. Catharsis appears once in the Poetics, unexplained; Politics 8.1341b–1342a describes a musical katharsis that relieves "as if by medical treatment". Bernays (1857) read purgation; Lessing purification; Golden and Nussbaum (The Fragility of Goodness, 1986) clarification; Halliwell (Aristotle's Poetics, 1986) a medical metaphor for emotions properly felt, not evacuated.

Where sources disagree. How far to trust it: it is the only criticism by someone who read hundreds of lost tragedies, and it ignores Dionysus, the festival, politics, the gods and the chorus (1456a25). Its model is Oedipus; it has no room for the trilogy, for Persians or for Bacchae. Halliwell defends it as a theory of a core type; Vernant and Goldhill call it a fourth-century misreading. The "unities" are not in it: 1449b12 only notes tragedy "tries" to stay within one day; Castelvetro invented the rest in 1570.

Old Comedy and Aristophanes

Comedy entered the Dionysia in 486 (Suda); Cratinus and Eupolis survive in fragments. Aristophanes (c. 446–c. 386) wrote about forty plays from 427; eleven survive, the only complete Old Comedies. Costume was padded belly and buttocks with a leather phallus; the chorus of twenty-four might be men, wasps, birds or clouds. The form has set parts: a prologue states a fantastic idea; the parodos brings on a usually hostile chorus; the agon is a formal debate the hero wins. Then the parabasis: with the actors gone, the chorus "steps forward" and addresses the audience in a fixed sequence (kommation; anapaests, often in the poet's own voice; pnigos; ode, epirrhema, antode, antepirrhema). Here Aristophanes talks about himself: Cleon's prosecution over Babylonians (Acharnians 628–64), his career (Knights 507–50), his third place with Clouds (518–62). Episodes then test the idea on a parade of intruders, and an exodos of feast or wedding closes. The parabasis shrinks in Frogs and vanishes in Assemblywomen and Wealth: Old Comedy turning Middle before our eyes.

The satire is personal, onomasti komoidein, abusing real men by name, above all Cleon. Yet Cleon was elected general weeks after Knights won, and Socrates lived twenty-four years after Clouds. The alleged decree of Syracosius (415) banning abuse by name rests on a scholion to Birds 1297 and may be invented.

Where sources disagree. Was Aristophanes a conservative with a programme, a festival safety-valve, or democratic accountability in costume? Jeffrey Henderson (1990) sees a citizen-adviser meant to be taken seriously; Stephen Halliwell stresses the ritual frame that made abuse unreal; Malcolm Heath (Political Comedy in Aristophanes, 1987) doubts persuasion was intended. Plato's Apology 18b–19c already names Aristophanes among Socrates's "old accusers".

Wealth388Chremylus, following Delphi's advice, takes home the blind god Wealth. Poverty argues she alone makes men work, and loses. Cured at Asclepius's shrine, Wealth enriches the just; informers, a hag's gigolo and a starving Hermes come begging. Quiet, moralising; the chorus barely sings.

Menander, New Comedy, and six plays to read first

By the 380s comedy had shed its political target, its parabasis and most of its chorus ("Middle Comedy": Antiphanes, Alexis). New Comedy, from about 320, is the comedy of private life in a city that no longer governs itself: a lover, a girl who proves to be a citizen's lost daughter, a soldier, a courtesan, a clever slave, an angry father, a recognition by tokens, a wedding. The chorus is a band of revellers whose entrances mark five acts (manuscripts write only XOPOY); prologues are spoken by Chance (Aspis) or Ignorance (Perikeiromene). Menander (342/1–291/0), pupil of Theophrastus, wrote over a hundred plays and won eight times; Aristophanes of Byzantium asked, "O Menander, O life, which of you imitated the other?" His text vanished from the Byzantine schools and returned on papyrus, above all the Bodmer codex (1958) with the complete Dyskolos (316; the misanthrope Cnemon falls down his well and is reconciled), most of Samia, and much of Epitrepontes. Through Plautus and Terence his plots reach Shakespeare and Molière; Menander, not Aristophanes, is the ancestor of European comedy.

Six to read first

  1. Aeschylus, Agamemnon, then the rest of the Oresteia: the only complete trilogy, the densest poetry, and the template every later Orestes answers.
  2. Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus: Aristotle's model; read it before the Poetics so you can test the theory against the play.
  3. Sophocles, Antigone: the cleanest clash of two kinds of right, and the tragedy later philosophy and politics have used most.
  4. Euripides, Medea: his whole method in one evening, prologue, debate, a woman at the centre, a superhuman exit, no consolation.
  5. Euripides, Bacchae: the one tragedy about the festival's god, with the chorus restored to power.
  6. Aristophanes, Frogs: the play that discusses the others, Aeschylus against Euripides judged by Dionysus, with every Old Comedy convention on show and the city about to fall.

A second six: Persians, Hippolytus, Trojan Women, Philoctetes, Lysistrata, Dyskolos.

Self-test

  1. In which months did the City Dionysia and the Lenaea fall, and why did that matter for the audience?
    Answer

    Dionysia in Elaphebolion (March/April), when the open seas brought allies and foreigners; Lenaea in Gamelion (January/February), Athenians only, as Acharnians 502–8 exploits.

  2. What did a choregos pay for, and what did Lysias 21 say a tragic chorus cost?
    Answer

    Training, costume, upkeep and victory feast of the chorus; about thirty minae. The state paid poet and actors.

  3. How were the ten judges chosen, and how many votes were counted?
    Answer

    One drawn at the festival from each of ten sealed tribal urns; only five of their ten tablets were drawn and counted.

  4. Which innovations does Aristotle give to Aeschylus and to Sophocles in Poetics 1449a?
    Answer

    Aeschylus: second actor, reduced chorus, primacy of speech. Sophocles: third actor and scene painting.

  5. What does the Marmor Parium tell us about Thespis, and what does Horace add?
    Answer

    A first tragic victory between 538 and 528, under Pisistratus. Horace (Ars Poetica 275–7) adds the wagon.

  6. Why do many scholars doubt that Aeschylus wrote Prometheus Bound?
    Answer

    Griffith (1977) showed its metre, vocabulary, chorus and stagecraft differ from the other six; West proposed Euphorion, c. 440–430. Antiquity never doubted it.

  7. Why do nineteen plays of Euripides survive against seven each of the others?
    Answer

    Seven come from the selected school edition like the other sevens; ten more (Helen to Hippolytus, with Cyclops) survived by chance in one volume of an alphabetical complete edition.

  8. What does hamartia mean in Aristotle, and what does it not mean?
    Answer

    An error made in ignorance of a particular fact, like Oedipus at the crossroads; not a moral "tragic flaw". Bremer and Stinton debate how far it reaches toward culpable error.

  9. Name the parts of a parabasis and say what Aristophanes uses it for.
    Answer

    Kommation, anapaests, pnigos, ode, epirrhema, antode, antepirrhema. The chorus speaks for the poet: Cleon's prosecution (Acharnians), his career (Knights), his defeat with Clouds.

  10. What replaced the chorus in New Comedy, and which Menander play survives complete?
    Answer

    Revellers whose entrances mark the five acts, noted only as XOPOY. Dyskolos (316), from the Bodmer papyrus, 1958.

Carry forward

  1. Attic drama was competitive civic worship of Dionysus, paid for by liturgy and judged by lot; read every play as one entry on one day of a festival the whole city attended.
  2. The three tragedians are three answers to the same inherited myths: Aeschylus's justice evolving across a trilogy, Sophocles's single will meeting its limit, Euripides's unconsoled scrutiny of cruelty and gods. Keep the Theban and Argive cycles as the spine on which all three hang their variations.
  3. Aristotle's Poetics is a fourth-century theory of one kind of plot; use it as a tool for Oedipus, not the law of the genre, and treat hamartia and catharsis as contested words, not settled doctrine.
