GREECE · UNIT 6 · The Classical age, 480 to 323 BC · 6.5 · 3,476 words

The Sophists, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle

The SophistsNomos, physis and fearSocrates: sources and methodThe trial of 399 and the deathPlato: Academy, dialogue, FormsThe Republic, the Symposium, the late dialoguesAristotleThe minor SocraticsSelf-testCarry forward

The Sophists

Sophistēs began as a compliment (Herodotus 1.29 uses it of Solon). By the 420s it meant a travelling professional who taught, for a fee, what a citizen needed in assembly and court: argument, speaking, general culture. The Sophists were not a school; they shared a market, not doctrines. Almost nothing they wrote survives whole; we read them through Plato, who made them his foils, and the fragments in Diels and Kranz (DK 80 to 90).

SophistOrigin and datesCharacteristic claimPrincipal sources
ProtagorasAbdera, c. 490 to c. 420Man the measure; two opposed arguments on every matterPlato, Protagoras, Theaetetus 152a; Diogenes Laertius 9.50 to 56; DK 80 B1, B4, B6a
GorgiasLeontini, c. 485 to c. 380Logos as a power that compels the soulEncomium of Helen, Defence of Palamedes; Plato, Gorgias, Meno 76c
ProdicusCeos, c. 465 to c. 395Precise synonyms; gods as deified useful thingsPlato, Protagoras 337a to c; Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21 to 34; Sextus, Against the Mathematicians 9.18
HippiasElis, c. 470 to after 399Polymathy; first Olympic victor listPlato, Hippias Major, Hippias Minor, Protagoras 337c to d; Plutarch, Numa 1.4
AntiphonAthens, fifth centuryLaw as convention against nature's necessityOn Truth, papyrus fragments (DK 87 B44)
ThrasymachusChalcedon, active c. 430 to 400Justice as the advantage of the strongerPlato, Republic 1.336b to 354c; Aristotle, Rhetoric 3.1, 3.8; DK 85 B1

Protagoras can be stated with most confidence. "Man is the measure of all things, of things that are that they are, of things that are not that they are not" (DK 80 B1). "Concerning the gods I am unable to know whether they exist or not" (B4). On every matter there are two opposed logoi (B6a). Plato's Protagoras adds the Great Speech (320c to 328d): justice and shame are given to all humans as the condition of city life, so virtue is teachable as a mother tongue is. He was no revolutionary; he wrote laws for Thurii in 444 (Diogenes Laertius 9.50).

Gorgias came to Athens on an embassy in 427 (Diodorus 12.53) and dazzled it with antithesis. His Encomium of Helen acquits her under every hypothesis and gives the first theory of speech as a drug: logos is "a great potentate, which with the smallest body accomplishes the most divine works" (Helen 8). On Not-Being, known through Sextus, argued that nothing exists, could not be known if it did, and could not be communicated if known. In the Meno (76c) he laughs at the idea he teaches virtue; he sold technique. Prodicus taught fine distinctions between words (Protagoras 337a to c), composed the Choice of Heracles (Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21 to 34), and held that early humans deified sun, rivers, bread and wine, whence Demeter and Dionysus (Sextus 9.18). Hippias compiled the Olympic victor list on which Greek chronology depended, and at Protagoras 337c to d calls "law, the tyrant of men", a force against nature. Antiphon's On Truth (DK 87 B44) says a man best serves himself by honouring law before witnesses and nature when alone; law's demands are adventitious, nature's necessary; Greeks and barbarians are by nature alike. Thrasymachus in Republic 1 calls justice "the advantage of the stronger" (338c) and "another's good" (343c): rulers legislate for themselves and the just obey at their own cost. The historical Thrasymachus was a stylist; his one real fragment (DK 85 B1) defends the ancestral constitution and sounds conservative.

Where sources disagree. Antiphon the Sophist and Antiphon of Rhamnus, the oligarch executed in 411, may be one man or two. Hermogenes separated them on style; Gagarin argues for one, Pendrick for two. If one, the theorist of law's artificiality was also an active anti-democratic politician. Unresolved.

Nomos, physis and fear

The fault line ran between nomos (law, custom) and physis (nature). Herodotus had shown through Darius's Greeks and Callatians (3.38) that customs differ and each people prefers its own; Ionian physics had dissolved the gods into process. If law is agreement and nature everywhere the same, which has authority? Protagoras: nomos makes the city possible and is good. Hippias and Antiphon leaned to nature. Callicles in Plato's Gorgias (482c to 486d) says laws are made by the weak many to tame the strong few. The Sisyphus fragment (DK 88 B25), Critias's or Euripides', has a clever man invent the gods to deter secret wrongdoing. The Dissoi Logoi (DK 90) argues both sides of every moral pair.

Four fears follow. Fees: Anytus in the Meno (91c) wishes no citizen would let a Sophist near his son. Religion: agnosticism in a city whose festivals were its politics. Courts: Aristophanes' Clouds (423) has the Worse Argument beat the Better and a son justify beating his father. Class: the pupils were rich, and the two most associated with Sophistic training were Alcibiades and Critias, traitor and leader of the Thirty. Protagoras himself (Protagoras 316c to 317c) admits the profession attracts envy.

Where sources disagree. Diogenes Laertius (9.54) says Protagoras was tried for impiety and his books burned; Plato's Meno (91e) says he died in high repute. Dover showed the fifth-century intellectual impiety trials rest on late evidence, and most scholars treat this one as fiction modelled on Socrates'. The rehabilitation of the Sophists begins with Hegel and Grote (1850); Kerferd's The Sophistic Movement (1981) is the standard case.

Socrates: sources and method

Socrates (469 to 399) wrote nothing. Aristophanes' Clouds, the only evidence from his lifetime, shows a natural philosopher teaching argument for money; it is comedy. Plato's Socrates says things in the Phaedo and Republic that the Socrates of the Apology disclaims. Xenophon's Memorabilia and Apology show a practical moral adviser hard to imagine being executed. Aristotle, the best external check, says Socrates dealt with ethics not nature, sought universal definitions, and did not separate them from particulars as Plato did (Metaphysics 1.6, 987b1 to 6; 13.4, 1078b17 to 32). Lost are the Socratic writings of Antisthenes and Aeschines, and Polycrates' hostile Accusation (c. 393), which Memorabilia 1.2 answers.

On the method, the elenchus, the witnesses converge. The interlocutor asserts a thesis; Socrates secures agreement to further propositions; these entail the thesis's negation; the interlocutor is left in aporia. Socrates insists he teaches nothing. The Apology gives the origin: Delphi said no one was wiser than Socrates, who set out to refute it by examining politicians, poets and craftsmen and found each thought he knew what he did not (21a to 23b). His wisdom is not to think he knows what he does not (21d); "I know that I know nothing" is a later slogan. The Laches, Charmides and Euthyphro show the method and end without a definition.

Positions that recur across the witnesses: virtue is a kind of knowledge; no one does wrong willingly (Protagoras 345d to e, 358c to d); it is better to suffer injustice than commit it, and never right to return a wrong (Gorgias 469c; Crito 49a to e); the soul outranks body and money (Apology 29d to 30b); a daimonion turns him back from actions (Apology 31c to d; Memorabilia 1.1.2 to 4). The ugly face and bare feet are attested (Symposium 215b, 220b); the shrewish Xanthippe is later embroidery.

Where sources disagree. Vlastos (Socrates: Ironist and Moral Philosopher, 1991) held that Plato's early dialogues preserve the real man's method and doctrines, the metaphysical Socrates being Plato's. Kahn (1996) replied that even the early dialogues are Plato's design; Dorion calls the Socratic problem unanswerable. Vlastos's "problem of the elenchus" also stands: showing beliefs inconsistent does not show which is false.

The trial of 399 and the death

The indictment, which Favorinus claimed to have read in the Metroon (Diogenes Laertius 2.40): "Socrates does wrong by not acknowledging the gods the city acknowledges and by introducing new divinities; he also does wrong by corrupting the young. Penalty: death." The prosecutor was Meletus, an obscure poet; behind him stood Anytus, a tanner and leader of the democratic restoration, and Lycon. Socrates says thirty votes the other way would have acquitted him (Apology 36a), implying roughly 280 to 220 of 500. He proposed free meals in the Prytaneum, then thirty minae guaranteed by Plato and Crito (38b). The jury chose death by a larger margin than it convicted.

The context governs the charges. In 404 the Thirty under Critias killed perhaps 1,500 citizens; Critias and Charmides, Socrates' associates and Plato's relatives, were among them, and Alcibiades had betrayed the city twice. The amnesty of 403 barred prosecution for acts before that year, so Socrates could not be charged with training oligarchs, and the case had to be religious. Aeschines (1.173) later said it plainly: "You put to death Socrates the sophist, because he was shown to have educated Critias." Socrates' refusal to arrest Leon of Salamis under the Thirty (Apology 32c to d) and his denial that he ever had pupils (33a to b) answer that unspoken charge.

Execution waited a month for the sacred ship from Delos (Phaedo 58a to c). The Crito refuses escape because fleeing would wrong the laws he had lived under. The Phaedo narrates the last day: the hemlock at sunset, numbness rising from the feet, the last words "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius" (118a). Plato was not there (59b); Xenophon was in Asia. The symptoms match Conium maculatum.

Where sources disagree. Xenophon says Socrates spoke with deliberate arrogance (megalēgoria) because he preferred death to decay; Plato gives a reasoned if provocative defence. Moderns divide between a genuine religious prosecution (Parker), a political purge under religious cover (Stone, 1988), and a scapegoat for 415 to 403 (Waterfield, 2009). The vote shows the city itself divided.

Plato: Academy, dialogue, Forms

Plato (c. 428 to 348/7) was an aristocrat related through his mother to Critias and Charmides. The Seventh Letter, of disputed authenticity but well informed, says he expected a political career and was repelled first by the Thirty, then by the democracy that killed Socrates. After travels, including Syracuse around 388, he taught in the gymnasium in the grove of Academus. The Academy was a circle, not a university: mathematics, dialectic and politics, with Eudoxus, Speusippus, Xenocrates and, from 367, Aristotle. Two more Syracusan visits (367, 361) to shape Dionysius II failed. The inscription about geometry at the door is attested only in the sixth century AD.

Plato never speaks in his own voice. Socrates leads most dialogues but yields in the late ones to an Eleatic visitor, a Locrian and an unnamed Athenian. The Phaedrus (274b to 278b) calls writing a dead image of speech; the Seventh Letter (341c) denies any treatise of Plato's on what matters most. Stylometry since Campbell (1867) fixes a late group (Sophist, Statesman, Philebus, Timaeus, Laws); the early and middle groups are broadly agreed, their internal order is not.

The theory of Forms is what Aristotle credits to Plato as distinct from Socrates. A Form is what a general term names: the Beautiful itself, the Equal itself. Forms are outside space and time, unchanging, grasped by thought; sensible things imperfectly participate in them. The Phaedo argues from recollection (72e to 77a): we judge sticks deficiently equal, which presupposes knowledge of Equality that sense never gave. Republic 5 to 7 add the epistemology: knowledge is of what is, opinion of what becomes, and the Good is to the intelligible what the sun is to the visible, "beyond being" (509b). In the Parmenides (130a to 135c) Plato raises the hardest objections, including the regress Aristotle called the Third Man (132a to b), and leaves them unanswered. Whether the late dialogues abandon, revise or restate the theory is disputed.

The Republic, the Symposium, the late dialogues

The Republic asks what justice is and whether it pays. Book 1 clears Thrasymachus. In Book 2 Glaucon's ring of Gyges (359d to 360b) restates the Sophistic challenge: show justice good for its possessor apart from reputation. Socrates founds a city in speech with three classes, producers, auxiliaries, rulers, and in Book 4 matches them to three parts of the soul, appetitive, spirited and reasoning, distinguished because one thing cannot at once want and refuse the same object (436b to 441c). Justice is each part doing its own work under reason (433a to b, 441d to e). Books 2 and 3 censor poetry that shows gods doing evil and install the noble lie of the metals (414b to c). Book 5 abolishes the guardians' families, admits women to rule, and declares that cities' ills will not end until philosophers rule (473c to d). Book 6 gives the ship of state and the Sun; Book 7 the Cave (514a to 517a), whose returning prisoner would be killed, an allusion to Socrates, then a mathematical curriculum ending in dialectic. Books 8 and 9 trace decline through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy and tyranny. Book 10 returns to poetry: imitation stands at third remove from the Form (597e), feeds the lower soul, and is exiled unless it can defend itself, "an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry" (607b).

The Symposium is set after Agathon's tragic victory of 416 and written around 385. Five speakers praise Eros, Aristophanes with his severed halves; Socrates reports Diotima: Eros is a daimōn, child of Resource and Poverty (203b to e), the desire to possess the good for ever, leading from one beautiful body to all, to souls, laws, knowledge, and the sight of the Beautiful itself (210a to 212a). Alcibiades bursts in drunk and praises Socrates instead, recounting his failed seduction and Socrates' courage at Potidaea and Delium (215a to 222b).

The late dialogues change register. The Theaetetus refutes Protagoras on his own terms (171a to c) and fails to define knowledge. The Sophist treats not-being as difference. The Statesman makes weaving the model of rule. The Philebus ranks pleasure and knowledge. The Timaeus has a Demiurge shape a receptacle after the Forms, the Plato the Middle Ages knew. The Laws, unfinished, describes Magnesia, a second-best city under law. Aristotle mentions Plato's "unwritten doctrines" (Physics 209b14 to 15); whether these were a systematic oral metaphysics (Krämer, Gaiser) or little beyond the Philebus (Cherniss) is unresolved.

Aristotle

Aristotle (384 to 322) was born at Stagira, son of a physician to Amyntas III of Macedon. He joined the Academy at seventeen and stayed twenty years. After Plato's death, with Speusippus as head, he left for Assos, then Mytilene, where much of the biology was done, then in 343/2 Macedon as tutor to Alexander; how much he shaped the boy is unknown (Plutarch, Alexander 7 to 8). In 335/4 he returned to teach in the gymnasium of Apollo Lyceius, the Lyceum. After Alexander's death in 323 he was charged with impiety (Diogenes Laertius 5.5) and withdrew to Chalcis, dying in 322; the line about not letting Athens sin twice against philosophy is Aelian's (Varia Historia 3.36) and probably invented. The surviving treatises are lecture material edited by Andronicus of Rhodes in the first century BC; the dialogues antiquity admired are lost.

The break with Plato was philosophical: where friends have introduced the Forms, truth must come before friends (Nicomachean Ethics 1096a11 to 17). Metaphysics 1.9 argues that separated Forms double the world without explaining it and cannot cause change. For Aristotle the primary realities are individual substances, compounds of form and matter; universals exist in particulars. Knowledge begins in perception and rises by induction to first principles (Posterior Analytics 2.19). Hence his work is a set of distinct sciences, not a single ascent to the Good.

The four causes (Physics 2.3, 194b16 to 195a3) are four answers to "why?". Of a statue: the bronze (material), the shape (formal), the sculptor (efficient), the purpose (final). Predecessors had found only the first and third, Plato the second; the final cause, which Aristotle makes central to nature, had been neglected.

The Nicomachean Ethics identifies the human good as eudaimonia via the function argument (1.7, 1097b22 to 1098a20): the human function is rational activity, so the good is rational activity done well, in accordance with virtue, over a whole life. Virtue of character is a disposition to choose, lying in a mean relative to us, determined by reason as the person of practical wisdom would determine it (2.6, 1106b36 to 1107a2). The mean is not moderation: courage is the right amount of fear for this situation, and some acts have no mean (1107a9 to 17). Book 7 rejects Socrates' denial of weakness of will (1145b22 to 27); Book 10 crowns the life of contemplation (1177a12 to 1178a8). The aim is to become good, not to know what goodness is (1103b26 to 29).

The Politics opens with the city as natural and the human as a political animal (1253a2 to 3). Book 1 defends slavery by nature while admitting the controversy (1255a3 ff.); Book 2 attacks the Republic's communism; Book 3 defines the citizen as one who shares in judging and ruling (1275a22) and sets out six constitutions, kingship, aristocracy and polity with their deviations tyranny, oligarchy and democracy (1279a22 to b10); Book 4 praises the middle class (1295b).

The Poetics answers Republic 10 without naming it. Tragedy is "an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, of a certain magnitude, through pity and fear accomplishing the katharsis of such emotions" (1449b24 to 28). Plot is its soul; the best plot moves through reversal and recognition to a fall caused by hamartia, an error not a vice (1453a7 to 17), as in the Oedipus Tyrannus. Katharsis, used once and unexplained, is read as purgation (Bernays), purification, or clarification (Golden, Nussbaum). The book on comedy is lost; the three unities are Castelvetro's (1570), not Aristotle's.

Biology fills more of the corpus than any other subject: History of Animals, Parts of Animals, Generation of Animals, some five hundred kinds. He divided animals into blooded and bloodless, separated dolphins from fish because they breathe and suckle, described the placenta-like attachment of the smooth dogfish embryo (HA 6.10), confirmed in 1842, and the octopus's hectocotylus arm (5.6), disbelieved until the nineteenth century. He also said men have more teeth than women (501b19). Parts of Animals 1.5 (645a) argues that even humble animals reward study because nature works to ends. Darwin told Ogle in 1882 that Linnaeus and Cuvier "were mere schoolboys to old Aristotle".

Where sources disagree. Jaeger (1923) read the corpus developmentally, from Platonist youth to empirical maturity; the thesis depends on dating treatises whose order cannot be fixed, and recent scholarship treats them as concurrent inquiries. The tale that the treatises lay in a cellar at Scepsis (Strabo 13.1.54) is doubted, since Hellenistic authors knew some of them.

The minor Socratics

Cynics. Antisthenes (c. 445 to 365), pupil of Gorgias then Socrates, taught that virtue suffices for happiness; "I would rather go mad than feel pleasure" (Diogenes Laertius 6.3). Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412 to 323) made it a way of life: the storage jar, public shamelessness, the lamp "looking for a human being" (6.41), "defacing the currency" of convention (6.20, 6.71), the first recorded kosmopolitēs (6.63). The Alexander anecdotes (Plutarch, Alexander 14) are legend. Zeno of Citium studied with Diogenes' pupil Crates before founding the Stoa (7.2 to 3), keeping the sufficiency of virtue and dropping the shamelessness.

Cyrenaics. Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 435 to 356) appears in Memorabilia 2.1 and 3.8 as a hedonist Socrates tries to correct; "I possess Laïs, I am not possessed" (Diogenes Laertius 2.75). The doctrine that the end is present bodily pleasure, and that only our own affections (pathē) are knowable, was probably systematised by his grandson. Epicurus despised them and built a hedonism of stable pleasure, but they made pleasure the candidate end every Hellenistic ethics had to address.

Megarians. Euclides of Megara, present at Socrates' death (Phaedo 59c) and host to Plato afterwards (Diogenes Laertius 2.106), fused Socratic ethics with Eleatic monism: the good is one thing under many names. His school turned to logic. Eubulides devised the Liar and the Heap (2.108); Stilpo taught apatheia and taught Zeno (7.2, 7.24); Diodorus Cronus and Philo, whom Sedley assigns to a separate Dialectical school, debated the conditional (Sextus, Outlines 2.110 to 112), and Diodorus's Master Argument (Epictetus, Discourses 2.19.1) forced the Stoics to build a modal theory. Stoic logic grew from this ground.

Where sources disagree. The succession Socrates, Antisthenes, Diogenes, Crates, Zeno is Hellenistic doxography, which wanted lineages. Dudley (1937) argued Antisthenes was no Cynic and that Diogenes barely met him; whether Cyrenaic epistemology is the elder Aristippus's or his grandson's is open. What is secure is that by 300 BC every Hellenistic position had a Socratic pedigree someone claimed.

Self-test

  1. Which three fragments carry most of what we know of Protagoras, and what do they say?
    Answer

    DK 80 B1, man is the measure of all things; B4, agnosticism about the gods; B6a, two opposed arguments on every matter.

  2. What is the nomos/physis distinction, and who took which side?
    Answer

    Law or convention against nature. Protagoras defended nomos as the basis of city life; Hippias, Antiphon and Plato's Callicles treated law as an artificial constraint on nature.

  3. Why is the report of Protagoras's impiety trial doubted?
    Answer

    It rests on Diogenes Laertius 9.54, conflicts with Meno 91e, and fits a pattern Dover showed was modelled on Socrates' trial.

  4. What does Aristotle say about Socrates that separates him from Plato?
    Answer

    That Socrates dealt with ethics not nature, sought universal definitions, and did not separate universals from particulars (Metaphysics 1.6, 13.4).

  5. What were the charges against Socrates, and why religious rather than political?
    Answer

    Not acknowledging the city's gods, introducing new divinities, corrupting the young. The amnesty of 403 barred prosecution for anything before that year, so his link to Critias and Alcibiades could not be charged directly.

  6. Name the three parts of the soul in the Republic and the argument that distinguishes them.
    Answer

    Appetitive, spirited, reasoning. One thing cannot at once want and refuse the same object in the same respect, so inner conflict proves distinct parts (436b to 441c).

  7. What is the Third Man argument and where does Plato raise it?
    Answer

    If the Form of Largeness is itself large, it and large things share a feature requiring a further Form, without end. Parmenides 132a to b.

  8. State Aristotle's definition of virtue and say why the mean is not moderation.
    Answer

    A disposition to choose, in a mean relative to us, determined by reason as the practically wise person would (NE 1106b36 to 1107a2). The mean is the right amount for the situation, which may be extreme; some acts have no mean.

  9. Give two biological observations of Aristotle confirmed only in modern times, and one error.
    Answer

    The dogfish embryo's placental attachment (1842) and the octopus hectocotylus. Error: men have more teeth than women.

  10. Through which two minor Socratics did Zeno of Citium train, and what did each give Stoicism?
    Answer

    Crates the Cynic, whose ethics of virtue as sufficient Stoicism kept; Stilpo the Megarian, whose school's logic fed Stoic dialectic.

Carry forward

  1. The nomos/physis question posed by the Sophists is the question every later Greek ethics answers: Plato by grounding justice in a nature the soul shares with the cosmos, Aristotle by making the city natural, the Cynics by rejecting nomos, the Stoics by identifying nature with reason and law.
  2. Socrates is reconstructed, not reported. Every claim about him must name its witness, and the four witnesses agree on method and manner far more than on doctrine. The same discipline applies to Pythagoras, Diogenes and every figure known through followers.
  3. Aristotle's break with Plato over separated Forms produced the model of knowledge as distinct sciences with their own principles and final causes central to nature. Transmitted through Andronicus, the Arabic commentators and the medieval universities, it is the framework later modules presuppose and the scientific revolution overturns.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Athenian philosophy from the Sophists to Aristotle. Cover: the Sophists (Protagoras, Gorgias, Prodicus, Hippias, Antiphon, Thrasymachus), the nomos/physis debate and why they were feared; Socrates: the problem of sources, the elenchus, the Apology, the trial of 399 in its political context after the Thirty, and his death; Plato: the Academy, the dialogue form, the theory of Forms, the Republic in outline (the tripartite soul, the philosopher-king, the cave, the critique of poetry), the Symposium, and the late dialogues in a paragraph; Aristotle: the Lyceum, the break with Plato, the four causes, the Nicomachean Ethics and the mean, the Politics, the Poetics, and his biology; the minor Socratics (Cynics, Cyrenaics, Megarians) as seeds of the Hellenistic schools. Keep each thinker's actual claims distinct from the legend. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 6 · The Classical age, 480 to 323 BC · 6.6 · 2,962 words

The fourth century: Sparta, Thebes, Philip

The Spartan hegemony and its abuses, 404–395The Corinthian War and the King's Peace, 395–387Sparta overreaches, 386–379The Second Athenian League, 378–Thebes: Epaminondas, Pelopidas and the Sacred BandLeuctra, Messenia, Megalopolis and Mantinea, 371–362Jason of PheraePhilip II: the army and the diplomacy, 359–352The Third Sacred War, Olynthus, and the war of words, 356–346Chaeronea, the League of Corinth and the assassination, 340–336Self-testCarry forward

The Spartan hegemony and its abuses, 404–395

When Lysander sailed into the Piraeus in spring 404 and the walls of Athens came down "to the music of flute-girls" (Xenophon, Hellenica 2.2.23), Sparta inherited an empire it had no apparatus to run. Lysander's answer was personal: in the former Athenian cities he installed boards of ten local oligarchs (dekarchies) backed by a Spartan governor, the harmost, with a garrison. Plutarch (Lysander 13) calls these regimes the harshest Greece had seen, and the harmosts quickly became a byword for brutality, extortion and lack of accountability. Tribute, which Sparta had gone to war promising to abolish, continued; Diodorus (14.10) puts it at more than a thousand talents a year.

At Athens, Lysander's protégés were the Thirty, whose rule (404–403) killed perhaps 1,500 citizens before Thrasybulus' return from Phyle and the amnesty of 403 (Xenophon, Hellenica 2.3–4). It was King Pausanias, not Lysander, who brokered that settlement: the Spartan establishment was already alarmed by Lysander's personal network and dissolved the dekarchies soon after. His scheme to make the kingship elective (Plutarch, Lysander 24–26) came to nothing, and he died at Haliartus in 395.

The deeper problem was structural. Sparta had perhaps 2,500 adult citizens by 400, a number that kept falling (oliganthropia); it could not garrison the Aegean, govern Asia Minor and hold down the Peloponnese at once. Agesilaus' Asian campaign of 396–394 provoked Persia into financing a coalition at home: the satrap Tithraustes' agent Timocrates carried gold to Thebes, Corinth and Argos (Xenophon, Hellenica 3.5.1–2).

Where sources disagree. Xenophon, hostile to Thebes, makes Persian bribery the cause of the Corinthian War. The Oxyrhynchus historian (Hellenica Oxyrhynchia 7) says anti-Spartan feeling at Thebes and Athens long preceded the gold, and that the Theban leaders deliberately engineered a border dispute between Phocis and Locris to force Sparta's hand. Most modern scholars follow the Oxyrhynchus account.

The Corinthian War and the King's Peace, 395–387

The coalition of Athens, Thebes, Corinth and Argos fought Sparta for eight years. On land Sparta won the set battles, at the Nemea River and Coronea in 394 (Xenophon, Hellenica 4.2–3), without being able to exploit them. At sea the decisive event was Cnidus (August 394), where the Athenian exile Conon, commanding a Persian fleet for Pharnabazus, destroyed the Spartan navy; the harmosts were expelled from the islands within months and Conon rebuilt Athens' Long Walls with Persian money (Xenophon, Hellenica 4.8.9–10). Iphicrates' peltasts destroyed a Spartan mora near Lechaeum in 390 (Hellenica 4.5.11–17).

Athens then overreached. Thrasybulus' campaigns of 389–388 revived a tithe at Byzantium and pushed Persia back to Sparta's side. The Spartan admiral Antalcidas blockaded the Hellespont, and the Greeks accepted Artaxerxes II's terms in 387/6. Xenophon preserves the text (Hellenica 5.1.31): the cities of Asia and Cyprus belong to the King; all other Greek cities, great and small, are to be autonomous, except that Athens keeps Lemnos, Imbros and Scyros; whoever refuses, the King will make war on "by land and by sea, with ships and with money".

The King's Peace, the first "common peace" (koine eirene), was a Persian document, but Sparta was its enforcer, and "autonomy" became a weapon: it dissolved the Boeotian federation and the union of Corinth and Argos while leaving the Peloponnesian League intact.

Sparta overreaches, 386–379

Agesilaus used the peace as licence. Mantinea was broken into villages in 385 (Xenophon, Hellenica 5.2.1–7); Phlius was besieged; a Spartan army marched north to dismantle the Olynthian federation (382–379). In 382, en route to Olynthus, Phoebidas accepted an invitation from the Theban oligarch Leontiades and seized the Cadmea, Thebes' acropolis, during the Thesmophoria (Xenophon, Hellenica 5.2.25–31). The democratic leader Ismenias was tried and executed; some 300 Thebans fled to Athens.

Where sources disagree. Xenophon says the Spartan authorities were angry and fined Phoebidas, but Agesilaus argued that only the outcome mattered ("was it useful?"), and Sparta kept the garrison. Diodorus (15.20) and Plutarch (Agesilaus 23–24, Pelopidas 6) report a widespread belief that Phoebidas acted on secret orders. Whether the seizure was policy or opportunism cannot be settled; that Sparta ratified it is not in doubt, and Xenophon himself (Hellenica 5.4.1) treats the fall of Spartan power as divine punishment for the oath-breaking.

In winter 379/8 the exiles struck back. Pelopidas and a handful of conspirators entered Thebes disguised, killed the pro-Spartan polemarchs at a drinking party, and with Athenian border forces in support forced the garrison to capitulate (Xenophon, Hellenica 5.4.2–12; Plutarch, Pelopidas 7–13). Then, in spring 378, the harmost Sphodrias launched an unprovoked night march on the Piraeus, failed to arrive before dawn, and was acquitted at Sparta through Agesilaus' influence (Hellenica 5.4.20–33). Athens, until then wavering, committed to Thebes.

The Second Athenian League, 378–

The league's charter survives on stone: the decree of Aristoteles (IG II² 43, 378/7). It is a point-by-point repudiation of the fifth-century empire: members are to be "free and autonomous", with no garrisons, governors or tribute; Athenians may not own land in allied territory; contributions were called syntaxeis, never phoros; a synod of allies sat at Athens alongside the assembly. Membership reached perhaps seventy cities, Thebes among the earliest, with the stated aim of compelling Sparta to let the Greeks live in peace under the King's Peace.

Where sources disagree. Xenophon (Hellenica 5.4.34) implies the Athenians built the league in reaction to Sphodrias' raid. Diodorus (15.28–29) places the founding before it. The inscription's dating by archon (Nausinicus, 378/7) fits either, and scholars divide between a league already in formation that the raid accelerated (Cawkwell) and one the raid created.

The league worked. Chabrias beat the Spartan fleet at Naxos in September 376, the first Athenian naval victory since the Peloponnesian War; Timotheus won at Alyzeia in 375, and Sparta accepted a renewed common peace recognising the league. But Theban strength now worried Athens as much as Spartan weakness pleased it.

Thebes: Epaminondas, Pelopidas and the Sacred Band

Theban power rested from 378 on three things. First, the re-founded Boeotian federation, now democratic, with seven elected boeotarchs. Second, the Sacred Band, 300 picked hoplites maintained at state expense on the Cadmea, organised, Plutarch says, in pairs of lovers (Pelopidas 18–19); Gorgidas had spread them along the front of the phalanx, Pelopidas concentrated them as one striking unit. Third, Epaminondas, a Pythagorean-trained aristocrat whom Nepos (Epaminondas) and Diodorus (15.39, 15.88) treat as the finest Greek of his age, and whom Xenophon almost ignores until 362.

At Tegyra in 375 Pelopidas with the Sacred Band and a few horsemen beat two Spartan morai in the open, killing both polemarchs (Plutarch, Pelopidas 16–17): the first time a Spartan force had been defeated by a smaller one. In 371 a peace conference at Sparta broke down when Epaminondas insisted on swearing for "the Boeotians", not "the Thebans", and Agesilaus struck Thebes from the treaty (Xenophon, Hellenica 6.3.18–20; Plutarch, Agesilaus 28).

Leuctra, Messenia, Megalopolis and Mantinea, 371–362

King Cleombrotus, already in Phocis, marched into Boeotia and met the Thebans at Leuctra in July 371. Xenophon (Hellenica 6.4.4–15) gives the fullest account. The Thebans put their phalanx fifty shields deep on the left, opposite the Spartan king, and left the rest of their line weak and held back; their cavalry drove the Spartan horse into their own infantry; Cleombrotus and 400 of the 700 Spartiates present fell. Diodorus (15.55–56) adds that Epaminondas deliberately refused battle with his right while his left advanced, the oblique order that later writers made his signature, and Plutarch (Pelopidas 23) has the Sacred Band charge at the run into the gap.

Where sources disagree. Xenophon never names Epaminondas at Leuctra and attributes the result to the cavalry mêlée and Spartan drunkenness at breakfast; Diodorus and Plutarch make it a tactical masterpiece. Numbers differ too: Diodorus gives the Spartans 10,000 against 6,000, Plutarch (Pelopidas 20) fewer. Modern debate (Cawkwell, Hanson, Buckler) turns on whether the deep left wing and the echelon were genuinely new or whether Xenophon's silence is simply his well-attested Theban bias.

Leuctra ended Spartan hegemony because Epaminondas followed it up. In winter 370/69 a Boeotian army with Arcadian, Argive and Elean allies invaded Laconia, the first enemy force there in centuries; unwalled Sparta survived because the Eurotas was in flood and Agesilaus held the city (Xenophon, Hellenica 6.5.22–32). Epaminondas then marched into Messenia, freed the helots who had worked Sparta's richest land for three centuries, recalled exiles from Italy, Sicily and Libya, and founded Messene on Mount Ithome (Diodorus 15.66; Pausanias 4.26–27). Sparta lost half its territory and the economic basis of the Spartiate way of life, and never recovered.

The Arcadians, encouraged by Thebes, had already united (370) and founded Megalopolis, a federal capital settled from some forty villages to block the road north from Sparta (Diodorus 15.72; Pausanias 8.27).

Where sources disagree. Pausanias dates Megalopolis to 371/0, immediately after Leuctra; Diodorus places it in 368. Whether Epaminondas personally planned the city, as Pausanias says, or merely approved an Arcadian initiative, is uncertain.

The Theban decade was never a hegemony in the Spartan sense. Epaminondas built a fleet in 364 and briefly won over Byzantium, Chios and Rhodes (Diodorus 15.78–79); Pelopidas was killed at Cynoscephalae the same year fighting Alexander of Pherae (Plutarch, Pelopidas 32). The Arcadians split over the use of sacred money from Olympia, and Mantinea went over to Sparta. Epaminondas marched south a fourth time in 362 and met Sparta, Athens, Mantinea and Elis at Mantinea; he won by the same deep left-wing attack and died of a spear wound as he did so (Xenophon, Hellenica 7.5.18–27; Diodorus 15.84–87). Xenophon ends his history there, judging that afterwards there was "even more confusion and disorder in Greece than before".

Jason of Pherae

The one new centralising power of the 370s was Thessalian. Jason, tyrant of Pherae, had by 375 made himself tagos, federal war-leader of all Thessaly, commanding (he claimed) 8,000 cavalry and 20,000 hoplites plus mercenaries. Xenophon reports his ambitions through his enemy Polydamas of Pharsalus, who went to Sparta for help and was told there was none to give (Hellenica 6.1.4–19). Jason arrived at Leuctra the day after the battle, allied to Thebes, and talked the Thebans out of storming the Spartan camp (Hellenica 6.4.20–26); they later suspected he wanted Sparta weakened, not destroyed. In 370 he announced he would preside over the Pythian festival with his whole army, and was assassinated by seven young men before he could go; many Greek cities honoured the killers (Hellenica 6.4.28–32). A northern monarch uniting Greece under a sacred festival and the prospect of a Persian war: Jason's project anticipates Philip's with uncanny precision, and his successors reduced Thessaly to a client of whoever could intervene, first Thebes, then Macedon.

Philip II: the army and the diplomacy, 359–352

Philip took power in 359 after his brother Perdiccas III and 4,000 Macedonians died fighting the Illyrians. Within two years he had bought off the Paeonians, beaten the Illyrian Bardylis (358) and taken Amphipolis (357), promising it to Athens and keeping it. Diodorus (16.3.1–2) says he at once reorganised the army and "devised the compact order and equipment of the phalanx". The infantry (pezhetairoi, "foot-companions") carried the sarissa, a pike of some 4.5 to 5.5 metres held in both hands, with a small shield slung from the shoulder, in files sixteen deep: five rows of points projected beyond the front rank. The Companion cavalry (hetairoi), heavy horse from the nobility, were the striking arm; the hypaspists linked them to the phalanx. Philip drilled year-round, banned wagons and most servants, and paid wages, creating something close to a professional national army. His engineers under Polyidus of Thessaly brought torsion catapults and siege towers to a new scale: Amphipolis, Methone (354, where Philip lost an eye), Olynthus and Perinthus were all besieged.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus credits the phalanx to Philip; a fragment attributed to Anaximenes credits an "Alexander" (probably Alexander II, Philip's elder brother) with naming the pezhetairoi. Whether Philip invented the sarissa phalanx or perfected it, and how much he owed to his years as a hostage in Thebes (Plutarch, Pelopidas 26) watching Epaminondas, remain contested; Hammond stressed the Theban debt, Ellis and Worthington Philip's originality.

His diplomacy was as inventive. He married seven times for policy: Phila of Elimeia, Audata the Illyrian, Philinna of Larissa, Olympias of Epirus (mother of Alexander, 357), Nicesipolis of Pherae, Meda of the Getae and, in 337, the Macedonian Cleopatra (Athenaeus 13.557b–e, quoting Satyrus). He bribed, promised, delayed and lied; Demosthenes' complaint that Philip took Pydna, Potidaea and Methone "while you were debating" (First Philippic 4.4–5) is also a tribute. The gold of Mount Pangaeum, won in 356, gave him a thousand talents a year (Diodorus 16.8.6–7).

The Third Sacred War, Olynthus, and the war of words, 356–346

In 356 the Amphictyonic Council fined Phocis for cultivating sacred land; Phocis under Philomelus seized Delphi and used its treasures to hire mercenaries (Diodorus 16.23–30). Thebes led the "Sacred War" against them, and Thessaly, ravaged by Phocian-backed Pherae, called Philip in. He was beaten twice by Onomarchus in 353, then crushed him at the Crocus Field in 352, drowning or crucifying 3,000 prisoners as temple-robbers (Diodorus 16.35), and was elected archon of Thessaly for life, acquiring its cavalry and its votes at Delphi. Athens blocked him at Thermopylae that summer.

In 349 Philip turned on Olynthus, head of the Chalcidian League, which had taken in his half-brothers. Demosthenes' three Olynthiacs begged Athens to send citizens, not mercenaries, and to touch the theoric fund. Athens sent too little, too late; Olynthus fell by treachery in 348 and Philip razed it and enslaved the population (Diodorus 16.53). In 346, while the Peace of Philocrates was being sworn, Philip marched through Thermopylae, accepted Phocian surrender, took Phocis' two Amphictyonic votes and presided at the Pythian Games (Diodorus 16.59–60; Demosthenes, On the Peace).

The intellectual argument was now clear. Demosthenes (First Philippic, 351; Second Philippic, 344; On the Chersonese and Third Philippic, 341) held that Philip was a barbarian despot, that every treaty was a stratagem, and that freedom meant a citizen army, war taxes and alliance with any Greek who would fight. Isocrates had called in the Panegyricus (380) for Athens and Sparta to lead a Persian crusade; in the Philippus (346) he urged Philip to reconcile Argos, Sparta, Thebes and Athens, lead them against Persia and settle Greece's landless mercenaries in Asia. Pan-Hellenism and Macedonian hegemony had converged.

Where sources disagree. Ancient judgement was divided: Theopompus called Philip the greatest man Europe had produced and also an incontinent drunk; Polybius (18.14) defended the Greeks who sided with Philip as patriots, not traitors, against Demosthenes' charge. Modern scholars split along the same line: Cawkwell saw Demosthenes as a brilliant orator and a disastrous strategist who misread Philip's limited aims in 346; Harris and Worthington are more sympathetic; Ellis argued Philip never sought to destroy Athens at all.

Chaeronea, the League of Corinth and the assassination, 340–336

War resumed in 340 when Philip seized the Athenian grain fleet at the Bosporus after failing to take Perinthus and Byzantium. In 339 an Amphictyonic dispute with Amphissa gave him a pretext to march south; he bypassed Thermopylae and seized Elatea. Demosthenes went to Thebes and, against Macedonian envoys and a century of enmity, secured the Theban alliance (On the Crown 18.169–179; Diodorus 16.84–85). At Chaeronea on 2 August 338 (Plutarch, Camillus 19) perhaps 35,000 allied Greeks faced Philip's 30,000 foot and 2,000 horse. Diodorus (16.85–86) has Philip on the right against the Athenians and the eighteen-year-old Alexander with the Companions against the Thebans; the Sacred Band died in place, and its grave beneath the lion monument yielded 254 skeletons in 1880 (Plutarch, Pelopidas 18; Pausanias 9.40.10). Athens lost 1,000 dead and 2,000 prisoners.

Where sources disagree. Polyaenus (4.2.2) says Philip feigned a retreat on his right to pull the Athenians forward and open the gap that Alexander exploited; Diodorus mentions no such manoeuvre, and Plutarch (Alexander 9) says only that Alexander "is said" to have been first to break the Sacred Band. The tactical detail of Chaeronea is reconstructed, not reported.

Philip garrisoned Thebes and installed an oligarchy; Athens, which had expected destruction, got its prisoners back without ransom and kept its fleet in exchange for dissolving the Second Athenian League (Diodorus 16.87). At Corinth in winter 338/7 he convened every mainland state except Sparta and created a common peace with a council (synedrion), a guarantee of existing constitutions, a ban on exile, confiscation and redistribution of land, and himself as hegemon of its forces; in 337 it voted war on Persia (Diodorus 16.89; IG II² 236). Autonomy, the slogan of 387, had become the legal basis of Macedonian control.

In 337 Philip married Cleopatra, niece of Attalus; Alexander and Olympias left court after the quarrel at the wedding (Plutarch, Alexander 9). In summer 336 at Aegae, during the wedding festival of his daughter to Alexander of Epirus, Philip entered the theatre without his guards and was stabbed by Pausanias of Orestis, a bodyguard who had been raped at Attalus' instigation and denied redress (Diodorus 16.91–94; Aristotle, Politics 1311b). Pausanias was killed as he reached his horse.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus and Aristotle treat the motive as personal. Justin (9.7) and Plutarch (Alexander 10) report suspicion of Olympias, who allegedly crowned the killer's corpse, and of Alexander; others pointed to Persian gold or to the Lyncestian brothers executed at Alexander's accession. No ancient source offers evidence beyond rumour, and modern opinion (Badian for conspiracy; Hammond, Ellis and Worthington for a lone killer with aristocratic grievances) remains unresolved.

Self-test

  1. What were the dekarchies and who installed them?
    Answer

    Boards of ten pro-Spartan oligarchs set up by Lysander in the former Athenian cities after 404, supported by a Spartan harmost and garrison; the Spartan authorities dissolved them within a few years out of suspicion of Lysander's personal power.

  2. Which sea battle ended Spartan naval supremacy in the Corinthian War, and who won it?
    Answer

    Cnidus, August 394: the Athenian Conon, commanding a Persian fleet with the satrap Pharnabazus, destroyed the Spartan fleet.

  3. State the two central provisions of the King's Peace of 387/6.
    Answer

    The Greek cities of Asia and Cyprus belong to the Persian King; all other Greek cities are to be autonomous (Athens keeping Lemnos, Imbros and Scyros), with the King threatening war on any who refuse.

  4. How was the Cadmea seized, and how did Agesilaus justify keeping it?
    Answer

    In 382 Phoebidas, invited by the oligarch Leontiades, occupied Thebes' acropolis during the Thesmophoria. Agesilaus argued that only whether the act was useful to Sparta mattered, so the garrison stayed, though Phoebidas was fined.

  5. Name three ways the Second Athenian League's charter differed from the fifth-century empire.
    Answer

    No garrisons, governors or tribute (contributions were called syntaxeis); members free and autonomous under their own constitutions; a ban on Athenians owning land in allied territory; and an allied synod sitting at Athens.

  6. What was tactically distinctive about the Theban deployment at Leuctra?
    Answer

    The phalanx was massed fifty deep on the left, opposite the Spartan king, while the weaker right was held back; the cavalry fought first and drove the Spartan horse into their own line. Diodorus and Plutarch credit Epaminondas with the oblique order; Xenophon does not name him.

  7. Why did the liberation of Messenia matter more than Leuctra itself?
    Answer

    Messenia's helot labour had funded the Spartiate way of life for three centuries; its loss, and the founding of Messene on Ithome, removed roughly half of Sparta's territory and made recovery of great-power status impossible.

  8. What did Jason of Pherae intend to do in 370, and what happened?
    Answer

    As tagos of Thessaly he announced he would preside over the Pythian festival at Delphi with his army; he was assassinated by seven young men before he could, and many Greek cities honoured the killers.

  9. What did Philip gain from the Third Sacred War beyond military victory?
    Answer

    Election as archon of Thessaly for life (its cavalry and Amphictyonic votes), the two Phocian votes on the Amphictyonic Council after 346, control of Thermopylae, and the presidency of the Pythian Games: a legal and religious standing inside Greece.

  10. What were the key terms of the League of Corinth?
    Answer

    A common peace among all mainland states except Sparta, a council (synedrion), guarantee of existing constitutions, prohibition of exile, confiscation and land redistribution, and Philip as hegemon commanding its forces; in 337 it voted war on Persia.

Carry forward

  1. "Autonomy" was the political vocabulary of the whole period, and every hegemon in turn, Sparta after 387, Thebes after 371 and Philip at Corinth in 338/7, used a common peace guaranteeing it as the legal instrument of control.
  2. Hegemony failed when it rested on a narrow citizen body: Spartan oliganthropia, Theban dependence on two men, and the fact that Philip's Macedon succeeded precisely because it was a monarchy with a mass, paid, professional army rather than a city-state.
  3. Our sources are partisan: Xenophon's silence on Epaminondas, Demosthenes' portrait of Philip and Diodorus' compression of Ephorus all shape what later generations, Alexander's historians included, took to be the facts of the fourth century.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Greece from 404 to 336 BC. Cover: the Spartan hegemony and its abuses (Lysander, the harmosts, the seizure of the Cadmea); the Corinthian War and the King's Peace of 387; the Second Athenian League; Thebes under Epaminondas and Pelopidas, the Sacred Band, Leuctra in 371 and the end of Spartan power, the liberation of Messenia and the founding of Megalopolis, Mantinea in 362; Jason of Pherae; the rise of Macedon: Philip II's reforms of the army (the sarissa phalanx, the Companions, siegecraft), his diplomacy and marriages, the Third Sacred War, Olynthus, Demosthenes and the Philippics versus Isocrates' pan-Hellenism, Chaeronea in 338, the League of Corinth, and Philip's assassination. Use Xenophon's Hellenica, Diodorus, Demosthenes and Plutarch. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
