The sources problem

Everything we read about Alexander was written more than two and a half centuries after his death. The contemporary accounts are lost: Callisthenes of Olynthus, the official historian who died in the army's custody in 327 or, by Chares' account, in 326/325; Ptolemy son of Lagus, writing as king of Egypt late in life; Aristobulus of Cassandreia, an engineer who began his history after 301 aged eighty-four (Lucian, Macrobii 22); Cleitarchus of Alexandria, whose colourful narrative became the most popular; Nearchus the admiral; Chares the chamberlain; and the Ephemerides, or Royal Diaries, whose authenticity is contested. What survives quarried these.

Surviving authorDateMain lost sourcesCharacter
Diodorus, Library 17c. 30 BCCleitarchusEarliest continuous narrative; the "vulgate"
Curtius Rufus, History of Alexander1st century AD (disputed)Cleitarchus, Ptolemy, TimagenesRhetorical, hostile to tyranny; books 1–2 lost
Plutarch, Life of Alexanderc. AD 100Over twenty, including letters, Chares, AristobulusBiography of character, not history
Arrian, Anabasisc. AD 140Ptolemy and Aristobulus (1 pref.)Military, sober, admiring; the standard account
Justin, Epitome of Trogus 11–122nd–4th century ADCleitarchus and othersBrief, hostile, often garbled

Arrian names his method: where Ptolemy and Aristobulus agree he follows them; where they differ he chooses the more plausible. Diodorus, Curtius and Justin draw mainly on Cleitarchus, hence "the vulgate tradition". The only strictly contemporary evidence is a handful of inscriptions, coins, and the Babylonian astronomical diaries, which fix the eclipse before Gaugamela and the day of his death.

Where sources disagree. Cleitarchus was long dated to c. 310–300 BC, almost a contemporary. A papyrus published in 2007 (P.Oxy. LXXI 4808) calls him tutor to Ptolemy IV, which would push him into the mid-third century and weaken the vulgate's independent authority. Curtius's date is equally open; both questions are argued in full in module 11.7.

Upbringing: Olympias, Philip, Aristotle

Alexander was born at Pella in July 356, the son of Philip II and Olympias, a Molossian princess of Epirus who claimed descent from Achilles (Plutarch, Alexander 2–3). Philip was turning Macedon into the dominant power in Greece, and his many marriages, seven by Satyrus's count in Athenaeus (13.557b–e), bred court factions in which succession was never automatic.

His tutors were Leonidas, an austere kinsman of Olympias, and Lysimachus of Acarnania, who cast the boy as Achilles (Plutarch, Alexander 5). From 343 to about 340 Aristotle taught him and a group of noble sons at Mieza (Plutarch, Alexander 7). What he taught is barely recoverable: Plutarch says Alexander loved medicine and kept Aristotle's recension of the Iliad under his pillow; the two later cooled, perhaps over Callisthenes, Aristotle's kinsman. Aristotle's advice to treat barbarians as a master treats slaves (Strabo 1.4.9) is quoted mainly to show Alexander ignoring it.

The rivalry with Philip shaped him. Alexander was regent at sixteen and led the Companion cavalry at Chaeronea in 338 (Diodorus 16.86). In 337 Philip married Cleopatra, niece of the general Attalus. At the wedding Attalus prayed for a legitimate heir; Alexander threw a cup at him, and Philip, drawing his sword, stumbled drunk, earning the jibe that the man who would cross to Asia could not cross from one couch to another (Plutarch, Alexander 9; Justin 9.7). Alexander and Olympias withdrew to Epirus and Illyria; a return was brokered, but the Pixodarus affair of 336, when Alexander secretly offered himself to the Carian dynast's daughter, shows he feared being set aside (Plutarch, Alexander 10). The sources paint Olympias as a scheming queen and her real influence is hard to measure; but Alexander's only recorded family quarrel was over Philip's new wife.

Accession and the destruction of Thebes

In October 336 at Aegae Philip was stabbed by Pausanias of Orestis, a bodyguard with a grievance against Attalus (Diodorus 16.93–94; Aristotle, Politics 1311b). Alexander, twenty, was acclaimed by the army. He then removed Amyntas IV, two Lyncestian princes and Attalus; Olympias is said to have killed Cleopatra and her infant (Justin 9.7; Pausanias 8.7.7).

Where sources disagree. Diodorus gives Pausanias a private motive. Plutarch (Alexander 10) says suspicion fell on Olympias and even on Alexander; Justin (9.7) states that Olympias arranged the murder and crowned the assassin's corpse. Alexander himself blamed Persia (Arrian 2.14.5). Badian and Bosworth find complicity plausible but unprovable; Hammond rejects it. Uncertain.

A rapid tour of Greece renewed the League of Corinth and Alexander's position as hegemon. In 335, while he campaigned in Thrace and Illyria, a rumour of his death set Thebes against the Macedonian garrison on the Cadmea. He appeared before Thebes in under a fortnight, before the city knew he was alive (Arrian 1.7). The city was stormed, allegedly after Perdiccas attacked without orders (Arrian 1.8, from Ptolemy; Diodorus 17.12 says Alexander planned it). About 6,000 Thebans were killed and 30,000 sold; the city was razed except for the temples and Pindar's house (Arrian 1.9; Diodorus 17.14). Arrian stresses that the formal decision was taken by the League allies, Plataeans, Orchomenians, Phocians and Thespians, with old scores to settle. Screen or not, no Greek city rose again until he was dead.

From the Granicus to Siwa, 334–331

Alexander crossed the Hellespont in spring 334 with about 32,000 foot and 5,000 horse, leaving Antipater as regent (Arrian 1.11; Diodorus 17.17). He sacrificed at Troy and took a shield from Athena's temple. The satraps of Asia Minor met him at the Granicus in May. Arrian (1.13–16) has him attack across the river against Parmenion's advice; Spithridates struck his helmet with an axe and Cleitus the Black severed the Persian's arm (1.15.8), a debt with a long shadow. The Greek mercenaries in Persian service were massacred as traitors to the League.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (17.19) has Alexander cross at dawn unopposed and fight on the far bank; Arrian, from Ptolemy, has the Companions fighting their way up a muddy bank in the afternoon. Some modern scholars prefer Diodorus as tactically more credible. The two cannot be reconciled.

Sardis, Miletus and Halicarnassus fell; the fleet was disbanded on the gamble that the Persian navy could be beaten by taking its harbours. At Gordium in 333 he cut, or according to Aristobulus unpinned, the knot of Midas's cart (Arrian 2.3). In November 333 Darius III brought the royal army behind him to the narrow plain of Issus. Alexander broke through on the right to the royal chariot; Darius fled, and his mother, wife and children were taken in the camp (Arrian 2.6–11; Curtius 3.8–12). Darius's offer of the lands west of the Euphrates was refused; Alexander's reply demanded to be addressed as king of Asia (Arrian 2.14).

Tyre, on its island, refused him entry to sacrifice to Melqart-Heracles. The siege lasted seven months of 332: a mole from the mainland, Phoenician and Cypriot fleets that came over after Issus, siege towers on ships, a breach on the south wall (Arrian 2.18–24; Diodorus 17.40–46). About 8,000 Tyrians died and 30,000 were sold; Curtius (4.4.17) adds 2,000 crucified along the shore. Gaza followed, and Curtius (4.6.29) alone says its governor Batis was dragged behind a chariot in imitation of Achilles.

Egypt submitted without a fight in late 332. Alexander sacrificed to Apis at Memphis and in early 331 founded Alexandria. The journey to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa is the campaign's most argued episode. Arrian (3.3–4) says he went to rival Perseus and Heracles and received the answer he wanted, unspecified. Plutarch (Alexander 27) reports that the priest greeted him as son of Zeus, or, in a rationalising variant, mispronounced paidion as pai Dios. Callisthenes, quoted by Strabo (17.1.43), gave the official line: the god acknowledged him as his son. From Siwa onward divine paternity is part of his repertoire.

Gaugamela, Babylon, Persepolis and the death of Darius, 331–330

A lunar eclipse on 20 September 331, recorded in the Babylonian diary and by Arrian (3.7.6), fixes Gaugamela, near Arbela, to 1 October. Darius had levelled the ground for scythed chariots and had a large numerical advantage. Alexander advanced obliquely to the right, drew the Persian left after him and charged the gap that opened when Darius's cavalry followed; Darius fled a second time (Arrian 3.11–15). On the left Parmenion was hard pressed, and Arrian has a message from him recall Alexander from the pursuit, an incident Callisthenes used against Parmenion (Plutarch, Alexander 33).

Babylon opened its gates under the satrap Mazaeus, whom Alexander kept in office with Macedonian officers beside him, the first clear instance of retaining Iranians (Arrian 3.16). Susa and its treasury followed. In January 330 he forced the Persian Gates and reached Persepolis, which was given to the troops to plunder (Diodorus 17.70). Some months later the palace of Xerxes burned.

Where sources disagree. Arrian (3.18.11–12) makes the fire deliberate policy, revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens, taken over Parmenion's objection. Diodorus (17.72), Curtius (5.7) and Plutarch (Alexander 38) describe a drunken revel in which the Athenian courtesan Thais urged him on. The treasury had been emptied first. Badian saw a political signal to Greece that the war of revenge was over; Bosworth thought a sober decision could hide behind the party; Hammond followed Arrian. Plutarch says Alexander soon regretted it.

Darius retreated east from Ecbatana. Near Hecatompylos in July 330 the Bactrian satrap Bessus arrested him and, as the Macedonians closed in, stabbed him and left him by the road (Arrian 3.21; Curtius 5.8–13). Alexander sent the body to Persepolis for royal burial and thereafter behaved as Darius's successor, adopting the diadem and the striped tunic while refusing the upright tiara and trousers (Diodorus 17.77; Plutarch, Alexander 45). The League allies were sent home with bonuses (at Ecbatana in Arrian 3.19.5, after Darius's death in Diodorus 17.74.3): the Hellenic war of revenge was formally over, and what followed was conquest on his own account.

Bactria and Sogdiana: Philotas, Cleitus, proskynesis, the pages, 330–327

The three north-eastern years were the hardest of the war and the most corrosive for the high command. In autumn 330 at Phrada a minor plot by one Dimnus was reported to Philotas, commander of the Companion cavalry and son of Parmenion, who sat on it for two days. Arrian (3.26) gives the bare account; Curtius (6.7–11) and Plutarch (Alexander 48–49) give the long version, with torture, a trial before the army and death by javelins. Alexander then sent riders to Ecbatana with orders to kill Parmenion, who controlled the treasury and the communications (Arrian 3.26.3–4). Philotas's guilt beyond arrogance and silence is unknowable; the effect is clear. The affair destroyed the most powerful family in the army, ended the collegial command inherited from Philip, and split the Companion cavalry between Hephaestion and Cleitus.

In 329 Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush and had Bessus delivered to him; Arrian (3.29–30) notes that Ptolemy claimed the capture and Aristobulus credited Spitamenes. A massacre at Cyropolis and the founding of Alexandria Eschate on the Jaxartes provoked a Sogdian revolt under Spitamenes that destroyed a Macedonian column at the Polytimetus (Arrian 4.5–6). Two years of garrisons and reprisals followed; Spitamenes was killed in 328, by the Massagetae in Arrian (4.17), by his own wife in Curtius (8.3).

At Maracanda in autumn 328, at a drinking party, Cleitus the Black, provoked by flattery of Alexander at Philip's expense, taunted the king with the hand that had saved him at the Granicus and was run through by Alexander with a guard's spear (Arrian 4.8–9; Plutarch, Alexander 50–51; Curtius 8.1–2). All record three days of remorse; Arrian adds that the philosopher Anaxarchus consoled him with the doctrine that whatever a king does is just. Cleitus had just been named satrap of Bactria, which is to say removed from the centre.

At Bactra in spring 327 Alexander tried to introduce proskynesis, the Persian obeisance before the king, among Macedonians and Greeks; to Greeks it implied worship. Arrian (4.10–12) gives a staged debate in which Anaxarchus proposed it and Callisthenes, who had himself written that Alexander was son of Zeus, refused on the grounds that gods and men are honoured differently; Chares, in Plutarch (Alexander 54), has guests bow and receive a kiss, and Callisthenes skip the bow and lose the kiss. The experiment was dropped for Macedonians. Soon afterwards the page Hermolaus, flogged for killing a boar before the king, plotted with other royal pages to kill Alexander in his sleep; it failed because he drank until dawn (Arrian 4.13–14; Curtius 8.6–8). The pages were stoned, and Callisthenes was arrested as their teacher.

Where sources disagree. Arrian (4.14.3) records that Ptolemy said Callisthenes was tortured and hanged, while Aristobulus said he was carried about in chains and died of disease. Curtius (8.8.21) and Chares in Plutarch (Alexander 55) favour imprisonment. If the two best-placed eyewitnesses could not agree on this, the limits of the whole tradition are plain; module 11.7 weighs the versions.

In the same season he took the Sogdian Rock and married Roxane, daughter of the Bactrian noble Oxyartes. Arrian (4.19) and Plutarch (Alexander 47) call it love; Curtius (8.4) stages a banquet. The political reading is obvious: the marriage ended the war by binding the Bactrian aristocracy. That Alexander's first marriage, at thirty, was to an Iranian was not lost on the army.

India, the Hyphasis and the Gedrosian desert, 327–325

Alexander entered India in 327 with an army swollen by Iranian cavalry. Taxiles submitted and asked for help against Porus across the Hydaspes (Jhelum). In May 326, in the monsoon, Alexander crossed upstream at night by a wooded island, leaving Craterus opposite the Indian camp, and defeated Porus's elephants in the only set battle of the campaign (Arrian 5.8–19; Curtius 8.13–14; Plutarch, Alexander 60). Porus asked to be treated "as a king" and was restored and enlarged. Bucephalas died after the battle.

At the Hyphasis (Beas) in late summer the army refused to go on. Arrian (5.25–29) gives Alexander a speech on glory and the end of Asia, answered by Coenus for men who wanted to see their homes; Alexander sulked for three days, took unfavourable omens and turned back, building twelve altars on the bank (Diodorus 17.93–95; Curtius 9.2–3). Some scholars, notably Spann, argue that Alexander, knowing of the Nanda power on the Ganges, wanted the retreat and let the army take the blame; most accept a genuine refusal. It was the first time anything had stopped him, and it was his own army.

The voyage down the Indus became a war of extermination against the Malli. At a Mallian town Alexander mounted the wall almost alone and took an arrow in the chest (Arrian 6.9–11). Arrian (6.11.8) notes that Cleitarchus placed Ptolemy at his side, and that Ptolemy himself wrote that he was elsewhere, a neat illustration of how the vulgate improved on the record. At Patala in summer 325 the force divided: Nearchus took the fleet along the coast, Craterus led the veterans by the Bolan pass, and Alexander marched with the rest through Gedrosia (the Makran) to dig wells for the fleet.

The sixty-day desert crossing in autumn 325 killed more of his people than any battle: sand, heat, night marches, a flash flood that swept away the camp followers (Arrian 6.22–26). Strabo (15.2.5) says Alexander undertook it to outdo Semiramis and Cyrus, who had failed there. Plutarch (Alexander 66) says only a quarter survived, which cannot be right since most of the army was not with him; the losses are uncertain. Badian read the executions of satraps and generals in 325–324, including Cleander who had killed Parmenion, as a "reign of terror" against men who had assumed he would not return; Bosworth saw genuine misconduct under a king restoring control. The treasurer Harpalus fled with 5,000 talents and 6,000 mercenaries (Diodorus 17.108.6) and reached Athens with about 700 of them.

Susa, Opis, Hephaestion and Babylon, 324–323

At Susa in spring 324 Alexander held the mass marriage. He took Stateira, elder daughter of Darius, and Parysatis, daughter of Artaxerxes III, marrying into both branches of the Achaemenid house, while Hephaestion married Stateira's sister (Arrian 7.4). Some eighty Companions received Iranian noblewomen in a five-day Persian ceremony described by Chares (Athenaeus 12.538b–539a); about ten thousand soldiers' unions with Asian women were registered and dowered. He also paid the army's debts and received the 30,000 Epigoni, Iranian youths trained in Macedonian arms (Arrian 7.6; Diodorus 17.108).

The Macedonian response came at Opis on the Tigris that summer. When Alexander announced that the old and unfit would go home with Craterus, the whole army took it as dismissal in favour of Persians and jeered at the son of Ammon. He had thirteen ringleaders executed, delivered the speech Arrian (7.9–10) wrote for him, shut himself away, and began giving Persians Macedonian commands and the title of kinsmen. The men broke. At the reconciliation banquet he prayed for "concord and partnership in rule between Macedonians and Persians" (Arrian 7.11.9). Ten thousand veterans left with Craterus, who was to replace Antipater. In the same year the Exiles' Decree ordered Greek cities to readmit their exiles, breaching the League's autonomy clause (Diodorus 18.8), and cities debated divine honours; Demosthenes said Alexander could be son of Zeus and Poseidon too, if he liked (Hyperides, Against Demosthenes col. 31).

At Ecbatana in October 324 Hephaestion died after a week of fever (Arrian 7.14; Plutarch, Alexander 72). Alexander's grief is drawn in Achillean terms: he lay on the body, cut his hair, crucified the doctor, ordered a pyre at Babylon costing 10,000 talents (Arrian 7.14.8; Plutarch, Alexander 72) or more than 12,000 (Diodorus 17.115) and obtained Ammon's sanction for a hero cult (Arrian 7.14.7, 7.23.6).

Alexander entered Babylon in spring 323 despite a Chaldaean warning (Arrian 7.16–17), received embassies from the Mediterranean and prepared an Arabian expedition. After a long party at the house of Medius he fell ill with fever. The Ephemerides, quoted by Arrian (7.25–26) and Plutarch (Alexander 76), record about eleven days of worsening illness and the army filing past his bed while he could still move his eyes. The Babylonian diary places his death on 29 Aiaru, 11 June 323. He was thirty-two.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (17.117) and Curtius (10.5) have Alexander hand his ring to Perdiccas and leave the kingdom "to the strongest"; Arrian and Plutarch, following the Diaries, give him no last words and dismiss the story that Antipater's son Iollas poisoned him (Arrian 7.27; Plutarch, Alexander 77). Whether the Diaries are genuine or a propaganda document from the succession struggle (Bosworth) is argued in module 11.7; the Antipater case in module 11.5. Modern diagnoses include malaria, typhoid, West Nile virus, pancreatitis and white hellebore. None can be tested.

His aims as historians have read them

The nineteenth century, led by J. G. Droysen, made Alexander the founder of Hellenism, the fusion of Greek and Oriental that prepared the ground for Christianity. W. W. Tarn's Alexander the Great (1948) took the line furthest: Alexander was the first to conceive the brotherhood of man, and the proof was the Opis prayer, the Susa marriages, the Iranian satraps and Plutarch's essay On the Fortune of Alexander (329c–d), which has him mixing the lives of men "as in a loving cup". Tarn dismissed the "last plans" in Diodorus 18.4, with their population exchanges between Europe and Asia, as a forgery, because they did not fit.

Ernst Badian's "Alexander the Great and the Unity of Mankind" (1958) dismantled Tarn source by source: the Opis prayer concerns Macedonians and Persians sharing rule, not mankind; Plutarch's essay is a rhetorical exercise; the marriages created a ruling caste, not a fused people. In "The Loneliness of Power" (1962) Badian drew the portrait that has dominated since: a king who destroyed Parmenion, Philotas, Cleitus and Callisthenes because they were in his way, and who ended his life isolated and feared. A. B. Bosworth's Conquest and Empire (1988) and Alexander and the East (1996), which sets the Indian campaign beside the Spanish conquest of Mexico, confirmed the realist reading with closer attention to body counts. Peter Green and Ian Worthington pushed the hostile reading further; N. G. L. Hammond and Robin Lane Fox defended a man of genuine vision shaped by Homer and Macedonian kingship. The present consensus is close to Bosworth: Alexander aimed at conquest and the kingship of Asia for its own sake, used Iranian nobles because he needed them, and claimed divinity because it worked.

Immediate legacy

Alexander left no adult heir: Roxane was pregnant and his half-brother Arrhidaeus was mentally incapable. The Babylon settlement (Curtius 10.6–10; Diodorus 18.2; Justin 13.2–4) made Arrhidaeus king as Philip III, added Roxane's son as Alexander IV, and gave Perdiccas the regency after infantry and cavalry had nearly fought over the corpse. The satrapies went to the marshals: Ptolemy took Egypt, Antigonus Phrygia, Lysimachus Thrace, Antipater Macedon. News of his death set off the Lamian War; Antipater crushed Athens in 322. Olympias was killed by Cassander in 316, Roxane and Alexander IV in 310 or 309; by 306–305 the surviving generals wore diadems. Ptolemy hijacked the funeral cortege in 321 and buried the body in Egypt.

The durable legacies were structural rather than ideological: Greek-speaking dynasties over the Persian empire for two to three centuries; a scatter of Alexandrias, most of them garrison towns; an Attic-weight silver coinage circulating from Macedon to India; the koine that would carry the Septuagint and the Gospels; and the Persian hoards released into the Mediterranean economy. Culturally he became the measure of kingship and ambition, imitated by Pompey, Caesar and Trajan, and in the Alexander Romance an everyman's hero across Europe and Asia. The historiographical legacy is the one this module began with: a man known almost entirely through the quarrels of those who claimed to have known him.

Self-test

  1. Which two lost historians does Arrian name as his principal sources, and why does he trust them?
    Answer

    Ptolemy son of Lagus and Aristobulus of Cassandreia (Arrian 1 pref.). Both served on the campaign, and Ptolemy, writing as a king, would in Arrian's view have found lying dishonourable.

  2. What happened at the wedding of Philip and Cleopatra in 337, and what did it reveal?
    Answer

    Attalus prayed for a legitimate heir; Alexander threw a cup at him and Philip drew his sword and stumbled drunk (Plutarch, Alexander 9). It showed Alexander's succession was not secure and depended on his and Olympias's standing.

  3. According to Arrian, who formally decided the fate of Thebes in 335?
    Answer

    The League of Corinth allies, in particular the Plataeans, Orchomenians, Phocians and Thespians, old enemies of Thebes (Arrian 1.9). Alexander could present the destruction as their decision.

  4. What debt did Alexander owe Cleitus the Black, and where did he repay it?
    Answer

    Cleitus severed the arm of Spithridates at the Granicus as the Persian was about to strike Alexander (Arrian 1.15.8). Alexander killed Cleitus with a spear at a drinking party in Maracanda in 328.

  5. Give the two main traditions for the burning of Persepolis.
    Answer

    Arrian: a deliberate act of policy, vengeance for Xerxes, over Parmenion's objection (3.18). Diodorus, Curtius and Plutarch: a drunken revel in which the courtesan Thais urged the king on.

  6. Why does the Philotas affair matter beyond the death of one officer?
    Answer

    It led to the murder of Parmenion at Ecbatana, destroyed the most powerful family in the army, ended the collegial command inherited from Philip, and split the Companion cavalry between Hephaestion and Cleitus.

  7. What was proskynesis, and who is said to have refused it?
    Answer

    The Persian gesture of obeisance before the king, which Greeks took to imply worship. Callisthenes refused it at Bactra in 327 (Arrian 4.10–12; Plutarch, Alexander 54) and was later arrested in the pages' conspiracy.

  8. What does the Babylonian astronomical diary contribute to the chronology of Alexander?
    Answer

    It records the lunar eclipse of 20 September 331 that fixes Gaugamela to 1 October, and the king's death on 29 Aiaru, 11 June 323.

  9. What did Alexander pray for at the Opis banquet, and why did Badian think Tarn misread it?
    Answer

    For concord and partnership in rule between Macedonians and Persians (Arrian 7.11.9). Badian argued this concerns two ruling peoples sharing power, not a brotherhood of all mankind.

  10. Who were the two kings proclaimed at Babylon in 323, and who held the regency?
    Answer

    Philip III Arrhidaeus, Alexander's half-brother, and the infant Alexander IV, son of Roxane. Perdiccas held the regency after the infantry and cavalry nearly fought.

Carry forward

  1. Every narrative of Alexander is late and partisan, resting on lost eyewitnesses who disagreed even about events they saw; Arrian's Ptolemy-Aristobulus line and the Cleitarchan vulgate must always be weighed against each other, never simply trusted.
  2. The conquest changed character at the death of Darius, from a Hellenic war of revenge into Alexander's personal kingship of Asia; every later crisis, Philotas, Cleitus, proskynesis, Opis, is a Macedonian reaction to that shift.
  3. The argument between Tarn's visionary and Badian and Bosworth's ruthless realist is an argument about how to read the same few texts, above all the Opis prayer and the Susa marriages; the Hellenistic world that followed was built by his generals out of the structures he left, not out of any plan he wrote down.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Alexander the Great, 356 to 323 BC. Cover: his upbringing, Aristotle, Olympias and the Philip rivalry; the accession and the destruction of Thebes; the campaign in order: Granicus, Issus, the siege of Tyre, Egypt and Siwa, Gaugamela, Babylon, the burning of Persepolis, the death of Darius, the Bactrian and Sogdian war, Roxane, the Philotas and Cleitus affairs, the proskynesis and the pages' conspiracy, India and the Hydaspes, the mutiny at the Hyphasis, the Gedrosian desert, Susa and the mass marriage, Opis, the death of Hephaestion, the death in Babylon; his aims as historians have read them (Tarn's brotherhood of man versus Badian and Bosworth's ruthless realist); the sources problem (Arrian, Curtius, Diodorus, Plutarch, Justin, all late, resting on lost Ptolemy, Aristobulus and Cleitarchus); and his immediate legacy. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 7 · Hellenistic and Roman Greece, 323 BC to AD 529 · 7.1 · 2,989 words

The Successors and the kingdoms

Babylon, June 323: the settlement that settled nothingPerdiccas, Antipater, Craterus and Eumenes, 323–316Antigonus and Demetrius, Cassander, and the end of the ArgeadsIpsus, 301, and Corupedium, 281Ptolemaic Egypt: Alexandria, the pharaoh-king and the Greek eliteThe Seleucid empire: cities, eastern losses, Antiochus III and IV, the MaccabeesAntigonid MacedonThe smaller powersRuler cult and the new idea of kingshipThe far edge: the Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek kingdomsSelf-testCarry forward

Babylon, June 323: the settlement that settled nothing

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 without a competent heir: his half-brother Arrhidaeus was mentally impaired and Roxane was pregnant. The narrative is Diodorus 18.2–4, with Arrian's Events after Alexander (in Photius' summary), Curtius 10.6–10 and Justin 13.2–4. The cavalry under Perdiccas, to whom the dying king had supposedly handed his ring, wanted to await Roxane's child; the infantry under Meleager proclaimed Arrhidaeus as Philip III. The compromise made both kings, with Perdiccas as chiliarch and effective regent; Meleager was soon executed. Ptolemy took Egypt, Antigonus Monophthalmus kept Greater Phrygia, Lysimachus got Thrace, Eumenes of Cardia the unconquered Cappadocia; Antipater stayed as general in Europe with Craterus, the army's favourite, awkwardly named his colleague. Seleucus received only the Companion cavalry. Roxane's son became Alexander IV.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus 17.117 and Curtius 10.5 have Alexander leave the kingdom "to the strongest" (tōi kratistōi), a pun on Craterus that ancient readers already noticed; Arrian, Anabasis 7.26, says he was speechless. Whether the ring was ever given to Perdiccas is unverifiable. The "last plans" he read out to be voted down (Diodorus 18.4) were rejected as forgery by Tarn; Badian and most recent scholars accept a genuine core.

Perdiccas, Antipater, Craterus and Eumenes, 323–316

Greece rose at once. In the Lamian War Athens trapped Antipater in Lamia until Craterus arrived with the veterans and crushed the Greeks at Crannon in 322 (Diodorus 18.9–18). Demosthenes took poison; Athens received a garrison and an oligarchic franchise, the pattern of Macedonian control for a century.

Perdiccas overreached. Married to Antipater's daughter, he began negotiating for Alexander's sister Cleopatra, a bid for the throne itself. Antigonus fled to Antipater; Ptolemy hijacked Alexander's funeral cortège to Egypt (Diodorus 18.26–28). Perdiccas invaded Egypt in 320, failed to force the Nile and was killed in his tent by his own officers, Seleucus among them (Diodorus 18.33–36). Two days later came news that Eumenes, the Greek secretary turned general, had defeated and killed Craterus in Asia Minor (Diodorus 18.30–32; Plutarch, Eumenes 5–7). At Triparadeisus (Diodorus 18.39) Antipater became regent, Antigonus general in Asia against Eumenes, and Seleucus satrap of Babylonia. Dying in 319, Antipater passed the regency to Polyperchon rather than his son Cassander; Cassander went to Antigonus and Ptolemy, and Polyperchon answered by proclaiming the freedom of the Greeks and recalling Olympias (Diodorus 18.55–56).

Eumenes led the royal cause in Asia with the Silver Shields, Alexander's veterans now in their sixties. He drew with Antigonus at Paraetacene (317); at Gabiene (winter 317/316) he won the infantry fight but lost the baggage with the veterans' wives and loot, and the Silver Shields handed him over to be killed (Diodorus 19.26–44; Plutarch, Eumenes 16–19). To hold officers who despised a Greek, he had held council before Alexander's empty throne and diadem in a tent (Diodorus 18.60–61; Plutarch, Eumenes 13): the dead king as political cult object.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus 18–20 derives largely from Hieronymus of Cardia, Eumenes' compatriot and later an Antigonid courtier, so Eumenes the loyalist and Antigonus the magnanimous are partisan portraits. The Babylonian Diadochi Chronicle (BCHP 3) is the independent check and has shifted the chronology of 323–319 towards the "low" scheme (Perdiccas' death 320, not 321); the question is not closed.

Antigonus and Demetrius, Cassander, and the end of the Argeads

Antigonus now held Asia from the Hellespont to Iran and in 316 drove Seleucus from Babylon; Seleucus fled to Ptolemy, who allied with Cassander and Lysimachus (Diodorus 19.55–57). In Macedon Olympias killed Philip III and Eurydice in 317; Cassander besieged her at Pydna, had her executed in 316 (Diodorus 19.11, 19.35–36, 19.49–51), and kept Alexander IV and Roxane under guard at Amphipolis.

At Gaza in 312 Ptolemy and Seleucus beat the young Demetrius (Diodorus 19.80–85). Seleucus rode back to Babylon with a thousand men and retook it; the Seleucid era was counted from autumn 312 or spring 311. The peace of 311 (Diodorus 19.105) recognised the dynasts as governors until Alexander IV came of age, which was the boy's death warrant. Cassander had him and Roxane murdered in 310 or 309; Polyperchon killed Heracles, Alexander's son by Barsine, in 309; Antigonus had Cleopatra killed at Sardis in 308 (Diodorus 20.20, 20.28, 20.37). No Argead with a claim survived. Seleucus fought Antigonus in a Babylonian War (311–309) known only from cuneiform sources, then around 305–303 ceded the Indian satrapies to Chandragupta Maurya for five hundred elephants (Strabo 15.2.9; Appian, Syriaca 55; Justin 15.4).

Demetrius freed Athens in 307 and destroyed Ptolemy's fleet off Cypriot Salamis in 306 (Diodorus 20.47–52); Antigonus took the diadem, gave his son one, and the other four followed (Plutarch, Demetrius 17–18). His invasion of Egypt failed on the Nile as Perdiccas' had. The siege of Rhodes (305–304; Diodorus 20.81–99) earned Demetrius the name Poliorcetes and ended in a draw; the Rhodians sold his abandoned engines to pay for the Colossus (Pliny, Natural History 34.41).

Ipsus, 301, and Corupedium, 281

Antigonus revived Philip II's Hellenic League in 302 to legitimise a drive on Macedon; Lysimachus crossed to Asia while Seleucus came from the east with his elephants. At Ipsus in Phrygia Demetrius' cavalry charge succeeded too well: Seleucus screened the gap with elephants, the Antigonid phalanx was surrounded, and the eighty-year-old king died under javelins still expecting his son's return (Plutarch, Demetrius 28–29). Seleucus took Syria, Lysimachus Asia Minor; Ptolemy, who had not fought, kept Coele-Syria, and the Seleucid claim to it as spear-won land (Polybius 5.67) poisoned the two dynasties for a century. Demetrius was left, in Plutarch's image, a wounded beast with a fleet and a few cities.

Cassander died in 297; in 294 Demetrius murdered his son Alexander V and took Macedon (Plutarch, Demetrius 36–37). Seven years building a fleet to reconquer Asia ended when Pyrrhus and Lysimachus invaded in 288 and his army deserted; he surrendered to Seleucus in 285 and drank himself to death in captivity (Plutarch, Demetrius 44–52). Lysimachus took Macedon, then at his wife Arsinoe's urging killed his heir Agathocles; Seleucus invaded, and at Corupedium in February 281 Lysimachus fell (Appian, Syriaca 62–64; Justin 17.1–2; Memnon, FGrH 434 F 5–8). Seleucus, last of Alexander's companions, crossed to claim Macedon and was stabbed near Lysimacheia by Ptolemy Ceraunus, his guest. Ceraunus died fighting the Galatians in 279; Demetrius' son Antigonus Gonatas beat them at Lysimacheia in 277 and secured Macedon for his line. Pyrrhus, after Italy (280–275), died in a street fight in Argos in 272 (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 34).

Where sources disagree. Plutarch, Demetrius 28, gives the allies 480 elephants at Ipsus against Antigonus' 75, implying Seleucus brought nearly all Chandragupta's gift across Iran intact; Bar-Kochva accepts it, others do not. Diodorus' account of the battle is lost with book 21.

Ptolemaic Egypt: Alexandria, the pharaoh-king and the Greek elite

Ptolemy I Soter (satrap 323, king 305/304, died 283/282) took the most defensible and richest prize and never seriously left it. Alexandria became the capital, with the Soma holding Alexander's body, the Museum and Library (Strabo 17.1.8; the Letter of Aristeas is unreliable on their founding) and the Pharos. Euclid, Callimachus and Eratosthenes worked under royal patronage, and Sarapis, Osiris-Apis in Greek dress, was promoted as a shared cult (Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris 28).

The kings ruled two ways at once. To Greeks they were basileis with a Macedonian court and Greek as the language of administration; the Zenon archive from the Fayum shows the finance minister Apollonius' estate run by Greek and Carian managers over Egyptian labour. To Egyptians they were pharaohs. The Satrap Stele of 311 already shows Ptolemy in pharaonic style before he took the title; kings were crowned at Memphis by the priests of Ptah, and the Rosetta Stone (196) records a priestly synod decreeing honours for Ptolemy V in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek. Ptolemy II married his full sister Arsinoe II around 275, a pharaonic rather than Greek precedent praised in Theocritus, Idyll 17. Ptolemy IV's enrolment of twenty thousand Egyptian phalangites for Raphia in 217 (Polybius 5.65, 5.107) was followed by the Great Revolt of the Thebaid (206–186) under native pharaohs. Polybius divided Alexandria's population into Egyptians, mercenaries and mixed "Alexandrians", and liked none of them (34.14, via Strabo 17.1.12).

Where sources disagree. Préaux and Rostovtzeff saw a colonial state in which Greeks ruled and Egyptians were taxed. Manning and Thompson argue from Demotic papyri that the Ptolemies ruled through the temples and Egyptian notables from the start and that the ethnic line blurred quickly in the countryside. Both agree few Egyptians reached the top before the second century.

The Seleucid empire: cities, eastern losses, Antiochus III and IV, the Maccabees

Seleucus I ruled from the Aegean to the Hindu Kush and answered the size by founding: Seleucia-on-Tigris (c. 305), Antioch, Apamea and Laodicea (300), and military colonies along the roads to Iran (Appian, Syriaca 57). Cuneiform archives show Babylonian satrapal and temple structures carrying on beneath. The founding story, Seleucus ceding his wife Stratonice to his lovesick son Antiochus I (Plutarch, Demetrius 38), is a parable of orderly succession in a world that rarely had one.

The east came loose in the 240s: Diodotus of Bactria struck his own coins around 250, and Arsaces' Parni took Parthia, conventionally in 247 (Justin 41.4; Strabo 11.9.2–3). Antiochus III (223–187) rebuilt. He lost Raphia in 217, then marched east from 212 to 205: Armenia submitted, Arsaces II accepted alliance, Euthydemus of Bactria withstood a two-year siege and kept his crown by treaty (Polybius 10.27–31, 10.49, 11.34). He took the title Great King and won Coele-Syria at Panium in 200. Then he crossed to Greece, lost Thermopylae in 191 and Magnesia in 190/189, and by the Peace of Apamea in 188 gave up everything north of the Taurus, his fleet, his elephants and 15,000 talents (Polybius 21.42; Livy 38.38). He died in 187 plundering a temple in Elymais to pay for it.

Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164), "Epimanes" to Polybius (26.1), had all but conquered Egypt when the Roman envoy Popilius Laenas drew a circle in the sand at Eleusis in 168 and demanded an answer before he stepped out (Polybius 29.27); the parade at Daphne in 166 (Polybius 30.25) was his reply to Roman triumphs. In Judaea he sold the high priesthood to Jason and then Menelaus, garrisoned the Akra, and in December 167 banned Jewish observance and set a pagan altar in the Temple (1 Maccabees 1; 2 Maccabees 4–6; Josephus, Antiquities 12.237–264; Daniel 11.31). Mattathias' revolt became Judas Maccabaeus' war: the rededication of the Temple in 164, death at Elasa in 160. His brothers exploited Seleucid civil wars; Jonathan became high priest in 152, Simon won independence in 142 (1 Maccabees 13.41), and the Hasmonean state outlived the dynasty.

Where sources disagree. Why Antiochus IV persecuted a religion, which no Hellenistic king had done, has no agreed answer. Tacitus, Histories 5.8, says he meant to civilise; Bickerman blamed Jewish Hellenising reformers around Menelaus; Tcherikover made the persecution a response to a rising already under way; Gruen sees a king punishing a rebellious temple-state in the usual way, with the religious ban as Maccabean framing. The dates of Arsaces' secession (247 or 238) and Diodotus' (256 or 246) are also uncertain.

Antigonid Macedon

Antigonus Gonatas (277–239) ruled a poor land and a Macedonian people, answered to an army assembly that acclaimed him and tried capital cases, and was never a god to his own subjects. A pupil of Zeno the Stoic, he called kingship "a noble servitude" (Aelian, Varia Historia 2.20). He held Greece by the "fetters", garrisons at Demetrias, Chalcis and Corinth (Polybius 18.11), and survived the Chremonidean War (268–261) against Athens, Sparta and Ptolemy II. Antigonus Doson (229–221) returned at Aratus' invitation, refounded a Hellenic League under Macedonian presidency in 224 and broke Cleomenes at Sellasia in 222.

Philip V (221–179) is Polybius' tragic figure, the gifted young king who turned tyrant. He made peace with Aetolia at Naupactus in 217 after Agelaus warned of "the cloud in the west" (Polybius 5.104), then allied with Hannibal in 215 (Polybius 7.9). Cynoscephalae in 197 showed the legion beating the phalanx on broken ground (Polybius 18.18–27); his son Perseus lost at Pydna in 168 (Livy 44.40–42; Plutarch, Aemilius Paullus 16–22), the monarchy was replaced by four republics, and in 148 Macedon became Rome's first eastern province.

Where sources disagree. Whether the Macedonian assembly had constitutional powers (Granier) or was acclamatory and summoned at the king's convenience (Errington; Hatzopoulos with reservations) turns on a few passages in Curtius and Polybius 5.27–29 and remains open.

The smaller powers

Pergamon. Philetaerus, Lysimachus' eunuch treasurer, took fortress and treasury over to Seleucus in 282 and kept both. Attalus I took the royal title after a Galatian victory around 238 and allied with Rome; Eumenes II fought at Magnesia, received most of Seleucid Asia Minor at Apamea and built the Great Altar. Attalus III willed the kingdom to Rome in 133 (Strabo 13.4.2).

Rhodes. The republic that defied Demetrius became arbiter of the Aegean, policing pirates and setting commercial law; when an earthquake around 227 toppled the Colossus every king sent aid (Polybius 5.88–90). Neutrality in the Third Macedonian War cost it Rome's favour, and the free port at Delos in 167 drained its harbour dues (Polybius 30.31).

The Leagues. The Aetolian League controlled Delphi, lived partly by licensed plunder and became Rome's first Greek ally in 211; Polybius, an Achaean, loathes it. The Achaean League, refounded in 280, grew when Aratus of Sicyon brought his city in (251) and seized Acrocorinth in 243 (Plutarch, Aratus 18–24). Polybius 2.37–44 describes a federal state with common citizenship, laws, coinage and an annual strategos, the nearest Greece came to one polis. Fear of Sparta drove Aratus into Doson's arms; quarrels with Rome ended in the sack of Corinth in 146.

Sparta. By 244 Sparta had perhaps seven hundred citizens. Agis IV (244–241) proposed debt cancellation and 4,500 citizen lots; the ephors and his co-king had him executed (Plutarch, Agis 5–20). Cleomenes III (235–222) used the army: after a coup in 227 he abolished the ephorate, cancelled debts, enfranchised perioikoi to make four thousand hoplites and restored the agoge, with the Stoic Sphaerus as adviser (Plutarch, Cleomenes 7–11). He beat the Achaeans repeatedly until Sellasia, fled to Alexandria and died in a failed rising there in 219 (Polybius 5.35–39).

Where sources disagree. Plutarch's Agis and Cleomenes follow Phylarchus, who admired the kings; Polybius 2.56–63 attacks Phylarchus by name and paints Cleomenes as a tyrant who nearly destroyed Achaea. Social revolution or a bid for a bigger army: the sources themselves pose the question.

Ruler cult and the new idea of kingship

Greeks had honoured a living man as a god once before, when Samos gave Lysander altars and paeans in 404 (Duris in Plutarch, Lysander 18); Alexander's request for divine honours in 324 still drew mockery (Hypereides, Against Demosthenes 31). After 323 cult became ordinary. Athens received Antigonus and Demetrius in 307 as Saviour Gods and named two new tribes after them (Plutarch, Demetrius 10–13; Diodorus 20.46); Rhodes founded a cult of Ptolemy Soter after the siege (Diodorus 20.100; Pausanias 1.8.6). The hymn sung for Demetrius in 290 gives the logic:

the other gods are far away, or have no ears, or do not exist (Athenaeus 6.253e)

Dynastic cult followed: Ptolemy II deified his parents as Saviour Gods and himself and Arsinoe as Sibling Gods; Antiochus III ordered a kingdom-wide cult of Queen Laodice in 193, attested on stone from Iran to Caria. Macedon alone did not follow.

The kingship itself was new. It was personal, not territorial: Antigonus was king of wherever his army stood. The Suda's entry on basileia preserves the doctrine that neither descent nor legitimacy gives men kingdoms but the ability to lead an army and manage affairs. Legitimacy came from victory (Nicator, Callinicus), spear-won land, benefaction (Euergetes, Soter) and a court of Friends (philoi) chosen by the king, not by birth. Plutarch, Demetrius 42, sets Demetrius, who threw petitions in the river, against Philip II, who read them; the kings who lasted learned that cities must be courted. Treatises On Kingship and Theocritus 17 describe the same ideal: the king as living law, generous, victorious, accessible.

Where sources disagree. Tarn and Taylor saw ruler cult as Oriental servility or cynical manipulation. Habicht showed it was a city's initiative, granted for concrete benefits; Price and Chaniotis treat it as the language of reciprocity, honours in a divine register because nothing less fitted the power. Whether anyone "believed" becomes the wrong question.

The far edge: the Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek kingdoms

When Diodotus I broke away around 250, Bactria had been Greek-ruled for eighty years; Strabo 11.11.1 calls it the land of a thousand cities, and Justin 41.1–6 gives the thin narrative. Euthydemus survived Antiochus III; his son Demetrius I crossed the Hindu Kush around 185 as the Mauryas collapsed and took Gandhara and the Punjab; Eucratides (c. 170–145) seized Bactria in civil war. Menander I (c. 155–130) debates a Buddhist monk in the Pali Milindapanha, and Plutarch, Precepts of Statecraft 821d, says his cities divided his ashes as relics. Coins became bilingual, Greek and Kharosthi, with Buddhist wheels beside Zeus; Heliodorus, envoy of King Antialcidas, raised a pillar to Vasudeva at Besnagar around 110. Ai Khanoum had a gymnasium, a theatre and Delphic maxims copied by Clearchus of Soli, beside a palace in Achaemenid style. Bactria fell to the Yuezhi between about 145 and 130; the last Indo-Greek, Strato III, held a sliver of the Punjab until about AD 10.

Where sources disagree. Almost all this chronology rests on coins. Tarn's Greeks in Bactria and India (1938) made an epic of Greek civilisation in the east; Narain's The Indo-Greeks (1957) replied that their history "is part of the history of India". The number of kings called Demetrius and whether Menander ruled Bactria at all remain uncertain.

Self-test

  1. Who were the two kings recognised at Babylon in 323, and who held real power?
    Answer

    Philip III Arrhidaeus and the infant Alexander IV; Perdiccas as chiliarch and regent held power until his murder in Egypt in 320.

  2. What did Eumenes set up in his camp to command Macedonian loyalty, and where is it reported?
    Answer

    Alexander's empty throne with diadem and sceptre, before which the council met; Diodorus 18.60–61 and Plutarch, Eumenes 13.

  3. Which battle in 312 allowed Seleucus to return to Babylon, and from when is the Seleucid era counted?
    Answer

    Gaza, where Ptolemy and Seleucus defeated Demetrius; the era runs from autumn 312 (Macedonian) or spring 311 (Babylonian reckoning).

  4. Name the Argead victims of Cassander, Polyperchon and Antigonus between 317 and 308.
    Answer

    Olympias (Cassander, 316); Alexander IV and Roxane (Cassander, c. 310/309); Heracles (Polyperchon, 309); Cleopatra (Antigonus, 308). Olympias herself had killed Philip III and Eurydice in 317.

  5. How did Demetrius lose Ipsus despite winning the cavalry fight?
    Answer

    He chased the enemy horse off the field; Seleucus placed elephants across his return path and the isolated Antigonid phalanx was surrounded (Plutarch, Demetrius 29).

  6. Why did Coele-Syria become a permanent quarrel after Ipsus?
    Answer

    The allies assigned it to Seleucus, but Ptolemy, who had not fought, occupied it; Seleucids claimed it as spear-won land (Polybius 5.67), producing six Syrian Wars.

  7. Who killed Seleucus I, where, and what had happened a few months earlier?
    Answer

    Ptolemy Ceraunus, near Lysimacheia in 281, after Seleucus had killed Lysimachus at Corupedium in February and crossed into Europe.

  8. What does the Satrap Stele of 311 show about Ptolemy's rule, and what does the Rosetta Stone add?
    Answer

    Ptolemy was presented in pharaonic style to Egyptians before taking the royal title; the Rosetta Stone (196) shows a priestly synod decreeing honours for Ptolemy V in three scripts, a king working through the temples.

  9. What were the terms of the Peace of Apamea (188), and what did they mean for Pergamon?
    Answer

    Antiochus III gave up Asia Minor north of the Taurus, his fleet and elephants, and paid 15,000 talents; most of the ceded land went to Eumenes II of Pergamon, Rome's ally.

  10. Why does Polybius' account of Cleomenes III differ so sharply from Plutarch's?
    Answer

    Plutarch follows Phylarchus, who admired the Spartan reformers; Polybius, an Achaean whose league Cleomenes nearly destroyed, attacks Phylarchus (2.56–63) and casts Cleomenes as a tyrant.

Carry forward

  1. Hellenistic kingship was personal and won by the spear: legitimacy came from victory, benefaction and the loyalty of an army and Friends, not from territory or descent, and ruler cult was the cities' way of bargaining with a power too large for ordinary honours.
  2. The three kingdoms ruled differently because they ruled different peoples: the Ptolemies as pharaohs and Greek kings in one body, the Seleucids through founded cities over inherited satrapies, the Antigonids as national kings answerable to a Macedonian assembly. Rome met each in turn.
  3. The source problem is structural: Diodorus 18–20 is Hieronymus' Antigonid-leaning narrative, Polybius is an Achaean writing for Romans, Plutarch moralises from both; cuneiform chronicles, papyri, inscriptions and coins are the independent checks, and for Bactria almost the only evidence.

GREECE · UNIT 7 · Hellenistic and Roman Greece, 323 BC to AD 529 · 7.2 · 2,878 words

Alexandria: science, scholarship and the new philosophies

Alexandria: the Museum and the LibraryEditing Homer: Zenodotus, Aristophanes, AristarchusHellenistic poetry: Callimachus, Theocritus, ApolloniusScience: measuring the worldStoicismEpicureanismScepticism and the CynicsKoine and the SeptuagintSelf-testCarry forward

Alexandria: the Museum and the Library

After Alexander's death in 323 BC his generals carved the conquered world into kingdoms, and the Ptolemies of Egypt decided that dynastic prestige could be bought in books. Ptolemy I Soter (king 305–282) founded the Museum (Mouseion, a shrine of the Muses) in the palace quarter of Alexandria; Ptolemy II Philadelphus (282–246) enlarged it. Strabo (Geography 17.1.8), who saw it in the 20s BC, describes a covered walk, an exedra, and a hall where salaried scholars dined together under a priest appointed by the king.

The innovation was royal money, a salaried scholarly community and a systematic hunt for texts. Galen (Commentary on Hippocrates' Epidemics 3) says ships entering the harbour were searched for books, and that Ptolemy III forfeited a fifteen-talent deposit rather than return the Athenian state copies of the tragedians. Callimachus produced the Pinakes, a 120-book catalogue of authors and works by genre, the ancestor of every bibliography. Ancient figures for the holdings run from 490,000 rolls (Tzetzes) to 700,000 (Aulus Gellius 7.17.3); many were duplicates.

A papyrus list (P.Oxy. 1241) gives the librarians: Zenodotus of Ephesus, Apollonius of Rhodes, Eratosthenes, Aristophanes of Byzantium, Apollonius "the classifier", Aristarchus of Samothrace. After Aristarchus fled the purges of Ptolemy VIII around 145 BC, scholarship dispersed to Pergamum, Rhodes and Rome.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch (Caesar 49) and Seneca (On Tranquillity 9.5, giving 40,000 rolls) say Caesar's fire of 48 BC destroyed the Library; Dio Cassius 42.38 says only harbour warehouses burned, and Strabo describes the Museum as functioning afterwards. The tale of Arab conquerors burning the books as bath fuel in 642 first appears six centuries later. Most historians now favour slow decline from the second century BC over any single catastrophe.

Editing Homer: Zenodotus, Aristophanes, Aristarchus

Ptolemaic papyri from before about 150 BC show a "wild" Homer, with extra lines and variant phrasing; after that date the papyri settle into the text the medieval manuscripts transmit. Something standardised Homer in the second century BC, and the three great librarians are the obvious candidates.

Zenodotus (fl. c. 280) made the first diorthosis, or corrected edition, of both poems. He marked suspect lines with a horizontal stroke (the obelos) rather than deleting them, and compiled a Homeric glossary; the division of each epic into twenty-four books is traditionally his. His readings often look like conjectures driven by taste: he objected to gods behaving undignifiedly and emended accordingly.

Aristophanes of Byzantium (c. 257–180) sharpened the tools: the system of accents and punctuation, the arrangement of lyric poetry in metrical lines (colometry), and more critical signs. Aristarchus of Samothrace (c. 216–144), his pupil, dominates the Homeric scholia preserved in the tenth-century manuscript Venetus A. He produced two editions and running commentaries (hypomnemata), and extended the marginal signs. His method, summarised by Porphyry as "clarifying Homer from Homer", settled a word's meaning by its usage elsewhere in the poems rather than by etymology or myth. He athetised lines he thought un-Homeric but kept them in the text, which is why the Iliad still contains lines its greatest ancient editor rejected.

Where sources disagree. Martin West (Studies in the Text and Transmission of the Iliad, 2001) argues the standard text was already circulating in the book trade and that Aristarchus' own readings rarely entered it; the disappearance of plus-verses reflects commercial copying from a good exemplar, not editorial decree. Others give the Library a larger role. The timing is clear from the papyri; the mechanism is uncertain.

Hellenistic poetry: Callimachus, Theocritus, Apollonius

The poets of Alexandria were also its scholars, and that explains their verse. Writing for readers who knew the classics in catalogued editions, they prized compression, allusion and the obscure version of a myth over the familiar one. Callimachus of Cyrene (c. 310–240) set out the aesthetic in the prologue to his Aetia (fr. 1 Pfeiffer), the "Reply to the Telchines": his critics complain that he has not written one continuous poem of thousands of lines about kings and heroes; he answers that poetry is judged by art, not length, and that Apollo told him to keep his Muse slender and drive on untrodden paths. Epigram 28 Pf. begins "I hate the cyclic poem".

The Aetia, four books of elegiac "causes" explaining obscure rites, survives in fragments; its "Lock of Berenice" (fr. 110) was translated by Catullus (poem 66). Theocritus of Syracuse (fl. 270s) invented the bucolic idyll: herdsmen competing in song (Idylls 1, 7), the lovesick Cyclops singing to Galatea (Idyll 11), two Syracusan housewives at Ptolemy's Adonis festival (Idyll 15). The monster of Odyssey 9 recast as a comic adolescent is the Hellenistic move in miniature.

Apollonius of Rhodes answered the call for brevity with an epic, but a short one: the Argonautica, four books and under six thousand lines against the Iliad's fifteen thousand. Jason is hesitant and amechanos, "at a loss"; the poem's centre is Book 3, where Medea's falling in love is traced with an inwardness no earlier epic attempted, in a passage Virgil reworked for Dido. It is thick with geography, aetiology and Homeric phrases redeployed in new contexts: epic turned into a scholar's game for readers who would notice.

Where sources disagree. The ancient Lives report a feud between Callimachus and Apollonius, with the lost invective Ibis aimed at his former pupil. Mary Lefkowitz (The Lives of the Greek Poets) argues the quarrel is a fiction spun from the Aetia prologue, whose Telchines are unnamed; the Argonautica shares Callimachus' aesthetic in most respects.

Science: measuring the world

Euclid taught in Alexandria under Ptolemy I (Proclus, Commentary on Euclid I, prologue 2). His Elements in thirteen books organised earlier Greek mathematics into a deductive system and remained the model of proof until the nineteenth century. Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212) found the volume and surface of the sphere (On the Sphere and Cylinder), bounded pi between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7 (Measurement of a Circle), founded hydrostatics (On Floating Bodies), and in the Method, recovered from a palimpsest in 1906, showed that he found results by mechanical reasoning before proving them geometrically. His death at the fall of Syracuse is in Plutarch (Marcellus 19) and Livy 25.31.

Eratosthenes of Cyrene measured the earth. Cleomedes (On the Heavens 1.7) gives the method: at midsummer the sun stood overhead at Syene while at Alexandria, assumed on the same meridian, a gnomon's shadow put it 1/50 of a circle from the zenith; the cities being 5,000 stades apart, the circumference was 250,000 stades, later rounded to 252,000 for divisibility. Whether the result is nearly exact or sixteen per cent too large depends on which stade he used, which is unknown.

Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230) proposed that the earth rotates and revolves around a stationary sun. We know this only from Archimedes (Sand-Reckoner 1.4–7) and Plutarch (On the Face in the Moon 6, where Cleanthes thinks he should be charged with impiety); his surviving treatise On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon is geocentric in frame. Hipparchus of Nicaea (c. 190–120) discovered the precession of the equinoxes, compiled a star catalogue, built the first table of chords and used Babylonian eclipse records; nearly all of it survives only through Ptolemy's Almagest (7.1–3).

In medicine, Herophilus of Chalcedon and Erasistratus of Ceos, in early third-century Alexandria, carried out systematic human dissection, forbidden by scruple elsewhere and again for over a millennium after. Herophilus described the brain's ventricles, distinguished sensory from motor nerves, and named the duodenum and prostate (fragments in von Staden). Celsus (On Medicine, preface 23–26) adds that they dissected living criminals from the royal prisons, which Tertullian (On the Soul 10) turns into the charge of butchery; whether vivisection occurred is debated.

Hero of Alexandria, whose Dioptra 35 describes an eclipse of AD 62, left the Pneumatica with its steam-driven aeolipile, temple automata and the Metrica; Roman in date, he is wholly Alexandrian in tradition. The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a shipwreck by sponge divers in 1900–1901, is the physical proof of what that tradition could build: a geared bronze device with Metonic and Saros dials, an Olympiad counter, and pin-and-slot gearing that reproduces the moon's variable speed on exactly Hipparchus' model (Freeth and colleagues, Nature 2006 and 2008). It dates from roughly 150–60 BC.

Where sources disagree. Cicero describes planetary spheres by Archimedes (On the Republic 1.21–22) and Posidonius at Rhodes (On the Nature of the Gods 2.88), and Rhodes was long the favoured origin of the mechanism; the Corinthian month-names on its dial point instead to a Corinthian colony, possibly Syracuse (Freeth and Jones 2012). The 2021 reconstruction of a full planetary display is hypothesis, since those gears do not survive.

Stoicism

Zeno of Citium (334–262), a Phoenician from Cyprus who studied under the Cynic Crates, began teaching in the Painted Colonnade (Stoa Poikile) in Athens around 300 BC. Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280–206) systematised the school in over seven hundred books, so that "had there been no Chrysippus, there would be no Stoa" (Diogenes Laertius 7.183). No Hellenistic Stoic work survives whole; the doctrines are reconstructed from Diogenes Laertius book 7, Cicero (On Ends 3, On Fate), Stobaeus, Plutarch and Galen.

In physics everything is body, and the cosmos is a single living thing pervaded by logos, divine reason, identified with god, fate, creative fire and the tensile breath (pneuma) that holds each thing together. The world is periodically consumed in conflagration and reborn identical in every detail. Fate is a seamless chain of causes, yet Chrysippus insisted that action remains "up to us": a pushed cylinder rolls because of its own shape (Cicero, On Fate 42–43). In logic they built the first propositional calculus and a theory of the "cognitive impression" that the sceptics attacked for two centuries.

The end is "living in agreement with nature", which for a rational being means living by reason. Virtue is the only good, vice the only evil; health, wealth, pain and reputation are "indifferent", though some indifferents are "preferred". The passions (pathe) are not forces overwhelming reason but false judgements, assents to the belief that an indifferent thing is good or bad; the sage, having no false beliefs, has no passions, only the rational "good feelings" of joy and caution. Cosmopolitanism is the political face of this: since reason is shared by all and one law governs the cosmos, the world is a single city of gods and men. Plutarch (On the Fortune of Alexander 329a–b) says Zeno's Republic dreamed of one way of life for all people as fellow citizens.

Where sources disagree. Zeno defined a passion as "an excessive impulse", Chrysippus as a judgement. Galen (On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato 4–5) reports that Posidonius rejected Chrysippus' intellectualism and reintroduced irrational parts of the soul to explain why passions persist against better judgement. Whether this was a return to Zeno or a Platonising departure is contested, as is Galen's reliability as a witness.

Epicureanism

Epicurus (341–270) bought a garden outside Athens in 306 and taught a community of friends, including women and slaves, for the rest of his life. Diogenes Laertius book 10 preserves three letters (to Herodotus on physics, Pythocles on meteorology, Menoeceus on ethics) and the forty Principal Doctrines; fragments of his On Nature survive charred from Herculaneum; Lucretius' On the Nature of Things gives the system in Latin hexameters.

The physics is Democritus revised: only atoms and void exist, worlds form and dissolve, and the soul is a fine atomic compound that disperses at death. To rescue free action from determinism the atoms occasionally "swerve" by a minimum (Lucretius 2.216–293; Cicero, On Fate 22). The gods exist, as universal belief attests, but are blessed and imperishable and take no interest in us (KD 1). Atomism removes the fear of death, since "death is nothing to us" (KD 2; Letter to Menoeceus 124–127): where death is, we are not, and the time before our birth troubled no one, as Lucretius' symmetry argument (3.830–1094) presses.

Pleasure is the end, but not the hedonist's. The limit of pleasure is reached when all pain is removed; "static" pleasure (aponia in the body, ataraxia in the mind) outranks the "kinetic" pleasures of variation (Diogenes Laertius 10.136). The wise person lives on little, prizes friendship, avoids politics ("live unnoticed") and knows that pain, if intense, is brief and, if long, mild (KD 4). Philodemus' "fourfold remedy" compresses it: nothing to fear in god, nothing to feel in death, good is easy to get, evil easy to endure.

Where sources disagree. On the "realist" reading (Konstan) Epicurus' gods are atomic compounds living between worlds; on the "idealist" reading (Long and Sedley) they are thought-constructs, idealisations of the blessed life. The texts support both. Whether the swerve was Epicurus' own idea or a later addition is also disputed, since it is absent from his surviving words.

Scepticism and the Cynics

Pyrrho of Elis (c. 365–275) accompanied Alexander to India and wrote nothing; his pupil Timon, in a summary preserved by Aristocles (Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 14.18), says he held things to be equally indifferent, unmeasurable and undecidable, and the outcome first speechlessness and then freedom from disturbance. The parallel with the Stoic and Epicurean goal of ataraxia is deliberate: Hellenistic philosophy, across its divisions, sells tranquillity.

The more consequential scepticism grew inside Plato's Academy. Arcesilaus (scholarch c. 268–241) turned the school to arguing against every thesis, attacking Zeno's cognitive impression: for any true impression an indistinguishable false one can be produced, so assent should be withheld (epoche). Asked how one then lives, he answered that "the reasonable" suffices for action (Sextus, Against the Mathematicians 7.158). Carneades of Cyrene (c. 214–129) refined this into a graded account of "persuasive" impressions that could guide life without claiming truth (Cicero, Academica 2.99–104); on an embassy to Rome in 155 BC he argued for justice one day and against it the next (Cicero, On the Republic 3, via Lactantius). Aenesidemus in the first century BC revived a "Pyrrhonism" of ten modes, which Sextus Empiricus codified around AD 200.

The Cynics were a way of life, not a school. Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412–323) took a dog's shamelessness as his emblem, lived in a storage jar, "defaced the currency" of convention, and, asked where he came from, said "I am a citizen of the world" (Diogenes Laertius 6.63), the first recorded kosmopolites. Zeno was the pupil of his successor Crates, and Stoicism carried the Cynic conviction that virtue alone matters into a system. Menippus turned Cynic preaching into the satire that Lucian and Rome inherited.

Where sources disagree. Diogenes Laertius makes Antisthenes the Socratic founder of Cynicism; Dudley (1937) and Goulet-Cazé argue this pedigree was constructed later and Diogenes is the real beginning. Richard Bett reads Timon's summary of Pyrrho as a metaphysical thesis that reality is indeterminate rather than a refusal to judge, so that Sextus' "Pyrrhonism" was largely Aenesidemus' creation.

Koine and the Septuagint

The medium of all this was a new Greek. Alexander's armies carried a simplified Attic across Egypt, Syria and Anatolia, where it became the "common" dialect, koine. It dropped the dual and most of the optative, regularised verbs and favoured prepositions over bare cases. Egyptian papyri show it as the language of tax, farming and letters; the Rosetta Stone (196 BC) shows it as the language of government. From the first century BC grammarians reacted with Atticism, a cult of the old dialect that split written from spoken Greek until 1976.

Its most consequential product was the Septuagint, the Greek Bible of Egyptian Jewry. The Letter of Aristeas, probably second century BC, tells how Ptolemy II, at Demetrius of Phalerum's suggestion, summoned seventy-two elders from Jerusalem who translated the Law in seventy-two days; Philo (Life of Moses 2.25–44) and Josephus (Antiquities 12.11–118) repeat it. The story is legend (Demetrius was exiled by Ptolemy II), but the Pentateuch was translated in third-century Alexandria, the rest over two centuries, for a community that no longer read Hebrew easily.

The Septuagint matters beyond itself for three reasons. It made Jewish scripture part of Greek literature: Ezekiel the Tragedian put the Exodus into iambic trimeters. It became the Bible of the early church and the New Testament's usual text for quotation, so Christian theology was built in koine. And it preserves a Hebrew text older than the medieval Masoretic one: the Greek Jeremiah is about an eighth shorter and differently ordered, and the Qumran fragment 4QJer-b agrees with the Greek, showing the translators worked from a different Hebrew rather than carelessly.

Where sources disagree. Alexandria or Palestine as the place; synagogue, schoolroom, royal library or Ptolemaic legal need as the motive; one event or several: all are debated. Later Jewish revisers (the "kaige" group, Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus) pulled the Greek towards the emerging standard Hebrew, and Origen laid them side by side in his Hexapla; the Septuagint we print is thus itself a layered text, like the Alexandrian Homer.

Self-test

  1. Which ancient author describes the Museum's buildings and communal dining from eyewitness knowledge, and where?
    Answer

    Strabo, Geography 17.1.8, who visited Alexandria in the 20s BC.

  2. What was Callimachus' Pinakes?
    Answer

    A 120-book catalogue of Greek authors and works arranged by genre, the first systematic bibliography, compiled at the Alexandrian Library.

  3. What is the obelos, who introduced it, and why does it matter that athetised lines were kept?
    Answer

    A marginal stroke marking a line as spurious, introduced by Zenodotus. Because Alexandrian editors marked rather than deleted, the vulgate still contains lines they rejected; the papyri show plus-verses vanishing after c. 150 BC, but whether editorial authority or book-trade copying caused this is disputed.

  4. Summarise the aesthetic programme of the Aetia prologue.
    Answer

    Callimachus answers the Telchines that poetry is judged by art, not length; Apollo tells him to keep his Muse slender and follow untrodden paths. Learned, small-scale, allusive verse over long heroic epic.

  5. How did Eratosthenes measure the earth, and why is the accuracy of his result uncertain?
    Answer

    He compared the sun overhead at Syene with its 1/50-circle angle from the zenith at Alexandria at midsummer and multiplied the 5,000-stade distance by 50 to get 250,000 (later 252,000) stades. Accuracy depends on the length of his stade, which is unknown.

  6. What is our evidence for Aristarchus of Samos' heliocentrism?
    Answer

    Reports in Archimedes, Sand-Reckoner 1.4–7, and Plutarch, On the Face in the Moon 6; his own surviving treatise on the sizes and distances of sun and moon is geocentric in frame.

  7. What does the Antikythera mechanism's pin-and-slot gearing reproduce, and what does that imply?
    Answer

    The moon's variable apparent speed on Hipparchus' lunar theory, showing Hellenistic astronomy and precision mechanics combined before 60 BC.

  8. Why is a passion a false judgement for Chrysippus, and what follows about the sage?
    Answer

    A passion is assent to the belief that an indifferent thing (wealth, pain, death) is good or bad; since virtue alone is good, the belief is false. The sage, holding no false beliefs, has no passions, only rational good feelings.

  9. State Epicurus' argument that death is nothing to us, and the extra argument Lucretius adds.
    Answer

    Good and evil consist in sensation; death ends sensation because the soul's atoms disperse; so death cannot be bad for the one who dies (KD 2; Letter to Menoeceus 124–127). Lucretius 3 adds the symmetry argument: we were untroubled by the time before birth, so should be by the time after death.

  10. What is the Letter of Aristeas, what does it claim, and what internal flaw exposes the claim as legend?
    Answer

    A Hellenistic Jewish text (probably 2nd century BC) claiming Ptolemy II commissioned seventy-two elders to translate the Law at Demetrius of Phalerum's suggestion. Demetrius had been exiled by Ptolemy II and could not have advised him; the Pentateuch was nonetheless translated in third-century Alexandria.

Carry forward

  1. The texts you read of Homer, and of the Hebrew Bible in Greek, are Hellenistic editorial products: Alexandria standardised the Iliad and created the Septuagint, and every later module that quotes either depends on choices made there.
  2. Hellenistic poetry retold myth for readers who already knew it, so allusion, variant versions and learned aetiology became the norm; Roman poets (Catullus, Virgil, Ovid) inherit this mode, not the archaic one.
  3. Stoics, Epicureans and Sceptics all promise tranquillity by correcting belief; their vocabulary (logos, ataraxia, cosmopolitanism, the fear of death) is what Rome, early Christianity and the Renaissance received as "Greek philosophy".
