First contact: Pyrrhus and the Illyrian wars (280–219)

Pyrrhus in Italy

Rome met the Hellenistic world in southern Italy, not Greece. In 281 Tarentum invited Pyrrhus of Epirus, a cousin of Alexander and the ablest general of his generation, to defend it against Rome. He landed in 280 with some 25,000 men and twenty elephants. He beat the legions at Heraclea (280) and Asculum (279), but each victory cost veterans he could not replace while Rome simply levied new legions. Plutarch, Pyrrhus 21, preserves the remark that gave us "Pyrrhic victory":

If we win one more battle against the Romans, we shall be utterly ruined.

After a Sicilian detour against Carthage (278–276) he returned, was checked at Beneventum (275) and sailed home; Tarentum fell in 272. The fuller accounts are Plutarch, Pyrrhus 13–26, and Appian, Samnite Wars 10–12. The lesson stood: a Hellenistic professional army could win battles against Rome and still lose the war to Roman manpower.

The Illyrian wars

Rome's first armed crossing of the Adriatic came in 229, against Queen Teuta of Illyria, whose fleets had been raiding Italian shipping. Polybius 2.2–12 presents the war as a police action against piracy; Rome crushed Teuta, installed Demetrius of Pharos as a client, and sent embassies to the Greek leagues announcing what it had done; Demetrius later switched to Macedon and was expelled in a second war (219), fleeing to Philip V.

Where sources disagree. Polybius' piracy explanation has been doubted. Maurice Holleaux (1921) held that Rome had no eastern policy before 200; W. V. Harris (War and Imperialism, 1979) saw habitual aggression; Erich Gruen (1984) a reactive Rome; Arthur Eckstein (2006) an anarchic interstate system in which every power behaved like this.

Philip V and the Second Macedonian War (215–196)

In 215 Philip V allied with Hannibal (treaty text in Polybius 7.9). Rome kept him busy through the Aetolians until the Peace of Phoenice (205), then returned in 200 on an appeal from Rhodes and Pergamon alarmed by a reported pact between Philip and Antiochus III to carve up the possessions of the child-king Ptolemy V (Polybius 15.20; Livy 31.14).

The decisive battle came at Cynoscephalae in Thessaly in 197. Polybius 18.18–27 and Livy 33.7–10 describe a confused engagement among foggy hills: Philip's right-wing phalanx drove the Roman left downhill, but his left never formed, and an unnamed tribune peeled twenty maniples off the victorious Roman right and struck the phalanx from behind. It could not turn; some 8,000 Macedonians died. Polybius 18.28–32 explains why the manipular legion, able to reform in sub-units on any terrain, beats a phalanx invincible only on flat ground.

At the Isthmian Games of 196 Titus Quinctius Flamininus had a herald proclaim that the Greeks formerly subject to Philip were to be "free, ungarrisoned, untaxed, and governed by their own laws" (Polybius 18.46; Livy 33.32; Plutarch, Flamininus 10–12). By 194 every Roman soldier had left Greece.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch and Livy present Flamininus as a sincere philhellene; Polybius, who admired him, notes his vanity. Ernst Badian (Foreign Clientelae, 1958) read "freedom" as the language of Roman patronage: the Greeks became clients bound by gratitude, a Roman and not a Greek notion of liberty. Gruen replied that Rome was borrowing an old Hellenistic slogan and meant roughly what the Antigonids and Ptolemies had meant by it.

Antiochus III and the Syrian War (192–188)

Antiochus III "the Great", fresh from reconquering Seleucid Iran and Coele-Syria, crossed to Thrace in 196 and was told by Roman envoys to leave Europe and free the Asian Greek cities. Talks failed; in 192 the Aetolians, disappointed in their reward from Rome, invited him into Greece. He came with only 10,000 men and was swept out of Thermopylae in 191 by Manius Acilius Glabrio, with Cato the Elder as legate.

Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with his brother Africanus as adviser, crossed the Hellespont and met Antiochus at Magnesia ad Sipylum in the winter of 190/189. Livy 37.37–44 and Appian, Syrian Wars 30–36, both resting on lost Polybius, describe scythed chariots panicking Antiochus' own left wing, Eumenes II of Pergamon's cavalry rolling it up, and the Seleucid centre of phalanx and elephants broken by missile fire. Livy's 50,000 Seleucid dead is a propaganda figure. The Treaty of Apamea (188; Polybius 21.42; Livy 38.38) pushed the Seleucids beyond the Taurus, imposed an indemnity of 15,000 talents, limited fleet and elephants, and demanded the surrender of Hannibal, at Antiochus' court since 195, who fled to Bithynia.

Perseus, Pydna and the end of the Antigonids (171–167)

Philip's son Perseus rebuilt Macedonian strength quietly. Eumenes denounced him in the Senate in 172 (Livy 42.11–13) and Rome declared war in 171; Livy 42.47 preserves older senators deploring the "new wisdom" of deceiving Perseus during negotiations.

Lucius Aemilius Paullus took command in 168. At Pydna on 22 June (the date is fixed by the lunar eclipse of the night before, which the tribune Sulpicius Gallus had predicted to the troops: Livy 44.37; Plutarch, Aemilius 17) the battle began by accident over a stray horse. The phalanx advanced magnificently across level ground, lost cohesion on broken terrain, and Paullus fed cohorts into the gaps. Plutarch, Aemilius 20, says 20,000 Macedonians died in an hour. Perseus surrendered on Samothrace and died in Italian custody. The monarchy founded by Antigonus Gonatas was abolished and Macedon split into four tributary republics (Livy 45.29). The same year, outside Alexandria, the envoy Popillius Laenas drew a circle in the sand around Antiochus IV and demanded an answer before he stepped out of it (Polybius 29.27). No Hellenistic monarch could now act without reference to Rome.

The settlement was brutal where it chose to be. On senatorial orders Paullus sacked seventy towns of Epirus in a day and enslaved 150,000 people (Polybius 30.15; Livy 45.34). In Achaea, technically loyal, the pro-Roman Callicrates supplied a list of a thousand leading men suspected of sympathy for Perseus; they were summoned to Rome "for trial" in 167 and detained in Italian towns for seventeen years without charge (Polybius 30.13, 30.32; Pausanias 7.10.7–12). Among them was Polybius of Megalopolis, former cavalry commander of the League. Kept in Rome through his friendship with Paullus' son Scipio Aemilianus (Polybius 31.23–25), he wrote the history that remains our best account of how Rome won. When the survivors were released in 150, fewer than 300 of the thousand were alive.

The last wars in Greece and the first provinces (150–129)

Andriscus and the province of Macedonia

In 149 a pretender, Andriscus, claiming to be Perseus' son, overran the four republics and beat a Roman praetor. Quintus Caecilius Metellus destroyed him in 148, and Macedonia became Rome's first province east of the Adriatic.

The Achaean War and the sack of Corinth

When Sparta tried to leave the Achaean League, the Senate (146) ordered the League to release not only Sparta but Corinth, Argos and other members; the assembly rioted, and the strategoi Critolaus and then Diaeus led the League into war. Metellus beat Critolaus at Scarpheia; Lucius Mummius destroyed Diaeus at Leucopetra, entered Corinth, killed the men, sold the women and children, shipped the art to Rome and burned the city (Polybius 38.9–18, 39.2–6; Pausanias 7.14–16; Strabo 8.6.23). Polybius was present and records seeing Roman soldiers using masterpieces as dice-boards. The League was dissolved; Polybius himself was asked to arrange the new order.

Where sources disagree. Whether "Achaea" became a province in 146 is uncertain. Pausanias 7.16.9–10 implies direct rule from then on, but no governor of Achaea is attested before Augustus constituted the province in 27 BC, and most scholars now think southern Greece was supervised by the Macedonian governor for a century, with free cities such as Athens and Sparta nominally autonomous.

The Attalid bequest

Attalus III of Pergamon died childless in 133 and left his kingdom to the Roman People by will (Strabo 13.4.2; Livy, Periochae 58–59; Justin 36.4). Tiberius Gracchus at once proposed using the Attalid treasure for his land commission (Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 14). A pretender, Aristonicus, was crushed by 129 and Pergamon became the province of Asia, the richest in the empire and the one whose tax-farmers would do most to make Mithridates welcome.

Where sources disagree. The letter of Mithridates in Sallust, Histories 4.69 M, alleges the will was forged by Rome. The Pergamene decree OGIS 338, passed within weeks of Attalus' death, refers to the will's ratification as fact, which most historians take as decisive; the motive, probably to pre-empt a succession war, remains conjecture.

Mithridates, Sulla and Pompey (89–63)

Mithridates VI Eupator of Pontus, Persian in descent and Greek in self-presentation, struck while Rome was distracted by the Social War. In 88 his armies overran Roman Asia and he ordered the massacre of every Italian resident in a single day: 80,000 according to Valerius Maximus 9.2 ext. 3 and Memnon (FGrH 434 F 22.9), 150,000 in Plutarch (Sulla 24); the cities' eager participation says how Roman rule had been experienced. His general Archelaus crossed to Greece, where Athens under the tyrant Aristion joined him.

Sulla arrived in 87, besieged Athens through the winter, felled the groves of the Academy and Lyceum for siege timber, and stormed the city on 1 March 86 (Plutarch, Sulla 12–14; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 30–39; Pausanias 1.20.4–7). The killing in the Kerameikos stopped, Plutarch says, when Sulla declared he forgave "the living for the sake of the dead". Sulla then beat Archelaus at Chaeronea and Orchomenus (86) and in 85 made the Peace of Dardanus, restoring Mithridates to Pontus because his own enemies in Rome mattered more. Among the spoils he shipped home was Apellicon's library, containing the manuscripts of Aristotle and Theophrastus (Strabo 13.1.54; Plutarch, Sulla 26): the Aristotelian corpus reached the Latin West as loot.

Two further wars followed. Lucullus drove Mithridates from Pontus (73–67) but lost control of his army; Pompey, given the command in 66, finished him in a year, and the king killed himself at Panticapaeum in the Crimea in 63 when his son Pharnaces revolted (Appian, Mithridatic Wars 111–113; Cassius Dio 37.11–14). Pompey then turned south. The Seleucid dynasty had shrunk to a few cities of northern Syria. In 64 Pompey declined to recognise Antiochus XIII Asiaticus, remarking that a king who could not hold his realm against Arabs and Jews was unfit to have it back, and annexed Syria as a province (Appian, Syrian Wars 49–50, 70; Justin 40.2). The house of Seleucus ended by administrative decision, without a battle.

Cleopatra, Actium and the end of Ptolemaic Egypt (51–30)

Egypt survived because it was rich and already half-controlled: Ptolemy XII had bought his throne back from Rome with 6,000 talents. His daughter Cleopatra VII, queen from 51, saw that the only path was personal alliance with whoever held Roman power. She bore Caesar a son, Caesarion, in 47, and after his murder allied with Mark Antony from 41. At the Donations of Alexandria in 34 Antony distributed eastern kingdoms to her children and proclaimed Caesarion Caesar's legitimate heir (Plutarch, Antony 54; Cassius Dio 49.41), a direct challenge to Octavian's adoptive legitimacy.

Rome declared war on Cleopatra, not Antony, in 32, and the fleets met off Actium on 2 September 31. Antony's larger ships, undermanned by disease and desertion, failed to break Agrippa's line; Cleopatra's squadron broke out and Antony followed, abandoning the rest (Plutarch, Antony 62–68; Cassius Dio 50.12–35). The army surrendered a week later. Octavian entered Alexandria on 1 August 30; Antony killed himself, and Cleopatra died about ten days later, aged thirty-nine. Egypt became the emperor's personal possession under an equestrian prefect. Horace, Odes 1.37, gives the Roman triumph and, remarkably, the queen's dignity:

No humble woman, she scorned to be led in a proud triumph.
Where sources disagree. Plutarch, Antony 86, admits no one knew how Cleopatra died: the asp was one story, a poisoned hairpin another; Strabo 17.1.10 likewise gives two versions. On the battle, W. W. Tarn (1931) argued that Actium was hardly fought, Antony's fleet being cover for a planned escape, and that Augustan poets (Virgil, Aeneid 8.675–713; Propertius 4.6) inflated it into a cosmic clash of East and West. Most recent accounts accept a real but short battle, decided when Cleopatra's departure broke Antony's nerve.

Captive Greece: the reverse conquest

Horace, Epistles 2.1.156–157, put the paradox in a line every educated Roman knew:

Captive Greece took captive her savage conqueror and brought the arts to rustic Latium.

Tutors and philosophers

Latin literature began as a Greek import: Livius Andronicus, a Greek from Tarentum, translated the Odyssey and staged the first Latin tragedies; Ennius, who said he had three hearts (Oscan, Greek, Latin), wrote the Annales in Homer's hexameter. The Athenian philosophers' embassy of 155 so alarmed Cato that he urged it be sent home before Roman youth forgot how to obey (Plutarch, Cato Maior 22). Within a generation the Stoic Panaetius lived in Scipio Aemilianus' house, and every senatorial boy had a Greek paedagogus and finished his education at Athens or Rhodes, as Cicero did.

Loot

The art came as spoil. Marcellus' sack of Syracuse in 211 filled Rome with Greek statues for the first time (Livy 25.40; Plutarch, Marcellus 21); Polybius 9.10 criticises the policy: a conqueror should take gold and leave the conquered their ornaments. Paullus' triumph of 167 took three days, the first for statues and paintings alone (Plutarch, Aemilius 32–33); Pliny, Natural History 35.24, records that when Attalus II bid 600,000 denarii at Mummius' Corinthian auction for a painting by Aristides, Mummius assumed it held some hidden virtue and withdrew it to dedicate in Rome. A century later Verres was prosecuted (Cicero, Verrines 2.4) for stealing Greek art privately: the loot was now understood.

Gods and ancestors

Roman religion had received Greek gods long before the conquest: Apollo in 431, Asclepius fetched from Epidaurus in 293 (Livy 10.47), the twelve-god lectisternium of 217 pairing Roman and Greek deities in six couples (Livy 22.10.9), the Great Mother in 204 (Livy 29.10–14). The interpretatio that identified Jupiter with Zeus, Juno with Hera, Minerva with Athena, Mars with Ares, Venus with Aphrodite, Mercury with Hermes, Neptune with Poseidon and Diana with Artemis was standard when Ennius listed the twelve Di Consentes. What Rome mostly took was not the gods but their stories: Latin cult had names, rituals and functions but little narrative, and Greek myth filled the vacuum.

The Trojan ancestry was the master-stroke. Hellanicus of Lesbos in the fifth century already had Aeneas founding Rome (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities 1.72), and Etruscan statuettes of disputed date from Veii show Aeneas carrying Anchises, so the legend was in Italy early. Naevius, Ennius and Cato's Origines built it into Roman history; the gens Iulia claimed descent from Aeneas' son Iulus and so from Venus; Virgil's Aeneid and Livy 1.1–3 fixed the canonical form. The genius of the choice is that Troy placed Romans inside the Homeric world as equals of the Greeks yet not Greeks, and even gave them a grievance. Andrew Erskine (Troy between Greece and Rome, 2001) shows Greek cities exploiting the kinship to win Roman favour.

Where sources disagree. Georges Dumézil held that early Rome was a society "without mythology", its gods abstract functions, which is why Greek myth was absorbed wholesale; T. P. Wiseman (The Myths of Rome, 2004) argued that Rome had plenty of native story, told in drama and ritual, which the literary record failed to preserve.

Why Rome won: Polybius' answer

Polybius opens his Histories (1.1.5) by asking who could be so idle as not to want to know "by what means and under what kind of constitution" the Romans subjected almost the whole inhabited world in less than fifty-three years (220–167). His answer in Book 6 is constitutional. Rome's politeia mixes monarchy (consuls), aristocracy (Senate) and democracy (assemblies), each checking the others (6.11–18), and this mixture resists anacyclosis, the natural cycle by which pure constitutions degenerate (6.3–9).

Three supporting arguments matter more to a modern reader. First, the army (6.19–42), with the phalanx comparison at 18.28–32 explaining Cynoscephalae and Pydna together. Second, culture: the aristocratic funeral with its ancestral masks (6.53–54) bred young men who would die for glory, and Roman religious scruple, which Polybius frankly calls deisidaimonia, superstition, kept the masses honest and magistrates accountable where Greek officials embezzled (6.56). Third, manpower: his census figures for 225 (2.24) give Rome and its allies over 700,000 foot and 70,000 horse, which is why Pyrrhus and Hannibal could win battles and still lose. What his later books show rather than say is that Rome also won by exploiting Greek states that could never combine against it, and after 168 by terror as policy.

Where sources disagree. Modern explanations divide along lines already met. Harris stresses an aristocracy whose careers required war; Gruen Roman reluctance to annex and the Greek habit of inviting Rome in; Eckstein argues that every Hellenistic state was equally bellicose and Rome simply had the deeper manpower base and a more inclusive citizenship, which is Polybius' own answer in modern dress. His constitutional thesis is now generally judged his weakest argument, his military and social observations his strongest.

Self-test

  1. Which two battles did Pyrrhus win against Rome, and which battle ended his Italian campaign?
    Answer

    Heraclea (280) and Asculum (279); he was checked at Beneventum in 275 and withdrew to Epirus.

  2. What Roman manoeuvre decided Cynoscephalae, and where does Polybius explain its general significance?
    Answer

    A tribune detached twenty maniples from the victorious Roman right and attacked the phalanx from behind; Polybius 18.28–32 explains why the flexible manipular legion beats the phalanx on uneven ground.

  3. What did Flamininus proclaim at the Isthmian Games of 196, and how have Badian and Gruen interpreted it differently?
    Answer

    That the Greeks formerly under Philip V were free, ungarrisoned, untaxed and self-governing. Badian saw Roman patronage creating client states; Gruen saw Rome borrowing a standard Hellenistic slogan in good faith.

  4. Name the treaty that ended the Syrian War and two of its terms.
    Answer

    The Treaty of Apamea (188): Antiochus III withdrew beyond the Taurus, paid 15,000 talents, limited his fleet and elephants, and was to surrender Hannibal.

  5. How is the date of Pydna fixed, and what happened to the Macedonian monarchy afterwards?
    Answer

    By the lunar eclipse of 21 June 168, the night before the battle. The Antigonid monarchy was abolished and Macedon divided into four tributary republics.

  6. Who compiled the list of the thousand Achaeans, how long were they held, and how many survived?
    Answer

    The pro-Roman Achaean politician Callicrates; they were held in Italy from 167 to 150, and fewer than 300 returned.

  7. What evidence supports the authenticity of Attalus III's will?
    Answer

    The Pergamene decree OGIS 338, passed just after his death in 133, treats the will and its ratification by Rome as fact; the forgery allegation appears only in Mithridates' letter in Sallust's Histories.

  8. What famous library reached Rome as a result of Sulla's sack of Athens?
    Answer

    Apellicon's library, containing the manuscripts of Aristotle and Theophrastus (Strabo 13.1.54; Plutarch, Sulla 26).

  9. How did the Seleucid dynasty end?
    Answer

    Without a battle: in 64 Pompey refused to recognise Antiochus XIII Asiaticus and annexed Syria as a Roman province.

  10. According to Polybius Book 6, what three elements made up Rome's mixed constitution, and what did he think its religion did?
    Answer

    Consuls (monarchic), Senate (aristocratic) and assemblies (democratic), each checking the others; Roman religious scruple, which he calls deisidaimonia, kept the masses in order and magistrates honest (6.56).

Carry forward

  1. Rome did not conquer the Greek world in one campaign but by a century of interventions, each invited or provoked by Greek states that would not combine against it; the step from arbitration to terror came in 168–146, with Epirus, the thousand Achaeans and Corinth.
  2. The Hellenistic monarchies ended differently: Macedon by battle and abolition, Pergamon by bequest, the Seleucids by Pompey's decree, Egypt by Actium and annexation to the emperor personally. Each became a province of a different legal shape.
  3. The conquest ran both ways. Greek literature, art, philosophy and myth became Rome's own, the Trojan ancestry letting Romans enter the Homeric world as rivals rather than pupils; Polybius, himself a hostage of the conquest, wrote the first serious analysis of why it happened.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Roman conquest of the Greek world, 280 to 30 BC. Cover: Pyrrhus in Italy; the Illyrian wars; the Macedonian Wars (Cynoscephalae in 197, Flamininus' "freedom of the Greeks" at the Isthmian Games, Pydna in 168 and the end of the Antigonids, the deportation of the thousand Achaeans including Polybius); the Syrian War and Magnesia; the Attalid bequest of Pergamon; the sack of Corinth in 146 and the province of Macedonia; Mithridates and the sack of Athens by Sulla in 86; Pompey and the Seleucid end; Cleopatra, Actium and the end of Ptolemaic Egypt. Then the reverse conquest: Horace's "captive Greece captured her savage conqueror", the Greek tutors, the looting of art, the Roman adoption of Greek gods and myths (Jupiter for Zeus, Aeneas as Trojan ancestor), and Polybius' explanation of why Rome won. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 7 · Hellenistic and Roman Greece, 323 BC to AD 529 · 7.4 · 2,691 words

Greece under the Empire and the end of antiquity

Achaea: a province of monuments and a town of lecture hallsHadrian and the PanhellenionThe Second SophisticPlutarch and Pausanias: the great witnessesGalen and PtolemyThe religious marketplaceNeoplatonismChristianity in the Greek citiesThe long ending, 391 to 529How the Byzantine scribes saved itSelf-testCarry forward

Achaea: a province of monuments and a town of lecture halls

Mainland Greece had been Roman since Mummius sacked Corinth in 146 BC; what changed in 27 BC was administrative. Augustus detached Achaea from Macedonia and made it a senatorial province governed by a proconsul of praetorian rank, seated at Corinth, which Caesar had refounded in 44 BC as the colony Laus Iulia Corinthiensis. Tiberius merged Achaea back into a large imperial command with Macedonia and Moesia in AD 15; Claudius returned it to the senate in 44 (Tacitus, Annals 1.76; Suetonius, Claudius 25). Nero's "liberation" of Greece in 67 lasted until Vespasian revoked it (Pausanias 7.17.3–4).

Augustus founded Nicopolis opposite Actium and settled veterans at Patrae; Strabo describes much of the Peloponnese as depopulated (8.6.20–23). The old cult centres survived on Roman money.

Athens had no political weight and immense cultural capital. Cicero's son and Horace (Epistles 2.2.45) had studied there; under the Empire this became institutional. Marcus Aurelius in 176 endowed salaried chairs at Athens for the four philosophical schools, Platonic, Peripatetic, Stoic and Epicurean, and for rhetoric (Dio Cassius 72.31.3; Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 566). The ephebate became a gentlemen's gymnasium for Athenian and foreign youths. The Herulian sack of 267 wrecked the lower city, yet the schools recovered and still drew Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus and the future emperor Julian in the 350s.

Hadrian and the Panhellenion

Hadrian (117–138) held the Athenian archonship in 112 and visited three times as emperor (124/5, 128/9, 131/2). He completed the Olympieion begun six centuries before, built the library north of the Roman Agora, reformed the olive-oil law (IG II² 1100) and was initiated at Eleusis. The arch near the Olympieion carries two inscriptions: "This is Athens, the former city of Theseus" on one face and "This is the city of Hadrian, not of Theseus" on the other.

In 131/2 he founded the Panhellenion, a league of cities that could prove Greek descent, with its council and temple at Athens and its own quadrennial games. Inscriptions show cities from Asia Minor, Crete and Cyrene submitting foundation myths as evidence; many Hellenistic foundations could not qualify. It lasted about a century and mattered less politically than as a formal audit of Greek identity under imperial patronage.

Where sources disagree. Spawforth and Walker (1985–86), who reconstructed the Panhellenion from epigraphy, read it as Hadrian's own design to bind the Greek East to Rome through a shared antiquarian ideal. Romeo (2002) and others have since argued that the initiative came from Greek cities, with Hadrian ratifying rather than inventing it. The literary sources (Dio Cassius 69.16; Pausanias 1.18.9) say only that Hadrian built the temple and founded the festival.

The Second Sophistic

The phrase is Philostratus' own. In his Lives of the Sophists (481), written in the 230s, he distinguishes the old sophistic of Gorgias from a "second" one he traces back to Aeschines, and which he treats as flourishing in his own age. Its practitioners were wealthy public speakers who declaimed on historical and mythical themes in Attic Greek, served as ambassadors to emperors and spent fortunes on buildings.

Dio of Prusa, "Chrysostom", exiled under Domitian and restored under Trajan, wrote the Olympic Oration (Or. 12), a theology of Phidias' Zeus, and the Euboean (Or. 7), idealising rural poverty. Aelius Aristides of Smyrna (117–after 181) wrote the Panathenaicus (Or. 1), a vast praise of Athens, To Rome (Or. 26) praising the empire, and the Sacred Tales (Or. 47–52), a diary of illness and dreams sent by Asclepius at Pergamum, our most intimate record of a pagan's religious life. Herodes Atticus (101–177), consul in 143 and tutor to Marcus Aurelius, rebuilt the Panathenaic stadium in marble and built the Odeion below the Acropolis; Philostratus (VS 545–566) gives him his longest life, including his trial before Marcus at Sirmium in 174. Lucian of Samosata (c. 120–after 180), a Syrian who learnt Greek as a second language, turned the same training to satire: Dialogues of the Gods, Zeus Rants, Alexander the False Prophet, On the Death of Peregrinus and A True Story mock gods, oracle-mongers and philosophers from inside their own idiom.

Where sources disagree. Bowersock (1969) treated the sophists chiefly as power brokers between cities and court. Bowie (1970) read their archaism as compensation for political loss. Swain (1996) and Whitmarsh (2001) see a confident negotiation of Greek identity within Rome rather than nostalgia. Brunt (1994) questioned whether "Second Sophistic" names a real movement at all or only Philostratus' canon.

Plutarch and Pausanias: the great witnesses

Plutarch of Chaeronea (c. 45–after 120), Roman citizen, Platonist and priest of Apollo at Delphi, is the single most important bridge between classical Greek religion and us. The Parallel Lives, twenty-three surviving pairs, preserve otherwise lost traditions on Theseus, Lycurgus and Numa; the preface to Theseus openly marks the boundary where history gives way to "the mythical and the tragic". The Moralia contains the Delphic dialogues (On the E at Delphi, On the Pythian Oracles, On the Obsolescence of Oracles), debating why the oracle now answers in prose and why shrines have fallen silent, and On Isis and Osiris, our fullest Greek account of Egyptian myth, read allegorically. The death of Pan announced to a ship off Paxi (De defectu 419b–d) and the Greek Questions show a man collecting a world he felt thinning.

Pausanias, probably from Lydia, travelled mainland Greece between about 150 and 180 and wrote the ten books of the Description of Greece, from Attica (1) through Olympia (5–6) to Delphi (10). He records sanctuaries, cult images, rituals and local myths told by priests and guides, with the Olympian Zeus of Phidias (5.11) and the Arcadian cults of Lycosura (8.37–38) among his most valuable passages. At 8.8.3 he says that he once dismissed Greek legends as foolishness but, at the Arcadian stage of his work, came to think them riddles of ancient wisdom.

Where sources disagree. Wilamowitz and much nineteenth-century scholarship treated Pausanias as an armchair compiler copying Hellenistic guidebooks. Habicht (1985) rehabilitated him as an autoptic traveller, and this is now the consensus, though how far his religious reflections are his own rather than conventional remains debated (Elsner, Hutton).

Galen and Ptolemy

Galen of Pergamum (129–c. 216) trained at Smyrna and Alexandria and from 169 served Marcus Aurelius and his successors in Rome. His output, roughly a tenth of all surviving Greek literature before AD 300, includes On Anatomical Procedures, On the Natural Faculties, On the Usefulness of the Parts and the autobiographical On My Own Books. He welded Hippocratic humoral theory, Platonic teleology and Aristotelian logic into a system that governed medicine until Vesalius and Harvey. He dissected apes and pigs, not humans, so his anatomy errs in ways his authority long concealed. His death date is uncertain: the Suda gives seventy years, Arabic sources eighty-seven.

Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170) worked at Alexandria. The Mathematical Syntaxis, known as the Almagest from its Arabic title, sets out in thirteen books a geocentric model with epicycles and the equant that predicted planetary positions well enough to stand for fourteen centuries. The Tetrabiblos systematised astrology; the Geography gave coordinates for eight thousand places; the Harmonics and Optics treated sound and refraction mathematically. Both men were Greek in language and Roman in patronage, and neither saw a tension.

Where sources disagree. R. R. Newton (1977) accused Ptolemy of fabricating observations to fit Hipparchus' parameters. Most historians of astronomy (Toomer, Jones, Swerdlow) reject fraud, reading the discrepancies as ancient practices of selecting and rounding data rather than modern dishonesty.

The religious marketplace

Civic cult continued, funded by the same families who paid for the sophists' buildings, with the imperial cult housed alongside the old gods. But the Empire made movement easy, and with movement came choice. Eleusis initiated Augustus, Hadrian, Lucius Verus and Marcus Aurelius (176), and Pausanias refuses to describe its interior rites (1.38.7). Isis had temples across the Greek world (Apuleius, Metamorphoses 11). Asclepius flourished at Epidaurus and Pergamum, where Aristides lived in the sanctuary for two years. Mithras barely appears in Greece itself. Delphi declined while Claros and Didyma answered theological questions about the highest god, and the Chaldaean Oracles of the late second century provided the Neoplatonists with scripture. Lucian's Alexander shows a new oracle of the snake-god Glycon being founded at Abonoteichus and acquiring Roman senatorial clients.

Where sources disagree. Nock (1933) and Cumont saw the "oriental" cults as a spiritual stepping stone toward Christianity. Burkert (1987) argued that the mysteries were options within polytheism, not religions of salvation competing with the Church. The "marketplace" model itself (North 1992) has been criticised for importing modern consumer assumptions into a world where civic cult was never optional.

Neoplatonism

Plotinus (204/5–270), an Egyptian who studied with Ammonius Saccas in Alexandria and taught at Rome from 244, reorganised Plato into a hierarchy: the One beyond being, from which Intellect and Soul emanate down to matter; the philosopher's task is return by contemplation. His treatises were edited after his death by Porphyry into six groups of nine, the Enneads, with a Life of Plotinus prefixed; Ennead I.6 On Beauty and VI.9 On the Good or the One are the best entry points. Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305) wrote the Isagoge that became the medieval logic primer, On the Cave of the Nymphs allegorising Odyssey 13, and fifteen books Against the Christians, burned in 448.

Iamblichus of Chalcis (c. 245–325), teaching at Apamea, answered Porphyry's sceptical Letter to Anebo with On the Mysteries, a defence of theurgy: ritual acts that draw the gods down rather than the soul up alone. The Athenian school, refounded by Plutarch of Athens (died 432) and led by Syrianus and then Proclus (412–485), made this the official philosophy of the Academy's last century. Proclus' Elements of Theology, Platonic Theology and commentaries on the Timaeus, Parmenides and Republic are systematic to the point of architecture; Marinus' Life of Proclus 30 shows him praying to Athena as her image left the Parthenon. The emperor Julian (361–363), pupil of Maximus of Ephesus, tried to make this tradition the state religion and died in Persia before it could take.

Where sources disagree. Dodds (1951) and most earlier scholarship read theurgy as Platonism's decline into magic. Shaw (1995) and Addey (2014) argue it is a coherent ritual theology grounded in the Timaeus. Whether Plotinus himself practised any rite remains uncertain: Porphyry reports a séance in the Iseum at Rome (Life 10) but also his master's indifference to civic cult.

Christianity in the Greek cities

Paul reached Greece around AD 49–51. Acts 17:16–34 places him at Athens disputing with Epicureans and Stoics, taken to the Areopagus, citing the altar "to an unknown god" and quoting Greek poetry (the line "in him we live and move and have our being" echoes Epimenides; "we are his offspring" is Aratus, Phaenomena 5). The response is polite indifference. At Corinth he stayed eighteen months, and the Delphi inscription dating Gallio's proconsulship to 51/52 fixes the chronology (Acts 18:12).

The Church's intellectuals were trained in the same schools as the sophists. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 2–8) tried Stoic, Peripatetic and Platonist teachers before conversion, and identified John's Logos with the Stoics'. Clement of Alexandria's Stromateis treats Greek philosophy as a tutor that led the Greeks to Christ as the Law led the Jews. Origen's Against Celsus preserves most of a Platonist's attack of around 178 by answering it. In the 350s Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus studied rhetoric at Athens (Gregory, Or. 43); Basil's Address to Young Men tells Christians to read Homer and Plato selectively, as bees take from flowers. In the early sixth century an anonymous Syrian writing as Dionysius the Areopagite recast Proclus' hierarchies as angelic orders; Koch and Stiglmayr demonstrated the dependence in 1895. Tertullian's "What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?" (De praescriptione haereticorum 7) is the Latin exception, not the Greek rule.

Where sources disagree. Harnack's thesis of the "Hellenisation of Christianity", a Greek metaphysical overlay on a Semitic gospel, dominated a century of scholarship. Recent work (Edwards, Boys-Stones) stresses that Second Temple Judaism was already Greek-speaking and philosophically engaged, so there was no un-Hellenised Christianity to corrupt.

The long ending, 391 to 529

The conventional endpoints are legal and symbolic rather than a single moment.

DateEventPrincipal source
Feb 391Theodosius I bans sacrifice and temple visitsCodex Theodosianus 16.10.10
Nov 392All pagan cult, including domestic, made treasonCod. Theod. 16.10.12
393 (traditional)Last Olympic GamesCedrenus; inference
396Alaric's Goths destroy EleusisEunapius, Lives of the Sophists 476
March 415Hypatia murdered at AlexandriaSocrates Scholasticus, HE 7.15
late 5th–6th c.Parthenon converted to a churchArchaeology; no dated text
529Justinian bans philosophy teaching at AthensMalalas 18.47; Cod. Just. 1.11.10

Theodosius' laws of 391 and 392 forbade sacrifice, divination and temple entry. Enforcement varied; Libanius (Or. 30) pleads against monks demolishing Syrian shrines, and Athens, with a pagan elite still in office, kept its festivals longer than most. Alaric burned Eleusis in 396 and the mysteries never resumed. Phidias' Zeus was taken to Constantinople and perished in the Lausus palace fire of 475.

At Alexandria, Hypatia, a Neoplatonist mathematician and daughter of Theon, was killed by a Christian mob in March 415 during the conflict between the prefect Orestes and the bishop Cyril. Socrates Scholasticus, a Christian historian, calls it a disgrace to the Church; Damascius (Life of Isidore) blames Cyril directly; the seventh-century John of Nikiu calls her a witch.

The Parthenon lost the statue of Athena before Proclus' death in 485, and at some point between the late fifth and late sixth century an apse was cut into its east end, the entrance reversed to the west, and it was dedicated to the Theotokos, the Mother of God. It served as a church for nearly a thousand years. In 529 Justinian forbade pagans to teach, and Malalas records an order to Athens that no one teach philosophy. Damascius, the last head of the Academy, and Simplicius went to the Persian court of Khusro I, returned under the peace of 532.

Where sources disagree. The 393 Olympic date rests on Cedrenus, who says only that the games ceased under Theodosius I; a bronze victor list found at Olympia in 1994 runs to 385, and some scholars (Lee, Remijsen) think the games continued until the Zeus temple burned under Theodosius II around 426. Alan Cameron (1969) argued the Academy was not actually closed in 529 and teaching persisted; Watts (2006) answers that the ban ended the school as an institution even if individuals lingered. Tardieu's Harran thesis for Simplicius is widely cited and widely doubted. The Parthenon's conversion date is uncertain by a century.

How the Byzantine scribes saved it

Everything in this course that is not inscription or papyrus reached us through Byzantine copyists. The shift from papyrus roll to parchment codex in the second to fourth centuries forced a first selection: what was not recopied was lost. Schooling narrowed the canon to seven plays each of Aeschylus and Sophocles, ten of Euripides, Homer, the orators and school prose. A second filter came in the ninth century when minuscule script replaced uncial; texts transliterated into the new hand in the next two centuries are the ancestors of our editions. Photius' Bibliotheca summarised 279 volumes he had read, many now lost. Arethas of Caesarea commissioned the Clarke Plato (Bodleian E. D. Clarke 39) from John the Calligrapher in 895; the Venetus A manuscript of the Iliad with its ancient scholia was written in the tenth century; Constantine Cephalas compiled the Palatine Anthology around 900; the Suda lexicon preserved thousands of fragments. The nine "alphabetic" plays of Euripides survive in a single manuscript, Laurentianus 32.2, copied about 1300. After 1204 and again before 1453 Byzantine scholars carried books to Italy, where Aldus Manutius printed the first editions of Aristotle, Aristophanes and Plato between 1495 and 1513. The classical world is, in a literal sense, what medieval Christian copyists chose to write out.

Self-test

  1. In which year did Augustus make Achaea a separate senatorial province, and what was its capital?
    Answer

    27 BC; Corinth, refounded by Caesar in 44 BC as Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis.

  2. What did Marcus Aurelius do for Athenian education in 176?
    Answer

    He endowed salaried chairs for the four philosophical schools (Platonic, Peripatetic, Stoic, Epicurean) and for rhetoric (Dio Cassius 72.31.3; Philostratus, VS 566).

  3. What was the Panhellenion, and what qualified a city to join?
    Answer

    A league of Greek cities founded by Hadrian in 131/2 with its temple and council at Athens; cities had to demonstrate Greek descent, often through foundation myths.

  4. Who coined the term "Second Sophistic", and in which work?
    Answer

    Philostratus, in the Lives of the Sophists (481), written in the 230s.

  5. Which work of Aelius Aristides records his dreams and cures from Asclepius?
    Answer

    The Sacred Tales (Orations 47–52).

  6. In which Plutarchan dialogue does the death of Pan story appear, and in which do his friends discuss why oracles have fallen silent?
    Answer

    Both are in On the Obsolescence of Oracles (De defectu oraculorum, the Pan story at 419b–d).

  7. Where does Pausanias say he changed his mind about the value of Greek myths?
    Answer

    In Book 8 on Arcadia (8.8.3), where he says he once thought the legends foolish but came to see them as riddles of ancient wisdom.

  8. What is the Isagoge, who wrote it, and why does it matter?
    Answer

    Porphyry's introduction to Aristotle's Categories; through Boethius' Latin translation it became the standard first logic text of the medieval West.

  9. Which two Theodosian laws, with dates, outlawed pagan sacrifice?
    Answer

    Codex Theodosianus 16.10.10 of February 391 and 16.10.12 of November 392, the latter extending the ban to domestic cult.

  10. Why is 393 as the date of the last Olympic Games disputed?
    Answer

    Cedrenus says only that the games ceased under Theodosius I; a victor list from Olympia runs to 385, and some scholars argue they continued until the temple of Zeus burned around 426.

Carry forward

  1. Roman Greece was not a decline but a reorganisation: political power left, cultural authority stayed, and the people who tell us most about classical cult and myth (Plutarch, Pausanias, the sophists) were Roman citizens writing under Roman peace.
  2. Christianity's Greek theologians were trained by the same schools, in the same texts, as the pagan philosophers they argued with; the Christian doctrine of God and the Neoplatonic One were built from one toolkit, which is why Proclus survives inside Pseudo-Dionysius.
  3. The ending was a process, not an event: laws in 391–392, a sack in 396, a murder in 415, a church in the Parthenon, a school closed in 529. And every text in this course exists only because Byzantine Christian scribes chose to copy it.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Greece and Greek culture under the Roman Empire, 30 BC to AD 529. Cover: Achaea as a province and Athens as a university town; Hadrian's philhellenism and the Panhellenion; the Second Sophistic (Dio Chrysostom, Aelius Aristides, Herodes Atticus, Lucian); Plutarch's Lives and Moralia and Pausanias' Description of Greece as our key witnesses to the old cults and myths; Galen and Ptolemy; the mystery cults and the religious marketplace; Neoplatonism (Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus); Christianity's spread through Greek cities, Paul at Athens, the Church Fathers' use of Greek philosophy; Theodosius' bans on pagan cult in the 390s, the end of the Olympic Games, the conversion of the Parthenon into a church, the murder of Hypatia, and Justinian's closing of the Athenian Academy in 529 as the conventional end; and how Byzantine scribes then preserved everything we have. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 8 · Religion and daily life · 8.1 · 2,907 words

Ritual practice: sacrifice, temples, priests, pollution

A religion with no nameAnimal sacrifice, step by stepPrometheus at MeconeLibations, votives and first-fruitsThe god's house, the altar outside, and the civic priestThe household cultsMiasma and purificationPrayer, oaths, curses and magicThe Athenian yearState, deme, household, individualSelf-testCarry forward

A religion with no name

Classical Greek had no word for "religion". It had ta hiera ("the sacred things"), ta nomizomena ("the customary things"), eusebeia (right conduct towards gods, parents and guests alike) and therapeia theon, "tending the gods". The gap in vocabulary reflects the absence of the thing. There was no scripture: Homer and Hesiod were poets, not revelation; it was they, Herodotus says, who "gave the gods their epithets and told the Hellenes where each came from" (Herodotus 2.53). There was no creed, because nobody was asked to believe anything, only to do the customary things; Socrates was charged with "not acknowledging the gods the city acknowledges" (Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.1.1), not with false belief. There was no priestly class with doctrine, because priests were office-holders attached to a single sanctuary. Myths contradicted one another freely; this troubled philosophers, not worshippers.

Walter Burkert's Greek Religion (1977; English 1985) starts here: Greek religion is ritual transmitted by imitation, with myth as loose commentary. Robert Parker (Polytheism and Society at Athens, 2005) adds that the rituals belonged to groups existing for other purposes: city, deme, phratry and household were the congregations. Herodotus defines Greekness by "common blood, common language, common shrines of the gods and sacrifices, and like customs" (Herodotus 8.144.2).

Where sources disagree. Burkert and Price treat ritual as primary and belief as nearly irrelevant. Henk Versnel (Coping with the Gods, 2011) and Julia Kindt (Rethinking Greek Religion, 2012) argue that Greeks held beliefs that shaped action, and that Socrates' trial shows belief could become a public issue. Parker is intermediate: belief existed but was never a test of membership.

Animal sacrifice, step by step

The central rite was thysia: slaughter of a domestic animal followed by a shared meal. The fullest early descriptions are Nestor's heifer for Athena (Homer, Odyssey 3.430–463) and the hecatomb at Chryse (Iliad 1.447–474); Aristophanes parodies it in Peace 948–1022.

  1. Procession. The garlanded animal is led to the altar; a girl carries the basket (kanoun) with the knife hidden under barley. The beast must seem willing.
  2. Lustral water (chernips). Carried round the altar; hands washed; the animal sprinkled, its start read as assent.
  3. Barley (oulai). Thrown at altar and victim; forehead hairs cut and burnt, the first offering and first violence.
  4. The prayer. Standing, arms raised: name the god, state the claim, make the request (model: Chryses, Iliad 1.451–456).
  5. The cut. Axe-blow, then the throat cut with head pulled back so blood sprays upward; the women raise the ololyge; blood splashed on the altar.
  6. The division. The splanchna (heart, liver, lungs, kidneys) are roasted at once and eaten by the inner circle. The thigh bones (meria) are wrapped in fat, topped with pieces from every limb and burnt. The rest is boiled and distributed equally or by lot; the hide went to the priest or was sold (dermatikon accounts, IG II² 1496).
  7. The gods' portion. Bones, fat, smoke (knise), and the tail and sacrum (osphys), whose curling in the fire was an omen. Menander's cook grumbles that men give the gods "the tail-end and the gall-bladder" (Dyskolos 447–453).

Sphagia before battle or at an oath drained blood into the earth uneaten; the holokaustos burnt the whole victim; enagismos for the dead and some heroes went into a pit.

Where sources disagree. Karl Meuli (1946) saw in thysia a survival of hunters' ritual, a "comedy of innocence" disclaiming guilt; Burkert's Homo Necans (1972) built on this: sacrifice channels aggression and binds the group through shared killing. Vernant and Detienne (The Cuisine of Sacrifice, 1979) read the rite instead as culinary and political, defining humans between beasts and gods. F. S. Naiden (Smoke Signals for the Gods, 2013) argues all of them overweight the killing; the guilt reading has little ancient support beyond the Bouphonia aetiology (Porphyry, On Abstinence 2.28–30). Whether the Olympian/chthonian split is an ancient category (Scott Scullion) or a modern schema (Renate Schlesier) is also open.

Prometheus at Mecone

Hesiod explains the division through a story. At Mecone, when gods and mortals were being separated, Prometheus set out two portions of an ox: the meat hidden in the stomach, and the white bones dressed in gleaming fat. Zeus, seeing through the trick (Hesiod insists), chose the bones, "and from this the tribes of men on earth burn white bones for the immortals" (Hesiod, Theogony 535–557). Zeus withholds fire, Prometheus steals it, and Zeus answers with Pandora and with Prometheus bound (Theogony 558–616; Works and Days 42–105).

The myth is a strict aetiology: it explains a rite whose logic looks odd (why do the gods get the inedible part?) and fixes sacrifice at the moment the human condition was set: men eat meat, cook with stolen fire, labour and die; the gods take the smoke. Burkert noted that Hesiod's insistence that Zeus was not fooled betrays the problem: the rite must honour the god, yet looks like a swindle.

Where sources disagree. The Theogony makes Prometheus's act the origin of sacrifice, the Works and Days the origin of toil and of woman, with no butchering. Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound drops the trick altogether; Apollodorus (Library 1.7.1) keeps only the fire theft. Whether Mecone (later identified with Sicyon) had a commemorative cult is unknown.

Libations, votives and first-fruits

Libation (sponde) was the commonest ritual act: a few drops of wine from a shallow phiale before drinking, at meals, departures, the symposium and treaties, which is why spondai came to mean "truce". The choe emptied the vessel completely, for the dead and the powers below; Odysseus pours milk-and-honey, wine and water into a pit (Odyssey 11.26–28). Wineless libations (nephalia) went to the Eumenides (Aeschylus, Eumenides 107; Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus 100, 481).

Votives (anathemata, "things set up") stayed with the god: statuettes, pots, weapons, clothing, hair, or Croesus's gold at Delphi (Herodotus 1.50–51). The logic was charis, pleasure that creates obligation: Hecuba promises Athena twelve heifers and a robe "if she will pity the city" (Iliad 6.302–311). Brauron's inventories list garments dedicated after childbirth (IG II² 1514–1531); Epidaurus and Corinth yield terracotta limbs recording cures.

First-fruits (aparchai) gave the god a share before humans took theirs: a handful of harvest, part of a catch, the first cut of hair. Athens made this policy: the Eleusinian decree (IG I³ 78, about 435–415) orders demes and allies to send a fraction of their grain to Eleusis, and one sixtieth of imperial tribute was an aparche to Athena. Hesiod's household version: "sacrifice to the immortals according to your means" (Works and Days 336–341).

The god's house, the altar outside, and the civic priest

A temple (naos) housed the god's image and treasure; it was not a hall for worshippers, and the cella was dark and often locked. Worship happened at the altar (bomos), outdoors before the east end, within the temenos. The altar is the older and indispensable element: Zeus at Olympia was worshipped for centuries at a mound of ash before any temple stood, and the ash altar remained the cult centre afterwards (Pausanias 5.13.8–11). Many cults never had a temple; Burkert calls the temple "a votive offering writ large". Inside stood the cult image, an ancient wooden figure like the olive-wood Athena Polias or a showpiece like Pheidias's Athena Parthenos (Pausanias 1.24.5–7): the god's presence, not the god.

Where sources disagree. No text records a priestess or regular sacrifice for the Parthenon, and the old image of Athena Polias was housed elsewhere. Some conclude the Parthenon was chiefly treasury and monument; others think the evidence is simply thin. Uncertain.

Priests (hiereis) and priestesses (hiereiai) belonged to one cult and were defined by office, not learning: they kept the keys, tended the image, presided at sacrifice and took perquisites. They did not preach or monopolise sacrifice; any head of household could kill for Zeus. Some priesthoods were hereditary in a genos (the Eteoboutadai for Athena Polias, the Eumolpidai and Kerykes at Eleusis); the priestess of Athena Nike was chosen by lot "from all Athenian women" (IG I³ 35, about 448); in some Ionian cities priesthoods were sold. Women held office on a scale unmatched elsewhere in public life; Lysimache served Athena Polias for sixty-four years (Pliny, Natural History 34.76). Beside priests stood manteis (seers) and exegetai (advisers on sacred law); the archon basileus oversaw the whole (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 57).

The household cults

The oikos had its own gods at boundary and centre. Archon-candidates were asked whether they had "an Apollo Patroos and a Zeus Herkeios, and where these shrines are" (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 55.3).

  • Zeus Herkeios, "of the fence", had his altar in the courtyard, the place of household sacrifice and refuge (Odyssey 22.334–336).
  • Hestia, the hearth, took the first and last libation at meals; newborn, bride and new slave were each brought to it and so admitted to the house. She has no myths and no temple of consequence; she is the fire.
  • Zeus Ktesios, "of possessions", lived in the storeroom as a wool-wreathed jar of water, oil and seeds (Autocleides' Exegetikon, at Athenaeus 11.473b–c).
  • Hermes at the door: a herm stood outside, often with an Apollo Agyieus pillar and a small Hecate shrine. Hipparchus set up herms along the roads (Plato, Hipparchus 228d–229a); their mutilation in 415 was sacrilege against the whole city (Thucydides 6.27).
  • Zeus Meilichios, the snake-form Zeus of wealth and purification, took ancestral family sacrifice; Xenophon, told he had neglected it, sacrifices whole pigs as his father did (Anabasis 7.8.1–6).

The kyrios conducted these rites. Plato's hostility to private shrines (Laws 909d–910e) shows how common and uncontrolled they were.

Miasma and purification

Pollution (miasma) was a condition, not a sin: a contagious disorder that made a person unfit to approach the gods and dangerous to others. Parker's Miasma (1983) is the standard study. Birth polluted mother and house: the Cyrene sacred law (SEG 9.72) rules that the woman in childbed pollutes the roof, and those in the house for three days; births and deaths were forbidden on Delos (Thucydides 3.104.2). Death polluted the household; a bowl of water from another house stood at the door for visitors (Euripides, Alcestis 98–100), and the funerary law of Iulis on Keos (IG XII.5 593) fixes who is polluted and for how long. Homicide was gravest: the killer was barred from shrines, market and city, and even unintentional killers went into exile (Demosthenes 23.72); the pollution attached to the land, as at Thebes under Oedipus (Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 95–101), and to Orestes until Apollo purifies him with pig's blood (Aeschylus, Eumenides 280–283). Athens even tried and expelled the axe or stone that had killed a man (Constitution of the Athenians 57.4). Sex polluted briefly: one washed before entering a sanctuary; priests in office observed stricter abstinence.

Purification (katharmos) used water (the perirrhanteria at sanctuary entrances, sea water for grave cases), sulphur (Odysseus fumigates his hall, Odyssey 22.481–494) and piglet's blood, dripped over the killer or carried round the Pnyx before the assembly met; scapegoats (pharmakoi) were driven out at the Thargelia. Athens purified Delos in 426/5 by removing its graves (Thucydides 3.104.1–2).

Where sources disagree. Louis Moulinier (1952) held that archaic pollution was quasi-physical dirt that later acquired moral content; E. R. Dodds (The Greeks and the Irrational, 1951) traced a shift from "shame-culture" to "guilt-culture". Parker, drawing on Mary Douglas's Purity and Danger (1966), rejected both: pollution and moral fault were entangled from the start but never identical. Ancient writers disagreed too: the Hippocratic On the Sacred Disease (1) mocks purifiers who treat epilepsy as pollution, and Euripides' Iphigenia asks why a goddess who shrinks from a mourner delights in human slaughter (Iphigenia in Tauris 380–391).

Prayer, oaths, curses and magic

Prayer was spoken aloud, standing, arms raised with palms to the sky (Iliad 1.450; Odyssey 9.526–527); to the powers below one pointed the hands down or struck the earth (Iliad 9.568–569). Kneeling was foreign or servile; Theophrastus's Superstitious Man, who kneels at crossroads and oils smooth stones, is ridiculous (Characters 16). The structure was invocation with cult titles, argument from charis, request.

An oath (horkos) was a conditional self-curse with the gods as enforcers; Hesiod makes Horkos a child of Strife, "who most afflicts men who swear falsely" (Theogony 231–232). Solemn oaths were sworn standing on the cut pieces (tomia) of a victim so the swearer's fate should match the beast's: the Areopagus oath over boar, ram and bull (Demosthenes 23.67–68); the truce-oath at Iliad 3.276–301, wine poured as the perjurer's brains should spill. The ephebic oath calls the boundary stones and crops as witnesses (Lycurgus, Against Leocrates 76–77).

Public curses were a state weapon: the Teos inscription (ML 30, about 470) curses poisoners and traitors with death for them and their line. Private curses took the form of binding tablets (katadesmoi): lead sheets inscribed "I bind X, his tongue, his hands, his soul" before a lawsuit, rivalry or love affair, rolled, sometimes nailed, and dropped into a grave of the untimely dead or a well. Over 1,600 are known, the earliest Sicilian of the later sixth century, with a dense Athenian cluster of legal curses. Plato knew the trade and the fear of it (Republic 364b–c; Laws 933a–e). Erotic spells like Simaetha's (Theocritus, Idyll 2) and itinerant purifiers (goetes) belong to the same world.

Where sources disagree. Frazer and Tylor opposed coercive magic to supplicatory religion; Fritz Graf (Magic in the Ancient World, 1997), Christopher Faraone and Versnel show that the tablets borrow prayer formulae and invoke the same gods, so the line is one of social approval, not technique. The Greek word mageia, from the Persian Magi, was polemical.

The Athenian year

The lunar year began with the first new moon after the summer solstice, with a thirteenth month intercalated as needed. Each month had fixed sacred days: the first (noumenia), the third for Athena, the fourth for Heracles, Hermes and Aphrodite, the sixth for Artemis, the seventh for Apollo, the eighth for Poseidon and Theseus. The state calendar stood on the Solonian axones, controversially revised by Nicomachus around 400 (Lysias 30). Jon Mikalson's Sacred and Civil Calendar of the Athenian Year (1975) is the guide; Parker counts roughly 120 festival days a year, as the "Old Oligarch" complained (Pseudo-Xenophon, Constitution of the Athenians 3.2).

Exact days are secure only where a literary or epigraphic source fixes them; the placing of the Oschophoria, Arrhephoria and Chalkeia is debated between Deubner (Attische Feste, 1932), Mikalson and Parker. Thucydides calls the Anthesteria "the older Dionysia" (2.15.4), yet its relation to the Lenaia and City Dionysia remains unclear.

State, deme, household, individual

The four levels nested, worshipping largely the same gods under local titles. The state was a corporate worshipper: the demos voted sacrifices, financed hecatombs, appointed hieropoioi and received the gods' charis for all. Impiety (asebeia) was a public crime because divine anger fell on the city. Christiane Sourvinou-Inwood's "polis religion" model (1990) made the city the frame within which all Greek religion had meaning.

The deme was a miniature polis. The Erchia calendar (SEG 21.541, early fourth century) lists some fifty sacrifices a year, roughly 550 drachmas, to gods from Zeus to local heroines. The Rural Dionysia was a deme affair, parodied in Dikaiopolis's private procession (Aristophanes, Acharnians 237–279). Phratries, gene and orgeones occupied the same middle ground.

The household had the kyrios as priest and the family dead tended at the Genesia. The individual had more room than the model allows: people vowed and dedicated, asked Dodona about marriage and money, slept in Asclepius's precinct for a dream cure, bought a binding tablet, or sought initiation into the Mysteries or a Bacchic group whose gold leaves promised a better lot below.

Where sources disagree. Kindt (2012) and Esther Eidinow argue that the polis-religion model marginalises what did not fit the city: magic, Bacchic initiation, private oracles, household superstition. Parker accepts much of this while holding that the city remained the dominant frame. Burkert treated the polis as a late container for rituals far older than any city.

Self-test

  1. Which Greek terms came closest to "religion", and what do they emphasise?
    Answer

    Ta hiera (the sacred things), ta nomizomena (the customary things), eusebeia (right conduct) and therapeia theon (tending the gods). All emphasise practice and custom, not belief or doctrine.

  2. In what order do the chief acts of a thysia occur?
    Answer

    Procession with garlanded animal, basket and water; lustral water and hand-washing; barley thrown and forehead hairs burnt; prayer with raised hands; the cut and the ololyge; roasting and sharing of the splanchna, burning of thigh bones in fat; boiling and distribution of the meat.

  3. What exactly do the gods receive from a sacrifice, and which text explains why?
    Answer

    The thigh bones wrapped in fat, the tail and sacrum, and the rising smoke. Hesiod, Theogony 535–557: Prometheus's division at Mecone, where Zeus took the bones dressed in fat.

  4. Distinguish sponde from choe.
    Answer

    A sponde pours a few drops of wine and the rest is drunk; it accompanies meals, departures and treaties. A choe empties the vessel completely and is poured for the dead and chthonic powers, often with milk, honey or water.

  5. Why is it misleading to call a Greek temple a place of worship?
    Answer

    The temple housed the image and treasure and admitted no congregation. Worship, above all sacrifice, happened at the altar outside, which was older and indispensable; many cults had an altar but no temple (Zeus's ash altar at Olympia).

  6. Give two ways a priesthood might be filled in classical Athens.
    Answer

    Hereditarily within a genos (Eteoboutadai for Athena Polias; Eumolpidai and Kerykes at Eleusis) or by lot from all citizens (priestess of Athena Nike, IG I³ 35). Elsewhere, by purchase.

  7. Which two household gods did an archon-candidate have to possess, and where did they stand?
    Answer

    Apollo Patroos and Zeus Herkeios (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 55.3). Zeus Herkeios had his altar in the courtyard.

  8. Name the four main sources of miasma and one purifying agent for each.
    Answer

    Birth (washing, waiting days per the Cyrene law); death (water bowl at the door, the fixed days of the Iulis law); homicide (exile, piglet's blood as for Orestes); sex (washing before entering a sanctuary).

  9. How was a solemn oath physically enacted, and what did the gesture mean?
    Answer

    The swearer stood on or touched the cut pieces (tomia) of a sacrificed animal, as in the Areopagus oath over boar, ram and bull (Demosthenes 23.67–68). The gesture is a conditional self-curse: may I perish like the beast if I swear falsely.

  10. In which Athenian month did the Eleusinian Mysteries fall, and in which the City Dionysia?
    Answer

    Boedromion (September/October) for the Mysteries; Elaphebolion (March/April) for the City Dionysia.

Carry forward

  1. Greek religion is a set of inherited practices, not a set of beliefs: judge later material (mystery cults, philosophy, Christian polemic) by asking what people did, not what they professed.
  2. Sacrifice is the master rite, and its structure (procession, prayer, kill, divide, eat) and its Promethean aetiology recur wherever gods and humans meet; the unburnt meat is the human share and the smoke is the divine one.
  3. The worshipping unit is a social unit that exists for other reasons (city, deme, phratry, house), so changes in Greek politics are always also changes in Greek religion, and pollution, oath and curse are the mechanisms by which the gods police those units.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the practice of ancient Greek religion. Cover: why there was no word for religion, no scripture, no creed, no priestly class with doctrine; the structure of animal sacrifice step by step (procession, lustral water, barley, the prayer, the cut, the division of the meat, the gods' portion) and the Prometheus myth as its explanation; libations, votives and first-fruits; the temple as the god's house, not a congregation hall, and the altar outside; priests and priestesses as civic offices; the household cults (Zeus Herkeios, Hestia, Hermes at the door); purity and pollution (miasma) from birth, death, murder and sex, and purification rites; curses, oaths, binding tablets and magic; prayer gestures; the calendar of an Athenian year; and how the state, the deme, the household and the individual each related to the gods. Draw on Burkert and Parker where relevant. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

Oracles and mystery cults

Delphi: the Pythia and the procedureDelphi: the gas theory, colonisation and politicsThe Amphictyony and the Sacred WarsDodona, Siwa, Trophonius and the AsclepieiaEleusisOrphism, the gold tablets and the PythagoreansDionysiac mysteries and maenadismSamothrace and the CabiriIsis, Cybele, Mithras: imports through a Greek filterSelf-testCarry forward

Delphi: the Pythia and the procedure

Delphi sits on the southern slope of Parnassus above the Pleistos gorge, in Phocis. Apollo's sanctuary there was active from the eighth century BC and functioned, with fluctuations, until the fourth century AD. The mouthpiece was the Pythia, a local woman of mature age who, after Delphi's prestige grew, was supplemented by two more so that consultations could run in shifts (Plutarch, De defectu oraculorum 414b). Our best witness is Plutarch himself, who held a priesthood at Delphi around AD 100 and wrote three dialogues set there; the price of his reliability is that he describes a diminished Roman-era oracle, not the archaic one.

Procedure, reconstructed from Plutarch, Euripides' Ion, Diodorus 16.26 and inscriptions: consultation originally fell once a year on the seventh of the month Bysios, Apollo's birthday, later on the seventh of every month outside the three winter months when Apollo was away and Dionysus held the sanctuary. The enquirer paid the pelanos (a cake-fee, with cities such as Phaselis and Sciathus negotiating fixed rates), sacrificed a goat, and waited in the order of promanteia, the right of priority that Delphi granted to favoured states such as Chios. Before the session the goat was sprinkled with cold water; if it failed to tremble, the day was unpropitious (Plutarch, De defectu 435b, 437a–b). The Pythia bathed at the Castalian spring, burned laurel and barley on the altar, and sat on the tripod in the adyton, the sunken inner room of the temple. The prophetai and the five hosioi, drawn from Delphian aristocratic families, managed the enquirer and transmitted the response.

Where sources disagree. Whether the Pythia raved or spoke lucidly is unresolved. Plato (Phaedrus 244b) and Plutarch treat her inspiration as a kind of divine madness, and Plutarch records a Pythia who was forced to prophesy on a bad day, shrieked, fled the adyton and died within days (De defectu 438a–b). Fontenrose (1978) argued from the catalogue of historically attested responses that she answered plainly and that the frenzied Pythia is a literary construct, largely Lucan's; Maurizio (1995) replied that spirit possession can be coherent and that the priests' alleged hexameter "versifying" of her words is a modern assumption with little ancient support. Uncertain, and probably varied over nine centuries.

Delphi: the gas theory, colonisation and politics

Strabo 9.3.5 and Diodorus 16.26 speak of a chasm beneath the tripod exhaling a pneuma enthousiastikon, and Plutarch's companions discuss a sweet fragrance that sometimes filled the room (De defectu 437c). The French excavators of the 1890s found no chasm, and Oppé (1904) dismissed the vapour as fiction. In 2001 de Boer, Hale and Chanton published geological work showing that two faults, the Delphi and the Kerna, intersect beneath the temple, that the bituminous limestone below is capable of releasing light hydrocarbons, and that spring water nearby contained ethylene, methane and ethane. Ethylene has a sweet smell and in low concentration produces a dissociated, euphoric state, which matched Plutarch suspiciously well.

Where sources disagree. The gas theory was widely reported as settled; it is not. Lehoux (2007) and Foster and Lehoux (2007) pointed out that the measured ethylene was far below any pharmacological threshold and that the adyton was not a sealed chamber. Etiope and colleagues (2006) proposed that methane and carbon dioxide, not ethylene, were the active agents, with oxygen depletion rather than intoxication at work. The ancient tradition itself is not unanimous: Plutarch's own speakers are divided over whether the pneuma matters at all, and no classical author before the Hellenistic period mentions a chasm. A fault zone and seeping gas are now established; what the Pythia breathed, and whether it mattered to the responses, remains uncertain.

Herodotus is the great storehouse of Delphic responses, and he uses them as plot. Croesus tests the oracles by asking what he is doing on a given day; only Delphi and Amphiaraus answer correctly (1.46–49). Delphi then tells him that attacking Persia will "destroy a great empire" (1.53) and that he need not fear until "a mule becomes king of the Medes" (1.55); after his fall the Pythia defends herself by explaining that the empire was his own and the mule was the half-Median Cyrus (1.91). The Spartans ask about conquering Arcadia and are told they may "dance on Tegea" in chains, which they do, as prisoners (1.66). Battus of Thera is ordered to found Cyrene and, after resisting, is punished with seven years' drought (4.150–157). In 481/480 the Athenians receive first a response telling them to flee to the ends of the earth and then, after supplication, the famous "wooden wall" and "divine Salamis" response that Themistocles reads as a reference to the fleet (7.140–143). Herodotus also records the oracle's corruptibility: the Alcmaeonids bribe the Pythia to urge Sparta to free Athens (5.63), and Cleomenes bribes her to declare Demaratus illegitimate (6.66).

Delphi's authority in colonisation is beyond doubt for the archaic period; Cyrene, Croton, Rhegium, Taras and Gela all carried foundation oracles, and Pindar's Pythian 4 and 5 celebrate Battus's commission. Malkin (1987) saw Apollo Archegetes as a genuine clearing-house for geographical knowledge gathered from enquirers; Londey (1990) and others treat many foundation oracles as later legitimation. Delphi's political alignments are easier to see: the Spartan constitution was attributed to Delphic sanction (Tyrtaeus fr. 4 West; Herodotus 1.65), the Spartan kings kept standing envoys, the Pythioi (Herodotus 6.57), and the oracle's discouraging responses to Greeks resisting Xerxes (7.140, 7.148 to Argos) left it open to the charge of medising.

The Amphictyony and the Sacred Wars

Delphi was not governed by Delphi. The Pylaean-Delphic Amphictyony was a league of twelve ethne (Thessalians, Boeotians, Dorians, Ionians, Perrhaebians, Magnesians, Locrians, Oetaeans, Phthiotic Achaeans, Malians, Phocians, Dolopians), each with two hieromnemones, meeting twice a year at Anthela near Thermopylae and at Delphi. Aeschines 2.115 quotes its oath: not to destroy any Amphictyonic city and not to cut off its running water. The league administered the sanctuary's funds, rebuilt the temple after the fire of 548 and the earthquake of 373, and ran the Pythian Games.
