Where sources disagree. Robertson (1978) argued that the First Sacred War never happened: no fifth-century author mentions it, and the story first appears in fourth-century orators who needed a precedent for the Third. Davies (1994) and most since accept a conflict over Crisa but admit that its scale and chronology are reconstructed backwards from Aeschines and the Pythian Games foundation dates.

Dodona, Siwa, Trophonius and the Asclepieia

Dodona in Epirus belonged to Zeus Naios and Dione. Homer already knows the Selloi, interpreters "with unwashed feet, sleeping on the ground" (Iliad 16.233–235), and Odysseus claims to have gone "to hear the will of Zeus from the high-leaved oak" (Odyssey 14.327–328). Herodotus 2.54–57 calls it the oldest oracle in Greece and tells of the prophetic doves, rationalising them as priestesses nicknamed peleiades; Plato pairs the Dodonaean priestesses with the Pythia as inspired madwomen (Phaedrus 244b). The excavations of Evangelidis and Dakaris, and the 2013 corpus of Dakaris, Vokotopoulou and Christidis, have produced over four thousand lead tablets inscribed with the enquirers' questions: whether to marry, whether a child is one's own, which god to sacrifice to, who stole the blankets. They are the single best evidence for what ordinary Greeks actually asked an oracle. The sanctuary was sacked by the Aetolians in 219 BC and never fully recovered.

Siwa, the oracle of Ammon in the Libyan desert, was Egyptian Amun identified with Zeus; Herodotus 1.46 lists it among the oracles Croesus tested, and Cyrene and Sparta both consulted it (Pausanias 3.18.3 on Lysander). The god answered through the movements of a statue carried in a boat by priests (Diodorus 17.50). Alexander's visit in 331 made it famous; Callisthenes (in Strabo 17.1.43), Arrian 3.3–4 and Plutarch Alexander 26–27 disagree about what he was told, Plutarch preserving the story that the priest's Greek slipped from o paidion to o pai Dios, "son of Zeus".

Trophonius at Lebadeia in Boeotia is the only oracle whose procedure we have from an initiate: Pausanias 9.39.5–14 describes his own consultation. The enquirer lodged for days in the house of Good Fortune and the Good Daimon, bathed in the river Hercyna, sacrificed repeatedly, drank from the springs of Forgetfulness and Memory, and was lowered feet first through a narrow hole into a chamber, carrying honey-cakes, to be swept away and shown or told the future. He returned stupefied and was seated on the Chair of Memory to dictate what he had experienced. The proverb "he has consulted Trophonius", said of a man who never laughs, was already current for Aristophanes (Clouds 508). Herodotus 8.134 has Mardonius's agent Mys consult it before Plataea.

Epidaurus and the other Asclepieia (Cos, Pergamon, Athens from 420/419, Rome's Tiber island from 293) were healing oracles working by enkoimesis, incubation: the patient slept in the abaton and the god, or his snakes and dogs, visited in dreams. The fourth-century iamata stelae from Epidaurus (IG IV² 1, 121–124; LiDonnici 1995) record some seventy cures: Ambrosia of Athens, blind in one eye, laughs at the cures and is healed anyway; Cleo, pregnant for five years, gives birth to a boy who walks at once. Aristophanes' Wealth 653–747 parodies an incubation at the Piraeus with a priest stealing the offerings, which shows the practice was familiar enough to mock by 388. Aelius Aristides' Sacred Tales are the second-century patient's view from Pergamon.

Eleusis

The Mysteries of Demeter and Kore at Eleusis, twenty kilometres west of Athens, were open to any Greek speaker of either sex and any status, slaves included, who was free of blood-guilt. The foundation charter is the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (seventh or sixth century), which ends with Demeter teaching her rites to the Eleusinian princes and the promise that whoever has seen them is olbios, blessed, while the uninitiated "has no share in such things" below (473–482). Pindar fr. 137 and Sophocles fr. 837 repeat the promise; Isocrates (Panegyricus 28) makes it the Athenian gift to mankind.

The calendar, reconstructed from inscriptions and scholia, is reasonably secure. The Lesser Mysteries at Agrai on the Ilissos, in Anthesterion (February–March), were a preliminary purification; the Greater fell in Boedromion (September–October). On the 14th the sacred objects (hiera) were carried from Eleusis to the Eleusinion in Athens. On the 15th, the agyrmos, the hierophant proclaimed the exclusion of the impure and of those "unintelligible of speech". On the 16th, "to the sea, initiates!", each candidate washed a piglet and himself. Sacrifices and a day of rest followed; on the 19th the great procession walked the Sacred Way with the statue of Iacchus, enduring ritual abuse at the Cephisus bridge (the gephyrismos), arriving by torchlight. The initiates then fasted and broke the fast with the kykeon, barley water flavoured with pennyroyal, as Demeter did in the Hymn (208–209). What happened in the Telesterion on the nights of the 20th and 21st was never to be spoken.

The Telesterion was a square hall, enlarged under Peisistratus and rebuilt under Pericles by Ictinus and others (Strabo 9.1.12; Plutarch, Pericles 13), seating thousands on stepped benches around a small inner chamber, the Anaktoron, which only the hierophant entered. He came from the Eumolpidae; the torch-bearer (dadouchos) and sacred herald from the Kerykes. The ancient grammarians divide the rite into things done, things said and things shown. Of the first, the Christian Clement (Protrepticus 2.21) quotes the password: "I fasted, I drank the kykeon, I took from the chest". Of the third, Hippolytus (Refutatio 5.8.39) says the hierophant displayed in silence a reaped ear of grain. Aristotle (fr. 15 Rose) said initiates were "not to learn but to experience"; Plutarch (fr. 178 Sandbach) compares dying to the initiate's passage from terror in the dark to light, meadows and voices. A second grade, epopteia, followed a year later.

Where sources disagree. Almost everything about the central night rests on hostile Christian writers of the second and third centuries AD, who may be reporting hearsay or conflating cults. Mylonas (1961) refused to use them; Clinton (1992) and Burkert use them cautiously. The suggestion of Wasson, Hofmann and Ruck (1978) that the kykeon contained ergot is unsupported by any ancient text and is rejected by most specialists.

In summer 415, on the eve of the Sicilian expedition and amid the mutilation of the Herms, informers accused Alcibiades and others of parodying the Mysteries in private houses (Thucydides 6.27–29, 6.53, 6.60–61; Andocides 1 On the Mysteries; Plutarch, Alcibiades 19–22). Alcibiades sailed, was condemned in absentia, had his property confiscated and his name cursed by the Eumolpidae and Kerykes; the stelae recording the sale of the condemned men's goods survive. When he returned in 408/7 he made amends by leading the procession overland under armed escort for the first time since the Spartan occupation of Decelea (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.4.20; Plutarch, Alcibiades 34). The cult survived Christian legislation until Alaric's Goths destroyed the sanctuary in 395/6 (Eunapius, Lives of the Sophists 7.3).

Orphism, the gold tablets and the Pythagoreans

"Orphism" names not a church but a body of poems attributed to Orpheus, a set of ritual experts who used them (Plato's orpheotelestai, Republic 364e), and a cluster of ideas about the soul: the body as a prison or tomb (Cratylus 400c), transmigration, purification by abstinence, and a judgement below. The Derveni papyrus, carbonised on a pyre near Thessaloniki around 330 BC and finally published in 2006, is an allegorical commentary on an Orphic theogony in which Zeus swallows the phallus of the sky-god and recreates the world; it proves that Orphic poetry and its exegesis were current in the fifth century.

The anthropogony most readers call Orphic runs: the Titans lure the infant Dionysus with toys, dismember and cook him; Zeus blasts them with lightning, and from the smoking remains humankind is born, carrying both a Titanic guilt and a Dionysiac spark. This explains Plato's reference to a "Titanic nature" (Laws 701c) and Pindar's "penalty for ancient grief" (fr. 133) that Persephone accepts before releasing souls.

Where sources disagree. The full myth, with humans made from the Titans' ashes, is first stated by Olympiodorus in the sixth century AD (On the Phaedo 1.3). Edmonds (1999, 2013) argues it is a Neoplatonic construction and that Pindar and Plato are being read backwards; Bernabé and Graf and Johnston (2007) hold that the Pelinna tablets and Pindar fr. 133 presuppose it. Genuinely open.

The gold tablets, some forty thin inscribed leaves placed in graves from the late fifth century BC to the second century AD, are the hard evidence. The Hipponion leaf (c. 400 BC) tells the dead to avoid the first spring, to say to the guardians "I am the child of Earth and starry Heaven", to drink from the lake of Memory, and to walk the road that "other mystai and bacchoi" walk. The Pelinna ivy leaves (late fourth century) say "tell Persephone that Bacchios himself has freed you" and "a bull you leapt into milk". Zuntz (1971) denied the tablets were Orphic at all; the Pelinna finds, naming Bacchus, and the Olbia bone plaques of the fifth century, which scratch "life death life" and "Dio(nysus) Orphikoi", have turned most scholars towards a Bacchic-Orphic milieu.

The Pythagorean overlap was noticed early. Herodotus 2.81 says that the rule against burial in wool is shared by "the so-called Orphic and Bacchic" rites, "which are really Egyptian and Pythagorean", and Ion of Chios claimed Pythagoras wrote poems under Orpheus's name. Both traditions taught transmigration, vegetarianism and ritual purity; Burkert (1972) treated Pythagoras as a shamanic figure in an Orphic world, while the Pythagorean political brotherhoods of Croton and the mathematical tradition belong elsewhere.

Dionysiac mysteries and maenadism

Ritual maenadism was a real institution, but a regulated one. Women's thiasoi left the city in alternate winters for oreibasia, dancing on the mountain, at Thebes, Delphi (the Thyiades; Plutarch, Mulierum Virtutes 249e–f) and elsewhere. A Milesian inscription of 276/5 BC (LSAM 48) has the public priestess of Dionysus licensing private initiations and reserving the right to throw in the omophagion, the raw-meat offering; a Magnesian inscription (I.Magnesia 215) records the city importing three maenads from Thebes, "of the race of Ino", on Delphic instruction to found three thiasoi. Henrichs (1978) used such texts to show that historical maenads were respectable citizen women performing a periodic rite, not hysterics; Dodds (1951) had taken ecstasy more literally.

Euripides' Bacchae (405 BC) gives the fullest literary picture and the greatest risk of confusion. Its chorus of Asian Bacchants describes genuine ritual: fawnskins, thyrsus, ivy, the mountain dances, "the joy of raw-eaten flesh" (138–139), and the blessedness of one who "knows the rites of the gods" (73). The messengers report miracles of milk, wine and honey and the tearing of cattle (677–774, 1043–1152). But the Theban women on Cithaeron are not initiates; they are driven mad as punishment for denying the god's birth, and Agave's killing of Pentheus is the myth of resistance, not the content of a mystery. The play tells us what Athenians found plausible about Bacchic worship and nothing certain about any initiation.

Private Dionysiac mysteries with a promise for the afterlife are better attested than the maenadic rites. Plato already quotes "many carry the thyrsus, few are bacchoi" (Phaedo 69c). Ptolemy IV ordered everyone initiating into Dionysus in Egypt to register and deposit a sealed copy of their sacred text (BGU VI 1211). The Roman senate's suppression of the Bacchanalia in 186 BC (Livy 39.8–19; CIL I² 581) shows initiation groups spreading through Italy; the Villa of the Mysteries frieze at Pompeii and the Torre Nova inscription of Agrippinilla's four-hundred-member thiasos (IGUR 160) show the cult as a graded, prosperous, imperial-age association.

Samothrace and the Cabiri

The Great Gods of Samothrace were never securely named in public; Greeks called them Cabiri by analogy with the Cabirion of Thebes (Pausanias 9.25.5–10) and Lemnos, and a scholiast on Apollonius (1.917, citing Mnaseas) gives the secret names Axieros, Axiokersa, Axiokersos and Kasmilos, with Kasmilos equated to Hermes. Herodotus 2.51 says the Pelasgians taught the Samothracians the ithyphallic Hermes and that "whoever has been initiated knows what I mean". Diodorus 5.47 reports that the ritual retained a non-Greek language, confirmed by inscriptions in an unidentified pre-Greek tongue. Unlike Eleusis, both grades could be taken on one visit at any time of year, by anyone; initiates wore a purple sash and an iron ring, and were promised safety at sea (Aristophanes, Peace 277–278; Diodorus 4.43). A confession of one's worst deed to a priest is recorded in the story of the Spartan who answered that if he had done anything bad the gods already knew (Plutarch, Apophthegmata Laconica 217c–d). Philip II is said to have met Olympias at the initiation (Plutarch, Alexander 2.2), and the Macedonian and Ptolemaic kings endowed the sanctuary's great buildings. Cole (1984) and Dimitrova's 2008 edition of the initiate lists are the standard studies.

Isis, Cybele, Mithras: imports through a Greek filter

The three great cults of the Roman Empire were not "oriental religions" imported wholesale, as Cumont framed them; Burkert (1987) showed that each was remodelled on the Greek mystery pattern, voluntary, individual, graded and promising personal benefit, before it reached Rome.

Isis: Herodotus 2.59 already equated her with Demeter. Under the Ptolemies she acquired a Greek consort, Sarapis, a hellenised Osiris-Apis whose cult statue came from Sinope (Plutarch, De Iside 28; Tacitus, Histories 4.83–84), and Greek aretalogies in which she speaks in the first person: "I am Isis, mistress of every land" (the Cyme text). Egyptians were allowed a temple in Piraeus by 333/2 BC (IG II² 337), and the Delian Sarapeia date from the third century. Her mysteries proper, with an initiation modelled on death and rebirth, are known from Apuleius, Metamorphoses 11, where Lucius says he "approached the boundary of death" and returned.

Cybele, the Phrygian Mountain Mother, was in Greek cities from the sixth century, with the Metroon in the Athenian Agora housing the state archive; Herodotus 4.76 has Anacharsis killed for celebrating her rites learned at Cyzicus. The castrated Galli and the Attis myth (Catullus 63) were a later, Hellenistic and Roman development; Rome formally imported her from Pessinus in 204 BC through Pergamene mediation (Livy 29.10–14). Roller (1999) traces how a Greek iconography of the enthroned goddess with lions preceded Roman reception.

Mithras carries an Iranian name and nothing securely Iranian in cult. The earliest notice is Plutarch's Cilician pirates performing his rites (Pompey 24); the mithraea, the bull-slaying image and the seven grades (Corax, Nymphus, Miles, Leo, Perses, Heliodromus, Pater: Jerome, Epistles 107.2; the Felicissimus mosaic at Ostia) appear from the late first century AD. The Greek intermediaries are visible in Commagene, where Antiochus I worshipped Apollo-Mithras-Helios-Hermes, in the Greek treatises of Eubulus and Pallas that Porphyry used (De abstinentia 4.16; De antro nympharum 6), and in the cult's Hellenistic astrology (Beck 2006).

Where sources disagree. Cumont's Iranian derivation of Mithraism was abandoned after the 1970s, but no replacement commands consent: Gordon and Clauss see a new Roman creation under a Persian label; Beck reads the tauroctony as a star map; Merkelbach proposed a single founder in Rome. The dependence on Greek astrology and Greek mystery form is the one point agreed.

Self-test

  1. On which day of the month did Delphic consultations take place, and why were three months unavailable?
    Answer

    The seventh of each month, Apollo's birthday; in the three winter months Apollo was held to be away and Dionysus occupied the sanctuary.

  2. What was the purpose of sprinkling the sacrificial goat with cold water?
    Answer

    If it trembled, the day was propitious; if not, consultation was refused (Plutarch, De defectu 435b, 437a–b).

  3. State the two main objections to the ethylene version of the gas theory.
    Answer

    Measured concentrations were far below any pharmacological threshold, and the adyton was not a sealed space; alternative proposals favour methane and carbon dioxide or doubt the pneuma mattered at all.

  4. Which three Herodotean responses did Croesus misread, and how did the Pythia defend herself?
    Answer

    The "great empire" he would destroy (his own), the "mule" king of the Medes (Cyrus, half Median), and the earlier test oracle; she replied that the god had spoken truly and Croesus had failed to ask follow-up questions (1.91).

  5. What did the Amphictyonic oath forbid, and who quotes it?
    Answer

    Destroying any Amphictyonic city or cutting off its running water; Aeschines 2.115.

  6. Why is Robertson's view of the First Sacred War significant?
    Answer

    He argued it was invented in the fourth century as a precedent for the Third, since no fifth-century author mentions it.

  7. What makes the Dodona lead tablets uniquely valuable?
    Answer

    They preserve thousands of actual questions from ordinary enquirers, showing the everyday business of an oracle rather than the literary set-pieces.

  8. Name the two Eleusinian priestly families and the offices each supplied.
    Answer

    The Eumolpidae supplied the hierophant; the Kerykes supplied the dadouchos (torch-bearer) and the sacred herald.

  9. Why does the Hipponion tablet matter for the "Orphic or Bacchic" debate?
    Answer

    It names the fellow travellers on the sacred road as mystai and bacchoi, tying the afterlife instructions to Dionysiac initiation, which undercut Zuntz's denial that the tablets were Orphic.

  10. In what sense is Mithraism "Greek-mediated"?
    Answer

    Its form is that of a Greek mystery cult, its astrology is Hellenistic, its first attested worshippers are in Greek-speaking Cilicia and Commagene, and its theology survives through Greek writers used by Porphyry; nothing securely Iranian survives in the cult.

Carry forward

  1. Greek oracles were institutions embedded in politics: Delphi's authority depended on the Amphictyony, on priority rights sold to cities, and on a reputation that Herodotus shows could be bought.
  2. Mystery cults were optional additions to civic religion, not rival religions: the same person could be a Spartan king, an Eleusinian initiate and a Samothracian ring-wearer, and the promise was personal benefit, not doctrine.
  3. Most of what we "know" about secret rites comes from hostile, late or literary witnesses; the inscriptions, tablets and papyri are the control, and where they are silent the honest answer is "uncertain".

Festivals and the games

The crown games and their cycleFounding mythsThe programme of eventsRules, truce, judges, nudityPrizes, rewards at home, and famous athletesWomen: exclusion and the HeraiaOlympia as a site, and Pindar's odeThe Athenian festival yearSpartan festivalsHellenistic and Roman afterlifeSelf-testCarry forward

The crown games and their cycle

Four festivals stood above all others because their only prize was a wreath: the stephanitic or crown games, together called the periodos (circuit). An athlete who won all four was a periodonikes. Olympia belonged to Zeus and gave a wreath of wild olive cut from the sacred tree behind his temple; Delphi's Pythian Games belonged to Apollo and gave bay laurel; the Isthmian Games near Corinth belonged to Poseidon and gave pine (dry wild celery for a period in the classical age, according to Plutarch, Table Talk 5.3); Nemea in the Argolid belonged to Zeus and gave fresh wild celery.

The cycle ran on a four-year frame, the Olympiad, which Greek historians from the late fourth century used as a common chronology. Olympia fell in year one, at the second full moon after the summer solstice; Nemea and Isthmia were biennial, held in years two and four (Isthmia in spring, Nemea in summer); the Pythian Games fell in late summer of year three. A serious competitor could therefore attend a crown festival every year and never clash.

FestivalGodCrownTraditional foundationPlace in Olympiad
OlympiaZeusWild olive776 BCYear 1, high summer
Pythia (Delphi)ApolloLaurel586 or 582 BCYear 3, late summer
Isthmia (Corinth)PoseidonPine (later celery, then pine)582/581 BCYears 2 and 4, spring
NemeaZeusWild celery573 BCYears 2 and 4, summer
Where sources disagree. The date 776 BC rests on the victor list compiled by Hippias of Elis around 400 BC, which Plutarch (Numa 1) already distrusted. Pausanias (5.8.6) says the stadion alone was run for the first thirteen Olympiads, which looks like back-projection to fill a gap. Excavation shows cult activity at Olympia from the eleventh century and a surge of dedications around 700, so most scholars now treat 776 as a rounded convention rather than a recorded event; some would lower the real start of regular games to c. 700.

Founding myths

Each site told more than one story. For Olympia, Pindar gives two in his own odes. Olympian 1 tells how Pelops won Hippodamia by beating her father Oenomaus in a chariot race, with horses from Poseidon; the Pelopion, a Bronze Age tumulus inside the Altis, was his tomb, and the games his memorial. Olympian 10 says instead that Heracles founded the festival and measured out the Altis after sacking Augeas of Elis. Pausanias (5.7.6–5.8.5) stacks up further layers: Cronus and Zeus wrestled there, the Idaean Heracles from Crete raced his brothers, and Iphitus of Elis revived lapsed games with the Spartan Lycurgus. The ancients themselves noticed the tension; Pausanias simply records each tradition.

Delphi's games commemorated Apollo's killing of the serpent Python, and began as a musical contest of hymns to the god (Pausanias 10.7.2); Strabo (9.3.10) describes the nomos Pythikos, a flute piece imitating the fight. Athletics arrived with the reorganisation after the First Sacred War. The Isthmian Games were funeral games for Melicertes, the son of Ino who was carried ashore by a dolphin and worshipped as Palaemon; Plutarch (Theseus 25) adds that Theseus refounded them in honour of Poseidon. Nemea's games were funeral games too, for the infant Opheltes (renamed Archemorus, "beginner of doom"), killed by a snake while his nurse showed the Seven against Thebes a spring; Apollodorus, Library 3.6.4 and Bacchylides 9 tell it, and the judges at Nemea wore black in mourning. A rival Nemean story credited Heracles after the lion. The pattern matters: Greek athletics was understood as a rite of death and memory, as in the games for Patroclus in Iliad 23, not as recreation.

The programme of events

Pausanias (5.8.6–5.9.2) supplies the traditional dates at which each event entered the Olympic programme. The core was footraces: the stadion (one length of the track, about 192 m at Olympia); the diaulos (two lengths, turning at a post); and the dolichos, a long race of between seven and twenty-four lengths, the figure uncertain and perhaps varying by site. Runners started standing, toes in grooves cut into a stone sill, held by a rope gate, the hysplex, that dropped at the signal; a false start earned a whipping.

The pentathlon (from 708 BC) combined stadion, long jump with hand-weights (halteres), discus, javelin thrown with a leather thong (ankyle) and wrestling. How the winner was decided remains the classic problem of Greek sport: a victor in three events won outright, but the procedure when no one managed three is nowhere stated clearly. The combat events were wrestling (three falls to win, 708 BC), boxing (688 BC; thongs of oxhide round the knuckles, no rounds, no weight classes, fought until a man was knocked out or raised a finger), and pankration (648 BC), an all-in fight in which only biting and gouging were forbidden, and the Spartans supposedly allowed even those at home (Philostratus, Gymnasticus 11). The hoplitodromos, a diaulos run in helmet and shield (greaves until the fifth century), was added in 520 BC and closed the athletic programme.

The hippodrome events were the aristocrat's domain: the four-horse chariot (tethrippon, 680 BC, twelve laps), the ridden horse (keles, 648 BC), the two-horse chariot (408 BC), races for foals, and for a time a mule-cart race, dropped in 444 BC as undignified. Crucially, the owner won, not the driver or jockey, which is how women and tyrants could be Olympic victors without competing in person. Boys' events ran alongside the men's from 632 BC.

Rules, truce, judges, nudity

Olympia was run by Elis. The Hellanodikai ("judges of the Greeks"), originally one, then two, then nine, ten and twelve, were chosen by lot from the Eleans, wore purple and trained for ten months in a special building at Elis before each festival (Pausanias 5.9.4–6, 6.24.1). Competitors arrived at Elis a month early, trained under the judges' eyes, and were sorted into men and boys at the judges' discretion, since no birth certificates existed. At Olympia, athletes, fathers, brothers and trainers swore over a boar's flesh before the statue of Zeus Horkios ("of the oath") that they would do nothing wrong (Pausanias 5.24.9). Cheating was fined and the fines paid for bronze Zeuses, the Zanes, lining the way into the stadium; Pausanias (5.21.2–18) read their inscriptions and names the bribers, beginning with Eupolus of Thessaly in 388 BC. Whip-bearing stewards enforced order on the spot, and a Hellanodikes could be appealed against to the Elean council, but his verdict stood.

The sacred truce (ekecheiria, "holding of hands") was announced by heralds and covered a month, later perhaps three, around the festival. Pausanias (5.20.1) saw the text on a bronze discus in the Temple of Hera, attributed to Iphitus and Lycurgus. It did not stop Greek wars; it protected pilgrims travelling to and from Olympia and placed Elis itself under protection. The clearest case is Thucydides 5.49–50: in 420 BC the Eleans fined Sparta two thousand minae for attacking Lepreum during the truce and barred Spartans from the festival; a Spartan who entered a chariot under another name was whipped.

Where sources disagree. Who first competed naked? Pausanias (1.44.1) names Orsippus of Megara, whose loincloth fell off in the stadion of 720 BC; Dionysius of Halicarnassus (7.72.3) names the Spartan Acanthus in the same year; Thucydides (1.6) says simply that the Spartans introduced it, "not many years ago" in his terms. Homer's wrestlers wear a zoma (Iliad 23.683, 710). Modern explanations range from ritual (Sansone) to a marker of citizen status distinguishing Greek from barbarian (Bonfante); the vase evidence suggests nudity was normal by the sixth century, whatever the origin.

Prizes, rewards at home, and famous athletes

At the crown games the prize was the wreath, a palm branch and a ribbon of wool. The real return came at home. Solon's Athens reportedly paid an Olympic victor 500 drachmas and an Isthmian victor 100 (Plutarch, Solon 23); a fifth-century decree (IG I3 131) gave victors in the crown games free meals in the Prytaneion for life. Cities granted front seats at the theatre, tax exemptions, statues in the agora and at Olympia, and odes. Croton kept a stable of champions; Astylus, who switched his allegiance from Croton to Syracuse to please Hieron, had his statue at home torn down and his house turned into a prison (Pausanias 6.13.1). Xenophanes (fr. 2 West) complained that a sprinter received honours above a wise man who did the city more good. Many lesser festivals were chrematitic, giving cash or goods; the Panathenaic prize list of the 380s (IG II2 2311) gives a hundred amphorae of oil to the winning stadion runner, a small fortune.

Three victors became legends. Milo of Croton won the wrestling at Olympia six times between about 540 and 516 BC (five as a man), and once more at each of the other crown games; stories tell of him carrying his own statue into the Altis, eating twenty pounds of meat a day, and dying when a tree trunk he was splitting closed on his hands and wolves found him (Pausanias 6.14.5–8; Strabo 6.1.12). Theagenes of Thasos won Olympic boxing in 480 and pankration in 476 and claimed 1,300 or 1,400 crowns across the circuit; after his death an enemy flogged his statue nightly until it fell on him, the statue was tried for murder and thrown in the sea, and after a famine the Delphic oracle ordered it fished out and worshipped as a healer (Pausanias 6.11.2–9; Dio Chrysostom 31.95). Diagoras of Rhodes, boxing champion of 464 BC, was celebrated in Pindar's Olympian 7, which the Rhodians inscribed in gold letters in the temple of Athena at Lindos; his sons Damagetus and Acusilaus won on the same day in 448 and carried him round the stadium while the crowd called out that he should die now, having nothing greater to live for; his third son Dorieus was a periodonikes three times in pankration (Pausanias 6.7.1–7).

Women: exclusion and the Heraia

Married women were barred from the Olympic festival on pain of being thrown from Mount Typaeon (Pausanias 5.6.7); the one exception was the priestess of Demeter Chamyne, who sat on an altar opposite the judges (Pausanias 6.20.9). Pausanias adds that unmarried girls were not forbidden to watch, a detail many scholars accept with caution, since it stands alone. The tale of Diagoras's daughter Callipateira (or Pherenice), who entered disguised as a trainer to see her son Peisirodus win, was caught and acquitted because her father, brothers and son were all victors, is told to explain why trainers thereafter attended naked (Pausanias 5.6.7–8). Women could nonetheless win as owners: the Spartan princess Cynisca took the four-horse chariot in 396 and 392 BC and set up a bronze chariot and a boastful epigram in the Altis (Pausanias 3.8.1, 6.1.6).

The Heraia, a separate festival for Hera at Olympia, is known almost entirely from Pausanias 5.16.2–8. A college of Sixteen Women of Elis wove a robe for the goddess every four years and organised footraces for unmarried girls in three age classes, run on the Olympic track shortened by one sixth, with hair loose, a short chiton above the knee and the right shoulder bared. Winners received an olive crown and a share of the cow sacrificed to Hera, and could dedicate painted portraits. Foundation was credited to Hippodamia; the bronze "Spartan girl runner" statuettes may show the costume.

Where sources disagree. Whether the Heraia was a pre-marital initiation rite (Scanlon, following Calame on girls' choruses) or simply a cult occasion with a race attached is undecided; its date is also unknown, and we cannot say if it was held before or after the men's games or in a different year. Pausanias's Elis and its Sixteen Women are second-century AD realities; how far they describe archaic practice is uncertain.

Olympia as a site, and Pindar's ode

The sanctuary grew around the Altis, a walled grove beside the Alpheios and Cladeos with the conical ash altar of Zeus, built up from centuries of burnt thighbones, at its centre. The Temple of Hera (c. 600 BC) is the oldest monumental building. Libon's Temple of Zeus (c. 470–457), paid for from Elis's spoils over Pisa, received Phidias's gold and ivory Zeus around 430; Phidias's workshop, with his named cup, was found in 1958 under a Byzantine church. Treasuries of colonial cities lined the northern terrace; the Bouleuterion held the oath statue; the Prytaneion housed the victors' feast. The stadium was moved three times, ending in the mid fourth century outside the Altis to the east, holding perhaps 40,000 standing spectators on earth banks with a single stone seat for the Demeter priestess. The Leonidaion guest house, the Philippeion of Philip II, the Palaestra and Gymnasium for training, and the Echo Colonnade followed in the fourth and third centuries; the hippodrome, with its ingenious staggered starting gate described by Pausanias (6.20.10–14), was long thought lost under the Alpheios but was traced by geophysical survey in 2008.

The epinikion, the choral victory ode, is the literary monument of the games. Simonides, Pindar and Bacchylides wrote them for pay, to be sung at the victor's homecoming or the festival itself. Pindar's forty-five surviving odes are grouped by festival: fourteen Olympians, twelve Pythians, eleven Nemeans, eight Isthmians. The standard shape names the victor, city and event, pivots to a myth tied to the family or city, dispenses maxims on mortality and divine favour, and returns to praise. Olympian 1, for Hieron of Syracuse's horse Pherenicus in 476, opens with water as the best of elements and gold as the brightest, then retells and corrects the Pelops story. Pindar insists victory is a gift of the gods and that the ode preserves it against oblivion: "fame is the one thing that lasts" is a fair summary of his creed, not a quotation. Whether the odes were sung by a chorus or performed solo by a kitharodos is disputed (Lefkowitz argued for solo performance; Carey and Burnett defended the choral tradition), and the question is open.

The Athenian festival year

Athens kept about 120 festival days a year. The Panathenaia (28 Hekatombaion, Athena's birthday, roughly August) was celebrated annually and, from 566/565 BC, as the Great Panathenaia every fourth year with games open to all Greeks. The peplos, a saffron and purple robe showing the Gigantomachy, was begun nine months earlier at the Chalkeia by the Arrephoroi and woven by girls called ergastinai; it was carried in the procession from the Dipylon gate to the Acropolis, in the Hellenistic age hoisted as a sail on a ship-cart, and draped on the ancient olive-wood statue of Athena Polias. The procession, with knights, hoplites, metics carrying trays, maidens with baskets, elders with olive branches and a hundred cattle for the hecatomb, is widely identified with the Parthenon frieze, though Connelly has argued the frieze shows the sacrifice of Erechtheus's daughters instead, a thesis most scholars reject. Events unique to the festival included the apobates (leaping on and off a moving chariot in armour), the Pyrrhic war dance, the euandria (manly beauty), torch race, boat race, and rhapsodic recitation of Homer in sequence (pseudo-Plato, Hipparchus 228b). Prizes were Panathenaic amphorae of olive oil.

The City Dionysia (10–14 Elaphebolion, March) began with the escort of Dionysus Eleuthereus's statue from the Academy and ended with the dramatic contests: three tragedians each with three tragedies and a satyr play, five comedies, and ten dithyrambic choruses from the tribes, all funded by wealthy choregoi and judged by ten citizens drawn by lot. The Rural Dionysia in Poseideon and the Lenaia in Gamelion completed the dramatic calendar. The Anthesteria (11–13 Anthesterion, February) was the oldest Dionysiac festival: Pithoigia (jar-opening of the new wine), Choes (pitchers, a drinking contest, children's first taste of wine, the archon basileus's wife "married" to Dionysus in the Boukoleion; pseudo-Demosthenes 59.73–78), and Chytroi (pots of grain boiled for Hermes Chthonios and the dead). It was an unlucky day; doors were tarred and buckthorn chewed against ghosts, and the proverb "Out, Keres, the Anthesteria is over" sent the spirits away.

Women dominated three festivals. The Thesmophoria (11–13 Pyanepsion, October) was for married citizen women only: Anodos (ascent to the Thesmophorion), Nesteia (fasting on the ground, with ribald abuse), Kalligeneia (fair birth). Women called antletriai had earlier thrown piglets and dough models into pits and now brought up the rotted remains to mix with seed-corn (scholiast to Lucian, Dialogues of the Courtesans 2.1); men were excluded, which Aristophanes's Thesmophoriazusae exploits. The Arrephoria in Skirophorion sent two girls aged seven to eleven, chosen from noble families and resident on the Acropolis, down a natural stair at night carrying covered objects they must not see to the sanctuary of Aphrodite in the Gardens, bringing other objects back (Pausanias 1.27.3); the underground passage survives. The Adonia was a private, mid-summer women's rite with no state funding: women, respectable and hetairai alike, lamented Adonis on the rooftops, planted "gardens of Adonis" in pots that sprouted and withered, and carried effigies to burial; Aristophanes (Lysistrata 387–398) and Plutarch (Nicias 13, Alcibiades 18) link its laments to the launch of the Sicilian expedition in 415.

The Apatouria (Pyanepsion) belonged to the phratries, the hereditary brotherhoods through which citizenship was recognised. On Dorpia men feasted; on Anarrhysis they sacrificed to Zeus Phratrios and Athena Phratria; on Koureotis fathers presented infants (meion) and adolescents cutting their hair (koureion) and swore to their legitimacy. The name was explained by the apate, trick, by which the Athenian Melanthus killed the Boeotian Xanthus.

Spartan festivals

Sparta's three great Apolline festivals shaped its military calendar. The Carneia, in the month Karneios (August–September), honoured Apollo Karneios with a camp-like feast in nine tents and the staphylodromoi, youths who chased a man wreathed in wool; catching him was a good omen for the harvest. Herodotus (6.106, 7.206) reports the Carneia as the reason the Spartans arrived late at Marathon and sent only Leonidas's three hundred to Thermopylae. The Hyacinthia at Amyclae, early summer, mourned the youth Hyacinthus whom Apollo loved and accidentally killed, with a day of grief and no bread or garlands, then days of boys' lyre-songs, girls' processions in wicker carts, and a feast for citizens and slaves (Athenaeus 4.139d–f, quoting Polycrates); Xenophon (Hellenica 4.5.11) records Amyclaeans leaving an army mid-campaign to attend. The Gymnopaidiai, in high summer, were dances by choruses of naked boys and men in the agora, an endurance test in the heat (Plato, Laws 633c); Xenophon (Hellenica 6.4.16) describes the ephors receiving news of Leuctra during the men's chorus and letting it finish. At the sanctuary of Artemis Orthia the diamastigosis, flogging of boys at the altar, grew in Roman times into a spectacle with a stone theatre; the classical form was a cheese-stealing contest at the altar (Xenophon, Constitution of the Lacedaemonians 2.9; Pausanias 3.16.9–11).

Hellenistic and Roman afterlife

From the third century onwards new festivals multiplied, many declared isolympic or isopythian (equal in status) by decree: the Ptolemaia at Alexandria (279/278 BC), the Soteria at Delphi, the Nikephoria at Pergamum, and scores of civic games across Asia Minor. Athletes became professionals organised in guilds under the patronage of Heracles, with imperial charters by the second century AD; the four old games remained the summit of prestige. Rome absorbed rather than suppressed this culture. Sulla moved the Olympic Games of 80 BC to Rome (Appian, Civil Wars 1.99), leaving only the boys' stadion at Olympia. Tiberius and Germanicus won chariot victories as owners. Nero had the games of AD 65 postponed to 67 so that he could compete, added musical contests, fell from a ten-horse chariot and was crowned anyway; the Eleans later annulled his Olympiad (Suetonius, Nero 24; Pausanias 10.7.1 for Delphi). Augustus founded the Actia at Nicopolis and the Sebasta at Naples (AD 2); Domitian the Capitoline Games (AD 86). Herodes Atticus gave Olympia its first aqueduct and nymphaeum in the 150s, and Pausanias, who saw the site intact, remains the best guide.

The end was slow. The last victor in the literary record is the Armenian prince Varazdates, boxing champion in AD 369. Theodosius I's laws of 391–392 (Theodosian Code 16.10.10–12) banned sacrifice and pagan cult, and the chronicler Cedrenus, writing in the eleventh century, says the games ceased after the Olympiad of 393. A bronze plaque from Olympia, however, lists victors to 385, and the workshop of Phidias was still in use. Theodosius II's order of 426 to destroy pagan temples, the fires that gutted the Temple of Zeus, Christian conversion of the site and the earthquakes of 522 and 551 completed the ruin; the Alpheios and Cladeos buried it under metres of silt until 1875.

Where sources disagree. No ancient text records an edict abolishing the Olympic Games. Cedrenus's 393 date is late and inferential; the Theodosian laws forbid sacrifice, not athletics. Recent work on the Olympia inscriptions (Ebert, Sinn) suggests contests of some kind continued into the fifth century, perhaps without the sacrifice to Zeus, and that the Antioch "Olympics" ran until 520. Whether the games "ended in 393" is therefore a modern convenience, not a fact.

Self-test

  1. Name the four crown games with their god and wreath.
    Answer

    Olympia, Zeus, wild olive; Pythia at Delphi, Apollo, laurel; Isthmia, Poseidon, pine (celery for a time); Nemea, Zeus, wild celery.

  2. How did the four fit into one Olympiad?
    Answer

    Olympia in year one, Nemea and Isthmia in years two and four, Pythia in year three, so a crown festival every year.

  3. What two different foundation myths for Olympia does Pindar himself give?
    Answer

    Pelops's chariot victory over Oenomaus (Olympian 1) and Heracles's foundation after defeating Augeas (Olympian 10).

  4. What was the hoplitodromos, and when was it added?
    Answer

    A race, usually a diaulos, run in helmet and shield (originally greaves too); added in 520 BC and closing the athletic programme.

  5. Who actually received the victory in the chariot race, and why did that matter for women?
    Answer

    The owner, not the driver; so Cynisca of Sparta could be Olympic victor in 396 and 392 BC without being present.

  6. What were the Zanes?
    Answer

    Bronze statues of Zeus paid for by fines on cheating athletes, lining the way into the stadium, inscribed with warnings; Pausanias names the offenders.

  7. Give one concrete reward an Athenian Olympic victor received at home.
    Answer

    500 drachmas under Solon's law (Plutarch, Solon 23), or free meals for life in the Prytaneion (IG I3 131).

  8. Describe the Heraia races.
    Answer

    Footraces for unmarried girls in three age groups on a track shortened by one sixth, hair loose, short chiton, right shoulder bare; olive crown and a share of the cow; organised by the Sixteen Women of Elis (Pausanias 5.16).

  9. What happened on the three days of the Thesmophoria, and who attended?
    Answer

    Anodos (ascent), Nesteia (fasting), Kalligeneia (fair birth); married citizen women only, with pig remains retrieved from pits to mix with seed-corn.

  10. Why is "the Olympics ended in 393" an oversimplification?
    Answer

    No edict abolishing the games survives; Theodosius banned sacrifice, Cedrenus's 393 date is late inference, and inscriptions and site evidence suggest contests continued into the fifth century.

Carry forward

  1. Greek athletics was cult first: every crown festival was a sacrifice to a god, grounded in a funeral or heroic myth, and the truce, nudity and oath belong to ritual as much as to sport.
  2. The wreath was symbolic but the system was not: cities, tyrants and families converted victory into cash, meals, statues and odes, so games are a window on how Greek elites competed for honour.
  3. Festivals organised time and membership: the Athenian calendar sorted citizens by sex, age and phratry, Sparta's shaped its wars, and the Olympiad became the Greeks' shared clock.

The Homeric psyche and the shadow-world

In Homer the psyche is not a soul in the later sense but the breath-life that leaves the body through mouth or wound and flies to Hades "bewailing its fate" (Iliad 16.856, 22.362). There it is an eidolon, an image keeping the dead person's shape but without strength or, usually, mind. Achilles cannot embrace the ghost of Patroclus; it slips through his arms "like smoke" (Iliad 23.99–101). The living person was a compound of body and several life-forces (thymos, menos, noos); what survives is the least of them.

Odyssey 11, the Nekyia, is the fullest picture. Odysseus does not descend; at the world's edge he digs a pit and lets sheep's blood run into it, and the shades must drink before they can speak. Teiresias alone keeps his wits by a gift of Persephone (11.90–96). Anticleia explains that once the fire has consumed flesh and bone the psyche "flutters away like a dream" (11.218–222). Achilles delivers the famous verdict that he would rather be a hired labourer on earth than king over all the dead (11.488–491). There is no judgement of ordinary lives; Tityus, Tantalus and Sisyphus (11.576–600) are mythical offenders against the gods, and Minos "giving judgements among the dead" settles disputes rather than assigning fates. Elysium is reserved for a few favoured heroes (Odyssey 4.561–569; Hesiod, Works and Days 167–173).

Where sources disagree. Scholars since the Alexandrians have treated the catalogue of heroines (225–332) and the vision of Minos, the great sinners and Heracles (565–627) as interpolated, since they sit oddly with the pit-side framing where shades come to Odysseus. Others defend the book's unity. The point matters because the "sinners" passage is the main evidence for any Homeric posthumous punishment.

Funeral rites from Homer to Solon

The ritual sequence barely changed in a thousand years, from the funerals of Patroclus and Hector (Iliad 23–24) to Lucian.

Prothesis

Women of the family washed, anointed and dressed the body and laid it on a bier inside the house, feet towards the door; an obol for Charon, unknown to Homer, appears from the fifth century. Funerary plaques and loutrophoroi show the standard tableau: women around the bier, hands to heads, men approaching with right arm raised in salute.

Ekphora

Before dawn the body was carried in procession to the cemetery outside the walls. Solon's legislation (Plutarch, Solon 21; Demosthenes 43.62) required the ekphora before sunrise, limited the women attending to close kin over sixty, forbade laceration of the flesh and set lamentation for persons outside the family, and capped grave goods at three garments and a modest offering of food and drink. Similar laws are attested at Delphi (the Labyad inscription), Ioulis on Keos (IG XII 5.593) and Gambreion. Their aim is debated: curbing aristocratic display, or disciplining the ritual power of women.

Cremation and inhumation

Homer knows only cremation; the pyre of Patroclus with its slaughtered horses, dogs and twelve Trojans (Iliad 23.166–177) exaggerates Iron-Age practice. Archaeologically the two rites alternate and coexist at Athens from the Protogeometric period to the Classical cemetery, with no demonstrable doctrinal difference; the choice was family tradition, cost and fashion. Children were almost always inhumed, often in jars.

Grave goods and the lekythos

Geometric graves held weapons and the great Dipylon amphorae as markers; after Solon and under the democracy goods shrink to pottery, strigils and mirrors. The characteristic fifth-century vessel is the white-ground lekythos, an oil flask painted with the tomb visit, the prothesis, Charon's boat or Hermes conducting the psyche. Many have a false inner cup so that a little oil appeared to fill the vase, a telling detail about the economy of grief.

Mourning, women and the politics of lament

Lament was women's work and women's power. The goos was the improvised wail of kin, the threnos a composed song, sometimes by hired professionals. Andromache, Hecuba and Helen each lead a lament over Hector (Iliad 24.723–776) in antiphony with the crowd. Tearing the hair and scratching the cheeks until they bled are the gestures the law tried to forbid. Offerings at the tomb on the third, ninth and thirtieth days and at the annual Genesia were also women's responsibility; the lekythoi show them bringing ribbons and cakes to the stele.

Tragedy stages this power and its danger: Antigone, Electra at Agamemnon's tomb in the Choephoroi, the Trojan women. Modern scholarship (Alexiou, Holst-Warhaft, Loraux) reads the sumptuary laws and the public funeral as a transfer of death from household to state: the funeral oration, delivered by a man over anonymous bones, replaces the women's goos over an individual body.

The Kerameikos and the grave stelai

The Kerameikos, the potters' quarter outside the Dipylon and Sacred Gates, was Athens' principal cemetery from the Submycenaean period. Along the road to the Academy lay the demosion sema, where each year's war dead were laid in common tombs after the funeral described by Thucydides (2.34); the Marathon dead were exceptionally buried on the battlefield.

Archaic Attica produced tall stelai crowned with sphinxes or palmettes and carved with the standing youth or girl, with name, patronymic and sometimes an epigram ("stand and mourn at the tomb of dead Kroisos"). Stelai almost vanish between about 500 and 430 and return as the family-group relief: Hegeso with her maid, Dexileos spearing a fallen enemy (dated by inscription to 394/3), Ampharete with her grandchild. They show the dead and living together, the handshake (dexiosis) disputed as farewell or reunion, and almost nothing of Hades. In 317 Demetrius of Phalerum restricted monuments to a small column or slab, and the series ends.

Where sources disagree. The gap in Attic grave reliefs has been attributed to a sumptuary law "some time after Solon" (Cicero, De legibus 2.64), to a shift of patronage towards public monuments, or to accidents of survival. No Athenian text records such a law; its date and existence are uncertain.

The evolution of afterlife belief

From Homer to the mysteries

Homer's grey democracy of shades was one view among several. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (480–482) already declares the uninitiated to have "no share of such good when dead"; Eleusis promised a better lot below for ritual purity, not moral conduct. Aristophanes' initiates in the Frogs (440–459) dance in sunlit meadows while the impious lie in mud, a pattern repeated in Plato and the gold leaves.

The Orphic-Bacchic gold tablets, from Hipponion (c. 400 BC) to Thessaly and Crete, instruct the dead: avoid the first spring, drink from the lake of Memory, say "I am the child of Earth and starry Heaven"; one from Pelinna announces "Tell Persephone that Bacchios himself freed you". Here the soul is divine, the body a tomb (soma sema, Plato, Cratylus 400c), and salvation comes by initiation. Transmigration, attributed to Pythagoras (Xenophanes fr. 7) and Empedocles (fr. 115, 117), belongs to the same current.

Pindar's Second Olympian

Pindar, writing in 476 for Theron of Acragas in Pythagorean Sicily, gives the earliest worked-out moral afterlife in mainstream poetry (Olympian 2.56–80). The dead are judged; the wicked suffer "toil not to be looked upon"; the good live without tears where the sun shines by night; those who thrice in each world have kept their souls from injustice travel the road of Zeus to the tower of Cronus and the Isle of the Blessed, with Peleus, Cadmus and Achilles. Fragment 133 adds rebirth as kings and sages for souls who have paid for "ancient grief". Other odes speak in Homeric terms; Pindar tailors eschatology to patron.

Plato's eschatological myths

Plato ends three dialogues with a judgement myth, each time calling it a mythos whose detail he will not defend while its lesson is "worth the risk" (Phaedo 114d). In the Gorgias (523a–527a) Zeus moves judgement to after death and strips the dead of their bodies so scarred souls are seen naked; the incurable hang in Tartarus as examples. In the Phaedo (107d–115a) each soul is led by its daimon to judgement, the true earth and its four rivers are mapped, and the purified philosopher lives bodiless. In the Republic (614b–621d) Er the Pamphylian revives on the pyre and reports the two openings, the thousand-year journey, the spindle of Necessity, the lottery of lives and the river of Forgetting. The choice of lives, with the former Odysseus picking a private man's life, turns eschatology into ethics.

The Epicurean denial

Epicurus cut the knot: the soul is atoms dispersed at death, and "what is dissolved has no sensation, and what has no sensation is nothing to us" (Principal Doctrines 2; Letter to Menoeceus 124–127). Fear of death is the chief disturbance of life. Lucretius' third book reads the Acheron of myth as the torment of the living: Tantalus is the man paralysed by fear, Sisyphus the office-seeker. The epitaph non fui, fui, non sum, non curo is found across the Empire.

Where sources disagree. How widespread were such beliefs? Rohde and Dodds saw a "Puritan" counter-religion of the soul from the sixth century; Burkert and Parker stress that the gold leaves are a few dozen among hundreds of thousands of graves and that most Athenians held vague, inconsistent expectations. Whether "Orphism" was ever a movement or only a label for texts and rites is contested.

Hero cult

A heros in cult is a dead mortal who retains power to help or harm from the grave. Ordinary dead receive nomima, the customary offerings; a hero receives priests, festivals and sacrifice, and his power is local, tied to the bones. The phenomenon appears archaeologically in the eighth century, when offerings begin at Mycenaean tombs (Menidi, Prosymna, Mycenae).

Ritual: enagismata and the heroic feast

The traditional distinction is between thysia to Olympians (throat up, meat shared at a raised altar) and enagismata to heroes and the dead (throat down into a pit or low hearth, blood poured into the earth, carcass burned whole, libations of water, milk, honey and wine). Pausanias 2.10.1 describes Heracles at Sicyon receiving part as hero and part as god; Herodotus 2.44 says the same of Thasos. Banquet reliefs show the hero reclining, cup in hand, with snake, horse and armour.

Where sources disagree. Gunnel Ekroth (2002) concluded that most Archaic and Classical hero sacrifice was ordinary thysia with dining, and enagismata the exception. The sharp Olympian/chthonian dichotomy inherited from Rohde and Nilsson is now widely regarded as overdrawn.

Who became a hero

Founders (oikistai) were buried in the agora of their colonies with annual rites, as Battus at Cyrene (Pindar, Pythian 5.93–95). Lawgivers and poets: Lycurgus had a shrine at Sparta (Herodotus 1.66), Archilochus a heroon on Paros, Sophocles cult as Dexion. Athletes: Cleomedes of Astypalaea vanished in a chest after killing an opponent and Delphi called him "the last of the heroes" (Pausanias 6.9.6–8); the statue of Theagenes of Thasos was tried for murder, drowned, recovered and given healing cult (Pausanias 6.11.2–9). The common factor is extraordinary power, not goodness; the violent and the murdered became heroes as readily as the virtuous.

The war dead

The Athenian war dead received annual games (Lysias 2.80 calls them "immortal honours"), and the Marathon fallen had cult as heroes into the second century AD (Pausanias 1.32.4, who adds that horses and fighting are heard there by night). Pericles' "most conspicuous grave, not that in which they lie" (Thucydides 2.43) substitutes civic memory for chthonian power.

Brasidas at Amphipolis

Thucydides 5.11 is the clearest text on heroisation in historical time. After Brasidas died defending Amphipolis in 422, the citizens buried him inside the city before the agora, "enclosed his tomb, and sacrifice to him as a hero, with games and yearly offerings". They demolished the buildings of Hagnon, the Athenian founder, and transferred his honours to Brasidas as "saviour". Heroisation is a political act: a new founder replaces the old, and the tomb sits inside the walls against the normal exclusion of the dead.

Bones as state relics

Herodotus 1.67–68: Sparta, failing against Tegea, was told by Delphi to fetch the bones of Orestes from "where two winds blow"; Lichas found a seven-cubit coffin in a smith's yard, and after the transfer Sparta prevailed. Size is the point: heroes were larger than men, and fossil or Bronze-Age bones were read accordingly. Cimon brought Theseus' bones from Scyros in 476/5 to the Theseion, an asylum for fugitive slaves (Plutarch, Theseus 36; Cimon 8); Tisamenus went from Helice to Sparta (Pausanias 7.1.8). The hero protects where his bones lie, so possessing them is possessing him.

Hero cult and the heroes of myth

The relation of cult heroes to epic heroes is the central problem. Rohde and Farnell saw faded gods or ancestor worship; Coldstream argued the eighth-century tomb cults were prompted by the spread of epic; Snodgrass and Antonaccio decoupled them, reading tomb cult as land claims by new communities that only later acquired epic names. Homer himself barely knows hero cult (Erechtheus, Iliad 2.550–551, is the sole clear case). By the Classical period the categories interpenetrate: Ajax is a tribal eponym at Athens, Achilles has cult at Troy and on the Black Sea, the Seven against Thebes at Eleusis, and Delphi chose the ten Cleisthenic tribal heroes from a hundred candidates (Aristotle, Constitution of Athens 21.6).

Ghosts and the restless dead

The unburied (ataphoi), the violently killed (biaiothanatoi), the untimely dead (aoroi) and the unmarried were held to wander, dangerous or useful. Patroclus demands burial so he may pass the gates of Hades (Iliad 23.71–74); Elpenor is the first shade Odysseus meets because unburied (Odyssey 11.51–80). Clytaemnestra's ghost rouses the Furies (Aeschylus, Eumenides 94–139); Darius is raised by libation (Persians 619–842); Polydorus opens Euripides' Hecuba. Pausanias 6.6.7–11 tells of the Hero of Temesa, a stoned sailor of Odysseus whose ghost demanded a maiden yearly until the boxer Euthymus expelled him.

Lead curse tablets, pierced with nails and deposited in graves of the untimely dead from the fifth century on, use them as couriers to Hermes and Persephone. Oracles of the dead at Ephyra, Tainaron, Heraclea Pontica and Avernus are attested by Herodotus 5.92, where Periander's wife Melissa complains of cold because her clothes were not burned with her. Psychagogoi ("soul-leaders", the title of an Aeschylus play) and the Attic Anthesteria, which ended with "Out of doors, Keres, the Anthesteria is over", managed the annual return. Plato, Phaedo 81c–d, rationalises ghosts as souls still weighted with body, flitting about tombs.

Where sources disagree. The Anthesteria formula survives in late lexica with the variant "Kares" (Carian slaves) for "Keres" (spirits); whether the festival originally involved the dead is uncertain. Johnston's picture of rising Classical anxiety about the restless dead, against an unanxious Homer, is questioned by those who note how little ghost-lore Athenian prose preserves.

The Roman-period shift to individual immortality

Under the Empire the centre of gravity moves to the salvation of the individual soul. Platonism (Plutarch, On the Delays of Divine Vengeance 563b–568a; Plotinus) makes astral immortality the educated default. Isis promises Lucius worship after death in the Elysian fields (Apuleius, Metamorphoses 11.6); Dionysiac sarcophagi carry the god's triumph; Mithras and Christianity compete. Epitaphs assert "I did not die but went to the gods", place the soul in the ether and the body in earth, and in Boeotia and Thessaly heros becomes an honorific for any dead man. Sarcophagi show Endymion, Alcestis and Persephone, myths of transit rather than judgement; Herodes Atticus heroised Regilla and his pupils, Hadrian deified Antinous.

The old apparatus persisted. Eleusis ran until Alaric; Pausanias describes hero cult as living practice; Lucian's On Mourning satirises the same prothesis, wailing and obol that Solon regulated. But the questions Plato asked in myth became ones a cult or philosophy had to answer plainly, and when Christianity made personal judgement and resurrection the common creed it built on four centuries of Greek expectation that death was a passage of the self, not the dissolution of a compound into breath, bone and shadow.

Where sources disagree. MacMullen and others warn that the "spiritualisation" of Roman epitaphs is a trend among the literate and wealthy; Epicurean formulae persist alongside astral ones, and whether belief or fashion changed cannot be settled from the stones alone.

Self-test

  1. In what state does Homer depict the psyche after death, and how does Teiresias differ from the other shades in Odyssey 11?
    Answer

    It is a witless image (eidolon) without strength or memory, needing to drink sacrificial blood to speak; Teiresias alone keeps his mind intact by Persephone's gift (11.90–96).

  2. Name the two stages of the Greek funeral before burial and say what Solon's laws regulated about each.
    Answer

    Prothesis (laying-out in the house) and ekphora (procession to the grave). Solon restricted the women attending to close kin over sixty, required the ekphora before sunrise, forbade self-laceration and lament for non-kin, and limited grave goods (Plutarch, Solon 21; Demosthenes 43.62).

  3. What is a white-ground lekythos and what tells us about its function?
    Answer

    A fifth-century Attic oil flask painted with funerary scenes (tomb visits, Charon, Hermes) and deposited at graves; many have a false inner cup so a small amount of oil appears to fill it.

  4. What was the demosion sema, and which Athenian dead were the exception to burial there?
    Answer

    The public cemetery along the road from the Kerameikos to the Academy where each year's war dead were buried collectively after the state funeral (Thucydides 2.34). The Marathon dead were buried on the battlefield.

  5. What does Pindar's Second Olympian say happens to souls who have thrice kept themselves from injustice?
    Answer

    They travel the road of Zeus to the tower of Cronus on the Isle of the Blessed, where Peleus, Cadmus and Achilles dwell (Olympian 2.68–80).

  6. In which dialogue does Zeus move judgement to after death so that souls are judged naked, and why?
    Answer

    The Gorgias (523a–524a): living judges were deceived by fine bodies, clothes and witnesses, so Zeus had the dead judged stripped of their bodies.

  7. State the Epicurean argument that death is nothing to us.
    Answer

    The soul is atomic and dispersed at death; what is dissolved has no sensation; what has no sensation is nothing to us (Principal Doctrines 2; Letter to Menoeceus 124–127).

  8. What did the Amphipolitans do after Brasidas died in 422, according to Thucydides 5.11?
    Answer

    Buried him inside the city in front of the agora, enclosed the tomb, sacrificed to him as a hero with games and annual offerings, and transferred to him the founder's honours of the Athenian Hagnon, whose buildings they demolished.

  9. Why did Sparta bring the bones of Orestes from Tegea, and how was his tomb identified?
    Answer

    Delphi told them they would defeat Tegea once they possessed the bones. Lichas identified the spot as a smith's yard ("where two winds blow", the bellows) and found a seven-cubit coffin (Herodotus 1.67–68).

  10. Which categories of dead were believed most likely to become restless ghosts?
    Answer

    The unburied (ataphoi), the violently killed (biaiothanatoi), the untimely dead (aoroi) and the unmarried; curse tablets were deposited in their graves to use them as couriers.

Carry forward

  1. Greek afterlife belief was plural and unsystematic: Homer's witless shades, the initiates' meadow, Pindaric and Platonic judgement and Epicurean dissolution all coexisted, and the same person could hold several at once. Later modules on tragedy, philosophy and early Christianity presuppose this plurality.
  2. Hero cult is worship of a powerful dead person tied to the physical location of the bones; it is a political instrument (founders, bone-transfers, Brasidas) and it is the hinge between the myths of the heroic age and the historical cities that claimed them.
  3. Death ritual was a contest over who controls the dead: the household and its women against the city and its men, visible in Solon's laws, the public funeral and tragedy. Keep this frame when reading Antigone and the funeral oration.
