The oikos and the kyrios

The unit of Greek social life was not the individual but the oikos: household understood as people, land, house, slaves and cult together. Aristotle builds the polis out of households (Politics 1.2, 1252a–1253b) and analyses the household as three relations of rule: master over slave, husband over wife, father over children (1.3, 1253b). The man at the top of all three is the kyrios. Every Athenian woman had one for life: father, then husband, then son or nearest male kin. He gave her in marriage, represented her in court and controlled her property; she could not contract for more than a medimnos of barley (Isaeus 10.10), about a week's food for a family.

The ideology is set out in Xenophon's Oeconomicus 7–10, where Ischomachus trains his wife, married before fifteen (7.5), to run the interior: stores, slaves, textiles. The god made the man for outdoors and the woman for indoors (7.22–30). A wife who ran a large household had real authority within it, but delegated authority, and the text is prescriptive, not descriptive.

Sparta inverts this. Men ate in common messes and lived in barracks until thirty; wives ran the estates, and Aristotle complains (Politics 2.9, 1269b–1270a) that Spartan women were licentious, held nearly two-fifths of the land and had ruined the state. Gorgo's reply that Spartan women rule their men "because we alone give birth to men" (Plutarch, Lycurgus 14.4) is a later anecdote, but it captures the Athenian view that Sparta had the household the wrong way up.

Where sources disagree. Sparta reaches us through Plutarch's Lycurgus (c. AD 100), Xenophon's admiring Constitution of the Lacedaemonians and Aristotle's hostile Politics 2.9. Since Ollier's Le mirage spartiate (1933) much of it is read as idealising construction. Hodkinson (Property and Wealth in Classical Sparta, 2000) holds that land was privately and unequally owned from the start, against the Plutarchan equal lots; Cartledge allows more of an archaic reform. Every "Spartan custom" below is contested.

Marriage, dowry, the epikleros, divorce

Athenian marriage was a transaction between two men. The kyrios pledged the woman in a betrothal (engye) before witnesses; Herodotus 6.130 gives the formula as Cleisthenes of Sicyon hands Agariste to Megacles "according to the laws of Athens". The gamos was the procession and handing over, not a religious rite. Girls married at fourteen or fifteen, men near thirty (Hesiod, Works and Days 695–698; Aristotle, Politics 7.16, 1335a recommends eighteen and thirty-seven). After Pericles' citizenship law of 451/0 (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 26.4) only children of two Athenians were citizens. Demosthenes 59 (Against Neaera) 122 states the purposes:

hetairai for pleasure, concubines for daily care, wives to bear legitimate children

The dowry (proix) went with the bride but never became the husband's outright. If the marriage ended he returned it or paid 18 per cent interest (Demosthenes 59.52; Isaeus 3.36): a large dowry made divorce expensive and gave her family leverage. Divorce itself was easy in law. A husband dismissed his wife with her dowry (apopempsis); a wife could leave by registering with the archon (apoleipsis), though Alcibiades dragging Hipparete home across the agora when she tried (Plutarch, Alcibiades 8) shows the cost. Adultery with a citizen wife was graver than rape because it threatened legitimacy: Lysias 1 defends Euphiletus for killing his wife's lover in the act, and the law then compelled divorce.

The epikleros shows the oikos outranking the woman. A daughter without brothers did not inherit; she went with the estate to the nearest male kinsman, who could claim her through the archon even if she or he was already married (Isaeus 3 and 10; Demosthenes 43). Her son would inherit as the dead man's heir and the line was repaired. Plutarch (Solon 20.2) records a rule that her husband must have intercourse with her three times a month, which shows the point. Sparta's patrouchos was adjudicated by the kings (Herodotus 6.57), but Spartan women could inherit in their own right. Spartan marriage by mock capture, with the bride's head shaved (Plutarch, Lycurgus 15), and the lending of wives to beget children for another man (Xenophon, Constitution of the Lacedaemonians 1.7–9) scandalised Athenians; moderns read them as eugenic policy or as misunderstood archaic survivals.

Women: law, practice, religion and voice

Pericles' funeral oration tells widows that a woman's glory is to be least talked of among men (Thucydides 2.45.2). Orators do not name respectable women; the ideal house had women's quarters, upstairs in Euphiletus' case (Lysias 1.9); women attended no symposia or assemblies, and probably not the theatre.

Two bodies of evidence cut against this. Poorer women worked: Euxitheus' mother sold ribbons in the agora and wet-nursed, which his enemies used against his citizenship (Demosthenes 57.30–35); Aristophanes is full of bread-sellers and garland-makers; grave stelai honour nurses and wool-workers (Brock, "The Labour of Women in Classical Athens", 1994). Seclusion was an ideal the leisured could afford. And religion was a genuine female public sphere: the priestess of Athena Polias was the city's most important religious officer; girls served as arrhephoroi and ran at Brauron; married women alone held the Thesmophoria for three days with their own officers. Connelly (Portrait of a Priestess, 2007) argues priesthoods gave women public honour and legal capacities denied them elsewhere.

Euripides lets a woman state the grievance. Medea (Medea 230–251) tells the Corinthian women they are the most wretched of creatures: they buy a master over their bodies with a dowry, cannot refuse him, cannot divorce without disgrace, and when a man is bored at home he goes out, while a woman must look to one soul alone. A man wrote it for men, which shows the audience knew the cost.

The hetaira, "companion", could attend the symposium, talk and be named because she was not a citizen wife. Aspasia of Miletus, Pericles' partner, was mocked in comedy as a brothel-keeper, credited by Plato (Menexenus 235e–236b) with teaching Socrates rhetoric, and reportedly tried for impiety (Plutarch, Pericles 24, 32); her son by Pericles was made a citizen by special decree after the plague.

Where sources disagree. Gomme (1925) argued from tragedy and vases that Athenian women were not oppressed; Pomeroy (Goddesses, Whores, Wives and Slaves, 1975) reasserted the legal disabilities; Cohen ("Seclusion, Separation and the Status of Women", 1989) proposed separate spheres rather than seclusion, with a female world of wells, neighbours and festivals. The evidence is male-authored and Athenian; conclusions about "Greek women" are conclusions about an ideology.

Childhood, exposure and education

A newborn was not yet a member of the oikos. The father decided within days whether to rear it; a rejected infant was exposed in a pot at a crossroads or shrine, to die or be raised as a slave, the plot of Menander's Epitrepontes and of Oedipus. Acceptance was marked by carrying the child round the hearth at the Amphidromia (Plato, Theaetetus 160e) and naming on the tenth day. Plato (Republic 460c) and Aristotle (Politics 7.16, 1335b) treat exposure of defective infants as policy; at Sparta the tribal elders, not the father, inspected the baby and had the weak thrown into the Apothetae (Plutarch, Lycurgus 16.1–2).

Where sources disagree. Golden (1981) argued from demography that 10 per cent or more of girls were exposed; Engels (1980) that widespread infanticide would have collapsed the population; Harris (1982) that modest rates were sustainable; Patterson (1985) that exposure was not killing in Greek eyes. The practice was legal and real; the numbers are unknown.

An Athenian boy of means went from about seven to the grammatistes for letters, the kitharistes for lyre and poets, and the paidotribes for exercise (Plato, Protagoras 325d–326c; Aristophanes, Clouds 961–983), escorted by a paidagogos, a household slave who carried his things and kept older men off. Socrates teases Lysis that a free boy is ruled by a slave (Plato, Lysis 208c). There was no state schooling; girls learned at home. From 335/4 Athens imposed two years of military training at eighteen (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 42).

Sparta made upbringing public. From seven the boy lived in herds under a paidonomos, barefoot, one cloak, underfed so he would steal and be whipped if caught (Plutarch, Lycurgus 16–18; Xenophon, Constitution of the Lacedaemonians 2–4). Girls trained in running, wrestling and discus to bear strong children (Plutarch, Lycurgus 14), which no Athenian girl did.

Slaves and metics

Slaves came from war, piracy and the markets fed from Thrace, Phrygia, Caria and the Black Sea; Solon had ended debt-bondage of Athenians. Numbers are unknown: Athenaeus (6.272c) reports a census giving 400,000 slaves in Attica, which nearly everyone rejects; estimates run from 60,000 to 150,000 against 30,000–40,000 adult male citizens.

The worst fate was the Laurium silver mines, worked by chained gangs in galleries a metre high. Nicias leased a thousand slaves to a contractor at an obol a day each (Xenophon, Ways and Means 4.14–15); more than twenty thousand slaves, mostly skilled, deserted to the Spartans at Decelea (Thucydides 7.27.5). Household slaves cooked, wove, nursed and fetched water, and the oligarch who wrote the Constitution of the Athenians attributed to Xenophon (1.10–12) complains one cannot strike a slave in the street because he dresses like a citizen. Aristotle's natural slave, a living tool without deliberative faculty (Politics 1.4–7), is the only extended justification, and he admits others thought slavery conventional and unjust (1253b20–23). Finley's answer ("Was Greek Civilisation Based on Slave Labour?", 1959) was yes: the citizen's leisure for politics, philosophy and the gymnasium rested on slaves, even though most farming was done by free smallholders.

Where sources disagree. Jameson (1977) argued that even small farmers normally owned a slave and that slavery was integral to peasant agriculture; Wood (Peasant-Citizen and Slave, 1988) that the independent working peasant, not the slave, was democracy's base; Ste Croix (1981) placed slavery at the centre of the propertied class's surplus. Archaeology cannot settle it; slaves leave few traces.

Spartan helots were different: a conquered Greek population, mainly Messenian, tied to the land, state-owned and assigned to individuals, paying a fixed share of produce. Two thousand helots promised freedom for bravery were made to vanish (Thucydides 4.80); the krypteia sent youths out to kill helots at night, and the ephors declared war on them annually (Plutarch, Lycurgus 28). Thucydides judged most Spartan institutions designed for security against them (4.80.3).

Free resident foreigners at Athens, the metics, registered with a citizen sponsor, paid twelve drachmas a year (six for an independent woman), served in the army and paid liturgies, but could not own land, marry citizens with legitimate issue or address the assembly. They ran trade, banking and crafts: Lysias and his father Cephalus, host of Plato's Republic, were metics. Whitehead (The Ideology of the Athenian Metic, 1977) showed how the city used them and kept them out. Sparta periodically expelled foreigners (Thucydides 1.144.2).

The symposium

The symposion was the central institution of elite male leisure. It met in the andron, the one room built for show, with off-centre door and a raised border for seven or eleven couches, as the houses at Olynthus show. Guests reclined two to a couch after the meal was cleared; a libation of neat wine to the Good Spirit and a paean opened proceedings, and the symposiarch fixed the mixture. Greeks never drank wine neat; Hesiod (Works and Days 596) gives three parts water to one, and the mixing-bowl, the krater, was the room's focus. Eubulus has Dionysus allot three kraters to the sensible, the fourth to hybris, the eighth to the police (Athenaeus 2.36b–c). Vases show the kottabos stand at which drinkers flicked wine-lees at a target, and the aulos-girls who were the only women present.

Entertainment was participatory: skolia sung in turn with a myrtle branch, verses capped, riddles set. The Harmodius song for the tyrannicides (Athenaeus 15.695a–b) was a political creed; much archaic lyric, Theognis to Cyrnus, Alcaeus' faction songs, Anacreon, Xenophanes fr. 1, was composed for this room. Plato's and Xenophon's Symposia are idealisations in which the aulos-girl is sent away and talk takes over; Alcibiades' drunken entrance (Plato, Symposium 212d) shows what was idealised away.

It was political because it bred the hetaireia, the sworn drinking group. Thucydides (8.54.4) has Peisander touring the clubs in 411 to arrange the oligarchic coup; the herm-mutilation of 415 was blamed on such a group (Andocides, On the Mysteries). Democracy distrusted the andron (Murray, Sympotica, 1990).

Sparta replaced the private party with the compulsory public mess: fixed monthly contributions of barley, wine, cheese and figs, black broth eaten in groups of about fifteen, boys present to listen, drunkenness forbidden (Plutarch, Lycurgus 12). Critias (fr. 6 West) praised Spartans for drinking from their own cup without toasts; helots were sometimes made drunk and paraded as a warning (Plutarch, Lycurgus 28.4).

Pederasty, same-sex relations, Sappho and prostitution

Elite Athenian pederasty joined an adult man (erastes) and an adolescent of citizen family (eromenos), roughly from first down to beard. The erastes courted with gifts (hares, cocks on vases), frequented the gymnasium and was expected to educate; the eromenos was to be reluctant, yield slowly, never for money, and not seek pleasure. Pausanias in Plato's Symposium (182a–185c) gives the code: honourable if the boy yields to a good man for virtue, shameful if quickly or for gain. Aeschines' Against Timarchus shows the law: a citizen who had prostituted himself lost his political rights, and Aeschines distinguishes his own honourable loves (1.136) from Timarchus' hired ones. Vase painting, read by Dover (Greek Homosexuality, 1978), shows a stylised courtship, the "up-and-down" gesture of chin and genitals, and consummation standing, between the thighs, never in black-figure the anal penetration of a citizen boy.

Where sources disagree. Dover and Foucault (History of Sexuality 2) read Greek sex as structured by penetration and domination, not by the partner's sex. Davidson (The Greeks and Greek Love, 2007) called this a modern obsession and stressed age-classes and gift-exchange; Lear and Cantarella (2008) re-read the vases. The firm negative is that "homosexual" and "heterosexual" are not Greek categories: men were expected to marry and to desire both, and the question was how, with whom and at what age, not whether.

Spartan evidence contradicts itself. Xenophon (Constitution of the Lacedaemonians 2.12–14) insists Lycurgus allowed love of a boy's soul but made physical relations as shameful as incest, and admits nobody believed him; Plutarch (Lycurgus 18) says every boy of twelve had a lover who shared his punishments. Female relations are attested at Sparta (Plutarch, Lycurgus 18.4) and in Alcman's maiden-songs (fr. 1 and 3), but above all in Sappho of Lesbos, c. 600 BC, whose fr. 1, 16 and 31 voice desire for named women in the first person. Whether her circle was a school, a cult group or aristocratic friendship is unknown; the sexual sense of "Lesbian" is nineteenth-century.

Prostitution was legal, taxed and graded. Tradition credited Solon with state brothels (Philemon fr. 3, Athenaeus 13.569d); the pornai there and in the Kerameikos were slaves or metics at a fixed price, while the hetaira sold company by the evening or the year and might, like Neaera (Demosthenes 59), buy her freedom. Male prostitutes served the same market; the law punished only the citizen who sold himself. Davidson's Courtesans and Fishcakes (1997) treats it as part of an economy of appetite.

Farm, agora, food, clothing, gymnasium

Most citizens farmed smallholdings of a few hectares: barley, some wheat, olives, vines, figs, goats and a few sheep, as Hesiod and Aristophanes' Dicaeopolis (Acharnians) assume. Hanson (The Other Greeks, 1995) argued this intensive family farming created the hoplite and the polis. Attica could not feed itself: the Bosporan kingdom alone sent 400,000 medimnoi of grain a year (Demosthenes 20.31–32), and The agora was market, court, cult-centre and gossip-exchange; everyone frequents some shop, Lysias 24.20 reminds a jury. Spartiates were forbidden crafts and trade, with an iron currency to make wealth useless (Plutarch, Lycurgus 9).

Food was barley cake or wheat bread with opson: olives, cheese, onions, figs, lentils and above all fish, the glutton's mark in comedy; meat came mainly from sacrifice. Plato's healthy city eats exactly this and drinks in moderation (Republic 372a–d). Spartan black broth was so bad that a Sybarite said he now saw why Spartans were willing to die (Athenaeus 4.138d).

Clothing was draped: a pinned rectangle, the chiton or woollen peplos, under a himation. Spartan women's open-sided peplos earned them the name "thigh-showers". Thucydides (1.6.3–5) says Spartans first adopted simple dress and stripped naked to exercise, a habit that spread to all Greeks and separated them from barbarians.

The gymnasium and its wrestling-ground, the palaestra, made and displayed the male body. Athens had three public ones, Academy, Lyceum and Cynosarges, which became philosophical schools because teachers went where young men were. Exercise was naked and oiled; the law fixed opening hours and kept adults from loitering with boys (Aeschines 1.9–12); Plato's Charmides opens with Socrates entering a palaestra to see who is beautiful. At Sparta the whole of male life was in effect the gymnasium, and the women joined it.

Self-test

  1. What were the three relations of rule within the oikos according to Aristotle?
    Answer

    Master over slave, husband over wife, father over children (Politics 1.3, 1253b).

  2. What happened to the dowry on divorce, and why did this matter?
    Answer

    It had to be returned or interest paid at 18 per cent a year; the cost deterred husbands and gave the wife's family leverage.

  3. Who was an epikleros and what could the nearest male kin do?
    Answer

    A brotherless daughter who passed with the estate; the nearest kinsman could claim her in marriage through the archon, even if either was already married.

  4. Name two pieces of evidence that Athenian women worked outside the home.
    Answer

    Euxitheus' mother selling ribbons and wet-nursing (Demosthenes 57); market-women in Aristophanes; grave stelai of nurses and wool-workers.

  5. What did Pericles' citizenship law of 451/0 require?
    Answer

    Both parents Athenian for a child to be a citizen (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 26.4).

  6. Who decided whether a newborn was reared in Athens, and who at Sparta?
    Answer

    The father in Athens; the tribal elders at Sparta (Plutarch, Lycurgus 16).

  7. What is Finley's answer to whether Greek civilisation depended on slavery?
    Answer

    Yes: citizen leisure for politics and culture depended on slave labour, even though most farming was done by free smallholders.

  8. What was the political danger of the symposium in democratic eyes?
    Answer

    It bred the hetaireia, the sworn drinking club, which organised the 411 coup (Thucydides 8.54) and was blamed for the herms affair.

  9. According to Pausanias in Plato's Symposium, when was a boy's yielding honourable?
    Answer

    When granted slowly, to a good man, for the sake of virtue, never for money or quickly (182a–185c).

  10. Why did Athenians regard adultery with a citizen wife as worse than rape?
    Answer

    Because it corrupted the wife's loyalty and threatened the legitimacy of heirs, the core of the oikos (Lysias 1).

Carry forward

  1. The oikos, not the individual, is the unit; women, children and slaves are defined by their relation to its kyrios, and the law's first concern is legitimate succession.
  2. Nearly all evidence is Athenian, male and often prescriptive; distinguish the ideology of seclusion from the practice of poorer households, and the Spartan mirage from Spartan reality.
  3. Greek sexuality is organised by age, status and conduct, not by the sex of the partner; never import modern identity categories into the symposium or the gymnasium.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Greek social life, centred on Classical Athens with Sparta as the contrast. Cover: the oikos and the kyrios; marriage, dowry, the epikleros, divorce; the legal and real position of women (seclusion versus the evidence of working women, religion as the female public sphere, Medea's speech, the hetaira and Aspasia); childhood, exposure, education and the paidagogos; slavery: sources of slaves, the silver mines, household slaves, the debate over whether Greek civilisation depended on it; metics; the symposium as institution (the andron, the krater, the games, the poetry, the politics); pederasty and its rules, the evidence of vases and the Symposium, and how not to read it with modern categories; male and female same-sex relations, Sappho; prostitution; the economy of the farm and the agora; food, clothing, the gymnasium. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 9 · Art, the ground, and the afterlife of it all · 9.1 · 2,987 words

Reading Greek art: temples, sculpture, vases

The three ordersAnatomy of a templeThe Parthenon's refinementsSculpture by periodLost bronzes, Roman copies, painted marbleVase paintingHow to read a mythological sceneThe great sculptural programmesSelf-testCarry forward

The three orders

An order is a grammar: a fixed set of parts whose proportions and ornament are agreed in advance, so that a trained eye reads a building as a reader scans a line of verse. Vitruvius (De architectura 4.1) gives the ancient account; his numbers are a Roman systematisation of looser Greek practice.

Doric is the mainland and western order, canonical by about 600 BC. Identify it by what is missing: the column has no base and rises straight from the stylobate. The shaft carries twenty shallow flutes meeting in sharp edges (arrises). The capital is a plain cushion (echinus) under a square slab (abacus). Above the architrave the frieze alternates triglyphs (three vertical bars) and metopes (square panels, often carved). Beneath the triglyphs hang guttae, the fossilised pegs of a timber ancestor. Early shafts at Paestum and Corinth are barely four lower diameters high.

Ionic comes from the eastern Aegean and the islands in the sixth century. The column stands on a moulded base; the shaft carries twenty-four flutes separated by flat fillets; the capital rolls into two volutes like a scroll laid over the shaft. The frieze is either continuous and sculpted (Attic practice) or replaced by a row of dentils (Asia Minor). Proportions are slender, around nine diameters, and the mouldings (egg-and-dart, bead-and-reel) are carved.

Corinthian is an Ionic variant distinguished only by its capital, a bell wrapped in two rows of acanthus leaves with small volutes at the corners. Vitruvius (4.1.9–10) credits its invention to the sculptor Kallimachos, moved by a basket left on a girl's grave through which acanthus had grown. The earliest surviving example is a single interior column at Bassae (late fifth century); the first exterior use is the Choregic Monument of Lysikrates in Athens (334 BC). Rome preferred it because the capital reads the same from every angle, which the Ionic volute does not.

Where sources disagree. Vitruvius (4.2) says Doric forms translate carpentry into stone: triglyphs are beam ends, guttae pegs. Barletta (The Origins of the Greek Architectural Orders, 2001) argues they were devised in stone, since no excavated wooden temple shows the prototype. Uncertain.

Anatomy of a temple

A temple is a house for a cult statue; sacrifice happened at the altar outside. The building is a box inside a colonnade on a platform.

PartWhat it isNotes
CrepidomaStepped platform, usually three stepsTop step is the stylobate; a levelling course (euthynteria) lies beneath
Peristyle (pteron)Colonnade around the buildingA temple with one ring is peripteral, with two dipteral; six columns on the front is hexastyle, eight octastyle
PronaosPorch before the cellaUsually framed by two columns between projecting walls (in antis)
Cella (naos)The closed hall holding the statueOften with interior colonnades; some have an inner room (adyton)
OpisthodomosRear porch, mirroring the pronaosNo door to the cella; used as a treasury at the Parthenon
EntablatureEverything carried by the columnsArchitrave (epistyle), then frieze, then cornice (geison)
FriezeMiddle band of the entablatureDoric: triglyphs and metopes; Ionic: continuous relief or dentils
PedimentTriangular gable at each endThe recessed field is the tympanon; statues stood on its floor; acroteria crowned the angles

The standard Doric plan by 500 BC is hexastyle with thirteen columns on the flank; the Parthenon is octastyle with seventeen. The Doric corner is the order's permanent headache: a triglyph should sit over each column and also close each end of the frieze, which at the corner it cannot, so architects narrowed the end intercolumniations (angle contraction).

The Parthenon's refinements

The Parthenon (447–432 BC; Iktinos and Kallikrates architects, Phidias overseeing according to Plutarch, Pericles 13) contains almost no straight line. Penrose measured this in the 1840s (Principles of Athenian Architecture, 1851), confirming hints in Vitruvius 3.3.13 and 3.4.5:

  • The stylobate rises in a convex curve, about 6 cm on the short sides and 11 cm on the long, carried up through the entablature.
  • Every column leans inward by about 7 cm; the corner columns lean on the diagonal.
  • The corner columns are some 4 cm thicker than the rest, and the end intercolumniations are narrower.
  • Each shaft swells slightly below the midpoint (entasis), so the profile is a curve rather than a cone.
  • A 4:9 ratio governs width to length, column diameter to interval, and façade height to width.
Where sources disagree. Vitruvius says the refinements correct illusions: a straight stylobate would appear to sag, a corner column against the sky would look thin. Since Goodyear (Greek Refinements, 1912) many reject this, because the curves are visible, and argue they give the building a muscular tension; others invoke drainage. The intention is uncertain; the precision is not.

Sculpture by period

Daedalic and Archaic, c. 680–480 BC

The earliest monumental style is called Daedalic after the mythical craftsman: frontal, flat figures with triangular faces and wig-like hair, such as the Auxerre Goddess (Louvre, c. 640) and the Nikandre from Delos (c. 650). Egyptian influence shapes the kouros, the standing nude youth with left leg advanced and arms at his sides, which appears about 600 BC (New York Kouros) and evolves over a century from diagram to anatomy: Kleobis and Biton at Delphi (c. 580; Herodotus 1.31), the Anavysos Kouros (c. 530, the tomb of Kroisos), the Aristodikos (c. 500). The kore, the draped maiden, shows the same trajectory through dress: the Peplos Kore (c. 530) and the Phrasikleia of Aristion of Paros (c. 540), whose epitaph says the gods gave her the name maiden in place of marriage.

The Severe style, c. 480–450 BC

After the Persian Wars the archaic smile vanishes. The Kritios Boy (Acropolis, c. 480) is the first surviving figure whose weight shifts onto one leg, tilting the hips: the beginning of contrapposto. The Tyrannicides by Kritios and Nesiotes (477/6; copies in Naples) replaced Antenor's group that Xerxes carried off (Pausanias 1.8.5; Arrian, Anabasis 3.16.7). The Charioteer of Delphi (c. 475) and the Artemision god (c. 460) are rare bronze originals. Faces are heavy-lidded and grave; drapery falls in columnar folds.

Polykleitos and the canon

Polykleitos of Argos (active c. 460–410) wrote a treatise, the Kanon, and made a statue to demonstrate it, almost certainly the Doryphoros (best copy in Naples). The treatise is lost; Galen (De placitis Hippocratis et Platonis 5) says it located beauty in the commensurability (symmetria) of finger to finger, hand to forearm and so on, and Philo Mechanicus quotes him:

Perfection comes about little by little through many numbers.
The Doryphoros systematises contrapposto into chiasmus: tensed leg under relaxed arm, relaxed leg under tensed arm. Pliny (Natural History 34.55–56) also lists his Diadoumenos.

Phidias

Phidias of Athens made the two most famous statues of antiquity, both lost: the gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos (dedicated 438; Pausanias 1.24.5–7, Pliny 36.18) and the seated Zeus at Olympia (Pausanias 5.11; Strabo 8.3.30 says that standing he would unroof the temple). His Olympia workshop, excavated in 1954–58, yielded drapery moulds and a cup scratched I belong to Phidias. Whether he carved any Parthenon marble is unknown; the style is nonetheless called Phidian: wet-looking drapery revealing the body beneath, faces of serene detachment.

Praxiteles

The fourth century softens the body into an S-curve and gives it a mood. Praxiteles (active c. 370–330) made the Aphrodite of Knidos, the first monumental female nude, which the Knidians refused to sell even for cancellation of their public debt (Pliny 36.20–21), and the Apollo Sauroktonos, a boy teasing a lizard (Pliny 34.70). Asked which marbles he valued most, he named those the painter Nikias had coloured (Pliny 35.133).

Where sources disagree. Pausanias (5.17.3) saw a Hermes with the infant Dionysus by Praxiteles in the Heraion at Olympia; a matching statue was found there in 1877. Whether it is the original, a later Praxiteles, or a Roman copy has been argued since Blümel (1927) from tool marks and the strut. Divided.

Lysippos

Lysippos of Sikyon (active c. 370–310), Alexander's portraitist (Plutarch, Alexander 4), made heads smaller and bodies slimmer than Polykleitos and represented men as they appeared rather than as they were (Pliny 34.65). His Apoxyomenos, an athlete scraping himself, reaches an arm into the viewer's space: the first statue that demands to be walked around.

Hellenistic baroque

Under the kings, sculpture turns theatrical: extremes of age, pain, sleep and movement. The Great Altar of Pergamon (c. 180–160 BC, under Eumenes II; Berlin) wraps its podium in a Gigantomachy over two metres high, gods treading on serpent-legged giants whose faces contort; the inner Telephos frieze tells the city's founding myth. The Laocoön (Vatican) shows the Trojan priest and his sons strangled by serpents; Pliny (36.37) names Hagesandros, Polydoros and Athenodoros of Rhodes. The Nike of Samothrace and the Dying Gaul share the sensibility.

Where sources disagree. The Laocoön, found in 1506, has been dated from c. 200 BC to the reign of Tiberius. Andreae sees a Roman marble version of a Pergamene bronze; others an original Rhodian work of the first century BC, when the same sculptors signed at Sperlonga. Unresolved.

Lost bronzes, Roman copies, painted marble

Most celebrated Greek statues were bronze, hollow-cast by the lost-wax method, with inlaid eyes, copper lips and silver teeth (all visible on the Riace warriors, c. 460–450). Bronze is money; nearly all was melted. What survives was lost at sea (Artemision, Antikythera) or buried (Delphi, Riace, Piraeus). Our image of Polykleitos, Praxiteles and Lysippos rests on Roman marble versions, made from plaster casts (a cache was found at Baiae in 1954) and burdened with tree-trunk supports and struts that bronze never needed. Furtwängler's Meisterwerke (1893) founded Kopienkritik, reconstructing lost originals by comparing copies.

Where sources disagree. Ridgway (Roman Copies of Greek Sculpture, 1984) and Marvin (The Language of the Muses, 2008) argue that many copies are Roman creations in a Greek manner, and that hunting a lost original behind each type misreads Roman taste. The Doryphoros is secure; many others are not.

Marble, too, was coloured. Plato (Republic 420c) speaks of statue-painters putting the finest colours on the finest parts; Euripides (Helen 262–3) has Helen wish her beauty wiped away like paint from a statue. Hair, lips, eyes, borders and often whole garments were painted; metal supplied spears, wreaths and jewellery. Brinkmann's reconstructions (Gods in Color, 2003 onwards), from ultraviolet and raking-light traces, restore the Peplos Kore and the Aegina archer to a brightness that still shocks viewers raised on white marble.

Vase painting

Pots survive because they are worthless to melt; they are the largest body of Greek narrative art.

  • Geometric (c. 900–700). Meanders, zigzags and concentric circles cover the surface in bands; late in the period silhouette figures appear. The Dipylon Amphora (Athens, c. 750) shows a laying-out of the dead with mourners tearing their hair: the owner's funeral, not myth.
  • Corinthian (c. 720–550). Corinth invents the black-figure technique about 700: figures painted in glossy slip, details incised with a point, red and white added. Protocorinthian miniaturists reach a peak on the Chigi Vase (c. 640), with its hoplite phalanx and Judgement of Paris; later Corinthian fills every space with animal friezes and rosettes.
  • Attic black-figure (c. 630–500). Athens takes over the technique and the market. The François Vase of Kleitias and Ergotimos (c. 570, Florence) carries over 200 named figures in six friezes. Exekias (c. 545–530), potter and painter, is the master: Achilles and Ajax absorbed over a board game (Vatican), Dionysus sailing alone across a cup (Munich), Ajax planting the sword on which he will fall (Boulogne). He paints the moment before the event.
  • Red-figure (c. 530 onwards). The Andokides Painter reverses the scheme, reserving figures in clay colour against black and drawing inner lines with a brush, which allows anatomy, foreshortening and expression. Euphronios and Euthymides, the Pioneers, compete openly; Euthymides writes on one amphora, as never Euphronios. The Berlin Painter (c. 505–460, named by Beazley after an amphora in Berlin) isolates one or two figures against unbroken black, with no ground line or frame: a kitharode mid-song, Hermes with a satyr, the pot itself the stage.
  • White-ground lekythoi (c. 470–400). Oil flasks for the grave, painted in matt colours on a white slip too fragile for use. The Achilles Painter shows a woman handing a soldier his helmet, a mourner at a stele, Charon waiting in his boat, in a register unlike symposium ware.
Where sources disagree. The painter-names rest on Beazley's connoisseurship (ABV 1956, ARV 1963), attributing unsigned pots by Morellian comparison of ears, knees and folds. Whitley (1997) questions its assumptions about individual genius; Vickers and Gill (Artful Crafts, 1994) argued painted pottery merely imitated silver and gold and was cheap. Most specialists accept the attributions and reject the metalware thesis.

How to read a mythological scene

Painters had no captions beyond occasional name-labels, so they built a vocabulary of attributes. Herodotus (2.53) says Homer and Hesiod gave the gods their forms; painters gave them their luggage.

FigureIdentifiers
ZeusThunderbolt, sceptre, eagle; mature, bearded, enthroned
PoseidonTrident; otherwise Zeus's twin, so labels help
HeraVeil, polos crown, sceptre, often beside Zeus
AthenaCrested helmet, spear, aegis with gorgoneion, owl
ApolloKithara or lyre, bow, laurel; beardless and long-haired
ArtemisBow, quiver, deer, torches
HermesKerykeion (herald's staff), petasos hat, winged boots, traveller's cloak
DionysusKantharos cup, thyrsos, ivy, vine; satyrs and maenads; bearded until c. 430, then youthful
AphroditeDove, Eros in attendance, mirror
HephaistosAxe or tongs, workman's cap, riding a mule
HeraclesLion skin (head as hood), club, bow; Athena usually at hand
TheseusYoung, beardless, sword or club; known only by what he is doing
PerseusWinged cap and boots, kibisis bag, sickle sword, averted gaze
OdysseusConical pilos cap, often with Athena

Then ask what the action is, who is present who need not be, and what the pot is for. A hoplite leaving home is generic; the same figure with a woman labelled Andromache is Hector. Gods standing by signal the weight of a duel. Heracles feasting on a drinking cup is a joke shared with the drinker.

Vases routinely show what no surviving text describes. Achilles and Ajax at their game appears on over 150 vases and in no literary source; Achilles' ambush of Troilos comes from the lost Cypria, Ajax carrying Achilles' corpse from the lost Aethiopis, both known through Proclus's summaries. Painters drew on oral tradition, local cult, lost epic and lyric, the stage, and their own invention, for an audience that knew the stories in versions Homer and Hesiod never fixed. Snodgrass (Homer and the Artists, 1998) showed how rarely archaic painters follow Homer's text even on Homeric subjects; Small (The Parallel Worlds of Classical Art and Text, 2003) treats image and text as largely separate traditions. A vase is evidence for a myth, not an illustration of a book.

The great sculptural programmes

The Siphnian Treasury at Delphi, c. 525 BC

Herodotus (3.57–58) says the Siphnians, rich from gold and silver mines, built their treasury from a tithe before Samian raiders humbled them. It is a small Ionic building with caryatid porch columns and a continuous frieze on all four sides, cut by two masters of different style. North: Gigantomachy, Apollo and Artemis shooting side by side. East: the gods in council while Greeks and Trojans fight over a body below. South: a chariot abduction. West: the Judgement of Paris. The east pediment shows Heracles trying to carry off the Delphic tripod while Apollo holds on and Zeus steps between. It is a statement of piety at a sanctuary that polices the boundary between hero and god: the greatest of men does not get to take Apollo's oracle.

The Temple of Zeus at Olympia, c. 470–456 BC

Built from the spoils of Elis's war against Pisa for control of the games. East pediment (Pausanias 5.10.6–8): the moment before the chariot race between Pelops and Oinomaos for Hippodameia, Zeus unseen between them, an old seer at the edge who already knows the outcome. West: centaurs assaulting the Lapith women at Peirithoos's wedding, Apollo calm at the centre. Twelve metopes over the porches show the labours of Heracles, the first appearance of the canonical twelve, with Athena assisting. The message is local and Panhellenic at once: Pelops is the founder-hero buried in the sanctuary, Heracles the founder of the games, and a race won through the perjury of Myrtilos warns athletes swearing before the altar of Zeus Horkios.

Where sources disagree. Pausanias attributes the pediments to Paionios (east) and Alkamenes (west). Both worked a generation too late; modern scholars speak instead of an anonymous Olympia Master, and argue from style whether one workshop or two carved the ends.

The Parthenon, 447–432 BC

Ninety-two metopes carry four battles: east, gods against giants; west, Greeks against Amazons; south, Lapiths against centaurs; north, the sack of Troy. One thought stated four ways: order defeats disorder, Greek defeats barbarian, and the Persian who burned the Acropolis in 480 is written into myth without being named. The east pediment showed the birth of Athena before the gods, framed by the chariots of Helios and Selene; the west, the contest of Athena and Poseidon for Attica (Pausanias 1.24.5). The Athena Parthenos inside repeated the programme: Amazonomachy on her shield, Centauromachy on her sandals, Pandora on the base. The frieze, 160 metres of horsemen, chariots, elders, musicians and sacrificial animals converging on seated gods and a folded cloth, has since Stuart and Revett (1787) been read as the Panathenaic procession, living Athenians on a temple for the first time.

Where sources disagree. Boardman (1977) counted 192 horsemen and read them as the Marathon dead heroised. Connelly (1996) argued the central scene shows Erechtheus preparing his daughter for sacrifice, the cloth her shroud, making the frieze mythological like every other. Most retain the procession reading; no ancient source mentions the frieze.

Self-test

  1. Name three features that distinguish a Doric from an Ionic column without looking at the frieze.
    Answer

    Doric has no base, twenty flutes meeting in sharp arrises, and a plain echinus-and-abacus capital; Ionic has a moulded base, twenty-four flutes separated by fillets, and a volute capital.

  2. What is the Doric corner problem and how was it solved?
    Answer

    A triglyph must sit over each column and also close the frieze at the corner, which is geometrically impossible; architects narrowed the end intercolumniations (angle contraction) so the last triglyph could reach the corner.

  3. Which part of a temple is the opisthodomos, and how does it differ from the pronaos?
    Answer

    The rear porch, mirroring the front porch (pronaos) but with no door into the cella; at the Parthenon it served as a treasury.

  4. List four optical refinements of the Parthenon.
    Answer

    Convex curvature of the stylobate and entablature, inward inclination of the columns, thickening of the corner columns with angle contraction, and entasis of the shafts.

  5. What was Polykleitos's Kanon, and how do we know anything about it?
    Answer

    A lost treatise on proportion demonstrated in a statue, probably the Doryphoros; known from quotations in Galen and Philo Mechanicus and from Pliny's notice.

  6. Why is almost every famous Greek statue known only through Roman marbles?
    Answer

    The originals were bronze and were melted for the metal; Roman workshops made marble versions from plaster casts, adding struts and tree-trunk supports that bronze did not need.

  7. What is the technical difference between black-figure and red-figure, and what did red-figure make possible?
    Answer

    Black-figure paints figures in slip and incises details; red-figure reserves figures in clay colour and paints the background black, drawing details with a brush, which permitted fluid anatomy, foreshortening and expression.

  8. What attributes identify Hermes, Heracles and Perseus?
    Answer

    Hermes: kerykeion, petasos, winged boots. Heracles: lion skin, club, bow. Perseus: winged cap and boots, kibisis, sickle sword, averted gaze.

  9. Give an example of a myth scene common on vases but absent from surviving literature, and explain why this happens.
    Answer

    Achilles and Ajax playing a board game (over 150 vases, no text). Painters drew on lost epic, oral and local tradition, and their own invention; image and text were largely parallel traditions.

  10. What single idea unites the four metope battles of the Parthenon?
    Answer

    Order defeating disorder and Greek defeating barbarian, read as a mythological statement of the Persian defeat; gods over giants, Greeks over Amazons, Lapiths over centaurs, Greeks over Trojans.

Carry forward

  1. Greek art is a grammar of fixed parts and attributes: the orders, the temple plan and the gods' identifiers are conventions learnt by the whole culture, so a building or a pot could be read at a glance.
  2. What survives is a distorted sample: marble and clay, not bronze and paint. Reconstruct the lost originals and the lost colour in your mind before judging any Classical work.
  3. Images are independent evidence for myth. Vase scenes and temple programmes preserve versions and emphases the texts do not, and their choice of subject is always a political and religious statement by whoever paid.

Reading a site: Athens on foot

The Acropolis, building by buildingThe slopesThe Areopagus and the PnyxThe AgoraThe Kerameikos and the DipylonOlympieion, Hadrian's Arch, the Roman Agora and the Tower of the WindsThe museums: objects and what they proveWalking ordersSelf-testCarry forward

The Acropolis, building by building

Everything standing on the rock belongs to one generation, roughly 447 to 406 BC, and sits on what the Persians burnt in 480 (Herodotus 8.51–55). Keep that double layer in mind: each Periclean building is a statement about the city that had just defeated Persia, built over the debris of the city Persia destroyed. Walk them west to east, as the ancient visitor did.

Propylaea

Mnesicles designed the gateway, built 437–432 BC and abandoned unfinished when the Peloponnesian War began; the lifting bosses were never trimmed off the walls. It is Doric outside with an Ionic interior, a mixing of orders the Parthenon shares. The north wing was the Pinakotheke, whose paintings Pausanias could still see (Pausanias 1.22.6). The political point is in the stone: a Pentelic-marble gatehouse on a scale no sanctuary had ever given an entrance, paid for from the same programme as the Parthenon.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch, Pericles 12 reports the charge that Pericles dressed the city "like a vain woman" with allied tribute. Many historians accept that League money funded the programme; Lisa Kallet and Aldo Giovannini argue the accounts (IG I³ 436–451) show Athena's own treasury paying and that the tribute story is partisan. Unresolved.

Temple of Athena Nike

On the bastion to your right as you climb stands the small Ionic temple of Athena as Victory, designed by Kallikrates under a decree of about 449/8 (IG I³ 35) but built around 427–424 BC. The bastion is Mycenaean and the Athenians left its masonry visible. Pausanias 1.22.4–5 says the statue was wingless so that Victory could never leave Athens, and places here the leap of Aegeus when he saw Theseus's black sail. The parapet Nikai, one adjusting her sandal, are in the museum. This is a war temple finished in wartime, with the plague and the Archidamian War both running.

Parthenon

Built 447–438 BC, sculpture finished by 432, by Iktinos and Kallikrates under Pheidias's direction (Plutarch, Pericles 13). Doric, eight columns by seventeen, with an Ionic frieze round the cella. It housed Pheidias's gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos, dedicated 438, described by Pausanias 1.24.5–7 and copied in the Varvakeion statuette in the National Museum. East pediment the birth of Athena, west pediment her contest with Poseidon; metopes with Gigantomachy, Amazonomachy, Trojan War and Centauromachy, four mythic defeats of barbarism read through 480. Note two anomalies: Pausanias never calls it a temple, and no altar or priestess of Athena Parthenos is attested; the ancient cult image stayed in the Erechtheion. The Parthenon was treasury and votive as much as cult building.

Where sources disagree. The frieze is usually read as the Panathenaic procession, which would make it the only Greek temple decorated with contemporary citizens. Joan Connelly (1996) argued it shows the sacrifice of the daughters of Erechtheus from Euripides' lost Erechtheus. Most specialists keep the procession; the peplos scene over the east door remains contested.

Erechtheion and the contest of Athena and Poseidon

The irregular Ionic building on the north side, built about 421–406 BC with a building inspection of 409/8 preserved on stone (IG I³ 474), is the religious heart of the rock. It held the olive-wood Athena Polias, Poseidon's saltwater "sea", the trident marks, the tomb of Erechtheus, altars of Poseidon-Erechtheus, Boutes and Hephaestus (Pausanias 1.26.5–27.1); the split levels answer the cults already in place. The Caryatid porch covers the tomb of Cecrops. The myth it encloses is told by Herodotus 8.55 and Apollodorus, Library 3.14.1: Poseidon struck the rock and produced the sea, Athena planted the olive, Cecrops witnessed and the gods judged for Athena; Poseidon flooded the Thriasian plain in anger. The political reading is the one Athenians made themselves: a city founded on the land's own gift, with the sea god reconciled and sharing the house, which is to say a land polity turned naval empire.

Pandroseion

The open court west of the Erechtheion is the precinct of Pandrosos, the daughter of Cecrops who alone did not open the basket holding the infant Erichthonius (Apollodorus 3.14.6; Pausanias 1.18.2, 1.27.2). Here grew the sacred olive, beside an altar of Zeus Herkeios; a young olive planted in 1917 marks the spot. This is autochthony in a courtyard: the first king born from the soil, nursed by Athena.

Old Temple foundations

Between Parthenon and Erechtheion lie the limestone foundations Wilhelm Dörpfeld uncovered in 1885–86, the Old Temple of Athena Polias, built in the late sixth century under either the Peisistratids or the young democracy and burnt in 480. Its marble Gigantomachy pediment is in the museum. From the Agora side, look at the north wall: column drums and triglyphs of the Older Parthenon, begun after Marathon and destroyed unfinished, were built in as a visible memorial of the sack.

Where sources disagree. Dörpfeld held that the Old Temple was repaired and stood until the fire of 406 (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.6.1). William Dinsmoor argued it was dismantled soon after 480. Whether the Erechtheion rose beside a standing ruin or an empty platform is still debated.

The slopes

Enter from the south-east gate and walk the Peripatos westward. The theatre of Dionysus Eleuthereus is where Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes were first staged, though the stone you see is the rebuilding of Lycurgus around 330 BC, seating perhaps 17,000, with Roman reworkings and the marble throne of the priest of Dionysus in the front row. The fifth-century theatre was wooden benches on the slope; the temple of Dionysus below holds the older cult brought from Eleutherae under the Peisistratids. West along the slope is the Asclepieion, founded in 420/419 BC by Telemachos of Acharnai after the plague, with its spring and the Doric stoa for incubation; the Telemachos monument (IG II² 4960) records the foundation, and tradition made Sophocles the god's first host (Plutarch, Numa 4). Below runs the Stoa of Eumenes II of Pergamon, a second-century BC promenade ending at the Odeon of Herodes Atticus, built about AD 160–174 in memory of his wife Regilla (Philostratus, Lives of the Sophists 2.1; Pausanias 7.20.6), roofed in cedar and burnt by the Heruli in 267. The slope is a four-century sequence: tyrant's cult, democratic festival, Hellenistic royal gift, Roman private benefaction.

The Areopagus and the Pnyx

The bare rock west of the Acropolis entrance is the Hill of Ares. Here Ares was tried for killing Halirrhothius, son of Poseidon, who had raped his daughter Alcippe (Apollodorus 3.14.2; Pausanias 1.28.5), and here Aeschylus, Eumenides 681–710 has Athena found the court for Orestes, with the rule that a tied vote acquits. The council of ex-archons sat here until Ephialtes's reforms of 462/1 stripped it of political power (Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 25), leaving homicide jurisdiction. The Persians camped on it in 480 (Herodotus 8.52); a plaque marks Paul's speech (Acts 17:22–34).

The Pnyx is twenty minutes south-west over the Hill of the Muses. The assembly met here from the Cleisthenic period until it moved to the theatre in the Hellenistic age. The rock-cut bema and the great retaining wall belong to the third phase; the auditorium held perhaps six thousand. There is nothing to see but the view, which is why it matters: this is the one place where you stand where the sovereign body stood.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch, Themistocles 19.4 says the Thirty turned the bema inland because sea-views bred democracy. Homer Thompson tied this to the second phase, about 404/3; others doubt the Thirty built anything, and the third phase has been dated both to Lycurgus and to Hadrian. The sequence is secure, the dates are not.

The Agora

Find the Panathenaic Way first: the gravel road running diagonally from the north-west corner to the Acropolis ramp, the route of the procession and the spine of the civic centre. Along its west side you pass the apparatus of the democracy. The Tholos, a round building of about 470–460 BC, is where the fifty prytaneis of the presiding tribe ate at public expense and a third of them slept, so that someone with authority was always on duty (Aristotle, Constitution 43.3); the official weights and measures were kept here. Behind it is the Bouleuterion: the old chamber of about 500 BC, built for Cleisthenes's Council of Five Hundred and later converted into the Metroon, the state archive, with the new chamber cut into the hill beside it about 415–406.

The Hephaisteion on the hill above is the best-preserved temple in Greece, Doric, six by thirteen, begun about 449 BC and finished with Alkamenes's bronze Hephaestus and Athena in 421–415 (Pausanias 1.14.6). Its metopes show Heracles and Theseus, hence its old name of Theseion. The Altar of the Twelve Gods, dedicated in 522/1 BC by the younger Peisistratos, son of Hippias (Thucydides 6.54.6–7), was the zero point of Attica, from which Herodotus 2.7 measures to Olympia, and a place of asylum (Herodotus 6.108); most of it lies under the railway cut of 1891. The Stoa of Attalos, gift of Attalos II of Pergamon (159–138 BC), rebuilt by the American School in 1953–56, is the museum. Do not miss the kleroterion for allotting jurors, the water clock that timed speeches, the bronze ballots, the ostraka naming Themistocles, the Spartan shield taken at Pylos in 425 and inscribed as such (Thucydides 4.38), and the law of Eukrates of 337/6 against tyranny with Democracy crowning the Demos. This is the democracy's hardware.

The Kerameikos and the Dipylon

Walk down Ermou to the potters' quarter, named for Keramos son of Dionysus and Ariadne (Pausanias 1.3.1). The Themistoclean wall of 479/8 can be seen built in the haste Thucydides 1.93.2 describes, with grave stelai reused in the lower courses. Two gates pierce it: the Sacred Gate, where the Sacred Way to Eleusis begins, and the Dipylon, the double gate on the road to the Academy, the largest in Greece in its fourth-century form. Between them stands the Pompeion, where the Panathenaic procession assembled (Pausanias 1.2.4). Outside the Dipylon ran the Demosion Sema, the public cemetery where the war dead were buried and the funeral orations given; Pericles' speech of 431/0 (Thucydides 2.34–46) was delivered here. The Street of Tombs has the fourth-century family plots: the monument of Dexileos, killed at Corinth in 394/3 aged twenty, the only Athenian grave inscription giving both birth and death years; the bull of Dionysios of Kollytos. The row ends abruptly because Demetrios of Phaleron's law of about 317 banned such monuments (Cicero, De legibus 2.66). The Dipylon vases were found here.

Olympieion, Hadrian's Arch, the Roman Agora and the Tower of the Winds

The Olympieion is a six-century project. The Peisistratids laid out a colossal Doric temple of Zeus about 515 BC; Aristotle, Politics 1313b lists it among the works tyrants build to keep subjects busy and poor. The democracy abandoned it. Antiochus IV of Syria resumed it about 174 BC in Corinthian marble with the Roman architect Cossutius (Vitruvius 7, pref. 15–17) and died in 164 with it unfinished; Hadrian completed it in AD 131/2 with a gold-and-ivory Zeus and statues of himself from every city of the Panhellenion (Pausanias 1.18.6). Fifteen of the 104 columns stand. Beside it Hadrian's Arch carries two inscriptions (IG II² 5185): towards the Acropolis "This is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus", towards the Olympieion "This is the city of Hadrian and not of Theseus".

Where sources disagree. Older scholarship read the arch as a boundary between the old town and a new Hadrianic quarter. Many now take it as an honorific set up by the Athenians presenting Hadrian as a second founder, with no boundary implied. Who paid for it is unknown.

North of the Acropolis the Roman Agora, a colonnaded market court, was built with money from Julius Caesar and Augustus; its Gate of Athena Archegetis is dated by inscription to 11/10 BC (IG II² 3175). It marks the moment commerce left the old Agora and the old Agora became a museum of itself. At its east end is the Tower of the Winds, the Horologion of Andronikos of Kyrrhos (Vitruvius 1.6.4; Varro, On Agriculture 3.5.17): an octagon of Pentelic marble with the eight winds in relief, a sundial on each face, a water clock inside fed from the Klepsydra, and once a bronze Triton weathervane. It is traditionally dated to the mid-first century BC because Varro knows it; Hermann Kienast argues for the second century.

The museums: objects and what they prove

Take the Acropolis Museum after the rock, because its Archaic gallery is the city the Persians destroyed. The Moschophoros (about 570), the Peplos Kore (about 530), the Rampin Horseman and the Old Temple's Gigantomachy pediment all come from the Perserschutt, the debris buried in 479 when the rock was tidied, which is why they are so fresh. The Kritios Boy, about 480, standing with his weight on one leg, is the first surviving statue to break the kouros stance. The Caryatids and the sandal-binding Nike are here; the top-floor Parthenon gallery hangs frieze and metopes in their original orientation, with white casts filling the gaps held in London, which makes the Elgin question visible rather than argued.

Where sources disagree. Lycurgus, Against Leocrates 81 and Diodorus 11.29.3 record an oath sworn before Plataea not to rebuild the burnt temples. Theopompus (FGrH 115 F 153) already called it a forgery, and the thirty-year gap before the Parthenon has been explained both by the oath and by lack of funds. The Perserschutt is real; the oath may not be.

The National Archaeological Museum needs a Metro ride north and half a day. The Mask of Agamemnon, from Shaft Grave V of Grave Circle A at Mycenae (Schliemann, 1876), dates to about 1550–1500 BC, three centuries before any plausible Trojan War: it proves the wealth of early Mycenaean kings and disproves Schliemann's label at once. The Antikythera mechanism, raised from a wreck in 1901, is a geared bronze calculator with Metonic, Saros and Olympiad dials, decoded from 2006 by the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project; it proves that the planetary devices Cicero attributes to Archimedes and Posidonius (De natura deorum 2.88) were real. The Artemision bronze, about 460 BC, from a wreck off Euboea, is one of very few large original bronzes of the Severe Style to escape the melting-pot. The Dipylon amphora, about 760–750 BC, 1.55 metres high, with its prothesis scene of mourners round a bier, is the return of the human figure to Greek art after the Dark Age, made within a generation of the Dipylon oinochoe nearby, which carries the oldest known Greek alphabetic inscription. The Thera frescoes from Akrotiri, the Boxing Boys, the Antelopes, the Spring Fresco, excavated by Spyridon Marinatos from 1967, prove a Cycladic court culture in close contact with Minoan Crete, frozen by the eruption.

Where sources disagree. William Calder suggested in 1999 that Schliemann tampered with or planted the Mask; most Aegean archaeologists reject this while granting that the mask is stylistically odd. The Artemision figure is Zeus with a thunderbolt for most, Poseidon with a trident for a minority. Radiocarbon puts the Thera eruption about 1620–1600 BC, Egyptian-anchored chronology about 1530–1500. The Antikythera mechanism has been dated anywhere between about 205 and 60 BC.

Walking orders

Both plans take the Acropolis at opening, when the light is low and the crowds absent. Everything in the centre is within twenty minutes' walk of everything else; the National Archaeological Museum is the one Metro ride.

SlotOne dayTwo days
Day 1, morningSouth slope: theatre of Dionysus, Asclepieion, Stoa of Eumenes, Odeon; Propylaea, Nike, Parthenon, Erechtheion, Pandroseion, Old Temple foundations; AreopagusSame route, taken slowly
Day 1, middayAgora: Stoa of Attalos, Hephaisteion, Tholos, Bouleuterion, Altar of the Twelve Gods; Roman Agora and Tower of the WindsPhilopappos Hill and the Pnyx; lunch in Koukaki
Day 1, afternoonAcropolis Museum; Hadrian's Arch and Olympieion before closingAcropolis Museum with the rock fresh in mind
Day 2, morning—Kerameikos at opening; Panathenaic Way into the Agora: Stoa of Attalos, Hephaisteion, Tholos, Bouleuterion, Altar of the Twelve Gods
Day 2, midday—Roman Agora, Tower of the Winds, Hadrian's Library; lunch in Plaka
Day 2, afternoon—Hadrian's Arch and Olympieion; Metro to the National Archaeological Museum
SkippedPnyx, Kerameikos, National Archaeological MuseumNothing on the list

The two-day order is chronological as well as geographical: the rock and its museum first, then the procession's road from the Dipylon into the civic centre, the Roman city, and finally the Bronze Age gold the classical Athenians never saw.

Self-test

  1. Why was the Propylaea left unfinished, and what physical trace of this can you still see?
    Answer

    Work stopped in 432 BC at the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War; the lifting bosses were never trimmed off the wall blocks.

  2. According to Pausanias, why was the statue of Athena Nike wingless, and what death does he locate on the Nike bastion?
    Answer

    So that Victory could never fly away from Athens; the leap of Aegeus when he saw Theseus's black sail (Pausanias 1.22.4–5).

  3. Give two reasons for doubting that the Parthenon functioned as an ordinary cult temple.
    Answer

    No altar or priestess of Athena Parthenos is attested, Pausanias never calls it a temple, and the ancient cult image of Athena Polias stayed in the Erechtheion; it served as treasury and votive.

  4. Which three physical tokens of the contest between Athena and Poseidon did the Erechtheion and Pandroseion contain?
    Answer

    Poseidon's saltwater "sea", the trident marks in the rock, and Athena's sacred olive in the Pandroseion (Herodotus 8.55; Pausanias 1.26.5–27.2).

  5. What did Pandrosos do, or not do, to earn her precinct?
    Answer

    Alone of the daughters of Cecrops she did not open the basket containing the infant Erichthonius (Apollodorus 3.14.6).

  6. Who founded the Asclepieion, when, and in what circumstances?
    Answer

    Telemachos of Acharnai in 420/419 BC, in the aftermath of the plague, as recorded on the Telemachos monument.

  7. What does Plutarch say the Thirty did to the Pnyx, and why is the claim doubted?
    Answer

    They turned the bema to face inland because sea-views bred democracy (Themistocles 19.4); the archaeology shows no phase securely datable to 404/3, and the later phases are themselves disputed.

  8. Who dedicated the Altar of the Twelve Gods, and what two civic functions did it serve?
    Answer

    The younger Peisistratos, son of Hippias, in 522/1 BC (Thucydides 6.54); it was the zero milestone of Attica (Herodotus 2.7) and a place of asylum (Herodotus 6.108).

  9. What do the two inscriptions on Hadrian's Arch say, and which way does each face?
    Answer

    Towards the Acropolis: "This is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus"; towards the Olympieion: "This is the city of Hadrian and not of Theseus".

  10. Why does the Mask of Agamemnon disprove its own name, and what does it prove instead?
    Answer

    Shaft Grave V dates to about 1550–1500 BC, roughly three centuries before any plausible Trojan War; it proves the wealth of early Mycenaean rulers, not the existence of Homer's king.

Carry forward

  1. The Acropolis is a double layer: every Periclean building stands on, and quotes, the ruins of 480 BC. The Perserschutt, the Older Parthenon drums in the north wall and the Oath of Plataea debate all turn on this.
  2. Athenian myth is political geography. Autochthony (Erichthonius, Cecrops, the olive) and the contest with Poseidon underwrite the claim to be both the oldest land and the master of the sea.
  3. Athens kept being rebuilt by outsiders who wanted to own its past: Attalos, Antiochus, Caesar and Augustus, Herodes Atticus and above all Hadrian. The Roman city is a commentary on the classical one.
