The prompt this answers
I have completed a 49-module course on Greek history and mythology covering sources, geography, the Bronze Age, Hesiod's cosmogony, the Olympians and lesser gods, the underworld, the heroes (Perseus, Heracles, Theseus, Jason, the Theban cycle, the secondary heroes, the metamorphoses), the full Trojan cycle including the Iliad, the lost Epic Cycle, the Odyssey and the house of Atreus, the Archaic age (the polis, colonisation, tyrants, Sparta, Athens to Cleisthenes, lyric and the Presocratics), the Classical age (Persian Wars, Athenian empire, Peloponnesian War, drama, philosophy, the fourth century, Alexander), the Hellenistic and Roman periods, religion and daily life, and art and reception. Give me a 40-question final examination that tests integration across modules rather than isolated facts: questions that require connecting a myth to the society that told it, a source to its bias, an event to its long consequences. Mix formats: 15 short-answer, 10 "explain the connection between X and Y", 10 "which source says this and why should we doubt it", 5 essay questions. Provide full model answers after the questions. Then list the ten topics where a reader of this course is most likely still to have gaps, with one follow-up prompt each.
GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.1 · 2,955 words

Achilles

Birth and the Thetis prophecyMaking him invulnerable: Styx versus firePelion and ScyrosThe two fates and the economy of kleosAchilles and PatroclusMenis, Briseis, and the ShieldHector, Priam, and the deathAfter death: games, arms, the shade and the islandReceptionWhat Achilles is forSelf-testCarry forward

Birth and the Thetis prophecy

Achilles exists because Zeus was frightened. The clearest statement is Pindar, Isthmian 8.26–48: Zeus and Poseidon both want the Nereid Thetis, and Themis stops them with a prophecy that any son Thetis bears to a god will be mightier than his father, wielding a weapon stronger than the thunderbolt or the trident. The solution is to marry her downwards, to the mortal Peleus, so that the child inherits a mortal ceiling. Achilles is therefore a contained cosmic threat: the god who never happened.

Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 755–770 and 907–927, makes the same prophecy the secret Prometheus withholds from Zeus until he is released; the lost Prometheus Unbound presumably traded the secret for his freedom. Apollodorus, Library 3.13.5, records both this and a rival explanation: Thetis refused Zeus out of loyalty to Hera, who had reared her, and was condemned to a mortal husband. Homer knows the second strand without the prophecy (Iliad 24.59–63; 18.432–434).

Where sources disagree. Pindar and Aeschylus make the marriage a precaution against a usurper; the Cypria (as reported in scholia) and Apollodorus' second version make it a punishment for refusing Zeus. The Iliad suppresses the succession theme almost entirely. Laura Slatkin (The Power of Thetis, 1991) argues the suppression is deliberate and audible: Thetis once saved Zeus from being bound (1.396–406), and her power to compel him for Achilles is the residue of a cosmic plot the poem declines to tell.

Making him invulnerable: Styx versus fire

The Styx-dipping is late. Its first surviving statement is Statius, Achilleid 1.133–134, where Thetis regrets that she did not arm him completely in the Styx's waters; the heel as the held, unwetted part is spelled out only by Servius (on Aeneid 6.57) and Fulgentius (Mythologiae 3.7). The older story is fire and ambrosia. Apollonius, Argonautica 4.869–879, and Apollodorus, Library 3.13.6, have Thetis burn away the infant's mortal part by night and anoint him with ambrosia by day, until Peleus sees the child in the flames and cries out; Thetis abandons both and returns to the sea. The template is Demeter's attempt on Demophoon in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter 231–262. A grimmer variant in Lycophron, Alexandra 178–179, with Ptolemy Hephaestion (via Photius, Bibliotheca 190), has Thetis destroy six sons in the fire; Achilles, the seventh, is snatched out with a burnt ankle, which Peleus replaces with the ankle-bone of the giant Damysus. That is the root of the vulnerable heel: not a dry spot but a graft.

Homer has none of this. His Achilles bleeds when Asteropaeus grazes his forearm (Iliad 21.166–167) and needs Hephaestus' armour because his body is ordinary. Invulnerability is a folk-tale accretion the epic resisted, and it makes the arrow story necessary: an unwoundable man needs a loophole.

Pelion and Scyros

After Thetis leaves, Peleus hands the boy to Chiron on Pelion. Pindar, Nemean 3.43–63, has the six-year-old killing lions and boars and dragging the carcasses to the centaur, who raises him with his wife Philyra. Apollodorus 3.13.6 adds the diet of lion and boar entrails and bear marrow, and a folk etymology: he is Achilles because his lips (cheile) never touched a breast. Homer keeps a thinner Chiron: the source of Peleus' ash spear (Iliad 16.143–144) and of Achilles' medicine (11.831–832). Statius, Achilleid 2.96–167, lets Achilles narrate his own curriculum.

Where sources disagree. Homer's Phoenix claims to have raised Achilles from infancy, cutting his meat and holding him on his knees (Iliad 9.485–495), a human nurture with no room for a centaur. The lyric tradition preferred Chiron because it makes Achilles half-wild from the start; the Iliad prefers Phoenix because its Achilles must be socialised enough to be persuadable.

Scyros is where the tradition contradicts itself most openly. Homer's Achilles took Scyros by force (Iliad 9.667–668) and left a son, Neoptolemus, raised there (19.326–327; Odyssey 11.506–509). The Cypria, per Proclus, has him land there after a storm and marry Deidamia, Lycomedes' daughter. The famous version, in which Thetis hides him dressed as a girl among Lycomedes' daughters and Odysseus unmasks him with a trumpet and a spear, is first attested in the lost Scyrians of Sophocles and Euripides, then in Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.162–170, Hyginus, Fabulae 96, Apollodorus 3.13.8, and above all Statius, Achilleid 1.207–960. The son's alternative name Pyrrhus derives from Achilles' alias Pyrrha. The concealment is incompatible with the Iliad's Achilles, who sailed knowing the two fates; a hidden boy does not choose.

The two fates and the economy of kleos

In the embassy scene Achilles reports his mother's words: he carries two fates (dichthadias keras) to his death; stay and fight at Troy and his homecoming is lost but his kleos is imperishable (kleos aphthiton); go home and the fame is lost but he lives long (Iliad 9.410–416). The passage sits inside a refusal of Agamemnon's gift list, and its real argument is at 9.401–409: no quantity of cattle or tripods is worth a life, because the psyche once past the teeth cannot be bought back.

This is a crisis in the heroic economy. The norm is Sarpedon's at 12.310–328: kings eat the fat and drink the sweet wine because they stand in the front line, and since death waits anyway, one should go and win glory or give it. Prizes (time) and song (kleos) are supposed to be one currency, honour paid now and honour paid forever. Agamemnon broke the exchange by taking Briseis, and Achilles discovers that the two cannot be reconverted: gifts cannot restore honour, and honour cannot be eaten. Gregory Nagy (The Best of the Achaeans, 1979) read kleos aphthiton as an inherited Indo-European formula for what epic itself confers, so that the choice of fates is the poem naming its own function; Margalit Finkelberg (1986) objected that the phrase is not formulaic in the strict sense. The dispute matters less than the fact that Achilles treats his fame as something he could decline.

The choice is never made in Book 9. Achilles says he will sail tomorrow and does not. The decision comes at 18.98–126, after Patroclus' death, and it is vengeance over life, not glory over life: he will accept death when Zeus wishes, provided he can first kill Hector. Glory is a by-product of grief.

Achilles and Patroclus

The Iliad never names the bond. It gives Patroclus as the older man sent to advise (11.786–787), as the one person Achilles weeps for without limit (18.22–35), as the subject of the vow to Menoetius that he would be brought home alive (18.324–327), and as the ghost who asks that their bones share one urn (23.83–92), honoured in Odyssey 24.76–77. Both men sleep with captive women on the same night (9.663–668). The words used are philos and hetairos, which cover kin, comrade and beloved without deciding.

The fifth century decided. Aeschylus' Myrmidons (frr. 135–136 Radt, in Athenaeus 13.601a–b) had Achilles address the corpse with the words sebas de meron, the reverence of your thighs, and reproach it for being ungrateful for many kisses. In Plato, Symposium 179e–180b, Phaedrus accepts the erotic reading but says Aeschylus talks nonsense in making Achilles the lover: Homer makes him the younger and more beautiful, so he was the beloved who died for his lover, the rarer and nobler act, rewarded with the Isles of the Blest. Xenophon, Symposium 8.31, has Socrates deny it: Homer shows Patroclus as a comrade, not a lover. Aeschines, Against Timarchus 141–150, quotes the laments of Books 18 and 23 and argues that Homer concealed the eros because educated hearers would understand.

Where sources disagree. Four readings coexist in antiquity: silence (Homer), lover Achilles (Aeschylus), beloved Achilles (Plato's Phaedrus), chaste comradeship (Xenophon). Moderns split the same way. W. M. Clarke (1978) and Kenneth Dover (Greek Homosexuality, 1978) see the Iliad as compatible with a sexual bond it does not name; David Halperin ("Heroes and their Pals", 1990) groups the pair with Gilgamesh and Enkidu and David and Jonathan as a type of heroic friendship that is intense, exclusive and not pederastic. The Iliad is undecidable here; the Athenian debate tells you about Athens.

Menis, Briseis, and the Shield

The poem's first word is menin. Leonard Muellner (The Anger of Achilles, 1996) showed that menis is not ordinary rage (cholos) but a sanction normally reserved for gods when cosmic order is breached: Apollo's at 1.75, Zeus', Demeter's. Applied to a mortal it belongs to Achilles alone. This is the theology of the plot. Apollo's menis over the dishonoured priest opens the poem, Achilles' over his dishonoured time mirrors it, and Thetis carries the second to Olympus where Zeus' nod (1.524–530) makes a mortal grudge an instrument of divine will. The man whose birth was arranged to keep him from threatening Zeus becomes the one mortal whose anger operates at Zeus' scale. He lays the menis down at 19.67–68 and then exceeds it.

Briseis is the price-tag that turns out to be a person. Taken from Lyrnessus after Achilles killed her husband Mynes (2.689–694; 19.291–296), she is led from the hut unwilling, aekousa (1.348). In Book 9 Achilles claims to have loved her from the heart although she was won by the spear (9.341–343). Her single speech, the lament over Patroclus (19.282–300), reveals that Patroclus had promised to make her Achilles' wedded wife in Phthia. The scholia name her Hippodameia; Briseis is a patronymic. Through Dictys, Benoit de Sainte-Maure and Boccaccio she becomes Briseida and then Chaucer's Criseyde, which is how she reaches Shakespeare detached from Achilles.

The Shield (18.478–608) is the poem's view of what the war excludes: cosmos, then two cities, one at peace with a wedding and a lawsuit over a killed man's blood-price (18.497–508), one at war with a siege and an ambush; then ploughing, reaping, vintage, lions on cattle, a dance, Ocean on the rim. Oliver Taplin (1980) read it as ordinary life carried into battle on the arm of the man who has left it; the lawsuit answers Ajax's complaint at 9.632–636 that even a brother's killer is forgiven once the poine is paid, which Achilles alone refuses.

Hector, Priam, and the death

Achilles' treatment of Hector is a sustained refusal of the shield's world. He pierces the ankles and drags the corpse (22.395–404), drags it three times round Patroclus' tomb each dawn (24.14–18), and is kept from succeeding only because Aphrodite and Apollo preserve the body (23.184–191). Apollo's indictment at 24.33–54 is the poem's verdict: Achilles has destroyed pity (eleos) and has no aidos. To Lycaon he had put it in his own terms: Patroclus died, who was far better than you, and I too shall die (21.99–113). The cruelty is a levelling: no death matters because his own does not.

Book 24 undoes this without cancelling it. Priam kisses the hands that killed his sons (24.478–479); the two men weep for different dead (24.507–512); Achilles speaks of the two jars of Zeus and of Peleus, who like Priam has one son who will not tend his old age (24.527–551). Colin Macleod's commentary (1982) treats this as the poem's real conclusion, pity learnt through a shared condition. But Achilles still warns Priam not to provoke him (24.559–570). Pity is a truce, not a conversion.

The death is outside the Iliad, which only predicts it: by a god and a man (19.416–417), by Apollo's arrows (21.277–278), by Paris and Apollo at the Scaean Gates (22.359–360). Proclus' summary of Arctinus' Aethiopis gives the sequence: Achilles kills Memnon, routs the Trojans, bursts into the city and is killed by Paris and Apollo; Ajax carries the body while Odysseus holds off the Trojans; Thetis, the Nereids and the Muses mourn; Thetis snatches him from the pyre to the White Island.

Where sources disagree. Neither Homer nor, as far as the summary shows, the Aethiopis mentions the heel. A Chalcidian amphora of about 540 BC showed the dead Achilles with an arrow in the ankle, so the motif is archaic in art; in texts it appears in Apollodorus, Epitome 5.3, Hyginus, Fabulae 107, Quintus Smyrnaeus 3.60–63 and Statius 1.134. Dictys and Dares replace the battlefield death with an ambush in the temple of Thymbraean Apollo, where Achilles is lured by a promise of Polyxena; this unheroic version dominated the medieval West and lies behind Shakespeare.

After death: games, arms, the shade and the island

Agamemnon's ghost describes the funeral at Odyssey 24.36–94: seventeen days of mourning, the Nereids, the Muses singing the dirge, the bones placed with Patroclus' in a golden amphora Dionysus gave Thetis, a tomb on the headland over the Hellespont, and prizes set out by Thetis for the games. The Aethiopis adds the quarrel of Odysseus and Ajax over the arms; the Little Iliad (scholia to Aristophanes, Knights 1056) has it settled by overhearing Trojan girls on the wall, Pindar, Nemean 8.23–34, by secret ballot, the Odyssey (11.543–567) by Trojan captives and Athena. The first act of Achilles' afterlife is the destruction of the second-best Achaean.

Two afterlives then compete. In Odyssey 11.467–540 the shade rejects consolation: he would rather be a hired labourer (thes) to a landless man than king over all the dead (11.488–491). The usual rendering "slave" is too strong; a thes is a free man with nothing, and that is the point. The Achilles who refused gifts because life cannot be bought confirms it from the other side. The other tradition removes him from Hades: the Aethiopis sends him to Leuke; Pindar puts him in the Isles of the Blest, taken there by Thetis (Olympian 2.79–80), or on a bright island in the Euxine (Nemean 4.49–50); Euripides, Andromache 1259–1262, has Thetis promise Peleus he will see their son living there.

Leuke is a real island, modern Zmiinyi off the Danube mouth, and the cult is documented. Arrian, Periplus of the Euxine 21–23, describes a temple, offerings left by sailors, and Achilles appearing in dreams to give sailing directions; Olbian inscriptions call him Achilles Pontarches; Alcaeus already called him lord of Scythia (fr. 354). Pausanias 3.19.11–13 tells of Leonymus of Croton, who saw Achilles on the island married to Helen; Philostratus, Heroicus 53–57, elaborates the household. Guy Hedreen (1991) and Hildebrecht Hommel (1980) debate whether this is hero-cult for a dead man or an originally divine Achilles the epic demoted.

Where sources disagree. His consort on the island is Helen in Pausanias and Philostratus; Medea in Ibycus (fr. 10) and Simonides, per the scholia on Apollonius 4.814, and Apollonius' Hera promises exactly that (4.811–815); Iphigenia, renamed Orsilochia, in Nicander as excerpted by Antoninus Liberalis 27. The Polyxena sacrifice attaches the tomb to this afterlife: Proclus' summary of the Iliou Persis ends with her slaughter at Achilles' grave, a Tyrrhenian amphora of about 570 BC shows Neoptolemus doing it, and Euripides, Hecuba 37–41 and 521–582, makes the ghost demand her as his prize. Whether he wanted a bride, a blood-offering or a wind is left open.

Reception

Alexander crossed to Troy in 334 BC and, according to Arrian, Anabasis 1.12.1, garlanded Achilles' tomb while Hephaestion garlanded Patroclus'; Plutarch, Alexander 15.8–9, adds that he anointed the stele, ran naked round it, and called Achilles fortunate to have had a faithful friend in life and a great herald after death. Olympias' Aeacid line claimed descent from Neoptolemus, and after Hephaestion's death Alexander cut his hair over the corpse as Achilles had (Arrian 7.14.4).

Catullus 64.338–370 gives the Fates' wedding-song for Peleus and Thetis and lets it prophesy the child: a hero who will choke the Scamander with corpses and whose final witness will be Polyxena, her blood soaking his high tomb. The whole career becomes an atrocity foreseen at the moment of joy. Statius' unfinished Achilleid (c. AD 95) turns to the boy: the dress, Deidamia, Odysseus' unmasking, the account of Chiron. P. J. Heslin (The Transvestite Achilles, 2005) reads it as a meditation on how masculinity is put on, and it is the main reason the Scyros story, not the fire or the Styx, dominated the medieval Achilles.

Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida (c. 1602) inherits the Dictys–Dares–Caxton Achilles: proud, idle, sulking for love of Polyxena, manipulated by Ulysses, and finally having his Myrmidons kill an unarmed Hector while he watches (5.8). Thersites calls Patroclus Achilles' "masculine whore" (5.1). This is Achilles with the kleos drained out. Madeline Miller's The Song of Achilles (2011) reverses the polarity: narrated by Patroclus, it assembles Chiron, Scyros and Deidamia from Statius and Apollodorus, follows Phaedrus in making Achilles the beloved rather than the lover, and ends with the shared urn. Its popularity shows which ancient reading the present prefers.

What Achilles is for

Achilles is the figure through whom Greek culture priced its own ideal. Sarpedon's logic is that since death is certain, the only rational use of a life is to spend it for honour. Achilles accepts the premise and tests the arithmetic, and the tradition keeps both results: the Iliad 9 Achilles who knows the fame is not worth it and takes it anyway for Patroclus' sake, and the Odyssey 11 Achilles who confirms from Hades that it was not. The island cult is the third answer, the one that cheats: the hero who did not really die. Socrates in Plato, Apology 28c–d, took the first Achilles as his model for refusing to abandon his post; Jean-Pierre Vernant's "La belle mort" (1982) named the ideology, the beautiful death that freezes a man at his peak and hands him to song. Achilles is for asking whether a short, remembered life beats a long, unremembered one, and for refusing to let either answer stand unchallenged.

Self-test

  1. Which source first states that Thetis' son by a god would overthrow his father, and how is the problem solved?
    Answer

    Pindar, Isthmian 8.26–48, where Themis prophesies it and advises marrying Thetis to the mortal Peleus so the son is mortal.

  2. Which version of Achilles' infancy is older, Styx-dipping or fire-and-ambrosia, and where is each first attested?
    Answer

    Fire-and-ambrosia is older (Apollonius, Argonautica 4.869–879; Apollodorus 3.13.6, modelled on the Demeter–Demophoon story). Styx-dipping first appears in Statius, Achilleid 1.133–134, with the heel specified only by Servius and Fulgentius.

  3. What is the strongest evidence that Homer's Achilles is not invulnerable?
    Answer

    Asteropaeus grazes his forearm and draws blood at Iliad 21.166–167, and he needs divine armour.

  4. How do Homer's and the later tradition's accounts of Achilles' arrival on Scyros conflict?
    Answer

    Homer says he conquered Scyros (Iliad 9.667–668); the Cypria has a storm landing; Sophocles, Euripides, Ovid, Hyginus and Statius have Thetis hide him there disguised as a girl, which is incompatible with his knowing choice of fates.

  5. In which book does Achilles actually commit to dying at Troy, and what motivates him?
    Answer

    Book 18 (18.98–126), after Patroclus' death; the motive is vengeance on Hector, not glory for its own sake.

  6. Name the four ancient positions on the Achilles–Patroclus bond and one source for each.
    Answer

    Silence or ambiguity (Homer); Achilles as lover (Aeschylus, Myrmidons); Achilles as beloved (Plato, Symposium 179e–180b); chaste comradeship (Xenophon, Symposium 8.31). Aeschines, Against Timarchus 141–150, holds Homer concealed an erotic bond.

  7. Why does the word menis matter theologically?
    Answer

    Following Muellner, menis is the anger of gods at breaches of cosmic order; Achilles is the only mortal to whom it is applied, so his wrath mirrors Apollo's and is ratified by Zeus' nod (1.524–530).

  8. What does the lawsuit on the Shield (18.497–508) have to do with Achilles' refusal in Book 9?
    Answer

    It shows a community settling a killing by blood-price, the ordinary poine that Ajax (9.632–636) says even a brother's killer accepts and that Achilles alone refuses.

  9. Where did the Aethiopis send Achilles after death, and which later text makes the shade regret death?
    Answer

    The Aethiopis has Thetis snatch him from the pyre to the White Island (Leuke); Odyssey 11.488–491 has the shade say he would rather be a landless man's hired labourer than rule the dead.

  10. What did Alexander and Hephaestion do at Troy in 334 BC, and who reports it?
    Answer

    Alexander garlanded Achilles' tomb and Hephaestion garlanded Patroclus' (Arrian, Anabasis 1.12.1); Plutarch, Alexander 15, adds the anointing and naked race.

Carry forward

  1. Achilles is a contained cosmic threat: the Thetis prophecy means his mortality is a design decision by Zeus, and the Iliad's menis is the residue of the god he was prevented from being.
  2. The two fates expose the heroic economy: time and kleos are supposed to be interchangeable, and Achilles' career, from refusing the gifts to the regretful shade in Odyssey 11, is the tradition's own audit of that exchange.
  3. Every later Achilles chooses among inherited variants rather than inventing: the Scyros concealment (Statius), the treacherous ambush (Dictys to Shakespeare), the beloved rather than lover (Phaedrus to Miller). Knowing which variant a text picks tells you what that culture wanted from him.

GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.2 · 3,190 words

Agamemnon and the kingship of the Atreids

The sceptre: a genealogy of authorityAnax andron and the Mycenaean wanaxThe limits of his authorityThe Catalogue of Ships as a political mapHomer's king and the tyrant of tragedyIphigenia: four moral weightsChryseis, Briseis, CassandraReturn, carpet, murder; and the shade in HadesCult, Sparta, and the archaeology that is not hisWhat does a king owe to those he commands?Self-testCarry forward

The sceptre: a genealogy of authority

When Agamemnon rises to speak in Iliad 2.100–108, the poet pauses over the object in his hand. Hephaestus made the sceptre and gave it to Zeus; Zeus to Hermes; Hermes to Pelops; Pelops to Atreus "shepherd of the people"; Atreus, dying, to Thyestes "rich in flocks"; Thyestes to Agamemnon, "to rule over many islands and all Argos". The authority is two steps from a god's forge, and the house of Pelops is an orderly succession.

That orderliness is the point. There is no golden lamb, no seduction of Aerope, no banquet of children, no curse of Myrtilus. Homer either does not know or deliberately excludes the Tantalid horrors that Aeschylus makes the engine of the Oresteia; Tantalus is never named in either epic. The Homeric sceptre carries only themistes, the ordinances of Zeus. Nestor states the theology: Zeus gave Agamemnon "the sceptre and the themistes, that you may take counsel for them" (9.98–99); Odysseus repeats it while restoring order, "let there be one lord, one king, to whom the son of Kronos gave sceptre and themistes" (2.204–206).

Yet the sceptre is also a stick. Achilles swears on his and hurls it down (1.234–246); Odysseus takes Agamemnon's from his hand (2.186) and uses it to beat the ranks back to assembly and then to beat Thersites (2.265–268). The emblem of Zeus-given rule is, in the same book, a bludgeon.

Where sources disagree. Pausanias (9.40.11–12) says Chaeronea worshipped a sceptre it called "the spear", claiming it was Homer's, with a priest and daily sacrifices; no other source corroborates this local appropriation. More seriously, every post-Homeric genealogist (Apollodorus, Epitome 2.10–15; the tragedians) has Thyestes and Aegisthus expel the Atreidae, with Agamemnon regaining the throne by force. Whether Homer suppressed the feud or whether it had not yet been invented is uncertain.

Anax andron and the Mycenaean wanax

Agamemnon's signature formula is anax andron, "lord of men", some forty times in the Iliad. Zeus, Apollo and Poseidon are anax, and metre lends the title to minor figures such as Anchises and Eumelus, but its concentration on Agamemnon is deliberate. It stands above basileus, the ordinary word Homer uses for every chieftain in the camp. Agamemnon is one basileus among many; he alone is habitually anax andron.

The Linear B tablets (thirteenth century BC) give the word's prehistory. The palace ruler at Pylos and Knossos is the wa-na-ka, wanax, whose initial w- Homeric metre still "hears" in hiatus. At Pylos his temenos is three times that of the lawagetas, "leader of the people" (PY Er 312); craftsmen are wa-na-ka-te-ro, "royal"; he appears in offering and initiation records. The qa-si-re-u (basileus) is a minor local official, in one case over a group of bronze-smiths. Homer preserves this hierarchy in fossil form: by the eighth century the wanax was a poetic word and basileus had risen to fill the vacancy. Agamemnon commanding a camp of basileis is the memory of a system, not the description of one.

Where sources disagree. L. R. Palmer read the Pylian wanax as a sacral king and saw Homer's divine anax as a trace of this. T. G. Palaima argues the word is probably non-Indo-European with real cultic associations but no divine kingship; P. Carlier (La royauté en Grèce avant Alexandre, 1984) stresses administration over cult. The tablets are too laconic to settle it.

The limits of his authority

The Iliad is an experiment on how far a paramount king's power reaches when he has no palace, bureaucracy or standing army behind him, only consent.

Book 1

Agamemnon's power is first shown as refusal: he threatens Chryses (1.26–32) and, when Calchas tells him to return the girl, demands an immediate replacement geras (1.118–120). Achilles calls him "most grasping of men" (1.122) and demoboros basileus, "people-devouring king" (1.231). Nestor's mediation (1.254–284) states the rule the poem will test: Achilles must not "strive against a sceptre-bearing king", but Agamemnon must not take the girl "whom the sons of the Achaeans gave him". Both halves are ignored. Agamemnon can take Briseis because nobody physically stops him; he cannot make Achilles fight.

Book 2: Diapeira and Thersites

Deceived by the Dream, Agamemnon "tests" the army by proposing flight (2.110–141). They bolt for the ships; only Athena, through Odysseus, turns them. The king does not know the mood of his own men. Then Thersites, "the ugliest man who came to Troy" (2.216), repeats Achilles' charges almost verbatim: Agamemnon's huts are full of bronze and women the army won for him; "let us sail home and leave him to digest his prizes" (2.236–238). Odysseus beats him and the army laughs. Order is restored, but the complaint has now been voiced by the best warrior and the worst, and refuted by neither.

Where sources disagree. W. G. Thalmann (1988) reads Thersites as a scapegoat through whom heroic ideology disciplines dissent by laughter; P. W. Rose reads the scene as the demos briefly speaking. The later tradition (Proclus on the Aethiopis; Apollodorus, Epitome 5.1) made him Diomedes' kinsman, killed by Achilles for mocking his grief over Penthesilea, which suggests more than a comic foil.

Book 9: the Embassy

Agamemnon weeps and proposes flight sincerely (9.17–28). Diomedes answers that Zeus "gave you the sceptre to be honoured above all, but not courage, which is the greatest power" (9.37–39). Nestor tells him he "dishonoured a mighty man" (9.109–111); he concedes, "I was blinded, I do not deny it" (9.115–116), lists a king's ransom (9.121–157), and ruins it: "let him yield to me, since I am more kingly (basileuteros) and older" (9.160–161). Odysseus silently omits that clause when he delivers the offer. Achilles refuses anyway. The king can command gifts; he cannot command what gifts are meant to buy.

Book 10: the Night Council

Sleepless, tearing his hair (10.3–16), Agamemnon convenes the chiefs by night and gives one instruction that reads as self-criticism: Diomedes must choose a companion by merit, "not looking to birth, even if he is more kingly" (10.237–239), a glance at Menelaus. The poem's one meritocratic sentence comes from the man whose rank is the problem. A scholion on 10.1 reports that the Doloneia was inserted by Pisistratus, and many analysts treat it as a later addition; its Agamemnon is nonetheless consistent with Books 2, 9 and 14.

Book 19

Achilles renounces his wrath in nine lines (19.56–73). Agamemnon's reply is long and evasive: Zeus, Fate and the Erinys blinded him, as Ate once blinded Zeus at the birth of Heracles (19.86–136). He re-offers the gifts and swears he never touched Briseis (19.258–265). Nowhere does he say, in the first person, that he did wrong. The reconciliation is Achilles' indifference, Odysseus's ceremony and Agamemnon's theology of excuse.

He proposes flight three times (2, 9, 14); on the third Odysseus says he should command "some other, inglorious army" (14.84). He insults Odysseus and Diomedes on review (4.338–400), fights magnificently once (Book 11), and is harsher to suppliants than any Greek (6.55–65; 11.122–147). Priam, from the wall, never saw a man "so kingly" (3.170). Appearance and performance diverge.

Is this a critique of kingship? Oliver Taplin ("Agamemnon's Role in the Iliad", 1990) argues Homer draws a deliberately inadequate king. Dean Hammer (The Iliad as Politics, 2002) and David Elmer (The Poetics of Consent, 2013) read the poem as working out when collective approval, epainos, may be withheld from a leader; Kurt Raaflaub sets it in the emergent eighth-century polis; Moses Finley denied it reflects stable institutions at all. The safe statement: the Iliad never questions that there should be a sceptre, only whether this man deserves to hold it.

The Catalogue of Ships as a political map

The Catalogue (2.494–759) lists twenty-nine contingents and about 1,186 ships. Agamemnon brings 100 (2.569–580), and the poet infers rank from number: "he was the best, since he led by far the most people". Nestor brings 90, Diomedes and Idomeneus 80, Menelaus 60, Achilles 50, Odysseus 12. Thucydides (1.9) reasoned from this that Agamemnon led through power and fear, not Tyndareus's oaths, backed by inherited Pelopid wealth and the strongest navy.

His territory is Mycenae, Corinth, Cleonae, Sicyon and the Achaean coast to Helice and Aegion: the north-east Peloponnese. Argos and Tiryns belong to Diomedes (2.559–568), contradicting "all Argos" at 2.108 and the Odyssey's "corner of horse-pasturing Argos" (3.263). The seven cities "near sandy Pylos" he offers Achilles (9.149–153) imply a reach into Messenia. The map is a composite of claims, not a survey.

Where sources disagree. Hope Simpson and Lazenby (1970) argued the Catalogue preserves Mycenaean geography, since it names places abandoned after the Bronze Age and omits Dorian centres; Giovannini (1969) and Visser (1997) argued for Archaic composition. The Boeotians coming first, with their sixty-man detail, has suggested a Boeotian origin. No consensus exists.

Homer's king and the tyrant of tragedy

The Homeric Agamemnon is anxious, generous, quick to despair, brutal in battle, insecure in council. He is never a tyrant, because the concept belongs to the seventh century. Tragedy, performed in a democracy that had expelled its tyrants before an audience that was itself an assembly, recast him. Aeschylus's Agamemnon thanks the gods and promises to purge the city "by cutting or burning" (Ag. 848–850), a man who rules by force; then resists the crimson cloths, "honour me as a man, not a god" (925), and yields in six lines. Sophocles' Ajax (1226–1315) shows him arrogant and legalistic, cowed by Odysseus. Euripides goes furthest: in Hecuba he will not help openly because "the army would say I did it for Cassandra's sake" (854–863); in Iphigenia at Aulis Menelaus accuses him of canvassing humbly for command and growing haughty once he had it (337–375), and he confesses "Hellas compels me" (1271–1275). The king who could not control the army has become the king controlled by it.

Iphigenia: four moral weights

Homer knows nothing of the sacrifice; Agamemnon offers Achilles one of three living daughters, Chrysothemis, Laodice and Iphianassa (9.144–145). The Cypria, in Proclus's summary, is the earliest source: Agamemnon shoots a deer at Aulis and boasts he surpasses Artemis; she sends contrary winds; Calchas prescribes the sacrifice; Iphigenia is lured by a false marriage to Achilles; Artemis substitutes a deer and makes the girl immortal among the Taurians. The Hesiodic Catalogue of Women (fr. 23a M-W) has "Iphimede" saved to become Artemis Einodia. The offence is a hunter's boast, the punishment divine, the girl does not die.

Aeschylus removes the rescue. The parodos (Ag. 184–247) gives the eagles and the pregnant hare, Artemis's anger half-explained, and quotes Agamemnon: "how can I desert the fleet and fail my allies?" (212–213). The chorus judges: he "put on the yoke of necessity" and "breathed an impious change of mind" (218–221); he "dared to become his daughter's sacrificer" (224–225). Then the gag, the saffron robe falling, the glance that struck each sacrificer "as in a picture" (231–247). Necessity is real and the choice is his; Clytemnestra's "he sacrificed his own child" (1415–1418) is the debt coming due.

Euripides wrote it twice. Iphigenia among the Taurians (c. 414) restores the rescue and tells it from the victim's side; she blames Helen, Calchas and Odysseus more than her father (354–377), who becomes a remote cause. Iphigenia at Aulis (405) inverts this: Agamemnon writes to stop her coming, recants, is caught by Menelaus, weeps, and yields once the army knows. Iphigenia, who begged for life at 1211–1252, volunteers at 1368–1401, "I give my body to Hellas". Moral agency passes from king to girl; the king is left with fear. Aristotle (Poetics 1454a) cited her reversal as inconsistent character.

Where sources disagree. The IA was produced posthumously and is the most interpolated Euripidean text; the messenger speech reporting the deer-substitution (1532–1629) is almost certainly spurious, so whether Euripides let her die is uncertain. Why Artemis is angry in Aeschylus is also unresolved: the hare omen is the surface motive, and some (Lloyd-Jones) see the Cypria's boast behind it.

Chryseis, Briseis, Cassandra

Three captured women mark Agamemnon's career, each a geras that signals his precedence over his peers. Chryseis, taken at Hypoplacian Thebe (1.366–369), he prefers to Clytemnestra "in form, stature, mind and work" (1.113–115); a god forces her return. Briseis, taken at Lyrnessus by Achilles, who killed her husband (2.689–693), he seizes as compensation and twice swears he never slept with her (9.132–134; 19.258–265). Her one speech, the lament for Patroclus (19.282–300), recalls his promise that Achilles would make her his wedded wife; she alone speaks of the geras economy from inside it.

Cassandra is his prize from the sack. In Homer she is betrothed to Othryoneus (13.365–369), first to see Priam bring Hector's body home (24.699–706), and killed over Agamemnon's body (Od. 11.421–423). Tragedy gives her the voice Briseis lacks: in Aeschylus (Ag. 1035–1330) she sees the murder before it happens; in Euripides' Trojan Women (353–405) she sings her own wedding song and prophesies that her marriage will destroy the house of Atreus. Each woman is the token of the king's status and the instrument of its undoing: Chryseis through Apollo, Briseis through Achilles, Cassandra through Clytemnestra.

Return, carpet, murder; and the shade in Hades

The Odyssey tells the homecoming three times before Agamemnon does. Zeus makes Aegisthus the paradigm of the warned transgressor (1.35–43). Nestor (3.254–312) says Aegisthus seduced Clytemnestra despite a bard set to guard her, killed Agamemnon, ruled seven years and died at Orestes' hand in the eighth. Proteus (4.512–537) has Agamemnon blown round Malea, landing in joy, ambushed at a banquet with twenty men. In every Homeric version Aegisthus kills and Clytemnestra assists.

Aeschylus reverses this. Clytemnestra kills, in the bath, with sword and entangling robe. Before it, the carpet scene (905–974): she spreads crimson cloths, he protests that such honours belong to gods, she argues him down, and he walks barefoot on the wealth of his house ("there is the sea; who shall drain it dry?", 958). Over the body she claims justice for Iphigenia (1372–1398). Pindar (Pythian 11.22–25) asks what the tradition never settled: was it the daughter's slaughter, or another man's bed?

Where sources disagree. Homer places the murder at Agamemnon's house in Mycenae or "Argos"; Stesichorus and Simonides (scholia on Euripides, Orestes 46) and Pindar (Pyth. 11.31–32) set it at Amyclae near Sparta; Aeschylus moved the Oresteia to Argos, almost certainly for Athens's alliance with Argos in 462/1. The weapon shifts from sword (Aeschylus) to axe (Sophocles, Electra 99; Euripides).

In Hades (Od. 11.385–464) Agamemnon died "like an ox at the manger", and draws the lesson: "never be gentle with your wife; do not tell her everything" (441–443), exempting Penelope; he urges Odysseus to land in secret (455–456). In Book 24 he envies Achilles' death at Troy (24.36–94) and contrasts Penelope's "gracious song" with Clytemnestra's "hateful song for women" (24.192–202). He is the Odyssey's negative template: the king who came home openly, trusted his house and died at dinner. Odysseus does everything he did not.

Cult, Sparta, and the archaeology that is not his

Pausanias (2.16.6–7) saw at Mycenae the tombs of Atreus, Agamemnon, Eurymedon, Cassandra's twins Teledamus and Pelops, and Electra, inside the walls; Clytemnestra and Aegisthus lay "a little outside, not deemed worthy". About a kilometre away the British School excavated (1950–53) the Agamemnoneion, a shrine with votives from the late eighth century and Hellenistic sherds inscribed to Agamemnon. Hero cult at Mycenae begins as the epics take fixed form.

Sparta claimed him too. Clytemnestra and Helen were Tyndareus's daughters; Euripides (IA 1148–1156) gives Clytemnestra a first husband, Tantalus son of Thyestes, whom Agamemnon killed with her infant. Pausanias (3.19.6) saw a tomb of Agamemnon and a shrine of Cassandra at Amyclae; Sparta fetched Orestes' bones from Tegea (Herodotus 1.67–68); Gelon mocked Spartan pride with "Agamemnon son of Pelops would groan" (Hdt. 7.159); Lycophron (Alexandra 1369) attests a Spartan Zeus Agamemnon. Argos and Sparta fought over the Pelopid inheritance as title to Peloponnesian hegemony, and the lyric poets who moved the murder to Amyclae took Sparta's side.

Then Schliemann. In 1876, following Pausanias literally, he dug inside the Lion Gate and found Grave Circle A: five shaft graves (a sixth by Stamatakis in 1877) with gold masks, diadems, inlaid daggers, and the mask from Grave V. The telegram line "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon" is probably apocryphal; the identification was his. It cannot stand. The shaft graves date to c. 1600–1450 BC, three to four centuries before any Trojan War date (Eratosthenes' 1184/3; Troy VIIa's fall c. 1180; Troy VI c. 1300). The Lion Gate and the wall extension that enclosed the old graves belong to c. 1250, the right century but anonymous: no Linear B tablet from Mycenae names a king. The "Treasury of Atreus" and "Tomb of Clytemnestra" are tholoi of c. 1250 and 1220, labelled by modern guides. Pausanias himself saw the Lion Gate (2.16.5); it was never lost. Schliemann found the graves of a dynasty the Mycenaeans venerated enough to wall in; its names are gone.

Where sources disagree. David Traill (Schliemann of Troy, 1995), with William Calder before him, questioned the mask's authenticity on its upturned moustache and Schliemann's record of fabrication at Troy; most specialists (Demakopoulou, Dickinson) accept it as genuine, while agreeing it is not Agamemnon's. The Hittite "king of Ahhiyawa" of the Tawagalawa letter (c. 1250) was treated as a Great King but is unnamed; Forrer's equation of Attarissiya with Atreus is generally rejected.

What does a king owe to those he commands?

The Iliad states the obligation in the mouth of a lie: the false Dream tells Agamemnon that "a man of counsel, to whom peoples are entrusted and so many cares, ought not sleep all night" (2.24–25). Nestor supplies the content: the sceptre brings themistes, so the king must "speak and listen, and carry out what another says for the good" (9.100–102). Diomedes adds that honour without courage is empty; Achilles, that a king who eats the people's winnings devours them. Assembled from its critics, the poem's answer is that a king owes counsel, restraint, a fair division of time, and the capacity to listen; he holds the sceptre on a consent he cannot compel.

Tragedy answers what the epic poses. Aeschylus takes the one act of command Homer never mentions, a child for a fleet, and makes it the unpaid debt collected in the bath; the cycle ends only when judgment leaves the house for the city's court in the Eumenides. Euripides pushes further: in the IA the king owes the army so much that nothing is left for his daughter, and the army, not Zeus, now holds the sceptre. Homer's Agamemnon could not make Achilles fight; Euripides' cannot make himself stop. Between them lies the Greek discovery that authority is a relation, not a possession, and that a sceptre handed down from Zeus is still a stick in the hand of a man who does not know what he owes.

Self-test

  1. Trace the sceptre's genealogy in Iliad 2.100–108 and say what is conspicuously absent from it.
    Answer

    Hephaestus to Zeus to Hermes to Pelops to Atreus to Thyestes to Agamemnon. Absent is any trace of the Pelopid feud: Atreus and Thyestes hand on peacefully, with no golden lamb, cannibal banquet or curse.

  2. What is the relationship between Homeric anax and basileus, and how do the Linear B tablets illuminate it?
    Answer

    In Homer anax is the grander title (gods, Agamemnon), basileus the ordinary word for any chieftain. In Linear B the wanax is the palace ruler with the largest temenos, the qa-si-re-u a minor local official. Homer preserves a Mycenaean hierarchy in fossil form.

  3. How many times does Agamemnon propose abandoning the war, and which proposal is insincere?
    Answer

    Three: Books 2, 9 and 14. Only the first, the Diapeira, is a test; the others are sincere and are rebuked by Diomedes and Odysseus respectively.

  4. What clause does Odysseus omit when conveying Agamemnon's offer to Achilles in Book 9, and why does it matter?
    Answer

    "Let him yield to me, since I am more kingly and older" (9.160–161). Agamemnon cannot separate compensation from submission, and Odysseus knows the demand would wreck the embassy.

  5. Which cities does Agamemnon lead in the Catalogue of Ships, and who holds Argos?
    Answer

    Mycenae, Corinth, Cleonae, Sicyon and the Achaean coast to Helice and Aegion, with 100 ships. Argos and Tiryns belong to Diomedes (80 ships), contradicting "all Argos" at 2.108.

  6. How does the Cypria explain Artemis's anger at Aulis, and how does Aeschylus differ?
    Answer

    In the Cypria Agamemnon shoots a deer and boasts he surpasses Artemis; she substitutes a deer and saves Iphigenia. Aeschylus gives the eagles-and-hare omen, leaves the motive obscure, and removes the rescue: the girl dies and the choice is Agamemnon's.

  7. In Homer, who kills Agamemnon, and how does Aeschylus change it?
    Answer

    In every Odyssey account (1.35–43; 3.254–312; 4.512–537; 11.405–434) Aegisthus kills him at a banquet with Clytemnestra's complicity. Aeschylus has Clytemnestra kill him herself, in the bath, with sword and robe, citing Iphigenia.

  8. What advice does Agamemnon's shade give Odysseus in Odyssey 11, and how does Odysseus act on it?
    Answer

    Not to trust his wife fully and to land in secret (11.441–456). Odysseus returns disguised and tests Penelope; Agamemnon is the negative template for the second half of the poem.

  9. Why can the "mask of Agamemnon" not be Agamemnon's?
    Answer

    It comes from the Grave Circle A shaft graves, c. 1600–1450 BC, three to four centuries before any plausible Trojan War date (c. 1300–1180). The Lion Gate (c. 1250) is the right century, but no name is attached to anyone at Mycenae.

  10. Name two ways Sparta laid claim to Agamemnon.
    Answer

    Any two of: Clytemnestra and Helen as Tyndareus's daughters; the tomb of Agamemnon and shrine of Cassandra at Amyclae (Pausanias 3.19.6), where Stesichorus, Simonides and Pindar set the murder; Orestes' bones fetched from Tegea (Hdt. 1.67–68); the cult of Zeus Agamemnon.

Carry forward

  1. Homeric kingship is a relation of consent, not a possession: the sceptre comes from Zeus, but the Iliad shows it cannot compel a peer, and the obligation it carries is counsel, restraint and a fair division of honour.
  2. Each age rewrites Agamemnon to answer its own question: Homer's anxious paramount chief becomes Aeschylus's debtor to his house and Euripides' politician captive to the army, and the Iphigenia story is the hinge on which that rewriting turns.
  3. Mycenae's archaeology confirms a thirteenth-century palace-state ruled by a wanax that venerated older royal graves, but attaches no name; Agamemnon is a figure of cult and poetry, claimed by Argos and Sparta alike, never of record.

GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.3 · 3,279 words

Hector, Priam and the Trojan side

The house of PriamThe senior TrojansHectorPriamHecuba and Andromache after TroyThe alliesAre the Trojans foreign?Wilusa and the Luwian hypothesisTroy to RomeThe poem's refusalSelf-testCarry forward

The house of Priam

Priam tells Achilles that he fathered fifty sons, nineteen "from one womb" and the rest by women of the palace (Homer, Iliad 24.495–497). That sentence fixes what the Greeks found most striking about the Trojan royal house: its size and its polygamy. Hecuba, daughter of the Phrygian Dymas (Iliad 16.718–719), is the matriarch; Laothoe is the named secondary wife, mother of Lycaon and Polydorus (21.84–91). The family descends from Dardanus through Ilus, the senior line, while the junior line of Assaracus runs to Anchises and Aeneas (20.215–240):

Zeus
└─ Dardanus
   └─ Erichthonius
      └─ Tros
         ├─ Ilus ─ Laomedon ─ Priam (and Tithonus, Lampus, Clytius, Hicetaon)
         └─ Assaracus ─ Capys ─ Anchises ─ Aeneas
ChildIn the IliadLater tradition
HectorCommander; killed Book 22Hero cult at Thebes (Pausanias 9.18.5)
Paris / AlexandrosDuel Book 3; archerKilled by Philoctetes (Little Iliad)
Helenus"Best of augurs" (6.76)Captured, reveals Troy's fate (Sophocles, Philoctetes 604–613); marries Andromache
DeiphobusHector's favourite brother (22.233–234)Marries Helen after Paris (Odyssey 8.517–520); mutilated by Menelaus (Virgil, Aeneid 6.494–534)
TroilusNamed once, already dead (24.257)Ambushed by Achilles at the Thymbraean Apollo (Cypria; François Vase); Troy stands if he reaches twenty (Plautus, Bacchides 953–954)
PolydorusSon of Laothoe, killed by Achilles (20.407–418)Son of Hecuba, murdered by Polymestor (Euripides, Hecuba)
CassandraFairest daughter (13.365–366); first to see Priam return (24.699–706); no prophecyApollo's cursed prophetess (Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1202–1212); raped by Ajax; killed with Agamemnon (Odyssey 11.421–423)
PolyxenaAbsentSacrificed at Achilles' tomb (Iliou Persis; Euripides, Hecuba 518–582)
LaodiceFairest daughter (3.124; 6.252), wife of HelicaonSwallowed by the earth at the sack (Apollodorus, Epitome 5.25)
Where sources disagree. The Iliad is inconsistent about which daughter is "fairest": Laodice in Books 3 and 6, Cassandra in Book 13. Polydorus has two incompatible mothers and deaths. Hecuba's father is Dymas in Homer but Cisseus in Euripides (Hecuba 3); Apollodorus (Library 3.12.5) lists both. Cassandra's prophetic gift is post-Homeric; the Iliad gives prophecy to Helenus, her twin only in later sources.

Two stories about this house were told as omens. Hecuba, pregnant with Paris, dreamed she bore a firebrand that burned the city (Pindar, Paean 8a; Euripides, Trojan Women 919–922). And Priam began as the thing ransomed: when Heracles killed Laomedon, the boy Podarces was bought back by his sister Hesione and renamed Priamos, read by Greeks as "the purchased one" (Apollodorus, Library 2.6.4).

The senior Trojans

Antenor is the elder statesman and the peace party. He hosted Menelaus and Odysseus when they came to demand Helen (Iliad 3.203–224) and tells the assembly of Book 7 that she and her goods should go back (7.347–353); Paris refuses. His wife Theano, priestess of Athena, leads the women's failed prayer (6.297–311). Later tradition turns his reasonableness into treason: the Greeks spare his house, marked with a leopard skin (Pausanias 10.27.3 on Polygnotus' painting), and he founds Patavium (Livy 1.1.1–3).

Anchises is in the Iliad only a horse-breeder (5.265–272); his seduction by Aphrodite on Ida belongs to the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite. Aeneas is treated with an oddly protective hand. Aphrodite and Apollo pull him away from Diomedes (5.311–346), Poseidon from Achilles (20.288–339), and Poseidon states why: Aeneas is fated to survive so that the line of Dardanus does not perish and "his children's children" will rule (20.302–308). Aeneas also resents Priam, who "did not honour him" (13.459–461). The poem knows a rival branch.

Where sources disagree. Whom did Poseidon mean? Demetrius of Scepsis, cited by Strabo (13.1.52–53), read the prophecy as referring to the Aeneadae who ruled at Scepsis in the Troad, which would make the lines local dynastic propaganda inside the poem. Rome's reading comes much later. The text names no place.

Polydamas, son of Panthous and born the same night as Hector (18.251), is the counsellor whose advice is sound and almost always rejected. He reads the omen of the eagle and the snake as a warning to withdraw (12.210–229), answered by Hector's "one omen is best: to fight for one's country" (12.243), and after Achilles reappears he urges retreat behind the walls (18.254–283), rejected by acclamation. He exists to make Hector's final error legible as a choice.

Hector

The aristeia and Book 6

Hector's great day runs from Book 8 to Book 17 with Zeus's explicit backing (11.186–194). Its peak is the smashing of the Achaean gate with a boulder "no two men could lift" (12.445–471), the firing of Protesilaus' ship (15.704–746) and the killing of Patroclus (16.818–867). Yet the poem frames the aristeia so that it never reads as pure triumph. Sarpedon tells Hector he leaves the allies to do his fighting (5.471–492); Glaucus calls him a coward for abandoning Sarpedon's body (17.142–168); Zeus, watching him put on Achilles' armour, pities a doomed man who will never return it to Andromache (17.198–208).

Book 6 is the poem's one domestic interlude and it is given to the Trojans. Hector refuses Hecuba's wine (6.264–268), rebukes Paris in his bedroom (6.325–331), and meets Andromache at the Scaean gate. She reminds us who she is: daughter of Eetion of Thebe-under-Placus, whose father and seven brothers Achilles killed in one day (6.414–428); Hector is "father and lady mother and brother" to her (6.429–430). He refuses her plea to fight defensively, foresees the city's fall and her slavery, and turns to the baby: Astyanax screams at the helmet's crest, both parents laugh, and Hector prays the child may be a better man than his father (6.466–481). No epic before the Iliad and few after it put a soldier's marriage at the centre.

Paris

Hector's dealings with Paris are a study in fraternal contempt without hatred. He calls him "Dyspari", evil Paris, "best in looks, woman-mad, seducer" (3.39; 13.769), and wishes he had never been born. Paris's answer is always the same: you are right, let me fight (3.59–75; 6.333–341). The wider tradition makes Paris the seducer and the archer who kills Achilles with Apollo's help (Aethiopis); the Iliad makes him something less comfortable, a brother who is charming, unreliable and not actually a coward.

Death and judgement

Does the poem judge Hector? Yes, and it has him do it first. Alone outside the wall in Book 22 he admits that Polydamas was right and that his own recklessness (atasthaliai, 22.104) destroyed the army. He considers surrendering Helen and half the city's treasure, dismisses it, resolves to fight, and then runs. Three circuits of the walls, Zeus's golden scales (22.209–213), Athena in the shape of Deiphobus promising support and vanishing (22.226–247, 294–299): the gods cheat, and the poem does not hide it. Dying, Hector asks for his body to be returned; Achilles says he wishes he could eat him raw (22.345–348).

Where sources disagree. James Redfield (Nature and Culture in the Iliad: The Tragedy of Hector, 1975) reads Hector as the poem's true tragic figure, culpable through error, not vice. Others stress the darker Hector: the boast over the dying Patroclus (16.830–842), the attempt to behead the corpse and feed it to dogs (17.125–127), the over-reading of Zeus's favour. Both camps read the same lines. The poem gives Hector the self-knowledge Achilles never quite reaches, and also the mistakes.

The funeral

The Iliad ends not with Troy's fall but with Hector's funeral (24.719–804): three laments, by Andromache, Hecuba and, last and most surprisingly, Helen (24.762–775), who says Hector alone never spoke a harsh word to her. Nine days gathering wood, the tenth burning, the eleventh building the tomb. The last line, "Thus they held the funeral of Hector, tamer of horses" (24.804), is a Trojan line. A variant preserved in the scholia continued, "and the Amazon came, daughter of great-hearted Ares", the splice to the Aethiopis; the tradition that fixed the text declined it.

Priam

Priam moves from pure passivity to action. He watches from the wall in Book 3 and asks Helen to name the Greek leaders (3.161–242); he leaves before the duel because he cannot bear to see his son fight (3.304–309); he pleads from the gate, tearing his hair, as Achilles approaches (22.33–78). In Book 24, after Zeus sends Iris and Hermes, he drives a mule-cart into the enemy camp at night and kisses the hands of the man who killed his sons (24.477–479). His speech asks Achilles to remember his own father and ends: "I have done what no mortal has done before" (24.505–506). The two weep together, then eat. The poem's last reconciliation is between a Greek and a Trojan, and it is private.

The death belongs to the Iliou Persis: in Proclus' summary Neoptolemus kills Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios in his own courtyard. Virgil (Aeneid 2.506–558) has the old man arm himself, see Polites killed in front of him, throw a useless spear, and be dragged through his son's blood to the altar.

Where sources disagree. Pausanias (10.27.2) records that the Little Iliad had Neoptolemus drag Priam from the altar and kill him at the doors, away from the sanctuary, whether to lessen the sacrilege or as a different local version is unknown. Pindar (Paean 6.112–117) keeps the altar and makes it the reason Apollo later kills Neoptolemus at Delphi.

Hecuba and Andromache after Troy

In the Iliad Hecuba is formidable within limits: she tries to hold Hector back by baring the breast that fed him (22.79–89), calls Priam's night journey madness (24.200–216), and says she would gladly "eat the liver" of Achilles (24.212–213). Euripides builds a play on that sentence. In Hecuba (c. 424 BC) she loses Polyxena to sacrifice and finds Polydorus' body washed up from Thrace; she lures the murderer Polymestor into the women's tent, blinds him and kills his sons. He prophesies that she will become a dog and name the headland Cynossema (1259–1273). Trojan Women (415 BC) gives her the other ending, grief without revenge, as Astyanax's body is brought in on his father's shield.

Andromache's later life is the cruellest symmetry in the cycle. She is allotted to Neoptolemus, who in the Little Iliad threw Astyanax from the wall. She bears him Molossus (three sons in Pausanias 1.11.1) and lives in Epirus under the jealousy of his Spartan wife Hermione. When Neoptolemus dies at Delphi, Thetis decrees that she marry Helenus and that Molossus found the Molossian dynasty (Euripides, Andromache 1243–1252). Virgil's Aeneas finds her at Buthrotum, in a replica Troy with a sham Simois, pouring libations at an empty tomb for Hector (Aeneid 3.294–355). Pausanias adds that she ended in Asia with Pergamus, founder of Pergamon, where she had a shrine.

Where sources disagree. Who killed Astyanax? Neoptolemus in the Little Iliad; Odysseus in the Iliou Persis; the whole army on Odysseus' advice in Euripides (Trojan Women 721–725). Who killed Neoptolemus is equally unstable: Orestes in Euripides, the Delphians in Pindar (Nemean 7.40–47), Apollo in Paean 6.

The allies

The Trojan catalogue (2.816–877) lists a west Anatolian coalition with Balkan support, but only the Lycians get full characters. Sarpedon, son of Zeus and Laodameia (6.198–199), delivers the clearest statement of aristocratic duty in the poem: Lycian kings enjoy their lands and wine precisely so that they will fight in the front line (12.310–328). Glaucus, grandson of Bellerophon, discovers an inherited guest-friendship with Diomedes and the two agree not to fight (6.119–236). The Trojan side contains men bound to Greeks by the same codes.

Sarpedon's death (16.419–507) matters for three reasons. Zeus weeps blood and wants to save him; Hera's answer, that every god would then rescue a favourite son and the order of things would fail, is the poem's statement of the limit on divine power (16.431–461). His body is carried by Sleep and Death to Lycia for burial (16.666–683), the only honour of its kind in the poem, painted by Euphronios on the krater of about 515 BC now at Cerveteri. And it is the template for Hector: Zeus weighs the same choice in Book 22 (22.168–181) and reaches the same answer.

Where sources disagree. Hesiod and Apollodorus (Library 3.1.2) make Sarpedon son of Zeus and Europa and brother of Minos, three generations too early; Diodorus (5.79.3) has Zeus grant him three lifetimes. Homer knows nothing of this.

Three allies stand outside the poem's main action. Rhesus, the Thracian with silver-white horses, is killed asleep by Diomedes on the night he arrives (10.469–525); scholia add that had his horses once drunk from the Scamander, Troy would never have fallen. The tragedy Rhesus under Euripides' name makes him son of the Strymon and a Muse; both its authorship and Book 10 itself, which scholia call a Pisistratean insertion, are disputed. Memnon, son of Eos and Priam's brother Tithonus, kills Antilochus and is killed by Achilles in the Aethiopis, where Eos wins him immortality; Aeschylus staged the weighing of the two souls in the lost Psychostasia. Penthesilea, the Amazon daughter of Ares, opens the same poem; Achilles kills her and then kills Thersites for mocking his grief over her body (Proclus; Quintus Smyrnaeus, Posthomerica 1). Exekias' amphora in the British Museum (c. 530 BC) shows the spear going in as their eyes meet.

Are the Trojans foreign?

Hector and Achilles converse without an interpreter. Trojans swear by Zeus, Athena has a temple on the citadel (6.297–311), Apollo defends the walls, and Hector's name is a Greek word, "the holder". Iris remarks that the allies are of "many tongues" (2.803–804; 4.437–438), but the Trojans themselves are never marked as speaking anything else. Edith Hall (Inventing the Barbarian, 1989) made the standard case that Homer has no concept of the barbarian: barbarophonos occurs once, of the Carians (2.867), and means only "odd-sounding".

What the poem marks is subtler. Trojans advance in a clamour like bleating sheep, Achaeans in silence (3.1–9; 4.428–438). Priam is polygamous; Paris fights with the bow, wears a leopard skin (3.17) and goes to bed with Helen in the afternoon; Hecuba is Phrygian and Priam once fought beside the Phrygians (3.184–189). Hilary Mackie (Talking Trojan, 1996) argued that Trojan speech is more lyrical and less given to blame. These are differences of texture, not of kind; whether they amount to an "orientalised" Troy is argued both ways.

The Trojans become barbarians after 480 BC. Aeschylus' Clytemnestra asks whether Cassandra speaks "an unknown barbarian tongue, like a swallow" (Agamemnon 1050–1051), and his lost Phrygians staged the ransom of Hector with a chorus in eastern dress. Euripides calls Trojans Phryges throughout, gives Orestes a cowardly Phrygian eunuch who sings his terror (1369–1502), and has Hermione sneer that barbarians sleep with their relatives (Andromache 173–176). Athenian painters, who in the sixth century drew Trojans as hoplites identical to Greeks, begin after the Persian Wars to give Paris a Phrygian cap, trousers and a Scythian bow; by the fourth century the cap is a Trojan uniform. Herodotus supplies the political logic: Xerxes sacrifices a thousand oxen to Athena at Ilion on his way to Greece (7.43), and the Persians count Asia and its peoples as their own (1.4.4). Troy had been re-filed under Asia.

Wilusa and the Luwian hypothesis

Hittite texts of the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BC know a kingdom in north-western Anatolia called Wilusa, once Wilusiya, among the Assuwa coalition defeated by Tudhaliya I/II around 1400 BC. A treaty of Muwatalli II (c. 1280 BC) binds its king Alaksandu as vassal and names an earlier king, Kukkunni. The Manapa-Tarhunta letter reports an attack on Wilusa by the renegade Piyamaradu; the Tawagalawa letter recalls a dispute over Wilusa between the Hittite king and the king of Ahhiyawa; the Milawata letter shows Tudhaliya IV restoring a deposed Wilusan king, Walmu.

The equations are phonologically attractive. Wilusa matches Greek Wilios, the form of Ilios with its original w-sound, still preserved in the metre of many Homeric lines; the neighbouring Taruisa matches Troia. Alaksandu looks like Alexandros. A god in the treaty's witness list, Appaliunas, has been read as Apollo. J. D. Hawkins' decipherment of the Karabel inscription (1998) fixed the kingdom of Mira and pushed Wilusa into the Troad, where most Hittitologists now place it.

The Luwian hypothesis goes further. Calvert Watkins (1986) drew attention to a Luwian song fragment embedded in a Hittite ritual text (KUB 35.102+103), ahha-ta-ta alati awienta Wilusati, "when they came from steep Wilusa", and suggested it might be the ghost of a Luwian Troy epic. In 1995 Korfmann's excavators found a Luwian hieroglyphic seal in Troy VIIb, still the only writing found on the site. Watkins also derived Priam from Luwian Pariya-muwa, "exceptionally brave".

Where sources disagree. None of this is settled. Alaksandu may be a Luwian name folk-etymologised by Greeks, or a Greek name borne by an Anatolian king with Aegean connections (Joachim Latacz argues the latter). Appaliunas is a damaged reading. One seal does not establish a city's language. Kolb's attack on Korfmann over the scale of Troy VI belongs to module 10.10; the Wilusa equation, while the majority view, has not persuaded everyone. What is secure: a kingdom with a name like Ilios existed where Troy stands, was a Hittite vassal, and was fought over in the thirteenth century.

Troy to Rome

Aeneas' westward journey is older than Rome's interest in it. Sixth-century Etruscan vases and fifth-century terracottas from Veii show him carrying Anchises; Hellanicus of Lesbos made him a founder of Rome with Odysseus (Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1.72.2); Thucydides (6.2.3) knows the Elymians of Sicily as Trojan refugees. Rome adopted the genealogy through Naevius and Ennius and used it in diplomacy: Ilion received Roman favour in the second century BC because the Romans were, formally, its colonists.

The Julii made it dynastic. Caesar's funeral oration for his aunt Julia derived the family from Venus through Aeneas' son Iulus (Suetonius, Divus Julius 6.1); he dedicated the temple of Venus Genetrix in 46 BC. Virgil's Jupiter spells out the line Aeneas–Iulus–Alba–Romulus–"Julius, a name descended from great Iulus" (Aeneid 1.267–288), and the Forum of Augustus set Aeneas with Anchises and Ascanius opposite Romulus. Lucretius had already called the Romans Aeneadae (1.1). To be Trojan was to be Roman, and the city the Greeks had barbarised became the ancestor of the people who ruled the Greeks.

The poem's refusal

The Iliad is a Greek poem about a Greek victory, and it never once asks us to hate the Trojans. The first death in the fighting is Simoeisios, a Trojan youth who never repaid his parents for rearing him, compared to a felled poplar (4.473–489). The only family we enter is Hector's. The city's women, children and old men are on the walls; the Greek camp has no women except captives. Priam gets the closing book. Simone Weil's observation in "The Iliad, or the Poem of Force" (1940) remains the sharpest: a reader who did not know would find it hard to tell whether the poet was Greek or Trojan.

This is not neutrality about the war's cause. The poem knows that Paris broke the laws of hospitality and that Troy, by keeping Helen, is complicit; Antenor says so. But it declines the step every later tradition took, in which an enemy's wrongdoing licenses contempt. The barbarian of Euripides, the treacherous Antenor, the effeminate Paris in his cap are answers to a question the Iliad refused to ask. Its Trojans are men who fight well, love their families, make wrong choices under pressure and die. That is also its description of the Greeks. The remarkable thing is not that the poet sympathised with the losers but that he saw no reason to write them differently.

Self-test

  1. How many sons does Priam claim, and how many by Hecuba? Cite the passage.
    Answer

    Fifty, nineteen "from one womb"; Iliad 24.495–497.

  2. Give the two incompatible accounts of Polydorus' parentage and death.
    Answer

    Iliad 20.407–418 and 21.84–91: son of Laothoe, killed by Achilles. Euripides, Hecuba: son of Hecuba, murdered by Polymestor in Thrace.

  3. Who in the Iliad is the prophet of Priam's house, and who takes over the role later?
    Answer

    Helenus, "best of augurs" (6.76). Cassandra acquires prophecy only post-Homerically, notably in Aeschylus' Agamemnon.

  4. What advice of Polydamas does Hector reject in Book 18, and where does Hector later admit the error?
    Answer

    To retreat inside the walls before Achilles returns (18.254–283). Hector admits it alone outside the gate, 22.99–107, calling it his own atasthaliai.

  5. Which three women lament Hector, in what order, and why is the third surprising?
    Answer

    Andromache, Hecuba, Helen (24.725–775). Helen is a Greek and the cause of the war; she says Hector alone never reproached her.

  6. At whose altar does Priam die according to Proclus' Iliou Persis, and how does the Little Iliad differ?
    Answer

    Zeus Herkeios, in his courtyard. Pausanias 10.27.2 reports that the Little Iliad had Neoptolemus drag him from the altar and kill him at the doors.

  7. Why does Hera stop Zeus saving Sarpedon, and where is the argument re-run?
    Answer

    Because every god would then rescue a favourite son and the order of things would fail (16.440–457). Zeus faces the same choice over Hector at 22.168–181.

  8. Name two markers by which Attic art and drama turned Trojans into barbarians after 480 BC.
    Answer

    The Phrygian cap and eastern dress on vases; the term Phryges and the cowardly Phrygian slave in Euripides' Orestes; Clytemnestra's "swallow" line in Agamemnon 1050–1051.

  9. What are the two Hittite place-names matched with Ilios and Troia, and which treaty names King Alaksandu?
    Answer

    Wilusa (Wilios) and Taruisa (Troia). The treaty of Muwatalli II, c. 1280 BC.

  10. How did the Julii connect themselves to Troy?
    Answer

    Through Iulus, identified with Aeneas' son Ascanius, and so to Venus; Caesar's funeral speech for Julia (Suetonius, Divus Julius 6) and Virgil, Aeneid 1.267–288.

Carry forward

  1. The Iliad's Trojans speak Greek, worship Greek gods and live by Greek codes; the barbarian Trojan in the Phrygian cap is an Athenian invention of the decades after the Persian Wars, and every later text that uses it must be read with that date in mind.
  2. Hector is judged by the poem through his own mouth, not the narrator's: good counsel rejected (Polydamas), then self-knowledge too late, is the shape Greek tragedy will take from epic.
  3. The Hittite Wilusa dossier and the Aeneas-to-Rome line are the two directions in which Troy escapes Greek ownership, backwards into Anatolian history and forwards into Roman ideology; both grow from the small protected space the Iliad gave to Aeneas and to the idea that Troy was not simply the enemy.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Trojans as the Iliad and the wider tradition present them. Cover: the house of Priam (Hecuba, the fifty sons, Hector, Paris, Helenus, Deiphobus, Troilus, Polydorus, Cassandra, Polyxena, Laodice) and the senior Trojans (Antenor, Anchises, Aeneas, Polydamas); Hector as the poem's second hero: his aristeia, Book 6 with Andromache and Astyanax, his relationship with Paris, his death and the question of whether the Iliad judges him, his funeral as the poem's last word; Priam: the ransom in Book 24 and the death at the altar; Hecuba from matriarch to Euripides' avenger; Andromache's afterlife with Neoptolemus and Helenus; the Trojan allies (Sarpedon and Glaucus of Lycia, Rhesus, Memnon, Penthesilea) and why Sarpedon's death matters; the language question: the Trojans speak Greek and worship Greek gods, so in what sense are they foreign, and when do Trojans become Phrygian barbarians (Aeschylus, Euripides, Athenian vase painting after the Persian Wars); the Hittite material: Wilusa, Alaksandu and the Luwian hypothesis for Troy's real identity; Troy as ancestor city for Rome (Aeneas) and for the Julii. End with the Iliad's refusal to make the Trojans villains and why that is the poem's most remarkable feature. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

Odysseus

A thief's grandson: ancestry, name and scar

Homer gives Odysseus a respectable father and a disreputable grandfather. Laertes is a minor Ithacan king who by the Odyssey's end digs his orchard in a patched tunic (Odyssey 24.226–231). Anticleia, who died of longing for her son (11.202–203), is the daughter of Autolycus, who surpassed all men in thievery and the oath, a gift from Hermes (19.394–398). Deceptive swearing is presented as a craft with a divine patron, and it sits in the bloodline.

The scar tells the inheritance. When Eurycleia recognises it, the narrative pauses for some seventy lines (19.392–466). Autolycus named the baby: having been angered by (or having angered) many, he called him Odysseus, punning on odussomai, "to be wrathful, to hate" (19.407–409). Whether the name means the man who gives pain or the man who suffers it is ambiguous, and the poem plays on both (1.62, 5.340). On a visit to Parnassus the youth was gashed by a boar: the scar marks initiation into his mother's family of tricksters, and it is also what breaks his disguise.

Later writers made the inheritance worse. Autolycus stole the cattle of Sisyphus, who had marked their hooves; Sisyphus then lay with Anticleia before her marriage, and Odysseus was his son (Hyginus, Fabulae 201). Tragedy uses this as an insult: "the Sisyphid" (Sophocles, Ajax 189), "son of Sisyphus" (Philoctetes 417, 1311; Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis 524, Cyclops 104).

Where sources disagree. Homer never hints at Sisyphus; Laertes is the father without qualification. The earliest surviving attestation is Aeschylus (fr. 175 Radt, from the Judgement of the Arms), so the story is at least as old as the early fifth century. W. B. Stanford (The Ulysses Theme, 1954) treated it as part of the post-Homeric hostile tradition, a bad father invented for a bad son once Autolycus' trickery was already in the epic; Timothy Gantz (Early Greek Myth, 1993) notes that nothing in the Cycle as summarised by Proclus has it, so a pre-Homeric folk version cannot be shown. The question stays open because the evidence between Homer and Aeschylus is lost.

The reluctant volunteer and the death of Palamedes

The Cypria, summarised by Proclus, records that Odysseus feigned madness to avoid the expedition and that the Greeks, on Palamedes' advice, seized the infant Telemachus to expose him. Later handbooks supply the scene: Odysseus yokes ill-matched animals and sows salt; Palamedes puts Telemachus before the plough (Hyginus, Fabulae 95) or draws a sword over him (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.7). The trickster is caught by another trickster, through his family.

His revenge is the first lasting stain on his name. Pausanias (10.31.2) says the Cypria had Odysseus and Diomedes drown Palamedes while he was fishing. The later standard version (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.8; Hyginus, Fabulae 105) has Odysseus forge a letter from Priam, bury gold in Palamedes' tent, and let the army stone him as a traitor. All three tragedians wrote a Palamedes (all lost; Euripides' was staged in 415 with Trojan Women), Gorgias wrote a Defence of Palamedes, and Plato's Socrates looks forward to meeting Palamedes and Ajax in Hades, men killed by unjust judgement (Apology 41b). The pattern of the hostile tradition is set: his victims are the honest and inventive, destroyed through rigged procedure.

Where sources disagree. Homer never mentions Palamedes. Ancient critics said Homer suppressed him out of partiality for Odysseus (Philostratus, Heroicus 25.13); most modern scholars think the inventor-hero is a later elaboration who grew because he made the perfect foil.

The Iliad's Odysseus

In the Iliad he is not yet a wanderer but an institutional man, often the poem's instrument of order.

The sceptre and Thersites

When Agamemnon's test of the army in Book 2 sends the men running for the ships, Athena dispatches Odysseus. He takes Agamemnon's ancestral sceptre (2.185–187): kings he persuades, commoners he strikes, for "the rule of many is not good; let there be one lord" (2.204). When Thersites repeats Achilles' charge that the war is Agamemnon's private profit, Odysseus beats him with the sceptre and the army laughs (2.211–277). Antiquity read this as royal correction; modern readers see class politics. Odysseus here enforces hierarchy, and democratic Athens remembered who held the stick. Antenor's portrait (3.216–224) adds the orator: he stood stiff, eyes down, like a fool, until words came "like winter snowflakes".

The Embassy (Book 9)

Odysseus repeats Agamemnon's gift-list almost verbatim (9.260–299) but quietly drops the demand that Achilles submit to the "more kingly" man (9.158–161): tactful editing, and the selective truth that defines him. Achilles answers that hateful as the gates of Hades is the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another (9.312–313). The line need not target Odysseus, but ancient readers took it so, and Plato's Hippias Minor rests on the contrast of truthful Achilles and polytropos Odysseus.

Where sources disagree. The embassy is described with dual verbs (9.182–198) though Phoenix, Ajax and Odysseus go. Explanations range from an older two-man version with Phoenix inserted (Page, History and the Homeric Iliad, 1959) to a loose archaic use of the dual (Hainsworth, The Iliad: A Commentary vol. 3, 1993); Nagy (The Best of the Achaeans, 1979) thinks the duals pointedly exclude Odysseus. There is no consensus.

The Doloneia (Book 10)

Odysseus and Diomedes capture the spy Dolon, extract information under an ambiguous promise of safety, and Diomedes kills him as he pleads; they then kill the sleeping Thracian king Rhesus and take his horses. It is the Iliad's only night raid and its only victory by stealth and near bad faith. A scholion on 10.1 reports that Homer composed it separately and Peisistratus inserted it; its style and loose fit persuade many modern scholars it is a later addition, though some defend its deliberate difference. Either way, it is the Iliadic seed of the Cyclic Odysseus: the night operative paired with Diomedes.

The funeral games

In Book 23 he wrestles Telamonian Ajax to a draw, cunning against bulk (23.700–739), and wins the footrace when Athena, answering his prayer, makes the lesser Ajax slip in dung (23.740–783). Both contests foreshadow the judgement of the arms. Small unresolved hints elsewhere complicate him: in Book 8 he does not respond to Diomedes' call to stand (8.92–98, the verb ambiguous between "did not hear" and "did not heed"); in Book 11, isolated, he reasons himself into holding his ground (11.401–410).

The Cyclic Odysseus: arms, Palladium, horse, child

The lost Epic Cycle, known chiefly through Proclus' summaries, supplies the episodes that later made him suspect.

EpisodeSourceOdysseus' role
Judgement of the armsAethiopis, Little IliadWins Achilles' arms; Ajax goes mad and kills himself
Capture of HelenusLittle IliadSeizes the seer who reveals how Troy can fall
Spying in TroyLittle Iliad; Odyssey 4.242–264Enters as a beggar; Helen recognises him and keeps silent
Theft of the PalladiumLittle IliadWith Diomedes
Wooden horseLittle Iliad, Iliou Persis; Odyssey 8.492–520Leads the men inside; Epeius builds it
Death of AstyanaxIliou PersisKills Hector's infant son

The Palladium and the horse are the two exploits the Cycle gave him outright. In the Little Iliad he and Diomedes steal the Palladium from Troy by night, in some versions by a sewer or over the wall, with Helen's or Theano's help; the Roman tradition later made Diomedes the thief and Odysseus the one who tried to kill him for the credit (the "Diomedean compulsion" below).
