The horse is Epeius' craft and Odysseus' command: he chooses the men, keeps them silent in the belly while Helen imitates their wives' voices, and stops Anticlus' mouth with his hands (Odyssey 4.271–289; 8.492–520, where Demodocus sings it at his request).

The arms defined him for the classical world. In the underworld Ajax's shade refuses to speak to him (Odyssey 11.543–567). A scholion on Aristophanes' Knights 1056 preserves a Little Iliad version in which Greek spies overhear Trojan girls debating who was braver, one arguing, with Athena's prompting, for Odysseus. The prize is settled by talk, by the wrong jury, against the man who fought best. A later story explaining the proverb "Diomedean compulsion" (Conon, Narrations 34; Suda s.v.) has Odysseus try to kill Diomedes from behind on the way back with the Palladium, to keep the credit.

Where sources disagree. Proclus' Iliou Persis has Odysseus kill Astyanax; a Little Iliad fragment (via Tzetzes) has Neoptolemus hurl him from the walls; in Euripides' Trojan Women the army decrees the death on Odysseus' motion (721–725). In every version his name attaches to the worst act of the sack, as killer or as the man whose argument made it policy.

Metis and the man of many turns

The Odyssey's first line names him only polytropos: "much-turned" (driven off course) or "of many turns" (versatile, wily). A scholion on 1.1, deriving from Porphyry, reports Antisthenes' defence: he knows many modes (tropoi) of speech for many kinds of hearer, a mark of wisdom. Plato's Hippias reads it the other way: Homer made Achilles true and simple, Odysseus polytropos and false (Hippias Minor 365b). The only other early use, of Hermes (Homeric Hymn to Hermes 13, 439), points towards cleverness and the grandfather's god. Emily Wilson's "complicated" (2017) refuses to choose.

His epithets polymētis, polymēchanos and polytlas name the cluster. Metis is the intelligence of the hunter, sailor and politician: disguise, delay, trap and turn. Detienne and Vernant (Les ruses de l'intelligence, 1974) showed that Greeks prized it but uneasily, as the weapon of the weaker party and the opposite of straight force and plain speech. Hesiod's Zeus swallows the goddess Metis to keep her power inside himself (Theogony 886–900); her daughter Athena embodies it. Hence Odyssey 13.287–310: having heard his lies, Athena smiles, strokes him, and says she is best among gods for metis as he is among mortals. The poem's patron goddess endorses the trickster as kin. The ambiguity is structural: the intelligence behind the "Nobody" trick is the one that forges the letter that kills Palamedes.

The Odyssey's lies, the slaughter, and death from the sea

The Cretan tales

On Ithaca he tells five false life stories: to the disguised Athena (13.256–286), to Eumaeus (14.192–359), to Antinous (17.415–444) and to Penelope (19.165–202), three of them Cretan (to Antinous he tells only of Egypt and Cyprus); and to Laertes (24.244–279), as Eperitus of Alybas. He "spoke many lies like the truth" (19.203), echoing Hesiod's Muses (Theogony 27). The tales are disguised autobiography (raider, wanderer, survivor of companions lost through folly); they test hospitality and loyalty; and they remind the audience that Books 9–12 are also his own unverifiable account. The poem never condemns them. The test of a lie here is whom it serves.

The ethics of the slaughter

The killing of the suitors is framed as justice from Zeus' opening speech on Aegisthus (1.32–43): men suffer beyond their share through their own recklessness, after warnings. But the cost shows. Leodes, the seer who disapproved of the suitors, begs and is beheaded (22.310–329), while Phemius and Medon are spared. Telemachus hangs the twelve disloyal slave women, denying them the sword-death his father ordered (22.457–473); Melanthius is mutilated (22.474–477). In Book 24 the suitors' kin take up arms, and only Athena and Zeus' decree of oblivion (24.482–486) prevent civil war. The poem admits the slaughter created a feud only gods could cancel.

Where sources disagree. The scholia on 23.296 report that Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus called that line the "end" (telos or peras) of the Odyssey; whether they meant its original ending or its fulfilment is disputed, and with it the status of Book 24. On the maids, older translations call them "sluts"; Wilson calls them slaves, and Atwood's The Penelopiad (2005) gives them the voice.

Death from the sea: the Telegony

Teiresias foretells an oar carried inland until mistaken for a winnowing fan, a sacrifice to Poseidon, then a gentle death ex halos in sleek old age (11.119–137). The phrase means "away from the sea" or "out of the sea". Eugammon of Cyrene's Telegony (known from Proclus) took the second sense: Odysseus marries Callidice of Thesprotia, returns, and is killed unknowingly by Telegonus, his son by Circe, with a spear tipped with a stingray's spine. Telegonus then marries Penelope and Telemachus marries Circe. Aeschylus' Psychagogoi apparently had a heron drop the spine on him; Sophocles wrote a lost Odysseus Akanthoplex.

Where sources disagree. Most scholars read Teiresias as promising a peaceful end away from the sea and treat the Telegony's grotesque irony as a later twist. The live question is whether the Odyssey poet knew a Thesprotian sequel: Alfred Heubeck (in Heubeck and Hoekstra, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey II, 1989, on 11.134–137) holds that the prophecy's vagueness is deliberate and presupposes no sequel, while Malcolm Davies (The Greek Epic Cycle, 1989) allows that Eugammon worked up older Thesprotian material the Odyssey already alludes to (14.315–335).

The fifth-century prosecution

Pindar announces the turn. In Nemean 7 (20–27) he suspects Odysseus' fame exceeds his sufferings through sweet-voiced Homer, whose lies have majesty; if the crowd could see the truth, Ajax would not have fallen on his sword. In Nemean 8 (23–34) the Danaans favoured Odysseus in "secret votes", and hateful deceit (parphasis) existed even then. For a poet of aristocratic victors, Odysseus is the man talk and ballots unjustly preferred.

Sophocles

In Ajax (probably 440s) Odysseus is the most humane figure on stage: shown his maddened enemy by a gloating Athena, he pities him, seeing that all men are shadows (121–126), and he wins Ajax burial from Agamemnon (1332–1373). In Philoctetes (409) he coaches Neoptolemus to deceive the marooned archer, asking for a brief shameless part of a day (83–85), since in life the tongue, not deeds, rules (96–99). Neoptolemus' nature rebels; only Heracles ex machina resolves the play.

Where sources disagree. Cedric Whitman (Sophocles, 1951) saw the Philoctetes Odysseus as a sophist and political operator, the play's villain; C. M. Bowra (Sophoclean Tragedy, 1944) stressed that he serves the gods' declared will and the common good, so the play indicts his methods, not his aims. The same split runs through Ajax 1332–1373: Bernard Knox ("The Ajax of Sophocles", 1961) reads Odysseus' plea for burial as the play's one act of humane reason, Whitman as calculation that keeps the army whole. The admirable Odysseus of Ajax shows that the fifth century did not speak with one voice.

Euripides

In Hecuba (c. 424) he persuades the army to sacrifice Polyxena. Hecuba recalls that he once entered Troy as a spy, was recognised, and begged her for his life (239–250), and denounces the ungrateful breed who court the mob (254–257); the chorus calls him a sweet-talking people-pleaser (131–133). In Trojan Women (415) Hecuba, allotted to him, laments serving a treacherous man with a double tongue (281–288), and he proposes Astyanax's death. Only the satyr play Cyclops keeps something of the Homeric hero.

Why Athens found him uncomfortable

Three pressures converged. Rhetoric: a democracy run by persuasion, with sophists selling it, saw in him speech detached from truth; Thucydides' Cleon calls the Athenians spectators of speeches (3.38). Voting: the judgement of the arms looked like a ballot, and its victim Ajax was a Salaminian hero who gave his name to the tribe Aiantis. War: Hecuba and Trojan Women were staged during the Peloponnesian War, the latter in the year after Melos, when expediency was beating pity in real assemblies. W. B. Stanford's The Ulysses Theme (1954) is still the classic account, though it perhaps overstates the uniformity.

Philosophers and Romans

Plato. In the Myth of Er (Republic 10.620c–d) Odysseus' soul draws the last lot, remembers its toils, is cured of ambition, and searches out the neglected life of a private man who minds his own business, saying it would have chosen the same had it drawn first. The man of many turns chooses the life with none.

Cynics and Stoics. Antisthenes' paired speeches of Ajax and Odysseus survive: Odysseus argues he endured disguise, beggary and beating for the common good while Ajax fought only by day for glory. The patient, self-sufficient beggar became a Cynic model. Stoics allegorised him into the sage: Cicero reads the Sirens as the lure of knowledge (De Finibus 5.49); Seneca asks not where Ulysses wandered but how we may stop wandering (Epistles 88.7); Epictetus holds up his wanderings as the model of the man at home anywhere under providence, while refusing him his tears for Penelope (Discourses 3.24.13–20). Porphyry's On the Cave of the Nymphs makes his homecoming the soul's return.

Rome. Claiming Trojan descent, Rome sharpened the hostile figure. Virgil's Sinon episode makes him scelerum inventor, "deviser of crimes" (Aeneid 2.164), and dirus Ulixes (2.261); Laocoon asks "is this how you know Ulysses?" (2.44); in Book 3 he has abandoned Achaemenides to the Cyclops. Seneca's Troades gives him the hunt for Astyanax (the Andromache act, 524–813). Horace offers both faces: the "useful exemplar" of virtue and wisdom who resisted Circe and the Sirens (Epistles 1.2.17–26), and the legacy-hunter of the parody Satires 2.5. Ovid stages the contest of arms (Metamorphoses 13.1–398) and lets eloquence win (13.382–383). This Latin Ulysses, not Homer's, reached medieval Europe.

The modern voyage: Dante to Kazantzakis

Dante, without Greek, knew him from Virgil, Ovid, Statius and Cicero. In Inferno 26 he burns in a twin flame with Diomedes among the fraudulent counsellors, for the horse, the deception of Achilles at Scyros and the Palladium. Yet the flame tells an invented last voyage: no love of son, father or Penelope could overcome his desire for experience; he urges his old crew past the Pillars of Heracles, "you were not made to live like brutes, but to pursue virtue and knowledge" (26.119–120), and after their "mad flight" (26.125) they sight Purgatory before a whirlwind sinks them. Romantic readers heard heroic aspiration; theological readers stress transgression and the eloquence that killed those it inspired. Dante leaves the tension live.

Tennyson's "Ulysses" (written 1833 after Arthur Hallam's death, published 1842) follows Dante: the old king leaves "an aged wife" and the prudent Telemachus, "to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield". Victorians heard heroism; many modern readers hear abandonment of duty. Joyce's Ulysses (1922) makes him Leopold Bloom on 16 June 1904; Joyce told Frank Budgen that Ulysses was literature's only "complete" man, son, father, husband, lover, and a soldier who tried to dodge the war. Bloom's metis is decency; there is no slaughter. Kazantzakis' The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel (1938), 33,333 lines, sends him out again to found and lose an ideal city in Africa and die on Antarctic ice, a Nietzschean hero of pure striving. Horkheimer and Adorno (Dialectic of Enlightenment, 1944) read him bound to the mast as the prototype of instrumental reason, surviving by cunning and self-denial.

Is Odysseus admirable?

Each era's answer reveals the answerer. Homer admires him because homecoming is the highest good in a dangerous world and metis is how the weaker survive; Athena's smile is the verdict. Pindar and the Athenian stage distrust him because they feared that persuasion could defeat merit in a vote and expediency silence pity; the Odysseus of Hecuba is a portrait of a politician. The philosophers keep his endurance and self-knowledge and strip the tricks. Rome hated the Greek deceiver and praised the Stoic wanderer in one generation. Dante condemns his fraud and is transfixed by his curiosity; the nineteenth century made him an explorer, the twentieth an ordinary man or the alienated rational self.

The constant is that Odysseus is a hero of means rather than ends. Achilles and Ajax are judged by the values they embody; Odysseus is judged by what one thinks intelligence is for. Where the purpose is trusted, home, city, the gods' will, his cunning is virtue. Where cleverness is suspected of serving only itself, he becomes the liar, the demagogue and the murderer of Palamedes. To ask whether he is admirable is to ask whether a society trusts its own cleverness.

Self-test

  1. What does the Odyssey say Autolycus excelled in, and who gave him the gift?
    Answer

    Thievery and the oath (deceptive swearing), a gift from Hermes (Odyssey 19.394–398).

  2. How does the Cypria explain Palamedes' death, and how does it differ from the later standard version?
    Answer

    According to Pausanias (10.31.2), the Cypria had Odysseus and Diomedes drown him while fishing; the later version (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.8; Hyginus) has Odysseus forge a letter from Priam and plant gold, so the army stones Palamedes as a traitor.

  3. What does Odysseus leave out when he repeats Agamemnon's offer to Achilles in Iliad 9?
    Answer

    Agamemnon's demand that Achilles yield and submit to him as the more kingly man (9.158–161).

  4. What ancient claim casts doubt on the authenticity of Iliad 10?
    Answer

    A scholion on 10.1 says Homer composed the Doloneia separately and Peisistratus inserted it; modern arguments from style and loose connection point the same way, though some defend it.

  5. In the Little Iliad version preserved by a scholion on Aristophanes' Knights, who decides the judgement of the arms?
    Answer

    Trojan girls, overheard by Greek spies, one of whom argues with Athena's prompting for Odysseus over Ajax.

  6. How did Antisthenes defend the epithet polytropos?
    Answer

    As versatility in modes of speech, adapting discourse to different hearers, a mark of wisdom rather than deceit (scholion on Odyssey 1.1).

  7. What does Athena say about herself and Odysseus after he lies to her in Odyssey 13?
    Answer

    That he is the best of mortals in counsel and speech, and she is famous among the gods for metis; she delights in his cunning as kin to her own.

  8. Why do Pindar's and Euripides' hostility to Odysseus converge on the same two things?
    Answer

    Both fasten on the vote and the tongue. Pindar (Nemean 7.20–27, 8.23–34) makes him the man whose fame outran his deeds because Homer's sweet speech and the Danaans' secret ballots favoured talk over merit, at Ajax's cost; Euripides (Hecuba, Trojan Women, Iphigenia at Aulis) makes him the demagogue whose persuasion wins assemblies and silences pity. For an aristocratic poet and a democratic dramatist alike, the danger is the same: cleverness that works through speech and procedure rather than deeds.

  9. What life does Odysseus' soul choose in the Myth of Er?
    Answer

    Drawing the last lot and cured of ambition, he chooses the neglected life of a private man who minds his own business, saying he would have chosen it even with the first lot (Republic 10.620c–d).

  10. For what sins is Dante's Ulisse punished, and what does his final speech urge?
    Answer

    Fraudulent counsel: the wooden horse, the deception of Achilles at Scyros, and the theft of the Palladium; he urges his men not to live like brutes but to pursue virtue and knowledge (Inferno 26.119–120).

Carry forward

  1. Odysseus is the hero of metis, a morally neutral intelligence: every era's verdict on him is really a verdict on whether cleverness can be trusted without a fixed loyalty to truth.
  2. The negative Odysseus comes mostly from outside Homer, from the Cycle (Palamedes, the arms, Astyanax) and from fifth-century Athens, where he became the image of the demagogue and sophist in a city ruled by persuasion.
  3. Later Europe inherited a Latin Ulysses (Virgil's deceiver, Horace's sage, Ovid's orator), and Dante's invented last voyage, not Homer's homecoming, became the template for the modern restless Ulysses.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Odysseus as a figure across the whole tradition, assuming I know the Odyssey's plot. Cover: his ancestry (Laertes, Anticleia, the thief-grandfather Autolycus, and the Sisyphus slander) and the scar; the feigned madness and Palamedes' exposure of it, then Palamedes' framing and death as the first stain on his reputation; the Iliad's Odysseus (Book 2 with the sceptre and Thersites, the Embassy in Book 9, the Doloneia in Book 10 and its problems, the funeral games); the Little Iliad and Iliou Persis: the arms, the Palladium, the horse, the killing of Astyanax in some versions; metis as his defining virtue and its ambiguity (polytropos, polymetis, the man of many turns); the Odyssey's handling of his lies, the Cretan tales, and the ethics of the suitors' slaughter; his death from the sea in the Telegony; the fifth-century turn against him: Pindar's suspicion, Sophocles' Ajax and Philoctetes, Euripides' Hecuba and Trojan Women, and why democratic Athens found him uncomfortable; Plato's Odysseus choosing a quiet life in the Myth of Er; the Stoic and Cynic Odysseus as sage; Ulysses in Rome (Horace, Ovid, the Ulysses of Virgil's Book 2); Dante's Ulisse, Tennyson, Joyce, Kazantzakis. End with the question of whether Odysseus is admirable and what each era's answer says about it. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.5 · 3,534 words

Helen, Menelaus and Sparta

Two mothers, two eggsTheseus, the suitors and the oathHelen in HomerThe phantom in EgyptGuilt as a set piece: Gorgias and SapphoThe sword that drops, and the goddess at TherapneMenelaus and his LaconiaAfterlives, and the problem Helen posesSelf-testCarry forward

Two mothers, two eggs

Homer knows Helen only as "daughter of Zeus" (Iliad 3.199, 3.418) and sister of Castor and Polydeuces, "whom one mother bore with me" (Iliad 3.238). He never mentions a swan or an egg, and in the underworld Leda's sons are Tyndareus' children (Odyssey 11.298–304). The swan is later. Euripides gives it in full while letting Helen doubt it: Leda bore her to Zeus in swan's form, "if the story is true" (Helen 17–21), and she calls her own egg-birth a teras, a monstrosity (Helen 257–9).

The rival genealogy is older and stranger. The Cypria (fr. 9 Bernabé, in Athenaeus 8.334b–d) made Helen the daughter of Zeus and Nemesis, who fled him through sea and land as fish and beast and conceived against her will; the egg she laid was found by a shepherd and given to Leda, who hatched it and reared the child as her own (Apollodorus, Library 3.10.7, reporting both versions). At Rhamnous the base of Agoracritus' Nemesis showed Leda leading Helen to her true mother (Pausanias 1.33.7–8); at Sparta an egg bound with ribbons hung in the sanctuary of the Leucippides, "said to be the one Leda laid" (Pausanias 3.16.1). The tidy scheme of two eggs, one divine (Helen and Polydeuces) and one mortal (Clytemnestra and Castor), is late systematising (Hyginus, Fabulae 77); Pindar divides the twins by father without needing an egg (Nemean 10.79–82). The theology matters more than the biology: a child of Retribution is a different person from a child of Leda, and the Iliad seems to hear the pun when the Trojan elders say it is ou nemesis, "no cause for blame", that two peoples suffer for such a woman (3.156–7).

Where sources disagree. A scholion on Pindar, Nemean 10.150a, claims Hesiod made Helen the daughter of Zeus and an Oceanid, with no Leda at all; the fragment is lost and the attribution uncertain. Whether the Cypria's Nemesis is older than the swan or a learned alternative to it cannot be decided.

Theseus, the suitors and the oath

Helen is abducted twice, the first time as a child of seven (Hellanicus) or ten (Diodorus 4.63), seized by Theseus and Peirithous while dancing at the sanctuary of Artemis Orthia (Plutarch, Theseus 31; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23). Theseus left her at Aphidnae with his mother Aethra and went to Hades; the Dioscuri sacked Aphidnae, recovered their sister and enslaved Aethra, which is why "Aethra, daughter of Pittheus" can stand among Helen's handmaids at Troy without explanation (Iliad 3.144). Alcman already sang the Dioscuri's raid on Attica (fr. 21 Page), and Herodotus reports that Sparta spared Decelea throughout the Peloponnesian War because the Deceleans had shown the Tyndaridae where Helen was hidden (9.73).

Where sources disagree. Stesichorus and Euphorion made Helen bear Iphigenia to Theseus and hand her to Clytemnestra (Pausanias 2.22.6–7), so that Aulis sacrifices the daughter for the mother. It never displaced the Homeric line in which Iphianassa is Agamemnon's own child (Iliad 9.145).

The wooing survives best in the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women (frr. 196–204 M–W). Suitors send gifts from all Greece; Odysseus sends none, knowing Menelaus will win (fr. 198); Achilles is a boy with Chiron, and had he come "neither Menelaus nor any other" would have had her (fr. 204.87–92). Agamemnon woos for his brother (fr. 197), and Tyndareus chooses Menelaus "because he gave the most" (fr. 204.85–7). First he binds every suitor to defend the chosen husband if Helen is taken (fr. 204.78–85; Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis 57–65). Apollodorus credits the idea to Odysseus, who traded it for help in winning Penelope (3.10.9); Pausanias places the ceremony at the Tomb of the Horse near Sparta, the suitors standing on the pieces of a sacrificed horse (3.20.9).

Where sources disagree. Thucydides 1.9 rejects the oath: Agamemnon raised the fleet "not so much through the oaths of Tyndareus as through superiority in power". Poetry needs the oath to explain why Odysseus and Achilles sailed; history needs hegemony.

Helen in Homer

Iliad 3: the weaver on the wall

Iris finds Helen weaving into a purple cloak "the many struggles of the Trojans and Achaeans, which they were suffering for her sake" (3.125–8): she is composing the war as art while it is still being fought. On the wall Priam calls her "dear child" (3.162); she answers that she wishes "evil death had pleased me" when she followed his son, and calls herself kunōpis, dog-faced (3.173–80). She identifies Agamemnon, Odysseus and Ajax, then looks in vain for her brothers and supposes they are ashamed of her; the poet corrects her in his own voice, "but the life-giving earth already held them" (3.243). Her sight is sharp, her knowledge partial. After the duel Aphrodite summons her to Paris' bed, and Helen does what no other mortal in the poem does: she tells the goddess to go and sit beside him herself (3.399–412). The threat that follows silences her; she goes, but only to tell Paris she wishes he had died (3.428–36). Agency and compulsion share one scene.

Iliad 6 and 24: the dog who will be a song

To Hector she is harsher than anyone else is to her, "brother-in-law of me, a dog, an evil-contriving abomination", wishing a storm had swept her into the sea at birth (6.344–8). Then: Zeus set an evil doom on her and Paris "so that in time to come we may be a song for men" (6.357–8). She is the only character in the Iliad who knows she is in the Iliad. At the funeral she laments last, after Andromache and Hecuba, and for herself as much as for Hector: twenty years since she left home, he alone never spoke harshly to her, and now "all shudder at me" (24.762–75). Over all this hangs the poem's phrase for the war's cause, "Helen's struggles and groans" (2.356, 2.590), which cannot tell us whether the groans are hers or caused by her.

Odyssey 4: the drug and the horse

At Sparta Helen enters "like Artemis of the golden distaff" (4.122), recognises Telemachus before her husband does, and when grief threatens drops into the wine a drug "banishing pain and anger, bringing forgetfulness of every ill", from Polydamna of Egypt (4.219–32). She tells her story: she alone recognised the disguised Odysseus in Troy, bathed him, swore silence, and rejoiced, because her heart had turned homeward and she mourned the madness Aphrodite gave her (4.240–64). Menelaus replies, "Yes, wife, all that you have said is correct", and tells another: inside the Horse she walked round calling each hero in his wife's voice, "and a god must have bidden you, who wished to give glory to the Trojans"; Odysseus had to clamp his hand over Anticlus' mouth (4.266–89). The panels are paired and unadjudicated, and the drug is precisely what lets the room sit through the second story. That Hermione is their only child, "for the gods gave Helen no more" (4.12–14), has been stated flatly before either speaks.

The phantom in Egypt

Stesichorus of Himera (sixth century) wrote a Palinode, a song of recantation, whose opening Plato preserves:

That story is not true; you did not go in the well-benched ships, nor reach the towers of Troy.

(fr. 192 PMG, at Plato, Phaedrus 243a.) Plato frames it with a blinding cured by recantation, repeated by Isocrates (Helen 64), and tells us what replaced her: men at Troy fought over "the eidolon of Helen, in ignorance of the truth" (Republic 586c). A commentary attributed to Chamaeleon reports two Palinodes, one rebuking Homer and one Hesiod (P.Oxy. 2506 fr. 26). Stesichorus had treated her guilt earlier: the Greeks were about to stone her after the fall and dropped the stones at her face (fr. 201 PMG).

Where sources disagree. A scholion on Lycophron 822 says Hesiod first put the phantom at Troy (Hesiod fr. 358 M–W), which would make Stesichorus populariser not inventor. Most scholars doubt the attribution, since nothing in the Catalogue supports it; the second Palinode is also contested.

Herodotus keeps Egypt and drops the phantom. Memphite priests told him Paris was blown to Egypt, where king Proteus confiscated Helen and the treasure and expelled him; the Greeks besieged Troy for ten years refusing to believe the Trojans did not have her; Menelaus recovered her after the war and repaid his host by sacrificing two Egyptian children for a wind (2.112–119). Homer, he argues, knew this and suppressed it as unepic, witness the Sidonian robes Paris collected en route (Iliad 6.289–92) and Helen's Egyptian drug (Odyssey 4.227–30). His verdict: the Trojans would certainly have given her back, and the god arranged their destruction to show that "great wrongs bring great punishments" (2.120). Helen is innocent and absent; the war is theodicy.

Euripides' Helen (412 BC) stages Stesichorus with Herodotus' map. Hera, cheated by Paris' judgement, fashions a Helen out of sky for him while Hermes carries the real one to Proteus (31–48). Proteus is dead; his son Theoclymenus wants to marry her; Teucer reports that Greece hates her; Menelaus arrives shipwrecked and in rags, and the phantom dissolves into air announcing that Tyndareus' daughter is blameless (605–15). The sophistic game runs in Gorgias' vocabulary: onoma against sōma, name against body (42–3, 588); seeming against being; a chorus asking "what is god, what is not god, what lies between?" (1137–8). Faced with two Helens, Menelaus trusts the memory of his labour over the fake more than his eyes. Aristophanes parodied it the next year (Thesmophoriazusae 850–928). Three years earlier Euripides had given the other Helen her trial in Trojan Women (914–1032), where she argues like a sophist and Hecuba answers that "your mind became Aphrodite" (988–9).

Where sources disagree. Verrall read Helen as comedy and the twentieth century called it tragicomedy or escape play; Allan and Wright argue that a play about a war fought for nothing, staged the year after the Sicilian disaster, is serious under its wit. At issue is whether Euripides endorsed the sophistic epistemology he dramatised or exposed it.

Guilt as a set piece: Gorgias and Sappho

Gorgias' Encomium of Helen (DK 82 B11), the oldest surviving defence of a mythological defendant, is a disjunction. Helen went for one of four reasons: the will of the gods and necessity; force; persuasion by speech; or love. Gods or force excuse the weaker party. Speech makes her a victim, because "speech is a great dynast, which with the smallest and least visible body accomplishes the most divine works" (B11.8) and acts on the soul as drugs on the body (B11.14). Love is either a god she could not resist or a human sickness to be pitied. The last sentence gives the game away: he wrote "an encomium of Helen and a plaything (paignion) for myself" (B11.21). Isocrates' Helen (c. 370) opens by objecting that Gorgias wrote an apologia, and that to defend is to concede the charge (10.14). Helen became the schools' standard exercise in making the weaker argument strong; the Encomium is also a claim that logos is a fourth cause of the war, which no epic poet had named.

Sappho fr. 16 (Voigt), a century and a half earlier, speaks from inside Helen's desire rather than about her culpability. Some say cavalry, some infantry, some ships are the finest thing on the black earth; Sappho says it is whatever one loves, and proves it by Helen, "who far surpassed all mortals in beauty, left her most noble husband and sailed to Troy, with no thought at all for child or dear parents", led astray by something the lacuna at 12–13 has swallowed. The example then dissolves into absent Anactoria, whose walk Sappho would rather see than all the chariots of Lydia. Helen is a subject who chooses, and her choice is the paradigm of the one thing worth having. No apology is offered because none is felt to be needed.

The sword that drops, and the goddess at Therapne

The reunion at the fall has a fixed archaic shape: Menelaus goes for Helen with drawn sword and drops it at the sight of her. Ibycus (fr. 296 PMG) and the Little Iliad are cited for the bared breasts; Aristophanes jokes about it as common knowledge (Lysistrata 155–6), and Peleus throws it at Menelaus: "when you saw her breast you threw away your sword and took her kiss" (Euripides, Andromache 627–31). Euripides tests the other ending twice. In Trojan Women Menelaus swears to kill her in Sparta and Hecuba warns him not to sail in the same ship, since "a lover never stops loving" (1049–59); in Orestes, Orestes and Pylades attack her in Argos and she vanishes from under the blade to be made a goddess by Apollo, a beacon for sailors beside her brothers (1629–42).

Goddess is what Sparta meant by Helen. At Therapne, on the bluff above the Eurotas, a nurse carried an ugly infant daily to "the shrine of Helen" until a woman appeared, stroked the child's head and promised she would be the most beautiful woman in Sparta; she became the mother of king Demaratus (Herodotus 6.61). Isocrates says the Spartans sacrifice there to Helen and Menelaus "not as heroes but as gods" (Helen 63); Pausanias was shown their tomb (3.19.9). Rhodes is darker: driven from Sparta after Menelaus' death by his bastard sons, Helen fled to Polyxo, widow of Tlepolemus, who sent maids dressed as Furies to hang her from a tree; the Rhodians worship her as Helen Dendritis, "of the Tree" (Pausanias 3.19.9–10). Hanging is a recurrent death for goddesses of young women (Artemis Apanchomene, Pausanias 8.23.6–7), and the tree returns in Theocritus' Spartan wedding song, where girls who ran oiled "like men" beside the Eurotas with Helen promise to garland a plane tree inscribed "Revere me: I am Helen's tree" (Idyll 18.22–48).

Alcman's Partheneion (fr. 1 Page), sung at dawn by a Spartan girls' chorus under Hagesichora and Agido, does not name Helen. Claude Calame (1977) argued that such choruses were the institutional form of girls' initiation, that Helen with the Leucippides and Artemis Orthia was among their patrons, and that Therapne was the terminus of the passage from parthenos to bride; Theocritus and the ugly child of Herodotus fit that reading exactly. Alcman does name Therapne elsewhere, with the Dioscuri (fr. 7 Page).

Where sources disagree. Calame's initiatory reading remains dominant, but the goddess of the Partheneion (Orthria or Aotis) is disputed, and Hutchinson and Ferrari see a wedding or an Orthia festival with no Helen at all. Her link to the Louvre Partheneion is inference, not text.

Menelaus and his Laconia

Menelaus brings sixty ships from "Lacedaemon of the many ravines", with Pharis, Sparta, Messe, Amyclae and Helos (Iliad 2.581–90). He is the lesser Atreid and the poem knows it: Agamemnon stops him facing Hector because he would die (7.104–21), Apollo taunts that Trojans once called him "a soft spearman" (17.588), Agamemnon grumbles that he slackens and leaves the work to his brother (10.114–23). The duel is his: he wins on points, his sword shatters on Paris' helmet, he drags him by the chin-strap until Aphrodite snaps it (3.340–82). His wounding by Pandarus' arrow, turned into his belt by Athena, is the poem's first real injury, and draws Agamemnon's cry that he would go home in disgrace with Menelaus' bones rotting in Troy (4.104–82). His aristeia is Book 17, over Patroclus' body: he kills Euphorbus in the scene of the uprooted olive sapling (17.45–60), is given by Athena "the courage of a fly" (17.570), and brings the corpse home with the Ajaxes and Meriones. His best moment is off the field, yielding a disputed prize to Antilochus, "for my heart is never arrogant or harsh" (23.566–613).

The Odyssey gives him Egypt and eternity. Becalmed at Pharos, helped by Eidothea, he ambushes Proteus under seal-skins and holds him through lion, serpent, leopard, boar, water and tree (4.351–461). Proteus tells him the fates of Ajax, Agamemnon and Odysseus, then his own: not death in Argos but the Elysian plain where Rhadamanthys is, "because you have Helen and are the son-in-law of Zeus" (4.561–9). It is Homer's only promise of a blessed afterlife to a living man, and it is earned by marriage, not merit. The wealth Telemachus marvels at (4.71–5) Menelaus would return for the lives it cost (4.97). Athenian tragedy was less kind: the Menelaus of Sophocles' Ajax and of Euripides' Andromache and Orestes is a Spartan in the Athenian sense, petty and cold.

The Menelaion and Mycenaean Laconia

The Menelaion sits on the Therapne ridge. British excavations (Dawkins 1909–10; Catling 1973–6 and 1985) found two successive Mycenaean mansions, the first built around 1450 BC and the last destroyed by fire around 1200, then no use until the seventh century, when cult appears: a bronze aryballos of about 650 BC inscribed "Deinis dedicated these to Helen, wife of Menelaus", a bronze meat-hook for Helen, a fifth-century stele to Menelaus and a monumental stepped platform. A visible Bronze Age ruin was given to the royal couple five centuries after its fall, the normal pattern of Greek hero-cult.

Where sources disagree. Catling saw the mansions as the seat of a Mycenaean ruler of Laconia. Since 2009 excavation at Ayios Vasileios near Xirokambi, 12 km south of Sparta, has uncovered a palatial complex with Linear B tablets destroyed around 1200 BC, now generally taken as the true palace of Mycenaean Laconia, with the Menelaion a subordinate residence. Whether either preserved any memory into Homer's age, rather than being reinvented by it, is uncertain.

Hermione, Orestes and Neoptolemus

Hermione was promised to Neoptolemus at Troy and Telemachus arrives during her wedding feast (Odyssey 4.3–9); Menelaus' other heir Megapenthes is a slave's son (4.10–12), and Hesiod's Nicostratus as Helen's son (fr. 175 M–W) contradicts the Odyssey's only child. Euripides' Andromache dramatises the sequel: Hermione, barren and jealous of Andromache's son by Neoptolemus, plots murder, is carried off by Orestes, who arranges Neoptolemus' death at Delphi. Pindar had told that death two ways, as Apollo's punishment for killing Priam (Paean 6.112–20) and as a quarrel over sacrificial meat (Nemean 7.34–47). Orestes and Hermione's son Tisamenus inherited Sparta over Menelaus' slave-born sons (Pausanias 2.18.6), the last Pelopid before the Heraclid return.

Where sources disagree. Whether Tyndareus first betrothed Hermione to Orestes (Euripides, Andromache 966–70; Orestes 1653–7; Sophocles' lost Hermione) or Menelaus gave her straight to Neoptolemus (Odyssey 4) decides who is the wronged party at Delphi. The Odyssey knows nothing of Orestes' claim.

Afterlives, and the problem Helen poses

Marlowe's Faustus asks "Was this the face that launched a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?" (Doctor Faustus, A-text 5.1), and the answer is no: the Helen he kisses is a devil in a woman's shape, Stesichorus' eidolon in a Lutheran key. Goethe built the third act of Faust II (1827) on Euripides: Helen before Menelaus' palace at Sparta, warned by Phorkyas-Mephistopheles that her husband means to sacrifice her, flees to Faust's Gothic castle, bears Euphorion, and when the boy falls dissolves, leaving robe and veil in Faust's arms. Yeats made the egg a political event, "the broken wall, the burning roof and tower / And Agamemnon dead" (Leda and the Swan, 1924). H.D.'s Helen in Egypt (1961), in three parts (Pallinode, Leuké, Eidolon), is the full modern Palinode: Achilles meets the real Helen on the Egyptian shore and the war is rebuilt from the woman who was never in it. Seferis' Helen (1953), spoken by Teucer on Cyprus, is the bitterest: so many dead "for an empty tunic, for a Helen". Christa Wolf's Kassandra (1983) rationalises as Herodotus did, with a twist: Paris returns without her and Troy fights to the death to protect a lie its leaders cannot admit. Giraudoux's The Trojan War Will Not Take Place (1935) has Helen bored on stage while men explain why she matters; Petersen's Troy (2004) restores her guilt by calling it love. Austin (1994), Hughes (2005), Maguire (2009) and Blondell (2013) agree on one thing: each age reinvents Helen by deciding how much agency it can bear to give her.

Antiquity had already split along that fault. One branch keeps her at Troy and clears her: Priam blames the gods (Iliad 3.164–5), Penelope says a god drove her (Odyssey 23.222), Gorgias proves no cause leaves her culpable. The other removes her and leaves a cloud or an Egyptian hostage in her place. Both solutions destroy the war they explain. If Helen is guiltless, ten years of dead men avenged nothing, because no wrong was done by the person for whom they died. If she was absent, they fought for a name, which is exactly what Euripides' Menelaus cannot accept when he weighs the woman in Egypt against his own toil. Homer's answer is the only one that does not flinch: Helen is at Troy, she chose and was compelled, she calls herself a dog and no one agrees, and she knows the whole thing exists so that there will be a song. The war was fought for a woman, and the woman was never adequate to the war. The Spartans, who built her a temple and brought her their ugly daughters, understood that this made her a goddess rather than a criminal.

Self-test

  1. Which two mothers does the tradition give Helen, and which text first makes Nemesis her mother?
    Answer

    Leda (the swan, Euripides Helen 17–21) and Nemesis, pursued by Zeus and laying an egg Leda hatched; first in the Cypria (fr. 9 Bernabé, in Athenaeus 8.334b–d), reported by Apollodorus, Library 3.10.7.

  2. How does Aethra, Theseus' mother, come to be at Troy in Iliad 3.144?
    Answer

    The Dioscuri enslaved her when they sacked Aphidnae to recover the child Helen whom Theseus had hidden there (Plutarch, Theseus 31; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.23).

  3. What does Thucydides think raised the army against Troy, and what does the poetic tradition say?
    Answer

    Thucydides 1.9 credits Agamemnon's power, not the oath of Tyndareus; the Hesiodic Catalogue (fr. 204), Euripides (IA 57–65) and Apollodorus (3.10.9) make the suitors' oath the binding mechanism.

  4. What is unique about Helen's exchange with Aphrodite at Iliad 3.399–412?
    Answer

    She is the only mortal in the poem to defy a god to her face, telling Aphrodite to go and sit beside Paris herself; Aphrodite's threat forces compliance.

  5. What two stories do Helen and Menelaus tell in Odyssey 4, and why does the drug matter?
    Answer

    Helen says she alone recognised the disguised Odysseus in Troy and helped him; Menelaus "agrees" and recounts how she circled the Wooden Horse imitating the heroes' wives. She has just drugged the wine with a pain-killing Egyptian pharmakon, so no one can react.

  6. What is the Palinode, and what evidence is there for a phantom Helen in Stesichorus?
    Answer

    Stesichorus' recantation (fr. 192 PMG, at Plato, Phaedrus 243a) denies Helen sailed to Troy; Plato, Republic 586c, says men fought over her eidolon "as Stesichorus says". P.Oxy. 2506 suggests two Palinodes.

  7. How does Herodotus' Egyptian Helen differ from Euripides'?
    Answer

    Herodotus (2.112–120) has no phantom: king Proteus detains Helen and the Greeks refuse to believe the Trojans lack her. Euripides (Helen, 412 BC) has Hera make a phantom of air for Troy while Hermes carries the real Helen to Proteus.

  8. Name Gorgias' four possible causes for Helen's going to Troy, and what he calls the speech at its end.
    Answer

    Gods and necessity; force; persuasion by speech; love. He calls it an encomium of Helen and a paignion, a plaything, for himself (DK 82 B11.21).

  9. Why does Proteus tell Menelaus he will go to Elysium?
    Answer

    Because he has Helen and is therefore Zeus' son-in-law (Odyssey 4.561–9); the reward is for the marriage, not for any deed.

  10. What did the Menelaion excavations find, and how does Ayios Vasileios change the picture?
    Answer

    Two Mycenaean mansions (c. 1450 to c. 1200 BC), a gap, then seventh-century cult including the Deinis aryballos "to Helen, wife of Menelaus". The palace with Linear B tablets at Ayios Vasileios, dug since 2009, is now taken as Mycenaean Laconia's centre, making the Menelaion a subordinate residence later claimed for hero-cult.

Carry forward

  1. Helen is the tradition's test case for responsibility: Homer gives her both choice and compulsion and refuses to resolve them, and every later author (Sappho, Stesichorus, Gorgias, Euripides) picks a side. Watch for the same move with Clytemnestra, Medea and Pandora.
  2. The phantom Helen lets the Trojan War be told as a war about nothing: a theodicy (Herodotus), a puzzle about names and bodies (Euripides), an allegory of propaganda (Wolf, Seferis). Keep the eidolon in hand for Plato's cave and the fifth-century debate on seeming and being.
  3. At Sparta Helen was a goddess with a cult at a Bronze Age ruin, patron of girls becoming women; the Menelaion is the model case of epic names attaching to Mycenaean remains, which recurs at Mycenae, Pylos and the eighth-century tomb cults.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Helen and the Spartan side of the Trojan War. Cover: Helen's birth (Leda and the swan, Nemesis and the egg, the two eggs with the Dioscuri); the abduction by Theseus and the rescue by her brothers; the suitors, the oath and Menelaus' selection; her agency in Iliad 3 and 6 and 24 (the teichoskopia, her self-reproach, her lament for Hector) and Odyssey 4 (the drug, the horse story, Menelaus' pointed reply); Stesichorus' Palinode and the phantom Helen in Egypt, Herodotus' Egyptian Helen, Euripides' Helen and the sophistic game it plays; Gorgias' Encomium of Helen and the question of her guilt as a rhetorical set piece; Sappho fr. 16; her reunion with Menelaus and the sword that drops; the Spartan cult of Helen at Therapne (the Menelaion), Helen Dendritis at Rhodes, Helen as a goddess of girls' initiation (Alcman); Menelaus himself: the lesser Atreid, his aristeia, the wounding, the wrestling with Proteus and Elysium as his reward for marrying Zeus' daughter; Mycenaean Laconia and the Menelaion site; Hermione, Orestes and Neoptolemus; Helen in Marlowe, Goethe's Faust, H.D., modern retellings. End with the problem Helen poses: a war fought for a woman who is either guiltless or absent. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.6 · 3,324 words

Reading the Iliad closely: Books 1, 6, 9, 16, 18, 22, 24

Book 1: the quarrelBook 6: Hector in the cityBook 9: the embassyBook 16: the PatrocleiaBook 18: grief and the ShieldBook 22: the death of HectorBook 24: the ransomHow the seven books speak to each otherThe translatorsReading the remaining seventeen booksSelf-testCarry forward

Book 1: the quarrel

The movement is a chain of refused supplications. Chryses comes with ransom for his daughter and is driven off (1.11–32); Apollo's plague follows; Calchas speaks only under Achilles' protection (1.74–100); Agamemnon, forced to give up Chryseis, takes Briseis; Achilles withdraws, and Thetis goes to Zeus. The book closes on Olympus with Hephaestus pouring wine and the gods laughing (1.595–611), a deliberate tonal drop after the human bitterness.

Achilles' first attack on Agamemnon (1.149–171) is forensic: he lists what he does and what he receives; the grievance is distributive. The second (1.225–244), with the sceptre oath, is where he stops arguing within the system and steps outside it. Nestor's mediation (1.254–284) fails because it treats the dispute as a seniority problem, which it no longer is. The epithets dios Achilleus and anax andrōn Agamemnōn set godlike excellence against institutional rank, which is exactly the quarrel. The one simile is Apollo's descent "like the night" (1.47); the sceptre "which will never again grow leaves" (1.234–237) brings in the cut tree that recurs in Book 6 and in Sarpedon's fall.

Rage. Sing, goddess, the rage of Peleus' son Achilles (1.1)
and the plan of Zeus was moving towards its end (1.5)
Wine-sack, with a dog's eyes and a deer's heart (1.225)
Mother, since you bore me to be short-lived (1.352)
Zeus nodded with his dark brows, and great Olympus shook (1.528–530)
Where sources disagree. Whether Achilles is right in Book 1 divides readers. Redfield (Nature and Culture in the Iliad) and Schein (The Mortal Hero) read his withdrawal as a legitimate protest against a broken honour economy; others, following Nestor's own verdict at 9.108–111 and Achilles' later self-reproach at 18.98–111, stress that both men are guilty. The poem itself gives no narrator's verdict.

Book 6: Hector in the city

Book 6 leaves the battlefield twice. First Diomedes and Glaucus meet, discover a hereditary guest-friendship, and exchange armour instead of blows (6.119–236). Then Hector enters Troy and meets, in order, his mother Hecuba (6.251–285), Paris and Helen (6.313–368), and Andromache with the child at the Scaean gate (6.390–502). The three encounters are graded: duty, contempt, love. Hector refuses wine from his mother because he is bloodied and must not pour to Zeus unclean; refuses to sit with Paris; refuses Andromache's plea to fight from the wall.

Glaucus's speech is the poem's great statement of mortality: the generation of leaves (6.146–149), which deliberately recalls the dead sceptre of Book 1. The homilia between Hector and Andromache is a ring: her plea, his reply, the child, her tears, his departure. Andromache's "you are father to me, and honoured mother, and brother" (6.429–430) is a woman who has already lost every other male relative to Achilles (6.414–428), a detail that makes Book 22 inevitable. Hector's reply moves from shame (aidōs) before the Trojans to a vision of Troy's fall and her enslavement, and ends in a prayer for his son that the audience knows is futile.

Hector is koruthaiolos, of the glancing helmet, and that helmet frightens Astyanax (6.467–470), so he takes it off: the formula briefly becomes a prop. Andromache is leukōlenos, white-armed, the formula for a protected woman, used again at 24.723 as she holds Hector's head.

As is the generation of leaves, so is that of men (6.146)
I would feel deep shame before the Trojans and the Trojan women with trailing robes (6.441–442)
The day will come when sacred Ilios will perish (6.448)
May men say of him one day, "He is far better than his father" (6.479)
she took him to her fragrant breast, laughing through her tears (6.483–484)
They mourned Hector in his house while he yet lived (6.500)

Book 9: the embassy

The movement is from the Achaean assembly at night (9.9–181), where Agamemnon offers gifts but no apology, through the embassy's three speeches and Achilles' three replies, back to the assembly where Diomedes dismisses the whole exercise (9.697–709). Odysseus speaks first (9.225–306) and repeats Agamemnon's catalogue of gifts word for word but silently drops Agamemnon's closing demand that Achilles submit to him as the greater man (9.160–161). Achilles' reply (9.308–429) is the longest and most disordered speech in the poem: he rejects the gifts, rejects the honour system that makes gifts meaningful (the coward and the brave man are held in one honour, 9.318–320), announces his departure, and reveals Thetis's prophecy of the two fates.

Phoenix (9.434–605) argues by paradigm: the allegory of the Prayers who follow Ruin (9.502–512) and the long story of Meleager, who withdrew in anger, refused gifts, and was finally persuaded by his wife Cleopatra when the enemy fired the city, but by then the gifts were gone. Achilles softens: he will decide at dawn whether to sail (9.618–619). Ajax (9.624–642) speaks shortest and in the plain idiom of the warrior: a man accepts blood-price even for a brother; Achilles has forgotten his philoi. Achilles yields furthest: he will stay, but not fight until Hector reaches the Myrmidons' ships (9.650–655).

Achilles' one simile, the mother bird feeding her chicks while she goes without (9.323–327), has the greatest warrior figure himself as a female bird; the image of care points forward to Patroclus.

Hateful to me as the gates of Hades is the man who hides one thing and says another (9.312–313)
My homecoming is lost, but my fame will be imperishable (9.412–413)
I count him at the worth of a splinter (9.378)
Not worth my life are all the possessions of Ilios (9.401)
as if I were some vagabond without honour (9.648)
Where sources disagree. At 9.182–198 the Greek uses dual forms ("the two of them went") although three ambassadors go. Page and the Analyst school read this as proof that Phoenix was added later to an embassy of two; Unitarians reply that Phoenix went ahead, or that the duals cover the two heralds, or that the poet counts Phoenix as one of Achilles' own household rather than an envoy. The question remains open. Separately, Nagy holds that kleos aphthiton (9.413) is an inherited Indo-European formula; Finkelberg argued it is a one-off phrase, which would make Achilles' choice of words his own.

Book 16: the Patrocleia

Patroclus comes weeping to Achilles (16.2–4, likened to a girl tugging at her mother's skirt, 16.7–11) and asks to borrow the armour. Achilles consents with a condition he repeats twice: drive them from the ships, then turn back (16.87–96). He prays to Zeus, who grants half (16.249–252). The Myrmidons go out like wasps (16.259–267). Patroclus kills Sarpedon, Zeus's son, whom Zeus considers saving and does not; the god weeps blood onto the earth (16.459–461). Patroclus forgets the condition, charges the wall three times, and is struck by Apollo, speared by Euphorbus, and finished by Hector (16.786–863).

The key speech is Patroclus's rebuke (16.21–45): Achilles is nēlees, pitiless; the grey sea and the cliffs bore him, not Peleus and Thetis. The narrator's comment is unlike anything else in the poem: "so he spoke, begging, the great fool; for it was his own death he was begging for" (16.46–47). Achilles' reply (16.49–100) is the moment where he half-chooses: he will not fight, he will not sail, he will send a proxy. His closing wish that all Achaeans and Trojans perish and only he and Patroclus survive to take Troy (16.97–100) is the ethical low point of his withdrawal.

Sarpedon falls like an oak, poplar or pine cut for ship-timber (16.482–484), the shipwright's world replacing the warrior's; the wrangle over his corpse rehearses Book 17. Patroclus's death is narrated in the second person (16.787), the narrator's only direct address to a dying character.

Peleus was not your father nor Thetis your mother; the grey sea bore you (16.33–34)
the father granted one part and refused the other (16.250)
he wept tears of blood down onto the earth (16.459)
Then, Patroclus, the end of life appeared to you (16.787)
You yourself will not live long; already death stands beside you (16.852–853)
his soul flew from his limbs to Hades, lamenting its fate, leaving manhood and youth (16.856–857)

Book 18: grief and the Shield

Antilochus brings the news; Achilles pours dust on his head and lies in it, "mighty in his mightiness" (18.26), the posture of a corpse. Thetis hears from the sea depths and comes with the Nereids, a catalogue of thirty-three names (18.39–49) that functions as a dirge. Achilles chooses death (18.90–126). Iris sends him unarmed to the trench, where Athena sets a flame on his head like a beacon from a besieged island city (18.207–214); he shouts three times and the Trojans break. The Trojan assembly follows: Polydamas urges retreat inside the walls, Hector refuses (18.243–313), the error that kills him. Then Hephaestus's forge, the Shield, and dawn.

Achilles' speech to Thetis is the pivot of the poem. He wishes Briseis had died rather than cause the quarrel (18.86–87); he calls himself a useless weight on the earth; he accepts the fate revealed in Book 9 as already chosen. The Meleager paradigm has come true: he returns, and the gifts no longer matter. Thetis's dysaristotokeia (18.54) is a word coined for the line.

The Shield (18.478–608) is the poem's largest simile in effect though not in form. Its rings are: cosmos (earth, sea, sky, sun, moon, constellations, 18.483–489); the city at peace with a wedding and a lawsuit over a blood-price (18.490–508); the city at war, besieged, with an ambush and a cattle-raid (18.509–540); ploughing, reaping, vintage (18.541–572); cattle attacked by lions (18.573–586); a sheepfold (18.587–589); a dance-floor like the one Daedalus made for Ariadne (18.590–606); Ocean around the rim (18.607–608).

unhappy mother of the best of men (18.54)
Let me die at once, since I was not to help my companion as he was killed (18.98–99)
I sit by the ships, a useless burden on the earth (18.104)
Not even mighty Heracles escaped death (18.117)
On it he made the earth, the sky, the sea, the untiring sun (18.483–484)
Where sources disagree. Lines 18.535–538, personifying Strife, Tumult and Death on the Shield, are nearly identical to Hesiod, Shield of Heracles 156–159, and were athetised by Alexandrian critics as an interpolation; most modern editors print them with brackets or a note. The lawsuit at 18.497–508 is also unclear: whether the two talents go to the judge who speaks straightest or to the winning litigant, and whether the defendant is offering a blood-price or refusing one, cannot be settled from the Greek.

Book 22: the death of Hector

Hector alone remains outside the wall. Priam (22.38–76) and Hecuba (22.79–89) plead; he deliberates (22.99–130), considers surrender, rejects it, and runs when Achilles arrives. Three circuits of the city, Zeus's scales (22.209–213), Athena disguised as Deiphobus, the duel, the prophecy, the mutilation, and three laments from the wall by Priam, Hecuba and Andromache.

Hector's monologue is the Trojan counterpart to Achilles' speech in Book 9: a hero reasoning his way through alternatives and ending up where honour requires. He imagines Polydamas's reproach (22.100), repeats his Book 6 shame formula word for word (22.105 = 6.442), fantasises surrendering Helen and half the city's wealth, and knows Achilles would kill him anyway. His last proposal to Achilles, a pact over the corpses (22.254–259), is refused in the poem's most savage speech: no oaths between lions and men (22.262–267). Hector dying asks only for burial; Achilles wishes he could eat him raw (22.346–348).

The similes are the richest in the poem and all drawn from peace or sport. Achilles approaching is the Dog Star, brightest and most baneful (22.26–32); his spear-point the evening star (22.317–319). The chase is a hawk and a dove (22.139–142), then horses racing round turning posts for a tripod or a woman as prize, "but they ran for the life of Hector" (22.162–166), then the dream in which pursuer never catches pursued (22.199–201). Andromache, hearing the cry, drops her shuttle: she had been weaving and heating Hector's bath (22.440–446). She runs out "like a maenad" (22.460) and throws off the headdress Aphrodite gave her on her wedding day (22.468–472).

No way now to talk sweetly with him, as a young man and a girl talk (22.126–128)
Let me not die without a struggle and without glory (22.304–305)
There are no trustworthy oaths between lions and men (22.262)
Paris and Phoebus Apollo will destroy you at the Scaean gates (22.359–360)
I will accept my death whenever Zeus and the other gods wish to accomplish it (22.365–366)
as if all Troy were burning from its summit (22.410–411)

Book 24: the ransom

Achilles cannot sleep and drags Hector's corpse round Patroclus's tomb each dawn; Apollo preserves the body. On the twelfth day Apollo protests to the gods (24.33–54): Achilles has destroyed pity and has no shame. Zeus sends Thetis to Achilles and Iris to Priam. Priam loads the ransom, quarrels with his sons, is escorted by Hermes disguised as a young Myrmidon, and enters Achilles' hut unannounced. He clasps Achilles' knees and kisses his hands (24.477–479). They weep together; Achilles speaks of the two jars of Zeus; a flash of the old anger (24.559–570); they eat; they sleep. Hector's body goes home and three women lament him: Andromache, Hecuba, Helen.

Priam's speech (24.486–506) is built on one word: remember your father. It is Phoenix's technique, argument by substitution, but the paradigm is now a living old man in the room. Achilles' reply (24.518–551) is the only place where he generalises about the human condition, with his own father's grief beside Priam's. With Niobe (24.602–617) Achilles uses the mythological paradigm himself, as Phoenix did to him, to persuade Priam to eat. Helen's lament (24.762–775), that Hector alone never spoke a harsh word to her, ends the human voices on gentleness. The one great simile is Priam's entrance: like a killer who comes as a suppliant to a rich man's house, so that amazement seizes those who see him (24.480–484); the roles are inverted, the killer is the host.

Achilles has destroyed pity, and has no shame (24.44–45)
Remember your father, godlike Achilles (24.486)
I have reached out my hand to the face of the man who killed my sons (24.506)
The gods have spun it so that wretched mortals live in grief, while they are free of care (24.525–526)
Now let us think of food. Even Niobe remembered to eat (24.601–602)
Thus they held the funeral of Hector, tamer of horses (24.804)
Where sources disagree. Nineteenth-century Analysts argued Book 24 was a late addition, pointing to its Odyssean vocabulary and to Hermes' escort. Whitman's Homer and the Heroic Tradition (1958) answered with the geometric argument: 24 answers 1 so precisely that the poem is unthinkable without it, and almost all scholars now treat it as integral. Whether its vision of shared grief amounts to a reconciliation or only a truce is still debated; the final line looks past the funeral to Troy's fall.

How the seven books speak to each other

Book 24 answers Book 1

Both open with an old father bringing ransom for a child; Chryses is refused and Priam accepted. Apollo opens both books (1.9, 24.33). Nine days of plague (1.53) answer nine days of mourning (24.664, 24.784); twelve days of divine absence (1.425) answer twelve days of Hector unburied (24.31). Thetis goes up to Zeus in 1 and comes down from him in 24. The quarrel over a prize of honour becomes a shared meal. Whitman called this geometric symmetry; Taplin (Homeric Soundings) prefers to see three movements, 1–9, 11–18, 19–24, each ending at night.

Book 6 sets up Book 22

Everything Andromache loses in 22 was shown in 6: the shame formula (6.442 = 22.105), the Scaean gate, the child, the vision of her slavery (6.454–465) which her lament repeats as fact (22.484–507). The maids who mourned Hector alive at 6.500 mourn him dead. In 6 Hector removes the helmet to comfort the child; in 22 the helmet flashes as he runs. He never comes home between the two books.

The three speeches of Book 9 and Achilles' three choices

Odysseus offers compensation; Achilles rejects it and declares he will sail. Phoenix offers the Meleager paradigm; Achilles wavers and in effect becomes Meleager, returning too late, in 18, when the gifts are worthless. Ajax appeals to the companions; Achilles concedes the condition that is fulfilled to the letter in 16, Hector at the Myrmidons' ships. The three answers map onto the three choices still ahead: send Patroclus (16), return for Patroclus (18), release Hector (24). Several scholars, Nagy among them, have noted that Cleopatra, the wife who moves Meleager, inverts the name Patroclus.

Book 16 mirrors Book 22

Both deaths begin with a warning ignored (Achilles to Patroclus, Priam to Hector). Both are killed by a god's intervention first, Apollo's blow and Athena's deceit, then by a man. Both victims prophesy their killer's death. The two lines for the departing soul are identical (16.856–857 = 22.362–363). Each killer answers the corpse: Hector refuses the prophecy (16.859–861), Achilles accepts it (22.365–366), and that difference is the difference between them. Hector dies wearing Achilles' own armour, which is why Achilles knows where the gap at the throat is (22.322–325).

The Shield and the world outside

The Shield gives the Iliad its missing half: harvest, law, marriage, dance, the whole seasonal and civic order that war interrupts. The lawsuit over a blood-price anticipates Ajax's argument and Priam's ransom; the besieged city is Troy seen from outside; the dancing-floor recalls Andromache's wedding veil. Taplin's reading is that the similes do piecemeal what the Shield does whole, keeping peace present in a poem of killing.

The translators

Lattimore (1951) uses a loose six-beat line, keeps every epithet and repetition, and translates mēnis as "anger"; he is closest to the Greek word order and still the standard for study, at the cost of some stiffness. Fagles (1990) opens "Rage—Goddess, sing the rage", expands freely, varies formulas, and gives the speeches theatrical energy; line numbers do not match the Greek. Lombardo (1997) is the most colloquial, sets each simile off in italics as a separate stanza, and was built for performance; purists object to its slang. Alexander (2015) is line-for-line and as faithful as Lattimore in modern diction, with a preference for "wrath"; the best choice for close reading alongside the Greek line numbers given here. Wilson (2023) writes strict iambic pentameter, which forces a longer poem than the original, flattens archaism, renders epithets variably by context, and translates the opening as "cataclysmic wrath". The disagreement is not about accuracy but about which Homeric quality to keep: formulaic repetition (Lattimore, Alexander), speed and voice (Fagles, Lombardo), or English metre (Wilson).

Where sources disagree. Translators split on whether the repeated formulas are meaning-bearing. Parry's oral-formulaic theory implies many epithets are metrical filler, which licenses Fagles, Lombardo and Wilson to vary or drop them. Lattimore and Alexander hold that the repetitions are heard as echoes, and the mirrored lines of Books 16 and 22 are strong evidence for that view.

Reading the remaining seventeen books

Read Books 2 to 5 fast: the Catalogue (2.484–877) only for names; Helen on the wall (3.121–244); Diomedes' aristeia (5) as the model Achilles will exceed. Skim 7 and 8. Book 10, the night raid, is probably a later insertion and can be skipped. In 11 read Nestor to Patroclus (11.655–803), which sets the proxy plan in motion; in 12 Sarpedon on why princes fight (12.310–328). In the long middle of 13 to 15 read the Deception of Zeus (14.153–351) and Zeus's plot summary at 15.59–71. In 17 read Zeus pitying the immortal horses (17.426–447); in 19 Briseis's lament (19.282–300) and the horse Xanthus speaking (19.404–417); skim 20; in 21 Achilles and Lycaon (21.34–135), the suppliant he kills, which 24 reverses; in 23 Patroclus's ghost (23.65–107) and Achilles' grace at the games, the first sign of the man Priam will meet. With the seven held, each passage locks in as a rung between them.

Self-test

  1. Which two refused or accepted ransoms frame the poem, and in which books?
    Answer

    Chryses' ransom for his daughter is refused by Agamemnon in Book 1; Priam's ransom for Hector is accepted by Achilles in Book 24.

  2. What formula does Hector repeat word for word in Books 6 and 22, and what does it express?
    Answer

    "I would feel shame before the Trojans and the Trojan women with trailing robes" (6.442 = 22.105); it expresses aidōs, the shame before one's community that overrides family pleas.

  3. What does Odysseus omit from Agamemnon's offer when he repeats it to Achilles?
    Answer

    Agamemnon's demand that Achilles submit to him as the greater and elder man (9.160–161).

  4. In what way does Achilles become Meleager?
    Answer

    Like Meleager he withdraws in anger, refuses gifts, and returns only when his own people are desperate, so the gifts no longer matter; Patroclus plays the role of Cleopatra.

  5. Which lines are identical in Books 16 and 22, and what do they describe?
    Answer

    16.856–857 and 22.362–363, the soul leaving the limbs and flying to Hades, lamenting its fate and leaving manhood and youth.

  6. How do Hector and Achilles respond differently to the dying prophecies they receive?
    Answer

    Hector denies that he need die (16.859–861); Achilles accepts his death whenever the gods will it (22.365–366).

  7. Name the main scenes on the Shield of Achilles in order.
    Answer

    Cosmos; city at peace (wedding, lawsuit); city at war (siege, ambush); ploughing, reaping, vintage; cattle and lions; sheepfold; dance; Ocean round the rim (18.483–608).

  8. What is the sceptre oath of Book 1 and what later image does it anticipate?
    Answer

    Achilles swears by the sceptre that will never again grow leaves (1.234–244); it anticipates Glaucus's generation of leaves (6.146–149) and the felled-tree simile for Sarpedon (16.482–484).

  9. Why can Achilles find the vulnerable spot on Hector so precisely in Book 22?
    Answer

    Hector is wearing the armour stripped from Patroclus, which is Achilles' own, so Achilles knows the gap at the collarbone (22.322–325).

  10. What was Andromache doing when she heard the cry from the wall?
    Answer

    Weaving a purple cloak and ordering a hot bath for Hector's return (22.440–446).

Carry forward

  1. The Iliad is built on ring composition and verbal echo: identical lines across books (6.442 and 22.105; 16.856 and 22.362) are deliberate signals, and any translation that varies formulas for elegance hides the structure.
  2. Achilles' arc is a sequence of choices about compensation, from refusing gifts in Book 9 to accepting Priam's in Book 24; the poem's ethics are worked out through what can and cannot be exchanged for a life, which Greek tragedy and Plato's Socrates will both take up.
  3. The similes and the Shield keep the world of peace present inside a poem of war; this Homeric habit of placing the heroic against the ordinary is the model for later Greek thinking about the limits of glory.

Written with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth close reading of the seven structurally critical books of Homer's Iliad, assuming I already have the plot. For each of Books 1, 6, 9, 16, 18, 22 and 24: the scene-by-scene movement, the key speeches and what each is doing rhetorically, the similes and what they bring in from outside the battlefield, the formulaic epithets that matter in context, the ring structures and echoes to other books, and four to six specific lines (quoted briefly in translation with book and line numbers) that I should be able to recognise. Then draw the connections: how Book 24 answers Book 1, how Book 6 sets up Book 22, how the three speeches of Book 9 anticipate Achilles' three choices, how Book 16 and Book 22 mirror each other in the deaths of Patroclus and Hector, what the Shield of Book 18 says about the world outside the poem. Discuss where translators differ significantly (Lattimore, Fagles, Lombardo, Wilson, Alexander) and why. End with how to read the remaining seventeen books efficiently once these seven are known. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.7 · 3,240 words

Reading the Odyssey closely: the Telemachy, the Apologoi, the Nekyia, the recognitions

The proem and the theodicy of Book 1The Telemachy (Books 1–4)Calypso, Nausicaa and the Phaeacians (Books 5–8)The Apologoi (Books 9–12) and the CyclopsThe Nekyia (Book 11)The slow recognitions (Books 13–24)The bow, the slaughter and the maids (Books 21–22)The ending: 23.296 and Book 24Against the Iliad: nostos, metis, the householdSelf-testCarry forward

The proem and the theodicy of Book 1

The first word is andra, "man"; the first epithet, polytropos, "of many turns", means much-travelled, versatile or elusive. Of the whole voyage the proem names only the cattle of Helios, and says the companions died "by their own recklessness" (atasthaliēisin). The poem opens by assigning blame.

"Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns." (1.1)
"They perished by their own recklessness, the fools." (1.7)
"From some point in it, goddess, tell us too." (1.10)

The Muse begins in medias res, and the hero is postponed until Book 5. The first divine speech supplies the moral frame: Zeus, musing on Aegisthus, just killed by Orestes, complains that mortals suffer "beyond their portion" (hyper moron) through their own folly, though Hermes was sent to warn him (1.37–43). The Oresteia becomes the poem's paradigm, repeated by Athena (1.298–302), Nestor (3.193–200) and Agamemnon's ghost in Books 11 and 24.

"How mortals blame the gods! They say evils come from us." (1.32)
"But they themselves, by their own recklessness, suffer beyond their portion." (1.33–34)

The pattern is exact: Aegisthus, the companions (11.104–115, 12.271–276) and the suitors (Halitherses, 2.161–176; Odysseus to Amphinomus, 18.125–150) are each warned, each consume what is not theirs, and each die.

Where sources disagree. Whether the Odyssey actually delivers the justice Zeus announces is contested. Lloyd-Jones (The Justice of Zeus, 1971) argued that the Iliad's Zeus already upholds justice and that the Odyssey only makes the theme explicit; Allan ("Divine Justice and Cosmic Order in Early Greek Epic", JHS 126, 2006) extended the case. Clay (The Wrath of Athena, 1983) reads the opening theodicy as a frame the narrative does not honour: Poseidon persecutes Odysseus for blinding a son who ate six of his men, which is vengeance, not justice; and the Phaeacians are punished for their hospitality, their ship turned to stone (13.125–187). The theodicy may be a programmatic claim the narrative only partly honours.

The Telemachy (Books 1–4)

For four books the hero is absent and the poem studies his absence: a house being eaten, a wife unable to choose, a son who does not know whether he has a father. Athena's stated aim in sending Telemachus away is not information but reputation, "that good fame (kleos) may be his among men" (1.95). The journey to Pylos and Sparta is an apprenticeship in speech, guest-friendship and bearing.

"My mother says I am his; no one knows his own begetting." (1.215–216)
"Speech shall be the concern of men, and mine most of all." (1.358–359)

That second line silences Penelope and is a pointed adaptation of Hector's "war shall be the concern of men" (Iliad 6.492); the formula returns at 21.352 with "the bow". Telemachus asserts manhood by imitating a fixed phrase, and the poem marks his growth by the occasions on which he uses it.

Sparta supplies competing images of the father and of marriage. Helen drugs the wine with nepenthes (4.220–221) and tells how she kept the disguised Odysseus' secret at Troy (4.240–264); Menelaus answers with Helen at the Wooden Horse imitating the Greeks' wives to lure them out (4.266–289). The stories disagree about Helen, and the poem lets them stand.

"You hold Helen, and to them you are son-in-law of Zeus." (4.569)

Proteus promises Menelaus an Elysian afterlife earned by marriage: an immortality Odysseus will refuse from Calypso.

Where sources disagree. Nineteenth-century analysts (Kirchhoff, Die homerische Odyssee, 2nd ed. 1879) treated the Telemachy as a separate poem stitched on, noting the duplicated divine council of Book 5. Unitarians (Klingner, "Über die vier ersten Bücher der Odyssee", 1944) reply that the doubled council handles simultaneous action and that the Telemachy sets the stakes, including the suitors' ambush plot (4.663–672). Most current scholarship is unitarian here, but the seams are real.

Calypso, Nausicaa and the Phaeacians (Books 5–8)

Odysseus is first seen weeping on a beach, his life "ebbing away" (5.152–153). Calypso, whose name suggests "concealer", offers immortality; his refusal is the poem's choice of mortal identity over oblivion. He answers with tact rather than passion: Penelope is lesser in looks, but he wants to go home.

"Even so I wish and long each day to reach my home." (5.219–220)
"Thrice blessed the Greeks who died at Troy." (5.306)

The second line, spoken on the raft, is an Iliadic wish for a hero's death and fame; the Odyssey's hero will have to survive instead. Washed up on Scheria, he hides under a double bush "like a brand in black ashes" (5.488–491), the seed of fire kept alive.

Nausicaa's episode is Homer's most delicate social comedy. A naked, brine-crusted man emerges "like a mountain lion" (6.130), supplicates with words rather than touch, and compares her to Artemis and a Delian palm (6.149–169). His blessing frames the poem's marriage plot.

"Nothing is better than when man and wife keep house with one mind." (6.182–184)
"Remember me at home, for you owe me your life first." (8.461–462)

Nausicaa's hope of such a husband (6.244–245) is quietly closed off. Scheria is a hinge between fairy-tale and Ithaca: Arete, not Alcinous, must be won over (6.310–315, 7.53–77), a rehearsal for Penelope.

Demodocus' songs of the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles (8.72–82) and of the Wooden Horse (8.499–520) make Odysseus weep, and the simile for his tears is the Odyssey's sharpest comment on the Iliad.

"As a woman weeps, flung on her husband's body, fallen before his city." (8.523–524)
"The gods spun ruin for men, so there might be song hereafter." (8.579–580)

The sacker of cities weeps like a captive widow of a sacked city. The reverse simile asks the listener to see the war from the side of its victims, and Alcinous' gloss turns suffering into material for poetry.

The Apologoi (Books 9–12) and the Cyclops

For four books Odysseus narrates his own adventures to the Phaeacians. No other witness survives to check him. He opens by naming himself with Iliadic pride.

"I am Odysseus son of Laertes, known to all for my wiles." (9.19–20)

The Cyclops read in full

The episode is framed by ethnography: no assemblies, no laws (themistes), no ships, no ploughing (9.106–115), and a goat island viewed with a colonist's eye (9.116–141). Odysseus brings Maron's strong wine (9.196–211), anticipating trouble. In the cave his men urge him to take cheeses and lambs and run; he stays, wanting guest-gifts.

"I would not listen, though it would have been far better." (9.228)

The narrator concedes his own error. Polyphemus inverts every rule of xenia: he asks the guests' names only after eating two of them, mocks Zeus (9.275–278), and promises Odysseus the "gift" of being eaten last (9.369–370). Odysseus' reply rests on a pun.

"Nobody is my name. Nobody they call me." (9.366)
"Nobody is killing me by trickery, not by force." (9.408)

The neighbours answer "if nobody (mē tis) is harming you", and Odysseus' heart laughs that his name and metis deceived them (9.410–414). The blinding uses similes of a shipwright's drill and a smith's quenching (9.384–394), civilised craft turned on the uncivilised. Triumph is then complicated by Polyphemus' tender speech to the ram hiding Odysseus (9.447–460). Finally Odysseus abandons outis for kleos and shouts name, patronymic and home (9.502–505), enabling the curse.

"Let him come late and badly, lose all his comrades, on another's ship." (9.534–535)

Polyphemus' prayer, ending "and find troubles in his house", is an exact summary of the rest of the poem. The episode dramatises the tension between the self-effacing cunning that saves Odysseus and the heroic need to be known that endangers him.

An unreliable narrator?

In the Ithacan half Odysseus tells long false autobiographies, the Cretan tales (13.256–286, 14.192–359, 19.165–202), and the narrator comments that "he told many lies like truths" (19.203), a line echoing Hesiod's Muses (Theogony 27). Alcinous, at the intermezzo, insists the opposite about the Apologoi.

"You have told your tale with skill, as a singer does." (11.367–368)
Where sources disagree. Most ("The Structure and Function of Odysseus' Apologoi", TAPA 119, 1989) reads the Apologoi as a performance tailored to win Phaeacian gifts and passage, perhaps embroidered. Richardson ("Truth in the Tales of the Odyssey", Mnemosyne 49, 1996) and others note that the primary narrator independently corroborates key facts (the cattle, 1.7–9; Poseidon's anger over the Cyclops' eye, 1.68–75), and that Alcinous' praise is designed to exclude the comparison with liars. Antiquity was split too: Juvenal (15.13–26) mocks the tall tales, and "a tale of Alcinous" became proverbial for a long improbable story (Plato, Republic 614b). The poem may want the question left open.

The Nekyia (Book 11)

Odysseus does not descend; he pours blood into a pit and the dead come up to drink. Elpenor comes first, unburied (11.51–80); then Tiresias, prophesying the inland journey with an oar and a gentle death ex halos, ambiguously "away from" or "out of" the sea (11.121–137); then Anticleia, dead of longing for him (11.197–203).

"Three times she flew from my hands like a shadow or a dream." (11.207–208)

The catalogue of women

Persephone sends a procession of heroines (11.225–332): Tyro, Antiope, Alcmene, Megara, Epicaste, Chloris, Leda, Iphimedeia, Phaedra, Procris, Ariadne, Maera, Clymene and Eriphyle.
