It is Hesiodic in form, close to the Catalogue of Women attributed to Hesiod, and it is aimed at its audience: when Odysseus breaks off, it is Arete who speaks first and claims him as "my guest" (11.336–341).

Where sources disagree. In the catalogue, Epicaste (Jocasta) hangs herself, but Oedipus goes on ruling in Thebes "suffering pains" (11.271–280); there is no self-blinding and no exile. This is earlier than, and different from, the version Sophocles made canonical.

Agamemnon and Achilles

Agamemnon tells his murder at a feast (11.405–434) and draws the moral that makes Penelope's fidelity the poem's measure. He praises her (11.444–446), then advises secrecy anyway.

"There is no more trusting women." (11.456)

Achilles' answer to Odysseus' consolation is the most quoted repudiation of the Iliad's value system in Greek.

"I would rather be a hired hand to a landless man, alive." (11.489–490)
"Than be lord over all the perished dead." (11.491)

The thēs was the lowest free labourer, below the oikos itself. Achilles is consoled only by news of Neoptolemus (11.538–540): kleos survives as a father's pleasure, not a dead man's compensation. Ajax's silent turning away (11.563–564) is the other answer.

Tityos, Tantalus, Sisyphus and Heracles' phantom

At 11.568 the scene changes. Odysseus, still at the pit, suddenly sees Minos judging, Orion hunting, Tityos with vultures at his liver (11.576–581), Tantalus reaching for water and fruit (11.582–592), Sisyphus pushing his stone (11.593–600), and Heracles.

"Then I saw mighty Heracles, his phantom; he himself is with the gods." (11.601–602)
Where sources disagree. The scholia report that 11.602–604, which split Heracles into a phantom below and a deified self married to Hebe on Olympus, were suspected as an insertion by Onomacritus, the Peisistratid editor. Aristarchus athetised the whole stretch from 11.568 to 627 (the scholia's objection is that Odysseus could not see into Hades from his pit), and modern analysts (Page, The Homeric Odyssey, 1955, among them) keep the suspicion on roughly 11.565–627: the viewpoint shifts from a pit to a tour of Erebus, and eternal punishment is otherwise absent from Homer. Defenders (Heubeck in the Oxford commentary, vol. 2, 1989) note that the sinners offended gods directly, an archaic idea, and that Heracles' labour in Hades (11.617–626) mirrors Odysseus' own. Interpolation of 602–604 is likely; of the larger passage, uncertain.

The slow recognitions (Books 13–24)

The second half is built from recognitions deliberately delayed and differentiated by character. Athena opens it by appreciating his lies, "crafty would he be who outdid you" (13.291), and claiming kinship in cunning (13.296–299). Telemachus recognises him only by being told.

"I am no god. Why liken me to the immortals? I am your father." (16.187–188)

Argos, neglected on the dung heap, recognises him first and unprompted, and dies (17.290–327). In the same scene Eumaeus, himself a nobleman's son sold into slavery (15.403–484), states the poem's harshest social axiom.

"Zeus takes half a man's worth the day slavery seizes him." (17.322–323)
"Death seized Argos, having seen Odysseus in the twentieth year." (17.326–327)

Eurycleia and the scar

Penelope orders the old nurse to wash the beggar's feet. As her hand touches the scar the narrative stops for some seventy lines (19.393–466) to tell how the boy was named by his grandfather Autolycus, "a man who has caused pain (odyssamenos) to many" (19.406–409), and gored by a boar on Parnassus. Only then does she drop his foot in the basin.

"You are Odysseus, dear child, and I did not know you." (19.474–475)

Erich Auerbach's "Odysseus' Scar" (Mimesis, 1946, ch. 1) made this the type of Homeric style, everything foregrounded, against the "fraught with background" Genesis 22. Critics object that the digression is placed with purpose: it gives the origin of the name at the moment identity is exposed. Odysseus then grips her throat (19.479–481): recognition is a danger, not a reward.

Penelope's tests

Penelope extracts gifts from the suitors as Odysseus watches approvingly (18.274–283), tells her dream of the eagle and geese (19.535–553), distinguishes the gates of horn and ivory (19.560–567), and announces the bow contest (19.572–581). After the slaughter she still withholds recognition until the test of the bed built round an olive trunk (23.177–204), the only time Odysseus is caught off guard. The embrace simile again reverses roles.

"As welcome as land to swimmers whose ship Poseidon has smashed." (23.233–234)
Where sources disagree. Does Penelope recognise Odysseus before Book 23? Harsh ("Penelope and Odysseus in Odyssey XIX", AJP 71, 1950) argued for an early, concealed recognition in Book 19; Winkler ("Penelope's Cunning and Homer's", in The Constraints of Desire, 1990) and Katz (Penelope's Renown, 1991) read her strategic indeterminacy as the point; Heubeck in the Oxford commentary (vol. 3, 1992) keeps her ignorant until the bed test. The text supports suspicion; it does not settle it.

Laertes

Odysseus finds his father digging in rags and tests him with "mocking words" (24.240): gratuitous cruelty to some readers, a release of grief to others. The scene completes the poem's pattern: every recognition has been a test, and the last is made of the one person who could never have been an enemy, so that the testing is shown as a habit of the man and not only a tactic. The proof is the trees Laertes gave the boy, thirteen pear, ten apple, forty fig (24.340–342): the orchard as inheritance.

"What a day, dear gods: son and grandson vie in courage." (24.514–515)

The bow, the slaughter and the maids (Books 21–22)

The suitors cannot string the bow; Odysseus does so like a singer stringing a lyre, and the string sings "like a swallow" (21.406–411). The simile completes the identification of hero and bard made in Book 11. Book 22 opens with him shedding his rags (22.1) and shooting Antinous through the throat mid-drink (22.8–21).

"You dogs, you thought I would never come home from Troy." (22.35)
"It is unholy to exult over slain men." (22.412)

The killing is sorted by status: the prophet Leodes dies despite supplication (22.310–329); the bard Phemius and herald Medon are spared (22.330–380). Eurycleia names twelve of fifty female slaves as disloyal (22.421–425). Odysseus orders them to clean the hall and be put to the sword; Telemachus changes the method.

"Let them not die a clean death, these who poured shame on us." (22.462–463)
"Their feet twitched for a little, not for long." (22.473)

The hanging is described with a simile of thrushes or doves caught in a net (22.468–472), after which Melanthius is mutilated (22.474–477). The scene was little discussed for centuries and is now one of the most discussed in the poem.

Wilson and the women and slaves

Emily Wilson's translation (Norton, 2017), widely billed as the first complete English Odyssey by a woman, kept the Greek line count in iambic pentameter and rendered andra polytropon as "a complicated man". Its larger effect was on the vocabulary of the household. Where earlier versions often said "maids" or "servants" for dmōai, Wilson says "slaves", and she pointed out that some modern translators had given the hanged women abusive labels ("sluts", "whores") absent from the Greek, which uses neutral demonstratives and a verb for sleeping with the suitors. She stressed how little choice unfree women had with their master's guests. Attention shifted from Penelope as the poem's only significant woman to the women whose bodies sustain the oikos and are destroyed by it. Margaret Atwood's The Penelopiad (2005), partly narrated by the maids, had prepared the ground.

Where sources disagree. The objections to Wilson's choices are three: "complicated" loses the travel sense of polytropos; the plain register flattens formula; and the contrast with earlier translators is overstated, since "servant" was often period convention, as Lattimore's and Fitzgerald's versions show. Few dispute that the poem presents the hanging as justified within its frame; the debate is how a translation should render that frame.

The ending: 23.296 and Book 24

"Gladly they went to the rite of their old bed." (23.296)

The scholia on this line report that Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus called it the peras or telos of the Odyssey. They also preserve objections, associated with Aristarchus, to the second Nekyia (24.1–204), where Agamemnon sets Penelope's undying kleos against Clytemnestra's infamy (24.192–198). Then come Laertes, the revolt of the suitors' kin under Eupeithes, and Athena's abrupt halt (24.531–548).

"Stop, men of Ithaca, from grievous war." (24.531)
Where sources disagree. Whether "telos" meant the textual end or the plot's fulfilment is itself disputed. Page (The Homeric Odyssey, 1955) argued the continuation is later, citing linguistic anomalies and Hermes' unusual role as escort of souls. Defenders, notably Wender (The Last Scenes of the Odyssey, 1978) and Heubeck in the Oxford commentary, answer that the poem has prepared Laertes (1.189–193, 11.187–196) and the blood-feud (20.41–43, 23.117–122), so stopping at 23.296 leaves a vendetta unresolved. Most now accept Book 24 as integral, if rougher; the abrupt divine halt still dissatisfies many.

Against the Iliad: nostos, metis, the household

Nostos against kleos

Achilles chooses between return without kleos and death at Troy with fame "unwithering" (Iliad 9.412–416). Odysseus refuses immortality, wishes once for Iliadic death (5.306), and hears Achilles call kleos worthless to the dead (11.489–491). Yet the boast to the Cyclops shows kleos still compelling, and the last word on fame goes to Penelope (24.196–198), whose kleos is won by staying.

Metis against bie

The Iliad knows that cunning beats strength (Nestor, Iliad 23.315–318), but its decisive acts are of force. Gregory Nagy (The Best of the Achaeans, 1979) read the poems as rival claims to be "best of the Achaeans", by bie or by metis; Demodocus' first song stages that quarrel (8.75–78). Yet the Odyssey ends in massacre, and the bow is both force and skill.

The household against the battlefield

The Iliad's house is Hector's, glimpsed in Book 6 and doomed. The Odyssey's subject is the oikos: stores, herds, slaves, bed, trees. Its values are hospitality and like-mindedness; its villains are guests who consume. The reverse similes carry war and shipwreck into the house, and Book 22's battle is fought in a dining hall. The cost of restoration falls on those who belonged to the household without owning anything in it.

Self-test

  1. Which single episode of the voyage does the proem name, and what moral word is attached to the companions' deaths?
    Answer

    The cattle of Helios (1.8–9); the companions died by their own recklessness, atasthaliēisin (1.7).

  2. What is the point of Zeus' speech about Aegisthus at 1.32–43?
    Answer

    Mortals suffer "beyond their portion" through their own recklessness despite divine warnings (Hermes warned Aegisthus); it frames the companions' and suitors' fates and makes the Oresteia the poem's recurring paradigm.

  3. Which Iliadic line does Telemachus adapt at 1.358–359, and where does the formula recur?
    Answer

    Hector's "war shall be the concern of men" (Iliad 6.492); Telemachus substitutes "speech" (mythos), and the formula recurs with "the bow" at 21.352.

  4. What does the simile at 8.523–531 do?
    Answer

    It compares Odysseus, weeping at the song of the Wooden Horse, to a woman mourning her husband killed defending their city: the sacker of cities likened to his victims.

  5. Explain the pun at 9.410–414.
    Answer

    The Cyclopes say "if nobody (mē tis) is harming you"; Odysseus laughs that his name and metis (cunning) deceived them. Outis/mē tis/metis fuse anonymity and intelligence.

  6. Why does Odysseus' boast at 9.502–505 matter for the rest of the poem?
    Answer

    By giving his full name he enables Polyphemus' curse to Poseidon (9.528–535), which predicts the late, solitary return on another's ship and trouble in his house.

  7. What does Achilles say at 11.489–491, and what consoles him?
    Answer

    He would rather be a hired labourer (thēs) to a landless man than rule all the dead; he is consoled only by news of his son Neoptolemus' prowess.

  8. Which lines of the Nekyia were suspected in antiquity, and on what grounds is a larger passage suspected now?
    Answer

    11.602–604 (Heracles' phantom and deified self), attributed in the scholia to Onomacritus; modern analysts suspect roughly 11.565–627 because Odysseus, fixed at the pit, suddenly views Erebus and its eternal punishments, otherwise un-Homeric.

  9. What did Auerbach argue from the scar digression (19.393–466), and what is the usual objection?
    Answer

    That Homer foregrounds everything with no background or suspense, unlike Genesis; critics reply that the digression on Odysseus' naming is purposefully placed at the moment of exposure of identity.

  10. What did Aristophanes and Aristarchus say about 23.296, and what is the main argument for Book 24?
    Answer

    They called it the telos or peras of the poem; defenders of Book 24 argue that the poem has prepared both the Laertes reunion and the blood-feud with the suitors' families, which require resolution.

Carry forward

  1. The Odyssey announces a moral frame at 1.32–34 (suffering through one's own recklessness after warning) and then tests it; read its justice, including the hanging of the slave women, as a claim the poem makes, not a fact it proves.
  2. Odysseus is a narrator as well as a hero; the poem identifies him with the bard (11.368, 21.406–411) and with the liar (19.203), so every first-person account in Greek literature after it inherits the question of reliability.
  3. The Odyssey defines itself against the Iliad: nostos over kleos, metis over bie, oikos over battlefield, yet it keeps the older values alive inside the new ones, and the cost of the restored household falls on those without power in it. Whether that contrast is allusion to a fixed text (Pucci, Odysseus Polutropos, 1987) or rivalry between two traditions still forming (Nagy, The Best of the Achaeans, 1979) is itself open.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth close reading of the structurally critical parts of Homer's Odyssey, assuming I already have the plot. Cover: the proem and the theodicy of Book 1 (Zeus on Aegisthus) as the poem's moral frame; the Telemachy (Books 1 to 4) and what it is for; the Calypso and Phaeacian books (5 to 8) and Nausicaa; the Apologoi (Books 9 to 12) as a first-person narration and the question of Odysseus as unreliable narrator, with the Cyclops episode read in full; the Nekyia (Book 11) in detail: the catalogue of women, Agamemnon, Achilles' reply, the Tityos-Tantalus-Sisyphus passage and its possible interpolation, Heracles' phantom; the slow recognitions of the second half (Argos, Eurycleia and the scar with its digression, Penelope's tests, Laertes); the bow and the slaughter in Books 21 and 22 and the hanging of the maids; the ancient athetesis of the ending after 23.296 and the modern debate about Book 24. Give four to six specific lines per section (quoted briefly in translation with book and line) that I should recognise. Discuss how Wilson's translation changed the conversation about the poem's women and slaves. End with the thematic contrasts to the Iliad: nostos against kleos, metis against bie, the household against the battlefield. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.8 · 3,936 words

The other Greeks at Troy

Diomedes: the hero who fights godsThe two AjaxesNestor: speech, Pylos and a cupPatroclus and Antilochus: the deaths that define AchillesIdomeneus, Menelaus and TeucerPhiloctetes and Neoptolemus: the men fetched lateCalchas, the seers, and ThersitesCults, colonies and the uses of TroySelf-testCarry forward

Diomedes: the hero who fights gods

Diomedes son of Tydeus is the Iliad's substitute Achilles. While Achilles sulks, Diomedes carries the Greek offensive, and the poem lets him do what no other mortal does: strike Olympians. In his aristeia (Homer, Iliad 5) Athena lifts the mist from his eyes so that he can tell gods from men (5.127–8), and tells him to spare every god except Aphrodite. He kills Pandarus, crushes Aeneas' hip with a stone, and when Aphrodite shields her son he wounds her on the wrist, drawing ichor (5.330–43). She flees to Dione, whose list of gods wounded by mortals (5.381–415) also works as a warning: men who fight gods do not live long. Later, with Athena driving his chariot, he spears Ares in the belly, and the war god bellows like nine or ten thousand men (5.855–63).

Book 6 reverses the mood. Meeting Glaucus, Diomedes asks his pedigree, and Glaucus answers that the generations of men are like leaves (6.146) before telling the Bellerophon story. Their grandfathers turn out to have been guest-friends, so the two refuse to fight and swap armour. Homer remarks that Zeus took Glaucus' wits away, since he gave gold for bronze, a hundred oxen's worth for nine (6.234–6). The scene shows xenia (guest-friendship) overriding the war, and lets the narrator make a dry joke at the Lycian's expense.

The night raid of Book 10, the Doloneia, pairs Diomedes with Odysseus. They capture the Trojan spy Dolon, get the dispositions of the camp out of him, kill him, then slaughter the newly arrived Thracian king Rhesus and take his horses. After Troy, the Little Iliad (in Proclus' summary) has the same pair steal the Palladium, the image of Athena whose presence protected the city. A later tale, the source of the proverb "Diomedean necessity", has Odysseus try to murder Diomedes on the way back with the image; it survives only in late compilers and is best treated as uncertain.

Where sources disagree. A scholion to Iliad 10.1 reports that Book 10 was composed separately and inserted into the poem under Peisistratus. Georg Danek (Studien zur Dolonie, 1988) and Bryan Hainsworth (The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 3, 1993) treat it as a late addition, pointing to its unusual vocabulary and its loose links to the plot. Casey Dué and Mary Ebbott (Iliad 10 and the Poetics of Ambush, 2010) defend it as a deliberately different, night-time kind of episode within the oral tradition. The question remains unresolved.

On the homecoming, Homer and the later tradition part ways. Nestor reports that Diomedes reached Argos safely on the fourth day (Odyssey 3.180–2). The later version, which a scholiast on Lycophron traces to Mimnermus, has Aphrodite take her revenge: his wife Aegialeia takes a lover (Cometes in Apollodorus, Epitome 6.9) and drives him out. He sails to Daunia in Apulia, helps King Daunus, and founds Argyrippa (Arpi), along with other towns, according to Strabo (6.3.9). His companions are turned into seabirds that nest on the Islands of Diomedes, the Tremiti, and are said to welcome Greeks and attack barbarians (Pliny, Natural History 10.126–7; Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.457–511). In Virgil (Aeneid 11.243–95) the old exile turns down the Latin request to fight Aeneas, having learned what fighting Trojans costs. Strabo records that the Heneti at the head of the Adriatic sacrificed a white horse to him (5.1.9). Pindar says Athena made him an immortal god (Nemean 10.7). Diomedes is therefore one of the few Homeric heroes who received cult as a god across a wide stretch of non-Greek Italy.

The two Ajaxes

Ajax son of Telamon

The greater Ajax is the defensive hero. His shield, made by Tychius from seven ox-hides with a bronze facing, is "like a tower" (Iliad 7.219). The image may preserve a memory of the Mycenaean body-shield, which had gone out of use long before Homer. In Book 7 he fights Hector in a formal duel that heralds stop at nightfall, and the two exchange gifts: Hector's silver-studded sword for Ajax's purple belt (7.303–5). In Sophocles that sword is the one Ajax later falls on. He is the only major Greek the Iliad never wounds. In Book 15 he holds the ships alone, striding from deck to deck with a pike twenty-two cubits long (15.674–88). Only when Hector cuts his spear through does he give way and let the fire in (16.102–23), which prompts Achilles to send Patroclus.

His defining story comes after the Iliad: the Judgement of the Arms. When Achilles dies, his armour is to go to the best of the Greeks, and Odysseus wins it. The Little Iliad had Trojan girls overheard comparing the two heroes. In Odyssey 11.543–64 the judges are "children of the Trojans and Pallas Athena", and Ajax's shade turns away from Odysseus in silence. Pindar returns to the episode repeatedly as an example of envy and of the lies that defeat merit (Nemean 7.20–30, 8.23–34). Sophocles' Ajax stages what followed. Athena drives him mad, he slaughters the army's cattle believing them to be the Atreidae, and when he recovers he kills himself on stage, which is rare in tragedy. The second half of the play is a quarrel over his burial that Odysseus settles in his favour. The play's question is whether a heroic code built on honour can survive a world run by votes and speeches.

His cult had a political role. Ajax came from Salamis, which Athens and Megara contested. Iliad 2.557–8 places his twelve ships beside the Athenians, and in antiquity the line was alleged to have been inserted by Solon or Peisistratus to support the Athenian claim (Plutarch, Solon 10; Strabo 9.1.10). When Cleisthenes created ten tribes, Delphi chose ten eponymous heroes, and Ajax was admitted as a "neighbour and ally" although he was a foreigner (Herodotus 5.66). The tribe Aiantis carried his name. Before the battle of Salamis the Athenians called on Ajax and Telamon for help (Herodotus 8.64), and they afterwards dedicated a captured Phoenician trireme to him (8.121). Miltiades' family, the Philaids, traced their line to him (Herodotus 6.35). His tomb mound at Rhoeteion in the Troad was still being visited under Hadrian.

Ajax son of Oileus

The lesser Ajax leads the Locrians: he is small, wears a linen corslet, surpasses all the Greeks with the spear (Iliad 2.527–30) and has no equal at running down men in flight (14.520–2). The Iliad already treats him as someone Athena dislikes. She makes him slip in dung during the footrace (23.773–83). At the sack of Troy he drags Cassandra away from Athena's image, which in some versions turns its eyes away. He escapes stoning by clinging to the goddess's altar (Proclus' summary of the Iliupersis). On the voyage home Poseidon saves him from the wreck, but when he boasts that he survived in spite of the gods, Poseidon splits the rock he is clinging to (Odyssey 4.499–511).

Where sources disagree. The early epic summaries describe a sacrilegious dragging from sanctuary. The explicit rape of Cassandra appears later, in Hellenistic and Roman authors such as Lycophron. Lycophron has Cassandra foretell her own violation (Alexandra 348–64) and Apollodorus states it outright (Epitome 5.22), while Proclus' summary of the Iliupersis speaks only of dragging her from the image. Whether the early epic implied the rape and was discreet, or later writers made the crime worse, is uncertain.

The crime was atoned for by a real ritual. For a thousand years, so the story ran, the Locrians sent two maidens of good family each year to Athena's sanctuary at Ilion. They had to slip in at night while the townsfolk tried to kill them, and then served barefoot with cropped hair (Lycophron, Alexandra 1141–73, with scholia; Aeneas Tacticus 31.24). An early-third-century BC inscription from western Locris (IG IX 1² 3, 706) sets out privileges for the families that supplied the girls, so the practice was historical. Plutarch speaks of it as having ended not long before his own time (On the Delays of Divine Vengeance 557d).

Where sources disagree. Polybius (12.5) and Timaeus argued over the tribute in connection with the origins of Locri in Italy. Strabo (13.1.40) says the maidens were first sent only in the Persian period, which contradicts the claim that the rite went back to the Bronze Age. Modern estimates of when it began range from the seventh century BC to a Hellenistic revival.

Nestor: speech, Pylos and a cup

Nestor has ruled over two generations of men and now rules the third (Iliad 1.250–2). His digressions are not filler. Each recalled exploit, whether against the Centaurs (1.260–72), the giant Ereuthalion (7.132–56) or the cattle raid on the Epeans (11.670–761, the longest in the poem), sets a precedent that the present generation is invited to live up to. His advice is mixed. He proposes marshalling the army by tribe and phratry (2.362–3) and suggests the embassy to Achilles. But his speech in Book 11 also gives Patroclus the idea of going into battle in Achilles' armour (11.796–803), so the counsellor sets the fatal chain in motion. His four-handled gold cup, decorated with doves, which other men can hardly lift (11.632–7), is a deliberately antique object. In Odyssey 3 he is home again, sacrificing to Poseidon on the shore at Pylos.

In 1939 Carl Blegen began digging at Ano Englianos in Messenia and found a Mycenaean palace, now called the Palace of Nestor, together with an archive of Linear B tablets. Once Ventris had deciphered the script in 1952, the tablets showed a palace economy with offerings to po-se-da-o (Poseidon) and a coastline organised against attack. The palace burned around 1180 BC. The rich Griffin Warrior grave nearby (found 2015) shows that the site already had elite wealth in the early Mycenaean period.

Where sources disagree. Even in antiquity it was unclear which Pylos was Nestor's. Strabo (8.3.7) quotes the saying that there is "a Pylos before Pylos" and argues for Triphylian Pylos. Blegen's identification (Blegen and Rawson, The Palace of Nestor at Pylos in Western Messenia, vol. 1, 1966) is a convention, not a proof.

The other Nestor relic is a clay drinking cup from Pithekoussai on Ischia. It is a Rhodian kotyle buried in a boy's cremation grave (no. 168) around 730–720 BC, and an inscription in Euboean script was cut into it after firing. After a damaged first line come two hexameters, which end:

whoever drinks from this cup, desire of fair-crowned Aphrodite will seize him

It is among the earliest Greek verse to survive in writing, and the joke works by contrast: an ordinary clay cup against the heavy golden one of legend.

Where sources disagree. The first line can be restored as "I am Nestor's cup" or "Nestor's cup was good to drink from, but…". Barry Powell (Homer and the Origin of the Greek Alphabet, 1991) takes the joke to show that our Iliad was known in the West by about 720 BC. Christopher Faraone ("Taking the Nestor's Cup Inscription Seriously", Classical Antiquity 15, 1996) reads the lines as a conditional incantation rather than a literary allusion, and others think the cup was already famous in pre-Homeric tradition, which would leave the date of the poem open.

Patroclus and Antilochus: the deaths that define Achilles

Achilles' story turns on two dead companions. Patroclus is the older of the pair (Iliad 11.786–7). He came to Peleus' house as a boy exile after killing a playmate in a quarrel over knucklebones (23.85–8). Wearing Achilles' armour, he kills Sarpedon. He is then stripped by Apollo, wounded by Euphorbus and finished off by Hector (16.786–857), and Achilles' grief and revenge drive the last third of the poem. His ghost asks for their bones to share one urn (23.82–92), and Odyssey 24.76–7 says that they do.

Where sources disagree. Homer never calls them lovers. Aeschylus' Myrmidons did, making Achilles the older lover. Phaedrus in Plato's Symposium (180a) objects that Achilles was the younger and more beautiful of the two. Modern readers remain divided on whether Homer implies an erotic bond: W. M. Clarke ("Achilles and Patroclus in Love", Hermes 106, 1978) argued that he does, K. J. Dover (Greek Homosexuality, 1978) that the pederastic reading is a fifth-century imposition.

Antilochus, Nestor's son, is the young man Achilles likes best after Patroclus (Odyssey 24.78–9). He brings Achilles the news of Patroclus' death (Iliad 18.1–21). In the chariot race he fouls Menelaus, and Achilles smiles at him and gives him a prize anyway (23.555–6). In the lost Aethiopis he dies saving his father from Memnon. Pindar (Pythian 6.28–42) holds him up as the model of a son's devotion. Achilles then kills Memnon, and soon afterwards dies himself, so Antilochus' death repeats the Patroclus pattern of a friend killed, revenge taken and Achilles' own death following.

Where sources disagree. Neoanalytic scholars such as Kakridis and Schadewaldt argued that the Iliad's Patroclus plot was modelled on an older Memnon–Antilochus story. Bernard Fenik (Typical Battle Scenes in the Iliad, 1968) replied that the shared scenes are typical patterns of the tradition, and others that the influence could have run the other way, or that both versions draw on a shared stock of motifs. Because the Aethiopis is lost, the question cannot be settled.

Idomeneus, Menelaus and Teucer

Idomeneus and the Cretans

Idomeneus, grandson of Minos, brings one of the largest contingents: eighty ships from Knossos, Gortyn, Lyktos, Phaistos and other towns (Iliad 2.645–52). The Catalogue calls Crete the island "of a hundred cities", while the Odyssey gives ninety (19.174), a discrepancy ancient critics already discussed. He is middle-aged and half-grey (13.361), and his aristeia in Book 13 is one of a veteran fighter. His squire Meriones wears the boar's-tusk helmet described at 10.261–5, an object archaeology has confirmed as Mycenaean. Homer brings Idomeneus home safely (Odyssey 3.191–2). The later tradition does not. In Servius (on Aeneid 3.121), Idomeneus vows in a storm to sacrifice the first thing he meets on landing, which turns out to be his son. Plague follows, and he is expelled and settles among the Sallentini of southern Italy (Aeneid 3.400–1). In another version his wife Meda is unfaithful with Leucus (Apollodorus, Epitome 6.10).

Menelaus as warrior

Menelaus is more than a wronged husband. He beats Paris in their duel until Aphrodite carries Paris away (Book 3), survives Pandarus' arrow (4.127–47), and volunteers to face Hector until Agamemnon holds him back (7.94–122). His real aristeia is the defence of Patroclus' body in Book 17: he kills Euphorbus over the corpse and strips him (17.43–60), holds the body against Hector until the Ajaxes arrive (17.106–39), and in the end carries it off with Meriones while the two Ajaxes cover them (17.715–61). Apollo, in disguise, there calls him a "soft spearman" (17.588), but the insult is answered by what Menelaus is shown doing in that book. The Odyssey promises him the Elysian plain because he is Helen's husband and so Zeus' son-in-law (4.561–9). He and Helen were worshipped at Therapne near Sparta (Herodotus 6.61), where excavation has found Archaic votives dedicated to Helen.

Teucer and Cypriot Salamis

Teucer, Ajax's half-brother by the Trojan captive Hesione, shoots from behind Ajax's shield "like a child under its mother" (Iliad 8.266–72). When he came home without his brother, Telamon banished him. Euripides' Helen (87–150) shows him on his way to found a new Salamis in Cyprus at Apollo's command. Pindar (Nemean 4.46–7) and Horace (Odes 1.7.21–32) tell the same story. The Teucrid kings of Cypriot Salamis claimed descent from him (Isocrates, Evagoras 18), and so did the priest-dynasts of Zeus at Olba in Cilicia (Strabo 14.5.10).

Where sources disagree. Einar Gjerstad ("The Colonization of Cyprus in Greek Legend", 1944) took the Teucer legend as a distant memory of real Aegean migration to Cyprus in the twelfth and eleventh centuries BC, supported by the Arcado-Cypriot dialect and Late Cypriot III material. Maria Iacovou (American Journal of Archaeology 112, 2008) reads the Hellenisation of Cyprus as a slow process that the founder legend compresses into one landing, which would make Teucer a later dynastic charter that happened to match the archaeology. The evidence fits both readings.

Philoctetes and Neoptolemus: the men fetched late

Philoctetes

Philoctetes holds the bow of Heracles, given to him for lighting the hero's pyre on Oeta. In the Catalogue he is already lying on Lemnos in agony from a water snake's bite, and the Argives "would soon remember" him (Iliad 2.721–5). The Cypria (in Proclus' summary) placed the bite on Tenedos and said he was left behind because of the stench of the wound. The Little Iliad told how the captured seer Helenus revealed that Troy could not fall without the bow. Philoctetes is fetched, healed by Machaon, and kills Paris.

Sophocles' Philoctetes (409 BC) sends Odysseus and the young Neoptolemus to bring him back. Odysseus wants to win him by a lie. Neoptolemus, who has his father's honest nature, goes along with it, then breaks off and returns the bow. Only the appearance of the deified Heracles brings the story to the outcome myth requires. The play sets persuasion against force and fraud, and asks whether a good end can justify deceiving a man who has been wronged. Dio Chrysostom (Oration 52) compares it with the lost versions by Aeschylus and Euripides, both of which had Lemnian choruses. Sophocles' deserted island is his own invention. Homer lists Philoctetes among those who got home safely (Odyssey 3.190). The western tradition has him driven out of Meliboea by civil strife instead. He then founds Petelia and Crimisa in Bruttium (Strabo 6.1.3; Aeneid 3.401–2) and dedicates the bow to Apollo Alaios (ps.-Aristotle, On Marvellous Things Heard 107). The temple of Apollo Alaios has been excavated at Punta Alice near Cirò Marina.

Neoptolemus

Achilles' son by Deidamia grew up on Scyros (Iliad 19.326–7). In the Little Iliad Odysseus fetches him and gives him his father's armour, and in Odyssey 11.505–37 Odysseus praises him to Achilles' ghost. At the sack he kills Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios and takes Andromache as his prize. Euripides' Andromache (1243–9) makes their son Molossus the ancestor of the Molossian kings, the dynasty that later produced Pyrrhus and Olympias.

Where sources disagree. Proclus' summary of the Iliupersis has Odysseus kill Astyanax. A fragment of the Little Iliad (quoted by Tzetzes on Lycophron 1268) has Neoptolemus throw the child from the walls. Euripides' Trojan Women presents the killing as a decision of the whole Greek army.

He died at Delphi. Pindar (Paean 6.112–20) says Apollo had sworn that the man who killed Priam at an altar would never reach home or old age, and that Neoptolemus was cut down in a quarrel over sacrificial meat. Euripides makes Orestes the planner of the murder (Andromache 1085–165). Nemean 7 (35–47) presents his death more favourably: he lies within the sanctuary as overseer of its rites. A scholiast says the ode was meant to mollify Aeginetans offended by the paean, but many modern scholars doubt that story. Pausanias saw his tomb, which received annual offerings (10.24.6), and reports that his ghost helped defend Delphi against the Gauls in 279 BC (1.4.4). The killer at the altar ended up guarding the sanctuary where he was killed.

Calchas, the seers, and Thersites

Calchas son of Thestor is "best of bird-interpreters", who knew what is, what will be and what was before, and guided the fleet to Troy (Iliad 1.69–72). He reads the omen of the snake and the nine sparrows at Aulis as nine years of war (2.299–330). In Book 1 he names Agamemnon's offence and is called a "prophet of evils" for it (1.106). The Cypria and Aeschylus (Agamemnon 104–257) make him the man who demands Iphigenia. His death fits the fate of seers: Hesiod's Melampodia, as cited by Strabo (14.1.27), has him die of grief at Claros after losing a contest in counting figs to Mopsus. Strabo (6.3.9) also records a hero-shrine of Calchas on a hill in Daunia, where people seeking oracles slept on the fleece of a black ram, with a shrine of the healer Podalirius nearby. The army's experts were a seer and two healers, Machaon and Podalirius (Iliad 2.729–33). Their later cults followed the same western routes as the warriors'.

Thersites is the only character in the Iliad whose ugliness is described in detail: bandy-legged, lame, hunched, with a pointed, balding head (2.216–19). His speech against Agamemnon repeats Achilles' grievances almost point for point (2.225–42). Odysseus beats him with the sceptre, and the army laughs and calls it the best thing Odysseus has ever done. The scene makes the same argument sound contemptible in the mouth of a man without status. In the Aethiopis Achilles kills him for mocking his grief over Penthesilea. In Plato's myth of Er his soul chooses to be reborn as an ape (Republic 620c).

Where sources disagree. Homer gives Thersites no father, and many critics read him as the voice of the common soldier being silenced. The later tradition makes him the son of Agrius and so a cousin of Diomedes' father Tydeus (Apollodorus 1.8.5–6), an Aetolian aristocrat. That turns the class reading into a question about manners within the elite.

Cults, colonies and the uses of Troy

Put the later fates side by side and a pattern appears. The heroes whose homecomings fail become founders. Diomedes' unfaithful wife, Idomeneus' vow, Philoctetes' expulsion and Teucer's exile all leave the hero unable to return home, so he goes west or east and settles somewhere new. In the stories that survive, Diomedes, Idomeneus, Philoctetes, Calchas and Podalirius, along with Epeius at Lagaria and Nestor's Pylians at Metapontum (Strabo 6.1.15), are spread along the coasts of southern Italy. Teucer goes to Cyprus, Mopsus and Amphilochus to Cilicia, and Neoptolemus to Epirus. Irad Malkin's The Returns of Odysseus argues that these nostoi served as a shared language between Greek newcomers and native peoples. A Daunian elite could take Diomedes as its own founder and so claim a place in Greek legend without being colonised, as Rome later did with the Trojan Aeneas.

At home, the same heroes supported land claims and political identities. Athens used a disputed line of Homer and Ajax's cult to claim Salamis, and his name for a Cleisthenic tribe. It argued over Sigeion with Mytilene by appeal to Trojan precedent (Herodotus 5.94–5). Spartan and Athenian envoys cited Agamemnon and the Catalogue to Gelon of Syracuse (Herodotus 7.159–61). Royal houses such as the Philaids, the Teucrids of Salamis and the Molossian Aeacids used the heroes as ancestors. Tombs anchored cult in a specific landscape: Ajax at Rhoeteion, Neoptolemus at Delphi, Calchas in Daunia.

Where sources disagree. Mycenaean pottery at Apulian and Calabrian sites such as Scoglio del Tonno and Roca Vecchia has been read as the basis for a Bronze Age memory behind the western nostoi, the view Malkin argues against. Malkin (The Returns of Odysseus, 1998) dates the stories as we have them to the Archaic and Classical periods. They were collected by Timaeus and turned into poetry by Lycophron, long after any such memory could have survived. What remains uncertain is how far native communities shaped these myths, rather than simply receiving them from Greeks.

The Trojan legend was flexible enough to be used in all these ways. The heroes it pushed into exile, defeat or sacrilege were especially useful for founding new communities, because their stories left them with nowhere to return to.

Self-test

  1. Why does Athena allow Diomedes to wound Aphrodite in Iliad 5, and which other god does he wound?
    Answer

    Athena clears his sight so he can recognise gods and tells him to fight none except Aphrodite, whom he wounds on the wrist (5.330–43). Later, with Athena as his charioteer, he also wounds Ares (5.855–63).

  2. What does the Glaucus–Diomedes exchange in Book 6 show, and what is the narrator's joke?
    Answer

    Guest-friendship inherited from their grandfathers outweighs the war, so they refuse to fight and exchange armour. The joke is that Zeus took Glaucus' wits, since he gave gold armour worth a hundred oxen for bronze worth nine (6.234–6).

  3. What ancient doubt attaches to Book 10, and who takes part in the raid?
    Answer

    A scholion says the Doloneia was composed separately and added under Peisistratus. Diomedes and Odysseus capture and kill Dolon, then kill Rhesus and take his horses.

  4. How does the Homeric account of Diomedes' return conflict with the later tradition?
    Answer

    In Odyssey 3.180–2 he reaches Argos safely. Later sources give him an unfaithful wife, Aegialeia, and exile to Daunia, where he founds Arpi, his companions become birds, and he is worshipped in Italy.

  5. How did Athens make political use of Ajax son of Telamon?
    Answer

    Through the disputed line Iliad 2.558 supporting the Athenian claim to Salamis, through the Cleisthenic tribe Aiantis (Herodotus 5.66), through calling on Ajax before the battle of Salamis (8.64), and through the Philaid claim of descent from him.

  6. What was the Locrian maidens' tribute, and what shows it was historical?
    Answer

    As atonement for the lesser Ajax's sacrilege against Cassandra, the Locrians sent two maidens each year to serve Athena at Ilion, entering at night at risk of their lives. An early-third-century BC Locrian inscription regulating the supplying families, together with Polybius, Strabo and Plutarch, shows the practice was real. Its date of origin is disputed.

  7. What does Nestor's cup from Pithekoussai say, and why is it debated?
    Answer

    It is a kotyle of about 730–720 BC whose inscription ends in two hexameters promising that the drinker will be seized by the desire of Aphrodite. Scholars debate whether its joke presupposes our Iliad (11.632–7) or an older traditional cup of Nestor.

  8. How does Antilochus' death relate to Patroclus', and what theory links them?
    Answer

    In the Aethiopis Memnon kills Antilochus while he saves Nestor, Achilles takes revenge, and Achilles' own death follows, which mirrors the Patroclus–Hector sequence. Neoanalysts argue that the Iliad adapted an earlier Memnon story. Critics dispute the direction of influence.

  9. What ethical problem does Sophocles' Philoctetes stage, and where did Philoctetes end up in the western tradition?
    Answer

    Whether a needed end justifies deceiving a wronged man: Neoptolemus' honesty against Odysseus' fraud, settled only by Heracles. In the West he founds Petelia and Crimisa in Bruttium and dedicates the bow to Apollo Alaios.

  10. How did Neoptolemus die, and what was his status at Delphi afterwards?
    Answer

    He was killed at Delphi, in a quarrel over sacrificial meat according to Pindar's Paean 6, or in a plot by Orestes according to Euripides. This was Apollo's punishment for killing Priam at an altar. He received annual hero cult at his tomb there (Pausanias 10.24.6) and was said to have helped defend the sanctuary against the Gauls.

Carry forward

  1. A failed homecoming is how the myth produces founders: heroes who cannot return home through exile, betrayal or vow found cities instead, so the nostoi serve as charter myths for the Greek and Italian West and for Cyprus.
  2. Homer and the later tradition often disagree about the same hero (Diomedes' safe return against his exile, Odysseus or Neoptolemus as killer of Astyanax), so always ask which source and which century a version comes from.
  3. Hero cult was real and had political uses: tombs, tribes, rituals and genealogies (Ajax at Athens, the Locrian maidens, Neoptolemus at Delphi, the Teucrids) turned epic figures into supports for land claims and dynastic legitimacy.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the secondary Greek heroes of the Trojan War, one profile each with sources and later fate. Cover: Diomedes (his aristeia in Book 5 including wounding Aphrodite and Ares, the exchange with Glaucus in Book 6, the Doloneia, the Palladium, his return to an unfaithful wife and his second life in Italy with cult in Apulia); Ajax son of Telamon (the duel with Hector, the defence of the ships, the shield like a tower, the Judgement of the Arms, the madness and suicide in Sophocles, his cult at Salamis and the Athenian tribe); Ajax son of Oileus (the rape of Cassandra, the shipwreck, the Locrian maidens' tribute to Athena at Troy as a historical ritual); Nestor (the garrulous counsellor, his Pylos and the Linear B palace, Nestor's cup from Pithekoussai); Patroclus and Antilochus as the two whose deaths define Achilles; Idomeneus and the Cretan contingent; Menelaus as warrior; Philoctetes (the bow of Heracles, Lemnos, Sophocles' play and its ethics, his Italian foundations); Neoptolemus (Scyros, the killing of Priam and Astyanax, Andromache, his death at Delphi and his cult there); Teucer and the founding of Cypriot Salamis; Calchas and the seers; Thersites as anti-hero. End with what the spread of these heroes' cults across the Greek and Italian world tells us about how the Trojan legend was used to found cities and claim land. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.9 · 3,599 words

The gods at Troy

The plan of ZeusZeus, Thetis and the scales of fateThe partisans and their reasonsDouble motivation: whose decision?Thetis, pity and the limits of immortalityOlympian comedy: deception, laughter, theomachyThe Odyssey's different theologyCritics and allegoristsIf the gods made it happen, who is responsible?Self-testCarry forward

The plan of Zeus

The Iliad's proem names a cause before it names a single action: the wrath of Achilles sent many souls to Hades, "and the plan of Zeus was being accomplished" (Dios d' eteleieto boulē, Iliad 1.5). The clause is grammatically parenthetical and thematically enormous. It places everything that follows under a divine design without saying what the design is.

Ancient readers gave two answers. The narrow one identifies the plan with the one Zeus forms in Book 1: to honour Achilles by giving the Trojans the upper hand until the Achaeans pay for Agamemnon's insult (1.508–10; 2.1–4, where Zeus "pondered how he might honour Achilles"). The broad one comes from the scholia on 1.5, which quote the Cypria (fr. 1 West). Earth, weighed down by the countless tribes of men, appealed to Zeus, who pitied her and resolved to lighten her load through "the great strife of the Iliac war". The same scholion reports that Momus advised Zeus against thunderbolts and floods and suggested instead that he marry Thetis to a mortal and father a beautiful daughter. Achilles and Helen become the two instruments of depopulation. Proclus' summary of the Cypria opens with Zeus planning the war with Themis. The idea had a long life: in Hesiod's Catalogue of Women (fr. 204.95–123 M–W) Zeus resolves to end the race of demigods, and Euripides uses the overpopulation motive at Helen 36–41 and Orestes 1639–42.

Where sources disagree. Nobody has settled whether the Iliad poet knew the Cypria plan, or meant it. Neoanalysts such as Wolfgang Kullmann argue that the Iliad presupposes a cyclic story of this kind, which is why 1.5 needs no gloss. The other side is Aristarchus' own, preserved in the scholia on 1.5: explain Homer from Homer, read the plan as the Thetis plan only, and note that the Iliad never mentions a burdened Earth. The Cypria as a poem is later than the Iliad, although its material may be older. Kirk (The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 1, 1985) on 1.5 takes a middle line: the phrase is deliberately open, and the local plan (Achilles' honour) is one phase of the larger one (the fall of Troy and the end of the heroes).

The consequence is what matters. If the war is Zeus' population control, the Iliad is a poem about mass death administered from above, and the causes the heroes argue over (Helen, Briseis, the insult) are surface. If the plan is only the Thetis plan, Zeus is a god who acts because a mother asked him to. The poem supports both readings, and much of its theology lives in the gap between them.

Zeus, Thetis and the scales of fate

Thetis' supplication (1.495–530) follows the ritual form exactly. She clasps Zeus' knees with one hand and his chin with the other, and she calls in a debt: Achilles has already told how she once saved Zeus, when Hera, Poseidon and Athena tried to bind him, by summoning the hundred-handed Briareus (1.396–406). Zeus' first reply is anxious, because Hera will scold. His second is absolute: the nod of his head cannot be revoked (1.524–30). From here on Zeus is bound by his own promise, and the middle books carry it out: the false dream sent to Agamemnon (2.1–40), the ban on divine intervention (8.1–27), the Trojan advance to the ships, and the death of Patroclus, which Zeus forecasts at 8.473–7 and 15.59–71.

Alongside the promise runs the language of fate (moira, aisa) and the golden scales. At 8.68–74 Zeus weighs the two armies; the Achaean fates sink, and he thunders against them. At 16.658 Hector, turning to flee, "recognised the sacred scales of Zeus", a metaphor that the earlier scene has made literal. At 22.208–13 Zeus weighs the death-fates of Achilles and Hector. Hector's sinks toward Hades, and Apollo leaves him. Odysseus' remark that Zeus tips the scales in battle (19.223–4) shows that the image was proverbial. The device probably comes from the Memnon story of the Aethiopis, in which Thetis and Eos watched the souls of their sons weighed. Aeschylus staged that weighing in his lost Psychostasia (Plutarch, How the Young Man Should Listen to Poems 17a).

The test cases are Sarpedon and Hector. At 16.431–61 Zeus, grieving for his son, asks whether he should snatch him from death. Hera answers that he may: "do it; but we other gods will not all approve" (16.443). Then she warns that every god will want to save a favourite. Zeus gives way and sheds a rain of blood. At 22.168–85 the exchange is replayed with Athena over Hector. Zeus yields again, and adds that he was not speaking in earnest.

Where sources disagree. Is Zeus subject to fate? Three positions have long competed. (1) Fate is an impersonal power above Zeus, and the scales are something he reads, not something he sets. This is the older view, found in W. C. Greene's Moira (1944). (2) Fate and the will of Zeus coincide. Homer speaks of "the aisa of Zeus" (17.321) and pairs Zeus with Moira (19.87), so the scales are a ritual of decision, not discovery (Lloyd-Jones, The Justice of Zeus, 1971; B. C. Dietrich, Death, Fate and the Gods, 1965, traces a more complex development). (3) The question is partly misplaced. Zeus could act "beyond fate" (hyper moron; cf. 2.155, 16.780, 20.30), but doing so would break the order the gods share, which is exactly Hera's argument at 16.443–9. Narratological readers add that fate is the shape of the tradition: Zeus "could" save Sarpedon in the way the poet "could" have the Achaeans sail home in Book 2, and these near misses are dramatic tension, not metaphysics (Janko, The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 4, 1992, on 16.431–61; J. V. Morrison, Homeric Misdirection, 1992). No single answer fits every passage, and that is probably the honest conclusion.

The partisans and their reasons

Iliad 20.33–40 gives the formal line-up. Hera, Athena, Poseidon, Hermes and Hephaestus side with the Achaeans; Ares, Apollo, Artemis, Leto, Xanthus and Aphrodite with the Trojans. Their motives are uneven: some come from myth, some from cult, some are purely personal.

GodSideReason, stated or impliedKey passages
HeraAchaeanThe Judgement of Paris. She will let Zeus destroy her own Argos, Sparta and Mycenae in return for Troy4.31–67; 24.25–30
AthenaAchaeanThe Judgement; patron of Diomedes, Odysseus and Achilles5.1–8, 5.825–63; 22.214–47
PoseidonAchaeanLaomedon cheated him and Apollo of their wages for building the wall and herding cattle, and threatened to cut off their ears21.441–60; 7.452–3
AphroditeTrojanThe Judgement; Paris is her favourite and Aeneas her son3.373–420; 5.311–430
ApolloTrojanHis cult at Troy (a temple on Pergamum, 5.446) and in the Troad; the honour of his priest Chryses1.33–52; 16.786–806; 24.33–54
AresTrojanNone given. Athena accuses him of breaking a promise to fight for the Achaeans5.832–4; 21.410–14

HermesAchaean (in name)None. He will not fight Leto, and he escorts Priam in Book 2421.497–501; 24.334–467
Xanthus (Scamander)TrojanThe local river, whose streams are choked with Achilles' dead21.211–382

Two of the partisans are worth a sentence beyond the table. Aphrodite is the only god the poem shows failing in battle: she carries Paris out of his duel in a mist (3.373–82) and is wounded in the wrist by Diomedes while rescuing Aeneas, so that Zeus tells her war is not her work (5.330–51, 5.426–30). Xanthus is the one partisan with no myth behind him, only a grievance of the present: Achilles chokes his streams with corpses, the river rises against him, and Hephaestus has to burn the water back (21.211–382), the Iliad's one fight between a man and a landscape.

Three points are worth pressing. First, the Judgement of Paris is the obvious explanation for Hera's and Athena's hatred, yet the Iliad names it only at 24.25–30. There Paris is said to have insulted the goddesses who came to his farmstead, and to have praised the one who gave him grievous lust. Everywhere else the poem treats their hatred as a given, and at 4.31–5 Zeus himself asks what Priam has done to deserve it.

Where sources disagree. Aristarchus athetised 24.25–30, partly because he held that Homer did not know the Judgement and partly because the word machlosynē ("lust") seemed un-Homeric. Karl Reinhardt (Das Parisurteil, 1938) argued the reverse: the poet knew the story and held it back until the end, when the gods' partisanship has to be accounted for before Hector is ransomed. Most scholars now accept the lines and treat the silence as deliberate. A minority still regards them as an intrusion.

Second, Poseidon's motive falls apart if pressed. Apollo suffered the same fraud from Laomedon and still defends Troy, and Poseidon himself rescues Aeneas at 20.293–308 because the line of Dardanus has to survive. Grudges in the Iliad are real, but they give way to destiny and to the gods' private attachments. Third, Ares is a war god without a cause. Zeus calls him the most hateful of the Olympians to him (5.890), and Athena wounds him twice: through Diomedes' spear in Book 5, and with a boundary stone thrown by her own hand at 21.403–8. The poem's sympathy runs with Athena's disciplined violence, not with violence for its own sake.

Double motivation: whose decision?

At 1.188–222 Achilles is divided in his heart: draw his sword and kill Agamemnon, or check his anger. As he draws, Athena seizes him by the hair. Only he can see her, and she tells him she has come to stop his fury, "if you will obey" (1.207). He obeys, saying that a man should listen to the gods. So whose restraint is it, his or hers?

The classic answer is Albin Lesky's "double motivation" (Göttliche und menschliche Motivation im homerischen Epos, 1961): Homer routinely gives an act both a human and a divine cause and sees no contradiction. The text supports him. Achilles' deliberation is narrated before Athena arrives. Her speech gives reasons, since gifts three times as great will come to him (1.213–14), and she makes her intervention depend on his consent. The goddess does not replace the man's decision. She makes it visible and gives it dignity.

Where sources disagree. Bruno Snell (Die Entdeckung des Geistes, 1946) argued that Homeric man lacks a unified self, so decisive turns of mind can only be represented as divine interventions. E. R. Dodds (The Greeks and the Irrational, 1951, ch. 1) read Agamemnon's apology, "I am not to blame, but Zeus and Moira and the Erinys" (19.86–7), as evidence of a shame culture that projected unwelcome impulses onto the gods. Bernard Williams (Shame and Necessity, 1993) attacked both. Homeric characters deliberate, decide and accept responsibility, and only the vocabulary differs from ours. Agamemnon, after all, still pays the compensation (19.137–8). In Homer, divine causation explains an act; it does not excuse it.

Ancient readers asked the same question in different terms. Heraclitus the Allegorist (Homeric Problems 17–20) read Athena's grip on Achilles' hair as reason taking hold of the head, the seat of thought. That is an allegorical version of the psychological reading Lesky would later give.

Thetis, pity and the limits of immortality

Thetis is the most important mother in the poem and arguably its most important god. Laura Slatkin (The Power of Thetis, 1991) showed how much the Iliad compresses into her. The courtship, Themis' prophecy and the marriage to Peleus are told in module 4.1; what matters here is the consequence: her son's mortality is the price of Zeus' continued rule. Her rescue of Zeus with Briareus hints at a cosmic power the poem otherwise keeps offstage, and it is the reason Zeus owes her. Whether that story is old is disputed: M. M. Willcock ("Mythological Paradeigma in the Iliad", 1964) argued that Achilles' tale of Briareus is the poet's ad hoc invention, made for the moment of the plea and attested nowhere else, which would make the "debt" a rhetorical fiction; Slatkin takes it as a compressed trace of a real cosmogonic tradition about Thetis. The poem's theology reads differently on each view.

Her scenes mark the poem's structure: the first plea (1.357–427, 1.495–530); her lament among the Nereids as "unhappy mother of the best of men" (dysaristotokeia, 18.54); her request for new armour (18.369–617); and her last errand, telling Achilles that Zeus wants Hector's body returned (24.77–140). She knows the choice her son faces, a long life without glory or a short one with it (9.410–16), and every intervention she makes brings closer the outcome she mourns. A goddess who cannot die watches the one thing she cares for become mortal.

Divine pity in the Iliad follows the same pattern: deep feeling with no power to undo. Zeus' rain of blood for Sarpedon (16.459–61) is the strongest case. At 17.198–208 he pities Hector as he puts on Achilles' armour, knowing that his death is near. At 17.441–7 he pities the immortal horses of Achilles (not Hector's), who weep for Patroclus, and regrets giving them to a mortal, since nothing is more wretched than man of all that breathes and creeps on the earth. Apollo, declining to fight Poseidon, states the theology behind this. Men are like leaves that flourish and then perish (21.462–7), and their fate is not worth a quarrel between gods.

Olympian comedy: deception, laughter, theomachy

The Deception of Zeus

The Dios apatē (14.153–353) is the poem's longest divine episode. To distract Zeus from the battle, Hera bathes and dresses, borrows Aphrodite's embroidered band (kestos himas, 14.214–17) under a false pretext, and bribes Sleep with the promise of the Grace Pasithea (14.267–9). Sleep is nervous, because the last time he helped her Zeus nearly threw him into the sea (14.249–62). On Ida, Zeus assures Hera that he has never desired anyone so much and then lists his previous lovers (14.315–28). The earth sends up flowers beneath them, and a golden cloud covers them (14.346–51). When he wakes in Book 15, Zeus reminds Hera of the time he hung her from the sky with anvils tied to her feet (15.18–24).

Where sources disagree. Is the scene comedy or cult? The flowers and cloud recall the sacred marriage (hieros gamos) of Sky and Earth. Jasper Griffin (Homer on Life and Death, 1980) reads the scene as comedy whose point is the contrast with the men dying below; Janko sets out the sacred-marriage parallels and takes the demonstration that desire can overpower even Zeus seriously. Aristarchus athetised the list of lovers (14.317–27) as unfitting. The episode also contains a theogony that is not Hesiod's, naming Ocean and Tethys as the origin of the gods (14.201, 14.246), which Plato noticed (Theaetetus 152e). Janko (vol. 4, 1992) reads the episode as both comic and cosmological.

Laughter

Book 1 ends with Hephaestus bustling round Olympus pouring nectar to defuse a quarrel between Zeus and Hera, and "unquenchable laughter rose among the blessed gods" (1.599). The joke depends on the gods' freedom from consequence: they can quarrel and laugh because nothing that happens among them is final. Demodocus' song of Ares and Aphrodite caught in Hephaestus' net (Odyssey 8.266–366) repeats the pattern, with the same laughter at 8.326.

The theomachy

In Book 20 Zeus lifts his ban and the gods go to war with one another. The opening is cosmic. Zeus thunders, Poseidon shakes the earth, and Hades leaps from his throne in fear that the ground will split and expose his house (20.54–66). Then the battle is postponed. When it resumes (21.385–513) it is farce. Athena fells Ares with a stone and knocks down Aphrodite. Apollo declines to fight Poseidon. Hera boxes Artemis' ears with her own bow, and Artemis runs weeping to her father's lap (21.489–513). Hermes concedes to Leto without striking a blow. Zeus watches, and his heart laughs with joy (21.389–90).

The meaning lies in the contrast with the plain below. On Olympus nobody dies: a wound heals and a defeat ends in a sulk. The theomachy sits between Achilles' fight with the river and his killing of Hector, so the gods' war reads as a parody of the human war around it. Pseudo-Longinus (On the Sublime 9.6–8) put the problem precisely: Homer makes his men gods and his gods men, and the battle of the gods is terrifying but, unless taken as allegory, wholly godless.

The Odyssey's different theology

The Odyssey opens on Olympus with a theodicy. Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for their troubles, when "they themselves, through their own recklessness, suffer beyond their portion" (1.32–4). His example is Aegisthus, whom Hermes warned and who went ahead anyway (1.35–43). The proem has already said that Odysseus' companions died "by their own recklessness" (atasthaliai, 1.7) when they ate the cattle of the Sun. The suitors' destruction makes the same point at length, and Laertes draws the conclusion: the gods still exist on Olympus, if the suitors have paid (24.351–2). Gods visit men in the guise of strangers to watch their violence and their good order (17.485–7).

Athena's patronage is different in kind as well. In the Iliad she favours heroes. In the Odyssey she has a sustained, almost collegial bond with Odysseus, founded on shared intelligence: she cannot abandon him, she says, because he is so smooth-spoken, quick-witted and shrewd (13.330–2). Against this stands Poseidon's grudge over the blinding of Polyphemus (1.68–75, with the curse at 9.526–36). That grudge is a personal vendetta, not justice, and Zeus indulges it by letting Poseidon turn the Phaeacian ship to stone (13.125–87).

Where sources disagree. How different is the Odyssey's theology? Kullmann ("Gods and Men in the Iliad and the Odyssey", 1985) argued for a real shift from a capricious Zeus to an ethical one. Lloyd-Jones (The Justice of Zeus, 1971), whom Kullmann was answering, had argued that the Iliad's Zeus already punishes crooked judgements (16.384–92) and broken oaths (4.160–8), so the difference is one of emphasis. Poseidon's grudge shows that the Odyssey has not fully moralised its gods either.

Critics and allegorists

Xenophanes and Plato

The philosophical attack begins with Xenophanes of Colophon in the late sixth century. Homer and Hesiod, he wrote, gave the gods everything that is shameful among men: theft, adultery and deceiving one another (fr. B11 DK; cf. B12). He added that men make gods in their own image (B15–16) and proposed instead a single god who does not move (B23–6). Plato's Republic (2.377d–383c, 3.386a–392c) turns the criticism into censorship. It bans Hephaestus' binding of Hera and the battles of the gods (378d), the two jars of Zeus (379d, quoting 24.527–33), Athena's prompting of Pandarus to break the truce (379e), the lying dream of Book 2 (383a), the gods' unquenchable laughter (389a) and the Deception (390b–c). Plato also rejects the defence that these stories carry hidden meanings (hyponoiai), because the young cannot tell allegory from literal sense (378d).

The Alexandrians

The Hellenistic editors (Zenodotus, Aristophanes of Byzantium and above all Aristarchus) dealt with the problem in the text itself. Lines judged unfitting (aprepes) for gods or heroes were marked with the obelos as suspect, among them the Judgement at 24.25–30 and Zeus' list of lovers at 14.317–27. Aristotle had already given a more relaxed answer: some things said about the gods are neither better nor true, "but that is what people say" (Poetics 25, 1460b35–1461a1, with a reference to Xenophanes).

Allegory

The other defence was allegory. Theagenes of Rhegium (c. 525 BC), the first Homeric critic we know of, read the theomachy in two ways, according to a scholion on Iliad 20.67 that goes back to Porphyry. Physically, it is a war of elements, with Apollo and Hephaestus as fire against Poseidon as water. Morally, it is a war of qualities, with Athena as wisdom against Ares as folly and Aphrodite as desire. Metrodorus of Lampsacus went further and turned the heroes into parts of the cosmos. The Stoics systematised allegory through etymology. Heraclitus' Homeric Problems (first century AD) states the stakes in its opening: if Homer meant nothing allegorically, he was impious throughout. Heraclitus reads the plague of Book 1 as summer sickness sent by the sun, and Hera hung between the anvils as the ordering of the elements. By the time of Porphyry's On the Cave of the Nymphs, the Neoplatonists had made Homer a theologian.

If the gods made it happen, who is responsible?

The poems ask this question before any critic does. On the wall Priam tells Helen, "you are not to blame in my eyes; the gods are to blame" (3.164). Helen blames herself (3.173–80, 6.344–8) and then gives the poem's most startling answer. Zeus laid an evil fate on her and Paris, she says, so that they might be a song for people yet to come (6.357–8). In the Odyssey Alcinous says the same of Troy (8.579–80). Agamemnon blames Zeus, Moira and the Erinys, and still pays.

Later writers kept pressing. Gorgias' Encomium of Helen argues that if the gods compelled her, she is blameless. In Euripides' Trojan Women Hecuba answers that "Aphrodite" is only a name for Helen's own folly: her mind saw Paris and became Cypris (987–90). Homer's position is neither of these. Divine causation and human responsibility run together, and the gods give suffering a purpose by making it worth singing about. That theodicy of song is the Iliad's answer, and its most disturbing one.

Self-test

  1. What does Iliad 1.5 assert, and what two identifications of the "plan of Zeus" did ancient readers offer?
    Answer

    That the plan (boulē) of Zeus was being accomplished through Achilles' wrath. The narrow reading identifies it with Zeus' promise to Thetis to honour Achilles (1.508–10, 2.1–4); the broad reading, from the scholia quoting the Cypria (fr. 1 West), identifies it with Zeus' plan to relieve the overburdened Earth by means of the Trojan War.

  2. In the scholion quoting the Cypria, what alternative methods did Momus advise against, and what did he propose instead?
    Answer

    He advised against thunderbolts and floods, and proposed marrying Thetis to a mortal and fathering a beautiful daughter, Helen. Achilles and Helen together would bring about the war that thins out mankind.

  3. Name the three passages in which Zeus' scales appear in the Iliad narrative, and what each decides.
    Answer

    8.68–74: the Achaean fates sink and Zeus thunders against them. 16.658: Hector recognises the turning of Zeus' sacred scales and flees. 22.208–13: the death-fates of Achilles and Hector are weighed; Hector's sinks and Apollo leaves him.

  4. What argument does Hera use at 16.443–9 to stop Zeus saving Sarpedon, and why does it matter to the question of fate?
    Answer

    She says he may do it, but the other gods will not approve, and every god will then want to save a favourite son. It suggests that Zeus can act "beyond fate" but refrains because doing so would destroy the shared divine order. Fate is binding as a social and cosmic constraint, not as a physical impossibility.

  5. Where is the Judgement of Paris mentioned in the Iliad, and how did Aristarchus and Reinhardt respond?
    Answer

    Only at 24.25–30. Aristarchus athetised those six lines, partly because he thought Homer did not know the story and partly because the word machlosynē seemed un-Homeric. Reinhardt (1938) argued the poet knew it and deliberately withheld it until the end.

  6. Why does Poseidon hate Troy, and what makes the motive awkward?
    Answer

    Laomedon cheated him and Apollo of their wages for building the wall and herding cattle (21.441–60). The awkwardness: Apollo suffered the same fraud yet defends Troy, and Poseidon himself rescues the Trojan Aeneas (20.293–308) because Dardanus' line must survive.

  7. What features of 1.188–222 support Lesky's double motivation over the view that Athena removes Achilles' agency?
    Answer

    Achilles' deliberation is narrated before she arrives; she gives him reasons (threefold gifts, 1.213–14); and she makes her intervention conditional, "if you will obey" (1.207). He then chooses to comply.

  8. How does the theomachy of Book 21 differ in tone from its opening in Book 20, and what was pseudo-Longinus' verdict?
    Answer

    Book 20 opens cosmically, with Hades leaping from his throne in fear that the earth will split (20.54–66); Book 21 is farce, with Hera boxing Artemis' ears with her own bow and Hermes conceding to Leto. Pseudo-Longinus (On the Sublime 9.6–8) said Homer makes gods into men, and the theomachy, unless taken as allegory, is wholly godless.

  9. What is the key claim of Zeus' speech at Odyssey 1.32–43, and what element of the poem resists a fully moral reading?
    Answer

    That mortals suffer beyond their portion through their own recklessness (atasthaliai), with Aegisthus as the example, warned by Hermes and ignoring him. Poseidon's personal grudge over Polyphemus, which Zeus indulges by letting him petrify the Phaeacian ship (13.125–87), is vendetta rather than justice.

  10. What did Theagenes of Rhegium and Heraclitus the Allegorist each do with Homer's gods?
    Answer

    Theagenes (c. 525 BC; scholion on Iliad 20.67) read the theomachy physically as elements in conflict and morally as qualities in conflict, Athena wisdom against Ares folly. Heraclitus (Homeric Problems, 1st century AD) argued that if Homer meant nothing allegorically he was impious throughout, and read, for example, Book 1's plague as sun-sent sickness and Athena's grip on Achilles' hair as reason.

Carry forward

  1. In Homer, divine and human causation are not alternatives. The gods explain an act without excusing it, and those who invoke them, like Agamemnon, still pay.
  2. Fate is the shape of the story. Zeus could overturn it but will not, because the cosmic order and the tradition both depend on it, and the gods' pity is real feeling without the power to undo mortality.
  3. Every later Greek answer to Homer's gods is one of three moves: moralise them (the Odyssey, Plato), correct the text (the Alexandrians), or allegorise them (Theagenes to Heraclitus). The same three moves recur throughout the rest of the course.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the role of the gods in the Trojan War tradition, centred on the Iliad. Cover: the Dios boule (the plan of Zeus) in the proem and the Cypria's version where the war relieves the earth of overpopulation; Zeus' promise to Thetis and the scales of fate (Books 8, 16, 22) and the long debate about whether Zeus is subject to fate; the partisans and their reasons: Hera and Athena (the Judgement of Paris, never named in the Iliad except once), Poseidon (Laomedon's cheat), Aphrodite, Apollo, Ares, Artemis, Hermes, Xanthus; divine interventions and the question of double motivation (does Athena's restraint of Achilles in Book 1 remove his agency?); the Deception of Zeus in Book 14 and its comedy; the theomachy of Books 20 and 21 and what it means that the gods fight each other; Thetis as the poem's most important mother; the gods' pity (Zeus for Sarpedon and Hector's horses) and their frivolity (the laughter at Hephaestus); the Odyssey's different theology: Zeus' speech in Book 1, Athena as patron, Poseidon's grudge, the gods as moral; Xenophanes, Plato and the Alexandrian critics on Homer's gods; allegorical readings from Theagenes to Heraclitus the Allegorist. End with the question the whole tradition keeps asking: if the gods made it happen, who is responsible? Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
