Troy the place: Hisarlik and the historicity question

Finding Hisarlik: Calvert, Schliemann and the rival sitesSchliemann's trench and Priam's TreasureThe nine citiesTroy VI and Troy VIIa: Dörpfeld, Blegen, KorfmannTroy in the Hittite textsWind, current and the economics of TroyDating the war and the scholarly positionsWhat archaeology can and cannot confirm about a poemSelf-testCarry forward

Finding Hisarlik: Calvert, Schliemann and the rival sites

The Greek town of Ilion stood on the mound now called Hisarlik ("place of fortresses"), about 6 km from the Dardanelles, and showed visitors the relics of Priam's city. Xerxes sacrificed a thousand oxen to Athena of Ilion (Herodotus 7.43); Alexander did the same in 334 BC. The doubt was ancient too. Demetrius of Scepsis, followed by Strabo (Geography 13.1.25–27, 13.1.35), placed Homer's Troy at the "Village of the Ilians" inland, because the plain before Ilion seemed too young and small for the Iliad's battles.

By the late eighteenth century the favourite candidate was Bunarbashi (Pınarbaşı), whose springs travellers matched to Iliad 22.147–56. Charles Maclaren argued for Hisarlik in 1822, but the groundwork was done by Frank Calvert, a British consular agent whose family owned part of the mound. Calvert dug trial trenches in 1863–65 and in 1868 persuaded Heinrich Schliemann, then touring the Troad with Bunarbashi in mind, that Hisarlik was the place. Schliemann's books played down Calvert's part; modern histories give him the credit.

Where sources disagree. Strabo and Demetrius denied that Ilion was Homer's Troy; the Ilians insisted it was. Modern archaeology has sided with the Ilians, but Strabo's point about the plain has been partly answered by geology: coring by John Kraft and colleagues showed that the Karamenderes delta has silted up since the Bronze Age, so the shoreline lay much closer to the citadel in the late second millennium.

Schliemann's trench and Priam's Treasure

Schliemann dug without a permit in 1870 and in proper campaigns in 1871, 1872 and 1873, returning in 1878–79, 1882 and 1890. Believing Homer's Troy lay at the bottom, he drove a great north–south trench to bedrock, cutting away much of the Late Bronze Age citadel that would later matter most. He identified Troy II, a burnt Early Bronze Age citadel, as Priam's city, its ramp as the Scaean Gate. He was wrong by more than a thousand years, and from 1882 his architect Wilhelm Dörpfeld began to correct him.

In 1873, beside the Troy II wall, Schliemann found the hoard he named Priam's Treasure: copper and silver vessels, a gold sauceboat, silver ingots, thousands of gold beads and two elaborate diadems. Photographs of Sophia Schliemann wearing the "Jewels of Helen" made it world-famous. He smuggled it to Athens and in 1881 gave his Trojan collection to Berlin. The treasure disappeared in 1945. Reports in 1991 traced it to Moscow, taken by a Soviet trophy brigade, and on 25 August 1993 the Russian culture minister Yevgenii Sidorov admitted it was there; the Pushkin Museum, which holds the gold, put it on display in 1996, and the Hermitage holds further material. Germany and Turkey both have claims; Russia treats it as compensation for wartime losses under its 1998 law on displaced cultural property.

The treasure belongs to Troy II, in the mid-third millennium BC (roughly 2500–2300 BC). It has nothing to do with Priam on any chronology.

Where sources disagree. Schliemann's account of the find is unreliable. He wrote that Sophia carried the objects away in her shawl, yet his own letters show she was in Athens at the time. William Calder ("Schliemann on Schliemann", Greek, Roman and Byzantine Studies 13, 1972) opened the case against Schliemann's own accounts, and David Traill (Schliemann of Troy: Treasure and Deceit, 1995) argued that Schliemann put the "treasure" together from several findspots, perhaps adding purchased pieces. Donald Easton ("Schliemann's mendacity: a false trail?", Antiquity 58, 1984; "Priam's gold: the full story", Anatolian Studies 44, 1994) and others accept that the core is a genuine Troy II hoard or hoards, with Schliemann dramatising the circumstances. The objects are genuinely Early Bronze Age; how they were found remains uncertain.

The nine cities

Dörpfeld divided the mound into nine main settlements; Carl Blegen's Cincinnati team (1932–38) split them into some fifty phases. Dates approximately follow Korfmann's Tübingen chronology; every boundary is debated.

CityApproximate dateKey features
Troy Ic. 2900–2550 BCSmall walled citadel about 90 m across; long megaron houses; handmade dark pottery
Troy IIc. 2550–2250 BCLarger citadel, monumental ramped gate, great megaron; wheel-made pottery; Priam's Treasure; ended in fire
Troy IIIc. 2250–2200 BCCrowded, poorer settlement rebuilt on Troy II; much continuity
Troy IVc. 2200–1900 BCLarger area, domed ovens; Anatolian rather than Aegean connections
Troy Vc. 1900–1750 BCNeater houses, new wall circuit; transition to the Middle Bronze Age
Troy VIc. 1750–1300 BCNew culture; great limestone walls with towers and gates; grey wheel-made ware, horse bones, imported Mycenaean pottery; lower city; end (VIh) in earthquake or attack
Troy VIIa (VIi)c. 1300–1180 BCSame people rebuild; small crowded houses against the walls, storage jars sunk into floors; destroyed by fire
Troy VIIbc. 1180–950 BCReoccupation; handmade "knobbed ware" with Balkan links (VIIb2); Luwian seal; gradual decline
Troy VIIIc. 950–85 BCGreek Ilion; sanctuary and later temple of Athena; visits by Xerxes and Alexander; sacked by Fimbria in 85 BC
Troy IX85 BC–c. AD 500Roman Ilium, rebuilt and favoured by Augustus as the city of Aeneas; declined in late antiquity

Only two layers are serious candidates for Homer's city: the end of Troy VI and the end of Troy VIIa. Both fall in the Late Bronze Age, when Mycenaean Greece was at its height and the Hittites were the great power of Anatolia.

Troy VI and Troy VIIa: Dörpfeld, Blegen, Korfmann

Dörpfeld's walls

In 1893–94 Dörpfeld exposed the walls of Troy VI on the south and east, beyond Schliemann's trench: dressed limestone faces that slope inwards, with shallow vertical offsets every nine or ten metres, a mudbrick superstructure, massive towers and several gates. The citadel, about 200 metres across, held large free-standing houses on terraces. Dörpfeld declared Troy VI Priam's city, because imported Mycenaean pottery lay in its levels and none in Troy II: the citadel that traded with the Greeks of the Late Bronze Age was the one the Greek story could be about. Andromache's warning that the wall is weakest by the fig tree (Iliad 6.433–39) has been matched to a weaker western stretch, but such matches prove little.

Blegen's earthquake and fire

Blegen concluded that Troy VIh ended by earthquake, not enemy action: toppled walls, shifted masonry, no general burning. Survivors built Troy VIIa among the ruins: small, packed houses against the citadel wall, with large pithoi sunk into the floors, which Blegen read as a population sheltering and storing food against a siege. Troy VIIa ended in a violent fire. Blegen found human remains in the streets and a bronze arrowhead of a type usually called Aegean; Korfmann's team later added a few more arrowheads and spearheads, piles of sling-stones and a partly burnt skeleton of a girl. Blegen named VIIa as Priam's Troy and dated its fall to about 1250 BC.

Where sources disagree. The earthquake that ended Troy VI is Blegen's reading (Troy III, 1953: leaning walls, fallen masonry, no burning); Penelope Mountjoy (Studia Troica 9, 1999) and others note that the evidence does not exclude human destruction following it, or both. The date of VIIa's fall has moved: on Mountjoy's study of the Mycenaean pottery it falls around 1190–1180 BC, after many Mycenaean palaces had already burnt. That is awkward for a grand expedition led from Mycenae. The arrowheads are too few to identify an attacker; the fire could be accidental, internal conflict, or raiders from anywhere.

Korfmann's lower city and the Kolb controversy

Manfred Korfmann of Tübingen excavated from 1988 until his death in 2005. Magnetometer survey revealed a ditch cut into bedrock about 400 metres south of the citadel, and later a second ditch further out. Korfmann argued that Troy VI had a lower city, the whole covering perhaps 27 hectares with several thousand inhabitants, and presented Troy as a regional capital and trading centre between the Aegean, the Black Sea and Anatolia. He also proposed renaming VIIa as VIi to stress continuity.

In 2001 the Tübingen ancient historian Frank Kolb attacked these claims: the lower city was barely attested by buildings, the ditch was no fortification, the reconstruction in the exhibition "Troia: Traum und Wirklichkeit" showed a dense town the evidence did not support, and large-scale trade was unproven. Troy, for him, was a modest provincial seat. The quarrel became public and personal; a symposium in Tübingen in February 2002 settled nothing.

Where sources disagree. Kolb and Dieter Hertel (Hertel, Troia: Archäologie, Geschichte, Mythos, 2001; Hertel and Kolb, "Troy in clearer perspective", Anatolian Studies 53, 2003) held that the plateau south of the citadel was all but empty before Hellenistic times and the population at most a few thousand; Donald Easton, J. David Hawkins, Andrew and Susan Sherratt ("Troy in recent perspective", Anatolian Studies 52, 2002) answered that a lower settlement of some kind is accepted by everyone and that the truth lies nearer Korfmann's end. Later work under Ernst Pernicka and Peter Jablonka uncovered Late Bronze Age houses in the lower city, and most archaeologists now accept that one existed. Its density, and therefore the population, remains uncertain. On trade, Kolb is partly right: imported Mycenaean pottery is only a small share of Troy VI ceramics, and direct evidence for Black Sea traffic in the Bronze Age is thin.

Troy in the Hittite texts

The strongest evidence that Troy mattered comes from the archives at Hattusa. Emil Forrer proposed in 1924 that Ahhiyawa was Homer's Achaioi and Wilusa was Ilios (originally Wilios); Ferdinand Sommer rejected both in 1932. In 1998 J. David Hawkins's reading of the Karabel inscription fixed Mira and the Seha River Land, leaving Wilusa in or near the Troad. Most specialists now accept both equations; the texts are collected in Gary Beckman, Trevor Bryce and Eric Cline, The Ahhiyawa Texts (2011).

Wilusa and Alaksandu

Wilusiya and Taruisa (perhaps Troia) appear among twenty-two places in the Assuwa coalition that Tudhaliya I/II defeated in the late fifteenth century. Around 1280 BC Muwatalli II made a treaty (CTH 76) with Alaksandu of Wilusa. It says Wilusa had been loyal to Hatti since early times, names an earlier king Kukkunni, binds Alaksandu to send troops for Hittite wars, and lists Wilusa's gods, including a deity whose name has been restored as Appaliunas and an underground watercourse (KASKAL.KUR). Korfmann's team then found a rock-cut water system under the edge of the Troy citadel. Alaksandu looks very like Alexandros, the second name of Paris.

Where sources disagree. Appaliunas is a partly restored reading (Beckman, Hittite Diplomatic Texts, 2nd ed. 1999, no. 13 prints the restoration), so the claim, pressed by Latacz (Troy and Homer, 2004), that it is Apollo rests on a damaged word. Alaksandu as a Greek name at Wilusa is striking but may reflect contact rather than a Greek dynasty, and no specialist identifies him with Homer's Paris. Taruisa as Troia is linguistically weaker than Wilusa as Ilios. The Luwian-language question (Watkins on the Trojans' speech) belongs to module 10.3.

Ahhiyawa, Piyamaradu and Millawanda

About thirty Hittite texts mention Ahhiyawa. Its king is addressed as a "brother", a great king, and its Anatolian foothold was Millawanda (Milawata), almost certainly Miletus, where a Mycenaean settlement has been excavated. It worked through clients and adventurers, above all Piyamaradu, a western Anatolian prince who raided Hittite vassals for decades with Ahhiyawan backing.

  • The Manapa-Tarhunta letter (CTH 191), probably to Muwatalli II from the vassal king of the Seha River Land, reports that Hittite troops have gone to attack Wilusa and that Piyamaradu has raided Lazpa (Lesbos), with men from there going over to Atpa, Piyamaradu's son-in-law, in Millawanda. Why Hittite troops were moving against Wilusa is not clear: to put down a revolt, or to drive off attackers.
  • The Tawagalawa letter (CTH 181), probably from Hattusili III around 1250 BC to an unnamed king of Ahhiyawa, complains that Piyamaradu escaped by ship from Millawanda and asks the Ahhiyawan king to hand him over or rein him in. It mentions Tawagalawa, the addressee's brother (perhaps Greek Etewoklewes, Eteocles). It also refers to "the matter of Wilusa" over which the two kings had been hostile and have now made peace.
  • The Milawata letter (CTH 182), probably from Tudhaliya IV to Tarkasnawa of Mira late in the thirteenth century, shows Millawanda now under Hittite control and concerns Walmu, a king of Wilusa who had been driven out; the Hittite king wants him restored as a vassal.

Tudhaliya IV's treaty with Sausgamuwa of Amurru lists the king of Ahhiyawa among the great kings and then strikes the name out, perhaps marking the end of Ahhiyawan power in Anatolia. The cumulative case is real: a Mycenaean power was active in western Anatolia for two centuries; Wilusa, a Hittite vassal on its edge, was attacked at least once, lost a king, and caused hostility between Hatti and Ahhiyawa.

The Luwian seal

In 1995 Korfmann's team found a small bronze biconvex seal in a Troy VIIb2 context of the twelfth century BC. It carries Luwian hieroglyphs, read by Hawkins and Donald Easton (1996) as a man's name with the title "scribe" on one side and a woman's name on the other. It is the only Bronze Age writing yet found at Troy. It shows someone at Troy used Anatolian writing, not that Trojans spoke Luwian, and its context postdates both candidate destructions. No archive has been found at Troy, so Wilusa's own side is missing.

Wind, current and the economics of Troy

Homer's stock epithet for the city, Ilios ēnemoessa, "windy Ilios", is accurate. Through most of the summer sailing season a strong north-easterly wind blows down the Dardanelles, and a surface current flows out of the Sea of Marmara towards the Aegean at one to three knots. A Bronze Age square-rigged ship, poor at sailing into the wind, could wait days or weeks for a southerly. Korfmann argued that ships anchored in Beşik Bay, south-west of Troy, where he excavated a Late Bronze Age cemetery with Mycenaean pottery, and that Troy grew rich by supplying, piloting or taxing them. The citadel also commanded the crossing between Europe and Asia.

Wealth also came from horses (horse bones appear in Troy VI; Homer's Trojans are "horse-tamers"), textiles (spindle whorls abound) and the plain's grain and fish. A strategic site on a contested frontier needs no stolen queen to explain a war; Herodotus already reported Persian and Phoenician versions that turned the abductions into tit-for-tat raiding (Herodotus 1.1–5).

Dating the war and the scholarly positions

Ancient and archaeological dates

Herodotus put the war rather more than 800 years before his time (2.145), around 1250 BC. The Parian Marble gives 1209/8, Duris of Samos 1334/3. Eratosthenes' 1184/3 became canonical. All rest on genealogies counted at fixed years per generation, not records. The archaeological windows are the end of Troy VIh around 1300 and the end of VIIa around 1190–1180 on current pottery dating. Eratosthenes' figure lands close to the second, but given his method that is probably coincidence.

Where sources disagree. Blegen's early date for VIIa (c. 1250) suited Herodotus and a Mycenaean expedition before the palaces fell. The later date (c. 1180) suits Eratosthenes but puts the destruction in the disorder of the collapse, when attackers were more likely to be refugees, raiders or northern newcomers than a coalition from Mycenae. The Hittite texts point to trouble over Wilusa in the early-to-mid thirteenth century, which fits neither destruction exactly.

Finley's scepticism

Moses Finley, in The World of Odysseus (1954) and the 1964 Journal of Hellenic Studies debate "The Trojan War" with John Caskey, Geoffrey Kirk and Denys Page, argued that Homer's society belongs to the tenth and ninth centuries, that oral tradition preserves little reliable over five centuries, and that the war should be removed from Greek history and treated as myth. His dating rested on institutions rather than objects: a world of gift exchange and the household (oikos), with no polis, no coinage and no writing, fits the Dark Age and not the palaces, so the poems could not be carrying a Bronze Age memory intact. That is the argument Latacz had to answer.

Latacz's maximalism

Joachim Latacz, in Troia und Homer (2001; English Troy and Homer, 2004), argued the reverse. With Wilusa equal to Ilios and Ahhiyawa equal to the Achaeans, he held that the Catalogue of Ships (Iliad 2.494–759) preserves a Mycenaean political map, that the hexameter tradition reached back into the Bronze Age, and that the story's core is historical: Greeks fought for Wilusa. Page, in History and the Homeric Iliad (1959), had made an earlier version of this case.

The middle ground

Most current specialists, for example Trevor Bryce in The Trojans and Their Neighbours (2006) and Eric Cline in The Trojan War: A Very Short Introduction (2013), take a middle position. The setting is historical: Troy was a substantial Late Bronze Age city, Achaeans were active in western Anatolia, and Wilusa was fought over. Whether any single event lies behind the Iliad cannot be shown, and there may have been several "Trojan Wars". Homer himself knows an earlier sack, by Heracles in the reign of Laomedon (Iliad 5.640–42).

What a historical kernel might look like

A plausible kernel is a series of conflicts in the thirteenth and early twelfth centuries: raids by Ahhiyawan lords and allies such as Piyamaradu, attacks on Wilusa, a dethroned king, perhaps a sack, with the Hittites as distant overlord. There is no evidence of a ten-year siege, a coalition of 1,186 ships under one high king, a war fought over one woman, or Greek-speaking Trojans who worship Greek gods. The poem's material world is also mixed: the boar's-tusk helmet (Iliad 10.261–65) and Ajax's tower shield are Bronze Age survivals, while cremation, iron and much of the social world belong to later centuries. Homer's Troy is a composite built up over five hundred years of performance.

What archaeology can and cannot confirm about a poem

Archaeology at Hisarlik has confirmed that the place existed where tradition put it, that it was large, walled and prosperous in the Late Bronze Age, that it had Mycenaean contacts, and that it was destroyed around 1300 and again around 1180. With the Hittite texts it shows Wilusa was a cause of dispute between great kings. That is more than Finley allowed.

What it cannot do is confirm events, agents or motives. A burnt layer does not record who lit it or why, and a few arrowheads do not identify an army. Even the texts name Wilusa but not Priam, Hector or Agamemnon. Agreement between poem and site is also partly circular: Schliemann's Troy II, Dörpfeld's VI and Blegen's VIIa were each "confirmed" by the excavator who wanted them. The lasting lesson is that oral poetry keeps names, places and a sense of former greatness much longer than it keeps narrative facts. Homer remembered that Ilios was rich, walled and windy and that Achaeans once fought there; the rest of the story is epic.

Self-test

  1. Who first dug at Hisarlik and convinced Schliemann it was Troy, and what rival site did many earlier travellers favour?
    Answer

    Frank Calvert, the British consular agent whose family owned part of the mound, dug trial trenches in 1863–65 and persuaded Schliemann in 1868. Many earlier travellers favoured Bunarbashi (Pınarbaşı), on the strength of its springs.

  2. Which ancient authors denied that Greek Ilion was Homer's Troy, and on what grounds?
    Answer

    Demetrius of Scepsis, followed by Strabo (Geography 13.1), placed Homer's Troy at the "Village of the Ilians", partly because the plain in front of Ilion seemed too new and small. Coring has since shown that the coastline was much closer to the mound in the Bronze Age.

  3. To which city does Priam's Treasure belong, roughly when, and where is it now?
    Answer

    Troy II, c. 2500–2300 BC, more than a thousand years before any Trojan War. Taken from Berlin by Soviet forces in 1945, the gold is in the Pushkin Museum in Moscow, with other material in the Hermitage.

  4. What did Blegen see as the cause of Troy VIh's end, and why did he think Troy VIIa was under siege?
    Answer

    An earthquake (collapsed masonry, no general fire). In VIIa he found small crowded houses against the walls with storage pithoi sunk into the floors, which he read as a population sheltering inside the citadel and stockpiling food. VIIa then burnt, with human remains and at least one arrowhead in the debris.

  5. Why is the newer date for the destruction of Troy VIIa awkward for a Mycenaean expedition?
    Answer

    Mountjoy's pottery dating puts it around 1190–1180 BC, after many Mycenaean palaces had already been destroyed, so a coalition led from Mycenae is unlikely at that point.

  6. What was Korfmann's main new claim about Troy VI, and what were Kolb's objections?
    Answer

    Korfmann argued from a bedrock-cut ditch found by magnetometry that Troy VI had a large lower city (about 27 hectares, several thousand people) and was a regional trading centre. Kolb said the lower city was barely attested, the ditch was not a fortification, the exhibition reconstruction was misleading and the trade was unproven.

  7. What does the Alaksandu treaty tell us, and which Homeric parallel does it suggest?
    Answer

    Around 1280 BC Muwatalli II bound Alaksandu of Wilusa as a loyal vassal who had to supply troops; it lists Wilusa's gods, perhaps including Appaliunas and an underground watercourse. The name recalls Alexandros, the other name of Paris.

  8. What is the significance of the Tawagalawa letter for the Trojan question?
    Answer

    Probably from Hattusili III to the king of Ahhiyawa, whom he treats as an equal "brother", it concerns the renegade Piyamaradu and refers to the matter of Wilusa over which the two had been hostile and have made peace, the nearest text to a Hittite-Ahhiyawan dispute over Troy.

  9. Why did the Dardanelles make Troy economically important?
    Answer

    Prevailing north-easterly winds and an outward current made the strait hard to enter under sail, so ships may have waited in Beşik Bay, and Troy could profit from servicing or taxing them, as well as from controlling the crossing to Europe.

  10. Contrast Finley's and Latacz's positions in one sentence each.
    Answer

    Finley held that Homeric society is post-Mycenaean and that the war should be treated as myth rather than history. Latacz held that the Hittite texts and the Catalogue of Ships show a historical Mycenaean conflict over Wilusa behind the epic.

Carry forward

  1. Troy (Hisarlik, Wilusa) was a real and substantial Late Bronze Age city on a contested frontier between the Hittite and Mycenaean worlds, and the Hittite texts show it was fought over.
  2. No layer, text or object confirms the Iliad's story; destructions around 1300 and 1180 BC have no named attackers, and Homer's Troy is a composite built up over centuries of oral poetry.
  3. Archaeology can confirm places, scale, dates and contacts but not agents, motives or plots; oral epic keeps names and a sense of former greatness much longer than it keeps events.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the archaeology of Troy and the question of whether the Trojan War happened. Cover: the identification of Hisarlik (Calvert, Schliemann), Schliemann's excavation and its destructions, Priam's Treasure and its true date and modern whereabouts; Dörpfeld and Troy VI, Blegen and Troy VIIa, Korfmann and the lower city, and the Korfmann-Kolb controversy about Troy's size and importance; the nine cities and their dates, the Troy VI walls and the earthquake, the Troy VIIa destruction by fire and the arrowheads; the Hittite texts in detail: Wilusa, Alaksandu, the Ahhiyawa letters, the Tawagalawa letter, Piyamaradu, Milawata, the Manapa-Tarhunta letter, and the case for a Mycenaean-Hittite conflict over western Anatolia; the Luwian seal from Troy; the Dardanelles winds and the economic logic of a Troy; the dating problem (Eratosthenes' 1184, Herodotus' 1250, the archaeological windows); the positions: Finley's scepticism, Latacz's maximalism, the middle ground; what a historical kernel might look like and how different it would be from Homer. End with the methodological lesson: what archaeology can and cannot confirm about a poem. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.11 · 2,734 words

Homeric society and Homeric warfare

How a Homeric battle worksThe economy of honourXenia, the oikos and the limits of powerSlavery and the fate of captured womenMarriage and the position of womenReligion as practisedWhich world? The historicity debateUsing Homer as a historical sourceSelf-testCarry forward

How a Homeric battle works

The Iliad looks like a string of single combats, but its battlefield is always crowded. The narrative follows the promachoi, the "fighters in front", who step out from the mass, throw their spears, kill or die, and fall back among their companions when pressed. The anonymous plēthus behind them fights as well. Joachim Latacz (Kampfparänese, 1977) and Hans van Wees (Status Warriors, 1992) argued that this fluid, open-order mass fighting is the poems' real tactical picture, and that the duels are close-ups within it.

An encounter follows a pattern. There is a boast or challenge, often with a genealogy (Glaucus at Iliad 6.145–211). Then comes a thrown spear, usually one of a pair, then a thrust, then the sword if the spear is lost. When weapons run out, heroes throw boulders. Diomedes lifts one "which two men could not carry, such as mortals are now" (5.302–304; compare 12.445–449). The phrase shows that the poet himself places his heroes in a stronger, vanished age.

Chariots, aristeiai and spoils

Chariots are mostly taxis. The hero rides up, dismounts, fights on foot, and keeps his driver close by for a quick retreat. The exception is telling. Nestor orders his Pylians to keep their chariots in line, saying "this is how men of old sacked cities" (4.297–309). The poet knows that chariots were once a massed arm but not how they worked. Linear B tablets from Knossos list hundreds of chariots, so the palaces certainly fielded them. Homer's taxi-chariot may be a memory that has lost its function, or, as P. A. L. Greenhalgh argued (Early Greek Warfare, 1973), the eighth-century practice of riding to battle projected back onto the past.

The aristeia, a run in which one hero dominates the field, structures the narrative: Diomedes in Book 5, Agamemnon in 11, Patroclus in 16, Achilles in 20–22. Each has an arming scene, a series of kills, a wound or a divine intervention, and a climax. Stripping armour is the visible proof of victory, and the struggle for corpses fills whole books. Book 17 is entirely about Patroclus' body, and Hector puts on the armour he has stripped from it (17.192–197). Nestor has to warn the Achaeans to kill first and strip later (6.66–71), which shows that the habit could become a tactical liability.

Anachronisms in both directions

Twice men stand packed "shield on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man" (13.130–133; 16.212–217), which is the language of close formation. Shields are often "round", as hoplite shields were. Yet Hector's shield bumps his neck and ankles as he walks (6.117–118), a Bronze Age body shield. Weapons are bronze, but iron appears in similes and tools, in one arrowhead (4.123), and as a prize at Patroclus' games (23.826–835).

Where sources disagree. Latacz took the massed passages as evidence that a phalanx already existed in the poet's day. Snodgrass ("The Hoplite Reform and History", Journal of Hellenic Studies 85, 1965) dated the hoplite panoply to c. 700–650, with the Chigi vase (c. 650) as the first clear image of a formation. Van Wees argues that the tight phalanx came later still, perhaps in the sixth century. Whether Homeric warfare is pre-hoplite, proto-hoplite or incoherent is uncertain.

The economy of honour

Timē means both honour and price, and in Homer it is material. It shows in the best meat, the front seat and the full cup (Iliad 12.310–321), and above all in the geras, the prize of honour that the army allots from the spoils. Iliad 1 is a dispute over geras. Agamemnon refuses to be left alone without a prize (1.118–120), and Achilles protests that he does the fighting and gets the smaller share (1.163–168). Taking Briseis publicly marks down Achilles' worth.

Kleos, "what is heard", is fame in song. Achilles chooses between a short life with kleos aphthiton, "unwithering fame", and a long life without it (9.410–416). Sarpedon sets out the bargain: privilege at home is paid for by risk at the front (12.310–328). Aidōs is the restraining sense of other people's eyes. Hector stays outside the walls from aidōs before the Trojans (22.105–107). Nemesis is the indignation others feel when the code is broken (6.350–351).

Where sources disagree. E. R. Dodds (The Greeks and the Irrational, 1951) called Homeric society a "shame culture". Douglas Cairns (Aidōs, 1993) and Bernard Williams (Shame and Necessity, 1993) argued that aidōs is internalised, an imagined audience the hero carries within him, and that the shame/guilt contrast distorts the poems.

Gifts as a social system

Moses Finley, following Marcel Mauss (Essai sur le don, 1925), put gift exchange at the centre of the Homeric world. A gift creates an obligation, and an unreturned gift is a debt of status.

  • Glaucus and Diomedes (Iliad 6.119–236). The two enemies find that their grandfathers were guest-friends, so they refuse to fight and exchange armour. Glaucus gives gold for bronze, "a hundred oxen's worth for nine" (6.236). The comment is read as irony: Zeus has taken Glaucus' wits, since a gold cuirass for a bronze one is no exchange between equals. Either way, hereditary xenia overrides the war.
  • The Embassy (9.121–157). Agamemnon offers tripods, gold, horses and women, returns Briseis under oath, and adds a daughter without bride-price and seven cities. He also says Achilles should yield "since I am more kingly" (9.160–161), and Odysseus leaves that line out when he relays the offer. Achilles refuses because accepting would confirm the hierarchy. A gift this large is an assertion of superiority.
  • Priam's ransom (24.228–237, 553–595). The poem opens with a father's ransom refused (Chryses, 1.12–32) and closes with one accepted. That ring frames the Iliad around whether goods can still buy back what violence has taken.

Xenia, the oikos and the limits of power

Xenia is the poems' international law. Zeus Xenios protects it (Odyssey 9.270–271), it passes down through families, and it has a protocol: welcome, bath and food come first, and questions about who the guest is come after (1.118–124; 3.69–74). It ends with guest-gifts, often heirlooms with pedigrees, such as the Sidonian mixing bowl Menelaus passes on (4.613–619). The Odyssey is a sequence of tests of xenia. The Phaeacians are ideal hosts. Polyphemus parodies the custom with his "gift" of eating Odysseus last (9.369–370). The suitors are permanent uninvited guests who eat the host's property. The war itself began when Paris stole his host's wife.

The basic unit is the oikos: land, herds, stored treasure (keimēlia), dependants and slaves. The suitors' crime is economic, the consumption of Odysseus' livelihood, and his wealth is counted in herds (14.96–104).

Basileis and the assembly

A basileus is a leading man among peers, not a monarch. Ithaca has many basileis (Odyssey 1.394–396), and Scheria has twelve, with Alcinous as the thirteenth (8.390–391). Agamemnon's authority rests on a sceptre said to come from Zeus (Iliad 2.100–108) and on the size of his contingent, not on any administration. Odysseus' "let there be one ruler" (2.204) is spoken just as one-man rule is visibly failing.

The agora matters but does not decide. The army shouts for Chryseis' return and Agamemnon overrides it (1.22–25). Thersites, the only commoner who speaks, is beaten to the army's laughter (2.211–277). Ithaca's assembly has not met in twenty years (Odyssey 2.26–27), and at the end of the poem it splits, with more than half arming against Odysseus (24.420–471). The Shield shows elders judging a blood-price case in the agora (Iliad 18.497–508). Hesiod's "gift-devouring basileis" (Works and Days 38–39, 263–264) show a similar world seen from below.

Where sources disagree. Kurt Raaflaub sees a polis in formation in these assemblies, in Scheria's walls and temples (Odyssey 6.7–10) and in the language of community. Finley saw a pre-political world of oikoi. The question is whether the scenes of communal action are vestigial or emergent.

Slavery and the fate of captured women

Slaves come through capture, purchase and birth. Eumaeus was a king's son, carried off by a Phoenician slave-woman and sold to Laertes (Odyssey 15.403–484). Slavery is a fall in status, not an innate condition. Eumaeus owns a slave himself (14.449–452) and hopes for a house, land and a wife (14.62–66), which Odysseus later promises him (21.213–216). He also states the system's ideology: Zeus takes away half a man's worth on the day he is enslaved (17.322–323).

Eurycleia cost Laertes twenty oxen, and he never slept with her for fear of his wife's anger (1.429–433). The line shows both the master's entitlement and the wife's power in the house. Twelve of the fifty maids took up with the suitors (22.421–425). Telemachus hangs them, choosing a death that is "not clean" (22.462–473). The poem presents this as justice, and modern readers find it the hardest scene in the epic.

For women in war, capture was the expected end. Agamemnon offers captive women as gifts (Iliad 9.128–140). Briseis lost her husband and brothers to Achilles. Her lament recalls Patroclus' promise to make her Achilles' wife (19.282–300), which was a captive's best hope. Andromache foresees herself at an Argive's loom (6.454–458). The victims' side is imagined most sharply in a simile. Odysseus weeps over the song of Troy like a woman dragged into slavery from her dying husband (Odyssey 8.523–531), so the sacker of cities weeps like the women he enslaved.

Marriage and the position of women

The marriage gifts do not form one system. Hedna usually means bride-price paid by the suitor. Iphidamas gave a hundred cattle (Iliad 11.241–245), Agamemnon offers a daughter anaednon, "without hedna" (9.146–148), and Hephaestus demands his hedna back after Aphrodite's adultery (Odyssey 8.317–320). But elsewhere Penelope's father "prepares the hedna" (1.277–278), and Telemachus speaks of Icarius endowing his daughter (2.52–54). That looks like dowry. Penelope also demands courtship gifts from the suitors (18.274–283).

Where sources disagree. Snodgrass ("An Historical Homeric Society?", Journal of Hellenic Studies 94, 1974) made the marriage gifts his star exhibit: no real society muddles bride-price and dowry, so the poems are an amalgam. Morris (1986) replied that real societies combine them, through indirect dowry and competitive courtship, so the "confusion" is aristocratic bargaining.

The women are elite women seen from inside the oikos, and they have more room to act than the rules suggest.

  • Andromache gives Hector tactical advice (Iliad 6.433–439) and is sent back to her loom: "war will be the concern of men" (6.492). Telemachus twice turns the line on Penelope (Odyssey 1.356–359; 21.350–353).
  • Penelope controls the timing of remarriage with the shroud trick (2.93–110) and sets the contest of the bow. She is the pivot of the succession.
  • Arete is the person Odysseus is told to supplicate (6.303–315; 7.53–77). She settles men's quarrels and is honoured "like a god".
  • Helen weaves the war into her web (Iliad 3.125–128) and drugs the wine at Sparta (Odyssey 4.219–232). She is the most self-aware figure in either poem.
  • Nausicaa thinks about marriage and fears gossip if she is seen with a stranger (Odyssey 6.273–288): aidōs governs where she goes.

Religion as practised

The gods are characters, but human cult is recognisably historical. Sacrifice follows a fixed order: barley, prayer, slaughter, thigh bones wrapped in fat for the gods, entrails tasted, meat shared (Iliad 1.447–474; Odyssey 3.418–463). Prayer is reciprocal: Chryses reminds Apollo of the temple he roofed for him (Iliad 1.37–42). Theano lays a robe on the knees of Athena's seated statue in a temple, and the goddess refuses (6.297–311). Temple and cult image together make this an eighth-century scene. Omens are read by seers or ignored. Hector answers Polydamas: "one omen is best, to fight for one's country" (12.243). Oaths are sacrifices with a curse attached: the oath-breakers' brains are to be poured out like the wine (3.264–301). The dead are cremated and become strengthless shades (Odyssey 11). Hero cult and Delphic consultation are almost absent, perhaps by deliberate archaism.

Which world? The historicity debate

After Schliemann, scholars read the poems as Mycenaean. Martin Nilsson (Homer and Mycenae, 1933), H. L. Lorimer (Homer and the Monuments, 1950) and Denys Page (History and the Homeric Iliad, 1959) catalogued the survivals. Linear B, deciphered in 1952, showed how much had been lost. The palaces ran scribal, redistributive economies. Homer has no palace administration, and he mentions writing once, in Bellerophon's "baneful signs" (Iliad 6.168–170).

The Mycenaean survivals

  • The boar's-tusk helmet (Iliad 10.261–265). It matches excavated examples, and the type was out of use by about the twelfth century.
  • Ajax's tower shield of seven hides and bronze (7.219–223). It matches Shaft Grave-era shields such as those on the Lion Hunt dagger.
  • Bronze weapons throughout, and Nestor's dove-handled cup (11.632–637).
  • The wanax. Linear B wa-na-ka was the palace king, and qa-si-re-u was a local official. Homer keeps anax as a title ("lord of men") but not the institution, and the basileus has risen to the top.
  • The Catalogue of Ships (2.494–759). Page read it as a Bronze Age map; Giovannini (Étude historique sur les origines du Catalogue des vaisseaux, 1969) derived it from seventh-century Delphic lists, and Visser (Homers Katalog der Schiffe, 1997) from the poet's own composition. The question is open.

Four modern positions

ScholarWorkClaimDate
Moses FinleyThe World of Odysseus (1954; rev. 1978)A coherent society of oikoi and gift exchange; Mycenaean elements are fossilsTenth to ninth century
Anthony Snodgrass"An Historical Homeric Society?" (1974)An amalgam of many centuries plus inventionNone
Ian Morris"The Use and Abuse of Homer" (1986)Oral poets must be intelligible, so institutions are contemporary and archaism is a distancing deviceEighth century
Kurt Raaflaub; Hans van Wees"A Historian's Headache" (1998); Status Warriors (1992)A broadly coherent society with an emerging polis, under heroic exaggerationc. 750–650

Finley's tenth century rested on absences: Homer has no polis, no colonisation and no hoplites. Morris inverted the argument. A tradition that stays intelligible keeps updating its social world, and what looks archaic is mostly material culture used to signal "long ago". Later archaeology also gave the eighth century texture: temples, colonial foundations like Scheria's, Phoenician traders, and the "Nestor's cup" from Pithekoussai (c. 725).

Where sources disagree. The date of the poems is itself contested. Richard Janko's linguistic statistics (1982) place the Iliad around 750–725. Martin West argued for c. 680–640 ("The Date of the Iliad", Museum Helveticum 52, 1995). Gregory Nagy's evolutionary model (Homeric Questions, 1996) has the text fixing gradually into the sixth century, which makes the search for a single date misguided.

Oral tradition and the compression of centuries

Milman Parry and Albert Lord (The Singer of Tales, 1960) showed that noun-epithet formulas are a technology for composing in performance. Formulas are conservative: a phrase that scans survives long after its referent has gone, which is how a boar's-tusk helmet lasts four centuries in verse. The dialect agrees. It is an artificial mix of Ionic, Aeolic and older forms, some close to Arcado-Cypriot, and no one ever spoke it.

The layers are uneven. Objects and the formulas attached to them hold the oldest material. Social relations, which the audience had to recognise, renew themselves fastest. On this view Snodgrass and Morris are less opposed than they seem: the material inventory is an amalgam, while the institutions are largely recent and touched up to look old.

Using Homer as a historical source

  1. Separate the layers. A weapon or title may be centuries older than its line. Material details are evidence of the tradition's memory, not of a period.
  2. Trust the incidental. Similes show the poet's world: iron tools, ploughing, horse-riding (Iliad 15.679–684). The plot's background assumptions are better evidence than the plot.
  3. Read the archaising filter. The poems exclude writing, coinage, Ionia and almost all Dorians (one mention, Odyssey 19.177). Something missing from Homer may still have existed in the poet's day.
  4. Remember whose voice it is. Thersites is mocked and slaves are loyal or punished. The poems give elite values, not a census.
  5. Avoid circularity. Date objects by excavation, then ask whether Homer knows them. Never date a site by the poem.
  6. Use controls. Where Homer agrees with Hesiod, Geometric art and early inscriptions, you are probably looking at the poet's present.

Self-test

  1. What are promachoi, and how did Latacz and van Wees change the standard picture of Homeric battle?
    Answer

    Promachoi are the "front fighters" who step out from the mass to fight and fall back when pressed. Latacz and van Wees argued that the anonymous mass is always present and fighting, so the poems describe fluid open-order mass combat, and the duels are close-ups within it rather than the whole of the battle.

  2. Why is Nestor's advice at Iliad 4.297–309 significant for the chariot question?
    Answer

    It is the one passage in which chariots fight as a massed arm, and Nestor presents it as the practice of "men of old". Everywhere else chariots act as taxis. The poet seems to remember that chariots were once a tactical force without knowing how they worked.

  3. Give two passages that look like anachronistic hoplite or phalanx features, and one Bronze Age feature they clash with.
    Answer

    The close formation "shield on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man" (Iliad 13.130–133; 16.212–217) and the "round" shield vocabulary. They clash with Hector's body shield, which bumps his neck and ankles (6.117–118), and with Ajax's tower shield (7.219–223).

  4. Explain the double meaning of timē and how it drives the quarrel in Iliad 1.
    Answer

    Timē means both honour and price or value. Honour is expressed in material shares, above all the geras. When Agamemnon takes Briseis, Achilles' geras, he publicly lowers Achilles' worth, so the quarrel is about status made visible in goods.

  5. Why does Achilles refuse the gifts in Iliad 9, given how large they are?
    Answer

    Accepting them would acknowledge Agamemnon's superiority. Agamemnon explicitly says Achilles should submit because Agamemnon is "more kingly" (9.160–161), a line Odysseus leaves out. A gift that large asserts hierarchy, and Achilles will not be bought back into subordination.

  6. What ring structure do the ransoms of Chryses and Priam create?
    Answer

    The Iliad opens with a father's ransom for his child refused (Chryses, Book 1) and closes with a father's ransom accepted (Priam, Book 24). The poem is framed by the question of whether gift exchange can still contain violence.

  7. What does the story of Eumaeus show about how a person became a slave in the Homeric world?
    Answer

    Slavery was a fall in status, not a hereditary caste. Eumaeus was a king's son kidnapped by Phoenicians and sold to Laertes. Slaves came through capture, trade and birth, and a favoured slave could own a slave himself and hope for a house, land and a wife.

  8. Why did Snodgrass treat the marriage gifts as evidence against an "historical Homeric society", and what was the reply?
    Answer

    Hedna sometimes runs from suitor to father, which is bride-price, and sometimes from father with daughter, which looks like dowry. Snodgrass argued that no real society works this way, so the poems are an amalgam. Morris replied that real societies do combine the two (indirect dowry, competitive courtship gifts), so the mixture reflects elite bargaining rather than compilation.

  9. Contrast Finley's dating of Homeric society with Morris's, and state the principle behind Morris's view.
    Answer

    Finley placed it in the tenth to ninth centuries because the poems lack the polis, colonisation and hoplites. Morris placed it in the eighth century, the poet's own, on the principle that oral tradition must stay intelligible to its audience, so institutions are contemporary and archaism is a deliberate distancing device.

  10. Name three Mycenaean survivals in Homer and explain why the wanax is a survival of a word rather than an institution.
    Answer

    The boar's-tusk helmet (Iliad 10.261–265), Ajax's tower shield (7.219–223) and the consistently bronze weapons (Nestor's cup is another). Linear B wa-na-ka was the palace king at the head of a scribal bureaucracy. Homer keeps anax as an honorific, but there are no palaces or scribes in the poems, and his basileis, who were minor officials in Linear B, are now the ruling class.

Carry forward

  1. Homer's layers are uneven. Objects and formulas preserve the Bronze Age, while social institutions mostly reflect the poet's eighth- or seventh-century present, dressed to look ancient.
  2. Homeric honour is material and relational. Timē, geras and gift exchange tie status to goods, and xenia structures relations between oikoi, a pattern that later Greek aristocratic culture inherits.
  3. Use Homer through controls: date things by archaeology, trust incidental details and similes over the plot, and read the poems as elite ideology rather than social description.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the society and warfare depicted in the Homeric poems and the debate about which real period they reflect. Cover: how a Homeric battle works (the promachoi and the mass, chariots as taxis, duels and aristeiai, spear and sword, the stripping of armour, the boulder-throwing, where the phalanx and the hoplite shield intrude as anachronisms); the economy of honour (time, geras, kleos, aidos, nemesis) and the gift exchange that structures it (Glaucus and Diomedes, the Embassy's gifts, Priam's ransom); xenia as institution; the oikos, the basileis, the agora and the limits of assembly; slavery in the poems (Eumaeus, Eurycleia, Briseis, the maids) and the fate of captured women; marriage, dowry and bride-price confusion; the position of women (Andromache, Penelope, Arete, Helen, Nausicaa); religion as practised in the poems (sacrifice, prayer, omens, oaths); the big debate: Finley's World of Odysseus and the tenth-century thesis, Snodgrass's amalgam, Morris's eighth-century thesis, Raaflaub, and the Mycenaean survivals (boar's-tusk helmet, Ajax's shield, bronze weapons, the wanax); the poems as oral tradition compressing centuries. End with the practical consequence: how to use Homer as a historical source without being fooled by him. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 10 · Deep dive I: the Trojan War · 10.12 · 3,899 words

Troy after antiquity

Rome: the city that chose to descend from the losersDares and Dictys: the eyewitnesses who outranked HomerMedieval Troy: romance, genealogy and the invention of CressidaEarly modern Troy: Shakespeare's anti-epic and Homer recoveredSchliemann and the Victorian TroyThe twentieth century: Troy against warThe women-centred retellings: what they correct and what they flattenTroy on screenWhy this war remains the West's master storySelf-testCarry forward

Rome: the city that chose to descend from the losers

The Roman claim on Troy rests on one Homeric hinge. In Iliad 20.302–308 Poseidon rescues Aeneas from Achilles because fate has decreed that he and his sons' sons will rule the Trojans. A survivor with a future was a gift to any people looking for a pedigree. Greek writers had already brought Aeneas west: Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities 1.72) reports that Hellanicus, in the fifth century BC, had Aeneas founding Rome, oddly in company with Odysseus. By the third century BC the Romans had made the story their own. Its political use is visible in the 260s and 240s BC, when Rome treated Ilion in the Troad as kin.

Where sources disagree. When Rome took Aeneas up is argued. Karl Galinsky (Aeneas, Sicily, and Rome, 1969) read the cult at Lavinium and the Etruscan Aeneas figurines as evidence that the legend was at home in Latium by the sixth century; Erich Gruen (Culture and National Identity in Republican Rome, 1992) argued that Rome adopted the Trojan pedigree late and deliberately, as a diplomatic instrument in its third-century dealings with the Greek world. The Lavinium evidence is real but does not show who told the story or why.

The first Latin poets built on this. Livius Andronicus translated the Odyssey (Odusia) into Saturnians for the schoolroom. Naevius, a veteran of the First Punic War, opened his Bellum Punicum with Aeneas leaving the burning city. The fragments survive mostly through Servius and Macrobius, and Macrobius says Virgil took the storm and Venus' complaint to Jupiter from Naevius. Ennius' Annales began with a dream in which Homer's shade told him that his soul had passed into Ennius, so the Roman epic would be Homer reborn. Lucretius (De rerum natura 1.117–126) mentions the dream with some irony. Ennius made Ilia, Aeneas' daughter, the mother of Romulus. Later antiquarians had to stretch a list of Alban kings to fill the four centuries between Troy's fall and 753 BC.

Virgil's Aeneid is a deliberate answer to Homer from the other side. Books 1–6 are an Odyssey of wandering and Books 7–12 an Iliad of war in Italy, but this time the Trojans win the Iliad. Book 2 tells the sack from inside the city. The Greeks become liars and butchers: Sinon's false story, Pyrrhus killing Priam at the altar. Laocoön's line sums up the Roman view of the enemy:

timeo Danaos et dona ferentes (Aeneid 2.49)

The dynastic point is made openly. In Jupiter's prophecy (1.267–288) Ascanius takes the name Iulus, and a Julius "whose name comes from great Iulus" will carry Rome's rule to the stars. Julius Caesar had already dedicated the temple of Venus Genetrix in 46 BC to honour his divine Trojan ancestress. Augustus made Troy ceremonial. The lusus Troiae, a cavalry display by noble boys, gets its origin story in Aeneid 5.545–603, where Virgil says Rome still calls the boys "Trojan". Suetonius (Julius 39.2; Augustus 43.2) records that both Caesar and Augustus staged it. Augustus gave it up after boys were injured and Asinius Pollio complained. Then comes Virgil's sharpest turn. In 12.819–828 Juno gives up her anger only on condition that Troy's name, dress and language disappear. Rome will be Trojan by blood and Latin by name. Troy survives by agreeing to die.

Where sources disagree. Whether the Aeneid celebrates the Augustan settlement or mourns what it cost is the oldest quarrel in Virgil scholarship. Adam Parry's "The Two Voices of Virgil's Aeneid" (1963) and the so-called Harvard school stress the private grief and the killing of Turnus that ends the poem. Readers such as Brooks Otis (Virgil: A Study in Civilized Poetry, 1964) and Francis Cairns (Virgil's Augustan Epic, 1989) stress its imperial teleology. Most current readers hold that both voices are present.

Nero took the Trojan connection to the stage. Suetonius (Nero 38.2) says that while Rome burned in AD 64 he sang The Sack of Ilium in stage costume. Tacitus (Annals 15.39) gives this only as a rumour and notes that Nero was at Antium when the fire started. Cassius Dio (62.18) repeats it. Nero also wrote a Troica, which Juvenal mocks in Satire 8. According to Servius (on Aeneid 5.370) it made Paris strong enough to beat Hector at the funeral games. That makes sense for an emperor who preferred the lyre-player prince to the warrior. Petronius' Eumolpus recites a Troiae Halosis (Satyricon 89), which is very likely a parody aimed at Nero's poem.

Dares and Dictys: the eyewitnesses who outranked Homer

Two short prose works shaped the Latin Middle Ages more than any epic. The Ephemeris belli Troiani of "Dictys of Crete" claims to be the war diary of a companion of Idomeneus. Its Latin version, by one Lucius Septimius, probably dates to the fourth century AD. A prefatory letter says shepherds found the text in a box in Dictys' tomb at Knossos after an earthquake in Nero's reign, written in Phoenician letters, and that it was translated into Greek for the emperor. The tale of the found manuscript is a forger's convention, but a Greek original did exist. A Tebtunis papyrus (P.Tebt. 2.268) of the early third century preserves part of it, and the Byzantine chronicler John Malalas used it. Dictys writes from the Greek side, rationalises the gods away, and has Achilles lured to his death by his love for the Trojan princess Polyxena.

The De excidio Troiae historia of "Dares the Phrygian" is shorter, flatter and pro-Trojan. It probably dates to the fifth or sixth century. A fake letter from Cornelius Nepos to Sallust says Nepos found it in Athens. Its author borrows the name of a minor Trojan priest of Hephaestus (Iliad 5.9). Dares gives brisk portraits of the main figures (chapters 12–13), which medieval poets copied almost word for word, and closes with an exact casualty count. Awkwardly for Rome, Dares has Aeneas and Antenor betray the city.

The Middle Ages trusted these texts over Homer for several reasons:

  • Eyewitness over poet. Medieval historiography ranked testimony above song. Isidore of Seville (Etymologies 1.42.1) names Dares as the first pagan historian, after Moses among the Hebrews, and claims he wrote on palm leaves. Homer was a later poet who, as the Nepos letter puts it, had been thought mad for showing gods fighting men.
  • No Greek. The Latin West could not read Homer. Its Homer was the Ilias Latina, a first-century abridgement of about 1,070 hexameters.
  • No gods. A war without divine meddling suited Christian readers better.
  • The right side. Dares favoured Troy, which mattered to nations that believed they were descended from it.
Where sources disagree. The papyrus proves the Greek Dictys. No Greek Dares has ever been found; Aelian (Varia Historia 11.2) says a Phrygian Iliad by Dares still existed in his day, and whether one did is uncertain. Dates for both Latin texts are estimates. The Greek Dictys is fixed only at one end: the Tebtunis papyrus (P.Tebt. 268) is of the early third century AD, so the Greek text is older than that; whether it was written under Nero, as its own preface claims by dating the "discovery" of the tin box to Nero's reign, or in the second century, is open.

Medieval Troy: romance, genealogy and the invention of Cressida

Benoît de Sainte-Maure's Roman de Troie (c. 1160–1170) runs to about 30,000 octosyllabic lines. It belongs with the Roman de Thèbes and the Eneas among the "romances of antiquity" written in the Plantagenet orbit. Its praise of a "riche dame de riche rei" is usually taken to mean Eleanor of Aquitaine, though this cannot be proved. Benoît follows Dares, then Dictys, and turns the war into chivalric romance. His great addition is the story of Troilus and Briseida. She is sent to the Greek camp in an exchange of prisoners, swears to stay faithful, and gives herself to Diomedes. A minor figure in Dares became the West's emblem of female inconstancy.

In 1287 Guido delle Colonne, a judge at Messina, produced the Historia destructionis Troiae. It is a Latin prose version of Benoît that never names Benoît, cites Dares and Dictys as its authorities, and scolds Homer for lying. Because it was in Latin and looked like history, Guido's text became the standard account and was translated across Europe; Lydgate's Troy Book (1412–20) is Guido turned into English verse at four times the length, with the moralising expanded. Boccaccio's Il Filostrato (c. 1335–1340) turned Briseida into Criseida and invented Pandaro as go-between. From Boccaccio came Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385). Chaucer credits an invented authority, "Lollius". His narrator sympathises with Criseyde and is reluctant to condemn her. The poem ends by lifting Troilus' soul to the eighth sphere, where he laughs at those who mourn him. Chaucer calls it a tragedy:

Go, litel bok, go, litel myn tragedye (Troilus 5.1786)

Robert Henryson's Testament of Cresseid answered Chaucer by striking her with leprosy. John Lydgate's Troy Book (1412–1420), written for Henry, Prince of Wales, put Guido into some 30,000 English lines. William Caxton's Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (Bruges, c. 1473–1474), a translation of Raoul Lefèvre, was the first book printed in English. Troy and English print began together.

Behind the romance sat genealogy. A Trojan ancestor made a people Rome's cousin rather than its subject.

PeopleTrojan founderKey source
RomansAeneas, IulusVirgil, Aeneid; Dionysius 1
FranksFrancio, kin of Priam; later Antenor's lineChronicle of Fredegar (7th c.); Liber Historiae Francorum (727)

NormansAntenor, via the "Dacians"Dudo of Saint-Quentin
Paduans, VenetiansAntenorAeneid 1.242–249
Norse godsThor as "Tror", grandson of PriamSnorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Prologue
Ottoman Turks"Teucri" as TurciKritoboulos on Mehmed II at Troy, 1462
Where sources disagree. Geoffrey claimed he was translating a "very ancient book" in British. William of Newburgh (Historia rerum Anglicarum, preface, c. 1196–1198) called him a liar, and J. S. P. Tatlock (The Legendary History of Britain, 1950) and most modern scholars regard the book as a fiction. The case for a real source rests on Geoffrey's use of Welsh names and genealogies that are not in Bede or Gildas; that shows Welsh material, not a book.

Early modern Troy: Shakespeare's anti-epic and Homer recovered

Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida (c. 1601–1602) drew on Chaucer, Caxton and Lydgate, and perhaps also on Chapman's 1598 Homer. It treats the whole tradition with contempt. The Prologue enters "armed" and starts in the middle of things, as epic should. The play then takes epic apart. Hector concedes that Helen ought to go back (2.2) and then argues for keeping her. Ulysses' great speech on "degree" (1.3) is followed by his cynical handling of Achilles. Helen chatters about love songs (3.1). Cressida's betrayal (5.2) is watched in layers: Troilus watches her, Ulysses watches Troilus, and Thersites watches them all and gives his verdict: "still wars and lechery". Achilles does not defeat Hector. His Myrmidons kill Hector while he is unarmed (5.8), a detail that comes from the medieval Achilles of Benoît, Guido and Lydgate, who kill Hector unguarded and send the Myrmidons against Troilus, never from Homer, nor from Dares, whose Achilles kills Hector in open battle (ch. 24). The play ends with Pandarus leaving the audience his venereal diseases.

Where sources disagree. The play's genre was unsettled from the start. The 1609 quarto exists in two states: one says it was acted at the Globe, and the other carries an epistle claiming it was never staged and calling it a comedy. The Folio printed it late, unpaginated, between the histories and the tragedies. F. S. Boas classed it as a "problem play" in Shakspere and His Predecessors (1896). Peter Alexander ("Troilus and Cressida, 1609", The Library, 1928) suggested it was written for an Inns of Court audience. That remains uncertain.

Homer himself came back slowly. Petrarch owned a Greek Homer he could not read. Leontius Pilatus made a crude Latin prose version for him and Boccaccio in the 1360s. The editio princeps appeared in Florence in 1488 under Demetrios Chalkokondyles. George Chapman published Seaven Bookes of the Iliades in 1598, the full Iliad in fourteeners in 1611, and the Odyssey in 1614–1615. He read Homer as Neoplatonic allegory and claimed Homer's spirit inspired him. Two centuries later Keats's sonnet "On First Looking into Chapman's Homer" (1816) recorded the shock of that rough energy. Alexander Pope's Iliad (1715–1720), in heroic couplets, earned enough by subscription to make him independent. His Odyssey (1725–1726) was partly farmed out to William Broome and Elijah Fenton. Richard Bentley's reputed remark, "a pretty poem, Mr Pope, but you must not call it Homer", is anecdote, but it names the problem: Homer made polite.

The deeper change concerned authority. Once Homer could be read, Dares was exposed as a late forgery, and the oldest text replaced the supposed eyewitness. Then the oldest text was itself questioned. Robert Wood's Essay on the Original Genius of Homer (1769) read the poems against the landscape of the Troad. F. A. Wolf's Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795) argued that "Homer" was a product of oral tradition and later editing. The question of whether there was a Homer reopened the question of whether there was a Troy.

Schliemann and the Victorian Troy

Victorian Britain took Homer as moral education. Gladstone wrote Studies on Homer and the Homeric Age (1858) out of office, between his two terms at the Exchequer (1855 and 1859). For Gladstone, Homer was close to a second revelation, a record of a moral order older than Greece; that is why the poems could carry the weight of a gentleman's education. Matthew Arnold's On Translating Homer (1861), answering F. W. Newman's ballad-metre version, demanded rapidity, plainness and nobility. Tennyson's "Ulysses" (1842) made the returned hero a restless imperial explorer. The habit ran deep in the public schools. In 1915, across the Dardanelles from Hisarlik, Patrick Shaw-Stewart wrote in his copy of Housman the lines "Stand in the trench, Achilles, / Flame-capped" (printed in Ronald Knox, Patrick Shaw-Stewart, 1920). Rupert Brooke, bound for Gallipoli, was buried on Skyros, the island where Achilles had been hidden.

The site itself was disputed. Late eighteenth-century travellers favoured Pınarbaşı. Charles Maclaren argued for Hisarlik in 1822, and Frank Calvert, who owned part of the mound, dug trial trenches there in the 1860s. Heinrich Schliemann used Calvert's ground and excavated from 1871. His great north–south trench destroyed much of the upper layers he was looking for. In 1873 he announced "Priam's Treasure" and photographed his wife Sophia wearing the gold. The hoard came from Troy II, about a thousand years before any plausible Trojan War. He smuggled it out of the Ottoman Empire. It went to Berlin, vanished in 1945, and in 1993 was acknowledged to be in the Pushkin Museum, Moscow.

His successors refined the picture. Wilhelm Dörpfeld identified the walls of Troy VI. Carl Blegen in the 1930s favoured Troy VIIa, whose fall he put at about 1250 BC; Penelope Mountjoy's pottery dating has since moved it to about 1190–1180 BC. From 1988 Manfred Korfmann traced a large lower town. Hittite texts name a western Anatolian state called Wilusa, widely equated with (W)ilios, and a treaty between Muwatalli II and its king Alaksandu (c. 1280 BC), a name that resembles Alexandros, Paris's other name.

Where sources disagree. Schliemann's treasure (Traill and Calder against Easton) is argued in module 10.10. The Kolb–Korfmann quarrel over the lower town is in module 10.10, the Wilusa equation in module 10.3. Whether any of this confirms a single war behind Homer is uncertain.

The twentieth century: Troy against war

After 1914 Troy became the West's way of thinking about its own wars. Jean Giraudoux's La guerre de Troie n'aura pas lieu (1935) shows Hector, back from war, trying to send Helen home and keep the Gates of War closed. In the central scene with Ulysses, the two men almost succeed. Then the warmonger poet Demokos lies with his dying breath, and the war happens anyway. Staged between Hitler's rise and Munich, its irony arrived on schedule. Christopher Fry translated it as Tiger at the Gates (1955).

Simone Weil wrote "L'Iliade ou le poème de la force" in 1939–1940 and published it in Cahiers du Sud (1940–1941) under the anagram Émile Novis. Her claim is that the real subject of the Iliad is force, which "turns anybody who is subjected to it into a thing" (Mary McCarthy's 1945 translation). In her reading Homer gives the same bitter pity to both sides, and only the Gospels match it.

Where sources disagree. Rachel Bespaloff's De l'Iliade (1943), written in the same years, reads the poem as tragic but also as a celebration of beauty and heroic life. Set against Weil, Bespaloff is the case that Weil underplays how fully the Iliad honours kleos, the glory a warrior wins by killing; the two essays were published together in English (War and the Iliad, 2005) because they are the two sides.

Christa Wolf's Kassandra (1983) is spoken by Cassandra at Mycenae in the hour before her death. It reimagines Troy as a militarised state with a security apparatus, under its official Eumelos, that silences its own prophet. Achilles is simply "the brute", and real hope lies in a community of women in the caves of Mount Ida. Published with Wolf's Frankfurt poetics lectures, during the NATO missile debate and under East German censorship, it reads as a feminist critique of a whole civilisation's investment in war.

Christopher Logue's War Music began in 1959 with a BBC commission. He knew no Greek, worked from cribs, and called his versions "accounts". He was still writing when he died in 2011, leaving the work unfinished. Its cinematic cutting, anachronistic similes and violent speed made the Iliad modern without the polish of Pope. Derek Walcott's Omeros (1990) moves Troy to St Lucia. The fishermen Achille and Hector fight over Helen, a waitress. Philoctete suffers a wound that will not heal. "Omeros" is Homer's name in modern Greek. Here the Trojan story belongs to the descendants of the enslaved, though the narrator keeps questioning whether a Caribbean life needs a Homeric frame at all.

The women-centred retellings: what they correct and what they flatten

Margaret Atwood's The Penelopiad (2005) has Penelope speak from Hades, with a chorus of the twelve maids whom Telemachus hangs in Odyssey 22. Pat Barker's The Silence of the Girls (2018) gives the Iliad to Briseis, and its opening lines mock the epic praise of Achilles ("Great Achilles. Brilliant Achilles"). Its sequels continue past the sack. Madeline Miller's The Song of Achilles (2011) is narrated by Patroclus as a love story, and Circe (2018) moves to the edge of the Odyssey, correcting the goddess into a person and flattening Odysseus into a guest who passes through. Natalie Haynes's A Thousand Ships (2019) gives the war to the Muse Calliope and dozens of women; it corrects the silence of Euripides' survivors into speech and flattens the men into a chorus of causes. Emily Wilson's Odyssey (2017) and Iliad (2023) are line-for-line translations, not retellings. Her opening "Tell me about a complicated man" and her decision to call the hanged women "slaves" rather than "maids" changed how the poem is read in English. Caroline Alexander's Iliad (2015) was the first complete English version by a woman.

What they correct is real. Enslaved women, rape as a spoil of war, and the fate of a captured city were the subject of the tradition, and the epic voice rarely lingered on them. What they claim to restore is older than they sometimes admit. The Iliad gives Briseis her own lament over Patroclus (19.282–300). It ends with three women's laments, by Andromache, Hecuba and Helen (24.723–776). Euripides' Trojan Women (415 BC) is a women-centred Troy staged two thousand four hundred years before Barker. The flattening is also real. Gods tend to vanish or shrink. Achilles becomes either a romantic lead or a thug. A modern therapeutic idiom replaces formulaic speech. A sharp line between victim and perpetrator crowds out the Iliad's hardest scene, in Book 24, where Priam and Achilles weep together for different dead.

Where sources disagree. The objection to Wilson is that "complicated" narrows polytropos, "of many turns", and that some of her plain diction loses the formulaic grandeur. Wilson's own answer, in her translator's note, is that older translations brought their own Victorian or Augustan values into the text unremarked. The disagreement is less about Greek than about whether any translation can be neutral.

Troy on screen

Film has kept the medieval habit of taking sides and trimming the gods.

ProductionApproachMain liberties
Helen of Troy (1956, dir. Robert Wise)Warner Bros. CinemaScope epic shot at Cinecittà; Rossana Podestà and Jacques SernasParis as a sincere peace envoy and Helen as a willing lover; greedy Greeks led by Agamemnon want plunder, not Helen; a pro-Trojan romance in Dares' tradition
Troy (2004, dir. Wolfgang Petersen; script David Benioff)"Inspired by" the Iliad; no gods on screen; Agamemnon's imperial ambition as the real motiveThe war seems to last weeks, not ten years; Hector kills Menelaus (who in Homer goes home, Odyssey 4) and Ajax; Briseis kills Agamemnon (Clytemnestra's deed in Aeschylus); Patroclus a "cousin"; Achilles dies inside the sacked city; Aeneas escapes with a Trojan sword, a nod to Virgil
Troy: Fall of a City (2018, BBC One and Netflix; David Farr)Eight episodes; gods present; Paris's shepherd youth and the Judgement shown at lengthHelen as an active agent of her own flight; Achilles and Patroclus explicitly lovers; long invented Trojan court politics

The BBC series drew racist abuse for casting black actors as Achilles, Patroclus, Zeus and Aeneas. Critics cited Homer's xanthos ("fair", "tawny") for Achilles' hair. Classicists replied that modern racial categories do not map onto Homeric colour terms. The row, more than the series, showed how much ownership some modern viewers still claim over Troy.

Why this war remains the West's master story

Several features explain its persistence. First, it has two sides, and either can be claimed. The Iliad grants the enemy full humanity, so Rome, the Franks, the Britons, Wolf's Cassandra and Walcott's fishermen could all take the losing side, the side of survivors and founders. Second, it is complete. A cause, a quarrel, the death of the best man, the fall of a city, captive women and homecomings that go wrong supply nearly every plot later literature needs, and Aeschylus, Euripides and Virgil all took their material from it. Third, its centre is almost empty. A war fought over one woman, or an insult, or a ghost, invites each age to name the real motive: honour, desire, trade, empire, oil, patriarchy. Fourth, it is probably real but cannot be proved. Hisarlik and Wilusa show that something was there without ever confirming Homer. Finally, the story is always a contest over who has the right to tell it: Dares against Homer, Guido against Benoît, Schliemann against the sceptics, Briseis against Achilles. Each age re-fights the Trojan War over the right to narrate it.

Self-test

  1. Which Homeric passage gives the Romans their opening, and what does it say?
    Answer

    Iliad 20.302–308: Poseidon saves Aeneas from Achilles because fate has decreed that Aeneas and his descendants will rule the Trojans.

  2. What condition does Juno set in Aeneid 12 before she gives up her anger, and why does it matter for Rome's Trojan identity?
    Answer

    Troy's name, language and dress must disappear and the new people must be called Latin. Rome is Trojan by descent but Italian by name, so Troy survives only by ceasing to exist.

  3. What was the lusus Troiae, and who records its staging?
    Answer

    A cavalry display by aristocratic boys, given an origin story in Aeneid 5.545–603. Suetonius (Julius 39; Augustus 43) records that Caesar and Augustus staged it, and that Augustus dropped it after injuries.

  4. How does Tacitus' account of Nero singing during the fire of 64 differ from Suetonius'?
    Answer

    Suetonius (Nero 38) states it as fact. Tacitus (Annals 15.39) reports it as a rumour and notes that Nero was at Antium when the fire began.

  5. What evidence shows that Dictys Cretensis had a Greek original?
    Answer

    A Tebtunis papyrus (P.Tebt. 2.268) of the early third century AD preserves part of the Greek text, and John Malalas used it. No comparable evidence exists for Dares.

  6. Give three reasons medieval readers preferred Dares and Dictys to Homer.
    Answer

    They claimed to be eyewitness prose history rather than later poetry (Isidore, Etymologies 1.42.1, calls Dares the first pagan historian); the Latin West could not read Greek; they removed the gods; and Dares took the Trojan side favoured by peoples claiming Trojan descent.

  7. Who first told the Troilus–Briseida story, and how did the woman's name reach Chaucer's form?
    Answer

    Benoît de Sainte-Maure, in the Roman de Troie (c. 1160–1170). Guido delle Colonne carried it into Latin prose. Boccaccio's Filostrato renamed her Criseida and added Pandaro, and Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde followed Boccaccio.

  8. In Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, how does Hector die, and why is that significant?
    Answer

    Achilles' Myrmidons kill him while he is unarmed. The treacherous Achilles comes from the medieval Benoît–Guido–Lydgate tradition, not Homer or Dares, and the scene demolishes epic heroism.

  9. What did Schliemann's "Priam's Treasure" turn out to be, and where is it now?
    Answer

    A hoard from Troy II, roughly a thousand years earlier than any plausible Trojan War. It was taken from Berlin in 1945 and has been acknowledged since 1993 to be in the Pushkin Museum, Moscow.

  10. What women-centred version of Troy existed long before the modern retellings?
    Answer

    The Iliad itself, with Briseis' lament (19.282–300) and the three women's laments that close the poem (24.723–776), and above all Euripides' Trojan Women (415 BC).

Carry forward

  1. Troy was a claim of descent before it was a story. From Rome to the Franks and Britons, the losing side was the prize because it supplied founders, not subjects.
  2. Each age fights over who has authority to tell the war: eyewitness forgery, then the oldest poem, then the excavated site, then the silenced voice. The way a culture tells Troy shows what it counts as truth.
  3. Homer and Euripides already contain most of the counter-voices later retellings claim to add. Reception usually amplifies what the old texts left at the margins rather than inventing it.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the reception of the Trojan War from Rome to the present. Cover: the Roman Troy (Naevius, Ennius, Virgil's Aeneid as a pro-Trojan answer to Homer, the Julian claim through Iulus, Augustus and the Troy Game, Nero's Troica); the late antique prose forgeries Dares Phrygius and Dictys Cretensis and why the Middle Ages trusted them over Homer; the medieval Troy: Benoît de Sainte-Maure's Roman de Troie, Guido delle Colonne, Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde, Lydgate, the Trojan ancestry claimed by Franks, Britons (Brutus of Troy) and others; Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida as anti-epic; the Renaissance recovery of Homer (Chapman, Pope); Schliemann and the Victorian Troy; Troy in the twentieth century (Giraudoux's La guerre de Troie n'aura pas lieu, Simone Weil's The Iliad or the Poem of Force, Christa Wolf's Cassandra, Logue's War Music, Walcott's Omeros); the recent women-centred retellings (Atwood's Penelopiad, Barker's Silence of the Girls, Miller, Haynes, Wilson's translations) and what they correct and what they flatten; Troy on screen (the 1956 Helen of Troy, Petersen's Troy, the BBC Troy: Fall of a City) and the historical liberties each takes. End with why this one war has stayed the West's master story.
