GREECE · UNIT 11 · Deep dive II: Alexander · 11.1 · 2,737 words

Macedon before Alexander

Land and dynastyKingship and courtGods and graves at AegaeFrom Archelaus to the crisis of the 360sPhilip II: building the instrumentPhilip's household and his deathGreek views and the Hellenicity questionWhat Alexander inheritedSelf-testCarry forward

Land and dynasty

Two Macedonias

Lower Macedonia was the alluvial plain at the head of the Thermaic Gulf, made up of Pieria, Bottiaea and Emathia and watered by the Haliacmon, Loudias and Axios. It had grain and horse pasture, but the good harbours belonged to Greeks for most of the period. Aegae, the old royal seat, sat where the Haliacmon leaves the Pierian hills. Pella was already the largest city by 382 (Xenophon, Hellenica 5.2.13). Archelaus is usually credited with moving the court there, but that is a modern inference, and Amyntas III is the alternative candidate.

Upper Macedonia was the ring of highland basins to the west: Elimeia, Orestis, Lyncestis, Eordaea, Tymphaea and Pelagonia. Thucydides (2.99.2) calls the Lyncestae and Elimiotae allies and subjects of the lowland kings who nevertheless "have kings of their own". Their position between the Illyrians and Paeonians made their loyalty negotiable. Binding them to the crown was Philip's first structural achievement. This is why Alexander's marshals include so many highlanders (Perdiccas and Craterus of Orestis, Coenus of Elimeia, Polyperchon of Tymphaea), and why phalanx battalions were still raised by region (Diodorus 17.57.2).

The Argead claim

The ruling house claimed descent from Temenus of Argos, and so from Heracles. In Herodotus' founding story (8.137–139), three exiled Temenid brothers serve a local king, and the youngest, Perdiccas, founds the line. Thucydides (2.99.3) accepts this. Justin (7.1) names Caranus as founder instead, and Euripides' lost Archelaus gave the founder the name of its royal patron (Hyginus, Fabulae 219). The genealogy was evidently flexible.

The key text is Herodotus 5.22. When Alexander I entered the stadion at Olympia, rivals objected that barbarians could not compete. He proved his Argive descent, the Hellanodikai admitted him, and he "tied for first". Herodotus endorses the claim:

That these descendants of Perdiccas are Greeks, as they say, I myself know.

Three points matter. The claim covers the dynasty, not the people. It had to be argued, so other Greeks did not take it for granted. And Alexander I had been a Persian vassal: his sister married the Persian Bubares (5.21), and he served as Mardonius' envoy in 479 (8.136). Badian ("Herodotus on Alexander I of Macedon", 1994) read Herodotus' flattering stories, the murdered Persian envoys (5.17–21) and the warning before Plataea (9.44–45), as the king's own post-war apologetics. The Olympic episode cannot be dated, and no victor list records him.

Where sources disagree. Appian (Syrian Wars 63) derives the Argeadae from Argos Oresticum in Upper Macedonia, not from Peloponnesian Argos. Hesiod's Catalogue (fr. 7) makes Makedon a son of Zeus, a cousin of Hellen's line rather than a member of it. The Peloponnesian pedigree may be fifth-century diplomacy built on a convenient name.

Kingship and court

The throne was hereditary within the Argead house, without primogeniture. Any adult Argead could claim it. The candidate who held the army and the great men at the moment of vacancy was acclaimed by the Macedonians under arms. Hammond treated this as quasi-constitutional and gave the army assembly real rights to acclaim kings and to try capital cases, citing Curtius 6.8.25, where treason was judged by the army "by ancient Macedonian custom". Errington ("The Nature of the Macedonian State", Chiron 1978) and Borza answered that these were customs a strong king used and a weak one could not avoid, not entitlements. Most recent scholars side with Errington.

The king was warlord: he fought in the front rank and carried the scars. Demosthenes (18.67) lists Philip's lost eye, broken collarbone and maimed hand and leg. He was priest: he made the state sacrifices daily, and Alexander kept them up even when dying (Arrian 7.25). He presided at rites such as the Xandika, an army purification (Livy 40.6, describing the Antigonid version). He was judge: in an anecdote also told of other kings, an old woman refused a hearing tells Philip "then stop being king" (Plutarch, Demetrius 42).

The hetairoi were the king's personal following. They hunted, drank and fought beside him and were paid in land. Theopompus, hostile and moralising, claims Philip's 800 Companions held as much land as 10,000 of the richest Greeks (FGrH 115 F225). Under Philip the name also passed to the heavy cavalry. The royal pages, sons of the nobility, guarded the king's sleep and hunted with him. Arrian (4.13.1) dates them "from Philip's time", which may mean Philip founded the institution or only that it existed under him. They were a school for officers and hostages for their fathers' loyalty.

The hunt conferred rank. Hegesander (in Athenaeus 1.18a) says no Macedonian reclined at dinner until he had killed a boar without a net. Aristotle (Politics 7.1324b) says a man who had killed no enemy wore a halter for a belt. The symposium was the arena of free speech among Companions, and the drinking was notorious. Theopompus calls Philip a drunkard, and Ephippus (FGrH 126) says the same of Alexander. Southern Greek sources exaggerate, but two decisive ruptures happened over wine: Attalus' wedding toast and the killing of Cleitus (Arrian 4.8).

Gods and graves at Aegae

The pantheon was Greek with a northern emphasis. There was Zeus Olympios at Dion, where Archelaus founded a festival with dramatic contests (Diodorus 17.16.3–4). Heracles Patroos was worshipped as the dynasty's ancestor. Dionysiac cult was strong: Plutarch (Alexander 2) has Olympias handling snakes in orgiastic rites. Philip's mother Eurydice made dedications to Eukleia at Aegae.

In 1977 Manolis Andronikos opened the Great Tumulus at Vergina, which Hammond had identified with Aegae in 1968. Tomb I was a looted cist with a painting of Hades seizing Persephone. Tomb III held a youth's remains, usually taken as Alexander IV. Tomb II, barrel-vaulted with a hunting frieze, was intact. In its chamber a gold larnax held a man's cremated bones with armour, an oak wreath and a gilded silver diadem. In the antechamber lay a woman with a myrtle wreath and a Scythian-style gorytos.

Where sources disagree. Andronikos and Hammond named the man in Tomb II as Philip II, and Musgrave, Neave and Prag (JHS 1984) reported damage to the eye socket. Lehmann (AJA 1980), Borza and Palagia argued for Philip III Arrhidaeus and Adea-Eurydice, buried at Aegae by Cassander in 316. They pointed to the vault (thought to be a post-Alexander eastern borrowing), the diadem (adopted after 330), the pottery and the Asian gear. Bartsiokas (Science 2000) found no eye wound. He and colleagues (PNAS 2015) then proposed that a leg in Tomb I, with a fused knee, belongs to Philip, who was lamed in 339. Each step is contested. The identification is uncertain and should carry no argument.

From Archelaus to the crisis of the 360s

Archelaus (c. 413–399) took the throne by murder. Plato makes him the model of the happy criminal (Gorgias 470d–471d). Thucydides (2.100.2) credits him with roads, forts, and more horses and arms than his eight predecessors combined. He built a Greek court deliberately. Zeuxis painted the palace (Aelian, Varia Historia 14.17), and Agathon and Timotheus came to Pella. Euripides, by tradition, wrote the Archelaus and perhaps the Bacchae there. Socrates declined an invitation (Aristotle, Rhetoric 2.23, 1398a). Archelaus was murdered by his lover Crataeus, a case Aristotle (Politics 5.1311b) files with other killings provoked by sexual insult, the same category in which he places Philip.

Where sources disagree. Scullion ("Euripides and Macedon, or the Silence of the Frogs", CQ 2003) argued that Euripides never went to Macedon, since the Frogs of 405 does not mention it, and that the stories are biographical fiction. Most still accept the visit, but its basis is thin.

Forty years of weak reigns followed. Amyntas III (393–370/69) lost his kingdom at least once. Then:

DateEventSource
368Pelopidas takes hostages, including Philip, to ThebesPlutarch, Pelopidas 26
368/7Alexander II murdered; Ptolemy of Alorus regentDiodorus 15.71
c. 367Iphicrates repels the pretender Pausanias at Eurydice's pleaAeschines 2.26–29
365Perdiccas III kills PtolemyDiodorus 16.2
360/59Perdiccas and about 4,000 Macedonians killed by Bardylis' IllyriansDiodorus 16.2.4–5

Philip took over with Illyrians and Paeonians invading, two pretenders (one backed by Athens) and no field army.

Where sources disagree. Justin (7.5.9–10) says Philip first ruled as guardian for his infant nephew Amyntas. Diodorus (16.1–2) has him king from the start. Whether there was a regency is uncertain.

Philip II: building the instrument

The hostage years. Philip lived in Thebes from about 368 to 365, in the house of Pammenes, when Thebes was at its peak after Leuctra. Plutarch (Pelopidas 26.5) calls him a zealous imitator of Epaminondas. Whether he learned specific tactics or a broader lesson, that a drilled infantry state could overturn the Greek order, is inference. Diodorus (16.2.2) and Justin (7.5.1–3) give confused sequences involving Illyrian hostage-taking as well.

The army. Diodorus (16.3.1–2) describes constant drill and new equipment from 359. Its parts:

  • Sarissa: a cornel-wood pike of up to 12 cubits, about 5.5 m (Theophrastus, Historia Plantarum 3.12.2). Polybius (18.29) gives 14 cubits for the later phalanx. It was held two-handed, so the shield was small. It was cheap, which meant a poor peasantry could be armed in mass.
  • Pezhetairoi, "Foot Companions", extending the Companion bond to the infantry. Demosthenes mentions them by 349 (2.17).
  • Hypaspists, mobile elite infantry hinging phalanx and cavalry, with the royal agema.
  • Companion cavalry in regional squadrons using the wedge, which Arrian (Tactica 16.6) attributes to Philip. Thessalian horse was added after 352.
  • Siege train under Polyidus of Thessaly, whose pupils Diades and Charias served at Tyre. The failures at Perinthus and Byzantium (340) show its limits.
  • Year-round war: Demosthenes (9.48–50) contrasts Philip, fighting summer and winter with light troops, cavalry and mercenaries, with old Spartan four-month seasons. Frontinus (Strategemata 4.1.6) says he banned wagons.
Where sources disagree. Anaximenes (FGrH 72 F4) credits an unspecified "Alexander" (I, II or III) with creating the Companions and pezhetairoi. Theopompus (F348) uses pezetairoi for a picked guard. Some therefore think the name began with the guard, spread to the whole phalanx, and the guard was then renamed hypaspists.

Gold. In 356 Philip took Crenides under Mount Pangaion, refounded it as Philippi and worked the mines to over 1,000 talents a year (Diodorus 16.8.6–7). The figure may be inflated, but the gold staters he struck circulated as far as Gaul. The money paid mercenaries, bought politicians and rewarded Companions. The milestones were Amphipolis (357), Methone and the lost eye (354), the Crocus Field and the Thessalian archonship (352), Olynthus (348), the Peace of Philocrates (346), Chaeronea (338) and the League of Corinth (337).

Philip's household and his death

Satyrus (in Athenaeus 13.557b–e) says Philip "always married in connection with a war":

WifeOriginChildren
AudataIllyrianCynane
PhilaElimeianone known
NicesipolisPheraeThessalonice
PhilinnaLarissaArrhidaeus
OlympiasMolossiaAlexander, Cleopatra
MedaGetic Thracenone known
CleopatraMacedonian, niece of AttalusEuropa

There was no fixed rank of queen. Carney (Women and Monarchy in Macedonia, 2000) shows that a wife's standing rested on her son, his prospects and her kin, so rivalry between wives was succession politics. Olympias, a Molossian princess claiming descent from Achilles, had the strongest son, but Alexander was never formally designated.

At Philip's wedding to Cleopatra in 337, Attalus prayed for a "legitimate" heir. Alexander threw his cup. Philip drew on him and fell, and Alexander jeered that the man who would cross into Asia could not cross from couch to couch (Plutarch, Alexander 9.6–11). Alexander took Olympias to Epirus and went to the Illyrians himself until Demaratus of Corinth reconciled them. Arrian (3.6.5) calls the bride Eurydice. Whether she was formally renamed is unknown. In the Pixodarus affair (Plutarch, Alexander 10.1–4), the satrap of Caria offered his daughter to Arrhidaeus. Alexander secretly offered himself instead through the actor Thessalus. Philip rebuked him and exiled Harpalus, Nearchus, Erigyius, Laomedon and Ptolemy.

Where sources disagree. The Pixodarus story is told only by Plutarch. Some scholars think it is misdated or apologetic invention. Others take it as proof that Alexander's position in 337/6 was genuinely insecure.

In 336, with Parmenion and Attalus already in Asia, Philip married his daughter Cleopatra to Alexander of Epirus at Aegae. His statue was carried into the theatre as a thirteenth beside the twelve Olympians (Diodorus 16.92.5). He entered without guards and was stabbed by his bodyguard Pausanias of Orestis (Diodorus 16.93–94). According to Diodorus, Attalus had made Pausanias drunk and handed him to muleteers to be raped, and Philip had refused redress. Aristotle (Politics 5.1311b), a contemporary, gives the same grievance. The theories:

  1. Pausanias alone: the only version with contemporary support.
  2. Olympias: Justin (9.7) has her ready horses, crown the corpse and force Cleopatra to suicide after killing her infant. This is likely hostile embroidery.
  3. Alexander: Plutarch (Alexander 10.6–7) says suspicion "touched" him. Badian ("The Death of Philip II", Phoenix 1963) made the classic case. Bosworth and Carney are sceptical.
  4. Persia: Alexander's letter to Darius blames him (Arrian 2.14.5). Convenient and unprovable.
  5. The Lyncestians: Arrhabaeus and Heromenes were executed. Their brother Alexander Lyncestes, first to hail the new king, was spared (Arrian 1.25.1–2).

The purge that followed is certain. Attalus was killed in Asia (Diodorus 17.2.4–6), and Amyntas son of Perdiccas was killed, as were Cleopatra and her child.

Greek views and the Hellenicity question

For Demosthenes Philip was not Greek, not kin to Greeks, not even a respectable barbarian, but (9.31)

a pestilent Macedonian, from where you could not once buy a decent slave.

It is polemic, but it worked in front of an Athenian assembly. Isocrates' Philippus (346) urges Philip, as a Heraclid, to unite the Greeks against Persia. Yet even he says the founder left Greece because Greeks would not bear monarchy, and ruled a people "not of the same stock" (5.105–108). Friend and enemy agree that the kings could be Greek while the Macedonians were something else.

The modern debate concerns the people:

  • Language. Hesychius' glosses and the use of b for ph (Bilippos; Plutarch, Moralia 292e) suggest a distinct speech. The Pella curse tablet is in north-west Doric Greek, and Hatzopoulos treats Macedonian as a Greek dialect. But Alexander shouted Makedonisti to his guards in the Cleitus crisis (Plutarch, Alexander 51.6), and Philotas' use of the "native tongue" became an issue at his trial (Curtius 6.9.34–36).
  • Hammond (A History of Macedonia, 1972–88) held that they were Greek speakers, northern cousins of the Dorians. Herodotus 1.56 calls the proto-Dorians the Makednon ethnos.
  • Borza (In the Shadow of Olympus, 1990) saw a distinct Balkan people with a Hellenised elite, and thought the question unanswerable on present evidence.
  • Badian ("Greeks and Macedonians", 1982) moved the question to perception: whatever they spoke, Greeks and Macedonians each treated the other as outsiders.
Where sources disagree. The dispute over the name of North Macedonia, settled at Prespa in 2018, charged this debate beyond what the evidence can bear. A fair summary has three parts. Macedonian was probably a Greek dialect or a close relative. The court was Greek in culture by 400. Many southern Greeks still did not count Macedonians as Greek. These statements do not contradict each other.

What Alexander inherited

At Opis Alexander reminded his army that Philip found them

wanderers without means, most of you dressed in skins

and brought them down from the hills to cities and laws (Arrian 7.9.2). Alexander did not have to invent:

  • A professional, year-round, combined-arms army of over 30,000 foot and 5,000 horse at the crossing (Arrian 1.11.3), with engineers.
  • Upper Macedonia bound to the crown, and a nobility trained as pages and paid as Companions.
  • Hegemony through the League of Corinth, a declared Panhellenic war of revenge (Isocrates' programme), and a bridgehead in Asia.
  • Heraclid and Aeacid ancestry, and the beginnings of divine honours: the thirteenth statue, and the Philippeion at Olympia with gold-and-ivory family statues by Leochares (Pausanias 5.20.9–10).
  • Aristotle's tutelage at Mieza (343–340), and the generals Antipater and Parmenion.

He did not inherit solvency or security. At Opis he says he found under sixty talents and debts of five hundred (Arrian 7.9.6). He took over a throne secured by killing rivals, and a Greece that revolted at once, so that Thebes was destroyed in 335. Philip left him the instrument but not the settlement.

Self-test

  1. What does Herodotus 5.22 actually claim about Macedonian Greekness, and why is its scope narrower than it first appears?
    Answer

    It claims that the Argead dynasty, the descendants of Perdiccas, were Greeks of Argive origin, as shown by Alexander I's admission to Olympia. It says nothing about the Macedonian people. It also shows that the claim had to be argued, and Badian suspected it of being Alexander I's own propaganda.

  2. How does Thucydides (2.99) describe the relationship between the lowland kings and Upper Macedonia?
    Answer

    The Lyncestae, Elimiotae and other upland peoples were allies and subjects of the lowland kings but had kings of their own. Until Philip II the uplands were semi-independent cantons.

  3. Summarise the Hammond–Errington debate on the Macedonian army assembly.
    Answer

    Hammond saw quasi-constitutional rights to acclaim kings and to try capital cases, citing Curtius 6.8.25. Errington and Borza saw customs that depended on the king's strength, so the monarchy was personal, not constitutional.

  4. Give two pieces of evidence that the hunt and killing conferred status in Macedonian society.
    Answer

    Hegesander (Athenaeus 1.18a): no reclining at dinner until a boar had been killed without a net. Aristotle (Politics 7.1324b): a man who had killed no enemy wore a halter for a belt.

  5. What are the main arguments for identifying the man in Vergina Tomb II as Philip III Arrhidaeus rather than Philip II?
    Answer

    The barrel vault, thought to be a post-Alexander borrowing; the diadem, adopted after 330; the pottery dates; the Asian-style gear; and Bartsiokas' finding of no eye wound. Arrhidaeus and Adea-Eurydice were buried at Aegae in 316. The question remains unresolved.

  6. What did Thucydides credit Archelaus with, and what cultural episode of his reign is now doubted?
    Answer

    Roads, forts, and more horses and arms than his eight predecessors combined (2.100.2). Euripides' residence at Pella, which Scullion (2003) argued never happened.

  7. Name four components of Philip's military reform and the ancient evidence for one of them.
    Answer

    Any four of: the sarissa phalanx, the pezhetairoi, the hypaspists, the Companion cavalry in the wedge, the siege train, and year-round campaigning. For example: Theophrastus HP 3.12.2 on the sarissa; Demosthenes 9.48–50 on year-round war; Demosthenes 2.17 on the pezetairoi; Diodorus 16.3 on the drill.

  8. According to Satyrus, what principle governed Philip's marriages, and why did the seventh threaten Alexander?
    Answer

    He "always married in connection with a war", so each marriage sealed an alliance. Cleopatra was a Macedonian noblewoman, niece of the powerful Attalus. A son by her could be presented as fully Macedonian and "legitimate", which undercut the son of the Epirote Olympias.

  9. What motive do Aristotle and Diodorus give for Pausanias' assassination of Philip, and which modern scholar argued most strongly for Alexander's involvement?
    Answer

    Personal outrage: Attalus had Pausanias raped, and Philip refused redress (Aristotle, Politics 5.1311b; Diodorus 16.93). E. Badian, "The Death of Philip II" (Phoenix 1963).

  10. How does Isocrates' Philippus, though pro-Macedonian, support the view that the Macedonian people were not considered Greek?
    Answer

    It treats Philip as Greek through his Heraclid ancestry but says the founder ruled a people "not of the same stock" (5.105–108). The dynasty is distinguished from the people.

Carry forward

  1. The Macedonian monarchy was personal and was won by force. Every succession, Alexander's included, went to whoever held the army and the Companions and removed his rivals first. This explains the purges, the conspiracies, and the break-up after 323.
  2. Philip built almost everything Alexander used: the army, the engineers, the officer class, a unified Upper Macedonia, hegemony over Greece, the Persian war and the first steps towards divine honours. Measure Alexander against an instrument already made.
  3. Whether the Macedonians were Greek depended on who was asking. The dynasty claimed Argive descent, the court was Greek in culture, and the language was probably Greek, yet southern Greeks often counted Macedonians as outsiders. That tension runs from the League of Corinth to Opis.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the kingdom of Macedon down to 336 BC as the context for Alexander. Cover: the geography of Upper and Lower Macedonia and the Argead claim to Heraclid descent from Argos (Alexander I at Olympia and the Hellenicity question, Herodotus 5.22); the kingship: hereditary but acclaimed by the army, the king as warlord, priest and judge, the Companions and the royal pages, the royal hunt, the symposium culture and the heavy drinking; Macedonian religion and the royal tombs at Aegae (Vergina), including the debate about Tomb II; Archelaus and the Hellenisation of the court (Euripides at Pella); the chaos of the 360s; Philip II in detail: the hostage years at Thebes, the army reforms (sarissa, pezhetairoi, hypaspists, Companion cavalry, siege train, the end of seasonal campaigning), the gold of Mount Pangaion, the seven marriages and the harem politics, Olympias, the Pixodarus affair and the quarrel with Alexander, Attalus and Cleopatra Eurydice, the assassination by Pausanias and the theories about who was behind it; Demosthenes' and Isocrates' opposite views of Macedon; the modern debate about whether the Macedonians were Greeks (language, Hammond, Borza, Badian). End with what Alexander inherited and what he did not have to invent. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 11 · Deep dive II: Alexander · 11.2 · 2,724 words

Alexander's generalship: the battles and sieges

The four battles at a glanceGranicus, 334 BCIssus, 333 BCGaugamela, 331 BCHydaspes, 326 BCThe siegesThe system behind the victoriesComparisons and the honest assessmentSelf-testCarry forward

The four battles at a glance

Tactical reconstruction rests on Arrian's Anabasis, which follows Ptolemy and Aristobulus. The "vulgate" (Diodorus 17, Curtius, Justin, largely from Cleitarchus) is more rhetorical but sometimes keeps what the court historians suppressed. Enemy totals below are as reported and not credible.

BattleDate and placeMacedonians (reported)Opponents (reported)Decisive moveLosses (reported)
GranicusMay 334 BC; Biga Çay, Hellespontine Phrygia30,000+ foot, 5,000+ horse (Arrian 1.11.3)20,000 horse, nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries (Arrian 1.14.4); Diodorus 10,000 horse, 100,000 footDiversionary attack, then Alexander's Companions crossing obliquely into the Persian horse on the bank25 Companions, about 60 other horse, 30 foot (Arrian 1.16.4); Persians 1,000 horse, mercenaries destroyed
IssusNovember 333 BC; river Pinarus, head of the Gulf of İskenderunNo reliable figure; perhaps 30,000–40,000600,000 (Arrian 2.8.8); Callisthenes 30,000 horse, 30,000 mercenaries (Polybius 12.18)Charge across the river against the Persian left, then a wheel onto Darius32 foot, 150 horse dead (Curtius 3.11.27); Persians 100,000 (Arrian 2.11.8)
Gaugamela1 October 331 BC; near Tell Gomel, east of Mosul7,000 horse, about 40,000 foot (Arrian 3.12.5)40,000 horse, 1,000,000 foot, 200 scythed chariots, 15 elephants (Arrian 3.8.6)Rightward drift opens a gap; Companion wedge with phalanx drives into itAbout 100 men (Arrian 3.15.6), under 300 (Curtius), 500 (Diodorus); Persians 300,000 (Arrian), 40,000 (Curtius)
HydaspesMay 326 BC (Arrian 5.19.3); river Jhelum, PunjabCrossing force 5,000 horse, 6,000 foot (Arrian 5.14.1); Craterus held the camp30,000 foot, 4,000 horse, 300 chariots, 200 elephants (Arrian 5.15.4)Night crossing upstream; cavalry attack on the Indian left while Coenus took the Indian horse from behindAbout 310 (Arrian 5.18.3); 980 (Diodorus 17.89); Indians 23,000 (Arrian)

Granicus, 334 BC

Situation. The western satraps rejected Memnon's advice to burn the land and starve the invader, since Arsites would not see his satrapy burned (Arrian 1.12.9–10). An early battle suited Alexander, whose treasury was nearly empty. Ground. A river with steep, broken banks. The Persians lined the bank with cavalry and held the Greek mercenary infantry back on the rise, a deployment often read as a deliberate bid to kill Alexander as he climbed out.

Course. In Arrian (1.13–16) Parmenion urges waiting for dawn and Alexander attacks that afternoon: phalanx centre, Parmenion and the Thessalians left, Companions right. A probe by the Paeonians, prodromoi and one Companion squadron drew the Persian horse onto it. Alexander then led the Companions across in a slanting line against the current and struck the disordered Persians. The fight on the bank was a cavalry melee. Alexander's helmet was split; Cleitus severed Spithridates' arm as he struck (Arrian 1.15.8; Plutarch, Alexander 16). When the Persian centre broke, the mercenaries were encircled and almost annihilated. Lysippus cast statues of the 25 Companions killed in the first clash; Aristobulus, in Plutarch, gives 34 dead in all.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (17.19) has an unopposed crossing at dawn and a battle on the plain. Peter Green took this as true: a failed afternoon assault, suppressed by Arrian's source, then the dawn crossing. Hammond and Bosworth defended Arrian, noting that Diodorus' version mirrors Parmenion's advice. Most follow Arrian; the question is open.

Issus, 333 BC

Situation. Delayed by illness at Tarsus, Alexander marched south towards Myriandrus. Darius crossed the Amanus by a northern pass, came down behind him at Issus, and killed the Macedonian sick (Arrian 2.7.1). Alexander confirmed it with a thirty-oared ship (2.7.2), turned about, and retook the pass by night. Ground. A narrow plain between sea and foothills along the Pinarus, where numbers counted for little.

Orders of battle. Darius massed heavy cavalry under Nabarzanes by the sea, Greek mercenaries and Cardaces in the centre, light troops on the hills to his left, and himself in the centre. Alexander deployed from column as the plain widened, sent the Thessalians behind the phalanx to Parmenion on the left, and cleared the hills with Agrianians and archers. Course. Alexander crossed the river at the run with Companions and hypaspists and broke the Persian left. The phalanx, disordered by the banks, opened a gap that the mercenaries exploited; Ptolemy son of Seleucus and about 120 notable Macedonians fell (2.10.7). Alexander wheeled onto the mercenaries' flank and towards Darius, who fled; the Persian right, holding the Thessalians, broke on the news. Alexander took a thigh wound, by Darius' hand according to Chares (Plutarch, Alexander 20).

Where sources disagree. The Pinarus is usually the Payas, though the Deli Çay has had defenders. Polybius (12.17–22) argued that Callisthenes' plain could not hold Callisthenes' numbers, so the topography was contested in antiquity. Curtius makes Darius flee early; Arrian only once his left had collapsed.

Gaugamela, 331 BC

Situation. Alexander refused Darius' offers, including everything west of the Euphrates (Arrian 2.25). Darius chose an open plain and levelled it for chariots. A captured Persian order of battle, cited from Aristobulus (Arrian 3.11.3), makes the Persian deployment unusually well known; an eclipse eleven days earlier fixes the date (3.7.6). Orders of battle. Bessus with Bactrians and Sacae on the Persian left, Mazaeus on the right, Darius in the centre with the Kinsmen, Greek mercenaries and elephants, chariots in front. Expecting envelopment, Alexander posted a second line able to face about and angled his flank guards back, forming something close to a hollow rectangle (3.12). He refused a night attack: he would not steal victory (3.10.2).

Course. Alexander inclined right, off the prepared ground. Bessus' horse extended to match, feeding squadrons in against Menidas and the mercenary cavalry. The chariots charged; Agrianians and javelin men shot the drivers, and the infantry opened lanes for the rest (3.13.5–6). As the Persian left stretched, a gap opened beside the centre. Alexander formed a Companion wedge, took the nearest phalanx battalions with him, and drove at Darius, who fled. On the left Mazaeus pressed Parmenion hard, and horsemen broke through a separate phalanx gap to the baggage, where the second line expelled them. Parmenion sent for help; Alexander turned back and collided with retreating Persian cavalry in the day's hardest fighting, losing 60 Companions (3.15.2). Darius escaped.

Where sources disagree. Callisthenes, via Plutarch (Alexander 33), blamed Parmenion as sluggish and envious, his appeal costing Alexander the king. Arrian is milder. Since Parmenion was murdered in 330, many scholars, Bosworth among them, see a hostile tradition built afterwards, and credit Parmenion with holding the wing on which the battle actually hung. Whether the pursuit could have caught Darius anyway is uncertain.

Hydaspes, 326 BC

Situation. Porus held the far bank of a river in spate, with elephants horses would not face. Alexander advertised that he would wait for low water while moving troops noisily along the bank night after night until Porus stopped reacting (Arrian 5.9–11). He then took a picked force about 150 stades upstream to a wooded headland and island, leaving Craterus in camp with orders to cross only if the elephants left. The crossing. Made at night in a thunderstorm; the force landed on a second island and forded the last channel chest-deep (5.13). Porus' son, sent to intercept, was killed and his chariots bogged.

Battle. Porus left a screen against Craterus and deployed elephants along his front, infantry behind and between, cavalry and chariots on the wings. Short of infantry, Alexander massed horse against the Indian left, led by the horse archers, and sent Coenus towards the other flank to fall on the Indian cavalry from behind once it engaged (5.16.3). The Indian horse, caught between them, sheltered among the elephants. The phalanx met the elephants with sarissas and javelins aimed at the mahouts; maddened animals trampled both sides, more often their own. Alexander's cavalry closed round the Indian mass, Craterus crossed, and the pursuit became slaughter. Porus surrendered and was kept as king (5.19.1–3). Bucephalas died soon after and gave his name to one of the two cities founded on the field. The battle was the army's last great victory: that summer, at the Hyphasis, the men refused to go further, and part of the reason was what elephants and monsoon fighting had cost them.

Where sources disagree. The crossing site is unresolved: Stein argued for Jalalpur, others for sites near Haranpur or Mong. Coenus' route is contested, round behind the Indian line or a direct attack on the Indian right; Arrian's text allows both. Plutarch's "letter of Alexander" (Alexander 60) differs on the son's force, and Arrian's Munychion date sits awkwardly with his own mention of solstice rains.

The sieges

Halicarnassus (334)

Memnon held the city with mercenaries and the Persian fleet at his back. Alexander filled the ditch, brought up towers and breached the wall; one night two drunk men of Perdiccas' battalion started an unplanned assault that nearly succeeded (Arrian 1.21.1). After a failed sortie Memnon fired the town and withdrew to citadels that held into 333: proof that a fortress supplied by sea could not be finished off from land.

Tyre (January to July/August 332)

Refused leave to sacrifice to Heracles-Melqart inside the island city (Arrian 2.15.7–16.8), Alexander argued that a Tyre left free gave the Persian fleet a base behind him (2.17). The mole. A causeway was built from the mainland across the four-stade channel. In deep water near the walls the builders came under fire, and two towers behind hide screens went up at its head. A fireship, a horse transport packed with combustibles, burned them (2.19). The naval war. Alexander widened the mole and went to Sidon, where the decisive change came: the Phoenician squadrons, their cities already surrendered, joined him, with 120 Cypriot ships (2.20). Outnumbered, Tyre closed its two harbours. Rams and towers. Rams were mounted on lashed ships and transports. The Tyrians sank stones to keep them off and cut anchor cables; the Macedonians answered with chains and cranes. A midday sortie from the northern harbour mauled the Cypriots until Alexander rounded the island and destroyed it (2.21–22). Assault and massacre. A breach was opened on the south side, bridges were dropped from ships, and the hypaspists went up under Admetus, who was killed, with Alexander beside them (2.23). Arrian counts 8,000 Tyrians killed, about 30,000 sold, and 400 Macedonian dead over the siege (2.24.4–5). Diodorus (17.46.4) and Curtius (4.4.17) add 2,000 men crucified along the shore; Arrian is silent.

Gaza (autumn 332)

The engineers judged the hill-top city impregnable. Alexander built a ramp round it, two stades wide and 250 feet high in Arrian (2.26.3), hauled up the Tyre machines, and took a catapult bolt in the shoulder (2.27.2). After about two months the men were killed and the women and children sold.

Where sources disagree. Curtius (4.6.29), like Hegesias of Magnesia, says the commander Batis was dragged alive behind Alexander's chariot in imitation of Achilles. Arrian omits it. Some scholars dismiss it as rhetoric; others suspect deliberate omission.

The Sogdian Rock (327) and Aornos (326)

Ariamazes' defenders jeered that Alexander needed winged soldiers. For a prize of twelve talents, 300 volunteers climbed the snow cliff at night with iron tent pegs and flax ropes; about 30 fell, and the garrison surrendered at dawn (Arrian 4.18.4–19.4; Curtius 7.11). Arrian puts Rhoxane's capture here; Strabo (11.11.4) puts it at another rock. Aornos, which legend said had defeated Heracles, fell after Alexander filled a ravine with a mound to bring artillery in range; the defenders slipped away by night and many were cut down (Arrian 4.28–30). Stein's identification with Pir-Sar (1926) is widely accepted but not certain. Each impossible fortress taken persuaded the next to negotiate.

The system behind the victories

Hammer, anvil and hinge

The sarissa phalanx (twelve cubits in Theophrastus, Enquiry into Plants 3.12.2) pinned the enemy centre; it needed only to hold. The Companion cavalry in wedges struck the weak point. Alexander attacked from his right, refused his left and advanced in echelon, so the enemy committed first; at Gaugamela he made the gap himself. The 3,000 hypaspists, faster than the phalanx and able to keep pace with the horse, were the hinge that stopped a gap opening between them and led assaults on walls. Agrianians, archers and javelin men cleared hills, killed chariot crews and screened flanks; they appear at every turning point.

Leadership and its costs

Leading the wedge gave Alexander local control and unlimited loyalty, but nobody commanded the whole field once he charged, hence the stranded left at Gaugamela. The wounds accumulated: the Granicus, Issus, Gaza, a stone to the head at Cyropolis (Arrian 4.3.3), and an arrow through the chest among the Malli (6.10) that nearly ended the expedition.

Intelligence and speed

He questioned prisoners and locals constantly and checked reports before acting. Speed was a weapon: in 335 he reached Boeotia from Illyria before Thebes believed him alive (Arrian 1.7.5); chasing Darius in 330 he covered about 400 stades in a night with mounted infantry (3.21).

Logistics: Engels

Donald Engels (Alexander the Great and the Logistics of the Macedonian Army, 1978) argued that food, water and fodder governed every movement. Philip had banned carts and made men carry their own flour (Frontinus, Stratagems 4.1.6), shrinking the train, but the army could still carry only a few days' supply. Hence its timing by harvests, its hugging of rivers and coasts with the fleet, and its reliance on surrenders negotiated in advance; Gedrosia becomes a failed rendezvous with Nearchus. Critics accept the framework but dispute many of his figures.

Engineers, Bematists, doctors

Diades, pupil of Philip's engineer Polyidus, served at Tyre; Vitruvius (10.13.3) credits him with sectional towers, the borer and a boarding bridge. The Bematists, among them Baeton and Diognetus (Pliny, Natural History 6.61), paced and recorded each march, data later used by Eratosthenes. Philip of Acarnania treated Alexander at Tarsus (Arrian 2.4.8–11); Critodemus of Cos, or Critobulus in Curtius (9.5.25), drew the Mallian arrow. No medical corps can be shown, but care was expected.

Persian failures

No unified command at the Granicus; Memnon's death in 333 ending the naval counter-stroke; cramped ground at Issus; faith in chariots at Gaugamela; and Darius twice fleeing while his right was winning. Briant and others rightly reject the "decadent empire": the cavalry was excellent. The structural gap was line infantry able to face the phalanx: the Greek mercenaries were too few and were lost at the Granicus and Issus, and the Cardaces never proved themselves. Persian command also centred on the king's person, so his flight dissolved the army in a way Alexander's wounds never did; Macedonian battalion and squadron commanders could fight on without orders.

Comparisons and the honest assessment

Philip, Epaminondas, Hannibal

Philip built the instrument: phalanx, expanded Companions, pay, the cart ban, engineers, combined arms (Diodorus 16.3). At Chaeronea his feigned withdrawal (Polyaenus 4.2.2) drew the Athenians on while Alexander broke through on the other wing (Diodorus 16.86). But Philip preferred diplomacy and limited war; Alexander made the decisive battle the aim. Epaminondas, watched by the hostage Philip at Thebes, supplied the weighted wing and refused flank: fifty shields deep at Leuctra (Xenophon, Hellenica 6.4.12), driving "like a trireme" at Mantinea (7.5.23). Alexander turned the infantry wedge into a cavalry wedge. Hannibal is the contrast: at Cannae (Polybius 3.113–117) he enveloped, letting the Romans push into the trap, while Alexander penetrated and hunted the enemy commander. Hannibal won with mercenaries, no support from home, commanding from behind the line. In the story of his talk with Scipio he ranks Alexander first (Livy 35.14; Plutarch, Flamininus 21), though the anecdote may be invented.

How much was Alexander?

The army and most of its 334 officers were Philip's; Parmenion, Craterus and Coenus ran independent commands well. Persian choices eased the Granicus and Issus, and Darius' flight turned a close fight at Gaugamela into a rout. Yet three things were Alexander's alone: his reading of ground and timing (the Hydaspes feints, the rightward drift, the swift turn at Issus); his range, beating cavalry armies, a sea fortress, elephants, mountain strongholds and steppe raiders within a decade, which no other ancient commander matches; and his will, which took Tyre and Aornos. Against that: risk out of proportion to gain, lost control once he charged, brutality at Tyre, Gaza and among the Malli, and ambitions the army finally refused at the Hyphasis. A fair verdict: a supreme tactician with a supreme instrument against an enemy whose king lacked nerve. Remove any one and the outcome changes, though not necessarily to defeat.

Self-test

  1. What advice did Memnon give the satraps before the Granicus, and why was it rejected?
    Answer

    He advised a scorched-earth retreat to starve the Macedonians. Arsites refused to see his own satrapy burned (Arrian 1.12.9–10), and the satraps chose to fight.

  2. State the Granicus timing problem in one sentence for each source.
    Answer

    Arrian: Alexander rejected Parmenion's advice to wait and attacked across the river the same afternoon. Diodorus: he crossed unopposed at dawn and fought on the plain beyond. Green favoured Diodorus; Hammond and Bosworth defended Arrian.

  3. How did Darius come to be behind Alexander at Issus, and how did Alexander confirm it?
    Answer

    Darius crossed the Amanus by a northern pass while Alexander moved south towards Myriandrus, and reached Issus on Alexander's line of communication. Alexander sent a thirty-oared ship up the coast to check (Arrian 2.7.2).

  4. Where did the Macedonian line come closest to breaking at Issus, and who paid for it?
    Answer

    In the centre, where the river banks broke up the phalanx and the Greek mercenaries drove into the gap. Ptolemy son of Seleucus and about 120 Macedonians of rank were killed (Arrian 2.10.7).

  5. How were the scythed chariots at Gaugamela neutralised?
    Answer

    The Agrianians and javelin men shot the drivers and horses, and the infantry opened lanes so that the surviving chariots passed through harmlessly to be dealt with in the rear (Arrian 3.13.5–6).

  6. What is the dispute over Parmenion's role at Gaugamela?
    Answer

    Callisthenes, via Plutarch (Alexander 33), portrays him as slow and his appeal for help as costing Alexander the capture of Darius. Many modern scholars see a tradition hostile to him, built up after his murder in 330, and credit him with holding the hard-pressed left wing.

  7. How did Alexander get across the Hydaspes?
    Answer

    Weeks of noisy feints along the bank dulled Porus' reactions. Alexander then took about 5,000 horse and 6,000 foot to a screened crossing about 150 stades upstream, crossed by night in a storm, and forded a final channel after landing on a second island, while Craterus held the main camp opposite Porus.

  8. What turned the naval situation at Tyre?
    Answer

    The Phoenician squadrons, whose home cities had already submitted, and 120 Cypriot ships came over to Alexander at Sidon (Arrian 2.20). That gave him command of the sea, allowed him to blockade both harbours, and let him use ship-mounted rams against the walls.

  9. What does Engels' study argue, and what is its main limitation?
    Answer

    That food, water and fodder dictated the army's routes and timing: soldiers carried their own rations, the army could carry only a few days' supply, and it therefore depended on rivers, coasts, the fleet, harvests and local surrenders arranged in advance. Critics accept the framework but question his figures for the army's size and train.

  10. How does Alexander's decisive method differ from Hannibal's at Cannae?
    Answer

    Hannibal enveloped the enemy and let them advance into a trap, commanding from behind his line. Alexander broke into the enemy line at a gap, usually with the Companion wedge he led himself, and went for the enemy commander.

Carry forward

  1. Alexander's battles follow one pattern: the phalanx fixes, the hypaspists hold the hinge, the light troops screen, and the Companion wedge led by Alexander breaks through a gap that the oblique approach has created, aimed at the enemy commander.
  2. Almost every tactical reconstruction depends on Arrian, writing from Ptolemy and Aristobulus. Where the vulgate (Diodorus, Curtius) differs, as on the Granicus timing, Parmenion, Batis or the Tyrian crucifixions, the disagreement is often about reputation as much as fact.
  3. The victories came from three causes together: Alexander's own reading of ground and timing, the army and officers Philip left him, and the Persians' strategic and personal failures, Darius' above all. A balanced judgement of him has to give weight to all three.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Alexander as a commander, battle by battle. Cover, for each of Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela and the Hydaspes: the strategic situation, the ground, the two orders of battle, the plan, the course of the fight phase by phase, the decisive moment, the casualties as reported and as plausible, and the main scholarly disputes (the Granicus dawn-versus-evening problem, Parmenion's role at Gaugamela, the Hydaspes crossing). Then the sieges: Halicarnassus, Tyre in detail (the mole, the naval war, the siege towers, the massacre), Gaza, the Sogdian Rock and Aornos. Then the system behind the victories: the hammer-and-anvil combination of phalanx and Companion cavalry, the oblique approach, the hypaspists as hinge, the use of light troops, Alexander's personal leadership and its costs, intelligence and speed; Engels on logistics and why the army could move as it did; the Persian failures; the engineers (Diades), the Bematists, the medical service. Compare his method with Philip's, Epaminondas' and Hannibal's. End with the honest assessment: how much was Alexander, how much was Philip's army, how much was Persian weakness? Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 11 · Deep dive II: Alexander · 11.3 · 2,748 words

The Achaemenid side

The empire Darius inheritedBagoas, the succession and the problem of DariusMemnon and the western strategyThe Persian decisions at Issus and GaugamelaPersepolis: the palace and the fireThe end of Darius and the eastern resistancePersian voices and Persian memoryWhy the empire fell so fastSelf-testCarry forward

The empire Darius inherited

In 336 the Achaemenid king ruled from the Aegean to the Indus. Power ran through about twenty-five satrapies, each under a satrap who was usually a Persian noble, often a royal kinsman. Garrison commanders and treasurers reported separately to the court as a check on him. Herodotus' list of twenty tribute districts (3.89–97), totalling 14,560 Euboean talents of silver, is schematic, but the Persepolis Fortification and Treasury tablets show tribute and rations being accounted for with great care. The empire was not living on credit. By the ancient figures, Alexander took about 50,000 talents at Susa (Arrian 3.16.7) and 120,000 at Persepolis (Diodorus 17.71.1).

The Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, with 111 staging posts (Herodotus 5.52–54), was one artery of a larger network. The tablets record travellers drawing rations on sealed authorisations as far as Arachosia and India, and relay couriers carried royal orders day and night (Herodotus 8.98). The "King's Eye" was probably a real office of royal inspection that Greek imagination turned into a secret police. Herodotus has the boy Cyrus appoint one in a game (1.114), Aristophanes mocks one on stage (Acharnians 91–125), and Xenophon expands it into a web of the king's "eyes and ears" (Cyropaedia 8.2.10–12).

Herodotus' 10,000 Immortals (7.83) had their successor in Alexander's day in the thousand melophoroi, the "apple-bearers" with golden apples on their spear-butts, who stood beside the king (Heracleides of Cyme in Athenaeus 12.514b; Arrian 3.11.5). Around them came Bactrian and Saka horsemen, Median and Armenian cavalry, scythed chariots and levies of uneven quality. Persia's chronic weakness was heavy infantry, so it hired Greeks. Arrian puts about 30,000 Greek mercenaries in Darius' centre at Issus (2.8.6).
