Bagoas, the succession and the problem of Darius

The empire of 336 had just been restored, not run down. Artaxerxes III Ochus (r. 359/8–338) burned rebel Sidon in 345, retook Egypt in 343/2 after some sixty years of independence (Diodorus 16.40–51), and ordered the satraps of Asia Minor to disband their private mercenary armies. His generals in Egypt were the eunuch Bagoas and Mentor of Rhodes, Memnon's brother.

According to Diodorus (17.5.3–6), Bagoas, by then chiliarch, poisoned Artaxerxes III in 338, crowned his son Arses (Artaxerxes IV), poisoned him in 336, and raised Darius from a collateral branch of the royal house. When Bagoas tried to poison the new king, Darius made him drink the cup himself. Darius therefore came to the throne almost at the same moment Philip II was murdered, with a Macedonian advance force already in Asia.

Where sources disagree. One Babylonian tablet says only that Artaxerxes III "went to his fate", a formula that does not imply murder, so the poisoning of 338 is uncertain. Darius' background is contested as well. Plutarch (On the Fortune or Virtue of Alexander 326F) makes him an obscure royal courier (astandes), and Strabo (15.3.24) says he was not of the royal family; both have Bagoas promote him. Diodorus (17.6.1–2) and Justin (10.3), who calls him Codomannus, credit him with killing a Cadusian champion in single combat. Both versions may be propaganda, one hostile and one legitimising.

The Greek Darius is the one in Arrian's obituary (3.22.2–6): "most cowardly and incompetent" in war, a man who fled twice and was betrayed by his own men. Pierre Briant (Darius dans l'ombre d'Alexandre, 2003; English translation 2015) argues that the Alexander historians built this Darius as a foil, the coward who makes the hero's courage visible. Briant sets against it what Darius did. He raised two complete imperial armies in three years, funded a serious naval war, chose good ground at Gaugamela and kept most of his nobility loyal almost to the end. Ernst Badian ("Darius III", Harvard Studies in Classical Philology 100, 2000) is harder on Darius as a commander. The current view is that Darius cannot be known from these sources, not that he was contemptible.

Memnon and the western strategy

When the western satraps met at Zeleia in 334, Memnon of Rhodes advised against battle. The Macedonian infantry was superior, he argued, while Alexander was short of money and supplies, so the Persians should burn the crops and carry the war to Macedon by sea. Arsites refused, saying he would not allow a single house of his subjects to burn (Arrian 1.12.9–10; Diodorus 17.18.2–3). Greek writers saw Persian pride in this, but it was also a rational choice for a satrap whose standing rested on protecting his own land.

At the Granicus the Persians lined the bank with cavalry and kept the Greek mercenaries in reserve. The nobles fought around Alexander and several satraps died. The mercenaries were then surrounded and massacred, and about 2,000 survivors were sent to Macedonia in chains (Arrian 1.16.2–6). Memnon held Halicarnassus through 334 and then took his own plan to sea. Darius gave him supreme command and funds; Memnon had already sent his family to court as guarantees (Diodorus 17.23.5). In 333 he took Chios and most of Lesbos and besieged Mytilene, but died of illness there (Arrian 2.1.1–3). Diodorus (17.29.4) says his death ended Darius' hopes in the west. Pharnabazus and Autophradates carried on and gave Agis III of Sparta money and ships (Arrian 2.13.4–6), but Darius now chose to fight on land and in person.

The Persian decisions at Issus and Gaugamela

Issus, November 333

The Athenian exile Charidemus advised Darius to send a smaller army under a Greek general and was executed for speaking too freely, a scene that may be a Greek moral fable (Diodorus 17.30; Curtius 3.2.10–19). The deserter Amyntas told Darius to wait on the open plain at Sochoi (Arrian 2.6.3–6). Darius instead crossed the Amanus and came out behind Alexander, cutting his communications. Strategically this was bold. Tactically it was fatal, because the narrow coastal plain at the Pinarus cancelled out his numbers. When the Persian left collapsed, Darius fled.

Where sources disagree. In Arrian (2.11.4; 3.14.3), Darius flees at the first danger in both battles. Diodorus (17.34; 17.60) and Curtius (3.11; 4.15) describe hard fighting around the royal chariot, and at Gaugamela a charioteer struck down and mistaken for the king, which started the panic. Numbers are worthless too. Arrian's million infantry at Gaugamela (3.8.6) is absurd, and Polybius (12.17–22) had already taken apart Callisthenes' account of Issus.

The women in the tent

The camp at Issus yielded Darius' mother Sisygambis, his wife Stateira, two daughters and a small son (Arrian 2.11.9). Alexander left them their royal titles and attendants. In the anecdote Arrian reports without vouching for it, Sisygambis bowed to Hephaestion by mistake and Alexander said he "too is Alexander" (2.12.6–8). Plutarch insists that Alexander never saw Stateira (Alexander 21). She died in captivity, apparently in childbirth, around 332/1 (Plutarch, Alexander 30; Curtius 4.10.18–34), a timing the sources leave unexplored. Keeping the royal household was also a way of taking over part of the king's legitimacy. In 324 Alexander married Darius' daughter Stateira at Susa, and her sister Drypetis married Hephaestion (Arrian 7.4.4–5).

The offers and Parmenion's remark

After Issus, Darius wrote asking for his family and for friendship; Alexander told him to address him as lord of Asia (Arrian 2.14). During the siege of Tyre, Darius offered 10,000 talents, everything west of the Euphrates and a daughter in marriage. Parmenion said he would accept if he were Alexander. Alexander replied that so would he, if he were Parmenion (Arrian 2.25.1–3; Plutarch, Alexander 29.7–8).

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (17.39; 17.54) and Curtius (4.5; 4.11) give three embassies, the last before Gaugamela offering up to 30,000 talents. Plutarch (Alexander 29.7–9) sets the exchange at Tyre in 331, after Egypt; Diodorus (17.54) and Curtius (4.11) move it to the eve of Gaugamela. The escalating series may be a literary device, but the core is plausible: a rational Achaemenid ruler would give up the west to save the Iranian heartland.

Gaugamela and the Babylonian diary

In 331 Darius did what the critics of Issus would have advised. He chose an open plain beyond the Tigris, levelled it for about 200 scythed chariots and brought in the eastern cavalry. Mazaeus, on the Persian right, nearly broke Parmenion, and Persian and Indian horse reached the Macedonian baggage. But the chariots failed, the attempt to outflank Alexander's right opened a gap in the line, and Alexander drove through it toward the king. Darius left, and his army fell apart.

For once there is an independent witness. A Babylonian astronomical diary (Sachs and Hunger, Astronomical Diaries I, year −330) records the lunar eclipse of 20 September, also noted by Arrian (3.7.6) and Plutarch (Alexander 31), and the fear that followed. It dates the battle to 24 Ulūlu, which is 1 October, and says the king's troops deserted him and he fled to the land of the Guti. It calls Alexander "king of the world" and records his message to Babylon:

Into your houses I shall not enter.

The diary confirms the Greek date and the result but says nothing of cowardice. It suggests that the army deserting the king mattered as much as the king's own choice.

Mazaeus withdrew to Babylon, surrendered the city and was made its satrap, the first Persian given a great satrapy by Alexander (Arrian 3.16.4; Curtius 5.1.17–23). Abulites did the same at Susa. The terms were plain: those who came over kept their rank and office.

Persepolis: the palace and the fire

Darius I and Xerxes built Persepolis as a ceremonial centre. The Apadana reliefs show subject peoples bringing gifts in order and harmony. Alexander forced the Persian Gates, entered in early 330, let the lower city be plundered and removed the treasure. Months later he burned the palace.

Arrian (3.18.11–12) presents the fire as policy: revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens, carried out over Parmenion's objection that Alexander was destroying his own property. Arrian himself thought it unwise. The vulgate (Diodorus 17.72; Plutarch, Alexander 38; Curtius 5.7.2–7) tells of a drunken feast at which the Athenian courtesan Thaïs urged the burning, and torch-carrying revellers followed her up the terrace. Plutarch adds that Alexander quickly regretted it. The Thaïs story probably goes back to Cleitarchus (Athenaeus 13.576d–e).

Where sources disagree. Eugene Borza ("Fire from Heaven: Alexander at Persepolis", Classical Philology 67, 1972) and others read the fire as deliberate. The treasury had been emptied first, and the burning was heaviest in the Apadana, the Hall of a Hundred Columns and the buildings of Xerxes. On this view the fire told the Greeks that the war of revenge was over and told the Iranians that Achaemenid rule had ended. A drinking party could still have been the occasion for a decision already taken. The question is open.

The end of Darius and the eastern resistance

Darius fell back on Ecbatana and then, in summer 330, toward Bactria to raise a third army. Near the Caspian Gates, Bessus, satrap of Bactria and a royal kinsman, together with the chiliarch Nabarzanes and Barsaentes of Arachosia, arrested him. Curtius says he was bound in golden fetters (5.12.20) and that the Greek mercenary captain Patron offered him a bodyguard, which he refused out of trust in his Persians (5.11). When the Macedonian cavalry closed in, in July 330, the conspirators stabbed him and left him in a wagon (Arrian 3.21.10). Plutarch's deathbed message, passed to a Macedonian soldier (Alexander 43), is probably embellishment. Alexander sent the body to Persepolis for royal burial (Arrian 3.22.1); the unfinished tomb south of the terrace is sometimes assigned to Darius, but this is uncertain. By burying the king and pursuing his killer, Alexander made himself Darius' avenger and successor.

Bessus put on the upright tiara and took the name Artaxerxes (Arrian 3.25.3). Among the Aramaic documents from Bactria published by Naveh and Shaked (2012) is one dated to "year 1 of Artaxerxes", which the editors take to be Bessus; if they are right, local administration recognised him as king. In 329 his officers Spitamenes and Dataphernes gave him up. He was mutilated in the Persian manner and executed at Ecbatana (Arrian 4.7.3). Spitamenes then led the Sogdian and Bactrian revolt of 329–328, destroying a Macedonian column at the Polytimetus (Arrian 4.5–6), the hardest fighting of the whole war. The outcome was settled by marriages: Alexander married the Sogdian Roxane, and Spitamenes' daughter Apame married Seleucus (Arrian 7.4.6), so the Seleucid kings descended from the rebel.

Where sources disagree. Arrian (3.30.5) notes that Ptolemy claims to have fetched Bessus himself, while Aristobulus says Spitamenes and Dataphernes handed him over. In Arrian (4.17.7) the Massagetae send Spitamenes' head to Alexander, but Curtius (8.3.1–15) says his wife killed him.

Persian voices and Persian memory

The Babylonian Dynastic Prophecy (Grayson, Babylonian Historical-Literary Texts, 1975) describes past reigns in the form of predictions. One passage appears to show a king, usually identified as Darius III, defeated by the "Hanaeans" (Macedonians), who then re-equips his army and, with divine help, overthrows them.

Where sources disagree. Grayson (1975) and Matthew Neujahr (Journal of Near Eastern Studies 64, 2005) read the reversal as a genuine hope, written down by Babylonians who expected Darius to return. Others, notably R. J. van der Spek (Achaemenid History XIII, 2003), see a text reworked in the age of the Successors and aimed at early Seleucid politics. The tablet is broken at the crucial point, so the question is unresolved.

The Zoroastrian priestly books, written down in Middle Persian in the early Islamic centuries from Sasanian traditions, call him "the accursed Alexander the Roman" (gizistag Aleksandar hrōmāyīg), an epithet otherwise used for the Evil Spirit. In the opening chapter of the Ardā Wirāz Nāmag he kills the priests and burns the Avesta, which had been written in gold on ox hides and kept at Istakhr. The Dēnkard repeats the charge. These texts serve the Sasanian claim to have restored a broken faith, but they may preserve a memory of the Persepolis fire.

The other tradition took him in. Through the Alexander Romance, Alexander became Iskandar. In Ferdowsi's Shāhnāmeh (c. 1010) he is the son of King Darab by a daughter of Filqus (Philip), and so half-brother to Dara. When Dara is murdered by his ministers, Iskandar cradles the dying king, avenges him and marries his daughter Roshanak. In Nizami's Iskandarnāmeh (c. 1200) he becomes a philosopher and sage. Iranian memory made him either destroyer or legitimate heir, never simply a foreign conqueror.

Why the empire fell so fast

The Greek explanation was decadence. Plato (Laws 3.694a–698a) blames heirs raised by women and eunuchs; the last chapter of Xenophon's Cyropaedia (8.8) portrays a Persia gone soft; Isocrates (Panegyricus 150–151) calls Persians servile. Darius' flights fitted the stereotype neatly. The evidence does not. The empire had just retaken Egypt, held huge reserves, kept functioning archives and mobilised Iran twice in three years. Heleen Sancisi-Weerdenburg's question, "decadence in the empire or decadence in the sources?" (Achaemenid History I, 1987), gave rise to a generation of work reading the empire from its own documents.

Better explanations are structural and contingent: a Macedonian army without equal, the loss of Memnon, and an ideology centred on the king, so that his departure from a battlefield could dissolve an army. Above all, Alexander offered the satrapal elite continuity, with the same offices and tribute under a new king. Briant's phrase for him, "the last of the Achaemenids", captures this. Where Persians did refuse, in Persis, Bactria and Sogdiana, the conquest was slow and bloody.

The lesson is that this war is known almost entirely from the winning side. Arrian follows Ptolemy and Aristobulus and the vulgate follows Cleitarchus, all writing for readers who wanted to see a coward lose to a hero. The Persian side survives only in fragments: a diary, a broken prophecy, some Aramaic receipts and the memories of priests and poets centuries later. Wherever the Greek account can be checked, it gets the dates right and the characters wrong.

Self-test

  1. What three sources does the Greek picture of the "King's Eye" mainly rest on, and what was it probably in reality?
    Answer

    Herodotus 1.114 (Cyrus' game), Aristophanes, Acharnians 91–125 (the comic "King's Eye") and Xenophon, Cyropaedia 8.2.10–12 (the king's "eyes and ears"). It was probably a royal inspector reporting directly to the king, enlarged by Greeks into a network of spies.

  2. Which recent achievements of Artaxerxes III undermine the idea that the empire was decadent in 336?
    Answer

    He crushed the Phoenician revolt and burned Sidon (345), reconquered Egypt in 343/2 after some sixty years of independence, (Diodorus 16.40–51), and forced the satraps of Asia Minor to disband their private mercenary armies.

  3. According to Diodorus, how did Darius III come to the throne, and why is the first link in that chain uncertain?
    Answer

    Bagoas poisoned Artaxerxes III and then Arses, raised Darius, and was forced by Darius to drink his own poison (Diodorus 17.5.3–6). A Babylonian tablet says only that Artaxerxes III "went to his fate", which does not necessarily mean murder.

  4. What strategy did Memnon propose at Zeleia, and why did Arsites reject it?
    Answer

    Avoid battle, burn the crops and countryside to starve Alexander's army, and take the war to Macedon by sea. Arsites refused to allow even one house of his subjects to burn (Arrian 1.12.9–10), a choice that reflected both pride and a satrap's duty to protect his own territory.

  5. Why was Darius' march to Issus strategically clever but tactically ruinous?
    Answer

    By crossing the Amanus he came out behind Alexander and cut his communications. But he gave up the open plain at Sochoi that Amyntas had recommended and fought on a narrow coastal plain where his greater numbers and cavalry could not deploy.

  6. How do Arrian and the vulgate differ on Darius' conduct in battle?
    Answer

    Arrian (2.11.4; 3.14.3) has him flee at the first danger. Diodorus (17.34; 17.60) and Curtius describe fierce fighting around the royal chariot and, at Gaugamela, a fallen charioteer mistaken for the king, which set off the rout.

  7. What did Darius offer during the siege of Tyre, and what did Parmenion and Alexander say?
    Answer

    10,000 talents, all land west of the Euphrates and a daughter in marriage. Parmenion said he would accept if he were Alexander; Alexander said so would he, if he were Parmenion (Arrian 2.25.1–3; Plutarch, Alexander 29).

  8. What does the Babylonian astronomical diary add to our knowledge of Gaugamela?
    Answer

    It independently confirms the lunar eclipse of 20 September and dates the battle to 24 Ulūlu (1 October 331). It records that the king's troops deserted him and that he fled to the land of the Guti, calls Alexander "king of the world", and records his promise not to enter Babylonian houses.

  9. Give the two versions of the burning of Persepolis and the archaeological argument for one of them.
    Answer

    Arrian (3.18.11–12) presents it as deliberate revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens, against Parmenion's advice. The vulgate (Diodorus 17.72; Plutarch, Alexander 38; Curtius 5.7) has the drunken feast and Thaïs. The treasury was emptied first and the burning is concentrated in Xerxes' buildings, the Apadana and the Hundred Columns Hall, which supports a planned act.

  10. How does Iranian tradition treat Alexander in the Zoroastrian books and in the Shāhnāmeh?
    Answer

    The Zoroastrian books (Ardā Wirāz Nāmag, Dēnkard) call him "the accursed Alexander the Roman", who killed priests and burned the Avesta. In Ferdowsi's Shāhnāmeh he is Iskandar, son of Darab and half-brother of Dara, who mourns the murdered king, avenges him and marries his daughter Roshanak, making him a legitimate Iranian successor.

Carry forward

  1. Darius III and the "decadent" Persia of the Greek writers are literary constructs. The empire of 336 had just been restored, was rich and well run, and fought hard. Its fall needs structural explanations (Macedonian military quality, an ideology centred on the king's person, the elite's willingness to switch sides) rather than moral ones.
  2. Alexander conquered by taking over the Achaemenid system: he kept the satrapal offices, reappointed defecting nobles such as Mazaeus, held the royal women, buried and avenged Darius, and married into the dynasty. The Persepolis fire is the exception that needs explaining.
  3. When the only full narrative comes from the victor, the best checks are independent and partial sources (Babylonian diaries, prophecies, Aramaic documents, archaeology) and the defeated side's later memory. These usually confirm the Greek dates and outcomes while undermining the Greek explanations and characters.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Persian Empire of Darius III and its war against Alexander, told from the Persian side as far as the sources allow. Cover: the Achaemenid empire around 336 (satrapies, the royal roads, tribute, the King's Eye, the multi-ethnic army, the Immortals, the Greek mercenaries); Artaxerxes III's reconquests and the murders by Bagoas that brought Darius III to the throne; Darius' character as the Greek sources and the modern rehabilitation (Briant) present it; Memnon of Rhodes and the scorched-earth strategy rejected at Granicus, the naval counter-offensive in the Aegean and Memnon's death; the Persian decisions at Issus and Gaugamela; the royal women captured at Issus and their treatment; Darius' peace offers and Parmenion's remark; the flight, Bessus, the murder of Darius and his royal burial by Alexander; the satraps who resisted (Spitamenes, Bessus as Artaxerxes V) and those who defected (Mazaeus at Babylon); Persepolis: the palace, the burning, the Thais story and the deliberate-policy reading; the Persian evidence (the Babylonian astronomical diaries on Gaugamela, the Dynastic Prophecy) and Persian memory of Alexander (the Zoroastrian tradition of the accursed Alexander, the later Iskandar); why the empire fell so fast and whether it was as decadent as Greek sources claim. End with the historiographical lesson: a war known almost entirely from the victor's side. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 11 · Deep dive II: Alexander · 11.4 · 2,920 words

Alexander and the gods

Two lines of descent: Heracles and AchillesPiety in practice: sacrifice, seers and omensEgypt, Siwa and BabylonProskynesis at BactraDionysus as model324: divine honours and HephaestionDid he believe it?Ruler cult and the new idea of a kingSelf-testCarry forward

Two lines of descent: Heracles and Achilles

Alexander inherited two heroic genealogies and used them differently. On his father's side the Argead kings of Macedon claimed descent from Temenus of Argos, a great-great-grandson of Heracles. The claim had been tested in public: Herodotus (5.22) reports that Alexander I was admitted to the Olympic games after proving his Argive ancestry. Heracles was the dynasty's god, and Alexander's tetradrachms carried his head in the lion-scalp across the empire. He was the mortal who earned Olympus by labour, and that was the point.

On his mother's side Olympias was a Molossian princess of the Aeacid house, which traced itself through Neoptolemus to Achilles and beyond him to Aeacus, a son of Zeus. Plutarch opens his life with both lines (Alexander 2.1). The Achilles line was literary and personal: he kept an Iliad annotated by Aristotle in a casket taken from Darius (8.2, 26.1–2).

Heracles was the ancestor he invoked to claim things: Tyre, where he demanded to sacrifice to Melqart, the Tyrian Heracles (Arrian, Anabasis 2.15.7–16.7), and Aornos, which Heracles had reputedly failed to take (4.28.1–4). Achilles was the model he invoked to explain himself: the brief glorious life, the beloved companion, the grief.

Troy, 334

The crossing was staged as religious drama. Alexander sacrificed at the tomb of Protesilaus, the first Greek to die at Troy, so that his own landing would be luckier (Arrian 1.11.5), and Diodorus (17.17.2) has him hurl a spear into Asian soil, claiming it as spear-won land.

At Ilium he sacrificed to Athena, dedicated his own armour in her temple and took in exchange arms said to survive from the Trojan War (Arrian 1.11.7–8). One of these, the sacred shield, was carried before him in battle, and in India in 325 Peucestas held it over him as he lay wounded in the Mallian town (6.10.2). He also sacrificed to Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios, where Neoptolemus had killed the old king, to avert Priam's anger from Neoptolemus' descendants (1.11.8). This is the Molossian genealogy taken literally: he carried the blood-guilt of his ancestor and paid it off.

He then crowned the tomb of Achilles and called him fortunate to have had Homer as herald of his fame (Arrian 1.12.1).

Where sources disagree. Arrian reports, with a "some say", that Hephaestion crowned the tomb of Patroclus. Plutarch (Alexander 15.8) instead has Alexander anoint himself and run naked round the tomb-stele with his companions, Hephaestion unnamed. Aelian (Varia Historia 12.7) pairs the two men explicitly. The famous image of the two lovers racing round the tombs of Achilles and Patroclus is a modern composite of these accounts; how far the Patroclus parallel was a public statement in 334, rather than a reading back from Hephaestion's death in 324, is uncertain.

Piety in practice: sacrifice, seers and omens

Whatever he believed about himself, his religious conduct was conventional and constant. Macedonian kings were their people's chief priests, and Alexander sacrificed daily; the Royal Journals extracted by Arrian (7.25.2–6) and Plutarch (76) have him carried out on a litter to sacrifice as he lay dying. Their authenticity is disputed, but nothing contradicts the habit.

His chief seer was Aristander of Telmessus, from a Lycian city famous for diviners. Aristander read Philip's dream of sealing Olympias' womb with a lion seal (Plutarch 2.5), the bird that dropped a stone on Alexander at Gaza (Arrian 2.26.4–27.2), the birds eating the barley meal that marked out Alexandria (3.2.1–2), and the eclipse before Gaugamela (3.7.6). On the Jaxartes in 329 he declared the omens bad and held to it, and Alexander was wounded as predicted (4.4.3–9).

Divination was a tool of command: at Tyre, Plutarch (25.1–2) says, Alexander altered the calendar so that Aristander's prophecy came true "this month". But the dependence was real and grew. After Hephaestion's death Plutarch (75.1–2) describes a palace full of sacrificers and purifiers. The Chaldaean warning not to enter Babylon (Arrian 7.16.5–17.6) and the stranger found on the throne (7.24.1–3), which some read as a garbled Babylonian substitute-king ritual (attractive but uncertain), belong here.

Egypt, Siwa and Babylon

The journey

In the winter of 332/1, after the foundation of Alexandria, Alexander went west along the coast to Paraetonium and then south across some 250 kilometres of desert to the oasis of Siwa. Arrian (3.3.1–2) gives the motive as a pothos, a longing, and adds two reasons: the oracle was reputed infallible, and Perseus and Heracles had consulted it, and Alexander "traced part of his birth to Ammon" as the myths traced theirs to Zeus. Ammon, the Egyptian Amun, had long been equated with Zeus through Cyrene; Pindar wrote him a hymn and Lysander consulted him.

Where sources disagree. On the desert crossing, water ran out and the guides lost the way. Rain fell. Then, according to Ptolemy, two talking snakes led the army; according to Aristobulus, two ravens (Arrian 3.3.4–6). Callisthenes also had birds. On the return, Aristobulus says Alexander went back the same way, Ptolemy that he struck straight across to Memphis (3.4.5). Ptolemy, whose dynasty later made the serpent a sign of Alexander's divinity, had his own reasons for snakes.

What the oracle said

The earliest account was Callisthenes', preserved in Strabo (17.1.43). Only Alexander was allowed into the temple in his own dress; the oracle usually answered by nods and tokens, not words as at Delphi; but the prophet told the king in so many words that he was the son of Zeus. Callisthenes added confirmations from Didyma and the Erythraean prophetess Athenais. Strabo calls this flattery, but it was the official version, written for the court within a year or two.

Arrian is strikingly reticent: Alexander asked his question and "received the answer his heart desired, as he said" (3.4.5). We are never told the question. Plutarch (27) offers the fuller tradition: the prophet greeted him as son of Zeus; Alexander asked whether any of his father's murderers had escaped and was told to mind his words, for his father was no mortal; he asked whether he would rule all mankind and was told yes. Plutarch also preserves the rationalising story that the prophet meant to say o paidion, "my child", and mispronounced it o pai Dios, "son of Zeus". Diodorus (17.51) and Curtius are similar. Alexander himself wrote to Olympias that he had received secret answers he would tell to her alone (Plutarch 27.8). He died without telling her.

Where sources disagree. The questions about Philip's murderers and world rule appear only in the later vulgate and look like elaboration of Callisthenes' core. What is secure is the greeting, which any Egyptian priest would give a pharaoh. Whether Alexander heard it in an Egyptian, a Greek or a deliberately ambiguous sense cannot be settled.

Olympias' snake

Siwa connected with stories already circulating. Plutarch (2–3) reports Olympias' dream of a thunderbolt striking her womb, Philip seeing a serpent beside her, and Delphi telling Philip to honour Ammon above all gods. Eratosthenes said Olympias told Alexander the secret of his birth; others had her protest, "Will Alexander never stop slandering me to Hera?" (3.3–4). The claim was argued over while people who knew the family were alive.

Pharaoh and king of Babylon

In Egypt divine sonship was a constitutional fact: every pharaoh was son of Ra and of Amun. Alexander's hieroglyphic titulary gave him the throne name Setepenre Meryamun, "chosen of Ra, beloved of Amun", and the barque shrine built in his name in Luxor temple shows him as pharaoh before Amun.

Where sources disagree. A formal coronation at Memphis appears only in the Alexander Romance (Pseudo-Callisthenes 1.34). Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus and Curtius do not mention one, and several modern scholars doubt it took place. The titulary shows that the priesthood treated him as pharaoh; it does not prove a ceremony.

At Babylon in 331 he sacrificed to Bel-Marduk on the instructions of the Chaldaeans and ordered the rebuilding of Esagila, which he believed Xerxes had destroyed (Arrian 3.16.4–5, 7.17.1–3). Babylonian documents, including the astronomical diaries, style him "king of the world", the old Mesopotamian royal title. Babylonian kingship was not divine, but the king held office from Marduk and stood at the centre of temple ritual. In both places Alexander found subjects ready to grant a sacred status that Macedonians and Greeks would not.

Proskynesis at Bactra

In 327, at Bactra, Alexander tried to extend Persian court ceremonial to his Macedonians and Greeks. Arrian (4.10.5–12.5) gives a set debate in which Anaxarchus argues that Alexander will be honoured as a god after death, so better now, and Callisthenes replies that honours to men and gods must be kept distinct; Curtius (8.5.5–8.6.1) has a similar one. These speeches are largely literary. The better evidence is the eyewitness chamberlain Chares of Mytilene, used by Plutarch (54.3–6) and Arrian (4.12.3–5). At a drinking party a cup was passed round; each guest drank, performed proskynesis, and received a kiss from the king. Callisthenes drank but skipped the bow, and was refused the kiss. "I go away the poorer by a kiss," he said. The experiment was dropped for Macedonians.

What the gesture meant

To a Persian, proskynesis was social. Herodotus (1.134) describes the scale: equals kissed on the lips, near-equals on the cheek, inferiors prostrated themselves. The Great King received it as the summit of a social hierarchy, not as a god; Achaemenid kings did not claim divinity. To a Greek the same act was what one did before a god. When the Spartan envoys Sperthias and Bulis refused to prostrate themselves before Xerxes, they said it was not their custom to worship a man (Herodotus 7.136). Isocrates (Panegyricus 151) mocks Persians for doing obeisance to a mortal and calling him a divinity. Callisthenes could therefore refuse in the name of Greek piety, and Alexander could deny that he was asking for worship, and both could be sincere.

Where sources disagree. Balsdon (1950) argued the attempt was about unifying court protocol and implied no claim to divinity. Bosworth and others reply that Alexander knew how Greeks would read the gesture. Callisthenes was arrested after the Pages' Conspiracy later in 327 and either hanged after torture (Ptolemy) or died in chains (Aristobulus) (Arrian 4.14.3). The same man had earlier reported the Siwa greeting and Alexander's prayer at Gaugamela to the gods "if he were really sprung from Zeus" (Plutarch 33.1). The court historian had promoted the sonship; he drew the line at its consequences.

Dionysus as model

From Bactria onward Dionysus joins Heracles, and the connection began with guilt. Thebes, Dionysus' birthplace, was razed in 335, and Plutarch (13.4) says Alexander later blamed the god's anger for the murder of Cleitus, killed in 328 on a day sacred to Dionysus when Alexander had sacrificed to the Dioscuri instead (Arrian 4.8.1–2, 4.9.5).

In 326, at Nysa, envoys led by Acuphis claimed their city had been founded by Dionysus. Ivy grew on the nearby mountain Meros, "thigh", recalling the god's birth from Zeus' thigh. Alexander spared the city and his officers held a Bacchic revel in ivy wreaths (Arrian 5.1.1–2.7). Arrian cites Eratosthenes' view (5.3.1–4) that the Macedonians invented such discoveries, like Heracles' failure at Aornos, to flatter Alexander. By 323 Arrian (7.20.1) reports him thinking himself worthy to be a third god of the Arabs beside Ouranos and Dionysus.

Where sources disagree. On the return through Carmania in 325, Plutarch (67) and Curtius (9.10.24–29) describe a seven-day drunken procession in imitation of Dionysus' triumph. Arrian (6.28.1–2) disbelieves it, since neither Ptolemy nor Aristobulus mentions it. Worse, Dionysus' conquest of India is not clearly attested before Alexander: Euripides' Bacchae (13–20) brings the god from Bactria and Persia. Probably, though not certainly, Alexander imitated a myth his own campaign helped create.

Bosworth ("Alexander, Euripides and Dionysos", 1996) made the Dionysus model central to the drive for divinity: a son of Zeus who wins recognition by conquering the East and punishing deniers. Others see a court theme pushed by flatterers.

324: divine honours and Hephaestion

In the summer of 324 Nicanor of Stagira read out at Olympia a royal letter ordering the Greek cities to take back their exiles (Diodorus 18.8.2–5; 17.109.1). This broke the League of Corinth's terms and threatened Athens' hold on Samos. In the same months the Greek cities debated granting Alexander divine honours, and in 323 sacred envoys came to him at Babylon wearing crowns, "as though to honour a god" (Arrian 7.23.2).

The responses survive as anecdote. At Sparta, Damis proposed: "Since Alexander wishes to be a god, let him be a god" (Plutarch, Moralia 219e; Aelian, Varia Historia 2.19). At Athens, Demades proposed the honours and was later fined for it (Athenaeus 6.251b; Aelian, Varia Historia 5.12; the sum varies). Lycurgus asked what kind of god one had to purify oneself after visiting (Plutarch, Moralia 842d). Demosthenes, who first opposed the honours, is quoted by his prosecutors as conceding that Alexander could be son of Zeus, and of Poseidon too if he liked (Hyperides, Against Demosthenes; Dinarchus, Against Demosthenes 1.94). Greeks found the honours absurd, conceded them anyway, and reversed them once he was dead.

Where sources disagree. No ancient source quotes a request from Alexander. Tarn (1948) argued he demanded deification as a constitutional device, since a god could issue orders like the Exiles' Decree that a League hegemon could not. Balsdon (1950) found no evidence of a request. Habicht argued the cities offered cult spontaneously, as to earlier benefactors. Something prompted the debates of 324; whether a royal letter, an informal signal or civic initiative is uncertain.

Hephaestion's heroisation

Hephaestion died at Ecbatana in autumn 324. Alexander cut his hair like Achilles over Patroclus (Arrian 7.14.4), planned a pyre at Babylon said to cost ten or twelve thousand talents (Diodorus 17.115; Plutarch 72), and sent to Siwa to ask what honours were due. Arrian (7.14.7, 7.23.6) says Ammon permitted sacrifice to Hephaestion as a hero, and quotes a letter to Cleomenes in Egypt ordering hero-shrines at Alexandria and on Pharos. A votive relief from Pella dedicated to Hephaestion as hero suggests the cult was actually practised.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (17.115.6) says Ammon allowed sacrifice to Hephaestion as a god. Arrian's "hero" is more cautious and fits the Pella evidence. Either way, Alexander treated Ammon as the authority who could raise a mortal above the human, a power he could hardly deny himself.

Did he believe it?

Ancient writers already argued the point. Plutarch (28) says he used the belief to dominate barbarians but was restrained with Greeks; wounded, he quoted Homer: this is blood, not the ichor of the gods (Iliad 5.340). Arrian's verdict (7.29.3) is cautious: referring his birth to a god was perhaps a device to impress his subjects, and not a great fault. Yet Arrian also says that a man so unlike others was born "not without the divine" (7.30.2).

The modern positions:

  • Tarn (Alexander the Great, 1948): a rationalist who used deification as a political instrument without literal belief.
  • Balsdon ("The 'Divinity' of Alexander", Historia 1950): deflationary; the evidence for official claims is thin and much is later invention.
  • Badian (from "Alexander the Great and the Loneliness of Power", 1962): the belief grew as power isolated him; a symptom of autocracy, not a calculation.
  • Fredricksmeyer ("Alexander, Zeus Ammon, and the Conquest of Asia", 1991): sincere conviction, rooted in Macedonian religion and Philip's precedent, that the sonship was real and divinity could be won by achievement.
  • Bosworth (Conquest and Empire, 1988): he came to believe himself son of Zeus and sought recognition as a god in his lifetime.

The choice between belief and policy is probably false. For a Greek, divine sonship did not exclude a mortal father, and divine honours could be earned by deeds, as Heracles earned them. A king could believe this and also see its political value. What the evidence shows is growth: Siwa in 331, Bactra in 327, the cult debates of 324.

Ruler cult and the new idea of a king

Alexander did not invent cult for the living. Lysander received altars, sacrifices and paeans at Samos (Plutarch, Lysander 18, citing Duris), and Philip had his statue carried as a thirteenth beside the twelve gods at Aegae on the day of his murder (Diodorus 16.92.5) and built the Philippeion at Olympia (Pausanias 5.20.9–10). Fredricksmeyer stresses these precedents. But Alexander made the practice general and permanent. Ptolemy hijacked his corpse and founded a state cult of Alexander at Alexandria; Lysimachus' coins showed him with Ammon's ram's horns. Within a generation the Athenians sang to Demetrius Poliorcetes, who was present and visible, that:

the other gods are far away, or have no ears

(Athenaeus 6.253d–f, from Duris). Seleucid and Ptolemaic dynastic cult, and in time the Roman imperial cult, descend from this.

Three things changed in the Greek idea of a king. First, legitimacy moved from ancestry to achievement. Homeric kings were "Zeus-nurtured" and the Argeads had their Temenid pedigree, but the Hellenistic king was Soter or Euergetes, saviour or benefactor, his divinity proved by victory and benefaction. Second, cult became a language between a city and a power it could not control: "godlike honours" let a free city acknowledge a master without formally surrendering autonomy, exactly as the Greeks handled Alexander in 324. Third, Greek kingship absorbed the sacred kingships of Egypt and Mesopotamia; pharaoh, king of the world and son of Zeus became one office. Alexander's empire broke up within a generation; his religious model of kingship lasted far longer.

Self-test

  1. Why did Alexander sacrifice to Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios at Troy, and which genealogy does this act take literally?
    Answer

    To avert Priam's anger from the descendants of Neoptolemus, who had killed Priam at that altar. It treats his maternal Molossian (Aeacid) descent from Achilles through Neoptolemus as real, including the inherited blood-guilt (Arrian 1.11.8).

  2. What happened to the sacred shield Alexander took from the temple of Athena at Ilium?
    Answer

    It was carried before him in battle, and in 325, in the Mallian town in India, Peucestas held it over him as he lay badly wounded (Arrian 6.10.2).

  3. Name three omens interpreted by Aristander of Telmessus.
    Answer

    Any three of: Philip's dream of the lion seal on Olympias' womb; the sweating statue of Orpheus; the bird dropping a stone at Gaza; the birds eating the barley meal at Alexandria; the lunar eclipse before Gaugamela; the eagle at Gaugamela; the unfavourable sacrifices at the Jaxartes.

  4. On the desert route to Siwa, what guided the army according to Ptolemy, and according to Aristobulus?
    Answer

    Ptolemy said two talking snakes; Aristobulus said two ravens (Arrian 3.3.4–6). Callisthenes also had birds.

  5. What does Callisthenes' account (in Strabo 17.1.43) say about how the Siwa oracle normally answered, and what exception did it make for Alexander?
    Answer

    It normally answered by nods and tokens rather than words, as at Delphi, but the prophet explicitly told Alexander in words that he was the son of Zeus.

  6. What is the o paidion story in Plutarch, and why does the Egyptian context make the greeting less surprising?
    Answer

    Plutarch reports that the prophet meant to say "my child" (o paidion) in Greek and mispronounced it as "son of Zeus" (o pai Dios). In Egypt any pharaoh was by definition son of Amun-Ra, so a priest greeting the ruler of Egypt as son of the god was following standard usage.

  7. Why could Callisthenes refuse proskynesis on grounds of piety while Alexander denied asking for worship?
    Answer

    For Persians, proskynesis was a social gesture of deference to a superior, and the Great King was not a god (Herodotus 1.134). For Greeks, prostration was an act of worship due only to gods (Herodotus 7.136; Isocrates, Panegyricus 151). The same act meant different things to the two peoples.

  8. Why does Arrian doubt the Carmanian revel, and what did Eratosthenes say about the Dionysus discoveries at Nysa?
    Answer

    Arrian notes that neither Ptolemy nor Aristobulus mentions the revel, so he does not believe it (6.28.1–2). Eratosthenes held that the Macedonians invented the traces of Dionysus, like Prometheus' cave and Heracles at Aornos, to flatter Alexander (Arrian 5.3.1–4).

  9. Give the Spartan and Demosthenic responses to the question of divine honours in 324.
    Answer

    Damis at Sparta: since Alexander wishes to be a god, let him be a god. Demosthenes, as his prosecutors quote him: let him be son of Zeus, and of Poseidon too if he likes. Both concede the honours while mocking them.

  10. How do Arrian and Diodorus differ on Ammon's reply about Hephaestion, and which version is better supported?
    Answer

    Arrian (7.14.7, 7.23.6) says Ammon allowed sacrifice to him as a hero; Diodorus (17.115.6) says as a god. Arrian's version is better supported by the letter to Cleomenes ordering hero-shrines and by the votive relief from Pella to Hephaestion as hero.

Carry forward

  1. Alexander's divinity was built in stages from inherited material: Heracleid and Aeacid descent, the Siwa greeting of 331, which was also standard pharaonic address, the proskynesis experiment of 327, and the cult debates of 324. Treat any single episode as a point on a curve, not as the whole claim.
  2. The same ritual meant different things to different peoples. Proskynesis, divine sonship and sacred kingship were ordinary in Persia, Egypt and Babylon and offensive or comic to Greeks, and much of the conflict came from that gap.
  3. Ruler cult was Alexander's most durable political invention. It moved Greek kingship from pedigree to achievement and benefaction, and gave cities a way to acknowledge masters they could not resist. Hellenistic and Roman monarchy grew directly from it.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Alexander's relationship with the divine. Cover: the Argead descent from Heracles and the maternal (Molossian) descent from Achilles through Neoptolemus, and how he used both; the visit to Troy in 334 (the sacrifice to Priam, the shield of Achilles, the race round the tomb with Hephaestion); his piety in practice (daily sacrifice, the seers Aristander, the attention to omens); Siwa in detail: the route, the oracle of Ammon, what was said and not said, the son-of-Zeus claim and Olympias' snake stories, Callisthenes' account and Plutarch's; the Egyptian pharaonic titulary and the Babylonian kingship; the proskynesis affair at Bactra and Callisthenes' refusal, and what proskynesis meant to Persians versus Greeks; Dionysus as model (Nysa, the Carmanian revel, the Indian campaign as imitation of Dionysus' conquest); the Exiles' Decree and the request for divine honours in 324, the Greek responses (Demades, Damis, Demosthenes' quip); Hephaestion's heroisation; whether Alexander believed it, the ancient debate (Arrian 7.29) and the modern (Tarn, Balsdon, Badian, Fredricksmeyer, Bosworth); ruler cult as his most durable political invention. End with what the religious dimension changed in the Greek idea of a king. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 11 · Deep dive II: Alexander · 11.5 · 2,752 words

The court: Companions, conspiracies and the orientalising policy

Two generations at one courtBreaking the old guard, 330–327The orientalising policyOpis, 324: mutiny and the prayer for homonoiaAfter India: purge, Harpalus, Greeks, HephaestionWomen at courtIntegration or autocracy, and what the Successors keptSelf-testCarry forward

Two generations at one court

Alexander's court was Macedonian in structure. The hetairoi (Companions) dined, hunted and drank with the king and expected to speak freely at his table. The seven somatophylakes (Bodyguards) held a rank more than a duty, and the royal pages were noble sons serving their apprenticeship at his side. The politics of the expedition is the story of Alexander replacing his father's generation with his own, and then trying to fit Persians into a structure built for Macedonians.

ManGenerationPosition and fate
ParmenionPhilip'sSecond-in-command, commanded the left in the set battles; killed 330
AntipaterPhilip'sRegent in Macedon; told to hand over to Craterus in 324
AntigonusPhilip'sSatrap of Greater Phrygia from 333; held Anatolia, far from court
Cleitus the BlackPhilip'sRoyal cavalry squadron; saved Alexander at the Granicus; killed 328
CoenusPhilip'sPhalanx commander, Parmenion's son-in-law; spokesman at the Hyphasis; died 326
CraterusBridgeSenior infantry general and voice of tradition; took the veterans home 324
HephaestionAlexander'sBoyhood friend; cavalry commander, then chiliarch; died 324
Ptolemy, NearchusAlexander'sExiled by Philip in 337; Bodyguard (from 330) and admiral respectively
Perdiccas, Leonnatus, LysimachusAlexander'sBodyguards; Perdiccas received the ring in 323
SeleucusAlexander'sCommander of the royal hypaspists; kept his Iranian wife
PeucestasAlexander'sShielded the king at the Mallian town; eighth Bodyguard; satrap of Persis

Age is not the whole line. Craterus became the traditionalists' champion, and Plutarch (Alexander 47) gives Alexander's own verdict: Hephaestion loved Alexander, Craterus loved the king. The young men owed their careers to Alexander personally. Several had been exiled by Philip for siding with the prince in the Pixodarus affair (Plutarch, Alexander 10; Arrian, Anabasis 3.6.5). Parmenion's eminence came from Philip and from a network of kin: his son Philotas led the Companion cavalry, another son, Nicanor, led the hypaspists, and Coenus was his son-in-law.

The rear: Antipater and Olympias

Antipater governed Macedon and crushed Agis III at Megalopolis (331 or 330; uncertain). Olympias refused to accept his authority, and both bombarded Alexander with accusations (Arrian 7.12.5–7). His reply to one long complaint from Antipater was that a single tear of his mother outweighed ten thousand letters (Plutarch, Alexander 39). By the mid-320s Olympias had withdrawn to Epirus (Plutarch, Alexander 68). In 324 Alexander summoned Antipater to Babylon. He sent his son Cassander instead, whom Alexander treated with contempt (Plutarch, Alexander 74). Another son, Iollas, was royal cupbearer.

Where sources disagree. The story that Antipater poisoned Alexander through Iollas appears in Arrian 7.27 and Plutarch, Alexander 77, both of whom doubt it. Plutarch says Olympias promoted it. Most scholars see Successor-war propaganda, though the summons of 324 was a real threat to Antipater.

Breaking the old guard, 330–327

Phrada: Philotas and Parmenion

After Darius' death Parmenion was left at Ecbatana with the treasury, detached from the main army. In autumn 330 at Phrada in Drangiana, a plot came to light. Curtius (6.7–7.2) is fullest; Arrian (3.26), Diodorus (17.79–80) and Plutarch (Alexander 48–49) are briefer. Dimnus, a minor officer, revealed a plan to kill the king to his lover Nicomachus. Nicomachus told his brother Cebalinus, who told Philotas. Philotas saw the king twice and said nothing, and Cebalinus eventually got word to Alexander through a page. Dimnus died resisting arrest. Philotas was charged with failing to report the plot, not with joining it.

The ground had been prepared. Since Egypt Craterus had been collecting reports from Philotas' captive mistress Antigone of his boasts that the victories were his and his father's. Curtius describes a night council where Craterus, Hephaestion and Coenus urged action. Philotas was tried before the army and condemned. Those three tortured him to extract a confession that implicated Parmenion, and he was then executed. Alexander Lyncestis, in custody since 333, was killed in the same sweep. Polydamas rode by racing camel to the generals at Ecbatana, Cleander, Sitalces and Menidas, and they stabbed Parmenion while he read his letters (Arrian 3.26.3–4). Arrian is candid that Alexander either thought him guilty or judged it unsafe to leave alive a father whose son he had executed.

Where sources disagree. Arrian, following Ptolemy and Aristobulus, says the proofs were clear. Ptolemy, made a Bodyguard in the aftermath (Arrian 3.27.5), was not neutral. Badian ("The Death of Parmenio", 1960) argued for a frame-up to break Parmenion's faction. Heckel accepts that Philotas' silence was real but its exploitation political. Whether trial before the army was ancestral custom (Curtius 6.8.25) is also disputed.

The consequences were structural. The Companion cavalry was split between Hephaestion and Cleitus (Arrian 3.27.4), soldiers' letters were opened, and grumblers were put in a separate disciplinary unit (Diodorus 17.80.4). This set the pattern: dissent was answered by dividing commands so that no subordinate could hold a following of his own. The last of Philip's men at court were then removed one at a time. Coenus, who had turned on his father-in-law in 330, voiced the army's refusal to go beyond the Hyphasis in 326 (Arrian 5.27) and died of illness a few weeks later (Arrian 6.2.1). Curtius (9.3.20) has Alexander remark that he had made a long speech for a few days' life. Foul play is suspected but unproven. Antigonus survived because he was never at court: from Celaenae he held Anatolia against the Persian counter-offensive after Issus and stayed out of the expedition's politics.

Maracanda: Cleitus and the symposium

The Macedonian symposium involved heavy, often unmixed, drinking and the performance of status. According to Hegesander (in Athenaeus 1.18a), a man could not recline until he had speared a boar without nets. The symposium was also where Companions exercised parrhesia, frank speech to the king. A drinking contest at Calanus' funeral in 324 killed forty-one men (Chares, in Plutarch, Alexander 70).

In autumn 328 Cleitus had just been named satrap of Bactria, which was both a promotion and a removal from court. At a feast in Maracanda flatterers set Alexander above the Dioscuri and Heracles and disparaged Philip (Arrian 4.8.2–3), and verses mocked officers beaten by the Sogdians (Plutarch, Alexander 50–51). Cleitus defended Philip, reminded Alexander that his hand had saved him at the Granicus, and quoted Euripides' Andromache:

Alas, how evil is the custom now in Greece.

The point of the lines is that soldiers do the work and the general takes the glory. Alexander shouted for the guard in Macedonian and ran Cleitus through with a spear, then lay three days without food. Anaxarchus consoled him with the doctrine that whatever a king does is just, since Justice sits beside Zeus (Arrian 4.9.7; Plutarch, Alexander 52).

Where sources disagree. Aristobulus (Arrian 4.8.9) blames Cleitus, who was hustled out by Ptolemy and came back to provoke the king. Curtius (8.1.19–52) and Plutarch make Alexander more culpable. Modern readers debate whether this was drunken temper or a real quarrel over Philip's legacy and Persian ways. It was probably both.

Bactra: proskynesis, the pages, Callisthenes

In 327 Alexander tried to extend proskynesis, the Persian gesture of obeisance, to Macedonians and Greeks. Chares (Plutarch, Alexander 54) describes the method: each guest drank, made the gesture and received the king's kiss. Callisthenes, Aristotle's relative and the official historian, omitted the obeisance and said he would leave the poorer by a kiss. Arrian's formal debate between Anaxarchus and Callisthenes (4.10.5–12.5) is a literary set piece.

Where sources disagree. Arrian (4.12.2) has Leonnatus mock a prostrating Persian; Curtius (8.5.22–24) names Polyperchon. Some scholars see a claim to divinity. Others, Briant among them, see an attempt at one court protocol, so that Persians did not perform alone a gesture their peers refused.

Soon afterwards the page Hermolaus was flogged for striking a boar before the king. With Sostratus and others he planned murder on a night they held the watch. Alexander drank until dawn and the plot leaked (Arrian 4.13–14; Curtius 8.6–8). Curtius gives Hermolaus a speech of grievances: Philotas, Parmenion, Cleitus, Persian dress, proskynesis. The speech is composed, but probably accurate in substance. Callisthenes, the pages' tutor, fell with them, though no source says they named him.

Where sources disagree. Ptolemy says Callisthenes was tortured and hanged; Aristobulus says he died in chains of illness (Arrian 4.14.3). Chares says he was held for trial before Aristotle and died in India, obese and lice-ridden (Plutarch, Alexander 55). Theophrastus' Callisthenes (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 3.21) began a lasting Peripatetic portrait of Alexander as corrupted by fortune.

The orientalising policy

From 330 Alexander wore the diadem, the white-striped tunic and the Persian girdle, but not the trousers, sleeved kandys or upright tiara (Plutarch, Alexander 45; Diodorus 17.77.4–7). The choice kept the symbols of Achaemenid kingship and avoided what Greeks found most effeminate. Curtius (6.6.6) says he sealed Asian letters with Darius' ring and European ones with his own. Asian subjects were received in an audience tent guarded by Macedonian hypaspists and Persian "apple-bearers" (Phylarchus, in Athenaeus 12.539). Chares bore the Achaemenid title eisangeleus, controller of access. In ceremony the monarchy was dual: a Macedonian king to Macedonians, a Great King to Asians.

Persians entered government early. Mazaeus became satrap of Babylon in 331, followed by Artabazus in Bactria and Atropates in Media, and Darius' brother Oxyathres was enrolled among the Companions. Native satraps, however, usually sat beside Macedonian garrison and finance officers. In 327 Alexander ordered 30,000 Iranian youths trained in Macedonian arms. They reached Susa in 324 as the Epigonoi, and Macedonians called them an antitagma, a counter-army (Arrian 7.6.1; Diodorus 17.108.1–3). Iranian cavalry were brigaded into the Companion hipparchies and nobles entered the royal squadron itself (Arrian 7.6.3–5).

At Susa in spring 324 Alexander married Stateira, Darius' daughter (Arrian 7.4.4 calls her Barsine), and Parysatis, daughter of Artaxerxes III, uniting himself with both Achaemenid lines. Hephaestion took Drypetis, so that their children would be cousins. Craterus married Amastris, Ptolemy and Eumenes married daughters of Artabazus, Nearchus a daughter of Barsine, and Seleucus Apame, daughter of Spitamenes. Arrian counts about eighty Companion brides. Some 10,000 soldiers with Asian partners received gifts, and the army's debts were paid.

Where sources disagree. The debt payment is 20,000 talents in Arrian (7.5.3), about 10,000 in Diodorus (17.109.2) and 9,870 in Plutarch (Alexander 70). Arrian notes that some Companions disliked the marriages (7.6.2). Only Seleucus is known to have kept his wife after 323.

Opis, 324: mutiny and the prayer for homonoia

At Opis Alexander announced the discharge of the old and unfit. The army read it as replacement by Persians and shouted that he should campaign with his father Ammon (Arrian 7.8.3). He had thirteen ringleaders executed, spoke (Arrian 7.9–10, largely Arrian's own composition) and withdrew. On the third day he gave Persians commands and announced Persian Companions, Persian foot-companions and Persian Silver Shields (Arrian 7.11.1–4). The Macedonians broke. Their spokesman Callines complained that only Persians were called the king's kinsmen and allowed to kiss him. Alexander declared them all his kinsmen.

A banquet for 9,000 followed, with Macedonians seated nearest the king, then Persians, then others (Arrian 7.11.8–9). Greek seers and Magi officiated, and Alexander prayed for homonoia and partnership in rule between Macedonians and Persians. About 10,000 veterans then left under Craterus. Their Asian-born children stayed, to be raised as Macedonians.

Where sources disagree. Tarn (1933; Alexander the Great, 1948) read the prayer as the birth of the brotherhood of mankind. He drew on Plutarch's rhetorical On the Fortune of Alexander (329), where peoples are mixed as in a loving-cup. Badian ("Alexander the Great and the Unity of Mankind", Historia 1958) showed that it concerns two peoples, not mankind. It was a reconciliation after mutiny, with a hierarchical seating plan, offering shared rule to conqueror and conquered aristocracy. Badian's reading has prevailed.

After India: purge, Harpalus, Greeks, Hephaestion

Emerging from Gedrosia, Alexander executed Cleander, Sitalces and Heracon (Parmenion's killers) for temple-robbery and abuses (Arrian 6.27.3–5; Curtius 10.1.1–8). Astaspes, the pretender Baryaxes, Orxines of Persis and Abulites of Susiana with his son followed (Arrian 6.29–30; 7.4.1; Plutarch, Alexander 68). Satraps were ordered to disband their mercenaries (Diodorus 17.106.3). Thousands of them gathered at Taenarum and later fought in the Lamian War.

Where sources disagree. Badian ("Harpalus", JHS 1961) saw a "reign of terror" by a shaken, suspicious king. Curtius (10.1.22–38) supports it for Orxines, framed, he says, by the eunuch Bagoas. Arrian presents genuine misrule by men who expected the king to die in India. Higgins (1980) and Heckel stress the modest numbers and plausible charges. Bosworth takes a middle line of real abuses punished with exemplary severity. The question is uncertain.

Harpalus, an Elimiote noble unfit for war, was treasurer. He had deserted once before Issus and been forgiven (Arrian 3.6.4–7). At Babylon he lived lavishly, raising monuments to his dead mistress Pythionice (Theopompus, in Athenaeus 13.595a–596b). In 324 he fled with about 5,000 talents and 6,000 mercenaries (Diodorus 17.108.6). Athens admitted him with a smaller sum, and 700 talents were deposited on the Acropolis, of which half vanished. The Areopagus inquiry convicted Demosthenes, who was fined fifty talents and went into exile (Plutarch, Demosthenes 25–26; Hyperides and Dinarchus, Against Demosthenes). Whether he took bribes or a war chest is uncertain. Harpalus was murdered on Crete by Thibron.

The Greek allies were auxiliaries, not partners. Their League contingents were paid off at Ecbatana in 330 (Arrian 3.19.5), and many re-enlisted as mercenaries. Greeks filled technical posts. Eumenes of Cardia ran the chancery and feuded with Hephaestion (Arrian 7.13.1). The Exiles' Decree of 324 (Diodorus 18.8.2–5) overrode the League's guarantees, and the Greek colonists in Bactria revolted in 325 and 323 (Diodorus 17.99.5–6; 18.7).

Hephaestion, now chiliarch, an Achaemenid title for the chief minister, died at Ecbatana in autumn 324 after fever and drinking. Alexander executed the physician Glaucias, cut his hair, and, Diodorus says (17.114.4–5), extinguished the sacred fires, which was normally done only at a king's death. Ammon allowed Hephaestion heroic cult, not divine (Arrian 7.14.7). The pyre cost 10,000 talents (Plutarch, Alexander 72) or 12,000 (Diodorus 17.115), and the chiliarchy kept his name (Arrian 7.14.10). Arrian grades the grief stories and admits he cannot sift them. The political loss was the one intermediary able to carry the king's policies through a reluctant court.

Women at court

Olympias alone had an independent Macedonian power base, and she later had Philip III killed before Cassander executed her in 316. Sisygambis, Darius' mother, was captured at Issus and bowed to Hephaestion by mistake; Alexander told her that he too was Alexander (Diodorus 17.37.5–6; Curtius 3.12.15–17). Curtius says (10.5.19–25) she starved herself when he died. Barsine, Artabazus' daughter and Memnon's widow, was his mistress from 333 (Aristobulus in Plutarch, Alexander 21). Her son Heracles was murdered in 309 (Diodorus 20.28). Tarn denied that he existed; Brunt (1975) and most since accept him. Roxane, daughter of the Bactrian Oxyartes, married Alexander in 327 to seal the Sogdian settlement (Curtius 8.4.21–30). She and Alexander IV were killed by Cassander around 310. Stateira and Parysatis brought Achaemenid legitimacy; Plutarch (Alexander 77) says Roxane had Stateira killed after 323. These women carried legitimacy, which is why the Successors eliminated those with claims.

Integration or autocracy, and what the Successors kept

One view sees a Macedonian-Iranian ruling class under construction, built through the Susa marriages, the Epigonoi, the mixed cavalry and the Opis prayer. Briant calls Alexander "the last of the Achaemenids", running Persia's imperial machine with a new elite on top. The other view, associated with Badian and in modified form with Bosworth, treats the Persians as a counterweight that freed the king from his own people. The sequence supports a combined reading. Proskynesis followed Cleitus, the Epigonoi were ordered after the pages, and Persian commands answered Opis. Integration served autocracy every time it was applied; whether it also served a larger vision remains open.

Macedon gave its own verdict at Babylon in 323. The infantry acclaimed Arrhidaeus because he was fully Macedonian, and in Curtius (10.6.13–14) Ptolemy objects to an heir of conquered blood. Nearly every Susa bride was repudiated. Peucestas, who learned Persian and wore Persian dress in Persis (Arrian 6.30.3), stayed unique. Seleucus kept Apame, so the Seleucids were half-Iranian from Antiochus I. The Successors kept the diadem, the court of philoi, Bodyguards and pages, and the use of local elites. Eumenes' tent with Alexander's empty throne (Diodorus 18.60–61) shows ceremonial being turned into legitimacy. They dropped proskynesis for Greeks, the joint aristocracy and the partnership in rule. Hellenistic kingdoms were Graeco-Macedonian courts over native subjects: heirs to Alexander's autocracy, not his integration.

Self-test

  1. What was Philotas formally accused of at Phrada in 330, and who conducted his torture?
    Answer

    Failing to report the Dimnus plot, which he had heard of through Cebalinus, rather than plotting himself. Curtius names Craterus, Hephaestion and Coenus (Parmenion's own son-in-law) as his torturers.

  2. How was Parmenion killed, and how does Arrian explain the decision?
    Answer

    Polydamas carried orders by racing camel to Cleander, Sitalces and Menidas at Ecbatana, who stabbed him while he read letters. Arrian (3.26.4) suggests either that Alexander believed him guilty or that a father whose son had just been executed was too dangerous to leave in command.

  3. Which institutional changes followed the Philotas affair?
    Answer

    The Companion cavalry was divided between Hephaestion and Cleitus, letters home were censored, and malcontents were put in a separate disciplinary unit (Diodorus 17.80; Curtius 7.2).

  4. What political quarrel sat underneath the drunken killing of Cleitus at Maracanda?
    Answer

    Philip's reputation against Alexander's claims to surpass him, court flattery, mockery of Macedonian officers, and the standing of the old Companions under an increasingly Persian kingship. The Euripides quotation made the point that soldiers did the work while the king took the glory.

  5. Give the three ancient versions of Callisthenes' death.
    Answer

    Ptolemy: tortured and hanged. Aristobulus: kept in chains and died of illness. Chares: held for trial before Aristotle and died in India of obesity and lice (Arrian 4.14.3; Plutarch, Alexander 55).

  6. What were the Epigonoi, and what did the Macedonians call them?
    Answer

    Thirty thousand Iranian youths ordered in 327 to be trained in Macedonian arms, who arrived at Susa in 324. The Macedonians called them an antitagma, a counter-army (Diodorus 17.108.3).

  7. Why did Alexander marry both Stateira and Parysatis at Susa?
    Answer

    Stateira was Darius III's daughter and Parysatis the daughter of Artaxerxes III, so the two marriages joined him to both lines of the Achaemenid house.

  8. State Tarn's and Badian's readings of the Opis prayer.
    Answer

    Tarn: a statement of the brotherhood of mankind. Badian: a prayer for concord and shared rule between Macedonians and Persians only, a political settlement after a mutiny with a seating order that kept Macedonians first. Badian's view is now standard.

  9. What is the "reign of terror" thesis, and what is the main objection to it?
    Answer

    Badian's view that the executions of 325–324 were the paranoid lashing-out of a shaken autocrat. Critics (Higgins, Heckel) argue that the numbers were modest and the charges of misrule plausible, against officials who had expected Alexander to die in India.

  10. Name two things the Successors kept from Alexander's court and two they dropped.
    Answer

    Kept: the diadem, the court of philoi with Bodyguards and pages, and royal ceremonial used for legitimacy (as in Eumenes' Alexander-tent). Dropped: proskynesis for Greeks and Macedonians, the mixed marriages (Seleucus excepted), and the joint Macedonian-Persian ruling class.

Carry forward

  1. Alexander's court politics was a generational replacement. Philip's men, bound by kinship, were broken in 330–328, and Alexander's personal friends took the great commands, which were divided so that no subordinate could build an independent power base.
  2. Each measure of Macedonian-Persian integration followed a Macedonian crisis, so integration and autocracy were two faces of one policy. Whether Alexander held a vision beyond his own power is the open question, and Badian's reading of Opis has replaced Tarn's.
  3. The Successors inherited the autocratic monarchy and its ceremonial but rejected the joint elite and every royal woman and child who carried mixed legitimacy. The result was Graeco-Macedonian dynasties ruling over Asian subjects, not a fused aristocracy.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Alexander's court and the politics within the expedition. Cover: the old guard he inherited from Philip (Parmenion, Antipater, Antigonus, Cleitus, Coenus, Craterus) and the young men around him (Hephaestion, Ptolemy, Perdiccas, Leonnatus, Lysimachus, Seleucus, Peucestas, Nearchus); Antipater and Olympias feuding in Macedon; the Philotas affair in 330 in full and the judicial murder of Parmenion; the killing of Cleitus at Maracanda and the drinking culture behind it; the pages' conspiracy and the fall of Callisthenes; the orientalising policy: Persian dress, the mixed court ceremonial, the Persian nobles admitted, the 30,000 Epigonoi, the Susa mass marriage and the Macedonian reaction to it, the Opis mutiny and the reconciliation banquet with its prayer for homonoia (Tarn's brotherhood of man against Badian's reading); the purge of the satraps in 325-324 and the reign of terror thesis; Harpalus' flight with the treasury and the Athenian scandal; Hephaestion's death and the grief; the position of the Greek allies and mercenaries; women at court: Olympias, Sisygambis, Barsine, Roxane, Stateira and Parysatis. End with the question of whether the court was moving towards an integrated Macedonian-Persian elite or towards autocracy, and what the Successors kept of it.
