GREECE · UNIT 11 · Deep dive II: Alexander · 11.6 · 2,888 words

The eastern campaign: Bactria, Sogdiana, India and the return

From avenger to heir: Hyrcania to Arachosia, 330The Hindu Kush and the end of Bessus, 329Sogdiana, 329–327: the guerrilla war and its settlementInto India, 327–326: Taxiles, the hill peoples, Aornos, NysaHydaspes and Hyphasis, 326Down the Indus and three routes west, 326–324The world as they imagined itAssessment: the war that became something elseSelf-testCarry forward

From avenger to heir: Hyrcania to Arachosia, 330

In summer 330 Bessus, satrap of Bactria, and his fellow conspirators stabbed Darius III and left him dying (Arrian, Anabasis 3.21.10; Curtius 5.13). That changed what the war was about. At Ecbatana Alexander had already sent home the allied Greek contingents (Arrian 3.19.5): the League of Corinth's war of revenge had in effect ended at Persepolis. Bessus then took the upright tiara and the throne name Artaxerxes (Arrian 3.25.3). That made him a usurper whom Alexander, as Darius' self-declared avenger and heir, could hunt in Achaemenid terms.

DateTheatreKey events
330Hyrcania, Aria, DrangianaSatibarzanes' revolt; Philotas affair at Phrada
Spring 329Hindu Kush, BactriaCrossing; Oxus; Bessus handed over
329–327SogdianaAlexandria Eschate; Polytimetus; Cleitus; the Rocks; Roxane
327–326Swat, PunjabMassaga, Aornos; Hydaspes; Hyphasis
326–325IndusMallian town; Patala
325–324Gedrosia, CarmaniaDesert march; Nearchus' voyage; Susa

Aria set the pattern for the next five years. Its satrap Satibarzanes submitted, was confirmed in post, then killed his Macedonian escort and went over to Bessus. A lightning return to Artacoana crushed him (Arrian 3.25.5–7). Arrian does not record the foundation of Alexandria in Areia, at or near Herat. It is known from Strabo (11.10.1), Pliny (Natural History 6.61) and Isidore of Charax. The city commanded the junction of the roads to Bactria and Drangiana. At Phrada in Drangiana Philotas was executed and Parmenion murdered (Arrian 3.26). The army wintered among the Ariaspians, whom Alexander honoured as "Benefactors" because they had fed Cyrus the Great's army (Arrian 3.27.4–5). Cyrus would return as a model again and again. In Arachosia Alexander founded the city Isidore calls Alexandropolis, usually placed at Old Kandahar.

Where sources disagree. The derivation of "Kandahar" from "Iskandar" is a popular etymology, not a proven one. Old Kandahar had an Achaemenid predecessor, and Ashoka's Greek edicts there show Greek readers by the mid-third century, but no ancient author describes the foundation. The identification is probable, not certain.

The Hindu Kush and the end of Bessus, 329

After wintering near Begram, where he founded Alexandria in the Caucasus, Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush in early spring 329, probably by the Khawak pass. The troops lived on raw meat from the pack animals, seasoned with silphium (Arrian 3.28.4–7; Curtius 7.3). Bessus had counted on the mountains. He scorched the country and retreated across the Oxus, burning his boats. The army crossed on tent-skins stuffed with chaff (Arrian 3.29.4), and the coalition broke up. Spitamenes and Dataphernes offered to give up Bessus. Ptolemy's own account turns the handover into a daring raid that he led. Aristobulus says Bessus was simply handed over (Arrian 3.29.6–30.5).

Bessus was set naked and collared by the roadside, asked why he had killed his king and kinsman, and flogged. At Bactra a council sentenced him to lose his nose and ear-lobes, and he was sent to Ecbatana to be executed before the Medes and Persians (Arrian 4.7.3). This was the punishment Darius I had inflicted on the rebel Fravartish, as recorded at Behistun. Arrian (4.7.4) condemns it as barbarian and links it to Alexander's adoption of Median dress. The point is the role it reveals: Alexander was punishing a rebel against the Great King as the Great King.

Where sources disagree. Arrian has mutilation followed by execution at Ecbatana. Curtius (7.10.10) has crucifixion. Diodorus (17.83.9) has Bessus handed to Darius' brother Oxyathres and cut to pieces.

Sogdiana, 329–327: the guerrilla war and its settlement

Bessus' fall did not pacify the north-east. In summer 329 Alexander founded Alexandria Eschate, "the Furthest", at Khujand on the Jaxartes (Syr Darya). Arrian (4.4.1) says its walls rose in twenty days. The Sogdian towns, Cyropolis among them, immediately rose. Alexander was wounded in the head and neck during the sieges, and crossed the river under a catapult barrage to beat the Saca horsemen. Meanwhile Spitamenes laid siege to Maracanda (Samarkand).

The Polytimetus

The relief column, under the Lycian interpreter Pharnuches with Andromachus, Menedemus and Caranus, was wiped out on the Polytimetus (Zeravshan) by horse-archers (Arrian 4.5–6; Curtius 7.7.30–39). Curtius gives about 2,000 infantry and 300 cavalry killed, and says Alexander ordered the survivors to keep silent. It was the worst defeat of the reign. Alexander answered by slaughtering the people of the valley (Arrian 4.6.5). From then on it was a war of terror and counter-terror. It produced the drunken killing of Cleitus at Maracanda in 328 (Arrian 4.8–9) and overlapped with the proskynesis crisis of 327 (4.10–14).

Where sources disagree. Arrian gives two versions. In the first, probably Ptolemy's, Pharnuches loses his nerve in open battle. In Aristobulus' version, there is an ambush and a chaotic river crossing ordered by Caranus with no agreed command. Both blame a non-Macedonian with a doubtful commission, which looks apologetic.

The Branchidae

Curtius (7.5.28–35) tells of a town of Greeks descended from the Branchidae, the priests of Apollo at Didyma, whose ancestors had supposedly handed the temple treasure to Xerxes and moved east with him. They welcomed Alexander. He had them massacred anyway, for their ancestors' sacrilege. Strabo (11.11.4) and Plutarch (Moralia 557b) know the story. Arrian is silent.

Where sources disagree. Tarn dismissed the story as fiction. Others accept it, perhaps as an atrocity justified by Callisthenes, who was promoting the revived Didyma oracle (Strabo 17.1.43). Herodotus (6.19) makes things worse: in his account Didyma was sacked by Darius' generals in 494, not betrayed to Xerxes. Uncertain.

Spitamenes, the Rocks and Roxane

In 328 five columns swept Sogdiana. After Coenus defeated Spitamenes at Gabae, Spitamenes' Massagetae allies sent his head to Alexander (Arrian 4.17.7). Curtius (8.3) says his wife killed him, a more novelistic version. The resistance ended at mountain fortresses. At the Sogdian Rock the defenders jeered that Alexander would need soldiers with wings. About three hundred volunteers climbed the cliff at night with tent-pegs and ropes, and some thirty fell to their deaths (Arrian 4.18.4–19.4). Among the captives were the family of the Bactrian noble Oxyartes.

Alexander married Oxyartes' daughter Roxane. Plutarch (Alexander 47.7–8) calls it a love match that also served his policy. Curtius (8.4.23–30) records the Macedonians' disgust that the king had taken a captive's daughter. The marriage tied the most powerful Bactrian family to the regime, and Oxyartes later became satrap of the Paropamisadae. It also made an Iranian woman the probable mother of the heir.

Where sources disagree. Curtius (7.11) dates the "Rock of Arimazes" to 329/8, while Arrian puts it in 327. Strabo (11.11.4) has Roxane captured at the rock of Sisimithres, whom Curtius seems to treat as Arrian's Chorienes. The order of the sieges cannot be fixed.

Cities as garrisons

Justin (12.5.13) credits Alexander with twelve foundations in Bactria and Sogdiana, and Strabo (11.11.4) with eight. Most were garrison towns, not poleis: veterans, mercenaries and local people placed on river crossings and oasis routes. Amyntas was left with 10,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry (Arrian 4.22.3). The settlers rose on a false report of Alexander's death in 325, and again in force in 323 (Diodorus 17.99.5–6; 18.7). Whether Ai Khanoum was Alexandria Oxiana or an early Seleucid city is uncertain.

Into India, 327–326: Taxiles, the hill peoples, Aornos, Nysa

The ruler of Taxila, called Taxiles by the Greeks (perhaps Ambhi; Curtius' Omphis), had already offered an alliance against his rival Porus (Diodorus 17.86.4). In 327 Hephaestion and Perdiccas took the Kabul valley road with Taxiles' help to bridge the Indus. Alexander turned north into the hills to secure the flank. Against the Aspasians he was wounded in the shoulder, and Ptolemy, who is again his own witness, killed their chief in single combat (Arrian 4.23–24). At Massaga, among the Assacenians, an arrow hit Alexander in the ankle. After the town surrendered, 7,000 Indian mercenaries agreed to serve him and were then cut down. Arrian (4.27.3–4) says they tried to desert. Diodorus (17.84) and Plutarch (Alexander 59.6–7) call it treachery against men under truce.

Aornos, a crag above the Indus, was said to have defeated Heracles himself. Arrian (4.28.1–2) suspects Macedonian boasting. Alexander filled a ravine and built a mound across to the summit, then took it as the defenders slipped away (4.29–30). Aurel Stein identified Aornos as Pir-Sar. More recent work in Swat favours Mount Ilam. It remains uncertain.

At Nysa the people, led by Acouphis, claimed Dionysus as their founder and pointed to the ivy on Mount Meros, whose name echoed mēros, the thigh of Zeus from which the god was born. Alexander, moved by pothos (Arrian 5.2.1), spared the city, and the Companions held a Bacchic revel. Arrian (5.1.2) advises against looking too closely into such stories, and Eratosthenes treated them as flattery (Arrian 5.3.1–4; Strabo 15.1.7–9). The expedition was starting to measure itself against gods.

Hydaspes and Hyphasis, 326

Porus held the swollen Hydaspes (Jhelum) with elephants that horses would not face. After many nights of feints, Alexander crossed upstream in a storm with about 5,000 cavalry and 6,000 infantry, leaving Craterus to hold the camp (Arrian 5.11–14). In the battle Coenus' cavalry took the Indians in the rear. The phalanx attacked the elephants' drivers and trunks until the maddened animals trampled their own side (5.15–18). Asked how he wished to be treated, the wounded Porus said "as a king" (5.19.2). Alexander restored him with more territory and reconciled him with Taxiles. A grateful Porus could hold the Punjab more cheaply than a satrap. Nicaea and Bucephala, named for the dead horse, were founded on the battlefield.

Where sources disagree. Arrian (5.14.3–6) sets Aristobulus' sixty chariots under Porus' son against Ptolemy's 2,000 cavalry and 120 chariots. Porus' elephants are put at 200 (Arrian 5.15.4), 130 (Diodorus 17.87.2) and 85 (Curtius 8.13.6).

The army pushed east past the Acesines and Hydraotes and stopped at the Hyphasis (Beas). It had had some seventy days of monsoon rain (Diodorus 17.94.3), and there were reports of the Nanda kingdom on the Ganges with thousands of elephants (Curtius 9.2; Plutarch, Alexander 62). In Arrian, Alexander argues that the eastern Ocean is near and that conquest has no limit but the earth's end (5.25–26). Coenus answers for the men: they have done enough, they want to see their parents, wives and children, and the finest success is knowing when to stop (5.27). Alexander sulked in his tent for three days. The sacrifices then proved unfavourable, and he turned back, leaving twelve altars as high as towers (5.28–29.1). Coenus died within weeks (6.2.1).

Where sources disagree. The speeches are Arrian's compositions. Most scholars read the episode as a real defeat of the king's will. Some, notably P. O. Spann, argue Alexander engineered or exploited the refusal and used the omens to save face.

Down the Indus and three routes west, 326–324

The Mallian town

In November 326 the fleet left the Hydaspes, with Nearchus as admiral and Onesicritus as royal helmsman. Ptolemy put it at nearly 2,000 craft (Arrian 6.2.4), Nearchus at 800 (Indica 19.7). The voyage was a campaign of conquest. At a town of the Malli, often identified with Multan but uncertainly, Alexander climbed onto the wall. The ladders broke behind him, and he jumped down inside with Peucestas, Leonnatus and Abreas. Abreas was killed. An arrow pierced Alexander's chest while Peucestas covered him with the sacred shield from Troy, until the army broke in and killed everyone (Arrian 6.9–11).

Where sources disagree. Arrian (6.11.3–8) corrects the record. Ptolemy was not present, whatever Clitarchus and Timagenes said, because Ptolemy himself wrote that he was elsewhere. Curtius (9.5.21) notes the same contradiction. Who removed the arrowhead (Critodemus of Cos or Perdiccas) is also disputed.

Further down, rulers who submitted and then revolted, such as Musicanus, were hanged, along with the Brahmans who had encouraged them (Arrian 6.17.2). At Patala, the head of the delta, in summer 325, the tides stranded the boats and astonished the Macedonians (6.19.1–2). In open sea Alexander poured a libation to Poseidon from a golden cup (6.19.5).

Craterus and Gedrosia

The force was split. Craterus, sent ahead with the elephants, baggage and veterans, took the inland route through Arachosia and Drangiana (Arrian 6.17.3). He brought the rebel Ordanes to Carmania in chains. Alexander took the coast through the Oreitae, leaving Leonnatus at a new Alexandria at Rhambacia, and then entered Gedrosia. The march to Pura took sixty days (6.24.1). Arrian gives two motives. The practical one was to dig wells and lay down depots for the fleet (6.23). The other, from Nearchus, was rivalry: Semiramis had come back that way with twenty survivors and Cyrus with seven, and Alexander wanted to outdo them (6.24.2–3; Strabo 15.1.5). Heat and thirst were followed by a night flash flood that swept away most of the women and children (6.25.5). Plutarch (Alexander 66.4–5) says barely a quarter of 135,000 men survived.

Where sources disagree. Donald Engels argued that the fighting force was far smaller than Plutarch implies and that most of the dead were non-combatants and animals. A minority, Peter Green among them, suspect the march was a punishment for the Hyphasis. Most see a sound plan ruined by the monsoon's timing and the fleet's delay, and treat the Cyrus and Semiramis motive as Nearchus' gloss.

Nearchus and Onesicritus

Driven out early by hostile locals, Nearchus sailed the Makran coast. His account survives in Arrian's Indica (20–42). It describes Fish-Eaters who made meal from dried fish and built houses of whale bones (29), a school of whales scattered by trumpets (30), and his refusal of Onesicritus' plan to sail for Cape Maketa (Musandam). His orders, he said, were to survey the coast, not to take risks (32.9–13). Reaching Harmozia, he went inland to Alexander, who wept because he thought the fleet lost (33–36). Arrian (6.2.3) accuses Onesicritus of claiming the command when he was only a helmsman, and Strabo (15.1.28) calls him the arch-pilot of marvels.

Carmania and Susa

The vulgate tradition describes a seven-day Bacchic procession through Carmania, in imitation of Dionysus' triumph (Plutarch, Alexander 67; Curtius 9.10.24–29; Diodorus 17.106.1). Arrian (6.28.1–2) rejects it because neither Ptolemy nor Aristobulus mentions it. The purge, by contrast, is certain. Cleander and Sitalces, Parmenion's killers, were executed (Arrian 6.27.4), and Harpalus fled. At Pasargadae Aristobulus was ordered to restore Cyrus' plundered tomb (6.29). At Susa in early 324 Nearchus and Onesicritus were crowned, and 30,000 Iranian Epigoni arrived, trained in Macedonian fashion (7.5.6; 7.6.1).

The world as they imagined it

The army set out with Aristotle's map. According to Aristotle, from the Hindu Kush, his "Parnassus", one could see the outer Ocean (Meteorologica 1.13). For Herodotus, India was the last inhabited land to the east (3.98). The Hindu Kush became the "Caucasus", complete with Prometheus' cave, which Eratosthenes dismissed as flattery (Arrian 5.3; Strabo 11.5.5). The Jaxartes became the Tanais, so that Alexander could be said to have reached Europe's edge. Arrian separates it from Herodotus' Tanais (3.30.7–9). Strabo (11.7.4) blames Polycleitus for merging the Caspian with the Sea of Azov to make this work. Alexander treats the Caspian as a gulf of Ocean (Arrian 5.26.1–2) and later sent Heraclides to check (7.16).

Crocodiles in the Indus and Egyptian beans on the Acesines convinced Alexander he had found the upper Nile. He wrote as much to Olympias, then deleted the passage when he learned the river reached the sea (Arrian 6.1.2–5; Strabo 15.1.25). He apparently ignored or did not know that Scylax had sailed from the Indus to Egypt for Darius I (Herodotus 4.44).

The legacy lasted. The bematists Diognetus and Baeton produced measured distances (Pliny 6.61). Nearchus charted the sea route from India to the Gulf. Megasthenes, around 300, opened up the Ganges, and India became a subcontinent instead of a fringe. Eratosthenes drew one continuous chain from the Taurus through the "Caucasus" to the Himalaya, and moved the eastern Ocean far beyond the Hyphasis. Patrocles still persuaded him that the Caspian opened into the northern Ocean (Strabo 11.11.6).

Assessment: the war that became something else

These six years strip the expedition of its first purpose in stages. The League of Corinth war ended when the Greeks were sent home from Ecbatana. The pursuit of Bessus was an Achaemenid war of succession, fought with Persian punishments. Sogdiana was a frontier pacification of the kind any Great King would have had to fight. Even the Indus valley could be presented as recovering the old satrapies of Gandhara and Hindush. The Hyphasis was the first point clearly beyond any Persian frontier, where only conquest for its own sake remained, and there the army refused to go on.

By then the explanations are heroic ones. Arrian calls it pothos. The landmarks are Heracles at Aornos, Dionysus at Nysa, Cyrus and Semiramis in Gedrosia, and Achilles' shield at the Mallian town. At the same time the army was turned into an imperial force: Iranian cavalry, Persian court dress, Roxane, the Epigoni. Cleitus, Callisthenes and Coenus each voiced the Macedonian protest. What reached Susa was the personal empire of a king whose authority rested on conquest and emulation of the gods, served by an army loyal to him rather than to Macedon.

Where sources disagree. Tarn saw a vision of human unity here. Bosworth (Alexander and the East) stresses massacre and the "tragedy of triumph". Briant sees the last of the Achaemenids. Holt emphasises how coercive and fragile the Bactrian settlement was.

Self-test

  1. Why did Darius' death change the basis of Alexander's war, and what event at Ecbatana marks the shift?
    Answer

    Bessus claimed the throne as Artaxerxes, so Alexander could hunt him as Darius' avenger and heir, which made it an Achaemenid war of succession. The dismissal of the allied Greek contingents at Ecbatana (Arrian 3.19.5) had in effect ended the League of Corinth's war of revenge.

  2. What was Persian about Bessus' punishment, and how does Arrian judge it?
    Answer

    Mutilation of the nose and ears, then execution before the Medes and Persians: Darius I's treatment of rebels, as at Behistun. Arrian (4.7.3–4) condemns it as barbarian and links it to Alexander's Median dress.

  3. How do Arrian's two sources explain the Polytimetus disaster?
    Answer

    The main version blames Pharnuches for losing his nerve in open battle. Aristobulus describes an ambush and a chaotic crossing ordered by Caranus with no agreed command. Both lay the blame on others, not Alexander.

  4. Why do scholars doubt the Branchidae massacre?
    Answer

    Arrian does not mention it. Herodotus 6.19 has Didyma sacked in 494, not betrayed to Xerxes. And it may come from Callisthenes' propaganda for the revived oracle. Its historicity is uncertain.

  5. What political purposes did the marriage to Roxane serve?
    Answer

    It bound Oxyartes' family, the leading Bactrian aristocrats, to the regime and helped end the Sogdian resistance. It also signalled that Iranian elites could join the ruling class, which offended the Macedonians.

  6. How does Arrian treat Heracles at Aornos and Dionysus at Nysa?
    Answer

    Sceptically. He suspects the Macedonians attached Heracles to Aornos to inflate the feat (4.28.1–2). He advises against looking too closely into the Nysa claims (5.1.2), and he records Eratosthenes' view that both were flattery.

  7. Why did Alexander restore Porus?
    Answer

    A powerful, grateful native king could hold the Punjab more cheaply than a satrap and would balance Taxiles. It also fitted the image of royal magnanimity in the "as a king" exchange.

  8. What did Coenus argue at the Hyphasis, and what is the modern debate?
    Answer

    That the army had done enough, wanted to go home to its families, and that knowing when to stop was the finest success. Most scholars see a real defeat of Alexander's will. Spann and others argue he engineered or exploited the protest and used omens to save face.

  9. What two motives does Arrian give for the Gedrosian march, and where does the Cyrus and Semiramis comparison come from?
    Answer

    Supporting the fleet with wells and depots, and outdoing Semiramis and Cyrus, who had barely got through. The comparison comes from Nearchus (Arrian 6.24.2–3; Strabo 15.1.5).

  10. Name two geographical misidentifications and one lasting gain for Greek geography.
    Answer

    The Jaxartes taken for the Tanais, the Indus for the upper Nile, the Hindu Kush called the Caucasus, the Caspian thought a gulf of Ocean. Lasting gains include the bematists' measured distances, Nearchus' survey of the sea route, and the later picture of India and the Ganges.

Carry forward

  1. After 330 the expedition's justification moved from Panhellenic revenge to Achaemenid succession, and at the Hyphasis to open-ended personal conquest. The army's refusal there is the first limit Alexander's own troops imposed on him.
  2. The eastern campaign comes to us through competing filters: Ptolemy's self-promotion, Aristobulus' apologetics, the rival accounts of Nearchus and Onesicritus, and the moralising vulgate. Arrian's corrections at the Mallian town and in Carmania show the source problem directly.
  3. Myth and geography worked together. Heracles, Dionysus, Cyrus and Semiramis gave the campaign its meaning. Misnamed rivers and mountains shaped its decisions. Its surveys founded Hellenistic geography.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Alexander's campaigns from the death of Darius to the return to Susa, 330 to 324 BC. Cover: the pursuit of Bessus through Hyrcania, Aria, Drangiana and Arachosia, and the foundations (Alexandria in Areia, Kandahar); the crossing of the Hindu Kush; Bessus' capture and mutilation; Spitamenes' revolt and the two years of guerrilla war in Sogdiana, the massacre at the Polytimetus, the Branchidae, the city foundations as garrisons; the Sogdian Rock and the marriage to Roxane as policy; the descent into India: the alliance with Taxiles, the Aspasians and Assacenians, the storming of Aornos, Nysa; the Hydaspes campaign and Porus restored; the march to the Hyphasis and the mutiny, Coenus' speech; the river voyage down the Indus, the Mallian town and the near-fatal wound; Patala and the division of the force; the Gedrosian desert march (why he chose it, the losses, the Cyrus and Semiramis comparison); Nearchus' voyage along the Makran coast to the Persian Gulf and Onesicritus; Craterus' route through Arachosia; the Carmanian revel. Then the geography: what Alexander and his men thought the world looked like (the Jaxartes as the Tanais, the Indus as the Nile, the eastern Ocean) and how the campaign changed Greek geography. End with an assessment of the eastern campaign as the place where the expedition stopped being a war of revenge and became something else. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 11 · Deep dive II: Alexander · 11.7 · 3,206 words

The sources for Alexander

A structural problem, not a gapThe lost first generationThe five surviving narrativesThe Vulgate versus ArrianDocuments, coins and imagesThe Alexander RomanceModern QuellenforschungReading an anecdote: a methodSelf-testCarry forward

A structural problem, not a gap

Every narrative of Alexander that survives was written at least 270 years after his death in Babylon in June 323 BC. The men who marched with him did write, and some wrote at length, but their books are lost. What remains are fragments quoted by later authors, mostly Strabo, Plutarch, Arrian and Athenaeus, collected by Felix Jacoby in Die Fragmente der griechischen Historiker (FGrH II B, beginning at no. 117). So the Alexander historian works at two removes. First, what did Ptolemy or Cleitarchus actually say? Second, why did they say it? A third hangs over both: how far did the surviving author, writing under Augustus, Claudius or Hadrian, reshape what he took over? There is no neutral base text.

The lost first generation

AuthorPositionWork and dateCharacter and known bias
Callisthenes of OlynthusOfficial historian; Aristotle's relativeDeeds of Alexander, written during the campaign; fragments do not clearly go beyond 331/330Panegyric for Greek readers: Alexander as son of Zeus, the sea bowing to him off Pamphylia
Ptolemy son of LagusBodyguard, general, later king of EgyptHistory, date disputed (see below)Military, sober in tone; promotes Ptolemy, belittles rivals such as Perdiccas
Aristobulus of CassandreiaEngineer and technicianWrote in old age; Lucian, Macrobii 22, says he began at 84Geography, botany, monuments; apologetic, softening drink and violence
Nearchus of CreteAdmiral of the fleet, Indus to Persian Gulf, 325/324Account of the voyageNavigation and ethnography; self-promoting against Onesicritus
Onesicritus of AstypalaeaCynic, pupil of Diogenes; helmsman of the royal shipOn the education of Alexander, modelled on Xenophon's Cyropaedia (Diogenes Laertius 6.84)Philosophical idealisation, Indian marvels; claimed to be admiral (Arrian 6.2.3 denies it)
Chares of MytileneRoyal usher (eisangeleus)Histories of Alexander, at least ten booksCourt ceremony, banquets, the Susa weddings; gossipy insider
Royal EphemeridesAttributed to Eumenes of Cardia and Diodotus of Erythrae (Athenaeus 10.434b)Court journal; cited only for the last illnessAuthenticity disputed (see below)
Cleitarchus of AlexandriaNot a participant; son of the Persian historian DeinonHistory in at least twelve books; date disputedVivid, sensational, rhetorical; the chief source of the "Vulgate"
Marsyas of PellaBoyhood companion; half-brother of Antigonus the One-EyedMacedonica, reaching Alexander's early reignMacedonian insider; very little survives
The Bematists (Baeton, Diognetus, Philonides, Amyntas)Professional pacers on the marchDistance tables and route notesTechnical; used by Eratosthenes, Strabo, Pliny (Natural History 6.61)

Callisthenes and his death

Callisthenes is the paradox of the tradition: the most contemporary narrator and among the most flattering. His surviving fragments make Alexander the son of Zeus at Siwa and have the waves of the Pamphylian sea do obeisance. Yet in 327 at Bactra he publicly refused proskynesis, the Persian prostration, and was soon implicated in the Pages' Conspiracy (Arrian 4.10–14; Plutarch, Alexander 53–55). His death made him a Peripatetic martyr, and a hostile picture of Alexander as a tyrant corrupted by fortune is often traced to that school's grievance, though how coherent this "Peripatetic portrait" was is debated: Tarn (Alexander the Great II, 1948) built a hostile Peripatetic school tradition out of it; Badian ("The Eunuch Bagoas", 1958) denied that any such school line can be shown.

Where sources disagree. Arrian 4.14.3 sets the versions side by side: Ptolemy says Callisthenes was tortured and hanged; Aristobulus that he was carried in chains with the army and died of illness. Chares (Plutarch, Alexander 55.9) says he was held in fetters for seven months and died of obesity and lice before he could be tried before Aristotle. Arrian admits that even the eyewitnesses could not agree.

Ptolemy and Aristobulus

Arrian's preface explains why he chose these two: both campaigned with Alexander, and Ptolemy, being a king, would find lying more disgraceful than other men. That is a weak argument. Ptolemy wrote as ruler of an Egypt whose legitimacy rested partly on Alexander's body, which he had hijacked in 321. R. M. Errington ("Bias in Ptolemy's History of Alexander", 1969) showed how consistently Perdiccas, Ptolemy's great enemy, is diminished: at Thebes in 335 Ptolemy has Perdiccas attack without orders (Arrian 1.8.1), where Diodorus 17.12 has Alexander direct the assault. Ptolemy's date of writing is uncertain: most put it late in his reign (after 301, perhaps after 285), but some argue for an early date as propaganda in the Successor wars.

Aristobulus is the gentler apologist. He claims Alexander drank long for companionship, not wine (Arrian 7.29.4). Lucian (How to Write History 12) has Alexander throw Aristobulus's book into the Hydaspes for inventing a single combat with Porus, a story probably itself invented.

Where sources disagree. At the Malli town in 325, Cleitarchus and Timagenes had Ptolemy saving Alexander's life. Curtius 9.5.21 notes that Ptolemy himself wrote he was absent elsewhere. Here the self-interested source declines credit: bias does not always run one way.

The Ephemerides and the forgery debate

Plutarch (Alexander 76–77) and Arrian (7.25–26) both quote the "Royal Diaries" for Alexander's final fever: day after day of bathing, sacrificing, sleeping in the bathhouse, briefing officers, then losing his voice. The quotation is tightly dated and sober, and it rules out poison.

Where sources disagree. Lionel Pearson ("The Diary and the Letters of Alexander the Great", 1955) argued the diaries were a later literary forgery. A. E. Samuel ("Alexander's 'Royal Journal'", 1965) and N. G. L. Hammond ("The Royal Journal of Alexander", 1988) defended a genuine court journal, perhaps on the Achaemenid model. A. B. Bosworth ("The Death of Alexander the Great: Rumour and Propaganda", 1971) took a middle line: a real-sounding document was produced or doctored soon after 323 to rebut the rumour that Antipater's sons poisoned the king. That nothing survives from it except the last days is itself suspicious. Uncertain.

Cleitarchus and the Alexandrian romantic tradition

Cleitarchus wrote at Alexandria, from participants' accounts and oral tradition, for a readership that wanted drama. Thaïs leading the drunken burning of Persepolis (Athenaeus 13.576d–e), the Amazon queen's visit, and huge Persian casualty figures are his signatures. Ancient critics judged him harshly. Quintilian (10.1.74) put it in five words:

Clitarchi probatur ingenium, fides infamatur.

"His talent is approved, his reliability condemned." Yet he was the most widely read Alexander historian in the Hellenistic and Roman world, which is why so much of him survives in derivative form.

Where sources disagree. The traditional date is c. 310 BC. W. W. Tarn pushed it after 280 to discredit him. A papyrus list of scholars (P. Oxy. 4808, published 2007) calls Cleitarchus tutor of Ptolemy IV Philopator, which would put him in the later third century. Some accept this; others, Luisa Prandi (2012) among them, think the papyrus has confused him with someone else. If late, he used Ptolemy and Aristobulus rather than preceding them. Unresolved.

The five surviving narratives

Author and workDateMain sources usedMain bias
Diodorus Siculus, Library book 17c. 60–30 BCCleitarchus, probably as main source; perhaps othersCompressed universal history; Fortune and moral exempla; one large lacuna covering 329–327
Quintus Curtius Rufus, Histories of Alexander (10 books, 1–2 lost)Probably Claudian (AD 41+); possibly Vespasianic or laterCleitarchus, with Ptolemy and Timagenes cited by nameRoman rhetoric; speeches; the king corrupted by fortune and Persian luxury
Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus, books 11–12Trogus Augustan; Justin 2nd–4th century ADTrogus, who drew on the VulgateHostile, moralising, often garbled by compression
Plutarch, Life of Alexander; On the Fortune or Virtue of AlexanderLife c. AD 100–120; the speeches earlierAbout two dozen named authors, plus letters attributed to AlexanderCharacter over events; philosophical; generally admiring with a theme of anger and drink
Arrian, Anabasis (7 books) and Indica2nd century AD; exact date disputedPtolemy and Aristobulus; Nearchus and Megasthenes for the IndicaMilitary, apologetic, consciously literary; eulogy with measured criticism

Diodorus is the earliest of the five and the least mediated: book 17 follows one main source closely enough that scholars reconstruct Cleitarchus largely from it, and its single large gap (the lacuna after 17.83, covering Bactria and Sogdiana in 329 to 327) is the biggest hole in the Vulgate. Justin is the last and the least reliable: Trogus wrote a full Augustan history in forty-four books, Justin cut it to anecdote and moral, and where he can be checked against Diodorus and Curtius the compression has often garbled sequence and names (the two Darius battles merged, officers confused), so a detail found only in Justin needs another witness.

Curtius: the rhetorician as historian

Curtius has suffered from his talent. His speeches are free compositions, and his Alexander follows a Roman tyrant-narrative: great gifts undone by success. Elizabeth Baynham's Alexander the Great: The Unique History of Quintus Curtius (1998) argued that he must be read as a literary artist with his own design, not mined as a conduit for Cleitarchus. Still, he preserves details no one else has, including on the Persian side, and he knows Ptolemy's account well enough to correct Cleitarchus by it.

Where sources disagree. Curtius' date rests mainly on 10.9.1–6, which praises a new emperor who saved Rome from civil strife after a night of turmoil, "like a new star". Most, with Elizabeth Baynham (Alexander the Great: The Unique History of Quintus Curtius, 1998), read Claudius after Caligula's murder in AD 41; others (J. R. Hamilton, "The Date of Quintus Curtius Rufus", 1988) argue for Vespasian after 69, and a minority for Severus Alexander or later.

Plutarch: lives, not histories

Plutarch is explicit about his aim (Alexander 1.2):

For it is not histories that we are writing, but lives.

A jest, he says, can reveal more than battles. He keeps anecdotes historians discard and names his authorities, which makes him invaluable for reconstructing lost sources. The letters he quotes are a problem: J. R. Hamilton's Plutarch, Alexander: A Commentary (1969) accepted some; others think most are rhetorical exercises. The two early speeches On the Fortune or Virtue of Alexander (Moralia 326d–345b) are display pieces arguing that Alexander was a philosopher in arms, who won by virtue rather than luck. They show the Alexander of the schools, not of the campaign.

Where sources disagree. On the Amazon queen, Plutarch (Alexander 46) lists those who told the story (Cleitarchus, Polyclitus, Onesicritus and others) and those who called it fiction (Aristobulus, Chares, Ptolemy and others). He adds that when Onesicritus read the episode to Lysimachus, the old king smiled and asked where he himself had been at the time.

Arrian: method and Xenophontic pose

L. Flavius Arrianus of Nicomedia, pupil of Epictetus, consul and governor of Cappadocia in the 130s, styled himself a new Xenophon. The title Anabasis, the seven books, the plain Attic prose and the soldier-philosopher persona all imitate Xenophon. His stated method (preface) is to record as true what Ptolemy and Aristobulus agree on, to choose the more credible when they differ, and to mark other material as legomena, "things said". In a second preface (1.12) he presents himself as the worthy chronicler Alexander lacked, a prose Homer for a new Achilles. The Indica, written in Ionic in imitation of Herodotus, paraphrases Nearchus' voyage (Indica 18–42) and Megasthenes on India.

Arrian is no neutral editor. He condemns the killing of Cleitus and the Persian dress (4.7–14) and closes with a eulogy excusing faults as youth and fortune (7.28–30). Bosworth (From Arrian to Alexander, 1988) showed him misreading, conflating and embellishing his sources. His date is uncertain: Bosworth argued for early composition, others for after the Cappadocian command.

The Vulgate versus Arrian

"Vulgate" is a modern label for the shared material in Diodorus, Curtius, Justin and the Metz Epitome, traced in large part to Cleitarchus. The older view, still common in popular books, treats Arrian as the good source and the Vulgate as romance. That ranking does not hold.

  • Arrian's sources were participants with interests, writing decades later. Arrian prefers them because they are respectable, not because he tested them.
  • The Vulgate preserves uncomfortable truths. Curtius on the Philotas affair or the dragging of Batis at Gaza (4.6.25–29) may be embellished, but Arrian's silence is not proof of innocence.
  • Both sides are processed. Arrian's Xenophontic restraint is as much a literary choice as Curtius' melodrama.
Where sources disagree. Persepolis, 330. Arrian 3.18.11–12 presents the burning of the palace as deliberate policy, revenge for Xerxes' sack of Athens, and adds his disapproval. Diodorus 17.72, Curtius 5.7 and Plutarch, Alexander 38 have a drunken revel at which the courtesan Thaïs throws the first torch. Many scholars suspect both: a policy decision staged as ritual, which Cleitarchus turned into a party and Ptolemy into statecraft. Excavation confirms deliberate destruction, not motive.

The Metz Epitome and the Liber de Morte

The Metz Epitome is a late-antique Latin summary covering 330 to 325, closely related to Curtius and Diodorus, which makes it a Vulgate control text. It survived in a single manuscript at Metz destroyed in 1944, so editions rest on earlier transcriptions. In the same manuscript stood the Liber de Morte Alexandri, a pamphlet narrating a poisoning plot by Antipater's family and a forged testament distributing the empire. A version of it is also embedded in the Alexander Romance (3.30–33).

Where sources disagree. Waldemar Heckel (The Last Days and Testament of Alexander the Great, 1988) traced the pamphlet to the circle of Polyperchon and Olympias, c. 317, to blacken Cassander. Bosworth ("Ptolemy and the Will of Alexander", 2000) placed it c. 309 in Ptolemy's interest, since the will flatters Ptolemy. Both agree it is Successor propaganda; the beneficiary is disputed.

Documents, coins and images

Non-literary evidence rarely resolves famous episodes, but it is free of narrative shaping and shows Alexander the administrator.

  • Babylonian astronomical diaries. The diary for 331 records the lunar eclipse of 20 September and Gaugamela on 1 October, with Darius' troops deserting him. The diary for 323 records, without comment, "the king died" on 29 Aiaru, 10 or 11 June, fixing the date independently of Greek tradition.
  • The Priene inscription. The temple of Athena Polias carries the dedication: "King Alexander dedicated the temple to Athena Polias", with an edict on Priene's status and taxes, now in the British Museum. It contrasts with Strabo 14.1.22, where Ephesus politely declined Alexander's offer to pay for its Artemision.
  • The letter to Chios and the Mytilene decree. Alexander's letter to Chios (c. 332) orders the return of exiles and a democratic constitution, with a garrison. Mytilene's reconciliation decree regulates returning exiles' property. Both show "liberation" of Greek cities working as direct royal intervention.
  • The Exiles' Decree inscriptions. Diodorus 18.8 reports the decree proclaimed at Olympia in 324; the Tegea inscription shows a city working through its consequences in property law.
  • Coins and the Porus medallions. Beyond the standard Heracles/Zeus tetradrachms, the "elephant medallions" (a horseman attacking an elephant; on the reverse, Alexander with a thunderbolt, crowned by Victory) are the only near-contemporary image of Alexander with divine attributes. Their mint (Babylon is likely) and date (323 or a little later) are debated (Frank Holt, Alexander the Great and the Mystery of the Elephant Medallions, 2003).
  • The Alexander Sarcophagus. Found at Sidon in 1887, now in Istanbul, probably made for Abdalonymus, the king Alexander installed there. Macedonians and Persians hunting together show the regime's image from a client king's side.
  • The Alexander Mosaic. From the House of the Faun at Pompeii (c. 100 BC), copying an early Hellenistic painting: evidence for how Alexander and Darius were imagined around 300, not for the battle.
Where sources disagree. The mosaic's original is often identified with the battle painting Philoxenus of Eretria made for Cassander (Pliny, Natural History 35.110); others suggest Apelles or Helen of Egypt. Whether it shows Issus or Gaugamela is uncertain.

The Alexander Romance

The Alexander Romance is falsely attributed to Callisthenes, so its author is called Pseudo-Callisthenes. The earliest recension (alpha) took shape in Alexandria around the third century AD from older materials: a novel in letters, Egyptian propaganda making Alexander son of the last pharaoh Nectanebo II, Indian wonder-tales, and the testament pamphlet. Its value for Alexander is almost nil; for how later cultures adopted him, enormous.

  • Latin and medieval Europe: Julius Valerius translated it in the early fourth century; Leo of Naples' tenth-century version (the Historia de Preliis) fed the Old French Roman d'Alexandre, whose twelve-syllable line named the "alexandrine". Walter of Châtillon's Alexandreis (c. 1180) follows Curtius instead.
  • Armenian and Syriac: an Armenian version by the fifth century; the Syriac Alexander Legend (c. 630) adds the gates against Gog and Magog.
  • Persian: Zoroastrian texts call him "the accursed", but Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (c. 1010) makes Sikandar Darius' half-brother and a legitimate Iranian king; Nizami (12th century) makes him sage and prophet.
  • Arabic: identification with Dhu'l-Qarnayn of Qur'an 18.83–98, traditional but disputed, carried him into Islamic romance.
  • Ethiopic: a Ge'ez version, via Arabic, makes him a chaste Christian ascetic.
Where sources disagree. The older view that the Syriac Romance was translated from a lost Middle Persian version, implying an early Iranian adoption, (Theodor Nöldeke, Beiträge zur Geschichte des Alexanderromans, 1890) has been challenged; Claudia Ciancaglini (2001) derives it directly from Greek. The route into Persian tradition remains disputed.

Modern Quellenforschung

Source criticism ("Quellenforschung") tries to assign each passage of the surviving authors to its lost origin. Hermann Strasburger's Ptolemaios und Alexander (1934) reconstructed Ptolemy from Arrian and set the agenda. Tarn (Alexander the Great, 1948) was partisan, dismissing anything unflattering as Vulgate distortion. Lionel Pearson's The Lost Histories of Alexander the Great (1960) gave cautious portraits of each lost author. Hammond (Three Historians of Alexander the Great, 1983; Sources for Alexander the Great, 1993) assigned passages to sources with a confidence many found excessive. Bosworth's Historical Commentary on Arrian's History of Alexander (vols. I–II, 1980 and 1995, unfinished) is the indispensable tool and treats Arrian as an author with his own errors; Baynham did the same for Curtius. The shift since the 1980s runs from naming the lost source behind a sentence to reading each surviving author as a writer with purposes.

Reading an anecdote: a method

  1. Find every version in Arrian, Plutarch, Curtius, Diodorus, Justin and the Metz Epitome. A story in both families outweighs one in a single Vulgate author.
  2. Look for a named source. A named eyewitness raises the stakes, not necessarily the reliability: ask what that witness gained.
  3. Ask who benefits: Ptolemy against Perdiccas, Aristobulus for the king, Cleitarchus for drama, Successors for legitimacy, Romans for a tyrant lesson.
  4. Strip the genre. Speeches, omens, encounters with philosophers and Amazons are literary forms. The bare act may survive; the words rarely do.
  5. Test against documents. Where inscriptions, diaries or coins overlap with narrative, they outweigh it.
  6. Watch for legend. Romance motifs (divine birth, wonder-voyages, poisoning plots) entered even sober texts early.
  7. Grade the result: secure, plausible, doubtful or legendary, and say which.

Take the Gordian knot. Arrian 2.3.7 gives both versions: most said Alexander cut it; Aristobulus said he drew the pin from the yoke-pole. The duller version comes from an apologist with no reason to invent it. The visit and oracle are plausible; the sword cut is probably legend.

Self-test

  1. Why did Arrian say he trusted Ptolemy and Aristobulus, and what is wrong with his reasoning?
    Answer

    Both campaigned with Alexander, and Ptolemy as a king would find lying especially shameful (Anabasis, preface). But both wrote decades later with clear interests: Ptolemy dynastic legitimacy and the diminishing of rivals such as Perdiccas, Aristobulus a defence of Alexander's character.

  2. Give the three versions of Callisthenes' death and their sources.
    Answer

    Ptolemy: tortured and hanged. Aristobulus: carried in chains and died of illness (both in Arrian 4.14.3). Chares: held in fetters for seven months and died of obesity and lice (Plutarch, Alexander 55).

  3. What is the Vulgate, and which surviving authors belong to it?
    Answer

    A modern label for the shared tradition traced mainly to Cleitarchus, found in Diodorus 17, Curtius, Justin's epitome of Trogus and the Metz Epitome. Plutarch draws on both it and the Arrian tradition.

  4. How does the Thebes episode of 335 illustrate Ptolemy's bias?
    Answer

    Ptolemy (Arrian 1.8.1) has Perdiccas attack without orders, which shifts blame for the slaughter to Ptolemy's later enemy. Diodorus 17.12 has Alexander directing the assault.

  5. What are the main positions in the Ephemerides debate?
    Answer

    Pearson: a later forgery. Samuel and Hammond: a genuine court journal. Bosworth: a document produced or doctored soon after 323 to rebut poisoning rumours. It is quoted only for the last illness, which is suspicious.

  6. Why does the date of Cleitarchus matter, and what new evidence complicated it?
    Answer

    An early date (c. 310) makes him independent of Ptolemy and Aristobulus; a late one means he may have used them. P. Oxy. 4808 calls him tutor of Ptolemy IV, implying a later third-century date, but some think the papyrus is mistaken.

  7. What passage is the main evidence for Curtius' date, and what are the options?
    Answer

    Curtius 10.9.1–6, praising a new emperor who ended civil turmoil. Most read Claudius (AD 41); alternatives are Vespasian (AD 69/70) or a later emperor.

  8. What does the Babylonian astronomical diary add to the record of Alexander's death?
    Answer

    An independent, contemporary cuneiform entry, "the king died", dated 29 Aiaru, 10 or 11 June 323, unaffected by Greek narrative shaping.

  9. How does Arrian present the Gordian knot, and how should we grade the versions?
    Answer

    Arrian 2.3.7: most said Alexander cut it; Aristobulus said he pulled the pin from the pole. The undramatic version from an apologist is more plausible; the sword cut is likely legend, though the visit and oracle are plausible.

  10. Name two ways the Alexander Romance was adapted outside Greek, and what each made of Alexander.
    Answer

    Any two, for example: Ferdowsi's Shahnameh made Sikandar half-brother of Darius and a legitimate Iranian king; Nizami made him sage and prophet; Arabic tradition linked him to Dhu'l-Qarnayn; the Ethiopic version made him a Christian ascetic.

Carry forward

  1. There is no neutral base text for Alexander: both the Arrian tradition and the Vulgate descend from interested, lost writers, and each surviving author reshaped them for his own age.
  2. Bias does not run in one direction. Eyewitnesses can omit and flatter, while sensational writers can preserve what eyewitnesses suppressed; judge each episode, not each author wholesale.
  3. Documents such as the Babylonian diaries, city inscriptions and coins are the only evidence free of narrative shaping, though not of self-presentation; use them to anchor narratives and to see Alexander the administrator behind Alexander the hero.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the source tradition for Alexander the Great. Cover: the lost primary sources (Callisthenes the court historian and his death, Ptolemy's memoir and its self-interest, Aristobulus the engineer, Nearchus, Onesicritus, Chares the chamberlain, the Royal Ephemerides and the forgery debate, Cleitarchus and the Alexandrian romantic tradition, Marsyas, the Bematists' distance tables); the surviving accounts: Diodorus book 17, Curtius Rufus (his date and rhetoric), Justin's epitome of Trogus, Plutarch's Life (and On the Fortune of Alexander), Arrian's Anabasis and Indica (his method, his reliance on Ptolemy and Aristobulus, his Xenophon imitation); the Vulgate versus Arrian and why neither is simply right; the Metz Epitome and the Liber de Morte; documentary and non-literary evidence (the Babylonian astronomical diaries, the Priene inscription, the Mytilene decree, the Exiles' Decree inscriptions, coins and the Porus medallions, the Alexander Sarcophagus, the Alexander Mosaic as a copy of a lost painting); the Alexander Romance of Pseudo-Callisthenes and its descent into Persian, Arabic, Syriac, Ethiopic and medieval European versions; Strasburger's Quellenforschung, Pearson, Hammond, Bosworth's commentary, Baynham. End with a method: how to read any Alexander anecdote and estimate its reliability. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 11 · Deep dive II: Alexander · 11.8 · 2,872 words

Death, body and afterlives

The last year: from Ecbatana to BabylonEleven days in DaesiusWhat killed himThe bodyImage as currency: the Successors and RomeJerusalem, the Quran, Persia, the medieval WestThe modern AlexandersWhy readers project onto AlexanderSelf-testCarry forward

The last year: from Ecbatana to Babylon

The Exiles' Decree

At the Olympic Games of 324 Nicanor of Stagira read out a royal letter to a crowd that Diodorus puts at over 20,000 exiles: the Greek cities were to take back their banished citizens, except those guilty of sacrilege or murder (Diodorus 18.8.2–5; 17.109.1; Curtius 10.2.4). The order overrode the autonomy guaranteed by the League of Corinth. It hit Athens hardest, because Athens would lose Samos, settled by its cleruchs since 365, and it hit the Aetolians, who would lose Oeniadae. Athens prepared for war while it debated divine honours for Alexander. The decree is the direct background to the Lamian War of 323–322.

Hephaestion

Hephaestion died of fever at Ecbatana in autumn 324, after eating a boiled fowl and drinking wine against his doctor's orders (Plutarch, Alexander 72; Arrian, Anabasis 7.14). Alexander had the physician Glaucias crucified, cut the manes of the horses, and ordered a pyre at Babylon: 12,000 talents in Diodorus (17.114–115), 10,000 in Plutarch. Plutarch presents the winter massacre of the Cossaeans as an offering to the dead man.

Where sources disagree. The oracle of Ammon was asked what honours Hephaestion should receive. Arrian (7.14.7; 7.23.6) says it allowed hero cult. Diodorus (17.115.6) says it allowed sacrifice as to a god. The difference bears on how far Alexander was then pressing claims to divinity.

Arabia and the "last plans"

At Babylon Alexander dug a harbour for a thousand ships and had vessels carried overland from Phoenicia to the Euphrates (Arrian 7.19.3–6). The target was Arabia. The pretext was that the Arabs had sent no embassy, and Arrian (7.20.1) reports that Alexander hoped to be worshipped as their third god, after Ouranos and Dionysus. After the death Perdiccas read the army Alexander's memoranda (hypomnemata; Diodorus 18.4.4–6): a thousand warships against Carthage, a road along North Africa to the Pillars of Heracles, six great temples, a pyramid for Philip, and exchanges of population between Asia and Europe. The army voted to cancel all of them.

Where sources disagree. Tarn called the last plans a forgery. Badian defended them, and most scholars now follow him. Even a genuine document reached us through a manoeuvre, however, since Perdiccas presented it in order to have it rejected.

The Chaldaeans and the omens

Chaldaean priests warned Alexander not to enter Babylon, or at least not facing west (Arrian 7.16.5–17.6, from Aristobulus; Diodorus 17.112). He suspected they wanted to keep the revenues of the temple of Bel (Marduk), whose rebuilding they had delayed. Even so, he tried to circle round to another gate and was blocked by the marshes. Then the omens began. A gust blew his diadem into the reeds by the Assyrian royal tombs, and the sailor who retrieved it put it on his own head (Arrian 7.22). The seer Peithagoras found a liver without a lobe (7.18). A tame ass kicked the king's finest lion to death (Plutarch 73). An unknown man sat on the empty throne wearing the royal robe and diadem and said only that the idea had come to him; he was executed (Arrian 7.24; Diodorus 17.116; Plutarch 73–74). Assyriologists have read this as a garbled memory of the substitute-king ritual (šar pūḫi), in which a stand-in absorbed an evil omen and was then killed. The idea is attractive but uncertain.

Eleven days in Daesius

The illness followed a drinking party given by Medius of Larissa. Arrian (7.25–26) and Plutarch (Alexander 76) both reproduce the Ephemerides ("Royal Journals"). Plutarch dates the entries by the Macedonian month.

DaesiusEvents (Plutarch 76, with Arrian 7.25)
18Feverish after drinking with Medius; sleeps in the bathing-room.
19–20Plays dice with Medius; sacrifices; listens to Nearchus' account of the Ocean voyage; fever each night.
21–22Fever worse; moved beside the great pool; discusses army appointments.
24Carried out to sacrifice; officers ordered to wait in the courtyard.
25–26Carried across the river to the palace; speechless; the soldiers force the doors and file past. Arrian says he acknowledged each with his eyes.
27Peithon, Seleucus and others sleep in the temple of "Sarapis" and are told to leave him where he is.
28Dies towards evening.

A Babylonian astronomical diary records the king's death on 29 Ayyaru, that is, 11 June 323 BC. It is the firmest date in his life.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch (75) also cites Aristobulus for a different ending: wine drunk in the fever, delirium, and death on 30 Daesius. The journal's status is contested. Pearson thought it a literary fake. Bosworth (1971) argued that it was published in the early Successor period to establish a natural death against the poison rumours. Hammond defended it as an authentic court record. The reference to Sarapis looks anachronistic, since the cult is usually thought to be Ptolemaic.

"To the strongest"

Asked who should have the kingdom, Alexander is said to have answered tōi kratistōi, "to the strongest", and to have foreseen great funeral games over his body (Arrian 7.26.3; Diodorus 17.117.4). Curtius (10.5.5) has optimo, "to the best". He gave his ring to Perdiccas (Curtius 10.5.4; Justin 12.15). Arrian offers the saying as hearsay, outside the journal, which has the king already speechless. It reads like an epigram composed afterwards to explain forty years of war among the Successors.

What killed him

All the accounts describe roughly twelve days of fever after heavy drinking, with growing weakness, loss of speech and terminal coma. Diodorus (17.117) and Justin (12.13) add a sudden stabbing pain after he drained a great cup of unmixed wine to Heracles. Plutarch (75) dismisses this as tragic embellishment.

TheoryBasisDifficulty
Falciparum malariaThe traditional default: marshes, early summer, fever.The fever pattern recorded is not clearly periodic.
Typhoid with ascending paralysisOldach et al., NEJM 1998; would explain the abdominal pain and loss of speech.Any diagnosis made so long after the event is speculative.
West Nile encephalitisMarr and Calisher, Emerging Infectious Diseases 2003; the ravens that fell dead at Babylon (Plutarch 73).Rests on an omen that may be literary.
Pancreatitis / alcoholThe binge, the sudden pain, and the court's drinking culture (Ephippus in Athenaeus 10).Plutarch rejects the pain; drink alone does not explain twelve days.
StrychnineGraham Phillips 2004, blaming Roxane.Kills in hours, with convulsions, and none are recorded.
Veratrum albumSchep et al., Clinical Toxicology 2014; known to Greek physicians; slow decline.Fits the course of the illness, but is purely circumstantial.

The ancient poisoning story is political. Antipater, about to be replaced as regent, sent his son Cassander with water from the Styx at Nonacris, so corrosive that only a mule's hoof could hold it. His younger son Iolaus, the royal cupbearer, poured it, and some versions say Aristotle advised, embittered by the death of his relative Callisthenes (Arrian 7.27; Plutarch 77; Curtius 10.10.14–17; Diodorus 17.118; Justin 12.13–14). The Liber de morte attached to the Alexander Romance names Medius' guests as conspirators. It is a pamphlet aimed at Antipater's house, probably from Perdiccas' or Polyperchon's circle.

Where sources disagree. Arrian (7.27.3) records the poison story only so as not to seem ignorant of it. Plutarch (77.5) says most writers think it invented. Diodorus claims that historians suppressed it out of fear of Cassander. Justin accepts it. Most modern scholars favour natural causes, made worse by drink, the chest wound at the Malli town, and exhaustion, though Bosworth kept poisoning open. The honest verdict is that the cause is unknown. The poisoning story tells us about Successor politics, not about toxicology.

The body

Curtius (10.10.9–13) says the corpse lay six days in the summer heat while the generals quarrelled and was found uncorrupted. Egyptian and Chaldaean embalmers then placed it in a gold coffin filled with spices. Building the funeral carriage took two years. Diodorus (18.26–28) describes a gold-roofed Ionic shrine on wheels, hung with bells and painted panels of the army and fleet and drawn by sixty-four mules. In 321 Ptolemy met it in Syria and took it to Egypt, with the connivance of Arrhidaeus, its escort, while Perdiccas' officers failed to stop him (Diodorus 18.28; Strabo 17.1.8; Arrian, Events after Alexander fr. 1.25). The body gave Ptolemy a claim to legitimacy, and it gave Perdiccas a reason to invade Egypt, where his own officers murdered him.

Where sources disagree. The intended destination was either Siwa (Diodorus 18.3.5) or the royal tombs at Aegae (Pausanias 1.6.3). Curtius (10.10.20) and Pausanias (1.7.1) put the body first at Memphis, with the move to Alexandria under Ptolemy II. Diodorus implies that Ptolemy I took it to Alexandria directly.

In Alexandria it lay in the Sema or Soma. Zenobius (3.94) says Ptolemy IV built a mausoleum there in which the Ptolemies were buried around Alexander. Strabo (17.1.8) says a later Ptolemy melted down the gold coffin and replaced it with one of glass or alabaster. The visitors are part of the story.

  • Caesar came in 48 BC. Lucan (10.14–52) makes the visit an indictment of both men.
  • Augustus crowned the body and strewed flowers (Suetonius, Augustus 18). Dio (51.16.5) adds that he broke off part of the nose. Offered the Ptolemies too, he said he had come to see a king, not corpses.
  • Caligula wore Alexander's breastplate from the tomb (Suetonius, Caligula 52). Septimius Severus closed the tomb to visitors (Dio 76.13.2).
  • Caracalla, in 215, left his cloak, rings and belt on the coffin (Herodian 4.8.9).

Possible ends for the tomb are Aurelian's destruction of the palace quarter in the 270s, the tsunami of 365, and the anti-pagan violence of the 390s. Libanius (Oration 49.12), writing around 390, implies the body was still on show. Within a few years John Chrysostom (Homily 26 on 2 Corinthians) could ask where the tomb was as though no one knew. More than 140 official searches, from the Nebi Daniel mosque to Siwa, have found nothing confirmed.

Image as currency: the Successors and Rome

The Successors

The generals ruled in the Argead name while it lasted, through Philip III Arrhidaeus and Alexander IV, both murdered by about 310. After that, Argead brides served instead. Cassander married Philip's daughter Thessalonike, and Alexander's sister Cleopatra was killed in 308 before she could marry a rival. Ptolemy encouraged the rumour that he was Philip's bastard (Pausanias 1.6.2; Curtius 9.8.22). Eumenes held councils before Alexander's empty throne (Diodorus 18.60–61). Coinage made the image portable. From about 319 Ptolemy's tetradrachms showed Alexander in an elephant scalp with the ram's horn of Ammon, and from 297 Lysimachus put the horned, diademed Alexander on silver that circulated for centuries. This horned image matters for the Quran debate below.

The Roman Alexander

  • Scipio Africanus was rumoured, like Alexander, to have been fathered by a serpent (Livy 26.19).
  • Pompeius took the name Magnus and copied Alexander's raised forelock (Plutarch, Pompey 2). At his triumph of 61 he wore a cloak said to be Alexander's (Appian, Mithridatic Wars 117).
  • Caesar, at Gades, wept before Alexander's statue at having achieved nothing at the age by which Alexander had conquered the world (Suetonius, Julius 7). Plutarch (Caesar 11) has him reading a book instead.
  • Antony named his son Alexander Helios and dressed him as a Macedonian at the Donations of Alexandria (Plutarch, Antony 54).
  • Augustus sealed with a sphinx, then with Alexander's head, and then with his own (Suetonius, Augustus 50; Pliny, Natural History 37.10).
  • Trajan, at the Persian Gulf in 116, said he would sail to India were he younger, and sacrificed in the room where Alexander died (Dio 68.29–30).
  • Caracalla raised a "Macedonian phalanx" of 16,000 and persecuted Alexandria's Aristotelians because Aristotle had supposedly poisoned Alexander (Dio 78.7–9; Herodian 4.8).

The moralists pushed back. Livy's digression (9.17–19) argues that Alexander would have lost to Rome's consuls, and it is aimed at Greeks who rated even the Parthians above Rome. Seneca makes Alexander the type of the man ruined by anger and appetite (De ira 3.17; De beneficiis 1.13; Epistles 94.62). Lucan (10.20–46) calls him the mad son of Philip and a fortunate brigand, standing in for Caesar.

Jerusalem, the Quran, Persia, the medieval West

In Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 11.317–345) the high priest Jaddus meets Alexander in white robes. The king bows to the divine name, recognises a figure from his dreams, sacrifices in the Temple and is shown Daniel's prophecy. No Greek historian mentions the visit, and the story is almost universally regarded as a legend that served as a charter for Jewish privileges.

Quran 18:83–98 tells of Dhul-Qarnayn, "the two-horned one", who travels to the setting and the rising sun and builds an iron barrier against Gog and Magog. Most classical exegetes took him to be Alexander. Kevin van Bladel and others point to close parallels with the Syriac Alexander Legend of about 630, in which Alexander builds a gate against the northern peoples.

Where sources disagree. Because Dhul-Qarnayn is a righteous monotheist, many Muslim scholars reject identifying him with a pagan son of Ammon. Abul Kalam Azad and Maududi proposed Cyrus the Great instead, and others decline to name any historical king. Whether the Syriac Legend came before or after the Quranic passage is itself disputed.

Zoroastrian texts such as the Arda Viraz Namag call Alexander "the accursed", the man who burned the Avesta. Firdausi's Shahnameh (around 1010) absorbs him instead. Iskandar is the son of the Persian king Darab by a daughter of Filqus (Philip), which makes him half-brother to Dara, so the conquest becomes a family succession. Nizami's Iskandarnameh (late twelfth century) goes further and makes him conqueror, then philosopher among the Greek sages, then prophet.

The medieval West received him through the Greek Alexander Romance (Pseudo-Callisthenes) in Latin versions by Julius Valerius and Leo of Naples, and through Curtius. Walter of Châtillon's Alexandreis and the Old French Roman d'Alexandre (late twelfth century) made him a chivalric hero who explores the sea in a glass bell and the sky in a griffin-drawn basket. The poem's twelve-syllable line gave French the alexandrine. In Jacques de Longuyon's Vœux du paon (1312) he stands among the Nine Worthies with Hector and Caesar, alongside three Jewish and three Christian heroes.

The modern Alexanders

Droysen (1833; Geschichte des Hellenismus, 1836–43) coined "Hellenism" for a fusion of Greek and Eastern culture that prepared the way for Christianity, and his Macedon unifying Greece looks very like Prussia. Tarn (1926, 1948) made Alexander a visionary of the unity of mankind, built largely on the prayer for homonoia at Opis (Arrian 7.11.9) and on Plutarch's rhetorical On the Fortune of Alexander. Badian demolished that view (Historia, 1958) and portrayed a paranoid autocrat who destroyed his marshals. Bosworth (Conquest and Empire, 1988; Alexander and the East, 1996) documented the massacres in Sogdiana and India. Green (1974) gave a brilliant, ruthless politician. Lane Fox (1973) gave a Homeric romantic driven by longing (pothos). Worthington (2004) stresses drink, megalomania and a drained Macedon. Cartledge (2004) offers a balanced portrait built around the problem of the sources. The post-colonial turn, led by Pierre Briant, makes Alexander "the last of the Achaemenids", who took over Persian structures, and shows how European empires used a civilising Alexander to justify themselves.

Where sources disagree. Tarn wrote amid the internationalism that followed 1918. Badian, a refugee from Nazi Austria, wrote with recent experience of charismatic dictators. Both men read the same Arrian. Current work largely abandons the choice between good and bad Alexander and asks how late sources constructed each portrait.

Oliver Stone's Alexander (2004), with Lane Fox as adviser, is narrated by an aged Ptolemy writing his memoirs, so the film stages the source problem. Greek lawyers threatened to sue over the treatment of Hephaestion.

In the Balkans Alexander became a matter of state. Greece contested the newly independent Macedonia's name and the Vergina Sun on its flag, which was dropped under the 1995 Interim Accord. VMRO-DPMNE governments from 2006 pursued "antiquisation": Skopje's airport was named for Alexander and a huge "Warrior on a Horse" went up in 2011. Rallies in Thessaloniki and Athens in 2018 answered with "Macedonia is Greek". The Prespa Agreement (2018, in force 2019) created North Macedonia. It states that the country's Slavic language and identity are unrelated to ancient Hellenic Macedonia, and the airport and statues were renamed.

Why readers project onto Alexander

The first reason is the sources. Nothing written in Alexander's lifetime survives intact. Ptolemy, Aristobulus, Callisthenes and Cleitarchus reach us through writers three to five centuries later, so every reconstruction means choosing between incompatible witnesses, and the choices reveal the historian making them. The second is the shape of the life. He conquered the known world and died at thirty-two with his plans open, leaving no old age to settle what he was. The third is need. The Successors needed legitimacy, Romans a rival and a warning, Jews a king who bowed to their God, Persians a lost son, Muslims a monotheist builder of walls, knights a model, Droysen a unifier, Tarn a brotherhood, Badian a tyrant, Briant an Achaemenid, and the Balkans an ancestor. With the body lost there is no fixed point, and every age has filled the empty tomb with its own Alexander.

Self-test

  1. What did the Exiles' Decree require, and why did it threaten Athens in particular?
    Answer

    Proclaimed at Olympia in 324, it ordered the Greek cities to take back their exiles, overriding the League of Corinth. Athens would have lost Samos, held by its cleruchs since 365. The decree helped bring on the Lamian War.

  2. On what point do Arrian and Diodorus disagree about Ammon's reply concerning Hephaestion?
    Answer

    Arrian says Ammon allowed hero cult; Diodorus says it allowed worship as a god.

  3. What did the Chaldaeans warn, and what motive did Alexander suspect?
    Answer

    Not to enter Babylon, or not facing west. He suspected they wanted to keep the revenues of the temple of Bel (Marduk) (Arrian 7.16–17).

  4. How have modern scholars interpreted the stranger who sat on Alexander's throne?
    Answer

    As a garbled memory of the Mesopotamian substitute-king ritual (šar pūḫi), in which a stand-in absorbed an evil omen and was then killed. The reading is plausible but uncertain.

  5. Which ancient authors preserve the Ephemerides, and what did Bosworth argue about them?
    Answer

    Arrian (7.25–26) and Plutarch (Alexander 76). Bosworth argued that the account was published early in the Successor period to establish a natural death against the poison rumours.

  6. Why is the Veratrum album hypothesis preferred to strychnine?
    Answer

    White hellebore was known to Greek medicine and produces a slow decline over days. Strychnine kills within hours with convulsions, and none are recorded.

  7. Outline the ancient poisoning story and Arrian's attitude to it.
    Answer

    Antipater sent Cassander with Styx water carried in a mule's hoof; Iolaus the cupbearer gave it to Alexander; some versions say Aristotle advised. Arrian records the story but does not believe it.

  8. Trace the body from Babylon to Alexandria and name one dispute about the route.
    Answer

    The funeral carriage left Babylon in 321 and was diverted by Ptolemy in Syria to Egypt. The body lay at Memphis, then in the Sema at Alexandria. Curtius and Pausanias date the move to Alexandria to Ptolemy II, while Diodorus implies that Ptolemy I took it there directly. Whether the intended destination was Siwa or Aegae is also disputed.

  9. What did Augustus and Caracalla do at the tomb?
    Answer

    Augustus crowned the body and strewed flowers (Suetonius); Dio says he broke off part of the nose. Caracalla left his cloak, rings and belt on the coffin (Herodian 4.8.9).

  10. How does Firdausi make Alexander an Iranian king?
    Answer

    He makes Iskandar the son of the Persian king Darab by a daughter of Philip, and so half-brother to Dara. This turns the conquest into a dynastic succession and reverses the Zoroastrian image of "the accursed".

Carry forward

  1. The stories of the death, including the omens, the journal, "to the strongest" and the poison plot, were shaped by Successor propaganda. Read each first as evidence for who needed it told.
  2. Alexander's corpse and portrait were political property. The pattern runs from Ptolemy's theft of the body and the horned coinage to Roman emperors at the Sema.
  3. Every reception rebuilt Alexander for its own needs, and the modern scholarly Alexanders belong to that history of reception rather than standing outside it.

Written with Opus 5.5 · flagged for Fable 5.1 review (unit 13 audit)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Alexander's death and reception. Cover: the last months (the Exiles' Decree, Hephaestion's funeral, the Arabian plans, the omens at Babylon, the Chaldaeans' warning); the final illness day by day from the Ephemerides tradition, the theories (malaria, typhoid, West Nile, pancreatitis, alcohol, poisoning by Antipater's sons with Aristotle's complicity, strychnine, Veratrum), and the ancient and modern verdicts; the 'to the strongest' story; the body: the embalming, the funeral carriage, Ptolemy's hijacking of it to Memphis and then Alexandria, the Soma, the visits by Caesar, Augustus (the broken nose), Caligula and Caracalla, its disappearance after the fourth century and the modern search; the Successors' use of his image (Ptolemy's coins, Lysimachus' horned Alexander, the Argead name); Alexander as Roman model: Scipio, Pompeius Magnus, Caesar at Gades, Antony, Augustus' seal, Trajan at the Persian Gulf, Caracalla's imitatio, and the Roman moralists (Livy's digression, Seneca, Lucan); Alexander in Jewish tradition (Josephus and the Jerusalem visit), in the Quran (Dhul-Qarnayn and the debate), in Persian epic (Firdausi's Iskandar), in Nizami and in medieval Europe (the Roman d'Alexandre, the Nine Worthies); the modern historians' Alexanders: Droysen's Hellenism, Tarn's idealist, Badian's and Bosworth's tyrant, Green, Lane Fox, Worthington, Cartledge, and the post-colonial reading; Alexander in Stone's film and in Greek and North Macedonian national politics. End with why Alexander remains the ancient figure most readers project onto. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 12 · Deep dive III: Greek philosophy · 12.1 · 3,472 words

The Presocratics

Fragments, testimonia and the making of a canonThe Milesians: arguing for a principleXenophanes and the PythagoreansHeraclitus: the argument behind the riddlesParmenides and ZenoMelissus and the road to atomismEmpedocles and the Strasbourg papyrusAnaxagoras and MindLeucippus and DemocritusThe Derveni papyrus as a reader of philosophySelf-testCarry forward

Fragments, testimonia and the making of a canon

Module 5.6 names the evidence base: Aristotle, Theophrastus, Simplicius and the DK numbers. No Presocratic book survives. What survives is quotation embedded in later authors, each chosen for the quoter's purpose, and summaries of doctrine further removed still.

The first layer is Aristotle. Metaphysics A (983a24–993a27) reads his predecessors as partial discoverers of his own four causes; early philosophy, he says, is like someone lisping (993a15–16). His pupil Theophrastus arranged earlier opinions by topic in the Physical Opinions, lost but for the extract On the Senses and passages in Simplicius. Hermann Diels' Doxographi Graeci (1879) derived the later handbooks from it through Aëtius, probably of the first century AD, whom he reconstructed from the pseudo-Plutarchan Placita and Stobaeus.

The quoters form a second layer. Simplicius, in the sixth century AD, copies out Parmenides at length because, he says, the book has become rare (Commentary on Aristotle's Physics 144.25–28); much of Parmenides, Melissus, Anaxagoras and Empedocles exists only because he did. Hippolytus quotes Heraclitus to convict a Christian heretic of pagan borrowing; Sextus Empiricus quotes Xenophanes and Democritus as ancestors of doubt.

Diels gathered both layers in Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker (1903); Walther Kranz revised it from the fifth edition (1934–37), and the sixth (1951–52) is cited. Each thinker has a chapter (Heraclitus 22, Parmenides 28, Democritus 68) divided into A, testimonia about life and doctrine; B, fragments held to be his own words; and C, imitations. Diels ordered Heraclitus' fragments alphabetically by citing author, so the numbers say nothing about the book's shape. André Laks and Glenn Most's Loeb Early Greek Philosophy (2016) replaces A and B with P (person), D (doctrine) and R (reception), conceding that words and report often blur; DK numbers remain the common currency.

Where sources disagree. Harold Cherniss (Aristotle's Criticism of Presocratic Philosophy, 1935) argued that Aristotle's reports are reconstructions shaped by his own problems, not history; W. K. C. Guthrie ("Aristotle as a Historian of Philosophy", 1957) replied that Aristotle declares his framework openly and his quotations can often be checked. Jaap Mansfeld and David Runia (Aëtiana, from 1997) have also qualified Diels' single Theophrastean stream: the tradition was reworked by many hands, and a report's Theophrastean origin must be argued case by case.

The Milesians: arguing for a principle

Module 5.6 asks why philosophy began in Ionia and gives the core claims: water, the boundless, air, the floating earth, equidistance, condensation and rarefaction.

For Thales there is only Aristotle's guess at an argument. Aristotle says Thales held that water is the principle, perhaps from seeing that the nourishment of all things is moist and that seeds are moist by nature (Metaphysics 983b20–27); the reasons are flagged as conjecture. He also reports that Thales' earth floats on water like wood, and objects that the water then needs a support of its own (On the Heavens 294a28–b1). Anaximander's earth, needing no support, removes the difficulty.

Anaximander's boundless is argued for. Aristotle reports, without naming him, a reason to make the principle something other than the elements: they are opposed, so a boundless one would long since have destroyed the rest (Physics 204b22–29). Elsewhere he says the boundless is ungenerated and imperishable and surrounds and steers all things, as Anaximander and most natural philosophers say (203b6–15). Simplicius, drawing on Theophrastus, preserves the one sentence in Anaximander's words (DK 12 B 1), in which things pay one another penalty for injustice: change is encroachment kept in balance by time, and the source must be neutral among the opposites. Aristotle called the equidistance argument clever but untrue, likening it to the claim that a man equally hungry and thirsty between food and drink must stay put (On the Heavens 295b10–34).

Anaximenes returned to a named stuff for the sake of mechanism. Theophrastus, through Simplicius (Commentary on the Physics 24.26–25.1), reports that air differs by rarity and density: rarefied it is fire; condensed, wind, cloud, water, earth, stone. Plutarch preserves the evidence: breath through pursed lips is cold, from an open mouth warm (On the Principle of Cold 947f; DK 13 B 1). One stuff and one process make every difference quantitative. The cost is Anaximander's worry: what is air when it is stone? Diogenes of Apollonia revived air in the fifth century, arguing that unlike things could neither mix nor act on one another unless all were forms of one substance (DK 64 B 2).

Xenophanes and the Pythagoreans

Module 5.6 gives Xenophanes' attack on Homer's gods (B 11, 15, 16), his one unmoving god (B 23–26), the sea-shells and B 34. The argument beneath B 14–16 is general: if the gods people picture always resemble the picturers, the picture is explained by the believer and is no evidence about its object. That removes the anthropomorphic gods but leaves Xenophanes' own god resting on what is fitting (B 26). B 18 makes inquiry progressive: the gods did not show mortals everything from the beginning, but by searching they find out better in time. B 38 makes perception relative: without honey, men would think figs far sweeter.
