Plato's Eleatic visitor traces the Eleatics back to Xenophanes (Sophist 242d), and Aristotle says Parmenides was said to be his pupil (Metaphysics 986b21–22): the undivided god became a template for what-is. Sextus quotes B 34 as an early statement of sceptical doubt (Against the Mathematicians 7.49), a line module 12.8 follows.

For Pythagoras module 5.6 gives transmigration, number and the dispute between Burkert and Zhmud. Plato names him once, as founder of a way of life (Republic 600a–b); Heraclitus says he practised inquiry beyond all men and made a wisdom of his own, much learning and bad craft (B 129); Aristotle's treatises speak almost always of the so-called Pythagoreans. The lives by Porphyry and Iamblichus are Neoplatonic hagiography. Iamblichus (On the General Mathematical Science 76) records a split between akousmatikoi, who kept the oral rules, and mathematikoi, who claimed the science and whose teaching, the former said, came from Hippasus.

Philolaus of Croton (c. 470–c. 385), whom Cebes and Simmias had heard at Thebes (Phaedo 61d–e), is the first Pythagorean whose words survive, and he argues in Eleatic terms. Nature was fitted together from unlimiteds and limiters (DK 44 B 1). Things are all limiting, all unlimited, or both (B 2); were all unlimited, nothing could be known (B 3); so both. Being unlike, they could not be ordered unless a harmonia came upon them (B 6), given by the octave ratios 2:1, 3:2, 4:3. Everything known has number, since without it nothing could be thought or known (B 4). Aristotle, who names Philolaus only once, reports of the Pythagoreans a central fire (On the Heavens 293a20–b1) circled by ten bodies, the tenth a counter-earth invented to reach the perfect ten (Metaphysics 986a8–12), and objects that heavy bodies cannot be built from weightless numbers (1090a30–35); later doxography (Aëtius 2.7.7) gives the system to Philolaus. Plato's Philebus (16c) takes over limit and unlimited (module 12.3).

Where sources disagree. Ingram Bywater ("On the Fragments Attributed to Philolaus the Pythagorean", 1868) showed that some fragments under Philolaus' name were spurious and inferred that all were. Burkert (Weisheit und Wissenschaft, 1962; English 1972) argued for a genuine core, now generally put at about eleven fragments (B 1–7, 6a, 13, 16, 17) and defended by Carl Huffman (Philolaus of Croton, 1993); the two still differ over B 6b and some testimonia.

Heraclitus: the argument behind the riddles

Module 5.6 gives the logos, the road, sea water, fire in measures, strife, the rivers and the flux dispute. The unity of opposites is several claims. Some opposites belong to one thing for different subjects: sea water is life to fish, death to men (B 61); donkeys prefer rubbish to gold (B 9). Some belong to one thing under different aspects: the road (B 60), the carding-comb's path straight and crooked (B 59). Some succeed one another and so are the same: living and dead, waking and sleeping, young and old (B 88). Some give each other value: disease makes health sweet (B 111); men would not know the name of Justice without injustice (B 23).

The conclusion is structural: a thing at variance agrees with itself, a back-turning harmony as of bow and lyre (B 51), whose opposed pulls make the instrument. Fire is the paradigm because it lives by consuming, and its turnings (B 31) and the soul's death into water (B 36) make cosmic and personal economy one. He prefers what is seen and heard (B 55), but eyes and ears are bad witnesses for those with barbarian souls (B 107), who cannot read the language they report.

Aristotle reports that some think Heraclitus says the same thing is and is not, and replies that nobody can believe it (Metaphysics 1005b23–26). His follower Cratylus, Aristotle adds, rebuked him for saying one cannot step twice into the same river, since one cannot do so once, and ended by only moving his finger (1010a10–15); Plato learned the Heraclitean view of sensible things from Cratylus (987a32–b1). The Stoics took his fire for their physics (module 12.7).

Where sources disagree. Parmenides scorns two-headed mortals for whom being and not-being are the same and not the same, and whose path is back-turning (DK 28 B 6.4–9). Jacob Bernays (1850) read this as an answer to Heraclitus' back-turning harmony, as Daniel Graham (2002) still does; Karl Reinhardt (Parmenides und die Geschichte der griechischen Philosophie, 1916) made Heraclitus the later thinker, and Eduard Zeller and Jaap Mansfeld (1964) held that neither knew the other. The echo hangs on a reading: Hippolytus (Refutation 9.9.2) gives B 51 as palintropos, Plutarch (On Isis and Osiris 369b) as palintonos.

Parmenides and Zeno

Module 5.6 gives the central inference, the Doxa and the monism dispute. B 8 shows how the deductions run. Against generation there are two arguments: coming-to-be from what is not cannot be said or thought (B 8.7–9); and what need would have roused it to grow later rather than sooner, starting from nothing (B 8.9–10)? The second is the principle of sufficient reason module 5.6 finds in Anaximander. So it must be wholly or not at all (B 8.11). It is indivisible because all alike (B 8.22–25), unmoving because Necessity holds it in bonds (B 8.26–31), complete like a well-rounded sphere (B 8.42–49). B 7 bids the hearer judge by reasoning (logos), not by aimless eye and echoing ear: reason against sense begins here.

What "is" means is the crux: existence, predication, or truth, the last Charles Kahn's reading (The Verb "Be" in Ancient Greek, 1973). On any reading every Milesian principle, becoming what it was not, is ruled out. Plato's Eleatic visitor answers with parricide, showing that what is not, as what is different, in a way is (Sophist 241d–259b; module 12.3). Aristotle answered that Parmenides took "is" to be said in one way when it is said in many (Physics 186a24–25), and that things come to be from a privation in a persisting subject, not from what is not without qualification (191a23–b34).

Zeno's purpose is stated in Plato's Parmenides (128c–e): his youthful book answered those who mocked Parmenides by showing that plurality led to worse absurdities. Module 5.6 gives the motion paradoxes and B 1–2. Two more show the method: if everything is in a place, place too will be in a place, without end (Aristotle, Physics 209a23–25); a bushel of millet makes a sound when poured, a single grain none (250a19–22). Aristotle first answered the Dichotomy by making time divisible like distance (233a21–31), then conceded that this answers the questioner, not the problem, and distinguished potential from actual division (263a4–b9). Convergent series show that the halves sum to a finite distance; whether that explains how a runner completes infinitely many tasks is still argued. The Arrow led Bertrand Russell (The Principles of Mathematics, 1903) to define motion as being at different places at different times, and nothing more.

Where sources disagree. Paul Tannery (1885) argued that Zeno's target was a Pythagorean number-atomism that built bodies from units with magnitude, and F. M. Cornford and, in Pythagoreans and Eleatics (1948), J. E. Raven built on it. G. E. L. Owen ("Zeno and the Mathematicians", 1958) showed that no early evidence attests such a doctrine and read Zeno as attacking plurality as everyone assumed it; most now follow Owen.

Melissus and the road to atomism

Melissus of Samos commanded the fleet that beat an Athenian squadron in the Samian revolt of 441/0 (Plutarch, Pericles 26). His prose, preserved by Simplicius, restates Parmenides as a plain chain, and changes it. Whatever is always was, since nothing comes from nothing (DK 30 B 1); without beginning or end it is boundless in magnitude (B 2–3), not a bounded sphere; if boundless, it is one, since two would limit each other (B 6). There is no void, for void is nothing; without void nothing moves, having nowhere to give way (B 7.7–10). And if there were many things, each would have to be as the One is; but we see hot become cold and iron worn away, so we did not see rightly (B 8).

Aristotle thought him crude (Metaphysics 986b26–27) and caught a fallacy: from "what came to be has a beginning" he infers "what did not come to be has none" (Physics 186a10–16). His clarity mattered more. B 8 states the condition a pluralist must meet, B 7 ties motion to void, and Aristotle's account of Leucippus (On Generation and Corruption 325a2–b5) takes both premises and reverses the conclusion: motion is evident, so there is void, and the many are uncuttable ones moving in it. The pseudo-Aristotelian treatise that preserves one version of Gorgias' On Not Being sets him beside Melissus and Xenophanes (module 12.2).

Empedocles and the Strasbourg papyrus

Module 5.6 gives the roots, Love and Strife, the wandering limbs, the pores, the exiled daimon and the ban on flesh. The answer to Parmenides is explicit: there is no birth of any mortal thing nor end in death, only mixing and exchange, and birth is a name men give (DK 31 B 8); nothing of the whole is empty or overfull (B 13). Kinds are fixed by ratio: bone is two parts earth, two water, four fire (B 96), which Aristotle read as a glimpse of form (Parts of Animals 642a17–24). Like knows like: by earth we see earth, by water water (B 109, quoted at On the Soul 404b11–15).

Aristotle objected that Love often separates and Strife combines (Metaphysics 985a21–29), and that a zoogony in which chance combinations survived if fit, like the man-faced ox-progeny (B 61), cannot explain why nature produces its results always or for the most part (Physics 198b16–199a8); hence final causes. Lucretius (Rome module 5.6) praised Empedocles as a poet (1.716–733) before dismantling his roots.

The Strasbourg papyrus is a roll copied in the late first century AD, whose strips were folded to back the bronze leaves of a funerary crown and bought at Akhmim, ancient Panopolis, in 1904. Alain Martin recognised Empedocles in 1990; he and Oliver Primavesi published L'Empédocle de Strasbourg in 1999. One group overlaps the end of B 17 and continues it, a marginal sign placing the quoted passage's end at line 300 of the first book. Another, ensemble d, sets the lament of B 139 for dreadful deeds done for food inside the physical narrative. Module 5.6 gives what that does to the two-poem question; the cycle's shape is a separate fight.

Where sources disagree. Denis O'Brien (Empedocles' Cosmic Cycle, 1969) and M. R. Wright (Empedocles: The Extant Fragments, 1981) reconstruct a symmetrical cycle with two cosmogonies and two zoogonies, one as Love advances and one as Strife does; Jean Bollack (Empédocle, 1965–69) and A. A. Long ("Empedocles' Cosmic Cycle in the 'Sixties'", 1974) allow one world and one zoogony. Simon Trépanier ("Empedocles on the Ultimate Symmetry of the World", 2003) reads ensemble d as a zoogony under Strife distinct from the one under Love; André Laks (2001) doubts that the fragments can bear that weight.

Anaxagoras and Mind

Module 5.6 gives no coming-to-be (B 17), everything in everything (B 11), Mind (B 12), the trial and the Phaedo. The argument for B 11 starts from nutrition: how could hair come from what is not hair, or flesh from what is not flesh (B 10)? If bread becomes flesh and nothing comes from nothing, flesh was in the bread. Infinite divisibility, Zeno's weapon against plurality, becomes a premise: there is no smallest, always a smaller (B 3), so the portions never run out, and each thing is most manifestly what it has most of (B 12). Mind alone is unmixed, by argument: mixed with anything, it would share in everything and be hindered from controlling anything (B 12).

Aristotle praised him as a sober man among random talkers for making Mind a cause (Metaphysics 984b15–18), then complained that he wheels Mind in only when at a loss (985a18–21), and objected that infinitely many ingredients make everything unknowable (Physics 1.4, 187a26–188a18). Aristotle's term for the stuffs, homoiomerē, like-parted (On Generation and Corruption 314a18–20), is not in the fragments. Diogenes Laertius says Anaxagoras foretold the stone that fell at Aegospotami (2.10), which Pliny dates to 467 (Natural History 2.149).

Leucippus and Democritus

Module 5.6 gives atoms and void, convention against reality (B 9), the senses' reply (B 125) and the indivisibility dispute. Aristotle makes atomism an Eleatic settlement (On Generation and Corruption 325a2–b5): Leucippus granted that motion needs void and that void is what-is-not, but held motion evident, and concluded that what-is-not exists no less than what-is. Democritus coined a word for it: "den" is no more than nothing (Plutarch, Against Colotes 1108f–1109a; DK 68 B 156). Each atom has the properties of Melissus' One, and there are infinitely many. Aristotle reports an argument for indivisibility (316a14–b16): divide a body through and through; what remains is either magnitudes, still divisible, or points or nothing, from which no body can be composed; so there are uncuttable bodies.

Leucippus' one fragment says nothing happens at random, but everything for a reason and by necessity (DK 67 B 2). Aristotle objected that the atomists lazily set aside where motion comes from (Metaphysics 985b19–20); Theophrastus examined point by point Democritus' theory of perception, in which tastes follow atomic shapes (On the Senses 49–83). The ethical sayings, mostly from Stobaeus (B 169–297), make the goal euthymia, settled cheerfulness through measure (B 191); whether they connect to the physics, as Gregory Vlastos argued (1945–46), is uncertain. Epicurus revised the system (module 12.6).

Where sources disagree. Sextus (Against the Mathematicians 7.135–139) quotes B 9 and its kin to make Democritus a forerunner of doubt; Diogenes Laertius (9.72) gives B 117, that in reality we know nothing, for truth is in the depth; and Metrodorus of Chios said none of us knows anything (DK 70 B 1). But Sextus also quotes B 11, which ranks a legitimate knowledge, reached by reasoning finer than the senses, above their bastard kind, and Aristotle took Democritus to equate thought with perception and so make appearance true (Metaphysics 1009b11–17).

The Derveni papyrus as a reader of philosophy

Modules 2.1 and 8.2 give the Derveni papyrus' Orphic theogony, the aidoion dispute and the roll's survival on a pyre near Thessaloniki. Here the point is the commentator, writing about 400 BC or a little earlier, as the oldest surviving reader of philosophy. He treats the poem as riddling and decodes it into physics: Zeus becomes air and Mind, the swallowing a gathering of matter, Moira the god's thought. The physics is Anaxagorean, Mind arranging particles separated from a prior mixture, and in places close to Diogenes of Apollonia's intelligent air. Column IV quotes Heraclitus on the sun, the width of a human foot, kept within its measures by the Erinyes, overlapping DK 22 B 3 and B 94: since the roll is the oldest surviving Greek book, this is the oldest manuscript witness to any Presocratic, and proof that Heraclitus was already a text cited in argument.

Where sources disagree. Walter Burkert (1986) proposed Stesimbrotus of Thasos as the author, Charles Kahn (1997) Euthyphro, the seer of Plato's dialogue, and Richard Janko ("The Physicist as Hierophant", 1997) Diagoras of Melos, the notorious atheist, reading the allegory as a physicist's demythologising. Gábor Betegh (The Derveni Papyrus: Cosmology, Theology and Interpretation, 2004) argues instead for an Orphic priest who used physics to explain the rites he performed.

Self-test

  1. Why must Aristotle's account of Thales at Metaphysics 983b20–27 be read in two layers?
    Answer

    Aristotle reports that Thales held water to be the principle, but the reasons (moist nourishment, moist seeds) are his own conjecture, marked "perhaps", and the frame of a material cause is his too. Thales left no words of his own.

  2. What do A and B mean in a DK reference, and why did Laks and Most abandon the division?
    Answer

    A marks testimonia, reports about a thinker's life and doctrine; B marks fragments held to be his own words. Laks and Most (2016) use P, D and R instead because the line between quotation and paraphrase is often unclear.

  3. Reconstruct the argument Aristotle reports for a principle distinct from the elements, and say why its attribution needs care.
    Answer

    The elements are opposed, so a boundless one would destroy the others; the source must therefore be something neutral (Physics 204b22–29). Aristotle does not name Anaximander there; the attribution is inferred.

  4. How does Philolaus argue that the cosmos is made of both limiters and unlimiteds, and what binds them?
    Answer

    Things are all limiting, all unlimited, or both (B 2); were all unlimited, nothing could be known (B 3); so both. Being unlike, they need a harmonia to be ordered, given by the octave ratios (B 6).

  5. Sort Heraclitus B 61, B 59, B 88 and B 111 by the kind of unity of opposites each shows.
    Answer

    B 61: one thing, opposite effects for different subjects (sea water). B 59: one thing under different aspects (the comb's straight and crooked path). B 88: opposites that succeed one another (living and dead). B 111: opposites that give each other value (disease and health).

  6. State Parmenides' two arguments against generation in B 8 and name the principle behind the second.
    Answer

    Coming-to-be from what is not cannot be said or thought (B 8.7–9); and nothing explains why what-is should start from nothing at one time rather than another (B 8.9–10). The second is a principle of sufficient reason.

  7. What was Aristotle's first answer to the Dichotomy, and why did he later call it inadequate?
    Answer

    That time is infinitely divisible like distance, so infinitely many stages are crossed in infinitely many moments (Physics 233a21–31). He later said this answers the questioner, not the problem, and appealed to the difference between potential and actual division (263a4–b9).

  8. Which two Melissan premises did the atomists take over, and how did they reverse his conclusion?
    Answer

    That motion requires void (B 7) and that each of many things would have to be like the Eleatic One (B 8). Holding motion evident, Leucippus inferred that void exists and made the many into uncuttable, unchanging atoms (On Generation and Corruption 325a2–b5).

  9. What do Aristotle's objections to Empedocles' zoogony and to Anaxagoras' Mind have in common?
    Answer

    Both fault the absence of a working final cause: chance survival cannot explain why nature achieves its results always or for the most part (Physics 198b16–199a8), and Anaxagoras introduces Mind but uses it only as a device when at a loss (Metaphysics 985a18–21).

  10. Why does the Derveni papyrus matter for the history of philosophy apart from its theogony?
    Answer

    Its commentator, writing about 400 BC, decodes the poem into Anaxagorean physics and quotes Heraclitus (column IV, overlapping B 3 and B 94), so it shows Presocratic texts being read and cited within the fifth century, in the oldest manuscript witness to any of them.

Carry forward

  1. Every Presocratic sentence reaches us through a reporter with a purpose: Aristotle's four causes, Simplicius' commentary, Hippolytus' heresy-hunting, Sextus' scepticism. Name the reporter and separate B words from A reports before arguing about doctrine.
  2. The Presocratics form a chain of arguments, not of guesses: each accepts most of a predecessor's premises and denies one, as the atomists took Melissus' void premise and reversed it. To understand a position, find the premise it rejects.
  3. Parmenides' rules (nothing from nothing, reason over the senses, no change without sufficient reason) set the terms for Plato's Sophist, Aristotle's Physics and the Hellenistic schools, and the Derveni commentator's habit of reading old poems as coded physics runs on into Stoic allegory.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Presocratic philosophers, extending module 5.6, which already gives each thinker's core claim with his key fragments, Parmenides' central inference, Zeno's four paradoxes of motion, the evidence base (Aristotle, Theophrastus, Simplicius, DK numbers) and the disputes over Pythagoras, Heraclitus' flux, Parmenides' monism and the Strasbourg papyrus, and asks why philosophy began in Ionia: point back to it for each, and give each thinker the full argument, the objections it met and what the next thinker made of it. Cover: the Milesians (Thales, Anaximander, Anaximenes); Xenophanes; Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans, with Philolaus; Heraclitus; Parmenides, Zeno's paradoxes and Melissus; Empedocles; Anaxagoras; Leucippus and Democritus; and the evidence problem: fragments and doxography (Aristotle, Metaphysics A; Theophrastus; Simplicius), Diels' Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker and the DK numbering, the Derveni papyrus as a witness to early philosophical reading (modules 2.1 and 8.2 cover its Orphic theogony: point back), and the Strasbourg Empedocles. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 12 · Deep dive III: Greek philosophy · 12.2 · 3,357 words

The Sophists and Socrates

Protagoras: the measure tested in the TheaetetusGorgias: On Not Being and the HelenProdicus, Hippias and ThrasymachusAntiphon's On Truth and the Dissoi LogoiWhich Socrates? The four witnesses weighedElenchus, paradoxes, irony and the signThe trial continued: Polycrates, Xenophon and the two ApologiesThe Crito and the Phaedo: Plato's portrait of the deathThe Socratic dialogue as a genreSelf-testCarry forward

Protagoras: the measure tested in the Theaetetus

Module 6.5 gives Protagoras' three fragments (DK 80 B 1, B 4, B 6a) and the Great Speech of Plato's Protagoras, whose myth module 2.4 reads against Hesiod. Of the book one sentence survives. Plato calls it Truth (Theaetetus 161c); Sextus says the measure sentence opened the Overthrowing Arguments (Against the Mathematicians 7.60). Its word hōs can mean "that" or "how": man measures that things are, or how they are. The fullest interpretation is Plato's.

The Theaetetus takes it up because Theaetetus' definition, knowledge is perception (151e), is the same claim: as each thing appears to me, so it is for me, and the wind is cold for the man who shivers and not for the other (152a–c). To make perception infallible, Socrates attaches a "secret doctrine" that Protagoras supposedly told only his pupils (152c–e): nothing is anything in itself, all things come to be from motion, and perception and its object are twin offspring of meeting motions, so that no two perceptions share an object (156a–157c).

After jibes he withdraws as unfair (why not a pig as the measure; why charge fees if no one is wiser, 161c–e), Socrates composes a Defence of Protagoras (166a–168c), the most generous Sophist in Plato. The wise man replaces not false beliefs, since none are false, but worse appearances with better, as a doctor alters a sick man's taste with drugs; whatever seems just to a city is just for it while it holds to it (167c). Then the reversal (170a–171c): most people think Protagoras wrong; on his principle their belief is true for them; so he must grant his own doctrine false. Protagoras, Socrates jokes, would pop up from the ground to the neck to protest (171d). The decisive objection is the future (177c–179b): whether a thing will prove healthy or advantageous is judged better by doctor or legislator than by layman, so not everyone is a measure. Last, extreme flux would make all speech impossible (181c–183c). The Cratylus (385e–386a) compresses the case: if things are for each as they appear, no one is wiser or worse than another, so things must have a stable being of their own (386d–e).

Where sources disagree. Plato's Theaetetus relativises truth to each judge; Sextus (Against the Mathematicians 7.389–390, crediting the reversal to Democritus and Plato) and Aristotle (Metaphysics 4.5, 1009a6–15) read Protagoras as saying every appearance is simply true. Burnyeat (Philosophical Review, 1976) argued that the later tradition flattened Plato's relativist into an infallibilist, and that the reversal still catches a relativist who asserts his doctrine to others. Fine (1998) reads Plato's Protagoras as an infallibilist throughout, since the qualifiers Socrates drops at 171a–c would otherwise make the refutation a cheap win.

Gorgias: On Not Being and the Helen

Gorgias' treatise survives in two paraphrases. Sextus (Against the Mathematicians 7.65–87; DK 82 B 3) titles it On Not-Being, or On Nature and casts it as an attack on the criterion of truth. The pseudo-Aristotelian On Melissus, Xenophanes and Gorgias (MXG 979a11–980b21), badly transmitted, adds critical comment and says Gorgias borrowed from Melissus and Zeno (979b). Behind module 6.5's three theses lie these arguments.

  1. Nothing is. If anything is, it is what-is, or what-is-not, or both. What-is-not is not, and nothing can be both (7.75–76). What-is is eternal or generated: if eternal it has no beginning, so is unlimited, and the unlimited is nowhere; if generated, it came from what-is or what-is-not, and neither is possible (Sextus 7.66–76).
  2. If anything is, it cannot be known. If things thought were things that are, a chariot racing on the sea would exist because someone thinks of it; and Scylla and Chimaera, which are not, are thought (Sextus 7.79–80; MXG 980a9–12).
  3. If known, it cannot be communicated. Speech is not the things it signifies; as sight does not hear sounds, speech cannot convey colours (Sextus 7.83–86). The MXG adds that one thing cannot be in two minds at once (980b).

This is Eleatic logic turned on Eleatic conclusions: Parmenides (module 12.1) exhausted the alternatives to reach one changeless being; Gorgias exhausts them to reach none.

Where sources disagree. Isocrates (Helen 3) treats "nothing exists" as a thesis Gorgias dared to maintain. Heinrich Gomperz (1912) read the treatise as a rhetorical jest, a parody of Eleatic dialectic with no place in the history of philosophy; since Calogero (1932) most readers take it as a serious argument about being, thought and language. Which paraphrase is closer is also argued: Caston (2002) holds that Sextus recasts the work as epistemology and misreads its logical form, which the MXG keeps, while granting Sextus' versions of single arguments their value.

The Encomium of Helen (DK 82 B 11) is the other half. Helen went to Troy by the will of gods and Necessity, or by force, or persuaded by speech, or conquered by love (6); on each hypothesis she is blameless. Speech acts on the soul as drugs act on the body, some curing, some killing (14), so persuasion is a form of compulsion and the persuaded are as innocent as the forced. The speech ends by calling itself Gorgias' plaything (paignion, 21). Plutarch preserves the matching view of tragedy: a deception in which the deceiver is more just than the non-deceiver, and the deceived wiser than the undeceived (On the Glory of the Athenians 5, 348c; DK 82 B 23). Beside On Not Being the position is coherent: if speech does not convey things, it works by effects, and the orator makes states of soul. Plato's Gorgias attacks exactly this: rhetoric produces conviction without teaching (454e–455a), and Gorgias, pressed, concedes he will teach justice to a pupil who lacks it (460a).

Prodicus, Hippias and Thrasymachus

Prodicus of Ceos sold the correctness of names. Plato's Socrates says he could afford only the one-drachma lecture, not the fifty-drachma course (Cratylus 384b). In the Protagoras he is called in to split "to become" from "to be" in Simonides' poem (340b–c), and Socrates, teasing, gets him to gloss Simonides' "hard" as "bad" (341a–c); the Laches calls him the best of the Sophists at distinguishing names (197d). The chorus of the Clouds heeds no sky-theorist but Prodicus, for his wisdom, and Socrates, for his swagger (360–363): the audience of 423 classed the two together.

Hippias of Elis came to Olympia, in Plato's telling, wearing nothing he had not made himself, from ring to belt, with epics and tragedies in his baggage (Hippias Minor 368b–d). His Collection (DK 86 B 6) gathered sayings of poets and prose writers by theme, perhaps the first anthology of earlier opinions. Xenophon gives him his best argument: how can laws be serious when their makers repeal them (Memorabilia 4.4.14)? Socrates answers with unwritten laws, such as honouring gods and parents, that hold everywhere and punish their breakers by themselves (4.4.19–24), adding divine law to module 6.5's nomos and physis.

Thrasymachus of Chalcedon was for Aristotle a stylist of rhythm and pity (Rhetoric 3.1, 1404a14; 3.8, 1409a2). Republic 1 makes him a theorist whose thesis hardens under pressure: the ruler, strictly speaking, never errs about his advantage (340d–341a); the shepherd fattens sheep for himself (343b); the perfectly unjust tyrant is happiest (344a–c). Socrates answers with craft analogies: every craft serves its object (341c–342e), and even thieves need justice among themselves (351c–352a). Thrasymachus blushes (350d), but Glaucon thinks him charmed rather than refuted (358b), which is why the Republic continues (module 12.3).

Antiphon's On Truth and the Dissoi Logoi

Antiphon's ethical argument survives in his own words on Oxyrhynchus papyri (P.Oxy. 1364 and 1797, with P.Oxy. 3647): DK 87 B 44. Module 6.5 states the central claim and the identity dispute; the argument is more careful than the slogan. Justice is defined conventionally, as not transgressing the laws of one's city. Law's demands are agreed, nature's necessary. Break a law unseen and you escape shame and penalty; strain against nature and the harm is the same seen or unseen, for one is harmed "not through opinion but through truth". Hence the title. The later columns turn to the victim: the man who only defends himself, or treats bad parents well, suffers more, and the law neither prevents the wrong nor gives him more persuasive power in court than his injurer. P.Oxy. 1797 makes a paradox of it: if justice is not wronging one who has not wronged you, the truthful witness against a harmless neighbour does injustice by obeying the law. Gagarin (Antiphon the Athenian, 2002) reads the whole as an exploration of problems in nomos, not a recommendation of crime; the immoralist Antiphon, kin to Plato's Callicles, rests on the first column alone.

The Dissoi Logoi (DK 90), "Twofold Arguments", is an anonymous Doric treatise preserved at the end of manuscripts of Sextus Empiricus. It cites the Spartan victory over Athens and her allies (1.8), so it is later than 404. It argues both sides of paired terms (good and bad, seemly and shameful, just and unjust, true and false), then asks whether virtue can be taught and attacks election by lot: Protagoras' two opposed arguments in classroom form. Death is bad for the dying and good for undertakers (1.3). If every people brought its shameful customs to one heap and took away what it thought seemly, nothing would be left (2.18), an argument out of Herodotus 3.38. It shows Sophistic method written by someone other than Plato.

Which Socrates? The four witnesses weighed

Module 6.5 introduces the four witnesses; here each is weighed. Of the four, Aristophanes alone wrote in Socrates' lifetime. The Clouds (423, later partly revised; plot in module 6.4) gives him a Thinkery, a basket in which he walks on air and contemplates the sun (225), experiments on the flea's leap (144–152) and the god Vortex in place of Zeus (380–381). Plato's Apology answers this picture by name (19c), denying that Socrates studied the heavens or took fees (19c–20c). Yet Plato's own Socrates admits a youthful keenness for natural inquiry (Phaedo 96a–99d). Dover's edition of the Clouds (1968) argued that Aristophanes built a composite intellectual from natural philosophers, Sophists and ascetics and gave it Socrates' face; the Frogs (1491–1499) still treats sitting chattering beside Socrates as a fashion.

Xenophon, born about 430, was in Asia with Cyrus' army at the trial, wrote decades later in exile, and claims to have attended conversations he was too young for (Symposium 1.1, set in 422). His Socrates is pious, practical and self-mastered. Russell's quip that a stupid man's report of a clever man is never accurate (A History of Western Philosophy, 1945) is the old prejudice; the better objection is that Xenophon writes apologetic and selects. Plato, about twenty-eight in 399, gave Socrates views that change between dialogues. Aristotle, born in 384, adds to module 6.5's universal definitions the inductive arguments (Metaphysics 13.4, 1078b27–29), the intellectualism (virtues are forms of knowledge, Nicomachean Ethics 6.13, 1144b17–30) and the questioning without answers, "for he confessed he did not know" (Sophistical Refutations 34, 183b7–8). But his "Socrates" in Politics 2.1 (1261a6) is explicitly the speaker of Plato's Republic: Aristotle too sometimes reports a character.

Where sources disagree. Burnet and A. E. Taylor held that Plato's Socrates, even the Socrates of the Phaedo and Republic with his Forms, was the historical man; Gigon (Sokrates, 1947) answered that every Socratic writing is fiction and the man irrecoverable. Schleiermacher's criterion stands between: ask what Socrates must have been, beyond Xenophon's portrait, to make Plato's possible. Aristotle's statement that the separated Forms were Plato's, not Socrates' (Metaphysics 1.6, 987b1–10; 13.4, 1078b30–32), weighs against Burnet and Taylor.

Elenchus, paradoxes, irony and the sign

The elenchus has rules. The answerer must say what he really believes (Crito 49c–d; Gorgias 495a–b), because a life is under examination, not a thesis; and one witness suffices, the opponent himself (Gorgias 472b–c). To the problem of the elenchus that module 6.5 notes, Vlastos (Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy, 1983) gave his own answer: Socrates assumes that anyone holding a false moral belief also holds true beliefs entailing its negation.

The paradoxes are conclusions of arguments. No one does wrong willingly: no one wants to be miserable, so whoever pursues the bad mistakes it for good (Meno 77b–78b). The Protagoras (352a–358d) argues it against the many: grant that the pleasant is the good, and "overcome by pleasure" means doing bad knowingly because overcome by the good, which is absurd; the real fault is mismeasuring near and distant pleasures, cured by an art of measurement (356c–357b). Irwin (Plato's Moral Theory, 1977) took the hedonism as Socrates' own; the Gorgias (495a–499b), refuting Callicles' identification of pleasure and good, is the main text against. Virtue is knowledge: health and wealth benefit only when wisdom uses them, so virtue, which always benefits, is wisdom (Meno 87c–89a). Doing injustice is worse than suffering it: Polus grants it is more shameful; the shameful is so by pain or harm; it is not more painful; so it is more harmful (Gorgias 474c–475e). Aristotle named the weak joint: the denial of weakness of will conflicts with what plainly appears (Nicomachean Ethics 7.2, 1145b21–28).

Irony. Attic eirōneia meant sly dissembling; eirōn is among the rogue's names Strepsiades will answer to (Clouds 449). Thrasymachus calls Socrates' ignorance his habitual irony (Republic 337a); Alcibiades says he spends his life being ironic (Symposium 216e). Aristotle makes him the graceful self-deprecator (Nicomachean Ethics 4.7, 1127b22–26). Vlastos (1991) called it complex irony: the disavowal is true of certain knowledge and false of the tested beliefs he lives by.

The sign. Plato's Socrates has a voice that always turns him back and never urges him on (Apology 31c–d), and which was silent on the day of the trial, proof that death is no evil (40a–c). Euthyphro (3b) and Xenophon (Memorabilia 1.1.2) link it to the "new divinities" of the charge.

Where sources disagree. Plato's sign only forbids. Xenophon's also commands: it told Socrates what to do and what not to do, and friends who followed its advice profited (Memorabilia 1.1.4). In Xenophon it forbids him to prepare a defence (Apology 4; Memorabilia 4.8.5), where Plato's is silent. Xenophon's sign is a private oracle; Plato's is a check on a reasoner.

The trial continued: Polycrates, Xenophon and the two Apologies

Module 6.5 gives the indictment, the vote and the amnesty argument. The fight over Socrates' memory continued in pamphlets. The rhetorician Polycrates published an Accusation of Socrates, now lost. Its charges are recovered from Xenophon's replies to "the accuser" (Memorabilia 1.2.9–64) and from Isocrates, who mocks Polycrates for making Alcibiades Socrates' pupil when no one had noticed (Busiris 5). They were political: contempt for election by lot (1.2.9), Hesiod's line that no work is a disgrace read as licence for crime (1.2.56), and the training of Critias and Alcibiades (1.2.12).

Where sources disagree. Hermippus, quoted by Diogenes Laertius (2.38), says Polycrates wrote the prosecution speech for the trial; others, Diogenes adds, gave it to Anytus. Favorinus (2.39) showed it was later, since it mentions Conon's rebuilding of the walls six years after Socrates' death. Most moderns follow Favorinus and take Polycrates as Xenophon's accuser; how far his charges echo what was said in 399 is uncertain.

Xenophon's answer on Critias and Alcibiades (1.2.12–48) concedes the facts: Critias was the greediest and most violent of the oligarchs, Alcibiades the most insolent of the democrats. Both, he argues, came to Socrates for power, behaved well while with him, and left once they thought themselves his superiors (1.2.14–16, 1.2.39). Socrates called Critias' pursuit of Euthydemus swinish (1.2.29–30); Critias, as one of the Thirty, banned the teaching of the art of words and with Charicles forbade Socrates to talk with the young (1.2.31–38). Alcibiades, not yet twenty, questioned Pericles until he admitted that what the majority imposes on the rich by force is violence, not law (1.2.40–46): he had learned argument and used it like a Sophist.

The two Apologies differ in kind. Plato's is a three-part speech by a writer who places himself in court (34a, 38b). Xenophon's is a short memoir from Hermogenes' report (Apology 2), written to explain the boastful tone: Socrates had decided that death now was better than old age (5–9). Plato's oracle says no one is wiser than Socrates (21a), launching a mission of examination; Xenophon's that no one is more free, more just or more sensible (Apology 14), a verdict on character. Plato's Socrates proposes free meals, then a fine; Xenophon's refuses any counter-penalty (23). Plato alone gives the argument that death is dreamless sleep or a journey to the dead, either a gain (40c–41c).

The Crito and the Phaedo: Plato's portrait of the death

The Crito opens before dawn, the ship from Delos sighted off Sunium (43c–d). Socrates answers Crito's pleas from two principles: heed the expert, not the many (47a–48a), and never return wrong for wrong, a view few hold (49a–e). Then the Laws speak (50a–54d): they begot and educated him; he must persuade them or obey (51b–c); by staying seventy years he agreed to their terms (52b–53a); escape would confirm the verdict (53b–c). The Apology's promise to disobey an order to stop philosophising (29c–d) sits uneasily with this; Kraut (Socrates and the State, 1984) reconciles them by reading "persuade" as leaving room for disobedience by one who argues his case before the city.

The Phaedo is Phaedo's report to Echecrates at Phlius (57a). Among the absent Phaedo notes that Plato, he thinks, was ill (59b), one of three places where Plato names himself. The proofs of immortality belong to module 12.3, the closing myth to module 8.4. The death scene (115b–118a) enacts the argument that philosophy is practice for dying (64a). Asked how he wants to be buried, Socrates says however they like, if they can catch him (115c); the jailer weeps (116b–d); he declines to wait for sunset (116e–117a) and rebukes his friends' tears (117d). Phaedo calls him the best, wisest and most just man of his time (118a). Nietzsche read the last words as a confession that life is a sickness (The Gay Science 340); Most (Classical Quarterly, 1993) tied the cock for Asclepius to Plato's illness.

Where sources disagree. Gill ("The Death of Socrates", Classical Quarterly, 1973) argued that Plato idealised the death, since hemlock poisoning is normally more violent than the quiet, rising numbness of the Phaedo. Bloch (2001) answered that Conium maculatum produces exactly the peripheral paralysis Plato describes. Accurate or not, the scene is chosen for its meaning: the body dies while the reasoning part talks to the end.

The Socratic dialogue as a genre

Aristotle names Socratic conversations (Sōkratikoi logoi) as a kind of prose imitation beside the mimes of Sophron and Xenarchus (Poetics 1, 1447b9–11). Diogenes Laertius records Socratic dialogues by Phaedo, Euclides, Crito, Simon the shoemaker and others (2.105–124). Aeschines of Sphettus, present at the trial and the death (Apology 33e; Phaedo 59b), wrote seven (Diogenes Laertius 2.61). In his Alcibiades Socrates says he could help the young man by no art, only through love and a divine dispensation (theia moira); in his Aspasia, Aspasia questions Xenophon and his wife by induction (Cicero, On Invention 1.51–53). Antisthenes wrote Socratic works on Heracles, Cyrus and Aspasia among many (Diogenes Laertius 6.15–18); only his speeches Ajax and Odysseus survive. Xenophon's four Socratic books span memoir, banquet, household dialogue and defence.

The genre is the key to the Socratic problem. Its authors shared scenes, interlocutors (Alcibiades, Aspasia, Callias) and themes, and invented freely within them, as Plato does in setting conversations in his own childhood. Kahn (Plato and the Socratic Dialogue, 1996), whose reply to Vlastos module 6.5 gives, built on this: the dialogues are a literary form, not minutes. The schools that Antisthenes, Euclides and Aristippus founded are the subject of module 12.5.

Self-test

  1. How does the Theaetetus make Protagoras' measure doctrine the same claim as Theaetetus' definition of knowledge, and what extra theory does Socrates need to sustain it?
    Answer

    If things are for each person as they appear, perception is always of what is and cannot be false, which is what "knowledge is perception" requires (151e–152c). To give each perception its own object, Socrates adds the "secret doctrine" of universal motion and the twin-offspring theory of perception (152c–e, 156a–157c).

  2. Why is the argument from the future (Theaetetus 177c–179b) harder for Protagoras to escape than the reversal at 170a–171c?
    Answer

    Against a relativist the reversal seems to need the qualifier "true for him" dropped at 171a–c, a move Burnyeat defends and Fine takes as a sign that Plato's Protagoras is an infallibilist. Judgements about what will prove healthy or advantageous are settled by events, and experts make them better than laymen, so not everyone is a measure even of his own future.

  3. State Gorgias' chariot argument and explain how it uses Eleatic method against Eleatic conclusions.
    Answer

    If what is thought were what is, a chariot racing on the sea would exist because someone thinks of it, so thought does not reach being (Sextus, Against the Mathematicians 7.79–80; MXG 980a). Parmenides had argued from the link between thought and being to one changeless being; Gorgias cuts the link and, by the same exhaustive disjunctions, reaches nothing.

  4. In what sense is the Helen the practical counterpart of On Not Being?
    Answer

    If speech cannot convey things, it acts on souls by its effects, as drugs act on bodies (Helen 14); persuasion is a kind of compulsion, so Helen is blameless. The orator manages states of soul rather than truths, which is what Plato's Gorgias attacks.

  5. What does Antiphon mean by saying one is harmed through truth, not opinion, and why does Gagarin deny that On Truth preaches immoralism?
    Answer

    Breaches of law harm you only if seen, through reputation and penalty; breaches of nature harm you whether seen or not, so nature is what holds in truth. Gagarin (2002) argues that the later columns, on the defenceless victim and the truthful witness, probe the incoherence of conventional justice rather than recommend crime.

  6. What evidence suggests that Aristophanes' natural-philosopher Socrates is not pure invention, and what caution did Dover add?
    Answer

    Plato's own Socrates admits a youthful keenness for natural inquiry (Phaedo 96a–99d), and the Frogs (1491–1499) still treats him as the type of the talking intellectual. Dover (1968) argued that the Clouds fuses traits of natural philosophers, Sophists and ascetics into one figure with Socrates' face.

  7. Reconstruct the Protagoras' argument that weakness of will is ignorance, and give Aristotle's objection.
    Answer

    If the pleasant is the good, "overcome by pleasure" means doing bad knowingly because overcome by the good, which is absurd; so the error is mismeasuring near and distant pleasures, curable by an art of measurement (352a–358d). Aristotle replies that the denial conflicts with what plainly appears (Nicomachean Ethics 7.2, 1145b21–28).

  8. How do Plato's and Xenophon's accounts of the daimonion differ, and how does each relate it to the charge?
    Answer

    Plato's sign only turns Socrates back and was silent on the day of the trial (Apology 31c–d, 40a–c); Xenophon's also gives positive advice to him and his friends and forbade him to prepare a defence (Memorabilia 1.1.4; Apology 4). Both Euthyphro (3b) and Xenophon (Memorabilia 1.1.2) connect it with the charge of new divinities.

  9. Whom is Xenophon answering in Memorabilia 1.2, and how does he defend Socrates over Critias and Alcibiades?
    Answer

    "The accuser", usually identified with Polycrates, whose pamphlet postdates Conon's walls (Diogenes Laertius 2.39). Xenophon argues that both men sought Socrates for political advantage, behaved while with him and went bad after leaving; Critias as one of the Thirty even banned him from talking to the young (1.2.12–48).

  10. Where do the Apology and the Crito appear to conflict, and how does Kraut reconcile them?
    Answer

    In the Apology (29c–d) Socrates says he will disobey an order to stop philosophising; in the Crito (51b–c) the Laws say he must persuade or obey. Kraut (1984) reads "persuade" as permitting disobedience by one who argues his case before the city, so the two are consistent.

Carry forward

  1. The Sophists' own texts (Gorgias' two treatises, Antiphon's papyrus, the Dissoi Logoi) are tougher philosophy than Plato's portraits suggest; when a Sophist reaches us through Plato, separate the fragment from the reconstruction and the reconstruction from the refutation.
  2. Socratic ethics is intellectualist: virtue is knowledge and wrongdoing is error. Plato's divided soul, Aristotle's account of weakness of will and the Stoic theory of passions as false judgements each define themselves by what they keep or reject of it.
  3. After 399 the trial became a literary war over whether Socrates made Critias and Alcibiades, fought by Polycrates, Xenophon and Plato in a genre of free invention; a Socratic text is a move in that war before it is evidence for the man.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Sophists and Socrates, extending module 6.5, whose outline is the floor: go deeper, and don't repeat its table of Sophists or its account of the indictment, the vote and the hemlock. Cover: Protagoras (man the measure as Plato's Theaetetus develops and refutes it, 152a–179b, with the Cratylus, 385e–386a; module 6.5 gives the Great Speech of Plato's Protagoras: point back); Gorgias (On Not Being in its two versions, Sextus and the pseudo-Aristotelian treatise, and the Helen); Prodicus, Hippias and Thrasymachus; Antiphon's papyrus On Truth on law and nature; the Dissoi Logoi; Socrates: the Socratic problem source by source (Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes' Clouds, Aristotle), the elenchus and the Socratic paradoxes as arguments, irony, the daimonion; the trial of 399 beyond module 6.5's amnesty argument and its religious-or-political dispute: Polycrates' lost Accusation of Socrates and Xenophon's answer on Critias and Alcibiades (Memorabilia 1.2.12–48), with Plato's and Xenophon's Apologies compared; the Crito and the Phaedo as Plato's portrait of the death; and the Socratic dialogue as a genre (Aeschines of Sphettus, Antisthenes, Xenophon), leaving the schools Socrates' followers founded to module 12.5. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 12 · Deep dive III: Greek philosophy · 12.3 · 3,392 words

Plato

Life, Sicily and the AcademyCanon and chronologyThe Forms under attack: Parmenides and SophistRecollection and the immortal soulThe Republic: the challenge and the answerLove in the Symposium and PhaedrusThe Timaeus' cosmosThe LawsThe unwritten doctrinesPlato's myths as methodSelf-testCarry forward

Life, Sicily and the Academy

Module 6.5 gives the outline, from the birth about 428 to the founding of the Academy. The details rest on Diogenes Laertius book 3, compiled from Hellenistic biographers, and on the Letters, whose authority is disputed. Diogenes says Plato was named Aristocles after his grandfather and called Plato for his breadth, of build or of style (3.4), that he burned his tragedies after meeting Socrates (3.5), and that after the execution he withdrew with other Socratics to Euclides at Megara (3.6).

Sicily is told from Plato's side. On the first visit, about 388/7, he won Dion, brother-in-law of Dionysius I, to philosophy (Seventh Letter 327a); Diogenes adds that the tyrant had him sold at Aegina (3.18–20), which the Letter omits. In 367 Dion summoned him to make Dionysius II a philosopher-king, and Plato went for fear of seeming to himself a man of words only (328c); within four months Dion was exiled (329c). In 361 Plato returned on the promise of Dion's recall, was held in virtual custody, and got away when Archytas of Tarentum sent a ship (350a–b). Dion took Syracuse in 357 and was murdered in 354 by the Athenian Callippus (Plutarch, Dion 54–57); the Letter insists that Dion's Athenian killers were his friends through hospitality and the Mysteries, not philosophy (333d–e). The Letter's digression (342a–344d) explains why Plato wrote no treatise: name, account, image and even knowledge show what a thing is like rather than what it is, so the thing itself is grasped only after long shared inquiry, suddenly, like light kindled from a leaping spark (341c–d).

Where sources disagree. Morrow (Studies in the Platonic Epistles, 1935) accepted the Seventh Letter, and Ledger's computer analysis (Re-counting Plato, 1989) found its style compatible with Plato's. Edelstein (Plato's Seventh Letter, 1966) read it as a later apologia for the Sicilian failure, and Burnyeat and Frede (The Pseudo-Platonic Seventh Letter, 2015) argued that its theory of knowledge is not Plato's. The claim that Plato withheld his deepest thought rests largely on this letter.

The Academy, a circle in module 6.5's phrase, did mathematics: Theaetetus worked on irrationals, as the dialogue named after him shows (147d–148b), and on the regular solids, and Eudoxus' concentric spheres answered the problem, which Simplicius reports Plato set, of what uniform circular motions would save the planets' appearances (Commentary on Aristotle's On the Heavens). It practised definition by division, which the comic poet Epicrates mocked with young Academics classifying a pumpkin while Plato mildly told them to start again (fr. 10, in Athenaeus 2.59c–f). It lent lawgivers to Arcadia, Elis and Pyrrha (Plutarch, Against Colotes 1126c). It had no orthodoxy: Aristotle reports that Speusippus posited a different series of substances beginning from the One (Metaphysics 1028b21–24) and that Eudoxus made pleasure the good (Nicomachean Ethics 1172b9–15). The sceptical Academy belongs to module 12.8.

Canon and chronology

Every work antiquity cited as Plato's survives, with some that are not his. Thrasyllus arranged thirty-six works, the Letters counted as one, in nine tetralogies (Diogenes Laertius 3.56–61). Modern doubt falls on the Alcibiades I (rejected by Schleiermacher, defended by Denyer, 2001), the Hippias Major (defended by Woodruff, 1982), the Epinomis, which some gave to Philip of Opus (3.37), several minor pieces and most of the Letters.

No ancient source dates the dialogues, but Diogenes says Philip transcribed the Laws from wax tablets (3.37), and Aristotle that it was written after the Republic (Politics 1264b26–27). Lewis Campbell, introducing his edition of the Sophist and Statesman (1867), took the Laws as fixed point and found its peculiar vocabulary in those two and the Philebus, Timaeus and Critias. Dittenberger (1881) tracked particle combinations such as ti mēn, and Lutosławski (The Origin and Growth of Plato's Logic, 1897) some five hundred features, claiming a full order. What survives scrutiny, in Brandwood's survey (The Chronology of Plato's Dialogues, 1990), is three groups, not a sequence: a large first group whose internal order style cannot settle; the Republic, Parmenides, Theaetetus and Phaedrus; and the late six, which also avoid hiatus. That the short Socratic dialogues come first is inferred from content, not style.

Schleiermacher, introducing his translation from 1804, made the form the method: a planned course, opening with the Phaedrus, that leaves readers to find the answers themselves; K. F. Hermann (1839) saw the record of a mind developing from Socratic beginnings.

Where sources disagree. Unitarians hold that Plato had one philosophy and chose what to show: Shorey (The Unity of Plato's Thought, 1903), and Kahn (1996), who reads the Socratic dialogues as proleptic, preparing readers for the Phaedo and Republic. Developmentalists hold that the doctrines changed, Vlastos (1991) most sharply; module 6.5 gives his exchange with Kahn. When Owen ("The Place of the Timaeus in Plato's Dialogues", 1953) moved the Timaeus among the middle dialogues on philosophical grounds, Cherniss (1957) replied, and most still place it late.

The Forms under attack: Parmenides and Sophist

Module 6.5 gives what a Form is, the Phaedo's sticks, the Sun and the Third Man. The dialogues never expound a theory; they use Forms as premises, as in the safe answer that beautiful things are beautiful by the Beautiful (Phaedo 100b–e). Aristotle supplies a genealogy they lack: Plato, familiar from youth with Cratylus and the Heraclitean flux of sensibles, accepted Socrates' search for definitions and concluded that definitions must be of other things, which he called Ideas (Metaphysics 987a32–b10).

The Parmenides puts the objections in the mouth of Parmenides, addressing a very young Socrates (127b–c). Are there Forms of hair, mud and dirt? Socrates denies it, uneasily (130b–e). A thing sharing a Form gets the whole or a part; Socrates' day present in many places becomes a sail spread over many people, each under a part (131a–e). After the Third Man (132a–b), Forms as thoughts fail, since a thought is of something (132b–c), and Forms as patterns regress through resemblance (132c–133a). The greatest difficulty is that Forms relate only to Forms, so knowledge itself is beyond us and the gods cannot know us (133b–134e). Yet without Forms thought has nothing to fix on and dialectic is destroyed (135b–c). Vlastos ("The Third Man Argument in the Parmenides", 1954) showed that the regress needs two premises, that the Large is itself large and that what makes things large is none of them, which are jointly inconsistent. The second part's deductions on the One (137c–166c) became Neoplatonist theology (module 12.8).

The Sophist answers the problem module 12.1 hands on. To say what is false is to say what is not, which Parmenides forbade (237a, quoting DK 28 B 7). The Eleatic visitor commits parricide (241d): complete being must include motion, life and mind (248e–249a); five greatest kinds blend selectively; and not-being is difference, not the contrary of being (257b), so "Theaetetus flies" says what differs from what is true of him (263a–b).

Where sources disagree. Ryle ("Plato's Parmenides", 1939) and Owen (1953) took the objections as real flaws Plato had found, after which the late dialogues work with kinds, not separated paradigms. Cornford (Plato and Parmenides, 1939) and Cherniss (1957) held that he never gave the Forms up, citing the Timaeus' fresh argument that if intelligence differs from true opinion there are Forms (51b–e).

Recollection and the immortal soul

The Meno poses the paradox of inquiry: one cannot search for what one knows, nor for what one does not, since one would not recognise it (80d–e). Socrates answers from priests and Pindar (81a–c; the fragment is in module 8.4): the immortal soul has learned everything, so learning is recollection. Meno's untaught slave, asked to double a square, doubles the side, is refuted, reaches perplexity, and by questions alone sees that the square on the diagonal is double (82b–85b). The true opinions were in him, stirred up as in a dream (85c–d). Knowledge is true opinion tied down by reasoning about the cause, like Daedalus' runaway statues tethered, and that tying is recollection (97d–98a).

The Phaedo gives the proofs module 12.2 hands on. Opposites come from opposites, so the living from the dead (70c–72e); recollection (72e–77a) proves only pre-existence; the soul resembles the invisible, unchanging things it knows (78b–80b). Simmias objects that the soul may be an attunement of the body (85e–86d), Cebes that it may outlast several bodies as a weaver outlasts several cloaks and still die (87b–88b). An attunement cannot rule its instrument, as soul rules body (92a–95a). For Cebes, Socrates recounts his disappointment with Anaxagoras' Mind (97b–99c) and his second sailing, taking Forms as hypotheses (99c–100b). Then the final argument: soul brings life wherever it is, as fire brings heat, so it cannot admit death, as three cannot admit the even (102a–107b). The weak step is from deathless to imperishable, asserted at 106b–e; Socrates grants that the first hypotheses need examination (107b).

The Phaedrus argues that what always moves itself cannot cease (245c–246a), a definition of soul the Laws reuses (896a); Republic 10, that injustice, the soul's own evil, does not destroy it (608d–611a). The Phaedo's soul is intellect hindered by the body; the Republic's has parts.

The Republic: the challenge and the answer

Module 6.5 outlines the Republic, and module 12.2 shows why Thrasymachus' defeat settles nothing. Glaucon sharpens the challenge (357b–358a): some goods are welcomed for themselves, some also for their results, like health, some only for results, like medicine. The many put justice in the third class; Socrates must show it belongs in the second. Justice, on the many's theory, is a compact of the weak (358e–359b); parents and poets, Adeimantus adds, praise only its wages (362e–367e).

The central books add the Divided Line to the Sun and Cave (509d–511e). Above the cut lie mathematical thought, which reasons from hypotheses down to conclusions with the help of diagrams, and understanding, which treats hypotheses as steps up to an unhypothetical principle and descends without images (510b–511c). Socrates will not say what that principle, the Good, is (506d–e). Philosophers must be compelled to return to the Cave, since law aims at the whole city's happiness (519c–520a), and they are just men receiving just orders (520e).

Book 9 proves the just life happier three times: the tyrannical soul is enslaved to its worst part (576c–580c); only the philosopher has tasted the pleasures of all three parts, so his verdict counts (580d–583a); and his pleasures are truer and purer, the king's life 729 times more pleasant than the tyrant's (583b–588a). Only then are the wages restored (612b–614a).

Where sources disagree. Sachs ("A Fallacy in Plato's Republic", 1963) objected that Plato proves the worth of psychic harmony, not of justice in Glaucon's sense, and never shows that the harmonious soul will refrain from theft, betrayal and oath-breaking. Vlastos ("Justice and Happiness in the Republic", 1971) answered that the text makes the link itself (442e–443b): the motives for such acts are disorders the just soul lacks. Whether that suffices, or Plato simply redefined justice, is still argued.

Love in the Symposium and Phaedrus

Module 6.5 gives the Symposium's setting, Aristophanes, Diotima's daimon and the ascent. An argument leads to it: love desires beauty, so lacks it (199c–201c). Diotima, probably Plato's invention, defines love as desire for the good to be one's own for ever (206a), working by begetting in the beautiful, in body or soul (206b–e): lovers of honour beget laws and poems, the children of Homer, Lycurgus and Solon (208c–209e). The ascent is the purest begetting, issuing in true virtue (212a).

The Phaedrus' palinode recants the case, Lysias' and Socrates' own, for the non-lover. Divine madness gives the greatest goods: prophecy, purification, poetry and love (244a–245c). Beauty seen here recalls the Beautiful seen before birth, and the soul's wings regrow (249d–252b). Unlike the ascent, the palinode keeps the beloved: the pair grow their wings together in philosophy (256a–b). The dialogue's critique of writing is in module 6.5.

Where sources disagree. Vlastos ("The Individual as an Object of Love in Plato", 1973) charged that Platonic love loves a person only as a bearer of beauty, never as a whole individual. Nussbaum (The Fragility of Goodness, 1986) replied that Plato knew it: Alcibiades' speech of love for one irreplaceable Socrates shows what the ascent leaves out, and the Phaedrus recants in favour of the particular beloved.

The Timaeus' cosmos

The Timaeus, read in the Latin West through Calcidius' partial translation, is Timaeus of Locri's monologue. What becomes is grasped by opinion and has a cause; the cosmos is visible, so it has become (27d–28c), and an account of a copy of an eternal model can only be a likely story (eikōs mythos, 29d). The maker, good and without envy, wished all things to be like himself (29e–30a). He made the world one living creature with soul and intellect (30b), its soul blended from Being, Sameness and Difference and divided by harmonic ratios into circles carrying stars and planets (35a–36d). Time is a moving image of eternity (37d).

Midway Timaeus starts again: the world is the work of Reason and Necessity, Reason ruling by persuasion (47e–48a). Beside model and copy stands the receptacle, nurse of becoming (49a), later called space (chōra) and grasped by a bastard reasoning (52a–b). The elements are geometry: the half-equilateral triangle builds the tetrahedron of fire, the octahedron of air and the icosahedron of water, which can change into one another; the isosceles right triangle builds earth's cube, which cannot (53c–57c).

Where sources disagree. Aristotle took the generation literally and objected that what came to be cannot be everlasting, rejecting the defence, which the commentators assign to Xenocrates, that it is told for teaching, as geometers draw figures (On the Heavens 279b32–280a1). Plutarch and Atticus read it literally, most later Platonists not. Vlastos ("The Disorderly Motion in the Timaios", 1939) defended a real pre-cosmic chaos; Cornford (Plato's Cosmology, 1937) and Tarán (1971) read a didactic myth.

The Laws

Module 6.5 calls Magnesia a second-best city under law. The Laws, Plato's longest work and the only one without Socrates, has an Athenian Stranger, the Cretan Cleinias and the Spartan Megillus talk on the road from Cnossus to the cave of Zeus (625a–b). The best city remains the one where friends hold all in common (739a–e); Magnesia, built for human beings, has 5,040 lots, a number divisible by every number from one to ten (737e–738b), and a constitution mixing monarchy and democracy (693d–e).

Law persuades before it compels: as a free doctor explains to free patients (720a–e), each law has a preamble (722d–723b). God, not man, is the measure of all things (716c), against Protagoras (module 12.2). Book 10 legislates theology. The beliefs that gods do not exist, do not care, or can be bribed (885b) are answered, the first by the argument that soul, self-moving motion, is older than body (891e–899d); the honest unbeliever gets at least five years in a house of correction, death if he relapses (908e–909a). A Nocturnal Council guards the laws (961a–968e).

Where sources disagree. Popper (The Open Society and Its Enemies, 1945) read the Republic and Laws as a programme for a closed society, citing the rule that no one should ever be without a commander (942a–c). Levinson (In Defense of Plato, 1953) answered him point by point. Book 10's penalties remain the hardest text for Plato's defenders.

The unwritten doctrines

Here Aristotle is the witness, and his reports must not be read into the dialogues. He mentions Plato's so-called unwritten teachings (agrapha dogmata, Physics 209b11–16) and reports what no dialogue states: the elements of the Forms are the One and the Great-and-Small; the Forms are numbers; and the objects of mathematics stand between Forms and sensibles (Metaphysics 987b14–988a17). Aristoxenus says Aristotle used to tell how hearers came to Plato's lecture On the Good expecting wealth or health, heard mathematics and at last that the Good is one, and left scornful (Elements of Harmonics 2.30–31). Simplicius says Aristotle, Speusippus and Xenocrates wrote the lecture up (Commentary on Aristotle's Physics 151.6).

The Tübingen school made this the key to Plato. Hans Joachim Krämer (Arete bei Platon und Aristoteles, 1959) and Konrad Gaiser (Platons ungeschriebene Lehre, 1963) reconstructed a system deriving Forms, numbers and world from the One, identified with the Good, and the indefinite dyad. Thomas Szlezák (Platon und die Schriftlichkeit der Philosophie, 1985) read the dialogues' deferrals, Republic 506d–e above all, as deliberate passages of reserve.

The Philebus, which module 12.1 hands on, offers a middle way. Its god-given method holds that whatever is said to be consists of one and many and contains limit and unlimitedness (16c–17a), Philolaus' pair (module 12.1); all things fall under the unlimited, limit, their mixture and the cause of mixing (23c–27c). Sayre (Plato's Late Ontology, 1983) argued that the theses of Metaphysics A are found here and in the Parmenides, the Great-and-Small being the unlimited.

Where sources disagree. Cherniss (The Riddle of the Early Academy, 1945) held that no oral system existed: Aristotle misread the dialogues through his own polemic, and the riddle is how his reports arose. Vlastos, reviewing Krämer (Gnomon, 1963), allowed some oral teaching but denied it could override the dialogues. The Tübingen side answers that Aristotle sat in the Academy for twenty years and that Aristoxenus had the lecture story from him.

Plato's myths as method

Module 8.4 reads the judgement myths of the Gorgias, Phaedo and Republic for the afterlife. As method they share three features. Each follows argument that has done what it can: Callicles is silenced but unpersuaded, the Phaedo's hypotheses await examination (107b), and justice has been proved good in itself. Each carries a disclaimer: the Gorgias tale is a logos Callicles will take for a mythos (523a); no sensible man would insist on the Phaedo's details, but believing them is a noble risk (114d); Er's tale can save us if we are persuaded (621b–c). Each turns the afterlife into a lesson about the present soul, above all the choice of lives: aitia helomenou, theos anaitios, the responsibility is the chooser's, god is blameless (617e). Edelstein ("The Function of the Myth in Plato's Philosophy", 1949) read the myths as addressed to the parts of the soul argument does not reach. The Laws states the premise: the tale of Cadmus' sown men shows that young souls can be persuaded of anything (663e–664a).

The Phaedrus' charioteer states the principle: to say what the soul is would take a divine account, what it is like a human one (246a). It is like a winged charioteer and team; ours has one horse upright, white and led by word alone, the other crooked, dark and insolent, barely yielding to the goad (253c–254e). In the gods' procession souls glimpse the colourless, shapeless being seen only by intellect (247c); those dragged down lose their wings and fall into bodies, ranked in nine lives from philosopher to tyrant (248c–e), and a philosopher who chooses that life three times running regains his wings after three thousand years, not ten thousand (248e–249a). The Republic's three parts become a picture, and the fall explains why love can recall the Forms.

Atlantis inverts the method. Critias says Solon heard at Saïs that nine thousand years earlier an island beyond the Pillars of Heracles, larger than Libya and Asia together, attacked Europe and Asia, that ancient Athens alone defeated it, and that in one day and night the island sank (Timaeus 20d–25d). Socrates welcomes it as no fabricated myth but a true account (26e). The Critias describes the island and breaks off as Zeus summons the gods to punish its decline (108e–121c).

Where sources disagree. Proclus reports that Crantor, the first commentator on the Timaeus, took the story as history (Commentary on the Timaeus), and Strabo (2.3.6) that Posidonius thought it might not be fiction. Vidal-Naquet ("Athènes et l'Atlantide", 1964) read Atlantis as a mirror of imperial, naval Athens beaten by the land-bound city of the Republic, and Gill (1977) as fiction given the form of history.

Self-test

  1. What fixes the late group of dialogues, and why can stylometry not order the first group?
    Answer

    Campbell (1867) took the Laws, transcribed from wax by Philip of Opus (Diogenes Laertius 3.37) and later than the Republic (Politics 1264b26–27), as fixed point and found its vocabulary in the Sophist, Statesman, Philebus, Timaeus and Critias. Stylometry measures closeness to that late style; the first group shows too little of it to be ordered, so its priority rests on content.

  2. Why does the authenticity of the Seventh Letter matter for the unwritten doctrines?
    Answer

    Its claim that Plato wrote no treatise on what matters most (341c–d) is the main written warrant for a withheld teaching. If Edelstein and Burnyeat and Frede are right that it is not Plato's, the Tübingen case rests on the Phaedrus and on Aristotle's reports.

  3. Which two premises does Vlastos find in the Third Man, and why does the Parmenides not abandon the Forms anyway?
    Answer

    Self-predication (the Large is large) and non-identity (what makes things large is none of them), which are jointly inconsistent. Parmenides himself says that without Forms thought has nothing to fix on and dialectic is destroyed (135b–c).

  4. What does the slave-boy episode show, and what does the Meno later add about knowledge?
    Answer

    Untaught, the boy reaches the square on the diagonal by questioning alone, so the true opinions were already in him (82b–85d). Knowledge is true opinion tied down by reasoning about the cause, and that tying is recollection (97d–98a).

  5. State Cebes' objection in the Phaedo and the step in the final argument most open to challenge.
    Answer

    A soul might outlast many bodies, as a weaver outlasts many cloaks, and still perish (87b–88b). The final argument shows soul cannot admit death while it exists; that the deathless is therefore imperishable is asserted (106b–e), and Socrates grants that the hypotheses need examination (107b).

  6. Where does Socrates place justice among Glaucon's goods, and why does Sachs think the Republic's answer misses its target?
    Answer

    Among goods welcomed both for themselves and for their results (357b–358a). Sachs (1963) argued that Plato proves psychic harmony good but not that the harmonious person will refrain from ordinary injustice; Vlastos (1971) replied that 442e–443b makes the link.

  7. How does the Phaedrus treat the beloved differently from Diotima's ascent, and why does that matter to Vlastos' charge?
    Answer

    The ascent passes from one body to beauty in general and leaves the individual behind; the palinode keeps lover and beloved together, growing their wings in a shared philosophical life (256a–b). Nussbaum reads this, with Alcibiades' speech, as Plato's own answer to the charge that he loves qualities, not persons.

  8. Why can fire, air and water change into one another in the Timaeus while earth cannot?
    Answer

    Their solids (tetrahedron, octahedron, icosahedron) are all built from the half-equilateral triangle, whose pieces can be regrouped; earth's cube is built from the isosceles right triangle, so it cannot become the others (53c–57c).

  9. How does the Laws combine persuasion and compulsion, and how does Book 10 apply the principle to the gods?
    Answer

    Each law has a preamble arguing for it, as a free doctor explains his treatment (720a–e, 722d–723b). Book 10 first argues that soul is older than body (891e–899d), then penalises the unpersuaded (908e–909a).

  10. What do the three judgement myths share as method, and how does Atlantis invert it?
    Answer

    Each follows an argument that has gone as far as it can, disclaims literal truth while affirming its lesson (Gorgias 523a, Phaedo 114d, Republic 621b–c), and turns the afterlife into a lesson about choosing now (617e). Atlantis is presented as a true account, not a myth (Timaeus 26e).

Carry forward

  1. Keep two Platos apart: the Plato of the dialogues, who argues from hypotheses he leaves exposed, and the Plato Aristotle reports, with Forms as numbers derived from the One and the Great-and-Small. Every claim about "Plato's doctrine" should name the witness it rests on, a discipline module 12.4 needs for Aristotle's criticisms.
  2. The dialogues end in admitted difficulties (the Parmenides' objections, the Phaedo's unexamined hypotheses, the Good left unsaid), and later Platonists split over what that means: a system withheld, as the Tübingen school and the Neoplatonists read it, or inquiry left open, as the sceptical Academy did (module 12.8).
  3. Plato's myths are a method: placed after argument, disclaimed in detail and affirmed in lesson. The charioteer, the Demiurge and the receptacle, and the judgement of souls passed into later Platonism and Christian theology as doctrine, so ask of any Platonic image whether Plato offered it as a likeness or an argument.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Plato, extending module 6.5, which gives the life and the Syracusan visits, the Academy, the stylometric groups, the Forms with recollection in the Phaedo and the Third Man, the Republic, Diotima's ascent and the late dialogues in outline: point back to it and go into the arguments. Cover: the life, Sicily and the Seventh Letter's authenticity; the Academy; the dialogue form and the chronology debate (stylometry); the Forms and the objections of the Parmenides; recollection and the immortal soul (Meno, Phaedo); the Republic beyond 6.5's outline; love in the Symposium and Phaedrus; the Timaeus' cosmos; the Laws; the unwritten doctrines; and Plato's myths: the judgement myths of the Gorgias, Phaedo and Republic (module 8.4 reads all three, Er included, for the afterlife: point back and read them as Plato's method), Atlantis in the Timaeus and Critias, and the Phaedrus' charioteer. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 12 · Deep dive III: Greek philosophy · 12.4 · 3,383 words

Aristotle

The life beyond the outlineLecture notes and the cellar at ScepsisLogic: categories, syllogism, demonstrationPhysics: nature, change and endsMetaphysics: substance and the unmoved moverThe biologist at Pyrrha and the soulThe Nicomachean Ethics beyond the meanHousehold, slavery and constitutionsRhetoric and PoeticsAfterlife: the commentators, Arabic and LatinSelf-testCarry forward

The life beyond the outline

Module 6.5 gives the frame, from Stagira in 384 to Chalcis in 322. The evidence is thin and late: Diogenes Laertius 5.1–35, with its gossip, catalogue and will; Dionysius of Halicarnassus (First Letter to Ammaeus 5), who dates each stage by Athenian archon; and the reverent Neoplatonic lives, all collected in Ingemar Düring's Aristotle in the Ancient Biographical Tradition (1957).

The Academy years (367–347) produced the published dialogues, now lost: the Eudemus on the soul, the Protrepticus, On Philosophy. Cicero's "golden river of speech" (Academica 2.119) probably praises them. Ingram Bywater (1869) recovered much of the Protrepticus from Iamblichus: it argues that thought is the end for which humans exist, a conviction Aristotle never dropped. Plato's death in 348/7 and Speusippus' succession ended his place in the school; whether the fall of Olynthus in 348 also made a man with Macedonian ties unwelcome in Athens is guessed, not attested.

Assos was a philosophers' court. Hermias, ruler of Atarneus and Assos, had taken in the Academics Erastus and Coriscus (Plato's Sixth Letter is addressed to all three); Aristotle and Xenocrates joined them, and Aristotle married Pythias, Hermias' niece or adopted daughter (Strabo 13.1.57; Diogenes Laertius 5.3). Around 341 the Persians seized Hermias by treachery and killed him; Aristotle's hymn to Virtue in his memory (Diogenes Laertius 5.7–8) was later used against him at Athens. Theophrastus of Eresus, his colleague for life, is first visible beside him here, and from about 345 the two worked on Lesbos.

Module 6.7 tells the years at Mieza, and modules 11.5 and 11.7 the fate of Aristotle's kinsman Callisthenes. A Delphic decree (FD III 1.400, before 329) crowns the two for compiling the list of Pythian victors; Aelian (Varia Historia 14.1) quotes a letter in which Aristotle takes the later loss of these honours calmly.

The Lyceum's novelty was organised research. Aristotle, a metic who could not own land, taught in a public gymnasium whose covered walk (peripatos) named the school (Diogenes Laertius 5.2). The catalogue lists the constitutions of 158 cities (5.27); the Constitution of the Athenians returned on a papyrus published in 1891, and P. J. Rhodes (1981) assigns it to a pupil. Other collections listed Olympic victors and dramatic productions, and the pupils divided the history of knowledge: Theophrastus on plants and physical opinions (module 12.1), Eudemus on geometry and astronomy, Meno on medicine. The will (Diogenes Laertius 5.11–16) names Antipater executor, provides for Herpyllis, his companion after Pythias died, and frees slaves.
