Where sources disagree. Werner Jaeger (Aristoteles, 1923; module 6.5) mapped the corpus on to the life: Platonist in the Academy, critic at Assos, empiricist at the Lyceum, with the biology last; F. Nuyens (1939; French edition 1948) applied the method to the theory of the soul. H. D. P. Lee (1948) answered that the biology's place-names cluster around Lesbos and the Troad, placing it in the middle years, and G. E. L. Owen (1960) reversed the direction: the early logic is the most anti-Platonic, and the Metaphysics moves back towards Plato. Most now read the treatises as courses revised over decades.

Lecture notes and the cellar at Scepsis

Aristotle refers to his "exoteric" discussions (Nicomachean Ethics 1102a26; Politics 1278b31), the published dialogues. What survives is the other half, treatises (pragmateiai) for use inside the school, and they show it: cross-references in both directions, doublets (Metaphysics K repeats parts of B, Γ, E and the Physics), a philosophical lexicon (Metaphysics Δ), and three books shared by the two Ethics (NE 5–7 are EE 4–6). The catalogue in Diogenes Laertius (5.22–27) lists nearly 150 titles, many unknown to us, and lacks several treatises we read.

Strabo (13.1.54; module 6.5) tells how they came down. Theophrastus left the library, Aristotle's books with his own, to Neleus of Scepsis. Neleus' heirs hid the books in a trench from the Attalid kings, who were collecting for Pergamum, and damp and worms damaged them. Apellicon of Teos later bought them, filled the gaps badly and published faulty texts; Sulla took his library to Rome (module 7.3), where Tyrannion the grammarian handled it. Strabo's point is that the Peripatetics after Theophrastus, with few books and those mostly exoteric, could not philosophise systematically and merely declaimed on set themes. Plutarch (Sulla 26) adds that Andronicus of Rhodes obtained copies from Tyrannion, published them and drew up the tables now current.

Porphyry (Life of Plotinus 24) says Andronicus divided the works of Aristotle and Theophrastus into treatises, gathering related material together; our groupings, logic first and the Metaphysics named for its place after the physical works, probably descend from him. His date is open: Moraux (1973) put the work in the late 70s BC, Gottschalk (1987) in the 60s, Düring (1957) after Cicero's death, since Cicero never mentions it.

Where sources disagree. Athenaeus (1.3a–b) says Neleus sold Aristotle's books to Ptolemy II for Alexandria, which contradicts the cellar; and some treatises were plainly read in the Hellenistic school, since Eudemus asked Theophrastus for a sound text of a passage of the Physics (Simplicius, Commentary on the Physics). Barnes ("Roman Aristotle", 1997) argued that the two stories can both be true. Primavesi (2007) defends a modified Strabo: treatises absent from the Hellenistic catalogue keep a pre-Hellenistic system of book labels, so they reached our corpus from a collection out of circulation until about 100 BC.

Logic: categories, syllogism, demonstration

The six logical works were later grouped as the Organon, the instrument. The Categories sorts what is said without combination into ten kinds, from substance, quantity and quality to acting and being acted on (1b25–27). Its ontology is anti-Platonic (module 6.5): primary substance is the individual, this man or this horse; species and genus are secondary substances (2a11–19); and if primary substances did not exist, nothing else could (2b5–6).

The Prior Analytics defines a deduction (syllogismos) as an argument in which, certain things being laid down, something else follows of necessity from their being so (24b18–20). Its subject is the categorical syllogism, two premises sharing a middle term. The first figure is perfect, its validity evident: if A belongs to every B and B to every C, A belongs to every C (25b37–39), the mood medieval mnemonics called Barbara. Moods of the second and third figures are proved by conversion into the first or by reduction to the impossible, and invalid ones are rejected by counterexample. Aristotle claimed that on reasoning he found nothing done before him (Sophistical Refutations 34, 184b1–3); Stoic propositional logic later grew beside his (module 12.7).

Where sources disagree. Jan Łukasiewicz (Aristotle's Syllogistic, 1951) read each syllogism as a single conditional proposition and the system as an axiomatic theory. John Corcoran (1974) and Timothy Smiley (1973) read syllogisms as arguments and the system as natural deduction, closer to the text's practice of deriving conclusions from premises; most logicians since follow them.

The Posterior Analytics turns deduction into science: to know is to know the cause, through demonstration from premises that are true, primary, immediate, better known than, prior to and causes of the conclusion (71b19–22). First principles are grasped by induction and nous (2.19; module 6.5). The Topics supplies dialectic, which reasons from endoxa, the opinions of all, of most or of the wise (100b21–23). The treatises often open so, setting out the appearances and the puzzles (Nicomachean Ethics 1145b2–7); Owen ("Tithenai ta phainomena", 1961) argued that "appearances" there means what is said, not what is observed.

Physics: nature, change and ends

Module 6.5 gives the four causes; the Physics begins with the principles of change. Every change needs a persisting subject and a pair of contraries, a form gained and its privation: the unmusical man becomes musical (1.7). This was the answer to Parmenides that module 12.1 sets out. Nature is an internal principle of motion and rest (192b21–23). Motion is the actuality of the potential as such (201a10–11); place is the inner limit of the containing body (212a20–21); time is the number of motion with respect to before and after (219b1–2); and there is no void (4.8).

Book 2 defends final causes. Against those who say rain falls of necessity and only happens to ripen the corn, Aristotle argues that what happens always or for the most part cannot be chance, and that nature, like art, acts for an end without deliberating (2.8, 198b16–199b33). Sedley ("Is Aristotle's teleology anthropocentric?", 1991) adds Politics 1256b15–22, where plants exist for animals and animals for humans; most readers confine natural ends to the good of each kind. The heavens are made of aether, which moves naturally in circles (On the Heavens 1.2–3). A thrown stone keeps moving, Aristotle had to say, because the air pushes it (Physics 8.10); John Philoponus' sixth-century objection, that the thrower imparts a power to the stone itself, began the line to medieval impetus theory.

Metaphysics: substance and the unmoved mover

The Metaphysics is fourteen books of uneven date under an editor's title. Γ announces a science of being as being (1003a21): being is said in many ways, but all with reference to one, as everything healthy is called so with reference to health (1003a33–b10), what Owen named focal meaning. Γ also defends the principle of non-contradiction, the firmest of all (1005b19–20), which cannot be demonstrated, only defended against anyone willing to say something meaningful (1006a11–24).

Book Z starts again at Metaphysics 1028a10: being is said in many ways, and the old question what being is, is just the question what substance is (1028b2–4). The candidates are essence, universal, genus and substrate (1028b33–36). The substrate, stripped of attributes, collapses into bare matter, which cannot be primary, since substance must be separable and a this (1029a10–28). No universal is substance, since a universal is common and substance belongs to its owner alone (1038b8–12). What survives is form, the essence that makes this matter a man and the cause of its being (1041b27–28). The Categories made the individual primary; Z makes primary the form within it. Θ adds that actuality is prior to potentiality (Θ8, 1049b4–5).

Where sources disagree. If form is primary substance and no universal is substance, form must be particular: Socrates' form is his alone. Michael Frede and Günther Patzig (Aristoteles 'Metaphysik Z', 1988) took that line. Alan Code (1986) and Michael Loux (Primary Ousia, 1991) held that form is universal, shared by every man but predicated of matter rather than of individuals, so that Z13 does not exclude it.

Book Λ reaches god. If all substances were perishable, everything would be; but motion and time cannot have begun or ended, and the only continuous eternal motion is circular. So there is an eternal mover whose substance is actuality, without matter or potentiality (1071b3–22). It moves without being moved, as an object of desire and thought moves: it moves by being loved (1072b3). It thinks the best object, itself: thinking of thinking (1074b34–35). Λ8 multiplies the movers to match the spheres of Eudoxus and Callippus, fifty-five or forty-seven, as merely probable (1073b1–1074a14). The universe's good is like an army's, in its order and in its general, but more in the general (1075a11–15).

The biologist at Pyrrha and the soul

Module 6.5 gives the dogfish, the hectocotylus, the dolphins and Darwin's verdict. The lagoon of Pyrrha, the modern Gulf of Kalloni on Lesbos, is where much of that looking was done: the History of Animals names it for the fish that leave it in winter and the starfish that plague its fishermen, and Armand Marie Leroi's The Lagoon (2014) reconstructs the fieldwork from such notices. The method is first to collect differences and attributes, then to seek causes (History of Animals 491a7–14). The chick embryo, opened day by day, shows the heart as a beating speck of blood by the third day (6.3).

The Parts of Animals puts the final cause first (639b11–21): necessity in nature is hypothetical, as a saw must be of iron if it is to cut (Physics 200a10–13). The Generation of Animals makes the male supply form and motion, the female matter (729a9–11), calls the female a deformed male (737a27–28), and says that intellect alone enters from outside (736b27–28).

On the Soul defines soul as the first actuality of a natural body that has life potentially, a body with organs (412a27–b6). There is no more need to ask whether soul and body are one than whether the wax and its shape are (412b6–9); if the eye were an animal, sight would be its soul (412b18–22). Plants nourish, animals also perceive, humans also think (2.3). Perception takes on form without matter, as wax takes the seal's imprint without the gold (424a17–24). Before it thinks, the mind is actually nothing, a writing tablet with nothing yet written on it (429a24, 430a1). Then come the few lines of 3.5 (430a10–25): one intellect becomes all things, another makes all things, like light, and this one is separable, unaffected, and alone immortal and eternal.

Where sources disagree. Alexander of Aphrodisias identified the productive intellect with god, the first cause, so that nothing personal survives; Averroes made the receptive intellect, too, one and separate for all humans. Aquinas, On the Unity of the Intellect against the Averroists (1270), argued that both are powers of each individual soul. Moderns divide over perception as well: whether the eye-jelly literally turns red (Sorabji, 1974) or simply becomes aware of red (Burnyeat, 1992).

The Nicomachean Ethics beyond the mean

Module 6.5 gives the function argument, the mean, weakness of will and contemplation. Book 1 first fixes what the final good must be: complete, chosen always for itself, and self-sufficient, making life choiceworthy on its own (1097a25–b21). Happiness is activity over a complete life, for one swallow does not make a spring (1098a18–20). Fortune matters: Priam, virtuous and ruined, is not called happy, though the good man will never become wretched (1100a5–9, 1101a6–8). Pleasure is no process but the completion of an unimpeded activity, supervening like the bloom on those in their prime (1174b31–33).

Friendship fills two books because the city depends on it: lawgivers care more for it than for justice (1155a22–26). Its three kinds follow the three lovable things, the useful, the pleasant and the good (1155b17–1156a10). Friendships of use and pleasure end with the advantage; the complete kind joins good people alike in virtue, each wishing the other's good for the other's sake (1156b7–12). A friend is another self (1166a31–32). Why should the self-sufficient man need one? Because we contemplate our neighbours' actions better than our own, and a good friend's are good and akin to ours (9.9, 1169b33–1170a4). Book 8 maps constitutions on to household bonds: kingship on to fatherhood, aristocracy on to marriage, timocracy on to brotherhood (1160a31–1161a9).

Book 10 ranks the lives. Contemplation is the activity of the best part of us, the most continuous, pleasant, self-sufficient and leisured; so far as we can, we should make ourselves immortal (1177b33), and the life of practical virtue is happy in a secondary degree (1178a9–10).

Where sources disagree. W. F. R. Hardie ("The Final Good in Aristotle's Ethics", 1965) distinguished a dominant end from an inclusive one and found Aristotle wavering between them. J. L. Ackrill ("Aristotle on Eudaimonia", 1974) read Book 1 inclusively: happiness contains every intrinsic good, so nothing added could make it better. Richard Kraut (Aristotle on the Human Good, 1989) took Book 10 at its word: perfect happiness is contemplation, and the moral life a secondary happiness.

Household, slavery and constitutions

Module 6.5 gives the political animal, natural slavery with its admitted controversy, the six constitutions and the middle class. Book 1 builds the city from the household: master and slave, husband and wife, father and children (1253b4–11). Rule over a wife is political, over children royal (1259a37–b17); the woman has the deliberative part but without authority (akuron), the child has it undeveloped, the slave not at all (1260a12–14).

The argument for natural slavery runs through tools. The slave is a living tool for action; if shuttles wove by themselves, masters would need no slaves (1253b33–1254a1). Some people share in reason enough to perceive it but not to have it (1254b20–23), and for them being ruled is just and beneficial. Aristotle concedes that nature often fails to mark slaves' bodies and free men's souls as it intends (1254b27–1255a1), and that war enslaves the well-born (1255a3–b4); he names no natural slaves beyond hinting that barbarians fit the type (1252b5–9). Usury, money breeding money, is the most unnatural acquisition (1258b2–8).

What really divides oligarchy from democracy is wealth, not number: the rich happen to be few and the poor many (1279b34–1280a6). Book 3 grants the many a claim, since a crowd judging together may surpass the few best, as a feast to which many contribute beats one man's dinner (1281a40–b10). Polity mixes oligarchy and democracy (1293b33–34). The best city of Books 7 and 8 denies citizenship to farmers and craftsmen, whose work leaves no leisure for virtue (1328b33–1329a2).

Rhetoric and Poetics

Plato's Gorgias denied that rhetoric was an art, calling it a knack (462b–465a). Aristotle's Rhetoric opens by calling it the counterpart of dialectic (1354a1) and defines it as the capacity to see the available means of persuasion in each case (1355b25–26). Persuasion comes through the speaker's character, the hearer's emotion and the argument itself (1356a1–4). The argument proper is the enthymeme, a rhetorical deduction from probabilities and signs (1356b4–5). Speeches are deliberative, forensic or epideictic (1358b6–8). Book 2 gives the first systematic analysis of the emotions, each defined by its cause and object: anger is a desire, with pain, for revenge for an apparent slight (1378a30–32).

Module 6.5 gives tragedy's definition, plot, hamartia and the katharsis dispute. Behind them lies a theory of imitation. Humans are the most imitative of animals and learn first by imitating, and they enjoy exact images of things painful to see, such as corpses, because they learn from them (1448b4–19). A plot is a whole with beginning, middle and end (1450b26–27). Poetry is more philosophical than history, because it speaks of universals, what such a person would probably or necessarily do, where history says what Alcibiades did (1451b5–11). The lost second book, on comedy, drives Umberto Eco's Il nome della rosa (1980); Richard Janko (Aristotle on Comedy, 1984) argued that the Tractatus Coislinianus summarises it.

Afterlife: the commentators, Arabic and Latin

The school declined after Theophrastus (head 322–c. 287), and Strabo blamed the lost books. Alexander of Aphrodisias, whose On Fate is addressed to Septimius Severus and Caracalla, taught Aristotle's philosophy around 200 (module 7.4 has the chairs Marcus Aurelius endowed). The Neoplatonists (module 12.8) made Aristotle the road to Plato: Porphyry's Isagoge introduced the Categories, and Philoponus attacked the eternity of the world. Boethius' Latin Categories and On Interpretation carried the old logic into the Latin Middle Ages; Rome module 13.3 takes the Peripatetics at Rome.

Module 9.3 gives the Baghdad translators and the Toledo route. Al-Farabi was called the Second Teacher, after Aristotle. Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980–1037) rewrote the system in his Healing, sharpening the distinction between essence and existence. Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) of Córdoba wrote short, middle and long commentaries, defending Aristotle against Avicenna's Platonising; the Latins called him the Commentator, and Dante set him in Limbo near the "master of those who know" (Inferno 4.131, 4.144).

Paris banned lectures on Aristotle's natural philosophy in 1210 and 1215; by 1255 its arts statutes prescribed nearly the whole corpus, which William of Moerbeke then translated or revised from the Greek. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) commented on the major treatises, called Aristotle simply the Philosopher, and rebuilt theology with his tools: the first of the five ways argues from motion to an unmoved first mover (Summa Theologiae I q.2 a.3). Where Aristotle conflicted with faith, Aquinas held that reason cannot settle the matter: the world's beginning in time is believed, not demonstrated (I q.46 a.2). In 1277 Bishop Tempier of Paris condemned 219 propositions, some of them Aristotelian. The physics fell in the seventeenth century; the logic lasted, and Kant could say it had not taken a step forward since Aristotle (Critique of Pure Reason, preface to the second edition, 1787).

Self-test

  1. How did Jaeger map the corpus on to the life, and how did Lee and Owen each undermine the map?
    Answer

    Jaeger (1923) placed a Platonist Aristotle in the Academy, a critic at Assos and an empiricist at the Lyceum, with the biology last. Lee (1948) argued that the biology's place-names point to Lesbos and the Troad in the middle years; Owen (1960) argued that the early logic is the most anti-Platonic and the Metaphysics moves back towards Plato.

  2. What does Strabo infer from the Scepsis story, and what evidence tells against the inference?
    Answer

    That the later Peripatetics, lacking the treatises, could not philosophise systematically (13.1.54). Athenaeus (1.3a–b) has Neleus sell the books to Ptolemy II, and Eudemus' request to Theophrastus for a sound text of the Physics shows treatises in use inside the school.

  3. How does Book Z of the Metaphysics revise the Categories on primary substance?
    Answer

    The Categories makes the individual, this man, primary substance and species secondary (2a11–19). Z rejects substrate and universal as candidates and makes form, the essence within the individual, primary substance and the cause of its being (1041b27–28), which raises the dispute whether form is particular or universal.

  4. Why is the first figure called perfect, and how are the other figures validated?
    Answer

    Its validity is evident without further steps, as in Barbara: if A belongs to every B and B to every C, A belongs to every C (Prior Analytics 25b37–39). Second- and third-figure moods are proved by converting premises into a first-figure syllogism or by reduction to the impossible.

  5. How does demonstration differ from dialectic, and what are endoxa?
    Answer

    Demonstration deduces conclusions from true, primary premises that are causes of the conclusion (Posterior Analytics 71b19–22); dialectic reasons from endoxa, the opinions of all, most or the wise (Topics 100b21–23). The treatises use dialectic to set out the appearances and puzzles; first principles themselves are grasped by induction and nous.

  6. Reconstruct the argument of Metaphysics Λ for an unmoved mover, and say how it moves the heavens.
    Answer

    Motion and time are eternal; the only continuous eternal motion is circular; so there must be an eternal mover whose substance is actuality without matter (1071b3–22). It moves as an object of love and thought moves those who desire it (1072b3), its own activity being thinking of thinking.

  7. Give three readings of the productive intellect of On the Soul 3.5.
    Answer

    Alexander of Aphrodisias identified it with god, the first cause. Averroes made the receptive intellect, too, one and separate for all humans. Aquinas (1270) made both powers of each individual soul.

  8. Why, by Nicomachean Ethics 9.9, does the self-sufficient happy man need friends?
    Answer

    Because we contemplate others' actions better than our own, and a good friend, another self, performs good actions akin to ours (1169b33–1170a4); the friend lets the good man see his own kind of activity.

  9. How does Aristotle argue for natural slavery, and what does he concede?
    Answer

    The slave is a living tool, and some people share in reason enough to perceive it but not to have it, so being ruled benefits them (1253b33–1254a1, 1254b20–23). He concedes that nature often fails to mark slaves and free men as it intends and that war enslaves the well-born (1254b27–1255b4).

  10. Why is poetry more philosophical than history, according to the Poetics?
    Answer

    Poetry speaks of universals, what such a person would probably or necessarily do, while history says what a particular person, such as Alcibiades, did (1451b5–11).

Carry forward

  1. The corpus is school material that came through a narrow, contested channel, from Theophrastus' library to Andronicus' arrangement. Read its doublets and tensions as stages of inquiry, and treat every developmental chronology as a hypothesis.
  2. Aristotle's method is to set out the appearances and opinions, find the puzzles and dissolve them by distinctions: being said in many ways, form and matter, potential and actual, the four causes. That vocabulary is what the Hellenistic schools, the commentators and the scholastics argued in.
  3. His most consequential texts are his shortest and most ambiguous: Λ on god and On the Soul 3.5 on intellect. Read as impersonal intellect by Alexander and Averroes, and as compatible with a personal soul and a creator by Aquinas, they decided what Aristotle meant to Islam and Christendom.

Give me an in-depth report on Aristotle, extending module 6.5, which already gives the life from Stagira to Chalcis, Andronicus' edition and the doubted Scepsis cellar (Strabo 13.1.54), the break with Plato, the four causes, the biology with its famous observations, the function argument and the mean, natural slavery and the six constitutions, the Poetics with the katharsis dispute, and Jaeger's developmental thesis: point back to it for each, and spend the words on what it leaves out. GREECE · UNIT 12 · Deep dive III: Greek philosophy · 12.5 · 2,747 words

Cynics, Cyrenaics and the other Socratic schools

Diogenes Laertius and the Socratic remainsAntisthenesDiogenes of Sinope: what can be knownThe doctrine under the anecdotesCrates and HipparchiaMenippus and Cynic writingAristippus and the CyrenaicsThe later Cyrenaics: Hegesias, Anniceris, TheodorusThe Megarians and dialecticThe Cynic as social critic, and the road to ZenoSelf-testCarry forward

Diogenes Laertius and the Socratic remains

Almost everything here reaches us through one compiler. Diogenes Laertius wrote his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers probably in the first half of the third century AD, some five and a half centuries after Diogenes of Sinope died. Book 2 holds the Socratics, among them Aristippus and the Cyrenaics (2.65–104) and Euclides and the Megarians (2.106–120). Book 6 holds the Cynics, from Antisthenes (6.1–19) and Diogenes (6.20–81) to Crates, Hipparchia and Menippus (6.85–101).

The order is an argument. His Ionian succession runs from Socrates through Antisthenes, Diogenes and Crates to Zeno (1.15), so the Cynics, set between the Socratics and the Stoics, become the Stoa's pedigree. His sources were Hellenistic compilers who thought in such lines (Sotion's Successions, Diocles of Magnesia, Hippobotus, Satyrus, Hermippus), and he sets their versions side by side without judging.

Most of book 6 is chreiai, pointed sayings or acts attached to a name, a form drilled in rhetorical exercise books such as Aelius Theon's Progymnasmata. Collections began early (Zeno compiled one, 6.91), and their contents drifted. In book 2 Diogenes, washing vegetables, mocks Aristippus for courting kings and Aristippus has the last word (2.68); in book 6 Plato mocks Diogenes over his lettuces and Diogenes has it (6.58). The retort belongs to whoever the chapter is about. The testimonia are gathered in Giannantoni's Socratis et Socraticorum Reliquiae (SSR, 1990): Aristippus is IV A, Antisthenes V A, Diogenes V B.

Antisthenes

Module 6.5 gives Antisthenes' dates, his training under Gorgias and his preference for madness over pleasure; module 12.2 lists his Socratic writings; module 10.4 reads his Ajax and Odysseus. Xenophon's Symposium gives him a speech on wealth and poverty as states of the soul (4.34–44): owning almost nothing, he is the richest man present because he has enough. Diogenes Laertius adds that virtue is teachable and sufficient for happiness, needing only "Socratic strength" (6.10–11), that toil (ponos) is a good, as Heracles and Cyrus show (6.2), and that the wise man lives by the law of virtue, not the city's (6.11).

Aristotle knew a logician. Antisthenes, he says, held that nothing can be said of a thing but its own proper account, one for one, so that contradiction is impossible and error nearly so (Metaphysics 1024b32–34; Topics 104b20–21); "the Antistheneans and such uneducated people" denied that one can define what a thing is, only say what it is like, as silver is like tin (Metaphysics 1043b23–28).

This adds to the founder dispute that modules 6.5 and 7.2 weigh. Aristotle, whose life overlapped with both men's, cites the Antistheneans for logic and "the Dog" for a joke and never connects them. And the name Cynic was traced both to the Cynosarges gymnasium where Antisthenes taught and to his nickname, "plain dog" (6.13): two aetiologies pinning the name on him, as a succession written backwards would need.

Diogenes of Sinope: what can be known

Two witnesses are Diogenes' contemporaries, though one reaches us only through book 6. Aristotle's Rhetoric quotes "the Dog" calling the taverns the common messes of Attica (1411a24–25; SSR V B 184), the oldest testimony to Diogenes and proof that the nickname was current in his lifetime. Theophrastus' Megarian said Diogenes found his way of life by watching a mouse that needed no bed, feared no dark and craved no delicacies (Diogenes Laertius 6.22).

The outline: son of Hicesias, a banker at Sinope on the Black Sea (6.20), he left after a scandal over the coinage, lived in Athens and Corinth, and died at Corinth nearly ninety (6.76–78). The three deaths on offer (raw octopus, held breath, a dog's bite: 6.76–77) and Demetrius' claim that he died on Alexander's day (6.79) are literature; so, probably, is his sale to Xeniades of Corinth (6.29–31, 6.74), told in Menippus' satire Sale of Diogenes. Whether he wrote was disputed: one list gives dialogues, a Republic and seven tragedies, while Sosicrates and Satyrus said he wrote nothing, and Satyrus gave the tragedies to his follower Philiscus (6.80). The Republic at least existed: Philodemus' On the Stoics rebukes Stoics who tried to disown it, and its doctrines (wives and children in common, the cosmos as the only true commonwealth) are summarised at 6.72.

Where sources disagree. Diocles says Diogenes' father adulterated the coinage and the son went into exile; a certain Eubulides says Diogenes did it himself; Diogenes is said to confess it in his Pordalus; another version makes it a misreading of Apollo's advice to alter the nomisma, custom as well as coin (6.20–21). Debased Sinopean coins of about 350–340 BC led Branham (1996) and Navia (2005) to give the story a historical core. If the coins date the exile, Diogenes reached Athens after Antisthenes' death, and those who keep the link must posit an earlier visit.

The doctrine under the anecdotes

Strip out the stories and a position remains, stated most fully at 6.70–72. Training (askēsis) is twofold, of soul and of body, and nothing in life succeeds without it; one should choose the toils that accord with nature instead of useless ones, and once practised, contempt for pleasure is itself most pleasant (6.70–71). The body is drilled to need little so that the soul is free. To deface the currency is to give custom less authority than nature (6.71); what is not shameful is not shameful in public, so if eating is not wrong it is not wrong in the agora (6.69). The instrument is frank speech, parrhēsia, which Diogenes called the finest thing among men (6.69). A syllogism supplies a theology: all things belong to the gods; the wise are friends of the gods; friends share; so all things belong to the wise (6.72).

Where sources disagree. Diogenes Laertius treats Cynicism as a school but concedes that some call it only a way of life (enstasis biou, 6.103), and Hippobotus' list of schools omits it (1.19–20). The emperor Julian (Orations 6 and 7) answered that it is a philosophy, in some ways universal and the most natural, and Goulet-Cazé (L'ascèse cynique, 1986) found in 6.70–71 a reasoned theory of training, though whether the wording is Diogenes' or a later compiler's is uncertain.

Crates and Hipparchia

Crates of Thebes flourished in the 113th Olympiad, 328–325 BC (6.87). A Hellenistic Antisthenes, author of Successions, says a beggared Telephus on the tragic stage converted him, and that he turned his estate into about two hundred talents and gave it to his fellow citizens (6.87). Hippobotus made him a pupil of Bryson the Achaean, not of Diogenes (6.85): even this link in the chain had a rival. He was called the Door-opener for walking into houses to admonish (6.86). Asked by Alexander whether he wanted Thebes rebuilt, he asked why, since another Alexander would raze it; his country was obscurity and poverty, and he a fellow citizen of Diogenes (6.93). His verse turned Homer's Crete "in the midst of the wine-dark sea" (Odyssey 19.172) into Pera, the beggar's wallet, a city in the midst of wine-dark smoke (6.85).

Hipparchia of Maroneia, sister of his pupil Metrocles, is the only woman given her own life by Diogenes Laertius (6.96–98). She threatened to kill herself unless she could marry Crates; he stripped before her and said this was the bridegroom and these his possessions (6.96). Sextus cites their open union as a custom flouted (Outlines 1.153). At a dinner she argued against Theodorus the atheist: what would not be unjust if Theodorus did it is not unjust if Hipparchia does it; Theodorus striking Theodorus is not unjust; so Hipparchia striking Theodorus is not. He pulled at her cloak and asked if this was the woman who had left her loom; she answered that time taken from the loom for education was not badly spent (6.97–98). The argument slides from striking oneself to striking another, deliberately: dialectic parodied, and turned on a Cyrenaic.

Menippus and Cynic writing

Cynics distrusted books and wrote many. Menippus of Gadara, a Phoenician and once a slave, said by Hermippus to have lent money by the day and hanged himself when he lost it (6.99–100), left thirteen books, among them a Nekyia, Wills and Letters from the Gods (6.101). None survives. Strabo calls him the serio-comic (spoudogeloios, 16.2.29), and his mixture of prose and verse mocking philosophers and gods outlived him: in Varro's Menippean Satires, which imitated rather than translated him (Cicero, Academica 1.8), in Seneca's Apocolocyntosis (Rome module 7.1), and in Lucian (module 7.4), who sends Menippus to Hades and to the moon. Around him ran the diatribe of Bion of Borysthenes, whom Diogenes Laertius files with the Academy (4.46–58) and whose sermons survive in Teles' excerpts in Stobaeus; the meliambi of Cercidas (P.Oxy. 1082); Onesicritus' romance of Alexander's education (module 11.7). A philosophy without treatises spread through parody, anecdote and sermon, forms that attach to any name.

Aristippus and the Cyrenaics

Aristippus of Cyrene came to Athens drawn by Socrates' fame (2.65) and was in Aegina when Socrates died (Phaedo 59c). He was the first Socratic to charge fees (2.65), and could suit himself to place, time and person, so that Diogenes called him the king's poodle (2.66). Xenophon has him refuse both to rule and to be ruled, a foreigner everywhere (Memorabilia 2.1.13); Aristotle counts him among the sophists who scorned mathematics for saying nothing of good and bad (Metaphysics 996a29–b1).

The school's doctrine (2.86–93) starts from two affections (pathē): pain, a rough motion, and pleasure, a smooth one. The end is the particular pleasure of the moment; happiness, the sum of such pleasures, is chosen for their sake, not they for its (2.87–88). Absence of pain is no pleasure but an intermediate state, like sleep (2.89–90). Bodily pleasures are the strongest (2.90), and pleasure is good even from a shameful source, though the wise man avoids wrongdoing for fear of penalty and opinion (2.88, 2.93). Beneath lies an epistemology: we grasp only our own affections, so the honest report is "I am being whitened", not "this is white" (Sextus, Against the Mathematicians 7.191–192; Plutarch, Against Colotes 1120d–e).

Where sources disagree. Diogenes Laertius says the founder made smooth motion the end (2.85). Aristocles of Messene, quoted by Eusebius (Preparation for the Gospel 14.18.31–32), says the elder Aristippus talked constantly of pleasure but never clearly defined the end, and that his grandson, "mother-taught" by Arete, first defined it as living pleasantly. Tsouna (Stanford Encyclopedia, "The Cyrenaics") concludes that the founder was no ethical hedonist and shows no interest in epistemology, against Rowe (2015), who takes him to be the source of the anonymous "subtler" thinkers of Plato's Theaetetus (156a; module 12.2); Mondolfo gave that role to the grandson.

The later Cyrenaics: Hegesias, Anniceris, Theodorus

Around 300 BC the school split three ways. Hegesias, the Death-persuader (2.86), argued that happiness is impossible, since the body is full of suffering, the soul shares it and fortune thwarts hope; life and death are equally choiceworthy, and the wise man aims only at freedom from pain (2.94–96). Cicero says his book The Man Who Starves Himself drove so many to suicide that a King Ptolemy forbade him to lecture (Tusculan Disputations 1.83–84); Tsouna judges the story apocryphal. Anniceris kept pleasure as the end but made room for friendship, gratitude, honour to parents and service to country: a friend is chosen for goodwill, not only for use (2.96–97). Theodorus made the ends joy, from wisdom, and grief, from folly, dismissed friendship, and allowed theft, adultery and sacrilege on occasion, since none is shameful by nature (2.98–99). Cicero ranks him among the atheists (On the Nature of the Gods 1.2, 1.63) and has him tell Lysimachus, who threatened him with the cross, that it is all one to Theodorus whether he rots in the ground or in the air (Tusculan Disputations 1.102). Pessimism, sociability, amoralism: the school had no stable centre, and the Garden took its ground. Epicurus' differences from it (10.136–137) belong to module 12.6.

The Megarians and dialectic

Module 6.5 gives Euclides at Socrates' death, his good that is one thing under many names, Eubulides' Liar and Heap, Stilpo's apatheia and Sedley's Dialectical school. Diogenes Laertius adds that Euclides' followers were called Megarians, then Eristics, then Dialecticians, from their question-and-answer method (2.106). Eubulides is credited with seven arguments: the Liar, the Disguised, the Electra, the Veiled, the Heap, the Horned and the Bald (2.108). The Veiled: you know your father; you do not know this veiled man; he is your father; so you know and do not know him. Identicals cannot always be swapped after "know". The Horned: what you have not lost you have; you have not lost horns; so you have horns. A presupposition is smuggled in. An invented epitaph has a "lying argument" killing Philitas of Cos (Athenaeus 9.401e), perhaps the Liar itself.

Diodorus Cronus was nicknamed "old fogey": Strabo says the name passed to him from his teacher Apollonius Cronus (14.2.21), Diogenes Laertius that Ptolemy I gave it when he failed to solve a puzzle of Stilpo's at the king's table (2.111–112). He argued that nothing is moving, though things have moved (Sextus, Against the Mathematicians 10), and, Boethius reports, defined the possible as what is or will be true. Against Philo, for whom a conditional is false only when it has a true antecedent and a false consequent, he required that it never could have one (Sextus, Outlines 2.110). His Master Argument (module 6.5) set three propositions against each other: every past truth is necessary; the impossible does not follow from the possible; something is possible which neither is nor will be true. One must go (Epictetus, Discourses 2.19.1).

Stilpo, asked by Demetrius Poliorcetes, who took Megara in 307, whether he had lost anything, said he had seen no one carry off knowledge (2.115); Seneca makes it "all my goods are with me" (Letters 9.18–19). He denied that one thing can be predicated of another, so that only "man is man" and "good is good" are safe (Plutarch, Against Colotes 1119c–1120b). Phaedo's school at Elis, moved to Eretria by Menedemus (2.105, 2.125–144), was the Megarians' smaller cousin.

Where sources disagree. Epictetus (Discourses 2.19.2–5) reports three answers: Diodorus denied the third proposition, Cleanthes the first, Chrysippus the second. He does not say how the three clash, and modern reconstructions, from Prior ("Diodoran Modalities", 1955) to Gaskin (The Sea Battle and the Master Argument, 1995), supply the missing steps differently. The Stoic answers belong to module 12.7.

The Cynic as social critic, and the road to Zeno

The Cynic criticised by example. Diogenes answered Plato's definition of man with a plucked chicken (6.40) and temple officials arresting a petty thief by calling them great thieves leading away a small one (6.45). Each target is a convention claiming nature's authority. Epictetus' ideal Cynic belongs to Rome module 13.6, and the imperial Cynics, Demetrius and Peregrinus, to Rome module 13.3. Foucault's last course at the Collège de France (1984; The Courage of Truth, 2011) read Cynic parrhēsia as truth told at the risk of one's life.

Where sources disagree. Diogenes applied to himself the tragic curse of the man without city or home (6.38), and Crates called his country obscurity and poverty (6.93): on this evidence "citizen of the world" (6.63) means a citizen of nowhere. Yet 6.72 also makes the cosmos the only right commonwealth, a positive claim the Stoics built on. Kleingeld and Brown (Stanford Encyclopedia, "Cosmopolitanism") find no unambiguous positive commitment and make the Cynic life itself the cosmopolitan example.

The road to the Stoa ran through Crates. Zeno of Citium, shipwrecked near Athens, read the second book of Xenophon's Memorabilia in a bookshop, asked where such men were to be found, and was told to follow Crates, who was passing (7.2–3); Crates cured his modesty with a pot of lentil soup carried through the Kerameikos and broken (7.3), and people joked that Zeno wrote his Republic on the dog's tail (7.4). Zeno also studied with Stilpo and in the Academy (7.2); his Stoa belongs to module 12.7. The Stoics never settled the debt: Apollodorus allowed that the sage might live as a Cynic, Cynicism being a short cut to virtue (7.121), while Cicero, probably following Panaetius, would reject the Cynic way entirely as an enemy of modesty (On Duties 1.148).

Self-test

  1. Why does the arrangement of Diogenes Laertius' books 2, 6 and 7 bear on the question of who founded Cynicism?
    Answer

    He follows an Ionian succession from Socrates through Antisthenes, Diogenes and Crates to Zeno (1.15), so placing the Cynics between the Socratics and the Stoics makes them the Stoa's pedigree. The arrangement presupposes the founder claim that modules 6.5 and 7.2 question.

  2. Which contemporary evidence is older than book 6's compilers, and how does it bear on Antisthenes' claim to be the first Cynic?
    Answer

    Aristotle quotes "the Dog" on taverns (Rhetoric 1411a24–25) and Theophrastus' Megarian gives the mouse (Diogenes Laertius 6.22). Aristotle treats Antisthenes and "the Antistheneans" as logicians (Metaphysics 1024b32–34, 1043b23–28) and never links them with the Dog.

  3. How do the versions of the coinage scandal at 6.20–21 show the difference between anecdote and evidence?
    Answer

    Diocles blames the father, Eubulides blames Diogenes, the Pordalus has Diogenes confess, and the oracle version makes it a misread command to alter the nomisma. The coins confirm that Sinope's currency was tampered with, but the oracle story looks like an aetiology of the slogan.

  4. What does the lettuce retort at 2.68 and 6.58 show about chreiai?
    Answer

    That they migrate: the same exchange gives the last word to Aristippus in his chapter and to Diogenes, against Plato, in his. No single anecdote can be trusted as biography.

  5. State the syllogism at 6.72 that gives Cynic poverty a theology.
    Answer

    All things belong to the gods; the wise are friends of the gods; friends hold things in common; so all things belong to the wise. The Cynic who owns nothing claims everything.

  6. Reconstruct Hipparchia's argument against Theodorus and say where it fails.
    Answer

    Whatever would not be unjust if Theodorus did it is not unjust if Hipparchia does it; Theodorus striking himself is not unjust; so Hipparchia striking Theodorus is not (6.97). It slides from striking oneself to striking another, deliberately: a parody of dialectic.

  7. What does Aristocles say about the two Aristippi, and why does it matter?
    Answer

    That the elder talked of pleasure but never clearly defined the end, and that his grandson, "mother-taught" by Arete, defined it as living pleasantly (Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 14.18.31–32). If so, systematic Cyrenaic hedonism is third-generation, and Tsouna denies the founder was an ethical hedonist at all.

  8. How do Hegesias, Anniceris and Theodorus each change Cyrenaic hedonism?
    Answer

    Hegesias: happiness is impossible, so the aim is freedom from pain and life and death are indifferent. Anniceris: friendship, gratitude and country count, and friends are chosen for goodwill. Theodorus: joy and grief, from wisdom and folly, are the ends, friendship is rejected and conventional crimes are sometimes allowed (2.94–99).

  9. What does Eubulides' Veiled argument show about the verb "know"?
    Answer

    You know your father and do not know the veiled man, who is your father, so substituting one name for another inside "know" can turn truth into falsehood. It isolates what logicians now call an opaque context.

  10. Give the three propositions of the Master Argument and the answers of Diodorus, Cleanthes and Chrysippus.
    Answer

    Every past truth is necessary; the impossible does not follow from the possible; something is possible which neither is nor will be true. Diodorus rejected the third, Cleanthes the first, Chrysippus the second (Epictetus, Discourses 2.19.1–5).

Carry forward

  1. Separate the chreia from the doctrine and date every witness: Aristotle and Theophrastus are contemporaries, Diogenes Laertius writes five and a half centuries later from compilers who wanted successions, and anecdotes move from name to name.
  2. Socrates' followers divided his legacy into self-sufficient virtue (Antisthenes, Diogenes, Crates), pleasure and the private affection (Aristippus' school) and refutation turned into logic (the Megarians). The Stoics took the first and third and Epicurus answered the second, so each Hellenistic school begins as a choice among Socratic inheritances.
  3. Cynicism argued by living: poverty, shamelessness and frank speech performed in public to expose convention's claim to be nature. Whether that is a philosophy or a way of life was asked in antiquity and is asked again wherever the Cynic reappears, in the Stoic sage, Epictetus' ideal Cynic and Foucault's parrhēsia.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the minor Socratic schools, extending modules 6.5 and 7.2. Module 6.5 has a section on the minor Socratics (Antisthenes, Diogenes' jar and lamp, Aristippus and Laïs, Euclides, Eubulides' Liar and Heap, Stilpo, the Master Argument and Sedley's Dialectical school, and Dudley on the Cynic succession), and module 7.2 introduces Diogenes and Crates and weighs Antisthenes' claim to have founded Cynicism: point back to both, and add to those disputes rather than restating them. Cover: Antisthenes; Diogenes of Sinope and the anecdote tradition (Diogenes Laertius book 6), and what can be known about the man; Crates and Hipparchia; Menippus and Cynic writing; Aristippus and the Cyrenaics on pleasure, and the later Cyrenaics (Hegesias, Anniceris, Theodorus); the Megarians and dialectic (Euclides, Eubulides' paradoxes, Diodorus Cronus and the Master Argument, Stilpo); Diogenes Laertius as a source and his limits; and the Cynic as social critic, and the road from Diogenes through Crates to Zeno (hand off to module 12.7). Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 12 · Deep dive III: Greek philosophy · 12.6 · 2,857 words

Epicurus and the Garden

Samos, Lampsacus and the GardenThe sources: letters, maxims and charred rollsThe canon: how anything is knownAtoms, void and the swerveThe soul and deathPleasure and the kinds of desireFriendship, and justice as a compactThe gods and the fourfold remedyDiogenes of Oinoanda's wallThe hostile traditionSelf-testCarry forward

Samos, Lampsacus and the Garden

Module 7.2 gives the dates (341–270), the garden bought in 306 and a community open to women and slaves. Epicurus was an Athenian of the deme Gargettus, brought up on Samos, where his parents Neocles and Chaerestrate had settled in the Athenian cleruchy (Diogenes Laertius 10.1). He came to Athens at eighteen, the age of ephebic service, then joined his father at Colophon after Perdiccas expelled the Athenians from Samos (10.1). He said he turned to philosophy at fourteen; Apollodorus says his schoolmasters could not tell him where Hesiod's Chaos came from (10.2; module 2.1 reads the line). He heard the Platonist Pamphilus and the Democritean Nausiphanes, then called himself self-taught and Nausiphanes a jellyfish (10.8, 10.13–14; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1.72–73).

He taught at Mytilene and Lampsacus, where he gathered the core of the school: Metrodorus, Polyaenus, Colotes, Idomeneus, Leonteus and Themista, with Hermarchus, his successor, from Mytilene. In 307/6 he returned to Athens (10.2) and bought a garden for eighty minae (10.10). He died of a kidney stone in 271/0, aged seventy-two (10.15), writing on his last day to Idomeneus that against his pains stood the joy of remembering their conversations (10.22); Cicero's version is addressed to Hermarchus (On Ends 2.96).

The members lived simply and did not pool property, since sharing implies distrust (10.11). The will (10.16–21) leaves the garden, through two trustees, to Hermarchus and his successors, funds Epicurus' birthday on the tenth of Gamelion and a meeting on the twentieth of every month, provides for Metrodorus' children and frees four slaves. Romans later wore his portrait on rings (Cicero, On Ends 5.3), kept the twentieth as a feast (Pliny, Natural History 35.5) and were told to act as if Epicurus were watching (Seneca, Letters 25.5).

The sources: letters, maxims and charred rolls

Epicurus wrote some three hundred rolls (10.26), among them thirty-seven books On Nature (10.27). What survives whole is what Diogenes Laertius copied into book 10, which he ends with the Principal Doctrines (Kyriai Doxai, KD) as the colophon of his work (10.138).

TextDiogenes LaertiusSubject
Letter to Herodotus10.35–83atoms, perception, soul
Letter to Pythocles10.84–116celestial and weather phenomena
Letter to Menoeceus10.122–135gods, death, desire, pleasure
Differences from the Cyrenaics10.136–138kinds of pleasure and pain
Principal Doctrines 1–4010.139–154forty maxims

The letters are epitomes, written so that the main heads could be held in memory (10.35–36) and practised day and night (10.135). The Vatican Sayings (SV), eighty-one maxims, were found by Carl Wotke in 1888 in a fourteenth-century manuscript (Vaticanus graecus 1950); some repeat the KD, and some are elsewhere ascribed to Metrodorus. The rest is carbonised. From 1752 the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum yielded an Epicurean library (Rome module 13.3 takes the villa, Philodemus and Piso). It held books of On Nature, among them book 25, on the mind and responsibility (PHerc. 419, 697, 1056, 1191, 1420, 1634), and book 28, on language and error (PHerc. 1479/1417), besides Philodemus' treatises, such as On Piety, On Signs (PHerc. 1065) and On Death (PHerc. 1050).

The canon: how anything is known

Epicurus replaced logic with "canonic", after his lost Kanon (The Rule). The criteria of truth are sensations, preconceptions (prolepseis) and feelings (pathe); dialectic is superfluous (Diogenes Laertius 10.31; Cicero, On Ends 1.22).

Every sensation is true. It adds nothing, and nothing can refute it: not a sensation of the same kind, which has equal standing, nor one of another kind, which judges different objects, nor reason, which depends on the senses (10.31–32). Error lies in added opinion (Letter to Herodotus 50–51). In Sextus' report of the Epicurean view (Against the Mathematicians 7.208–209), a distant square tower looks round: the sensation truly reports an image worn round in transit; the belief that the tower is round is false. An opinion is true if evident experience attests it or, for things unseen, does not contest it (7.211–216). Void passes, since without it motion, which is evident, would be impossible.

A preconception is a general notion laid down by repeated perception; without it we could not even seek what we seek (10.33), Epicurus' answer to the puzzle of Plato's Meno (80d–e). Celestial events may have several explanations consistent with appearances, and to insist on one is to fall into myth (Letter to Pythocles 86–87). Here Epicurus parted from Democritus' doubts about the senses (module 12.1; DK 68 B 9), and Plutarch defends Democritus against his Epicurean heirs (Against Colotes 1108f–1111e). KD 23 states the principle: fight all your sensations and you have no standard for judging even those you call false.

Atoms, void and the swerve

Module 7.2 gives the outline; module 12.1 hands on the system Epicurus revised. The Letter to Herodotus argues that nothing comes from or perishes into what is not (38–39); that the whole is bodies, attested by sensation, and void, inferred because bodies must have somewhere to move (39–40); and that atoms, void and worlds are unlimited (41–45).

The revisions answer objections. To Aristotle's complaint that the atomists never explained motion (module 12.1), Epicurus gives atoms weight besides shape and size (Letter to Herodotus 54); Aetius (1.3.18) calls weight his addition to Democritus. Atomic shapes are inconceivably many but not unlimited (42). Each atom has minimal parts, the smallest magnitudes, which cannot exist apart (56–59); David Furley (Two Studies in the Greek Atomists, 1967) read these as a reply to Aristotle's argument that no magnitude is built from partless points (Physics 6.1).

The swerve is not in the surviving letters. Lucretius (2.216–293) gives it two jobs: without it atoms would fall like raindrops and never collide, and the mind would be bound by fate. Cicero mocks an uncaused motion invented to save free will (On Fate 22–23; On Ends 1.19); Diogenes of Oinoanda credits Epicurus by name with the free movement in atoms that Democritus missed (fr. 54 Smith). Epicurus' target shows in the Letter to Menoeceus: better to follow the myths about the gods than be enslaved to the fate of the natural philosophers (134). Book 25 of On Nature, like SV 40, argues that the determinist refutes himself, since in arguing he treats his opponent as responsible for his beliefs.

Where sources disagree. Cyril Bailey (The Greek Atomists and Epicurus, 1928) read Lucretius as placing a swerve of the mind's atoms in every act of will. Furley (1967) answered that swerves are rare and serve only to save the will from necessity, so that action flows from character, as in Aristotle. David Sedley ("Epicurus' refutation of determinism", 1983), reading On Nature 25, makes the self an emergent cause and the swerve the physical condition that leaves room for it. Module 7.2's other question, whether the swerve is Epicurus' own, turns on Cicero and Diogenes of Oinoanda, who say it is.

The soul and death

Modules 7.2 and 8.4 give KD 2 and the Letter to Menoeceus (124–127), and module 7.2 Lucretius' symmetry argument. Beneath them lies the physics. The soul is a body of fine particles spread through the frame, most like breath mixed with heat (Letter to Herodotus 63); Aetius (4.3.11) adds a nameless fourth component that produces sensation. The soul perceives only while housed in the body and scatters when the body breaks up (64–66); it cannot be incorporeal, since only void is, and void neither acts nor is acted on (67).

Since all good and bad lies in sensation, death, its privation, is nothing to us (Letter to Menoeceus 124–125), and to fear its prospect is to be pained in vain (125). Unlimited time holds no more pleasure than limited time, if reason measures pleasure's limits (KD 19–20), so a complete life needs no more years. Against death, says SV 31, we all live in a city without walls. Thomas Nagel ("Death", 1970) revived the objection that death harms by deprivation; James Warren (Facing Death: Epicurus and His Critics, 2004) reconstructs the Epicurean replies.

Pleasure and the kinds of desire

Pleasure is the beginning and end of the blessed life (Letter to Menoeceus 128), and the cradle argument adds that animals seek it by nature from birth (Diogenes Laertius 10.137; Torquatus in Cicero, On Ends 1.30). Pleasures are weighed against pains (129–130). The end is not the profligate's pleasures but freedom from pain in the body and from disturbance in the soul; bread and water please most when one is in want, and sober reasoning, not drinking parties, makes life pleasant (131–132). Practical wisdom (phronesis) is the greatest good, since one cannot live pleasantly without living wisely, honourably and justly (132; KD 5).

The removal of all pain is the limit of pleasure (KD 3); after it bodily pleasure is only varied (KD 18). The scholion on KD 29 sorts desires: natural and necessary (drink when thirsty), natural but not necessary (costly food), neither (crowns and statues). Nature's wealth is limited and easy to get, the wealth of empty opinion unlimited (KD 15); whoever is not hungry, thirsty or cold, and expects to stay so, could rival Zeus in happiness (SV 33).

Module 12.5 gives the Cyrenaic doctrine and module 7.2 the two kinds of pleasure; Diogenes Laertius records the break. The Cyrenaics admit only pleasure in motion; Epicurus admits both kinds, quoting his On Choices: freedom from disturbance (ataraxia) and from pain (aponia) are katastematic, static, pleasures, while joy and delight are kinetic, in activity (10.136). The Cyrenaics hold bodily pains worse; Epicurus holds mental pains worse, since the flesh suffers only the present, the soul past, present and future (10.137). The deathbed letter is the doctrine at work.

Where sources disagree. Torquatus holds that the removal of all pain is itself the highest pleasure (Cicero, On Ends 1.37–38); Cicero answers that nobody calls painlessness pleasure and that Epicurus slides between two senses of the word (2.9–10). Bailey and John Rist (Epicurus: An Introduction, 1972) take Diogenes Laertius 10.136 as Epicurus' doctrine, static pleasure being the enjoyment of a sound body and mind. J. C. B. Gosling and C. C. W. Taylor (The Greeks on Pleasure, 1982) doubted the division, and Boris Nikolsky ("Epicurus on Pleasure", 2001) traced it to Carneades' classification of ends, reaching Cicero through Antiochus: Epicurus spoke of one pleasure with two aspects.

Friendship, and justice as a compact

Of all that wisdom provides for a blessed life, friendship is by far the greatest (KD 27). It begins in benefit but is choiceworthy for itself (SV 23, where the manuscript reads arete, "virtue", and editors commonly print hairete, "choiceworthy"); we need less our friends' help than confidence in it (SV 34). Torquatus reports three Epicurean accounts, from friendship valued for use, to friendship loved for itself once formed, to a compact among the wise (Cicero, On Ends 1.65–70).

Justice is a pledge of advantage, not to harm one another or be harmed (KD 31), and there is none with creatures that cannot make such compacts (KD 32); it is nothing in itself, but a compact (syntheke) made in some place at some time (KD 33). Injustice is bad only through the fear of detection (KD 34), and no secret violator can be sure of escaping (KD 35). A law that ceases to be useful ceases to be just (KD 37–38). This is Glaucon's contract (Republic 358e–359b; module 6.5 tells the ring of Gyges) with his conclusion reversed: the just man is the least disturbed, the unjust the most (KD 17), so the wise keep their compacts. Security comes from a quiet life withdrawn from the many (KD 14), the wise man stays out of politics (10.119), and the maxim "live unnoticed" survives because Plutarch wrote an essay against it.

The gods and the fourfold remedy

Module 7.2 gives KD 1. The Letter to Menoeceus adds that god is an imperishable and blessed living being, as the common notion outlines; that the gods exist, since knowledge of them is evident, but are not as the many think; and that the impious man is the one who fastens the opinions of the many on the gods (123–124). Universal belief is evidence because it springs from a preconception nature has given every people (Velleius in Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1.43–45). The gods are grasped by the mind through fine images and have not body but a sort of body, not blood but a sort of blood (1.49). A scholion on KD 1 says that some are numerically distinct and others exist by likeness of form, from a continuous flow of similar images to one place (10.139). Philodemus' On Piety records Epicurus taking part in the city's festivals and sacrifices.

Lactantius (On the Anger of God 13.20–21) ascribes to Epicurus the dilemma that god either wishes to remove evils and cannot, or can and will not, or neither, or both; only the last befits a god, so whence evils? Reinhold Glei ("Et invidus et inbecillus: das angebliche Epikurfragment bei Laktanz, De ira dei 13,20–21", Vigiliae Christianae 42, 1988) traced the argument to an Academic source, not to Epicurus.

Where sources disagree. Module 7.2 sets out the realist and idealist readings. A. A. Long and David Sedley (The Hellenistic Philosophers, 1987) revived the idealist one, the gods as our own idealisation of the blessed life, which the scholion's likeness of form suits, and Sedley ("Epicurus' theological innatism", 2011) adds that our preconception of the gods is innate, not drawn from experience. David Konstan ("Epicurus on the gods", 2011) defends the realist one: the gods are atomic compounds, and the physics can explain both how we come to know them and why they never perish.

Module 7.2 gives the fourfold remedy in English. Philodemus states it (tetrapharmakos, a doctors' word for a four-ingredient salve) in a work whose title survives only as Pros tous [...] (PHerc. 1005, column 5): aphobon ho theos, anypopton ho thanatos, kai tagathon men eukteton, to de deinon euekkartereton; god presents no fears, death no worries; the good is easy to get, the terrible easy to endure. The four clauses follow KD 1–4 in order. Diogenes of Oinoanda calls the same fears, of gods, death and pain, with desires beyond nature's limits, the roots of all evils (fr. 34 Smith).

Diogenes of Oinoanda's wall

In the second century AD, under Hadrian on epigraphic grounds, Diogenes of Oinoanda (Latin Oenoanda), in the uplands of northern Lycia, paid for a stoa wall inscribed with Epicurean philosophy: about 25,000 words over some 260 square metres, on Martin Ferguson Smith's estimate. The first blocks were found in 1884; Smith's Diogenes of Oinoanda: The Epicurean Inscription (1993) numbers the fragments. The wall held treatises on physics, ethics and old age, letters, and maxims of Epicurus along its lower margin (fr. 29 carries KD 1).

Diogenes explains why a doctrine of withdrawal needed a monument. Near the sunset of his life he wished to set out the remedies of salvation for the well-disposed, now and to come (fr. 3), and for so-called foreigners, since the whole earth is one country for all and the world one home (fr. 30). He asks that statues of the gods be made genial and smiling, so that we smile back instead of fearing them (fr. 19), and foresees a time when the life of the gods will pass to men, everything full of justice and mutual love, with no need of walls or laws (fr. 56).

The hostile tradition

Hostility began inside the school. Timocrates, Metrodorus' brother, defected and alleged gluttony, and Diotimus the Stoic circulated fifty obscene letters in Epicurus' name (10.3, 10.6); Cicero's Cotta sneers that even the courtesan Leontion dared to write against Theophrastus (On the Nature of the Gods 1.93).

In book 1 of On Ends Lucius Manlius Torquatus expounds the ethics (1.29–72); in book 2 Cicero replies that Epicurus equivocates on pleasure, that infants seek pleasure in motion, not painlessness (2.31–32), and that Torquatus' ancestors acted for honour (2.60–61; Rome module 3.2). Yet he allows that the dying Epicurus was better than his theory (2.96–99). Plutarch's Against Colotes (Moralia 1107d–1127e) answers Colotes' book arguing that one cannot even live by the doctrines of the other philosophers, and turns the charge round. Dante puts Epicurus and his followers, who make the soul die with the body, among the heretics (Inferno 10.13–15). Rome module 5.6 reads Lucretius, and Rome module 13.3 takes Philodemus, Cassius, Atticus and the other Roman Epicureans.

Where sources disagree. Cicero (On Ends 2) takes Epicurus' pleasure at its word and finds either vulgarity or equivocation. Seneca, a Stoic who quotes Epicurus throughout the early Letters, calls his precepts upright and, seen close, austere, and says the school is maligned for its name (On the Happy Life 12–13). Plutarch argues that Epicureans could not live by their principles; Diogenes Laertius, our main source, defends the man against the slanders (10.9–11).

Self-test

  1. Why does Epicurus hold that every sensation is true, and where does error come in?
    Answer

    A sensation adds nothing, and nothing can refute it: not a sensation of the same kind (equal standing), nor one of another kind (different objects), nor reason (which depends on the senses) (Diogenes Laertius 10.31–32). Error lies in the opinion added, as when the image of a distant square tower, worn round in transit, is taken to show a round tower.

  2. Name three ways Epicurus revised Democritus' atomism and the objection each answers.
    Answer

    Weight, against Aristotle's complaint that the atomists never explained motion (Letter to Herodotus 54; Aetius 1.3.18); minimal parts, against Aristotle's argument that magnitudes cannot be built from partless points (Furley); and truthful sensation, against Democritus' own doubts about the senses (DK 68 B 9). The swerve, against determinism, is a fourth.

  3. What two jobs does the swerve do in Lucretius, and why is its attribution to Epicurus questioned?
    Answer

    It lets falling atoms collide, and it breaks the chain of fate so that the mind is free (Lucretius 2.216–293). It appears nowhere in Epicurus' surviving letters; the attribution rests on later witnesses, Cicero (On Fate 22–23) and Diogenes of Oinoanda (fr. 54 Smith).

  4. Why, on Epicurus' account, can the soul neither survive the body nor be incorporeal?
    Answer

    It is a body of fine particles spread through the frame, which perceives only while housed in the body and scatters when the body breaks up (Letter to Herodotus 63–66). The only incorporeal is void, which neither acts nor is acted on, so an incorporeal soul could neither feel nor act (67).

  5. Classify desires with Epicurus' examples, and say why the classification matters for happiness.
    Answer

    Natural and necessary (drink when thirsty), natural but not necessary (costly food), neither (crowns and statues), in the scholion on KD 29. Natural wealth is limited and easy to get, while empty desires have no limit (KD 15), so happiness depends on satisfying the first and dropping the last.

  6. On which two points does Diogenes Laertius say Epicurus differed from the Cyrenaics?
    Answer

    They admitted only kinetic pleasure, he static pleasure (ataraxia, aponia) as well (10.136). They held bodily pains worse; he held mental pains worse, since the soul suffers past, present and future, the flesh only the present (10.137).

  7. What is justice for Epicurus, and why should the wise keep the compact even when they could break it unseen?
    Answer

    A compact for mutual advantage, not to harm or be harmed (KD 31, 33). Injustice is bad only through fear of detection, and no one can be sure of escaping (KD 34–35), so the unjust live in disturbance and the just in calm (KD 17).

  8. State the fourfold remedy as Philodemus gives it and relate it to the Principal Doctrines.
    Answer

    In PHerc. 1005, column 5: god presents no fears, death no worries; the good is easy to get, the terrible easy to endure. The clauses summarise KD 1–4 in order: the gods, death, the limit of pleasure, the endurance of pain.

  9. What are the realist and the idealist readings of the Epicurean gods, and who holds each?
    Answer

    For realists such as Konstan (2011) the gods are compounds of fine atoms whose indestructibility the physics can explain. For idealists, Long and Sedley (1987) and Sedley (2011), they are our own idealisation of the blessed life, a reading the scholion on KD 1, with gods existing by likeness of form, suits.

  10. Why is Diogenes of Oinoanda's inscription a paradox for the Garden, and how did he justify it?
    Answer

    A school that taught "live unnoticed" was proclaimed on a public wall. Diogenes says that near the end of his life he wished to set out the remedies of salvation for his own and future generations (fr. 3) and for foreigners, since the earth is one country for all (fr. 30).

Carry forward

  1. Epicureanism was built for memory and community: epitomes, forty maxims led by the fourfold remedy, a founder's birthday and portrait. Lucretius' poem and the wall at Oinoanda are delivery systems for a fixed core, and later Epicurean texts should be read as transmitting it.
  2. Epicurus' physics serves his ethics: weight, minimal parts, the swerve and truthful senses answer named objections, and an understanding of atoms and void is meant to remove the fear of gods and death that the remedy's first two clauses name.
  3. Most of the evidence is hostile (Cicero, Plutarch, Lactantius), late (Diogenes Laertius, Oinoanda) or charred (Herculaneum). Keep the reporter apart from the claim, as with the problem of evil that Lactantius ascribes to Epicurus and the division of pleasures that may belong to Cicero's sources.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Epicurus and his school, extending module 7.2, which outlines the system, gives the sources, 'death is nothing to us' with Lucretius' symmetry argument, static and kinetic pleasure and Philodemus' fourfold remedy, and carries the disputes over the gods and the swerve, and module 8.4, which reads the Epicurean denial of an afterlife: point back to them for each and go deeper. Cover: the life, Samos and Lampsacus, and the Garden as a community; the sources: the three letters and the Principal Doctrines (Diogenes Laertius book 10), the Vatican Sayings, On Nature from the Herculaneum papyri; the canon and the theory of knowledge; atoms, void and the swerve; the soul and death ('death is nothing to us': Letter to Menoeceus and Principal Doctrines 2); pleasure as the absence of pain, and the kinds of desire; friendship, and justice as a compact; the gods; the fourfold remedy as Philodemus states it; Diogenes of Oenoanda's wall inscription; and the hostile tradition (Cicero, On Ends 2, answering Torquatus' exposition in book 1; Plutarch, Against Colotes). The Stoa from Zeno to Posidonius

Zeno of Citium and the Painted Stoa

Module 12.5 tells how Zeno came to philosophy: the shipwreck, the bookshop, Crates and the lentil soup (Diogenes Laertius 7.2–3). Diogenes adds Stilpo the Megarian and, in the Academy, Xenocrates and Polemo (7.2). From Crates came the sufficiency of virtue, from the Megarians compressed argument: what uses reason is better than what does not, nothing is better than the cosmos, so the cosmos uses reason (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.21). Cicero's On Ends 4, arguing Antiochus' case, presses that Zeno changed the Academy's words and kept its things.

He taught in the Stoa Poikile on the north side of the Agora, a public portico of the 460s hung with panels of Oinoe, the Amazons, fallen Troy and Marathon (Pausanias 1.15); his followers, first called Zenonians, became Stoics from the building (Diogenes 7.5). A public building gave the school no property to bequeath, unlike the Academy and the Garden. Athens voted Zeno a gold crown and a public tomb because his life matched his teaching (decree in Diogenes 7.10–12).

His most notorious book, the Republic, answered Plato's. Its hostile reporters describe a city of the wise without temples, law courts or coinage, where men and women dress alike and the wise hold wives in common (Diogenes 7.32–33, 7.131), bound by Eros as a god of friendship and concord (Athenaeus 13.561c). His pupils already disagreed: Aristo of Chios denied that any indifferent is preferred (7.160), and Herillus made knowledge the end (7.165).

Where sources disagree. Some later Stoics, Philodemus reports (On the Stoics), disowned the Republic as spurious or juvenile, and Athenodorus, keeper of the library at Pergamum, cut its offending passages from the school's books (Diogenes Laertius 7.34); Chrysippus went further in his own On the Republic (7.188). Plutarch read it as a dream of one world-city (module 7.2); Malcolm Schofield (The Stoic Idea of the City, 1991) argues for a community of the wise bound by concord and Eros, a rival to Plato's city rather than a world government.
