Cleanthes, the Hymn to Zeus and Heraclitus' fire

Cleanthes came to Athens a boxer, drew water for gardeners by night to study by day, and was called the Ass for his slowness and endurance (Diogenes Laertius 7.168–170). His physics is where the Stoics took Heraclitus' fire (module 12.1). Zeno had defined nature as a craftsmanlike fire proceeding methodically to generation (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.57); Cleanthes wrote an Interpretation of Heraclitus in four books (7.174), made the sun the ruling part of the cosmos (Cicero, Academica 2.126), and called tension a stroke of fire (Plutarch, On Stoic Self-Contradictions 1034d).

The Hymn to Zeus, thirty-nine hexameters preserved by Stobaeus (Anthology 1.1.12; SVF 1.537), is the one early Stoic text that survives whole. Zeus steers everything by law, and the cosmos obeys his ever-living thunderbolt, Heraclitus' thunderbolt that steers all things (DK 22 B 64). Nothing happens without him except what the bad do in their folly; yet he fits good and bad together, so that one logos of all things exists for ever (lines 15–21). The bad flee this common logos, like Heraclitus' many who live as though they had a private understanding (B 2), and the poem prays Zeus to rescue them from ignorance. Evil is human, and the whole absorbs it. Cleanthes' short prayer asking Zeus and Destiny to lead him survives in Epictetus (Handbook 53; SVF 1.527); Seneca's Latin of it belongs to Rome module 13.2.

Where sources disagree. Did the Stoics find the conflagration in Heraclitus or put it there? Aristotle, before the Stoa, says Heraclitus has all things become fire at some time (Physics 205a3–4), and Zeller accepted a Heraclitean world-fire. Burnet (Early Greek Philosophy) and Kirk (Heraclitus: The Cosmic Fragments, 1954) argued that a fire kindled and quenched in measures (B 30) excludes a total conflagration, and that Clement and Hippolytus read Heraclitus through Stoic eyes.

Chrysippus: propositions and arguments

Chrysippus of Soli heard Cleanthes and, in the Academy, Arcesilaus and Lacydes (Diogenes Laertius 7.183). He told Cleanthes to give him the doctrines and he would find the proofs (7.179); of his 705 books (7.180) we have quotations and a charred roll of his Logical Questions from Herculaneum.

Aristotle's syllogistic (module 12.4) relates terms; Chrysippus' logic relates whole propositions. What is true or false is a sayable (lekton), the incorporeal content of a sentence; a complete sayable that is true or false is a proposition (axiōma: 7.65). Connectives make conditionals, conjunctions and exclusive disjunctions. Five indemonstrable forms need no proof (7.79–81; Sextus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism 2.157–158):

  1. If the first, the second; the first; therefore the second.
  2. If the first, the second; not the second; therefore not the first.
  3. Not both the first and the second; the first; therefore not the second.
  4. Either the first or the second; the first; therefore not the second.
  5. Either the first or the second; not the first; therefore the second.

Rules called themata reduce other valid arguments to these. Module 12.5 gives Philo's and Diodorus' conditionals; a stricter view, usually credited to Chrysippus, required that the contradictory of the consequent conflict with the antecedent (Outlines 2.111).

Chrysippus' possible, in Diogenes' wording, is what admits of being true and is not prevented by external circumstances (7.75). Against the Master Argument, which module 12.5 hands on, he denied that the impossible cannot follow from the possible. "Dion has died" is possible, but "this man has died", said pointing at Dion, can never be true, since at Dion's death the "this" loses its object; yet it follows (Alexander of Aphrodisias, On Aristotle's Prior Analytics 177–178). Cleanthes instead gave up the necessity of every past truth (Epictetus, Discourses 2.19.2–4). The criterion was Zeno's cognitive impression: from what is, stamped in accordance with it, and such as could not come from what is not, the last clause added against Arcesilaus (Cicero, Academica 2.77), whose attack, and Carneades', is module 12.8's.

Where sources disagree. Carl Prantl's Geschichte der Logik im Abendlande (1855) dismissed Stoic logic as barren formalism. Jan Łukasiewicz (1935) recognised in the indemonstrables a logic of propositions two millennia before Frege, and Benson Mates (Stoic Logic, 1953) set it out in modern notation. How far it is a propositional calculus in the modern sense is still argued, since Chrysippus' conditional was not the truth-functional one.

Chrysippus: pneuma, mixture, fate and the conflagration

There are two principles, active (god, reason) and passive (unqualified matter), both bodies (Diogenes Laertius 7.134), since only body acts or is acted on; void, place, time and sayables are incorporeals that subsist without existing (Sextus, Against the Mathematicians 10.218). Chrysippus supplied the mechanism for module 7.2's outline. God is pneuma, fire and air, whose tensile motion runs inward and outward at once, giving each body its unity and qualities (Nemesius, On the Nature of Man 2). Grades of tension make the scale of nature: cohesion (hexis) in stones, growth (physis) in plants, soul in animals, reason in humans (Philo, Allegorical Interpretation 2.22–23).

Pneuma pervading matter means two bodies in one place. Chrysippus distinguished juxtaposition, as of grains; fusion, in which the ingredients perish into a new stuff; and total blending, in which each extends through the whole of the other and keeps its qualities, as wine in water or soul in body (Alexander of Aphrodisias, On Mixture 216–218). A drop of wine, he said, will blend with the whole sea (Diogenes 7.151); Alexander and Plutarch found this absurd.

Fate is the chain of causes, and divination its evidence (Cicero, On Divination 1.125–127). The Lazy Argument objected that if you are fated to recover you will recover whether or not you call the doctor. Chrysippus answered that recovery is co-fated with calling the doctor, as Oedipus' birth with Laius lying with a woman (Cicero, On Fate 28–30). He divided causes into perfect and principal, and auxiliary and proximate (41–43): an impression is only the proximate cause of assent, the principal cause being the mind's own character, as the cylinder's shape, not the push, makes it roll (module 7.2). Action is fated and still ours, because it runs through us.

Against evil, Chrysippus argued that opposites need each other, so there is no justice without injustice, and that some harms are by-products of good design, as the thin bones that suit the skull make it fragile (Gellius 7.1); even bedbugs serve, by waking us (Plutarch, On Stoic Self-Contradictions 1044d). Periodically the whole returns to fire, god alone remaining, and the same world is reborn with the same Socrates (Nemesius, On the Nature of Man 38).

Where sources disagree. Cicero presents Chrysippus as an honorary arbiter between those who put everything under fate and those who freed the mind's motions from it (On Fate 39); Alexander of Aphrodisias (On Fate) replies that responsibility without the power to do otherwise is responsibility in name only. Susanne Bobzien (Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy, 1998) argues that Chrysippus was not answering that question: "up to us" meant action that comes about through our own assent.

Chrysippus: oikeiosis and the end

Stoic ethics begins with the newborn. An animal's first impulse, Chrysippus wrote in book 1 of On Ends, is to preserve itself, since nature makes it from the start appropriated (oikeion) to itself and aware of its own constitution; pleasure, the Epicurean first object (module 12.6), is a by-product that supervenes once it has what suits it (Diogenes Laertius 7.85–86; SVF 3.178; LS 57A). Cicero's Cato traces the development (On Ends 3.16–22): from self-preservation to selecting what accords with nature, then to seeing order and agreement in conduct, which the agent values above everything that first attracted him (3.21), as one may value a person more than the friend who introduced him (3.23). Extended through love of offspring, the impulse grounds justice and the community of rational beings (3.62–64); Hierocles' circles are Rome module 13.2's.

The end was restated generation by generation. Diogenes Laertius (7.87) gives Zeno "living in agreement with nature"; Stobaeus (2.75–76) says Zeno said only "living in agreement" and Cleanthes added "with nature". Chrysippus glossed it as living according to experience of what happens by nature (7.87). Zeno had coined kathēkon, appropriate action, an act with a reasonable justification (7.107–108); done perfectly, from virtue, it is a katorthōma, open only to the sage. Chrysippus' passions, with his runner who cannot stop at will (Galen, On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato 4.2), are what Posidonius attacked.

Diogenes of Babylon and Antipater of Tarsus

After Chrysippus and Zeno of Tarsus came Diogenes of Seleucia, called the Babylonian. His Art of Voice supplied Diogenes Laertius' Stoic grammar (7.55–58), and his books on music and rhetoric survive through Philodemus' replies at Herculaneum; his embassy to Rome in 155 with Carneades and Critolaus belongs to Rome modules 4.5 and 13.1. He defined the end as reasoning well in selecting what accords with nature (7.88). His pupil Antipater, who wrote so much against Carneades and debated him so little that he was called the pen-shouter (Plutarch, On Talkativeness), made it living continuously selecting what accords with nature and rejecting what does not (Stobaeus 2.76). Cicero's archer, who does all he can to hit the mark while the aiming, not the hit, is what counts (On Ends 3.22), states the position; A. A. Long ("Carneades and the Stoic Telos", 1967) reads both restatements as answers to Carneades.

The two argue in Cicero, On Duties 3.50–57. A merchant brings grain to famine-struck Rhodes knowing more ships are coming: must he say so? Diogenes says keeping silent is not concealing; Antipater that a man bound into the human community may not profit from his neighbours' ignorance. Cicero sides with Antipater.

The sources

Hans von Arnim's Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta (1903–1905; index volume by Maximilian Adler, 1924) gathers Zeno and his pupils, Chrysippus' logic and physics, and his ethics with the successors through Antipater; Panaetius and Posidonius have editions of their own. Long and Sedley's The Hellenistic Philosophers (1987) translates the core texts by topic.

Diogenes Laertius book 7 gives Zeno's life, a long doxography (7.38–160), partly quoted word for word from Diocles of Magnesia (7.48), and lives of Cleanthes and Chrysippus; it breaks off in Chrysippus' book list. Stobaeus keeps the Hymn and an epitome of Stoic ethics usually credited to Arius Didymus (2.7). Cicero expounds the system through spokesmen, Cato in On Ends 3 and Balbus in On the Nature of the Gods 2, and attacks it in his own voice in On Ends 4. The longest verbatim quotations come from enemies: Plutarch's On Stoic Self-Contradictions and On Common Conceptions quote Chrysippus to convict him of inconsistency, and Galen's On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato quotes pages of his On Passions to refute them, with Posidonius as witness. Doctrine and hostile frame must be separated every time.

Panaetius and Posidonius: the hinge to Rome

Panaetius of Rhodes, pupil of Diogenes and Antipater, lived for years in Scipio Aemilianus' house (module 7.3) before heading the school at Athens. He dropped what critics found hardest to believe. He held the cosmos everlasting and doubted the conflagration (Diogenes Laertius 7.142; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.118), as Boethus of Sidon had (Philo, On the Eternity of the World 76); he alone of the Stoics rejected astrology, and he doubted divination (Cicero, On Divination 2.88, 1.6); and he argued that the soul, being born, must die, though he called Plato the Homer of philosophers (Tusculan Disputations 1.79). Cicero says he always had Plato, Aristotle, Xenocrates, Theophrastus and Dicaearchus on his lips (On Ends 4.79). His three books On Proper Functions were the model of Cicero's On Duties (Letters to Atticus 16.11.4); the four personae are Rome module 13.2's.

Posidonius of Apamea studied with Panaetius, settled at Rhodes and went as its envoy to Rome in 87/86 (Plutarch, Marius 45; EK F255). He travelled to Gades and Gaul, where he grew used to heads nailed over doorways (Strabo 4.4.5; EK F274). His Histories, fifty-two books continuing Polybius from 146 (Suda; EK T1), included the satire on Athenion, the Peripatetic who took Athens over to Mithridates in 88 (Athenaeus 5.211d–215b; EK F253), the prelude to Sulla's siege in module 7.3; whether he is the tyrant Aristion of Plutarch and Appian, as module 7.3 names him, or Aristion's predecessor is disputed. He measured the earth from the height of Canopus: 240,000 stades in Cleomedes (On the Heavens; EK F202), 180,000 in Strabo (2.2.2). Strabo found in him much hunting of causes and much Aristotelising, which Stoics avoid (2.3.8).

On the passions he turned Chrysippus' admissions against him, as Galen reports (On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato 4–5; module 7.2). Why does grief fade with time while the belief that one has suffered an evil remains, as Chrysippus conceded (4.7; EK F165)? Why do children and animals, without reason, have passions? His answer was that the soul has irrational powers, spirited and appetitive, whose affective movements must be trained by habit, rhythm and music rather than refuted; he claimed Cleanthes, and behind him Pythagoras and Plato, for the view (5.6). His end was to live contemplating the truth and order of the whole, in no way led by the irrational part of the soul (Clement, Stromateis 2.21). What Romans heard from the two is Rome modules 13.1 and 13.2.

Where sources disagree. Galen makes Posidonius a Stoic converted to Plato on the soul, while conceding that he spoke of powers of one soul, not of parts. Karl Reinhardt (Poseidonios, 1921) built an original system-maker from passages in Cicero, Seneca and others that do not name him; Ludwig Edelstein (1936) admitted named fragments only, the rule of the Edelstein–Kidd edition (1972), and Kidd's commentary (1988) reads the result as a Stoic who widened his school's search for causes without leaving it. Willy Theiler's edition (1982) admits much unnamed material and keeps the larger figure.
Where sources disagree. "Middle Stoa" is a modern period, fixed by August Schmekel's Die Philosophie der mittleren Stoa (1892) for a softened, Platonising phase between Chrysippus and the Roman Stoics. Brad Inwood (Later Stoicism 155 BC to AD 200, 2022) rejects any middle period and begins a later Stoicism with Antipater; his reviewer Jacob Klein (Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2025.01.21) answers that Diogenes Laertius has Panaetius and Posidonius deny that virtue suffices for happiness (7.128), which looks like a real departure under Academic pressure.

Self-test

  1. What did Zeno take from Crates and from the Megarians, and what charge does Cicero's On Ends 4 bring against his borrowing from the Academy?
    Answer

    From Crates the sufficiency of virtue, from the Megarians compressed argument. Cicero, arguing Antiochus' case, says Zeno changed the Academy's words and kept its substance.

  2. Why did some Stoics want to be rid of Zeno's Republic, and how do Plutarch and Schofield read its city differently?
    Answer

    It abolished temples, courts and coinage and held wives in common among the wise (Diogenes Laertius 7.32–33, 7.131), so Athenodorus cut such passages at Pergamum (7.34). Plutarch saw a single world-city; Schofield a community of sages bound by concord and Eros.

  3. How does Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus square providence with evil, and where does Heraclitus show through?
    Answer

    Nothing happens without Zeus except what the bad do in their folly, and Zeus fits good and bad into one logos of the whole (lines 15–21). The steering thunderbolt (DK 22 B 64) and the common logos the many ignore (B 2) are Heraclitean.

  4. Why is Chrysippus' logic called a logic of propositions, and what is the form of the second indemonstrable?
    Answer

    Its units are whole propositions joined by connectives, where Aristotle's syllogistic relates terms. The second: if the first, the second; not the second; therefore not the first.

  5. Which premise of the Master Argument did Chrysippus deny, and how does the Dion example support him?
    Answer

    That the impossible cannot follow from the possible. "Dion has died" is possible, but "this man has died", pointing at Dion, can never be true, yet follows from it (Alexander, On Aristotle's Prior Analytics 177–178).

  6. Why did Stoic physics need total blending, and how does it differ from fusion?
    Answer

    Pneuma, a body, must pervade matter, another body, so two bodies must occupy one place. In total blending each ingredient keeps its qualities through the whole (wine in water); in fusion the ingredients perish into a new stuff.

  7. How did Chrysippus answer the Lazy Argument, and how do principal and proximate causes keep action "up to us"?
    Answer

    Recovery is co-fated with calling the doctor, so effort is not idle (Cicero, On Fate 28–30). The impression is only the proximate cause of assent; the principal cause is the agent's own character, as the cylinder's shape makes it roll (41–43).

  8. What is the first impulse of an animal for Chrysippus, and why does that matter against Epicurus?
    Answer

    Self-preservation, from being appropriated to one's own constitution (Diogenes Laertius 7.85–86). Pleasure is only a by-product, so it cannot be the natural end, as Epicurus claimed.

  9. Why must Plutarch's and Galen's quotations of Chrysippus be handled with care, and why are they indispensable?
    Answer

    Both quote him to refute him, choosing and framing passages to show inconsistency or error. Yet they give the longest verbatim extracts we have, from works such as On Passions.

  10. Name two doctrines Panaetius gave up or doubted, and one argument Posidonius used against Chrysippus on the passions.
    Answer

    Any two of the conflagration, divination and astrology, and the soul's survival. Posidonius: grief fades with time though the judgement of evil remains, as Chrysippus admitted (Galen 4.7); or children and animals have passions without reason.

Carry forward

  1. Stoicism is one system: fate needs the physics of pneuma, responsibility needs the theory of assent, and the end needs a providential cosmos. Romans who kept the ethics and left the rest, as Rome module 13.1 asks why, inherited conclusions without their supports.
  2. The early Stoa survives almost wholly in reporters, many hostile; name the reporter for every doctrine (Diogenes, Stobaeus, Cicero's spokesmen, Plutarch, Galen) and strip the frame before judging the claim.
  3. The school changed under attack: Antipater's restated end, Panaetius' doubts on conflagration and divination, Posidonius' irrational powers. Whether or not that makes a "Middle Stoa", the Stoicism Rome met at Rhodes and in Scipio's house was the revised one.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Stoic school from Zeno to Posidonius, extending module 7.2, which outlines the physics and the ethics and Posidonius' quarrel with Chrysippus over the passions: point back to it and go deeper. Cover: Zeno of Citium, his Cynic training and his Republic; the Painted Stoa; Cleanthes and his Hymn to Zeus; Chrysippus' system in detail: the logic (propositions and the indemonstrable arguments), the physics of pneuma, tension and mixture, fate, providence and the conflagration, and the ethics of oikeiosis; Diogenes of Babylon and Antipater of Tarsus; the sources: von Arnim's Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, Diogenes Laertius book 7, Stobaeus, Cicero, and the polemics of Plutarch and Galen; and Panaetius and Posidonius as the hinge to Rome (module 7.3 has Panaetius in Scipio's house): hand off to Rome modules 13.1 and 13.2 for what Romans made of them. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
GREECE · UNIT 12 · Deep dive III: Greek philosophy · 12.8 · 2,828 words

Sceptics and Neoplatonists: the late schools to 529

Pyrrho and TimonArcesilaus and Carneades: the Academy turnsClitomachus, Philo and AntiochusAenesidemus and Sextus EmpiricusMiddle Platonists and PlotinusPorphyry, Iamblichus and ProclusHypatia as a philosopher529, Damascius and the road to PersiaSelf-testCarry forward

Pyrrho and Timon

Module 7.2 gives Pyrrho's journey with Alexander and Timon's summary. The life is Diogenes Laertius 9.61–108, drawn largely from the biographer Antigonus of Carystus. Pyrrho of Elis began as a painter and followed Anaxarchus east, where he met the Indian naked sages and the Magi (9.61); an Indian's rebuke of Anaxarchus for courting kings sent him into private life (9.63). Elis made him high priest (9.64). He lived with his sister, a midwife, and took poultry and pigs to market; frightened by a dog, he said it was hard to strip off the human being entirely (9.66). He wrote nothing.

Timon of Phlius (c. 320–230), a former dancer, studied with Stilpo and then with Pyrrho (9.109–112); his Silloi mock every dogmatist except Pyrrho (9.65, 9.111). The summary comes through a chain of reporters: Eusebius (Preparation for the Gospel 14.18.1–5) quotes the hostile Peripatetic Aristocles, who quotes Timon, who reports Pyrrho. Things are equally indifferent, unmeasurable and undecidable; for this reason our perceptions and opinions neither tell the truth nor lie; so we should trust neither, but say of each thing that it no more is than is not, or both, or neither. The outcome is speechlessness, then freedom from disturbance; Aenesidemus, Aristocles adds, said pleasure (14.18.4).

Where sources disagree. Antigonus said Pyrrho avoided neither carts nor cliffs and was kept alive by friends; Aenesidemus answered that he suspended judgement in philosophy but was not improvident in daily life (Diogenes Laertius 9.62). Moderns divide over Aristocles' text. Its manuscripts make the nature of things the reason why perceptions are neither true nor false, and Bett (Pyrrho, his Antecedents, and his Legacy, 2000), whose metaphysical reading module 7.2 gives, keeps them. Zeller emended "for this reason" to "because", and Stopper (1983) defended the change: things are undecidable for us because the senses fail, and Pyrrho becomes Sextus' epistemic sceptic.

Arcesilaus and Carneades: the Academy turns

Module 7.2 outlines Arcesilaus' attack on Zeno, his "reasonable" and Carneades' persuasive impressions. What needs explaining is why Plato's school turned. Arcesilaus of Pitane (c. 316–241), head from about 268, wrote nothing (Diogenes Laertius 4.28–45). Cicero, speaking for the New Academy, says he denied that anything can be known, not even the one thing Socrates had left himself (Academica 1.45), and adds that Plato's books affirm nothing (1.46): the reading of the dialogues that module 12.3 sets against the Neoplatonists'.

His method was to argue against any thesis until the sides balanced, and his target was the Stoa. Zeno defined the cognitive impression as one that comes from what is, stamped exactly in accordance with it; Cicero says he added, under Arcesilaus' pressure, that it must be such as could not come from what is not (Academica 2.77). Arcesilaus answered that any true impression could have an indistinguishable false twin, and turned the Stoic premise that the wise man never opines against its owners: if nothing is cognitive, the wise man assents to nothing (Against the Mathematicians 7.150–157). Plutarch reports the reply that action needs impression and impulse, not assent (Against Colotes 1122a–d).

Carneades of Cyrene (214/13–129/8) reportedly said that without Chrysippus there would have been no Carneades (Diogenes Laertius 4.62). Sextus gives his graded criterion: an impression may be persuasive; persuasive and unreversed; or persuasive, unreversed and tested, the higher grades being for weightier matters (Against the Mathematicians 7.166–189). He turned the method on Stoic theology, with a sorites from Zeus to the gods of rivers (9.182–184), and on fate, arguing against the Epicureans that a voluntary motion of the mind needs no swerve, being its own cause (Cicero, On Fate 23). His embassy to Rome in 155 is in Rome module 4.5.

Where sources disagree. Did the Academics hold their scepticism or only argue it? Sextus says Arcesilaus called suspension good, which is a kind of dogma, and repeats a rumour that he was a Platonist testing his pupils (Outlines of Pyrrhonism 1.232–234). Clitomachus never discovered what Carneades approved; Metrodorus and Philo said he let the wise man opine, and Cicero, trusting Clitomachus, thinks this was argued rather than approved (Academica 2.78, 2.139). Couissin (1929) and Striker (1980) read the arguments as dialectical, drawn from Stoic premises the Academics did not share; Frede (1979, 1984) and Cooper (2004) think the Academics came to hold, without claiming knowledge, the views their arguments left them with.

Clitomachus, Philo and Antiochus

Clitomachus, a Carthaginian named Hasdrubal, wrote more than four hundred books (Diogenes Laertius 4.67); Cicero follows one of them for two kinds of assent, withheld in the strict sense but given to the persuasive in action (Academica 2.98–104). Philo of Larissa (159/8–84/3), head from 110/09, moved from that line to a scepticism that allowed opinion. The Mithridatic war drove him to Rome in 88 (Cicero, Brutus 306), where his Roman Books denied that there had ever been two Academies (Academica 1.13) and held things inapprehensible by the Stoic criterion but apprehensible in their own nature (Sextus, Outlines 1.235).

His pupil Antiochus of Ascalon read them at Alexandria, answered with a book called Sosus (Academica 2.11–12) and returned to doctrine: Plato, Xenocrates, Polemo and Aristotle had shared one philosophy, the Old Academy, whose terms Zeno revised (Academica 1.15–42). He accepted the cognitive impression and demanded that the Academics at least grasp their own thesis that nothing can be grasped (2.28–29). Cicero calls him, but for a very few changes, a most genuine Stoic (2.132). His Roman following belongs to Rome module 13.3.

Where sources disagree. The Roman Books are lost, recovered from Antiochus' outrage as Cicero reports it and from one sentence of Sextus. Tarrant (Scepticism or Platonism?, 1985) read them as a turn towards a Platonist theory of knowledge; Brittain (Philo of Larissa: The Last of the Academic Sceptics, 2001) reads them as fallibilism, knowledge without the Stoic guarantee that an impression could not be false. Either way the sceptical Academy ended with Philo as a school; its heir was Aenesidemus.

Aenesidemus and Sextus Empiricus

Aenesidemus dedicated his Pyrrhonian Discourses to the Academic Lucius Tubero and complained, Photius reports, that the Academics of his day were Stoics fighting Stoics (Bibliotheca 212). If Tubero is Cicero's friend, as usually assumed, the break belongs to the first century BC; Aristocles calls the revival recent and places it in Alexandria (Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 14.18.29). Aenesidemus took Pyrrho's name for a scepticism that would not assert even that things are inapprehensible, and collected the modes, argument-forms that produce suspension: ten in Diogenes (9.79–88), nine in Aristocles (14.18.11), and eight more against causal explanation in Sextus (Outlines 1.180–186).

Sextus Empiricus, last but one in Diogenes' succession of Pyrrhonists (9.116), was a doctor of the Empiric school and wrote about AD 200, a guess. Besides the three books of Outlines, Against the Mathematicians 1–6 attacks the arts and books 7–11 the dogmatists' logic, physics and ethics. Scepticism is an ability to oppose appearances and thoughts so that, from the equal force of the opposed accounts, we reach first suspension and then tranquillity (Outlines 1.8). Tranquillity follows by luck, as when the painter Apelles, failing to paint a horse's foam, threw his sponge at the picture and produced it (1.28–29). The sceptic lives by appearances, nature, feeling, custom and craft (1.23–24), granting that honey appears sweet and doubting only whether it is (1.20). His slogans expel themselves like purgatives (1.206), and the argument against proof is kicked away like a ladder once climbed (Against the Mathematicians 8.481).

Sextus quotes Xenophanes' fragment DK 21 B 34 as, on some readings, a denial that anything can be grasped, likening inquirers to men hunting gold in a dark room who cannot know when they hold it (Against the Mathematicians 7.49–52). Yet he refuses Xenophanes the name, since his one god is dogma, and quotes Timon calling him only half free of vanity (Outlines 1.224–225). The ten modes, in Sextus' order (1.35–163):

ModeOutlines 1Example
1. Differences among animals40–78Hemlock feeds quails and kills men
2. Differences among humans79–90Alexander's servant Demophon shivered in the sun
3. Differences among the senses91–99Is an apple one quality or many?
4. Circumstances100–117Sleep, sickness, age, love, hunger
5. Positions, distances, places118–123A colonnade seen from one end tapers
6. Admixtures124–128Nothing reaches the senses unmixed
7. Quantities and compositions129–134Goat's horn filings look white, the horn black
8. Relativity135–140Everything appears relative to the judge and to its company
9. Frequency and rarity141–144A comet astonishes; the sun does not
10. Customs, laws, myths, dogmas145–163Peoples' beliefs about the gods conflict

The five modes of "the more recent sceptics" (1.164–169), whom Diogenes heads with Agrippa (9.88), are sharper: disagreement, regress, relativity, hypothesis and circularity. Any proof rests on an endless chain, an assumption or itself.

Where sources disagree. Sextus says the sceptic holds no belief in the sense of assent to what is unclear, but does not reject what appearances force on him (Outlines 1.13). Burnyeat ("Can the Sceptic Live His Scepticism?", 1980) took this to rule out belief altogether, so that the Pyrrhonist cannot live his scepticism consistently; Frede ("Des Skeptikers Meinungen", 1979) argued that only theoretical belief is renounced and everyday belief remains. Barnes (1982) called the two Pyrrhonists rustic and urbane; Sextus can be cited for each.

Middle Platonists and Plotinus

Between Antiochus and Plotinus Platonism became dogma again. Alcinous' Handbook of Platonism makes the first god an intellect thinking itself and the Forms its thoughts (9–10), the Timaeus fused with Aristotle's god. Plutarch (module 7.4) read the Timaeus' creation literally (module 12.3) and traced disorder to a pre-cosmic irrational soul (On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus). Numenius of Apamea set a first god above the Demiurge and asked, Clement reports, what Plato is but Moses speaking Attic (Stromateis 1.22).

Module 7.4 gives Plotinus' hierarchy and the edition; here are the arguments. Plotinus (204/5–270) found in Ammonius Saccas the teacher he sought, followed Gordian III east to learn Persian and Indian wisdom, and settled at Rome at forty (Porphyry, Life of Plotinus 3). He called himself an exegete: the Parmenides distinguishes a first One, a One-many and a One-and-many, so the three hypostases are Plato's (Enneads 5.1.8). That is the Neoplatonist theology module 12.3 hands on.

The One is argued from unity. Everything that is, is by being one; an army or a house ceases to be when its unity goes (6.9.1). The composite depends on what makes it one, so the first must be simple. Intellect cannot be first, because thinking is two, thinker and thought, even in Aristotle's self-thinking god (5.3.10–11; treatise 5.6). The first is beyond being, as Plato said of the Good (Republic 509b), and beyond speech.

Why does anything come from it? Whatever is perfect produces, as fire warms and snow cools (5.4.1); each thing has an activity that is its being and one that goes out from it (5.4.2). The One gives without loss, like the light round the sun (5.1.6), and what proceeds is constituted by turning back: Intellect is a sight that becomes seeing by looking towards the One (5.3.11). Intellect is the world of Forms, which are not outside it, or it would hold images, not truth (treatise 5.5). Soul stands to Intellect as spoken word to thought (5.1.3) and thinks one thing after another, where Intellect is all things at once (5.1.4); so it orders the cosmos in succession, and time is its life passing from one thing to the next (3.7.11). At the bottom is matter, privation and evil itself (treatise 1.8). The descent maps the return: the last treatise ends with the flight of the alone to the alone (6.9.11), and Porphyry says Plotinus reached union four times in their six years together (Life 23).

Porphyry, Iamblichus and Proclus

Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305), whose works module 7.4 lists, hesitated over ritual: Augustine reports that he let theurgy purify the lower, "spiritual" soul but not the intellect (City of God 10.9). His Letter to Anebo put his doubts to an Egyptian priest, and Iamblichus (c. 245–c. 325) replied in a priest's name with On the Mysteries. Its decisive argument: thought does not join the theurgist to the gods, or philosophers would be joined by theorising; the performance of ineffable acts and symbols understood by the gods alone does (2.11).

Where sources disagree. Plotinus, daring, he says, to speak against the opinion of others, held that part of our soul never descends but stays always in the intelligible (Enneads 4.8.8). Iamblichus rejected this, and Proclus states the rejection as a theorem: every particular soul descends entire (Elements of Theology, prop. 211). The stakes are practical: if the higher soul never fell, contemplation can reach the One unaided; if the whole soul fell, it needs help from above, which is theurgy's case. Module 7.4 has the modern quarrel over whether theurgy was magic or theology.

Proclus (412–485), head at Athens after Syrianus, built the system as geometry. The Elements of Theology proves 211 propositions in order: every manifold participates in unity (prop. 1); every productive cause is superior to its product (prop. 7); every effect remains in its cause, proceeds from it and reverts upon it (prop. 35), so causation is a circle, not a chain. Between the One and Intellect he set the henads, gods as unities beyond being, which brought the pantheon inside the system. Marinus' Life of Proclus shows the practice: hymns, Chaldaean rites, and a wish that of all ancient books only the Chaldaean Oracles and the Timaeus might survive.

Hypatia as a philosopher

Module 7.4 tells Hypatia's murder in 415. Her father Theon headed his commentary on book 3 of Ptolemy's Almagest as an edition revised by his daughter, the philosopher Hypatia, and the Suda credits her with commentaries on Diophantus and on Apollonius' Conics. Socrates Scholasticus says she succeeded to the Platonic school descended from Plotinus (Church History 7.15); Damascius, through the Suda, that she expounded Plato and Aristotle in the philosopher's cloak to anyone who wished. Her pupil Synesius of Cyrene, later a bishop, calls her mother, sister and teacher and sends her his books for judgement.

Where sources disagree. Socrates Scholasticus, a Christian, makes her the heir of Plotinus' school; Damascius, a pagan writing a century later, says Isidore differed from her not only as a man from a woman but as a genuine philosopher from a geometer. Watts (Hypatia, 2017) takes her for a Platonist who kept theurgy out of her teaching, which would explain why Christians such as Synesius studied with her. No philosophical writing of hers survives to test either verdict.

529, Damascius and the road to Persia

Module 7.4 gives the measure and the dispute between Cameron and Watts over whether it closed the school. Malalas says that in the consulship of Decius (529) a decree went to Athens that no one should teach philosophy or expound the laws (Chronicle 18.47); Justinian's Code barred pagans from teaching (Codex Justinianus 1.11.10). Alexandria shows what the measure missed. Ammonius son of Hermias had come to terms with the bishop there, as Damascius sneers (Life of Isidore); the Christian John Philoponus published Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World in 529 itself; and the pagan Olympiodorus was still lecturing on Plato and Aristotle after 565.

Damascius, the last head at Athens, pushed past Proclus' first principle. His Problems and Solutions concerning First Principles opens with a dilemma: if the principle of all things is one of them, it is not the principle of all; if it is beyond them, "all" is not all. Above the One he set the wholly ineffable. Simplicius, pupil of Ammonius and of Damascius, wrote his commentaries on Aristotle, usually dated after 532, attacking Philoponus on the eternity of the world and preserving much of the Presocratics (module 12.1).

Agathias, writing in the 570s, names the seven who went to Khusro I: Damascius, Simplicius, Eulamius, Priscian of Lydia, Hermias, Diogenes and Isidore of Gaza. Disliking the prevailing belief about the divine and hearing that Persia had a philosopher-king, they found the Persians arrogant and lawless, and came home under a clause of the peace of 532 that let them keep their beliefs unmolested (2.30–31).

Where sources disagree. Agathias makes Khusro a philosophical pretender, dazzled by a Syrian charlatan named Uranius, and the visit a disillusionment. Two survivals tell against the caricature: Priscian's Solutions to the Problems Raised by Khosroes, extant in Latin translation, answers the king's questions on the soul, sleep, the tides and other matters of natural philosophy, and Paul the Persian dedicated a treatise on Aristotle's logic to him. Whether Khusro's interest was serious or a court fashion, the sources do not settle.

Self-test

  1. Through whom does the summary of Pyrrho's philosophy reach us, and what textual choice divides Bett from Stopper?
    Answer

    Eusebius quotes the hostile Peripatetic Aristocles, who quotes Timon, who reports Pyrrho (Preparation for the Gospel 14.18.1–5). The manuscripts make the indeterminacy of things the reason why perceptions are neither true nor false, which Bett keeps as a metaphysical thesis; Zeller's emendation to "because", defended by Stopper, makes things undecidable for us because the senses fail.

  2. How did Arcesilaus use the Stoics' own premises to reach universal suspension?
    Answer

    The Stoics held that the wise man never opines and assents only to cognitive impressions. Arcesilaus argued that for any true impression an indistinguishable false one is possible, so nothing is cognitive; by the Stoic premise the wise man must then assent to nothing (Against the Mathematicians 7.150–157).

  3. What are Carneades' grades of persuasive impression, and what objection do they answer?
    Answer

    Persuasive; persuasive and unreversed; persuasive, unreversed and tested, the higher grades used for weightier matters (Against the Mathematicians 7.166–189). They answer the charge that a sceptic who withholds assent cannot act, by offering a guide to action that claims no truth.

  4. What does Cicero report about Carneades and opinion, and why does it matter for the dialectical reading?
    Answer

    Metrodorus and Philo said Carneades let the wise man opine; Clitomachus said he never discovered what Carneades approved, and Cicero sides with Clitomachus that the thesis was argued, not approved (Academica 2.78, 2.139). If Clitomachus is right, Carneades' positions may all be dialectical, as Couissin and Striker hold.

  5. What did Philo's Roman Books claim, and how did Antiochus respond?
    Answer

    That there had only ever been one Academy (Academica 1.13), and that things are inapprehensible by the Stoic criterion but apprehensible in their own nature (Outlines 1.235). Antiochus answered with the Sosus (2.11–12) and returned to doctrine: one Old Academy whose terms Zeno revised, which made him, Cicero says, nearly a genuine Stoic (2.132).

  6. What does Proclus' proposition 35 assert, and why does it make causation a circle rather than a chain?
    Answer

    Every effect remains in its cause, proceeds from it and reverts upon it (Elements of Theology, prop. 35). The product is never cut off from its source, and its return completes the movement its procession began.

  7. How does Sextus define scepticism, and how does tranquillity follow from it?
    Answer

    As an ability to oppose appearances and thoughts so that, from the equal force of opposed accounts, we reach suspension and then tranquillity (Outlines 1.8). Tranquillity is not argued for but follows suspension by luck, like Apelles' sponge producing the foam he could not paint (1.28–29).

  8. What does Alexandria show about the reach of Justinian's measure of 529?
    Answer

    Malalas' decree went to Athens (Chronicle 18.47). At Alexandria Ammonius had come to terms with the bishop, Philoponus published Against Proclus in 529, and the pagan Olympiodorus still lectured on Plato and Aristotle after 565, so the measure struck Athens and left Alexandria teaching.

  9. Why, for Plotinus, can Intellect not be the first principle?
    Answer

    Whatever is, is by being one (Enneads 6.9.1), so the first must be simple. Thinking always involves the duality of thinker and thought, even when it thinks itself (5.3.10–11; treatise 5.6), so the first is beyond thought and being, as Plato said of the Good.

  10. On what do Plotinus and Proclus disagree about the soul, and why does it bear on theurgy?
    Answer

    Plotinus held that part of the soul never descends (Enneads 4.8.8); Proclus, following Iamblichus, that every particular soul descends entire (Elements of Theology, prop. 211). A wholly fallen soul cannot rise by thought alone and needs the rites and symbols Iamblichus defends (On the Mysteries 2.11).

Carry forward

  1. Whether the soul can rise by thought alone, as Plotinus' undescended soul allows (Enneads 4.8.8), or fell entire and needs rites given from above (Iamblichus; Proclus, Elements of Theology, prop. 211), is the late form of the question of philosophy's relation to religion; Iamblichus' answer made the last pagan schools communities of cult as well as of study.
  2. Ancient scepticism was a technique before it was a thesis: argue from the opponent's premises, set equal accounts against each other, and expose regress, assumption or circularity in any proof. Through the Latin Outlines of 1562 it returned to Montaigne and Descartes.
  3. The late Platonist universe of procession and return (Elements of Theology, prop. 35) outlived the schools: it passed into Christian theology through the pseudo-Dionysius and into Arabic and Latin philosophy through the Theology of Aristotle and the Book of Causes, while the closure of 529 struck Athens and left Alexandria teaching.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Greek scepticism and the later Platonists, from Pyrrho to AD 529, extending modules 7.2 and 7.4, which outline both, carry the disputes over Pyrrho, over theurgy and over the closing of the Academy, and already tell Hypatia's death and the journey of Damascius and Simplicius to Khusro's court and back in 532: point back to them and go deeper. Cover: Pyrrho and Timon; the Academy's sceptical turn (Arcesilaus, Carneades, Clitomachus, Philo of Larissa) and Antiochus of Ascalon's return to doctrine; Aenesidemus and Sextus Empiricus (Outlines of Pyrrhonism and the modes); Middle Platonism in a paragraph (Plutarch and Alcinous); Plotinus (the Enneads, Porphyry's Life of Plotinus), with the One, Intellect and Soul argued rather than listed; Porphyry, Iamblichus and theurgy, and Proclus; Hypatia as a philosopher (module 7.4 tells her death); Justinian's measure of 529 and the argument over what it did; and Damascius, Simplicius and the philosophers who went to the Persian court (Agathias 2.30–31). Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
HISTORY · COURSE 2 · ROME · Personal Mythology · IN PROGRESS

Roman history and mythology

Four parts and three deep dives, 79 modules, plus a quality audit. History and myth are interleaved more tightly than in the Greek course, because Rome told its myths as history: the legends sit inside the periods that produced them. Every module is a long-form report with named primary sources, the places where the accounts disagree, a ten-question self-test and three ideas to carry forward.

The late Republic that most people mean by "ancient Rome" is the thin red slice: about a century. The kings in the gold band were written about by Romans living in it, five hundred years after the fact. The eastern empire that kept the Roman name until 1453 runs off the right-hand edge.

  • Iron Age Italy1000 BC – 753 BCmodules 1.1 and 1.2

How to read it

five rules
  1. Parts I to IV in order. Each report assumes the ones before it. Part I matters more here than in Greece: the evidence for Rome's first four centuries is late and partisan, and every later report assumes you know how late. Part IV ends with a capstone exam.
  2. Deep dives when you want them. Unit 11 (the fall of the Republic) extends unit 5; unit 12 (the Aeneid) extends module 6.3 and, for Aeneas, module 1.3; unit 13 (Roman philosophy) extends modules 4.5, 5.6, 7.3 and 10.2. Take each straight after the material it extends, or after the capstone.
  3. Greece behind you. Rome points back to the Greek course instead of repeating it: Greek 7.3 and 7.4 for the Greek side of the conquest, 2.2 for the Olympians, 9.3 and 10.12 for reception. Open the Greek module when a report names it.
  4. One or two a sitting, self-test before moving on. Under 7 of 10, re-read. The carry-forward ideas are the ones later reports lean on.
  5. A study text, not scripture. Citations are given so you can check them against the primary sources. Where sources disagree, the report says so in a red-edged box.

The reading spine

primary and secondary

The reports keep naming these. Read the primary ones at least once each, in this order, any decent translation: Livy, books 1 to 5 and then 21 to 30 · Polybius, books 1 to 6 · Virgil, Aeneid (book 8 with module 1.3) · Ovid, Fasti, then Metamorphoses · Sallust, The War with Catiline · Caesar, The Gallic War · Cicero, selected letters (Shackleton Bailey's translation) and the Second Philippic · Plutarch's Roman Lives as each name comes up · Augustus, Res Gestae · Tacitus, Annals · Suetonius, The Twelve Caesars · Seneca, Letters to Lucilius (a selection), Epictetus, Handbook, and Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (with deep dive 13) · Ammianus Marcellinus, books 14 to 31.

Secondary, three only: T. J. Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome; Mary Beard, John North and Simon Price, Religions of Rome; Mary Beard, SPQR, with Peter Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire.

The course, module by module

This is the complete syllabus the reports were generated from. Each module has its drop-in prompt; copy it into a new chat to regenerate a report yourself, extend one, or compare a fresh answer against the one here. Where a report exists it is linked.

How to run it

  1. Do the modules in order. Each prompt assumes the ones before it, and the Greek course before that: where Rome touches Greece, the prompt points back to the Greek module instead of repeating it.
  2. Tap copy prompt, paste the prompt into a new chat here, read the report, do the self-test at the end. If you score under 7/10, re-read before moving on.
  3. Tick the box when done. Progress is stored on this phone only.
  4. Every prompt asks for named primary sources and for the places where the accounts disagree. For early Rome that matters more than it did for Greece: almost everything before 300 BC reached us through writers of the first century BC, and the question is always what they could have known.

Units 11, 12 and 13 are deep dives: optional, and best taken after the core material they extend (unit 5; module 6.3; modules 4.5, 5.6, 7.3 and 10.2) or after the capstone.

Honest scoping: no syllabus gets you all of it. Rome left more words than Greece and fewer stories, and its stories come disguised as history. What this gets you is the skeleton, the main sources read in the right order, and enough structure that anything you meet later snaps into place.

UNIT 0

Foundations

Three modules that fix the evidence, the land and the dates before any story is told. Rome is a harder case than Greece: its early history was written down centuries late, by Romans with something to prove.

0.1

How we know anything: the sources

Livy wrote about Romulus seven centuries after the fact. Know what that means before you read a word of him.

Give me an in-depth report on the sources for Roman history and mythology, with the emphasis on the problem that defines the subject: Rome's early history was written down centuries after the events, by Romans with agendas. Cover: the first Roman historians, who wrote in Greek (Fabius Pictor, writing around 200 BC; Cincius Alimentus) and why they did; Cato's Origines and the Latin annalists (Cassius Hemina, Calpurnius Piso, Valerius Antias, Claudius Quadrigarius, Licinius Macer), known only in fragments, and the charge that they invented; the raw material they claimed to use (the Annales Maximi of the pontiffs, the lists of consuls and triumphs, family archives, funeral orations) and the complaints Cicero and Livy themselves make about it; the surviving narratives: Polybius (the outsider's analysis), Livy (Ab urbe condita, 142 books of which 35 survive, and his preface on legend), Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities, and his thesis that Rome was a Greek city), Diodorus, Plutarch's Roman Lives, Appian and Cassius Dio for the later Republic; the antiquarians (Varro, Verrius Flaccus through Festus, Aulus Gellius, Macrobius) for religion and custom; and the imperial historians in outline (Velleius, Tacitus, Suetonius, the Historia Augusta, Ammianus). Material sources: inscriptions (the Lapis Niger, the Duenos vase, the Satricum stone, the Scipio epitaphs, the Res Gestae, Claudius' speech on the Lyon tablet), coins as propaganda, the Pyrgi tablets, and archaeology in the Forum and on the Palatine. Then the method: the hypercritical tradition from Niebuhr and Mommsen to Pais and Forsythe, the more trusting positions of Cornell and Carandini, Wiseman's view of the early stories as dramatic inventions, and how to judge a story first found in Livy. End with the main traps: treating Livy book 1 as history, treating Dionysius as independent of Livy, trusting the Historia Augusta, and reading Roman myth only through Ovid. Point back to Greek module 0.1 for the Greek sources rather than repeating them. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
read the report
0.2

Italy and the Mediterranean: the shape of Rome's world

A city on a river crossing, between Etruria and Campania, in the middle of a peninsula in the middle of a sea.

Give me an in-depth report on the geography of Italy and the Mediterranean and how it shaped Roman history and myth. Cover: the site of Rome itself (the Tiber crossing at the Tiber Island, the salt route of the Via Salaria, the hills and what the number seven meant, the marshy Forum valley and its drainage, the Campus Martius); Latium and the Alban Hills; the regions of Italy and their peoples (Etruria, Umbria, the Sabine country, Samnium, Campania, Apulia, Lucania, Bruttium, Cisalpine Gaul and the Po valley) and the spine of the Apennines; why Italy, unlike Greece, could be unified by land; the islands (Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica) and the sea lanes to Carthage and Greece; the roads as the skeleton of conquest (Appia, Flaminia, Aemilia, Egnatia); the Mediterranean as mare nostrum, the provinces in outline and the frontiers on the Rhine, the Danube and the Euphrates; and which myths are pinned to which places (the Palatine and the Lupercal, the Capitol and the Tarpeian Rock, the Aventine, Lavinium, Alba Longa, Lake Nemi, Cumae and the Sibyl, Lake Regillus). Include a text description of a mental map I can memorise. Point back to Greek module 0.2 for the Greek world rather than repeating it. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
read the report
0.3

The timeline spine, 1000 BC to AD 476

About eighteen dates to hang everything on, and the eastern empire that kept going to 1453.

Give me an in-depth report that builds a memorisable timeline of Roman history from the Italian Early Iron Age, c. 1000 BC, to the deposition of the last western emperor in AD 476, with a closing note on the eastern empire to 1453. Cover: the standard period names and their date ranges (Iron Age Italy, the regal period, the early, middle and late Republic, the Principate, the third-century crisis, the late empire or Dominate) and why the boundaries fall where they do; the 15 to 20 anchor dates every educated person should know, each with one sentence on why it matters; how the Romans themselves dated things (consular years and the Fasti, years from the foundation of the city and the competing foundation dates of Timaeus, Ennius, Fabius Pictor, Cincius, Cato, Polybius and Varro, emperors' regnal years, the indiction); the big chronological problems (the foundation date, seven kings for 244 years, the 'dictator years' and the Varronian chronology, 390 or 387 BC for the Gallic sack, the date of the first consuls and the Capitoline temple, when the Republic 'ended'); and why AD 476 is a convention and 1453 a different kind of end. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, a clean dated list I can copy out by hand, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

UNIT 1

Italy before Rome and the founding legends

The peoples Rome grew out of and the stories it told about its birth. Archaeology and legend are read side by side, because for this period neither can be read alone.

1.1

The peoples of Iron Age Italy

Villanovans, Latins, Sabines, Samnites and Greek colonists: the crowded peninsula Rome came out of.

Give me an in-depth report on the peoples of Italy in the Iron Age, c. 1000 to 500 BC, the world Rome emerged from. Cover: the Final Bronze Age background (the Terramare, the Proto-Villanovan cremation cemeteries) and the Villanovan culture of Etruria and Bologna (biconical urns, hut urns, the shift to inhumation, the rise of a warrior elite); the Latial culture and its phases, the early cemeteries of Rome (the Forum burials, the Esquiline) and of the Alban Hills, and Osteria dell'Osa near Gabii as the best-excavated Latin community; the Latins as a people and their shared cults (the Latin festival on the Alban Mount, Diana at Aricia, the thirteen altars at Lavinium) and the Latin League; the Sabines, the Oscan- and Umbrian-speaking peoples (the Samnites, the Iguvine Tables as a window on Umbrian religion), the Veneti, Ligurians, Messapians and Picenes; the languages of Italy, Indo-European and not, and what the spread of the alphabet shows; the Greek colonies of the south (Pithekoussai and Cumae, then Magna Graecia and Sicily) seen from the Italian side, with the Nestor cup and the first writing in Latium; and the Phoenicians in the west. Point back to Greek module 5.2 for Greek colonisation itself. End with the Sabines as the first case of the course's method: what archaeology and language allow us to say about a people that Roman legend (module 1.4) made into Rome's co-founders. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

The Etruscans

Rome's teachers and first foreign kings, whose language we can read aloud but barely understand.

Leave Mastarna and the François Tomb to module 1.5. UNIT 2

The gods of Rome

Roman religion was a system of obligations, not a body of stories. Learn how it worked before the Republic, which ran on it, and before the Greek gods it absorbed.

2.1

What Roman religion was

Pax deorum, ritual exactness, and why the Romans are said to have had no mythology.

Cover: religio and superstitio, and why 'belief' is the wrong question; the pax deorum and the contractual logic of do ut des, vows and their fulfilment; ritual exactness and instauratio, the repetition of a flawed rite; the state as the religious actor and magistrates as officiants; prodigies and their expiation as Livy records them year by year; Varro's three theologies (mythical, natural, civil) as Augustine preserves them in City of God book 6, and Varro's claim that Rome worshipped without images for 170 years; numen, the 'animism' theory and its collapse; Dumézil's three functions and the archaic triad of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus; the old claim that the Romans had no mythology of their own and the modern answers to it (Dumézil's myths turned into history, Wiseman's lost dramatic myths, Feeney's Literature and Religion at Rome, Beard, North and Price's Religions of Rome); and how religion and politics were one activity, from augury in elections to Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods and On Divination. ROME · UNIT 0 · Foundations · 0.1 · 3,367 words

How we know anything: the sources

The defining problem: a past written down lateThe first historians: Roman history in GreekCato and the Latin annalistsThe raw material, and what the Romans said about itThe surviving narrativesThe antiquarians: religion, custom and wordsThe imperial historians in outlineMaterial sourcesMethod: how far to trust the traditionThe main trapsSelf-testCarry forward

The defining problem: a past written down late

Varro dated Rome's foundation to 753 BC; the first history of Rome by a Roman was written about 200 BC. Romulus reached the page five and a half centuries after his supposed date, the first consuls three centuries after theirs. Most of what we read is later still: Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus wrote under Augustus, seven centuries after Romulus; Plutarch nearly eight and a half. In between lay the Gallic sack of about 390 BC, which Livy says destroyed most of the records (6.1.2).

The writers who filled the gap were senators or their dependants, writing for families that competed through ancestral glory, and they made the early centuries an argument about the present: liberty against tyranny, patricians against plebeians, ancestral virtue against decline. The Roman problem is the reverse of the Greek one. Greek myth survives as many contradictory poems with no canon; Greek module 0.1 covers those sources, and they are not repeated here. Roman tradition survives as one apparently continuous prose history, dated year by year and largely constructed in its details. The task is not to choose between versions but to strip one back to what lies beneath.

Where sources disagree. Whether Rome had a mythology of its own is disputed. H. J. Rose held that Romans had gods without stories and borrowed myths from Greece; Georges Dumézil (Mythe et épopée, 1968–73) and T. P. Wiseman (The Myths of Rome, 2004), in different ways, find Roman myth told as history. Module 2.1 weighs the answers.

The first historians: Roman history in Greek

Poets came first: Naevius' Punic War (late third century) and Ennius' Annales (c. 180s–170s BC) made Romulus Aeneas' grandson (Servius on Aeneid 1.273), and Cicero quotes Ennius' augural contest of the twins (On Divination 1.107–108).

Prose began with Quintus Fabius Pictor, a senator of the patrician Fabii, who fought the Gauls in 225 (Orosius 4.13.6) and was sent to Delphi after Cannae (Livy 22.57.5; 23.11.1–6). His history, written in Greek around 200 BC, ran from Aeneas to his own day. Lucius Cincius Alimentus, praetor in 210 and once Hannibal's prisoner (Livy 21.38.3), wrote a similar Greek work. Dionysius says both were exact on what they had witnessed and summary on the centuries after the foundation (1.6.2): an hourglass, full at the origins and the present, thin between.

Why Greek? Latin had no prose literature, and Greek was the language of history and of the Mediterranean public that judged Rome. Like Berossus for Babylon and Manetho for Egypt, Fabius presented his people to the Hellenistic world in its own idiom, answering historians who wrote from Carthage's side: Philinus of Acragas, and Silenus and Sosylus in Hannibal's camp. He took the foundation story itself from a Greek, Diocles of Peparethus (Plutarch, Romulus 3.1). The habit lasted: Aulus Postumius Albinus, consul in 151, wrote in Greek and apologised for his Greek, earning Cato's mockery (Polybius 39.1).

Where sources disagree. Polybius calls Fabius a partisan who blamed the Second Punic War on Hasdrubal's ambition (1.14.1–3; 3.8–9); Dionysius treats Fabius and Cincius as careful witnesses of their own times. Matthias Gelzer ("Römische Politik bei Fabius Pictor", Hermes 1933) read Fabius as propaganda aimed at Greeks; Dieter Timpe ("Fabius Pictor und die Anfänge der römischen Historiographie", ANRW I.2, 1972) replies that the Roman elite read Greek and was itself the first audience.

Cato and the Latin annalists

Cato the Elder's Origines, begun after 168 and unfinished at his death in 149, was the first history in Latin prose: the kings in book 1, the origins of Italian peoples and towns in books 2–3 (hence the title), then Rome's wars to his own day, with his speeches inserted. He named no generals, only their offices (Nepos, Cato 3.4), though he named a Carthaginian elephant, Surus (Pliny, Natural History 8.11). The fragments of all these writers are in T. J. Cornell (ed.), The Fragments of the Roman Historians (2013).

The annalists, who arranged events year by year under the consuls, came in two waves:

  • Lucius Cassius Hemina (mid-second century) wrote from the origins with an antiquarian bent.
  • Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi (consul 133) moralised, dating the onset of decline to 154 BC (Pliny, Natural History 17.244), and rationalised: his Tarpeia tries to trick the Sabines out of their shields (Dionysius 2.38–40).
  • Quintus Claudius Quadrigarius (Sullan era) began with the Gallic sack, as if conceding that what lay before was unknowable.
  • Valerius Antias, his contemporary, wrote at least 75 books; Livy catches him "exaggerating the number of everything without limit" (33.10).
  • Gaius Licinius Macer (tribune 73) cited the "linen books" kept in the temple of Juno Moneta (Livy 4.7.12; 4.20.8), yet disagreed with Aelius Tubero, who cited the same books (4.23.1–3); Livy discounts him for seeking glory for his own family (7.9.5).

The charge is invention. The further the annalists stood from the early Republic, the more they knew: speeches, casualty figures, family heroes, political struggles that read like their own. Valerii loom large in Antias, Licinii in Macer. Ernst Badian ("The Early Historians", 1966) traced how each generation lengthened the early centuries.

Where sources disagree. Badian and, later, Gary Forsythe treat the annalists as free inventors. Wiseman (Clio's Cosmetics, 1979) recasts the charge: ancient historiography expected plausible "creative reconstruction", so they filled gaps by convention rather than lying. Cornell and Stephen Oakley (A Commentary on Livy Books VI–X, 1997–2005) see elaboration around a transmitted core of lists, laws, buildings and cults.

The raw material, and what the Romans said about it

The Annales Maximi. Each year, Cicero says, the pontifex maximus wrote up the year's events on a whitened board at his house, until Publius Mucius Scaevola's time, about 130 BC (On the Orator 2.52); an edition in eighty books followed (Servius on Aeneid 1.373). The entries were magistrates, prodigies, famines and eclipses. Cato would not copy "how often grain was dear, how often darkness obscured the moon or sun" (Gellius 2.28.6); Cicero found nothing "more jejune" (On the Laws 1.6). Even this record was reconstructed at its start: the first eclipse actually entered fell around 400 BC, and earlier ones, including one under Romulus, were calculated backwards (Cicero, On the Republic 1.25).

Lists. The consular and triumphal fasti survive chiefly in the Augustan Fasti Capitolini, found in the Forum in 1546. The triumphal list opens with Romulus over the Caeninenses, a record no one could have kept.

Documents. A few survived: Polybius read the Carthage treaties in the aediles' archive (3.22–26), and Cicero learnt the Twelve Tables by heart as a boy (On the Laws 2.59).

Families. Noble houses kept wax ancestor masks (imagines) captioned with offices held; at funerals actors wore them while a son praised the dead and his forebears (Polybius 6.53–54). Cicero says these eulogies filled Roman history with errors:

false triumphs, too many consulships, false genealogies too (Brutus 62)

Livy agrees that the record was "corrupted by funeral eulogies and false captions on the masks", and notes that no writer contemporary with those times survives (8.40.4–5). Cato recalled songs in praise of great men once sung at banquets, lost by his day (Cicero, Brutus 75).

Where sources disagree. The traditional view, broadly shared by Cornell, is that Scaevola published the eighty books around 130 BC and the annalists mined them. Bruce Frier (Libri Annales Pontificum Maximorum, 1979) argued that the edition was an Augustan reworking and that its role in shaping the tradition has been exaggerated. How much of the chronicle reached Livy is uncertain.

The surviving narratives
