Polybius, a Greek hostage in Rome after 167, asked an outsider's question: how did Rome conquer nearly the whole inhabited world in under fifty-three years (1.1.5)? His answer, the constitution and army of book 6, is analysis, not tradition. Livy follows him from the fourth decade, calling him "not an unreliable authority" (33.10).

Livy (c. 59 BC–AD 17) wrote Book 1 between 27 and 25 BC: it has Augustus closing the temple of Janus once, not twice (1.19.3). His preface will neither affirm nor refute stories from before the city's foundation, being

more fitting for poets' tales than for the incorrupt records of history (Preface 6)

Antiquity may mingle human and divine to make the beginnings of cities more august (Preface 7); history supplies examples to imitate and to avoid (Preface 10). But the line falls at the foundation: from Romulus on Livy narrates as history, hedged with "they say", and even offers the rationalised version in which the she-wolf was a prostitute (1.4.7). He worked from the annalists, rarely from documents.

Dionysius came to Rome in 30 BC and published in 7 BC (1.7.2; 1.3.4). His thesis is that Rome was a Greek city, founded by successive waves of Greeks (1.5.1; 1.89–90), an argument to reconcile Greek readers to Roman rule; module 1.3 takes up its content. He is fuller than Livy because more rhetorical, and he names the same annalists (1.7.3).

Diodorus gives sparse Roman notices for the fifth and fourth centuries, with a chronology often at odds with Livy's. Plutarch's Roman Lives (Romulus, Numa, Publicola, Coriolanus, Camillus for the early period) collect variants; he admits he learnt Latin late (Demosthenes 2.2–4). For the later Republic, Appian's Civil Wars is the only continuous narrative from the Gracchi to Sulla, and Dio's surviving books run from 69 BC to AD 46.

Where sources disagree. Mommsen, and later Otto Leuze (1909), held that Diodorus' Roman notices descend from Fabius Pictor and so preserve the tradition before annalistic expansion. Gerhard Perl traced the consular list to a separate magistrate list, Andrew Drummond treats anomalies as Diodorus' own errors, and Cornell leaves the question open.

The antiquarians: religion, custom and words

For religion and custom the key writers are antiquarians. Varro (116–27 BC) wrote the Antiquities Human and Divine in 41 books, 25 human and 16 divine (Augustine, City of God 6.3), the divine part dedicated to Caesar as pontifex maximus. It is lost, known mainly through Augustine, who quotes it to demolish it, including its three theologies: mythical (the poets'), natural (the philosophers') and civil (the city's) (City of God 6.5). Books 5–10 of On the Latin Language survive, rich in etymologies of hills, gates and festivals.

Verrius Flaccus, Augustan freedman and tutor to Augustus' grandsons, set up an annotated calendar at Praeneste (Suetonius, On Grammarians 17), fragments of which survive as the Fasti Praenestini. His lexicon On the Meaning of Words survives only through Festus' abridgement, itself in one fire-damaged manuscript, and Paul the Deacon's eighth-century epitome of Festus. Aulus Gellius' Attic Nights (later second century AD) quotes Cato, the annalists and the Twelve Tables verbatim. Macrobius' Saturnalia (early fifth century) explains the calendar and festivals in book 1.

The antiquarians' facts about ritual are often old and good; their explanations are scholarship, frequently etymological guesswork, not memory.

The imperial historians in outline

Velleius Paterculus published a compressed history in two books in AD 30, a soldier's panegyric of Tiberius. Tacitus (c. AD 56–c. 120) wrote the Histories (AD 69–96) and the Annals (AD 14–68), each surviving in part: senatorial, hostile to the principate, and supremely artful. Suetonius, imperial secretary under Hadrian, wrote the Lives of the Caesars from Julius to Domitian, arranged by topic, quoting Augustus' letters. The Historia Augusta gives lives of emperors and usurpers from Hadrian to Carinus (AD 117–284) under six names, with forged documents and a gap for 244–260. Ammianus Marcellinus, a Greek from Antioch writing Latin in Rome around 390, covered AD 96–378; books 14–31 (353–378) survive, much of it eyewitness.

Where sources disagree. Hermann Dessau (1889) showed that the Historia Augusta's six "authors" under Diocletian and Constantine are one writer of the late fourth century; Ronald Syme (Ammianus and the Historia Augusta, 1968) called him a rogue grammarian. Arnaldo Momigliano (1954) urged caution, but the single late author is now consensus. The live question is how much sound material the main lives take from Marius Maximus and the lost imperial history posited by Alexander Enmann (1884).

Material sources

Inscriptions. The Lapis Niger, a black paving in the Comitium found by Giacomo Boni in 1899, covers a cippus inscribed boustrophedon in archaic Latin around 570–550 BC (CIL I² 1). It names recei, "to the king", a herald (kalatorem) and a curse on violators (sakros esed): contemporary proof of a rex, whether king or the priestly rex sacrorum. The Duenos vase, a triple pot found near the Quirinal in 1880 (CIL I² 4), carries a sixth-century text that includes "Duenos made me". The Satricum stone, inscribed around 500 BC and found in 1977 reused in a temple's foundations, names the companions (suodales) of Poplios Valesios, perhaps the consul Publius Valerius (module 1.6). The Scipio epitaphs on the Via Appia are family self-advertisement in Saturnian verse. The Res Gestae, Augustus' own account set up before his Mausoleum (Suetonius, Augustus 101.4) and best preserved at Ancyra, claims he freed the republic from "the domination of a faction", leaving Antony unnamed (1.1). Claudius' speech of AD 48 on admitting Gallic nobles to the senate, on the bronze found at Lyon in 1528 (ILS 212), can be set beside Tacitus' version (Annals 11.24): same argument, wholly rewritten, a measure of what historians' speeches are.

Where sources disagree. The epitaph of Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus, consul 298 (CIL I² 7), says he took Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium and subdued all Lucania; Livy gives him Etruria that year and Samnium to his colleague (10.12). Either the family inflated the record, as Cicero and Livy complain, or the annalists confused the provinces. The text's date is debated too: traditionally a later replacement for an erased epitaph, it is original in Rudolf Wachter's analysis (1987).

Coins. A didrachm of about 269–266 BC already shows the wolf and twins. From the 130s BC the annual moneyers advertised their families: Sextus Pompeius Fostlus set Faustulus beside the wolf, punning on his name (c. 137 BC; RRC 235/1), and Caesar issued Aeneas carrying Anchises. Under the emperors the centre chose every type, though how much users noticed is debated (A. H. M. Jones, "Numismatics and History", 1956).

The Pyrgi tablets, three gold sheets found in 1964 at the port of Caere, two in Etruscan and one in Phoenician, record a dedication to Uni-Astarte around 500 BC by Thefarie Velianas, called king in the Phoenician text. Their bearing on Rome's first treaty with Carthage, which Polybius dates to 508/7 (3.22), is weighed in module 1.6.

Archaeology. In the Forum Boni found an Iron Age cemetery; the valley became a public square only after drainage, landfill and a first pavement in the later seventh century. On the Palatine, Iron Age hut post-holes lie near the "hut of Romulus" Romans preserved (Dionysius 1.79.11), and Andrea Carandini dated a wall at the hill's foot to about 730–720 BC (module 1.4). Sant'Omobono and the Regia show a monumental sixth-century city. Archaeology gives settings and sequences, not names.

Method: how far to trust the tradition

The hypercritical tradition

Louis de Beaufort (1738) first argued that the first five centuries were uncertain. Barthold Niebuhr (Römische Geschichte, 1811–32) derived the legends from lost banquet ballads; the theory is abandoned, his separation of source layers is not. Theodor Mommsen (Römische Geschichte, 1854–56) set the regal narrative aside and rebuilt early Rome from institutions and law. Ettore Pais (Storia di Roma, 1898–99) went furthest, reading Tarpeia and others as faded deities and much of the fifth century as doublets of later events. Gary Forsythe (A Critical History of Early Rome, 2005) restates the position: the fasti, a few documents and archaeology are usable; the narrative before the fourth century is reconstruction.

Cornell, Carandini, Wiseman

Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) separates structural facts (institutions, cults, treaties, the sequence of kings, the Servian reforms) from narrative superstructure. The first survived through institutions and monuments and fits the archaeology of a large sixth-century city; plebeian names in the early consular list are not what a patrician forger would invent. Carandini (La nascita di Roma, 1997; Remo e Romolo, 2006) goes further, treating the Palatine wall as evidence of a deliberate eighth-century foundation and legend as compressed memory; Wiseman ("Reading Carandini", 2001) rejects this as reading archaeology through Livy. Wiseman's own view (Remus, 1995; Roman Drama and Roman History, 1998) is that many early stories were created in the fourth and third centuries as dramatic performances at the games, Remus himself entering the story late. Plutarch already reports that some found the Romulus story "dramatic and fictitious" (Romulus 8).

Where sources disagree. Wiseman points to stage games at Rome from 364 BC (Livy 7.2) and to lost plays on Roman subjects such as Naevius' Romulus; critics reply that hardly any are attested before the late third century, and Cornell's structural memory needs no stage.

Judging a story first found in Livy

  1. Count the centuries. Name the earliest witness and its date; a story first found in Livy has passed through Fabius, the annalists and Livy's rhetoric.
  2. Separate structure from narrative. A law, cult, temple or name in the fasti may be old; a speech, motive or casualty figure is not.
  3. Look for aetiology. The Lacus Curtius has a Sabine Mettius Curtius (Livy 1.13.5), a self-sacrificing Marcus Curtius of 362 (7.6.1–6) and a consul fencing off a lightning strike (Varro, On the Latin Language 5.148–150): three explanations of one monument.
  4. Look for Greek models. Tarquin's poppies (Livy 1.54.6) are Thrasybulus' advice to Periander (Herodotus 5.92); Sextus Tarquinius at Gabii is Zopyrus at Babylon (Herodotus 3.153–158). In Cicero's Brutus (41–43) Atticus teases him for giving Coriolanus a Themistocles-like suicide, since rhetoricians may lie in histories.
  5. Look for later politics and family interest. Spurius Cassius and Spurius Maelius, would-be tyrants offering land or grain, read like the Gracchi; the 306 Fabii dying at the Cremera (Livy 2.48–50) are a family epic Fabius Pictor was placed to shape.
  6. Seek an outside control. Aristotle knew the Gauls took Rome but named its saviour Lucius, not Marcus Camillus (Plutarch, Camillus 22.4); an inscription, treaty or stratum can confirm or contradict.

The main traps

Treating Livy book 1 as history. Livy suspended judgement only on the stories before the foundation; the kings he narrates as history, seven centuries late. Seven kings filling 244 years, each founding a neat set of institutions, is a scheme. Read Book 1 for what Augustan Romans believed, and for the structural facts that survive scrutiny.

Treating Dionysius as independent of Livy. They were contemporaries in the same city, using the same annalists. Their agreement is one tradition reported twice; Dionysius' extra detail is usually extra rhetoric.

Trusting the Historia Augusta. It is a late fourth-century fiction on a factual spine. Use it only where Dio, Herodian, coins or inscriptions confirm it.

Reading Roman myth only through Ovid. Greek module 0.1 warned against treating Ovid as Greek; the Roman trap is the mirror image. The Metamorphoses ends with Roman stories, Vertumnus and Pomona (book 14) and Numa as Pythagoras' pupil (book 15), a link Livy rejects as chronologically impossible (1.18.2); the Fasti, an often playful calendar poem, covers only January to June. Roman myth lives in Livy, Dionysius, Virgil, Propertius book 4, the antiquarians, cult and topography.

Self-test

  1. Why did Fabius Pictor write Roman history in Greek around 200 BC?
    Answer

    Latin had no prose tradition; Greek was the language of history and of the Mediterranean public whose opinion mattered during the Hannibalic war, and Fabius was answering pro-Carthaginian Greek historians such as Philinus and Silenus.

  2. What does Dionysius 1.6.2 reveal about the shape of the earliest Roman histories, and why does it matter?
    Answer

    They were detailed on the origins and on their own times but summary on the centuries between. The full year-by-year narrative of the early Republic in Livy must therefore have been added later, largely by the annalists.

  3. What did Cicero and Livy say had corrupted the record of early Rome?
    Answer

    Family funeral eulogies and the captions on ancestral masks, which invented triumphs, consulships and genealogies (Cicero, Brutus 62; Livy 8.40.4–5); Livy adds the loss of records in the Gallic fire (6.1.2).

  4. How does Cicero's eclipse passage (On the Republic 1.25) undermine trust in the pontifical chronicle's early entries?
    Answer

    It shows that the first eclipse actually recorded fell around 400 BC and that earlier ones, including one under Romulus, were calculated backwards. The early part of the chronicle was itself reconstructed.

  5. What does Livy's preface claim about legend, and where does he draw the line?
    Answer

    He will neither affirm nor refute stories from before the foundation, which suit poetry better than history (Preface 6–7). From Romulus on he narrates as history, with hedges such as the rationalised she-wolf (1.4.7).

  6. Why is agreement between Livy and Dionysius not corroboration?
    Answer

    They wrote at the same time in the same city from the same annalistic sources, which Dionysius names (1.7.3). Two reports of one tradition are not two witnesses.

  7. What does the Lapis Niger prove, and what does it not?
    Answer

    It proves that a rex functioned in the Comitium around 570–550 BC, in contemporary Latin. It does not prove any named king of the tradition, and recei may mean the rex sacrorum.

  8. What does the Barbatus epitaph, set against Livy 10.12, teach about Roman sources?
    Answer

    A family record in stone and Livy's annalistic narrative disagree about where the consul of 298 fought. Either family display inflated the claim or the annalists confused the provinces; neither can be trusted by default.

  9. State Cornell's distinction and give one argument he uses for the authenticity of the early fasti.
    Answer

    Structural facts (institutions, cults, treaties, the sequence of kings) can be old; narrative detail is later elaboration. The plebeian names in the early consular list are not what a patrician forger would have inserted.

  10. Who exposed the Historia Augusta, and what did he show?
    Answer

    Hermann Dessau (1889): its six supposed authors of the Diocletianic and Constantinian age are one writer of the late fourth century who invented sources and documents.

Carry forward

  1. Keep the date of the event and the date of the source apart: everything before about 300 BC reached the page at least a century later, the kings five to eight centuries later, and the fullest accounts are the latest.
  2. Separate structure from narrative. Institutions, cults, treaties, monuments and names in the lists may preserve something old; speeches, motives, numbers and heroics belong to the annalists and their successors.
  3. Roman tradition is history-shaped and agenda-laden: ask whose family, faction or regime a story served when it was first told, and look for an outside control in an inscription, a coin, a Greek witness or a stratum.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the sources for Roman history and mythology, with the emphasis on the problem that defines the subject: Rome's early history was written down centuries after the events, by Romans with agendas. Cover: the first Roman historians, who wrote in Greek (Fabius Pictor, writing around 200 BC; Cincius Alimentus) and why they did; Cato's Origines and the Latin annalists (Cassius Hemina, Calpurnius Piso, Valerius Antias, Claudius Quadrigarius, Licinius Macer), known only in fragments, and the charge that they invented; the raw material they claimed to use (the Annales Maximi of the pontiffs, the lists of consuls and triumphs, family archives, funeral orations) and the complaints Cicero and Livy themselves make about it; the surviving narratives: Polybius (the outsider's analysis), Livy (Ab urbe condita, 142 books of which 35 survive, and his preface on legend), Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities, and his thesis that Rome was a Greek city), Diodorus, Plutarch's Roman Lives, Appian and Cassius Dio for the later Republic; the antiquarians (Varro, Verrius Flaccus through Festus, Aulus Gellius, Macrobius) for religion and custom; and the imperial historians in outline (Velleius, Tacitus, Suetonius, the Historia Augusta, Ammianus). Material sources: inscriptions (the Lapis Niger, the Duenos vase, the Satricum stone, the Scipio epitaphs, the Res Gestae, Claudius' speech on the Lyon tablet), coins as propaganda, the Pyrgi tablets, and archaeology in the Forum and on the Palatine. Then the method: the hypercritical tradition from Niebuhr and Mommsen to Pais and Forsythe, the more trusting positions of Cornell and Carandini, Wiseman's view of the early stories as dramatic inventions, and how to judge a story first found in Livy. End with the main traps: treating Livy book 1 as history, treating Dionysius as independent of Livy, trusting the Historia Augusta, and reading Roman myth only through Ovid. Point back to Greek module 0.1 for the Greek sources rather than repeating them. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

Italy and the Mediterranean: the shape of Rome's world

The shape of Italy: a mental map

Greek module 0.2 laid out the Aegean triangle, Magna Graecia and Sicily from the Greek side; none of that is repeated here. Hold Rome's world as a peninsula pushed into the middle of one sea, a mountain seam down its length, and the city halfway down the western side, on the shin of the boot.

Read it in three vertical bands. West: a chain of volcanic plains facing the Tyrrhenian (Etruria, Latium, Campania), with Rome at the joint of the first two. Middle: the Apennine spine, its upland peoples in long parallel valleys. East: a narrow Adriatic strip, poor in harbours, that widens only into Apulia. Cap the bands with the Po plain under the Alps, Rome's "Gaul this side of the Alps". Hang Corsica and Sardinia off Etruria and Latium, and Sicily under the toe like a ball kicked towards Africa, with Cape Bon in Africa 140 kilometres from its western cape. Then widen the view. The Mediterranean is two basins joined at the Sicilian Channel, with Italy across the waist; round the rim, clockwise from Spain, run Gaul, Italy, Illyricum, Greece, Asia Minor, Syria, Egypt and Africa; beyond the rim the empire stopped at Ocean, the Rhine and Danube, the Euphrates and the Sahara.

The site of Rome: ford, salt and hills

Rome stands where the lower Tiber is crossed. About 25 kilometres from the sea the river divides round the Tiber Island, the first point upstream where it could be forded and then bridged, so the land route between Etruria and Latium passed here. Beside it lay the Forum Boarium, cattle market and landing place, where Euboean pottery arrives in the eighth century and the Ara Maxima served Hercules, a god of traders. Livy gives the first bridge, the wooden Pons Sublicius, to Ancus Marcius (1.33.6). Cicero (On the Republic 2.5–11) praised the site as wisely chosen; Strabo (5.3.2) thought it taken "more by necessity than choice".

The crossing was also a salt road. Salt beds lay at the river mouth, and the Via Salaria ran north-east into the Sabine hills, named, Pliny says, for the salt carried to the Sabines along it (Natural History 31.89). Salt made Rome a middleman between coast and Apennines and set it against Veii, which held the right bank; Plutarch has Romulus take the salt-works from the Veientines (Romulus 25).

The canonical seven hills are the Palatine, Capitoline, Aventine, Caelian, Esquiline, Viminal and Quirinal (Varro, On the Latin Language 5.41–54). Stand on the Tiber Island facing east: the Capitol is on your left, the Palatine ahead, the Aventine on your right, the Caelian behind the Palatine; the Esquiline, Viminal and Quirinal are tongues of a plateau running in from the north-east. Seven is an ideal, not a survey. Virgil's Rome "ringed seven citadels with a single wall" (Georgics 2.535), and Revelation 17:9 turned the image against the city.

Where sources disagree. Varro derived the December festival of the Septimontium from "these seven hills on which the city stands" (On the Latin Language 6.24). Festus, quoting Antistius Labeo, lists eight places, mostly spurs and districts (Palatium, Velia, Fagutal, Subura, Cermalus, Oppius, Caelius, Cispius), without the Capitol, Quirinal or Aventine. Most scholars take the festival to belong to an early league of Palatine and Esquiline communities, and the canonical seven to be a later rationalisation.

Between Capitol, Palatine and Velia lay a low valley draining through the Velabrum to the river. Ovid remembered it as swamp (Fasti 6.401), and the Lacus Curtius at its centre kept the memory. It was a cemetery from the tenth century; in the later seventh it was raised with fill and given its first floor, the moment Rome acquires a public centre. Livy, writing more than five centuries later, credits Tarquinius Priscus with draining it (1.38.6) and Tarquinius Superbus with the Cloaca Maxima (1.56.2).

Where sources disagree. Albert Ammerman (American Journal of Archaeology, 1990) argued from cores that the valley was seasonally flooded ground rather than a permanent marsh, and that the decisive work was a deliberate landfill. John Hopkins (The Genesis of Roman Architecture, 2016) accepts an archaic open channel but notes that the vaulted Cloaca visible today is largely Republican. Livy may be right about the first canal and wrong about the sewer.

North-west of the Capitol, in a loop of the river, lay the flood-plain of the Campus Martius. It was outside the pomerium, the sacred boundary within which military command could not be exercised (Tacitus traces Romulus' line in Annals 12.24). So the comitia centuriata, the people voting as an army, met there, and generals awaited their triumphs there. Livy makes it the Tarquins' land, consecrated to Mars at their fall (2.5.2), and the place where Romulus vanished, at the Goat's Marsh (1.16.1). Augustan monuments later filled it (Strabo 5.3.8).

Latium and the Alban Hills

Old Latium, Latium vetus, is the coastal plain south of the Tiber, closed by the Sabine and Aequian hills to the north-east, the Volscian Lepini to the south-east, and the promontory of Circeii, where Greeks placed Circe. Its centre is the Alban Hills, a dormant volcano some 20 kilometres south-east of Rome, with the crater lakes of Albano and Nemi on its south-western side. Tuff gave building stone and fertile soil. The summit, the Alban Mount, held the Latins' common shrine of Jupiter Latiaris, and Pliny lists the vanished populi Albenses who once shared its sacrificial meat (Natural History 3.68–70). The Latin towns ring the hills: Tibur, Praeneste, Tusculum, Aricia, Lanuvium, Lavinium, Ardea, Gabii; their cults and league belong to module 1.1. Two works show Romans handling this landscape: the tunnel that drained Lake Albano, dug, Livy says, because an oracle tied the fall of Veii to it (5.15–16, 5.19), and the Pontine Marshes, which defeated drainage from Caesar's plan (Suetonius, Julius 44) until the 1930s.

The regions of Italy and the Apennine spine

The Apennines run about 1,200 kilometres from Liguria, swing east almost to the Adriatic at Ariminum, then run south-east down the middle and into the toe. They lie nearer the Adriatic, so the west has the broad plains and long rivers (Arno, Tiber, Liris, Volturnus). Polybius describes the peninsula in 2.14–17, Strabo in Books 5 and 6, Pliny in Natural History 3.38–138.

RegionPeoplesLandscapeRome's dealings
EtruriaEtruscans (module 1.2)Tiber to Arno; metals of ElbaVeii taken 396; the rest allied by the early third century

The pattern has three tiers. Plains peoples were urban, rich and reachable. Apennine peoples lived in villages and hill-forts, moved flocks between summer mountain and winter plain, and fought Rome longest; Livy's Samnite Wars (Books 7–10), written three centuries later, are a war of plain against mountain. The Po plain was Celtic, conquered late and colonised hard.

Why Italy, unlike Greece, could be unified by land

Greek module 0.2 argued that Greek mountains and sea favoured many small states without forcing them. Italy differed in three ways. Its plains are continuous along the western side, so a power in Latium could reach Etruria and Campania without crossing water or a range, and Rome sat at the middle of that chain. The Apennine valleys run lengthwise, and the mountain peoples needed lowland winter pasture and markets, so upland and plain were bound together by drove roads and by war. And there is no inner sea: an army could march from Rhegium to the Po. Mommsen's version is that Greece faces east and Italy west. Manpower followed: Polybius counts more than 700,000 foot and 70,000 horse available to Rome in 225 (2.24), a reservoir no Greek state approached.

Where sources disagree. Ancient writers made the geography providential: Strabo (6.4.1) lists the climate, harbours and central position that fitted Italy to rule, and Pliny calls it a land "chosen by the will of the gods" (Natural History 3.39). Modern historians are warier. W. V. Harris (War and Imperialism in Republican Rome, 1979) located the drive to expand in Roman society, T. J. Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) in the alliance system that turned defeated enemies into soldiers. Geography made unification possible; institutions made it happen.

The islands and the sea lanes

Rome came late to the sea. The Tyrrhenian was an Etruscan, Greek and Carthaginian water: off Alalia in Corsica, about 540, Etruscans and Carthaginians together fought the Phocaeans (Herodotus 1.166–167), and the first Roman treaty with Carthage (module 1.6) divides trading zones. Sicily lies three kilometres from Italy at the Straits of Messina and about 140 from Cape Bon; it is both bridge and barrier between the two basins, which is why Rome and Carthage collided there over Messana in 264 (Polybius 1.10–11). It became the first province in 241, and Cato called it the state's storehouse (Cicero, Verrines 2.2.5). Sardinia and Corsica, seized from Carthage in 238 while it fought its mercenaries, closed the Tyrrhenian triangle. The eastern lane ran from Brundisium across the Strait of Otranto, about 70 kilometres at its narrowest, to Apollonia and Dyrrhachium; the First Illyrian War (229) was fought to secure it.

The roads as the skeleton of conquest

A Roman road was first a military work: it ran from Rome to a colony, fixed the line of march, and moved an army in any season. Dionysius counts roads, with aqueducts and sewers, as Rome's three most magnificent works (3.67.5).

  • Via Appia, 312: the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, from Rome across the Pontine Marshes to Capua (Livy 9.29.6), in the middle of the Second Samnite War; extended by stages to Beneventum, Tarentum and Brundisium. Diodorus (20.36) says he exhausted the treasury on it.
  • Via Flaminia, 220: Gaius Flaminius as censor, from Rome through Umbria over the Apennines to Ariminum, the gate to the Po plain.
  • Via Aemilia, 187: the consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, from Ariminum along the edge of the Po plain to Placentia (Livy 39.2.10); Emilia keeps his name.
  • Via Egnatia, c. 146–120: named from the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius on a milestone found near Thessalonica, it crossed the Balkans from Dyrrhachium and Apollonia to Thessalonica, later Byzantium (Strabo 7.7.4, from Polybius). It turned the Adriatic crossing into a land route east, the road to Philippi.

The sequence tracks the conquest: Campania and Samnium, then the Adriatic, then the Po, then Macedonia. Colonies came first or with the road (Cales 334, Venusia 291, Ariminum 268, Placentia and Cremona 218), and the road tied them to Rome.

Mare nostrum, the provinces and the frontiers

"Our sea" is a Republican phrase (Caesar, Gallic War 5.1; Sallust, Jugurtha 17). It became literally true when Pompey cleared the pirates in three months of 67 under the Gabinian law (Plutarch, Pompey 24–28). The provinces came in rough rings round the sea:

  • The western islands and Spain: Sicily 241, Sardinia and Corsica 238, the two Spains 197.
  • The settlement of 146: Macedonia and Africa, the territory of destroyed Carthage.
  • The east by bequest and annexation: Asia 133, Cilicia c. 102, Bithynia and Cyrene 74, Crete 67, Syria 64.
  • The north-west: Transalpine Gaul c. 121, Caesar's Gaul 58–50.
  • Octavian, Augustus and after: Egypt 30, Galatia 25, the Alpine and Danubian provinces, Britain AD 43, Dacia and Arabia 106.

Beyond the coasts the empire ended at rivers. Caesar reached the Rhine in 58–55; Augustus pushed to the Elbe (Res Gestae 26) and gave it up after Varus lost three legions in AD 9. The Danube was reached in the Augustan wars in Illyricum and crossed for good only by Trajan into Dacia. The Euphrates faced Parthia: Crassus died beyond it at Carrhae in 53, Augustus recovered the standards by diplomacy in 20, and Hadrian gave up Trajan's Mesopotamia in 117. Tacitus describes the empire of AD 14 as "fenced by Ocean or distant rivers" (Annals 1.9) and records Augustus' advice to keep it within its limits (1.11).

Where sources disagree. Edward Luttwak (The Grand Strategy of the Roman Empire, 1976) read the rivers and walls as a planned defensive system. Benjamin Isaac (The Limits of Empire, 1990), C. R. Whittaker (Frontiers of the Roman Empire, 1994) and Susan Mattern (Rome and the Enemy, 1999) answered that Romans had neither the maps nor the doctrine for such a plan, that rivers were highways and zones of exchange rather than lines, and that halts followed defeats and costs.

Myths pinned to places

Roman myth is topographical: the stories were told at the spots they explained, and the spots were kept to prove the stories. Most of it reaches us through Livy, Dionysius and Virgil, five to seven centuries after the events.

PlaceMythMain sourcesWhat was shown
Palatine and LupercalThe she-wolf suckles the twins at a cave under the Cermalus; Romulus founds the cityLivy 1.4–7; Dionysius 1.79The cave, the fig tree, the hut of Romulus; Augustus lived beside them and rebuilt the Lupercal (Res Gestae 19). Module 1.4
Capitol and Tarpeian RockTarpeia betrays the citadel to the Sabines; a head in the temple foundations makes Rome "head of the world"; the geese, 390Livy 1.11.6–9, 1.55.5–6, 5.47The cliff from which traitors were thrown, Manlius, saviour of the Capitol, among them (Livy 6.20.12)
AventineRemus' augury; Hercules kills Cacus in his cave; Servius' temple of Diana for the LatinsLivy 1.6.4, 1.45; Virgil, Aeneid 8.190–267Outside the pomerium until Claudius, which Gellius (13.14) ties to Remus' bad omen
LaviniumAeneas lands, marries Lavinia, brings the PenatesLivy 1.1–2; Dionysius 1.55–64Thirteen altars (module 1.1) and a heroon (module 1.3)
Alba LongaFounded by Ascanius; Rome's mother city; destroyed by Tullus HostiliusLivy 1.3, 1.29Nothing: never located
Lake NemiDiana of the grove; the rex Nemorensis, a runaway slave who rules until killed; Hippolytus revived as VirbiusStrabo 5.3.12; Virgil, Aeneid 7.761–782The sanctuary; Caligula's ships; the opening of Frazer's Golden Bough (1890)
CumaeThe Sibyl's cave of a hundred mouths; Aeneas' descent near Avernus; the Sibylline Books sold to TarquinVirgil, Aeneid 6.9–155; Dionysius 4.62The oldest Greek city in Italy (Strabo 5.4.4); a gallery found by Amedeo Maiuri in 1932
Lake RegillusRome beats the Latins and Tarquins, c. 496; Castor and Pollux fight for Rome and water their horses at Juturna's springLivy 2.19–20; Dionysius 6.13The spring in the Forum and the temple of Castor, dedicated 484 (Livy 2.42.5). Module 1.6

Two patterns recur. The city's myths cluster at the crossing and its hills, each an aetiology for something a Roman could walk past: cave, hut, fig, rock, spring. The myths of Latium cluster on the Alban Hills and the coast and tell of a Latin headship passing from Lavinium to Alba to Rome; Cumae is the Greek door through which prophecy and the alphabet came in.

Where sources disagree. Even the hills were not fixed to the twins: Ennius has Romulus, not Remus, take the auspices on the Aventine (module 1.4). The places are uncertain too: Alba Longa has been sought at Castel Gandolfo and Palazzolo without a city being found, Lake Regillus has never been securely identified, and the "Sibyl's cave" that Maiuri matched to Aeneid 6.42–44 is read by many archaeologists as a defensive gallery of the fourth or third century BC.

Self-test

  1. Why did Rome grow at the Tiber Island rather than at the river mouth?
    Answer

    The island split the river at the first point upstream where it could be forded and bridged, so the land route between Etruria and Latium crossed there and the Forum Boarium beside it became market and landing. Cicero (On the Republic 2.5–11) praises the inland site as safe from pirates; Strabo (5.3.2) thought it chosen by necessity.

  2. What does the name of the Via Salaria reveal about early Rome's economy and its first great rival?
    Answer

    It was the road by which salt from the Tiber mouth went up to the Sabines (Pliny, Natural History 31.89), making Rome a middleman between coast and Apennines. Control of the salt beds set it against Veii on the right bank; Plutarch (Romulus 25) has Romulus seize them.

  3. Why is the canonical list of seven hills unlikely to be the original sense of the Septimontium?
    Answer

    Festus, quoting Antistius Labeo, gives eight places for the festival, mostly spurs of the Palatine and Esquiline, and omits the Capitol, Quirinal and Aventine. The seven-hilled city is a later ideal, fixed in Varro (On the Latin Language 6.24) and the Augustan poets.

  4. How does archaeology modify Livy's story of the draining of the Forum?
    Answer

    The valley was a cemetery, then in the later seventh century was raised by deliberate fill and floored; Ammerman (1990) argued it was seasonally flooded ground rather than a marsh. An archaic channel may go back to the kings, but the vaulted Cloaca Maxima seen today is largely Republican.

  5. Why did the comitia centuriata meet in the Campus Martius?
    Answer

    It was the people voting as an army, and military command could not be exercised inside the pomerium; the Campus lay outside it. Generals awaiting a triumph waited there for the same reason.

  6. Give three geographical reasons why Italy, unlike Greece, could be unified by land.
    Answer

    The western plains form a continuous chain with Rome at its middle; the Apennine valleys run lengthwise and their peoples depended on lowland pasture and markets; and no inner sea divides the peninsula. Greek module 0.2 gives the contrasting Aegean pattern.

  7. Match each road to its builder, date and endpoints, and say what links them.
    Answer

    Appia: Appius Claudius Caecus, 312, Rome to Capua, later Brundisium. Flaminia: Gaius Flaminius, 220, Rome to Ariminum. Aemilia: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, 187, Ariminum to Placentia. Egnatia: Gnaeus Egnatius, c. 146–120, Dyrrhachium to Thessalonica. Each follows the front of conquest and ties colonies to Rome.

  8. Why was Sicily Rome's first province, and what did it supply?
    Answer

    Three kilometres from Italy and about 140 from Africa, it is the hinge between the two Mediterranean basins, where Roman and Carthaginian interests met at Messana in 264; Rome took it in 241. It supplied grain: Cato called it the state's storehouse (Cicero, Verrines 2.2.5).

  9. What does Tacitus say about the empire's limits in AD 14, and how do Luttwak and his critics read the river frontiers?
    Answer

    He describes an empire fenced by Ocean or distant rivers (Annals 1.9) and Augustus' advice to keep it within its limits (1.11). Luttwak (1976) saw a planned grand strategy; Isaac, Whittaker and Mattern see rivers as zones of contact and halts as the result of defeats and costs.

  10. Which myth is pinned to Lake Regillus, and how did the Forum preserve it?
    Answer

    The battle of c. 496 in which Rome beat the Latins and the Tarquins The battle of c. 496 in which Rome beat the Latins and the Tarquins (Livy 2.19–20); in Dionysius (6.13) Castor and Pollux fought on its side.. The twins were seen watering their horses at Juturna's spring in the Forum (Dionysius 6.13), beside which stood the temple of Castor, dedicated in 484.

Carry forward

  1. Rome is a river crossing and a market before it is anything else: the Tiber Island ford, the salt road and the Forum Boarium explain why a city grew on low, flood-prone hills between Etruria and Latium, and why its oldest myths cluster round that crossing.
  2. Italy's geography made unification by land possible (continuous western plains, a lengthwise Apennine spine, no inner sea), and roads and colonies made it actual; the same method, exported round the Mediterranean and halted at the Rhine, the Danube and the Euphrates, is the shape of the empire.
  3. Roman myths were pinned to visible places by writers centuries after the events; always ask who tied the story to the spot and when, because the topography (the Lupercal, the hut of Romulus, Juturna's spring) was curated to prove the story.

The timeline spine, 1000 BC to AD 476

The periods and why the boundaries fall where they doThe anchor dates: a list to copy outConsuls and the FastiYears from the founding: seven ancient answersEmperors' years and the indictionThe big chronological problemsWhy 476 is a convention and 1453 is notSelf-testCarry forward

The periods and why the boundaries fall where they do

None of these period names is Roman. "Early", "middle" and "late" Republic are modern; the contrast of Principate and Dominate was sharpened by nineteenth-century German constitutional history; "third-century crisis" is a twentieth-century label. Each boundary marks a change of regime, of evidence, or both.

PeriodConventional rangeBoundary markers
Iron Age Italy (Latial culture)c. 1000–c. 730 BCHut villages, graves in the Forum valley; ends as the orientalising phase begins (module 1.1)
Regal period753–509 BCVarro's foundation to the expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus; both traditional
Early Republic509–264 BCFirst consuls to the first war outside Italy; some end it at 287
Middle Republic264–133 BCPunic Wars and conquest, to the killing of Tiberius Gracchus
Late Republic133–31 or 27 BCPolitical violence and civil war, to Actium or Augustus' settlement
Principate27 BC–AD 235Augustus to the murder of Severus Alexander
Third-century crisisAD 235–284Short reigns, usurpers, Persian and Gothic wars, breakaway Gaul and Palmyra
Late empire (Dominate)AD 284–476Diocletian to Romulus Augustulus in the West; the East continues

The line at 509 is Livy's own: Book 2 opens with a free people under annual magistrates (2.1.1). The line at 264 is Polybius', who began with the first Roman crossing to Sicily, where Timaeus had stopped (1.5.1); the evidence also improves there, since Fabius Pictor, Polybius' source for that war, wrote within living memory of it. The line at 133 follows Plutarch, for whom Tiberius Gracchus' death was the first civil strife since the kings to end in bloodshed (Tiberius Gracchus 20.1), and Appian, whose Civil Wars start there. In January 27 BC Octavian returned the provinces and became Augustus (Res Gestae 34); Tacitus says he took over a world worn out by civil war "under the name of princeps" (Annals 1.1). The murder of Severus Alexander in 235 ended the last stable dynasty; Diocletian's accession in 284 began the rebuilt state of module 8.2. "Dominate" comes from dominus, "lord", since late emperors were greeted by prostration; most historians now say "late empire", because the contrast with a constitutional Principate was overdrawn.

Where sources disagree. Karl-Joachim Hölkeskamp (Die Entstehung der Nobilität, 1987) dates the formation of the patricio-plebeian nobility, and so the classic Republic, to the decades between the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 and the lex Hortensia of 287. Harriet Flower (Roman Republics, 2010) divides the span into several successive republics and ends the republic of the nobles with Sulla's march in 88. The three-part scheme is a teaching convenience, not a finding.

The span falls into five blocks of roughly a quarter-millennium: kings 753–509 (244 years), early Republic 509–264 (245), conquest and civil war 264–27 (237), Principate 27 BC–AD 235 (261), crisis and late empire 235–476 (241). The first block's length is an artefact of the tradition, but the rhythm is a usable peg.

Consuls and the Fasti

A Roman year had a name, not a number: "the consulship of" two men. To place it you needed the list, the fasti consulares, by which the pontiffs' annual records were organised (module 0.1) and along which Livy's narrative moves. The best copy, the Fasti Capitolini, was inscribed in the Forum under Augustus, probably about 18 BC, with a list of triumphs; its fragments, found in 1546, are in the Capitoline Museums. As Greek module 0.3 showed for archons and Olympiads, chronology means reconciling lists.

There are two traps. The consular year began on 1 January only from 153 BC; before that, usually 15 March, and earlier the day shifted several times, so a consular year straddles two of ours. And the pre-Julian calendar drifted, by about three months before Caesar's reform of 46 BC (module 2.3). Under the emperors the year still bore the names of the consules ordinarii of 1 January, though replacements followed within months. The last private citizen to name a year was Basilius in AD 541; later documents counted years "after the consulship of Basilius".

Where sources disagree. Tim Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) defends the fifth-century list: it contains families that later vanished and plebeian names that contradict the later belief that plebeians were barred from the consulship before 367. Hypercritics from Ettore Pais onwards held that annalists padded or reconstructed it. The usual view accepts the names from about 500 BC and doubts the arithmetic.

Years from the founding: seven ancient answers

Counting ab urbe condita, "from the founding of the city", was a historian's device, not a civil one: Livy has the decemvirs take office "in the three hundred and second year" (3.33.1), and Orosius in the fifth century AD built a whole history on it. It needed a zero point the Romans did not have. The first historians, writing in Greek about 200 BC, five and a half centuries after the supposed event, had to convert a consular list and a king list into Olympiads. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, under Augustus, sets out the results (Roman Antiquities 1.74).

AuthorityFoundationBasis
Timaeus of Tauromenium (c. 350–260 BC)814/13 BCWith Carthage, 38 years before the first Olympiad (1.74.1)
Ennius, Annales (early 2nd century BC)c. 875 BC?"Seven hundred years, a little more or less" (quoted by Varro, On Agriculture 3.1.2); speaker and date uncertain
Fabius Pictor (c. 200 BC)748/7 BCOlympiad 8.1 (1.74.1)
Cincius Alimentus (c. 200 BC)729/8 BCOlympiad 12.4 (1.74.1)
Cato, Origines (c. 168–149 BC)752/1 BC432 years after Troy, which Dionysius makes Olympiad 7.1 (1.74.2)
Polybius (c. 200–118 BC)751/0 BCOlympiad 7.2 (1.74.3)
Varro (116–27 BC)753 BC, 21 AprilOlympiad 6.3, on the Parilia; Tarutius cast Romulus' horoscope for him (Plutarch, Romulus 12)

Set Timaeus and Ennius aside and the dates fall between 753 and 728, which suggests a common method: count the consular colleges back to the first consuls, then add a royal span of about 240 years agreed in advance. Timaeus' date pairs the two powers of the west; Ennius' belongs with the version in which Romulus was Aeneas' grandson (module 1.3). Varro's won by authority: Atticus used it in his Liber annalis of 47 BC, the Augustan Fasti a reckoning one year lower (752), and Censorinus in AD 238 called his year the 991st by Varro's count (De die natali 21). Modern books still convert with it.

Emperors' years and the indiction

Under the empire a second count ran beside the consuls. Egyptian papyri date by "year 15 of Tiberius Caesar Augustus", and Luke 3:1 dates the Baptist's preaching to "the fifteenth year" of Tiberius. Coins and inscriptions count annual renewals of tribunician power: Augustus' began in 23 BC and stood at thirty-seven when he finished the Res Gestae (4). With numbered consulships, these titles date most imperial inscriptions to the year.

The indiction grew out of Diocletian's tax assessments and became, under Constantine, a fifteen-year cycle counted from 1 September 312. Documents give the year within the cycle, never the cycle, so an indiction alone is ambiguous. Justinian made the full formula compulsory in 537: regnal year, consul, indiction, month and day (Novel 47). Constantinople kept the indiction to the end, beside an era of the world from 5509 BC. Our own era is a late arrival: Dionysius Exiguus devised Anno Domini for Easter tables in 525, and Bede's Ecclesiastical History (731) made it the historian's era in the West.

The big chronological problems

The foundation date

The archaeology recognises no foundation event. Graves in the Forum valley go back to about 1000 BC, the Palatine had huts in the eighth century, and the first Forum paving, implying one community managing the valley, belongs to the later seventh. Andrea Carandini dated a wall at the foot of the Palatine to the eighth century and read it as Romulus' circuit (La nascita di Roma, 1997); most archaeologists accept the wall but not the reading. The story is module 1.4; for chronology, 753 is a calculated date attached to a process.

Seven kings for 244 years

The traditional reigns, Romulus (753–716) to Tarquinius Superbus (534–509), average thirty-five years, in a line where one king vanished in a storm, one was struck by lightning, two were murdered and one was expelled. Long dynasties seldom average much above twenty. Dionysius saw part of the difficulty: he refused to make Superbus the son of Tarquinius Priscus, as Fabius had, because the dates would not allow it (Roman Antiquities 4.6–7). Most likely the span was fixed first, by setting a computed foundation against a Republic dated from the consular list, and the remembered kings were stretched to fill it (module 1.5). Livy and Dionysius wrote some five centuries after the last king.

The dictator years and the Varronian chronology

Count the consular pairs between the first consuls and about 300 BC and there are fewer than Varro's dates require. The Augustan Fasti fill the gap with four "dictator years", 333, 324, 309 and 301, in which a dictator and his master of horse appear with no consuls. Livy knows nothing of them, and modern scholars almost all regard them as insertions. A second elastic stretch is the "anarchy" of the 370s, when tribunes blocked curule elections: five years in Livy (6.35.10), one in Diodorus. The result is the Varronian chronology in which modern books give every date before about 300 BC: consistent, and probably about four years too early in the fourth century. "509" and "390" are positions in a system, not Julian years.

390 or 387: the Gallic sack

This is the one early Roman event Greeks recorded near the time: Aristotle had heard that Rome was taken by Celts and saved by a certain Lucius (Plutarch, Camillus 22.4). Polybius dates it by the King's Peace and the siege of Rhegium, 387/6 (1.6.1–2); Dionysius of Halicarnassus puts it in Pyrgion's archonship, 388/7 (1.74.4). Varro's 390 is higher because of the dictator years. The day is secure: 18 July, the unlucky dies Alliensis. Books use 390 in Roman narrative and 387/6 when synchronising with Greece.

The first consuls and the Capitoline temple

Three indications point to the end of the sixth century. Polybius dates the first treaty with Carthage to the consuls who dedicated the Capitoline temple, twenty-eight years before Xerxes crossed to Greece: 508/7 (3.22.1–2). Pliny records that Cn. Flavius as aedile in 304 BC dedicated a shrine of Concord 204 years after the Capitoline dedication (Natural History 33.19). Livy cites a law that the chief magistrate drive a nail into the temple wall each Ides of September, a count of years (7.3.5–7). The details conflict: Livy dedicates the temple in the Republic's first year (2.8.6–8), Tacitus in Horatius' second consulship (Histories 3.72), and Livy's first year has five consuls, as if several traditions had been stacked. Gjerstad's lowering of the end of the monarchy to about 450, and the suspicious closeness of 509 to Athens' 510, are weighed in module 1.6.

When did the Republic end?

Sallust (Catiline 10) and Velleius (2.1) put the moral turn at 146, when fear of Carthage was removed; Appian and Plutarch start the violence in 133. Augustus claimed no ending: in the Res Gestae he wrote that in 28–27 BC he had "transferred the res publica" to the Senate and people (34). Cassius Dio says monarchy strictly began in 27 (53.17); Tacitus asks how many were left in AD 14 "who had seen the Republic" (Annals 1.3). Modern candidates add 88, 60, 49, 43 and 23 BC. The convention of 31 or 27 marks the end of rival dynasts, not a day Romans thought the Republic gone.

Where sources disagree. Ronald Syme (The Roman Revolution, 1939) saw an oligarchy destroyed by revolution between 60 BC and AD 14. Erich Gruen (The Last Generation of the Roman Republic, 1974) argued that the institutions worked until 49 and that civil war caused the fall rather than resulting from it. Flower ends the traditional republic in 88. Module 11.8 takes it further.

Why 476 is a convention and 1453 is not

In 476 Odoacer, commanding the barbarian troops in Italy, killed the patrician Orestes and deposed his son, the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus, pensioning him off to Campania. He named no successor and sent the regalia to Zeno at Constantinople, with a senatorial message that one emperor sufficed (Malchus); Zeno replied that the West still had a lawful emperor, Julius Nepos, alive in Dalmatia until 480. Odoacer ruled as king, the Senate met, western consuls were named until 534, and Theoderic's Ostrogoths governed Italy on Roman lines from 493. Western contemporaries barely registered 476.

It became an ending fifty years later, in the East. Marcellinus Comes, writing at Constantinople, entered under 476 that "the western empire of the Roman people" perished with Augustulus (Chronicle, s.a. 476). Brian Croke ("A.D. 476: the manufacture of a turning point", Chiron, 1983) argued that the idea took shape in early sixth-century Constantinople and suited Justinian's claim to Italy as a lost province. It labels a transition running from the Vandal capture of Carthage (439) to the Lombard invasion (568).

Where sources disagree. Whether anything "fell" is the live question. Peter Brown (The World of Late Antiquity, 1971) and Walter Goffart (Barbarians and Romans, 1980) stressed transformation and accommodation; Peter Heather (The Fall of the Roman Empire, 2005) and Bryan Ward-Perkins (The Fall of Rome, 2005) restored violence and material collapse. Module 8.5 weighs them.

1453 is a different kind of end. On 29 May Mehmed II took Constantinople by assault and Constantine XI Palaiologos died at the walls: a capital, a siege, a last emperor and a date recognised everywhere at once. That state claimed an unbroken line from Augustus, interrupted only by the Latin occupation of 1204–1261; its people called themselves Rhomaioi, Romans, and "Byzantine" is a label popularised by Hieronymus Wolf in 1557. Fragments survived briefly (the Morea to 1460, Trebizond to 1461; module 8.6). The year 476 marks a western office that lapsed; 1453 marks the conquest of the Roman state itself.

Self-test

  1. Why does the Varronian date for the Gallic sack (390) differ from Polybius' (387/6)?
    Answer

    Polybius fixed it by Greek synchronisms, the King's Peace and the siege of Rhegium (1.6.1–2). The Varronian system, as on the Augustan Fasti, includes four inserted dictator years (333, 324, 309, 301), which push every earlier date back by about four years.

  2. What does Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities 1.74, show about the foundation date?
    Answer

    That it was computed, not remembered: Timaeus 814/13, Fabius Pictor 748/7, Cincius 729/8, Cato 432 years after Troy, Polybius 751/0, each converting Roman lists into Olympiads by a different reckoning.

  3. Why is the regal period of 244 years suspect, and what is the likeliest explanation?
    Answer

    Seven reigns averaging thirty-five years is implausible for a line with three or four violent ends. The span was probably fixed first, by setting a computed foundation date against a Republic dated from the consular list, and the remembered kings were stretched to fill it (module 1.5).

  4. Give two independent ancient indications that the Capitoline temple was dedicated around 509–507 BC.
    Answer

    Any two of: Polybius 3.22.1–2, dating the first Carthage treaty to the consuls who dedicated the temple, 28 years before Xerxes; Pliny, Natural History 33.19, Flavius' shrine of 304 BC built 204 years after the dedication; the annual nail in the temple wall (Livy 7.3.5–7).

  5. What two traps make it hard to convert a Republican consular year into a modern date?
    Answer

    The consular year began on different days until 1 January became fixed in 153 BC, so each straddles two of ours; and the pre-Julian calendar drifted, by about three months before Caesar's reform of 46 BC.

  6. Why does the line between the early and middle Republic usually fall at 264 BC?
    Answer

    It is Rome's first war outside Italy and Polybius' chosen starting point, where Timaeus had stopped (1.5.1); it is also where the evidence improves, since Fabius Pictor wrote within living memory of it.

  7. What was the indiction, and why does an indiction date alone not fix a year?
    Answer

    A fifteen-year fiscal cycle, counted under Constantine from 1 September 312. Documents give only the year within the cycle, never which cycle, so the same number recurs every fifteen years; Justinian's Novel 47 (537) required it alongside regnal year and consul.

  8. Who first treated 476 as the end of the western empire, and why is that suspicious?
    Answer

    Marcellinus Comes at Constantinople, some fifty years later (Chronicle, s.a. 476). Croke (1983) argued the idea suited Justinian's case for reconquering Italy; western contemporaries barely noticed, and Julius Nepos was still the lawful emperor until 480.

  9. Give three different ancient answers to when the Republic declined or ended.
    Answer

    Sallust (Catiline 10) and Velleius (2.1): 146 BC, with the fall of Carthage. Plutarch and Appian: 133, the death of Tiberius Gracchus. Cassius Dio (53.17): monarchy from 27; Augustus himself claimed to have transferred the res publica to the Senate and people (Res Gestae 34).

  10. In what sense is 1453 a different kind of end from 476?
    Answer

    In 1453 a capital fell by assault, a last emperor died and a continuous Roman state ended, recognised at once by contemporaries. In 476 no state ended: a western office lapsed and the date became an ending only in retrospect.

Carry forward

  1. Every Roman date before about 300 BC is a Varronian label, produced by counting a list back to a computed foundation; treat 753, 509 and 390 as positions in a system, and always ask who computed them and how many centuries after the event.
  2. The Romans dated by names, not numbers: consuls, then emperors' years and indictions. Counting "from the founding" was a historian's tool, so Roman chronology, like Greek, is built by reconciling lists.
  3. Period boundaries mark changes of regime or of evidence and are mostly modern; 476 is a retrospective convention and 1453 an event, and the Roman state outlived Rome's western empire by nearly a thousand years.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report that builds a memorisable timeline of Roman history from the Italian Early Iron Age, c. 1000 BC, to the deposition of the last western emperor in AD 476, with a closing note on the eastern empire to 1453. Cover: the standard period names and their date ranges (Iron Age Italy, the regal period, the early, middle and late Republic, the Principate, the third-century crisis, the late empire or Dominate) and why the boundaries fall where they do; the 15 to 20 anchor dates every educated person should know, each with one sentence on why it matters; how the Romans themselves dated things (consular years and the Fasti, years from the foundation of the city and the competing foundation dates of Timaeus, Ennius, Fabius Pictor, Cincius, Cato, Polybius and Varro, emperors' regnal years, the indiction); the big chronological problems (the foundation date, seven kings for 244 years, the 'dictator years' and the Varronian chronology, 390 or 387 BC for the Gallic sack, the date of the first consuls and the Capitoline temple, when the Republic 'ended'); and why AD 476 is a convention and 1453 a different kind of end. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, a clean dated list I can copy out by hand, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 1 · Italy before Rome and the founding legends · 1.1 · 2,739 words

The peoples of Iron Age Italy

Before the Iron Age: Terramare and Proto-VillanovanThe Villanovan cultureLatial culture: Rome, the Alban Hills and Osteria dell'OsaThe Latins: shared cults and the LeagueSabellic Italy and the other peoplesLanguages and alphabetsGreeks and Phoenicians, seen from ItalyThe Sabines: a first exercise in methodSelf-testCarry forward

Before the Iron Age: Terramare and Proto-Villanovan

Rome's neighbours were not newcomers in 1000 BC. In Emilia and southern Lombardy the Terramare (from terra marna, the black earth later farmers dug from the mounds as fertiliser) were villages of the Middle and Recent Bronze Age, c. 1650–1150 BC: banked, moated, laid out on regular plans, with houses on piles and cremation cemeteries outside. Around 1150 the system collapsed and the central plain emptied; Andrea Cardarelli blames over-exploitation and climate, not invasion. The Final Bronze Age, c. 1200–950, is called Proto-Villanovan because it anticipates the Iron Age rite. From the Po delta to Sicily cremation cemeteries appear with striking uniformity: ashes in a biconical urn capped by a bowl, set in a small pit, with few goods. Frattesina in the Polesine (a workshop centre for glass and amber), Pianello di Genga in the Marche, Allumiere in the Tolfa hills and Timmari near Matera are the reference sites.

Where sources disagree. Wolfgang Helbig (Die Italiker in der Poebene, 1879) and Luigi Pigorini made the Terramare folk the ancestral Italic people, who moved south and became the Latins, and read the urnfields as immigrants from central Europe. Renato Peroni and Anna Maria Bietti Sestieri replaced migration with local development: the rite spread through elite networks over a continuous pattern of settlement. Small-group movement remains possible.

The Villanovan culture

The name comes from Villanova near Bologna, where Count Giovanni Gozzadini excavated a cemetery in 1853. "Villanovan" labels the Early Iron Age, c. 900–720 BC, of the lands that became Etruscan: Etruria, Bologna and Verucchio, Fermo in the Marche, and Campania (Capua, Pontecagnano). It is the Etruscans before writing; their origins are module 1.2. The signature is the biconical urn, a hand-made vessel of two cones with one handle, incised with meanders and swastikas, capped by a bowl or, for some men, a crested helmet, and set in a pit. Some ashes went instead into a hut urn, a clay model of an oval hut with door and smoke-hole that matches the post-holes of real huts; hut urns are commoner still in Latium.

Two changes run through the ninth and eighth centuries. In southern Etruria inhumation in trench graves gained ground from the later ninth century and dominated by the late eighth, while cremation persisted at Bologna and Clusium. And the small villages were abandoned for a few huge plateaus, Veii (about 190 hectares), Tarquinia, Caere and Vulci, each the footprint of a future city. The graves show a warrior elite forming: at Quattro Fontanili at Veii the early burials are nearly uniform, but by the mid eighth century a minority of men lie with sword, shield, crested helmet and horse-bits, and women with heavy fibulae and weaving gear, beside Euboean cups. The Warrior Tomb at Tarquinia (late eighth century) is the type.

Where sources disagree. Velleius Paterculus (1.7.2–4), writing under Tiberius, reports Cato's date for the Etruscan foundation of Capua, 260 years before its capture in 211, and prefers a date near 800 BC. Capua's ninth-century Villanovan graves support Velleius; whether their people were Etruscan settlers or Campanians sharing Etruscan culture is still argued.

Latial culture: Rome, the Alban Hills and Osteria dell'Osa

South of the Tiber the Latial culture, defined by Giovanni Colonna and refined by Bietti Sestieri, began with the miniature: the cremated dead went into a hut urn or jar with tiny vessels and, for men, tiny weapons and offering-figurines, all packed into a storage jar (dolium) in a shaft. The miniatures mark ritual roles, not wealth.

PhaseConventional dates BCMarkers
Ic. 1000–900Miniature cremations, hut urns
IIAc. 900–830Inhumation normal; cremation for a few men
IIBc. 830–770First Greek imports; the Osa graffito
IIIc. 770–730/720Sharper ranking; only infants buried in the Forum
IVAc. 730/720–640/630Princely tombs: Praeneste, Castel di Decima
IVBc. 640/630–580Chamber tombs; grave goods dwindle

In Rome, Giacomo Boni found the Forum cemetery beside the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina from 1902: some forty graves, Latial I cremations in dolia, then inhumations. In 2006 a cremation of about 1000 BC turned up under the Forum of Caesar. When adults ceased to be buried in the valley, the valley had joined the settlement. The main cemetery moved to the Esquiline, dug hastily in the 1870s and 1880s and catalogued by Giovanni Pinza (1905), with graves from the ninth century into the orientalising period. The Palatine huts are module 1.4. In the Alban Hills, heartland of Latial I, hut urns found near Marino in 1817 beneath a layer of peperino were published by Alessandro Visconti as coming from "near ancient Alba Longa"; the cemeteries of Castel Gandolfo, Marino and Grottaferrata show small communities clustered round the lake, but no city of Alba.

Osteria dell'Osa, beside Gabii, is the best-excavated Latin community: some 600 graves of the ninth to seventh centuries, dug by Bietti Sestieri in the 1970s and 1980s (The Iron Age Community of Osteria dell'Osa, 1992). In phase IIA two clusters, which she reads as descent groups, each have a few cremated adult men with hut urns and miniature weapons at the core, ringed by inhumed men, women and children: cremation marks the heads of lineages, not a separate people. In a woman's grave of about 775 BC lay a local flask scratched with five letters, read as Greek eulin: the first writing in Latium.

Where sources disagree. The dates above rest on Greek pottery cross-dated to the Aegean. Radiocarbon and dendrochronology, pressed by Albert Nijboer and Johannes van der Plicht, raise the early phases by fifty to a hundred years; Bietti Sestieri and most Italian scholars keep the lower dates. The oldest Forum graves thus precede Varro's 753 by two and a half centuries, or by up to three and a half.

The Latins: shared cults and the League

The Latins saw themselves as one people, the nomen Latinum, with mutual rights of trade and marriage (commercium, conubium) and cults no single city owned.

  • The Latin festival on the Alban Mount, for Jupiter Latiaris: each member people received a share of a white bull. Dionysius (4.49), writing five centuries later, credits Tarquinius Superbus with founding it for forty-seven peoples; the Alban setting points to an older cult. Pliny (Natural History 3.69) lists some thirty populi Albenses who once took meat there, most vanished by his day.
  • Diana at Aricia, by Lake Nemi. A fragment of Cato's Origines, written some three and a half centuries after the event, records that Egerius Baebius of Tusculum, "Latin dictator", dedicated the grove for eight peoples: Tusculum, Aricia, Lanuvium, Laurentum, Cora, Tibur, Pometia and Ardea. Rome is absent.
  • Lavinium, seat of "our Penates" (Varro, On the Latin Language 5.144). Ferdinando Castagnoli's excavations from the late 1950s found thirteen altars, built and rebuilt from the mid sixth century into the fourth, and a bronze plaque of about 500 to Castorei Podlouqueique qurois, "Castor and Pollux, the kouroi" (Weinstock, 1960): a Greek cult reaching Latium directly. Aeneas' shrine there is module 1.3.

The Latin League was the political shadow of these cults. The Latins met at the grove of Ferentina; the antiquarian Cincius, quoted by Festus, says they shared command there "from the destruction of Alba" until 340 BC. Cato's "Latin dictator" shows a federal office. Romans dated the formal alliance to Spurius Cassius' treaty of 493 (Dionysius 6.95), whose bronze column Cicero remembered behind the Rostra (Pro Balbo 53); everything earlier is reconstructed backwards.

Where sources disagree. Andreas Alföldi (Early Rome and the Latins, 1965) argued that the annalists inflated Rome: leadership passed from Alba to Lavinium and Aricia, and Rome was a minor member until after 500, as Cato's list implies. Tim Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) answers with the first Carthage treaty, dated by Polybius (3.22) to 508/7, in which Rome speaks for Ardea, Antium and Laurentum; Cato's dedication then marks a league formed against Rome after the Tarquins fell.

Sabellic Italy and the other peoples

East and south of the Latins lived speakers of Sabellic (Osco-Umbrian) languages. Ancient writers derived them from the Sabines through the ver sacrum: a community vowed all born in one spring and sent the grown children out behind an animal, a bull for the Samnites, a woodpecker (picus) for the Picentes, a wolf (hirpus) for the Hirpini (Strabo 5.4.2, 5.4.12). These are aetiologies of names, but the link is real: the Samnites called their land Safinim. The Samnites are archaeologically thin before 500; their expansion is fifth-century, when Oscan speakers took Capua (423) and Cumae (421; Livy 4.37, 4.44).

The Umbrians of the upper Tiber left the Iguvine Tables, seven bronzes found at Gubbio in 1444 and engraved in the third to first centuries BC, in Umbrian and Latin letters: the rites of a priestly college, the Atiedian Brethren. Tablets VIa–VIb purify the citadel. Auspices are taken from named birds within a marked space, as in the Roman templum; sacrifices are made at three gates to Jupiter, Mars and Vofionus, all "Grabovius", and to a second triad including Fisus Sancius, cousin of Rome's Semo Sancus; then the people are purified and the neighbouring Etruscans and Naharci cursed. The prayers pile up paired synonyms exactly as Cato's farmer does (On Agriculture 141). The text is Hellenistic, so how much Iron Age ritual it preserves is unknown; Dumézil's reading of its triad is weighed in module 2.1.

  • Veneti, at Este and Padua: figured bronze buckets (situlae), and alphabet tablets dedicated to the goddess Reitia. Livy, a Paduan, makes the Trojan Antenor their founder (1.1).
  • Ligurians, in the north-west, known from place-names and statue-stelae; Cato called them "illiterate and liars" (quoted by Servius on Aeneid 11).
  • Messapians, in the Salento heel, Cretans by Herodotus' account (7.170), which records their slaughter of the Tarentines c. 473.
  • Picenes, on the middle Adriatic, with weapon-heavy graves at Novilara and Numana and the sixth-century Warrior of Capestrano, inscribed in South Picene.

Within Italic the split is sharp: Latin keeps qu where Sabellic has p (Latin quis, Oscan pis). Giacomo Devoto thought the two groups arrived separately and converged; Helmut Rix and most Indo-Europeanists posit one Proto-Italic parent. The alphabet's route maps the contacts. Euboean Greeks brought a western alphabet; the Etruscans had it by about 700 (the model alphabet on the Marsiliana ivory tablet) and passed it to Umbrians, Oscans, Picenes, Veneti and Lepontii, while the Messapians took theirs from Taras. Latin wrote C for /k/ and /g/ alike, as Etruscan did, implying an Etruscan teacher, yet kept B, D and O, which Etruscans never used, implying Greek contact too. Writing arrived as an elite skill, naming owners and givers on gifts.

Where sources disagree. Livy (1.7.8) honours Evander for teaching letters; Tacitus (Annals 11.14) has the Etruscans taught by Demaratus of Corinth and the Aborigines by Evander. The supposed earliest Latin text, the Praeneste fibula reading Manios med fhefhaked Numasioi, "Manius made me for Numerius", was denounced as a forgery by Margherita Guarducci (1980); analysis by Daniela Ferro and Edilberto Formigli (2011) supports authenticity, though doubts persist.

Greeks and Phoenicians, seen from Italy

For Greek colonisation itself, see Greek module 5.2. From Italy the Greeks appeared first as traders: Euboean cups reached Veii early in the eighth century, and Eugenio La Rocca published eighth-century Greek pottery from Sant'Omobono at Rome's river harbour. Pithekoussai on Ischia (c. 770; Strabo 5.4.9) was placed for Etruscan metal and worked Elban iron. Giorgio Buchner's excavation of its cemetery from 1952 (published with David Ridgway, 1993) showed a mixed population: Greeks, Levantines who scratched Semitic letters on amphorae, and Italian women who had married in. Grave 168 held the Nestor cup, a Rhodian cup of the later eighth century inscribed in the Euboean alphabet: "Nestor's cup, good to drink from", then two hexameters promising the drinker desire for "fair-crowned Aphrodite". It is a symposium joke on Iliad 11.632–637.

Where sources disagree. Whether the joke presupposes our Iliad is Greek module 10.8. Buchner took the bones for a boy of about twelve; Gigante and colleagues (PLoS One, 2021) found at least three people, apparently none a child.

Cumae (c. 750), planted on a native site, was the nearest Greek city for Etruscans and Latins: the source of their alphabet, the reclining banquet, Apollo and the Sibyl, and Tarquinius Superbus' last refuge (module 1.6). The cities of Magna Graecia and Sicily, from Naxos (734) and Syracuse (733; Thucydides 6.3), took Italian land; yet at L'Amastuola near Taras, Gert-Jan Burgers and Jan Paul Crielaard found Greek and native houses side by side c. 700–650. Latin loanwords show the channels: oliva from archaic elaiwa, machina from Doric machana.

The Phoenicians were in the west as early. Timaeus, writing around 300 BC (in Dionysius 1.74.1), put Carthage in 814/813, Rome's year too, and radiocarbon from the earliest levels comes close. The Nora stone names Sardinia in the ninth or eighth century; Sulcis, Tharros and Motya followed, and Thucydides (6.2.6) says Phoenicians once ringed Sicily. Nuragic bronzes in ninth-century graves at Vulci show a Tyrrhenian network before any colony. In the seventh century Phoenician silver bowls filled the princely tombs of Caere and Praeneste, and the orientalising style came through Phoenician and Greek hands alike. Ancient writers put Gadir near 1100 BC; tenth- and ninth-century Phoenician pottery at Huelva (González de Canales, 2004) has narrowed a gap once dismissed as legend.

The Sabines: a first exercise in method

In legend (module 1.4) the Sabines are Rome's co-founders: the seized women, Titus Tatius of Cures as joint king, Numa from Cures, and the citizens called Quirites after Cures (Livy 1.13.5). The story is first attested in Fabius Pictor (Plutarch, Romulus 14.1), more than five centuries after the supposed events, and told in full by Livy and Dionysius, seven centuries after.

Archaeology finds a Sabine country but no distinct Sabine people. The lower Sabina by the Tiber (Cures, Eretum, Poggio Sommavilla) shares its pottery and luxuries with Faliscans and Latins; the inland basins of Reate and Amiternum look to the Abruzzo. Nothing in Rome marks a Sabine quarter. An older reading took the Forum's cremations for Latins and the Esquiline inhumations for Sabines; Osteria dell'Osa disposes of it, since there both rites coexist within one kin group. What the ground does show is traffic along the Tiber corridor.

Language cuts both ways. Sabine is almost lost; a flask from Poggio Sommavilla (c. 600) carries a short text whose language is disputed. Ancient "Sabine" words come mostly through Varro, a man of Reate, who says the altars Tatius vowed "smell of the Sabine tongue" (On the Latin Language 5.74), then lists Saturn, Diana, Vulcan and Sol among them. Genuine Sabellic loans in Latin exist, bos, lupus, rufus, but could have entered at any date: they prove contact, not a joint foundation.

The story must be explained as well as weighed. It accounts for things Romans saw: the name Quirites, the tribe of Titienses named from Tatius (Livy 1.13.8), Sabine-seeming cults on the Quirinal, and real Sabine families such as the Claudii, said to have arrived with Attus Clausus in 504 (Livy 2.16.4–5). It served moralists: Livy's Numa learned "the grim and austere discipline of the ancient Sabines" (1.18.4). And Rome conquered the Sabines in 290, less than a century before Fabius Pictor wrote. The method: keep ground, language and story apart, and date each witness.

Where sources disagree. Jacques Poucet (Recherches sur la légende sabine des origines de Rome, 1967) argued that the Sabine element in early Rome was largely built in the fourth and third centuries, after Rome absorbed the Sabines. Dumézil read the Sabine war as myth joining the third function, wealth, to the first two. Cornell keeps a middle line: the synoecism is myth, but Sabine clans in early Rome, like the Claudii, are plausible in a world of horizontal mobility.

Self-test

  1. Why is the uniformity of Proto-Villanovan cremation no longer taken as proof of an invasion?
    Answer

    Helbig and Pigorini read it as migrants from the Terramare or central Europe; Peroni and Bietti Sestieri showed continuity of settlement and explained the rite as spreading through elite networks. A shared burial custom need not mean a new people.

  2. What evidence in Villanovan cemeteries shows a warrior elite forming in the eighth century?
    Answer

    Early graves at Quattro Fontanili (Veii) are nearly uniform; by the mid eighth century a minority of men have swords, shields, crested helmets and horse-bits, women rich fibulae and weaving gear, with Greek imports, as in the Warrior Tomb at Tarquinia.

  3. At Osteria dell'Osa, who was cremated in phase IIA, and what does that imply about rite and identity?
    Answer

    A few adult men, with hut urns and miniature weapons, at the core of each cluster of inhumations. The rite marked rank within a kin group, so a difference of burial rite is not a difference of people.

  4. Why does the end of adult burial in the Forum valley matter for the history of Rome?
    Answer

    Once adults were buried on the Esquiline and only infants in the valley, the valley had become part of the settlement: the hill villages were becoming one community.

  5. What does Pliny's list of populi Albenses tell us about early Latium?
    Answer

    About thirty peoples once shared the sacrificial meat on the Alban Mount (Natural History 3.69), most vanished by Pliny's day: Latium was once a mosaic of small communities bound by a cult older than Rome's leadership.

  6. Why is Rome's absence from Cato's record of the dedication at Aricia significant, and how do Alföldi and Cornell read it?
    Answer

    It shows a federal Latin act without Rome. Alföldi takes it as proof that Rome was a minor member before 500; Cornell, citing the Carthage treaty in Polybius 3.22, reads it as a league formed against a strong Rome after the Tarquins fell.

  7. What does the Castor and Pollux plaque at Lavinium show?
    Answer

    A Greek cult, with the Greek title kouroi written qurois, was established at a Latin sanctuary by about 500 BC, so Greek religion reached Latium directly and not only through Rome.

  8. What do the Iguvine Tables reveal about Umbrian religion, and what caution applies?
    Answer

    Auspices in a marked space, sacrifices to triads at the citadel gates, purification of the people and cursing of neighbours, with prayers like Cato's (On Agriculture 141). But the tablets date from the third to first centuries BC, so their Iron Age antiquity is assumed, not shown.

  9. What does Latin's use of C, and its keeping of B, D and O, suggest about where Latins learned to write?
    Answer

    C for both /k/ and /g/ follows Etruscan practice and implies Etruscan mediation; B, D and O, unused by Etruscans, imply direct contact with Greeks, most likely at Cumae. Probably both channels operated.

  10. On the Sabines, what can archaeology and language establish, and what can they not?
    Answer

    They show a Sabellic-speaking hill population in close exchange with Latins, Sabellic loanwords in Latin, and traffic along the Tiber. They cannot confirm a Sabine half of Rome or a joint foundation; the old cremation-Latin, inhumation-Sabine reading fails.

Carry forward

  1. Rome was one Latin community among many, sharing language, burial rites and federal cults (the Alban Mount, Aricia, Lavinium) older than its own leadership; every claim of early Roman primacy should be read against that crowded Latium.
  2. Iron Age Italy was multilingual and connected before it was colonised: Phoenicians, Euboeans, Sardinians and Etruscans traded through the Tyrrhenian, writing arrived as an elite import via Cumae and Etruria, and Rome's culture was hybrid from the start.
  3. Keep the ground, the language and the story apart, and date each witness: archaeology shows rank and period more readily than ethnicity, and ethnic labels in legend (Sabine, Trojan, Etruscan) usually explain later institutions and family claims.
