188At Apamea Ilium receives Rhoeteum and Gergis "in memory of origins"Livy 38.39.10
Where sources disagree. Maurice Holleaux (1921) rejected the Acarnanian appeal and the Seleucus letter as later fictions, and a letter produced under the antiquarian emperor Claudius invites suspicion. Gruen and Erskine accept that kinship was argued by the late third century, usually by Greek cities rather than by Rome.

The Julii, an Alban family (Tacitus, Annals 11.24), claimed descent from Iulus. Livy keeps his distance:

Iulum eundem Iulia gens auctorem nominis sui nuncupat (Livy 1.3.2)

Their clan altar at Bovillae honoured Vediovis "by Alban law". In 69 Caesar told the mourners of his aunt Julia that the Julii descended from Venus (Suetonius, Julius 6.1), and his denarius of 47–46 shows Aeneas carrying Anchises and the Palladium. Varro's lost De familiis Troianis catalogued the other Trojan clans. Greek module 10.12 follows the story through Venus Genetrix and the lusus Troiae, Greek module 7.3 narrates the conquest of the East in which the kinship was invoked, and the Aeneid itself belongs to deep dive unit 12.

Self-test

  1. What did Hellanicus, as Dionysius 1.72 reports him, say about Rome's foundation, and why is the phrase "with Odysseus" a problem?
    Answer

    Aeneas came from the Molossians into Italy with Odysseus and named the city after Rhome, a Trojan woman who led the burning of the ships. Making two enemies co-founders is odd, so some editors emend to "after"; Solmsen defended the text, and others doubt the ascription because Hellanicus' Troika left Aeneas at Pallene.

  2. How does Aristotle's version differ from Hellanicus', and what motif do they share?
    Answer

    Aristotle's settlers are Achaeans blown to "Latinion", not Trojans, so the city would be Greek (Dionysius 1.72.3–4). Both use Trojan women burning the ships to explain why wanderers stayed.

  3. Name three things Timaeus contributed to the Greek picture of early Rome.
    Answer

    A foundation date of 814/3, synchronised with Carthage (Dionysius 1.74.1); the October Horse as a memorial of the Wooden Horse (Polybius 12.4b–c); and the report of heralds' staffs and Trojan pottery among the holy objects of Lavinium (Dionysius 1.67.4).

  4. Give three different fathers ancient sources assign to Latinus, and say what the variety shows.
    Answer

    Odysseus (Hesiod, Theogony 1011–1016), Hercules (Dionysius 1.43) and Faunus (Virgil); Hyginus adds Telemachus. Latinus was an eponym of the Latins, attached to whichever founding story a writer favoured.

  5. What marked the cult of the Ara Maxima as foreign, and what happened to it in 312?
    Answer

    A Greek rite with the head bare, exclusion of women, a tithe, and service by two families, the Potitii and Pinarii; Livy calls it the only foreign rite Romulus adopted (1.7.3, 1.7.15). In 312 Appius Claudius transferred it to public slaves and the Potitii died out (Livy 9.29.9–11).

  6. Which Homeric passage made Aeneas usable as a founder, and how was it bent for Rome?
    Answer

    Iliad 20.307–308: Aeneas and his sons' sons will rule the Trojans. Strabo (13.1.53) reports a reading in which he rules "over all", adjusted to fit Roman power, while he himself kept Aeneas' heirs in the Troad.

  7. What did Sommella find at Lavinium, and why is its identification as Aeneas' heroon uncertain?
    Answer

    A seventh-century tumulus remodelled as a shrine in the fourth century, matching Dionysius' heroon by the Numicus (1.64.4–5). Nothing names Aeneas; the inscription Dionysius quotes names a "father and god", and the remodelling may reflect Rome's settlement of 338 rather than an older cult.

  8. Why did the Alban king list become necessary, and how do Livy and Dionysius differ over its first link?
    Answer

    Naevius and Ennius made Romulus Aeneas' grandson, but once Troy's fall was set at 1184/3 and Rome's foundation in the eighth century, some 430 years had to be filled. Livy makes Silvius Ascanius' son; Dionysius makes him Aeneas' son by Lavinia, preferred over Iulus, ancestor of the Julii (1.70.3–4).

  9. Give two reasons Rome preferred a Trojan ancestor to a Greek one, and one risk.
    Answer

    Troy gave Rome Homeric antiquity without colonial dependence on a Greek mother city, and it tied Rome to the Latin cult at Lavinium and to western peoples such as the Elymians. The risk was descent from the losers, and Greek versions in which Aeneas betrayed Troy (Dionysius 1.48.3).

  10. How did Pyrrhus and Flamininus use the same legend from opposite sides?
    Answer

    Pyrrhus, descended from Achilles, cast his war as a new sack of Troy against a Trojan colony (Pausanias 1.12.1). Flamininus called himself "great leader of the Aeneadae" at Delphi while proclaiming Greek freedom, so Trojan descent became a Roman credential in Greece (Plutarch, Flamininus 12).

Carry forward

  1. Rome's prehistory was a Greek product before it was a Roman one. For any "Roman" legend, ask which Greek first wrote it, how many centuries after the event, and what Roman writers from Fabius to Varro chose to keep.
  2. Rome took Greeks as precursors (Evander, Hercules) and Trojans as ancestors: kinship with the Homeric world without subordination to it, which is why the claim worked in diplomacy with Greek cities as well as against Greek kings.
  3. Chronology drives myth. Once the foundation was fixed in the eighth century, invented Alban kings filled the gap, and the Julii's Iulus shows genealogy staying open to political adjustment into the Augustan age.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the legends of Rome before Romulus and on how the Trojan claim was built. Cover: the Greek writers who first gave Rome a past (Hellanicus as Dionysius 1.72 reports him, Damastes, the Aristotelian story of the Achaeans and the burnt ships, Heraclides Ponticus calling Rome a Greek city, Callias, Timaeus and the Trojan relics at Lavinium) and the rival Greek founders (Rhomos, the sons of Odysseus and Circe, Latinus in Hesiod's Theogony 1011–1016); Saturn and the Golden Age in Latium, Janus, Picus and Faunus; Evander's Arcadians on the Palatine, Hercules and Cacus, and the Ara Maxima; Aeneas in Greek tradition (Iliad 20.307–308, the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite), the Etruscan vases and statuettes of Aeneas carrying Anchises, and the heroon at Lavinium identified as his tomb; the Roman version as it settled in Fabius Pictor, Naevius, Ennius, Cato and Varro (the landing, Latinus and Lavinia, Turnus and Mezentius, Lavinium, Ascanius and Alba Longa, and the invented Alban king list that fills the four centuries between the fall of Troy and 753); why Rome chose a Trojan ancestor rather than a Greek one; and how the claim was used in diplomacy (Segesta, Ilium, the Acarnanians, Flamininus at Delphi, Pyrrhus as a new Achilles) and by the Julii through Iulus. Point back to Greek modules 7.3 and 10.12 for the Roman Troy in reception, and leave the Aeneid itself to deep dive unit 12. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 1 · Italy before Rome and the founding legends · 1.4 · 3,321 words

Romulus and Remus

Sources: a founder written down five centuries lateAlba, the Vestal and the wolfRecognition, augury and the death of RemusThe asylum, the Sabine women and Titus TatiusThe vanishing king and QuirinusVariants: other founders, other parents, a wolf who was a womanThe earliest evidenceWhat the story is doingWhat the ground showsSelf-testCarry forward

Sources: a founder written down five centuries late

Varro's date for the foundation, 21 April 753 BC, became canonical; the rival dates belong to module 0.3. No Roman wrote the story down until about 200 BC, five and a half centuries later. Quintus Fabius Pictor, a senator writing Greek prose around the Second Punic War, gave the first Roman narrative. Plutarch says he followed the Greek Diocles of Peparethus in most points (Romulus 3.1); Dionysius says Cincius Alimentus, Cato and Calpurnius Piso followed Fabius (Roman Antiquities 1.79.4). Ennius' Annales, of the 180s and 170s BC, put the story into Latin verse. The full narratives are Augustan or later: Livy 1.3.10–16.8, written about 27–25 BC, seven centuries after the date he accepts; Dionysius, Roman Antiquities 1.76–90 and 2.1–56, published from 7 BC; and Plutarch's Romulus, about AD 100, paired with Theseus (Greek module 3.3). Ovid's Fasti ties episodes to festivals. All of them knew the versions conflicted.

Alba, the Vestal and the wolf

Proca, king of Alba Longa, left the throne to his elder son Numitor. Amulius, the younger, drove him out, killed his male offspring and made his daughter Rhea Silvia a Vestal, ending her hope of children "under the appearance of honour" (Livy 1.3.10–11). Raped, she bore twins and named Mars as their father, "whether she believed it, or because a god was a more honourable author of the fault" (1.4.2). Dionysius (1.77.1) reports that others blamed a suitor, or Amulius himself in armour. She was chained in custody (Livy 1.4.3); in Fabius' version Amulius' own daughter Antho begged for her life (Plutarch 3).

The twins were ordered drowned, but the Tiber was in flood and the servants left the basket in the shallows by the fig tree later called Ruminalis, at the foot of the Palatine. A she-wolf coming down to drink heard the crying, suckled them and licked them (Livy 1.4.4–6). Plutarch adds the woodpecker, sacred to Mars, which brought them food, and derives the fig's name from ruma, the teat (4). The royal herdsman Faustulus took the boys to his wife Larentia (Livy 1.4.7). In Dionysius' Fabian version he watches the wolf suckling them before a cave, the Lupercal, where a bronze group "of ancient workmanship" stood in Dionysius' own day (1.79.6–8). Livy (1.5.1–2) traces the Lupercalia to Evander's Arcadian rite of Lycaean Pan (modules 1.3 and 2.3). The boys grew up hunting and raiding brigands (Livy 1.4.8–9).

Where sources disagree. The mother's name and fate vary. Livy's Rhea Silvia stays in prison; Dionysius (1.78–79) records that she was killed at once, or hidden until her sons freed her. Naevius and Ennius call her Ilia, daughter of Aeneas, and Ennius has her thrown into the river, whose god takes her as wife, the version Horace's "uxorious" Tiber presupposes (Odes 1.2.17–20). Ovid calls her simply Silvia (Fasti 3.11).

Recognition, augury and the death of Remus

In Livy (1.5.3–7) brigands ambushed the twins during the Lupercalia and took Remus, who was handed to Numitor for punishment. Numitor, struck by his age and bearing, suspected the truth; Faustulus told Romulus; the brothers killed Amulius and restored Numitor (1.6.1–2). Dionysius (1.79–83) makes the trigger a quarrel over pasture. Plutarch (8) admits that the story looks "dramatic and fictitious", but fortune, he says, is sometimes a poet.

Wishing to found a city where they had been raised, the twins fell into "the ancestral evil, desire for kingship" (avitum malum, regni cupido, Livy 1.6.4). Neither was senior, so they asked the gods. Romulus took the Palatine for his observation post, Remus the Aventine. Remus saw six vultures first; Romulus then saw twelve. Each side hailed its man king, one claiming priority, the other number, and Remus fell in the brawl (1.6.4–7.1). "The more common story" (1.7.2) is that Remus jumped the new walls in mockery and Romulus killed him, adding:

So perish whoever else shall leap over my walls. (Livy 1.7.2)

Dionysius (1.85–87) has Romulus claim birds before he had seen any; Remus died in the fighting, Faustulus with him, and Romulus buried his brother at Remoria. Plutarch (9–10) offers two killers: Romulus, or his companion Celer, who fled to Etruria and gave his name to the celeres, the swift. In Ovid, Celer strikes with a spade and Romulus weeps (Fasti 4.837–852); Remus' ghost later gives the Lemuria its name (5.451–484). Plutarch (11) describes the rite: Etruscan experts, a pit (mundus) filled with first-fruits and soil, and a bronze ploughshare drawn by a bull and a cow to cut the line of the wall, lifted where gates would stand. The day was the Parilia, 21 April (Plutarch 12).

Where sources disagree. Ennius' augury (Annales, quoted by Cicero, On Divination 1.107–108) puts Romulus, not Remus, on the Aventine, frames the contest as Roma against Remora, and makes Romulus' twelve birds a clear sign; Livy, Dionysius and Plutarch put Romulus on the Palatine. Livy leaves the result open, while Dionysius and Plutarch (9) report that Romulus cheated. The killer is a nameless brawler in Livy's first version, Romulus in his second, Celer in Ovid and Plutarch.

The asylum, the Sabine women and Titus Tatius

The city needed people. Romulus opened an asylum "between the two groves" on the Capitol for any man, free or slave, without question (Livy 1.8.5–6; Plutarch 9.3). It also needed women. When the neighbours refused intermarriage, Romulus held games for Neptune Equester, the Consualia, and at a signal the young Romans seized the visiting girls of Caenina, Crustumerium, Antemnae and the Sabines (Livy 1.9). Livy gives no number; Plutarch (14) reports thirty, 527 from Valerius Antias and 683 from Juba.

Romulus killed Acron, king of Caenina, with his own hand and dedicated the armour to Jupiter Feretrius, whose precinct was the first temple in Rome (Livy 1.10.4–7; Plutarch 16). These were the first spolia opima, spoils taken by a Roman commander from an enemy commander killed in single combat. Only Aulus Cornelius Cossus, against Lars Tolumnius of Veii (Livy 4.19–20), and Marcus Claudius Marcellus in 222 BC repeated the feat.

The Sabines of Cures under Titus Tatius came last. Tarpeia, daughter of the citadel's commander, let them in for "what they wore on their left arms", meaning their gold bracelets, and they crushed her under their shields (Livy 1.11.6–9). In the battle in the valley Romulus vowed a temple to Jupiter Stator, the Stayer, and the Romans held (1.12.3–7). Then the Sabine women, hair unbound, ran between their fathers and their husbands (1.13.1–3). Peace made one people: a joint kingship, Rome the seat, the citizens called Quirites after Cures (1.13.4–5); the curiae belong to module 1.5. Some years later Tatius was killed at Lavinium after his kinsmen abused Laurentine envoys, and Romulus was "less troubled than was proper" (1.14.1–3).

Where sources disagree. Tarpeia's motive was argued over from the start. Fabius and Cincius, says Dionysius, made it gold; Calpurnius Piso (in Dionysius 2.38–40) had her ask for the shields in order to disarm the enemy, which would explain the yearly libations at her tomb. Propertius (4.4) makes her a Vestal in love with Tatius; the Greek poet Simylus (in Plutarch 17) moved her treachery to the Gallic sack.

The vanishing king and Quirinus

Romulus, dearer to the people than to the senators (Livy 1.15.8), was reviewing the army at the Goat's Marsh on the Campus Martius when a storm and thick cloud wrapped him; when it cleared he was gone (1.16.1). The senators said he had been taken up; the people hailed him a god; some muttered that the senators had torn him apart (1.16.4). Proculus Julius swore that Romulus had come down from the sky at dawn and declared that Rome would be capital of the world (1.16.5–7). Plutarch (27) sets the killing in Vulcan's precinct, each senator carrying a piece out under his robe, and has Romulus tell Proculus that he is now Quirinus (28). Ennius already had Romulus living in heaven "with the gods who begot him"; Cicero tells the eclipse and the vision in On the Republic 2.17–20. Quirinus himself was an old god with his own flamen and his festival on 17 February (Ovid, Fasti 2.475–512; module 2.2).

Where sources disagree. Livy calls the murder an obscure rumour; Dionysius (2.56) says the more plausible writers have Romulus killed by his own citizens for his harshness; Plutarch (28) argues that only souls, not bodies, rise to heaven. When Romulus became Quirinus is uncertain. Cicero is the earliest surviving author to state it outright; Ennius' prayer to "father Quirinus" may presuppose it, or may address the old god alone.

Variants: other founders, other parents, a wolf who was a woman

Plutarch opens the Life with a catalogue (1–2). Rome was named from the Pelasgians' strength (rhōmē); from Rhome, a Trojan woman who burned the ships; from Romanus, son of Odysseus and Circe; from Romus, sent from Troy by Diomedes; or from Romis, a Latin tyrant. Those who do name Romulus make him son of Aeneas and Dexithea, or of Mars by Aeneas' daughter Aemilia. Dionysius (1.72–73) gives a parallel list; Wiseman (Remus, 1995) catalogues sixty-one Greek and Roman versions in all.

Promathion, an author of unknown date, told the strangest version (Plutarch 2). A phantom phallus rose from the hearth of Tarchetius, a cruel king of Alba; an oracle ordered a virgin to lie with it, and the king's daughter sent her maid instead. Vesta forbade Tarchetius to kill them, so he set them weaving a web to earn their freedom and had it unpicked each night. The maid's twins were left by the river, suckled by a she-wolf, fed by birds and raised by a cowherd; grown, they overthrew him. There is no Mars and no Rhea: the father is a power of the hearth, the mother a slave. The same hearth-birth is told of Servius Tullius (Dionysius 4.2; Pliny, Natural History 36.204) and of Caeculus of Praeneste, which suggests an old Latin pattern for the birth of kings.

Acca Larentia has three faces. She is Faustulus' wife. She is the wolf rationalised, since lupa also meant prostitute (whence lupanar, a brothel), and Livy (1.4.7), Dionysius (1.84.4) and Plutarch (4) report that some called her the wolf because she sold herself to the shepherds. And she is a second Larentia, a courtesan of Ancus Marcius' day, won at dice by Hercules' temple-keeper, who left her estates to the Roman people and was honoured at the Larentalia on 23 December (Plutarch 5; Gellius 7.7; Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.10.11–17). Masurius Sabinus (in Gellius 7.7.8) and Pliny (Natural History 18.6) make her the mother of twelve sons, the first Arval Brothers, with Romulus taking a dead son's place. Many scholars see an old goddess behind all three; uncertain.

The earliest evidence

The Roman literature begins about 200 BC. Objects take the wolf and twins a century further back.

ObjectDateWhat it shows
Bronze mirror reportedly from Bolsena (Volsinii), Antiquarium Comunale, Romelater 4th century BCShe-wolf suckling twins below a rock, with onlookers, a lion and two birds
Statue group of the Ogulnii at the Ruminal fig (lost)296 BCThe infant founders under the wolf's teats (Livy 10.23.12)
Silver didrachm, legend ROMANO (Crawford, RRC 20/1)c. 269–266 BCHead of Hercules; wolf and twins, on some of Rome's first silver
Denarius of Sextus Pompeius Fostlus (RRC 235/1)137 BCWolf, twins, fig tree with birds and Faustulus, a pun on the moneyer's name
Capitoline wolflong dated c. 480–470 BC; now 11th–12th century ADThe wolf alone; the twins were added after 1471

In 296 BC the brothers Gnaeus and Quintus Ogulnius, plebeian curule aediles who as tribunes in 300 had opened the pontificate and augurate to plebeians (Livy 10.6–9), set up the twins under the wolf from fines levied on moneylenders (10.23.11–12). In 65 BC lightning struck a gilded wolf with the infant Romulus on the Capitol (Cicero, Against Catiline 3.19). Neither group survives.

Where sources disagree. The mirror is the earliest image, but of what? Adam and Briquel (1982) read it as Praenestine work showing the twins in a Latin rather than Etruscan setting, and most still see Romulus and Remus with Faustulus or a Lupercus. Wiseman (1993) made the twins the Lares Praestites and the onlookers Mercury and Lara, their parents, which would leave the Ogulnii group as the first certain Romulus and Remus.

The Capitoline wolf stood at the Lateran in the Middle Ages, where courts sat "at the wolf"; Sixtus IV gave it to the people of Rome in 1471, and the twins were added soon after, perhaps by Antonio del Pollaiuolo. Winckelmann judged it Etruscan, and later scholars dated it about 480–470 BC. Restoring it in 1997, Anna Maria Carruba found it cast in a single pour, a technique she argued was medieval (La lupa capitolina: un bronzo medievale, 2006). Radiocarbon tests at the University of Salento, on organic residue in the casting core, gave a date of about 1021–1153 at 95 per cent confidence; thermoluminescence on the core agreed.

Where sources disagree. Adriano La Regina backed the medieval date on grounds of style, comparing Carolingian and Romanesque bronzes. Defenders of antiquity cited a lead-isotope study co-authored by the Capitoline curator Claudio Parisi Presicce (2005) tracing the copper to a Sardinian mine; later analyses have not confirmed the match. Most specialists now accept a medieval wolf, perhaps copying an ancient one.

What the story is doing

Why Remus?

Remus is the puzzle: a twin whose only act is to die before the city exists. Theodor Mommsen ("Die Remuslegende", Hermes 16, 1881) read the twins as a projection of the two consuls; Mary Beard objects that consuls did not kill each other. Hermann Strasburger (1968) argued that so discreditable a tale, with its raped priestess, beast's milk, fratricide, runaways and stolen wives, must have begun as Greek anti-Roman propaganda; yet Romans displayed the wolf with evident pride. Jaan Puhvel (1975) derived Remus from *Yemo-, "twin", the being sacrificed at creation, like Norse Ymir; Jan Bremmer (1987) read exposure and wild youth as a pattern of initiation. T. P. Wiseman (Remus: A Roman Myth, 1995) dated Remus to the fourth century. The twins mirror the power-sharing of patricians and plebeians in the consulship; Remus is the latecomer, from remorari, "to delay"; and his murder enters the story about 295 BC, after Sentinum, as the memory of a human sacrifice to protect the walls, spread by plays staged at the games.

Where sources disagree. Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) treats the twin story as old and indigenous, and in reviewing Wiseman objected that Remus' death is told as murder, not sacrifice. Beard treats his reconstruction of lost plays as largely speculative. Carandini, at the other extreme, reads the legend as the memory of a real eighth-century founding. The evidence settles none of these.

A brother's blood

In the civil wars the fratricide became the city's original sin. Horace's seventh Epode, written in the triumviral civil wars, asks what madness drives Romans to arms and answers with bitter fates "and the crime of a brother's murder" (scelusque fraternae necis, 7.18): innocent Remus' blood, shed on the earth, is a curse on his descendants (7.19–20). Lucan (1.92–95) makes the first triumvirate an image of the first walls, "wet with a brother's blood". Tacitus has many excuse Nero's murder of Britannicus by "a kingship that cannot be shared" (Annals 13.17); Augustine pairs Romulus with Cain as founders by fratricide (City of God 15.5). Virgil's answer is "Quirinus with his brother Remus" giving laws (Aeneid 1.292–293): civil war over, the brothers reconciled.

A model and a warning

Romulus offered founder, conqueror and god; he also offered king, fratricide and a ruler killed by senators. In 45 BC Caesar's statue was set up in the temple of Quirinus (Dio 43.45.3), and Cicero wrote that he would rather Caesar shared a temple with Quirinus than with Salus, Safety (Letters to Atticus 12.45), a joke about how Romulus ended. The Lupercalia of 44, where Antony offered the diadem, was Romulus' festival (module 5.4). Twelve vultures greeted Octavian's first consulship in 43, as they had Romulus (Suetonius, Augustus 95). In 27 he passed over the name Romulus for Augustus, which Suetonius glosses with Ennius' line on Rome founded "by august augury" (Augustus 7.2); Dio says he feared the suspicion of kingship (53.16.7). He lived beside the hut of Romulus, rebuilt the Lupercal and the temples of Quirinus and Jupiter Feretrius (Res Gestae 19), denied Marcus Crassus the spolia opima in 29 BC (Dio 51.24.4), and set Romulus with the spoils opposite Aeneas in his Forum (Ovid, Fasti 5.563–566; module 6.2).

What the ground shows

The huts and the hut of Romulus

Rome was inhabited long before 753. Bronze Age pottery comes from the Capitol and the Forum Boarium, and the Forum cemetery begins in the tenth century (module 1.1). On the Cermalus, the south-western corner of the Palatine, twentieth-century excavations found Iron Age hut floors cut into the tufa, with post-holes and drainage gutters, of the eighth century in their visible phase; they match the hut-shaped urns of Latial burials. The Romans kept a casa Romuli there, repaired but never enlarged (Dionysius 1.79.11), and another on the Capitol (Vitruvius 2.1.5); Dio records fires in the Palatine hut (48.43, 54.29). Augustus' house stood alongside. The huts prove a village, not a founder.

Carandini's wall

From 1985 Andrea Carandini excavated the north slope of the Palatine above the Sacra Via, and in 1988 his team reported an earth-and-timber wall on a stone footing, rebuilt into the sixth century, its first phase in the mid- or later eighth. He read a gap as the Porta Mugonia, a girl's grave goods under its threshold as a foundation deposit, and the line as the boundary Tacitus traces round the foot of the Palatine (Annals 12.24). In La nascita di Roma (1997) and Rome: Day One (2011) it became a real founder's rite of about 750 BC.

Where sources disagree. Wiseman ("Reading Carandini", JRS 91, 2001, and later reviews) accepts the finds but not the story: turning a wall into Romulus needs texts written five centuries later, and since 753 is a construct of third-century chronographers, its match with the pottery is "no more than an accident". Adam Ziółkowski argues that the walls are too flimsy for defences and that the gate cannot be demonstrated.

The Lapis Niger and the tomb of Romulus

Festus records a black stone in the Comitium marking a place of ill omen, meant, some said, for Romulus' tomb but used for Faustulus or for Hostus Hostilius (s.v. niger lapis); Varro, in Porphyrio's note on Horace's "bones of Quirinus" (Epodes 16.13), put the tomb behind the Rostra. In 1899 Giacomo Boni found the black pavement and beneath it an archaic altar, a column stump and a sixth-century cippus naming a rex (module 1.5). Coarelli identifies the complex with the Volcanal, where Plutarch's senators killed Romulus. In 2020 a sixth-century tufa chest found beneath the steps of the Curia was hailed in the press as the tomb of Romulus; it was empty, and at most it marks a cult place.

The Lupercal of 2007

In 2007 Irene Iacopi announced a domed chamber some 15 m below the House of Augustus, encrusted with shells and mosaic and crowned by a white eagle, and it was hailed as the Lupercal that Augustus rebuilt.

Where sources disagree. Adriano La Regina, Fausto Zevi and Henner von Hesberg replied that the chamber is a nymphaeum or dining room of Nero's time, and that the ancient sources put the Lupercal at the foot of the hill (Dionysius 1.32.3–5, 1.79.8), not high inside it. Most topographers now look lower, towards Sant'Anastasia. The chamber is real; its name is not established.

Self-test

  1. Who wrote the first Roman narrative of the foundation, when, and how long after the traditional date?
    Answer

    Fabius Pictor, in Greek, about 200 BC: some five and a half centuries after 753. Plutarch says he followed Diocles of Peparethus in most points (Romulus 3.1), and Dionysius that Cincius, Cato and Piso followed him (1.79.4).

  2. What are the competing accounts of how Remus died?
    Answer

    Livy gives a brawl after the disputed augury and, as "the more common story", Romulus killing him for leaping the new walls (1.7.1–2). Dionysius has him die in the fighting with Faustulus; Ovid and Plutarch name Romulus' companion Celer as the killer.

  3. How does Ennius' augury differ from Livy's?
    Answer

    Ennius (in Cicero, On Divination 1.107–108) puts Romulus on the Aventine, makes the contest about the name Roma or Remora, and gives Romulus a clear sign. Livy puts Romulus on the Palatine and Remus on the Aventine and leaves the result disputed between priority and number.

  4. What were the spolia opima, and why did they matter to Augustus?
    Answer

    Spoils taken by a Roman commander from an enemy commander killed in single combat, dedicated to Jupiter Feretrius; Romulus won the first from Acron (Livy 1.10). Octavian rebuilt the temple and in 29 BC denied Crassus the honour; as Augustus he displayed Romulus carrying the spoils in his Forum.

  5. Why was Acca Larentia called lupa, and who is the other Larentia?
    Answer

    Lupa meant prostitute as well as she-wolf, and Livy 1.4.7, Dionysius 1.84 and Plutarch 4 report that some explained the wolf as Faustulus' wife, who sold herself to shepherds. The other Larentia is the courtesan of Ancus' day who left her estates to the Roman people and was honoured at the Larentalia (Plutarch 5; Gellius 7.7).

  6. What is distinctive about Promathion's version, and what does it connect with?
    Answer

    The twins are born to a slave girl and a phallus risen from the hearth of the Alban king Tarchetius, with no Mars and no Rhea Silvia (Plutarch 2). The hearth-birth matches the stories of Servius Tullius and Caeculus of Praeneste, suggesting a Latin pattern for royal births.

  7. Why can the Capitoline wolf no longer serve as early evidence, and what is the earliest secure evidence instead?
    Answer

    Its single-pour casting and a radiocarbon date of about 1021–1153 make it medieval, and the twins are fifteenth-century additions. The earliest images are the later fourth-century mirror, if it shows Romulus and Remus, the Ogulnii group of 296 BC (Livy 10.23.12) and the ROMANO didrachm of about 269–266.

  8. Summarise Wiseman's explanation of Remus and one objection to it.
    Answer

    Remus entered the story in the fourth century as an image of patrician and plebeian power-sharing, the "delayer" from remorari, and his death was added about 295 BC from a human sacrifice for the walls. Cornell objects that the death is told as murder, not sacrifice; Beard, that the lost plays it relies on are largely conjecture.

  9. How do Horace, Lucan and Virgil use the fratricide?
    Answer

    Horace (Epodes 7.17–20) makes Remus' blood the curse that drives Romans to civil war; Lucan (1.95) makes the first walls wet with a brother's blood an image of Rome shared among three masters. Virgil (Aeneid 1.292–293) answers with Quirinus and Remus giving laws together under Augustus.

  10. What do Carandini's wall and the 2007 cave prove, and what do they not?
    Answer

    The wall shows an eighth-century boundary on the Palatine's north slope, not that Romulus built it; Wiseman notes that 753 is a later construct and its match with the pottery accidental. The cave is a real decorated chamber, but La Regina, Zevi and von Hesberg date it to Nero's time and place the Lupercal lower, at the foot of the hill.

Carry forward

  1. The foundation story was first written down by a Roman about 200 BC, five and a half centuries after its date, and never settled into one version: names, parents, hills and killers all vary. For every early Roman story, ask who first tells it, when, and what was at stake in Rome at that moment.
  2. Romulus is double-edged: founder, conqueror and god, but also fratricide, king and a ruler perhaps murdered by senators. Caesar and Augustus had to claim him while avoiding his fate, and from Horace to Augustine the twins stand for civil war.
  3. Archaeology confirms an eighth-century Palatine village with huts and a boundary wall, but it cannot reach a named person, and a rough match between pottery and a chronographers' date is no proof of a legend. Module 1.5 applies the same test to the kings.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Romulus and Remus and the foundation of Rome. Cover: the story in full as Livy book 1, Dionysius books 1 and 2 and Plutarch's Romulus tell it (Rhea Silvia and Mars, Amulius and Numitor, the exposure, the she-wolf and the woodpecker, Faustulus and Acca Larentia, the Lupercal, the recognition, the augury contest on the Palatine and the Aventine, the wall and the death of Remus, the asylum, the rape of the Sabine women, Tarpeia, Titus Tatius and the joint kingship, the first spolia opima, the disappearance in the storm and the deification as Quirinus); the variants (Remus killed by Celer, the competing parents and names, Plutarch's catalogue of versions including Promathion's, Acca Larentia as lupa, 'she-wolf' and prostitute); the earliest evidence (the statue group set up by the Ogulnii in 296 BC, the Etruscan mirror from Bolsena, the first coins with the wolf and twins, and the Capitoline wolf, whose scientific dating made it medieval); what the story is doing (the explanations for Remus from Mommsen to Wiseman, the fratricide as an image of civil war in Horace's Epodes 7 and Lucan, Romulus as a model and a warning for Caesar and Augustus); and what the ground shows (the Iron Age huts on the Palatine and the 'hut of Romulus', Carandini's Palatine wall of the later eighth century and its critics, the Lapis Niger and the 'tomb of Romulus', the Lupercal cave claimed in 2007). Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 1 · Italy before Rome and the founding legends · 1.5 · 3,395 words

The seven kings

The seven and who tells themRomulus to Ancus: founder, priest, warrior, builderThe Tarquins and Servius in the traditionSeven reigns for 244 yearsServius Tullius as the Etruscan MastarnaThe great Rome of the TarquinsThe Servian reformsThe nature of the kingshipHow much is history: the modern positionsSelf-testCarry forward

The seven and who tells them

The canonical list runs from Romulus to Tarquinius Superbus: seven kings across 244 years, 753–509 BC on the Varronian count (module 0.3 has the variants). Every narrative is late. The first Roman historian, Fabius Pictor, wrote in Greek around 200 BC, three centuries after the last king and five after the first; he survives only in fragments quoted by later writers. Livy's Book 1 dates from about 27–25 BC, Dionysius of Halicarnassus' Roman Antiquities books 2–4 from 7 BC on, Cicero's sketch in On the Republic 2 from the 50s BC, Plutarch's Numa from around AD 100. Livy admits that most records perished when the Gauls burned the city (6.1.2). Between the kings and their historians lie family tradition, antiquarian aetiology, priestly lists of uncertain age, and monuments that carried a king's name.

KingTraditional reign BCOrigin in the traditionCredited with
Romulus753–716Alban, son of MarsSenate of 100, thirty curiae, three tribes, lictors, the Celeres
Numa Pompilius715–673Sabine of Curespriesthoods, calendar, gate of Janus
Tullus Hostilius673–642Roman, grandson of Hostus Hostiliusconquest and destruction of Alba, Curia Hostilia
Ancus Marcius642–617grandson of Numafetial law, Janiculum, Pons Sublicius, prison, Ostia
Tarquinius Priscus616–579Tarquinii; son of Demaratus of Corinth100 new senators, Circus Maximus, drainage, Capitoline temple begun
Servius Tullius578–535son of the captive Ocresia; or the Etruscan Mastarnacensus, classes and centuries, tribes, wall, Aventine Diana
Tarquinius Superbus534–509son or grandson of PriscusCapitoline temple, Cloaca Maxima, colonies at Signia and Circeii

Romulus to Ancus: founder, priest, warrior, builder

Romulus (his story is module 1.4) is the author of the political frame. He creates a hundred senators, the patres, whose descendants are the patricians (Livy 1.8.7); twelve lictors on the Etruscan model (1.8.2–3); thirty curiae named after the Sabine women and three centuries of cavalry, Ramnenses, Titienses and Luceres (1.13.6–8); and a bodyguard of 300 Celeres (1.15.8). The curiae were real: they voted the lex curiata into the late Republic, by then through thirty lictors, and the few names known, Faucia (Livy 9.38.15), Foriensis and Veliensis, look like places or clans, not abducted brides. Varro reports that the three tribe names were Etruscan (On the Latin Language 5.55).

Numa, chosen after a year's interregnum, is the priest-king: inaugurated by an augur on the Capitol (Livy 1.18.6–10), he closes the gate of Janus (1.19.2), divides the year into twelve lunar months with intercalation and fixes the days for public business (1.19.6–7), and founds the flamines of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus, the Vestals, the twelve Salii and the pontiff (1.20). His authority comes from night meetings with the nymph Egeria in a grove outside the Porta Capena (1.21.3; Plutarch, Numa 4, 8). The institutions are genuinely archaic; unit 2 (module 2.3) treats them. Their gathering under one founder is the move Sparta made with Lycurgus (Greek module 5.3). The "books of Numa" found on the Janiculum in 181 BC and burned (Livy 40.29.3–14) show claims on him still being made in the Republic.

Where sources disagree. Some made Numa a pupil of Pythagoras. Livy 1.18.2 and Cicero, On the Republic 2.28–29, reject it on chronology, since Pythagoras came to Italy under Servius Tullius (Livy) or Tarquinius Superbus (Cicero); Plutarch, Numa 1 and 8, reports both sides. The legend probably grew when Rome set up a statue of Pythagoras in the Comitium during the Samnite wars (Pliny, Natural History 34.26).

Tullus Hostilius, "fiercer even than Romulus" (Livy 1.22.2), fights Alba Longa. The war is settled by champions, three Roman Horatii against three Alban Curiatii; one Horatius survives (1.24–25). He kills his sister for mourning her betrothed Curiatius, is condemned for perduellio, appeals to the people and is acquitted (1.26), which supplies aetiologies for provocatio and the Tigillum Sororium, the "sister's beam" he passed under in expiation. When the Alban dictator Mettius Fufetius betrays Rome, Tullus has him torn apart by chariots (1.28), razes Alba except its temples, moves the Albans to the Caelian and builds the Curia Hostilia (1.29–30). He dies by Jupiter's lightning after a botched rite (1.31.8). Alba itself is module 1.3.

Where sources disagree. Livy himself says sources differ on which triplets were Roman, though most call the Horatii Roman (1.24.1). The combat of champions is a type: Herodotus 1.82 has 300 Spartans fight 300 Argives for Thyrea. Georges Dumézil read Horatius as the Indo-European warrior who defeats a triple foe and must be purified of his fury; critics prefer Roman aetiology of a beam, a tomb and a legal procedure.

Ancus Marcius, Numa's grandson, combines both predecessors (Livy 1.32). He institutes the fetial ritual for declaring war (1.32.5–14), conquers Latin towns and settles their people on the Aventine, fortifies the Janiculum, builds the wooden Pons Sublicius and the prison (1.33.1–8), and carries Roman territory to the sea, founding Ostia and its salt-works (1.33.9). The excavated castrum at Ostia is no older than the fourth century BC, so a regal Ostia, if real, was control of the salt beds at the river mouth rather than a town. The plebeian Marcii Reges claimed descent from him (Suetonius, Julius 6.1) and had reason to enlarge him.

The Tarquins and Servius in the tradition

Tarquinius Priscus is a Corinthian's son. Demaratus, a Bacchiad, fled when Cypselus seized Corinth (Greek module 5.3), settled at Tarquinii and married there (Livy 1.34.2; Dionysius 3.46–47; Cicero, On the Republic 2.34). The craftsmen Pliny puts in his train, Eucheir, Diopos and Eugrammos (Natural History 35.152), "Skilled-hand", "Line-sight" and "Fine-drawer", are too apt to be true. His son Lucumo, barred from honour at Tarquinii as an immigrant's son, comes to Rome with his wife Tanaquil; at the Janiculum an eagle lifts his cap and replaces it, and Tanaquil, versed in Etruscan augury, reads kingship (1.34.8–9). As Lucius Tarquinius he becomes guardian of Ancus' sons, then the first king to canvass for the throne (1.35.2). He adds a hundred senators from "lesser families", lays out the Circus Maximus and the Roman Games (1.35.6–9), drains the low ground and lays the Capitoline foundations (1.38.6–7). Ancus' sons have him murdered, and Tanaquil installs Servius (1.40–41).

Servius Tullius was born in the palace to Ocresia, a captive of Corniculum; a flame played round the sleeping boy's head (1.39.1–4). Livy argues against the slave birth his name suggested (1.39.5–6); others had him fathered by a phallus rising from the hearth (Dionysius 4.2; Ovid, Fasti 6.627–636) and loved by Fortuna. He reigns "without the people's order, by the will of the senators" (Livy 1.41.6), takes the census, creates classes, centuries and tribes (1.42–43), counts 80,000 citizens on Fabius Pictor's authority (1.44.2), extends the pomerium and walls, and builds the Aventine temple of Diana as a shrine for the Latins on the model of Ephesus (1.45.2). His daughter Tullia and her husband Lucius Tarquinius have him killed, and she drives her carriage over his body (1.48.7).

Tarquinius Superbus rules "neither by order of the people nor with the senators' authority" (1.49.3). He finishes the Capitoline temple with Etruscan workmen and plebeian labour, digs the Cloaca Maxima and plants colonies at Signia and Circeii (1.55–56). He is drawn as a Greek tyrant: his capture of Gabii is built from Herodotus (module 1.6), and the forced building matches Aristotle's list of tyrants' devices for keeping subjects poor and busy (Politics 5.1313b). His tyranny and fall belong to module 1.6.

Where sources disagree. Fabius Pictor made Superbus the son of Priscus. Dionysius 4.6–7 objects that the ages cannot work, since Priscus died old in 579 and Superbus lived until 495 (Livy 2.21.5), and follows Calpurnius Piso in making him a grandson; Livy 1.46.4 notes the doubt and keeps "son" with the majority. The chronology has been stretched to fill the space.

Seven reigns for 244 years

Seven reigns in 244 years average thirty-five years each. That is implausible in any monarchy, more so in an elective one choosing grown men, in which five of the seven vanished, were killed or were expelled. Well-documented dynasties average around twenty years a reign; module 0.3 states the problem, and here it is weighed. Either kings have dropped out, the foundation date is too early, or both. The date of 753 is a computation; the archaeology (below) puts the urban transformation in the later seventh century; and the end around 509 is anchored by the consular lists and the Capitoline dedication (module 1.6). Most modern accounts therefore compress the regal period, or treat its start as unknowable.

The first four kings look schematic. Warlike Romulus is paired with peaceful Numa, warlike Tullus with Ancus who combines both; Latin alternates with Sabine; each king owns a sphere: politics, religion, war, expansion and the plebs. Dumézil (Mitra-Varuna, 1940, and later work) mapped them onto the Indo-European functions: Romulus and Numa as the violent and the juridical sides of sovereignty, Tullus as the warrior, Ancus as the third function of wealth and people. The Tarquins double each other: both fight Latins and Sabines, both drain the city, both build the Capitol.

Where sources disagree. Momigliano's objection is weighed in module 2.1. Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) offers a different defence of the list: Numa, Tullus and Ancus are first names no Republican Roman used, and no later forger would choose them. The stories may be invented while the names are remembered.

Servius Tullius as the Etruscan Mastarna

In AD 48 the emperor Claudius urged the senate to admit nobles from Gallia Comata, arguing that Rome had always taken in outsiders, even as kings. The bronze text was found at Lyon in 1528 (CIL XIII 1668); Tacitus gives a reworked version (Annals 11.24). Claudius, who had written twenty books of Etruscan history (Suetonius, Claudius 42.2), says that by Roman authors Servius was born of the captive Ocresia, but by Etruscan ones he was the faithful companion of Caelius Vivenna, led the remnant of his army to Rome, occupied the Caelian and named it after his leader, and changed his name:

"Tusce Mastarna ei nomen erat": in Etruscan his name was Mastarna.

The François Tomb at Vulci, found by Alessandro François in 1857 and painted about 340–310 BC, shows the episode. Facing Achilles' slaughter of Trojan prisoners, a local scene: Macstrna cuts the bonds of Caile Vipinas; Larth Ulthes stabs Laris Papathnas Velznach, "of Volsinii"; Rasce kills Pesna Arcmsnas Sveamach; Avle Vipinas kills a third captor; Marce Camitlnas raises his sword over Cneve Tarchunies Rumach, "Gnaeus Tarquinius of Rome". Prisoners break free and kill captors drawn from several cities, one a Roman Tarquin.

The Vibennae are not fiction. A bucchero vessel dedicated by Avile Vipiienas at the Portonaccio sanctuary of Veii dates to the second quarter or middle of the sixth century. Roman antiquarians named the Caelian after Caeles Vibenna (Varro, On the Latin Language 5.46; Tacitus, Annals 4.65), and derived the Capitol from the head of Olus found in its foundations (Arnobius, Against the Pagans 6.7). Macstrna looks like Latin magister with an Etruscan suffix: a title, "the master", perhaps the magister populi that the early dictator was called.

Where sources disagree. Livy and Dionysius never mention Mastarna, and Roman tradition is unanimous for a Latin mother from Corniculum. Andreas Alföldi (Early Rome and the Latins, 1965) took the Etruscan version as the truth Roman patriotism suppressed. Momigliano and Cornell judge the equation to be Claudius' learned combination of two traditions; Cornell thinks Servius and Mastarna were probably different men. The identification is uncertain; the world it implies is not.

The great Rome of the Tarquins

Giorgio Pasquali's phrase of 1936, "la grande Roma dei Tarquini", became the title of the 1990 Rome exhibition. The archaeology supports it in outline.

  • The Forum. The valley between Palatine and Capitol held Iron Age burials and huts. It was raised by deliberate fill, up to two metres in places (Ammerman 1990), and received its first gravel floor in the later seventh century, about 650–600 BC; Gjerstad's date was c. 575.
  • The Regia. At the Forum's east end Frank Brown excavated in the 1960s a sequence of buildings from the late seventh century to the later sixth, ending in the irregular plan the Regia kept to the end. A bucchero bowl fragment of about 530–500 found there in 1899 bears the word rex. Tradition made it Numa's house (Plutarch, Numa 14; Ovid, Fasti 6.263–264); it was too small for a palace and reads better as the king's cult house.
  • The Comitium and the Lapis Niger. The assembly place before the Curia was first floored in the later seventh century. Beneath a late Republican pavement of black stone, Giacomo Boni found in 1899 an altar, a column stump and a tufa cippus inscribed boustrophedon on four faces and a bevelled edge (CIL I² 1), of about 570–550 BC. The text is a sacred law: sakros esed, "let him be accursed"; recei, "to the king", the dative of rex; kalatorem, "the herald"; iouxmenta, "yoked beasts". The ancient identifications of the spot are module 1.4.
  • Sant'Omobono. By the river harbour stand the temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta that tradition gives to Servius (Dionysius 4.27; Livy 5.19.6). Cult begins in the late seventh or early sixth century; the first temple, usually dated to the early sixth, was rebuilt about 540–530 with terracotta decoration including Hercules led by Minerva, a theme popular in Peisistratid Athens. The temple went down about 500 under a great fill. Imported Greek pottery and an ivory lion with an Etruscan name show the harbour's reach.
  • The Capitoline temple. Foundations of cappellaccio tufa, about 54 by 62 metres, were re-exposed in the 1990s and 2000s in the Capitoline Museums' garden. Three cellae for Jupiter, Juno and Minerva; a terracotta Jupiter by Vulca of Veii (Pliny, Natural History 35.157, citing Varro); dedication by the consul Horatius in the Republic's first year (Livy 2.8.6–8). At full size it rivalled the Heraion of Samos and Peisistratid Athens' unfinished Olympieion.
  • The Cloaca Maxima. Livy credits Priscus with draining the low ground (1.38.6) and Superbus with the great sewer (1.56.2). The surviving vaulted conduit is mid-Republican or later; the sixth-century work was an open, stone-lined channel along the Forum stream to the Velabrum.
Where sources disagree. John Stamper (The Architecture of Roman Temples, 2005) reads the foundations, and Dionysius' 200 feet a side (4.61), as a platform carrying a temple of roughly 34 by 38 metres. Anna Mura Sommella, Gabriele Cifani and John Hopkins (the last in The Genesis of Roman Architecture, 2016) accept the full size. On the cippus, most take recei as a real king, since the stone predates 509; Gjerstad, who lowered the end of the monarchy to about 450, and others who doubt the date allow the rex sacrorum.

The ground confirms the tradition's structure: between about 625 and 500 a village cluster became a city with paved public spaces, monumental temples, drainage, Greek imports and Etruscan craftsmen. It confirms no individual king.

The Servian reforms

Livy 1.42–43, Dionysius 4.16–21 and Cicero, On the Republic 2.39–40, describe a census of property dividing citizens into classes, each class into centuries of iuniores (17–46) and seniores, armed according to wealth.

ClassCensus (asses, Livy)CenturiesArms
I100,00080helmet, round shield, greaves, cuirass, spear, sword
II75,00020oblong shield, no cuirass
III50,00020no greaves
IV25,00020spear and javelin
V11,00030slings and stones

Eighteen centuries of cavalry, a few of engineers and musicians and one of those below the census brought the total to 193 (Dionysius 4.16–18; Livy differs in detail). Voting ran from the top, so cavalry and first class held a majority and the poor rarely voted (Livy 1.43.10–11). Servius also replaced Romulus' three tribes with four urban tribes, Suburana, Palatina, Esquilina and Collina, and rural ones; by 495 there were twenty-one (Livy 2.21.7).

Rome struck no coin before about 300 BC, so the figures in asses are anachronistic. The 193-century assembly as described is that of the third century. No army was ever drawn up in five graded panoplies. Plinio Fraccaro (1931) found the original underneath: the old distinction between classis and those infra classem (Gellius 6.13), and sixty junior centuries in the first three classes matching a legion of 6,000 hoplites. A sixth-century Servius could plausibly have created a single hoplite classis levied through territorial tribes, as Greek cities did in the same century; Solon's property classes and Cleisthenes' territorial tribes are the obvious parallels (Greek module 5.5).

Where sources disagree. Cornell (1995) accepts a Servian core: territorial tribes, a census and a hoplite army in the sixth century, with the voting assembly developing from the army later. Gary Forsythe (A Critical History of Early Rome, 2005) and others put the class system in the fifth or fourth century, with military pay from 406 BC. The tradition has the centuriate assembly elect the first consuls in 509 (Livy 1.60); few modern scholars think a voting assembly of 193 centuries existed under any king.

The nature of the kingship

No king succeeded his father. On a king's death the patres took turns as interrex for five days each (Livy 1.17.5–6); the interrex proposed a candidate, the people in their curiae voted, the patres ratified, the augur inaugurated him (1.18.6–10), and Cicero has each king confirm his power by a curiate law (On the Republic 2). The interrex survived into the Republic, last attested in 52 BC. The kingship was open to outsiders: a Sabine, a Corinthian's son, the son of a captive. Carmine Ampolo's studies of archaic social mobility treat this as normal for central Italy: Demaratus moves to Tarquinii, his son to Rome, and in 504 the Sabine Attus Clausus arrives with his clients (Livy 2.16.4).

The Tarquins break the procedure. Priscus canvasses; Servius rules without the people's vote; Superbus without either. Elective sacral kingship gives way to something like Greek tyranny, a non-hereditary sole rule backed by force and public works (Greek module 5.3). Sixth-century Rome was a prize for warlords with armed companions: the Vibennae and Mastarna, Gnaeus Tarquinius, and Porsenna of Clusium, who in one tradition took the city (module 1.6).

The sacral side outlived the kings. Livy says the Republic created a rex sacrorum to perform the kings' rites, subordinate to the pontifex maximus so that the name should not threaten liberty (2.2.1–2). Patrician and barred from other office, he kept the king's calendar rites, among them the Regifugium of 24 February and the days marked Q.R.C.F., "when the king has attended the assembly". He is the strongest proof of a priest-king. Some suggest the split began under the Etruscan rulers, a war-leader or magister holding power beside an old sacral rex; it cannot be shown.

How much is history: the modern positions

Barthold Niebuhr (1811–12) imagined lost banquet ballads behind Livy. Ettore Pais (Storia di Roma, 1898–99) led the hypercritics: most kings were gods, doublets or annalists' inventions. Einar Gjerstad (Early Rome, 1953–73) used his Forum stratigraphy to argue that the city was founded about 575 and the monarchy ran on to about 450. Alföldi (1965) made sixth-century Rome a small dependency of Etruscan cities and its regal hegemony in Latium Fabius Pictor's patriotic invention.

Cornell (1995) shifted the debate by separating the narrative superstructure, largely fiction, from the structural facts: institutions, topography, the Etruscan dynasty, the size of late sixth-century Rome. Those, he argues, came down independently and are confirmed by archaeology and by documents such as the Carthage treaty. Andrea Carandini (La nascita di Roma, 1997; Roma: il primo giorno, 2007) goes furthest: a Palatine wall of the later eighth century and a regal house by the Vesta temple make even Romulus and Numa historical figures, not personifications.

Where sources disagree. T. P. Wiseman, reviewing Carandini ("Reading Carandini", Journal of Roman Studies 2001), argued that the excavations are read through Livy and so cannot confirm him; Christopher Smith (Early Rome and Latium, 1996) and Francesca Fulminante see a gradual process of urbanisation from the ninth century to the sixth, not a foundation by a founder. The consensus, such as it is, lies between Cornell and the sceptics: the last three kings belong to history, the first four to aetiology, with names that may be old.

Self-test

  1. Why is it hard to treat Livy's account of the kings as testimony?
    Answer

    He wrote Book 1 around 27–25 BC, about five centuries after the last king; the first Roman historian, Fabius Pictor, wrote around 200 BC, and Livy says most records perished in the Gallic sack (6.1.2).

  2. What is wrong with seven reigns for 244 years, and what are the possible solutions?
    Answer

    An average of thirty-five years a reign is implausible, especially in an elective monarchy with several violent deaths. Either kings have been lost from the list, the foundation date is too early, or both.

  3. Give two signs that the first four kings are schematic, and one argument that their names are nonetheless old.
    Answer

    They alternate warlike and peaceful, Latin and Sabine, and each owns one sphere (politics, religion, war, expansion), which Dumézil read as Indo-European functions. Cornell notes that Numa, Ancus, Tullus and Servius are archaic names out of use in the Republic, which no forger would pick.

  4. What did Claudius claim about Servius Tullius, and where?
    Answer

    In his speech of AD 48 on the Lyon tablet (CIL XIII 1668) he said that Etruscan authors made Servius the companion of Caelius Vivenna, who brought Caelius' army to the Caelian and changed his Etruscan name, Mastarna.

  5. What does the François Tomb show, and why does the figure of Cneve Tarchunies Rumach matter?
    Answer

    Macstrna freeing Caile Vipinas while companions kill captors from several cities, painted at Vulci about 340–310 BC. "Gnaeus Tarquinius of Rome" is a Tarquin unknown to Livy, which suggests the two-Tarquin tradition simplifies a more crowded history.

  6. What is the Lapis Niger cippus, and what does recei tell us?
    Answer

    A tufa pillar of about 570–550 BC under the black pavement of the Comitium, inscribed boustrophedon with a sacred law (CIL I² 1). Recei, "to the king", shows a rex with a herald acting in the Comitium before 509, unless it means the rex sacrorum.

  7. What does the archaeology of the period 625–500 BC confirm, and what can it not confirm?
    Answer

    It confirms an urban transformation: the paved Forum and Comitium, the Regia, the Sant'Omobono temple, a huge Capitoline platform and drainage. It cannot confirm any individual king or deed.

  8. Why is the centuriate assembly as Livy describes it anachronistic for Servius?
    Answer

    Its census figures are in coined asses, unknown before about 300 BC, and its 193 centuries match the third-century assembly. Fraccaro's single hoplite classis of sixty centuries is the plausible sixth-century core.

  9. How was a king chosen, and how did the Tarquins depart from it?
    Answer

    Interreges from the patres in turn; a candidate proposed, voted by the curiae, ratified by the patres and inaugurated. Priscus canvassed, Servius ruled without the people's vote (Livy 1.41.6) and Superbus without either (1.49.3).

  10. What is the rex sacrorum evidence for?
    Answer

    That the king had sacral duties important enough to be kept after 509 by a priest bearing his title, deliberately subordinated to the pontifex maximus and barred from politics (Livy 2.2.1–2).

Carry forward

  1. Separate the narrative from the structure: the stories of the kings are late and shaped by aetiology, family pride and Greek models, but institutions, names and monuments can carry older information, and archaeology tests the structure, not the stories.
  2. Late sixth-century Rome was a large, Etruscanised city open to mobile warlords and their armed bands; the Tarquins, Mastarna and Porsenna belong to that world, and the Republic was born out of it rather than out of a tidy expulsion.
  3. Roman institutions are routinely projected back onto founders (Numa's priesthoods, Servius' centuries); before believing any "regal" institution, ask what form it took in the age of the historian who describes it.
