The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the seven kings of Rome and what archaeology allows of them. Cover: each king as the tradition presents him, with the institutions credited to him (Romulus' Senate and curiae; Numa, Egeria, the priesthoods and the calendar; Tullus Hostilius, the Horatii and Curiatii and the destruction of Alba; Ancus Marcius and Ostia; Tarquinius Priscus from Tarquinii and his Corinthian father Demaratus; Servius Tullius' census, centuries and tribes; Tarquinius Superbus and the Capitoline temple); the chronological problem of seven reigns for 244 years (module 0.3 states it: point back and weigh it here) and why the first kings look schematic; Servius Tullius as the Etruscan Mastarna, from Claudius' speech on the Lyon tablet and the François Tomb painting of the Vibenna brothers; 'the great Rome of the Tarquins' in the archaeology: the first paving of the Forum, the Regia, the Comitium and the Lapis Niger inscription with its word for king, the Sant'Omobono temples, the platform of the Capitoline temple, the Cloaca Maxima; the Servian reforms and whether the centuriate assembly can be so early; the nature of the kingship (election, the interrex, the rex sacrorum, Etruscan warlords such as the Vibennae and Porsenna seizing the city); and the modern positions, from the hypercritics to Cornell and Carandini, on how much of the regal tradition is history. Leave Lucretia and the fall of the monarchy to module 1.6. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 1 · Italy before Rome and the founding legends · 1.6 · 2,859 words

The fall of the monarchy: Lucretia, Brutus and Porsenna

Tarquinius Superbus: the tyrant's portraitDelphi, Lucretia and the oath on the daggerThe first year: Brutus' sons, Collatinus and PublicolaPorsenna of Clusium: heroes and a surrenderAristodemus of Cumae, Aricia and Lake RegillusThe documentary evidenceAthens 510, Rome 509Lucretia as political mythSelf-testCarry forward

Tarquinius Superbus: the tyrant's portrait

Every narrative of these events is late. Livy wrote Books 1–2 around 27–25 BC and Dionysius of Halicarnassus published his Roman Antiquities from 7 BC, both nearly five centuries after 509 and both dependent on annalists from Fabius Pictor (about 200 BC) onward (module 0.1). What they offer is a finished portrait, and it should be read as one.

Lucius Tarquinius, who took the throne by murdering Servius Tullius (module 1.5), is a tyrant by checklist. Livy 1.49 has him deny his predecessor burial, keep a bodyguard, kill leading senators without replacing them, judge capital cases alone, and make war and treaties without senate or people; hence Superbus, "the Proud". He drove the plebs to forced labour on the Capitoline temple and the Cloaca Maxima (1.56.1–3). He was also an effective general who led the Latin league and took Suessa Pometia from the Volsci (1.50–53).

Gabii fell to a trick (Livy 1.53.4–54.10; Dionysius 4.53–58). Sextus Tarquinius fled there complaining of his father's cruelty (in Dionysius after a public scourging staged for the purpose, 4.55), won command of the Gabine forces, and sent to ask what next. Tarquin said nothing to the messenger and walked in his garden striking off the tallest poppy heads (Livy 1.54.6); Sextus killed or exiled the leading men. Both halves are Herodotean. The self-maimed deserter is Zopyrus at Babylon (Herodotus 3.153–158); the wordless advice is Thrasybulus lopping the tallest ears of corn for Periander (5.92). Yet Dionysius saw the resulting treaty, written on an ox-hide stretched over a wooden shield in the temple of Dius Fidius (4.58.4).

Livy omits the Sibylline Books. In Dionysius (4.62) and Gellius (Attic Nights 1.19) an old woman offers Tarquin nine books of oracles, burns three and then three more when he refuses her price, and sells him the last three for the original sum. They were kept beneath the Capitoline temple and consulted only on the senate's order. Varro, quoted by Lactantius (Divine Institutes 1.6), made the buyer Priscus: the story followed whichever Tarquin was credited with the Capitol.

Delphi, Lucretia and the oath on the dagger

A snake glided from a wooden column in the palace, and Tarquin sent his sons Titus and Arruns to Delphi with their cousin Lucius Junius, who had survived the king's purge by playing the fool; hence Brutus, "dullard" (Livy 1.56.4–8). His gift to Apollo was a hollow cornel-wood staff filled with gold, an image of his own mind. The oracle promised supreme power to whoever first kissed his mother. Brutus stumbled on purpose and kissed the earth, the common mother of all mortals (1.56.9–12).

At the siege of Ardea the princes and their kinsman Tarquinius Collatinus wagered on their wives and rode out to look. The royal wives were feasting; Lucretia, at Collatia, sat spinning among her maids late at night (1.57). Days later Sextus returned alone, was received as a kinsman, and at night entered her room armed. The threat of death did not move her. The threat to kill a slave beside her and leave her seeming an adulteress did, and she submitted (1.58.1–5).

She summoned her father, Spurius Lucretius, and her husband, each with one friend: Publius Valerius and Lucius Brutus. She told them, made them swear vengeance, and refused their answer that the mind sins, not the body:

No unchaste woman shall live by Lucretia's example.

Then she stabbed herself (1.58.6–12). Brutus drew out the knife and swore by her blood to pursue the king, his wife and his children with fire and sword and to suffer no king at Rome; Collatinus, Lucretius and Valerius swore after him (1.59.1–2). As tribune of the Celeres, Brutus had the people revoke the king's power and exile the family. Tarquin found the gates shut and went to Caere, Sextus was killed at Gabii, and the centuriate assembly elected Brutus and Collatinus consuls (1.59.7–60.4).

Where sources disagree. Dionysius moves the climax to Rome: Lucretia drives to the city in mourning and dies in her father's house before kin and leading men (4.66–67). His Delphic embassy concerns a plague (4.69), and his Tarquin flees to Gabii (4.85). Ovid's Regifugium (Fasti 2.685–852) follows Livy but adds her care, even dying, to fall modestly. Guest, threat, testimony, suicide and oath never vary.

The first year: Brutus' sons, Collatinus and Publicola

Livy opens Book 2 by defining the new liberty: annual office, not any reduction of royal power (2.1.7). A rex sacrorum, barred from other office, took over the king's rites (2.2.1–2). Collatinus fell first. The people could not bear the name Tarquinius in power, so he resigned and retired to Lavinium, and the whole gens was exiled (2.2.3–11); Valerius replaced him. When royal envoys came to reclaim Tarquin's property, young nobles, the Vitellii, the Aquilii and Brutus' sons Titus and Tiberius among them, plotted a restoration, and the slave Vindicius informed (2.3–4). Brutus watched his sons flogged and beheaded, his father's feeling visible through the public office (2.5.8).

Veii and Tarquinii marched for the king. At the Silva Arsia, Brutus and Arruns Tarquinius charged each other and fell together; at night a voice from the wood, thought to be Silvanus', declared that the Etruscans had lost one man more (2.6–7.2). The matrons mourned Brutus for a year. Valerius, suspected of aiming at kingship because of his house on the Velia, pulled it down, lowered the fasces before the assembly and carried laws granting appeal to the people (provocatio) and outlawing would-be kings, earning the name Publicola (2.7.5–8.2). The year's fifth consul, Marcus Horatius Pulvillus, dedicated the Capitoline temple (2.8.4–8).

Where sources disagree. Dionysius (5.9–12) and Plutarch (Publicola 7) put the conspiracy first and have Collatinus deposed for pleading for the Aquilii, his sister's sons; Livy's Collatinus is exiled for his name alone. Dionysius says Brutus left no children (5.18), but Posidonius, cited by Plutarch (Brutus 1), had a third son survive to found the Junii Bruti, a claim that served Caesar's assassin. The appeal law recurs in 449 and 300 (Livy 10.9.3–6), and its 509 version is generally treated as a retrojection.

Porsenna of Clusium: heroes and a surrender

Tarquin then turned to Lars Porsenna, king of Clusium (Livy 2.9). The Etruscans took the Janiculum. Horatius Cocles held the far end of the Pons Sublicius, first with Spurius Lartius and Titus Herminius, then alone, until the bridge fell behind him, and swam back in armour (2.10). Gaius Mucius entered Porsenna's camp to kill him, stabbed the king's secretary by mistake, and when taken held his right hand in an altar fire, warning that three hundred young men had sworn the same oath; Porsenna released him, and the left-handed hero became Scaevola (2.12). Peace brought hostages and the return of land taken from Veii. The hostage Cloelia led the girls back across the Tiber, and Porsenna, after demanding her return, let her free half the hostages; she chose the boys (2.13).

Where sources disagree. Polybius, writing some 350 years after the event, has Horatius drown by choice (6.55); Livy has him swim to safety, Dionysius survive lamed (5.24–25). Each hero had a monument, and Ogilvie (A Commentary on Livy Books 1–5, 1965) and others read the tales as their aetiologies: Horatius' statue was moved after a lightning strike to the precinct of Vulcan, the lame god (Gellius 4.5), and the "Cloelia" on the Sacred Way was claimed for Valerius' daughter (Plutarch, Publicola 19). Dumézil (Mitra-Varuna, 1940) instead saw one-eyed Cocles and one-handed Scaevola as an inherited pair, like Odin and Tyr.

A rival tradition has Porsenna win. Tacitus, six centuries later, says that neither Porsenna, "when the city was surrendered", nor the Gauls had violated the Capitoline temple (Histories 3.72). Pliny had read Porsenna's treaty, which forbade the Romans to use iron except in farming (Natural History 34.139), a conqueror's disarmament clause. Dionysius has the senate send Porsenna an ivory throne, sceptre, gold crown and triumphal robe (5.35), and the old auction formula "the goods of King Porsenna are sold" (Livy 2.14.1) sounds like booty. Porsenna's son Arruns then attacked Aricia: the Etruscan objective was Latium, not Tarquin's restoration.

Where sources disagree. Alföldi (Early Rome and the Latins, 1965) took the capture as fact and made Porsenna, not Brutus, the man who ended the Tarquin monarchy. Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) and most recent historians accept the occupation but leave open whether Porsenna came for Tarquin or for himself. Livy and Dionysius keep the honourable peace; the surrender is the version no Roman had reason to invent.

Aristodemus of Cumae, Aricia and Lake Regillus

Dionysius' digression on Aristodemus of Cumae (7.3–12) derives, most scholars think, from a Cumaean Greek chronicle independent of the Roman annalists. Aristodemus, nicknamed Malakos, "the Soft", won fame when Cumae beat an Etruscan and Umbrian army in 524 (7.3–4). In the twentieth year after, about 504, he led the Cumaeans to relieve Aricia and killed the Etruscan commander himself (7.5–6), whom Dionysius elsewhere names as Arruns (5.36; compare Livy 2.14.5–9). Back home he massacred the aristocracy and ruled as tyrant. Tarquin died at his court in 495 (Livy 2.21.5), and Aristodemus, as his heir, later held Roman grain ships (2.34.4). The Greek dates corroborate the Roman structure: an Etruscan army in Latium after Tarquin's fall, broken by Latins and Greeks.

The last throw came through Tarquin's son-in-law Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, who led the Latins at Lake Regillus against the dictator Aulus Postumius; Mamilius fell and Tarquin was wounded (Livy 2.19–20). Postumius vowed a temple to Castor, dedicated in 484 (2.20.12, 2.42.5). Dionysius (6.13) adds that two horsemen of superhuman stature led the Roman charge and that evening watered their horses at the spring of Juturna in the Forum, announced the victory and vanished. A bronze plaque from Lavinium of about 500, dedicated to Castor and Pollux as kouroi (module 1.1), shows the cult was already in Latium.

Where sources disagree. Livy places the battle in 499 but notes that others put it in 496, Dionysius' year (Livy 2.21.3–4; Dionysius 6.2). Livy omits the epiphany, which Cicero (On the Nature of the Gods 2.6) and Plutarch (Coriolanus 3) know. The twins had already ridden for Locri at the river Sagra, the news of victory reaching Greece the same day (Justin 20.3): the Roman story fits a Greek template.

The documentary evidence

The first treaty with Carthage

Polybius (3.22) quotes a treaty dated to Lucius Junius Brutus and Marcus Horatius, "the first consuls after the expulsion of the kings", twenty-eight years before Xerxes crossed to Greece: 508/7. Writing some 350 years later, he worked from the bronze kept beside the Capitoline temple (3.26.1), in Latin so archaic that experts could barely construe it. Romans are not to sail beyond the Fair Promontory unless forced; trade in Libya and Sardinia requires a herald; Carthage must not harm Ardea, Antium, Laurentum, Circeii, Tarracina or other subject Latins, nor build a fort in Latium. The Republic had inherited the Tarquins' coastal hegemony intact.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (16.69) calls the treaty of 348, also in Livy (7.27.2), the first between Rome and Carthage, and Mommsen (Römische Chronologie, 1859) identified Polybius' text with it. Beaumont ("The Date of the First Treaty between Rome and Carthage", JRS 1939) and Cornell keep 509/8: Polybius saw the bronze, its language was archaic, and Antium and Tarracina as Roman dependants fit the sixth century, not the fourth. The early date is the majority view.

The Satricum stone

In 1977 Dutch excavators at Satricum in southern Latium found a stone reused in the foundations of the second temple of Mater Matuta, inscribed about 500 BC: the suodales of Poplios Valesios set it up to Mars (Mamartei) (Stibbe, Colonna, De Simone and Versnel, Lapis Satricanus, 1980). That he is Publicola is possible, not provable. The key word is suodales: companions bound to a leader, not a city. With the clan army of the Fabii at the Cremera in 477 (Livy 2.48–50) and the Vibenna brothers (module 1.5), it points to a world of warlords, in which 509 may have been one aristocratic following displacing another.

The Pyrgi tablets

The Pyrgi tablets (module 1.2) record about 500 BC that Thefarie Velianas dedicated a holy place to Uni, equated with Astarte, in the third year of his rule. The Phoenician calls him king over Caere; the Etruscan uses zilac, a magistrate's title. Superbus' neighbour and contemporary thus ruled in a form between king and magistrate, with Carthaginian ties public enough to inscribe, as Caere's alliance with Carthage at Alalia (Herodotus 1.166–167) would predict.

The consular lists

The magistrate lists in Livy, Dionysius, Diodorus and the Augustan Fasti Capitolini all begin with Brutus and Collatinus. Two items anchor them: Polybius' treaty, and the shrine of Concord dedicated by Cn. Flavius in 304, inscribed as built 204 years after the Capitoline dedication, again 508/7 (Pliny, Natural History 33.19). Livy (7.3.5–8) knew an archaic law making the praetor maximus drive a nail into the temple each September. Cornell argues the early lists are substantially authentic, since they contain families later plebeian that no patrician forger would have inserted; Beloch (Römische Geschichte, 1926) held them heavily interpolated. Whether the first magistrates were paired consuls or a praetor maximus with junior colleagues is uncertain.

Athens 510, Rome 509

Greek module 5.5 covers the fall of Hippias; here only the comparison. Pliny noted that the Athenian tyrannicide statues went up in the year Rome expelled its kings (Natural History 34.17).

FeatureAthensRome
Sexual outrage as triggerHipparchus insults Harmodius' sister (Thucydides 6.56)Sextus and Lucretia (Livy 1.58)
DelphiAlcmaeonids bribe the Pythia (Herodotus 5.63)Brutus' oracle (Livy 1.56)
Kinsman removed for the connectionHipparchus son of Charmus ostracised, 487Collatinus exiled for his name
Foreign attempts at restorationCleomenes, 508–506; Hippias at Marathon, 490Veii and Tarquinii; Porsenna; the Latins at Regillus
The exile's endHippias dies in Persian serviceTarquin dies at Cumae, 495
Liberators honouredTyrannicide statues in the AgoraBrutus' statue among the kings on the Capitol (Plutarch, Brutus 1)

Superbus also matches the Greek theory of the tyrant. Otanes' monarch violates women and kills men untried (Herodotus 3.80.5); Aristotle lists tyrannies overthrown for outrages against subjects, the Peisistratids included (Politics 1311a), and great building works as a device for keeping subjects poor and busy (1313b). Livy's king fulfils every item.

Where sources disagree. Gjerstad lowered the end of the monarchy to about 450 (module 1.5), and Alföldi argued that Fabius Pictor, writing in Greek for Greeks, shaped early Rome to Greek patterns. Cornell answers that the Greek colouring is literary but the date is anchored by the treaty and Flavius' inscription, and that the coincidence reflects a real wave of tyrannies across Greece and Etruria around 500. The best reading is a real event of 509–504 told in borrowed forms.

Lucretia as political myth

Livy's preface states the method: history sets every kind of exemplum on a monument, from which "you may choose for yourself and your state what to imitate" (praef. 10). Lucretia's last words name herself as one. The story makes a citizen wife's chastity the boundary of Roman liberty, and Livy repeats it for 449, when Verginius kills his daughter to save her from the decemvir Appius Claudius and the decemvirate falls (3.44–58; unit 3). Sandra Joshel ("The Body Female and the Body Politic", 1992) reads both as stories in which a woman must die so that men can act.

Augustine, writing after the sack of 410 and for Christian women raped in it, attacks the exemplum (City of God 1.19). He cites a declaimer, "there were two, and only one committed adultery", and sets the dilemma:

If adulterous, why praised? If chaste, why killed?

Chastity lives in the will (1.18); Lucretia, he argues, killed an innocent woman out of the Roman love of praise and fear of being thought complicit. Machiavelli returned the story to politics: Brutus was wise to feign folly (Discourses 3.2), and Tarquin lost his kingdom by breaking the laws, not through his son's crime (3.5).

Later artists choose between the private story and the public one. Shakespeare's The Rape of Lucrece (1594), 1,855 lines of rhyme royal dedicated to the Earl of Southampton, confines the politics to its prose Argument and last stanza, where the Romans consent "to Tarquin's everlasting banishment"; the poem itself is Tarquin's self-debate, Lucrece's complaints against Night, Opportunity and Time, and her long gaze at a painting of Troy. Titian's Tarquin and Lucretia (1571, Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge), painted for Philip II, isolates the assault without any civic frame. Botticelli's panel of about 1500 (Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, Boston) had placed her body in a forum with Brutus calling Rome to arms, a republican reading for Florence after the Medici fell in 1494. Britten's chamber opera The Rape of Lucretia (Glyndebourne, 1946; libretto by Ronald Duncan after André Obey) sets the story between a Male and a Female Chorus who comment as Christians and close by answering her death with Christ's: Augustine's frame, inside the opera.

Self-test

  1. Which elements of the Gabii story come from Herodotus, and what keeps the episode from being pure invention?
    Answer

    Sextus' false desertion copies Zopyrus at Babylon (Herodotus 3.153–158), and the poppy heads copy Thrasybulus' ears of corn (5.92). But Dionysius saw a treaty with Gabii on an ox-hide shield in the temple of Dius Fidius (4.58.4), so a real relationship lies behind the literary dress.

  2. How do Livy and Dionysius differ over where Lucretia died, and why does it matter?
    Answer

    Livy has her die at Collatia, so the revolt begins there before Brutus carries it to Rome (1.58–59). Dionysius has her drive to Rome and die in her father's house before leading citizens (4.66–67), making the revolution an urban, civic act from the start.

  3. What is Livy's definition of the new liberty, and how does the first year test it?
    Answer

    Liberty begins with annual consular power, not with any reduction of royal power (2.1.7). The year tests it through a consul exiled for his name, a father executing his sons, and Valerius demolishing his house and lowering the fasces to dispel suspicion of kingship.

  4. Give the two ancient explanations for Collatinus leaving office.
    Answer

    Livy 2.2: the people could not tolerate a Tarquinius in power, so he went for his name alone. Dionysius 5.9–12 and Plutarch, Publicola 7: he pleaded for his nephews the Aquilii after the conspiracy and was deposed.

  5. State three versions of Horatius' fate and one modern explanation of the legend.
    Answer

    Polybius 6.55: he drowns by choice; Livy 2.10: he swims to safety; Dionysius 5.24–25: he survives lamed. Either an aetiology of a statue later set in Vulcan's precinct (Gellius 4.5), or, for Dumézil, an inherited Indo-European one-eyed hero.

  6. What evidence suggests Porsenna actually took Rome?
    Answer

    Tacitus, Histories 3.72, speaks of the city surrendered to him; Pliny, Natural History 34.139, cites a treaty forbidding iron except in farming; Dionysius 5.35 has regalia sent to him; the formula for selling his goods (Livy 2.14.1) suggests booty.

  7. Why does Dionysius' account of Aristodemus matter for Roman history?
    Answer

    It comes from a Greek source independent of the annalists and dates the Etruscan defeat at Aricia to about 504, twenty years after Cumae's victory of 524 (7.5). It confirms an Etruscan campaign in Latium after Tarquin's fall and explains Tarquin's last refuge at Cumae.

  8. What are the arguments for dating Polybius' first treaty to 509/8 rather than 348?
    Answer

    Polybius dates it to Brutus and Horatius and worked from the bronze; its Latin was archaic; it treats Antium and Tarracina as Roman dependants, which fits before the fifth-century Volscian advance. Mommsen followed Diodorus 16.69 in preferring 348.

  9. Name three parallels between the fall of the Peisistratids and of the Tarquins, and the main argument against wholesale borrowing.
    Answer

    A sexual outrage as trigger, a Delphic role, and foreign attempts to restore the tyrant, who dies in exile under a foreign patron. Against borrowing: the date is anchored independently by Polybius' treaty and Flavius' inscription (Pliny, Natural History 33.19), and tyrannies were really falling across the region around 500 (Cornell).

  10. State Augustine's dilemma about Lucretia and the situation that prompted it.
    Answer

    If adulterous, why praised; if chaste, why killed (City of God 1.19)? He wrote after the sack of 410 for Christian women raped in it, arguing that chastity resides in the will and that Lucretia's suicide sprang from the Roman love of glory.

Carry forward

  1. The narrative of 509 is a literary construction, written about five centuries later and shaped by Greek models (Herodotus, the tyrant topos, the Dioscuri), yet a few documents (Polybius' treaty, Flavius' inscription, the Satricum stone, the Pyrgi tablets) anchor a real change around 509–504. Separate the frame from the anchors.
  2. The fall of the monarchy was a regional event: Porsenna, Aristodemus, the Latins and Carthage all had a hand in it, and the early Republic emerges in a Tyrrhenian world of tyrants and warlords with private followings, which the Fabii and Coriolanus of unit 3 continue.
  3. Lucretia and Brutus define Roman libertas as annual office, an inviolable citizen household and the state placed above family. The pattern of an outraged woman toppling a tyranny returns with Verginia in 449, and the myth was reused by Caesar's assassins, Augustine, Machiavelli and the Renaissance.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the fall of the Roman monarchy and the birth of the Republic. Cover: the story as Livy 1.53 to 2.15 and Dionysius tell it (Tarquinius Superbus' tyranny, Gabii and the poppy heads, the Sibylline Books, the embassy to Delphi and Brutus' feigned stupidity, the rape and suicide of Lucretia, the oath on the dagger, the expulsion, Brutus executing his own sons, Collatinus exiled for his name, Valerius Publicola, the battle of the Silva Arsia and Brutus' death); Porsenna of Clusium and the legends of resistance (Horatius at the bridge, Mucius Scaevola, Cloelia) against the alternative tradition that Porsenna actually took Rome (Tacitus, Histories 3.72; Pliny, Natural History 34.139); Aristodemus of Cumae and the battle of Aricia, and the Tarquins' last throw at Lake Regillus with the Dioscuri; the evidence: the first treaty with Carthage in Polybius 3.22 and its date, the Satricum stone naming the companions of Publius Valerius, the Pyrgi tablets and Thefarie Velianas of Caere as a parallel, the earliest consular lists; the parallels with the fall of the Peisistratids at Athens in 510 and whether they were borrowed; and Lucretia's afterlife as a political myth (Livy's preface on exempla, Augustine's critique in City of God 1.19, Shakespeare's The Rape of Lucrece, Titian, Britten's opera). Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 2 · The gods of Rome · 2.1 · 2,789 words

What Roman religion was

Religio, superstitio and the question of beliefThe pax deorum, do ut des and the vowRitual exactness and instauratioThe state as worshipperProdigies and their expiationVarro's three theologies and the gods without imagesOrigins: numen and the three functionsA people without myths?One activity: religion and politicsSelf-testCarry forward

Religio, superstitio and the question of belief

Latin had a word Greek lacked (Greek module 8.1), but religio did not name a faith. Its core sense is scruple: a felt obligation before what must be done or must not be touched. A day could carry religio; a tomb was religiosus, left to the gods below (Gaius, Institutes 2.4). Cicero's Stoic speaker claims that Romans surpass all peoples in religio, "that is, the worship of the gods" (On the Nature of the Gods 2.8).

The same speaker derives religiosi from relegere, to go over again, because they carefully retraced everything belonging to the gods' worship, and superstitiosi from those who prayed all day that their children might survive them (superstites) (2.72). Lactantius, a Christian, preferred religare, to bind (Divine Institutes 4.28). Superstitio was excess: fear of the gods beyond custom, private and anxious where religio was public and measured. Cicero ends On Divination urging that superstition be uprooted and religion kept (2.148–149); under the empire the word labels foreign cults (module 2.5).

Hence the claim that belief is the wrong question. No Roman assented to a creed; what was required was correct performance by the right person at the right time. John Scheid's title puts it: Quand faire, c'est croire (2005), when doing is believing. Beard, North and Price (Religions of Rome, 1998) call belief as an inner test of membership a Christian category read backwards.

Where sources disagree. Charles King (Classical Antiquity, 2003) and Denis Feeney reply that Romans held beliefs, only unsystematic ones that nobody policed. Cicero's pontiff Cotta says he must believe (credere) the ancestors even without a reason (On the Nature of the Gods 3.5–6). The issue is whether belief was ever the test, not whether it existed.

The pax deorum, do ut des and the vow

Public cult aimed at the pax deorum, the peace of the gods: a state of agreement in which they were well disposed to the community. Livy, writing some three and a half centuries later, says the lectisternium of 364 BC was held to secure it (7.2.2); plague, defeat or prodigy showed it broken, and ritual repaired it. The logic was reciprocal. Cicero's dialogue defines piety as justice towards the gods (On the Nature of the Gods 1.116):

Est enim pietas iustitia adversum deos.

Justice gives each his due; piety gives the gods theirs. Modern scholars call this do ut des, "I give so that you may give". Cato's farm prayers (On Agriculture 132, 139, 141) name the god, state the offering and attach the request "for the sake of this thing". The vow (votum) made the bargain conditional. The vower was voti reus, answerable; when the god delivered he was voti damnatus, condemned to pay like a debtor, and thousands of inscriptions end V.S.L.M., votum solvit libens merito, "paid the vow willingly and deservedly". After Trasimene in 217 BC, since the pontifex maximus ruled that it could not be vowed without them, the people voted a "sacred spring": every pig, sheep, goat and ox born that spring if the state survived five years, with clauses saving the vow if a beast was stolen, died or was offered on the wrong day (Livy 22.10).

Where sources disagree. Warde Fowler (The Religious Experience of the Roman People, 1911) and Kurt Latte (Römische Religionsgeschichte, 1960) read the contract as cold legalism that lost its hold on feeling and decayed in the late Republic. Beard, North and Price reject both coldness and decline, tracing the decline story to Christian polemic and Roman nostalgia. The contract was lopsided anyway: the human party was bound, the god free to refuse.

Ritual exactness and instauratio

A relationship founded on performance required exact performance. When the highest magistrates prayed, Pliny says, one man read the formula ahead from a text so that no word was skipped or misplaced, another checked it, a third ordered silence, and a flute-player drowned ill-omened sounds (Natural History 28.11). A god of uncertain identity was addressed "whether god or goddess" (Cato, On Agriculture 139).

A flawed rite was void and had to be done again: instauratio. If the dancer stopped, the flute-player fell silent, the boy with both parents living let go of the sacred cart, or the aedile slipped in a word or with the ladle, the games were not duly performed, and the gods were appeased by repeating them (Cicero, De haruspicum responso 23). Livy often records games repeated once, twice or more in a year; Plutarch knew of a sacrifice performed thirty times because faults kept appearing (Coriolanus 25.3). The sacred spring of 217, paid in 195, was judged improperly performed by the pontiffs and done again in 194 (Livy 33.44; 34.44). A flaw (vitium) in election auspices likewise forced magistrates to resign (below).

The state as worshipper

The religious actor that mattered was the Roman people. Sacra publica were rites performed at public expense for the people (Festus); households and clans had their own (module 2.4). Magistrates took the auspices before every public act, sacrificed, vowed and dedicated temples, presided at games and carried out expiations; the senate decided, with the priestly colleges as expert advisers (module 2.3). Priests were not a caste but senators, often the same men who held consulships; Cicero praised the ancestors for putting the same men in charge of the worship of the gods and the highest interests of the state (De domo sua 1). In the plague of 363 BC a dictator was appointed solely to drive a nail into the Capitoline temple (Livy 7.3). Neglect was a public fault: Gaius Flaminius left Rome in 217 without taking the auspices or pronouncing the vows on the Capitol (Livy 21.63), and after Trasimene the dictator Fabius told the senate that Flaminius had erred more by neglecting ceremonies and auspices than by rashness (22.9.7). Unlike the Greek city, whose priests belonged to sanctuaries (Greek module 8.1), Rome put the auspices in the hands of elected magistrates.

Where sources disagree. Beard, North and Price make the community the frame of Roman religion, as Sourvinou-Inwood's "polis religion" does for Greece. Andreas Bendlin (2000) and Jörg Rüpke (2016) reply that this marginalises individual choice, private vows, healing cults and magic, always present but less documented.

Prodigies and their expiation

A prodigy was an event against nature showing the pax deorum disturbed. It foretold no particular future; it demanded a remedy. Livy lists prodigies year by year, usually at the start of the consular year before the consuls left Rome: lightning on temples and walls, rains of stones, blood or milk, sweating statues, an ox that spoke, monstrous births. In the winter of 218/17 a six-month-old in the vegetable market shouted the triumphal cry, and an ox climbed to a third floor in the cattle market and threw itself down (21.62).

The procedure was public. Reports came from Rome and the Italian towns; the senate decided which to accept (suscipere); the pontiffs, the decemvirs with the Sibylline Books or Etruscan haruspices prescribed the remedy; the consuls performed it with full-grown victims, supplication at all the gods' couches, a lectisternium or a new cult (module 2.5). A rain of stones required nine days of rites, a rule Livy, writing some six centuries later, traces to Tullus Hostilius (1.31.4).

Livy reflects on his lists. The neglect that now makes men think the gods portend nothing, he says, has stopped prodigies being reported; but writing of old things his mind grows old-fashioned, and a scruple (religio) keeps him recording them (43.13.1–2). That year two were refused, one on private ground, one on foreign soil (43.13). Julius Obsequens, a late antique excerptor, extracted the lists into a Book of Prodigies that survives from 190 BC into Augustus' reign.

Where sources disagree. Bruce MacBain (Prodigy and Expiation, 1982) saw reports cluster in crises and allied prodigies expiated at Rome, and read the system as a way of binding Italy and managing senatorial tension. Veit Rosenberger (Gezähmte Götter, 1998) and Susanne Rasmussen (Public Portents in Republican Rome, 2003) see a working method for turning anxiety into prescribed action. Whether the thinner late Republican lists mean less fear or less recording is uncertain.

Varro's three theologies and the gods without images

Varro's Antiquities (module 0.1) is lost; its divine books survive in Augustine's City of God, books 4, 6 and 7, quoted for demolition. Varro put human things before divine because, as the painter precedes the painting, cities precede the rites they establish (6.4). His frame was a threefold theology (6.5). The mythical belonged to poets and theatre and was full of things unworthy of gods: births from heads and thighs, thefts, adulteries. The natural belonged to philosophers asking what the gods are, fire, numbers or atoms, a discussion for the schools, not the forum. The civil belonged to cities: what citizens and priests should know and do, which gods to worship publicly and with which rites. The pontifex maximus Quintus Mucius Scaevola had already distinguished the gods of poets, philosophers and statesmen, and thought it expedient for cities to be deceived in religion (4.27). Augustine replies that civil theology cannot be separated from mythical: the games were rites, and the gods of the temple were mocked on the stage (6.6–8).

Varro, writing some five centuries after the period, also claimed that Romans worshipped without images for over 170 years, that the gods would be worshipped more purely had this lasted, and that those who introduced images removed fear and added error (4.31). Plutarch, some eight centuries after Numa's supposed reign, credits him, in agreement with Pythagoras, with the ban (Numa 8). Counted from 753, the 170 years end about 583, under Tarquinius Priscus, to whom Pliny, citing Varro, assigns Vulca's terracotta Jupiter (module 1.5).

Where sources disagree. Warde Fowler and the numen school (below) read the imageless Rome as memory; it may instead be philosophy, echoing the Stoic and Pythagorean critiques of images that Varro and Plutarch share. Some cults did use objects instead of images: the flint of Jupiter Feretrius, the spears of Mars in the Regia, Vesta's fire, which Ovid says had no statue (Fasti 6.295–298). Whether these are remnants of a general rule or local peculiarities is uncertain.

Origins: numen and the three functions

The animism theory and its collapse

For much of the twentieth century the standard account began with numen. Warde Fowler, H. J. Rose ("Numen inest", 1935) and Hendrik Wagenvoort (Roman Dynamism, 1947) held that the earliest Romans worshipped impersonal powers in places, objects and acts, a Latin mana on the model of R. R. Marett's "pre-animism"; personal gods with images came later from Etruria and Greece. The evidence: Varro's 170 years, the aniconic cults, the "god or goddess" formula and swarms of functional gods. Servius' expanded commentary lists, from Fabius Pictor, twelve gods invoked at the sacrifice to Tellus and Ceres, one for each farming task from breaking the fallow to bringing grain out of store (on Georgics 1.21); Augustine mocks the door shared by Forculus, Cardea and Limentinus (City of God 4.8).

The theory collapsed on its key word. Numen comes from nuere, to nod; Varro glosses it as command, named from the nod (On the Latin Language 7.85). In Republican Latin it is almost always the numen of a named god, his expressed will; numen as a free-standing divinity is Augustan and later. Dumézil (La religion romaine archaïque, 1966; English 1970) pressed the linguistic case; anthropologists abandoned mana as a universal stage; and archaeology found anthropomorphic, Greek-influenced gods in sixth-century Latium, from the Sant'Omobono terracottas to a Lavinium bronze of about 500 BC dedicated to Castor and Pollux as qurois, Greek kouroi. The functional gods now look like pontifical classification, not fossils of a primitive mind.

Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus

Dumézil replaced primitive powers with an inheritance. Indo-European societies, he argued (Jupiter Mars Quirinus, 1941), thought through three functions: sovereignty, magical and juridical; force; and fertility, wealth and the people. At Rome he found them in a triad older than the Capitoline one (module 2.2). The three major flamines served Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus, ranked after the rex and before the pontifex maximus (Festus, under ordo sacerdotum); a law ascribed to Numa gave the first spoils of honour to Jupiter Feretrius, the second to Mars, the third to Quirinus (Plutarch, Marcellus 8; Festus, quoting the law, has Janus Quirinus); and the Umbrian Iguvine Tables name Jupiter, Mars and Vofionus, all called Grabovius (module 1.1).

Where sources disagree. Quirinus is the weak point: armed, god of the citizen body in its curiae, a "tranquil Mars" for Servius (on Aeneid 1.292), he fits the third function only by argument. Momigliano (History and Theory, 1984) objected that the system cannot be falsified and ignores Roman evidence that does not fit. Most historians accept an early grouping of the three gods while doubting the Indo-European ideology built on it.

A people without myths?

The old claim had an ancient root. Dionysius of Halicarnassus praises Romulus for rejecting Greek myths of castration, swallowed children and gods at war (Greek module 2.1): Roman gods are not wounded, chained or mourned (Roman Antiquities 2.18–19). Modern scholars from Rose to Latte made this a thesis: Rome had cult without stories and borrowed a mythology from Greece. The modern answers take four forms (module 0.1 gave the source problem and a first sketch of this debate).

  • Dumézil: the myths were turned into history. The one-eyed Horatius Cocles and the one-handed Mucius Scaevola answer to Odin and Tyr (Mitra-Varuna, 1940; module 1.6); the gods lost their stories and the city's past gained them.
  • Wiseman (The Myths of Rome, 2004): Rome had abundant myths, of Faunus and Picus, Hercules and Cacus, Remus and the Lupercalia, staged at the games from the fourth century and lost with the drama that carried them.
  • Feeney (Literature and Religion at Rome, 1998): the question assumes a Greek definition. Roman myth was entangled with Greek from the start, and literature was itself a religious voice; following Paul Veyne, Feeney argues that Romans kept the poet's gods and the cult's gods in separate compartments.
  • Beard, North and Price: myths were embedded in places and rituals, told as the origin of a festival or monument, and concerned the city more than the gods' private lives.

Varro's scheme explains the impression: myth was filed under the poets, so anyone looking for it in civil cult found none.

One activity: religion and politics

Because magistrates held the auspices, every assembly was also a rite. Lightning on the left, otherwise the best of omens, stopped an assembly, a rule Cicero says was made for the state's sake so that the leading men should interpret it (On Divination 2.74). An augur or magistrate could announce adverse signs (obnuntiatio) and dissolve the meeting; Cicero counts the augur's power to halt public business with the words "another day" among the greatest in the state (On the Laws 2.31). Flaws voided results: Tiberius Gracchus, the father, presiding as consul in 163 BC, later found from the augural books that he had erred in taking the auspices, and the consuls he had returned resigned (On the Nature of the Gods 2.10–11). Bibulus' sky-watching against Caesar in 59 was the same weapon at full stretch (module 5.4).

Cicero, augur from 53, theorised the system. On the Nature of the Gods (45 BC) sets the Epicurean Velleius and the Stoic Balbus against the Academic Cotta, himself a pontiff; Cicero warns that without piety, good faith, human society and justice may vanish (1.4), and ends finding the Stoic case nearer the likeness of truth (3.95). On Divination (44 BC) gives his brother Quintus the Stoic defence and himself the demolition, with Cato wondering that one haruspex could see another without laughing (2.51); yet augury is kept out of respect for popular opinion and its great service to the state (2.70).

Where sources disagree. Polybius thought Roman fear of the gods a device to control the masses and the cement of the state (6.56.6–12). Mary Beard ("Cicero and Divination", Journal of Roman Studies, 1986) and Malcolm Schofield in the same volume argue that On Divination is no confession of disbelief: the dialogue puts both cases in play and makes divination a subject of Latin rational argument. Manipulation, in any case, works only in a system others take seriously.

Self-test

  1. How did Cicero and Lactantius derive religio, and what does each derivation reveal about its author?
    Answer

    Cicero's Stoic derives it from relegere, to go over again, so religion is scrupulous attention to rites (On the Nature of the Gods 2.72); Lactantius from religare, to bind, so religion is a bond with God (Divine Institutes 4.28). The first is a Roman's religion of practice, the second a Christian's of relationship.

  2. Why do Scheid and Beard, North and Price call belief the wrong question, and what text best answers them?
    Answer

    Membership required correct performance, not assent to a creed, and belief as an inner test is a Christian category. Cotta's statement that he must believe the ancestors even without a reason (On the Nature of the Gods 3.5–6) shows that belief existed, though not as a test.

  3. What do voti reus and voti damnatus tell you about the logic of a vow?
    Answer

    The vower is bound once he vows, and when the god grants the request he is "condemned" to pay like a debtor. The vow is a conditional contract in which only the human party is obliged; V.S.L.M. inscriptions record the payment.

  4. What is instauratio, and why could a flawed rite not simply be accepted?
    Answer

    The repetition of a rite, often games, spoiled by a fault such as a dancer stopping or an aedile's slip (Cicero, De haruspicum responso 23). A rite was valid only if performed exactly, so a flawed one counted for nothing, as with the sacred spring repeated in 194 (Livy 34.44).

  5. Describe the path of a prodigy from report to expiation, and give Livy's reasons for refusing two.
    Answer

    Reported from Rome or Italy, accepted by the senate as public business, referred to pontiffs, decemvirs or haruspices, and expiated by the consuls with victims, supplications or new rites. In 169 one was refused because it happened on private ground, the other because it was on foreign soil (Livy 43.13).

  6. Name Varro's three theologies and state Augustine's objection to the scheme.
    Answer

    Mythical (the poets'), natural (the philosophers') and civil (the cities') (City of God 6.5). Augustine argues that civil theology cannot be separated from mythical, since the games were rites and the gods of the temple were the gods mocked on the stage (6.6–8).

  7. What did Varro claim about images, and why is the claim doubted?
    Answer

    That Rome worshipped without images for over 170 years and that images added error (City of God 4.31). It fits a Stoic and Pythagorean ideal of pure worship too well, and the aniconic cults (Jupiter's flint, Mars' spears, Vesta's fire) may be local peculiarities rather than relics of a general rule.

  8. What was the numen theory, and what linguistic fact undid it?
    Answer

    That the earliest Romans worshipped impersonal powers like mana before personal gods (Rose, Wagenvoort). Numen means the nod or will of a god (Varro, On the Latin Language 7.85) and in Republican Latin belongs to a named god; the free-standing numen is Augustan.

  9. What is the evidence for an archaic triad of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus, and where is Dumézil's reading weakest?
    Answer

    The three major flamines and their rank in the order of priests (Festus), the three grades of spoils of honour (Plutarch, Marcellus 8), and the Umbrian triad of the Iguvine Tables. Quirinus fits the function of fertility and the people only by argument, since he is also armed.

  10. Give two ways augury made elections religious events, and say how Cicero justifies keeping augury in On Divination.
    Answer

    Lightning or an announcement of adverse signs could halt an assembly, and a flaw in the presiding magistrate's auspices forced elected consuls to resign, as in 163 (On the Nature of the Gods 2.10–11). Cicero keeps augury out of respect for popular opinion and for its service to the state (On Divination 2.70).

Carry forward

  1. Roman religion is a relationship with the gods maintained by exact performance on behalf of the community: for any rite, ask who performed it, for whom, and whether it was done right, before asking what anyone believed.
  2. Religion and politics were one activity carried on by the same men under the same rules; every prodigy, vow and auspice in Livy or Cicero is also a political act, and manipulating the system presupposed that others took it seriously.
  3. Roman religion reaches us through systematisers and critics (Varro through Augustine, Livy's archaising lists) and through modern theories (numen, the three functions) that have risen and fallen; separate the attested practice from the frame laid over it.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the nature of Roman religion. Cover: religio and superstitio, and why 'belief' is the wrong question; the pax deorum and the contractual logic of do ut des, vows and their fulfilment; ritual exactness and instauratio, the repetition of a flawed rite; the state as the religious actor and magistrates as officiants; prodigies and their expiation as Livy records them year by year; Varro's three theologies (mythical, natural, civil) as Augustine preserves them in City of God book 6, and Varro's claim that Rome worshipped without images for 170 years; numen, the 'animism' theory and its collapse; Dumézil's three functions and the archaic triad of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus; the old claim that the Romans had no mythology of their own and the modern answers to it (Dumézil's myths turned into history, Wiseman's lost dramatic myths, Feeney's Literature and Religion at Rome, Beard, North and Price's Religions of Rome); and how religion and politics were one activity, from augury in elections to Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods and On Divination. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 2 · The gods of Rome · 2.2 · 3,377 words

The gods of Rome and their Greek doubles

Jupiter is not Zeus: names and layersThe Capitoline gods: Jupiter, Juno, MinervaMars, Quirinus and JanusHearth, seed and grain: Vesta, Saturn, CeresVenus, Apollo, Diana and MercuryNeptune, Vulcan, Hercules and the DioscuriThe system: triad, twelve and the lectisternium of 217Interpretatio graeca and interpretatio romanaGods with no Greek doubleSelf-testCarry forward

Jupiter is not Zeus: names and layers

Jupiter and Zeus are the same word: Iuppiter is *Dyeu-pater, "Father Sky", cognate with Greek Zeu pater and Sanskrit Dyaus pitar. Yet the Capitoline Jupiter had no succession myth, no amours and, in cult, no children. Each Roman god has two layers: an Italic power known from its name, priest, calendar day and cult titles, and a Greek identity added later, which brought images, genealogy and stories. Epithets are the best evidence of function. Temple dates before about 300 BC come from Livy and Dionysius, writing four to five centuries later. Greek module 2.2 profiles the Olympians themselves; module 2.1 covers the archaic triad of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus; module 2.3 the priests and festivals.

The Capitoline gods: Jupiter, Juno, Minerva

Jupiter

Origin and cult. The inherited sky father, guarantor of oaths: the fetial struck the victim with a flint, praying Jupiter to strike Rome likewise if it broke faith (Livy 1.24.8). The Ides of every month were his. The temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, "Best and Greatest", shared with Juno and Minerva, was begun by the Tarquins and dedicated in 509 by the consul M. Horatius (Livy 2.8.6–8, nearly five centuries later; Polybius 3.22.1 also links Horatius to it). Vulca of Veii made its terracotta image (Pliny, Natural History 35.157); the triumph ended at its steps, and its birthday, the Ides of September, carried the Ludi Romani.

Epithets. Feretrius, from ferre or ferire, to carry or to strike (Plutarch, Romulus 16), received the spolia opima, arms a Roman commander took from an enemy commander he had killed; Livy makes his shrine Romulus' foundation and Rome's first temple (1.10.5–7). Stator, "the stayer", halted the Romans' flight from the Sabines (Livy 1.12.3–6), but his temple was vowed by M. Atilius Regulus in 294 (10.36.11). Latiaris was the god of the Latin League on the Alban Mount, where the consuls had to celebrate the Latin Festival, which Dionysius ascribes to Tarquinius Superbus (4.49), before taking the field.

Greek double. Zeus matched at once and gave Jupiter a family: Saturn as father, Juno as wife, the amours Plautus staged in the Amphitruo. The match hid a civic god whose priest, the Flamen Dialis, lived under taboos no Greek priest knew (module 2.3).

Where sources disagree. All Livy's sources made A. Cornelius Cossus, the second winner of the spolia opima, a military tribune, yet Augustus told him the linen corselet in the temple named Cossus consul (4.20.5–11). Hermann Dessau (1906) tied the claim to Octavian's refusal of the honour to M. Licinius Crassus in 29 BC (Dio 51.24.4); Harriet Flower (2000) argued that the canonical three winners were themselves shaped by Marcellus' publicity after 222.

Juno

Origin. Italic, worshipped across Latium. The name is usually linked with iuven-, youthful vigour, as the woman's Juno answered the man's Genius (module 2.4). The Kalends were hers; her Etruscan form, Uni, is in module 1.2.

Epithets and cult. Regina, queen, shared the Capitol with Jupiter; a second Regina, called out of Veii, received an Aventine temple in 392 (Livy 5.31.3; module 2.5). Moneta had a temple on the Arx, dedicated in 344 on the site of M. Manlius' razed house (Livy 7.28.4–6), with the mint beside it: hence "money". Lucina, who brings the child into the light, had an Esquiline temple of 375 (Pliny, Natural History 16.235), whose birthday, 1 March, married women kept as the Matronalia. Sospita, saviour of Lanuvium, wore goatskin and carried spear and shield (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1.82); in 338 her cult was made common to Lanuvium and Rome (Livy 8.14.2).

Greek double. Hera, reached through Uni, brought marriage to Jupiter and a hatred of Troy that made Rome's queen goddess the enemy of its ancestors; Ennius had her reconciled to Rome in the Hannibalic war (Servius on Aeneid 1.281; deep dive module 12.6). Sospita and Moneta have no Hera behind them.

Where sources disagree. Cicero derives Moneta from monere, to warn, citing a voice from her temple before an earthquake (On Divination 1.101). Livius Andronicus, however, used Moneta to render Mnemosyne, Memory, and Andrew Meadows and Jonathan Williams (2001) read her as a goddess of remembrance, a fitting patron for coins as monuments.

Minerva

Origin and cult. Old Latin Menerva, from the root of mens: mind and skill. Her Quinquatrus of 19 March, named as the fifth day after the Ides, grew into a five-day feast of craftsmen, doctors and teachers (Ovid, Fasti 3.809–848). Her Aventine temple became the guild house of writers and actors in honour of Livius Andronicus' hymn of 207 (Festus, s.v. scribas).

Greek double. Athena came early, through Etruscan Menrva, who already wears the aegis on mirrors. The armour came with her; Roman cult stayed in the workshop.

Mars, Quirinus and Janus

Mars

Origin and cult. Archaic Mavors, Oscan Mamers, of unknown etymology: father of the twins (module 1.4) and lord of the month that opened the old year. His altar stood in the Campus Martius, outside the boundary, where the army mustered; his first temple, outside the Porta Capena, was dedicated in 388 (Livy 6.5.8). His festivals bracket the campaigning season, from the March horse races and Salian dances to the purification of arms on 19 October and the October Horse (module 2.3).

Greek double. Ares, the god Zeus calls most hateful (Greek module 2.2), was the worst of matches. Seated with Venus in 217, Ares' adultery became Rome's genealogy: the two parents of the nation through Romulus and Aeneas (Lucretius 1.31–40).

Where sources disagree. Cato's farmer asks Mars Pater to keep disease and storm from his fields and herds (On Agriculture 141). W. Warde Fowler (The Roman Festivals, 1899) took Mars for a farm god turned war god; Georges Dumézil (1966) read the prayer as a warrior guarding the boundary against enemies seen and unseen.

Quirinus

Origin and cult. The god of the Quirites, the citizen body, the name usually derived from *co-viria, "assembly of men", like curia; Ovid offered Sabine Cures or a Sabine word for spear (Fasti 2.475–480). L. Papirius Cursor dedicated his Quirinal temple in 293 (Livy 10.46.7). The Quirinalia fell on 17 February.

Greek double. None. Greeks glossed him as Enyalios (Dionysius 2.48; Polybius 3.25), and by Cicero's day he was the deified Romulus (On the Republic 2.20).

Janus

Origin and cult. From ianus, archway, and ianua, door: the god of passages and beginnings, named first in prayer (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.67), owner of January and of the Agonium of 9 January. His shrine was a gate, the Janus Geminus in the Forum, open in war and shut in peace (Livy 1.19.2–3; Res Gestae 13); C. Duilius added a temple after Mylae in 260 (Tacitus, Annals 2.49). His myth is in module 1.3.

Greek double. None, as he tells Ovid:

nam tibi par nullum Graecia numen habet (Fasti 1.90)

Hearth, seed and grain: Vesta, Saturn, Ceres

Vesta

Origin and cult. Perhaps cognate with Hestia. Her round Forum shrine, ascribed to Numa, kept the form of a hut, was no inaugurated templum (Gellius 14.7.7) and had no image, for the goddess was the fire (Ovid, Fasti 6.295–298). Its storeroom held the Palladium. The fire was renewed on 1 March; the Vestalia fell in June; the Vestals are module 2.3's.

Greek double. Hestia, a match so close it changed nothing, since neither had myths; Ovid had to borrow one for Vesta (Fasti 6.319–348).

Saturn

Origin and cult. A Latin sowing god to Varro (module 1.3 tells his myth), paired with Ops. His temple below the Capitol held the state treasury. Its image, filled with oil (Pliny, Natural History 15.32), had woollen bonds on its feet, loosed only at the Saturnalia of 17 December (Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.8), and he was worshipped in the Greek manner, head bare.

Greek double. Kronos, with the Golden Age and the Athenian Kronia, which Accius already called the Saturnalia's model (Macrobius 1.7.36–37). In 217 the Saturnalia was refounded with a public banquet (Livy 22.1.19–20). No Kronos kept a treasury.

Where sources disagree. Livy dates the dedication to 497 under the consuls Sempronius and Minucius (2.21.1–2); Varro, via Macrobius (1.8.1), credits Tarquinius Superbus and the dictator T. Larcius; Dionysius divides the honour (6.1.4). All wrote four or five centuries later and agree only on the years around 500.

Ceres, Liber and Libera

Origin and cult. Ceres, from the root of creare and crescere, had an Oscan form and a minor flamen; Liber was an Italic god of seed and wine, Libera his pair. A. Postumius vowed them a temple in a famine, on the Sibylline Books' advice, and Sp. Cassius dedicated it at the foot of the Aventine in 493 (Dionysius 6.17, 6.94, nearly five centuries later). Greek artists decorated it (Pliny, Natural History 35.154), and it became the plebeians' sanctuary and archive (Livy 3.55.7, 3.55.13). The Cerialia ran on 12–19 April, the Liberalia, when boys took the toga of manhood, on 17 March (module 2.4).

Greek double. Dionysius calls the three Demeter, Dionysus and Kore. A Greek rite of Ceres served by priestesses from Naples or Velia (Cicero, Pro Balbo 55) was apparently in place by 216 (Livy 22.56.4). Liber's double proved dangerous: the Bacchic cult of 186 was Dionysus outside the Aventine (module 2.5).

Where sources disagree. Cicero makes Libera Proserpina (Verrines 2.4.106); Ovid makes her Ariadne, renamed by Bacchus (Fasti 3.459–516). Whether the triad was Greek from the start or acquired Greek identities later is uncertain.

Venus, Apollo, Diana and Mercury

Venus

Origin and cult. First a common noun, "charm", akin to venerari, to worship, and venia, the gods' favour (Robert Schilling, La religion romaine de Vénus, 1954). Varro found no trace of her under the kings (Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.12); her early cult was Latin, at the federal sanctuary near Lavinium (Strabo 5.3.5). Rome's first temple, to Venus Obsequens (the epithet is Servius', on Aeneid 1.720), was paid for in 295 by fines on adulterous matrons (Livy 10.31.9). Venus of Eryx came to the Capitol by Sibylline order after Trasimene, vowed in 217 and dedicated in 215 (Livy 22.9.10, 23.31.9), and took over the Vinalia of 23 April; Caesar's Venus Genetrix followed in 46.

Greek double. Aphrodite, through Eryx and Aeneas (module 1.3), changed everything: a grace became a mother, Aeneadum genetrix (Lucretius 1.1).

Apollo

Origin and cult. None in Italy: Apollo is the one great god Rome never renamed. He came early, through Etruscan Aplu and Greek Cumae, source of the Sibylline Books (module 2.3). His temple in the Flaminian meadows was vowed in a plague in 433 and dedicated in 431 (Livy 4.25.3, 4.29.7); the Ludi Apollinares began in 212 (Livy 25.12).

Greek double. No pairing, only a narrowing. Rome's Apollo was long the healer, Apollo Medicus to the Vestals (Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.17.15); the god of music and poetry arrived with literature and with Augustus (module 6.2).

Diana

Origin and cult. Italic, from dius, bright: goddess of the wild margin, childbirth and slaves. Her grove at Aricia by Lake Nemi had a runaway slave as priest, who held office by killing his predecessor (Strabo 5.3.12). Servius Tullius, say Livy and Dionysius, founded her Aventine temple as a shrine of all the Latins (Livy 1.45.2–3; Dionysius 4.26), though Cato's list of the Latins who dedicated the Arician grove omits Rome. The temple's birthday, 13 August, was a slaves' holiday (Plutarch, Roman Questions 100).

Greek double. Artemis, through an Aventine image copied from the Ephesian Artemis of Massalia (Strabo 4.1.5), fixed by the couch shared with Apollo in 217.

Mercury

Origin and cult. From merx, merchandise: trade and nothing else, without flamen or old festival. His temple by the Circus Maximus was dedicated on 15 May 495 by a centurion, M. Laetorius, who was also put in charge of the grain supply and a merchants' guild (Livy 2.21.7, 2.27.5–6). On that day merchants sprinkled their goods from his spring and asked pardon for their lies (Ovid, Fasti 5.663–692).

Greek double. Hermes, probably from the start, adding messenger, guide of souls and patron of eloquence.

Neptune, Vulcan, Hercules and the Dioscuri

Neptune

Origin and cult. Italic, Etruscan Nethuns, of uncertain etymology. The Neptunalia of 23 July, kept in leafy shelters in the summer drought, suggests a god of springs before the sea. His one temple, by the Circus Flaminius, is attested from 206.

Greek double. Poseidon, matched by 217 at the latest, brought sea, trident and horse: Livy calls the Consualia a feast of Neptune Equester (1.9.6), and Sextus Pompeius styled himself Neptune's son.

Vulcan

Origin and cult. Volcanus had a minor flamen and an open precinct, the Volcanal, above the Comitium. He was fire as danger. At the Volcanalia of 23 August the people threw animals into the fire on their own behalf (Varro, On the Latin Language 6.20); live fish were given him in place of human lives (Festus, s.v. piscatorii ludi); and Vitruvius records the Etruscan rule that his temples stand outside the walls (1.7.1).

Greek double. Hephaestus, matched with him by 217, made a fire to be appeased into a smith with a forge, Cyclopes and the shield of Aeneas (Virgil, Aeneid 8).

Hercules

Origin and cult. Greek, through Etruscan Hercle; the Ara Maxima and its rite are in module 1.3; its feast fell on 12 August. Generals and merchants paid him a tithe of booty or profit, and Crassus feasted the people at ten thousand tables (Plutarch, Crassus 12). Temples multiplied: the round marble Hercules Victor in the Forum Boarium, Hercules of the Muses built by M. Fulvius Nobilior after 189.

Greek double. None needed. Rome added the invincible general's god and, later, the model of a man deified for his labours.

Castor and Pollux

Origin and cult. Greek, taken directly: a bronze plaque from Lavinium, of the sixth or early fifth century, dedicates an offering Castorei Podlouqueique qurois, to Castor and Pollux the kouroi. A. Postumius vowed them a temple at Lake Regillus, and his son dedicated it in the Forum in 484 (Livy 2.20.12, 2.42.5, nearly five centuries later). The epiphany at Juturna's spring and its Greek model at the Sagra are module 1.6's. The knights paraded past it every 15 July.

Greek double. They came as themselves; Rome made them patrons of its cavalry and gave the temple to one twin, as Bibulus complained (Suetonius, Julius 10.1). Women swore by Castor, men by Hercules (Gellius 11.6).

The system: triad, twelve and the lectisternium of 217

The Capitoline triad. Jupiter, Juno and Minerva shared one temple of three cellae, displacing the archaic triad of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus (module 2.1); an older shrine of the three stood on the Quirinal (Varro, On the Latin Language 5.158). Servius cites Etruscan doctrine that a proper city needed temples to the three (on Aeneid 1.422), and builders, image and temple form were Etruscan. Yet no Etruscan temple to Tinia, Uni and Menrva together is securely known (module 1.2), and Greece had no such trio: the triad may be Roman in Etruscan dress. Capitolia later rose in colonies and provincial cities from Cosa to Thugga.

Ennius' twelve. A couplet of Ennius' Annales, preserved by Apuleius (On the God of Socrates 2), fits twelve gods into two hexameters (fr. 240–241 Skutsch):

Iuno Vesta Minerva Ceres Diana Venus Mars / Mercurius Iovis Neptunus Volcanus Apollo

Varro knew them as the twelve Di Consentes, whose gilded statues, six male and six female, stood in the Forum (On Agriculture 1.1.4); their portico was restored in AD 367 by the pagan prefect Praetextatus.

The lectisternium. A lectisternium set couches and a meal before images of the gods, like the Greek theoxenia. The first, in a plague of 399, honoured three pairs: Apollo and Latona, Hercules and Diana, Mercury and Neptune (Livy 5.13.5–8). After Trasimene in 217 the Sibylline Books prescribed six couches for Ennius' twelve (Livy 22.10.9):

Roman godGreek doubleCouch-mate in 217First cult place at Rome
JupiterZeusJunoCapitol, 509
JunoHeraJupiterCapitol, 509
NeptunePoseidonMinervaCircus Flaminius, by 206
MinervaAthenaNeptuneCapitol, 509
MarsAresVenusCampus Martius altar; temple 388
VenusAphroditeMarsObsequens, 295
ApolloApolloDianaFlaminian meadows, 431
DianaArtemisApolloAventine, ascribed to Servius Tullius
VulcanHephaestusVestaVolcanal, ascribed to Romulus
VestaHestiaVulcanForum, ascribed to Numa
MercuryHermesCeresCircus Maximus, 495
CeresDemeterMercuryAventine, 493

The pairs follow Greek myth, not Roman cult: spouses, the rivals for Attica, the lovers of Odyssey 8, the twins, the two fires; only Mercury and Ceres, trade and grain, look Roman. The same consultation vowed a temple to Mens, Right Thinking, beside Venus Erycina's. In 217 the state's priests seated Rome's gods as Greek couples.

Where sources disagree. Varro's Forum statues and the Etruscan council gods that Arnobius calls Consentes (Against the Nations 3.40) suggest an older Italian twelve, so 217 may have formalised rather than invented. Rome's list also has Vesta and not Liber, the Hestia version of Greek module 2.2 rather than the Parthenon's, and its model is uncertain.

Interpretatio graeca and interpretatio romana

The modern phrase interpretatio graeca, formed on Tacitus' interpretatio romana, names an old habit of reading foreign gods under one's own names. Herodotus made Amun Zeus (2.42); Polybius and Dionysius wrote Zeus for Jupiter. Romans did it to themselves when they began to write: Livius Andronicus' Latin Odyssey turned the Muse into a Camena and Moira into Morta (Gellius 3.16.11). The equation transferred what Roman cult lacked: Greek images, genealogies, marriages, myths. It left the priest, the day and the rite alone, so Rome had gods of the pontiffs and gods of the poets under one set of names, which Varro's three theologies tried to keep apart (module 2.1). It also hid functions with no Greek match: Sospita's goatskin, Vulcan as mere fire, Diana of slaves.

Turned outward, the habit became interpretatio romana. Tacitus says that by Roman interpretation the twin gods of the Naharvali are Castor and Pollux, though they are called Alcis (Germania 43); Caesar gives the Gauls Mercury, Apollo, Mars, Jupiter and Minerva (Gallic War 6.17). In the provinces the double name became the cult: Sulis Minerva at Bath, Mars Lenus at Trier.

Where sources disagree. Georg Wissowa (1916) treated interpretatio Romana as Roman names laid over native gods. Jan Assmann (Moses the Egyptian, 1997) saw translatability as a premise of ancient polytheism, which took gods to be the same cosmic powers everywhere. Clifford Ando (2005) stresses how provisional Roman equations were: Tacitus offers a reading and keeps the native name.

Gods with no Greek double

Janus and Quirinus are profiled above. Three more show what Rome kept for itself.

Terminus. The boundary stone as god, honoured at the Terminalia on 23 February (Ovid, Fasti 2.639–684). When Tarquin cleared the Capitol, the birds allowed every shrine to be moved except his (Livy 1.55.3–4), so his stone stayed inside Jupiter's temple under a hole in the roof (Ovid, Fasti 2.667–672): a sign, Romans said, that their frontiers would never retreat.

Bellona. Old Latin Duellona, war itself. Ap. Claudius Caecus vowed her temple in battle in 296 (Livy 10.19.17). It stood outside the boundary, so the Senate met there with envoys and with generals seeking triumphs, and before it a fetial threw the spear that opened a war (Ovid, Fasti 6.205–208). Greek Enyo was a name more than a cult; when Romans met the Cappadocian goddess Ma they called her Bellona, and Plutarch could not decide whether she was Selene, Athena or Enyo (Sulla 9).

Fides. Good faith, which bound treaties, clients and those who surrendered into Rome's fides. Numa, Livy says, had the flamens sacrifice to her with the right hand wrapped (1.21.4). Her temple stood beside Jupiter's on the Capitol, built by A. Atilius Calatinus and rebuilt by M. Aemilius Scaurus (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.61). Greek Pistis had almost no cult.

The gods without doubles guard the community's procedures: the gate, the citizen body, the boundary, the declaration of war, the sworn word.

Self-test

  1. In what sense is Jupiter the same god as Zeus, and in what sense is he not?
    Answer

    Both names descend from *Dyeu-pater, the Indo-European sky father. But Roman cult gave Jupiter no succession myth, amours or children; he was a god of Roman places and offices (the Capitol, the spolia opima, the Latin Festival, the fetial oath), and his Greek family came later through literature.

  2. What do the titles Regina, Moneta, Lucina and Sospita tell you about Juno, and which least resembles Hera?
    Answer

    Queenship beside Jupiter, warning or memory (and later the mint), childbirth, and armed protection of Lanuvium. Sospita, in goatskin with spear and shield (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1.82), has no Hera behind her.

  3. Why is the temple of Saturn a good example of the problem of early foundation dates?
    Answer

    Livy gives a dedication by the consuls of 497 (2.21.1–2), Varro via Macrobius gives Tarquinius Superbus and the dictator Larcius (1.8.1), and Dionysius divides the credit. All wrote four or five centuries later and agree only on the years around 500.

  4. What happened at the lectisternium of 217, and why does it mark the official pairing of the Greek twelve?
    Answer

    After Trasimene the Sibylline Books prescribed a banquet for twelve gods on six couches (Livy 22.10.9): Jupiter and Juno, Neptune and Minerva, Mars and Venus, Apollo and Diana, Vulcan and Vesta, Mercury and Ceres. The state's priests arranged Rome's gods as Greek mythological couples.

  5. How does the lectisternium of 399 differ from that of 217?
    Answer

    In 399 three couches held Apollo and Latona, Hercules and Diana, Mercury and Neptune (Livy 5.13.5–8), an ad hoc appeal to Greek-friendly gods in a plague. In 217 the full twelve were seated as a system, matching Ennius' list.

  6. Why was Ares a poor double for Mars, and what did the pairing produce?
    Answer

    Ares was despised in Greek myth, while Mars was father of Romulus and guardian of army and fields (Cato, On Agriculture 141). Seated with Venus in 217, the Odyssean adultery became the parentage of the Roman people, celebrated by Lucretius (1.31–40).

  7. What did Rome first want from Apollo, and what is unusual about his name?
    Answer

    Healing: his first temple was vowed in a plague of 433 (Livy 4.25.3), and the Vestals invoked him as Apollo Medicus (Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.17.15). He is the one great god Rome never renamed, since no Italic god matched him.

  8. What does the Lavinium plaque to Castor and Pollux show, and how does it bear on the Regillus story?
    Answer

    It names the twins and calls them qurois, kouroi, in archaic Latin, so their cult reached Latium directly from Greeks by about 500 BC. That makes Postumius' vow plausible, though the epiphany at Juturna's spring (Dionysius 6.13) may be borrowed from the Sagra (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.6).

  9. What is the difference between interpretatio graeca and interpretatio romana, and what does Tacitus' Naharvali passage show?
    Answer

    The first reads foreign gods, Rome's included, by Greek names; the second reads foreign gods by Roman names. Tacitus calls the twins Castor and Pollux by Roman interpretation yet records their native name, Alcis (Germania 43): a reading, not a claim of identity.

  10. Name three gods with no Greek double and say what they have in common.
    Answer

    Any three of Janus, Quirinus, Terminus, Bellona and Fides. They govern the community's procedures (thresholds, the citizen body, boundaries, the declaration of war, the sworn word), for which Greek myth had no figures.

Carry forward

  1. Every Roman god has two layers: an Italic cult (priest, calendar day, epithet, place) and a Greek identity (image, family, myth). Read cult evidence for function and literature for the overlay, and never assume one tells you the other.
  2. The equation was a dated process, not a fact of nature: some gods arrived already Greek (Apollo, Hercules, Castor), others were matched by stages through Etruria, Cumae, Sicily and the poets, and 217 is the year the state seated its twelve as Greek couples.
  3. Interpretatio joins and hides at once. The gods with no double (Janus, Terminus, Fides) or a bad one (Mars, Venus, Vulcan) mark what was specifically Roman, and the same habit turned outward built the double-named pantheons of the provinces.
