ROME · UNIT 2 · The gods of Rome · 2.3 · 2,864 words

Priests, augury and the calendar

Priests without a priestly casteThe king's heirs: rex sacrorum, pontifex maximus, flaminesThe Vestal VirginsThe brotherhoods: Salii, Arvals, Luperci, fetialsAugury and the auspicesHaruspices in Roman serviceThe calendar from Romulus to CaesarA year of festivals, and how to read OvidSelf-testCarry forward

Priests without a priestly caste

Rome had no clergy. Its senior priests were senators holding a priesthood for life beside their magistracies: Caesar was pontifex maximus while consul, Cicero an augur from 53 BC. Priests advised; the Senate decided and magistrates acted (module 2.1). Tradition, written down five to seven centuries later, gave nearly every priesthood to Numa (Livy 1.20; module 1.5), but the colleges grew with the governing class.

CollegeSizeCharge
Pontifices4; 8 from 300 BC (Livy 10.6–9); 15 under Sullasacred law, calendar, burial, adoption, the annual record (module 0.1)
Augures4; 9 from 300 BC; 15 under Sullalaw of signs, inauguration, rulings on flawed auspices
Viri sacris faciundis2; 10 from 367 BC, half plebeian (Livy 6.42.2); later 15the Sibylline Books; cults performed by Greek rite
Epulones3 from 196 BC (Livy 33.42.1); later 7the feast of Jupiter at the games, taken over from the pontiffs

These were the "four most ample colleges" of the Res Gestae (9.1). They co-opted their members until 104 BC, when the tribune Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus gave the choice to seventeen of the thirty-five tribes drawn by lot, a minority so that the people did not formally confer a sacred office (Cicero, De lege agraria 2.18); the college then co-opted the winner. Sulla abolished the law; Labienus restored it in 63 BC (Dio 37.37.1), and Caesar was at once elected pontifex maximus. Tenure was for life: even a convicted augur kept his office (Plutarch, Roman Questions 99).

The Sibylline Books, bought by a Tarquin in the story of module 1.6, lay under the Capitoline temple and were opened only on the Senate's decree; the cults they prescribed (the Magna Mater of module 2.5) were performed by Greek rite. Burned with the temple in 83 BC, they were replaced from Erythrae and elsewhere (Tacitus, Annals 6.12), and Augustus shut the purged collection under the base of Palatine Apollo (Suetonius, Augustus 31.1).

The king's heirs: rex sacrorum, pontifex maximus, flamines

The pontifical college also held the rex sacrorum, fifteen flamines and the Vestals, all under the pontifex maximus, who lived in the domus publica beside the Regia. Festus' order of precedence (s.v. ordo sacerdotum) seats the rex first, the flamines of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus next, the pontifex maximus fifth. Power ran the other way. Module 1.5 introduced the rex as the king's substitute (Livy 2.2.1–2); his duties show what kingship had been. On the Kalends a junior pontiff watched for the new moon and called out (calare, hence Kalendae) the days to the Nones; on the Nones the rex proclaimed the month's festivals (Varro, On the Latin Language 6.27–28). The king had kept the city's time. Barred from office and from addressing the people, the rex sacrificed in the Comitium and then fled the Forum (Plutarch, Roman Questions 63). Athens kept a sacral king too, the archon basileus of Greek module 8.1, but as an annual magistrate. Nobody ambitious wanted the Roman post: in 180 BC Lucius Cornelius Dolabella preferred a fine to resigning a naval command for it (Livy 40.42).

Each flamen served one god: three major and patrician (Dialis, Martialis, Quirinalis: Dumézil's triad, module 2.1), twelve minor. Livy has Numa create the Flamen Dialis so that the king's rites would not lapse while kings were at war (1.20.1–2). Gellius 10.15, citing Fabius Pictor among others, lists his rules. He might not ride a horse, see an army in battle array or swear an oath; he wore no knot and no ring unless pierced; a man in chains entering his house was freed and the fetters drawn up through the roof opening and let down into the street. He might not touch or name a she-goat, raw meat, ivy or beans, never went outdoors without his cap, and every day was a holy day for him. Plutarch calls him an animate and sacred image (Roman Questions 111). The cost was political: after Lucius Cornelius Merula killed himself in 87 BC the post stood empty; the young Caesar was designated and then removed by Sulla (Suetonius, Julius 1), and Augustus filled it only in 11 BC (Dio 54.36.1).

The Vestal Virgins

Six Vestals kept the fire in Vesta's round temple beside the Regia, where there was no image: Vesta is "nothing but living flame" (Ovid, Fasti 6.291). Gellius (1.12), citing the jurists Labeo and Capito, gives the rules of selection: a girl of six to ten, both parents living, without defect of body, speech or hearing. The pontifex maximus took her from her father with the words te, Amata, capio (1.12.14); she left her father's power without emancipation and could make a will. She served thirty years, ten learning, ten performing, ten teaching (Dionysius 2.67.2).

The Vestals renewed the fire each 1 March, made the salted meal sprinkled on public victims, and guarded a store that included the Palladium (Livy 26.27.14). Their privileges were a man's: a lictor, testimony without oath, custody of wills (Suetonius, Julius 83.1), the power to save a condemned man met by chance (Plutarch, Numa 10; Gellius 10.15.31 for the oath). If the fire went out, the pontifex maximus flogged the Vestal responsible (Livy 28.11.6). An unchaste Vestal was carried in a closed litter through a silent Forum to the Colline Gate and sealed in an underground chamber with a lamp and a little food (Plutarch, Numa 10; Dionysius 2.67); her lover was flogged to death. Ovid explains that she is given to the Earth she violated, Earth and Vesta being one (Fasti 6.457–460). Livy records Opimia and Floronia after Cannae (22.57.2–3); under Domitian the chief Vestal Cornelia went down protesting her innocence (Pliny, Letters 4.11).

Where sources disagree. Mary Beard (Journal of Roman Studies 1980) read the Vestal as ambiguous by design, at once virgin, matron and almost male; she later retreated from that scheme (1995). Holt Parker (American Journal of Philology 2004) argued that her intact body stood for the city's, so that trials cluster in crises such as 216 and 114 BC. Pliny would not say whether Cornelia was guilty, "I do not know whether she was innocent, but she was certainly led out as if innocent" (4.11.9), and made her burial Domitian's theatre; Suetonius (Domitian 8.3–4) presents a strict emperor restoring discipline.

The brotherhoods: Salii, Arvals, Luperci, fetials

The Salii were two companies of twelve patricians: the Palatine Salii of Mars, ascribed to Numa (Livy 1.20.4), and the Colline Salii of Quirinus, vowed by Tullus Hostilius (1.27.7). In March and again in October they danced through the city in bronze breastplates, beating figure-of-eight shields (ancilia); one had fallen from heaven, and Mamurius made eleven copies so that no thief could find it (Ovid, Fasti 3.259–392). Their hymn was barely understood by its own priests (Quintilian 1.6.40), yet in 29 BC the Senate had Octavian's name inserted into it (Res Gestae 10.1; Dio 51.20.1). The two outings frame the season of war.

The Arval Brothers, twelve senators, worshipped Dea Dia in a grove on the Via Campana. Augustus refounded them, and their minutes were cut on marble there from 21 BC to AD 304: co-optations, the May festival, vows for the emperor's safety each 3 January, sacrifices for accessions and foiled conspiracies, expiations whenever iron entered the grove. The entry for AD 218 preserves the hymn they danced, read from booklets, beginning enos Lases iuvate, "help us, Lares" (CIL VI 2104). John Scheid (Romulus et ses frères, 1990) used the records to show an archaic rite turned into a register of loyalty to the dynasty. The Luperci, two companies joined by the Iuliani in Caesar's honour in 44 BC (Suetonius, Julius 76.1), were to Cicero "a wild brotherhood, plainly pastoral and rustic" (Pro Caelio 26).

The fetials handled dealings with other peoples. In Livy's procedure (1.32.5–14), set down some six centuries after Ancus' supposed reign, the envoy calls Jupiter and the boundaries to witness at the frontier and demands restitution. If nothing is returned within thirty-three days and the Senate votes for war, a fetial throws a spear tipped with iron, or of fire-hardened cornel stained with blood, into enemy land before at least three adult witnesses. Treaties were struck by killing a pig with a flint (1.24.7–8). For distant enemies a column before Bellona's temple stood in for the frontier (Ovid, Fasti 6.205–208); Octavian threw the spear there against Cleopatra in 32 BC (Dio 50.4.5). The rite's place in decisions for war is module 4.4.

Where sources disagree. Livy gives the fetial law to Ancus Marcius (1.32.5), Dionysius to Numa (2.72), Cicero to Tullus Hostilius (On the Republic 2.31). Thomas Wiedemann (Classical Quarterly 1986) argued that the spear at Bellona's column was Octavian's antiquarian revival, and John Rich (1976) that ordinary envoys made the demands in the middle Republic; Alan Watson (International Law in Archaic Rome, 1993) took Livy's formulae for archaic law.

Augury and the auspices

The auspices, literally "bird-watching", belonged to the magistrates: a consul took them before every assembly, levy or battle. The augurs held the law of signs, inaugurated priests and places, and ruled whether a fault (vitium) had occurred; an augur's alio die, "on another day", could dissolve an assembly (Cicero, On the Laws 2.31). Its political use is module 2.1. Signs were sought or sent unasked; Festus lists five kinds, from the sky, birds, feeding chickens, four-footed animals and ill-omened accidents. Left was lucky for a Roman augur, right for a Greek (Cicero, On Divination 2.82). A templum was not a building but a space marked out by spoken formula (Varro, On the Latin Language 7.6–9); the Senate could decree validly only in one (Gellius 14.7.7), and Vesta's shrine was not one (Servius on Aeneid 7.153).

In the field generals consulted caged chickens: if they ate so greedily that grain fell from their beaks, the sign was perfect, and Cicero objected that hungry birds always eat (On Divination 2.71–74). At Aquilonia in 293 BC the keeper reported a good sign the birds had not given; Papirius Cursor said a false report fell on the reporter and put him in the front line, where a spear killed him (Livy 10.40). The sign was what was announced. In 249 BC Publius Claudius Pulcher, told before Drepana (module 4.2) that the chickens would not eat, threw them overboard: "let them drink, since they will not eat" (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.7). He lost most of his fleet and was tried.

Where sources disagree. Polybius, writing about a century after Drepana, blames Claudius' rashness and says nothing of chickens (1.49–52). The story appears in Cicero, two centuries on, then in Livy (Periochae 19), Valerius Maximus 1.4.3 and Suetonius (Tiberius 2.2), where it marks the arrogance of the Claudii. Whether it was invented to explain the defeat, or omitted by a Greek who thought Roman religion a device for managing the crowd (Polybius 6.56), is uncertain.

Haruspices in Roman service

The haruspices were Etruscan experts, not a Roman priesthood; their discipline is module 1.2. The Senate summoned them to read prodigies, and Romans argued back. In 163 BC, when the man reporting the first century's vote dropped dead at the consular elections, they declared the presiding consul, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, improper; he called them Etruscan barbarians, then found in his augural books that he had indeed erred, and the consuls of 162 resigned (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.10–11). Roman augural law decided; the outsiders were merely right. In 56 BC a reply blaming polluted sacred places became Clodius' weapon against Cicero's house, answered in De haruspicum responso.

The calendar from Romulus to Caesar

How Roman years convert into ours is module 0.3; here the calendar is a religious instrument. Writers of six to ten centuries later gave Romulus ten months, March to December, 304 days (Censorinus, De die natali 20.2–3; Ovid, Fasti 1.27–44), which is why September to December are the seventh to tenth. Numa added January and February and set the months by the moon, with intercalation (Livy 1.19.6). The republican year had 355 days, in months of 29 or 31, odd numbers being lucky, and a February of 28. Days were counted back from the Kalends, Nones and Ides; an eight-day market cycle ran alongside, and each day was marked F if legal business was allowed, N if not, C if assemblies could meet.

Every second year the pontiffs inserted a month of 22 or 23 days after 23 February, and they granted or refused it for political favour (Censorinus 20.7; Suetonius, Julius 40.1): Curio, tribune in 50 BC, went over to Caesar when refused one (Caelius in Cicero, Letters to Friends 8.6.5). By 46 BC the calendar ran about three months ahead of the sun. Caesar, pontifex maximus, advised by the astronomer Sosigenes (Pliny, Natural History 18.211), gave 46 BC 445 days, then from 1 January 45 BC a year of 365 with a leap day every fourth year. The pontiffs miscounted, intercalating every third year, until Augustus suspended leap years (Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.14.13–15). The system ran until 1582.

One pre-Julian calendar survives: the Fasti Antiates Maiores, painted on plaster between 84 and 55 BC, found at Antium in 1915 and now in the Palazzo Massimo. Thirteen columns give the twelve months and the intercalary month, with market letters, day marks, the old festivals in large capitals and later temple anniversaries in small letters. The forty or so other surviving calendars, Verrius Flaccus' at Praeneste among them (module 0.1), are Julian.

Where sources disagree. Censorinus reports that Licinius Macer and Fenestella gave Rome twelve months from the start, against Junius Gracchanus, Fulvius Nobilior and Varro, whom he follows (20.2); Tuditanus and Cassius Hemina credited intercalation to the decemvirs, not Numa (Macrobius 1.13.21). Agnes Kirsopp Michels (The Calendar of the Roman Republic, 1967) dated the republican calendar to the decemvirs; Jörg Rüpke (The Roman Calendar from Numa to Constantine, 2011) ties the written calendar to Gnaeus Flavius' posting of the fasti in 304 BC (Livy 9.46.5). A 304-day year may be an antiquarian inference from the month names.

A year of festivals, and how to read Ovid

FestivalDateWhat was doneMain sources
Lupercalia15 Februarygoats and a dog killed at the Lupercal; Luperci in goatskins run striking women with thongs for fertilityOvid, Fasti 2.267–452; Plutarch, Romulus 21
Parilia21 Aprilshepherds' feast of Pales: flocks purified with smoke, leaps over burning straw; later Rome's birthdayFasti 4.721–862
Vestalia9 Junematrons barefoot to the temple; millers' donkeys garlanded; on 15 June the temple swept and the refuse taken to the TiberFasti 6.249–468
Consualia21 August, 15 DecemberConsus' buried altar in the Circus uncovered; races; horses and mules garlanded and rested; the Sabine women seizedLivy 1.9.6; Dionysius 2.31
October Horse15 Octoberright-hand horse of the winning chariot speared to Mars; Sacra Via and Subura fight for the head; the tail's blood dripped on the Regia's hearthFestus, s.v. October equus; Plutarch, Roman Questions 97
Saturnalia17 December, later longersacrifice and public banquet at Saturn's temple; slaves feast with masters; gifts of candles and figurinesLivy 22.1.19–20; Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.7–10

The priests tied the year together. The Vestals made the Parilia's smoke from the ash of unborn calves, the blood of the October Horse and bean-straw (Fasti 4.731–734): Mars' autumn victim purified the shepherds' spring. Festivals also changed. The Saturnalia was reorganised in 217 BC with the shout io Saturnalia (Livy 22.1.19–20), and the Lupercalia lasted until Pope Gelasius protested around AD 495. Athens' great festivals centred on contests in which citizens competed (Greek modules 8.1 and 8.3); Rome's games, most added during the Republic, were shows that citizens watched.

Ovid's Fasti, written about AD 2–8 and revised in exile (module 6.3), is the one sustained ancient guide, and it sets traps. It covers only January to June, so the Consualia, October Horse and Saturnalia come from Varro, Festus, Plutarch and Macrobius. It is late and Augustan, the new dates crowding the old. It multiplies causes: for the Lupercalia Ovid offers Arcadian Pan, Faunus tricked in the tale of Hercules and Omphale, Romulus and Remus chasing rustlers, and a Juno oracle on fertility, learned display on the model of Callimachus' Aitia. It historicises: the Regifugium becomes Tarquin's expulsion (2.685–852), though the rite was the rex sacrorum's flight. And its witness may be a persona when Ovid says he carried the purifying ash himself (4.725–728). Trust the actions, dates and materials over the reasons.

Where sources disagree. Timaeus explained the October Horse as revenge for the Trojan horse, and Polybius mocked him (12.4b). James Frazer, who edited the Fasti (1929), mined it for primitive agrarian magic, the horse as corn-spirit; Georges Dumézil compared it to the Vedic royal horse sacrifice. Mary Beard ("A complex of times", Proceedings of the Cambridge Philological Society 1987) replied that festivals had no single original meaning: the Parilia, a shepherds' rite turned Rome's birthday, was reinterpreted in every generation, and Ovid records one stage, not the origin.

Self-test

  1. Why is it misleading to speak of a Roman clergy, and how were members of the great colleges chosen by the late Republic?
    Answer

    Priests were senators holding a priesthood for life beside magistracies; they advised while the Senate decided and magistrates acted. Co-optation gave way in 104 BC to election by seventeen of thirty-five tribes chosen by lot, followed by formal co-optation; Sulla abolished this and Labienus restored it in 63 BC, when Caesar won the office of pontifex maximus.

  2. In what sense is the rex sacrorum the king's religious ghost?
    Answer

    He ranked first in Festus' order of precedence and kept the king's time-keeping rites, proclaiming each month's festivals on the Nones and fleeing the Comitium after his sacrifice (Plutarch, Roman Questions 63). But he was barred from office and from speaking to the people, and real authority lay with the pontifex maximus; Dolabella in 180 BC preferred a fine to the post (Livy 40.42).

  3. What do the Flamen Dialis' taboos have in common, and what did they cost the state?
    Answer

    They keep him free of every bond (knots, closed rings, chains), of war (horses, armies) and of oaths, and bind him to his god every day of the year (Gellius 10.15). He could not command or swear the magistrate's oath, so the post was hard to combine with a career and stood empty from 87 to 11 BC.

  4. How did a Vestal's legal position differ from that of other Roman women, and how has it been read?
    Answer

    She left her father's power without emancipation, could make a will, had a lictor and testified without oath (Gellius 1.12; Plutarch, Numa 10). Beard read this mix of virgin, matron and male privilege as a deliberately ambiguous status, a reading she later qualified.

  5. Why, on Parker's argument, do Vestal trials cluster in years of crisis?
    Answer

    Because the Vestal's intact body stood for the city's integrity, so a disaster such as Cannae in 216 BC prompted a search for her violation, with live burial as the repair. Pliny's doubts about Cornelia under Domitian show such trials could also be political theatre.

  6. Describe the fetial declaration of war and the modern doubts about it.
    Answer

    Demands at the frontier with Jupiter as witness, thirty-three days' grace, then a bloodied spear thrown into enemy land before three witnesses (Livy 1.32.5–14), later at Bellona's column, as Octavian did in 32 BC. Wiedemann thought that version an Augustan revival and Rich that envoys did the work in the middle Republic; Watson defended the formulae as archaic.

  7. Distinguish the auspices from augury, and explain what the Aquilonia episode shows.
    Answer

    Magistrates took the auspices before public acts; augurs held the law of signs, inaugurated, and ruled on faults. At Aquilonia Papirius held that a falsely reported sign stood for the general and fell on the reporter (Livy 10.40): a sign was a formal announcement, with responsibility attached.

  8. What does the episode of 163 BC show about the standing of the haruspices?
    Answer

    The Senate used them but did not defer to them: Gracchus abused them as Etruscan barbarians, and only his own reading of the augural books persuaded him of a fault, after which the consuls of 162 resigned (Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.10–11). Roman augural law, not Etruscan expertise, was decisive.

  9. Why had the calendar drifted by 46 BC, and how did Caesar fix it?
    Answer

    The 355-day year depended on intercalation decided by the pontiffs, who granted or withheld it for political ends (Censorinus 20.7; Curio in 50 BC), so it ran about three months ahead. Caesar made 46 BC 445 days long and then fixed 365 days with a leap day every fourth year; Augustus corrected the pontiffs' miscount.

  10. What traps does Ovid's Fasti set for anyone reconstructing a festival?
    Answer

    It covers only January to June; it is late and overlaid with Augustan dates; it piles up rival explanations that are learned display rather than cult testimony; it historicises rites, turning the Regifugium into Tarquin's flight; and its first-person witness may be a persona. Trust the actions and materials more than the reasons.

Carry forward

  1. Roman priests were the governing class in another capacity: senators holding priesthoods for life, increasingly by election, advising a Senate that decided. Religious authority and political competition were one system, which is why the emperors absorbed the priesthoods (module 6.2).
  2. Rome preserved ritual fossils whose meaning had gone: the rex sacrorum, the Flamen Dialis' taboos, the Salian and Arval hymns. Read the rite as old and the explanation as late, whether the explainer is Livy, Plutarch or Ovid.
  3. Time was administered by priests: the pontiffs controlled the calendar until Caesar replaced their discretion with a rule, and festivals kept their dates while their meanings changed, so a shepherds' Parilia could become Rome's birthday on the same day.

Give me an in-depth report on Roman priesthoods, divination and the religious calendar. Cover: the great colleges (the pontifices under the pontifex maximus, the augurs, the quindecimviri sacris faciundis with the Sibylline Books, the epulones) and how their members were chosen; the flamines, especially the Flamen Dialis and his taboos (Gellius 10.15); the rex sacrorum as the king's religious ghost; the Vestal Virgins, their selection, privileges, the sacred fire and the live burial of the unchaste; the Salii, the Arval Brothers and their inscribed records, the Luperci, and the fetials with their spear-throwing declaration of war; augury and the auspices, the templum, the sacred chickens and Claudius Pulcher at Drepana; haruspices and the Etruscan discipline; the calendar from the ten-month year of Romulus and Numa's reform to the late Republic's confusion and Caesar's Julian reform, with the Fasti Antiates Maiores as the only surviving pre-Julian calendar; and a year of festivals (Lupercalia, Parilia, Vestalia, Consualia, the October Horse, Saturnalia), read with Ovid's Fasti and its traps. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

House, family and the dead

The household as a congregationThe Lares: house and crossroadsPenates, Vesta, the Genius and the JunoRites of passageThe aristocratic funeral and the ancestor masksBurning, burial and the street of tombsThe Manes and the days of the deadGhostsPrivate magicSelf-testCarry forward

The household as a congregation

Roman religion had two arenas: sacra publica, performed for the people at public expense, and sacra privata, for individuals, families and gentes (Festus s.v. publica sacra). Module 2.1 deals with the first. The second had its own priest, the paterfamilias, and its own congregation, the familia of wife, children, slaves and freedmen, whose law belongs to module 9.3.

Cato's farm manual, of the mid-second century BC, shows the system at work. The master arriving at his villa first greets the household Lar (On Agriculture 2.1); the slave overseer may sacrifice only at the Compitalia, at the crossroads or the hearth, and must consult no haruspex or Chaldaean (5.3–4); his wife crowns the hearth on the Kalends, Nones and Ides and prays to the Lar (143.2). Private rites were property: Cicero's law code makes them perpetual and binds them to the estate (On the Laws 2.22, 2.47–53). A gens had rites of its own: Livy (5.46.2–3) has Gaius Fabius Dorsuo walk through the Gallic lines in 390 BC to perform his clan's sacrifice on the Quirinal, a story written down some three and a half centuries later.

The Lares: house and crossroads

The prologue of Plautus' Aulularia, staged about 200 BC from a Greek original, is spoken by the Lar familiaris, who has guarded a pot of gold under the hearth for generations and will reveal it because the daughter of the house honours him daily with incense, wine and garlands. In Plautus and Cato the household Lar is singular. The pair of dancing youths raising a drinking horn is the image of the crossroads Lares; in the surviving house shrines, almost all from Pompeii's last decades, it has replaced the single Lar of the texts.

Pompeii and Herculaneum preserve several hundred shrines (lararia): niches, painted walls and small aediculae in atria, gardens and above all kitchens, where slaves tended them. The standard painting shows the Genius of the master, togate and veiled, pouring a libation between the two Lares; below, one or two great snakes glide towards an altar laid with eggs or a pine cone. The snakes are the genius of the place, usually shown, Servius says, as a serpent; when a snake glides from Anchises' tomb to taste the offerings, Aeneas cannot tell whether it is that or his father's attendant (Virgil, Aeneid 5.84–96).

The Lares compitales lived at the compita, shrines where neighbourhood roads met. At their winter festival, the Compitalia, households hung woollen dolls for each free member and woollen balls for each slave, so that the Lares would take the effigies and spare the living (Festus s.v. pilae). The compital associations were political: dissolved by the senate in 64 BC, they were revived by Clodius for his street following (deep dive module 11.3). In 7 BC Augustus divided the city into fourteen regions and their neighbourhoods (vici), 265 of them by Vespasian's census (Pliny, Natural History 3.66), each with a crossroads shrine where elected magistri, mostly freedmen, served the Lares Augusti with the Genius of Augustus between them (Ovid, Fasti 5.145–146). Module 6.2 follows the politics.

Where sources disagree. Were the Lares the dead? Apuleius (On the God of Socrates 15) calls the kindly ancestral soul a Lar familiaris and the restless one a larva, and Ernst Samter (1901) built an ancestor theory on such texts. Georg Wissowa made the Lares gods of farmland, and Harriet Flower (The Dancing Lares and the Serpent in the Garden, 2017) argues that they were gods of place, and the Lares Augusti the old compital Lares renamed, not a cult of Augustus' Genius.

Penates, Vesta, the Genius and the Juno

The Penates were the gods of the penus, the household store; Cicero gives that etymology or one from penitus, "deep within" (On the Nature of the Gods 2.68). Nameless and plural, they were statuettes in the lararium and a presence in hearth and table; a portion of each meal went into the fire. The Penates of the Roman people at Lavinium are the household cult enlarged to the state (module 1.3). Vesta was the hearth fire itself, the focus; her priestesses belong to module 2.3.

The Genius was a man's divine double, the god under whose protection, Censorinus says, each person lives from birth (De die natali 3.1). The name belongs with gignere, "to beget"; the marriage bed was the lectus genialis. On the master's birthday the household honoured his Genius, and slaves swore by it; places, guilds and legions had Genii too. A woman had her Juno: Seneca says the ancients gave each person a Genius or a Juno (Letters 110.1), and Pliny mocks a crowd of gods larger than the human race (Natural History 2.16).

Where sources disagree. Censorinus (2.2–3), writing in AD 238, says the Genius received no blood on the birthday, so that no life was taken on the day one received it; Horace promises his a two-month-old pig (Odes 3.17.14–16), though in Epistles 2.1.143–144 farmers give it flowers and wine. The woman's Juno is attested almost only in imperial sources; whether it is old or a late analogy to the Genius is uncertain.

Rites of passage

On the dies lustricus, the eighth day for a girl and the ninth for a boy, the child was purified and named (Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.16.36). A freeborn boy wore the bulla, a protective locket, gold for the rich and a knot of leather for the poor (Juvenal 5.164–165). At fifteen or sixteen he put off the purple-bordered toga praetexta, hung up the bulla for the Lares (Persius 5.30–31) and was escorted to the Forum in the plain toga virilis, often at the Liberalia on 17 March (Ovid, Fasti 3.771–788). A girl's coming of age was her wedding.

Gaius, in the second century AD, lists three ways a wife entered her husband's manus (Institutes 1.110–113): usus, a year's cohabitation, interrupted if she stayed away three nights; coemptio, a ritual sale with scales and bronze; and confarreatio, the patrician sacrifice to Jupiter Farreus with a cake of spelt (far) before ten witnesses, to which later sources add the pontifex maximus and the Flamen Dialis. The major flamens and the rex sacrorum had to be born of such a marriage and to make one; by AD 23 so few patricians used it that the rules for the Flamen Dialis were eased (Tacitus, Annals 4.16). Most marriages were by then without manus (module 9.3).

Whatever the form, the bride's hair was parted with a spear-point (Plutarch, Roman Questions 87); she wore the flame-coloured flammeum. After the joining of right hands and a sacrifice, a torchlit procession with obscene Fescennine verses took her to her new home (Catullus 61). She wound the doorposts with wool, was lifted over the threshold and was received with fire and water. Varro, quoted by Nonius, says she brought three coins: for her husband, for the Lar of the house, and for the Lar of the nearest crossroads. Marriage was entry into a new set of gods.

The aristocratic funeral and the ancestor masks

Death began with the conclamatio, calling the dead by name. The body was washed and laid out in the atrium, feet to the door. The Twelve Tables, of about 450 BC and known through Cicero four centuries later, forbade burial or burning inside the city, limited flute-players to ten and forbade women to tear their cheeks (On the Laws 2.58–59); Cicero says the decemvirs took these rules almost word for word from Solon (2.59, 2.64), whose laws Greek module 8.4 covers.

Polybius, a Greek hostage at Rome from 167 BC, explains the noble funeral for Greek readers (6.53–54). The body is carried to the Rostra, usually upright, and a son or kinsman recounts the dead man's virtues and deeds. Afterwards his mask, closely reproducing features and complexion, is set in a wooden shrine in the most public part of the house. At later funerals the masks are worn by men of similar build, dressed in the toga of each ancestor's highest office: purple-bordered for a consul or praetor, purple for a censor, gold-embroidered for a triumphator. They ride behind the fasces and sit in ivory chairs on the Rostra while the speaker recounts each ancestor's deeds, oldest first. No sight, Polybius concludes, could be finer for a young man who loves glory.

Pliny describes wax faces in cupboards round the atrium, linked by painted lines into a family tree (Natural History 35.6); Sallust's Fabius Maximus and Scipio said the sight of them set their hearts on fire (Jugurtha 4.5–6). Absence spoke too: at Junia's funeral in AD 22 Cassius and Brutus outshone the rest because their images were not carried (Tacitus, Annals 3.76). Augustus' funeral carried images of Romulus and of Pompey (Dio 56.34).

Where sources disagree. Were the masks taken from the corpse? Older scholarship treated them as death masks and as the origin of the "veristic" Republican portrait (module 10.3). Harriet Flower (Ancestor Masks and Aristocratic Power in Roman Culture, 1996) argues that they were made in life, once a man reached the aedileship or higher, so that display followed office, not birth. Polybius says nothing of casting.

Burning, burial and the street of tombs

Rome practised both rites from the start (module 1.1). By the late Republic cremation was normal. The patrician Cornelii kept to inhumation until Sulla, who had his body burned so that it could not be dug up as he had dug up Marius' (Cicero, On the Laws 2.56–57; Pliny, Natural History 7.187). Even after burning, a bone was buried in earth to end the household's pollution (Varro, On the Latin Language 5.23). From the second century AD inhumation in carved sarcophagi returned.

The dead lined the roads out of the city: the tomb of the Scipios on the Via Appia, where the sarcophagus of Scipio Barbatus, consul in 298 BC, bears an epitaph in Saturnian verse; the baker Eurysaces' tomb, carved with his ovens. Epitaphs address the passer-by and wish that the earth lie light. One sums up the female ideal: Claudia loved her husband, bore two sons, kept the house, worked wool (CIL VI 15346). Slaves and freedmen of great houses went into columbaria, chambers lined with urn niches like dovecotes. Burial clubs pooled costs: the club at Lanuvium inscribed its entry fee, dues and funeral grant in AD 136 (CIL XIV 2112). The poorest went into pits on the Esquiline (Horace, Satires 1.8.8–16).

Where sources disagree. Why did the empire turn from burning to burial? Christianity cannot explain a change that began in the second century. Arthur Darby Nock ("Cremation and Burial in the Roman Empire", 1932) argued for a change of fashion led from the top, with no change of doctrine; Ian Morris (Death-Ritual and Social Structure in Classical Antiquity, 1992) traces a social shift spreading outward from Rome. Ancient writers give no reason.

The Manes and the days of the dead

The Romans called the dead collectively di Manes, "the good gods", a euphemism; from the first century AD epitaphs open D M, Dis Manibus. Cicero's code says: hold your dead kin as gods (On the Laws 2.22). The dead were a plural divinity, met at fixed times and kept at a distance.

DayDateRiteMain source
Parentalia13–21 FebruaryOfferings at family tombs; temples shut, no weddingsOvid, Fasti 2.533–570
Feralia21 FebruaryPublic close of the Parentalia; the Tacita spellFasti 2.569–616
Caristia22 FebruaryFamily meal, quarrelsome kin excluded; offerings to the LaresFasti 2.617–638
Lemuria9, 11, 13 MayMidnight expulsion of the restless deadFasti 5.419–492
Mundus patet24 August, 5 October, 8 NovemberThe pit opened; battle, levies and weddings avoidedFestus; Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.16.16–18

Ovid's Parentalia asks little: a garlanded tile, grain, salt, bread soaked in wine, violets (Fasti 2.535–542). Once, during a war, the rites lapsed and the dead howled through the streets until they resumed (2.547–556). On the Feralia an old woman binds hostile tongues for Tacita, the silent goddess, with thread, lead and a fish's head sewn shut (2.571–582): a binding spell inside the state calendar.

In May the dead came uninvited. At midnight on the Lemuria the father rises barefoot, washes his hands and throws black beans behind him without looking, saying nine times that with these he redeems himself and his own; the shade gathers them. He clashes bronze and nine times bids the ghosts go: Manes exite paterni (Fasti 5.429–444). Ovid derives the name from Remus' ghost (module 1.4), almost certainly wrongly. Beans belonged to the dead; the Flamen Dialis might not even name them (Gellius 10.15.12). Three times a year the mundus was opened, and then, says Varro, a door of the grim gods below stood open (in Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.16.18).

Where sources disagree. Plutarch (Romulus 11), eight centuries on, puts Romulus' foundation pit, filled with first-fruits and soil, in the Comitium; Festus, citing Ateius Capito and Cato, gives the three opening days and says the mundus was shaped like the vault of the sky. Whether these are one structure is unknown, and no excavated pit is securely identified. Warde Fowler ("Mundus patet", 1912) noted that the dates fit the farming year and conjectured a store-pit for seed corn that later acquired its underworld meaning.

Against Greek module 8.4, the Twelve Tables echo Solon, the Lemuria recalls the close of the Anthesteria, and the Parentalia does the work of the Genesia. But Rome had no hero cult tied to bones: a noble's ancestors acted through faces and offices paraded in the Forum. Nor had Rome its own map of the underworld; Virgil's is Greek in plan (deep dive module 12.5).

Ghosts

Roman ghosts are the family dead of the festivals and the murdered or unburied who haunt one place. Plautus' Mostellaria, adapted about 200 BC from a Greek comedy, makes farce of the second: the slave Tranio keeps his returning master out of the house by claiming that a guest murdered and buried there without rites has complained in a dream that Acheron will not take him, since he died before his time.

Pliny the Younger asks Licinius Sura whether ghosts exist (Letters 7.27). A house at Athens was haunted by an old man in chains until the philosopher Athenodorus rented it, followed the ghost to a spot in the courtyard and had it dug: chained bones were found and buried, and the haunting ceased; Lucian tells a Greek twin (Lover of Lies 30–31). Suetonius says Caligula's half-burned body haunted the Lamian gardens until his sisters cremated and buried it properly (Caligula 59).

Private magic

The Twelve Tables punished anyone who charmed away another's crops or chanted a malum carmen, as Pliny cites them five centuries later (Natural History 28.17–18). His book 30 opens with a history of magic, "the most fraudulent of arts" (30.1), a Persian invention; he credits the senate's decree of 97 BC against human sacrifice (30.12) and tells how Nero found magic empty (30.14–17). Yet his medical books record charms without censure, and amulets were respectable: the bulla, and the phallic fascinum hung on infants and under the triumphing general's chariot (28.39).

Lead curse tablets (defixiones) carry the Greek practice (Greek module 8.1) into Latin. They bind charioteers, opponents at law, lovers and above all thieves: some 130 from the sacred spring at Bath hand stolen goods over to Sulis Minerva. In Germanicus' house at Antioch in AD 19 were found human remains, spells and lead tablets bearing his name (Tacitus, Annals 2.69). Horace's witch Canidia pours a black lamb's blood into a pit on the Esquiline to call up the shades (Satires 1.8.23–33).

Apuleius' Apology is the only surviving speech of a man tried for magic. About AD 158–159, at Sabratha, his wife Pudentilla's relatives accused him of winning the rich widow by spells: he had bought rare fish, a boy collapsed in his presence, he kept something wrapped in linen among a household's Lares, and he worshipped a skeletal figure they said he called basileus, king. He replied as a philosopher: in Persian a magus is a priest (25–26), the fish were for dissection, the figure a Mercury. Rome had no crime called magic; the charge ran under Sulla's law of 81 BC on assassins and poisoners. The case shows how thin the line was between philosopher, priest and sorcerer.

Where sources disagree. Pliny read the Twelve Tables' malum carmen as a spell; Cicero (On the Republic 4.12, preserved by Augustine, City of God 2.9) took it as defamatory verse. James Rives ("Magic in Roman Law: The Reconstruction of a Crime", 2003) argues that magic became a distinct crime only under the empire, as jurists stretched the law on poisoning. For Fritz Graf, "magic" labels disapproved ritual, not a separate technique.

Self-test

  1. What do Cato's instructions for the farm show about who performed household religion?
    Answer

    The paterfamilias was its priest, greeting the Lar on arrival (On Agriculture 2.1), but cult was delegated to slaves under his control: the overseer might sacrifice only at the Compitalia (5.3) and his wife crowned the hearth and prayed to the Lar on fixed days (143.2).

  2. Why does the pair of dancing Lares in Pompeian kitchens not straightforwardly represent the household Lar of Plautus and Cato?
    Answer

    The early texts know a single Lar familiaris; the dancing pair is the iconography of the crossroads Lares, and the surviving lararia date almost entirely from Pompeii's last decades, when the domestic shrine had taken over the street image.

  3. What did Augustus change at the crossroads in 7 BC, and how does Flower read it?
    Answer

    He organised the city into fourteen regions and their vici, each crossroads shrine tended by elected magistri, mostly freedmen, for the Lares Augusti and the Genius of Augustus. Flower argues these were the old compital Lares renamed, not a cult of the emperor's Genius.

  4. What were the Penates, and how did the household honour them?
    Answer

    The nameless, plural gods of the household store (penus; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.68), kept as statuettes and present in hearth, table and salt-cellar; a portion of each meal was burned for them.

  5. Why is the Genius's birthday offering a point of disagreement?
    Answer

    Censorinus (2.2–3) says no blood was shed for the Genius on the birthday, but Horace promises his a young pig (Odes 3.17.14–16), though in the Epistles (2.1.143–144) farmers give it flowers and wine.

  6. Name the three forms of marriage with manus, and say why the decline of confarreatio was a religious problem.
    Answer

    Usus, coemptio and confarreatio (Gaius, Institutes 1.110–113). The major flamens and the rex sacrorum had to be born of and married by confarreatio, so when patricians abandoned it the rules for the Flamen Dialis had to be eased in AD 23 (Tacitus, Annals 4.16).

  7. According to Polybius 6.53–54, how were the ancestor masks used at a funeral, and why did he think it mattered?
    Answer

    Men of similar build wore them in the insignia of each ancestor's highest office, rode behind the fasces and sat on ivory chairs at the Rostra while the eulogist recited each ancestor's deeds. Polybius saw it as the finest school of ambition for the young.

  8. What did Tacitus mean by saying Cassius and Brutus outshone everyone at Junia's funeral?
    Answer

    Their masks could not be carried because they were Caesar's murderers, and the gap was conspicuous to everyone (Annals 3.76). The parade of masks was a political statement, and so was an absence from it.

  9. What does the Lemuria rite imply about the family dead?
    Answer

    At midnight the father throws black beans behind him nine times as ransom for himself and his own, clashes bronze and nine times orders the ghosts of his fathers out (Ovid, Fasti 5.429–444). The family dead are dangerous visitors to be paid off and expelled, not welcomed.

  10. On what legal basis was Apuleius prosecuted, and what was his defence?
    Answer

    Rome had no crime of magic as such; the charge ran under Sulla's law on assassins and poisoners. He argued that a magus is properly a Persian priest (Apology 25–26) and gave a philosopher's explanations for the fish, the boy's collapse and the statuette.

Carry forward

  1. The household was a miniature state: the paterfamilias was its priest, the familia including slaves its congregation, and the Lares, Penates, Vesta and Genius its gods. Augustus' crossroads reform shows how easily the domestic model could be enlarged into a cult centred on the ruler.
  2. The Roman dead were a collective divinity, the Manes, to be fed in February and expelled in May; the aristocratic dead, through masks, eulogies and offices, were also a political resource, and Roman nobility was a claim about ancestors displayed in public.
  3. Magic in Rome was defined by harm and social disapproval, not by technique: the curse tablet, the Feralia spell and the amulet use the same means as religion, and the label fell on whatever was foreign, secret or aimed at others.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Roman domestic religion and the cult of the dead. Cover: the paterfamilias as priest of the household; the Lares (the household Lar, the lararia of Pompeii and their painted snakes, the Lares of the crossroads and Augustus' reorganisation of them), the Penates and Vesta at the hearth, the Genius of the master and the Juno of the woman; the rites of passage (the naming day, the bulla, the toga of manhood, marriage by confarreatio and its alternatives); the aristocratic funeral as Polybius 6.53–54 describes it, with the ancestor masks, the eulogy and the parade of ancestors; cremation and inhumation, tombs along the roads, columbaria and epitaphs; the Manes, the Parentalia and Feralia in February, the Lemuria and the black beans, and the mundus; ghosts in Plautus' Mostellaria and Pliny's Letters 7.27; and private magic: curse tablets, amulets, and the line between religion and magic in Pliny's Natural History book 30 and Apuleius' Apology. Point back to Greek module 8.4 for the Greek comparison. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 2 · The gods of Rome · 2.5 · 2,736 words

New gods: Cybele, Bacchus, Isis, Mithras and the Christians

Evocatio: calling a god out of an enemy city

Conquest posed a religious problem: an enemy city had gods with a claim on it, and Rome would have to live beside them. Evocatio, "calling out", settled it. Before the final assault the commander invited the city's protecting deity to desert it for better cult at Rome: a transfer, not a defeat, on the do ut des logic of module 2.1.

The classic case is Juno Regina of Veii in 396 BC. Module 3.3 narrates the siege; the rite is told by Livy some 370 years later. Camillus prays to Juno Regina, "who now dwells at Veii", to follow the victors to a city soon to be hers, where a temple worthy of her will receive her (5.21.3). After the sack, young men bathed and dressed in white entered her temple in awe, since by Etruscan custom only a priest of one family touched the image. One asked, from inspiration or in jest,

Do you want to go to Rome, Juno?

and the others cried that she had nodded. She proved light to carry, as if willing, and went to the Aventine, where Camillus dedicated her temple in 392 (5.22.3–7, 5.31.3).

The formula itself survives for Carthage in 146 (Macrobius, Saturnalia 3.9.7–8): it addresses the power "whether god or goddess" protecting the city, asks it to desert the people and come to Rome, and promises temples and games. An inscription from Isaura Vetus in Asia Minor shows P. Servilius Vatia paying a vow to that town's god or goddess in 75 BC. Hence, Pliny says, Rome kept its own guardian's name secret (Natural History 28.18).

Where sources disagree. Beard, North and Price (Religions of Rome, 1998) treat evocatio as a regular instrument of expansion, practised more often than recorded, and modern lists add Vortumnus from Volsinii in 264. Blomart (1997) finds very few secure cases among the many uses of the verb evocare, and some read the Isaura text as a plain vow. Gustafsson (Evocatio Deorum, 2000) reads each account as the story of a unique crisis, not an instance of a fixed rite.

Invited gods: the Sibylline route and Aesculapius

Most new gods were invited, through the Sibylline Books, opened only on the senate's order (module 2.3): crisis, consultation, prescription. Apollo's temple was vowed for plague in 433 (Livy 4.25.3, writing four centuries later); Venus of Eryx received one on the Capitol after Trasimene (22.9–10, 23.31.9). Greek books prescribed Greek gods.

A plague of 293 sent the senate to the Books, which named Aesculapius of Epidaurus (Livy 10.47.6–7). The rest fell in Livy's lost book 11 and survives in its epitome (Periocha 11), in Valerius Maximus (1.8.2) and in Ovid (Metamorphoses 15.622–744), all nearly three centuries later. The envoys brought back a sacred snake, which swam from the ship to the Tiber Island, and the temple was dedicated on 1 January, conventionally in 291. The cult kept its Greek incubation (Greek module 8.2), and the island became a refuge: Claudius ruled that slaves abandoned there who recovered were free (Suetonius, Claudius 25.2).

Where sources disagree. Wissowa (Religion und Kultus der Römer, 1912) held that imported gods were housed outside the pomerium, the sacred boundary, and Juno on the Aventine and Aesculapius on the island fit. Orlin (Foreign Cults in Rome, 2010) points to Castor in the Forum, Venus Erycina on the Capitol and the Magna Mater on the Palatine, and argues that the senate sited each god case by case.

The Magna Mater, 204 BC

In 205, with Hannibal still in Italy, a shower of stones prompted a consultation: a foreign invader could be driven out if the Idaean Mother were brought from Pessinus to Rome (Livy 29.10.4–5). Attalus I of Pergamon, Rome's ally, handed the envoys the sacred stone the locals called the Mother of the Gods (29.11.7). Publius Scipio Nasica, judged the best man in the state, received her at Ostia; the leading matrons passed her hand to hand into the city, and on 12 April 204 she was lodged in the temple of Victory on the Palatine, the day made a holiday (29.14.5–14); the Megalesia of the calendars opened on 4 April. Her temple followed in 191 (36.36.3–4).

Livy gives Claudia Quinta one clause: a doubtful reputation made illustrious by her chastity (29.14.12). The miracle is Ovid's (Fasti book 4): the ship grounds in the Tiber, and Claudia, praying to be followed if she is chaste, draws it free alone. Herodian (1.11) makes her a Vestal.

Rome divided the cult. Magistrates gave the goddess Roman games and sacrifice, and aristocratic dining clubs feasted at her festival (Cicero, On Old Age 45). Her priests were the Galli, self-castrated devotees of Attis who processed with drums and cymbals collecting alms; by law and senatorial decree, Dionysius says, no native Roman joined their procession or rites (2.19.4–5). In 77 BC a consul denied the Gallus Genucius an inheritance as neither man nor woman (Valerius Maximus 7.7.6).

Where sources disagree. Livy's goddess comes from Pessinus, Varro's from Pergamon (On the Latin Language 6.15). Gruen (Studies in Greek Culture and Roman Policy, 1990) read the import as diplomacy, a claim on the Greek East through Attalus and Aeneas' Trojan descent; Beard (1994) argued that the cult was built to stay foreign, so that Rome could define itself against it. Attis figurines from Republican levels of the Palatine sanctuary show that her consort came with her from the start.

The Bacchanalia, 186 BC

Livy's account (39.8–19), written about 170 years later, is a comedy turned melodrama. A Greek sacrificer and seer brought nocturnal rites to Etruria and then Rome, where wine and darkness bred debauchery, forged wills and poisonings (39.8). The consul Spurius Postumius learns of it through young Publius Aebutius, whose mother and stepfather want him initiated to hide their embezzlement, and his lover, the freedwoman courtesan Hispala Faecenia. She testifies that the Campanian priestess Paculla Annia had turned a women's rite held three days a year into nocturnal initiations five times a month, admitting men and no one over twenty, until the initiates were almost a second people (39.9–14). Postumius told the assembly that nothing is more deceptive than a depraved religion (39.16.6). Over seven thousand were implicated, and more were executed than imprisoned (39.17.6, 39.18.5).

The consuls' letter relaying the senate's decree survives on a bronze found at Tiriolo in Bruttium in 1640 (CIL I² 581).

IssueLivyTiriolo bronze
Chargessexual crime, forgery, poisoning, a conspiracynone named
The cultshrines destroyed; rites only by licence of the urban praetor and a senate of 100the same licensing
Organisationno common fund, no master or priest (39.18.9)no male priest; no master or officer; no common fund; no oaths or mutual pledges
Meetingsno more than fiveno more than five, two men and three women; no rites in secret

Livy's summary of the decree agrees with the bronze; what the bronze lacks is every crime in his story. The cult survived, licensed and small.

Where sources disagree. North ("Religious toleration in Republican Rome", 1979) argued that the senate struck at an autonomous organisation with its own priests, funds and oaths, cutting across family and state, not at Bacchus. Gruen (1990) saw the senate asserting authority over Italy and over its own members; Walsh (1996) showed how much of Livy's narrative is stage comedy.

Expulsions: astrologers, Jews and Egyptians

Rome seldom banned a god; it removed practitioners, and every expulsion lapsed.

DateTargets and measureSource
