Astrologers could predict a ruler's death: a breed, Tacitus says, always banned at Rome and always retained (Histories 1.22).

Where sources disagree. Suetonius' Chrestus is usually read as Christ under a common slave name, the riots as synagogue quarrels over Christian preaching; Acts 18.2 has Aquila and Priscilla leave Rome after the expulsion. Orosius (7.6.15) dates it to 49; Dio says that in 41 Claudius did not expel the Jews but forbade their meetings. Lüdemann (1980) dates the measure to 41; Riesner (1994) defends 49. Uncertain.

Isis and Serapis

Isis came in the Ptolemaic form of Greek module 8.2, with Serapis, through traders: a Serapeum stood at Puteoli by 105 BC. After the demolitions of the 50s politics reversed policy. The triumvirs voted her a temple in 43 (Dio 47.15.4); Actium made Egypt suspect; under the Flavians the cult was imperial. Vespasian and Titus spent the night before their triumph of 71 at the Iseum (Josephus, Jewish War 7.123), and Domitian rebuilt the Iseum in the Campus Martius. At Pompeii a freedman's six-year-old son, Numerius Popidius Celsinus, rebuilt the temple after the earthquake of 62 and was made a councillor for it (CIL X 846).

Apuleius' Metamorphoses, the Golden Ass, of the later second century AD, ends with the only first-person account of a pagan initiation. Isis rises from the sea at Cenchreae and names herself the one goddess whom other peoples call Mother of the Gods, Minerva, Venus or Ceres (11.5); at her festival of the ship Lucius eats the priest's roses and becomes human again (11.13). After abstinence and fees he is initiated by night, approaching the boundary of death and passing through the elements (11.23):

At midnight I saw the sun gleaming with brilliant light.

Two more initiations follow at Rome (11.26–30), and a priest's dream expects a man of Madauros, Apuleius' own town (11.27).

Where sources disagree. Griffiths (The Isis-Book, 1975) read book 11 as sincere and largely autobiographical, the Madauros slip as the author's signature. Winkler (Auctor and Actor, 1985) argued that the novel leaves the reader unable to decide, and that a Lucius paying for three initiations may be the last dupe in a book of dupes. The ritual details match other evidence either way.

Mithras: the bull, the cave and the grades

Greek module 8.2 covers the cult's Greek mediation; here the Roman evidence. Statius gives the first notice of the bull-slaying, about AD 90 (Thebaid 1.719–720). The tauroctony is standard from Britain to Syria: Mithras in a Phrygian cap kneels on the bull and stabs it, looking away; dog and snake go for the blood, a scorpion for the genitals; Sol, Luna and a raven watch; two torch-bearers flank the scene. The mithraeum imitated a cave (Porphyry, On the Cave of the Nymphs 6): a vaulted room with benches for a shared meal, holding twenty to forty men, who rose through seven grades from Raven to Father (Jerome, Letters 107.2). They were soldiers, imperial slaves and freedmen, customs officials; women were excluded.

Under Santa Prisca on the Aventine, excavated by Vermaseren and van Essen, paintings of about AD 200 show the grades in procession with verses of disputed reading. Under San Clemente, beneath two superimposed churches, a mithraeum with its tauroctony altar was fitted into a first-century building around the same date.

Where sources disagree. Justin (First Apology 66) and Tertullian (Prescription against Heretics 40) said demons had imitated Christian sacraments in Mithras' bread and cup, and Renan (Marc-Aurèle, 1882) suggested that had Christianity been halted the world would have become Mithraist. Clauss (Mithras: Kult und Mysterien, 1990) and most specialists answer that small, all-male groups without public temples could never have become a mass religion.

The "oriental religions" since Cumont

Franz Cumont's Les religions orientales dans le paganisme romain (1906) made Cybele, Isis, the Syrian gods and Mithras one wave of eastern salvation religions that filled the void of a cold civic cult and prepared the way for Christianity. Each element has fallen. The cults reached Rome already Hellenised and differed in structure (Burkert, Ancient Mystery Cults, 1987; Greek module 8.2). None was exclusive: Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, who died in 384, was pontiff, augur and Mithraic Father of Fathers (CIL VI 1779). The cold civic religion was a Protestant caricature (J. Z. Smith, Drudgery Divine, 1990). Beard, North and Price prefer "elective" cults, joined by choice rather than birth.

Where sources disagree. The centenary conference of 2006 (published 2009 by Bonnet, Pirenne-Delforge and Praet) largely retired the category. Alvar (Romanising Oriental Gods, 2008) defends a revised one: the three cults share a soteriology and values distinct from civic cult, and Romans marked them as foreign. Versluys replies that their easternness was itself a Roman construction.

Jews at Rome

Judaism was the one foreign worship Romans met as a people's inheritance rather than a cult to be joined. A community existed by the second century BC; Pompey's captives enlarged it, and in 59 Cicero complained of the Jewish crowd at Flaccus' trial (Pro Flacco 66–69). Caesar exempted their associations from his ban on collegia (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 14.213–216); Augustus, Philo says, held their grain over when the distribution fell on the Sabbath (Embassy to Gaius 155–158). Horace jokes about the Sabbath (Satires 1.9.69–70); Tacitus is hostile (Histories 5.4–5). After 70 every Jew paid two drachmas a year to Jupiter Capitolinus (Josephus, Jewish War 7.218). Catacomb epitaphs name about a dozen synagogues.

Where sources disagree. Older handbooks call Judaism a religio licita with a charter from Caesar. The phrase is a Christian polemicist's (Tertullian, Apology 21.1), and Rajak ("Was there a Roman charter for the Jews?", 1984) showed that the privileges were grants to particular communities, renewed and contested city by city.

First encounters with the Christians

Christians were in Rome by the 50s, when Paul wrote to them. To Romans they were a superstitio (module 2.1) with no ancestral people behind it.

Tacitus, writing about fifty years after the fire of 64 (module 7.1), says Nero fastened the blame on people hated for their outrages, whom the crowd called Christians, followers of a Christus executed by Pontius Pilatus. They were convicted less of arson than of hatred of the human race, and were torn by dogs, crucified, or burned as night-lights in Nero's gardens (Annals 15.44.2–5). Suetonius lists their punishment among Nero's police measures, without the fire (Nero 16.2).

Where sources disagree. Shaw ("The myth of the Neronian persecution", 2015) argued that the name Christian was not current in Rome in 64 and that Tacitus projected the conflicts of his own day onto the fire. Jones (2017) defended the traditional reading; Suetonius' independent notice is its strongest support.

Pliny, governing Bithynia-Pontus about 110–112, asked Trajan whether the name itself was punished or only the crimes attached to it (Letters 10.96). He had asked the accused three times whether they were Christians and executed those who persisted, for their obstinacy; he released those who invoked the gods, offered incense and wine to Trajan's image and cursed Christ. The lapsed said they had met before dawn to sing a hymn to Christ as to a god and swore an oath against theft and adultery, then shared ordinary, harmless food. Two slave women called ministrae, tortured, revealed only a depraved and excessive superstition.

Trajan replied (10.97) that Christians were not to be sought out; if accused and convicted they were to be punished, but one who sacrificed was pardoned, and anonymous accusations were "not of our age". Tertullian asked why the guilty were not hunted and the innocent were punished (Apology 2.6–9). The rescript held until Decius' order of 250 (module 8.1).

Where sources disagree. De Ste. Croix ("Why were the early Christians persecuted?", 1963) argued that the charge was the name itself, standing for a refusal of the gods that endangered the pax deorum. Sherwin-White (1964; commentary on the letters, 1966) stressed the governor's discretionary coercion and the Christians' contumacia, defiance of his order, which is what Pliny says he punished.

Self-test

  1. What did evocatio assume about the bond between a god and a city, and what evidence outside Livy shows the rite was real?
    Answer

    That a god's protection was a relationship that could be renegotiated and transferred by the promise of better cult at Rome. Macrobius preserves the formula used at Carthage in 146 (Saturnalia 3.9.7–8), the Isaura Vetus inscription of 75 BC repeats its "god or goddess" hedge, and Pliny (Natural History 28.18) explains Rome's secret tutelary name by the same logic.

  2. How did Aesculapius come to Rome, and why does his island not prove a rule that foreign gods stayed outside the pomerium?
    Answer

    After the plague of 293 the Sibylline Books prescribed him; envoys brought a sacred snake from Epidaurus, which chose the Tiber Island (Periocha 11; Valerius Maximus 1.8.2). Castor in the Forum, Venus Erycina on the Capitol and the Magna Mater on the Palatine break Wissowa's rule, so Orlin argues for case-by-case siting.

  3. What did the oracle of 205 promise, and why was the import useful beyond the war?
    Answer

    That a foreign invader of Italy could be driven out if the Idaean Mother were brought from Pessinus (Livy 29.10.4–5). It also tied Rome to Attalus of Pergamon and to the Trojan ancestry of Aeneas, a claim on standing in the Greek East (Gruen).

  4. How did Rome accept the Magna Mater while keeping her priests at arm's length?
    Answer

    Magistrates gave her Roman games and sacrifice and aristocrats feasted at the Megalesia, but her eunuch Galli were Phrygian and citizens were barred by law and decree from joining their procession or rites (Dionysius 2.19.4–5). The Genucius case of 77 BC (Valerius Maximus 7.7.6) shows a Gallus losing civic capacity.

  5. What does the Tiriolo bronze show about the senate's aims that Livy's narrative obscures?
    Answer

    It names no crime and regulates structure: no male priests, no masters or officers, no common fund, no oaths, no secret rites, no more than five worshippers, all subject to licence (CIL I² 581). The cult was licensed and shrunk, not abolished, which supports North's view that independent organisation was the target.

  6. What did astrologers, Isiacs and Jews have in common as targets of expulsion, and how lasting were the measures?
    Answer

    Each formed a group outside civic control, perceived as foreign and low, and astrologers could also predict a ruler's death. The measures were temporary and repeated, as Tacitus admits of the astrologers, a breed always banned and always retained (Histories 1.22).

  7. Why is Metamorphoses 11 both the best and the most hazardous source for the mysteries of Isis?
    Answer

    It is the only first-person account of a pagan initiation, with details of abstinence, fees, the night rite and the festival that match other evidence. But it closes a comic novel, and Winkler showed that its sincerity cannot be settled against Griffiths' autobiographical reading.

  8. State Cumont's thesis about the oriental religions and two objections to it.
    Answer

    That Cybele, Isis, the Syrian gods and Mithras formed one wave of eastern salvation religions filling the void of cold civic cult and preparing for Christianity. Against it: each cult reached Rome already Hellenised and differed in structure (Burkert), none was exclusive, as Praetextatus' priesthoods show, and the cold civic religion is a Protestant caricature (J. Z. Smith).

  9. Why is religio licita a misleading description of the Jews' position at Rome?
    Answer

    The phrase is Tertullian's, not a Roman legal term, and Rajak showed that Jewish privileges were specific grants to communities, renewed and contested. Rome tolerated Judaism because it was the ancestral worship of a people, as Caesar's exemption of their associations shows.

  10. What did Pliny ask Trajan, and why did Tertullian find the answer incoherent?
    Answer

    Whether the name of Christian was punishable in itself or only the crimes attached to it (Letters 10.96). Trajan ruled that Christians were not to be sought out but were to be punished if accused and persistent, and pardoned if they sacrificed (10.97); Tertullian asked why the guilty were not hunted and the innocent were punished (Apology 2.6–9).

Carry forward

  1. Roman polytheism was absorptive by design: gods could be captured by evocatio, invited through the Sibylline Books or tolerated as a people's ancestral worship, and in each case the senate decided. Newness itself was never the offence.
  2. Repression targeted organisation, secrecy and allegiance, not belief: priests, funds and oaths outside the state's control in 186 BC, prophecy about the ruler, and finally refusal of the common cult, which Pliny turned into a sacrifice test. Watch the same logic harden into the persecutions of unit 8.
  3. "Oriental religions" is a modern category. Read each cult as a specific Roman construction (Roman games beside Phrygian eunuchs, an Egyptian style made in Italy, a Persian name on a Latin mystery) and keep each source's problem in view: Livy's melodrama, Apuleius' novel, Tacitus' hindsight.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on how Rome took in, regulated and resisted foreign gods. Cover: evocatio and the calling out of Juno from Veii in 396 BC (Livy 5.21–22); Aesculapius brought from Epidaurus to the Tiber Island in 291 BC; the Magna Mater brought from Asia Minor in 204 BC on the advice of the Sibylline Books, Claudia Quinta and the ship, the Megalesia, the eunuch Galli and the ban on citizens joining them; the Bacchanalia affair of 186 BC as Livy 39.8–19 tells it and as the bronze decree of the Senate found at Tiriolo records it; the expulsions of astrologers, Jews and worshippers of Isis; Isis and Serapis under the late Republic and the empire, with Apuleius' Golden Ass book 11 as the one insider's account; Mithras, the bull-slaying and the mithraea under Santa Prisca and San Clemente; the 'oriental religions' and the debate since Cumont over whether the category exists; Judaism at Rome; and the first encounters with Christians (Tacitus, Annals 15.44 on Nero's fire; Pliny, Letters 10.96–97 and Trajan's reply), stopping before the great persecutions and Constantine, which unit 8 covers. Point back to Greek module 8.2 for the Greek mysteries. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 3 · The early Republic and the conquest of Italy, 509 to 264 BC · 3.1 · 2,832 words

The Struggle of the Orders

Patricians and plebeians: what the distinction wasThe first secession and the plebeian state, 494–471Debt-bondage: nexumThe Decemvirate and the Twelve Tables, 451–449From the Valerio-Horatian laws to the consular tribunes, 449–367From the Licinio-Sextian laws to the lex Hortensia, 367–287The settlement: nobility, magistrates, Senate and assembliesLivy books 2 to 10 and the Gracchan lensSelf-testCarry forward

Patricians and plebeians: what the distinction was

Every narrative of the conflict is late. Livy wrote books 2 to 10, covering 509 to 293, in the 20s BC, three to five centuries after the events; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, fuller on the fifth century in books 5 to 11, published from 7 BC (module 0.1). Both inherited from annalists of the second and first centuries BC a contest between two orders: patricians who monopolised office and priesthood, plebeians who fought their way in.

The ancient explanation is genealogical: Romulus' hundred senators were the patres, their descendants the patricians (Livy 1.8.7), and Dionysius (2.9–10) makes everyone else their clients. What the patricians demonstrably held was religious. The auspices reverted to them when the magistracies lapsed, so the interrex was patrician; their senators ratified decisions by the patrum auctoritas; the rex sacrorum, the major flamines and the Salii stayed patrician to the end. The order was open early: Attus Clausus joined it with his clients in 504 (Livy 2.16.4–5).

The plebs was never a class: it held indebted smallholders and also rich families who later reached the consulship. It is defined by exclusion and, after 494, by its own organisation. Several consuls before 486 bear names later plebeian, Junius and Cassius among them; such names then vanish for decades, and the Twelve Tables forbade patrician-plebeian marriage. Many now speak of a "closing" of the patriciate in the early fifth century rather than of a primeval caste.

Where sources disagree. Niebuhr made the plebs a conquered people, like the Latins Ancus settled on the Aventine (Livy 1.33.2); Mommsen, nearer Dionysius, derived it from clients and outsiders. Momigliano and Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) see in the patriciate a religious and political elite that closed itself after 509, the plebs being everyone it excluded. Richard Mitchell (Patricians and Plebeians, 1990) reads the distinction as religious and military in origin and denies a conflict of hereditary orders from the start.

The first secession and the plebeian state, 494–471

In Livy debt drives the crisis. In 495 an old centurion, scarred in front and scourged behind, showed the Forum what his creditor had done to him (2.23.3–7). Relief was promised and refused, and in 494 the army, still bound by its oath, marched to the Sacred Mount beyond the Anio and camped there (2.31–32): a refusal to fight, not an assault. The Senate sent Menenius Agrippa, dear to the plebs as a man of plebeian origin (2.32.8). He told a fable. The limbs, resenting the idle belly, refused to feed it and the whole body wasted, until they saw that the belly also served, returning food to every part as blood (2.32.9–12; Dionysius 6.86). The plebs returned with magistrates of their own, tribunes to bring help (auxilium) against the consuls (2.33.1–3).

The plebs, not the community, created that power. Tribunes were sacrosanct by a collective oath, a lex sacrata making whoever harmed them sacer, killable without guilt; the jurists of Livy's day still held that their inviolability came from the oath, not from statute (3.55.10). From the inviolable body set between magistrate and citizen grew the veto. Two plebeian aediles kept the plebs' temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Aventine, dedicated in 493 (Dionysius 6.90, 6.94) and later its archive (Livy 3.55.13). From 471 the Publilian law had the tribunes elected by the plebs voting in tribes (Livy 2.56–58). With its own officers, assembly, cult centre and resolutions (plebiscita), the concilium plebis was a state within the state.

Where sources disagree. Livy notes that Calpurnius Piso put the secession on the Aventine (2.32.3). Livy gives two first tribunes who co-opted three (2.33.2–3), Dionysius five (6.89); Piso had the number raised from two to five only in 471 (Livy 2.58.1), and ten came in 457 (3.30.7). The fable is Greek in form, close to an Aesopic tale and to Socrates' brothers made to work together like hands and feet (Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.3.18).

Debt-bondage: nexum

Nexum, "binding", was a loan made by the ritual of bronze and scales in which the borrower pledged his person; a defaulter could be chained and worked by his creditor without any judgment. Republican jurists already disagreed on the term: Manilius applied it to every bronze-and-scales transaction, Mucius Scaevola only to those creating an obligation (Varro, On the Latin Language 7.105). Debt frames the period, from the centurion of 495 to the secession of 287, also over debts (Periocha 11).

Livy dates abolition to 326. Gaius Publilius, bound for his father's debt, was flogged by the moneylender Lucius Papirius for refusing his advances; the outcry carried a law that a debtor's goods, not his body, answer for money lent (8.28), velut aliud initium libertatis, "as it were a second beginning of liberty" (8.28.1). Solon had banned loans on the person at a stroke in 594/3 (Greek module 5.5). Rome needed nearly 170 years from the first secession, and the remedy came from a plebeian counter-state, not a mediator.

Where sources disagree. Varro (On the Latin Language 7.105) puts the abolition under the dictator Gaius Poetelius Libo Visolus, in 313, against Livy's 326. Tacitus (Annals 6.16) credits the Twelve Tables with the first ceiling on interest; Livy (7.16.1) gives it to a tribunician law of 357.

The Decemvirate and the Twelve Tables, 451–449

From 462, Livy says, tribunes demanded that consular power be defined in writing (3.9). An embassy went to Athens in 454 to copy Solon's laws (3.31.8), and for 451 consuls and tribunes gave way to ten patrician decemviri charged with writing laws. Their ten tables passed the centuriate assembly: fons omnis publici privatique iuris, the source of all public and private law (3.34.6). A second board under Appius Claudius added two (3.37.4), including the marriage ban Cicero calls "a most inhuman law" (On the Republic 2.63).

That board ruled as a tyranny and would not leave office (3.36–38). Livy tells its fall through Verginia (3.44–48). Appius had a client claim the centurion Verginius' daughter as his slave and, judging the case himself, gave interim custody to the claimant against his own law. Her father killed her in the Forum rather than surrender her; the armies mutinied, the plebs seceded again, to the Aventine and the Sacred Mount (3.50–52), and the decemvirs abdicated. Diodorus (12.24) tells the story briefly; module 3.2 treats Verginia as exemplum.

No text survives. The bronze tables (Livy 3.57.10) are reconstructed from quotations, often modernised, in Cicero, who learned them by heart as a boy (On the Laws 2.59), in Festus, Gellius, Pliny and Macrobius, and in the jurists, chiefly Gaius' commentary excerpted in the Digest. The table numbers are modern, from Jacques Godefroy (1616); Crawford's Roman Statutes (1996) reorders much.

What survives is procedure and private law for a farming community of households. Litigation begins with self-help: si in ius vocat, ito, "if he summons to court, let him go". A judgment debtor, after thirty days' grace and sixty in chains, was shown at three markets, and then (Gellius 20.1.48–49):

tertiis nundinis partis secanto. si plus minusve secuerunt, se fraude esto.

"On the third market day let them cut shares; if they cut more or less, let it be no offence"; or he was sold across the Tiber. A son sold three times is free of his father (Gaius, Institutes 1.132); a patron who cheats his client is sacer (Servius on Aeneid 6.609); assault costs twenty-five units of bronze as poena, a Greek loanword (Gellius 20.1.12); charming away a neighbour's crops is a crime (Pliny, Natural History 28.17–18); funeral display is capped, on Solon's model, Cicero says (On the Laws 2.59–64). Two clauses are constitutional: no laws against individuals, and capital cases only before the centuriate assembly (On the Laws 3.44). The plebeian gain was publication, though the forms of action stayed with the pontiffs until Gnaeus Flavius published them in 304 (Livy 9.46.5).

Where sources disagree. Ettore Pais and Édouard Lambert (1902) dismissed the Tables as a later compilation, Lambert's by Sextus Aelius Paetus about 200 BC; Wieacker, Watson and Crawford accept a fifth-century code on the evidence of its archaic language and society. The Athenian embassy is widely doubted, Greek influence much less: Pomponius (Digest 1.2.2.4) and Pliny (Natural History 34.21) name Hermodorus of Ephesus as adviser, and Gaius matched a boundary rule to Solon's (Digest 10.1.13). Most think the models came through southern Italy.

From the Valerio-Horatian laws to the consular tribunes, 449–367

The consuls of 449, Lucius Valerius and Marcus Horatius, carried three laws (Livy 3.55): that what the plebs resolved by tribes should bind the people; that no magistracy without appeal (provocatio) be created, renewing Publicola's law of 509 (module 1.6); and that whoever harmed tribunes or aediles should forfeit his head to Jupiter.

In 445 the tribune Gaius Canuleius repealed the marriage ban against patrician warnings that the auspices would be confounded (Livy 4.1–6). A bill to open the consulship produced a compromise: from 444 military tribunes with consular power, three at first and six from 405, replaced the consuls in about two years out of three until 367, with plebeians eligible (4.6.8). The patricians kept the census in a new censorship (443; 4.8), and the quaestorship was opened in 421 (4.43). Yet plebeians first won it in 409 (4.54.2–3), and the first plebeian consular tribune, Publius Licinius Calvus, came in 400 (5.12.9): eligibility did not win elections in assemblies weighted towards the rich.

Where sources disagree. Livy gives two reasons for the consular tribunate: to keep plebeians from the consulship (4.6.8), or, in some authors, too many simultaneous wars for two consuls (4.7.2). Forsythe (2005) links it to a military reorganisation that also produced the censorship; Cornell (1995) finds neither explanation convincing, since dictators were still named for wars and plebeians appear so late. Uncertain.

From the Licinio-Sextian laws to the lex Hortensia, 367–287

Livy's book 6 makes the decisive episode a ten-year struggle (6.34–42), sparked when Fabia, married to a plebeian, envied her sister, a consular tribune's wife, as the lictor's rod rapped at the door (6.34.5–10). In 376 the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus proposed that interest paid be deducted from debts; that no one hold more than 500 iugera of public land; and that one consul be plebeian (6.35.4–5). They blocked curule elections for five years (6.35.10), an anarchy the Varronian chronology must absorb (module 0.3). The laws passed in 367 with a half-plebeian board for the Sibylline Books. Lucius Sextius was consul in 366, and the patricians took compensation in a praetor for jurisdiction and two curule aediles (6.42).

300lex Ogulnia; lex Valeriapontiffs four to eight, augurs four to nine, new places plebeian (10.6–9); appeal re-enacted (10.9.3–6)
287lex Hortensiaplebiscites bind all citizens

The Ogulnian law opened the colleges that interpreted sacred law and the auspices, the patricians' last argument; Livy gives Appius Claudius the opposition and Decius Mus the reply (10.7–8). The last secession, to the Janiculum over debts, ended when the plebeian dictator Quintus Hortensius carried a law that what the plebs ordered should bind all Romans (Periocha 11; Pliny, Natural History 16.37). Livy's book 11 is lost; jurists writing four centuries and more later confirm that plebiscites had not bound patricians before (Laelius Felix in Gellius 15.27.4; Gaius, Institutes 1.3).

Where sources disagree. Three laws, of 449, 339 and 287, make plebiscites binding. Beloch, Ogilvie and Forsythe treat the first two as anticipations of the Hortensian law; Cornell argues that statutes were often re-enacted and that the earlier laws carried conditions, perhaps the patrum auctoritas, removed by stages. The consulship clause is doubted too: two patrician consuls appear in several years from 355 to 343 and never after 342, so von Fritz (1950) read 367 as an administrative reform, and many make the Genucian law the real guarantee.

The settlement: nobility, magistrates, Senate and assemblies

The result was a merged elite, not a plebeian victory. The leading plebeian families, Licinii, Genucii, Marcii, Publilii, Decii, shared the consulship with the surviving patrician clans and soon their interests: Licinius Stolo was fined under his own law for holding a thousand iugera (Livy 7.16.9). Gelzer (1912) defined the nobiles as families with a consul among their ancestors; Hölkeskamp (Die Entstehung der Nobilität, 1987) dates the formation of this patricio-plebeian nobility to the generations after 367 (module 0.3). The tribunate became a rung for young nobles. The patricians kept the interregnum and the old priesthoods; both consuls were first plebeian in 172.

The Senate of about three hundred was enrolled by the censors under the Ovinian law, of uncertain date before 312, from the best men of every order (Festus, s.v. praeteriti senatores); in practice it became a body of former magistrates, whose decrees were advice with customary authority. Of the three assemblies, the curiate survived to confer imperium. The centuriate, weighted by wealth (module 1.5), elected consuls, praetors and censors, declared war and heard capital cases. The tribal assembly elected quaestors and curule aediles and legislated; the plebeian council was the same tribes without patricians, and after 287 its plebiscites carried most legislation. No law yet fixed the cursus honorum: the Genucian ten-year rule restrained iteration, yet Valerius Corvus held six consulships. Rank was already ordered, the censorship normally going to former consuls, but the sequence stayed a matter of custom until the lex Villia annalis of 180 set minimum ages for each office (Livy 40.44.1; deep dive module 11.1). Cato called Rome's constitution the work of many men over centuries, not of one lawgiver (Cicero, On the Republic 2.2), the reverse of Athens under Solon and Cleisthenes. Polybius' mixed constitution is module 4.5; the system at its height, deep dive module 11.1.

Livy books 2 to 10 and the Gracchan lens

The framework is suspiciously late-Republican: agrarian bills almost yearly in books 2 to 4, debt relief, an obstructive Senate, secessions, appeals. Livy's named sources besides Fabius Pictor, Piso, Valerius Antias, Claudius Quadrigarius, Licinius Macer and Aelius Tubero, wrote after 133: Piso amid the Gracchan crisis, the rest after Sulla had curbed the tribunate (modules 5.1 and 5.2). Macer, tribune in 73, campaigned for its restoration (Sallust, Histories 3) and, Livy complains, sought praise for his family (7.9.5); Licinii supply a first tribune, the first plebeian consular tribune and the laws of 367. The appeal law was carried three times, Livy notes, semper a familia eadem, "always by the same family", the Valerii (10.9.3), and Valerius Antias is suspected of flattering his namesakes.

Specific projections show. Spurius Cassius' land bill of 486 includes Latins and Hernici (Livy 2.41), like Gaius Gracchus' programme for the allies; Mommsen read Cassius, Maelius and Manlius as Gracchan demagogues (module 3.2). The 500-iugera limit is Tiberius Gracchus' figure. Camillus' temple of Concord for 367 (Plutarch, Camillus 42) recalls Opimius' Concord after Gaius Gracchus' death in 121; Momigliano ("Camillus and Concord", 1942) judged the earlier one invented. The speeches, Canuleius' (Livy 4.3–5) or Dionysius', speak first-century idiom (Gabba, Dionysius and the History of Archaic Rome, 1991).

Against wholesale projection stand the lists: named laws, the Fasti's firsts and the odd colleges of consular tribunes, which no Gracchan pamphleteer needed, and the Twelve Tables' fifth-century world of debt and patronage. Cato's speech for the Rhodians of 167 cites a penalty for wanting more than 500 iugera (Gellius 6.3.37). Livy says the record grows clearer and surer after the Gallic sack (6.1.2–3). The skeleton is old, the flesh late.

Where sources disagree. Forsythe (A Critical History of Early Rome, 2005) treats much of the fifth-century narrative as reconstruction; Mitchell (1990) doubts a struggle of hereditary orders at all. Cornell (1995) and Raaflaub (Social Struggles in Archaic Rome, 1986; 2nd edn 2005) accept a real conflict in two phases, poorer plebeians seeking protection and debt relief in the fifth century and rich plebeians seeking office in the fourth, which the annalists fused. Module 0.1 gives Wiseman's case that such reconstruction was accepted method.

Self-test

  1. What did the patricians demonstrably hold that plebeians did not, and why do the early Fasti matter to the debate on the orders' origin?
    Answer

    The auspices (hence the patrician interrex), the patrum auctoritas and certain priesthoods such as the rex sacrorum and major flamines. Consuls with later plebeian names before 486 suggest that the patriciate closed itself in the early fifth century rather than being a primeval caste (Cornell).

  2. On what did the tribunes' sacrosanctity rest, and why does that make the office revolutionary?
    Answer

    On the plebs' collective oath, a lex sacrata making anyone who harmed a tribune sacer; Livy says the jurists still held this in his day (3.55.10). The power was created by a part of the community against the magistrates, not granted by the community's law.

  3. What was nexum, and how and when did it end?
    Answer

    A loan by bronze and scales in which the debtor pledged his person and could be bound by the creditor without judgment. The lex Poetelia, of 326 in Livy (8.28) or 313 in Varro (On the Latin Language 7.105), made the debtor's goods, not his body, answerable.

  4. How do the Twelve Tables survive, and why should you not trust a reference such as "Table VIII.21" too far?
    Answer

    Only as quotations and paraphrases in Cicero, Festus, Gellius, Pliny, Macrobius and the jurists, Gaius above all, via the Digest. The assignment to numbered tables is a modern reconstruction from Godefroy (1616), and Crawford's 1996 edition reorders much of it.

  5. Give three provisions of the Tables and what each shows about early Roman society.
    Answer

    Creditors may cut a judgment debtor into shares or sell him across the Tiber (Gellius 20.1.48–49): debt was enforced on the body. A son sold three times is free of his father (Gaius 1.132): paternal power was near absolute. A patron who defrauds his client is sacer (Servius on Aeneid 6.609): clientship was a sacred bond.

  6. What part does Verginia play in Livy's constitutional narrative?
    Answer

    Her case is the decemvirs' fall: Appius Claudius breaks his own law on interim custody, her father kills her, the armies mutiny and the plebs secede a second time (Livy 3.44–52). The abdication leads directly to the Valerio-Horatian laws of 449, as Lucretia's death led to the consulship.

  7. Why were the military tribunes with consular power created, and what shows that eligibility did not bring plebeians office?
    Answer

    Livy offers a political motive, to keep plebeians out of the consulship (4.6.8), and a military one, too many wars for two consuls (4.7.2); moderns divide. The first plebeian consular tribune was elected only in 400 (5.12.9) and the first plebeian quaestors in 409 (4.54.2–3): forty-four and twelve years after the two offices were opened.

  8. What did the Licinio-Sextian rogations propose, and what did the patricians gain in return?
    Answer

    Relief of debts by deducting interest paid, a limit of 500 iugera of public land, and the end of consular tribunes with one consul plebeian (Livy 6.35.4–5), plus a half-plebeian board for the Sibylline Books. The patricians obtained the new praetorship and the curule aedileship (6.42.11–14).

  9. Why do three laws (449, 339, 287) each make plebiscites binding, and what did the Hortensian law certainly do?
    Answer

    Either the first two are annalistic anticipations (Beloch, Ogilvie, Forsythe) or each carried conditions, such as patrician ratification, removed by stages (Cornell). The Hortensian law made plebiscites bind all citizens, patricians included (Gellius 15.27.4; Gaius, Institutes 1.3).

  10. Give two signs that Livy's account is coloured by the Gracchan age and two arguments that its skeleton is nonetheless old.
    Answer

    Spurius Cassius' land bill including Latins and Hernici (2.41) and the 500-iugera limit mirror Gracchan proposals, and Licinius Macer and Valerius Antias promoted their own families. But the laws' names and the Fasti's firsts are list data, the Twelve Tables are fifth-century, and Cato's speech of 167 already knows a 500-iugera penalty (Gellius 6.3.37).

Carry forward

  1. The Struggle of the Orders produced a broadened aristocracy, not a democracy: the patricio-plebeian nobility of 367–287 governed through Senate and magistracies, and the tribunate was absorbed into the state. Read Polybius' mixed constitution and the Millar debate (module 4.5 and deep dive module 11.1) against that outcome.
  2. The tribunate kept its revolutionary origin: sacrosanct by oath, armed with help, veto and the binding plebiscite, it lay dormant until the Gracchi used it in 133; and the annalists who wrote after 133 painted the early tribunes in Gracchan colours, so the traffic between 494 and 133 runs both ways.
  3. Separate skeleton from flesh: named laws, the Fasti's firsts and the Twelve Tables are early evidence; speeches, motives and the two-bloc drama were written three to five centuries after the events, through late-Republican concerns.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Struggle of the Orders and the making of the Republic's constitution, 509 to 287 BC. Cover: patricians and plebeians and the debate over what the distinction originally was; the first secession of 494 BC, Menenius Agrippa's fable of the belly, the tribunes of the plebs and their sacrosanctity, the plebeian council and the aediles; debt-bondage (nexum); the Decemvirate and the Twelve Tables of 451–450 BC (what survives, how it survives, and what it shows of early Roman society), Appius Claudius and Verginia, the second secession; the Valerio-Horatian laws, the Canuleian law on intermarriage, the military tribunes with consular power; the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 BC and the first plebeian consul; the lex Ogulnia opening the priesthoods; the lex Hortensia of 287 BC; and the result: the patricio-plebeian nobility, the consuls, praetors, censors and dictator, the Senate and the three assemblies, and the cursus honorum taking shape. Then the question of reliability: how much of Livy books 2 to 10 is the conflicts of the Gracchan age projected backwards. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 3 · The early Republic and the conquest of Italy, 509 to 264 BC · 3.2 · 2,759 words

The legends of the early Republic

Coriolanus and his motherCincinnatus and the FabiiThree men who aimed at kingshipTorquatus, the Decii and CurtiusThe women in the storiesThe exemplum as Roman mythFamilies, funerals and the stageGreek modelsValerius Maximus: the stock as a handbookSelf-testCarry forward

Coriolanus and his mother

Every story here reaches us through Livy's books 2–8, written in the 20s BC, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus' Roman Antiquities, published from 7 BC: three to five centuries after the events, and for the fifth century nearly three after Fabius Pictor, the first Roman historian (module 0.1).

Gnaeus Marcius took the Volscian town of Corioli in 493 and was named for it. Livy concedes that the consul in command would be forgotten had the bronze column of the Latin treaty not recorded his absence at the war (2.33.5–9): memory had already gathered round the hero. In the famine of 491 Marcius urged that Sicilian grain be sold cheap only if the plebs gave up their tribunes; summoned to trial, he went into exile with Attius Tullius of the Volsci (2.34–35). In 488 he led a Volscian army to the Cluilian trench, five miles from Rome, and sent back embassies of senators and priests (2.39).

Then the matrons gathered at the house of his mother Veturia and his wife Volumnia (2.40.1), and the women went to the camp with his sons. Veturia asks whether she has come to an enemy or a son, as captive or as mother; had she borne no son, Rome would not be besieged (2.40.5–8). He withdrew. The men of Rome, Livy says, did not begrudge the women their praise, and a temple of Fortuna Muliebris, Women's Fortune, was dedicated (2.40.11–12) at the fourth milestone of the Via Latina (Valerius Maximus 1.8.4).

Dionysius gives most of book 8 to the episode: Valeria, Publicola's sister, proposes the embassy (8.39), Veturia's pleading fills most of chapters 46–53, and the temple's statue speaks to approve the matrons' dedication (8.56.2). Plutarch's mother is Volumnia and his wife Vergilia (Coriolanus 33–36), names Shakespeare took from him (module 10.4).

Where sources disagree. Livy found in Fabius Pictor, "by far the oldest authority", that Marcius lived into old age in exile (2.40.10–11). Dionysius (8.57–59) and Plutarch (Coriolanus 39) have Tullus' faction kill him; Cicero gave him a suicide, and Atticus mocked him for it (Brutus 42). Even the praenomen varies: Gnaeus in Livy, Gaius in Dionysius and Plutarch.

Cincinnatus and the Fabii

In 458 the Aequi trapped the consul Minucius on Mount Algidus, and the senate named Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus dictator. Livy offers the scene to those who despise everything human beside wealth (3.26.7). The envoys found him on his four iugera across the Tiber, digging or ploughing, Livy cannot say which; his wife Racilia fetched his toga from their hut (3.26.8–10). He surrounded the Aequi by night, sent them under the yoke, triumphed and laid down a six-month office on the sixteenth day (3.29.7). Livy explains the poverty: the sureties forfeited when his son Kaeso fled trial were exacted from him (3.13.8–10). At over eighty he was dictator again, against Maelius (4.13–14). The Algidus wars are real; the plough, the toga and the sixteen days are what an age of great estates wished its ancestors had been.

The Fabii make a clan epic. A Fabius was consul every year from 485 to 479. In 479 the family offered to fight Veii at its own cost, and 306 Fabii marched out through the right-hand arch of the Porta Carmentalis, thereafter an unlucky gate (Livy 2.48–49; Ovid, Fasti 2.201–204), with some 4,000 clients and friends (Dionysius 9.15.3). From a fort on the Cremera they raided for two years until, in 477, an ambush killed them all (Livy 2.50). One boy, too young to march, survived at Rome to carry on a line that would one day save the state (2.50.11): the line of Fabius Maximus.

Where sources disagree. Ovid sets the disaster on the Ides of February (Fasti 2.193–196), Livy on 18 July, the day of the Allia (6.1.11). Dionysius rejects the lone survivor: Roman law made men marry and rear children, so 306 grown Fabii must have left sons, and the tale resembles the fictions of myth and the stage (9.22.1–3). Livy undercuts himself by making the survivor consul in 467 (3.1.1).

Three men who aimed at kingship

Cicero names the set: Spurius Cassius, Spurius Maelius and Marcus Manlius, killed on suspicion of seeking kingship (Philippics 2.114).

Cassius, consul in 486, proposed the first agrarian law, sharing public land with the plebs and the Latins (Livy 2.41.1–3). Either his father tried him at home, had him scourged to death and consecrated his property to Ceres, or the quaestors prosecuted him for treason before the people and his house was razed (2.41.10–12). The site lay before the temple of Tellus (Cicero, De domo sua 101), where the censors of 158 melted down his statue (Pliny, Natural History 34.30).

Maelius, a rich equestrian, gave away grain bought in Etruria during the famine of 440. Accused of arming his house, he was cut down by Gaius Servilius Ahala, master of horse to the dictator Cincinnatus; his levelled site became the Aequimaelium, and the informer Minucius received a gilded ox outside the Porta Trigemina (Livy 4.13–16).

Manlius Capitolinus, saviour of the Capitol in 390 (module 3.3), is Livy's first patrician turned popular leader (6.11.7): he paid debtors' debts and accused the senate of hiding the Gallic gold (6.14). Tried in 384, he pointed to the Capitol, and the assembly had to move out of its sight to condemn him. Thrown from the Tarpeian Rock, he made one place a monument of outstanding glory and of final punishment (6.20.10–12); his house was razed, and the Manlii resolved that none of them should again be called Marcus (6.20.13–14).

Mommsen (1871) first grouped the three; Lintott (1970) read them as post-Gracchan. Land for the poor and the Latins and cheap grain are the programmes of the Gracchi, debt relief that of Catiline, and the kingship charge was the smear used against Tiberius Gracchus (Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 19). What survives is topographical, and orators used it: Cicero set his own demolished house beside these razed houses in 57 (De domo sua 101) and cited Ahala against Catiline (Against Catiline 1.3).

Where sources disagree. Dionysius reports that Cincius and Calpurnius Piso knew no dictator in 439: the senate chose the young Servilius, who stabbed Maelius in the street and reported that he had killed the tyrant at the senate's command (12.4.2–5). Piso was consul in 133, when the private citizen Scipio Nasica led the killing of Tiberius Gracchus, and the version reads like a precedent for him. Yet if this Cincius is the annalist of about 200, as Dionysius' editors assume, the private killing predates the Gracchi.

Torquatus, the Decii and Curtius

Titus Manlius took the cognomen Torquatus from the torque of a Gaul he killed in single combat in 361 (Livy 7.9–10; Claudius Quadrigarius in Gellius 9.13). As consul in 340, against Latins alike in arms and language, he forbade fighting outside the line. His son accepted a Tusculan's challenge, killed him and brought the spoils; the father had him beheaded before the army (8.7). Livy is divided: the "Manlian orders" horrified at the time and left a grim example (8.7.22), yet made the army obedient (8.8.1). The exemplum absorbed rivals: Livy rejects a like tale of Postumius Tubertus because the orders are called Manlian, not Postumian (4.29.5–6).

In the same campaign both consuls dreamt that the general of one side and the army of the other were owed to the gods below and Earth (8.6.9–10). When his wing gave way at Veseris, Publius Decius Mus had a pontifex dictate the formula: Janus, Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus, Bellona, the Lares and other gods down to the Di Manes are asked for victory, and the enemy's legions are devoted with Decius to the gods below (8.9.6–8). Veiled, in the purple-bordered toga girt in the Gabine manner, standing on a spear, he rode into the Latins and died. Livy records the words because ancestral rite is forgotten (8.11.1) and adds the rules: a commander may devote any legionary instead; if the devoted man survives, a seven-foot image is buried (8.10.11–12). The son did the same at Sentinum in 295 (10.28; module 3.4), and Cicero adds a grandson at Asculum in 279 (Tusculan Disputations 1.89; module 3.5). Virgil sets the Decii beside Torquatus with his savage axe (Aeneid 6.824–825).

In 362 a chasm opened in the Forum that would close, the seers said, only when Rome offered what its strength lay in. Marcus Curtius, answering that this was arms and courage, rode armed into it (Livy 7.6.1–5). Livy keeps this explanation of the Lacus Curtius against its rivals (module 0.1) only because antiquity has removed certainty (7.6.6). It is a devotio without a battle, and the place kept its charge: under Augustus every order threw coins into it yearly for his health (Suetonius, Augustus 57.1).

Where sources disagree. The grandson's devotio is doubtful (module 3.5 sets out the evidence). Skutsch placed Ennius' devotio prayer (Annals 191–194) at Asculum, which would put the story into Latin verse within about a century; Cornell (1987) disagreed. Many critics suspect the father's devotio of 340 of copying the son's in 295.

The women in the stories

Women act in these legends as mothers and wives standing between houses, or die as daughters whose bodies mark the limit of power. Veturia replays the Sabine women who ran between their fathers and their husbands (Livy 1.13; module 1.4). In both, women loyal to the house of birth and the house of marriage end a war the men cannot end, and both close in women's institutions: the Matronalia (Ovid, Fasti 3.167–258) and Fortuna Muliebris.

Verginia is the other type. In 449 a client of the decemvir Appius Claudius claimed her as his slave, and her father, the centurion Verginius, killed her in the Forum with a butcher's knife, the only way, he said, to make her free (Livy 3.44–48; Dionysius 11.28–37). Module 3.1 takes the politics, module 1.6 the pairing with Lucretia. A second Verginia, patrician wife of a plebeian consul, was barred from the shrine of Patrician Chastity in 296 and founded an altar of Plebeian Chastity in her own house (Livy 10.23.1–10): the struggle of the orders told through a matron's honour.

Three of these stories are anchored in women's cults (Fortuna Muliebris, the Matronalia, the chastity shrines) rather than in family eulogy, which points to a channel of transmission beside the funeral: the yearly rite at which a cult's story was retold.

The exemplum as Roman myth

Livy's preface sets out the use: history displays every kind of example on a conspicuous monument, to imitate, or to avoid as foedum inceptu, foedum exitu, foul in beginning and in outcome (Preface 10; module 1.6). These legends supply both kinds, often in one man: Manlius saved the Capitol and died from its rock; Torquatus' severity was hateful and effective.

This is the work Greek myth did: charter, model, warning. Roman exempla do it in historical dress, dated by consuls and fixed to cognomina (Coriolanus, Capitolinus, Torquatus), to places (the Lacus Curtius, the Aequimaelium, the unlucky gate), to rites and to families. Quintilian puts it plainly: as much as the Greeks are strong in precepts, the Romans are in examples, which is greater (12.2.30). Matthew Roller (Models from the Past in Roman Culture, 2018) analyses the exemplum as deed, judging audience, monument and imitation; Jane Chaplin (Livy's Exemplary History, 2000) shows Livy's characters citing exempla themselves, as the younger Decius cites his father.

The late Republic used the stock as argument. Sallust's Cato cited Torquatus in 63 to justify executing the Catilinarians, calling him Aulus and placing the case in a Gallic war (Catiline 52.30); Cicero's Epicurean Torquatus explains his ancestor by utility, and Cicero answers with the Decii (On Ends 1.23–24, 2.60–61). Augustus' Forum, lined with statues of the men who had made Rome great (Suetonius, Augustus 31.5), each above an inscribed summary of his deeds, made the stock a canon.

Families, funerals and the stage

Module 0.1 gave the ancient complaints that funeral praises corrupted the record, and module 2.4 describes the funeral. Polybius, about 150 BC, already counts these types among its lessons: men who fought single combats to decide battles, and magistrates who put their own sons to death against all law and custom (6.54.4–5).

The families worked their stories. The Fabii had the first historian, a survivor whose line produced Fabius Maximus, and descent from Hercules (Ovid, Fasti 2.237; Plutarch, Fabius Maximus 1.2). The Torquati re-enacted theirs: the consul of 165 condemned his own son for extortion in 140 and stayed away from his funeral (Valerius Maximus 5.8.3), and later moneyers of the family set a torque round their coins. The Decii made devotio hereditary. Marcus Brutus put his ancestors, the first Brutus and Ahala, on a denarius in 54 BC. An exemplum kept a family in office.

Wiseman (Roman Drama and Roman History, 1998; The Myths of Rome, 2004) adds the stage. Stage games began in 364 (Livy 7.2), and stories built as scenes, with a crowd, a confrontation, a mother's plea and a reversal, look like performances before they were history. Ancient writers sensed it: Dionysius likens the Fabian survivor to stage fiction (9.22.3), and Livy calls a tale from Veii's siege ad ostentationem scaenae gaudentis miraculis aptiora quam ad fidem, fitter for a stage that delights in marvels than for belief (5.21.9). Plays on Roman subjects (fabulae praetextae) are attested: Naevius' Romulus, Ennius' Sabinae, and Accius' Aeneadae or Decius on Sentinum.

Where sources disagree. Harriet Flower ("Fabulae praetextae in context", 1995) argues that such plays were few, occasional pieces for triumphs, funerals and dedications, mostly on recent events; Cornell (2003) counts ballad, epic and play among the possible pre-literary carriers of the Coriolanus story. Wiseman replies that most performances were never written down, so lists of titles cannot measure them.

Greek models

Cicero drew the Coriolanus parallel himself: Marcius and Themistocles, contemporaries, were driven out by ungrateful peoples, joined the enemy and ended their anger by death (Brutus 41–42). Atticus' reply exposes the method: rhetoricians may lie in histories, as Clitarchus gave Themistocles bull's blood where Thucydides had illness (Brutus 42–43; Thucydides 1.138.4). Plutarch's Marcius sits veiled at Tullus' hearth (Coriolanus 23), as Themistocles sat at the Molossian king's (Thucydides 1.136–137). The annalists synchronised with Greek history, sometimes badly: Dionysius faults Licinius Macer and Gellius for sending the famine grain from Dionysius I of Syracuse instead of Gelon (7.1.4–6).

The 306 Fabii fall three years after Thermopylae, a few against a host with a lone survivor, like Leonidas' 300 (Herodotus 7.202, 7.229–231): a fit model for a family that claimed Hercules, as Leonidas did. Pairing became a genre. The Pseudo-Plutarchan Parallela minora matches Curtius with Anchurus, who rode into a chasm in Phrygia (5), and Decius with Codrus, the Athenian king who sought death because an oracle promised victory to the side whose king fell (18). The consuls' dream before Veseris has Codrus' logic.

Where sources disagree. Mommsen (1870) treated Coriolanus as a late fiction on Greek patterns. Cornell ("Coriolanus: myth, history and performance", 2003) argues for a core: an exile leading Volscians into Latium in the 490s fits the Volscian advance known on other grounds, and the Greek parallels are costume, not source.

Valerius Maximus: the stock as a handbook

Valerius Maximus completed the transformation. His Memorable Deeds and Sayings, nine books dedicated to Tiberius and written after Sejanus' fall in 31 (9.11.ext.4), files about a thousand exempla under rubrics of religion, institutions, virtues and vices, Roman cases before foreign. The preface promises a selection from famous authors that spares those seeking examples long research. Cut from its narrative, each story serves one virtue: Coriolanus piety towards parents (5.4.1), not treason; Cincinnatus poverty (4.4.7); Curtius and the Decii love of country (5.6.2, 5.6.5–6); Torquatus military discipline (2.7.6). Spurius Cassius appears under the severity of fathers, in the domestic version, the one that fits (5.8.2). Epitomised in late antiquity by Julius Paris and Januarius Nepotianus, the book was widely read through the Middle Ages and the Renaissance and carried the stock to later Europe.

Where sources disagree. Bloomer (Valerius Maximus and the Rhetoric of the New Nobility, 1992) reads a declaimer's sourcebook that gave men without ancestral masks a shared stock of ancestors; Skidmore (Practical Ethics for Roman Gentlemen, 1996), a moral guide for general readers. Langlands (Exemplary Ethics in Ancient Rome, 2018) sees clashing cases meant to be thought through, not simply obeyed.

Self-test

  1. What does Livy's citation of Fabius Pictor on Coriolanus' death suggest about the later versions?
    Answer

    The oldest authority had Marcius live to old age in exile (Livy 2.40.10–11). The murder by Tullus' faction (Dionysius 8.57–59; Plutarch, Coriolanus 39) and Cicero's suicide (Brutus 42) look like later elaboration for drama or for the Themistocles parallel.

  2. How does Livy frame the Cincinnatus story, and how does his own narrative explain the hero's poverty?
    Answer

    He offers it to those who value wealth above everything (3.26.7): a lesson in virtue without riches. The poverty comes from the forfeited sureties for his son Kaeso, which were exacted from him (3.13.8–10).

  3. Give two reasons to doubt the lone surviving Fabius, and say what the motif does for the family.
    Answer

    Dionysius notes that Roman law obliged men to marry and rear children, so 306 Fabii must have left sons (9.22.1–3); Livy makes the survivor consul in 467, ten years later (3.1.1). The motif guarantees the continuity of the gens that produced Fabius Maximus.

  4. What links Cassius, Maelius and Manlius, and why do many scholars treat them as retrojections?
    Answer

    Each championed the poor with land, grain or debt relief, was killed on suspicion of seeking kingship (Cicero, Philippics 2.114) and had his house razed. Their programmes and the charge of kingship match late-Republican politics from the Gracchi to Catiline (Lintott 1970).

  5. Why does the Cincius and Piso version of Maelius' death matter?
    Answer

    In it there is no dictator, and Servilius kills Maelius as a private citizen at the senate's bidding (Dionysius 12.4.2–5), a precedent for Scipio Nasica in Piso's consulship of 133. If Cincius is the annalist of about 200, the version predates the Gracchi, which complicates the retrojection theory.

  6. Describe the devotio as Livy records it.
    Answer

    Prompted by a pontifex, the commander prays to a list of gods from Janus to the Di Manes and devotes the enemy's legions with himself to the gods below; then, veiled, in the purple-bordered toga girt in the Gabine manner and standing on a spear, he rides into the enemy (8.9.6–9). If a devoted man survives, a seven-foot image is buried (8.10.11–12).

  7. In what sense is Torquatus' execution of his son both a model and a warning, and how was it used in 63 BC?
    Answer

    Livy calls the Manlian orders horrifying at the time and a grim example for later ages (8.7.22), yet credits them with restoring discipline (8.8.1). Sallust's Cato cited the case to justify executing the Catilinarians, calling him Aulus Manlius (Catiline 52.30).

  8. How does Veturia's embassy rework the Sabine women, and what commemorated it?
    Answer

    In both, women standing between the house of birth and the house of marriage stop a war that men cannot stop (Livy 1.13; 2.40). The matrons' temple of Fortuna Muliebris on the Via Latina commemorated it (2.40.12; Dionysius 8.55–56).

  9. State Wiseman's theory, two ancient items that fit it, and the main objection.
    Answer

    Many early legends were first performed as drama at the games before historians wrote them down. Dionysius likens the Fabian survivor to stage fiction (9.22.3), and Accius' Aeneadae or Decius staged the devotio at Sentinum. Flower (1995) replies that historical plays were few, occasional and mostly about recent events.

  10. How did Valerius Maximus change the stories by arranging them?
    Answer

    He cut them from their narratives and filed each under a single virtue, choosing the version that fitted: Coriolanus under piety towards parents (5.4.1), Spurius Cassius under paternal severity in the domestic version (5.8.2). His preface offers the collection as a saving of research for those who want examples.

Carry forward

  1. The exemplum is the Roman form of myth: a deed dated by consuls, fixed to a place, a cognomen, a rite or a family, and judged as a model or a warning. Read every early-Republican legend as an argument about conduct, and expect one exemplum to justify opposite acts.
  2. These legends travelled through identifiable channels: family display (funerals, masks, coins, a Fabius as first historian), cult and topography (Fortuna Muliebris, the Lacus Curtius, razed houses), probably the stage, and Greek historiography, which supplied the shapes. Ask of each story which channel made it.
  3. Much of the early-Republican narrative is the late Republic arguing with itself: the would-be kings resemble the Gracchi, and Ahala, Torquatus and the Decii were cited in 63 and after. Valerius Maximus fixed the stock as a handbook of virtues, and that is the form in which later Europe received it.
