The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the heroic legends of the early Republic as Livy books 2 to 8 and Dionysius tell them, and on how Romans used them. Cover: Coriolanus and his mother; Cincinnatus called from the plough; the 306 Fabii destroyed at the Cremera; Spurius Cassius, Spurius Maelius and Manlius Capitolinus as men killed for aiming at kingship; Manlius Torquatus executing his son; the self-sacrifice (devotio) of the Decii; Marcus Curtius leaping into the chasm in the Forum; and the women in these stories (Coriolanus' mother and wife, Verginia, the Sabine mothers). Horatius, Mucius Scaevola and Cloelia belong to module 1.6, and the geese of the Capitol to 3.3. Then the analysis: the exemplum as the Roman form of myth and Livy's preface on examples to follow and avoid; family traditions and funeral orations as the source of many stories; Greek models (Coriolanus and Themistocles, the Fabii and the three hundred Spartans); Wiseman's theory of historical drama on the Roman stage; and how Valerius Maximus turned the whole stock into a handbook. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 3 · The early Republic and the conquest of Italy, 509 to 264 BC · 3.3 · 2,708 words

Veii, the Gauls and Camillus

The Latin alliance and the hill peoplesVeii: the ten-year siegeWhat Veii did for RomeVeii in the groundThe Gauls in Italy and the AlliaThe sack, the Capitol and the goldWhat the Greeks heard and what the ground showsRebuilding: the wall and the second founderThe Latin War and the settlement of 338Self-testCarry forward

The Latin alliance and the hill peoples

Livy, books 2 to 8, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, whose account after 443 survives only in excerpts, wrote between three and four and a half centuries after these events, from annalists who began about 200 BC. Diodorus' book 14, thought to draw on an older and sparer source, and Plutarch's Camillus, of about AD 100, are the other narratives. Dates before 300 are Varronian (module 0.3).

After Lake Regillus (module 1.6) the consul Spurius Cassius made a treaty with the Latins in 493 (Livy 2.33). Dionysius gives its terms (6.95): peace while heaven and earth keep their places; no passage for each other's enemies; full aid to a partner attacked; equal shares of booty; contract disputes settled within ten days. Cicero remembered its bronze column behind the Rostra (Pro Balbo 53). The league's older history is module 1.1. The Hernici joined in 486 (Livy 2.41), and colonies were planted on the front, such as Signia, Norba and Ardea; Livy calls them Roman, but they became Latin states and were probably joint foundations.

The enemies were Sabellic-speaking hill peoples. The Aequi came down from the upper Anio each summer through the Algidus pass; the Volsci spread from the Liri valley to the coast, taking Antium, Velitrae, Satricum and Tarracina. At Satricum, Marijke Gnade's Dutch team found burials of a new type from the early fifth century, which fits Livy's Volscian conquest. The Sabines fought sporadically; in 460 the Sabine Appius Herdonius seized the Capitol with exiles and slaves and was dislodged with Tusculan help, as the treaty required (Livy 3.15–18). Coriolanus and Cincinnatus belong to module 3.2. The turn came in 431, when the dictator Aulus Postumius Tubertus beat Aequi and Volsci on the Algidus (4.26–29); Tarracina fell in 406 (4.59).

Where sources disagree. Livy expected readers to wonder where the Volsci and Aequi kept finding soldiers after so many defeats (6.12.2–5). R. M. Ogilvie (A Commentary on Livy Books 1–5, 1965) traced the stock scenes, and Gary Forsythe (A Critical History of Early Rome, 2005) treats most of the fighting as invention. Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) keeps the pattern of mountain pressure and a defensive alliance, supported by Satricum and by the Tabula Veliterna, a third-century bronze from Velitrae in Volscian.

Veii: the ten-year siege

Veii, 16 km north of Rome, is described as an Etruscan city in module 1.2. In Livy's first war with it the Fabii fell at the Cremera (module 3.2); in the second, about 437, Aulus Cornelius Cossus killed its king Lars Tolumnius (4.17–20). The third, 406–396, Livy tells as Rome's Trojan War (5.1–23), and his own speaker draws the comparison (5.4.11). Two institutional details are probably sound: pay for citizen soldiers from 406 (4.59–60), funded by a war tax, and winter campaigning (5.2).

In 398 the Alban lake rose to an unheard-of height without rain. A Veientine haruspex let slip that Veii would not fall until the water was let out; Delphi agreed, and the Romans drew it off on to the fields (5.15–16, 5.19.1). The outlet, the emissarium, a tunnel over a kilometre long through the crater rim, still drains the lake.

In 396 Marcus Furius Camillus, named dictator (5.19), drove a tunnel (cuniculus) towards the citadel and prayed twice: to Pythian Apollo, promising a tenth of the spoils, and to Juno Regina, Veii's protectress, that she follow the victors to a worthier temple (5.21.1–3). The tunnel came up in her temple. Livy adds that the Romans snatched the entrails from the king's sacrifice, a tale he calls fit for the stage and not worth affirming or refuting (5.21.8–9). The free population was sold (5.22.1; Diodorus 14.93.2). Her consent, a nod in Livy and speech in later tellers (5.22.3–7), and her Aventine temple of 392 belong with the rite in module 2.5.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus says only that Veii fell through an underground passage (14.93.2), so the tunnel stood in the earliest version; the haruspex, the lake and the entrails are fuller annalistic growth, which Plutarch (Camillus) tells with more wonder than Livy. Cornell (1995) accepts the fall in 396 and doubts the ten years. The lake story may be an aetiology of the emissarium, and the tunnel an inference from the drainage cuniculi that riddle Veii's countryside.

What Veii did for Rome

Camillus triumphed behind white horses, likening himself to Jupiter (5.23.5–6); a tenth of the booty went to Delphi as a golden bowl (Diodorus 14.93.3–5), and in 391 a tribune's prosecution over the spoils drove him into exile at Ardea (Livy 5.32.7–9). The real prize was land, the ager Veientanus. Stephen Oakley calls it the largest single increase in Roman territory; Lily Ross Taylor reckoned it added about half. In 393 every plebeian, children included, was voted seven iugera, about 1.75 hectares (5.30.8); Diodorus gives four plethra or, in other accounts, twenty-eight (14.102.4). Veientine deserters received citizenship and land (6.4.4); in 387 four new rural tribes raised the total to twenty-five (6.5.8); Latin colonies at Sutrium and Nepet, the gates of Etruria (6.9.4), held the frontier. Rome now outweighed any combination of Latin states, and a treaty of equals could not survive that.

Veii in the ground

Juno Regina's temple has never been securely identified. The best-known sanctuary lies below the western edge at Portonaccio, outside the walls. Votives name Menerva, and a sixth-century bucchero vessel was given there by Avile Vipiienas, the Aulus Vibenna of Roman tradition (module 1.5). Its temple, of about 510 BC, carried life-size painted terracotta figures along its roof-ridge. In 1916 Giulio Quirino Giglioli found the Apollo, striding in contest with Hercules over the hind, with a goddess holding a child and a head of Hermes; they are in the Villa Giulia. Pliny names a Veientine sculptor, Vulca, as maker of the Capitoline Jupiter (Natural History 35.157); giving him the Apollo is a modern guess. Propertius hears a shepherd's horn within Veii's walls (4.10.27–30), but votive deposits run on into the third century and Augustan Veii was a municipium: the ghost town is rhetoric.

The Gauls in Italy and the Allia

Livy gives two accounts of the Gauls' arrival (5.33–35). In one, Arruns of Clusium, wronged by his ward Lucumo, lured them over the Alps with wine (5.33.2–4; Plutarch, Camillus 15). In the other they crossed two centuries earlier, under Tarquinius Priscus, and settled in waves: Insubres round Mediolanum, Cenomani, Boii and Lingones, and last the Senones on the Adriatic (5.34–35). Polybius describes unwalled villages and wealth in cattle and gold (2.17). From about 400 La Tène graves appear in the Po plain and the Marche, as in the Senonian cemetery at Montefortino, and Etruscan Felsina became Bononia of the Boii.

Where sources disagree. Polybius and the Arruns story make the occupation recent; Livy's preferred chronology puts it about 600 (5.34). Archaeology allows both: Celtic speakers of the Golasecca culture were writing Lepontic by the sixth century (module 1.1), while La Tène material marks a new movement shortly before 400. Livy, nearly four centuries later, may have fused the two.

In 391 the Senones besieged Clusium, which appealed to Rome. Three Fabian envoys joined the fighting and one killed a chieftain, breaking the law of nations; asked to surrender them, the people elected them consular tribunes (Livy 5.35–36; Diodorus 14.113). On 18 July, ever after the unlucky dies Alliensis (Livy 6.1.11), the Gauls met the Roman army at the Allia, eleven miles north of Rome; it broke at the first shout and most survivors fled to Veii (5.37–38). Diodorus puts the battle on the Tiber's right bank (14.114). The year is 390 for Varro and 387/6 by Polybius' synchronisms (1.6.1–2); module 0.3 explains the gap, and this module uses 390.

The sack, the Capitol and the gold

Livy's sack (5.39–55), written some 360 years later, is his most finished set-piece. The Vestals carried the sacred objects to Caere in the cart of a plebeian, Lucius Albinius, who had put his family down to make room (5.40.7–10). The old men who had held curule office sat in their courtyards in their robes, on ivory chairs; the Gauls took them for statues until one stroked the beard of Marcus Papirius, who struck him with his ivory staff, and the killing began (5.41). The city was plundered and burned.

The Capitol held. Gaius Fabius Dorsuo walked through the Gallic lines to perform his clan's sacrifice on the Quirinal and back (5.46.1–3). When the Gauls climbed by night, the dogs were silent, but Juno's sacred geese, spared despite the famine, gave the alarm, and Marcus Manlius threw down the first Gaul (5.47; Diodorus 14.116). A yearly rite crucified dogs (Pliny, Natural History 29.57) and carried a goose in state (Plutarch, On the Fortune of the Romans). Manlius' later fall is module 3.2.

Famine forced terms: a thousand pounds of gold. When the Romans protested at false weights, the chief Livy calls Brennus threw his sword on the scale with vae victis, woe to the conquered (5.48.8–9). At that moment Camillus, recalled as dictator, arrived with the army from Veii, declared that Rome would be recovered with iron, not gold, and routed the Gauls in the city and again at the eighth milestone on the road to Gabii (5.49.1–6). The matrons who had given gold won funeral eulogies (5.50.7), and Caere public guest-friendship (5.50.3).

Where sources disagree. Polybius knows no rescue: threatened at home by the Veneti, the Gauls made a treaty and left with their plunder after seven months (2.18.3, 2.22.5). Diodorus has the gold paid and later recovered by Camillus from Gauls besieging Veascium (14.116.7, 14.117.5); Strabo credits the Caeretans (5.2.3); Suetonius says a Livius Drusus brought the Senones' gold back from Gaul, and that Camillus had not, as the story went, wrested it back (Tiberius 3.2). Mommsen ("Die gallische Katastrophe", 1878) took Diodorus for the oldest Roman version and Livy's rescue for patriotic growth; most since agree.

What the Greeks heard and what the ground shows

The sack is the first Roman event recorded by outsiders near the time. Heraclides Ponticus, Plato's pupil, wrote that an army from the Hyperboreans had taken a Greek city called Rome by the great sea (Plutarch, Camillus 22.2); Aristotle knew that Celts took it and one Lucius saved it (22.4); Theopompus, says Pliny, recorded only its capture by Gauls (Natural History 3.57). None names Camillus. Justin has Gauls who had burned Rome months before seeking alliance with Dionysius I of Syracuse (20.5), and Diodorus sends them on to Iapygia (14.117.7): a war band heading south, perhaps for mercenary service, with Rome a rich stop on the way. Livy's claim that most records burned (6.1.2) sits beside his report that the treaties and the Twelve Tables were recovered (6.1.10; module 0.1).

Where sources disagree. Livy burns the whole city (5.42–43); Diodorus spares a few houses on the Palatine (14.115.6); Polybius speaks of occupation, not destruction (2.18.2). Early excavators took a layer of burnt roof tiles in the Comitium for the Gallic fire (Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome, 1929); it is now usually dated earlier, and Cornell (1995) finds no destruction horizon securely attributable to the Gauls, though traces of fire of about this date have been reported on the Palatine. On a site of timber and mud-brick rebuilt for twenty-four centuries, absence of evidence is weak evidence of absence.

Rebuilding: the wall and the second founder

Tribunes urged migration to Veii, its buildings intact; Camillus answered, in the book's longest speech, that Rome's gods and rites were bound to its soil (Livy 5.51–54), and a centurion's order to his standard-bearer, hic manebimus optime, here we shall do best to stay, settled it (5.55.1–2). Rebuilding was hasty: public tiles, free quarrying, sewers left under private houses, a city that looked occupied rather than laid out (5.55.2–5; Diodorus 14.116.8–9).

The lasting answer was the wall. In 378 the censors let a contract for one of squared stone (6.32.1). Most of the surviving circuit, about 11 km long and enclosing some 426 hectares on the usual modern reckoning, is of Grotta Oscura tufa quarried in Veii's former territory: the conquest built the defence. Masons' marks in Greek letters suggest Greek contractors. "Servian" comes from Livy's report that Servius Tullius walled the city (1.44.3; module 1.5).

Where sources disagree. Gösta Säflund (Le mura di Roma repubblicana, 1932) dated the Grotta Oscura circuit after 390 and left the older stretches in cappellaccio tufa as fragments of earlier defences. Gabriele Cifani (Architettura romana arcaica, 2008) assigns the cappellaccio work to a sixth-century circuit on much the same line, giving the Servian name a real core. Livy has both a regal wall (1.44) and a fourth-century one (6.32).

Livy hails Camillus as a Romulus, father of his country and second founder of the city (5.49.7). Plutarch counts five dictatorships and four triumphs, yet no consulship (Camillus 1). Livy wrote book 5 when some proposed calling Octavian Romulus as a second founder (Suetonius, Augustus 7.2), and his pious, exiled, temple-restoring Camillus has an Augustan profile. His temple of Concord of 367 is probably invented (module 3.1). The man and the conquest of Veii are secure; the saviour of 390 is not.

The Latin War and the settlement of 338

Defeat loosened the alliance: Latins and Hernici broke away (Livy 6.2) and Praeneste fought Rome. Rome answered with incorporation: in 381 Tusculum received full citizenship while keeping its own magistrates, the first municipium (6.25–26). Gallic raids drove the Latins back, and the treaty was renewed in 358 (7.12); the Carthage treaty of 348 envisaged raids on Latin towns not subject to Rome (Polybius 3.24), implying a claim to the rest. The Samnite wars are module 3.4.

In 340 the Latin praetors Lucius Annius of Setia and Lucius Numisius of Circeii demanded one consul and half the Senate (8.3–6). Latins, Campanians, Volsci, Sidicini and Aurunci fought together and lost at Veseris, the battle of Decius' devotio and of Torquatus' execution of his son (8.7–10; module 3.2), and at Trifanum (8.11). In 338 the consuls Lucius Furius Camillus and Gaius Maenius finished the war at Pedum and the Astura (8.13); the beaks of Antium's warships were fixed to the speakers' platform, thereafter the Rostra (8.14.12). Livy sets out the settlement community by community (8.14):

CommunityTreatment
Lanuviumfull citizenship; its cults returned, the grove and temple of Juno Sospita shared with the Roman people
Aricia, Nomentum, Pedumfull citizenship
Tusculumcitizenship kept; the ringleaders punished
Velitraewalls razed, senators deported across the Tiber, colonists settled on their land
Antiumcitizen colony; warships removed and the sea forbidden
Tibur, Praenesteland confiscated, partly for an old alliance with the Gauls; allies still under treaty
The other Latinsintermarriage, trade and common councils with one another forbidden
Capua, Fundi, Formiae, Cumae, Suessulacitizenship without the vote

The league ceased as a political body; only the Latin festival on the Alban Mount continued. In its place stood bilateral ties, each community bound to Rome and barred from combining with the others. Three statuses resulted: full citizens in self-governing municipia; citizens without the vote (cives sine suffragio), who served in the legions and paid tax but could not vote at Rome; and allies such as Tibur, Praeneste and the Latin colonies, keeping rights of intermarriage, trade and migration with Rome. Those Latin rights soon came loose from descent: from Cales in 334, new Latin colonies across Italy held them as a legal status (module 3.4). Rome had learned at Veii to annex and at Tusculum to incorporate; in 338 it combined both into a system it could extend.

Where sources disagree. Gellius (16.13.7) makes Caere the first community without the vote, rewarded for sheltering the sacred objects in 390; Strabo (5.2.3) treats the status as a slight, and the censors' "Caeretan tablets" became a list of disfranchised citizens. A. N. Sherwin-White (The Roman Citizenship, 1939) read it as an honour grown from reciprocal hospitality that hardened into subjection; Michel Humbert (Municipium et civitas sine suffragio, 1978) saw it from the start as a means of incorporation carrying the burdens of tax and levy.

Self-test

  1. What did the Foedus Cassianum provide, and what does it imply about Rome's standing among the Latins in 493?
    Answer

    Perpetual peace, mutual aid, no passage for enemies, equal shares of booty and quick settlement of private contracts (Dionysius 6.95). It is a treaty between Rome and the Latins as equal parties, not an instrument of Roman rule, which is why the growth of Rome after Veii strained it.

  2. Why is Livy's annual chronicle of Volscian and Aequian wars suspect, and what supports its broad pattern?
    Answer

    It repeats stock scenes, and Livy himself wondered how the enemy kept finding soldiers (6.12.2–5). The pattern of Sabellic pressure is supported by the Volscian text from Velitrae, the new burials at Satricum and the joint colonies on the front.

  3. Which elements of the fall of Veii stand in Diodorus' spare account, and which appear only in the fuller tradition?
    Answer

    Diodorus has the dictator, the underground passage, the sale of the population and the bowl for Delphi (14.93). The Alban lake prophecy, the snatched entrails and the nodding Juno belong to the fuller annalistic version in Livy and Plutarch.

  4. Which details of the siege of Veii are probably sound, and what shaped the rest?
    Answer

    Pay for citizen soldiers from 406, funded by a war tax (Livy 4.59–60), and winter campaigning (5.2) are institutional details. The ten years and the Trojan comparison drawn by Livy's own speaker (5.4.11) are literary shaping; Cornell accepts the fall in 396 but doubts the ten years.

  5. What did the annexation of Veii's territory change for Rome?
    Answer

    In Oakley's judgement it was the largest single increase in Roman territory, and on Taylor's reckoning it added about half: allotments of seven iugera per plebeian (Livy 5.30.8), four new tribes in 387 (6.5.8) and colonies at Sutrium and Nepet. It also made Rome larger than any Latin combination, undermining the treaty of equals.

  6. What does the Portonaccio sanctuary show, and why is the Apollo's attribution to Vulca uncertain?
    Answer

    A rich extra-mural cult of Menerva, a temple of about 510 BC with life-size terracotta figures on its roof, and votive use continuing after 396. Pliny (35.157) names Vulca only as maker of the Capitoline Jupiter; linking him to the Apollo is a modern guess.

  7. Compare how Polybius, Diodorus and Livy have the Gauls leave Rome.
    Answer

    Polybius: they made a treaty and went home because the Veneti threatened their land (2.18.3). Diodorus: they took a thousand pounds of gold, which Camillus later recovered at Veascium (14.116–117). Livy: Camillus arrived during the weighing and defeated them on the spot (5.49).

  8. What do the Greek notices of the sack tell us, and what do they leave out?
    Answer

    Heraclides, Aristotle and Theopompus show that the capture of Rome by Celts was known in Greece within a generation or two (Plutarch, Camillus 22; Pliny 3.57). None mentions Camillus; Aristotle's saviour is a Lucius.

  9. Why is the "Servian" wall so called, and what does its stone reveal?
    Answer

    Livy credits Servius Tullius with walling the city (1.44.3), but the main circuit matches the contract of 378 (6.32.1). It is built of Grotta Oscura tufa from Veii's former territory, so the conquest supplied the stone for the post-sack defence.

  10. Name the three statuses produced by the settlement of 338, with an example of each.
    Answer

    Full citizenship (Lanuvium, Aricia, Tusculum); citizenship without the vote (Capua, Fundi, Formiae); allied Latin status under treaty (Tibur, Praeneste and the Latin colonies). The remaining Latins were forbidden intermarriage, trade and councils with one another (Livy 8.14).

Carry forward

  1. For Rome before 300 BC the nearer witnesses (the Greek notices, Polybius, Diodorus) are the sparer ones; prodigies, rescues and saviours accumulate in the later annalists, so test each Livian set-piece against the barest version.
  2. Veii set the pattern of Roman expansion: conquered land became allotments, tribes and colonies for citizens, and each gain moved Rome further from partner to master of its allies.
  3. The settlement of 338 turned peoples into legal statuses: full citizenship, citizenship without the vote and Latin rights detached from Latium, each tied to Rome alone. That template governs Italy until the Social War.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Rome's wars with its neighbours from the treaty with the Latins to the Latin settlement, c. 493 to 338 BC. Cover: the Foedus Cassianum and the wars with the Aequi, Volsci and Sabines; the ten-year siege of Veii and its fall to Camillus in 396 BC (the tunnel, the evocatio of Juno, which module 2.5 explains, the draining of the Alban lake), what Veii's territory did for Rome, and the archaeology of Veii (the Portonaccio sanctuary, the Apollo of Veii); the Gauls in Italy, the Allia and the sack of Rome (390 BC in Varro, 387/6 in Polybius), Brennus and 'woe to the conquered', the geese and Marcus Manlius, the senators in their chairs, Camillus' rescue and the gold, and the early Greek notices of the sack in Aristotle and Heraclides; whether the archaeology shows a destruction; the rebuilding, the 'Servian' wall in tufa from Veii's quarries, Camillus as second founder; and the Latin War of 340–338 BC and the settlement that dissolved the league into separate treaties, citizenship without the vote and colonies. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

The Samnite Wars and the Roman system in Italy

The sources and the SamnitesThe First and Second Samnite Wars, 343–304Sentinum and the end of Samnite independence, 298–264Appius Claudius CaecusColonies and roads as instruments of controlThe alliance system and the formula togatorumThe manipular legionThe manpower of 225 BCWhy Rome united Italy and no Greek city united GreeceSelf-testCarry forward

The sources and the Samnites

The conquest has one continuous narrative: Livy books 7 to 10, written in the 20s BC, about three centuries after the events, and ending in 293. After that come the summaries of his lost books (Periochae 11–15), fragments of Dionysius and of Appian's Samnite History, and Polybius' digression on the Gallic wars (2.18–23). Diodorus books 19 and 20 keep a thinner annalistic line that sometimes contradicts Livy. Livy's sources, from Fabius Pictor about 200 BC to Valerius Antias in the first century, embroidered battles and casualty figures; the skeleton of consuls, triumphs, colonies and treaties is sound. S. P. Oakley's commentary on books 6–10 separates the two.

Module 1.1 traced the Samnites' Sabellic origins. By 343 they held the central and southern Apennines, the largest state in Italy by area, and it was no city-state. The unit was the touto, "people", under an annual magistrate, the meddix tuticus, with rural districts, villages and hill-forts such as Monte Vairano beneath it. Four peoples formed the core: the Pentri round Bovianum, the Caudini in the west, the Hirpini round Maleventum, and the small Carricini. They shared a name, a language and sanctuaries such as Pietrabbondante, where captured arms were dedicated. Transhumance to the winter plains of Apulia and Campania kept them in contact, and in conflict, with the lowlands.

Where sources disagree. E. T. Salmon (Samnium and the Samnites, 1967) reconstructed a Samnite League with a federal council and a single war-leader. Emma Dench (From Barbarians to New Men, 1995) and Rafael Scopacasa (Ancient Samnium, 2015) answer that it rests mainly on Livy's habit of writing "the Samnites" as one state, while the archaeology shows a looser, regionally varied society. Whether Samnium had federal institutions or only wartime coalitions is uncertain.

The First and Second Samnite Wars, 343–304

A treaty of 354 (Livy 7.19.4; Diodorus 16.45.8) broke down in 343 when, Livy says, the Samnites attacked the Sidicini, Capua sent help and was beaten, and the Campanians surrendered themselves to Rome outright, so that Rome would be defending its own (7.29–31). Peace came in 341, and within a year Samnites were fighting beside Rome against the Latins (module 3.3). Diodorus says nothing of this war, and the surrender of Capua looks like a later legal justification.

The real contest began with Rome's push to the Liris and into Campania: a Latin colony at Fregellae (328) on land the Samnites claimed (8.22–23), and the siege of Neapolis in 327–326, during which Publilius Philo's command was extended beyond his year, the first prorogation (8.23.12). War followed in 326.

In 321 both consuls, Veturius Calvinus and Postumius Albinus, marching for Luceria, were trapped in a wooded defile near Caudium by the Samnite general Gavius Pontius (Livy 9.2–6). His father, Livy says, advised releasing them with kindness or killing them all (9.3); Pontius chose the middle course. The army gave up its arms and 600 equites as hostages; the consuls promised peace and the evacuation of Samnite land; then every man passed, in his tunic, under the yoke, two spears upright and one across (9.5–6). The rite unmade an army: the defeated passed beneath the victor's weapons as through a gate. The Senate repudiated the terms as a personal pledge of the commanders, not a treaty of the people, and handed Postumius over bound; he struck the fetial and declared himself a Samnite, so that a renewed war would be just (9.8–11).

Where sources disagree. Livy insists the peace was made by pledge (sponsio), "not, as is commonly believed and as even Claudius writes, by treaty" (9.5.2), and then avenges it at once at Luceria in 320 (9.12–15). Salmon and T. J. Cornell (The Beginnings of Rome, 1995) think the peace was real and kept until 316, and that the pledge and the revenge were built to clear Rome of perjury and shame.

When war resumed, Rome lost again at Lautulae in 315, a defeat Diodorus reports plainly (19.72) and Livy blurs (9.23). Recovery came by method: Latin colonies at Luceria behind Samnium (314) and along its western edge (313–312), the Via Appia (312), alliances in Apulia. Bovianum fell in 305 and peace in 304 restored the old treaty (9.44–45). By 302 the Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini, Frentani and Vestini were allies (9.45; 10.3), which cut Samnium off from the north.

Sentinum and the end of Samnite independence, 298–264

The Third War began in 298, and the Samnite strategy was not to fight Rome alone. In 296 Gellius Egnatius took an army north to join the Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls (Livy 10.16–18). In 295 the consuls Fabius Rullianus and Decius Mus met the coalition at Sentinum in Umbria, after raids on Clusium had drawn the Etruscans and Umbrians home (10.27). On the left Decius' line broke before the Gallic chariots, and he devoted himself and the enemy to the gods below, as his father had done at Veseris in 340, and rode to his death; Fabius won on the right and Egnatius fell (10.28–29). Livy gives 25,000 enemy dead against 8,700 Romans (10.29). The devotio as moral example is module 3.2.

Where sources disagree. Polybius (2.19.5–6), probably following Fabius Pictor, names only Samnites and Gauls. Duris of Samos, a contemporary Greek, put the dead at 100,000 (Diodorus 21.6.1), while Livy rejects writers who swelled the enemy to fantastic numbers (10.30). The epitaph of Scipio Barbatus, consul in 298, contradicts Livy's provinces for that year (module 0.1).

Livy ends at Aquilonia (293), where the Samnite elite had sworn in a linen-screened enclosure never to flee (10.38–42). Curius Dentatus forced peace in 290 and conquered the Sabines (Periochae 11). The Senones were expelled from the Adriatic coast and a citizen colony planted at Sena Gallica; Boii and Etruscans were beaten at Lake Vadimon in 283 (Polybius 2.19–20). Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttians joined Pyrrhus (module 3.5) and were reduced by 272. The ring of Latin colonies closed round Samnium: Venusia (291), Paestum and Cosa (273), Beneventum and Ariminum (268), Aesernia (263). Picenum fell in 269–268 and Volsinii in 264. Everything south of the Arno and Ariminum was bound to Rome.

Appius Claudius Caecus

The Second War's most consequential Roman won no great battle. Appius Claudius, later Caecus, "the Blind", was censor in 312 (Livy 9.29–34, 9.46; Diodorus 20.36). His road ran straight across the Pontine plain to Capua, giving armies a route to Campania clear of the exposed inland Via Latina. His aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, ran 11,190 paces from springs off the Via Praenestina, all but about sixty of them underground; Frontinus dates it to "the thirtieth year of the Samnite war" (On Aqueducts 5). He enrolled freedmen's sons in the Senate and spread the humble (humiles) through all the tribes, until the censors of 304 confined them to the four urban tribes (9.46.10–15). He transferred the cult of the Ara Maxima from the clan of the Potitii to public slaves (9.29.9–11). His speech against Pyrrhus is module 3.5.

Where sources disagree. Mommsen read Appius as a democratic reformer arming the urban poor; E. S. Staveley (1959) as an aristocrat building a clientele, which suits a man who opposed opening the priesthoods to plebeians in 300 (Livy 10.7–8). T. P. Wiseman (Clio's Cosmetics, 1979) traced Livy's arrogant Claudii to late-Republican invention, and the elogium of the Forum of Augustus, known from a copy at Arretium, lists his offices, Samnite towns taken, a Sabine and Etruscan army routed, peace with Pyrrhus prevented, the road, the water and the temple of Bellona, but nothing of freedmen or the Potitii.

Colonies and roads as instruments of control

Module 0.2 surveyed the roads. Rome planted two kinds of colony.

  • Citizen colonies: about 300 Roman families as a coastal garrison (Livy 8.21.11, for Tarracina), at Antium (338), Tarracina (329), Minturnae and Sinuessa (296) and Sena Gallica. Guarding the shore was their service, and they still claimed exemption from the legions in 207 (Livy 27.38).
  • Latin colonies: 2,500 to 6,000 men with their families (2,500 at Cales, Livy 8.16; 6,000 at Alba Fucens, 10.1), drawn from Romans, Latins and other allies. A Roman who enrolled became a Latin. The colony was a separate state with its own magistrates, laws and often coinage, linked to Rome by the Latin rights (intermarriage, trade, migration to Rome) and by the duty to send soldiers. About nineteen were founded between 334 and 263.

The sites state the purpose: Fregellae on the Liris crossing, Luceria behind Samnium, Sora and Interamna on its western edge, Alba Fucens and Carseoli on the route through the Marsi, and Venusia, Beneventum and Aesernia round the rest. Each stood on confiscated land, so the defeated paid for their own surveillance; to Cicero they seemed not towns of Italy but bulwarks of empire (De lege agraria 2.73). Individual allotments did the same work without a colony, organised into new rural tribes until the total reached thirty-five in 241. The roads, built by censors and consuls, joined the colonies to Rome: a colony in hostile country had only to hold out until an army came down them.

Where sources disagree. Aulus Gellius called colonies "little images and likenesses" of the Roman people (16.13.9), and Salmon (1969) saw a planned state strategy. Edward Bispham (2006) and Guy Bradley argue that this projects later practice backwards: early colonies had mixed populations, and the monumental centres excavated at Cosa and Alba Fucens are largely later than the foundations.

The alliance system and the formula togatorum

By 264 Rome had a separate treaty with nearly every community in the peninsula. The settlement of 338 (module 3.3) supplied the categories.

StatusExamples by 264RightsObligations
Roman citizensRome; Tusculum, Aricia; Sabines from 268Vote and office at RomeLegions; war tax (tributum)
Citizens without the voteCapua, Cumae, Formiae, ArpinumRoman private law; local self-governmentLegions and tax, without vote or office
LatinsTibur, Praeneste; the Latin coloniesIntermarriage and trade with Romans; migration to RomeTroops on the formula, at own cost
Allies (socii)Samnites, Etruscan cities, Lucanians, Greek citiesInternal autonomy; no tributeTroops or ships on the formula

The allies owed men. None paid tribute. Each sent a contingent at its own expense, under its own officers and Roman prefects; Rome fed it free, where legionaries had grain deducted from their pay (Polybius 6.39.15). Allied infantry equalled the Roman and allied cavalry outnumbered it (3.107.12); Greek coastal cities sent ships, and lent them to Rome for the crossing of 264 (1.20.14). The allies surrendered their foreign policy, sometimes under a clause binding them to uphold the majesty of the Roman people (Cicero, Pro Balbo 35–36), but kept their laws, magistrates, cults and languages. In return they had security, a share of booty and, through the Latin colonies, of land, and Roman backing for their ruling families, as at Arretium in 302 (Livy 10.3–5) and at Volsinii in 264, where former slaves had seized power. Cornell draws the consequence: since the only obligation was to fight, the system worked only when Rome was at war.

The register was the formula togatorum, the list of "men of the toga" from whom Rome could demand soldiers; the phrase survives in the agrarian law of 111 BC. Its working shows in 209, when twelve of the thirty Latin colonies refused their contingents, while eighteen, led by Fregellae, said their men were ready according to the formula and more besides (Livy 27.9–10). In 204 the twelve were made to supply double their largest levy (29.15).

Where sources disagree. Arnold Toynbee (Hannibal's Legacy, 1965) took the formula to fix a maximum each community could be asked for. P. A. Brunt (Italian Manpower, 1971) argued for a sliding scale, each year's demand set in proportion to the legions raised and to each ally's registered manpower.

The manipular legion

The instrument was the manipular legion, described by Polybius in the mid second century (6.19–42; module 9.2) and confusedly by Livy for 340 (8.8). Behind light-armed velites stood three lines, the hastati, the principes and the veteran triarii, each of ten maniples ("handfuls") with gaps between them, the second line covering the gaps of the first. The front lines threw heavy javelins (pila) and closed with sword and oval shield (scutum); the triarii knelt in reserve with the thrusting spear. The hoplite phalanx was one deep line that won by cohesion and push, with no reserve and no way to turn. A legion could relieve a tired line through the gaps, detach maniples to a flank and cross broken ground in order. Polybius, comparing it with the Macedonian phalanx after Cynoscephalae, says the phalanx needed level ground while the Romans could fight anywhere (18.28–32). Valleys, passes and hill-forts were the ground of the Samnite Wars.

Where sources disagree. In the anonymous Greek Ineditum Vaticanum a Roman tells a Carthaginian in 264 that Rome fought the Etruscans in their own phalanx, then took the oblong shield and javelin from the Samnites; Sallust's Caesar says the Romans took their arms from the Samnites (Catiline 51.38). Livy instead ties the change to the scutum to the introduction of pay at Veii (8.8.3). Such schematic sources cannot settle whether the system was borrowed or evolved.

The manpower of 225 BC

Polybius gives the balance sheet for the Gallic emergency of 225: the men in the field and the lists of men fit to serve that every ally returned (2.23–24), probably from Fabius Pictor, who fought in the war.

Group (Polybius 2.24)InfantryCavalry
Four legions with the consuls20,8001,200
Allies with the consuls30,0002,000
Sabines and Etruscans in the fieldover 50,0004,000
Umbrians and Sarsinates; Veneti and Cenomani20,000 each, all armsincluded

Two legions in Sicily and Tarentum8,400400
Lists: Latins80,0005,000

Lists: Marsi, Marrucini, Frentani, Vestini20,0004,000
Lists: Romans and Campanians250,00023,000
Total able to bear armsover 700,000about 70,000

Citizens of both grades, in the field and on the lists, make about 325,000 of some 770,000: three-fifths of Rome's strength was allied. The Samnites alone listed 77,000 men; Rome had not destroyed its most dangerous enemy but enrolled it. Hannibal invaded with fewer than 20,000 (2.24); he could destroy armies but not the lists, unless the allies left Rome, which is why his strategy aimed at them (module 4.3). Brunt took the lists as genuine but incomplete: the Bruttians and Greek cities are missing.

Why Rome united Italy and no Greek city united Greece

Module 0.2 gave the geographical half of the answer. The institutional half lies in the treatment of the conquered.

  1. Citizenship. Rome made defeated peoples Roman by grades (Tusculum in 381, much of Latium and Campania in 338, the Sabines in 290 and 268) and made citizens of freed slaves. Athens confined citizenship to children of two Athenians in 451/0 (Greek module 6.2), and Sparta's citizens fell from about 8,000 (Herodotus 7.234) to under a thousand (Aristotle, Politics 1270a). Aristotle's polis had to be small enough for citizens to know one another (Politics 1326b). Philip V, urging Larisa about 215 to enrol new citizens, cited the Romans, who admit freed slaves and have sent colonies to nearly seventy places (Syll.3 543); Dionysius (2.16–17) and Tacitus' Claudius (Annals 11.24) say Sparta and Athens fell by treating the conquered as aliens.
  2. Colonies. A Greek colony was an independent polis from birth (Greek module 5.2), and Corcyra fought Corinth; a Latin colony was defined by its rights at Rome and its duty to Rome. The nearest Greek equivalent, the Athenian cleruchy, was resented as confiscation, renounced in the charter of the Second Athenian League in 377 and revived at Samos in 365.
  3. Men, not money. Delian tribute paid Athenian rowers and Athenian buildings (Greek module 6.2), and every Athenian defeat invited revolt. Rome's allies paid nothing and fought beside Romans for shared spoils: a heavy burden, but a partnership in conquest.
  4. Separate treaties and local elites. Athens imposed democracies and drew allied lawsuits to its own courts; Rome left internal government alone, backed the propertied everywhere, and gave the allies no common council in which to combine.
Where sources disagree. Salmon (The Making of Roman Italy, 1982) described a gradual, largely consensual unification. Henrik Mouritsen (Italian Unification, 1998) argues that "unification" was written after the Social War made the allies citizens; in 264 Italy was a hegemony of unequal treaties, and the defections after Cannae (module 4.3) and the revolt of 91 (module 5.2) show how conditional consent was. Both sides agree that the Latin colonies, none of which defected after Cannae, were the system's spine.

Self-test

  1. Why can Livy books 7–10 not be read as a plain record of the Samnite Wars, and which parts of them are most trustworthy?
    Answer

    Livy wrote about three centuries after the events, from annalists who elaborated battles and inflated figures. The skeleton of consuls, triumphs, colonies and treaties is sound; battle narratives and casualty totals are not, and the Scipio Barbatus epitaph contradicts Livy 10.11–12 on 298.

  2. What was a touto, and why do scholars disagree over a Samnite League?
    Answer

    The Samnite "people", the basic state under an annual meddix tuticus, with districts, villages and hill-forts beneath it. Salmon reconstructed a federal league with a war-leader; Dench and Scopacasa argue the evidence is mostly Livy's habit of treating "the Samnites" as one state.

  3. What did the yoke at the Caudine Forks signify, and how did Rome escape the agreement?
    Answer

    Passing disarmed beneath the victor's spears was a rite of submission that unmade the army. The Senate called the terms a personal sponsio of the commanders and handed them over, and Postumius struck the fetial to make a new war just (Livy 9.5–11); Livy's denial that it was a treaty (9.5.2) shows the tradition was contested.

  4. Who fought at Sentinum, and how do Polybius and Duris complicate Livy's account?
    Answer

    Rome under Fabius Rullianus and Decius Mus against Samnites and Gauls, the Etruscans and Umbrians having been drawn away (Livy 10.27–29). Polybius (2.19.5–6) names only Samnites and Gauls; Duris' 100,000 dead (Diodorus 21.6.1) dwarfs Livy's 25,000.

  5. Name three acts of Appius Claudius' censorship and say why his road mattered in the war.
    Answer

    Any three of: the Via Appia, the Aqua Appia, freedmen's sons in the Senate, the humble spread through all the tribes, the transfer of the Ara Maxima cult (Livy 9.29, 9.46). The road gave armies a direct, all-weather route to Campania clear of the exposed Via Latina.

  6. How did a Latin colony differ from a citizen colony?
    Answer

    A citizen colony was some 300 Roman families guarding a coast, who claimed exemption from the legions; in 207 the Senate upheld the claim only for Antium and Ostia (Livy 27.38). A Latin colony had 2,500 to 6,000 men, whose Roman members gave up citizenship, and formed a separate state with Latin rights that owed troops to Rome.

  7. What did Rome's allies owe and not owe, and what does the episode of 209 show about the formula togatorum?
    Answer

    They owed soldiers or ships at their own expense and gave up independent foreign policy; they paid no tribute and kept their own laws. In 209 twelve Latin colonies refused their contingents while eighteen declared men ready according to the formula (Livy 27.9–10): a register of obligations that Rome enforced on the twelve in 204 (29.15).

  8. How did the manipular legion differ from the hoplite phalanx, and why did that suit Samnite warfare?
    Answer

    Three lines of small units with gaps, pila and scutum, and veterans in reserve, against a single deep line relying on cohesion. The legion could relieve tired troops, detach units and move over rough ground, which valleys and hill-forts demanded; Polybius makes the comparison at 18.28–32.

  9. What do Polybius' figures for 225 show about the composition of Rome's strength?
    Answer

    Of some 770,000 men able to bear arms (2.24), about three-fifths were allies, and the Samnites alone listed 77,000. Rome's power was the alliance, which is why Hannibal had to detach allies rather than simply win battles.

  10. Give two institutional reasons, each with a Greek counterpart, why Rome could unite Italy when no Greek city united Greece.
    Answer

    Rome extended citizenship by grades and even to freed slaves, while Athens closed it in 451/0 and Sparta's shrank (Greek module 6.2; Philip V in Syll.3 543). Rome took soldiers, not the tribute that made Athens' allies resent paying for another city, and its colonies extended the state rather than becoming independent poleis (Greek module 5.2).

Carry forward

  1. Rome conquered Italy by turning defeated enemies into allies who owed soldiers, not tribute; since the only obligation was war, the system needed war to work, and its manpower (three-fifths allied in 225) is the reserve that outlasted Pyrrhus and Hannibal.
  2. Colonies on confiscated land, roads that tied them to Rome, and a ladder of statuses (ally, Latin, citizen without the vote, full citizen) were instruments of control: each community had something to hope for and no common council in which to combine.
  3. The difference from Greece was institutional, an elastic citizenship and dependent colonies against the closed polis and the independent colony; but "unification" is partly a later story, and the allies' exclusion from citizenship is the fault line that opens in the Social War.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the conquest of central and southern Italy, 343 to 264 BC, and on the system that held it. Cover: the Samnites and their federation; the three Samnite Wars, the Caudine Forks in 321 BC and the yoke, Sentinum in 295 BC against Samnites, Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians and the devotio of Decius Mus; Appius Claudius Caecus, the Via Appia of 312 BC and the first aqueduct; Latin and citizen colonies and the roads as instruments of control; the alliance system, what the allies owed and what they got, and the list of allied obligations (formula togatorum); the manipular legion and how it differed from the phalanx; the Roman and allied manpower figures for 225 BC in Polybius 2.24; and why Rome united Italy when no Greek city could unite Greece, comparing how each handled conquered peoples (point back to Greek modules 5.2 and 6.2). Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

Pyrrhus and the Greek south

A Greek war in Roman memory

No Roman narrative of the war survives whole. Livy's books 12–15 are lost, and the Periochae give a line or two per event. The one connected account is Plutarch's Pyrrhus (about AD 100, nearly four centuries later), which follows Pyrrhus' contemporary Hieronymus of Cardia and the king's own memoirs; Greek module 7.3 summarises the campaign from that side. The Roman tradition survives in pieces: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities books 19–20, in Byzantine excerpts; Appian's fragmentary Samnite History; Cassius Dio, in fragments and in Zonaras' twelfth-century epitome (8.2–6); and the handbooks of Valerius Maximus, Florus and Eutropius. Behind them stand Ennius, who gave the war book 6 of his Annales about a century after it, and annalists such as Claudius Quadrigarius and Valerius Antias, two centuries after, whom Aulus Gellius sets against each other (3.8). The battles reach us from Greek witnesses; the moral legends were made by Romans long afterwards.

Tarentum and the soiled toga (282)

The road to Tarentum ran through Thurii. Pressed by the Lucanians, that Greek city appealed to Rome, and in 282 Gaius Fabricius relieved it (Livy, Periochae 11; Valerius Maximus 1.8.6). The same year ten Roman ships appeared off Tarentum. The Tarentines, watching from their theatre, cited an old treaty barring Roman ships from sailing beyond the Lacinian promontory, put out, sank several and killed the commander; then they expelled the Roman garrison from Thurii (Livy, Periochae 12; Appian, Samnite History 7; Zonaras 8.2).

Rome sent envoys under Lucius Postumius Megellus, who were received in the theatre. Postumius spoke Greek, and his mistakes were laughed at; then a drunk named Philonides soiled his toga. Postumius told the Tarentines they would wash it out with much blood (Dionysius 19.5; Appian, Samnite History 7). The story does Roman work: a violated envoy made the war just in fetial terms (modules 2.3 and 4.4), and the setting pits Greek wine and theatre against the Roman toga. It also shows a senator able to address Greeks in Greek.

Where sources disagree. Appian names the admiral Cornelius and says he was sightseeing along the coast; Dio and Zonaras call him Lucius Valerius. The Lacinian treaty is known only from Appian and is commonly placed about 303, when the Spartan Cleonymus was in Italy, but that is inference. Whether the fleet's entry was a tour or a deliberate breach is uncertain; the Roman tradition answers by shifting the weight of the story to the theatre.

Heraclea and Asculum as Rome remembered them (280–279)

Pyrrhus landed in 280 after a storm scattered his fleet (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 15); the size of his army is in Greek module 7.3. The Roman tradition kept moments, not tactics. Before Heraclea the consul Publius Valerius Laevinus caught a spy of Pyrrhus, paraded the army before him and sent him back to invite the king to come and see Roman strength openly (Dionysius 19.11). Pyrrhus, viewing the Roman camp, judged that the order of these barbarians was not barbarian (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 16). The elephants, which no Roman had seen, panicked the Roman horse and decided the day (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 17). Romans called them Lucanian oxen (Varro, On the Latin Language 7.39; Pliny, Natural History 8.16). Defeat was turned into credit: Pyrrhus found every Roman dead wounded in front and said that with such soldiers he could have ruled the world (Eutropius 2.11).

At Asculum in 279 the consuls brought an answer to the elephants. Dionysius (20.1) describes three hundred ox-wagons fitted with iron spikes, scythes and fire-bearing grapnels; his narrative covers a single day, while Plutarch, following Hieronymus, has two (Pyrrhus 21). The cost of the second day produced the remark behind "Pyrrhic victory" (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 21), quoted in Greek module 7.3.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch gives two sets of figures for Heraclea: Dionysius' nearly 15,000 Roman and 13,000 Epirote dead, Hieronymus' 7,000 and under 4,000 (Pyrrhus 17). For Asculum he gives Hieronymus' 6,000 Romans and, from Pyrrhus' memoirs, 3,505 of the king's men (21). The Roman-derived figures inflate both sides and so make each victory costlier for Pyrrhus; the Greek ones are lower and precise, which does not make them neutral.
Where sources disagree. Did a third Decius Mus devote himself at Asculum, as his grandfather had at Veseris in 340 and his father at Sentinum in 295 (modules 3.2 and 3.4)? Cicero counts the consul of 279 among the Decii who died for Rome (Tusculan Disputations 1.89). Dio and Zonaras (8.5) say Pyrrhus ordered his men to take alive any Roman in the ritual dress, and that Decius survived; Dionysius mentions no devotio. Patrick Kent (A History of the Pyrrhic War, 2020) treats it as family legend completing a triad.

Cineas, the blind censor and the assembly of kings

After Heraclea Pyrrhus sent Cineas, a Thessalian orator whose words, the king said, had won him more cities than his arms (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 14). His gifts were refused by the senators and, Livy's Cato later boasted, by their wives (Livy 34.4.6). The terms were moderate: friendship with Pyrrhus and Tarentum, freedom for the Italian Greeks, and the return of what Rome had taken from the Samnites, Lucanians, Bruttians and Daunians (Appian, Samnite History 10). The Senate inclined to accept.

Appius Claudius Caecus, censor in 312 (module 3.4), old and blind, had his sons carry him into the Curia. He wished he were deaf as well as blind: Romans who had boasted that they would have beaten Alexander now trembled before Chaonians and Molossians, and there could be no talk of peace while Pyrrhus stood in Italy (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 18–19). Ennius put the speech into verse, and Cicero quotes two of Ennius' lines (On Old Age 16); Cicero also read a prose text of it (Brutus 61), the earliest Roman speech known to have circulated in writing. Cineas reported that the Senate seemed a council of many kings, and that fighting Rome was like fighting the Lernaean hydra (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 19). Appius' principle, no negotiation with an invader on Italian soil, became doctrine; the Senate's refusal to ransom the prisoners of Cannae is its sequel (module 4.3).

Where sources disagree. Plutarch and Appian place the embassy after Heraclea. Justin (18.2) narrates it after Asculum and the arrival of a Carthaginian fleet of 120 ships under Mago, which offered help at Ostia (Valerius Maximus 3.7.10) and belongs to 279/8. Modern accounts therefore either posit two embassies or move the decisive refusal later. The text Cicero read may also have been a later composition under Appius' name.

Fabricius: gold, an elephant and a poisoner

Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, consul in 282 and 278 and censor in 275, became the war's Roman hero without beating Pyrrhus in battle. Sent to ransom the prisoners after Heraclea, he was offered enough gold to outdo any Roman in wealth; Dionysius gives him a speech on honourable poverty in reply (19.13–18). Plutarch adds an elephant trumpeting from behind a curtain, at which Fabricius smiled (Pyrrhus 20). Pyrrhus let the prisoners home for the Saturnalia on parole, and all came back.

In 278 the king's physician offered to poison him. The consuls Fabricius and Quintus Aemilius Papus warned Pyrrhus by letter, and he freed the prisoners in return (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 21). Cicero made the episode his proof that the honourable and the advantageous coincide (On Duties 3.86–87); Eutropius (2.14) has Pyrrhus say the sun could sooner be turned from its course than Fabricius from honour.

Where sources disagree. Gellius (3.8) shows the annalists at odds. Valerius Antias named the would-be poisoner Timochares of Ambracia, a friend of the king; Claudius Quadrigarius insisted it was Nicias and quoted the consuls' letter, in which Rome wishes to win by arms, not bribes or tricks. Plutarch's version, a letter from the king's physician, is closer to Quadrigarius'. The letter is rhetoric, not an archive document; that some offer was made is possible and unprovable.

The enemy was ennobled to make the virtue worth more. Ennius' Pyrrhus refuses ransom, proposing that both sides decide by iron, not gold, a sentiment Cicero calls worthy of the Aeacids (On Duties 1.38). The domestic half followed. As censor Fabricius expelled Publius Cornelius Rufinus, twice consul, from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate (Gellius 4.8), and Manius Curius was found cooking turnips when he refused Samnite gold (Plutarch, Cato Maior 2). These portraits were fixed in the second century, as eastern wealth poured in and Livy's older senators could deplore a "new wisdom" of deceit (Livy 42.47; Greek module 7.3). Fabricius was the past the age of Cato needed, and Valerius Maximus filed him under abstinence and justice (4.3, 6.5; module 3.2).

Sicily, Beneventum and elephants at Rome (278–275)

In 279/8 Rome and Carthage renewed their treaty with clauses against Pyrrhus (Polybius 3.25; module 4.1). Pyrrhus spent 278–276 in Sicily (Greek module 7.3) and, leaving, called it a wrestling ground for Carthaginians and Romans (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 23), the cue for module 4.2. On his way back he stripped Persephone's treasury at Locri; a storm wrecked the ships carrying it and he restored it in fear (Dionysius 20.9). In 204 the Locrians retold the story in the Senate against a Roman legate who had robbed the same temple (Livy 29.18), so a Greek tale of royal sacrilege became a charge against Romans.

In 275 Manius Curius Dentatus met Pyrrhus near Maleventum. A night march to surprise the Roman camp lost its way; at dawn Curius attacked, and the elephants were driven back through Pyrrhus' own lines (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 25). Dionysius (20.12) adds a wounded elephant calf that threw the beasts into confusion. A painted plate from Capena, now in the Villa Giulia, shows a war elephant with a tower followed by its calf, and is usually connected with the battle. When a colony was planted in 268 the ill-omened Maleventum became Beneventum (Pliny, Natural History 3.105). Curius' triumph showed Rome its first elephants (Pliny, Natural History 8.16), and his spoils paid for the Anio Vetus aqueduct (Frontinus, On Aqueducts 6).

Where sources disagree. Frontinus says Pyrrhus first enclosed a whole army in one camp and that the Romans learned the method from his camp captured near Maleventum (Stratagems 4.1.14); Livy's Hannibal agrees that Pyrrhus first taught camp-making (35.14.8). Plutarch's Pyrrhus instead admires the Roman camp at Heraclea (Pyrrhus 16), and Polybius describes the camp as a Roman institution (6.27–42). The Roman fortified camp was probably older; the story flatters Rome as a pupil of the best.

Tarentum, Rhegium and the settlement of the south (272–264)

Pyrrhus left his officer Milo in the citadel of Tarentum. After the king's death at Argos in 272 Milo surrendered it to the consul Lucius Papirius Cursor for safe passage, and the city gave up its arms and ships and became an ally (Zonaras 8.6). A Carthaginian fleet appeared off the harbour at the same moment (Livy, Periochae 14; Orosius 4.3.1–2), later read as a breach of treaty (module 4.2). Locri, back on the Roman side, struck a silver stater showing a seated Roma crowned by Pistis, Good Faith, both named in Greek: among the earliest images of Roma, and a Greek city's statement of what the new relationship should be.

Rhegium was the scandal. It had asked for a Roman garrison, and a legion of Campanians under Decius Vibellius was sent. Imitating the Mamertines across the strait, they killed or expelled the men and took the women and property (Polybius 1.7.6–8; Appian, Samnite History 9). In 270 Rome retook the city. The prisoners were flogged and beheaded in the Forum, burial was refused, and Rhegium was returned to its citizens (Polybius 1.7.10–13; Valerius Maximus 2.7.15). Polybius notes that Rome, having so punished its own men, then helped the Mamertines who had done the same (1.10.4).

Where sources disagree. Polybius says more than 300 were taken alive and executed (1.7.12); Livy's Scipio, rebuking mutineers in 206, makes it 4,000 beheaded (28.28), a number that suits a deterrent speech. Polybius ties the garrison to Pyrrhus' crossing in 280 (1.7.6–7); Dionysius ties it to a consulship of Fabricius (20.4). The year is uncertain; Polybius is the soberer witness.
