What Greek Italy gave Rome before 240

Between Heraclea and the first Latin play Rome took the south's equipment as well as its cities.

Money. Rome's first silver coins were didrachms on the standard of Naples, inscribed ROMANO. The earliest, with a helmeted Mars and a horse's head, was probably struck at a southern Greek mint; its date is disputed, about 310–300 for Andrew Burnett ("The first Roman silver coins", Numismatica e Antichità Classiche 1978) and Historia Numorum: Italy (2001), 280–276 for Crawford (Roman Republican Coinage, 1974, no. 13). A later issue shows Hercules and the she-wolf suckling the twins, the foundation story's first appearance on a coin (module 1.4). One series of cast bronze bars carries an elephant on one face and a sow on the other, usually read as a memory of Pyrrhus' beasts and of the squealing pigs said to have routed them (Aelian, On Animals 1.38).

Where sources disagree. Pliny dates Roman silver to 269 and attaches it to the denarius (Natural History 33.44); Livy, Periochae 15 says the people first used silver that year. The excavations at Morgantina showed the denarius began about 211, and the didrachms are earlier than 269. Most numismatists connect Pliny's year with the Hercules and wolf issue (Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage, 1974, no. 20, dated 269–266), so that it marks a new phase, perhaps the first silver minted at Rome itself, rather than a beginning.

Cults and clocks. Ceres' Greek rites were served by priestesses chosen from Naples or Velia and given citizenship (Cicero, Pro Balbo 55). During a Samnite war Rome set up statues of Pythagoras and Alcibiades, wisest and bravest of the Greeks, in the Comitium at Apollo's command (Pliny, Natural History 34.26), the same prestige that made Numa a pupil of Pythagoras (module 1.5). In 263 Manius Valerius Messalla brought a sundial from Catana; it was set for Sicily, and Rome kept time by it for ninety-nine years (Pliny, Natural History 7.214).

Ships and letters. The crossing of 264 went in fifty-oared ships and triremes lent by Tarentum, Locri, Velia and Naples (Polybius 1.20.14), allies whose service was ships rather than soldiers. Livius Andronicus, a Greek from Tarentum, staged the first Latin plays in 240 (Cicero, Brutus 72); Accius' claim that he came as a captive in 209 is refuted there, and the usual link with 272 is inference. Ennius, born at Rudiae in Calabria in 239, wrote this war into Latin epic. Their work belongs to module 4.5.

Achilles against Troy, and the Greek world looks west

Module 1.3 has Pyrrhus' framing of the war as Achilles' descendant against a colony of Trojans (Pausanias 1.12.1). His Italian coinage made it visible: a didrachm probably struck at Locri shows a helmeted Achilles and Thetis on a sea-horse bringing his shield. Rome kept the epic frame and reversed its outcome. Ennius gave Pyrrhus his ancestral name in the Delphic answer:

aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse (Cicero, On Divination 2.116)

The Latin means either that Pyrrhus can conquer the Romans or that the Romans can conquer him; Cicero objects that Apollo never spoke Latin. Virgil completed the reversal: a Roman will overthrow Argos, Mycenae and the Aeacid himself, usually taken as Perseus of Macedon, avenging his Trojan ancestors (Aeneid 6.836–840; deep dive module 12.5).

The war also made Rome a Greek subject. Pyrrhus dedicated spoils "from the Romans and their allies" to Zeus at Dodona (Syll.³ 392). Dionysius names Hieronymus as the first Greek to touch on Roman antiquities and Timaeus as the next, in his general history and in a separate work on the wars with Pyrrhus (1.6.1); Timaeus ended where Polybius begins, in 264 (Polybius 1.5.1). In 273 Ptolemy II sought friendship; the Roman envoys sent in return handed his gifts to the treasury and were allowed to keep them (Dionysius 20.14; Valerius Maximus 4.3.9). When young Romans struck envoys from Apollonia, the Senate surrendered them to that city (Valerius Maximus 6.6.5): the insult of 282, reversed for display.

Lycophron's Alexandra puts the new power into Cassandra's prophecy: Aeneas' descendants will take the sceptre and monarchy of land and sea (1226–1230), and a kinsman will later end the strife of Europe and Asia (1435–1450).

Where sources disagree. If the poet is Lycophron of Chalcis at Ptolemy II's court, these lines are Greek recognition of Rome in the 270s; Arnaldo Momigliano ("Terra marique", Journal of Roman Studies 1942) took the silence about the First Punic War as a sign of that date. Beloch and Simon Hornblower (edition, 2015) date the poem to about 190, and Hornblower, like Gruen, makes the kinsman Flamininus. On that view the Alexandra answers Cynoscephalae, not Pyrrhus.

Self-test

  1. What happened to Lucius Postumius at Tarentum, and what work does the story do in the Roman tradition?
    Answer

    Received in the theatre, he was mocked for his Greek and his toga was soiled by Philonides; he promised it would be washed in blood (Dionysius 19.5; Appian, Samnite History 7). A violated envoy made the war just, and the setting contrasts Greek levity with Roman gravity, displacing the question of whether the Roman fleet broke the Lacinian treaty.

  2. Why does Plutarch give two sets of casualty figures for Heraclea, and what is the pattern?
    Answer

    He cites Dionysius (nearly 15,000 Roman and 13,000 Epirote dead) and Hieronymus (7,000 and under 4,000) side by side (Pyrrhus 17). The Roman-derived figures inflate both sides, making Pyrrhus' victories look ruinous.

  3. Why is the devotio of a third Decius at Asculum doubted?
    Answer

    Dionysius' full account omits it, and Dio and Zonaras (8.5) have Decius survive after Pyrrhus prepared against the rite; only vaguer notices such as Cicero's make him die. It looks like family tradition completing the deaths at Veseris and Sentinum.

  4. What did Appius Claudius Caecus argue, and why is his speech important to Latin literature?
    Answer

    That Rome must not negotiate while Pyrrhus remained in Italy (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 18–19). Cicero read a written text of it (Brutus 61), making it the earliest Roman speech known to have circulated in writing; Ennius versified it (Cicero, On Old Age 16).

  5. What did Cineas report about the Senate, and what chronological problem surrounds his embassy?
    Answer

    That it seemed a council of many kings, and Rome a hydra (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 19). Plutarch and Appian put the embassy after Heraclea; Justin narrates it after Asculum and the arrival of Mago's fleet at Ostia in 279/8, so some posit two embassies.

  6. How do Quadrigarius and Antias differ over the poisoning offer, and what did Cicero make of it?
    Answer

    Antias named Timochares of Ambracia; Quadrigarius named Nicias and quoted the consuls' letter (Gellius 3.8). Cicero used it to show that the honourable and the advantageous coincide (On Duties 3.86–87).

  7. Why did Roman writers ennoble Pyrrhus himself?
    Answer

    A chivalrous enemy made Roman virtue worth more: Ennius' Pyrrhus will decide by iron, not gold (Cicero, On Duties 1.38), and his praise of Fabricius and of the Roman dead (Eutropius 2.11, 2.14) turns battlefield defeats into moral victories.

  8. What did the Campanian legion do at Rhegium, and how was it punished?
    Answer

    Sent as a garrison, it killed or expelled the citizens and seized the city in imitation of the Mamertines. In 270 Rome retook Rhegium, flogged and beheaded the survivors in the Forum (more than 300 in Polybius 1.7.12, 4,000 in Livy 28.28), and restored the city to its citizens.

  9. What is wrong with Pliny's date for Roman silver, and what do the coins show?
    Answer

    Pliny (Natural History 33.44) puts silver and the denarius in 269, but the denarius dates to about 211 (Morgantina), and ROMANO didrachms on the Neapolitan standard are earlier than 269. His year probably marks the Hercules and wolf issue, a new phase rather than a beginning.

  10. How do Pyrrhus' Achilles coins and Ennius' oracle show Rome answering his claim?
    Answer

    Pyrrhus advertised Achilles and Thetis on his Italian silver; Ennius kept the epic frame but gave the Aeacid an ambiguous oracle that could predict his defeat (Cicero, On Divination 2.116), and Virgil turned the conquest of Greece into Troy's revenge (Aeneid 6.836–840).

Carry forward

  1. The Pyrrhic war comes in two registers: battle accounts from Greek witnesses such as Hieronymus, and moral legends (Postumius, Appius, Fabricius, Curius) fixed by Roman annalists one to two centuries later. Read the first for events and the second for what second-century Romans wanted to have been.
  2. Rome's method in the south was to refuse terms while an invader stood in Italy, absorb defeats with manpower, and bind Greek cities by fides, ships and colonies, punishing breaches of faith even by its own soldiers; that is the posture it carried to Messana in 264.
  3. By 264 Rome had become a Greek subject and a Greek-equipped state: Greek coins, cults, clocks and ships at home, and Greek historians and poets abroad placing it in the Trojan scheme that Pyrrhus had tried to turn against it.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Rome's war with Pyrrhus and the absorption of Magna Graecia, 282 to 264 BC, from the Roman side. Cover: Tarentum and the insult to the Roman envoy in the theatre; Pyrrhus' landing, Heraclea in 280 and Asculum in 279 BC, the elephants and the 'Pyrrhic victory' (Plutarch, Pyrrhus 21); Cineas' embassy and the Senate as 'an assembly of kings', and Appius Claudius Caecus' speech; Fabricius and the offer to poison Pyrrhus, and the Roman self-image it served; Pyrrhus in Sicily and Beneventum in 275 BC; the fall of Tarentum in 272, the Campanian garrison at Rhegium and its punishment, and Rome's first silver coinage on the Greek model, whose date is disputed; Pyrrhus' Achillean claim against a Trojan Rome (module 1.3 lists it among the uses of the Trojan claim: point back, and read Pausanias 1.12.1 here); what Greek Italy gave Rome in the generation before Latin literature began; and how the war made the Greek world notice Rome (Timaeus, Lycophron's Alexandra). Point back to Greek module 7.3, which covers Pyrrhus from the Greek side, and concentrate on the Roman sources and their legends. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 4 · Carthage and the Mediterranean, 264 to 133 BC · 4.1 · 2,800 words

Carthage and Dido

Tyre and the Phoenician westQart-hadasht: the date of the foundationElissa before VirgilVirgil's Dido and an impossible meetingThe Carthaginian stateAn empire of coastsGods and the tophetThe treaties with RomeCarthaginian voicesPunica fides: the Roman stereotypeSelf-testCarry forward

Tyre and the Phoenician west

Carthage was a colony of Tyre and never forgot it. The Phoenician cities of the Levant coast, Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and Arwad, were small, rich and short of land, living by cedar, purple dye, metalwork and shipping. Tyre, an island city, rose to primacy under Hiram I in the tenth century, Solomon's partner in the Hebrew Bible (1 Kings 5). Assyrian demands for tribute in silver drew Tyrian ships west: copper from Cyprus, where Kition became a Tyrian foundation, then silver from the ores behind Huelva in southern Spain, the Greeks' Tartessos. Gadir (Cádiz), beyond the Strait, housed the great temple of Melqart; Strabo (3.5.5) tells how Tyre founded it at the third attempt, on an oracle's instruction. Utica, Lixus in Morocco, Motya in Sicily, and Nora and Sulcis in Sardinia made a chain of harbours.

Where sources disagree. Velleius Paterculus (1.2.3) puts Gades about eighty years after Troy's fall, around 1100, with Utica shortly after, and Pliny (Natural History 16.216) claims Utica's temple kept cedar beams 1,178 years old. Nothing Phoenician in the west is so early. Fernando González de Canales and colleagues (2004) dated Phoenician pottery at Huelva to about 900; María Eugenia Aubet placed settlement proper in the eighth century, after a phase of "precolonial" trade. The twelfth-century dates tie the west to the age of Troy.

Qart-hadasht: the date of the foundation

The Phoenician name was Qart-hadasht, "New City"; Greeks made it Karchedon, Romans Carthago. It sat on a peninsula in the Gulf of Tunis with a defensible hill, the Byrsa. Timaeus of Tauromenium, writing in the early third century, five and a half centuries after the date he gave, put the foundation 38 years before the first Olympiad, 814/813 BC, the same year as Rome (Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1.74.1; module 1.3). Menander of Ephesus, quoted by Josephus from what he presents as Tyrian annals, places Elissa's flight in King Pygmalion's seventh year, 143 years and eight months after Hiram began Solomon's temple (Against Apion 1.125–126): again the late ninth century. Justin (18.6.9) makes Carthage 72 years older than Rome; Appian (Punica 1) puts it before the fall of Troy.

The ground does not quite reach 814. The earliest securely dated finds, Greek cups of Euboean type and Phoenician wares from below the Byrsa and from Bir Massouda, found by excavations led by Hans Georg Niemeyer and Roald Docter, belong to the mid-eighth century; the oldest tophet deposit, the "Chapelle Cintas", is usually put in the second half of the eighth century.

Where sources disagree. Docter and colleagues (2008) obtained radiocarbon dates on animal bone from the lowest levels that reach into the later ninth century. Those who trust the Tyrian king list see near-confirmation of 814; those who weight the pottery prefer about 760, with Timaeus' year a learned synchronism. The gap is two or three generations, and the question is open.

Elissa before Virgil

The earliest surviving version is Timaeus', preserved in an anonymous Greek treatise On Women (FGrHist 566 F 82). Her Phoenician name was Elissa, and she was the sister of Pygmalion, king of Tyre. When Pygmalion killed her husband she fled by ship with some citizens and, after many hardships, reached Libya, where the Libyans called her Dido "because of her wandering". A Libyan king sought to marry her. She refused; pressed by the citizens, she feigned a rite to release her from an oath, built a pyre beside her house, lit it and threw herself in.

Pompeius Trogus, a Gaul writing under Augustus, eight centuries after the event, told the full story; it survives in Justin's epitome (18.4–6). Elissa marries her uncle Acherbas, priest of Hercules (Melqart) and second man in Tyre, and her brother Pygmalion murders him for his hidden gold. She loads the treasure on ships, then has sacks of sand thrown overboard as if they were the gold, so that the king's servants, fearing punishment, must flee with her. At Cyprus a priest of Jupiter joins on condition that his line keeps the priesthood, and some eighty girls, taken from the shore where they earned dowries by prostitution, become wives for her young men.

In Africa she buys as much land as an ox's hide can cover, cuts the hide into strips and encloses a hill: hence Byrsa, Greek for "hide". The settlers dig up an ox's head, sign of a fertile but servile city, and move; a horse's head promises a warlike and powerful one. Then Iarbas, king of the Maxitani, demands her in marriage under threat of war. His envoys trap her: he wants a Carthaginian, they say, to teach his people a civilised life, but who would live among savages? She rebukes their cowardice, and they reveal that the duty is hers. She takes three months, builds a pyre at the city's edge, sacrifices as if to her husband's shade, climbs it with a sword, tells the people she goes to her husband as they wished, and kills herself. While Carthage stood unconquered she was worshipped as a goddess (18.6). This Elissa is a chaste widow who dies to keep faith with the dead and to save her city. She never meets a Trojan.

Where sources disagree. Timaeus' Elissa leaps into the fire; Trogus' uses a sword on the pyre, the combination Virgil keeps. Timaeus glosses Dido as "wanderer"; Servius says it was Punic for a woman of manly courage. "Byrsa" is probably a Greek pun on a Semitic word for citadel. Whether a real princess lies behind her is uncertain: Menander makes Pygmalion a plausible historical king, but Elissa's cult may have generated her biography rather than the reverse.

Virgil's Dido and an impossible meeting

Virgil took Trogus' story almost whole into Venus' account at Aeneid 1.340–368, renaming the husband Sychaeus, then turned it inside out. The chaste widow breaks her vow for Aeneas; Iarbas becomes a rejected suitor (4.196–218); pyre and sword remain, but the motive is desertion; and her curse calls up an avenger from her bones (4.622–629), making Hannibal a Trojan inheritance. Naevius may already have brought Aeneas to Carthage, and Varro said it was Anna who died for love of him (Servius on Aeneid 4.682).

The ancients saw the difficulty: Eratosthenes put Troy's fall in 1184/3, some 370 years before Timaeus' Carthage. Macrobius (Saturnalia 5.17.5–6) calls wanton Dido a story the whole world knows is false, yet artists treat as true. A Greek epigram on her statue (Planudean Anthology 16.151), put into Latin by Ausonius, has Dido protest that she never saw Aeneas, and Jerome (Against Jovinian 1.43) praises Elissa's widowed chastity. Book 4 belongs to deep dive module 12.4.

The Carthaginian state

Aristotle, writing in the 330s, is the earliest analyst. In Politics 2.11 (1272b24–1273b26) he ranks Carthage's constitution with Sparta's and Crete's: the people stay loyal, and there has been no serious civil strife and no tyrant. He names "kings", a council of elders, a Hundred and Four comparable to the Spartan ephors but chosen on merit, and self-recruiting boards of five that elect them. When kings and elders agree, they decide whether to consult the people; when they disagree, the people decide, and any citizen may speak against a proposal, as at Sparta none could. His criticisms concern oligarchy: wealth counts in elections, the highest offices can be bought, and one man may hold several. Discontent is drained by sending citizens out to grow rich in the subject cities.

The "kings" are the suffetes (šptm, "judges"), two annual chief magistrates attested in Punic inscriptions and in Livy, who shows Hannibal as chief magistrate in 196 attacking the life tenure of the order of judges (33.46–47). Generals were separate, elected for a war and answerable to a court of a hundred judges created, Justin says, to restrain them (19.2); failed generals were sometimes crucified. Polybius (6.51) calls the constitution well designed but past its prime by the Hannibalic war: at Carthage the people had the greatest say, at Rome the Senate, so Rome deliberated better.

Two families dominate. The Magonids descend from Mago, who in the mid-sixth century first gave Carthage an ordered army (Justin 18.7, 19.1); a Magonid Hamilcar fell at Himera in 480 (Herodotus 7.165–167). The Barcids, Hamilcar Barca ("lightning") and his sons, built a near-monarchy in Spain after 237 (modules 4.2 and 4.3).

Where sources disagree. Herodotus (7.166) says Hamilcar was made king for his valour; Aristotle's kings are elected and not tied to one family. Whether a Magonid monarchy gave way to paired suffetes, or Greeks always styled elected magistrates kings, is uncertain, as is whether the Hundred and Four is Justin's court of a hundred.

An empire of coasts

When Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years in the early sixth century, Carthage took over the mother city's role in the west. Its empire was naval and coastal. In Sicily the Phoenicians held Motya, Soloeis and Panormus, near the Elymians and the short crossing to Africa (Thucydides 6.2.6); Carthage led them against the Greeks, losing at Himera in 480 and replacing Motya, destroyed by Dionysius I in 397 (Diodorus 14.47–53), with Lilybaeum. Off Corsica about 540 Carthaginian and Etruscan fleets fought the Phocaeans at Alalia (Herodotus 1.166); the gold tablets of about 500 from Pyrgi, Caere's port, with a dedication in Etruscan and Phoenician, show Carthage's Etruscan ties. Sardinia was conquered in the later sixth century after hard fighting (Justin 19.1). In Spain Carthage inherited Gadir and colonised Ebusus (Ibiza), 160 years after its own foundation by Diodorus' reckoning (5.16); the land empire there was Barcid. In Africa Carthage paid the Libyans rent for its site until the fifth century (Justin 19.1–2), then took the hinterland and taxed the Libyans hard; Agathocles of Syracuse, landing in 310, showed how thinly it was held.

Gods and the tophet

The chief god was Baal Hammon, whom Greeks called Kronos and Romans Saturn; the African Saturn of Roman times continues him. Beside him from the fifth century stands Tanit, "Tanit face of Baal" on thousands of stelae, with her sign of triangle, bar and disc; Romans identified her with Juno Caelestis, which is why Virgil's Carthage is Juno's city. Melqart, "king of the city", whom Greeks called Heracles and Romans Hercules, tied colony to mother city: Carthaginian envoys were at his festival in Tyre when Alexander besieged it (Arrian, Anabasis 2.24.5). Names carry the theology: Hannibal, "grace of Baal"; Hasdrubal, "Baal helps".

Greek and Roman writers accused Carthage of sacrificing children. Diodorus (20.14.4–6), writing nearly three centuries after the event, reports that in 310, with Agathocles in Africa, the Carthaginians blamed their disasters on Kronos, whom they had cheated with bought children; they sacrificed two hundred children of the noblest families, and at least three hundred others offered themselves. Each child rolled from the sloping hands of a bronze statue into fire. Plutarch (On Superstition 13) adds a mother standing by without tears while flutes and drums drowned the cries; Tertullian (Apology 9.2) says the rite lasted in Africa until a proconsul crucified its priests.

In 1921 stelae on the antiquities market led François Icard and Paul Gielly to a precinct in the Salammbô quarter. Dug since by Francis Kelsey, Pierre Cintas and, in 1976–79, Lawrence Stager's team, it held thousands of urns of burnt bones of infants and of lambs and kids, under stelae to Baal Hammon and Tanit recording vows the god "heard"; Stager estimated 20,000 urns for 400–200 alone. Archaeologists borrowed the biblical word tophet (Jeremiah 7.31); similar precincts exist at Motya, Sulcis and Tharros, none in Phoenicia. The inscriptions call the offering mlk, which Otto Eissfeldt (1935) showed is a sacrificial term, not a god "Moloch".

Where sources disagree. Sabatino Moscati (1987), M'hamed Fantar and Hélène Bénichou-Safar read the tophet as a cemetery for infants who died naturally and the classical reports as propaganda; Jeffrey Schwartz and colleagues (2010) found many of the infants prenatal or newborn. Patricia Smith, Stager and colleagues (2011) replied that the ages cluster at one to two months, unlike natural mortality, and Paolo Xella, Josephine Quinn and others (2013) set the vow formulae beside the texts. Opinion now leans to sacrifice; its frequency and scale remain disputed.

The treaties with Rome

Polybius copied three treaties from bronze tablets in the treasury of the aediles beside the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus (3.26.1); the first was in Latin so archaic that the best-informed Romans understood it only with effort (3.22.3).

TreatyPolybius' dateMain terms
First (3.22–23)consuls Brutus and Horatius, 28 years before Xerxes crossed to Greece: 508/7 (509 in Varro's reckoning)Romans not to sail beyond the Fair Promontory unless forced, and then to leave within five days; trade in Libya and Sardinia only before a herald or clerk; equal terms in Carthaginian Sicily; Carthage not to harm Ardea, Antium, Circeii, Tarracina or other Latins subject to Rome, nor build a fort in Latium
Second (3.24)undated; usually 348 (Livy 7.27.2; Diodorus 16.69.1)Tyre and Utica join Carthage; Mastia of Tarseion added as a western limit; Romans barred from Sardinia and Libya; trade open at Carthage and in Carthaginian Sicily
Third (3.25)Pyrrhus' invasion, 279/8earlier terms confirmed; any alliance with Pyrrhus to leave room to help the other; Carthage to supply ships

Carthaginians swore by their ancestral gods, Romans by Jupiter Lapis, the oath-taker casting a stone and praying to be cast out likewise if he broke faith (3.25.6–9). The pattern is clear: Carthage guards a trading monopoly in Africa and Sardinia and treats Rome as a Latin power whose coast it will leave alone. Polybius cites the treaties against Philinus of Agrigentum, who claimed that one barred Romans from Sicily and Carthaginians from Italy, so that Rome broke it by crossing in 264; Polybius says no such document exists (3.26). The crossing itself belongs to module 4.2.

Where sources disagree. Diodorus (16.69.1) calls the treaty of 348 the first; module 1.6 sets out why most, Beaumont and Cornell among them, keep Polybius' date near 509. Livy (9.43.26) records a renewal "for the third time" in 306 that Polybius omits, and some identify it with the treaty Philinus cited (module 4.2).

Carthaginian voices

Carthage's literature is lost. In 146 the Senate gave its libraries to African kings but had Mago's twenty-eight books on agriculture translated into Latin (Pliny, Natural History 18.22); Cassius Dionysius of Utica made a Greek version (Varro, On Agriculture 1.1.10), and Columella calls Mago the father of farming (1.1.13). The fragments, on vines, olives, bees and oxen, speak for a landowning elite: whoever buys land should sell his town house (Pliny, Natural History 18.35).

Hanno's Periplus survives in Greek, essentially in one ninth-century manuscript at Heidelberg, claiming to translate the account that Hanno, "king of the Carthaginians", set up in the temple of Kronos. He sails past the Pillars with sixty penteconters and thirty thousand settlers to found towns, then south past a burning mountain, the Chariot of the Gods, to hairy people his interpreters called Gorillai; Pliny says their skins hung in Juno's temple at Carthage until its fall (6.200).

The longest Punic text in Latin letters is in Plautus' Poenulus, adapted from a Greek Karchedonios: the Carthaginian Hanno enters praying in Punic (930–949) before switching to Latin. He is a pious father seeking his kidnapped daughters, though the prologue says he knows every language and pretends not to: "Poenus plane est" (113). Polybius' Greek text of Hannibal's oath with Philip V (7.9) and thousands of votive inscriptions complete the record.

Where sources disagree. Gilbert Germain (1957) judged the Periplus a Greek literary fiction; most scholars accept a Punic core, perhaps reworked. Its date is uncertain, and its furthest point is placed anywhere from Mount Cameroon to southern Morocco, Raymond Mauny doubting that ancient ships could return past Cape Bojador. Pliny (2.169) even has Hanno sail round Africa to Arabia.

Punica fides: the Roman stereotype

Romans made Carthage a proverb. Sallust (Jugurtha 108.3) suspects Bocchus of "Punic faith"; Livy gives Hannibal "perfidia plus quam Punica" (21.4.9). Cicero (De lege agraria 2.95) blames place, not race: harbours full of traders made Carthaginians liars. The type is older than Rome: Homer's Phoenician is a guileful trader (Odyssey 14.288–289), and Polybius says that at Carthage nothing profitable was thought shameful (6.56). Yet Polybius calls Rome's seizure of Sardinia in 238 contrary to all justice (3.28.1–2), and Rome's conduct in 149 (module 4.4) was no model of good faith. The stereotype is the victor's: Carthage left no history of its wars, and its treaties show a state that renewed terms with Rome for more than two centuries. Jonathan Prag (2006) and Josephine Quinn (In Search of the Phoenicians, 2018) add that "Punic" and "Phoenician" were outsiders' labels; Carthaginians named themselves by their city.

Self-test

  1. What dates did ancient writers give for the foundation of Carthage, and how does the archaeology compare?
    Answer

    Timaeus gave 814/813, synchronised with Rome (Dionysius 1.74.1), and Menander's Tyrian list via Josephus points to the late ninth century; Appian put it before the Trojan War. The earliest pottery belongs to the mid-eighth century and the Chapelle Cintas to its second half, though radiocarbon dates reach into the late ninth, so the gap is two or three generations and still debated.

  2. How does Elissa die in Timaeus, and how does Justin's version differ?
    Answer

    In Timaeus she refuses a Libyan king, pretends a rite to release an oath, builds a pyre beside her house and leaps into it (FGrHist 566 F 82). In Justin 18.6 she asks three months, builds a pyre at the city's edge, sacrifices to her husband's shade and kills herself with a sword on the pyre.

  3. How did Elissa trick Pygmalion's servants into joining her flight?
    Answer

    At sea she had sacks of sand thrown overboard as if they were Acherbas' gold; the servants, fearing the king's punishment for its loss, had to flee with her (Justin 18.4).

  4. What does the oxhide story explain, and why is it probably not an old Carthaginian tradition?
    Answer

    It explains the name of the citadel, Byrsa, which in Greek means "hide". The name is probably a Semitic word for citadel reinterpreted by a Greek pun, so the story was built on the etymology.

  5. What did Virgil change in the Elissa story, and what objection did ancient readers raise?
    Answer

    He made her Aeneas' contemporary and lover, broke her vow to Sychaeus, motivated her suicide by desertion and gave her a curse that founds the Punic wars. Troy fell about 370 years before Carthage was founded; Macrobius (Saturnalia 5.17.5–6) says the whole world knows the story is false, and a Greek epigram has Dido deny she ever saw Aeneas.

  6. Name the parts of the Carthaginian constitution in Aristotle and the feature of its assembly he contrasts with Sparta and Crete.
    Answer

    "Kings" (the suffetes, a pair in Punic and Latin evidence), a council of elders, the Hundred and Four, the boards of five, and the people. When a matter came before the people any citizen could speak against it (Politics 2.11).

  7. Why, according to Polybius 6.51, was Rome better placed than Carthage at the time of the Hannibalic war?
    Answer

    Both had mixed constitutions, but Carthage's had passed its prime: the people had the greatest voice there, while at Rome the Senate still guided deliberation.

  8. What does Diodorus 20.14 report, and what should a reader note about its date?
    Answer

    That in 310, during Agathocles' invasion, the Carthaginians sacrificed two hundred noble children to Kronos (Baal Hammon), with three hundred more volunteering, rolling them from a bronze statue's hands into fire. Diodorus wrote nearly three centuries later, from a Greek tradition hostile to Carthage.

  9. What evidence do the two sides of the tophet debate rely on?
    Answer

    The urns of infant and animal bones and the stelae with vow formulae and the term mlk. Schwartz and colleagues stress prenatal and newborn ages consistent with natural death; Smith, Stager and colleagues find ages clustered at one to two months, and Xella, Quinn and others combine inscriptions and texts to argue for sacrifice.

  10. What did the first two treaties in Polybius protect for each side, and what did the third add?
    Answer

    Carthage kept a trading monopoly in Libya and Sardinia behind the Fair Promontory and Mastia; Rome secured its Latin coast and equal access to Carthaginian Sicily. The third, at Pyrrhus' invasion, confirmed the earlier terms, let each side help the other against him and had Carthage supply the ships (3.25).

Carry forward

  1. Carthage is known almost entirely through its enemies, Greek historians, Roman annalists and a comic poet; read every verdict on it (Punic faith, child sacrifice, its constitution) by asking who wrote it, when and for whom, and treat the treaties, Mago, Hanno and the inscriptions as the nearest thing to Carthaginian testimony.
  2. The founding queen has two layers: the Tyrian Elissa of Timaeus and Trogus, a chaste widow who dies rather than marry Iarbas, and Virgil's Dido, made Aeneas' contemporary against a chronology the ancients knew, so that the Punic wars begin in her curse.
  3. Rome and Carthage were treaty partners with complementary spheres for more than two centuries before 264; the wars that follow broke a long arrangement, and who broke faith was argued from the start, by Philinus against Polybius.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Carthage and on the legend of its founding queen. Cover: the Phoenician expansion west and Tyre; the foundation of Carthage (Timaeus' date of 814/813 BC against the archaeology of the eighth century); Elissa-Dido before Virgil (Timaeus, Justin's epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.4–6, the oxhide and the Byrsa, her suicide to avoid marrying Iarbas) and Virgil's rewriting of her into Aeneas' lover, with the chronological impossibility the ancients already noticed; the Carthaginian state as Aristotle (Politics 2.11) and Polybius 6.51 describe it: suffetes, council and assembly, the Magonids and the Barcids; the empire in Africa, Sardinia, Spain and western Sicily; religion (Baal Hammon, Tanit, Melqart) and the tophet controversy over child sacrifice, from Diodorus 20.14 to the excavations at Salammbô and the modern argument; the treaties with Rome in Polybius 3.22–26; the Carthaginian voices that survive (Mago's agronomy, Hanno's Periplus, the Punic speeches in Plautus' Poenulus); and the Roman stereotype of Punic faithlessness. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 4 · Carthage and the Mediterranean, 264 to 133 BC · 4.2 · 2,842 words

The First Punic War

Polybius' war and its partisansMessana, 264: a hesitant Senate and a people that votedHiero changes sides; AgrigentumA fleet from a wreck: Mylae and the corvusEcnomus and Regulus in AfricaRegulus returns to Carthage: the making of an exemplumThe sea as enemy: storms and DrepanaHamilcar Barca and the Aegates IslandsThe Mercenary War, Sardinia and Corsica, and the first provinceThe cost in Polybius' figuresSelf-testCarry forward

Polybius' war and its partisans

The war survives as a connected story only in Polybius book 1, written after 167, a century after the events, as background to his fifty-three years from 220 (module 4.4). He starts in 264 because Timaeus stopped there and because the Romans then first crossed the sea (1.5, 1.12.5–9). His main sources were two contemporaries he distrusts: Philinus of Agrigentum, whose city Rome sacked in 261, and Fabius Pictor, the senator who wrote in Greek about 200 (module 4.5). Each wrote like a lover, Philinus finding wisdom and courage only in Carthaginians, Fabius only in Romans (1.14).

The rest is later and broken. Diodorus, writing about 30 BC, survives here in Byzantine excerpts (books 23–24) and cites Philinus by name (23.8). Cassius Dio, early in the third century AD, survives in fragments and in the twelfth-century epitome of Zonaras (book 8). Livy's books 16–19 are lost but for the late antique Periochae. Naevius, a veteran of the war (Gellius 17.21.45), made it a Latin epic (module 4.5).

Messana, 264: a hesitant Senate and a people that voted

Leaving Sicily in 276, Pyrrhus called it a wrestling ground for Carthaginians and Romans (module 3.5). The bout began at Messana. The Mamertines, "men of Mars", were Campanian mercenaries of Agathocles who seized the city after his death in 289, killing or expelling its men and taking their wives and property (Polybius 1.7.2–4). Hiero, general and then king of Syracuse, beat them at the Longanus river (1.9.7–8). Divided, one faction let a Carthaginian garrison into the citadel; the other offered the city to Rome and asked help as kinsmen (1.10.1–2).

Polybius presents a dilemma. Rome had just executed its own garrison at Rhegium for the same crime (module 3.5), and helping its imitators was inconsistent (1.10.3–4). Against that stood fear: Carthage held Africa, much of Spain and the western islands, and with Messana would hold the bridge to Italy (1.10.5–9). The Senate never gave its sanction. The people, worn out by recent wars, listened to the commanders, who promised plunder, and voted to send help under the consul Appius Claudius Caudex (1.11.1–3). The Mamertines got the Carthaginian commander out of the citadel; Carthage crucified him (1.11.4–5), allied with Hiero and besieged Messana. Appius crossed at night in ships lent by the Greek allies (1.20.13–14) and beat Hiero, then the Carthaginians (1.11.9–12.4).

Where sources disagree. Polybius' version, probably Fabian, puts reluctance in the Senate and greed in the people. W. V. Harris (War and Imperialism in Republican Rome, 1979) reads it as an alibi for an aristocracy that lived on military glory. B. D. Hoyos (Unplanned Wars, 1998) argues that Rome voted to help the Mamertines against Hiero, not for war with Carthage. Philinus had Appius beaten twice, a version Polybius shows to be self-contradictory (1.15).

The treaties Polybius copied from bronze tablets on the Capitol (3.22–26) are module 4.1; one disputed clause bears on war guilt.

Where sources disagree. Philinus said a treaty barred Romans from Sicily and Carthaginians from Italy, so that the crossing broke an oath; Polybius says no such document ever existed (3.26.2–5). Yet Livy's tradition made a Carthaginian fleet off Tarentum in 272 a breach of treaty (Periochae 14), and Servius (on Aeneid 4.628) knew a clause keeping each power off the other's shores. Hoyos ("Treaties True and False", CQ 1985) found most historians following Philinus and argued that he erred.

Hiero changes sides; Agrigentum

In 263 both consuls crossed with four legions and Sicilian cities came over (1.16.1–3), Segesta with its claim of Trojan kinship (module 1.3). Hiero asked for peace, returning prisoners and paying 100 talents (1.16.9); Diodorus gives a quarter of that sum and a fifteen-year term (23.4.1). Rome accepted because, with Carthage holding the sea, its army needed Syracusan grain (1.16.6–8). Hiero stayed loyal until his death in 215. Manius Valerius took the name Messalla from Messana and hung a painting of his victory on the Curia Hostilia (Pliny, Natural History 35.22).

Agrigentum fell in 261 after a long siege, and its people were sold, more than 25,000 by Diodorus' count (Polybius 1.19.15; Diodorus 23.9.1). The Senate now aimed to drive Carthage out of the island (1.20.1–2): the war for Messana had become a war for Sicily.

A fleet from a wreck: Mylae and the corvus

Land victories could not win Sicily while Carthage held the sea and raided Italy (1.20.5–8). In 261 Rome ordered 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes, though it had never built a quinquereme. The model, Polybius says, was a Carthaginian decked ship captured when it ran aground in 264, and crews learned to row on benches set up on land (1.20.9–21.2). The first seventeen ships, under the consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio, were trapped at Lipara and taken with him (1.21.4–8).

Because the new ships were slow, someone proposed the raven (korax, Latin corvus): a gangway about 1.2 metres wide and 11 long, pivoting on a pole in the bow, dropped so that an iron spike pinned the enemy deck and marines ran across (1.22). Off Mylae in 260 Hannibal's 130 ships came on in contempt. The first thirty were grappled and taken, among them his flagship, a "seven" that had belonged to Pyrrhus; ships trying the flanks met ravens swung round to face them, and Carthage lost fifty ships (1.23). Gaius Duilius held Rome's first naval triumph (Periochae 17) and was escorted home from dinner for life by a torch and a piper (Cicero, On Old Age 44). The inscription of his column of ships' beaks survives in an archaising imperial copy (CIL I² 25).

Where sources disagree. The captured-model story (Polybius 1.20.15–16) makes Rome a nation of amateurs, yet its Greek allies had built warships for centuries, the ground on which Thiel (1954) and Goldsworthy (2000) doubt it. The Punic warship excavated off Marsala, its timbers marked with Punic letters for assembly, shows building methods that could be copied. The corvus appears only in Polybius and leaves his narrative after 256; its weight in the bow has been blamed for losses in heavy seas, though a calculation in H. T. Wallinga's The Boarding-Bridge of the Romans (1956) found it unlikely to upset a quinquereme seriously. Eutropius gives Mylae as 31 ships taken and 14 sunk (2.20).

Ecnomus and Regulus in Africa

In 256 the consuls Marcus Atilius Regulus and Lucius Manlius Vulso sailed for Africa with 330 ships, each carrying 300 rowers and 120 marines, about 140,000 men; Hamilcar and Hanno met them off southern Sicily with 350 ships and over 150,000 (1.25.7–26.9). The Romans came in a wedge, with the horse transports in tow (1.26.10–16). In the separate fights the ravens told: Rome lost 24 ships sunk, Carthage more than 30 sunk and 64 taken (1.28.14).

The army landed at Aspis, and the Senate recalled Manlius with the fleet, leaving Regulus 15,000 infantry and 500 cavalry (1.29.9). He beat a Carthaginian army at Adys on hills where its elephants were useless and took Tunis (1.30). Hoping to finish before a successor came, he offered terms so harsh that Carthage chose to fight (1.31.4–8); Dio's list in Zonaras (8.13) amounts to surrender. Carthage hired Xanthippus, a Spartan who blamed its generals rather than Roman quality (1.32). With 12,000 foot, 4,000 horse and nearly 100 elephants on open ground in 255, he broke the Roman army; about 2,000 escaped and Regulus was taken with 500 (1.34). Polybius draws Euripides' lesson that one wise counsel defeats many hands (1.35). Appian (Punica 4) and Valerius Maximus (9.6 ext. 1) say Carthage had Xanthippus drowned on his voyage home.

Where sources disagree. If Polybius' totals stand, Ecnomus may have involved more men than any other sea battle. W. W. Tarn ("The Fleets of the First Punic War", JHS 1907) and J. H. Thiel (A History of Roman Sea-Power before the Second Punic War, 1954) reduced his largest Roman fleets as implausible; Tipps ("The Battle of Ecnomus", Historia 1985) defended them, and Goldsworthy (The Punic Wars, 2000) advises broad acceptance. H. H. Scullard (Cambridge Ancient History VII.2, 1989) judged Dio's terms for Regulus scarcely reliable.

Regulus returns to Carthage: the making of an exemplum

Polybius says nothing of Regulus after his capture; the Roman tradition kept him alive. Livy's book 18, in the Periochae, had him kill a monstrous serpent by the Bagradas, whose 120-foot skin Tubero says went to Rome (Gellius 7.3). About 250 Carthage sent him to Rome to negotiate peace or an exchange of prisoners, on oath to return if he failed. He urged the Senate to refuse both, went back, and was put to death. Tuditanus, consul in 129, had him kept awake until he died; Tubero, in the first century BC, had his eyelids sewn open against the sun (Gellius 7.4). Cicero, two centuries on, made him the proof that an oath to an enemy binds (On Duties 3.99–111); Horace's Regulus pushes away wife and sons and leaves as if for a country holiday (Odes 3.5.13–56).

Where sources disagree. Polybius, who admired Roman good faith, is silent. Diodorus (24.12) tells how the mother of the Atilii, angry at her husband's death, had her sons torture two Carthaginian prisoners until one died and the tribunes intervened. In Tuditanus it is Regulus' sons who shut Carthaginian captives in a spiked chest (Gellius 7.4); in Augustine Regulus himself dies in one (City of God 1.15). The cruelty migrated, and most modern historians treat the torture as family legend.

The sea as enemy: storms and Drepana

In 255 a rescue fleet took 114 Carthaginian ships off the Hermaean promontory (1.36.11). Returning along southern Sicily against its pilots' advice, between the risings of Orion and Sirius, it met a storm off Camarina: of 364 ships 80 survived, the greatest disaster at sea Polybius knew (1.37.1–4). He blamed the consuls and a Roman habit of meeting every obstacle with force, which works against men but not against wind and water (1.37.7–10). Rome built 220 ships in three months and took Panormus (1.38); in 253 another storm sank more than 150, and the Senate gave up the sea for a time (1.39.6–8). Lucius Scipio, consul in 259, whose epitaph records Corsica taken, also gave a temple to the Storms, the Tempestates (CIL I² 9). The war turned to land: at Panormus in 250 Lucius Caecilius Metellus broke Hasdrubal's elephants against a ditch, and the siege of Lilybaeum began (1.40–48).

In 249 Publius Claudius Pulcher tried to surprise Adherbal at Drepana. The Carthaginian slipped out as the Roman column entered, pinned it against the shore and took 93 ships (1.49–51). Later writers remembered the sacred chickens Claudius drowned (module 2.3); Polybius blamed rashness. Claudius named a man of the lowest standing as dictator, who was forced to resign (Periochae 19), and was fined heavily (1.52.2–3). His colleague Lucius Junius Pullus anchored his convoy on a rocky coast to avoid Carthalo, and a storm destroyed it (1.54).

Where sources disagree. Diodorus has 340 warships lost off Camarina (23.18.1) against Polybius' 284; Claudius losing 117 ships and 20,000 men (24.1.5) against 93 ships; and two warships surviving of 105 in Junius' storm (24.1.9). If Diodorus follows Philinus and Polybius here follows Fabius, each source had reason to bend the numbers.

Hamilcar Barca and the Aegates Islands

In 247, the eighteenth year of the war, Carthage gave the Sicilian command to Hamilcar Barca (1.56.1–2). He held Heircte, a mountain stronghold near Panormus, for three years and raided Italy as far as Cumae (1.56). In 244 he took the town of Eryx, between a Roman garrison by the summit sanctuary of Venus Erycina (module 1.3) and a Roman army at the foot, and held it two years more (1.58). Polybius compares the struggle to champion boxers and to game-cocks fighting on when their wings fail (1.57–58), and names Hamilcar the best general of the war (1.64.6). He was unbeaten but could not win while Carthage kept few ships at sea.

Rome's last fleet was privately funded: leading citizens, singly or in twos and threes, each provided a quinquereme, to be repaid after victory; 200 were built on the model of the ship of Hannibal the Rhodian, captured running the blockade of Lilybaeum (1.59.6–8). In March 241 Hanno brought ships loaded with supplies, meaning to unload at Eryx and embark Hamilcar's best men. The consul Gaius Lutatius Catulus caught him off the Aegates islands, attacking though the wind favoured the enemy; the heavy Carthaginian ships with raw crews lost 50 sunk and 70 taken, with nearly 10,000 prisoners (1.60–61). Diodorus has 117 Carthaginian ships lost and 80 Roman ships destroyed or damaged, and Philinus 6,000 prisoners (24.11).

Where sources disagree. Surveys off Levanzo led by Sebastiano Tusa with the RPM Nautical Foundation have recovered more than twenty bronze rams, with helmets and amphorae; Latin inscriptions on several name the quaestors who passed them (Jonathan Prag, JRA 2014). The rams are uniform and small: William Murray judges from their size that they come from ships smaller than "fours", not Polybius' quinqueremes. Either Polybius used "quinquereme" loosely, or the rams found so far come from the smaller ships in each fleet; the question is open.

Diodorus (24.13) and Nepos (Hamilcar 1) say the Romans first demanded Hamilcar's arms and deserters, and he refused. Lutatius agreed that Carthage would leave Sicily, make no war on Hiero, return all prisoners without ransom, and pay 2,200 Euboean talents over twenty years (1.62.8–9). The Roman people refused to ratify; ten commissioners added 1,000 talents payable at once, cut the term to ten years and took the islands between Sicily and Italy (1.63.1–3). Each side was barred from the other's allies (3.27.2–6).

The Mercenary War, Sardinia and Corsica, and the first province

Carthage could not pay the roughly 20,000 mercenaries brought home from Sicily (1.66–67). They mutinied, Libyan subjects squeezed by wartime levies joined them (1.72), and under Spendius, a Campanian runaway slave, and Matho, a Libyan, they besieged Utica and threatened Carthage, striking coins inscribed "of the Libyans". Polybius calls it the truceless war, unmatched in cruelty and lawlessness (1.65, 1.88.7): the rebels mutilated and killed the envoy Gisgo and some 700 prisoners (1.79–80); Hamilcar trapped one army at the Saw, where the starving men ate their prisoners and slaves (1.84–85); Matho was tortured to death in Carthage (1.88.6). It lasted three years and four months.

Rome at first behaved correctly, freeing Carthaginian prisoners and refusing Utica's surrender (1.83.5–11). Hiero supplied Carthage on a principle Polybius states as a rule: never help a power grow so great that no one can dispute even its acknowledged rights (1.83.3–4). Then, in 238 or 237, mercenaries expelled from Sardinia invited Rome in. When Carthage prepared to recover the island, Rome voted war; Carthage gave up Sardinia and paid 1,200 talents more (1.88.8–12). Polybius calls this contrary to all justice (3.28.1–4) and counts it the second cause of the Hannibalic war, after Hamilcar's anger (3.10); Hamilcar's departure for Spain in 237 is module 4.3. Corsica, not named in the cession, was subdued in the 230s (Periochae 20).

Sicily outside Hiero's kingdom passed to Rome; the former Carthaginian cities probably paid Rome the grain tithe they had paid Carthage. Cicero calls Sicily the first of all to be called a province (Verrines 2.2.2). In 227 the praetors were raised to four (Periochae 20), giving Sicily and Sardinia governors.

Where sources disagree. Modern textbooks date the first province to 241, but no regular governor is attested before 227, and provincia meant a magistrate's task before it meant a territory. J. S. Richardson (The Language of Empire, 2008) traces that shift; on this view 241 began Roman taxation in Sicily, and 227 the governed province.

The cost in Polybius' figures

The war lasted twenty-four years without a break, counting inclusively, the longest and greatest Polybius knew; the Romans lost about 700 quinqueremes, the Carthaginians about 500 (1.63.4–6).

YearEventRoman ships lostCarthaginian ships lostPolybius
260Lipara; Mylae17 taken501.21–23
256Ecnomus24 sunkover 30 sunk, 64 taken1.28
255Hermaeum; storm off Camarinaabout 284 wrecked114 taken1.36–37
253Storm on the voyage to Romeover 150none1.39
