Polybius, Cato and the Greek invasion of Rome

Polybius: hostage, tutor, witnessBook 6: three powers in one stateCamp, funeral and the fear of the godsJudging the analysisLatin literature begins as translationComedy in Greek dress: Plautus and TerenceGreek history and Latin prose: Fabius Pictor and CatoPhilosophers in the Senate, 155 BCThe "Scipionic circle" and captive GreeceSelf-testCarry forward

Polybius: hostage, tutor, witness

Polybius was born at Megalopolis around 200 BC, son of Lycortas, a leading Achaean statesman. He carried Philopoemen's urn at his funeral in 182 (Plutarch, Philopoemen 21) and was the League's cavalry commander in 170/169 (Polybius 28.6). In 167 he was among the thousand Achaeans deported to Italy; Greek module 7.3 tells how few came home. He stayed in Rome because of a friendship. The sons of Aemilius Paullus had borrowed books from him, and the younger, Scipio Aemilianus, then about eighteen, asked why Polybius always addressed his brother: did he too think him idle and un-Roman? Polybius promised to help him speak and act worthy of his ancestors (31.23–24).

He was more than a tutor. He helped the Seleucid hostage Demetrius escape in 162 (31.11–15). When the detainees were freed in 150, Cato told him that asking for their old honours too was like Odysseus going back into the Cyclops' cave for his cap and belt (Plutarch, Cato Maior 9). In 146 he stood beside Scipio as Carthage burned (38.21–22), and after Corinth the Roman commissioners left him to settle the Achaean cities' laws (39.5). He died at eighty-two after a fall from his horse (Pseudo-Lucian, Long Lives 22). His forty books, planned to end in 167 and extended to 146 (3.4), are treated as a source in module 0.1.

Where sources disagree. Was Polybius Rome's analyst or its apologist? F. W. Walbank (Polybius, 1972) saw a Greek statesman who came to accept Roman rule and wrote to explain it to Greeks. Craige Champion (Cultural Politics in Polybius's Histories, 2004) reads a double message: Romans praised as near-Greeks for Roman readers, their barbarian traits left visible for Greek ones.

Book 6: three powers in one state

Polybius asks how, and under what constitution, Rome conquered almost the whole inhabited world in under fifty-three years (1.1.5). Greek module 7.3 gives the answer in brief; here it is in full. Book 6 answers by interrupting the narrative after Cannae, because a constitution, like a man's character, is proved in reversal (6.2).

The theory comes first (6.3–10). Three good simple constitutions, kingship, aristocracy and democracy, each decay into a corrupt twin: tyranny, oligarchy and mob rule (ochlokratia). The sequence, anacyclosis, runs by nature: kings' heirs become tyrants, the nobles who expel them rule as an aristocracy until their sons make it an oligarchy, the people who expel those found a democracy, and their grandsons, bored with equality, corrupt it until violence returns everything to a master. Only a mixture halts the wheel. Lycurgus designed one for Sparta by reasoning; the Romans reached it through many struggles, learning from each disaster (6.10).

The description follows (6.11–18). The consuls, commanding armies and presiding over Senate and assemblies, look like kings; the Senate, controlling the treasury and receiving embassies, like an aristocracy; the people, who confer honours and punishments, elect magistrates, pass laws and decide on war and peace, like a democracy. Even Romans could not say which the state was (6.11.11). Each part checks the others. A consul in the field needs the Senate for supplies and any extension of command, and the people to ratify his treaties and judge him afterwards; a single tribune can stop the Senate meeting; the people depend on the Senate for public contracts and judges (6.15–17).

Comparisons close the case. Athens is a ship without a master (6.43–44); Sparta's mixture kept it free but could not sustain conquest (6.48–50); Carthage had passed its prime, its people having gained the chief say where at Rome the Senate still held it, and it fought with mercenaries where Rome fought with citizens (6.51–52; module 4.1).

Camp, funeral and the fear of the gods

The other half of the argument is custom. Module 9.2 treats the army; here the camp is evidence. A Roman army built the same camp every night, laid out like a city with streets and fixed quarters (6.27–32), where Greeks fitted a camp to the ground (6.42). A sentry who failed was cudgelled to death by his comrades, a unit that fled was decimated, and men who fought when not obliged received spears, cups or crowns before the assembled army (6.37–39). Public reward and punishment made the legion a school of ambition and fear.

The funeral is the famous passage (6.53–54). A dead noble was carried to the Rostra and a son praised his deeds before the people. The family kept wax masks (imagines) of ancestors who had held office; at the funeral men of matching build wore them, in the robes of the offices each had held, and sat on ivory chairs while the speaker recounted every ancestor's achievements. No finer sight, Polybius says, could meet a young man in love with glory (6.53.10). Good men's fame was renewed, and the young were readied to endure anything for the common good.

Money and religion complete the case (6.56). A Greek official trusted with a talent cheats despite ten clerks and as many seals; a Roman magistrate handling vast sums keeps faith because of his oath. The reason is deisidaimonia, fear of the gods, which Greeks thought a weakness and Polybius calls what held Rome together: a fickle crowd must be restrained by invisible terrors and solemn display. A state of wise men would not need it.

Judging the analysis

Ancient readers saw the problems. Tacitus thought a blended constitution easier to praise than to create, and short-lived if created (Annals 4.33). Cicero adopted the theory in On the Republic but gave it a Roman turn through Cato, who said Rome's state excelled because it was built by many men over centuries, not by one lawgiver (2.1–2). Ennius had given the native answer in one hexameter: moribus antiquis res stat Romana virisque, the Roman state stands on ancient customs and on men (Cicero, On the Republic 5.1).

Modern critics add three points. The theory is incoherent: the mixture escapes a law of nature, yet 6.57 predicts Rome's own slide into mob rule once prosperity breeds luxury, a strain set out in Walbank's Historical Commentary on Polybius (1957–79). The account is formal, listing powers but omitting the nobility's grip on office, patronage, an assembly weighted by wealth and the allies. And it is Greek theory fitted to a foreign state. Its strength is the chapters on custom.

Where sources disagree. Fergus Millar ("The Political Character of the Classical Roman Republic", 1984) took Polybius' democratic element at its word: the people elected, legislated and judged, so Rome was in a real sense a democracy. Karl-Joachim Hölkeskamp (Reconstructing the Roman Republic, 2010) and Henrik Mouritsen (Plebs and Politics in the Late Roman Republic, 2001) reply that assemblies voted only on what magistrates proposed, in small crowds, so power stayed with the nobility. The debate in full, with North and Morstein-Marx, is deep dive module 11.1.

Latin literature begins as translation

As Denis Feeney stresses (Beyond Greek, 2016), no other ancient people set out to translate Greek literature into its own language. Rome began in 240 BC, the year after the First Punic War, when Livius Andronicus staged a play at the Roman Games (Cicero, Brutus 72); module 3.5 gives his Tarentine origin. He wrote tragedies and comedies on Greek models and the Odusia, the Odyssey in native Saturnian verse, whose first line survives (Gellius 18.9.5):

Virum mihi, Camena, insece versutum

Homer's Muse becomes a Latin Camena, polytropos becomes versutus. Horace still remembered it beaten into him at school (Epistles 2.1.69–71).

Gnaeus Naevius, a Campanian veteran of the First Punic War, staged his first play in 235 (Gellius 17.21.45). He is credited with inventing the play on Roman history (fabula praetexta), with a Clastidium on Marcellus' victory of 222, and wrote the Bellum Punicum, a Saturnian epic of his own war that reached back to Aeneas (Greek module 10.12). Gellius has him jailed for abusing leading men (3.3.15).

Quintus Ennius (239–169), from Rudiae in the heel of Italy, said he had three hearts, Oscan, Greek and Latin (Gellius 17.17.1). Cato brought him to Rome from Sardinia in 204 (Nepos, Cato 1.4); Fulvius Nobilior took him to Aetolia in 189, which Cato denounced (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 1.3); and Fulvius' son made him a citizen in 184 (Cicero, Brutus 79). His Annales, eighteen books from Troy to his own day, replaced the Saturnian with Homer's hexameter, invoked the Greek Muses where Livius had a Camena, and opened with a dream in which Homer's soul passed into Ennius. The old Saturnians he dismissed as what Fauns and seers once sang (Cicero, Brutus 71). He also put Euripides on the Roman stage.

Where sources disagree. Cicero (Brutus 72) makes the play of 240 the beginning of Latin literature; Livy 7.2, probably following Varro, makes it one stage in a native theatre that had grown from Etruscan dancers in 364. Feeney treats 240 as a deliberate choice of the Roman elite after victory over Carthage; T. P. Wiseman (module 0.1) argues for a lost drama on Roman themes before and beside it.

Comedy in Greek dress: Plautus and Terence

Surviving Roman comedy is the palliata, played in the Greek cloak and set in Greek cities. Titus Maccius Plautus, from Sarsina in Umbria, wrote from about 205 until his death in 184, the year of Cato's censorship (Cicero, Brutus 60); twenty-one plays survive. He adapted Menander, Diphilus and Philemon, and said so with a joke at Rome's expense: Philemo scripsit, Plautus vortit barbare, Philemon wrote it, Plautus turned it into barbarian (Trinummus 19). Barbarian means Latin: Romans saw themselves through Greek eyes even while laughing. On his stage pergraecari, to play the Greek, means to carouse (Mostellaria), and clever slaves outwit fathers in an Athens full of Roman jokes and magistrates.

Publius Terentius Afer, born at Carthage according to Suetonius' life and freed by a senator, wrote six plays (166–160) that follow Menander and Apollodorus of Carystus closely in purer Latin. His prologues answer the charge of spoiling Greek plays by combining two (Andria 9–21) and the rumour that noble friends wrote for him, which he took as praise (Adelphoe 15–21). The Adelphoe was staged in 160 at the funeral games of Aemilius Paullus, given by his sons, Scipio Aemilianus among them. Caesar later called Terence half-Menander, pure but lacking force (Suetonius, Life of Terence).

Where sources disagree. How much of Plautus is Plautus? Gellius (2.23) set Caecilius beside his Menandrian original and found the Latin poorer, and nineteenth-century scholars mined Plautus for lost Greek plays. Eduard Fraenkel (Plautinisches im Plautus, 1922) identified systematic Plautine additions, and a papyrus of Menander's Dis Exapaton, presented by Eric Handley in 1968, confirmed against Bacchides that Plautus cut scenes, rewrote speeches and set dialogue to music.

Greek history and Latin prose: Fabius Pictor and Cato

History came to Rome in Greek. Quintus Fabius Pictor, senator and envoy to Delphi after Cannae, wrote around 200 BC in Greek for a Mediterranean public that read no Latin; module 0.1 covers the work and Polybius' criticism (3.8–9). A Roman who wished to explain Rome did it in the language of the world Rome was about to conquer.

Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149), a new man from Tusculum, made hostility to Greek manners his public character. Plutarch says he learned Greek late (Cato Maior 2) yet shows him at Athens in 191 speaking Latin through an interpreter though he could have spoken Greek (Cato Maior 12). To his son he wrote that the Greeks were a worthless and unteachable race who would corrupt everything once they gave Rome their literature, worse still if they sent their doctors, and that they called Romans barbarians (Pliny, Natural History 29.14). He called Socrates a babbler and said Rome would lose its empire once infected by Greek letters (Plutarch, Cato Maior 23). Yet his Origines, the first history in Latin prose, took its subject from the Greek genre of foundation stories and made the Aborigines, Rome's predecessors in Latium, Greeks from Achaea (Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1.11.1). On Agriculture, the earliest Latin prose work to survive whole, is a self-portrait in curt commands: its preface ranks the farmer above the trader and the moneylender and says the bravest soldiers come from farmers (preface 1–4); module 4.4 uses the estate as evidence.

The censorship of 184 made the persona policy (Livy 39.40–44; Plutarch, Cato Maior 16–19). Cato and Lucius Valerius Flaccus expelled seven senators, among them Lucius Quinctius Flamininus, brother of the liberator of Greece, for killing a man at a banquet to please a favourite; took the public horse from Lucius Scipio; assessed women's clothing, jewellery and carriages at ten times their value for tax; cut off public water piped to private houses; and built the Basilica Porcia. Luxury and the Scipios were linked targets: as quaestor in 204 Cato had attacked Scipio Africanus' spending and his hours in the palaestra at Syracuse (Plutarch, Cato Maior 3).

Where sources disagree. Plutarch and Cicero's On Old Age (26) have Cato learn Greek only in old age. Alan Astin (Cato the Censor, 1978) argued that he knew Greek literature throughout his career and attacked Greek manners in Roman leaders, not Greek learning. Erich Gruen (Culture and National Identity in Republican Rome, 1992) went further: his anti-Hellenism was a performance by which a Hellenised elite defined Romanness against a Greek foil.

Philosophers in the Senate, 155 BC

In 155 Athens sent the heads of three schools, Carneades of the Academy, Diogenes of Babylon of the Stoa and Critolaus of the Peripatos, to plead against a fine of five hundred talents for plundering Oropus; the Senate cut it to a hundred (Pausanias 7.11). They addressed the Senate through the senator Gaius Acilius as interpreter (Plutarch, Cato Maior 22) and lectured while they waited. On one day Carneades, whose scepticism Greek module 7.2 explains, praised justice; on the next he argued that justice is either nothing or the height of folly, and that Romans who wished to be just would have to give back their conquests and return to their huts. Cicero reworked the pair in book 3 of On the Republic, known for this part chiefly through Lactantius' Divine Institutes book 5. Cato urged the Senate to send the envoys home quickly, so that Roman youth would listen to the laws and magistrates as before (Plutarch, Cato Maior 22). The Senate had let a praetor expel philosophers and rhetoricians in 161 (Gellius 15.11.1), and in 181 had burned books ascribed to Numa, Greek works of philosophy that Valerius Antias called Pythagorean, a claim Livy rejects (40.29). Neither measure kept Greek thought out.

The "Scipionic circle" and captive Greece

Scipio Aemilianus kept Polybius and the Stoic Panaetius with him at home and on campaign (Velleius Paterculus 1.13.3); his friend Gaius Laelius was called the Wise; the satirist Lucilius, who served under him at Numantia, mocked Romans who affected Greek (Cicero, On Ends 1.9). Cicero made these men the cast of On the Republic and On Friendship, Greek learning lightly worn, and followed Panaetius in On Duties. Modern scholars named them the "Scipionic circle", a coterie of philhellene nobles. No ancient writer uses the phrase.

Where sources disagree. Hermann Strasburger ("Der Scipionenkreis", 1966) and James Zetzel ("Cicero and the Scipionic Circle", 1972) argued that the circle is largely Cicero's creation, a past built to dignify his own union of politics and learning; Alan Astin (Scipio Aemilianus, 1967) found no cultural programme or faction. Polybius, Velleius and Terence's prologues still attest the friendships; their coherence is what is doubtful.

Horace, writing to Augustus, put the century in a line: Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit et artis intulit agresti Latio, captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive and brought the arts to rustic Latium (Epistles 2.1.156–157). Greek module 7.3 uses it to frame loot, tutors and gods; in context it is narrower. Horace is arguing against admirers of the old Latin poets: the rough Saturnian gave way to elegance, yet traces of the farm remained, because the Roman turned late to Greek books, only in the peace after the Punic Wars (2.1.157–163). The epigram concerns literary taste, and its chronology is vague: post Punica bella fits Livius' first play of 240 only if Horace meant the first war.

Where sources disagree. Romans could not agree when Greek luxury began to corrupt them: Livy dated it to Manlius Vulso's army returning from Asia in 187 with bronze couches and lute-girls (39.6.7), Polybius to the years after Pydna (31.25), Calpurnius Piso to 154 (Pliny, Natural History 17.244), Sallust to the fall of Carthage in 146 (Catiline 10). Gruen and Andrew Wallace-Hadrill (Rome's Cultural Revolution, 2008) replace capture with choice: an elite switching between Greek and Roman codes as the setting required.

Self-test

  1. How did Polybius come to Rome, and why did he stay in the city rather than in an Italian town?
    Answer

    He was one of the thousand Achaeans deported after Pydna in 167. The sons of Aemilius Paullus, above all Scipio Aemilianus, sought his company, and he promised to help Scipio become worthy of his ancestors (Polybius 31.23–24).

  2. What is anacyclosis, and how did Sparta and Rome escape it according to Polybius?
    Answer

    The natural cycle in which kingship, aristocracy and democracy decay into tyranny, oligarchy and mob rule and give way to one another. A mixed constitution balances the three good forms; Lycurgus designed Sparta's by reasoning, while Rome reached its mixture through struggle and the lessons of disaster (6.3–10).

  3. Give two ways in which, for Polybius, one part of the Roman state checks another.
    Answer

    Any two of: the Senate controls a consul's supplies and the extension of his command; the people ratify his treaties and judge his conduct; one tribune can stop the Senate meeting; the Senate controls the public contracts and supplies judges on which the people depend (6.15–17).

  4. Why did Polybius think the aristocratic funeral was a cause of Roman strength?
    Answer

    Actors wearing the ancestral masks and insignia of office, and a eulogy of the dead man and every ancestor, kept the fame of good men alive and made the young ready to endure anything for the common good (6.53–54).

  5. What did Polybius claim Roman religion did, and what was his own attitude to it?
    Answer

    Fear of the gods (deisidaimonia) held the state together: oaths kept magistrates honest with public money, and invisible terrors restrained a fickle crowd. He treats it as a useful device that a state of wise men would not need (6.56).

  6. State one ancient and two modern objections to Polybius' constitutional analysis.
    Answer

    Tacitus (Annals 4.33) thought a mixed constitution easier to praise than to create, and short-lived. Modern critics note that a natural cycle and an escape from it sit uneasily together, especially as 6.57 predicts Rome's decline, and that the account is formal, omitting the nobility, patronage and the weighted assemblies.

  7. What does the first line of Livius Andronicus' Odusia show about early Roman translation, and how did Ennius change the approach?
    Answer

    Livius naturalised Homer: the Muse became a Latin Camena, polytropos became versutus, and the metre was the native Saturnian. Ennius invoked the Greek Muses, adopted Homer's hexameter and claimed to be Homer reborn.

  8. What does Plautus vortit barbare reveal about Roman comedy?
    Answer

    Plautus openly adapted Greek New Comedy and called his Latin version "barbarian", taking over the Greek view of Romans as a joke. Cato made the same complaint about Greek contempt in earnest (Pliny, Natural History 29.14).

  9. Why do Astin and Gruen doubt that Cato simply rejected Greek culture?
    Answer

    He knew Greek well, chose to speak Latin at Athens, brought Ennius to Rome and gave Rome's predecessors Greek origins in the Origines (Dionysius 1.11.1). His attacks targeted Greek manners in Roman leaders, and served to define Roman identity against a Greek foil.

  10. What happened during the philosophers' embassy of 155, and why did Cato want it ended quickly?
    Answer

    Carneades, Diogenes and Critolaus came to plead against the Oropus fine and lectured while waiting; Carneades argued for justice one day and against it the next. Cato feared that the young would prize eloquence over deeds and urged the Senate to send them home (Plutarch, Cato Maior 22).

Carry forward

  1. The first systematic explanation of Rome's success was Greek: Polybius' mixed constitution and his chapters on custom. Cicero took over the frame, and the modern argument over how democratic Rome was still begins from Book 6.
  2. Latin literature began as translation sponsored by the Roman elite at state festivals: Greek forms carrying Roman content. Every later Roman poet works inside this double inheritance, where allusion to a Greek model is the norm.
  3. Roman identity was defined against Greece by Romans who were themselves Hellenised. Cato's invective, the expulsions of philosophers and the dates of moral decline are ways of managing Greek culture, not refusing it; "captive Greece" is a metaphor, not a description.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on how Rome explained its own success and how Greek culture conquered it in the third and second centuries BC. Cover: Polybius' life as hostage and friend of Scipio Aemilianus; his book 6: the mixed constitution (consuls as monarchy, Senate as aristocracy, people as democracy), the cycle of constitutions, the army camp and the aristocratic funeral as causes of Rome's strength, and the criticisms of his analysis; the beginnings of Latin literature: Livius Andronicus' Odusia and his first plays in 240 BC, Naevius' Punic War, Ennius' Annales and the Latin hexameter, Plautus and Terence and their Greek originals; Fabius Pictor writing history in Greek; Cato the Elder as the anti-Hellene who knew Greek, his Origines, On Agriculture and censorship of 184 BC; the philosophers' embassy of 155 BC and Carneades arguing both sides of justice; the 'Scipionic circle' and its modern critics; and Horace's 'captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive' (Epistles 2.1.156). Point back to Greek module 7.3 for the Greek side. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 5 · The fall of the Republic, 133 to 30 BC · 5.1 · 2,853 words

The Gracchi

The land question as Appian and Plutarch tell itThe modern revision: a vanishing peasantry?Tiberius' law and the deposition of Octavius, 133Pergamon, a second tribunate and the killing on the CapitolThe land commission and its boundary stonesGaius Gracchus' programme, 123–122The final decree and the death of Gaius, 121CorneliaHeroes or demagoguesWhy 133 looked like the beginning of the endSelf-testCarry forward

The land question as Appian and Plutarch tell it

The continuous narratives are late and Greek: Plutarch's paired Lives, early in the second century AD, and Appian's Civil Wars, about AD 160, some 290 years after 133. Both drew on lost Latin historians, and both inherited a story the Gracchi first told. Contemporary evidence is thin: fragments of Gaius' speeches, the land commission's boundary stones, an extortion law on bronze.

Appian (1.7) gives the problem in one movement. As Rome conquered Italy it confiscated land, and it opened what war had left uncultivated to anyone who would farm it, for a tenth of the grain and a fifth of the fruit. The rich took most of this public land (ager publicus), added their poor neighbours' plots by purchase or by force, and worked the whole with slaves, who were exempt from the levy and multiplied, while the Italians dwindled under poverty, taxes and service. An old cap of 500 iugera a holder was ignored (1.8); Livy dates such a cap to 367 (module 3.1), and module 4.4 describes the slave-run estate itself.

Plutarch (Tiberius Gracchus 8) adds that the dispossessed lost interest in serving and in raising children, and quotes a pamphlet of Gaius: crossing Etruria on his way to Numantia in 137, Tiberius found the land worked by foreign slaves and almost empty of free men (8.7). Tiberius' own words survive in paraphrase: Italy's wild beasts have their lairs, but the men who fight and die for Italy have air and light and nothing else, masters of the world without a clod of earth of their own (9.4–5). Appian's Tiberius argues from manpower: a kindred people was sinking into poverty and fewness, and slaves, useless in war, had lately risen in Sicily (1.9). Appian speaks of Italians, Plutarch of Romans; whether allies could receive land is uncertain.

The modern revision: a vanishing peasantry?

Twentieth-century historians built this into a model. Arnold Toynbee (Hannibal's Legacy, 1965), P. A. Brunt (Italian Manpower, 1971) and Keith Hopkins (Conquerors and Slaves, 1978) argued that long service overseas ruined soldiers' farms, that the rich bought them with the profits of empire and stocked them with captives, and that the pool of propertied men liable for the legions shrank.

The model has been dismantled from several sides. Nathan Rosenstein (Rome at War, 2004) argued that the levy fell on young men who married late and whose labour their families could spare, so that service did not in itself wreck farms; the crisis of the 130s came from population growth and partible inheritance, too many heirs for too little land. Luuk de Ligt ("Poverty and demography: the case of the Gracchan land reforms", Mnemosyne, 2004; Peasants, Citizens and Soldiers, 2012) likewise traced the rural misery to continuing population growth rather than to slaves replacing citizens. Survey archaeology has found small rural sites persisting through the second century in many districts, though Dominic Rathbone ("Poor peasants and silent sherds", 2008) has pressed the question of how far the rural poor are visible to survey at all. What survives of the old picture is real poverty and a recruiting problem; its cause, slaves displacing citizens or too many sons for too few fields, is open.

Where sources disagree. Appian (1.7) and Plutarch (Tiberius Gracchus 8) describe a shrinking free population, but the census totals in Livy's Periochae barely move, 317,933 citizens in 136/135 (56) and 318,823 in 131/130 (59), then jump to 394,736 in 125/124 (60). The traditional reading, Brunt's among them, credits the jump to the commission's allottees, who now had property to declare; another reads the flat figures as men evading the census to escape the levy, corrected in 125/124.

Tiberius' law and the deposition of Octavius, 133

Tiberius was the son of a twice-consul of the same name and of Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus. As quaestor in 137 he negotiated the Numantine treaty that the Senate repudiated (module 4.4), the root of his breach with the Senate according to Cicero (De haruspicum responso 43) and Velleius (2.2.1). Plutarch (8) adds the Stoic Blossius of Cumae and Cornelia's complaint that she was still called Scipio's mother-in-law, not mother of the Gracchi.

As tribune for 133 he drafted his bill with his father-in-law Appius Claudius Pulcher, leader of the Senate, with Publius Licinius Crassus Mucianus and with the consul Publius Mucius Scaevola (Plutarch 9.1). It touched public land only. Each holder kept 500 iugera, now secure, and 250 for each son; the excess went to poor citizens in allotments that could not be sold, assigned by three commissioners (Appian 1.9–10). He took it straight to the plebeian council, legal since 287 (module 3.1) but without the customary prior approval of the Senate.

His colleague Marcus Octavius vetoed it. Tiberius suspended public business by edict and sealed the treasury (Plutarch 10.5), then asked the tribes to depose Octavius. When seventeen of the thirty-five had voted, he begged his colleague to yield; Octavius refused, the eighteenth tribe made a majority, and he was dragged from the Rostra (Appian 1.12; Plutarch 12). The law passed, with Tiberius, Gaius and Appius as commissioners. A tribune who works against the people, Tiberius said, is no tribune (Plutarch 15); Plutarch himself, comparing the Gracchi with Agis and Cleomenes, calls the deposition the gravest charge against him (Comparison 5.1).

Where sources disagree. Appian (1.9) gives 500 iugera plus 250 a son; the Periochae (58) give a ceiling of 1,000, perhaps the same rule with two sons counted. Only Plutarch has a first, milder draft that paid the occupiers the value of what they surrendered (9.2), replaced after the veto by a harsher bill (10.3). Whether that draft existed, or was invented to make Octavius the aggressor, is uncertain.

Pergamon, a second tribunate and the killing on the Capitol

That spring Attalus III of Pergamon died and left his kingdom to the Roman people. Tiberius proposed that the royal money stock the new farms and that the people, not the Senate, decide about the kingdom's cities (Plutarch 14.1), striking at the Senate's control of finance and foreign affairs; Quintus Pompeius claimed that the envoy Eudemus had brought Tiberius a diadem and a purple robe (14.2). Then he stood again for 132, which his enemies called unlawful (Appian 1.14).

On election day the Senate met in the temple of Fides. Tiberius touched his head to signal danger to his life; his enemies said he was asking for a crown (Plutarch 19.2). The consul Scaevola refused to kill a citizen without trial. Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, pontifex maximus and Tiberius' cousin, called on all who would save the state to follow him (19.3), and senators and their attendants went up the Capitol with clubs and bench legs. A fellow tribune, Publius Satureius, struck Tiberius down (19.6). Plutarch counts more than three hundred dead, none killed with iron (19.6); Appian (1.16) says only that many died. The bodies went into the Tiber. For Plutarch this was the first civil strife since the kings to end in bloodshed (20.1).

A special inquiry in 132 executed the rhetorician Diophanes (Plutarch 20.3); Blossius said he would have done anything Tiberius asked, even burned the Capitol (Cicero, On Friendship 37). Scipio Aemilianus, at Numantia, quoted Athena on Aegisthus, "so perish any other who does such things" (Odyssey 1.47; Plutarch 21.4), and later said that Tiberius was justly killed if he had meant to seize the state (Velleius 2.4).

Where sources disagree. Appian (1.16) and Plutarch have Nasica draw his toga over his head, and Appian offers three explanations: a signal to followers, a battle sign, or shame before the gods. Velleius (2.3.1) and Valerius Maximus have it wrapped round his left arm. Donald Earl read the veiling as the dress of sacrifice; Jerzy Linderski ("The Pontiff and the Tribune", 2002) argued instead for consecratio capitis, the pontiff handing a would-be king over to the gods, with human hands executing their anger.

The land commission and its boundary stones

The commission outlived Tiberius. Crassus took his place, and after Crassus and Appius died Marcus Fulvius Flaccus and Gaius Papirius Carbo joined Gaius (Appian 1.18). Its title survives on boundary stones from Campania, Lucania and Apulia: IIIviri agris iudicandis adsignandis, three men for judging and assigning land. Judging came first, since every holder had to prove what was private and what public. No source gives the number or size of the allotments.

A road inscription from Polla in Lucania has an unnamed magistrate claim to be the first to make shepherds give way to ploughmen on public land: primus fecei ut de agro poplico aratoribus cederent paastores. It has been assigned to Publius Popillius Laenas, consul in 132 and Tiberius' persecutor, and to Titus Annius Rufus, praetor by 131; its date and its link to the Gracchan scheme are disputed.

The allies, whose leading men held much of the land under review, complained. In 129 Scipio Aemilianus had the commission's judicial power transferred to a consul, who promptly left for Illyricum (Appian 1.19). Scipio was found dead soon after, and suspicion fell on his wife Sempronia, the Gracchi's sister (Periochae 59; Appian 1.20).

Gaius Gracchus' programme, 123–122

Gaius had served on the commission and as quaestor in Sardinia; Cicero reports, from Coelius Antipater, his dream of Tiberius warning that he would die the same death (On Divination 1.56). The allies' grievance had sharpened: as consul in 125 Flaccus proposed citizenship for them (Appian 1.21), and that year the Latin colony of Fregellae revolted and was razed by the praetor Lucius Opimius (Periochae 60). Tribune for 123 and 122, Gaius was the greatest orator of his day. The order of his laws is uncertain.

  • Protection. No citizen was to be tried on a capital charge without the people's order (Cicero, Pro Rabirio perduellionis reo 12); Popillius went into exile.
  • Grain. Every citizen might buy a monthly ration at 6⅓ asses a modius (Periochae 60) from public granaries; Appian (1.21) wrongly makes it free. Peter Garnsey and Rathbone (Journal of Roman Studies, 1985) saw it as giving Rome's supply regularity and storage after shortages in 142, 138 and 129, not as a response to Mediterranean-wide prices. Piso Frugi, who had opposed it, queued for his share (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 3.48).
  • Land and colonies. The agrarian law was renewed; colonies went out to Scolacium and Tarentum (Velleius 1.15), and the tribune Rubrius' law founded Junonia at Carthage, the first colony overseas, with 6,000 settlers from all Italy, more than the law allowed (Appian 1.24).
  • Soldiers and provinces. Soldiers were clothed at public expense and none conscripted under seventeen (Plutarch, Gaius Gracchus 5); the tithe of Asia was auctioned by the censors at Rome (Cicero, Verrines 2.3.12), a vast contract for the publicani (module 4.4).
  • Juries. The extortion court passed to the equites (Appian 1.22). Gaius said he had broken the Senate; Varro said he made the state two-headed, a source of civil discord (in Nonius).

The citizenship bill of 122 broke him. Appian (1.23) has full citizenship for the Latins and the vote for the other allies; Velleius (2.6) has citizenship for all Italians. The consul Gaius Fannius warned the citizens that the Latins would leave them no room at assemblies and games, and non-citizens were ordered out of the city for the vote (Appian 1.23). The tribune Marcus Livius Drusus vetoed it and outbid Gaius with twelve colonies of 3,000 poor citizens each, in Plutarch's figure (9), apparently never founded. After seventy days in Africa (Plutarch 11), Gaius failed to win a third tribunate. Deep dive module 11.3 follows the grain laws to Clodius.

Where sources disagree. Appian (1.22) and the extortion law on the bronze Tabula Bembina, usually identified with the Acilian law of 123 or 122, give the juries to non-senators: 450 jurors a year, senators and their relatives excluded. Plutarch (Gaius Gracchus 5) has 300 equites joined to the 300 senators, and the Periochae (60) have 600 equites enrolled in the Senate itself. Most follow the inscription; Plutarch may preserve an earlier proposal.

The final decree and the death of Gaius, 121

Opimius was consul for 121, and a bill was brought to repeal the Junonia law. During a sacrifice on the Capitol a consular attendant, Antyllius, was killed by Gracchans (Plutarch 13; Appian 1.25). The Senate decreed that the consul should see to it that the state suffer no harm (Cicero, Against Catiline 1.4); Caesar later called this the extreme and final decree (Civil War 1.5). It gave no new legal power, only the Senate's backing for whatever the consul did: where Scaevola in 133 had refused to kill without trial, Opimius now had cover.

Gaius and Flaccus held the Aventine. Opimius attacked with armed senators, equites and Cretan archers (Plutarch 16); Flaccus was killed, and Gaius fled across the Tiber to a grove of Furrina, where a slave killed him at his order and then himself. Opimius had promised the heads' weight in gold (Appian 1.26), strangled accomplices in prison and built a temple of Concord (module 3.1); someone wrote under its inscription that mad discord had produced a temple of Concord (Plutarch 17.6). He was acquitted in 120 (Periochae 61). Within a few years, Appian says (1.27), the allotments were made saleable and distribution stopped.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch counts 3,000 dead in 121 (17.5), names the slave Philocrates (17.2) and has Septimuleius fill Gaius' head with lead so that it weighed 17⅔ pounds (17.4); Valerius Maximus (9.4.3) also tells the Septimuleius story. Appian (1.26) gives no total and leaves the slave unnamed; Velleius (2.6) calls him Euporus. Deep dive module 11.3 treats the decree as legalised violence.

Cornelia

Cornelia bore the elder Tiberius Gracchus twelve children, three of whom grew up: Tiberius, Gaius and Sempronia. Widowed, she refused a king of Egypt (Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 1). Her letters were read as prose: Cicero (Brutus 211) judged that her sons were raised less in their mother's lap than in her speech. Pliny saw her seated statue (Natural History 34.31), and a base survives inscribed Cornelia Africani f. Gracchorum, daughter of Africanus, mother of the Gracchi. Deep dive module 11.4 goes further.

Two extracts of a letter to Gaius survive among the fragments of Cornelius Nepos. Written, it seems, before his first tribunate, it begs him not to stand: apart from Tiberius' killers no enemy has caused her such grief; when she is dead he may invoke her as a parent-god; will the family's madness never end?

Where sources disagree. Plutarch (Gaius Gracchus 13.2) knew letters of Cornelia that some read as hinting that she sent hired men to Rome disguised as harvesters to back Gaius, while others said she disapproved of him; the Nepos extracts are pure disapproval. Hans Ulrich Instinsky (Chiron, 1971) warned that genuine or forged is too crude a choice: the letter may be a fiction in the work of a historian close to the Gracchi's time, deceiving only once detached from its context.

Heroes or demagogues

Cicero's verdict follows his audience. To the people the brothers were two most distinguished and gifted men, most devoted to the plebs (De lege agraria 2.10). In the philosophical works Tiberius tried to seize kingship, or rather reigned a few months (On Friendship 41); Nasica served the state as well as Scipio did at Numantia (On Duties 1.76); and the brothers are counted among the justly killed (2.43). Sallust (Jugurtha 42) has them assert the liberty of the plebs against a guilty nobility, yet lack moderation in their desire to win. Velleius gives Tiberius a blameless life and upright intentions, then has him desert the good cause (2.2), praises Nasica (2.3), and calls Gaius' overseas colonies his most pernicious measure (2.7). Plutarch's pairing with Agis and Cleomenes, Spartan kings who died trying to restore land to citizens, makes them noble natures spurred by love of honour, and his comparison ranks Tiberius first of the four in virtue (Comparison 5.6). Tacitus files them among the agitators of the plebs (Annals 3.27).

Why 133 looked like the beginning of the end

Appian (1.1–2) states the thesis: earlier quarrels of people and Senate had ended in concession, Coriolanus apart, and the sword was never carried into the assembly until Tiberius Gracchus fell. Velleius (2.3.3) calls 133 the beginning of civil bloodshed and of swords unpunished, after which right was overwhelmed by force; Cicero's Laelius says that Tiberius' death, and before it his whole tribunate, split one people into two parts (On the Republic 1.31). The date is a construction: the theories of moral decline put the rot earlier (module 4.5), module 5.6 reads Sallust's, and deep dive module 11.8 weighs the explanations. Yet it names something real. A tribune used the plebeian council's legal sovereignty against senatorial custom, and senators answered with force, authorised by 121. Annalists writing after 133 also carried the quarrel back into the early Republic (module 3.1).

Self-test

  1. How do Appian and Plutarch explain the agrarian problem, and why should the picture of an empty Etruria be read with caution?
    Answer

    The rich occupied public land and absorbed small farms, worked them with slaves exempt from service, and the free population dwindled (Appian 1.7; Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 8). The Etruria scene comes from a pamphlet by Gaius (8.7): partisan testimony relayed by Plutarch some two and a half centuries later.

  2. What do Rosenstein and de Ligt put in place of the decline model?
    Answer

    Rosenstein (2004): late-marrying young men could be spared for the army, so service did not ruin farms; the crisis came from population growth and partible inheritance. De Ligt (2004, 2012): rural misery from continuing population growth, not slaves displacing citizens.

  3. What did Tiberius' law provide according to Appian, and how do Livy's epitome and Plutarch differ?
    Answer

    Holders of public land kept 500 iugera plus 250 per son; the surplus went in inalienable allotments to poor citizens through a board of three (Appian 1.9–10). The Periochae (58) give a ceiling of 1,000; Plutarch alone has a first draft with compensation, withdrawn after Octavius' veto (9.2, 10.3).

  4. Which actions of Tiberius in 133, beyond the land law, broke with senatorial custom?
    Answer

    Deposing his colleague Octavius by vote of the tribes (Appian 1.12; Plutarch 12); proposing that Attalus' money fund the new farms and that the people decide on the Pergamene cities (Plutarch 14.1), invading the Senate's control of finance and foreign affairs; and standing for a second consecutive tribunate (Appian 1.14).

  5. Who led the attack on Tiberius, how many died, and how has Nasica's gesture been read?
    Answer

    Scipio Nasica, pontifex maximus, after the consul Scaevola refused to act. Plutarch counts more than 300 dead (19.6); Appian says only that many died (1.16). The veiled head (Appian, Plutarch) has been read as the dress of sacrifice (Earl) or as consecratio capitis of a would-be king (Linderski, 2002); Velleius has the toga wrapped round his arm.

  6. What do the boundary stones and the Polla inscription show about the commission?
    Answer

    The stones, from Campania, Lucania and Apulia, give the board's title, IIIviri agris iudicandis adsignandis, and its changing membership, so it was surveying and judging land across the south. The Polla stone's claim to have made shepherds yield to ploughmen on public land may refer to the same policy, but its author (Popillius Laenas or Annius Rufus) and date are disputed.

  7. Name four of Gaius' measures and the group each served.
    Answer

    Any four of: grain at 6⅓ asses a modius for citizens (Periochae 60); colonies, including Junonia at Carthage, for the landless; extortion juries for the equites (Appian 1.22); the Asian tithe let at Rome for the publicani (Cicero, Verrines 2.3.12); clothing and no conscripts under seventeen for soldiers (Plutarch, Gaius Gracchus 5); citizenship for the Latins (Appian 1.23).

  8. What was the Senate's decree of 121, and what changed between 133 and 121?
    Answer

    That the consul see to it that the state suffer no harm (Cicero, Against Catiline 1.4), Caesar's "extreme and final decree". In 133 the consul refused to kill without trial and Nasica acted as a private citizen; in 121 the Senate gave the consul Opimius cover to use force, and his acquittal in 120 (Periochae 61) confirmed it.

  9. What does the letter attributed to Cornelia say, and why is its authenticity uncertain?
    Answer

    Preserved among Nepos' fragments, it begs Gaius not to seek the tribunate and says that no enemy except Tiberius' killers has caused her such grief. Plutarch knew letters read as showing her complicity (Gaius Gracchus 13.2), and Instinsky (1971) suggested a fiction in the work of a historian close to the Gracchi's time.

  10. Which ancient writers made 133 the beginning of the end, and on what grounds?
    Answer

    Appian (1.1–2): the first time the sword entered the assembly. Velleius (2.3.3): the beginning of civil bloodshed and unpunished violence. Cicero (On the Republic 1.31): one people split into two. Plutarch (Tiberius Gracchus 20.1): the first civil strife since the kings to end in bloodshed.

Carry forward

  1. The agrarian crisis as Appian and Plutarch tell it is Gracchan rhetoric relayed by imperial Greek writers; modern work (Rosenstein, de Ligt) makes it a crisis of rural poverty and population rather than of a vanishing peasantry. Either way the landless citizen soldier became the problem that later generals solved with land for their veterans.
  2. The Gracchi showed that the tribunate and the plebeian council could legislate over the Senate's head on land, money, courts and empire; the Senate answered with force, private in 133 and authorised by the final decree in 121. Every later crisis of the Republic repeats both moves.
  3. Whether the Gracchi were martyrs or demagogues depended on who was speaking and to whom: Cicero praised them to the people and damned them in his philosophical works. Read every source on them, and every source that starts the fall in 133, for its side.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, 133 to 121 BC. Cover: the agrarian problem as Appian (Civil Wars 1.7–13) and Plutarch describe it, and the modern revision of it (the debate over the decline of the peasantry: Rathbone, Rosenstein, de Ligt); Tiberius' land law, the deposition of the tribune Octavius, the Pergamene bequest, and his killing by Scipio Nasica and the senators; the land commission and its boundary stones; Gaius' programme (the grain law, the equestrian juries, colonies, citizenship for the Latins), the first 'final decree' of the Senate and his death in 121 BC; Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, and the letter attributed to her; the Gracchi as heroes or demagogues in Cicero, Sallust, Velleius and Plutarch; and why ancient writers saw 133 as the beginning of the end. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 5 · The fall of the Republic, 133 to 30 BC · 5.2 · 3,224 words

Jugurtha and Sallust's case against the nobility (118–105 BC)

Micipsa of Numidia died in 118, leaving his kingdom jointly to his sons Adherbal and Hiempsal and to his adopted nephew Jugurtha, who had served under Scipio at Numantia (Sallust, Jugurtha 7–11; module 4.4). Jugurtha had Hiempsal killed and drove Adherbal out; a Senate commission under Lucius Opimius split the kingdom in 116 and gave him the richer west (16). In 112 he took Cirta and killed Adherbal with every adult Numidian and Italian trader in it (26). The tribune-elect Gaius Memmius forced a war, but the consul Bestia made a quick peace in 111 (28–29). Summoned to Rome to testify, Jugurtha was silenced by a bribed tribune and had a rival murdered; leaving, he called Rome "a city for sale, and doomed to perish quickly if it finds a buyer" (32–35). In 110 Aulus Albinus' army passed under the yoke (38), and a tribune's law of 109, the lex Mamilia, set up a court that condemned Opimius, Bestia and others for taking the king's money (40; Cicero, Brutus 128).

Quintus Caecilius Metellus, consul in 109, restored discipline and beat Jugurtha on the Muthul (44–53). His legate Gaius Marius asked leave to stand for the consulship and was told to wait until Metellus' son, then about twenty, could stand with him (64). Marius was elected for 107, and a plebiscite gave him Numidia over the Senate's prorogation of Metellus (73). The war ended by diplomacy: his quaestor Lucius Cornelius Sulla persuaded Bocchus of Mauretania to hand Jugurtha over in 105 (102–113). Jugurtha walked in Marius' triumph on 1 January 104 and died in prison (Plutarch, Marius 12). Sulla wore a signet ring showing the surrender, and Plutarch dates their feud from it (Marius 10).

Sallust wrote about 41–40 BC, some sixty-five years later, as a Caesarian ex-governor of Africa accused of plundering it (Cassius Dio 43.9). He chose the war, he says, because it was great and savage, and because "then for the first time the arrogance of the nobility was opposed" (5.1). Bribery drives his plot, and his digression on parties traces the rot to the removal of the fear of Carthage (41; module 5.6). His chronology is loose, and the Senate's reluctance to send legions to Africa while the Cimbri threatened the north needs no bribe to explain it.

Marius, the new man, and the "Marian reforms"

Marius was born about 157 near Arpinum to an equestrian family with no senatorial ancestors (Velleius 2.11.1); Plutarch makes his parents poor labourers (Marius 3). As tribune in 119 he narrowed the gangways voters crossed to cast their ballots, making them harder to pressure (Cicero, On the Laws 3.38), and he married Julia, sister of Julius Caesar's father (Marius 6). Sallust gives him a new man's manifesto as consul-elect: the nobles despise his newness, he their idleness; he has no ancestral masks, only decorations and scars (Jugurtha 85). He was consul seven times: in 107, in five successive years from 104 to 100, the first in his absence and all against the rules on repeated office, and in 86.

The "Marian reforms" are a modern bundle. Sallust says that in 107 Marius enrolled volunteers, most of them from the capite censi, citizens registered by head alone because they owned too little for a property class (Jugurtha 86). Plutarch adds soldiers carrying their own kit, "Marius' mules" (Marius 13), and a pilum whose wooden pin snapped on impact (25); Pliny makes the eagle the sole legionary standard from 104 (Natural History 10.16). No ancient source credits Marius with the cohort, which Polybius already describes in 206 (11.23). Whether a client army followed is deep dive module 11.2; the army as an institution is module 9.2.

Where sources disagree. Emilio Gabba (1949) read the falling property minimum, 11,000 asses for the fifth class in Livy (1.43), 400 drachmas in Polybius (6.19.2), 1,500 asses in Cicero (On the Republic 2.40), as reductions that had already filled the legions with the poor, so that Marius only completed a process. John Rich (1983) denied the manpower shortage behind it, and François Cadiou (L'armée imaginaire, 2018) calls the post-Marian proletarian army a historiographical mirage. Sallust describes one emergency levy, not a law.

The Cimbri and Teutones

The Cimbri and Teutones, migrating peoples from the north, routed the consul Carbo at Noreia in 113 (Livy, Periochae 63); in 107 their allies the Tigurini killed the consul Lucius Cassius and sent his army under the yoke (Caesar, Gallic War 1.7, 1.12). In 106 Quintus Servilius Caepio took Tolosa, whose temple gold vanished and became a proverb (Strabo 4.1.13). On 6 October 105 at Arausio on the Rhône, Caepio as proconsul refused to combine with the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus, a new man, and both armies were destroyed (Plutarch, Lucullus 27; Periochae 67).

The Cimbri turned to Spain, and Marius trained a new army in southern Gaul. In 102 he destroyed the Teutones and Ambrones near Aquae Sextiae, where the Massiliots later fenced their vineyards with the bones (Marius 18–21). In 101 he and Quintus Lutatius Catulus annihilated the Cimbri, who had crossed the eastern Alps, on the Raudine Plain near Vercellae, a site still uncertain (Velleius 2.12.5; Marius 25–27). Marius was hailed as Rome's third founder (27).

Where sources disagree. Livy's epitomator, citing Valerius Antias, gives 80,000 soldiers and 40,000 servants and camp followers dead at Arausio (Periochae 67). For Aquae Sextiae the Periochae give 200,000 enemy dead and 90,000 captured (68), Plutarch more than 100,000 taken or killed (Marius 21); for Vercellae, 160,000 dead and 60,000 captured (Periochae 68) against Plutarch's 60,000 captured and twice as many dead (Marius 27). Livy distrusted Antias' numbers (33.10); none can be checked.

Saturninus and 100 BC

Marius' veterans needed land. Lucius Appuleius Saturninus, tribune in 103, carried allotments in Africa for them. In 100, tribune again, with Marius consul for the sixth time and Gaius Servilius Glaucia praetor, he passed a law distributing land in Gaul and founding colonies, and made every senator swear within five days to obey it; Metellus Numidicus refused and went into exile (Appian, Civil Wars 1.29–31). At the elections for 99 his men killed Gaius Memmius, Glaucia's rival for the consulship (1.32). The Senate passed its final decree (module 5.1), and Marius as consul besieged his allies on the Capitol and accepted their surrender. Appian has a crowd stone them with roof tiles in the Senate house (1.32), Plutarch kill them in the Forum (Marius 30). Marius had saved an order he had bypassed and pleased no one. He went east, and told Mithridates of Pontus to be stronger than Rome or obey it in silence (31). Saturninus' grain law and the politics of the street are deep dive module 11.3.

Livius Drusus and the Social War (91–88 BC)

The Italian allies fought Rome's wars and shared little of the profit. The lex Licinia Mucia of 95 expelled Italians passing as citizens; Asconius calls it perhaps the chief cause of the war (on Cicero, Pro Cornelio). In 92 an equestrian jury in the extortion court (module 4.4) condemned Publius Rutilius Rufus, who had protected Asia from the tax-farmers (Velleius 2.13.2). In 91 the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus proposed juries drawn from a Senate enlarged by three hundred equestrians, colonies, and citizenship for the Italians (Appian, Civil Wars 1.35). The Senate annulled his laws "by one little line" (Cicero, On the Laws 2.14), and an assassin stabbed him in his house (1.36).

The revolt began at Asculum late in 91 with the killing of every Roman in the town (1.38). Marsi, Paeligni, Samnites, Lucanians and others formed a state with its capital at Corfinium, renamed Italia, a senate of five hundred, two consuls and twelve praetors (Diodorus 37.2; Strabo 5.4.2). Its denarii, struck on the Roman standard (Alberto Campana, La monetazione degli insorti italici durante la guerra sociale, 1987), read ITALIA in Latin or Víteliú in Oscan; one type shows warriors swearing an oath over a pig, another the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf, and some name the Samnite consul Papius Mutilus in Oscan as embratur, imperator.

In 90 a consul was killed and Marius, serving as a legate, withdrew pleading age (Plutarch, Marius 33). Rome conceded. The lex Julia of 90 enfranchised Latins and allies who had stayed loyal (Civil Wars 1.49); the lex Plautia Papiria of 89 any man enrolled in an allied community who registered with a praetor at Rome within sixty days (Cicero, Pro Archia 7). Force did the rest. Pompeius Strabo took Asculum in 89, with the young Pompey on his council (ILS 8888), and Sulla, as legate, won the grass crown at Nola (Pliny, Natural History 22.12). Samnites and Lucanians held out until 82. The new citizens were confined to a few tribes, ten new ones voting last in Appian (1.49), eight existing ones in Velleius (2.20.2), and their distribution became the issue of 88.

Where sources disagree. Appian presents the war as a fight for citizenship (Civil Wars 1.34–39), and Velleius calls the allies' cause most just, since they asked for the citizenship of the empire they defended (2.15). P. A. Brunt ("Italian Aims at the Time of the Social War", 1965) argued that they wanted citizenship as protection and a share of empire; Henrik Mouritsen (Italian Unification, 1998) that they fought for independence, a state called Italia with its own coins being no lobby for enfranchisement.

Mithridates and the march on Rome (88 BC)

Mithridates VI Eupator of Pontus had built an empire round the Black Sea. In 89 the Roman envoy Manius Aquillius pushed Nicomedes IV of Bithynia to raid Pontus; in 88 Mithridates overran the province of Asia, welcomed by cities squeezed by tax-farmers, and killed Aquillius by pouring molten gold down his throat (Appian, Mithridatic Wars 11–21). From Ephesus he ordered the cities to kill on a single day every Roman and Italian, with their wives, children and Italian freedmen (22–23).

Where sources disagree. Valerius Maximus (9.2 ext. 3) and Memnon of Heraclea (22.9) give 80,000 dead; Plutarch gives 150,000 (Sulla 24). Appian, who describes the killing city by city, gives no total. No one could have counted, and the figures measure Roman outrage better than they measure people.

At Rome the consul Sulla held the command. The tribune Publius Sulpicius proposed to spread the new citizens through all thirty-five tribes and, to carry it, allied with Marius, who wanted the war. When the consuls suspended public business, Sulpicius' gangs rioted and drove Sulla to take refuge, Plutarch says, in Marius' house; the law passed and the command went to Marius (Plutarch, Sulla 8–10; Appian, Civil Wars 1.55–56). Sulla told his six legions at Nola that the eastern plunder would go to other men. They stoned Marius' officers and marched; all Sulla's officers but one quaestor refused to follow, and he told envoys he came to free Rome from tyrants (1.57). His men fought their way in by the Esquiline, the first Roman army to take the city as an enemy's (1.58–60). Marius, Sulpicius and ten others were outlawed. Sulpicius was killed; Marius escaped through the marshes of Minturnae to Africa and bade a messenger report that he had seen Marius sitting among the ruins of Carthage (Marius 37–40). Sulla let Lucius Cornelius Cinna be elected consul for 87 on an oath to respect his settlement, and sailed for Greece (Sulla 10).

Marius, Cinna and the peace of Dardanus (87–84 BC)

Cinna broke his oath, was driven out by his colleague Gnaeus Octavius after a battle in the Forum, and was deposed by the Senate (Civil Wars 1.64–65). He won over the army at Nola; Marius landed in Etruria and joined him, and Rome, blockaded, surrendered late in 87. Octavius' head was displayed on the Rostra, the first consul's to be (1.71). The orator Marcus Antonius was beheaded, Catulus suffocated himself with charcoal fumes, and a slave bodyguard killed whomever Marius did not greet (Plutarch, Marius 43–44). Marius entered his seventh consulship in January 86 and died within the month (45). Cinna was consul every year until his own troops killed him at Ancona in 84 (Civil Wars 1.78); his regime also let debtors pay a quarter of what they owed (Velleius 2.23.2).

Sulla's war, the sack of Athens in 86 and the victories at Chaeronea and Orchomenus, is told in Greek module 7.3. The Roman point is that he fought it as an outlaw: Cinna's government declared him a public enemy and sent its own army east, whose commander Flaccus was murdered by his legate Fimbria; in 85 Fimbria's army went over to Sulla (Appian, Mithridatic Wars 51–60). Needing to go home, Sulla made peace with Mithridates at Dardanus in 85. The king gave up his conquests and kept Pontus; Plutarch says he paid 2,000 talents and surrendered seventy ships (Sulla 22), Memnon 3,000 talents and eighty ships (25.2). Asia was fined 20,000 talents (Sulla 25); its later debts belong to module 5.3.

Civil war, the Colline Gate and the proscriptions (83–81 BC)

Sulla landed at Brundisium in 83. Metellus Pius, Crassus and the young Pompey, with three legions raised in Picenum on his own authority, joined him (Plutarch, Pompey 6; module 5.3 follows his rise). He beat one consul, Norbanus, and took over the army of the other, Scipio, without a fight (Civil Wars 1.84–85); on 6 July the Capitol burned (1.86; Julius Obsequens 57 for the day). In 82 he shut Marius' son, consul at under thirty, in Praeneste. On 1 November the Samnite Pontius Telesinus attacked Rome at the Colline Gate, saying the wolves would prey on Italy until their forest was cut down (Velleius 2.27.1–2). Sulla's left broke; Crassus won on the right (Plutarch, Crassus 6). Afterwards the prisoners were butchered while Sulla addressed the Senate in the nearby temple of Bellona, telling startled senators that some criminals were being corrected (Sulla 30): 6,000 in Plutarch, 8,000 who had surrendered, killed in the Villa Publica, in Livy's epitomator (Periochae 88). Praeneste fell, young Marius killed himself, and Sulla took the name Felix (Velleius 2.27.5).

The proscriptions made vengeance a procedure. Sulla posted eighty names, then 220 on each of the next two days (Sulla 31). Killers were paid two talents, property was auctioned, and the victims' sons and grandsons were barred from office (Sulla 31; Velleius 2.28). A law closed the lists on 1 June 81 (Cicero, Pro Roscio Amerino 128), but names were added for profit: Cicero's client Sextus Roscius had lost his father to the list after the deadline, so that Sulla's freedman Chrysogonus could buy an estate worth six million sesterces for two thousand (6). Crassus built his fortune at the auctions (Crassus 2).

Where sources disagree. Plutarch's lists total 520 (Sulla 31). Appian starts with about forty senators and 1,600 equestrians (Civil Wars 1.95) and sums the victims as ninety senators, fifteen ex-consuls and 2,600 equestrians, exiles included (1.103); Valerius Maximus gives 4,700 proscribed (9.2.1). François Hinard (1985) put the formal lists at a little over 520 and could name about seventy-five victims; the larger totals probably include the war dead.

The dictator's settlement, retirement and death

With both consuls of 82 dead, the interrex Lucius Valerius Flaccus carried a law making Sulla dictator for writing laws and setting the state in order, without time limit (Civil Wars 1.98–99); Cicero called it the most unjust of laws (De lege agraria 3.5). The aim was to make the Senate the government again and to close the routes by which the Gracchi, Saturninus, Sulpicius and Sulla himself had gone round it.

  • Senate. About three hundred equestrians enrolled (1.100); twenty quaestors a year, entering it automatically (Tacitus, Annals 11.22).
  • Courts. Juries back to senators (Velleius 2.32.3); standing courts for extortion, treason, bribery, embezzlement, murder and poisoning, and forgery.
  • Magistrates. Eight praetors; quaestorship, praetorship and consulship in that order, with ten years between repeated tenures (1.100); governors forbidden to leave their province or make war without authorisation (Cicero, Against Piso 50).
  • Tribunes. No right to propose laws (Periochae 89), a veto only to protect individuals, no higher office afterwards: in Cicero's words, the power to help without the power to harm (On the Laws 3.22).
  • Priests and people. Colleges enlarged to fifteen and filled by co-optation (module 2.3); grain distributions ended (Sallust, Histories 1, speech of Lepidus).
  • Veterans. Twenty-three legions settled on confiscated land in Etruria and Campania, 120,000 men in Appian (1.100, 1.104); ten thousand slaves of the proscribed freed as Cornelii (1.100).

Sulla was consul again in 80 and laid down the dictatorship at a date modern scholars place between 81 and 79; Appian puts it in 79 and has him offer in the Forum to account for his acts (1.103–104). He retired to Puteoli and died in 78, aged sixty, two days after he stopped writing the twenty-second book of his memoirs (Plutarch, Sulla 37). His epitaph claimed that no friend had outdone him in kindness and no enemy in harm (38). Lepidus' attack on his system is where module 5.3 begins.

Where sources disagree. Appian marvels that a man with a tyrant's power gave it up unasked (Civil Wars 1.3, 1.104); Caesar said that Sulla did not know his ABC when he laid down the dictatorship (Suetonius, Julius 77). Arthur Keaveney (Sulla: The Last Republican, 1982) reads the retirement as the act of a conservative who wanted the Senate restored, not a monarchy. Either way the method outlived the system, whose main pieces were gone by 70 (module 5.3).

Sulla's memoirs and Plutarch

Livy's books on the period survive only in the Periochae, Sallust's Histories begin in 78, and Appian gives the one continuous narrative (module 0.1). Sallust thought Sisenna's lost history the best account of Sulla, though not frank enough (Jugurtha 95.2). Much of the rest goes back to Marius' enemies: Rutilius Rufus, whose quarrel with Marius Plutarch notes (Marius 28); Catulus, in a book on his consulship (Cicero, Brutus 132); and Sulla, in twenty-two books of memoirs dedicated to Lucullus (Plutarch, Lucullus 1).

Plutarch read the memoirs and cites them often. Sulla presented himself as fortune's favourite: his boldest unplanned ventures went best and the gods spoke in dreams (Sulla 6); Plutarch adds, as hearsay, that a goddess from Cappadocia handed him a thunderbolt before the march on Rome (9); hence Felix, and Epaphroditus in Greek (34). He kept score too. At Chaeronea only fourteen of his men were missing, and two of them returned that evening (19); at Vercellae Marius' army lost its way in the dust while the Cimbri fell on Catulus' troops, with whom Sulla served (Marius 26–27). The grass crown at Nola comes from the same books. Plutarch notes that Sulla credits fortune more than ability and reports Vercellae as a claim, and for Marius' last days he names Posidonius and the historian Gaius Piso (Marius 45). Sallust's sketch is the counterweight: learned, eloquent, a man whose luck never outran his industry until the civil war, after which Sallust could not decide whether shame or disgust kept him silent (Jugurtha 95.3–4).

Self-test

  1. What two reasons does Sallust give for writing about the Jugurthine War, and how does the Mamilian court fit his theme?
    Answer

    The war was great and savage, and it was the first time the arrogance of the nobility was opposed (Jugurtha 5.1). The lex Mamilia of 109 set up a court that condemned Opimius, Bestia and others for taking Jugurtha's money (40; Cicero, Brutus 128), the popular counter-attack his bribery plot leads up to.

  2. How did Marius obtain the Numidian command in 107, and why was the method dangerous?
    Answer

    Elected consul despite Metellus' contempt, he was given Numidia by a plebiscite overriding the Senate's prorogation of Metellus (Jugurtha 73). It made a command something the assembly could transfer, the precedent Sulpicius used against Sulla in 88.

  3. Which of the "Marian reforms" have ancient attestation, and what do modern critics doubt?
    Answer

    Volunteers from the capite censi in 107 (Jugurtha 86), soldiers carrying their own kit (Marius 13), the modified pilum (25) and the eagle as sole standard (Pliny 10.16); the cohort is not credited to him. Gabba saw the change as the end of a long slide; Rich denies the manpower shortage behind it, and Cadiou doubts that the army became proletarian at all.

  4. Why did Arausio happen, and what did it do to the constitution?
    Answer

    The proconsul Caepio refused to cooperate with the consul Mallius, a new man, and both armies were destroyed on 6 October 105. Rome responded by electing Marius consul five years running, 104–100, against the rules on repeated office.

  5. What did the Italian rebel state look like, and what does its coinage suggest?
    Answer

    Its capital was Corfinium, renamed Italia, with a senate of five hundred, two consuls and twelve praetors (Diodorus 37.2). Its denarii carry ITALIA or Oscan Víteliú, an oath scene and the bull goring the wolf, which Mouritsen reads as a claim to independence rather than a demand for Roman citizenship.

  6. Which laws enfranchised the Italians, and how was the value of the vote limited?
    Answer

    The lex Julia of 90 (loyal Latins and allies) and the lex Plautia Papiria of 89 (registration with a praetor within sixty days; Cicero, Pro Archia 7). New citizens were confined to a few tribes: ten new ones voting last in Appian (1.49), eight existing ones in Velleius (2.20.2).

  7. What made it possible for Sulla to march on Rome in 88, and how did his own side react?
    Answer

    Sulpicius' law transferred the Mithridatic command to Marius, and Sulla persuaded his six legions at Nola that the eastern plunder would go to others; they stoned Marius' officers. All his officers except one quaestor refused to follow him (Appian, Civil Wars 1.57).

  8. How did the Sullan proscriptions work as a procedure?
    Answer

    Lists of names were posted (Plutarch's three total 520), killers were paid two talents, property was auctioned and descendants barred from office (Sulla 31). A law closed the lists on 1 June 81, though Cicero's Pro Roscio Amerino shows names added later for profit.

  9. What did Sulla do to the tribunate and the courts?
    Answer

    Tribunes lost the right to propose laws, kept the veto only to protect individuals, and were barred from higher office: power to help without power to harm (Cicero, On the Laws 3.22). Juries went back to senators (Velleius 2.32.3), and standing courts were created for the main crimes.

  10. How do Sulla's memoirs shape what we know, and give one example of Plutarch using them.
    Answer

    Plutarch drew on them, with the hostile accounts of Rutilius and Catulus, for much of Marius' and Sulla's careers, so the record leans to Marius' enemies. Examples: Sulla's claim that only fourteen men were missing at Chaeronea (Sulla 19), or that Marius lost his way in the dust at Vercellae (Marius 26).

Carry forward

  1. Between 107 and 82 the decisive political fact became who held a command and whether his soldiers would follow him: the plebiscite of 107, the transfer of 88 and Sulla's march turned armies into political actors, and every later dynast started from that precedent.
  2. The Social War made Italy Roman in law at the cost of a war against Rome, and the fight over how the new citizens would vote drove the violence of 88–87; Sulla's colonies and proscriptions then remade the landowning class of Italy.
  3. Sulla's settlement, the most thorough attempt to restore senatorial government, was imposed by the first march on Rome and secured by proscription; the method outlived the system, and the record of it comes largely from the memoirs of the men who won.

Give me an in-depth report on Marius, the Social War and Sulla, 112 to 78 BC. Cover: the Jugurthine War as Sallust tells it and his theme of senatorial corruption; Marius the new man, his seven consulships and the 'Marian reforms' with the modern doubts about them; the Cimbri and Teutones, Arausio, Aquae Sextiae and Vercellae; Saturninus and 100 BC; the Social War of 91–88 BC, Livius Drusus, the Italian state with its capital at Corfinium and its coins, and the citizenship grants; Mithridates and the massacre of Romans in Asia; Sulla's march on Rome in 88 BC, the first by a Roman army, Marius' return and the terror of 87, Cinna; Sulla's war in the East (point back to Greek module 7.3 for the sack of Athens), his return, the Colline Gate, the proscriptions, the dictatorship and its reforms, his retirement and death; and Sulla's lost memoirs and how Plutarch used them.
