Pompey, Crassus, Cicero and Catiline

Sulla's system under attack: Lepidus and SertoriusSpartacus, 73–71 BCThe year 70: Pompey, Crassus and the end of Sulla's constitutionThe great commands: the Gabinian and Manilian lawsPompey's settlement of the EastCicero's consulship and CatilineCaesar before 60, and Clodius at the Bona DeaPompey's return and the alliance of 60Self-testCarry forward

Sulla's system under attack: Lepidus and Sertorius

Sulla died in 78, where module 5.2 ends. His settlement had handed the courts to the Senate, gagged the tribunes and planted veterans on confiscated land; within eight years most of it was gone, undone by men he had raised. The narrative rests on the fragments of Sallust's Histories (78–67), Plutarch's Lives, Appian's Civil Wars and Cassius Dio, now joined by a contemporary, Cicero; module 0.1 surveys the later narratives and module 5.6 introduces Sallust and Cicero as writers.

Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, consul in 78, had been elected with Pompey's support against Sulla's wishes (Plutarch, Pompey 15). He opposed Sulla's state funeral and promised to restore the confiscated land (Appian, Civil Wars 1.105, 1.107). Sent to suppress dispossessed farmers who had killed Sullan colonists at Faesulae, he joined them, and in 77 marched on Rome demanding a second consulship. The Senate passed its final decree; Sallust gives the speeches of Lepidus and of Philippus, who moved it (Histories 1.55 and 1.77 M). Catulus beat Lepidus outside the city, and Pompey had Lepidus' legate Marcus Brutus, father of the tyrannicide, killed after he surrendered at Mutina (Pompey 16).

In Spain the Marian Quintus Sertorius had held out since 80 with Lusitanian support, wearing down Metellus Pius by guerrilla war, forming a senate of exiles and schooling chiefs' sons at Osca as hostages (Plutarch, Sertorius 14, 22). The Senate sent Pompey, twenty-nine and holding no office, with proconsular command: not as proconsul, Philippus said, but in place of both consuls (Cicero, Philippics 11.18). Sertorius beat him at Lauron in 76, and the war dragged on until his officer Perperna murdered him in 73 or 72 (Sertorius 18, 26). Pompey executed Perperna and burnt Sertorius' letters unread, sparing the senators who had written them (Pompey 20).

Spartacus, 73–71 BC

In 73 gladiators broke out of Lentulus Batiatus' school at Capua: seventy-eight in Plutarch (Crassus 8), about seventy in Appian (Civil Wars 1.116), sixty-four in Velleius (2.30.5). Their leader Spartacus was a Thracian who, Appian says, had fought Rome and been captured and sold; Plutarch makes him intelligent and humane, more Greek than Thracian. Runaway slaves and rural poor joined them, and through 72 they beat praetors and both consuls (Appian 1.116–117).

Late in 72 Marcus Licinius Crassus, Sulla's richest lieutenant, took command and revived decimation: on five hundred men who had fled, in Plutarch (Crassus 10); on two legions, in Appian (1.118). Pushed into Bruttium, Spartacus paid Cilician pirates to ferry men to Sicily; they took the money and sailed away. He broke through Crassus' ditch across the peninsula, and in 71, with Pompey returning from Spain, Crassus forced the last battle. Spartacus died fighting his way towards Crassus (Crassus 11). The Livian epitome claims 60,000 dead (Periochae 97); Appian alone reports six thousand prisoners crucified along the road from Capua to Rome (1.120). Pompey cut down five thousand fugitives, by Plutarch's count, and claimed to have torn the war out by the roots (Pompey 21). Crassus received only an ovation.

No slave speaks in the sources. Sallust's Histories, written a generation later, were the fullest and probably lie behind Plutarch, but survive in scraps; Plutarch and Appian wrote two centuries on; the epitome, Florus and Orosius descend from Livy. Cicero, a contemporary, mentions the war only in passing, as when he mocks Verres' claim to have kept it out of Sicily (Verrines 2.5).

Where sources disagree. Plutarch's Spartacus marches north meaning to cross the Alps and send his men home, until they refuse (Crassus 9); Appian's sets out for Rome with 120,000 foot, then turns back because his men are ill-armed and no city has joined him (1.117). Velleius gives 90,000 in the last battle (2.30.6); none of these figures is likely to rest on a count. Marx, writing to Engels in 1861, saw in Spartacus a representative of the ancient proletariat; Keith Bradley (Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World, 1989) argued that the slave revolts sought escape, not abolition. Module 9.3 places the revolt within the institution.

The year 70: Pompey, Crassus and the end of Sulla's constitution

Crassus and Pompey kept their armies near Rome and stood together for the consulship of 70. Pompey, thirty-five, had held no magistracy and was not a senator; the rules were waived (Cicero, De imperio Cn. Pompei 62). Pressure to restore the tribunate had been constant since 78, and Sallust gives the tribune Licinius Macer a speech demanding it in 73 (Histories 3.48 M). In 70 the consuls restored the tribunes' veto and right to legislate. The praetor Lucius Aurelius Cotta divided the juries among senators, equites and tribuni aerarii. The revived censors expelled sixty-four senators (Periochae 98), among them Gaius Antonius and Lentulus Sura, both heard of again in 63. Pompey paraded before them as a knight leading his horse; Crassus feasted the people at ten thousand tables (Plutarch, Pompey 22; Crassus 12). Sulla's enlarged Senate, standing courts and colonies survived; his government without tribunes did not.

Verres and the Verrines

Gaius Verres, governor of Sicily 73–71, was prosecuted for extortion that summer by Cicero, a new man from Arpinum who had been quaestor in Sicily. His advocate Hortensius, consul-elect for 69, played for delay into that year; Cicero replaced the long opening with a short speech, called his witnesses at once, and after the first hearing Verres went into exile at Massilia (Plutarch, Cicero 7). The five books of the Actio secunda were published, never delivered.

They are unique evidence: a governor's year rebuilt from city accounts, tithe records and testimony. Verres sold verdicts (2.2), rigged the grain tithe (2.3), stripped temples of their statues (2.4) and crucified a Roman citizen, Gavius, as he cried "civis Romanus sum" (2.5.162). Cicero claimed forty million sesterces (Verrines 1.56); Plutarch says Cicero assessed the damages at 750,000 denarii and was suspected of a bribe for keeping them low (Cicero 8). This is prosecution oratory, and every figure is the prosecutor's. It made Cicero the first advocate in Rome.

The great commands: the Gabinian and Manilian laws

By 68 pirates had destroyed a consular fleet at Ostia and kidnapped two praetors (Cicero, De imperio 32–33; Plutarch, Pompey 24). In 67 the tribune Aulus Gabinius proposed one commander for three years over the whole sea and fifty miles inland, with imperium equal to the governors' there (Velleius 2.31.2). The bill named no one; everyone knew whom it meant. When the tribune Trebellius vetoed, Gabinius began to have the tribes depose him, as Tiberius Gracchus had Octavius (module 5.1), and he gave way. Grain prices fell on the day of the appointment (Plutarch, Pompey 26). Cicero says Pompey began the war in early spring and finished it by midsummer (De imperio 35); surrendered pirates were resettled as farmers at Soli, renamed Pompeiopolis (Pompey 28).

Where sources disagree. Plutarch says Gabinius' bill offered two hundred ships and fifteen legates (Pompey 25), and that Pompey was then given five hundred ships, 120,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry and twenty-four legates (26). Appian gives 270 ships, 120,000 foot, 4,000 horse, twenty-five legates and 6,000 talents (Mithridatic Wars 94). Plutarch has the western sea cleared in forty days, Appian forty days in the west and as many in the east (95), the Livian epitome the whole sea in forty days (Periochae 99). The totals were probably authorisations rather than ships at sea.

Lucullus had driven Mithridates from Pontus (Greek module 7.3) and in 69 taken Tigranes' capital, Tigranocerta, but his curbs on interest in Asia angered the tax-farmers, and in 68–67 his army mutinied, stirred by his brother-in-law Publius Clodius (Plutarch, Lucullus 20, 34). In 66 the tribune Gaius Manilius transferred the war to Pompey. Cicero, praetor, spoke for the law in his first speech from the Rostra: a general needs knowledge of war, courage, authority and luck (De imperio 28), Pompey alone has all four, and the revenues of Asia and the equites' money there are at stake (14–19).

Pompey's settlement of the East

Pompey beat Mithridates in 66, and Tigranes surrendered and kept Armenia on payment of 6,000 talents (Plutarch, Pompey 33). Syria was annexed in 64 and the Seleucids ended without a battle, as Greek module 7.3 tells. In 63 Pompey took the Temple at Jerusalem after a three-month siege and entered the Holy of Holies, leaving its treasure untouched (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 14.72); Hyrcanus II became high priest without the royal title. Pontus was joined to Bithynia as a province, Cilicia was enlarged, and client rulers bound to Pompey personally, Deiotarus in Galatia and Ariobarzanes in Cappadocia, filled the gaps.

The totals differ by source. Plutarch reports triumphal tablets claiming a thousand strongholds, nearly nine hundred cities, eight hundred pirate ships, thirty-nine cities founded, revenues raised from fifty to eighty-five million drachmas and twenty thousand talents for the treasury (Pompey 45). Pliny quotes a dedication: 12,183,000 people defeated, killed or received in surrender, 846 ships sunk or taken, 1,538 towns and forts (Natural History 7.97–98). These are claims, not audits.

Cicero's consulship and Catiline

Lucius Sergius Catilina, a patrician and a killer in Sulla's proscriptions (Asconius, on Cicero's In a White Toga), lost the election for 63 to Cicero and Gaius Antonius, and in 63 lost again on a promise to cancel debts. Cicero, the first new man made consul in a very long time (De lege agraria 2.3), bought Antonius' loyalty with Macedonia and presided at the elections wearing a breastplate (Pro Murena 52).

In Etruria a Sullan centurion, Manlius, raised veterans and ruined farmers, and in late October the Senate passed its final decree. After a plot to kill Cicero at his morning reception was betrayed by Fulvia, mistress of a conspirator (Sallust, Catiline 28), Cicero denounced Catiline in the Senate on 8 November, and Catiline left for Manlius' camp. In Rome, Lentulus Sura, now praetor, and Cethegus approached envoys of the Allobroges, who told their patron, who told Cicero; arrested with sealed letters in the night of 2–3 December, they turned evidence (Sallust 40–41, 44–45). On 5 December Silanus, consul-elect, proposed death. Caesar, praetor-elect, argued against killing citizens untried; his speech in Sallust warns that bad precedents begin as good ones (51.27). Cato, tribune-elect, carried the house (52). Five men were strangled in the Tullianum that evening, and Cicero announced it in one word, vixerunt, they have lived (Plutarch, Cicero 22). Catiline fell at Pistoria in January 62 with an army that, Sallust says, died with its wounds in front (61).

Fourth5 DecemberSenateSteer the debate on punishment

Cicero published the speeches in 60 among his consular orations (Letters to Atticus 2.1.3), when the executions had become a liability; how far he revised them is uncertain. They argue the consul's case: a monster from whom Cicero alone saved Rome. Sallust's Catiline, written about 42–41, gives Catiline a voice (20, 35), treats the plot as a symptom of a society corrupted by wealth and ambition, and makes the climax the debate of Caesar and Cato (51–54), giving the First Catilinarian one sentence (31.6). The two agree on outline and dates and part on motive and blame. Module 5.6 reads Sallust as a writer; deep dive module 11.4 takes up Sallust's Sempronia.

Where sources disagree. Sallust (18–19) and Suetonius (Julius 9) report an earlier plot of 66–65 to murder the consuls; Robin Seager ("The First Catilinarian Conspiracy", 1964) argued that it was a fiction built from electoral slander. Sallust reports and rejects charges against Crassus (48) and Caesar (49), which Suetonius, citing Caesar's enemies, takes more seriously. Whether 63 was a coherent revolution or the desperation of bankrupt nobles and veterans, enlarged by the consul who crushed it, is still argued.
Where sources disagree. Sallust (51.43) and Cicero (Against Catiline 4.7–10) make Caesar's proposal permanent custody in Italian towns; Plutarch (Caesar 7) and Appian (Civil Wars 2.5–6) make it custody until Catiline was beaten, then trial. The difference is the legal point. Gaius Gracchus' law forbade executing a citizen without the people's verdict; Cicero replied that a public enemy is no citizen (4.10), and the final decree, like Opimius' in 121 (module 5.1), claimed that emergency suspended the rule. Clodius tested that claim in 58 (deep dive module 11.3).

Caesar before 60, and Clodius at the Bona Dea

Gaius Julius Caesar, born in 100 to an old patrician house, was Marius' nephew by marriage and Cinna's son-in-law. He refused Sulla's order to divorce Cinna's daughter and was spared with the warning that the boy held many Mariuses (Suetonius, Julius 1). Captured by pirates, he promised to crucify them and did (Plutarch, Caesar 2). He then ran a popular line: Marius' images at his aunt's funeral in 69, 320 pairs of gladiators as aedile in 65, and Marius' trophies restored to the Capitol (Caesar 5–6). In 63 he backed a treason charge against the aged Rabirius for the killing of Saturninus in 100, a challenge to the final decree; Cicero defended Rabirius (Dio 37.26–28). The same year, deep in debt, he beat Catulus to the office of pontifex maximus (Plutarch, Caesar 7). Before he could leave for Spain in 61, Crassus stood surety for 830 talents of his debts (Caesar 11).

In December 62 the women's rites of the Bona Dea were held in the pontifex maximus' house. Publius Clodius Pulcher got in dressed as a female lute player and was caught (Plutarch, Caesar 9–10). Tried for sacrilege, he claimed to have been at Interamna; Cicero testified that he had seen him in Rome that day (Plutarch, Cicero 29). The jury acquitted by thirty-one votes to twenty-five, and Cicero blamed bribery (Letters to Atticus 1.16.5). Caesar divorced his wife Pompeia because his household must be free of suspicion (Suetonius, Julius 74). Clodius never forgave Cicero; his tribunate of 58 and Cicero's exile belong to deep dive modules 11.3 and 11.5.

Pompey's return and the alliance of 60

Pompey landed at Brundisium in December 62 and dismissed his army (Velleius 2.40.3). He asked two things: ratification of his eastern acts as a whole, and land for his veterans. The Senate, led by Lucullus, Cato and Metellus Celer, whose half-sister Pompey had divorced, insisted on examining the acts one by one and blocked a land bill in 60 (Dio 37.49–50). Cato also opposed the Asian tax-farmers, whom Crassus backed, in their plea to cancel a third of their contract; Cicero complained that Cato spoke as if in Plato's Republic, not the dregs of Romulus (Letters to Atticus 2.1.8). Caesar, back from Spain in 60, could not both await a triumph outside the city and declare his candidacy within it; Cato talked out an exemption, and Caesar chose the consulship (Plutarch, Caesar 13; Suetonius, Julius 18). He then reconciled Pompey and Crassus in a compact that nothing should be done in the state that displeased any of the three (Julius 19). In December 60 Caesar's agent Balbus invited Cicero in (Letters to Atticus 2.3.3); he declined.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch (Caesar 13–14), Appian (Civil Wars 2.9) and the Livian epitome (Periochae 103) put the compact before Caesar's election in 60; Dio has him win both men over before it but narrates the compact after (37.54–58), Suetonius sets it after the election (Julius 19), Velleius in the consulship (2.44.1). Cicero's letter of December 60 shows an understanding with Pompey forming, Crassus not yet in it. Asinius Pollio began his history of the civil wars in 60 (Horace, Odes 2.1.1), dating the Republic's end to the compact.

The ancient accounts call it a pact or, in Velleius, a partnership in power (2.44.1); Varro called it a three-headed monster (Appian, Civil Wars 2.9). The surviving accounts do not call it a triumvirate. A triumvirate was a board created by law, like that of Antony, Lepidus and Octavian under the lex Titia of 43 (module 5.5); the arrangement of 60 had no law, title, term or office. "First triumvirate" reads the legal junta of 43 back into a private alliance of three men who distrusted one another.

Self-test

  1. Why did Lepidus' revolt start at Faesulae, and what did it reveal about Sulla's settlement?
    Answer

    Farmers dispossessed for Sullan colonists rose and killed the settlers; Lepidus, sent to suppress them, joined them. The confiscations had created a constituency for revolt, which Lepidus courted by promising to restore the land (Appian, Civil Wars 1.107).

  2. Why can no figure for Spartacus' army be trusted, and whose figures are they?
    Answer

    No slave source survives, the near-contemporary Sallust is in fragments, and the narratives are two centuries later. Appian gives 70,000 and then 120,000, Velleius 90,000 in the last battle, the Livian epitome 60,000 dead; Appian alone gives the six thousand crucified.

  3. What did the consuls of 70 undo of Sulla's system, and what survived?
    Answer

    The tribunes' veto and right to legislate were restored, Cotta's law shared the juries among senators, equites and tribuni aerarii, and the revived censors purged sixty-four senators. The enlarged Senate, the standing courts and the veteran colonies survived.

  4. Why did Cicero shorten his opening in the Verres trial, and what limits the Verrines as evidence?
    Answer

    Hortensius aimed to delay the trial into 69, when he would be consul; Cicero called witnesses at once and Verres fled after the first hearing. The speeches rest on documents and testimony but argue a prosecutor's case, and the Actio secunda was published, never delivered.

  5. What made the Gabinian law unprecedented, and what earlier tribunician tactic did Gabinius use?
    Answer

    One commander, three years, the whole sea and fifty miles inland, imperium equal to the governors' (Velleius 2.31.2), and resources beyond any magistrate's. Faced with Trebellius' veto, he began to have the tribes depose him, as Tiberius Gracchus had Octavius.

  6. How should the figures for Pompey's eastern conquests be read?
    Answer

    As self-advertisement, attributed to their reporters: Plutarch's triumphal tablets with a thousand strongholds and thirty-nine cities founded (Pompey 45), and Pliny's dedication with 12,183,000 people and 1,538 towns and forts (Natural History 7.97–98). They are claims, not audits.

  7. How do Cicero's four speeches and Sallust's Catiline differ as evidence for 63?
    Answer

    Cicero's are contemporary but were published in 60, perhaps revised, and argue the consul's case. Sallust wrote about twenty years later, gives Catiline a voice, makes the plot a symptom of moral decay and builds the climax on the debate of Caesar and Cato, passing over the First Catilinarian in a sentence (31.6).

  8. On what grounds were the conspirators executed, and what was the legal objection?
    Answer

    On the Senate's vote under the final decree, with Cicero arguing that public enemies forfeit citizenship (Against Catiline 4.10). Gaius Gracchus' law forbade executing citizens without the people's verdict, the point of Caesar's proposal, whose terms Sallust and Plutarch report differently.

  9. Why did the Bona Dea scandal matter beyond the sacrilege?
    Answer

    Clodius' acquittal by 31 votes to 25 amid bribery (Letters to Atticus 1.16.5) showed that a court could be bought, and Cicero's testimony against his alibi made Clodius his enemy, with consequences in 58 (deep dive modules 11.3 and 11.5).

  10. Why is "first triumvirate" a misleading name for the alliance of 60?
    Answer

    A triumvirate was a board created by law, as by the lex Titia of 43. The compact of 60 was private, with no title, term or office; ancient writers called it a pact or a partnership in power (Velleius 2.44.1), and Varro a three-headed monster.

Carry forward

  1. The extraordinary command became the normal answer to crisis: Pompey's career from 77 to 62 was a run of commands, the greatest of them voted by the people over senatorial objection, with resources and imperium no annual magistrate held, and the dynasts of the 50s and 40s built on that model.
  2. Sulla's settlement failed because it could not exclude the tribunate and the people. Once the tribunes were restored in 70 the assemblies were again the road to power, and the Senate's counter, the final decree, was itself put in question by the execution of the Catilinarians.
  3. This period has contemporary evidence for the first time, but it is advocacy: one interested witness shaped the whole tradition of 63, and every figure, from Spartacus' army to Pompey's conquests, belongs to the writer who gives it.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Roman politics from Sulla's death to the alliance of 60 BC. Cover: Lepidus' revolt and Sertorius in Spain; Spartacus' slave war of 73–71 BC and its sources; the consulship of Pompey and Crassus in 70 BC and the dismantling of Sulla's system; Verres and Cicero's Verrines; the Gabinian and Manilian laws and Pompey's commands against the pirates and Mithridates, his settlement of the East and the end of the Seleucids (point back to Greek module 7.3); Cicero's consulship and the Catilinarian conspiracy of 63 BC, comparing Sallust's Catiline, Cicero's four speeches and the execution of the conspirators without trial; Caesar's early career; Clodius and the Bona Dea scandal; and the alliance of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar in 60 BC, and why 'first triumvirate' is a modern label. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

The consulship of 59: Bibulus watches the sky

Module 5.3 ended with the private alliance of 60; the consulship of 59 made it public. Caesar's colleague was Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, Cato's son-in-law. Caesar had the proceedings of Senate and people published daily (Suetonius, Julius 20.1), then brought an agrarian law for Pompey's veterans and the urban poor. When Cato talked it out in the Senate, Caesar had him led towards prison (20.4) and took the bill to the people. Bibulus came to the Forum to block the vote; a basket of dung was emptied over his head and his fasces were broken (Plutarch, Pompey 48; Dio 38.6).

For the remaining eight months Bibulus stayed at home and issued edicts that he was watching the sky (servare de caelo) on every assembly day (Julius 20.1): the augural weapon of module 2.1, by which a magistrate's report of adverse signs halted public business. Caesar ignored him and legislated through the people. Wits dated documents to the consulship of Julius and Caesar (20.2).

The laws served all three partners. Pompey's eastern settlement was ratified; the tax-farmers of Asia, Crassus' clients, had their contract cut by a third (Julius 20.3); the Campanian land went to fathers of three or more children; a law on extortion by governors outlasted the Republic. Pompey married Caesar's daughter Julia, and Caesar married Calpurnia, daughter of Lucius Piso, his successor as consul (21). The tribune Vatinius' law gave Caesar Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum for five years, and the Senate added Transalpine Gaul (22.1). As pontifex maximus Caesar presided over the adoption that made Publius Clodius a plebeian; his tribunate of 58 and Cicero's exile are deep dive modules 11.3 and 11.5.

Where sources disagree. Whether Bibulus' edicts voided the year's laws was never settled. Cicero argued that Clodius' adoption, carried while Bibulus watched the sky, was invalid (De domo sua 39–40), an argument that reached every law of 59; in 58 two praetors demanded an inquiry into Caesar's acts, which the Senate would not take up (Julius 23.1). Many modern scholars doubt that a notice sent from home, rather than announced in person, counted as obnuntiatio at all, and Robert Morstein-Marx (Julius Caesar and the Roman People, 2021) argues that Bibulus stretched obstruction past its customary limits and that the acts of 59 stayed formally valid. The open question is one reason Caesar would never face Rome as a private citizen.

Gaul in outline, 58–50

The Gallic War, seven books by Caesar and an eighth by his officer Aulus Hirtius, is almost the only narrative, so the outline below is Caesar's account of Caesar, with his own figures. The campaigns, the ethnography and the archaeology of Alesia are deep dive module 11.6.

YearCampaignCaesar's figures (Gallic War)
58Helvetii turned back at Bibracte; the German king Ariovistus driven over the Rhine368,000 Helvetii and allies set out, 110,000 went home (1.29)
57The Belgae; the Nervii at the Sambre; the AtuatuciNervii cut from 60,000 men to 500 (2.28); 53,000 Atuatuci sold (2.33)
56The Veneti beaten at seatheir council executed, the rest sold (3.16)
55Usipetes and Tencteri; first Rhine bridge; first landing in Britain430,000 Germans (4.15)
54Second British expedition; Sabinus and Cotta destroyed at Atuatucaa legion and five cohorts lost (5.24–37)
53Second Rhine bridge; the Eburones hunted downnone given
52Vercingetorix; Avaricum, Gergovia, Alesiaof 40,000 at Avaricum, 800 escaped (7.28); a relief army of 250,000 foot and 8,000 horse (7.76)
51–50Last resistance; Uxellodunumdefenders' hands cut off (8.44)

The Rhine bridge of 55, built in ten days and broken down after eighteen (4.17–19), and the British landings were addressed to Rome as much as to the enemy: the Senate voted fifteen days of thanksgiving for 57, more than anyone had received (2.35), and twenty after 55 and 52 (4.38, 7.90). In 52 Vercingetorix of the Arverni united most of Gaul and repulsed Caesar at Gergovia. At Alesia Caesar ringed him with siege lines facing both inwards and outwards, beat off the relief army and took his surrender (7.68–89); Vercingetorix walked in the triumph of 46 and was then executed (Dio 43.19). Gaul paid 40 million sesterces a year in tribute (Suetonius, Julius 25.1).

Later writers gave totals. Velleius Paterculus: more than 400,000 killed and more captured (2.47.1). Plutarch: three million fought, a million killed, a million captured (Caesar 15). Appian: over four million fought, a million killed and as many captured (Gallic History 1). Pliny the Elder: 1,192,000 killed in Caesar's battles outside the civil wars, which he refuses to count as glory, calling it a great wrong to the human race (Natural History 7.92). Romans objected at the time too: when Caesar attacked the Usipetes and Tencteri while their envoys were in his camp, Cato proposed handing him over to the Germans (Plutarch, Caesar 22).

Where sources disagree. Every count goes back to Caesar, who had reasons to inflate, and historians since Hans Delbrück have cut his Helvetian and German figures on grounds of supply and terrain. Pliny's precise total looks like a sum of official reports and covers wars outside Gaul; the round millions of Plutarch and Appian are two or three times Velleius' figure. The charge of genocide built on these numbers is weighed in deep dive module 11.6.

Luca, Julia and Carrhae

By 56 the alliance was fraying, and Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, candidate for 55, promised to take Caesar's army from him (Suetonius, Julius 24.1). Caesar met Crassus at Ravenna and Pompey at Luca in April; Plutarch counts 200 senators come to pay court (Caesar 21). Pompey and Crassus were consuls again in 55. Their law extended Caesar's command for five years, and the tribune Trebonius gave Pompey the Spains, which he governed through legates while staying near Rome, and Crassus Syria. Cicero's forced change of course is deep dive module 11.5.

Two deaths followed. Julia died in childbirth in 54 (Plutarch, Pompey 53); Caesar offered Pompey his great-niece Octavia (Julius 27.1), but Pompey married Cornelia, daughter of Metellus Scipio. In 53 Crassus invaded Parthia. At Carrhae the general Surena's horse archers, resupplied from a camel train, and his armoured lancers destroyed the army; Crassus' son Publius died fighting, and Crassus was killed at a parley. Plutarch gives 20,000 dead and 10,000 captured (Crassus 31). Lucan's image is the ancient verdict: Crassus had been the isthmus that kept two seas apart, and Julia might have held husband and father together (Civil War 1.98–120).

The breakdown with Pompey and the Rubicon

In January 52 Clodius was killed by Milo's men and his followers burned the Senate house as his pyre (deep dive module 11.3). On Bibulus' motion Pompey became consul without a colleague (Plutarch, Pompey 54). A law of the ten tribunes let Caesar stand for the consulship in absence, and Pompey's law requiring candidates to appear in person had an exemption for him added after it was already engraved (Julius 26.1, 28.3).

Caesar meant to pass straight from his command to a consulship in 48, since Cato had sworn to prosecute him once he dismissed his army (Julius 30.3). In 50 the tribune Curio, his debts paid by Caesar, vetoed every move to recall him and proposed that both dynasts disarm. On 1 December the Senate agreed by 370 votes to 22 (Appian, Civil Wars 2.30), but the consul Gaius Marcellus went out to hand Pompey a sword and the defence of the state (Plutarch, Pompey 59). On 7 January 49 the Senate passed the final decree, and the tribunes Antony and Quintus Cassius fled to Caesar (Civil War 1.5).

Caesar crossed the Rubicon, the stream at the edge of his province, with one legion (Civil War 1.7.8) a few days later. Suetonius has him hesitate, see an apparition piping on the bank, and say "the die is cast" (Julius 31–33); Plutarch says he spoke it in Greek, with Asinius Pollio beside him (Pompey 60; Caesar 32); the Greek tag is a line of Menander. Caesar's own Civil War never mentions the river and moves straight to Ariminum (1.8). His case, his dignitas, the tribunes' rights and the people's freedom from a faction (1.9, 1.22), is read as propaganda in module 5.6.

Where sources disagree. No ancient source states when Caesar's command legally ended, and the question Mommsen posed in Die Rechtsfrage zwischen Caesar und dem Senat (1857) has yielded dates across 50 and 49 without agreement. The ancient verdicts divide as sharply. Pollio's Caesar blamed his enemies; Cicero, trying to mediate, wrote that each side had sought domination (Letters to Atticus 8.11.2); Lucan, that Caesar could bear no superior and Pompey no equal (1.125–126).

Civil war: Italy, Spain, Dyrrachium, Pharsalus

Pompey had boasted that he need only stamp on the ground for legions to rise in Italy (Plutarch, Pompey 57). Instead he abandoned Rome and then Italy, crossing from Brundisium in March 49. At Corfinium Caesar released the captured Domitius and his officers (Civil War 1.16–23) and wrote that this would be a new way of conquering, to make oneself safe by mercy and generosity (Cicero, Letters to Atticus 9.7C). To the pardoned, clemency was a master's gift. Caesar took the reserve treasury from the temple of Saturn over a tribune's protest (Plutarch, Caesar 35), then marched on Pompey's legions in Spain. At Ilerda he forced Afranius and Petreius to surrender by cutting them off from water, without a pitched battle (Civil War 1.37–87). In Africa Curio died with his army fighting King Juba of Numidia (2.23–44).

In January 48 Caesar crossed to Epirus past Bibulus' fleet. At Dyrrachium he tried to wall in a larger army, his men living on bread made from a root (3.48), until Pompey broke out in July; the enemy, Caesar said, would have won that day had they had a commander who knew how to win (Plutarch, Caesar 39). At Pharsalus in Thessaly, on 9 August 48 by the unreformed calendar, cohorts held back as a fourth line routed Pompey's cavalry and turned his flank (Civil War 3.88–99). Viewing the dead, Caesar said, by Pollio's report, "they wanted it": after such deeds he would have been condemned had he not turned to his army (Suetonius, Julius 30.4).

Where sources disagree. Caesar gives Pompey 45,000 men to his own 22,000 (Civil War 3.88–89) and claims 15,000 Pompeians killed and more than 24,000 surrendered, for a loss of 200 soldiers and 30 centurions (3.99). Asinius Pollio, an officer on Caesar's side, put the Pompeian dead at 6,000, as Plutarch reports him (Caesar 46). Caesar's own losses look improbably low, and the gap lies within the Caesarian camp itself.

Civil war: Egypt, Africa, Munda

Pompey fled to Egypt, where the advisers of the boy king Ptolemy XIII had him stabbed as he landed at Pelusium in September 48, by the Egyptian Achillas and a Roman who had served under him (Plutarch, Pompey 77–80); Caesar, arriving days later, wept over his signet ring (Caesar 48). Drawn into Ptolemy's quarrel with his sister Cleopatra VII, he was besieged in the palace quarter of Alexandria until March 47. Cleopatra reached him carried in a bedding sack, not the carpet of later legend (Caesar 49). Fire from the burning ships spread into the city; whether it reached the Library is argued in Greek module 7.2. Ptolemy drowned after a battle by the Nile, and Cleopatra was restored. She toured the Nile with Caesar (Suetonius, Julius 52.1) and bore a son, Caesarion, whom Caesar's friend Oppius later wrote was not his (52.2). The queen herself belongs to module 5.5 and Greek modules 7.1 and 7.3.

Caesar beat Pharnaces of Pontus at Zela in August 47: veni, vidi, vici, in a letter according to Plutarch (Caesar 50), on a triumphal placard according to Suetonius (Julius 37.2). After a mutiny in Italy (deep dive module 11.2) he defeated Metellus Scipio and King Juba at Thapsus on 6 April 46. At Utica Cato saw the others safe, read Plato's Phaedo and stabbed himself, tearing open the wound when it was bound (Plutarch, Cato Minor 66–70). Caesar said he begrudged Cato his death, as Cato had begrudged him the saving of his life (72). Dead, Cato became a cause: Cicero's Cato and Caesar's Anticato fought over him (module 5.6).

Four triumphs in 46, over Gaul, Egypt, Pontus and Africa, paraded Vercingetorix and Cleopatra's sister Arsinoe (Julius 37; Dio 43.19). Pompey's sons Gnaeus and Sextus then raised Spain. At Munda on 17 March 45 Caesar had often fought for victory, he said, but this time fought for his life (Plutarch, Caesar 56); the Spanish War and Plutarch agree on about 30,000 Pompeian dead to 1,000 Caesarian (Spanish War 31; Caesar 56). Sextus escaped (module 5.5). A triumph over fellow citizens followed, and offended.

The dictator's reforms

Caesar was dictator for eleven days in 49, for a year after Pharsalus, for ten years from 46, and from early 44 for life, dictator perpetuo on his coins; he was consul in 48, 46, 45 and 44. In the months between campaigns he legislated more widely than anyone since Sulla.

  • Calendar. The Julian year from 1 January 45 (module 2.3) replaced the pontiffs' political discretion with a rule.
  • Colonies. Some 80,000 citizens were settled overseas (Suetonius, Julius 42.1), among them at Carthage and Corinth, both destroyed in 146 (Plutarch, Caesar 57); the charter of one, Urso in southern Spain, survives on bronze tablets.
  • Rome. The free grain list was cut from 320,000 to 150,000 (Julius 41.3), the collegia dissolved except the ancient ones (42.3), debts settled at pre-war valuations (42.2), and the Forum of Caesar with its temple of Venus Genetrix dedicated in 46.
  • Senate and citizens. The Senate grew to about 900 (Dio 43.47), the quaestors to forty and the praetors to sixteen (43.51.3–4); the Transpadanes became citizens (Dio 41.36).

The watchword was clemency. The Senate voted a temple to Caesar's Clemency, and he restored Pompey's fallen statues, which, said Cicero, fixed his own (Plutarch, Caesar 57). Pardoned Pompeians, Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius among them, were praetors in 44.

Where sources disagree. The hostile tradition filled the new Senate with soldiers, freedmen's sons and Gauls: Suetonius quotes a lampoon of Gauls who took off their trousers to put on the senator's broad stripe (Julius 80.2), and Dio names soldiers and freedmen's sons (43.47). Ronald Syme ("Caesar, the Senate and Italy", Papers of the British School at Rome 1938) examined the known names and found mostly landed men of the Italian towns, knights and officers. The "Gauls" were most likely from Cisalpine or Narbonese Gaul, and the jokes were propaganda against a Senate opened to Italy.

Honours that looked like kingship

After Munda Caesar accepted honours that Suetonius calls too great for a mortal: the dictatorship for life, the prefecture of morals, Father of his Country, a statue among the kings, a golden chair in the Senate house, his image carried with the gods' at the games, temples, a priest of his own, and a month, Iulius (Julius 76.1). Antony was named his flamen (Cicero, Philippics 2.110), and early in 44 Caesar became the first living Roman portrayed on Rome's coins. Stefan Weinstock (Divus Julius, 1971) read the whole as a planned cult of the living ruler; the reconstruction has been widely doubted, notably in John North's review "Praesens divus" (Journal of Roman Studies 1975).

He received the Senate without rising from his seat (Julius 78.1). In January 44 the tribunes Marullus and Flavus removed a diadem placed on his statue and arrested the man responsible, and Caesar had them deposed (79.1); hailed as king, he answered that he was Caesar, not Rex, a Roman surname (79.2). At the Lupercalia on 15 February (module 2.3) Antony, consul and running with the Luperci, twice offered him a diadem; Caesar twice refused and sent it to Jupiter on the Capitol (Plutarch, Caesar 61; Julius 79.2). A rumour followed that the Sibylline books allowed only a king to conquer Parthia, and that the title would be proposed on 15 March, three days before Caesar left for a Parthian war (79.3; Appian, Civil Wars 2.110). He had already dismissed his bodyguard (Julius 86.1).

Where sources disagree. Cicero, attacking Antony, makes the offer Antony's own act and says Caesar had his refusal entered in the calendar (Philippics 2.84–87). Nicolaus of Damascus, writing in Augustus' circle, has a Licinius and Cassius present the diadem before Antony, implicating a future assassin; Plutarch says the applause for the offer was thin and planted (Caesar 61); Dio reports the suspicion that Caesar arranged it all (44.11). A test of opinion, Antony forcing the issue, or a trap: the sources allow each.

The Ides of March in outline

More than sixty conspired (Julius 80.4), led by two pardoned Pompeians, Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius, and two of Caesar's own officers, Decimus Brutus and Gaius Trebonius. Their motives are deep dive module 11.7, Servilia, Brutus' mother and Caesar's lover, deep dive module 11.4. The omens, the haruspex Spurinna's warning and Calpurnia's dream, were collected afterwards (Julius 81). On 15 March 44 the Senate met in the hall of Pompey's theatre, the Senate house still being rebuilt. Trebonius kept Antony talking outside (Cicero, Philippics 2.34). Tillius Cimber seized Caesar's toga and Casca struck first. Caesar took twenty-three wounds, of which, the physician Antistius judged, only the second was mortal; Suetonius says he only groaned, though some wrote that he said to Brutus, in Greek, "you too, child?" (Julius 82.2–3). He covered his head and fell at the base of Pompey's statue (Plutarch, Caesar 66). The senators fled. The conspirators went out with drawn daggers, calling the citizens to liberty, and made for the Capitol (Caesar 67).

Caesar as author and as legend

The Gallic War and the unfinished Civil War are commentarii, notes nominally left for historians to work up, told in the third person; the Alexandrian, African and Spanish War were added by his officers. Lost is On Analogy, a treatise on correct Latin written while crossing the Alps (Suetonius, Julius 56.5). What Cicero and Asinius Pollio thought of the Commentaries, and how their plain style argues Caesar's case, is module 5.6; deep dive module 11.6 tests them against the conquest.

The legend began at once. Cicero's On Duties made Caesar the man who overturned all law, divine and human, for a supremacy he had imagined (1.26). Octavian made him a god: the comet at the games of July 44 was read as his soul received into heaven (Julius 88), and he was deified in 42. Velleius praised a spirit raised above human nature (2.41); Lucan made him a thunderbolt beside Pompey's withered oak (Civil War 1.129–157); Pliny admired a mind that could dictate four letters at once (7.91); Plutarch paired him with Alexander; Suetonius judged that he abused his power and was justly killed (Julius 76.1). His name became the emperors' title and, as Kaiser and tsar, outlived Rome; Shakespeare's Caesar and his successors are deep dive module 11.7 and module 10.4.

Self-test

  1. What was Bibulus doing when he "watched the sky" in 59, and why did it still matter after his consulship?
    Answer

    He announced by edict from his house that he was observing the heavens on assembly days, a form of obnuntiatio that, if valid, halted public business (Suetonius, Julius 20.1). Caesar legislated anyway, so his acts were open to the charge of invalidity (Cicero, De domo sua 39–40; Julius 23.1), one reason he feared returning to Rome as a private citizen.

  2. Why should Caesar's figures for the Gallic dead be treated with caution, and how far apart are the later totals?
    Answer

    They come almost entirely from Caesar, who had reasons to inflate, and modern historians cut his largest counts (368,000 Helvetii, 430,000 Usipetes and Tencteri). Velleius gives over 400,000 killed (2.47.1); Plutarch (Caesar 15) and Appian (Gallic History 1) a million killed and a million captured; Pliny 1,192,000 killed in all Caesar's foreign wars (Natural History 7.92).

  3. What was agreed after Luca, and which two deaths broke the alliance?
    Answer

    Pompey and Crassus took the consulship of 55, Caesar's command was extended for five years, and Pompey received the Spains and Crassus Syria. Julia's death in 54 cut the marriage tie, and Crassus' death after Carrhae in 53 removed the third partner, Lucan's isthmus between two seas (1.98–120).

  4. What did Caesar need in 50–49, and what did the Senate vote on 1 December 50?
    Answer

    He needed to pass straight from his command to a second consulship in 48, as the law of the ten tribunes allowed, because as a private citizen he faced prosecution (Julius 30.3). The Senate voted 370 to 22 that both he and Pompey give up their armies (Appian, Civil Wars 2.30), but the consul Gaius Marcellus ignored the vote and turned to Pompey.

  5. How do Suetonius, Plutarch and Caesar himself treat the crossing of the Rubicon?
    Answer

    Suetonius has hesitation, an apparition and "the die is cast" (Julius 31–33); Plutarch has it spoken in Greek, with Pollio present (Pompey 60; Caesar 32). Caesar's Civil War omits the river altogether and moves straight to Ariminum (1.8).

  6. Compare Caesar's and Pollio's figures for Pharsalus.
    Answer

    Caesar claims about 15,000 Pompeians killed and more than 24,000 surrendered for a loss of some 200 men and 30 centurions (Civil War 3.99). Pollio, also on Caesar's side, put the Pompeian dead at 6,000, as Plutarch reports (Caesar 46).

  7. Why did Cato's death at Utica make him more dangerous to Caesar than he had been alive?
    Answer

    By choosing death over Caesar's pardon (Plutarch, Cato Minor 66–72) he exposed clemency as a master's gift and became a martyr of liberty. Cicero's Cato and Caesar's Anticato made his memory a political battleground.

  8. Name three reforms of the dictatorship and the problem each addressed.
    Answer

    Any three of: the Julian calendar, ending the pontiffs' politically driven intercalation (module 2.3); 80,000 citizens sent to overseas colonies such as Carthage and Corinth, providing for veterans and the urban poor (Julius 42.1); the grain list cut from 320,000 to 150,000 (41.3), curbing the cost and abuse of free grain; debts settled at pre-war valuations; a Senate enlarged to about 900 with more magistracies, rewarding supporters and admitting Italian notables.

  9. What happened at the Lupercalia of 44, and why is its meaning disputed?
    Answer

    Antony, consul and Lupercus, twice offered Caesar a diadem, and Caesar refused and sent it to Jupiter on the Capitol. Cicero makes it Antony's act with the refusal recorded in the calendar (Philippics 2.84–87); Nicolaus implicates Cassius; Dio reports the suspicion that Caesar staged it (44.11).

  10. How did Romans judge Caesar after the Ides, from Cicero to Suetonius?
    Answer

    Cicero made him the man who overturned all law, divine and human, for a supremacy he had imagined (On Duties 1.26); Octavian had him deified in 42, with the comet of 44 read as his soul in heaven (Julius 88); Velleius praised a spirit raised above human nature (2.41); Suetonius concluded that he abused his power and was justly killed (Julius 76.1).

Carry forward

  1. Caesar's career after 59 was driven by legal exposure: laws passed against the auspices and the threat of prosecution meant he could never safely become a private citizen, and the civil war began over whether a proconsul could be forced to be one.
  2. Almost every number and motive in this story comes from Caesar himself or from writers using partisan witnesses (Pollio, Oppius, Cicero) generations later; always ask whose figure or verdict you are reading before you use it.
  3. The dictatorship joined lasting reform (calendar, colonies, an Italian Senate) to honours indistinguishable from kingship and to a clemency that made the pardoned into dependants; the conspirators removed the man, not the problem of one man's supremacy, which modules 5.5 and 6.1 take up.
