After the Ides: the amnesty, the will and the funeral

Module 5.4 ends at the murder. For 44–30 the narrative rests on Appian, Civil Wars 3–5 (to 35; his Egyptian books are lost), Cassius Dio 44–51, Plutarch's Antony, Brutus and Cicero, Suetonius' Augustus and Velleius 2.58–87, all written under the victor's successors or long after. Cicero's letters and speeches, which stop in mid-43, are the only contemporary voice not writing for the winner.

The conspirators had planned the killing, not the day after. Antony, as consul, held Caesar's papers and money, and Lepidus had a legion on the Tiber Island (Appian 2.118). On 17 March the Senate, meeting in the temple of Tellus, compromised: the assassins were amnestied, and Caesar's acts, on which many senators' offices and provinces depended, were confirmed. Cicero claimed the amnesty as his, an Athenian precedent (Philippics 1.1; Greek module 6.3 covers the amnesty of 403). The price was the will and a public funeral. The will made Gaius Octavius, Caesar's great-nephew, heir to three quarters of the estate and adopted him; it left the people gardens across the Tiber and 300 sesterces a man (Suetonius, Julius 83). At the funeral the crowd burned the body in the Forum and went for the conspirators' houses with torches. What Antony said there differs between Appian 2.143–147 and Suetonius, Julius 84; deep dive module 11.7 compares the versions. Within a month Brutus and Cassius had left Rome for good.

Caesar's heir and Cicero's war: Octavian and Mutina

Antony had the dictatorship abolished for ever (Cicero, Philippics 1.3), but enacted measures he claimed to find in Caesar's papers and drew on Caesar's reserve in the temple of Ops, which Cicero puts at 700 million sesterces (Philippics 2.93). A plebiscite in June gave him the two Gauls in place of Macedonia; Brutus and Cassius were fobbed off with grain commissions and left Italy in August.

Octavius, eighteen and studying at Apollonia, came to Italy, accepted the inheritance and called himself Gaius Julius Caesar; "Octavian" renders the Octavianus of Cicero's letters (Letters to Atticus 15.12.2), a name he never used. Antony would not release Caesar's money, so the heir paid the people's legacy himself and in July held Caesar's victory games, when a comet appeared that the people, Augustus later wrote, took for Caesar's soul received among the gods (Pliny, Natural History 2.93–94). In the autumn he did what no private citizen could lawfully do: he recruited Caesar's veterans in Campania at 500 denarii a man (Cicero, Letters to Atticus 16.8), and two of Antony's legions, the Martian and the Fourth, came over to him. The Res Gestae opens with it: at nineteen, "by private decision and at private expense", he raised the army that freed the Republic (1.1).

Cicero made the young man his instrument. His fourteen Philippics, from September 44 to April 43 (deep dive module 11.5 treats them as oratory), had one political aim: Antony declared a public enemy and Octavian's army made the Senate's. In January 43 Octavian received propraetorian command and joined the consuls Hirtius and Pansa to relieve Decimus Brutus, besieged by Antony in Mutina. Antony was beaten in April at Forum Gallorum and at Mutina, but both consuls died; Tacitus, Annals 1.10, records the rumour that Octavian arranged it. The Senate then slighted him, and Cicero's quip reached him: the young man was to be praised, honoured and tollendum, "raised up" or "removed" (Decimus Brutus in Cicero, Letters to Friends 11.20.1). Antony, joined in Gaul by Lepidus, Plancus and Pollio, recovered; Decimus was killed in flight. Octavian marched on Rome and was made consul on 19 August 43, aged nineteen (deep dive module 11.2 takes the march and its army).

The triumvirate and the proscriptions

That autumn Antony, Lepidus and Octavian met on a river islet between Mutina and Bononia and divided the western provinces (Appian 4.2). The lex Titia of 27 November made them triumviri rei publicae constituendae, three men for setting the state in order, for five years, with power to legislate and appoint magistrates. Unlike the private pact of 60 (module 5.3), this was an office.

The proscription edict, which Appian gives in Greek (4.8–11), argued that killing was safer than Caesar's mercy, which had cost him his life; in practice the lists settled hatreds and raised money for the legions. Heads carried a price, slaves who killed their masters were promised freedom, and estates went to auction. When money still fell short, the triumvirs taxed the 1,400 richest women until Hortensia, the orator's daughter, protested in the Forum and the levy was cut (Appian 4.32–34; deep dive module 11.4).

Cicero headed Antony's list; Octavian, Plutarch says, held out for him for two days (Cicero 46). On 7 December 43 he was overtaken near Formiae and put his head out of his litter to the sword (Plutarch, Cicero 48). Antony had the head and the writing hands fixed to the Rostra. The man who had armed Octavian against Antony died with Octavian's consent.

Where sources disagree. Appian 4.5 gives about 300 senators and 2,000 equestrians proscribed; Livy, Periochae 120, 130 senators; Plutarch a little over 200 (Cicero 46) or 300 (Antony 20). The lists grew in stages, and some totals may include those who escaped. Blame is disputed too: Velleius 2.66 lays Cicero's death on Antony alone, while Suetonius, Augustus 27, says Octavian resisted at first but, once begun, was harsher than either colleague.

Philippi, 42

Brutus and Cassius had taken over the eastern provinces and their armies. In October 42 they met Antony and Octavian on the Via Egnatia at Philippi: nineteen legions on each side by Appian's count, with 20,000 cavalry against the triumvirs' 13,000 (4.108). In the first battle Brutus stormed Octavian's camp while Antony took Cassius', and Cassius, believing all lost, had his freedman kill him (Plutarch, Brutus 43). Some three weeks later Brutus offered battle, lost and fell on his sword. Antony covered the body with his own cloak (Plutarch, Antony 22); Octavian sent the head to Rome to be laid at Caesar's statue (Suetonius, Augustus 13). Philippi made Antony the first soldier of the Roman world.

Where sources disagree. Where was Octavian when his camp fell? Pliny, Natural History 7.148, lists among his humiliations three days hiding sick in a marsh, as Agrippa and Maecenas admitted. His own memoirs, cited by Plutarch, Brutus 41, and followed by Suetonius, Augustus 91, said his doctor Artorius dreamed a warning and had him carried out just before the camp was taken. The dream is the official version; an admission from Octavian's own friends is harder to dismiss.

Perusia, Brundisium and Sextus Pompey

Antony took the East and its revenues; Octavian took the task of settling veterans on land confiscated from eighteen Italian towns (Appian 4.3), whose dispossessed owners haunt Virgil's first and ninth Eclogues. Antony's brother Lucius, consul in 41, and his wife Fulvia championed the dispossessed and Antony's interest, and Octavian starved them out of Perusia in the winter of 41–40. Sling bullets from the siege carry obscenities about Fulvia and Octavian (CIL XI 6721). Fulvia died in Greece in 40 (deep dive module 11.4 takes her further).

Where sources disagree. Suetonius, Augustus 15, reports that "some write" that 300 men of both orders were sacrificed at an altar of the deified Julius on the Ides of March 40; Dio 48.14 tells the same story. Appian 5.48–49 has Octavian pardon most of the citizens and execute the councillors, and Velleius 2.74 blames the soldiers' anger, not their commander. Many modern historians treat the "Perusine altars" as hostile tradition, though executions there certainly were.

The soldiers would not fight each other, and the Treaty of Brundisium in autumn 40 gave Antony the East, Octavian the West and Lepidus Africa; Antony married Octavian's sister Octavia. Virgil's fourth Eclogue, with its child of a returning golden age, belongs to that hopeful season.

Sextus Pompey, Pompey's younger son, held Sicily with a fleet, sheltered the proscribed and runaway slaves, and starved Rome of grain. Bought off at Misenum in 39, he was at war again in 38 and beat Octavian at sea, until Agrippa built and trained a new navy and destroyed him at Naulochus on 3 September 36; Antony had lent ships at Tarentum in 37, when the triumvirate was renewed for five years. Lepidus then claimed Sicily, his legions deserted, and he was stripped of power but kept the chief priesthood (Appian 5.123–126). The Res Gestae calls the war a clearing of the seas of pirates and boasts of returning some 30,000 slaves to their owners for punishment (25.1).

Antony in the East: Cleopatra, Parthia and the Donations

Cleopatra VII, queen since 51, was the last of a Macedonian dynasty that ruled Egypt as Greek kings and as pharaohs; Greek module 7.1 describes that double kingship and Greek module 7.3 her alliance with Caesar. Summoned to Tarsus in 41, she came up the Cydnus as Aphrodite visiting Dionysus (Plutarch, Antony 26), and Antony wintered with her in Alexandria. In 37/36 Antony acknowledged their twins and gave Cleopatra Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, Cyprus and much of Cilicia (Plutarch, Antony 36), much of what Ptolemy II had held. Her aim was any Ptolemy's, the old kingdom restored through a Roman protector; Romans saw provinces handed to a foreign mistress.

His legate Ventidius Bassus had thrown back a Parthian invasion of Syria (Plutarch, Antony 33–34); in 36 Antony invaded Media through Armenia with, by Plutarch's count, 60,000 Roman infantry besides cavalry and allies (Antony 37). The siege train was destroyed, the siege of Phraaspa failed, and the retreat took twenty-seven days; Plutarch counts 20,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry lost, more than half to disease (Antony 50). Octavia came east in 35 with troops and supplies; Antony told her to stay in Athens, and she went home (Antony 53). In 34, in the Gymnasium of Alexandria, came the Donations: Cleopatra was proclaimed queen of Egypt, Cyprus, Libya and Coele-Syria with Caesarion, called Caesar's son, as co-ruler; Armenia, Media and Parthia, not yet conquered, went to Alexander Helios, Phoenicia, Syria and Cilicia to the infant Ptolemy (Plutarch, Antony 54). Proclaiming Caesarion struck at the one asset Octavian had that Antony lacked: Caesar's name.

Cleopatra is the clearest case of the victor writing the record. The Roman Cleopatra is Egyptian, though she was a Macedonian Greek; drunk, lustful, a sorceress who drugged Antony, set on ruling from the Capitol (Dio 50.5). Plutarch, less hostile, says her beauty was not beyond compare but her conversation irresistible, and that she was the first of her line to learn Egyptian (27). Her own hand may survive once: a papyrus of 33 granting tax privileges to Antony's general Publius Canidius ends with the Greek for "let it be done", which its editor, Peter van Minnen (2000), took to be her autograph. Maria Wyke (The Roman Mistress, 2002) reads the Augustan Cleopatra as a construction of Roman ideas about women and the East; Duane Roller (Cleopatra: A Biography, 2010) reconstructs a capable Hellenistic ruler.

The war of words, the will and the declaration

From 33 the two men fought with pamphlets and letters. Octavian's charges survive best: Antony was the drugged slave of an Egyptian woman, giving away Roman lands (Plutarch, Antony 60). Antony's survive in Suetonius: Octavian's ancestry was base and his adoption bought with his body (Augustus 2, 68). Antony's answer to the moralising is quoted there too: what had changed Octavian, that Antony slept with the queen? "She is my wife", or, as some editors punctuate it, "Is she my wife?" (Augustus 69).

In 32 both consuls were Antonians; after a clash in the Senate they and many senators left for Antony (Dio 50.2), though Octavian later claimed more than 700 senators under his own standards (Res Gestae 25.3). The defectors Plancus and Titius revealed that Antony's will was lodged with the Vestals; Octavian seized it and read to the Senate the clause that Antony, even if he died in Rome, was to be buried beside Cleopatra in Alexandria (Plutarch, Antony 58). All Italy swore an oath to Octavian "of its own accord" (Res Gestae 25.2). The Senate stripped Antony of the consulship he was to hold in 31 and declared war on Cleopatra alone, Octavian hurling the fetial spear at the temple of Bellona (Dio 50.4). A war on a foreign queen was not a civil war; if Antony stood by her, he made himself the enemy.

Where sources disagree. Plutarch, Antony 58–59, says senators thought it monstrous to call a living man to account for his will, and that most of the further charges brought by Calvisius were thought false. Dio 50.3 reports the will's contents, adding the recognition of Caesarion and legacies to Cleopatra's children, without doubt. Ronald Syme (The Roman Revolution, 1939) found the discovery suspiciously opportune; J. R. Johnson (1978) argued that the will was genuine and that its legal flaws tell for its authenticity.

Actium and Alexandria, 31–30

Plutarch, Antony 61, gives Antony 500 warships, 100,000 infantry and 12,000 cavalry against Octavian's 250 warships and 80,000 infantry; Orosius 6.19 gives Antony 170 ships against Octavian's 230. In spring 31 Agrippa took Methone and cut the supply route from Egypt, Octavian camped north of the strait at Actium, and Antony's fleet was penned in the Ambracian Gulf. Through the summer, blockade, malaria and desertion did the work (Plutarch, Antony 63; Dio 50.13).

On 2 September Antony brought the fleet out, having burned all the Egyptian ships but sixty and ordered the sails taken aboard, on the pretext, Plutarch says, that no fleeing enemy must escape (Antony 64). In the afternoon Cleopatra's sixty ships hoisted sail and broke through, and Antony followed with a handful of companions (Antony 66). The rest fought on or surrendered; Augustus' memoirs, cited by Plutarch, gave not more than 5,000 dead and 300 ships captured (Antony 68). The army surrendered within a week. Octavian founded Nicopolis, Victory City, by his camp, with a memorial set with captured rams whose sockets, studied by William Murray and Photios Petsas (1989), show ships of very large classes.

Where sources disagree. Was Actium a battle lost or an escape achieved? Plutarch, Antony 66, and Velleius 2.85 tell of flight: Cleopatra lost her nerve, and Antony deserted men still dying for him. Dio 50.15 says the pair had already resolved to break out for Egypt, and the sails point the same way; most modern accounts accept a planned breakout that half succeeded, while Carsten Lange (2011) argues that Antony fought to win. Tarn's view that the fleet hardly fought is in Greek module 7.3.

In summer 30 Octavian advanced on Egypt. On 1 August, as his fleet and cavalry deserted, Antony stabbed himself and died in Cleopatra's arms (Plutarch, Antony 76–77). She was taken alive and died about ten days later, by asp or poison: Plutarch, Antony 86, admits that no one knew (Greek module 7.3). Caesarion was killed on the advice that too many Caesars was not good (Antony 81). Egypt was annexed under an equestrian prefect and closed to senators without leave (Tacitus, Annals 2.59): "I added Egypt to the empire of the Roman people" (Res Gestae 27.1). What Octavian built on the victory is module 6.1.

The poets' Actium

The poets made a blockade and a breakout into the battle of the age. Horace's ninth Epode, probably of 31, is close to the event: Roman soldiers serving a woman and her wrinkled eunuchs, a mosquito net among the standards. Odes 1.37, written after her death, opens nunc est bibendum, "now we must drink". The queen is unnamed and Antony absent; "scarcely one ship" escapes the flames (13), against Plutarch's sixty, and Caesar pursues her like a hawk after doves (17–20), though he reached Egypt only the next summer. Then the poem turns: the "deadly monster" (21), "no humble woman" (32), chooses death over a triumph.

Virgil, Aeneid 8.675–713, sets Actium at the centre of Aeneas' shield: Augustus leads the Italians with the Senate, the people and the great gods (678–679), Antony brings the wealth of the East, "and, shame, his Egyptian wife follows" (688), and Actian Apollo's bow routs Egypt's monstrous gods (698–706). Deep dive module 12.3 reads the shield in its book. Propertius makes Cleopatra the harlot queen of Canopus (3.11) and in 4.6 turns the battle into a hymn for Palatine Apollo. Module 6.3 sets these poets in their Augustan context.

The pattern is plain. A civil war becomes a foreign war, as the declaration of 32 had made it; Antony shrinks or vanishes; a campaign decided by Agrippa's seamanship, disease and desertion becomes a clash of gods, West against East. The poets gave Octavian's official version the form in which it would be remembered.

Self-test

  1. What did the Senate decide on 17 March 44, and why did the compromise fail to protect the conspirators?
    Answer

    An amnesty for the assassins and confirmation of Caesar's acts (Cicero, Philippics 1.1), at the price of reading the will and holding a public funeral. The will's gifts to the people (Suetonius, Julius 83) and the funeral turned the city against the conspirators, who left Rome within a month.

  2. How did a nineteen-year-old with no office come to command an army, and how was it made legal?
    Answer

    Caesar's will adopted him; he recruited Caesar's veterans in Campania at 500 denarii a man (Cicero, Letters to Atticus 16.8) and won over two of Antony's legions. In January 43, at Cicero's urging, the Senate gave him propraetorian command.

  3. What was the political aim of Cicero's Philippics, and how did the policy end?
    Answer

    To have Antony declared a public enemy and use Octavian's army as the Senate's weapon. After Mutina both consuls were dead, the Senate slighted Octavian, he took the consulship by force and joined Antony and Lepidus, and Cicero was proscribed and killed on 7 December 43.

  4. How did the triumvirate of 43 differ from the alliance of 60?
    Answer

    It was a magistracy created by law, the lex Titia of 27 November 43, for five years, with power to legislate and appoint magistrates; the alliance of 60 was a private agreement with no legal standing.

  5. Why do the ancient totals for the proscribed differ so widely?
    Answer

    Appian 4.5 gives about 300 senators and 2,000 equestrians, Livy, Periochae 120, 130 senators, Plutarch 200 or 300. The lists were issued in stages, many escaped, and the writers may be counting the listed, the killed or both.

  6. Why was Philippi Antony's victory, and how did Augustus' memoirs handle his own part?
    Answer

    Antony took Cassius' camp in the first battle and won the second, while Octavian's camp fell to Brutus. The memoirs said his doctor Artorius' dream had him carried out of the camp in time (Plutarch, Brutus 41); Pliny 7.148 has him hiding sick in a marsh for three days.

  7. What was at stake in the war with Sextus Pompey, and how does the Res Gestae describe it?
    Answer

    Rome's grain supply and control of the western seas; Agrippa's fleet won it at Naulochus in 36, and Lepidus was removed in the aftermath. The Res Gestae 25.1 calls it a war on pirates and boasts of returning some 30,000 slaves to their owners for punishment.

  8. What happened at the Donations of Alexandria, and why was the treatment of Caesarion so provocative?
    Answer

    In 34 Antony proclaimed Cleopatra queen of Egypt, Cyprus, Libya and Coele-Syria with Caesarion as co-ruler, and gave eastern kingdoms, some unconquered, to her sons by him (Plutarch, Antony 54). Presenting Caesarion as Caesar's son challenged Octavian's standing as Caesar's heir.

  9. Why did Rome declare war on Cleopatra alone in 32, and what prepared opinion for it?
    Answer

    A war on a foreign queen was not a civil war, and it left Antony to make himself the enemy by standing with her. The will's burial clause, read to the Senate (Plutarch, Antony 58), and the oath of Italy (Res Gestae 25.2) prepared it; Octavian declared it by the fetial rite (Dio 50.4).

  10. Give two ways Horace, Odes 1.37, departs from the historical Actium, and say what it concedes to Cleopatra.
    Answer

    It has "scarcely one ship" escape where Plutarch, Antony 66, has sixty; it has Caesar pursue her at once, though he reached Egypt only in 30; and it leaves Antony out. It concedes her a defiant death: "no humble woman", she refuses to be led in triumph.

Carry forward

  1. Between 44 and 30 Caesar's name was the decisive political asset: Octavian's adoption, the comet, the veterans' loyalty and the rivalry with Caesarion show legitimacy passing by inheritance and army rather than by office.
  2. The triumvirate was a dictatorship by commission, and its instruments (private armies, proscriptions, confiscations, the oath of Italy) are what the Principate was built from; the Res Gestae rewrites each of them as service to the Republic.
  3. Actium as Octavian framed it, a foreign war fought by Italy and its gods against an Eastern queen, became the founding myth of the new order; read every Augustan Cleopatra and Antony against the declaration of 32 that created it.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the last civil wars of the Republic, 44 to 30 BC. Cover: the aftermath of the Ides, the funeral and the will; Octavian's arrival as Caesar's heir and his private army; Cicero's Philippics and the war of Mutina; the triumvirate of 43 BC, the proscriptions and Cicero's death; Philippi in 42 BC and the deaths of Brutus and Cassius; Perusia, Fulvia, Brundisium, Sextus Pompey and Naulochus; Antony in the East, the Parthian disaster and the Donations of Alexandria; Cleopatra as Ptolemaic queen and as Roman propaganda made her (point back to Greek modules 7.1 and 7.3); the propaganda war, Antony's will and the declaration of war on Cleopatra alone; Actium in 31 BC, the deaths of Antony and Cleopatra in 30 BC and the annexation of Egypt; and the poets' Actium (Virgil's shield, Horace's Cleopatra ode 1.37, Propertius) against what the battle actually was. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 5 · The fall of the Republic, 133 to 30 BC · 5.6 · 2,826 words

Writing in a falling Republic

Writers who were also the stateLucretius: physics against fearCatullus and the new poetsCicero: orator, philosopher, correspondentVarro and Nepos: putting the past in orderCaesar: the general as stylistSallust: decline as a thesisWhat was going wrong: the authors disagreeWhat this generation did to LatinSelf-testCarry forward

Writers who were also the state

Latin literature began as the work of outsiders: a freedman from Tarentum, a client from Rudiae, comic poets from Umbria and Carthage (module 4.5). The generation born between about 116 and 84 BC changed that. A consul (Cicero), a dictator (Caesar), an expelled senator who became a Caesarian governor (Sallust), a Pompeian legate (Varro) and two men of means from the Po valley who never held office (Catullus, Nepos) wrote in their own names, in Latin, about their own world. Lucretius, whose life is almost unknown, addressed his poem to a praetor.

They wrote while the institutions they took for granted failed, and much of it was made possible by the failure: the forum closed, and writing became the public service left. A senator's leisure (otium) needed a defence, and each supplied one.

Lucretius: physics against fear

Jerome's Chronicle, under 94 BC, says Titus Lucretius Carus was driven mad by a love potion, wrote in lucid intervals, had his books corrected by Cicero and killed himself in his forty-fourth year. Donatus (Life of Virgil 6) has him die in 55 BC, on the day Virgil took the man's toga. The dates conflict, and the madness is usually dismissed as legend. The earliest notice is Cicero's remark to his brother in February 54 that the poems show many flashes of genius and much art (Letters to Quintus 2.10.3).

On the Nature of Things sets out Epicurus' physics in six books of hexameters, about 7,400 lines, for Gaius Memmius, praetor in 58. Greek module 7.2 gives the doctrine; what is Lucretius' own is its use. The poem opens with a hymn to Venus, mother of Aeneas' people, begging her to calm Mars, since the poet cannot work with an even mind patriai tempore iniquo, in his country's time of trouble, nor can Memmius fail the common safety (1.41–43). Book 3 traces greed and the blind desire for office to the fear of death, and makes civil bloodshed their fruit (3.59–86); Sisyphus is the candidate who seeks the fasces from the people and always loses (3.995–1002). Book 5 concludes that it is better to obey in quiet than to wish to rule (5.1127–1128). The crisis, for Lucretius, is a disease of belief, and the cure is physics, its bitterness disguised by the honey of verse (1.936–950).

Epicureanism had reached Rome earlier in Latin prose: Cicero sneers that Amafinius' books took over Italy because they were easy (Tusculan Disputations 4.6–7). Philodemus taught under the patronage of Piso, Caesar's father-in-law. Not every Roman Epicurean withdrew. Cassius, the tyrannicide, was one (Plutarch, Brutus 37), and Sallust gives Caesar an Epicurean argument in the Senate in 63: death is rest from troubles, not punishment, and beyond it there is no place for grief or joy (Catiline 51.20).

Where sources disagree. How Roman is the poem? David Sedley (Lucretius and the Transformation of Greek Wisdom, 1998) reads Lucretius as a fundamentalist working from Epicurus' own On Nature and indifferent to later debate. Benjamin Farrington (Science and Politics in the Ancient World, 1939) took its assault on religion as an attack on the state cult that Polybius praised as a means of control, and Don Fowler ("Lucretius and Politics", 1989) argued that its images of ambition and civil war answer the Roman crisis directly.

Catullus and the new poets

Gaius Valerius Catullus came from a leading family of Verona; his father entertained Caesar, who forgave the son's verses on Mamurra and asked him to dinner the same day (Suetonius, Julius 73). The poems mention Caesar's Britain (11) and Pompey's second consulship (113), so Jerome's dates (87–57) are too early. He served under Memmius in Bithynia in 57–56 and complained that it made no one rich (10, 28).

The label is Cicero's. In 50 BC he quoted a spondaic hexameter built round a Greek place-name and told Atticus to sell it as his own to one of the neoteroi (Letters to Atticus 7.2.1); later he spoke of the poetae novi (Orator 161) and the "singers of Euphorion" (Tusculan Disputations 3.45). Catullus' friends include Calvus (50) and Cinna, whose miniature epic Zmyrna took nine years and will outlast the annals of Volusius, "shitty paper" (95, 36). Their creed is Callimachus' (Greek module 7.2): short, learned, polished poems against bulky epic. Poem 64, on the wedding of Peleus and Thetis with Ariadne's desertion set inside it as the picture on a coverlet, is the Alexandrian epyllion in Latin.

Lesbia, a name metrically equal to Clodia, was a Clodia according to Apuleius (Apology 10); whether the Clodia of Cicero's Pro Caelio is the problem of deep dive module 11.4. The poems run from kisses counted in thousands (5) to "I hate and I love" (85), and their novelty is vocabulary: the affair is measured in the words Cicero's letters use for political alliance, fides, foedus, amicitia, bene velle (72, 76, 87, 109). The code of obligation failing in the forum becomes the standard by which a private love fails.

The politics is open. Poem 29 asks who can bear to see Mamurra hold the wealth of Gaul and Britain, and ends on Caesar and Pompey: socer generque, perdidistis omnia, father-in-law and son-in-law, you have ruined everything (29.24). Poem 49 thanks Cicero as the best of advocates from the worst of poets, perhaps ironically. Poem 64 closes with its own theory of decline: since crime stained the earth and brothers killed brothers, the gods no longer visit men (64.397–408).

Where sources disagree. Was there a school? Cicero treats the new poets as a recognisable set, and R. O. A. M. Lyne ("The Neoteric Poets", 1978) read the line parodied at Letters to Atticus 7.2.1 as an exact caricature of a shared manner. The old picture of the grammarian Valerius Cato as the group's leader has been given up, and sceptics such as Edward Courtney (The Fragmentary Latin Poets, 1993) doubt that the category existed at all; many prefer a loose network of friends to a movement with a programme.

Cicero: orator, philosopher, correspondent

Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43) made Latin prose. Fifty-eight speeches survive whole or in part, each a political act revised for readers; the speeches against Catiline belong to module 5.3. The Pro Sestio (56) defined the optimates as all honest men of every order and their goal as cum dignitate otium, peace with standing (96–98). On the Orator (55), the Brutus and the Orator (both 46) made the ideal orator a statesman schooled in law, history and philosophy.

Pushed aside by the alliance of 60, he turned to political theory. On the Republic (54–51) adapts Polybius' mixed constitution (module 4.5) and imagines a guiding statesman, the moderator rei publicae, against whom Cicero later measured Pompey and found him wanting (Letters to Atticus 8.11.1–2). Its fifth book quoted Ennius on ancient customs and men, then gave the verdict: through our own vices, not by chance, we keep the republic in name and have long since lost it in fact (5.2, preserved by Augustine, City of God 2.21).

The great burst came in 45–44, with Caesar ruling and Cicero's daughter Tullia dead in February 45. In some eighteen months he wrote the Consolation and the Hortensius (both lost), the Academica, On Ends, the Tusculan Disputations, On the Nature of the Gods, On Divination, On Fate, On Old Age, On Friendship and, late in 44, On Duties for his son. His reason: since the state had to be governed by one man's counsel, teaching philosophy to Romans was the public service left to him (On the Nature of the Gods 1.7; On Divination 2.1–7). The form was the dialogue: Roman nobles argue the Stoic, Epicurean and Academic cases, and Cicero, an Academic sceptic, leaves the verdict to the reader.

The letters, some 900 including about 90 written to him, were not composed for publication. Nepos said that whoever read those to Atticus would hardly need a history of the times (Atticus 16.3). Deep dive module 11.5 reads them.

Where sources disagree. Cicero told Atticus the dialogues were copies made with little labour: he supplied only the words, of which he had plenty (Letters to Atticus 12.52.3). In On Ends (1.6) he claims instead not to act as a translator but to add his own judgement and arrangement. Nineteenth-century source critics took the first statement at its word and mined the dialogues for lost Hellenistic originals; the essays in J. G. F. Powell (ed.), Cicero the Philosopher (1995), read them as philosophy in their own right.

Varro and Nepos: putting the past in order

Marcus Terentius Varro of Reate (116–27) was a Pompeian, legate against the pirates and in Spain in 49, and the satirist who called the alliance of 60 the Three-Headed Monster (Appian, Civil Wars 2.9). Caesar pardoned him and charged him with assembling Rome's first public library (Suetonius, Julius 44.2); Antony proscribed him in 43. By his seventy-eighth year he had written 490 books (Gellius 3.10.17), nearly all lost. The Antiquities Human and Divine (module 0.1) survives through Augustine, who reports Varro's fear that the gods would perish not by enemy attack but by the citizens' neglect, and his claim to rescue them as Aeneas saved the Penates from Troy (City of God 6.2). Six books On the Latin Language and On Agriculture, written at eighty (1.1.1), survive. Cicero put the tribute in a dialogue: Romans wandering like strangers in their own city were led home by Varro's books, so that they could recognise who and where they were (Academica 1.9).

Cornelius Nepos (c. 110–c. 25), from the Po valley (Pliny, Natural History 3.127), held no office and was a friend of Cicero and Atticus. Catullus praised his Chronica, which alone of Italians dared unfold all history in three learned volumes (1.5–7). His On Famous Men paired Roman lives with foreign ones; the surviving book On Foreign Generals runs from Miltiades to Hannibal. The Atticus, begun in its subject's lifetime and finished after his death in 32, portrays a man who survived every civil war by refusing office and helping each side in turn (6–11); Fergus Millar ("Cornelius Nepos, 'Atticus' and the Roman Revolution", 1988) read it as a guide to how a private man lived through the revolution. Varro, Nepos and Atticus, whose one-volume chronology prompted Cicero's Brutus (13–15), answered disorder by cataloguing dates, names, lives and words.

Caesar: the general as stylist

Caesar wrote his wars as commentarii, notes nominally meant as material for a historian: seven books on Gaul and three on the civil war, in the third person. Cicero called them bare, upright and graceful, stripped of ornament like a body of its clothes (Brutus 262); Asinius Pollio thought them careless and not always true (Suetonius, Julius 56.4). The plain style was itself an argument, since a narrative without rhetoric reads as a report of fact. The Civil War makes Caesar the defender of the tribunes, of his own dignitas, dearer to him than life (1.9.2), and of a Roman people "oppressed by a faction of the few" (1.22.5). He also wrote On Analogy, dedicated to Cicero, and an Anticato (Suetonius, Julius 56.5), both lost. Cicero's Cato of 46 praised the dead man; Caesar's reply praised Cicero's eloquence and life, likening him to Pericles and Theramenes, while it blackened Cato (Plutarch, Cicero 39; Caesar 54). Module 5.4 treats Caesar as author and legend; deep dive module 11.6 takes the Commentaries apart.

Sallust: decline as a thesis

Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–35), a Sabine from Amiternum, was tribune in 52, expelled from the Senate by the censors in 50 (Dio 40.63.4), and governed Caesar's new province of Africa in 46–45, coming home rich and charged but not condemned (Dio 43.9.2–3). After the Ides he withdrew. His preface confesses youthful ambition and claims a mind now free of hope, fear and party (Catiline 3–4). He wrote the Catiline (about 42–41), the Jugurtha (about 41–40) and the Histories of 78–67, which survive in speeches, letters and fragments.

The monographs rest on a theory. Early Rome was held together by concord and fear of enemies; when Carthage, rival of Roman power, was destroyed root and branch, fortune began to rage, and first the desire for money grew, then the desire for power, the material of all evils (Catiline 10). The Jugurtha names the mechanism: metus hostilis, fear of the enemy, kept the city to good practices; once it was gone, the nobility turned its standing and the people their liberty into licence (41.2–5). Module 4.5 lists the rival ancient dates for the onset of decline; deep dive module 11.8 weighs the theory as an explanation.

As literature, the thesis organises everything. The Jugurthine War is chosen because then the arrogance of the nobility was first opposed (Jugurtha 5.1). In the Catiline, Cicero gives a speech "brilliant and useful to the state" (31.6) and little more; the climax belongs to Caesar and Cato, men of great virtue and different character (53–54). Sallust's Cato complains that Romans have lost the true names of things, calling the squandering of others' goods generosity and recklessness courage (52.11), the corruption of words Thucydides found in civil war (3.82; Greek module 6.3). In the Histories, written under the triumvirs, the thesis darkened: discord now ran back to the Republic's beginning, and the best morals lay only between the second and third Punic Wars (fragments 1.11–12 Maurenbrecher).

Where sources disagree. Can a corrupt man write moral history? The hostile tradition, Varro's story that Milo caught Sallust in adultery and had him flogged (Gellius 17.18), the forged Invective against Sallust under Cicero's name and Dio's account of Africa, makes him a hypocrite. D. C. Earl (The Political Thought of Sallust, 1961) and Ronald Syme (Sallust, 1964) took him seriously as a political thinker, and Syme rejected reading the monographs as pamphlets for Caesar's party.

What was going wrong: the authors disagree

Lucretius and Sallust both blame avarice and ambition, but Lucretius makes them symptoms of a false belief that physics can cure, Sallust the consequence of an event, the end of fear, that nothing can reverse. Cicero looks for a person, a statesman backed by the honest classes; Caesar's narrative supplies one and calls its opponents a faction, the word Augustus reused in the first sentence of the Res Gestae (module 0.1). Catullus and Nepos decline the question: one turns the language of obligation inward, the other shows a man surviving by staying out.

What this generation did to Latin

Lucretius complained of the poverty of his native tongue (1.139, 1.832, 3.260). Cicero answered that Latin was richer than Greek (On Ends 1.10) and proved it by coining: qualitas for Greek poiotes (Academica 1.25), moralis "to enlarge the Latin language" (On Fate 1), beatitas and beatitudo, both harsh until use softened them (On the Nature of the Gods 1.95). Much of Europe's philosophical vocabulary passed through his Latin, and his rhythmic periodic sentence became the model of prose for Quintilian (10.1.112) and for the Renaissance. Caesar argued for purity: avoid an unheard-of word as you would a reef (Gellius 1.10.4, from On Analogy). Catullus brought fashionable Rome's diminutives and slang into lyric metres and made the elegiac couplet a vehicle for personal poetry, the form the elegists inherited (module 6.3); with Lucretius he made the hexameter supple enough for Virgil. Sallust built a counter-style, abrupt and archaic, with Thucydides as model (Quintilian 10.1.101) and Cato's old words as material, for which Asinius Pollio mocked him (Suetonius, On Grammarians 10) and Augustus mocked his imitators (Suetonius, Augustus 86); Tacitus followed it.

Where sources disagree. Calvus called Cicero loose and nerveless, Brutus "broken and loinless" (Tacitus, Dialogue on Orators 18.5), and men of his own day, Quintilian reports, called him swollen, Asian and redundant (12.10.12): these self-styled Atticists wanted Lysias' plainness.. Cicero replied in the Brutus and the Orator that Demosthenes, master of every register, was the true Attic orator. Posterity sided with Cicero; Sallust's success shows the rival taste survived.

Self-test

  1. What do Jerome, Donatus and Cicero each tell us about Lucretius, and why should the reader trust Cicero most?
    Answer

    Jerome (Chronicle, under 94 BC) gives madness from a love potion, Cicero's correction of the books and suicide at forty-three; Donatus (Life of Virgil 6) puts his death in 55, which Jerome's dates do not allow. Cicero's letter of February 54 (Letters to Quintus 2.10.3) is the earliest witness and the only contemporary verdict on the poem, and it says only that the poems combine genius and art.

  2. How does Lucretius connect political ambition with the fear of death?
    Answer

    Book 3 makes greed and the blind desire for office products of the fear of death, ending in civil bloodshed (3.59–86), and turns Sisyphus into the perpetual losing candidate (3.995–1002). Since Epicurean physics removes that fear, it removes the root of the political disease; quiet obedience beats ruling (5.1127–1128).

  3. Where do the terms for the "new poets" come from, and what aesthetic did Catullus and his friends share?
    Answer

    From Cicero's sneers: neoteroi (Letters to Atticus 7.2.1), poetae novi (Orator 161), "singers of Euphorion" (Tusculan Disputations 3.45). The shared aesthetic was Callimachus': short, learned, laboured poems, as in Cinna's nine-year Zmyrna (Catullus 95) and Catullus' poem 64, against long annalistic epic.

  4. What is new about the language of Catullus' Lesbia poems, and how does it connect them to the political crisis?
    Answer

    He describes love in the vocabulary of aristocratic alliance (fides, foedus, amicitia, bene velle: 72, 76, 87, 109). The code that was failing in public life becomes the measure of a private betrayal, while poems such as 29 attack Caesar and Pompey openly.

  5. Why did Cicero write most of his philosophy in 45–44 BC, and what form did he choose?
    Answer

    Caesar's rule left him no public role and Tullia died in February 45; he says that, with the state governed by one man, teaching Romans philosophy was his remaining service (On the Nature of the Gods 1.7; On Divination 2.1–7). He wrote dialogues in which Romans argue the Greek schools' positions, leaving the reader to judge in the Academic manner.

  6. What did Varro believe threatened Roman religion, and what was his answer?
    Answer

    Not enemies but the citizens' own neglect, which would let the gods be forgotten. He set out to rescue them in the Antiquities, as Aeneas saved the Penates from Troy (Augustine, City of God 6.2): record as preservation.

  7. What does Nepos' Atticus offer as a response to the civil wars?
    Answer

    A model of survival: Atticus refused office and helped each side in turn, from Brutus' friends to Fulvia and the proscribed (Atticus 6–11). Millar (1988) read it as a document of how a private man lived through the Roman Revolution.

  8. How does the plain style of Caesar's Commentaries serve his political case?
    Answer

    Stripped of rhetoric (Cicero, Brutus 262), the third-person narrative reads as a neutral report. Within it Caesar presents himself as defending his dignitas, the tribunes and a people "oppressed by a faction of the few" (Civil War 1.9.2, 1.22.5), a claim Pollio doubted (Suetonius, Julius 56.4).

  9. State Sallust's theory of moral decline, and say how the Histories changed it.
    Answer

    Fear of the enemy (metus hostilis) kept Rome united and virtuous; after Carthage fell in 146, avarice and then ambition grew, and nobles and people abused standing and liberty (Catiline 10; Jugurtha 41). The Histories push discord back to the Republic's beginning and confine the best morals to the interval between the second and third Punic Wars.

  10. How did Lucretius and Cicero disagree about the Latin language, and what did Cicero do about it?
    Answer

    Lucretius lamented the poverty of his native tongue (1.139, 1.832); Cicero held Latin richer than Greek (On Ends 1.10). He coined the words philosophy needed, such as qualitas (Academica 1.25), moralis (On Fate 1) and beatitudo (On the Nature of the Gods 1.95).

Carry forward

  1. The writers of the late Republic were participants: consuls, generals, partisans and their friends. Even a turn away from politics, Lucretius' withdrawal or Sallust's and Cicero's otium, is a position in the crisis, and should be read as one.
  2. They disagreed about the disease: false belief, the end of fear after 146, the want of good men, forgetting, faction. The Augustan settlement borrowed from all of them, from Caesar's language of faction in the Res Gestae to Varro's restored gods and Sallust's decline in Livy's preface.
  3. This generation made Latin able to carry Greek philosophy, Alexandrian poetry and serious history: Cicero's vocabulary and periodic prose, Catullus' elegiacs and Lucretius' hexameter are the instruments that Virgil, Horace, Livy and Ovid took up (module 6.3).

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the literature of the late Republic. Cover: Lucretius' On the Nature of Things and Epicureanism at Rome; Catullus, the 'new poets' and Lesbia; Cicero as orator, philosopher and letter writer, with the dialogues of 45–44 BC that put Greek philosophy into Latin; Varro's antiquarian encyclopaedia, mostly lost; Caesar's Commentaries as style and as propaganda (deep dive module 11.6 takes them further); Sallust's monographs and his theory of moral decline after 146 BC; Cornelius Nepos; and what this generation did to the Latin language. Read each against the political crisis around it, and show where the authors disagree about what was going wrong. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 6 · Augustus, 31 BC to AD 14 · 6.1 · 2,838 words

From Octavian to Augustus

From Actium to the sixth consulship, 31–28 BCThe settlement of January 27 BCThe crisis of 23 BC and the second settlementRefusals and the father of his countryThe Res Gestae: Augustus' own accountThe inner circle and the problem of successionAD 14 and Tacitus, Annals 1.2–10Syme and the favourable readingsWhy the arrangement workedSelf-testCarry forward

From Actium to the sixth consulship, 31–28 BC

Module 5.5 ends with Egypt annexed in 30. The only continuous narrative of what follows is Cassius Dio, books 51–56, written two centuries later by a senator who thought monarchy the only workable government for an empire; Livy's books on these years are lost. Velleius Paterculus (2.88–123) wrote under Tiberius as an admirer, Suetonius' Augustus arranges its matter by topic, and Tacitus looks back from the opening of the Annals. Augustus' own Res Gestae is the fullest witness and the least neutral.

In August 29 Octavian held three triumphs on successive days, for Illyricum, Actium and Egypt (Suetonius, Augustus 22), and the temple of Janus was shut: closed, the Res Gestae boasts, only twice since the foundation before his birth and three times while he was princeps (13). As consul for the sixth time in 28, with Agrippa as colleague, he took the first completed census since 70 and revised the Senate roll (Res Gestae 8). In this consulship, Tacitus says, he annulled what he had ordered as triumvir (Annals 3.28), and an aureus of 28, published by John Rich and Jonathan Williams in 1999, proclaims that he restored to the Roman people their laws and rights. Legality was being rebuilt before the grand gesture.

The settlement of January 27 BC

On 13 January 27 Octavian, consul for the seventh time, laid down his powers before the Senate. Dio composes a long speech for him (53.3–10); the Res Gestae needs one sentence: having ended the civil wars, and being by universal consent in control of all affairs, he transferred the res publica from his own power to the judgement of the Senate and people (34.1). The senators begged him to keep a share. He accepted for ten years a single provincia of Spain, Gaul and Syria, with Egypt already his: the regions where most of the legions stood. The peaceful provinces went to proconsuls chosen by lot (Dio 53.12–13; Strabo 17.3.25). Dio saw the point: under pretence of taking the burden, he left the senators unarmed and kept the soldiers (53.12.3). His own legates governed his provinces, the legions swore to him, the grant was renewed until his death, and after Balbus' triumph in 19 BC no one outside his family triumphed. Module 6.4 takes the two kinds of province as administration.

On 16 January, by the Praenestine calendar (Ovid, Fasti 1.587–590, puts it on the Ides), the Senate on the motion of Munatius Plancus named him Augustus (Suetonius, Augustus 7.2). Romulus had been proposed, but Romulus was a king and a fratricide. The new name carried no power. Augustus meant hallowed, akin to augur, and Suetonius quotes Ennius on Rome founded by august augury (7.2). An oak crown over his door and a golden shield in the Senate house proclaiming his valour, clemency, justice and piety came with it (Res Gestae 34.2). His style was now Imperator Caesar Augustus: a victor's acclamation, a murdered dictator's name and a word with no constitutional meaning.

The theory came later. After that time, he wrote, he excelled all in auctoritas, influence, but had no more potestas, legal power, than his colleagues in each magistracy (Res Gestae 34.3); the word was long restored as dignitas until the copy from Pisidian Antioch settled it. True of each office, the claim is false of the whole, for no colleague held a consulship, the great provinces and the legions at once. Princeps, "first man", was a courtesy, not an office.

Where sources disagree. Velleius says that in 27 the ancient form of the res publica was recalled, with force restored to the laws and majesty to the Senate (2.89.3–4); Dio dates monarchy in the strict sense from the same moment (53.17.1). E. A. Judge ("Res publica restituta: a modern illusion?", 1974) argued that no Augustan text claims to have restored "the Republic" as a constitution: res publica meant the commonwealth, and what was restored was its order and legality, a reading the aureus of 28, published in 1999, fits.

The crisis of 23 BC and the second settlement

The settlement of 27 rested on a consulship Augustus held every year from 31 to 23, which left the nobility one consulship a year instead of two. In 23 he nearly died. Expecting the end, he gave his fellow consul Piso a record of the forces and revenues and Agrippa his signet ring, naming no successor (Dio 53.30.1–2). His doctor Antonius Musa's cold baths saved him (Suetonius, Augustus 81.1), but not his nephew and son-in-law Marcellus, who died late in the year. About this time Marcus Primus, governor of Macedonia, on trial for an unauthorised war, claimed instructions from Augustus or Marcellus; his advocate Murena, Maecenas' brother-in-law, was soon condemned with Fannius Caepio for conspiracy and killed (Dio 54.3).

In the summer of 23 Augustus resigned the consulship, so that more men could hold it, Dio says (53.32.3), and received two powers in its place (53.32.5). Tribunicia potestas for life gave him a tribune's rights without the office: to summon Senate and people, propose laws, veto and protect any citizen. He numbered his years by it (Res Gestae 4.4), and Tacitus calls it the title for supreme power that Augustus devised so as not to take the name of king or dictator (Annals 3.56). Proconsular imperium that did not lapse inside the city, and was greater than that of any proconsul, secured the provinces and armies. Agrippa went east with imperium of his own.

Where sources disagree. Dio puts Primus' trial and the conspiracy in 22, after the new settlement (54.3). But the list of consuls for 23 names a Varro Murena as Augustus' colleague, replaced by Piso, and many modern historians move the conspiracy into 23 and make it, with the illness, a cause of the resignation; others keep Dio's date and doubt that consul and conspirator were one man. Whether greater imperium came in 23 or later is argued too; a papyrus of Augustus' funeral speech for Agrippa shows such greater imperium voted to Agrippa by law by 13 BC.

Refusals and the father of his country

In 22, amid plague, flood and famine, the people shut the senators in their meeting-place and threatened to burn them unless they made Augustus dictator (Dio 54.1). He knelt, Suetonius says, and begged with bared breast to be spared (Augustus 52). The Res Gestae records the refusal and, in the same breath, the charge he did accept: the grain supply, by which at his own expense he freed the city from fear within a few days (5.1–2). He also refused a perpetual consulship (5.3) and, in 19, 18 and 11, the supervision of laws and morals, as an office contrary to ancestral custom; what the Senate wanted done he did through tribunician power (6). Caesar had accepted the dictatorship for life and the prefecture of morals (module 5.4). Augustus declined each title that looked like kingship and kept its function. The chief priesthood waited for Lepidus' death (module 6.2).

Where sources disagree. Against Res Gestae 6, Dio says that in 19 he accepted the supervision of morals for five years and consular power for life (54.10.5), and Suetonius that he received the supervision of morals and laws for life (Augustus 27.5). Most modern historians trust Augustus on the title and read the others as describing what he did. The lifelong consular power remains disputed, though the Res Gestae says he took two censuses "with consular imperium" (8.3–4).

On 5 February 2 BC the Senate, the equestrian order and the whole people hailed him pater patriae, father of his country, the honour on which the Res Gestae ends (35.1). Suetonius has the plebs offer it twice before Valerius Messalla spoke for the Senate and Augustus answered in tears that his prayers were fulfilled (Augustus 58). Cicero had been so hailed after 63 (Against Piso 6), and Caesar had borne the title (module 5.4); this father was the living patron of every citizen. Within months he exiled his daughter.

The Res Gestae: Augustus' own account

Augustus left with his will an account of his achievements to be inscribed on bronze before his Mausoleum (Suetonius, Augustus 101.4); module 0.1 introduces the text and its best copy, at Ancyra. It dates itself to his seventy-sixth year (35.2) and runs from honours (1–14) through spending (15–24) and conquests (25–33, module 6.4) to the constitutional claim (34–35). Module 5.5 has set its account of 44–30 against the record.

It tells few direct lies; it lies by arrangement and silence. Antony is only "a faction" (1.1); Lepidus is the colleague who seized the chief priesthood in a time of civil disturbance (10.2). Caesar's killers went into exile "by lawful judgements" (2), which means the court of the lex Pedia and then Philippi. The proscriptions, Perusia and the confiscations are absent; the triumvirate gets one sentence (7.1). He spared all citizens who asked for pardon (3.1), where Suetonius says that once the proscription began he was harsher than either colleague (Augustus 27.1). Gaius and Lucius appear as "my sons, whom fortune snatched from me" (14.1), Tiberius as stepson and then son, Marcellus only as the name on a theatre (21.1); Julia, Postumus and Varus' lost legions do not.

The inner circle and the problem of succession

Three people stood closest. Marcus Agrippa, of a family so obscure that he dropped its name Vipsanius, won Naulochus and Actium, was consul three times and rebuilt Rome's water supply. Maecenas, an equestrian of Etruscan royal descent (Horace, Odes 1.1.1), held no office yet ran Rome and Italy in Octavian's absences and patronised the poets; his eclipse after the Murena affair is in module 6.3. Livia, married to Octavian in 38 while pregnant by her first husband (deep dive module 11.4), held no office but unusual standing: sacrosanctity from 35 (Dio 49.38.1), and a husband who wrote out beforehand anything serious he meant to say to her (Suetonius, Augustus 84.2).

The Principate was not an office and could not be inherited, and Augustus had no son. Each plan tied a man to Julia, his only child, and gave him a share of the powers (Tacitus, Annals 1.3).

Agrippa's marriage was a necessity: Maecenas warned, Dio reports, that Augustus had made him so great that he must become his son-in-law or be killed (54.6.5). When Lucius and Gaius died within eighteen months, by fate's haste or their stepmother Livia's guile, as Tacitus insinuates (Annals 1.3), only Tiberius was left. On 26 June AD 4 Augustus adopted him, swearing that he did it for the sake of the state (Suetonius, Tiberius 21.3), and made him adopt Germanicus, soon to marry Augustus' granddaughter Agrippina, to keep Augustus' blood in the succession.

Julia's fall in 2 BC belongs here; the adultery law is module 6.2's. Augustus denounced her adulteries to the Senate by letter (Suetonius, Augustus 65.2) and sent her to the island of Pandateria. Her lovers were exiled, and Iullus Antonius, Antony's son and consul in 10 BC, died by his own hand in Velleius' account (2.100.4), by execution in Tacitus' (Annals 4.44). Augustus called Julia, her daughter and Postumus his three boils and three cancers (Suetonius, Augustus 65.4).

Where sources disagree. Velleius (2.100) and Seneca (On Benefits 6.32) tell a scandal of lust, with revels on the Rostra from which her father had proposed his adultery law. Pliny pairs her adultery with plans of parricide (Natural History 7.149), Dio says Iullus aimed at the monarchy (55.10.15), and Tacitus that Augustus charged adultery as sacrilege and treason (Annals 3.24). Syme (The Crisis of 2 B.C., 1974) read a conspiracy over the succession; others take the scandal as reported. Uncertain.

AD 14 and Tacitus, Annals 1.2–10

Augustus died at Nola on 19 August AD 14, having asked his friends whether he had played the comedy of life well (Suetonius, Augustus 99–100). Tacitus says Livia guarded the house and roads until his death and Tiberius' succession could be announced together, and that some suspected her of hastening the end (Annals 1.5). The will named Tiberius and Livia heirs (Suetonius, Augustus 101.2), and the first crime of the new principate was the killing of Agrippa Postumus (Annals 1.6). Tiberius' accession is module 7.1.

Where sources disagree. Tiberius claimed his father's standing order for Postumus' death. Tacitus thinks Tiberius' fear and Livia's hatred nearer the truth (Annals 1.6); Suetonius leaves open whether Augustus or Livia gave the order and whether Tiberius knew (Tiberius 22); Dio says Tiberius had it done (57.3.6).

Tacitus wrote a century later, a senator who had held office under Domitian. His first movement (1.2) is a cold narrative: with his rivals dead or stripped of power, Octavian dropped the title of triumvir and was content with tribunician power to protect the plebs; he won the soldiers with gifts, the people with grain and everyone with the sweetness of peace, and drew to himself the functions of Senate, magistrates and laws, unopposed, since the boldest had fallen and the surviving nobles found servility profitable. The second (1.3) traces the dynastic plans and ends: the magistracies kept their names, and how few were left who had seen the res publica?

The third (1.9–10) is the verdict of men talking at the funeral. For him: civil war forced on him by duty to his father, neither kingship nor dictatorship but a princeps, an empire bounded by ocean and rivers, the city adorned, force used rarely. Against him: duty a pretext for power, bribed veterans, the proscriptions, Sextus, Lepidus and Antony deceived in turn, the bloody peace of Lollius and Varus, temples to himself, and Tiberius chosen so that a worse successor would make him shine. The hostile case is longer and comes last; Tacitus never says which he believes, and the arrangement judges for him. Dio's obituary concludes the reverse: by mixing monarchy with democracy Augustus kept the Romans free and safe (56.43).

Syme and the favourable readings

Ronald Syme's The Roman Revolution (1939), written as Europe's dictators rose and in a Tacitean style, told the Principate as the victory of a faction: Caesar's generals and the new families of the Italian towns took the state from the old nobility, and the settlements of 27 and 23 were a facade over army, money and clients. His method was prosopography, and constitutional law counts for little beside who held which post. Deep dive module 11.8 places him among the explanations of the Republic's fall.

The favourable readings start from the forms. Mommsen's Römisches Staatsrecht called the Principate a dyarchy of princeps and Senate. Andrew Wallace-Hadrill ("Civilis princeps: between citizen and king", 1982) argued that the emperor's citizen manners (Suetonius, Augustus 53–56) were the price of aristocratic cooperation and a working part of the system, not a disguise. Karl Galinsky (Augustan Culture, 1996) made auctoritas an authority that drew consent, so that Augustan culture was made with him, not imposed. Syme asks who held power; his critics ask how a monarch made Romans willing to be governed.

Why the arrangement worked

Augustus ruled for forty-four years after Actium; Caesar lasted five after the Rubicon.

  • The army was his alone. It stood in his provinces under his legates, and from AD 6 its discharge bounties came from his military treasury (module 6.4). No senator could again raise a private army, as Octavian had in 44.
  • The forms survived. King and dictator were refused, each power had a republican name, Senate and magistrates went on working, and the consulship stayed a prize.
  • Exhaustion. After twenty years of civil war, peace, property and grain outweighed the liberty of a nobility the wars had thinned.
  • A wider governing class. Italian new men became consuls; equestrians became prefects of Egypt, the guard and the grain supply.
  • Flexibility and time. Powers were revised as needed, and by AD 14 few remembered anything else.

The succession failed. Powers voted to a person carried no rule of inheritance, only the family and the soldiers' loyalty to it.

Self-test

  1. What did Octavian give up in January 27 BC, what did he receive, and why did the division of provinces matter more than the gesture?
    Answer

    He transferred the res publica to the Senate and people (Res Gestae 34.1) and received for ten years Spain, Gaul and Syria, besides Egypt, governed by his own legates, while proconsuls chosen by lot took the rest (Dio 53.12–13; Strabo 17.3.25). His provinces held most of the legions, so, as Dio saw, the senators were left unarmed and the army stayed his (53.12.3).

  2. What did the name Augustus and the claim to auctoritas add to his position?
    Answer

    No legal power. The name came from religion, the hallowed, akin to augur (Suetonius, Augustus 7.2), and avoided Romulus' associations with kingship. Auctoritas was influence rather than potestas (Res Gestae 34.3): true for each office, misleading for a man who held consulship, provinces and legions at once.

  3. Why did Augustus give up the consulship in 23 BC, and what replaced it?
    Answer

    Holding one consulship every year blocked the nobility's highest prize, and his near-fatal illness and, on the modern dating, the Murena conspiracy exposed the regime's fragility. He received tribunician power for life and proconsular imperium that held inside Rome and was greater than any proconsul's (Dio 53.32.5); Tacitus calls tribunician power a name for supremacy that avoided king and dictator (Annals 3.56).

  4. How do the refusals in Res Gestae 5–6 answer Caesar's honours, and what complicates the record?
    Answer

    Caesar took the dictatorship for life and the prefecture of morals (module 5.4); Augustus refused the dictatorship in 22, a perpetual consulship and the supervision of laws and morals, accepting only the grain supply and acting through tribunician power. Dio 54.10.5 and Suetonius, Augustus 27.5, say he did accept the supervision of morals.

  5. Why is 2 BC a revealing year for the regime?
    Answer

    On 5 February Augustus was hailed father of his country by Senate, equestrians and people (Res Gestae 35.1; Suetonius, Augustus 58), the climax of his honours. In the same year he exiled Julia, the mother of his heirs, and Iullus Antonius died, a scandal that Pliny 7.149, Dio 55.10.15 and Tacitus, Annals 3.24, hint was also a political plot.

  6. Give three omissions in the Res Gestae and what each conceals.
    Answer

    Antony is only "a faction" and Lepidus unnamed (1.1, 10.2), hiding that his enemies were Romans and colleagues; the proscriptions and Perusia are absent, though Suetonius, Augustus 27.1, makes him the harshest triumvir; Julia, Postumus and Varus are absent, hiding the failures of the family and the frontier.

  7. What method lay behind the succession plans from Marcellus to Tiberius?
    Answer

    Each candidate was bound to Julia by marriage or descent, or adopted, and given a share of Augustus' powers, tribunician power or greater imperium, to mark him as successor to something that was not an office. Marcellus, Agrippa, Lucius and Gaius died in turn, leaving Tiberius, adopted in AD 4 for the sake of the state, as Augustus swore (Suetonius, Tiberius 21.3).

  8. How does Tacitus pass judgement on Augustus in Annals 1.2–10 without stating his own?
    Answer

    His narrative in 1.2 shows power gathered by gifts, grain and peace while the nobles were dead or servile. In 1.9–10 he gives two verdicts at the funeral; the hostile one is longer and comes last, ending with Tiberius chosen so that a worse successor would flatter Augustus' memory.

  9. How does Syme's reading of the Principate differ from the more favourable modern ones?
    Answer

    Syme (The Roman Revolution, 1939) made it the victory of a faction of generals and Italian new men, with the settlements a facade over army, money and clients. Mommsen read a constitutional dyarchy, Wallace-Hadrill (1982) citizen manners as a working part of the system, and Galinsky (1996) auctoritas as authority that drew consent.

  10. Why did the Augustan arrangement last where Caesar's did not, and where did it fail?
    Answer

    He monopolised the army while refusing the names of king and dictator, kept Senate and magistracies working, widened the governing class, and revised his powers as needed, among people exhausted by civil war. It failed on succession: powers voted to a person gave no rule of inheritance beyond family and the soldiers' loyalty.

Carry forward

  1. The Principate was a bundle of separately voted powers, provincial imperium, tribunician power and greater imperium, dressed in republican names with the army underneath; every later accession repeats the pattern, with the Senate voting the powers and the soldiers deciding who receives them.
  2. Augustus governed by refusing titles and keeping functions, and the Res Gestae lies by arrangement and silence rather than by statement; read every imperial claim as true word by word and test it as a whole.
  3. The succession was never solved: because power attached to a person, every transfer turned on adoption, the women of the family and the army's loyalty, which is the question the Julio-Claudians after AD 14 pose.
