ROME · UNIT 6 · Augustus, 31 BC to AD 14 · 6.2 · 2,860 words

The city of marble and the restored religion

Brick and marbleThe house on the Palatine and the temple of ApolloThe Forum of Augustus and Mars UltorThe Campus Martius: Mausoleum, obelisk and Ara PacisThe Prima Porta statue and the image of the princepsThe restored religion: temples, priesthoods, pontifex maximusThe Secular Games of 17 BCMarriage, adultery and the failure of lawGenius, Lares and divus: the cult of the princepsSelf-testCarry forward

Brick and marble

Suetonius ends his survey of Augustus' building with the emperor's own boast. Rome had been unworthy of the empire's majesty and exposed to flood and fire; he improved it so far that he could justly claim

marmoream se relinquere, quam latericiam accepisset (Suetonius, Augustus 28.3)

that he left of marble a city he had found of brick. The inventory is his own: Res Gestae 19–21 lists the Curia, the temples of Apollo, the deified Julius, Jupiter Feretrius, Jupiter Tonans, Quirinus and Magna Mater, the Lupercal, the Capitol and Pompey's theatre restored without his name, aqueducts and roads, and a forum on his own land. Others built at his urging, Agrippa most of all (Suetonius, Augustus 29.5). Each project argued that the new order was the old one restored. Style is module 10.3, the walk module 9.5; this module reads the argument.

Where sources disagree. Suetonius takes the boast literally. Dio sets it among Augustus' last words and says he meant the strength of the empire, not its buildings (56.30.3–4). Since much Augustan building was tufa, travertine and concrete faced with marble, even the literal claim was partly a figure.

The house on the Palatine and the temple of Apollo

Octavian lived on the Palatine in the orator Hortensius' former house, modest, with short colonnades of Alban stone and no marble floors (Suetonius, Augustus 72.1). After Naulochus in 36 BC he bought neighbouring houses; when lightning struck part of the property, the haruspices declared that the god wanted it, and he made it public and vowed a temple to Apollo (Velleius 2.81.3; Suetonius, Augustus 29.3). Dedicated on 9 October 28 BC, it shared the hilltop with his house, and in its Greek and Latin libraries the ageing princeps often held the Senate.

Propertius describes it (2.31): the daughters of Danaus between the columns of a golden portico, Myron's cattle round the altar, ivory doors carved with the Gauls hurled from Parnassus and Niobe's dying children, and inside Apollo the lyre-player between his mother and sister. Actian Apollo (module 5.5) was now the princeps' neighbour, and his doors showed what befell those who insulted him.

The house became a monument too, with laurels at the doorposts and the oak crown over the door from 27 BC (Res Gestae 34.2). Pontifex maximus from 12 BC and bound to live in a public house, Augustus made part of his own public and gave the house of the rex sacrorum, which adjoined their quarters, to the Vestals (Dio 54.27.3); a shrine of Vesta was dedicated in his home, so that, in Ovid's arithmetic, Phoebus held one part, Vesta a second and Caesar the third (Fasti 4.949–954). Below stood the hut of Romulus and the Lupercal (module 1.4). The hill's name, Palatium, became the word for a ruler's residence.

The Forum of Augustus and Mars Ultor

Before Philippi in 42 BC Octavian vowed a temple to Mars the Avenger if he punished his father's murderers (Suetonius, Augustus 29.2; Ovid, Fasti 5.569–578). He built it, with a forum round it, on private land from the spoils of war (Res Gestae 21.1), keeping the square narrower than he wished rather than evict owners (Suetonius, Augustus 56.2). It was dedicated in 2 BC (Velleius 2.100.2), the year of the title Father of his Country, inscribed beneath his chariot group in the square (Res Gestae 35.1). There the Senate would debate wars and triumphs, governors set out and victors bring back their insignia (Suetonius, Augustus 29.2); the temple held the standards recovered from Parthia (Res Gestae 29.2). The colonnades' upper storey carried copies of the Erechtheum caryatids and shields with the head of Jupiter Ammon, the god of Alexander's sonship (Greek module 11.4).

The exedrae held the argument. On one side stood Aeneas carrying Anchises and leading Ascanius, with the Alban kings and the Julii; on the other Romulus with the spolia opima and the great men of the Republic (Ovid, Fasti 5.563–566; modules 1.3 and 1.4). Each statue stood above an inscription of name, offices and deeds; fragments survive, with copies at Arretium and Pompeii, Marius among them. Suetonius gives no total; he says Augustus honoured these leaders next to the gods and declared by edict that citizens should hold him, and later principes, to their standard (Augustus 31.5). The Julian descent from Venus and the Republic's roll of honour faced each other as one story, ending in the man in the chariot.

Where sources disagree. Suetonius and Ovid make Mars the avenger of Caesar. Dio says that in 20 BC a temple of Mars Ultor was decreed on the Capitol to receive the standards (54.8.3), and coins show a small round one; yet the Res Gestae puts the standards in the Forum temple. Ovid fuses the two causes, making Mars twice avenger (Fasti 5.579–596). Whether the Capitoline temple was ever built is uncertain.

The Campus Martius: Mausoleum, obelisk and Ara Pacis

In 28 BC Octavian built his tomb between the Via Flaminia and the Tiber (Suetonius, Augustus 100.4). Antony had asked to be buried in Alexandria (module 5.5); the largest tomb Rome had seen declared where the new dynasty belonged. Strabo describes a mound on a high marble base, planted with evergreens and crowned by a bronze Augustus (5.3.8). Marcellus entered it first in 23 BC, and the Res Gestae was set up in bronze before it (Suetonius, Augustus 101.4). Its models were probably both Italic tumuli and Hellenistic royal tombs, above all Alexander's, whose body Octavian had crowned in 30 BC, declining to view the Ptolemies because he had come to see a king, not corpses (18.1).

In 10 BC an obelisk from Heliopolis, dedicated to the Sun on the conquest of Egypt and now at Montecitorio, became the gnomon of a pavement inlaid with bronze rods on which its noon shadow measured the length of the days (Pliny, Natural History 36.72–73). In 1979–80 a stretch of the line was found under the Via di Campo Marzio, with Greek labels for signs of the zodiac and the seasons.

Where sources disagree. Edmund Buchner (Die Sonnenuhr des Augustus, 1982) reconstructed a vast sundial whose shadow reached the Ara Pacis on Augustus' birthday, 23 September, binding birth, Sun and peace. Peter Heslin (Journal of Roman Studies 2007), following Michael Schütz, argued for a meridian line only, the excavated stretch being Flavian; Bernard Frischer's computer simulations (2013–2017) found that Buchner's alignment fails.

On Augustus' return from Spain and Gaul in 13 BC the Senate decreed an altar of Augustan Peace, at which magistrates, priests and Vestals were to sacrifice every year (Res Gestae 12.2); it was dedicated on 30 January 9 BC (Ovid, Fasti 1.709–722). The peace was one won by victories (Res Gestae 13). On the long sides of the enclosure a life-size procession moves: Augustus with lictors, flamines in spiked caps, Agrippa veiled with a small boy clutching his toga, the women and children of the house. The short sides carry the Lupercal, Roma, a seated goddess and a sacrifice. The goddess holds two infants and fruit, with an ox and a sheep at her feet. The sacrificer is bearded and veiled, with attendants leading a sow and a shrine with two seated figures above: traditionally Aeneas sacrificing the sow of Lavinium, with the Penates in their shrine (Virgil, Aeneid 8.81–85). Reassembled in 1938 for Mussolini's bimillenary of Augustus' birth, away from its original site, the altar we see is a modern reconstruction.

Where sources disagree. Paul Rehak ("Aeneas or Numa?", Art Bulletin 2001) argued that the sacrificer is Numa, older, bearded and unarmed, the founder of peace and cult answering Romulus, the founder in war, opposite. For the goddess, Karl Galinsky argued for Venus (1966), Nancy de Grummond for Pax (1990) and Barbette Spaeth for Ceres (1994); the old name Tellus, Earth, survives, and many now read her as several at once.

The Prima Porta statue and the image of the princeps

The statue was found in 1863 at Livia's villa at Prima Porta, where an eagle had dropped into her lap a white hen holding the laurel sprig from which the triumphal laurels grew (Pliny, Natural History 15.136–137). It shows the general addressing his troops, cuirassed, right arm raised. But the feet are bare, as a hero's or god's, and a Cupid on a dolphin names his ancestress Venus. Stance and proportions follow Polykleitos' Doryphoros. Paul Zanker (The Power of Images in the Age of Augustus, 1988) read this classicism as policy: Octavian's early portraits had the agitation of Hellenistic kings, while the type adopted about 27 BC is calm and ageless, and stayed unchanged until his death at seventy-five. Suetonius' real man was short, with decayed teeth and eyebrows that met (Augustus 79). The breastplate, a Parthian handing back a standard, is module 6.4. Whether the marble copies a bronze of about 20 BC or was made for Livia after AD 14, when bare feet would suit a god, is uncertain.

The same man appears veiled for sacrifice on the Ara Pacis, and the golden shield set in the Curia named his courage, clemency, justice and piety (Res Gestae 34.2). General, priest and moral exemplar: the images assign roles, not powers.

The restored religion: temples, priesthoods, pontifex maximus

In 28 BC, consul for the sixth time, Octavian repaired eighty-two temples in the city, by his own count passing over none that needed it (Res Gestae 20.4). Livy calls him founder or restorer of every temple (4.20.7); Horace warns the Roman that he will pay for his fathers' sins until he rebuilds the gods' crumbling shrines (Odes 3.6.1–4). New temples tied gods to his life: he vowed Jupiter Tonans when lightning killed the slave lighting the way before his litter in Spain, and later called it Capitoline Jupiter's doorkeeper (Suetonius, Augustus 29.3, 91.2).

He sat in all four great colleges and among the fetials, Arvals and Titii (Res Gestae 7.3; the colleges are module 2.3). He revived the augury of Safety, the Flamen Dialis, the Lupercalia, the Secular Games and the Compitalia (Suetonius, Augustus 31.4), and had his name sung in the Salian hymn (Res Gestae 10.1). He refused to take the chief pontificate from the living Lepidus and was elected at his death in 12 BC by a crowd from all Italy (10.2); he then burned more than two thousand unreliable prophetic books (Suetonius, Augustus 31.1). In 8 BC Sextilis became Augustus (Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.12.35). Head of state and head of state religion were henceforth one man.

Where sources disagree. The Augustans wrote of decay: Varro composed his Divine Antiquities lest the gods perish through neglect (Augustine, City of God 6.2), and Livy laments the neglect of the gods in his own age (3.20.5). Beard, North and Price (Religions of Rome, 1998) treat the decline as largely the restorers' own story: republican nobles had competed for priesthoods and vowed temples, and Augustus rebuilt religion around himself.

The Secular Games of 17 BC

A saeculum was the longest human life, set at 110 years by the Sibylline oracle preserved in Zosimus (2.6) and by Horace (Carmen Saeculare 21–22). The republican games had honoured Dis Pater and Proserpina at night at the Tarentum in the Campus (Zosimus 2.1–3). In 17 BC the quindecimviri, with Augustus and Agrippa presiding, fixed the date, and the jurist Ateius Capito expounded the rules (Zosimus 2.4.2). The inscribed record, found by the Tiber in 1890 (CIL VI 32323), gives the programme. On three nights Augustus sacrificed by Greek rite to the Moerae, the Ilithyiae of childbirth and Terra Mater; on three days he and Agrippa offered to Jupiter and Juno on the Capitol, while 110 matrons prayed, and to Apollo and Diana on the Palatine. The prayers asked that the empire of the Roman people grow and that the Latin should always obey. Then twenty-seven boys and twenty-seven girls sang a hymn on the Palatine and the Capitol; Quintus Horatius Flaccus composed the song, the record notes (module 6.3). Underworld gods had given way to Fates, birth and Earth; expiation became the inauguration of an age, and the rite ended at the princeps' own Apollo.

Where sources disagree. Censorinus (De die natali 17) sets the quindecimviri's 110-year series, leading to 17 BC, beside that of Valerius Antias, Varro and Livy, with games in 249 and 149 or 146 BC, a century apart. Claudius reverted to the century in AD 47, and those who had seen Augustus' games laughed at the herald's promise of a spectacle no one had seen or would see again (Suetonius, Claudius 21.2).

Marriage, adultery and the failure of law

The Julian laws on the marriage of the orders and on adultery came in 18 BC (Dio 54.16.1–2); the Papian-Poppaean law of AD 9 was carried by two consuls who were both unmarried and childless (Dio 56.10.3). The unmarried could not inherit from outside their kin, the childless took half, and lapsed shares could fall to the treasury; parents gained precedence in office, and a freeborn mother of three escaped guardianship. Adultery became a public crime with its own court: the husband had to divorce or face a charge of pandering, and the guilty were relegated to islands (Digest 48.5). Horace's hymn asks the goddess to prosper the senators' decrees on marrying women (Carmen Saeculare 17–20). Equestrians demanded repeal; Augustus displayed Germanicus' children at them (Suetonius, Augustus 34.2). His daughter Julia was exiled for adultery in 2 BC (module 6.1) and his granddaughter in AD 8. Tacitus' verdict, from AD 20: marriage and child-rearing grew no commoner, and informers had made every household a target (Annals 3.25).

Where sources disagree. Propertius rejoices that a law which would have parted him from Cynthia was lifted (2.7); Gordon Williams took it for a marriage law withdrawn about 28 BC, while Ernst Badian ("A Phantom Marriage Law", 1985) denied that any such law existed or that the poem was evidence for one. On purpose, Dio's Augustus speaks of a shrinking citizen body (56.2–9), Tacitus of the treasury; Andrew Wallace-Hadrill (1981) noted that the sanctions work through inheritance, making the laws chiefly about how property passed within the propertied orders.

Genius, Lares and divus: the cult of the princeps

At Rome the princeps was honoured in existing forms. In 30 BC the Senate ordered libations to Octavian at all banquets (Dio 51.19.7), and Horace's farmer mingles his divine power with the Lares (Odes 4.5.31–35). Module 2.4 describes the crossroads reform of 7 BC and the freedmen serving the Lares Augusti and the Genius of Augustus; Dio adds that these officials wore magistrate's dress with two lictors in their own districts on set days (55.8.6–7). A household honoured its master's Genius; freedmen now honoured Augustus' across a city treated as his household, as the title Father of his Country made explicit.

Caesar's deification in 42 and his comet are modules 5.4 and 5.5. Octavian became son of a god, and in 29 BC dedicated the temple of the deified Julius on the site of the pyre, with prows from Actium (Dio 51.19.2, 51.22.2). For himself he refused a temple in Rome and melted his silver statues to pay for golden tripods for Apollo (Suetonius, Augustus 52); when Agrippa wished to set his statue in the Pantheon he declined, so Caesar stood inside and Augustus in the porch (Dio 53.27.3).

In 29 BC Octavian allowed Romans at Ephesus and Nicaea precincts to Roma and the deified Julius, and Greeks temples to himself and Roma at Pergamum and Nicomedia (Dio 51.20.6–7). In 9 BC Asia began its year on his birthday, the decree found at Priene calling the god's birth the beginning of good news for the world. At Lugdunum an altar of Roma and Augustus received an Aeduan priest (Livy, Periochae 139); it was dedicated in 12 BC according to the epitome and Dio (54.32.1), on 1 August 10 BC according to Suetonius (Claudius 2.1).

The idiom was Hellenistic. Greek cities had given kings cult for benefactions, as Athens did Antigonus and Demetrius in 307 (Greek module 7.1), and Smyrna gave the goddess Roma a temple in 195 BC (Tacitus, Annals 4.56). Augustus borrowed Alexander's apparatus with care: Alexander's head on his seal (Suetonius, Augustus 50), and a tale that Apollo as a serpent fathered him on Atia (94.4), answering Olympias' snake (Greek module 11.4). What he added was gradation: god in the East, Roma and Augustus in the provinces, a Genius at Rome, divinity at death. In AD 14 a senator swore he had seen him ascend, as Proculus had seen Romulus (Dio 56.46.2; module 1.4).

Where sources disagree. Suetonius says he refused such honours in the city (Augustus 52), and Dio that no one in Rome or Italy dared them (51.20.8). Tacitus' critics at the funeral say he wished to be worshipped with temples, images, flamines and priests (Annals 1.10.6), and the temple to Rome and Augustus at Pola, built in his lifetime within Augustan Italy, supports them. The line between Genius and person, city and province, leaked.

Self-test

  1. What did Augustus mean by leaving a city of marble, and how does Dio's version change the claim?
    Answer

    Suetonius takes it literally: Augustus adorned a city unworthy of the empire and boasted that he left it of marble (Augustus 28.3). Dio sets it among his last words and says he meant the strength of the empire, not its buildings (56.30.3–4).

  2. Why did the princeps' house on the Palatine become a religious site after 12 BC?
    Answer

    As pontifex maximus he had to live in a public house, so Augustus made part of his own public, gave the house of the rex sacrorum, which adjoined their quarters, to the Vestals (Dio 54.27.3) and housed a shrine of Vesta, so that Apollo, Vesta and Caesar shared it (Ovid, Fasti 4.949–954). His temple of Apollo already stood beside it, built on ground struck by lightning.

  3. What did the two exedrae of the Forum of Augustus show, and what argument did they make?
    Answer

    Aeneas carrying Anchises with the Alban kings and the Julii on one side, Romulus with the spolia opima and the great men of the Republic on the other (Ovid, Fasti 5.563–566). Family and Republic became one history culminating in Augustus, who by edict made them the standard for himself and his successors (Suetonius, Augustus 31.5).

  4. Why is Mars Ultor twice an avenger?
    Answer

    He was vowed at Philippi as avenger of Caesar, and the standards recovered from Parthia were later housed in his Forum temple (Res Gestae 29.2). Ovid combines the two (Fasti 5.579–596), though Dio reports a separate Capitoline temple decreed for the standards in 20 BC (54.8.3).

  5. What is the case for reading the sacrificer on the Ara Pacis as Numa rather than Aeneas?
    Answer

    Rehak (2001) pointed out that the figure is older, bearded and unarmed, and that Numa, founder of peace and cult, would answer Romulus, the founder in war, on the opposite panel. The traditional reading sees Aeneas sacrificing the sow of Lavinium, with the Penates in their shrine.

  6. What did Buchner claim about the obelisk in the Campus Martius, and what have his critics said?
    Answer

    That it was the gnomon of a vast sundial whose shadow reached the Ara Pacis on Augustus' birthday. Schütz and Heslin argue from Pliny (Natural History 36.72–73) and the excavation for a meridian line, the excavated stretch being Flavian, and Frischer's simulations found that the birthday alignment fails.

  7. Which features of the Prima Porta statue go beyond the portrait of a general?
    Answer

    The bare feet of a hero or god, the Cupid on a dolphin naming Venus as ancestress, and the Polykleitan model that makes the face calm and ageless. Zanker read this classicism as a deliberate break with the agitated Hellenistic royal portrait.

  8. How did the Secular Games of 17 BC change the republican rite?
    Answer

    The night offerings went to the Moerae, Ilithyiae and Terra Mater instead of Dis Pater and Proserpina, day sacrifices to Jupiter, Juno, Apollo and Diana were added, and the rite ended with Horace's hymn at Palatine Apollo (CIL VI 32323). A rite of expiation became the inauguration of an age, on a 110-year cycle built to fit 17 BC (Censorinus, De die natali 17).

  9. How did the marriage laws try to compel marriage, and why did Tacitus think they failed?
    Answer

    Mainly through inheritance: the unmarried could not inherit from outside their kin and the childless took half, while parents gained privileges. Tacitus says that by AD 20 marriage and children were no commoner and that informers had made every household a target (Annals 3.25).

  10. How did cult of the princeps differ between Rome and the provinces, and where did the provincial forms come from?
    Answer

    At Rome he received libations and Genius worship at the crossroads but no temple (Suetonius, Augustus 52); in the provinces Greeks had temples to Roma and Augustus at Pergamum and Nicomedia (Dio 51.20.6–7), and the Gauls an altar at Lugdunum. These continued the cults Greek cities had offered to Hellenistic kings (Greek module 7.1) and to Roma since 195 BC.

Carry forward

  1. Augustus argued through places: a house shared with Apollo and Vesta, a forum where Roman history ended in his chariot, and a Campus binding tomb, sun and peace. Read later imperial building as the same kind of claim.
  2. The religious restoration was a relocation: priesthoods, calendar, games and crossroads were renewed with the princeps at their centre, and from 12 BC the head of state religion and the head of state were one man.
  3. Ruler cult was graded by place and time: god in the Greek East, Roma and Augustus in the provinces, Genius and son of the deified at Rome, divus after death. Law could not achieve what images and ritual did, as the marriage laws showed in his own family.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Augustan Rome as an argument in stone and ritual. Cover: 'found a city of brick and left it of marble' (Suetonius, Augustus 28); the Forum of Augustus and the temple of Mars Ultor with its gallery of great Romans and the Aeneas and Romulus statue groups; the Ara Pacis and its reliefs (Aeneas or Numa, Tellus or Pax, the procession); the Mausoleum, the sundial and the Campus Martius; the house on the Palatine beside the temple of Apollo; the Prima Porta statue and the image of the princeps; the religious restoration (eighty-two temples repaired, the revived priesthoods, Augustus as pontifex maximus from 12 BC, the Secular Games of 17 BC and Horace's Carmen Saeculare); the laws on marriage and adultery and their failure; the Lares Augusti and the Genius of Augustus at the crossroads; and divus Julius and the beginnings of the imperial cult in the provinces, read against Hellenistic precedents (point back to Greek modules 7.1 and 11.4). Virgil, Horace, Livy and Ovid: the Augustan myth

Maecenas and the friendship of poets

Gaius Maecenas descended from Etruscan kings, as Horace never tired of saying (Odes 1.1.1; Satires 1.6.1–4), and never held a magistracy. He stayed an equestrian while acting as Octavian's negotiator in the triumviral years and his deputy in Rome during the Actium campaign (Velleius 2.88).

Patronage was friendship between unequal men, not employment. It meant dinners, introductions, protection and gifts of property: Horace's Sabine farm (Odes 2.18.14; Satires 2.6). Virgil and Varius presented Horace; Maecenas said little and sent for him nine months later (Satires 1.6.54–62). The poets paid in dedications. Each book of the Georgics names Maecenas, and the third calls its theme tua, Maecenas, haud mollia iussa, "your far from easy commands" (3.41); the first poems of Horace's Satires, Epodes, Odes and Epistles all address him; Propertius addresses him in 2.1 and 3.9. The friendship allowed refusal. In Epistles 1.7 Horace tells Maecenas he would hand everything back rather than lose his freedom, and Suetonius' Life of Horace records that he declined Augustus' offer of the post of private secretary without offence.

Maecenas was not the only patron. Asinius Pollio, consul in 40, protected the young Virgil (Eclogues 3 and 4) and wrote a history of the civil wars that Horace called a work full of dangerous hazard (Odes 2.1.6). Messalla Corvinus, once Brutus' officer, kept Tibullus, his niece Sulpicia and the young Ovid, who called him the instigator of his studies (Epistulae ex Ponto 2.3). Maecenas' own influence faded after 23 or 22, when he warned his wife Terentia that her brother Murena was under suspicion (Suetonius, Augustus 66.3); Tacitus says he kept the appearance of the princeps' friendship rather than its power (Annals 3.30). He died in 8 BC, leaving Augustus his heir. Horace died weeks later and was buried near him on the Esquiline.

Where sources disagree. Ronald Syme's chapter "The Organization of Opinion" (The Roman Revolution, 1939) set Maecenas and his poets beside coins and buildings as instruments of a managed consensus. Peter White (Promised Verse, 1993) replied that the "circle of Maecenas" is a modern construction: the poets had several patrons, gifts were the ordinary currency of Roman friendship, and no source shows Augustus or Maecenas prescribing content. The "commands" of Georgics 3.41 can be read either way.

Virgil before the Aeneid: the Eclogues and Georgics

Virgil's life belongs to deep dive module 12.1. The ten Eclogues, Theocritean pastoral in Latin, put the land confiscations of 41 inside the shepherds' world. In the first, Meliboeus is driven from his farm while Tityrus has been left in peace by a young man at Rome whom he will honour as a god: deus nobis haec otia fecit (1.6). In the ninth, Moeris has been evicted and songs have not saved Menalcas. Ancient commentators read Tityrus as Virgil and the god as Octavian; the poem names neither. The fourth Eclogue's child goes to deep dive module 12.1, and module 5.5 places it in the hopeful season of Brundisium.

The four books of the Georgics, finished in 29, were read to Octavian at Atella on his return from the East, Maecenas taking over when Virgil's voice failed (Donatus, Life 27). Book 1 closes with the portents after Caesar's murder, Philippi, and a prayer that the young man be allowed to rescue an age in which right and wrong are reversed, the world a chariot that no longer answers the reins (1.498–514). Book 3 promises a temple at Mantua with Caesar at its centre and, later, an epic of his battles (3.10–48). Book 4 ends with Caesar thundering at the Euphrates while the poet idles at Naples (4.559–566). The promised poem on Caesar's wars became, instead, a poem about his ancestor.

Where sources disagree. Servius (on Eclogue 10.1 and Georgics 4.1) says the second half of Georgics 4 once praised Cornelius Gallus and was replaced at Augustus' order by Aristaeus and Orpheus after Gallus' fall. Franz Skutsch (Aus Vergils Frühzeit, 1901) defended the story; W. B. Anderson ("Gallus and the Fourth Georgic", 1933) and most since doubt it, since Donatus is silent and Orpheus is integral to the book's design.

The Aeneid in outline and its Augustan programme

The Aeneid, twelve books left unrevised at Virgil's death, gives the legend traced in module 1.3 its final form. Books 1–6 are the Odyssean half: storm, Carthage and Dido, the fall of Troy, the wanderings, the underworld. Books 7–12 are the Iliadic half: Latium, Allecto's war, Evander's Palatine, Pallas killed, and the duel that ends with Turnus' death. Deep dive modules 12.2 and 12.3 take it book by book; Greek module 10.12 shows how it answers Homer from the Trojan side. Propertius greeted it in progress: something greater than the Iliad is being born (2.34.65–66). Three passages carry its Augustan programme, and each is prophecy, Roman history seen forward from the mythic past.

Jupiter's prophecy (1.257–296). To console Venus, Jupiter unrolls a timetable: three years of Aeneas' rule, thirty of Ascanius, three hundred of Alba until Ilia bears the twins, then Romulus and the Romans, to whom he sets no limits of space or time, imperium sine fine dedi (1.279). Juno will come round and cherish Romanos, rerum dominos gentemque togatam (1.282). Then a Trojan Caesar, Iulius from great Iulus (1.286–290; Greek module 10.12 covers the naming), and a world at peace: Fides and Vesta, Remus beside his brother Quirinus giving laws, the gates of war shut, and impious Furor chained inside on a heap of weapons, roaring with bloody mouth (1.291–296). Each detail points at 29 BC: Janus closed, religion restored, fratricide ended. But Furor is bound, not dead.

Where sources disagree. Which Caesar is meant at 1.286? Most commentators since Heyne take him as Augustus, since the closing of Janus follows directly. Servius, and in a full modern defence Robert Dobbin (1995), argue for Julius Caesar, whose name Iulius the line presses and whose reception in heaven matches the deified dictator. The ambiguity may be deliberate: the heir's legitimacy rested on the god.

The parade of heroes (6.756–892). Anchises shows Aeneas the souls waiting to be born. Augustus appears out of sequence, straight after Romulus: Augustus Caesar, divi genus, who will found again the golden age in Latium and carry empire past the Garamantes and Indians, further than Hercules or Bacchus travelled (6.791–805). What follows is not simple praise. Brutus, who executed his own sons, is infelix (6.822); Caesar and Pompey are begged not to turn their strength on their country (6.826–835). The precept to spare the conquered (6.851–853) belongs to deep dive module 12.5. The parade ends not on Augustus but on Marcellus, his nephew and heir, dead in 23 BC (6.860–886); Donatus says Octavia fainted at the reading (Life 32).

The shield (8.626–728). Vulcan engraves Roman history: the wolf and twins, the Sabine women, Cocles and Cloelia, Manlius and the geese, Catiline punished in Tartarus and, among the righteous, his dantem iura Catonem (8.670), probably Caesar's enemy, as their lawgiver. At the centre is Actium (8.675–713), which module 5.5 reads; then the triple triumph of August 29, Caesar seated at the threshold of Apollo's temple as the conquered nations file past (8.714–728). Aeneas lifts it onto his shoulder, rerumque ignarus imagine gaudet (8.730): he rejoices in the image without knowing the events.

The technique is the programme. History becomes fate, foreseen by gods and ancestors, and every line ends at Augustus; the cost (chained Furor, the dead heir, the hero who cannot read what he carries) is written into the same passages. Whether that cost undermines the celebration is the debate between Augustan and pessimistic readers that deep dive module 12.7 runs.

Horace: lyric for the res publica

Quintus Horatius Flaccus, a freedman's son from Venusia, fought for Brutus at Philippi as a military tribune and made a joke of his lost shield (Odes 2.7.9–10). Pardoned, he bought a treasury clerkship. The three books of Odes, published in 23, claimed to have brought Aeolian song to Italian measures (3.30.13–14): Alcaeus and Sappho made Latin. In 1.2 Mercury takes the form of the young Caesar to avenge the murdered dictator; 1.37 celebrates Cleopatra's death (module 5.5).

The six "Roman Odes" that open book 3 (the label is modern) share one metre, the Alcaic, and one voice, the poet as priest of the Muses: odi profanum vulgus et arceo (3.1.1). Their themes are the regime's. Contentment over ambition (3.1); military hardiness, with dulce et decorum est pro patria mori (3.2.13); the just man, among whom Augustus will drink nectar with the gods, and Juno's speech forbidding Troy ever to be rebuilt (3.3.18–68), apt when rumour had Caesar planning to move the capital east (Suetonius, Julius 79.3). In 3.4 the Giants fall, since vis consili expers mole ruit sua, force without judgement collapses under its own weight (3.4.65). In 3.5 Augustus will be held a present god once Britons and Persians are added to the empire (3.5.2–4). In 3.6 Romans will pay for their fathers' sins until they repair the temples, and each generation is worse than the last. The cycle preaches the restoration that module 6.2 traces in stone.

The Carmen Saeculare was a commission. The inscribed record of the Secular Games of 17 BC states carmen composuit Q. Horatius Flaccus (CIL VI 32323); twenty-seven boys and twenty-seven girls sang it on the Palatine and the Capitol. Module 6.2 covers the ritual; as a poem it is a hymn in Sapphic stanzas to Apollo and Diana that compresses the Augustan myth into prayers: bless the senators' decrees on marriage (17–20); if Rome is your work and Trojans reached the Etruscan shore (37–38), grant the princeps, clarus Anchisae Venerisque sanguis (50), his asks; Fides, Pax, Honos, Pudor and neglected Virtus dare to return (57–59). Horace later made the commission his title to fame: the girl in the chorus will remember, married, that she learned the hymn of the bard Horace (Odes 4.6.41–44). Suetonius says Augustus also pressed for a fourth book of odes to celebrate Tiberius' and Drusus' Alpine victories (4.4, 4.14).

Livy: a history for these times

Titus Livius of Patavium held no office and had no known patron. Module 0.1 treats him as a source for early Rome, quotes the preface on poets' tales and dates book 1 by its single closing of Janus (1.19.3); here he is an Augustan author. The preface frames the whole work as a history of decline. Readers will hurry to recent times, in which a long-dominant people's strength destroys itself (Preface 4); Livy turns to antiquity to avert his eyes from what his own age has seen (5). Morals slid, then sank, then fell headlong, until haec tempora quibus nec vitia nostra nec remedia pati possumus, these times in which we can endure neither our vices nor their remedies (9). No state was ever greater or richer in good examples, nor so late in admitting greed and luxury (11).

The first decade, to 293 BC, offers founders. Romulus is taken up to heaven, though Livy reports that some even then believed the senators had torn him apart (1.16.4); Augustus considered the name Romulus before choosing his own (Suetonius, Augustus 7.2; Dio 53.16.7). Camillus, after the Gallic sack, is hailed as Romulus ac parens patriae conditorque alter urbis (5.49.7), and his speech keeps the Romans from migrating to Veii (5.51–54), the same refusal to abandon the city that Horace gives Juno. Most telling is the digression on Cossus (4.20.5–11). All Livy's sources made Cossus a military tribune when he won the spolia opima; Augustus told Livy he had read "consul" on the linen corslet in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius. The point was live, since Crassus had claimed the spoils as a mere proconsul in 29 (Dio 51.24; module 2.2 gives the modern dispute). Livy prints the princeps' testimony, judges it almost sacrilege to deny Cossus such a witness, and leaves his sources standing beside it.

Where sources disagree. Cremutius Cordus, in Tacitus, says Livy praised Pompey so warmly that Augustus called him a Pompeian, without harm to their friendship (Annals 4.34.3); Seneca reports him uncertain whether Caesar's birth helped or harmed the state (Natural Questions 5.18.4). Syme ("Livy and Augustus", 1959) concluded that Livy was an independent republican moralist; readers who stress Cossus and Camillus see a willing contributor to the image of the refounder. The remedies of Preface 9 may be moral legislation or, as John Moles read them, one-man rule itself.

Propertius and Tibullus: love instead of war

Latin love elegy had its first master in Cornelius Gallus, whose four books are lost but for a few lines on papyrus; Ovid gives the canon as Gallus, Tibullus, Propertius and himself (Tristia 4.10.53–54). The form came from Catullus (module 5.6). Its stance was a refusal: the lover is a slave to his mistress, his service is a campaign (militat omnis amans, Ovid, Amores 1.9.1), and the career of office and arms is declined. Gallus' fate shadowed the genre: prefect of Egypt, he boasted of his deeds, lost Augustus' friendship and killed himself in 27–26 (Dio 53.23.5–7; Suetonius, Augustus 66.2).

Propertius' first book, about 29, ends on the Perusine graves and an unburied kinsman (1.21–22): the civil war seen from the losing town. Taken up by Maecenas, he offered the patron a recusatio: were he able, he would sing Caesar's wars, but his gift is narrow (2.1). In 2.7 Cynthia rejoices that a law that would have parted them has been lifted, and he asks why he should supply sons for his country's triumphs: nullus de nostro sanguine miles erit (2.7.14). If all lived like lovers, the sea at Actium would hold no Roman bones (2.15). Book 4, about 16, turns to Roman aetiology as the "Roman Callimachus" (4.1.64): Tarpeia in love, Hercules and Cacus, the spolia opima, Actium (4.6, module 5.5).

Tibullus, Messalla's poet, sets the lover on a poor farm while his patron wages war by land and sea (1.1), and curses the inventor of the sword (1.10.1). He celebrated Messalla's triumph of 27 (1.7) and gave the Sibyl a prophecy of Rome to Aeneas (2.5), yet nowhere names Augustus.

Where sources disagree. Hans-Peter Stahl (Propertius: "Love" and "War", 1985) read the poems as an individual's resistance to the state's claims on him; Francis Cairns (Sextus Propertius: The Augustan Elegist, 2006) set Propertius within Maecenas' patronage and his book 4 as its natural product. Whether the law lifted in 2.7 ever existed is weighed in module 6.2.

Ovid: the calendar, the changes and Tomis

Publius Ovidius Naso was born at Sulmo in 43, the year both consuls fell at Mutina (Tristia 4.10.6). He declined a senatorial career and only saw Virgil: Vergilium vidi tantum (4.10.51). He was the first Augustan poet with no adult memory of civil war. The Ars Amatoria taught seduction in the city of the Julian adultery law, its first book sending readers to Pompey's portico, the theatres and Augustus' mock sea battle of 2 BC.

The Fasti, which module 2.3 reads as a source for festivals, is also an Augustan poem: an elegiac calendar after Callimachus' Aitia, six books for January to June, dedicated to Augustus (Tristia 2.551–552) and rededicated in exile to Germanicus (Fasti 1.3). Ovid calls it his military service: haec mea militia est (2.9). The new dates crowd the old. On 13 January the provinces were returned and Octavian named Augustus, a name shared with sacred things (1.587–616). On 5 February Augustus became father of his country, and Ovid compares him with Romulus to Romulus' cost: the founder took wives by force, the princeps makes them chaste (2.119–144). On the Ides of March Vesta says she snatched her priest Caesar away and left only his image to the daggers (3.697–710); in April she is lodged in Augustus' Palatine house (4.949–954); in May Mars Ultor inspects his new forum (5.545–598).

Where sources disagree. Geraldine Herbert-Brown (Ovid and the Fasti, 1994) reads the poem as a courtier's tribute alert to dynastic politics. Alessandro Barchiesi (The Poet and the Prince, 1997) and Carole Newlands (Playing with Time, 1995) find its Augustan days undercut by juxtaposition, an elegiac voice too light for its subject and an unfinished shape.

The Metamorphoses, fifteen books of hexameter from Chaos to Caesar's apotheosis, ends with Jupiter ruling the heavens and Augustus the earth, each father and ruler (15.858–860), then claims a fame that neither Jupiter's anger nor fire nor sword can destroy (15.871–872). Greek module 3.7 treats Ovid's handling of the Greek myths and the council of the gods; module 10.1 takes the poem further.

In AD 8 an edict of Augustus relegated Ovid to Tomis on the Black Sea. He insists he was relegated, not exiled, and kept his property (Tristia 2.135–138). Two crimes ruined him, carmen et error (2.207): the poem was the Ars; the mistake he will not name, saying only that he saw something, like Actaeon (2.103–108). He was never recalled and died at Tomis under Tiberius.

Where sources disagree. Ovid's relegation coincided with that of Augustus' granddaughter Julia (Tacitus, Annals 4.71), and many link the mistake to her adultery or to her brother Agrippa Postumus; others propose forbidden rites. John Thibault (The Mystery of Ovid's Exile, 1964) surveyed the theories and found none proven; A. D. Fitton Brown (1985) argued that the exile was a literary fiction, a view few accept.

Propaganda, collaboration or something freer?

The evidence for direction is thin and specific. Augustus commissioned the Carmen Saeculare, pressed for Odes 4 and asked for drafts of the Aeneid; Suetonius says he fostered the talents of his age, and objected to being written about except seriously and by the best writers (Augustus 89.3). Against that stand the refusals: the recusatio in Virgil (Eclogue 6.3–5), Horace and Propertius, Horace's declined secretaryship, Tibullus' silence, Livy's Pompeian sympathies. Repression came late. In Augustus' last years Titus Labienus' histories were burned by senatorial decree (Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 10 preface 5), Cassius Severus' libels drew the first use of the treason law against writing (Tacitus, Annals 1.72), and Ovid went to Tomis.

Syme's "organisation of opinion" makes the poets part of the apparatus. White denies any apparatus. Karl Galinsky (Augustan Culture, 1996) describes an evolving culture of shared values, in which the poets were participants with minds of their own. Duncan Kennedy (1992) argued that "Augustan" and "anti-Augustan" are readers' terms of reference, positions taken by critics, not properties of texts.

The texts themselves suggest a sequence. Virgil and Horace had lived through confiscation and Philippi and wrote as survivors for whom the peace was a deliverance with a price, which their poems name. The elegists declined the public voice, then borrowed it. Ovid, born into the settlement, played with its myths as if they were already literature, which by then they were. "Collaboration" fits the myths better than the men: Aeneas' piety, the returning golden age, Actium as foreign war and the refounder's line were made by these writers, and the regime quoted them back in its forum and on its altars (module 6.2). The poets made the Augustan myth more than Augustus made the poets.

Self-test

  1. What did Maecenas' patronage consist of, and what evidence shows that it left room for refusal?
    Answer

    Friendship with gifts, dinners, introductions and protection, such as Horace's Sabine farm (Odes 2.18.14), repaid by dedications. Horace tells Maecenas he would return everything rather than lose his freedom (Epistles 1.7) and declined Augustus' offer of a secretaryship (Suetonius, Life of Horace).

  2. How do the first and ninth Eclogues register the confiscations of 41, and why should Tityrus not simply be equated with Virgil?
    Answer

    Meliboeus and Moeris lose their land while Tityrus keeps his farm thanks to a young "god" at Rome (1.6). The equation of Tityrus with Virgil and the god with Octavian comes from ancient commentators; the poems name neither.

  3. What do Jupiter's prophecy, the parade of heroes and the shield have in common as narrative devices?
    Answer

    All three are prophecy: Roman history is seen forward from the mythic past as fate, and each line leads to Augustus (1.286–296; 6.791–805; 8.714–728). Each also writes in a cost: Furor bound but alive, Marcellus dead, Aeneas ignorant of what he carries (8.730).

  4. Why is the identity of the Caesar at Aeneid 1.286 disputed?
    Answer

    The name Iulius and the reception in heaven fit the deified Julius Caesar, as Servius and Dobbin argue; the closing of the gates of war that follows fits Augustus, the view of most commentators since Heyne. The overlap may be intended, since Augustus' standing rested on his divine father.

  5. How does the parade in Aeneid 6 complicate its own praise of Augustus?
    Answer

    Augustus is placed beside Romulus as refounder of the golden age (6.791–805), but the procession includes the infelix Brutus (6.822), Caesar and Pompey begged to lay down arms (6.826–835), and ends on Marcellus, the heir who died in 23 BC (6.860–886).

  6. Name three themes of the Roman Odes and say how 3.3 uses Juno.
    Answer

    Any three of contentment, military virtue and loyalty (3.2.13), the just man and Augustus among the gods, the fall of the Giants (3.4.65), Augustus as a present god after conquest (3.5.2–4), temple repair and moral decline (3.6). Juno forbids Troy ever to be rebuilt (3.3.18–68), a warning against moving the capital east.

  7. What makes the Carmen Saeculare different from the other Odes, and how did Horace present it afterwards?
    Answer

    It was a state commission, recorded in the inscribed acts of the Games (CIL VI 32323), sung once by a chorus of boys and girls, and its prayers set out the Augustan programme: marriage laws, Trojan origins, the returning virtues (17–20, 37–59). Horace later claimed it as his fame in Odes 4.6.41–44.

  8. What does the Cossus digression (Livy 4.20.5–11) reveal about Livy's relation to Augustus?
    Answer

    Livy reports Augustus' claim to have read "consul" on Cossus' corslet, a claim that helped deny Crassus the spolia opima, while leaving all his own sources, which made Cossus a tribune, beside it. He defers to the princeps without suppressing the conflict.

  9. In what ways did Propertius and Tibullus refuse the regime's values, and how did Propertius' fourth book change course?
    Answer

    They chose love over office and war: Propertius will father no soldiers (2.7.14) and declines epic for Maecenas (2.1); Tibullus curses the sword (1.10.1) and never names Augustus. Propertius' book 4 turns to Roman aetiology as the "Roman Callimachus" (4.1.64), including Actium (4.6).

  10. What does Ovid say caused his relegation in AD 8, and what changed in the regime's treatment of writers in its last decade?
    Answer

    A poem and a mistake (Tristia 2.207): the Ars Amatoria and something he saw but will not name (2.103–108). In the same years Labienus' books were burned (Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 10 preface 5) and Cassius Severus was prosecuted under the treason law for libel (Tacitus, Annals 1.72).

Carry forward

  1. The Augustan myth was made in words before it was quoted in stone: Aeneas' piety, the returning golden age, Actium as a foreign war and the refounder after Romulus and Camillus come from Virgil, Horace and Livy, and the Forum of Augustus and the Ara Pacis set them in stone (module 6.2).
  2. The characteristic Augustan device is prophecy: history told as fate from the mythic past, every line ending at Augustus. Later writers who attack the regime attack that teleology, and the cost the Augustan texts themselves record is where the attack begins.
  3. Patronage was friendship, not employment, and the recusatio let poets praise while declining; the space narrowed only in the reign's last decade. "Augustan" and "anti-Augustan" are labels the texts resist, so ask what each voice does within a work.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Augustan writers and the myths they made for the new order. Cover: Maecenas and patronage; Virgil's Eclogues and Georgics, and the Aeneid in outline (deep dive unit 12 takes it book by book), with Jupiter's prophecy (1.257–296), the parade of heroes (6.756–892) and the shield (8.626–728) as the poem's Augustan programme; Horace's Odes, the 'Roman Odes' of book 3 and the Carmen Saeculare; Livy's preface and his first decade as the regime's history or its quiet critique; Propertius and Tibullus and the elegists' refusal of war; Ovid's Fasti as a calendar of Augustan Rome, the Metamorphoses (module 10.1 takes it further), the 'poem and a mistake' and the exile to Tomis in AD 8; and whether 'Augustan literature' was propaganda, collaboration or something more independent. Point back to Greek modules 3.7 and 10.12 rather than retelling the Greek myths these poets reworked. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

Empire without end

Empire without end, empire within limitsThe standing armySpain, the Alps and the DanubeEgypt, the emperor's provinceThe standards from ParthiaGermany: Drusus, Tiberius and VarusClient kings and the provinces of the Senate and of CaesarThe Res Gestae's map of the worldSelf-testCarry forward

Empire without end, empire within limits

In the first book of the Aeneid Jupiter consoles Venus with the future of her son's line:

his ego nec metas rerum nec tempora pono: imperium sine fine dedi.

"For these I set no bounds in space or time: I have given empire without end" (1.278–279). The coming Caesar's empire is bounded only by Ocean (1.287). Module 6.3 reads the prophecy as the poem's programme; Tacitus supplies the counter-claim. After the funeral in AD 14 Tiberius had Augustus' handwritten summary of the state's resources read in the Senate: soldiers, fleets, kingdoms, provinces and taxes.

addideratque consilium coercendi intra terminos imperii, incertum metu an per invidiam.

He had added advice to keep the empire within its limits, "whether from fear or from jealousy is uncertain" (Annals 1.11.4). Suetonius describes the summary without the advice (Augustus 101.4). Dio has it, and claims that Augustus always followed it in deed as well as word, having declined much barbarian land (56.33.5–6). The reign refutes Dio. Augustus annexed more territory than any Roman before him, and the advice came after the Pannonian revolt of AD 6–9 and the loss of three legions in Germany.

Where sources disagree. P. A. Brunt ("Augustan Imperialism", Journal of Roman Studies 1963) took the poets' universal empire as Augustus' real aim, abandoned only when the disasters of AD 6–9 exhausted his manpower. Erich Gruen ("The Imperial Policy of Augustus", 1990) set an ideology of world rule, aimed at opinion at home, against a practice of piecemeal, opportunistic expansion.

The standing army

Octavian came out of Actium with more legions than the state could pay. The Res Gestae puts some 500,000 citizens under his oath in his lifetime, more than 300,000 of them settled in colonies or sent home with land or money (3.3), at a cost of about 860 million sesterces for land in 30 and 14 BC and 400 million in cash between 7 and 2 BC (16). The rest became a permanent army, paid by the state, enlisted for fixed terms, stationed in the provinces and sworn to one man; its background is module 5.2 and deep dive module 11.2. Augustus stopped addressing soldiers as commilitones, fellow-soldiers, and called them milites (Suetonius, Augustus 25.1). Pay stayed at Caesar's 225 denarii a year, the ten asses a day that the mutineers of AD 14 set against the guard's two denarii, complaining too that discharged men were kept on under the banner (Tacitus, Annals 1.17). Glory was centralised. Wars were fought under his auspices, and after Cornelius Balbus' triumph of 19 BC no one outside the family triumphed; generals received triumphal ornaments instead, given, Suetonius says, to rather more men than the thirty-odd full triumphs Augustus had voted (Augustus 38.1).

Legions25 in AD 23 (Tacitus, Annals 4.5)16 years from 13 BC (Dio 54.25.6); 20 years and 12,000 sesterces from AD 5 (Dio 55.23.1)
Praetorian cohortsNine (Annals 4.5), three kept in Rome (Suetonius, Augustus 49.1); two equestrian prefects from 2 BC (Dio 55.10.10)12 years from 13 BC; 16 years and 20,000 sesterces from AD 5 (Dio)
AuxiliariesAlae and cohorts roughly as strong as the legions (Annals 4.5)Unknown under Augustus; regular citizenship on discharge came later (module 9.2)
Where sources disagree. Dio, under AD 5, gives twenty-three or, as others say, twenty-five legions (55.23.2); Tacitus counts twenty-five in AD 23 (Annals 4.5). The familiar twenty-eight is a modern sum, Tacitus' total plus Varus' three legions, whose numbers were never reused, and it holds only if no legion was raised in the emergencies of AD 6–9, which Dio's lower figure leaves open.

The military treasury

In AD 6 Augustus founded the aerarium militare to pay bounties after twenty years' service, putting in 170 million sesterces from his patrimony (Res Gestae 17.2). Dio adds gifts in his and Tiberius' names, contributions from kings and cities but none from private citizens, and three ex-praetors chosen by lot to run the fund (55.25.2–3). Its income came from a five per cent tax on inheritances, sparing near kin and the poor (Dio 55.25.5), and a one per cent tax on sales that Tiberius refused to abolish in AD 15 because the treasury depended on it (Annals 1.78). Italy, free of direct tax since 167 BC (module 4.4), now paid for the army.

Spain, the Alps and the Danube

Suetonius says Augustus fought only two foreign wars in person, the Dalmatian as a young man and the Cantabrian (Augustus 20). In 26 BC he campaigned against the Cantabrians and Asturians of the north-west, fell ill and withdrew to Tarraco (Dio 53.25). Janus was closed in 25 (53.26.5), but the mountain peoples rose again and again until Agrippa ended the war in 19, after enslaved prisoners had killed their masters and gone home and his own troops had wavered (Dio 54.11). Velleius calls Spain pacified after two hundred years of war (2.90); three legions still stood there in AD 23 (Annals 4.5).

In the Alps Varro Murena crushed the Salassi of the Aosta valley in 25 BC, selling 36,000 by Strabo's figure (4.6.7). In 15 BC Drusus from Italy and Tiberius from Gaul took Raetia and Vindelicia in a single summer (Dio 54.22; Velleius 2.95), and Horace celebrated each (Odes 4.4, 4.14). Cottius was kept on as prefect of his Alpine peoples, as his arch at Susa records, and the trophy at La Turbie, dedicated in 7/6 BC, listed the conquered tribes (Pliny, Natural History 3.136–137). The Alps secured the routes between Italy and the northern armies.

On the Danube Marcus Crassus beat the Bastarnae in 29–28 and killed their king with his own hand, but was refused the spolia opima because he had not fought under his own auspices (Dio 51.24). Tiberius conquered Pannonia in 12–9 BC (Velleius 2.96). In AD 6, as he moved against the Marcomannic king Maroboduus in Bohemia, the Pannonians and Dalmatians rose. Velleius, who served there, gives the rebels 200,000 infantry and 9,000 cavalry (2.110.3) and has Augustus warn the Senate that they could be in sight of Rome within ten days (2.111.1); Suetonius calls it the gravest foreign war since the Punic Wars (Tiberius 16.1). The Res Gestae claims Illyricum carried to the Danube (30.1).

Egypt, the emperor's province

Module 5.5 tells how Egypt was taken in 30 BC. Augustus says he added it to the empire of the Roman people (Res Gestae 27.1), but it was his. An equestrian prefect, holding in Strabo's phrase the rank of the king, governed it and, uniquely for a knight, commanded legions: three in Strabo's day (17.1.12), two by Tacitus' count in AD 23 (Annals 4.5). Senators and leading knights needed leave to enter, one of the secrets of domination, lest anyone seize the province and starve Italy (Annals 2.59). A late epitome credits Augustan Egypt with twenty million modii of grain a year for Rome (Epitome de Caesaribus 1.6). The first prefect, the poet Cornelius Gallus, boasted on a trilingual stele at Philae in 29 BC of leading an army beyond the cataract; by 26 he had been renounced by Augustus and had killed himself (Dio 53.23). In the temples, as at Dendur, Augustus appeared as pharaoh. From Egypt Aelius Gallus marched into Arabia and Gaius Petronius against Kush as far as Napata (Res Gestae 26.5; Strabo 17.1.54). A bronze head of Augustus that the Kushites carried off, buried beneath a temple stair at Meroe, is now in the British Museum.

The standards from Parthia

Three Roman armies had lost standards to Parthia: Crassus' at Carrhae in 53 (module 5.4), Decidius Saxa's in 40 and Antony's in 36. In 20 BC, with Augustus in the East and Tiberius leading an army into Armenia, Phraates IV returned the standards and prisoners. Armenia, which Augustus says he could have made a province, went by ancestral example to a king, Tigranes (Res Gestae 27.2). No battle was fought; the presentation made it a conquest. Coins showed a kneeling Parthian offering a standard, Horace has Phraates accept Caesar's rule on his knees (Epistles 1.12.27–28), and the Res Gestae says Augustus compelled the Parthians to return the standards of three armies and to seek friendship as suppliants, and laid them in the temple of Mars Ultor (29.2; module 6.2).

The Prima Porta statue carries the scene on its cuirass. At the centre a bearded, trousered Parthian hands an eagle standard to a Roman in armour. Above, Caelus spreads the sky and the Sun drives his chariot; at the sides sit two mourning subject peoples, often identified as Gaul and Spain; below are Apollo on a griffin, Diana on a stag and Earth with a cornucopia. A negotiated exchange sits at the centre of an ordered cosmos. Whether the Roman is Tiberius, Mars Ultor or a figure for the army is uncertain; module 6.2 reads the statue as a whole.

Where sources disagree. The Res Gestae says Phraates later sent his sons and grandsons to Italy not because he was beaten in war but to seek Roman friendship through pledges (32.2), and Suetonius has the Parthians return the standards on demand and offer hostages besides (Augustus 21.3). Strabo says Phraates gave up the princes to rid himself of rivals around whom revolt could gather (16.1.28), and Tacitus that he acted less from fear of Rome than from distrust of his own people (Annals 2.1).

Germany: Drusus, Tiberius and Varus

Suetonius counts only two serious defeats in the reign, both in Germany: Lollius' loss of an eagle in 16 BC (Velleius 2.97.1), more disgraceful than damaging, and Varus', almost fatal (Augustus 23.1). From 12 BC Drusus campaigned beyond the Rhine and in 9 BC reached the Elbe, dying on the return, after a fall from his horse in Livy's epitome (Periochae 142), of disease in Dio (55.1.4). Tiberius, in Velleius' words, reduced the country almost to a tributary province (2.97.4). At Waldgirmes in the Lahn valley a Roman town begun about 4 BC, with a forum and a gilded equestrian statue of Augustus, was abandoned unfinished; Dio describes cities being founded and Germans learning to hold markets (56.18.2).

In AD 7 Publius Quinctilius Varus took command; Dio says he exacted money as from subjects (56.18.3). Arminius, a Cheruscan noble with Roman citizenship and equestrian rank (Velleius 2.118.2), led the conspiracy. In autumn AD 9 Varus, marching from summer camp to deal with a reported rising, was caught in forest and bog; he killed himself, and his head reached Augustus by way of Maroboduus (2.119.5). Velleius counts three legions, three alae and six cohorts lost (2.117.1); Suetonius, three legions with the commander, his legates and all the auxiliaries (Augustus 23.1). Reckoning from paper strengths, Michael McNally (Teutoburg Forest AD 9, 2011) puts Varus' force at about 17,000 soldiers and 3,800 servants. The legions were the Seventeenth, Eighteenth and Nineteenth; the cenotaph of Marcus Caelius at Xanten commemorates a centurion of the Eighteenth who fell in the Varian war (CIL XIII 8648).

Augustus, Suetonius says, left hair and beard uncut for months and struck his head against a door, crying Quintili Vare, legiones redde, "Quintilius Varus, give back the legions" (Augustus 23.2). Dio adds conscription by lot, the enrolment of veterans and freedmen, and the German bodyguard sent away to islands (56.23.2–4); Tiberius was sent back to Germany (Velleius 2.120.1). An empire that had not stopped at the shore of Ocean, Florus wrote, stopped at the bank of the Rhine (2.30). Germanicus' campaigns of AD 14–16 are module 7.1.

Where sources disagree. Velleius has the army trapped by forests, marshes and ambush (2.119.2), and Dio a running fight of several days through rain and broken country (56.19–22). Florus instead has the Germans fall on an unsuspecting camp while Varus summoned litigants to his tribunal (2.30), which suits his theme of a governor playing judge. Tacitus' account of the field, a first camp built by three legions and then a half-ruined rampart where the remnant stood (Annals 1.61), supports a battle on the move.

In 1987 Tony Clunn, a British officer with a metal detector, found Roman coins at Kalkriese, north of Osnabrück, where Mommsen had placed the battle in 1885. Excavation in the narrow passage between the Kalkrieser Berg and the Great Bog has produced a turf wall, a silvered cavalry face mask, an almost complete segmented cuirass, pits of human and mule bones buried some years after death, and coins that end in the first years AD, some countermarked VAR.

Where sources disagree. Most specialists accept Kalkriese as part of the Varian battlefield. Reinhard Wolters argued that the coins cannot exclude a later date, since bronze circulating on the lower Rhine was old stock, and proposed Caecina's fight at the pontes longi in AD 15 (Tacitus, Annals 1.63–68); David Wigg-Wolf replied that the profile of the coin finds separates a Varian horizon from a Germanicus horizon, and Kalkriese belongs to the first. The turf wall, long read as a German ambush rampart, has been re-examined since 2016 as possibly a Roman emergency camp.

Client kings and the provinces of the Senate and of Caesar

Suetonius says Augustus restored kingdoms or gave them to other foreigners, and treated all the kings as membra partisque imperii, limbs and parts of the empire (Augustus 48). Tacitus speaks of an old Roman habit of using even kings as instruments of servitude (Agricola 14). Herod, made king of Judaea by the Senate in 40 BC, was confirmed by Octavian at Rhodes in 30 (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 15.187–201), built Caesarea with a temple of Rome and Augustus, and executed three sons; Augustus reportedly said it was better to be Herod's pig than his son (Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.4.11). After his death in 4 BC the kingdom was divided, and in AD 6 Judaea became a province under an equestrian prefect (Jewish Antiquities 18.1–2). Galatia was annexed when its king Amyntas died in 25 BC (Dio 53.26.3). Kings cost no legions and were provinces in waiting.

Module 6.1 treats the division of January 27 BC as a constitutional act; this is how it worked. The people's provinces, Africa, Asia, Achaea, Macedonia, Sicily, Baetica and others (Dio 53.12), went by lot to former magistrates for a year, ex-consuls to Africa and Asia and ex-praetors elsewhere, all styled proconsul and, once Illyricum passed to Caesar in 11 BC (Dio 54.34.4), without legions outside Africa. Caesar's provinces, the rest of Spain, the Gauls, Syria and later conquests, went to senators of his choice, legati Augusti pro praetore, who served at his pleasure and commanded the legions, while equestrian procurators handled his revenues. Suetonius' reason is practical: Augustus kept the provinces that annual governors could not safely hold (Augustus 47). The line was no wall. The Cyrene edicts of 7/6–4 BC show Augustus instructing the proconsul of a public province on juries and extortion, and Fergus Millar ("The Emperor, the Senate and the Provinces", 1966) argued that communities in both kinds of province dealt directly with the emperor. The Republican governor is module 4.4; later government, module 7.5.

The Res Gestae's map of the world

Chapters 26–33 of the Res Gestae, copied in Latin and Greek at Ancyra in annexed Galatia, are a tour of the world. They open with the claim that Augustus extended the boundaries of every province bordering peoples not subject to Rome (26.1), then go west and north: Gaul, Spain and Germany to the mouth of the Elbe pacified, the Alps pacified without unjust war, a fleet sent to the Cimbri (26.2–4). Then south to Ethiopia and Arabia (26.5), east to Egypt, Armenia and the recovered provinces (27), and on to colonies (28), standards (29) and the Danube (30). The outer ring comes last: Indian embassies never before seen with a Roman general (31), suppliant kings, two of them British (32), and kings given to the Parthians and Medes (33).

The map has no frontier. Power shades outward from provinces to kings to peoples seeking friendship, each grade an acknowledgement of the princeps. It is also selective: Germany pacified to the Elbe stands in a text finished five years after Varus, and Aelius Gallus' march, which his friend Strabo admits failed (16.4.22–24), appears as an advance. Claude Nicolet (Space, Geography, and Politics in the Early Roman Empire, 1991) set the text beside the census and Agrippa's map of the world in a Roman portico (Pliny, Natural History 3.17), and argued that the regime made geographical knowledge an instrument of rule.

Where sources disagree. Module 0.2 sets out the general quarrel over Roman frontiers. For Augustus it turns on intent. Edward Luttwak (The Grand Strategy of the Roman Empire, 1976) read the Julio-Claudian empire as a design, client kings absorbing lesser threats while concentrated legions served as a striking force; Benjamin Isaac and C. R. Whittaker, whose books module 0.2 cites, denied any such doctrine. The Res Gestae, in which boundaries exist to be extended (26.1, 30.1), and a halt that followed Varus rather than a plan, suit the critics better.

Self-test

  1. What does Jupiter promise at Aeneid 1.278–279, and how does Tacitus' report of Augustus' last advice qualify it?
    Answer

    Empire without bounds of space or time. Tacitus says Augustus' summary of the empire ended with advice to keep it within its limits, adding that it was uncertain whether from fear or jealousy (Annals 1.11.4); Dio's claim that he always practised this (56.33.5–6) is contradicted by the conquests of the reign.

  2. How did Augustus turn the armies of the civil wars into a standing army, and what does Suetonius' detail about commilitones show?
    Answer

    He discharged more than 300,000 of some 500,000 men who served under his oath, paying for land and cash bounties (Res Gestae 3.3, 16), and kept the rest as a permanent, paid, fixed-term force in the provinces. Dropping "fellow-soldiers" for "soldiers" (Augustus 25.1) marks the shift from a general's partisans to an emperor's servants.

  3. Where does the figure of twenty-eight legions come from, and why is it not certain?
    Answer

    Tacitus counts twenty-five in AD 23 (Annals 4.5); adding the three lost with Varus, whose numbers were never reused, gives twenty-eight. Dio's figure for AD 5, twenty-three or twenty-five (55.23.2), leaves open whether legions were raised in the crises of AD 6–9.

  4. What did a legionary serve and receive after AD 5, and how was his bounty funded?
    Answer

    Twenty years, pay of 225 denarii a year (the ten asses a day of Annals 1.17) and 12,000 sesterces on discharge (Dio 55.23.1). The military treasury of AD 6 began with 170 million sesterces from Augustus (Res Gestae 17.2) and lived on a five per cent inheritance tax (Dio 55.25.5) and a one per cent sales tax (Annals 1.78).

  5. Why was Egypt governed by an equestrian prefect and closed to senators?
    Answer

    Whoever held Egypt, with its legions and grain, could starve Italy (Tacitus, Annals 2.59), so it went to a knight who depended on Augustus and could not aspire to rule. Even so, Cornelius Gallus claimed too much glory and was destroyed in 26 BC (Dio 53.23).

  6. How were the Parthian standards recovered in 20 BC, and how was the event represented?
    Answer

    By negotiation with Phraates IV, backed by Augustus' presence in the East and Tiberius' army in Armenia, without a battle. Coins with a kneeling Parthian, Horace's king on his knees (Epistles 1.12.27–28), the Res Gestae's "compelled" (29.2) and the Prima Porta breastplate turned it into a submission within a cosmic order.

  7. What did Rome lose with Varus according to Velleius and Suetonius, and how did Augustus respond?
    Answer

    Velleius: three legions, three alae and six cohorts (2.117.1); Suetonius: three legions with the commander, legates and all the auxiliaries (Augustus 23.1). Augustus mourned publicly, conscripted by lot, enrolled veterans and freedmen, sent away his German guard (Dio 56.23) and sent Tiberius to the Rhine.

  8. What links Kalkriese to AD 9, and what was Wolters' objection?
    Answer

    Military equipment, bone pits of men and mules, and coins that end in the first years AD, some countermarked VAR. Wolters argued that old bronze stock could not exclude AD 15 and proposed Caecina's battle at the pontes longi (Annals 1.63–68); Wigg-Wolf answered that the coin profile is Varian.

  9. How did the provinces of the people and of Caesar differ in administration, and where did client kings fit?
    Answer

    Proconsuls chosen by lot for a year, mostly without legions, against legates chosen by Augustus who served at his pleasure and commanded the legions, with equestrian procurators and prefects (Suetonius, Augustus 47). Kings such as Herod governed at no cost to Rome and were replaced by provinces when convenient, as in Galatia in 25 BC and Judaea in AD 6.

  10. What is the structure of the map in Res Gestae 26–33, and what does it leave out?
    Answer

    It moves from provinces whose boundaries were extended, through conquests west, north, south and east, to colonies and standards, then to an outer ring of embassies, suppliant kings and kings given to Parthia and Media: graded acknowledgement with no frontier. It claims Germany pacified to the Elbe after Varus and presents Aelius Gallus' failed Arabian march as an advance.

Carry forward

  1. Augustan ideology promised empire without end while the paid army and its treasury set a finite scale; the advice of AD 14 records the moment the two met, and every later emperor who annexed or withdrew was choosing between them.
  2. Augustus made the army permanent, salaried and bound to the princeps, with its pensions paid from taxes on citizens; from now on whoever paid and commanded the legions and the guard held the state, which is the question the Julio-Claudians and their successors keep answering.
  3. Roman power was graded, not bounded: provinces of the people and of Caesar, client kingdoms waiting to be annexed, and peoples who sent embassies; the Rhine after Varus was where expansion stopped, not a line anyone had drawn in advance.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Augustan empire, its army and its frontiers. Cover: Jupiter's promise of 'empire without end' (Aeneid 1.279) against Augustus' advice to keep the empire within its limits (Tacitus, Annals 1.11); the professional army Augustus created (twenty-eight legions, the auxiliaries, the praetorian guard, the military treasury and the terms of service); the conquest of north-west Spain, the Alps and the Danube lands; Egypt as the emperor's personal province; the recovery of the Parthian standards in 20 BC and the Prima Porta breastplate; Germany, Drusus and Tiberius, and the loss of three legions with Varus in AD 9, with the battlefield at Kalkriese; client kings such as Herod; the provinces of the Senate and of Caesar; and the Res Gestae's map of the world. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 7 · The Principate, AD 14 to 235 · 7.1 · 3,363 words

The Julio-Claudians

The sources reign by reignTiberius: accession, mutiny and GermanicusTiberius: Sejanus, Capri and the treason trialsGaius Caligula: the first years and the turnClaudius: the guard's emperorNero: the good years and the murder of AgrippinaNero: Boudica, the fire and the Golden HouseNero: conspiracy, the Greek tour and the endWhen the princeps is badSelf-testCarry forward

The sources reign by reign

Module 0.1 introduces Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio. For the four reigns after Augustus none is complete, and each emperor's reputation shifts with whichever survives. Tacitus wrote the Annals early in the second century, year by year and from the Senate's benches; Suetonius arranged each life by topic, virtues before vices; Dio, a senator of the early third century, survives in his own words, with gaps, to AD 46 and then only in Byzantine epitome.

ReignTacitus, AnnalsDioOther early witnesses
Tiberius, 14–37books 1–6; the fall of Sejanus lostbooks 57–58Velleius 2.124–131 (AD 30); the decree on Piso
Gaius, 37–41lostbook 59Philo; Seneca; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18–19
Claudius, 41–54books 11–12, from 47book 60the Lyon tablet; the letter to the Alexandrians; Seneca

Tiberius: accession, mutiny and Germanicus

Power came before the vote. On Augustus' death Tiberius gave the watchword to the praetorians as imperator and wrote to the armies as princeps (Tacitus, Annals 1.7.5); only then did he hesitate before the Senate over accepting the whole (1.11–13), holding, Suetonius has him say, a wolf by the ears (Tiberius 25.1). Velleius, who had served under him, makes the reluctance sincere (2.124.2); Tacitus reads it as a mask, and Dio opens his book on a man who never said what he wanted (57.1).

The armies tested the reign at once. The Pannonian legions mutinied over pay and service (module 6.4 quotes their complaints, 1.17) and were calmed by Tiberius' son Drusus (1.16–30). The four legions of the lower Rhine offered the empire to their commander Germanicus, Tiberius' nephew and adopted son, who threatened to kill himself rather than break faith, bought peace with a letter written as if from Tiberius, and let the loyal soldiers butcher the ringleaders (1.31–49). His small son Gaius, the soldiers' pet, was nicknamed Caligula for his boots (1.41).

Germanicus then took the army across the Rhine for three seasons, in 16 with a fleet Tacitus puts at a thousand ships (2.6). He recovered two of Varus' three eagles (1.60, 2.25), buried the bones of Varus' legions, which Tiberius thought improper for an augur (1.61–62), and beat Arminius at Idistaviso (2.16–18). But Caecina's army was nearly lost at the pontes longi in 15 (1.63–68; module 6.4 asks whether Kalkriese is that battle), and a North Sea storm wrecked the fleet (2.23–24). Tiberius recalled him, writing that Germany could be left to its own quarrels (2.26), and gave him a triumph in 17. Sent east with authority over every governor there (2.43), Germanicus quarrelled with Gnaeus Piso, governor of Syria, and died at Antioch in 19, sure he had been poisoned; lead curse tablets bearing his name were found in his house (2.69–73; module 2.4). Piso, tried before the Senate, killed himself before the verdict (3.15).

Where sources disagree. Suetonius reports the belief that Germanicus died by Tiberius' design and Piso's agency (Caligula 2); Tacitus lets the rumour stand while admitting that the poisoning charge failed (Annals 3.14.1). The Senate's own decree, dated 10 December 20 and found near Seville, names Piso as the cause of the death only in Germanicus' own testimony, condemns Piso for leaving his province and trying to retake it by force, and spares his wife Plancina at Livia's request, as Tacitus reports (3.17).

Tiberius: Sejanus, Capri and the treason trials

Tacitus makes AD 23 the turn, when fortune began to make trouble and Tiberius to rage or lend his strength to others' rage (4.1). The agent was Sejanus, an equestrian from Volsinii and prefect of the guard, who gathered its cohorts into a single camp (4.2). Drusus, Tiberius' heir, died that year; in 31 Sejanus' divorced wife revealed that Sejanus and Drusus' wife Livilla had poisoned him (4.3, 4.11). Sejanus persuaded Tiberius to live away from Rome (4.41), and from 27 the emperor stayed on Capri (4.67). After Livia's death in 29 Germanicus' widow Agrippina and her two elder sons were destroyed. In 31 Sejanus was consul with Tiberius; on 18 October a long letter from Capri was read in the Senate (Juvenal 10.71), the guard having passed to Macro, and Sejanus was executed that day (Dio 58.9–11). Velleius, publishing in 30, had praised him as Tiberius' tireless helper (2.127–128); Valerius Maximus, soon after, cursed an unnamed would-be parricide (9.11.ext.4; module 3.2).

Where sources disagree. Tiberius wrote that he punished Sejanus for raging against Germanicus' children (Suetonius, Tiberius 61.1); Josephus has Antonia warn him of a plot (Jewish Antiquities 18.181–182); Dio's Sejanus reaches for the throne. Edward Champlin (Tiberius and His Age, 2024) draws an equestrian who modelled himself on Agrippa and may have been seen as a serious candidate for the succession. Whether there was a conspiracy is uncertain.

The instrument of fear was the law of maiestas, which Augustus had stretched from deeds to words and writings (1.72.3). With no public prosecutor, informers brought charges for a share of the estate, "a breed of men invented for the public ruin" (4.30.3). In 25 the historian Cremutius Cordus, accused of praising Brutus and Cassius, starved himself and his books were burned; punishing talent, Tacitus answers, increases its authority (4.34–35). Tacitus also shows Tiberius quashing early charges (1.73) and muttering at the senators, "men ready for slavery" (3.65.3). After 31 the trials became a massacre (6.19).

Capri is Suetonius' showpiece of sexual vice (Tiberius 43–45); Tacitus is vaguer (6.1). Champlin calls these stories incoherent fictions, probably by one skilled writer who hated Tiberius, and finds behind them a learned emperor absorbed in astrology and myth. Tiberius died at Misenum in March 37: smothered by Macro in Tacitus (6.50), by Gaius and Macro in Dio (58.28), by one of several means in Suetonius (Tiberius 73). Tacitus' obituary traces stages of declining concealment until, fear and shame gone, he followed only his own nature (6.51).

Gaius Caligula: the first years and the turn

Gaius, Germanicus' last surviving son, was twenty-four, and the Senate set aside Tiberius' will, which had made Tiberius' grandson Gemellus joint heir (Suetonius, Caligula 14.1). Suetonius counts more than 160,000 victims sacrificed for joy in under three months (14.1); exiles were recalled, accounts published, Cordus' books allowed back (15–16). Philo remembers seven golden months ended by a grave illness in autumn 37 (Embassy to Gaius 8–21). Within a year Gemellus had been killed and Macro forced to suicide (Dio 59.8–10).

Dio dates the open break to 39, when Gaius praised Tiberius in the Senate, read out the senators' own attacks on Tiberius' victims from papers he had claimed to burn, and restored treason charges (59.16); a plot by the commander in Upper Germany and Gaius' brother-in-law followed (59.22). Then come the stories of madness: the seashells gathered as spoils of Ocean (Suetonius, Caligula 46), incest with his sisters (24), the horse he is said to have meant to make consul (55.3; Dio 59.14.7), a temple to his own divinity (Caligula 22). Suetonius marks the turn in his own text: so much for the princeps, the rest must be told of a monster (22.1). He supplies causes too, epilepsy, insomnia and a love potion (50); Seneca uses the cruelties as moral examples (On Anger 3.18–19).
