Where sources disagree. Philo places the change in the illness of 37, Dio in the quarrel of 39. Arther Ferrill (1991) took the madness as real. Anthony Barrett (Caligula: The Corruption of Power, 1989; revised as Caligula: The Abuse of Power, 2015) denies insanity and finds a capable young man so absorbed in his own importance that he lost all sense of moral responsibility. Aloys Winterling (Caligula, 2003) argues that from 39 Gaius refused the double-speak by which senators treated a monarch as a fellow citizen while flattering him as a god: he took the flattery literally, and the horse insulted the Senate.

The Jews of Alexandria and Philo's embassy

In 38 the Greek crowd of Alexandria mocked the Jewish king Agrippa I, set up images of Gaius in the synagogues, and the prefect Flaccus declared the Jews foreigners and aliens and penned them into one quarter, where they were looted and killed (Philo, Against Flaccus 25–72). Both communities sent embassies, the Jewish one led by the aged Philo (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.257–260). Gaius heard the Jews while touring the gardens of Maecenas and Lamia, ordering refurbishments, asked why they did not eat pork, and dismissed them as more unfortunate than wicked for not believing him a god (Embassy to Gaius 349–367). Meanwhile he had ordered his statue set up in the Temple at Jerusalem; the legate of Syria delayed, Agrippa interceded, and Gaius' death ended the danger (Embassy 188–348; Jewish Antiquities 18.261–309). Claudius' letter of 41, preserved on papyrus (P.Lond. 1912), told the Greeks to leave Jewish worship alone and the Jews not to seek more than they had in a city not their own.

Where sources disagree. Josephus quotes an edict of Claudius granting Alexandria's Jews civic rights equal to the Greeks' from the earliest times (Jewish Antiquities 19.280–285). The papyrus, untouched by copyists, says a city not their own and bars them from the gymnasium's games. How far the Jews sought full citizenship, rather than security as a community, is still argued.

Gaius was killed in a palace passage on 24 January 41 by guard officers led by Cassius Chaerea, whom he had mocked with obscene watchwords (Suetonius, Caligula 56–58; Dio 59.29). Josephus gives the fullest narrative (Jewish Antiquities 19.1–273).

Claudius: the guard's emperor

While the consuls held the Capitol and the Senate debated liberty (Suetonius, Claudius 10.3; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 19.158–184), a soldier found Germanicus' brother Claudius hiding behind a curtain in the palace and the guard took him to its camp (Claudius 10.1–2). He promised each guardsman 15,000 sesterces in Suetonius' figure, the first Caesar to buy the soldiers' loyalty (10.4), 5,000 drachmas in Josephus' (19.247). The Senate, without troops, voted the powers. The guard chose; the Senate ratified.

Claudius was fifty, lame and stammering, an antiquarian who had written Etruscan and Carthaginian histories (Claudius 30, 42), and for Suetonius the servant of his wives and freedmen (29.1). Freedmen ran the secretariats, Narcissus the correspondence and Pallas the accounts (28); module 7.5 asks how much of a bureaucracy this was. In 43 Aulus Plautius invaded Britain, and Claudius came for sixteen days, with elephants, to take the surrender of Camulodunum (Dio 60.19–23). His arch claimed, on the usual restoration, eleven kings surrendered without loss (CIL VI 920), and his son became Britannicus.

Tacitus' Claudius, from book 11, is a court drama of wives. In 48 Messalina went through a public marriage with the consul designate Gaius Silius; Narcissus stampeded Claudius into having her killed, and the emperor, told at dinner, called for more wine (11.26–38). Tacitus concedes the tale will seem fabulous (11.27). In 49 Claudius married his niece Agrippina (12.5–7), who had Seneca recalled (12.8), her son adopted as Nero (12.25) and Burrus put over the guard (12.42). Claudius died in October 54.

Where sources disagree. Tacitus has Agrippina poison a dish of mushrooms (12.66–67); Pliny the Elder names Agrippina's mushroom (Natural History 22.92); Suetonius says all agree on poison but not on where or by whom (Claudius 44.2); Josephus says only that some said so (Jewish Antiquities 20.148). Seneca's satire has him die listening to comic actors. A sick man of sixty-three could die naturally; the case rests on motive, with Britannicus near manhood.

The Lyon tablet

In 48, as censor, Claudius proposed that the nobles of Gallia Comata be allowed to hold magistracies and so enter the Senate. The bronze from Lyon (CIL XIII 1668) preserves part of the speech; module 1.5 uses it for Mastarna, and module 0.1 sets it beside Tacitus' version. The argument is an antiquarian's. Outsiders have always ruled Rome: the Sabine Numa, Tarquinius Priscus, son of a Corinthian, Servius the captive's son or Etruscan Mastarna. The constitution has always changed, from kings to consuls, dictators, tribunes and decemvirs. Augustus and Tiberius admitted the best men of the colonies and towns, and Vienne already sends senators; against Caesar's ten years of war Gaul sets a hundred years of loyalty. Tacitus reports the objection that these were heirs of the Gauls who had besieged Caesar at Alesia (11.23); his Claudius answers more sharply that Athens and Sparta fell because they treated the conquered as aliens, Romulus made enemies citizens on the same day, and what is now defended by precedent will itself become precedent (11.24).

Seneca's satire on the deification

Claudius was made a god, and the senators laughed when Nero's funeral speech, written by Seneca, praised his foresight (Annals 13.3). Seneca also wrote the satire Dio calls the Apocolocyntosis, the "pumpkinification" (60.35.3). It sends Claudius limping to heaven, where Augustus lists his murders to the gods (10–11), then to the underworld, where he is convicted without a hearing, as he had convicted others, and handed to a freedman as a law clerk (14–15). Every joke is the senatorial case: rule by freedmen and wives, trials unheard, senators killed. Seneca's life is deep dive module 13.5.

Nero: the good years and the murder of Agrippina

Nero was sixteen at his accession. His first speech to the Senate, written by Seneca according to Dio (61.3.1), promised no more trials behind closed doors and a household kept apart from the state (Annals 13.4). Asked to sign a death warrant, he wished he had never learned to write (Suetonius, Nero 10.2); in 58 he proposed abolishing the indirect taxes (Annals 13.50). Trajan was later said to have rated five years of Nero above any emperor's (Aurelius Victor, Caesares 5.2). Yet Britannicus was poisoned in 55 (13.15–17; module 1.4).

The coins chart Agrippina's fall: in 54 her head faces her son's, in 55 it sits behind his. In March 59 Nero sent her home from Baiae in a boat built to collapse; she swam ashore, and the fleet prefect came to her villa to kill her (14.1–8). Nero's letter to the Senate accused her of plotting; Thrasea Paetus walked out (14.10–12), the first gesture of a resistance that deep dive module 13.4 follows to his death in 66.

Where sources disagree. Tacitus makes Poppaea's taunts the motive (14.1) and names his authorities on the rumoured incest, Cluvius Rufus blaming Agrippina and Fabius Rusticus Nero (14.2). Barrett (Agrippina, 1996) finds the Poppaea motive weak, since Nero married her only in 62, and argues that Agrippina remained a force to the end and that the good years coincided with her influence. Champlin (Nero, 2003) shows Nero later singing Orestes on stage (Suetonius, Nero 21.3), turning the crime into tragedy.

Nero: Boudica, the fire and the Golden House

In Britain in 60 or 61 Prasutagus, king of the Iceni, died leaving Nero co-heir with his two daughters. The procurator's men plundered the kingdom, flogged his widow Boudica and raped the daughters, and the Trinovantes, dispossessed by the veterans of Camulodunum, joined the rising (Annals 14.31). Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium were burned, about 70,000 citizens and allies dying by Tacitus' figure (14.33), 80,000 by Dio's (62.1.1). Suetonius Paullinus won the final battle; Tacitus gives a little under 80,000 British dead against about 400 Roman, and has Boudica take poison (14.37). Module 7.5 takes the revolt as a limit of the system.

Where sources disagree. Tacitus' Agricola makes the rising a general revolt against occupation (15–16), the Annals a reaction to particular outrages (14.31). Dio, in epitome, adds that Seneca had called in forty million sesterces of loans at once (62.2.1), gives Boudica a long speech and an omen from a released hare, and has her die of illness (62.12.6).

On 19 July 64 fire broke out by the Circus Maximus and burned for six days; of Rome's fourteen regions three were levelled and seven gutted (Annals 15.38–40). Nero opened his gardens to the homeless, cut the price of grain (15.39), and rebuilt with wider streets, lower blocks and fireproof stone (15.43). To end the rumour of his guilt he punished the Christians, which module 2.5 examines with Annals 15.44.

Where sources disagree. Tacitus leaves open whether the fire was chance or the emperor's malice, since writers gave both (15.38.1), and reports only a rumour that Nero sang of Troy's fall (15.39.3). Suetonius (Nero 38) and Dio (62.16–18) make him the arsonist, and Pliny the Elder, who lived through it, mentions the fires with which Nero burned the city (Natural History 17.5). Champlin argues for Nero's guilt; Barrett (Rome Is Burning, 2020) judges the origin undetermined and the guilt mostly legend.

On the cleared ground rose the Golden House. Suetonius describes a colossal statue of Nero 120 feet high, a mile-long portico, a lake like a sea, fields and woods, and Nero saying he could at last live like a human being (Nero 31); Tacitus describes landscapes contrived by its architects Severus and Celer (15.42); Martial, under the Flavians who built over it, says one house had filled the city (On the Spectacles 2). A wing survives under Trajan's baths; Roman painting is module 10.3. Champlin reads it as public in spirit, a seaside villa brought into the city for the people.

Nero: conspiracy, the Greek tour and the end

In 62 Burrus died, Tigellinus took the guard, Seneca withdrew, Octavia was divorced and killed, and the treason law returned (Annals 14.48–64). In 65 a conspiracy around Gaius Calpurnius Piso was betrayed; the guard tribune Subrius Flavus told Nero he had begun to hate him when he became the murderer of his mother and wife, a charioteer, an actor and an arsonist (15.67). Seneca was ordered to die (15.60–64; deep dive module 13.5), and the poet Lucan too (15.70; module 10.2). In 66 Thrasea followed (16.21–35), and there the Annals break off.

In 66–67 Nero toured Greece, competing at festivals crowded into one year; at Olympia he fell from his chariot and was crowned anyway (Suetonius, Nero 23–24). At the Isthmus he proclaimed the province free (IG VII 2713), a gift Vespasian revoked (Greek module 7.4). The general Corbulo, summoned to Greece and ordered to die, said only that he deserved it (Dio 63.17.5–6).

In March 68 Vindex, governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, rose, and Galba in Spain answered his call (Suetonius, Galba 9–10); module 7.2 begins with Galba's reign. The guard went over to Galba, and the Senate declared Nero a public enemy (Nero 49.2) and recognised Galba (Plutarch, Galba 7.1). Nero fled to a freedman's villa, lamented what an artist was dying in him, and with his secretary's help stabbed himself in June 68 (49). Flowers were laid on his tomb for years, and false Neros appeared in the East (57). Champlin's Nero starts from that afterlife: a showman whose popularity with the plebs and the Greeks the senatorial tradition buried.

When the princeps is bad

The Principate had no way to remove a bad emperor. His powers were voted for life, and the Senate could act only when armed men had decided, as it did against Nero once the guard deserted him. Gaius died by his guard officers, Claudius perhaps by his wife, Nero when governors and guard abandoned him; none of it touched the system. Government continued: Britain was conquered under Claudius, Corbulo fought for Armenia under Nero, and Tacitus wrote that there can be great men even under bad emperors (Agricola 42.4). "Bad" was also a senator's measure, applied to emperors who killed senators, while the plebs mourned Nero. Tacitus gives a Roman general the provincial lesson: bear the greed of rulers as you bear barren years and floods (Histories 4.74). He gives Galba the dynastic one, adoption of the best man in place of inheritance (Histories 1.16), the remedy module 7.3 follows. Winterling's Gaius suggests a structural answer: the Principate ran on the pretence that the monarch was a citizen, and the emperors remembered as monsters were those who stopped pretending.

Self-test

  1. What had Tiberius done before the Senate debated his position in AD 14, and how do Velleius and Tacitus read his hesitation?
    Answer

    He had given the watchword to the praetorians as imperator and written to the armies as princeps (Annals 1.7.5), so the vote ratified power already held. Velleius, his officer and admirer, takes the reluctance as sincere (2.124.2); Tacitus reads it as a mask (1.11–13).

  2. Why did Tiberius recall Germanicus in 16, and what does the Senate's decree on Piso add to the story of his death?
    Answer

    Tiberius wrote that Germany could be left to its quarrels (Annals 2.26), after heavy losses at the pontes longi and in the North Sea storm. The decree of December 20 condemns Piso for leaving his province and trying to retake it by force, names Piso as the cause of the death only in Germanicus' own testimony, and records Livia's protection of Plancina, matching Tacitus' admission that the poisoning charge failed (3.14.1, 3.17).

  3. How did Sejanus rise and fall, and why is his motive uncertain?
    Answer

    As prefect he concentrated the guard in one camp (Annals 4.2), induced Tiberius to withdraw to Capri, and was destroyed by a letter read in the Senate on 18 October 31 after the guard had passed to Macro (Dio 58.9–11). Tacitus' account is lost; Tiberius' memoir (Suetonius, Tiberius 61.1), Josephus' story of Antonia's warning and Dio give different motives, and Champlin sees a credible successor rather than a usurper.

  4. How did a treason trial work under Tiberius, and what does the case of Cremutius Cordus show?
    Answer

    Maiestas now covered words and writings (Annals 1.72.3), and with no public prosecutor informers brought charges for a share of the estate (4.30). Cordus, accused in 25 of praising Brutus and Cassius, starved himself and his books were burned; Tacitus comments that punishing talent increases its authority (4.34–35).

  5. Where do Philo, Dio and Suetonius place the change in Gaius, and how do Barrett and Winterling explain his conduct?
    Answer

    Philo in the illness of autumn 37 (Embassy to Gaius 14–21), Dio in the quarrel with the Senate in 39 (59.16); Suetonius gives no date but turns to the "monster" at Caligula 22.1 and blames disease and a potion (50). Barrett finds a sane autocrat without moral responsibility; Winterling a rational ruler who exposed the Senate's double-speak by taking its flattery literally.

  6. What happened to the Jews of Alexandria in 38, and what did Claudius' letter of 41 decide?
    Answer

    Images of Gaius were set up in the synagogues and Flaccus declared the Jews aliens, confining them to one quarter amid killing and looting (Philo, Against Flaccus 25–72). Claudius' letter (P.Lond. 1912) told the Greeks to respect Jewish worship and the Jews to seek no more in a city not their own, which contradicts Josephus' version of his edict (Jewish Antiquities 19.280–285).

  7. How did Claudius become emperor, and what precedent did it set?
    Answer

    Soldiers found him in the palace after Gaius' murder and took him to the praetorian camp, where he promised a donative (15,000 sesterces a man in Suetonius, Claudius 10.4; 5,000 drachmas in Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 19.247) while the Senate debated liberty. The Senate then voted him the powers: the guard could make an emperor and the Senate would ratify.

  8. What were the arguments of Claudius' speech on the Gallic nobles, and how did Tacitus rework them?
    Answer

    The bronze argues from history: Rome's kings were outsiders, its constitution always changed, Augustus and Tiberius admitted provincial elites, and Gaul had been loyal a hundred years (CIL XIII 1668). Tacitus compresses this, adds Athens and Sparta, ruined by excluding the conquered, and ends that today's innovation will become precedent (Annals 11.24).

  9. What does Seneca's Apocolocyntosis accuse Claudius of, and why is its authorship awkward?
    Answer

    Of rule by freedmen and wives, of judging without a hearing, and of killing senators and kin, which Augustus lists in the gods' debate (10–11); he is convicted unheard and made a freedman's law clerk (14–15). Seneca also wrote the funeral speech in Claudius' praise that made the Senate laugh (Annals 13.3).

  10. Who blames Nero for the fire of 64, who does not, and where do Champlin and Barrett stand?
    Answer

    Suetonius (Nero 38), Dio (62.16–18) and Pliny the Elder (Natural History 17.5) blame him; Tacitus says writers gave both chance and malice (Annals 15.38.1). Champlin (2003) argues for Nero's guilt; Barrett (2020) thinks the origin undetermined and the guilt mostly legend.

Carry forward

  1. The Senate voted the powers, but the guard, the armies and the family chose the man: Claudius was made in the praetorian camp and Nero unmade by governors and the guard, and every succession after 68 turns on the same fact.
  2. Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio wrote from the Senate's injuries, generations later; documents (the Piso decree, the Lyon tablet, Claudius' letter), contemporaries (Velleius, Philo, Seneca) and the modern revisions (Barrett, Champlin, Winterling) show competence, popularity or calculation behind the monsters, so read every portrait for whom the emperor harmed.
  3. A bad princeps could be removed only by murder or rebellion, yet the empire kept being governed; the age's answers, Seneca's education of the prince, Tacitus' endurance as of bad weather and Galba's choice by adoption, frame the politics of the next century.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Julio-Claudian emperors after Augustus, AD 14 to 68. Cover: Tiberius (Germanicus, Sejanus, Capri, the treason trials); Gaius Caligula (the first years and the turn, the stories of madness, the Jews of Alexandria and Philo's embassy, the assassination); Claudius (made emperor by the guard, the freedmen, the conquest of Britain, Messalina and Agrippina, the Lyon tablet, Seneca's satire on his deification); and Nero (the good first years, Agrippina's murder, the fire of 64 and the Christians, the Golden House, Boudica, the Pisonian conspiracy and the deaths of Seneca and Thrasea Paetus in outline (deep dive modules 13.5 and 13.4 take them further), the Greek tour, the end in 68). For each, compare Tacitus' Annals, Suetonius and Cassius Dio, and show where the modern revisions (Barrett, Champlin, Winterling) differ. End with the question these reigns pose: what the Principate does when the princeps is bad. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 7 · The Principate, AD 14 to 235 · 7.2 · 2,734 words

The year of four emperors and the Flavians

Galba and the secret of empireOtho, Vitellius and the burning of the CapitolThe law on Vespasian's powersThe Jewish War and the fall of JerusalemVespasian and TitusDomitian and the senatorial memory of terrorAgricola in BritainRehabilitating DomitianThe Flavian poetsSelf-testCarry forward

Galba and the secret of empire

Module 7.1 ends with Nero's death in June 68 and the Senate's recognition of Servius Sulpicius Galba, governor of Nearer Spain. The narrative rests on Tacitus' Histories (module 0.1), which survive only for 69–70; on Plutarch's Galba and Otho; on Suetonius; and on Dio in Byzantine epitome. For 69 the first three agree so closely that a lost common source is usually assumed.

Galba, an old noble of severe reputation, lost it within months. He refused the donative promised in his name: he chose his soldiers, he said, and did not buy them (Tacitus, Histories 1.5; Suetonius, Galba 16.1). On 1 January 69 the legions of Upper Germany refused their oath, and the next day Lower Germany hailed its governor, Aulus Vitellius (Histories 1.55–57). Galba adopted a young noble, Piso Licinianus. Marcus Salvius Otho, who had expected the honour, bought the praetorians instead, and on 15 January Galba and Piso were cut down in the Forum (1.41–43). All would have judged him capable of ruling, Tacitus says, had he not ruled (1.49).

evulgato imperii arcano, posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri.

"The secret of empire was out: an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome" (Histories 1.4). Galba was made in Spain, Vitellius on the Rhine, Vespasian in Egypt and Judaea; only Otho was made in the city, by the guard. Module 6.1 closes on a succession that rested only on the family and the soldiers' loyalty to it; 69 showed that any provincial army could decide.

Otho, Vitellius and the burning of the Capitol

Otho reigned three months. Vitellius' generals crossed the Alps and in April beat his army at the first battle of Bedriacum, near Cremona. Otho, his forces still intact, killed himself to end the bloodshed: by two deeds, one most shameful and one most noble, Tacitus says, he earned as much good fame as bad (Histories 2.50). Vitellius reached Rome in July, a glutton in Tacitus and Suetonius alike, and filled a new guard from his German legions.

On 1 July the prefect of Egypt, Tiberius Julius Alexander, swore his legions to Titus Flavius Vespasianus, commander against the Jewish revolt; Judaea and Syria followed (Histories 2.79–81). Vespasian came of a Sabine family without ancestral masks (Suetonius, Vespasian 1.1). The Danube legions joined him and Antonius Primus invaded Italy; in late October the Vitellians were broken near Cremona, and the city was sacked for four days (Histories 3.33).

In Rome Vitellius agreed to abdicate, then could not carry it through. Vespasian's brother Flavius Sabinus, prefect of the city, seized the Capitol with his followers and the young Domitian. On 19 December the Vitellians stormed it and the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest burned: for Tacitus the most lamentable and disgraceful crime since the city's foundation, committed with no foreign enemy at the gates (3.72). Sabinus was killed; Domitian escaped disguised as a worshipper of Isis (Suetonius, Domitian 1.2), a cult whose Flavian fortunes module 2.5 follows. Next day the Flavians fought their way in, and Vitellius was killed and thrown on the Gemonian steps (Histories 3.84–85). The Druids, Tacitus reports, read the fire as a sign that empire was passing to the peoples beyond the Alps (4.54).

The rebuilding began in June 70 on the old foundations (4.53). Vespasian carried rubble on his own neck and had copies sought of three thousand bronze tablets of laws and decrees lost in the fire (Suetonius, Vespasian 8.5).

Where sources disagree. Who lit the fire is unclear. Tacitus gives two versions: the attackers threw torches onto the roofs, or, the commoner report, the besieged fired the buildings to drive them back (Histories 3.71). Suetonius blames Vitellius' men, with Vitellius dining and watching from the palace (Vitellius 15.3). On Tacitus' commoner report, the dynasty that restored the Capitol rose through a fire its own partisans set.

The law on Vespasian's powers

With Vitellius dead, the Senate voted Vespasian "everything customary for emperors" (Histories 4.3), and an assembly made the decree law. Its end survives on a bronze tablet that Cola di Rienzo displayed in the Lateran in the 1340s as proof of the Roman people's lost sovereignty (ILS 244; CIL VI 930). Module 6.1 shows Augustus' powers voted piece by piece over decades; here the bundle arrives in one law. Its clauses allow Vespasian to make treaties; to convene the Senate and have its decrees passed; to have candidates he commends considered out of turn; to extend the pomerium; and to do whatever he judges in the interest of the state and the majesty of things divine and human, public and private. They also free him from the laws from which his predecessors were freed.

The precedents named are Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius only; Gaius, Nero and the emperors of 69 vanish. The last clause validates everything done by Vespasian or at his order before the law, as if by the people's command. He counted his reign from 1 July, the day of the Alexandrian oath (Suetonius, Vespasian 6.3), not from the Senate's vote. The law shows both faces of the Principate: the powers remain a legal bundle conferred by Senate and people, and the conferring follows the army's choice. Ulpian built on it: what pleases the emperor has the force of law, because by the law on his imperium the people confers on him all its own imperium and power (Digest 1.4.1).

Where sources disagree. Read alone, the discretionary clause looks like a blank cheque and the law like a new constitution for a family without Julio-Claudian blood. P. A. Brunt ("Lex de imperio Vespasiani", Journal of Roman Studies 1977) argued that its wording was inherited, probably from the grant to Gaius in 37, with prerogatives added since Claudius; that only the final clause may be new; and that it is the basis of the jurists' doctrine. Whether the lost opening conferred tribunician power and imperium is unknown.

The Jewish War and the fall of Jerusalem

The revolt began in 66, when the procurator Gessius Florus took seventeen talents from the Temple treasury (Josephus, Jewish War 2.293) and the Temple captain Eleazar son of Ananias stopped the sacrifices for the emperor, which Josephus calls the foundation of the war (2.409). The governor of Syria, Cestius Gallus, was routed at Beth Horon. Nero gave the war to Vespasian, who with his son Titus reduced Galilee in 67. At Jotapata the Galilean commander, the priest Joseph son of Matthias, surrendered and told Vespasian he would be emperor (3.399–408; Suetonius, Vespasian 5.6).

Titus besieged Jerusalem from the spring of 70 with four legions; the Temple burned in August and the upper city fell in September. Josephus gives 1,100,000 dead in the siege and 97,000 captives in the whole war (Jewish War 6.420), Tacitus 600,000 besieged (Histories 5.13): both more than the city could have held. Masada fell in 73 or 74 (Jewish War 7.252–406).

Josephus is almost the only narrative. Freed, he took the name Flavius and lived on a pension in Vespasian's former house (Life 423), and Titus signed the copies of the War for publication (Life 363). In his account the revolt is the work of brigands and tyrants, not of the nation or its priestly elite, and God has gone over to Rome. Tessa Rajak (Josephus: The Historian and His Society, 1983) reads him as the voice of that elite rather than a mere Flavian mouthpiece; Steve Mason stresses the irony and rhetoric of a work shaped for Roman readers.

Where sources disagree. Josephus has Titus resolve in council to spare the Temple and a soldier throw a firebrand unordered (Jewish War 6.236–266). Sulpicius Severus, about 400, has Titus urge its destruction to uproot the religion of Jews and Christians alike (Chronicle 2.30); Jacob Bernays (1861) argued that Severus drew on the lost part of Tacitus' Histories. T. D. Barnes ("The Fragments of Tacitus' Histories", 1977) accepted the passage as Tacitean; whether it records Titus' decision or Tacitus' reading of it is still argued.

In 71 Vespasian and Titus triumphed with the Temple's golden table and lampstand; Simon son of Gioras, a leader of the defence, was executed (Jewish War 7.123–157), and the vessels went into the new Temple of Peace (7.158–162). An arch in the Circus Maximus, of 80–81, claimed that Titus destroyed Jerusalem, which all before him had attacked in vain or never attempted (CIL VI 944): Pompey had taken it in 63 BC. The surviving Arch of Titus on the Sacred Way, dedicated to the deified Titus (CIL VI 945), shows the spoils carried in triumph and Titus crowned by Victory; module 10.3 reads it as art. Géza Alföldy's reconstruction (1995) of the Colosseum's dedication, from the dowel holes of its lost bronze letters, has it built from spoils (ex manubis), presumably this war's. The Temple tax diverted to Jupiter Capitolinus is module 2.5's.

Vespasian and Titus

An unexpected new emperor, Suetonius says, lacked authority and majesty, and they came to Vespasian at Alexandria when he healed a blind man and a lame man (Vespasian 7.2–3; Tacitus, Histories 4.81). In Rome he said forty thousand million sesterces were needed to set the state on its feet (Vespasian 16.3), raised taxes, and told Titus that money from the tax on urine did not smell (23.3). As censor in 73–74 he refilled the senatorial and equestrian orders from Italy and the provinces, and he gave Latin rights to all Spain (Pliny, Natural History 3.30), whose charters module 7.5 reads. Helvidius Priscus, who would not treat him as more than a private citizen, was exiled and killed (Vespasian 15), and philosophers were expelled (Dio 66.13); deep dive modules 13.4 and 13.6 take both further. His sons would succeed him, he told the Senate, or no one (Vespasian 25). He died in June 79, the first emperor followed by his own son.

Titus, his father's praetorian prefect, had been feared as another Nero and loved Queen Berenice, sister of Agrippa II, who lived with him on the Palatine from 75 (Dio 66.15). As emperor he sent her away, "he unwilling, she unwilling" (Suetonius, Titus 7.2), and ruled so mildly that Suetonius calls him the love and delight of the human race (1).

Within months Vesuvius buried Pompeii, Herculaneum and Stabiae. Pliny the Younger wrote two letters for Tacitus' Histories (Letters 6.16.1). In 6.16 his uncle, the elder Pliny, commander of the fleet at Misenum, sees a cloud shaped like an umbrella pine, turns a scholar's outing into a rescue, saying fortune favours the brave (6.16.11), and dies on the shore at Stabiae, his body later found intact (6.16.20). In 6.20 the seventeen-year-old nephew reads Livy at Misenum (6.20.5), then flees with his mother through a darkness like a closed room with the lamp out, among people who thought it the world's last, eternal night (6.20.14–15).

Where sources disagree. The oldest manuscript of Letters 6.16, the ninth-century Medicean, gives the ninth day before the Kalends of September, 24 August; other copies point to November. Autumn fruit and braziers at Pompeii, and a charcoal graffito found in 2018 dated 17 October without a year, have persuaded many to prefer 24 October. A coin naming Titus imperator for the fifteenth time is disputed evidence.

In 80 Titus dedicated the amphitheatre his father had begun on the drained lake of Nero's Golden House (Martial, On the Spectacles 2), with a hundred days of games in which Dio counts nine thousand animals killed (66.25); the games are module 9.4's. Titus died in September 81, aged forty-one.

Domitian and the senatorial memory of terror

Domitian reigned fifteen years, longer than anyone since Tiberius. From 85 he was censor for life and used the office on the Senate and on morals; module 2.3 tells how the chief Vestal Cornelia was buried alive. He raised legionary pay by a third, the first rise since Caesar's (Suetonius, Domitian 7.3; module 6.4). After a triumph over the Chatti in 83, two commanders died in Dacia (Domitian 6.1), and the peace of 89 paid King Decebalus subsidies. In January 89 Antonius Saturninus, governor of Upper Germany, rebelled at Mainz and was crushed within weeks.

The senatorial memory concentrates on 93–96. After Agricola's death, Tacitus writes, soldiers besieged the Senate house; Arulenus Rusticus and Herennius Senecio were killed for praising Thrasea and Helvidius, their books burned, and philosophers expelled (Agricola 2, 45; deep dive modules 13.4 and 13.6). Tacitus confesses complicity, "our hands dragged Helvidius to prison" (45.1), and calls the reign fifteen years of silence (2.3–3.2). Suetonius has Domitian complain that no one believes in a conspiracy against an emperor until he is killed (Domitian 21) and dictate a letter as "our lord and god" (13.2); Juvenal has Rome slave to a bald Nero (4.38). After he executed his cousin Flavius Clemens in 95 (15.1), Stephanus, steward of Clemens' widow Domitilla, stabbed him on 18 September 96 in a plot of palace staff (17). The Senate erased his name, while the soldiers wanted him deified (23.1). Module 7.3 begins with Nerva.

Agricola in Britain

Gnaeus Julius Agricola, from Forum Iulii, had served in Britain in the year of Boudica (module 7.1) and governed it for seven seasons; Tacitus, his son-in-law, wrote his life in 98. Agricola took Anglesey (Agricola 18), reached the Tay and garrisoned the Forth–Clyde isthmus (22–23), and thought Ireland could be held with one legion and some auxiliaries (24.3). In the last season he beat the Caledonians at Mons Graupius, where Tacitus gives their leader Calgacus the charge that Romans make a desolation and call it peace (30) and counts ten thousand enemy dead to 360 Roman (37.6). The fleet then rounded the north and proved Britain an island (38.4).

Domitian recalled him with honours and coldness, from envy, Tacitus says (39). Within a few years the north was given up, the legionary fortress at Inchtuthil dismantled unfinished and a legion sent to the Danube: Britain conquered and at once let go (Histories 1.2).

Where sources disagree. Tacitus, the son-in-law, makes the recall Domitian's envy (Agricola 39–42). Yet seven seasons was already a long command, and the withdrawal from the north followed the Dacian disasters Suetonius records (Domitian 6.1), so policy may explain what Tacitus calls envy. The governorship is dated 77–83 or 78–84, and Mons Graupius has no secure site.

Rehabilitating Domitian

The hostile portrait was written after 96 by men who had prospered under him. Tacitus owed his career to all three Flavians, Domitian most (Histories 1.1); Pliny held office to the end, and his Panegyricus praises Trajan by blackening his predecessor. Suetonius concedes that magistrates and governors were never more restrained or just (Domitian 8.2). The physical record is of a builder: the Capitol, the Palatine palace, the stadium preserved as Piazza Navona. Ian Carradice (Coinage and Finances in the Reign of Domitian, 1983) found the denarius' silver raised in 82 and lowered in 85: finance strained but managed.

Where sources disagree. Stéphane Gsell's Essai sur le règne de l'empereur Domitien (1894) began the reassessment, and K. H. Waters ("The Character of Domitian", Phoenix 1964) sifted the hostile stories for a credible character. Brian Jones (The Emperor Domitian, 1992) presents a benevolent despot whose personal monarchy met no widespread discontent for most of the reign. Pat Southern (Domitian: Tragic Tyrant, 1997) strips away the sensational detail but holds that the suffering he caused was real and must be explained. Sceptics add that good administration and terror are compatible.

The Flavian poets

Module 10.2 takes them as literature. Valerius Flaccus' unfinished Argonautica hails Titus black with the dust of Jerusalem (1.12–14); Quintilian lamented his recent death (10.1.90). Silius Italicus, consul in 68, wrote the Punica, seventeen books on the Second Punic War, the longest surviving Latin poem; he kept Virgil's tomb as a shrine and starved himself to death at seventy-five (Pliny, Letters 3.7). Statius' Thebaid ends by telling itself to follow the Aeneid at a distance (12.816–817), and his Silvae include Domitian's equestrian colossus (1.1). Martial wrote of an edict of "our lord and god" (5.8) and, after 96, that he would call no one that (10.72). The court had a culture as well as a terror.

Self-test

  1. What did Tacitus mean by the "secret of empire" (Histories 1.4), and how did the emperors of 69 illustrate it?
    Answer

    That an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome, by a provincial army. Galba was proclaimed in Spain, Vitellius on the Rhine and Vespasian in Alexandria and Judaea; only Otho was made in the city, by the praetorians who killed Galba.

  2. Why did Galba fall so quickly?
    Answer

    He refused the promised donative, saying he chose soldiers and did not buy them (Histories 1.5), and lost the German legions on 1–2 January 69. His adoption of Piso passed over Otho, who bought the guard; Galba was killed on 15 January (1.41).

  3. Who burned the Capitol in December 69?
    Answer

    Uncertain. Tacitus gives both versions and calls the commoner one the besieged Flavians firing the buildings to repel the attack (Histories 3.71); Suetonius blames Vitellius' men (Vitellius 15.3). Tacitus calls it the worst crime since the city's foundation (3.72).

  4. How does the law on Vespasian's powers both confirm and qualify the idea of the Principate as a bundle of voted powers?
    Answer

    It lists the powers with Augustan, Tiberian and Claudian precedents, voted by Senate and people (ILS 244; Histories 4.3). But its last clause validates everything done before the vote, and Vespasian dated his reign from the army's oath of 1 July (Suetonius, Vespasian 6.3): the legal grant ratified the soldiers' choice.

  5. Why must Josephus' account of the Temple's destruction be read with caution, and what is the alternative version?
    Answer

    He was a surrendered rebel general living on Flavian patronage, and Titus approved the publication (Life 363). He has Titus try to save the Temple (Jewish War 6.236–266); Sulpicius Severus, probably following Tacitus as Bernays argued, has Titus urge its destruction (Chronicle 2.30).

  6. Name three ways the Flavians turned the Jewish War into legitimacy at Rome.
    Answer

    Any three of: the joint triumph of 71 with the Temple spoils (Jewish War 7.123–157); the Temple of Peace housing the vessels; the Circus Maximus arch claiming Jerusalem never taken before (CIL VI 944); the Arch of Titus (CIL VI 945); the Colosseum built from spoils, on Alföldy's reconstruction.

  7. What do Pliny's Letters 6.16 and 6.20 describe, and why is the date of the eruption disputed?
    Answer

    6.16 tells the elder Pliny's rescue voyage and death at Stabiae; 6.20 the nephew's own flight from Misenum in darkness. The oldest manuscript gives 24 August, but other copies, autumn finds and a charcoal graffito of 17 October found in 2018 favour 24 October.

  8. What did Agricola achieve in Britain, and why did it not last?
    Answer

    Anglesey, an advance to the Tay, a garrisoned Forth–Clyde line, victory at Mons Graupius and the circumnavigation (Agricola 18, 22–23, 29–38). After his recall the north was abandoned, Inchtuthil dismantled and a legion sent to the Danube crisis: conquered and at once let go (Histories 1.2).

  9. On what grounds have modern historians rehabilitated Domitian's government, and what is the objection?
    Answer

    The hostile writers served him and wrote after 96 (Histories 1.1); Suetonius admits his governors were never more just (Domitian 8.2); building and coinage show competent rule (Carradice; Jones' benevolent despot). The objection is that efficient administration and terror against the Senate can coexist.

  10. What do the Flavian poets show about the regime, and how did Martial's position change after 96?
    Answer

    Valerius Flaccus, Silius, Statius and Martial show a court culture of epic and panegyric around the dynasty, from Titus at Jerusalem to Domitian's colossus (Silvae 1.1). Martial, who had written of "our lord and god" (5.8), declared after 96 that he would call no one that (10.72).

Carry forward

  1. The year 69 exposed the Principate's base: provincial armies chose emperors, and the Senate and people then voted the powers, as the law on Vespasian's powers did, retroactively. Every accession by force afterwards, 193 above all, replays this sequence.
  2. A new family could manufacture legitimacy: the Flavians built theirs from a foreign victory turned into triumph, arches, temples and an amphitheatre, from miracles and a restored Capitol, and from succession by blood sons, which failed when Domitian left no heir.
  3. The "bad emperor" is largely a senatorial verdict written after the fact by men who had served him: read Tacitus, Pliny and Suetonius on Domitian as evidence for the Senate's relationship with the princeps, and test it against inscriptions, coins, buildings and the provinces.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on AD 69 and the Flavian dynasty, 69 to 96. Cover: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian, and Tacitus' 'secret of empire, that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome' (Histories 1.4); the burning of the Capitol; the law on Vespasian's powers; the Jewish War and the fall of Jerusalem in 70, with Josephus as a source and the Arch of Titus; Titus, Berenice, Vesuvius in 79 with Pliny's Letters 6.16 and 6.20, and the opening of the Colosseum; Domitian, the senatorial memory of terror, the expulsions of philosophers and the younger Helvidius Priscus in outline (deep dive modules 13.4 and 13.6 take them further), Agricola in Britain, and the modern rehabilitation of his government; and the Flavian poets (Statius, Martial, Silius Italicus, Valerius Flaccus). Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 7 · The Principate, AD 14 to 235 · 7.3 · 3,342 words

The adoptive emperors

Sources, and Nerva, 96–98Adoption as ideology and as accidentTrajan, 98–117Hadrian, 117–138Antoninus Pius and the quiet reign, 138–161Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, 161–180Commodus, 180–192Gibbon's verdict and what it leaves outSelf-testCarry forward

Sources, and Nerva, 96–98

The second century has no Tacitus. Cassius Dio's books 68–73 survive only in the eleventh-century epitome of John Xiphilinus and in Byzantine excerpts, and Xiphilinus' copies already lacked the reign of Antoninus Pius (Dio 70.1.1). Dio sat in the Senate under Commodus and writes those years as an eyewitness, and is cited here by the Loeb book numbers, with Boissevain's in brackets where they differ. Herodian, a Greek of the next generation, begins at Marcus' death. The Historia Augusta has a life of every emperor from Hadrian on; module 0.1 sets out the problem of its single late author. Its lives of Hadrian, Antoninus and Marcus rest on good early material and are mostly sober; the Verus is fair; the lives of Aelius and Avidius Cassius are padded with invention and forged letters; the Commodus is hostile but sound in outline. Pliny, Fronto, the late epitomes, coins, inscriptions and two sculpted columns supply the rest.

On 18 September 96, the day Domitian was killed (module 7.2), the Senate made Marcus Cocceius Nerva emperor: a childless senator in his sixties, consul with Vespasian in 71 and with Domitian in 90, a safe man. He recalled exiles, stopped the treason trials and executed slaves who had informed on their masters (Dio 68.1.2). Tacitus, writing in 98, credits him with combining two things once irreconcilable, principate and liberty (Agricola 3.1). The army had not been consulted. In 97 the praetorians under Casperius Aelianus besieged the palace and forced Nerva to surrender the men Aelianus demanded (Dio 68.3.3), Domitian's killers Petronius Secundus and Parthenius (Epitome de Caesaribus 12.8). In October, when a laurelled dispatch arrived from Pannonia, Nerva went up to the Capitol and announced that he adopted Marcus Ulpius Traianus, governor of Upper Germany (Pliny, Panegyricus 8; Dio 68.3.4). He died in January 98. The first "adoptive" succession was a frightened old man borrowing an army.

Adoption as ideology and as accident

The regime made a doctrine of the event. Pliny, thanking Trajan as consul in 100 in a speech later expanded for publication (Letters 3.18), says Trajan was adopted not to please a wife, nor by a stepfather, but by a princeps (Panegyricus 7.4), and that he who is to rule all should be chosen from all (7.6). Tacitus gives Galba the same argument in 69: Rome had been one family's inheritance, and "that we have begun to be chosen will stand in place of liberty" (Histories 1.16.1). Dio's Hadrian, adopting Antoninus, says nature gives whatever son it pleases while adoption lets a man choose (69.20). Machiavelli made it a law of history: emperors who inherited were bad, Titus excepted, and the five adopted "from Nerva to Marcus" good (Discourses on Livy 1.10).

The facts tell another story. Nerva, Trajan and Hadrian had no sons; Antoninus' sons died young. Every choice followed blood or marriage. Hadrian was the son of Trajan's cousin and the husband of his great-niece Sabina. Hadrian's first choice, Aelius Caesar, died on 1 January 138; Hadrian then adopted Antoninus on condition that he adopt Marcus, his wife's nephew, and Aelius' son Lucius (Historia Augusta, Hadrian 24.1). The first emperor of the line with a surviving son made that son his colleague. Adoption was the expedient of childless men and the language of a Senate that wished to believe it had a voice.

Where sources disagree. Hadrian's own adoption is doubtful. Dio, citing his father Apronianus, who governed Cilicia where Trajan died, says Trajan never adopted him: Plotina hid the death for several days until the adoption was announced, and signed the letters to the Senate herself (69.1). The Historia Augusta reports that some said a man was hidden to speak in the dying emperor's voice, others that Trajan meant to name Neratius Priscus or no one (Hadrian 4.8–10). Hadrian kept 9 August, when he learnt of his adoption at Antioch, as its anniversary (4.6).

Trajan, 98–117

Optimus princeps

Trajan, born at Italica in Baetica to a family of Italian settlers, was the first emperor from a province. He reached Rome only in 99 and entered on foot among the senators (Pliny, Panegyricus 22). The Panegyricus is the regime's manifesto, built on antithesis to Domitian: a princeps who behaves as a citizen, submits to the laws and lets senators speak. It praises the support of Italian children (26–28), the scheme whose loans to landowners are recorded on the bronze tablet of Veleia. Optimus, "best", already in Pliny's mouth, became an official title in 114. Pliny's letters from Bithynia belong to module 7.5, and his exchange with Trajan on the Christians (Letters 10.96–97) to module 2.5. In the late fourth century the Senate still hailed new emperors as "luckier than Augustus, better than Trajan" (Eutropius 8.5.3).

The Dacian Wars and the Column

Domitian had ended his Dacian war in 89 by paying Decebalus subsidies (Dio 67.7). Trajan reversed the settlement. The first war, 101–102, imposed terms that Decebalus soon broke; Apollodorus of Damascus then bridged the Danube at Drobeta (Dio 68.13 describes the bridge; Procopius, Buildings 4.6.12–13 names the architect). In the second, 105–106, the capital Sarmizegetusa fell and Decebalus killed himself; the tombstone of Tiberius Claudius Maximus, found near Philippi, records the cavalryman who carried his head to Trajan. Dacia became a province, settled with colonists from "the whole Roman world" (Eutropius 8.6.2). Its loot is a figure with a pedigree: John Lydus, citing Trajan's doctor Crito, gives five million pounds of gold and ten million of silver (On the Magistracies), which Jérôme Carcopino cut to a tenth. By Dio's count the victory games lasted 123 days, with 11,000 beasts killed and 10,000 gladiators fighting (68.15.1).

The Column, dedicated in 113 in Trajan's forum, is the main visual source for the wars. Its inscription says it shows the height of the hillside cut away for the forum, and its base later received Trajan's ashes. The spiral frieze tells both wars in sequence, but as evidence it is double-edged: soldiers build, march and listen to the emperor far more often than they fight, and whether it follows Trajan's lost war commentaries or arranges stock scenes is argued. Module 10.3 reads it as art.

Parthia and the greatest extent

Arabia was annexed in 106 (Dio 68.14.5). In 114 Trajan deposed Parthia's candidate in Armenia, Parthamasiris, and made the kingdom a province (68.19–20). In 115–116 he took Mesopotamia and the Parthian capital Ctesiphon and reached the Persian Gulf, where, Dio says, he watched a ship leave for India and wished he were young like Alexander (68.29.1). Eutropius names three new provinces, Armenia, Assyria and Mesopotamia (8.3.2), though whether Assyria was ever organised is doubted. This greatest extent lasted months. In 116 the conquered cities rose and a Jewish revolt spread through Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus, for which Dio claims 220,000 dead in Cyrene and 240,000 in Cyprus (68.32). Trajan failed before Hatra (68.31), fell ill and died at Selinus in Cilicia in August 117.

Hadrian, 117–138

Giving up the East

Hadrian gave up Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria at once. The Historia Augusta says he followed Cato, who declared the Macedonians free because they could not be protected (Hadrian 5.3); Eutropius blames envy of Trajan's glory and adds that friends dissuaded him from abandoning Dacia, lest its settlers be handed to the barbarians (8.6.2). The retreat applied Augustus' advice to keep the empire within its limits (Tacitus, Annals 1.11.4; Dio 56.33), discussed in module 6.4; the modern quarrel over frontier strategy is in module 0.2. In 118 four consulars, among them Trajan's marshals Palma and Lusius Quietus, were executed for conspiracy; Hadrian disowned the deed and swore never to punish a senator without the Senate's verdict (Hadrian 7; Dio 69.2), but the Senate did not forget.

The travelling emperor

Hadrian spent most of 121–132 away from Rome, in Gaul, Germany, Britain, Spain, Africa, Greece, Asia, Syria and Egypt. He inspected camps and tightened discipline (Dio 69.9); his speeches to the army of Africa at Lambaesis in 128 survive on stone, and his coins honoured the provinces one by one. Tertullian called him an explorer of every curiosity (Apology 5.7). In Britain, from about 122, he built the Wall; module 7.5 treats it with the frontier army in peacetime. The travel was government: the emperor went to the provinces instead of waiting for them to come to him.

Antinous

Antinous, a youth from Claudiopolis in Bithynia and the emperor's favourite, drowned in the Nile in October 130. Hadrian wept for him "like a woman" (Hadrian 14.5), founded Antinoopolis at the place and declared him a god; his cult and idealised portraits spread across the Greek East.

Where sources disagree. Hadrian wrote that Antinous fell into the Nile; Dio says the truth was that he was sacrificed, Hadrian being given to divination and magic (69.11.2–3). The Historia Augusta mentions a story that he gave his life for Hadrian (Hadrian 14.6), and Aurelius Victor makes it a voluntary death to lengthen the emperor's life (Caesares 14.7–9). The evidence cannot decide between accident, suicide and sacrifice.

The Bar Kokhba war

Jerusalem had lain in ruins since 70 (module 7.2); after Hadrian's visit in 130 it was to be refounded as a Roman colony, Aelia Capitolina. In 132 Judaea rose under Simon ben Kosiba, known from his own letters, found in caves of the Judaean desert, and from coins overstruck on Roman silver with "Year one of the redemption of Israel". Rabbi Akiva, a later tradition says, hailed him with "a star shall come out of Jacob" (Numbers 24:17), whence Bar Kokhba, "son of the star" (Jerusalem Talmud, Ta'anit 4.5). Rome needed three years and Julius Severus, brought from Britain (Dio 69.13.2). Dio counts fifty fortresses and 985 villages destroyed and 580,000 killed in the fighting, and notes that Hadrian omitted from his letter to the Senate the customary assurance that he and the army were well (69.14.1–3). Betar fell in 135; Jews were barred from Jerusalem (Eusebius, Church History 4.6), and the province became Syria Palaestina.

Where sources disagree. Dio makes the foundation of Aelia Capitolina, with a temple of Jupiter where the Temple had stood, the cause of the war (69.12.1–2); the Historia Augusta blames a ban on circumcision (Hadrian 14.2); Eusebius has the colony founded after the war (Church History 4.6). Werner Eck ("The Bar Kokhba Revolt: The Roman Point of View", 1999) argued from the transfer of Severus and the decorations awarded that Rome treated it as a grave crisis, against those, G. W. Bowersock (1980) among them, who held the threat grossly exaggerated.

Builder and philhellene

Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon under the original builder's name (Hadrian 19.9–10), so that the porch still says Marcus Agrippa made it; Lise Hetland ("Dating the Pantheon", 2007) argued from brick stamps that work began under Trajan, about 114–116, and module 10.3 takes the building. Dio tells that Apollodorus, who had mocked the emperor's architectural drawings, was banished and later killed (69.4), perhaps senatorial malice. At Tibur Hadrian built a villa the size of a town and named its parts the Lyceum, the Academy, the Prytaneum, Canopus, the Painted Stoa and Tempe (Hadrian 26.5). He was the first emperor portrayed with a full beard and as a young man was nicknamed Graeculus, "the little Greek" (1.5). His Athenian archonship, the Olympieion, the arch with its two inscriptions, the Panhellenion and Herodes Atticus belong to Greek module 7.4.

Antoninus Pius and the quiet reign, 138–161

Hadrian died at Baiae on 10 July 138, addressing his soul in verse, animula vagula blandula (Hadrian 25.9). The Senate, remembering the executions, was reluctant to deify him; Antoninus insisted, one of several explanations the Historia Augusta gives for his name Pius (Antoninus 2.3–7). He was a rich, mild consular of fifty-one from a family of Nemausus (Nîmes).

Of the next twenty-two years almost nothing is told. Antoninus never left Italy, saying that a prince's retinue burdened the provinces (Antoninus 7.11). His legate Lollius Urbicus built a second, turf wall in Scotland (5.4); his deified wife Faustina, who died in 140, gave her name to a foundation for poor girls and, with him, to the temple that still stands in the Forum; Aelius Aristides praised the empire as one well-ordered city (Greek module 7.4). He died in March 161, giving the guard the watchword aequanimitas (12.6). The quiet is partly an artefact. Dio's account was lost before Xiphilinus, the Historia Augusta's life is short and admiring, and even it records wars with Britons, Moors, Germans and Dacians and risings among the Jews and in Achaea and Egypt, all handled by legates (5.4–5).

Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, 161–180

Marcus at once made his adoptive brother Lucius his equal as Augustus, the first time Rome had two emperors (Historia Augusta, Marcus 7.5–6). His life and inner history are deep dive module 13.7; this is the reign in outline, and it was almost continuous war.

Parthia and the plague. Vologaeses IV took Armenia and destroyed a Roman army at Elegeia (Dio 71.2). Lucius went east and, in the Historia Augusta's portrait, enjoyed Antioch while his generals fought: Avidius Cassius sacked Seleucia on the Tigris and burned the palace at Ctesiphon in 165–166. Lucius died of a stroke early in 169. The army brought home an epidemic; Roman tradition said soldiers at Seleucia had opened a golden casket in a temple of Apollo and let it out (Verus 8.1–2; Ammianus 23.6.24). Galen describes fever, diarrhoea and a dark pustular rash, usually taken for smallpox. It returned for a generation: under Commodus, Dio says, 2,000 people often died at Rome in a single day (73(72).14.3).

Where sources disagree. No ancient source gives a total. J. F. Gilliam ("The Plague under Marcus Aurelius", 1961) thought the literary picture overdrawn; R. J. and M. L. Littman (1973), reading Galen's symptoms as smallpox, estimated 7–10 per cent of the population dead, 13–15 per cent in cities and armies. Richard Duncan-Jones ("The impact of the Antonine plague", 1996) read sudden breaks in building, inscriptions, coinage and Egyptian papyri as signs of catastrophe; each series can be explained otherwise, and estimates still range widely.

The northern wars. About 170 the Marcomanni and Quadi broke into Italy, besieged Aquileia and destroyed Opitergium (Ammianus 29.6.1). Rather than raise taxes, Marcus auctioned the palace furnishings in Trajan's Forum (Marcus 17.4–5), and he enlisted slaves, gladiators and brigands (21.6–7). He spent most of the 170s on the Danube, at Carnuntum and Sirmium, against the Marcomanni, the Quadi and the Iazyges. The rain miracle, Avidius Cassius' revolt of 175 and Commodus' elevation in 177 belong to deep dive module 13.7. A second expedition was under way when Marcus died on 17 March 180 (Dio 72(71).33), at Vindobona according to Aurelius Victor (Caesares 16.14), at Sirmium according to Tertullian (Apology 25). The Historia Augusta says he meant to make provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia (Marcus 24.5).

The column. The column of Marcus in the Piazza Colonna was finished by 193, when an inscription records that its custodian Adrastus might build a lodge beside it. Its frieze borrows Trajan's form and changes the tone: villages burned, prisoners beheaded, women dragged away. Module 10.3 reads it as art. In the same camps Marcus kept a Greek notebook whose manuscripts place one book "among the Quadi on the Granua" and another "at Carnuntum": the Meditations, which deep dive module 13.8 takes up.

Commodus, 180–192

Commodus, Augustus since 177, was eighteen when his father died. He made peace with the Marcomanni and Quadi on terms that included grain, recruits and a cleared strip along the river (Dio 73(72).2), and went home to Rome. In 182, at his sister Lucilla's instigation, Claudius Pompeianus Quintianus drew a dagger on him, crying that the Senate had sent it, and was seized before he could strike (73(72).4.4). Government passed to favourites: the prefect Perennis, surrendered in 185 to 1,500 javelin-men sent by the army of Britain (73(72).9–10), and the freedman Cleander, who sold offices and made twenty-five consuls in one year (73(72).12.4), until a crowd angry at a grain shortage forced Commodus to have him killed in 190 (73(72).13).

In his last years Commodus presented himself as Hercules. He renamed Rome the Colonia Commodiana and the twelve months after his own titles (Dio 73(72).15.2–3), and the bust from the Esquiline, now in the Capitoline Museums, shows him in the lion skin with the club and the apples of the Hesperides. He fought in the arena as a secutor, charging the gladiatorial fund a million sesterces a day (73(72).19.3). Dio sat among the senators obliged to watch; when Commodus cut off an ostrich's head and waved it at them, Dio chewed laurel leaves from his garland to keep from laughing, which would have been fatal (73(72).21.1–2).

He meant to enter 193 as consul from the gladiators' barracks (73(72).22.2). On the night of 31 December 192 his mistress Marcia, his chamberlain Eclectus and the prefect Laetus gave him poisoned beef; when he vomited it, the athlete Narcissus strangled him in his bath (73(72).22.4–5). Herodian adds that Marcia had found her own name on his list of those to die (1.17). The conspirators already had a successor, the city prefect Pertinax, whose reign and the auction that followed open module 7.4.

Where sources disagree. Dio, who watched as a senator, and Herodian, writing a generation later, give the same portrait of a frivolous tyrant, and Dio dates the decline from the accession, when history descends "from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust" (72(71).36.4). Olivier Hekster (Commodus: An Emperor at the Crossroads, 2002) looked for method in the madness: the Herculean imagery arrived suddenly after Cleander's fall, and the arena won acclamation from people and soldiers over the Senate's head. The senators who wrote the history were the audience it bypassed.

Gibbon's verdict and what it leaves out

Near the end of his third chapter Gibbon wrote the sentence that named the age: "If a man were called to fix the period in the history of the world, during which the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous, he would, without hesitation, name that which elapsed from the death of Domitian to the accession of Commodus." The empire, he went on, "was governed by absolute power, under the guidance of virtue and wisdom" (Decline and Fall, chapter 3). His period ends in 180, not 192. The verdict has ancient parents: Tacitus on the rare happiness of a time when one might think what one liked and say what one thought (Histories 1.1.4), Aristides' world as one city, Dio's kingdom of gold. All are the view of senators and of the cities' governing class, and Gibbon himself saw that a happiness depending on one man's character was unstable. What the sentence leaves out:

  • The provinces that paid. Dacia conquered for its gold; the diaspora revolt of 115–117 ending in massacre; Judaea losing, on Dio's count, 580,000 men and 985 villages.
  • Plague and invasion. Both fall inside Gibbon's dates. Joseph McConnell and colleagues (2018) found that lead pollution in Greenland ice, a proxy for Roman silver mining, fell sharply with the plague and stayed low.
  • Slaves, captives and the persecuted. The 10,000 gladiators of 107, the prisoners of Dacia and Parthia, the slaves on the estates behind the senators' villas, and the Christians executed under Trajan's rescript (module 2.5) and at Lyon in 177 (deep dive module 13.7).
  • The succession. The happiness rested on four childless emperors in a row; the first with a son gave the empire to him.

What Gibbon saw was real for the class that left the evidence: no civil war between 69 and 193 beyond two failed usurpations, cities building in marble from Britain to the Euphrates, emperors who answered petitions. His sentence describes that class's experience and calls it the condition of the human race.

Self-test

  1. How did Nerva come to adopt Trajan, and why do the circumstances matter for reading adoption as a principle?
    Answer

    The praetorians under Casperius Aelianus besieged the palace and forced Nerva to surrender Domitian's killers (Dio 68.3.3); he then announced on the Capitol the adoption of the governor of Upper Germany (Pliny, Panegyricus 8). A threatened emperor acquired an army; the doctrine of choosing the best came afterwards.

  2. What did Pliny, Tacitus' Galba and Dio's Hadrian claim for adoption, and what facts undercut the claim?
    Answer

    That choosing the best man from all replaces inheritance and even stands in place of liberty (Panegyricus 7.4–6; Histories 1.16.1; Dio 69.20). But Nerva, Trajan and Hadrian had no sons and Antoninus' died, each choice followed kinship or marriage, and the first emperor with a surviving son, Marcus, made him his heir.

  3. Why is Hadrian's adoption doubtful, and where does the doubt come from?
    Answer

    Dio, citing his father Apronianus, governor of Cilicia, says Plotina concealed Trajan's death so that an adoption could be announced first and signed the letters to the Senate herself (69.1). The Historia Augusta adds the story of a man impersonating the dying emperor's voice (Hadrian 4.10).

  4. Why is Trajan's Column double-edged evidence for the Dacian wars?
    Answer

    It is a contemporary narrative of both wars set up in 113, but a commissioned monument: it shows building, marching and imperial speeches far more than fighting, and its sequence may follow Trajan's lost commentaries or simply arrange stock scenes. It records what the regime wished remembered.

  5. What was the empire's greatest extent, why did it not last, and how do the ancient sources explain Hadrian's withdrawal?
    Answer

    By 116 Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria had been declared provinces (Eutropius 8.3.2) and Trajan reached the Gulf. Revolts in the conquered cities and the diaspora, failure at Hatra and his death undid it. The Historia Augusta cites Cato's precedent with Macedonia (Hadrian 5.3), Eutropius envy of Trajan (8.6.2); either way it fits Augustus' advice to keep within limits (module 6.4).

  6. What three ancient explanations of the Bar Kokhba war are there, and what suggests its seriousness for Rome?
    Answer

    Dio blames the foundation of Aelia Capitolina (69.12.1–2), the Historia Augusta a ban on circumcision (Hadrian 14.2), and Eusebius makes the colony a consequence of the war (Church History 4.6). Julius Severus was brought from Britain, and Hadrian dropped the formula that he and the army were well (Dio 69.13–14); Eck reads Rome's response as that to a grave crisis.

  7. In what sense is Antoninus' reign "quiet", and how far is that an artefact of the sources?
    Answer

    He never left Italy (Antoninus 7.11), fought no war in person and faced no succession crisis. But Dio's account was lost before Xiphilinus (70.1.1) and the Historia Augusta is brief, and even it records wars in Britain and Mauretania and risings in several provinces (5.4–5).

  8. Name three crises of Marcus' reign and two measures he took to pay for the northern wars.
    Answer

    Any three of: the Parthian war and the defeat at Elegeia; the plague from 165–166; the invasion of Italy and siege of Aquileia about 170; the revolt of Avidius Cassius in 175. He auctioned the palace furnishings in Trajan's Forum (Marcus 17.4–5) and enlisted slaves, gladiators and brigands (21.6–7).

  9. How do Dio and Hekster read Commodus' Hercules and his arena appearances differently?
    Answer

    Dio, an eyewitness, sees degradation, from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust (72(71).36.4), and records the ostrich scene and his laurel leaves (73(72).21). Hekster (2002) sees a deliberate programme after 190 that sought acclamation from people and soldiers and bypassed the Senate, whose members wrote the history.

  10. What period does Gibbon actually name, and what does his verdict leave out?
    Answer

    From the death of Domitian to the accession of Commodus, 96–180 (Decline and Fall, chapter 3). It leaves out the cost at the edges (Dacia, the diaspora revolt, Judaea), the plague and invasion inside its own dates, slaves, captives and Christians, and the dependence of the whole arrangement on childless emperors; it generalises the experience of the governing class.

Carry forward

  1. The "adoptive" succession was the expedient of childless emperors dressed as a principle of choosing the best; power still passed through family, marriage and the army's acceptance, and the doctrine ended the moment an emperor had a son. Later dynasts will still borrow the Antonine name to claim legitimacy.
  2. The second-century peace was made at the edges: conquest in Dacia, withdrawal from Mesopotamia, devastation in Judaea, and from 165 plague and invasion. The empire's greatest extent on the map (116) and its high point in reputation (Gibbon's 96–180) are different measures.
  3. Our picture of the century is senatorial and damaged: Dio in epitome, a Historia Augusta of uneven worth, a panegyric and Herodian. Emperors are judged by how they treated the Senate, and a silence such as Antoninus' may be a loss of evidence rather than an absence of events.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the emperors from Nerva to Commodus, AD 96 to 192. Cover: adoption as ideology and as accident; Trajan (the Dacian Wars and the Column, the Parthian war and the empire's greatest extent, Pliny's Panegyricus); Hadrian (the abandonment of the eastern conquests, the travels, the Wall, Antinous, the Bar Kokhba war, the Pantheon and the villa at Tivoli, his philhellenism; point back to Greek module 7.4); Antoninus Pius and the quiet reign; Marcus Aurelius' reign in outline (the Antonine plague, the Marcomannic wars, the column, Lucius Verus; deep dive modules 13.7 and 13.8 take his life and the Meditations further); Commodus as gladiator and Hercules, and his murder; and Gibbon's verdict that this was the period in which 'the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous', with what it leaves out. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 7 · The Principate, AD 14 to 235 · 7.4 · 2,836 words

The Severans and the citizenship of 212

193: the murder of Pertinax and the auction of the empireSeptimius Severus: Lepcis, the civil wars and the armyThe arch, Plautianus and the death at YorkJulia Domna and the Syrian womenCaracalla: fratricide, erasure and the bathsThe edict of 212Macrinus and ElagabalusSeverus Alexander, Mamaea and the SasaniansPapinian, Ulpian and PaulCassius Dio and Herodian as witnessesSelf-testCarry forward

193: the murder of Pertinax and the auction of the empire

Module 7.3 ends with Commodus strangled on the last night of 192. His killers made the city prefect Pertinax emperor; on 28 March 193 the praetorians, resenting his discipline, killed him in the palace after eighty-seven days (Dio 74(73).10). Dio is cited here by the Loeb book numbers with Boissevain's in brackets, since the two editions number these books differently.

Dio, a senator in Rome at the time, tells what followed as a bidding war. Pertinax's father-in-law Sulpicianus, inside the camp, and the rich senator Didius Julianus, at the wall, raised their offers until Sulpicianus reached 20,000 sesterces a man and Julianus jumped at once by 5,000 (74(73).11.2–5). Herodian has the soldiers cry the empire for sale from the walls (2.6). Dio then sat in the Senate as Julianus addressed it, ringed by soldiers (74(73).12).

Where sources disagree. Dio's 25,000 sesterces is the bid. The Historia Augusta says Julianus promised 25,000 and paid 30,000 (Didius Julianus 3.2); Herodian, that he could not pay what he had promised because the money was not there (2.7.1). The same biography calls false the story, which Dio tells (74(73).13), that he dined luxuriously while Pertinax's body lay in the palace (Didius Julianus 3.8).

The provincial armies refused the sale. Pescennius Niger was hailed in Syria; Clodius Albinus in Britain was bought off with the title of Caesar (Herodian 2.15); and on 9 April Septimius Severus, governor of Upper Pannonia, the army nearest Rome, was proclaimed at Carnuntum. The Senate deposed Julianus, who was killed in the palace after sixty-six days (Dio 74(73).17.4–5).

Septimius Severus: Lepcis, the civil wars and the army

Severus was born at Lepcis Magna in Tripolitania on 11 April 145 (Dio 77(76).17.4), into a Punic family whose forebears, the Historia Augusta says, were Roman knights before the citizenship was given to all (Severus 1.2); he kept an African ring in his voice into old age (19.9).

Before entering Rome he had the praetorians parade unarmed, surrounded them and banished them beyond the hundredth milestone (Dio 75(74).1.1–2; Herodian 2.13). The new guard came from the legions instead of Italy, Spain, Macedonia and Noricum, and Dio complained that Italian youth turned to banditry and the arena (75(74).2.4–6).

Niger was beaten at Cyzicus, Nicaea and Issus in 193–194 and killed in flight (Dio 75(74).6–8; Herodian 3.2–4); Byzantium held out until 195 or 196 (Dio 75(74).10–14). In 195 Severus declared himself son of the deified Marcus and brother of Commodus; his elder son, renamed Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and nicknamed Caracalla, was soon made Caesar. Albinus, displaced, was hailed Augustus. At Lugdunum on 19 February 197 each side had, by Dio's figure, 150,000 men (76(75).6.1). Albinus killed himself, and in the Senate Severus praised the severity of Sulla, Marius and Augustus, defended Commodus, released thirty-five senators accused of siding with Albinus, and put twenty-nine men to death, Sulpicianus among them (76(75).8.1–4).

He then sacked Ctesiphon (76(75).9.4) but failed twice before Hatra (76(75).10–12). Mesopotamia became a province under an equestrian prefect, held by two new legions, I and III Parthica; the third, II Parthica, was stationed at Albanum in the Alban hills, the first legion based in Italy under the emperors, and all three had equestrian commanders. Dio called the conquests "a source of constant wars and great expense to us" (75(75).3.2–3).

The army was his constituency. Herodian says he gave the soldiers large sums, was the first to increase their ration allowance, and let them wear gold rings and live with their wives, things earlier emperors had thought fatal to discipline (3.8.4–5). The legionary's pay had stood at 300 denarii a year since Domitian (Suetonius, Domitian 7.3); module 9.2 takes the army as an institution.

Where sources disagree. Herodian blames Severus for corrupting discipline (3.8.5), and Gibbon concluded that posterity justly considered him "the principal author of the decline of the Roman empire" (Decline and Fall, chapter 5). Against this, pay had not risen for over a century, soldiers' families already existed outside the law, and armies had made emperors since 69 (module 7.2). The size of the rise is unknown: J. Jahn (1984) and M. A. Speidel (1992) argued for a doubling; others assume a rise of half, to 450 denarii.

The arch, Plautianus and the death at York

The arch the Senate and people dedicated in the Forum in 203 honours Severus and his sons for restoring the state and extending the empire; its four panels map the Parthian campaigns, and module 10.3 sets out how to read historical relief. In its inscription the fourth line, which named Geta, was recut after 211 as "best and bravest princes", and the dowel holes of the bronze letters still show the lost name.

Gaius Fulvius Plautianus, praetorian prefect from 197 and Severus' fellow townsman, married his daughter to Caracalla in 202 and, in Dio's portrait, wielded power equal to the emperors' own, with more and larger statues than theirs (76(75).14.6). On 22 January 205 he was killed in the palace on Caracalla's charge of a plot (Dio 77(76).3–4; Herodian 3.11–12), and Papinian took the prefecture. From 208 Severus campaigned in northern Britain; Dio's 50,000 Roman dead (77(76).13.2) cannot be checked. He died at York on 4 February 211, telling his sons, in Dio's version, "Be harmonious, enrich the soldiers, and scorn all other men" (77(76).15.2).

Julia Domna and the Syrian women

Severus' second wife, Julia Domna, came from Emesa (Homs) in Syria, from the family that held the priesthood of its sun god Elagabal; the Historia Augusta has him choose her for a horoscope promising a royal husband (Severus 3.9). From 195 she was mother of the camps, the first empress so styled since Faustina the Younger, and under Caracalla mother of the Senate and the fatherland as well. Dio says Plautianus' hostility drove her to philosophy (76(75).15.6–7), and Philostratus wrote his Life of Apollonius at her request (1.3). Under Caracalla she handled petitions and correspondence in both languages (Dio 78(77).18.2), the business module 7.5 describes, and after his murder she starved herself (79(78).23–24).

Her sister Julia Maesa and Maesa's daughters, Soaemias and Mamaea, carried the dynasty once its men were dead. Dio and Herodian treat their power as a symptom of disorder; coins and inscriptions show the dynasty advertising it.

Caracalla: fratricide, erasure and the baths

Severus left two Augusti who hated each other; Herodian has them consider dividing the empire until their mother asked how they would divide her (4.3.5–9). In December 211 Caracalla had centurions kill Geta in her arms (Dio 78(77).2.3–4), ran to the praetorian camp crying conspiracy, and promised each man 2,500 denarii and half as much again on his ration (Herodian 4.4.7). Dio puts Geta's partisans killed afterwards at about 20,000 (78(77).4.1).

To speak or write Geta's name became a capital offence (Dio 78(77).12.5). It was chiselled from inscriptions, and his face was scraped from a painted wooden tondo of about 200, probably from Egypt and now in Berlin, which shows Severus and Julia Domna behind their two sons: three faces and a blank. Dieter Metzler suggested instead that the erased boy is Caracalla, defaced in Egypt after his massacre of 215.

Caracalla spent most of his reign with the armies, imitating Alexander the Great down to a Macedonian phalanx (Dio 78(77).7–8), and in 215 had the young men of Alexandria massacred for their mockery (78(77).22–23; Herodian 4.9). Dio's account of his finances is a list of exactions: crown gold, new taxes and doubled ones, the soldiers paid without limit. Reproached by his mother, he pointed to his sword and said they would not lack money while they had this (78(77).9–10). In 215 he issued the radiate coin modern numismatists call the antoninianus (module 8.1 follows the debasement). His baths, inaugurated in 216, had 1,600 marble seats by the count of the fifth-century historian Olympiodorus, and yielded the Farnese Bull and Hercules in the 1540s (module 10.3). On 8 April 217, near Carrhae, a soldier stabbed him at the prompting of the praetorian prefect Macrinus (Dio 79(78).5; Herodian 4.13).

The edict of 212

Ulpian, writing within a few years, states the fact:

in orbe Romano qui sunt ex constitutione imperatoris Antonini cives Romani effecti sunt.

"Those who are in the Roman world were made Roman citizens by a constitution of the emperor Antoninus" (Digest 1.5.17). A damaged Greek papyrus at Giessen, P.Giss. 40 col. I, is usually taken as a copy of the edict. The emperor thanks the gods who preserved him, which most connect with Geta's alleged plot, and grants the citizenship of the Romans to all [foreigners] in the world, with an exception restored as the dediticii, probably freedmen of criminal status or surrendered barbarians. After 212 the papyri swarm with Aurelii, new citizens taking their benefactor's family name.

Module 3.4 describes the graded statuses of Republican Italy; after the Social War (module 5.2) the empire ran on a cruder division between citizens and peregrines, with Latin rights as a step for provincial towns. Myles Lavan (Past & Present, 2016) judged it extremely unlikely that more than a third of free provincials were citizens on the eve of the grant: the edict was a break, not a formality.

Much did not change. Local law persisted beside Roman, as Ludwig Mitteis showed from the papyri (Reichsrecht und Volksrecht, 1891), and Junian Latins survived until Justinian. Penalties already followed rank, honestiores against humiliores, more than citizenship (Peter Garnsey, Social Status and Legal Privilege, 1970). But every free provincial could now enter a legion, and the line between legions and auxiliaries lost its legal basis (module 9.2).

Where sources disagree. Dio's motive is fiscal: Caracalla doubled the taxes on inheritances and manumissions to ten per cent and made everyone a citizen so that everyone paid them (78(77).9.4–5). The papyrus speaks of thanks to the gods, and later writers lost even the author: Aurelius Victor credits Marcus Aurelius (Caesares 16.12), Justinian credits Antoninus Pius (Novel 78.5).
