Kostas Buraselis (Theia Dorea, 1989) read it through Severan ruling ideology and judged it far more important than earlier scholars allowed; Alex Imrie (2018) combines the motives, more taxpayers and more men eligible for the legions, presented as piety and generosity after the fratricide.

Macrinus and Elagabalus

Macrinus, a Moor from Caesarea in Mauretania (Dio 79(78).11), was the first emperor who had not been a senator, which Dio held against him (79(78).41). After an indecisive battle at Nisibis he bought peace from the Parthian king Artabanus for 200 million sesterces (79(78).26–27). In a letter to the city prefect Maximus, as Dio reports, he put the cost of Caracalla's pay rise at 280 million sesterces a year (79(78).36.3), and he enlisted recruits on the old terms fixed by Severus (79(78).28). Julia Maesa used her fortune and the claim that her grandson, the god's boy priest at Emesa, was Caracalla's son to win the legion camped nearby on 16 May 218 (79(78).31–32; Herodian 5.3), and Macrinus was beaten near Antioch on 8 June (79(78).38–40).

The boy reigned as Marcus Aurelius Antoninus; Elagabalus is his god's name, and the god was a black conical stone. Module 2.5 covers the eastern cults that reached Rome with traders and soldiers; this one arrived as the emperor's own, and that was the scandal. Herodian says he sent ahead a portrait of himself in Syrian priestly robes to hang above the statue of Victory in the Senate house, so that senators would grow used to it (5.5.6–7). He married the god to Urania of Carthage (5.6.3–5) and at midsummer ran backwards before its chariot through the city (5.6.6–8). He took the title of priest of the invincible Sun god Elagabal, and his coins show the stone in a chariot. He married a Vestal Virgin (Dio 80(79).9.3). For Dio the offence lay not in bringing a foreign god to Rome but in placing him above Jupiter and having himself voted his priest (80(79).11.1). Maesa had him adopt his cousin, renamed Alexander, as Caesar in 221; when he turned against the boy, the guard killed him and his mother Soaemias in March 222 (80(79).17–20).

Where sources disagree. Dio, Herodian and the Historia Augusta built Elagabalus from the stock vices of the tyrant and the effeminate easterner. Leonardo de Arrizabalaga y Prado (The Emperor Elagabalus: Fact or Fiction?, 2010) tested each claim against coins, inscriptions and papyri, found the sexual and violent stories unconfirmed, and calls him by his boyhood name Varius. Martijn Icks (The Crimes of Elagabalus, 2011) takes the cult and the priestly role as real and as the cause of his fall, while doubting most of the scandal.

Severus Alexander, Mamaea and the Sasanians

Alexander was thirteen. Herodian says his grandmother and mother chose sixteen senators as his council (6.1.2); after Maesa's death Mamaea ruled, and she summoned Origen to Antioch (Eusebius, Church History 6.21.3–4). The guard remained master. Dio says the praetorians killed Ulpian, Alexander's prefect and chief minister, at night in the palace before the emperor and his mother (80(80).1.1, 2.2), and that he himself, hated by them for disciplining the Pannonian legions, was told to spend his second consulship, held with the emperor in 229, outside Rome (80(80).4.2–5.1).

Meanwhile Ardashir, a Persian dynast from Fars, killed the Parthian king Artabanus about 224 and founded the Sasanian empire. Dio, writing as it happened, reports his threat to win back everything the ancient Persians had held as far as the Greek sea, and fears him less for his own strength than for the state of the Roman armies (80(80).3–4). Alexander went east in 231 and invaded in three columns in 232.

Where sources disagree. Herodian makes the campaign a humiliation: the southern army destroyed, the northern wasted in the Armenian mountains, the emperor, held back by fear or by his mother, never advancing (6.5–6). The Historia Augusta has Alexander read the Senate a dispatch announcing a crushing victory (Severus Alexander 55–57). Ardashir's quiet for several years afterwards suggests a costly stalemate rather than either version.

Then the Germans crossed the Rhine. At Mainz Alexander tried to buy peace (Herodian 6.7); the troops despised a youth ruled by his mother, and in March 235 the recruits proclaimed their trainer, Maximinus, and killed Alexander and Mamaea in their tent (6.8–9). Module 8.1 begins with him.

Papinian, Ulpian and Paul

The Severan age is the summit of Roman jurisprudence, and its jurists held the highest equestrian office. Papinian, prefect from 205, wrote the Quaestiones and Responsa that the Law of Citations of 426 made decisive in a tie. He was killed in the purge after Geta's murder, with an axe, as Dio notes (78(77).4.1); the Historia Augusta's story that he refused to defend the fratricide (Caracalla 8) is probably invention. Paul records a document read in Papinian's auditorium (Digest 12.1.40): the jurists sat as the prefect's and the emperor's councillors. Ulpian of Tyre (Digest 50.15.1) died at the guard's hands as prefect; a papyrus showing his killer Epagathus already prefect of Egypt in 224 led J. Modrzejewski and T. Zawadzki (1967) to date his death to 223 rather than 228. Paul's own prefecture rests on late, doubtful sources. Ulpian is the largest single source of Justinian's Digest, and his sentences that the princeps is released from the laws (1.3.31) and that what pleases the princeps has the force of law (1.4.1) became texts of absolutism. Module 9.1 takes their law further.

Cassius Dio and Herodian as witnesses

Cassius Dio of Nicaea, a senator's son, came to Rome around 180 and held office from Commodus to Alexander, from praetor in the 190s to consul with Alexander in 229 (module 0.1 introduces his history). A pamphlet on the portents of Severus' rise led to a history of the civil wars and then, at a dream's bidding, to the whole of Roman history: ten years of collecting to Severus' death and twelve of writing (73(72).23). He saw what he describes: Julianus' Senate, Severus' entry, the speech of 197, Caracalla's court. His standard is senatorial, his hostility to Caracalla and Elagabalus open, his verdict on Severus mixed. A Vatican manuscript keeps his own text for 217–219; the rest of these books survive in the eleventh-century epitome of John Xiphilinus and in Byzantine excerpts, and for Alexander's reign he warns that he was seldom in Rome (80(80).1.2–3).

Herodian, of uncertain origin, says he wrote of events he saw or shared in imperial and public service (1.2.5); his eight books run from 180 to 238. He has the better scenes and the worse facts: vague dates, invented speeches, a moral thread of boy emperors and greedy soldiers. Whether he read Dio is disputed. The Historia Augusta draws on Herodian and on the lost Marius Maximus; its life of Alexander, the longest in the collection, gives him a private shrine holding Christ, Abraham, Orpheus and Apollonius (Severus Alexander 29.2). Module 0.1 explains why it is not to be trusted.

Self-test

  1. How does Dio's account of the auction of 193 differ from Herodian's and the Historia Augusta's, and why does Dio's carry particular weight?
    Answer

    Dio has a bidding war in which Julianus beat Sulpicianus' 20,000 sesterces by jumping 5,000 (74(73).11); Herodian has the empire cried for sale from the walls and says Julianus could not pay (2.6, 2.7.1); the Historia Augusta says he promised 25,000 and paid 30,000 (Didius Julianus 3.2). Dio was a senator in Rome and sat through Julianus' first Senate meeting.

  2. What did Severus change in the guard and the legions, and why did Dio object?
    Answer

    He disbanded the old praetorians and recruited the new guard from the legions of every province (Dio 75(74).1–2), raised three Parthian legions under equestrian commanders and stationed II Parthica at Albanum. Dio complained that Italian youth, shut out of the guard, turned to banditry and the arena.

  3. Why did Herodian and Gibbon blame Severus for the decline, and what can be said against them?
    Answer

    Herodian says his money, rations, rings and wives corrupted discipline (3.8.5), and Dio's deathbed advice to enrich the soldiers (77(76).15.2) sums up the policy; Gibbon called him the principal author of the decline. Against this, pay had stood still since Domitian, soldiers' families already existed, and armies had made emperors since 69; the size of the rise is unknown.

  4. Where can the erasure of Geta still be seen, and what made it necessary?
    Answer

    In the recut fourth line of the arch in the Forum and the blank face on the Severan tondo in Berlin. Caracalla had Geta killed in December 211 (Dio 78(77).2), presented it as self-defence against a plot, and made speaking or writing his name a capital offence (78(77).12.5).

  5. What roles did Julia Domna, Julia Maesa and Julia Mamaea play in the dynasty?
    Answer

    Domna was mother of the camps and of the Senate, patron of Philostratus and Caracalla's manager of petitions and correspondence (Dio 78(77).18.2). Maesa used her fortune and a claimed paternity to make Elagabalus emperor in 218 and replaced him with Alexander in 222. Mamaea governed for Alexander and died with him in 235.

  6. What motives do Dio and P.Giss. 40 give for the edict of 212, and how does Imrie combine them?
    Answer

    Dio: revenue, since new citizens became liable to the inheritance and manumission taxes he had doubled (78(77).9.4–5). The papyrus: thanks to the gods for the emperor's preservation, probably from Geta. Imrie (2018) sees more taxpayers and more men eligible for the legions, presented as piety and generosity after the fratricide.

  7. What did the edict end, and what did it leave untouched?
    Answer

    It ended the division between citizens and peregrines that had replaced the graded statuses of Republican Italy (module 3.4), enfranchising a majority: Lavan puts citizens at no more than a third of free provincials before it. Local law persisted (Mitteis), Junian Latins and probably the dediticii remained, and penalties followed rank, honestiores and humiliores (Garnsey).

  8. How did army pay bring down Macrinus?
    Answer

    Caracalla's rise cost, by Macrinus' reckoning in Dio, 280 million sesterces a year (79(78).36.3), on top of a peace with Parthia bought for 200 million. Macrinus put new recruits back on Severus' terms (79(78).28), alarming the soldiers, and Maesa's money and her claim that Elagabalus was Caracalla's son won the Syrian legion in May 218.

  9. What exactly was Elagabalus' offence in Dio's eyes, and what does the non-literary evidence confirm?
    Answer

    Not importing a foreign god but placing Elagabal above Jupiter and having himself voted his priest (Dio 80(79).11.1), with the marriage to a Vestal as sacrilege. Coins and inscriptions confirm the god's primacy and the priestly title; the sexual stories are unconfirmed, as Arrizabalaga y Prado (2010) argued.

  10. Why did the rise of Ardashir matter, and how do the sources judge Alexander's response?
    Answer

    The Sasanians replaced a weakened Parthian dynasty with one that claimed the old Persian lands to the Greek sea (Dio 80(80).3–4). Herodian makes the campaign of 232 a humiliation (6.5–6), the Historia Augusta a victory (Severus Alexander 55–57); the outcome was probably a costly stalemate, and on the Rhine his attempt to buy peace cost him his life in 235.

Carry forward

  1. The Severans made explicit what Augustus had disguised: the emperor ruled because he paid the army. Each pay rise drove new taxes, the fiscal side of 212 and the debasement of the coinage, and the cycle of soldier emperors after 235 follows from it.
  2. The edict of 212 made nearly every free inhabitant a Roman citizen, ending the graded citizenship that had built Roman Italy; from now on "Roman" names a subject of the empire, while real status runs through rank, wealth and office, and local law lives on beneath.
  3. The dynasty's legitimacy ran through invented descent and through women, from Severus' self-adoption into the Antonines to Maesa's claim that Elagabalus was Caracalla's son; its history is told by senators who measured emperors by senatorial and Roman norms, so read the scandals of Elagabalus and the rule of women as judgements, not reports.

Give me an in-depth report on the Severan age, AD 193 to 235. Cover: the auction of the empire in 193; Septimius Severus from Lepcis Magna, the civil wars against Niger and Albinus, the army and its pay, the Parthian campaign, the arch in the Forum and the death at York; Julia Domna and the Syrian women of the dynasty; Caracalla, the murder of Geta and his erasure from the Severan tondo, the Constitutio Antoniniana of 212 and its purpose, the baths; Macrinus; Elagabalus and the god of Emesa as Roman scandal; Severus Alexander and Julia Mamaea, the rise of the Sasanians and the assassination of 235; the great jurists (Papinian, Ulpian, Paul) at the Severan court, with module 9.1 taking their work; and Cassius Dio and Herodian as contemporary witnesses. ROME · UNIT 7 · The Principate, AD 14 to 235 · 7.5 · 3,253 words

How the empire worked

The emperor at work: petition and responseSenators, knights and government without bureaucracyThe governor on the spot: Pliny in BithyniaThe cities as the governmentTaxes, census and coinThe frontiers and the army in peacetime"Romanisation" and the quarrel over the wordThe Greek East under RomeThe limits of the systemSelf-testCarry forward

The emperor at work: petition and response

Module 6.1 showed what the princeps was: a bundle of powers voted by the Senate, with the army beneath. Fergus Millar's The Emperor in the Roman World (1977) asked what he did all day, and answered from inscriptions, papyri and the law codes rather than from the court historians. His formula is that the emperor was what he did, and what he did was mostly respond. Cities sent embassies with loyal decrees and requests for privileges; individuals handed up petitions (libelli); governors wrote for rulings; litigants appealed. The emperor heard, judged and replied. Answers to petitions were written beneath them as subscriptions and posted in public; answers to cities and officials went as letters, which the cities cut in stone. Initiative came from below, and the rhythm of government was the queue.

Dio gives the norm in an anecdote. A woman stopped Hadrian on a journey; he said he had no time; she cried that then he should stop being emperor, and he turned and heard her (69.6.3). About 181 the tenants of an imperial estate in Africa, the saltus Burunitanus, petitioned Commodus that the lessee and the procurators had sent soldiers to beat them, Roman citizens among them; his reply, inscribed on the estate, ordered the procurators to exact no more labour days than the standing rules allowed (CIL VIII 10570). Antoninus Pius wrote to Ephesus in 145 rebuking the citizens for undervaluing Vedius Antoninus, a benefactor who preferred buildings to shows. Embassies were constant and costly: Byzantium, Pliny found, paid 12,000 sesterces a year to send a man to greet the emperor with a decree (Letters 10.43).

The paperwork passed through palace offices: ab epistulis for letters, a libellis for petitions, a rationibus for accounts. Under the Julio-Claudians imperial freedmen held them (module 7.1). Vitellius gave palace posts to knights (Tacitus, Histories 1.58), and the Historia Augusta makes Hadrian the first to put equestrians in charge of letters and petitions (Hadrian 22.8); the biographer Suetonius was his ab epistulis.

Where sources disagree. Keith Hopkins ("Rules of Evidence", Journal of Roman Studies 1978) attacked the book's method, an accumulation of evidence without an explicit model, and its picture of the emperor as administrator and judge, which left war, the army and money at the margins. Millar's case rests on the documents, which overwhelmingly record requests and replies. The reactive model fits the civil sphere best: Trajan's Dacian conquest and Hadrian's Wall answered no petition.

Senators, knights and government without bureaucracy

The emperor's officers came from two orders. Augustus cut the Senate to about six hundred (Dio 54.14) and fixed a property qualification of a million sesterces in Dio's account, 1.2 million in Suetonius' (Augustus 41.1). Pliny's career, set out on an inscription from his home town of Comum (CIL V 5262), shows the senatorial ladder: a minor judicial board, military tribune in Syria, quaestor, tribune of the plebs, praetor, prefect of the military treasury and then of the treasury of Saturn, consul in 100, augur, curator of the Tiber's banks and the city's sewers, and finally legate of Bithynia. Each post lasted a year or a few. The consulship, now shared among several pairs of suffects each year, was the rank that qualified a man for the great military provinces; the proconsulships of Asia and Africa crowned a career.

Knights, with a fortune of 400,000 sesterces, served as prefects and tribunes of auxiliary units, then as procurators graded by salary at 60,000, 100,000 and 200,000 sesterces. They managed imperial revenues and estates, governed small provinces such as Judaea before 66, and filled the great prefectures of the watch, the grain supply, Egypt and the guard. H.-G. Pflaum's count of procuratorial posts (Les procurateurs équestres, 1950) rises from about 25 under Augustus to about 136 under Commodus. Promotion ran on recommendation. Pliny asks Trajan for senatorial rank for Voconius Romanus, whose mother had made over four million sesterces to qualify him (10.4), and Richard Saller (Personal Patronage under the Early Empire, 1982) argued that patronage, not seniority, moved careers.

Set these men against Bruce Frier's estimate of some 61 million people by AD 164 (Cambridge Ancient History XI, 2000): a few dozen governors with their legates and quaestors, a little over a hundred procurators, the imperial slaves and freedmen who kept the accounts. Peter Garnsey and Richard Saller called the chapter on it "Government without bureaucracy" (The Roman Empire, 1987). Amateurs on short terms, advised by their friends, presided; the cities and the army did the work.

The governor on the spot: Pliny in Bithynia

Module 4.4 described the Republican governor: a magistrate for a year with a quaestor, a few legates and his friends, answerable only on his return. Module 6.4 showed Augustus dividing the provinces between proconsuls chosen by lot and his own legates. What changed afterwards was supervision. Legates of Caesar served for several years under written instructions (mandata); procurators reported separately on revenue; provincials could go over the governor's head. The Senate still judged extortion: Pliny prosecuted Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa, in 100 (Letters 2.11).

Book 10 of Pliny's letters is the only surviving file of a governor's correspondence with an emperor. Bithynia-Pontus was a public province, but about 110 Trajan sent Pliny as his own legate with consular power to put the cities' finances in order. Module 2.5 reads the letters on the Christians (10.96–97); the rest show the work.

  • Money. Nicomedia had spent 3,318,000 sesterces on an aqueduct left unfinished and 200,000 more on a second, also abandoned (10.37). Nicaea's theatre had swallowed more than ten million and was cracking. Trajan replies that Pliny is on the spot and should decide, and adds that the little Greeks love their gymnasia (10.39–40).
  • Experts. Asked for a surveyor, Trajan says he barely has enough for works at Rome and near it, and every province has its own (10.17b–18).
  • Associations. After a fire at Nicomedia Pliny proposes a guild of 150 firemen. Trajan refuses: whatever the name, men gathered for a common purpose soon become political clubs (10.33–34).
  • Local law. Apamea, a colony, claims the right to run its own accounts (10.47–48); Amisus, free by treaty, may keep its benefit societies under its own laws (10.92–93); on entry fees for town councillors no general rule can be laid down (10.112–113).
  • Feuds. When Dio of Prusa is accused of setting the emperor's statue near the graves of his wife and son, Trajan refuses to let reverence for his name be won by fear and treason charges (10.81–82).

The emperor's style is consistent: refer to local law, refuse precedents, keep soldiers with the standards. So is the governor's poverty of means. Pliny had no engineers, police or fire service of his own; his staff was his friends, a few freedmen and soldiers seconded from the army.

The cities as the government

The empire was a federation of self-governing cities, each responsible for its territory, its courts of first instance, its public works and the collection of its taxes. In the Greek East the cities were old. In the West Rome made them, by founding colonies and by turning tribal centres into towns with charters.

The fullest charter was found in 1981, by men with metal detectors, near El Saucejo in the province of Seville: six of the ten bronze tablets of the lex Irnitana, the law of the small municipium Flavium Irnitanum. Vespasian had given the Latin right to all Spain (Pliny, Natural History 3.30), and Irni's law is a copy of a standard Flavian municipal statute, known before only in fragments from Malaca and Salpensa found in 1851. A letter of Domitian of AD 91, pardoning marriages contracted irregularly under the Latin right, is appended. The law sets out a council of decurions (it assumes sixty-three), annual elections of duoviri, aediles and quaestors, the oath, public slaves, finances, festivals, manumission and guardianship. Chapter 21 gives Roman citizenship to those who have held a magistracy, with their parents, wives and children. Chapter 84 caps the magistrates' civil jurisdiction at 1,000 sesterces; bigger cases went to the governor. Its courts follow the edict of the provincial governor (ch. 85), itself modelled on the praetor's at Rome. A small Spanish town ran itself on Roman law, and its leading men became Roman citizens by doing so.

The system rested on local wealth. Councillors paid an entry fee (summa honoraria), and magistrates were expected to give: buildings, oil for the baths, games, feasts. Paul Veyne made "euergetism", a word coined by French scholars before him, the standard name for the habit (Le pain et le cirque, 1976). Pliny gave Comum a library, baths and a fund for the children of its plebs (CIL V 5262); in Lycia Opramoas of Rhodiapolis paid for rebuilding after the earthquake of 141 and had the emperor's letters of thanks inscribed on his tomb. Generosity bought honour and kept the cities solvent, but competition led to the half-built aqueducts Pliny inspected. From about Trajan's time emperors appointed curators (curatores rei publicae) to supervise individual cities' finances, a sign that the model strained.

Taxes, census and coin

Provincials paid two direct taxes, on land (tributum soli) and on persons (tributum capitis); Italy paid neither. Indirect taxes included customs dues (portoria), at a fortieth in the Gauls, the five per cent on the freeing of slaves, and the inheritance and sales taxes that funded the military treasury (module 6.4). Cities collected the direct taxes under procurators' eyes; companies of publicani still farmed customs. In 58 Nero proposed abolishing all indirect taxes, was talked out of it by older advisers who warned that the empire would dissolve, and ordered the tax regulations published instead (Tacitus, Annals 13.50–51).

Direct tax needed a census, and censuses were provincial. Augustus held one in Gaul in 27 BC (Dio 53.22.5); the form Ulpian describes required each field's name, district and neighbours, its arable sown in the last ten years, and the number of vines and olive trees (Digest 50.15.4). Quirinius' census of Judaea in AD 6, when it became a province, provoked Judas the Galilean's revolt (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.1–10). Luke places Jesus' birth at this census, ordered, he says, for the whole world (Luke 2.1–2), while Matthew puts it under Herod, who died in 4 BC; no empire-wide census is attested. In Egypt households declared every fourteen years, and Roger Bagnall and Bruce Frier built The Demography of Roman Egypt (1994) from the surviving returns. In 127 Babatha, a Jewish woman of Maoza, registered her date groves in the census of the new province of Arabia (P.Yadin 16).

The coinage tied the system together: an aureus of 25 denarii, a denarius of four sesterces, a sestertius of four asses, struck chiefly at Rome. Nero cut the weight of gold and silver in 64, and the denarius lost silver again under Marcus and Severus. The East kept its own silver at Alexandria and Antioch, and hundreds of cities struck bronze with the emperor's head and their own gods. Reverse types announced victories, virtues and provinces, Hadrian's tours among them. A. H. M. Jones ("Numismatics and History", 1956) doubted that users read them, against C. H. V. Sutherland's view of the types as instruments of policy (Coinage in Roman Imperial Policy, 1951).

Where sources disagree. Keith Hopkins ("Taxes and Trade in the Roman Empire", Journal of Roman Studies 1980) built a model: money taxes raised in the rich inner provinces were spent in Rome and on the frontier armies, so the taxed provinces had to sell goods to earn the coin back, and taxation drove trade and monetisation. Richard Duncan-Jones (Structure and Scale in the Roman Economy, 1990) found taxation in money less general than this assumes, and taxation in kind, Egypt's grain above all, more widespread.

The frontiers and the army in peacetime

Most soldiers in most years fought no battle. The army built roads and forts, guarded governors and prisons, escorted grain, policed roads and markets and kept the governor's office; its clerks and orderlies were the nearest thing the provinces had to a civil service. Trajan resisted every drain on it. Prisons should be guarded by public slaves, not soldiers (Pliny, Letters 10.19–20). Byzantium had a legionary centurion because of the crowds passing through, but Juliopolis would not, for every town would then ask (10.77–78). Agrippa, in the speech Josephus gives him in AD 66, says the Gauls were held by 1,200 soldiers, hardly more than their cities (Jewish War 2.345–401): rhetoric, but the point was that obedience did not depend on garrisons. Pay, service and discharge are module 9.2's.

Hadrian, the Historia Augusta says, was the first to build a wall, eighty miles long, to separate barbarians from Romans (Hadrian 11.2). Begun about 122, under the governor Aulus Platorius Nepos named on its building inscriptions, it ran from Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness on the Solway: stone in the east, turf in the west, a fortlet with a gate at every Roman mile and two turrets between, forts added during construction, and the ditch and mounds of the Vallum behind. Legionaries of the Second, Sixth and Twentieth built it; auxiliaries manned it. Under Antoninus Pius the governor Lollius Urbicus advanced to a turf wall between Forth and Clyde (Historia Augusta, Antoninus Pius 5.4); within a generation the army was back on Hadrian's line. David Breeze and Brian Dobson (Hadrian's Wall, 1976) read it as a means of controlling movement, a line of gates, not a fighting platform. Module 0.2 holds the argument over frontier strategy.

Vindolanda, a fort on the road behind the later Wall, has since 1973 produced hundreds of ink tablets of about 85 to 130, excavated by Robin Birley and edited by Alan Bowman and David Thomas. They show the army running a province. A strength report of the First Cohort of Tungrians (Tab. Vindol. II 154) counts 752 men, of whom 456 were absent, 46 as the governor's guards and 337 at Coria (probably Corbridge); of the 296 present, 31 were sick, wounded or had inflamed eyes. A civilian contractor writes that he has bought some 5,000 modii of grain and needs cash, and that the roads are too bad to move hides (II 343). A memorandum notes that the "little Britons", Brittunculi, do not mount to throw javelins (II 164). A man from overseas, beaten with rods, petitions "your majesty" for redress (II 344): petition and response reached the edge of the province.

"Romanisation" and the quarrel over the word

Tacitus describes his father-in-law in Britain about 79 urging the Britons to build temples, fora and houses, educating chiefs' sons in the liberal arts, until they took to the toga, porticoes, baths and elegant dinners (Agricola 21). He ends:

idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset.

"The innocent called it civilisation, when it was part of their slavery." Module 7.2 has Agricola's campaigns. The passage frames a modern argument over what happened when provincials took up Roman towns, villas, Latin, bath-houses and gods, and over whether "Romanisation" is the right word for it. Archaeology supplies most of the evidence, and the West, where Latin replaced local languages, is its main field.

Where sources disagree. Francis Haverfield, lecturing in 1905, described a civilisation spreading from Rome through which western provincials, Britons included, came to share Roman speech and ways; Richard Hingley (Roman Officers and English Gentlemen, 2000) showed how closely this mirrored the British Empire's view of itself. Martin Millett (1990) made native elites the agents: with little administration, Rome governed through tribal aristocracies who adopted Roman culture to keep their status. Greg Woolf (Becoming Roman, 1998), working on Gaul, treated Roman culture as a changing structure of differences rather than a package, remade as provincials joined it. David Mattingly (Imperialism, Power, and Identity, 2011) wants the term dropped: it implies one culture and a benign process, and hides power, exploitation and the discrepant identities of soldiers, townsmen, peasants and slaves; Jane Webster (2001) proposed creolisation instead.

The argument changes the question rather than the evidence. A bath-house in a Gallic town is a fact; whether it marks emulation, coercion or a new provincial culture is the dispute. Citizenship advanced by grant, army service and municipal office until the edict of 212 (module 7.4).

The Greek East under Rome

Greek module 7.4 covers Achaea, Athens as a university town, Hadrian's Panhellenion and the Second Sophistic. The administrative point is that Rome governed the East in Greek. Governors and emperors wrote to Greek cities in Greek, and the cities kept their councils, assemblies and magistrates. Plutarch tells a Greek magistrate to remember the Roman shoe above his head and not to run to the governor with every local quarrel (Precepts of Statecraft 813–815). Rivalry was channelled into status: in AD 26 eleven cities of Asia competed before the Senate for the right to build a temple to Tiberius, and Smyrna won (Tacitus, Annals 4.55–56); module 6.2 has the imperial cult's provincial forms. Woolf's formula for the East is "becoming Roman, staying Greek" (Proceedings of the Cambridge Philological Society, 1994): the elites took citizenship, office and senatorial rank, and kept Greek culture as their claim to distinction.

The limits of the system

Government by consent of local elites failed where its levers bit too hard, and the great revolts read as a list of them. In Britain in 60–61 the annexation of a client kingdom, a veterans' colony on native land, a temple of the deified Claudius seen as the citadel of perpetual domination (Tacitus, Annals 14.31), a procurator reclaiming Claudius' gifts and Seneca calling in his loans (Dio 62.2) all fed Boudica's revolt, which module 7.1 tells. In Judaea in 66 a procurator's raid on the Temple treasury and the ending of the sacrifices for the emperor began the war of module 7.2. The diaspora rising of 115–117 in Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus (Dio 68.32) and the Bar Kokhba war of 132–135 (module 7.3) followed.

Banditry was the chronic limit. Ulpian tells the governor to purge his province of the sacrilegious, kidnappers, thieves and bandits (Digest 1.18.13). Pliny writes of a knight who vanished on the road near Ocriculum and of a townsman of Comum who disappeared with his slaves (Letters 6.25), and epitaphs record men killed by latrones. Under Commodus the deserter Maternus led a band through Gaul and Spain (Herodian 1.10). Under Severus Bulla Felix ran six hundred men in Italy for two years; captured, he was asked by the prefect Papinian why he was a bandit, and answered: why are you a prefect? (Dio 77(76).10). Josephus calls the Jewish rebels "bandits"; the word was a label as much as a trade.

Where sources disagree. Brent Shaw ("Bandits in the Roman Empire", Past and Present 1984) argued that banditry was endemic and structural, a sign of how thinly the state reached the countryside, and that latro was a relation to power that could fit a rustler, a local strongman, a rebel or a usurper. Thomas Grünewald (Räuber, Rebellen, Rivalen, Rächer, 1999; English 2004) sorted the evidence into types and treated the noble robber of the stories, Bulla among them, as a literary figure rather than Hobsbawm's social bandit.

Self-test

  1. What does Millar mean by government through petition and response, and give two pieces of evidence for it.
    Answer

    That the emperor mostly reacted to initiatives from below: embassies, petitions, governors' questions and appeals, answered by subscription or letter. Evidence: Dio's woman who told Hadrian to stop being emperor if he had no time (69.6.3); the African tenants' petition to Commodus and his inscribed reply (CIL VIII 10570); Pliny's file of questions to Trajan.

  2. What did Hopkins object to in Millar's book?
    Answer

    Its method, an accumulation of evidence without an explicit model, and its emphasis on the emperor as administrator and judge, which pushed war, the army and money to the margins ("Rules of Evidence", 1978).

  3. How did senatorial and equestrian careers differ?
    Answer

    Senators climbed the magistracies (quaestor, praetor, consul) and alternated them with legionary commands and governorships, ending in great consular provinces or the proconsulships of Asia and Africa. Knights served in auxiliary commands, then as salaried procurators graded at 60,000 to 200,000 sesterces, rising to the prefectures of the watch, the grain supply, Egypt and the guard.

  4. Why is "government without bureaucracy" a fair description of the second-century empire?
    Answer

    Some 61 million people on Frier's estimate were governed by a few dozen governors, about a hundred procurators on Pflaum's count, and imperial slaves and freedmen; the cities collected taxes and judged small cases, and soldiers did the clerical and police work (Garnsey and Saller, 1987).

  5. What do Pliny's letters on the Nicomedia fire brigade and the surveyor reveal?
    Answer

    Trajan feared associations as political clubs even when their purpose was useful (10.33–34), and the centre had no technical staff to spare: provinces must find their own surveyors (10.17b–18). Security outranked efficiency, and expertise was local.

  6. What did the lex Irnitana provide, and how did it bind local elites to Rome?
    Answer

    A standard Flavian constitution for a Latin town: council, elections, magistrates, finances, festivals, and procedure following the governor's edict, with civil jurisdiction capped at 1,000 sesterces (ch. 84). Chapter 21 made ex-magistrates and their families Roman citizens, so local office became the road to Roman status.

  7. Why is Luke's census a problem, and what do Babatha and the Egyptian returns show about real censuses?
    Answer

    Luke 2.1–2 has a census of the whole world under Quirinius, which Josephus dates to AD 6 in Judaea alone, while Matthew puts the birth under Herod, dead by 4 BC. Real censuses were provincial: Babatha registered her groves in Arabia in 127 (P.Yadin 16), and Egyptian households declared every fourteen years.

  8. State Hopkins's taxes-and-trade model and Duncan-Jones's objection.
    Answer

    Money taxes from the inner provinces were spent in Rome and on the frontiers, so the taxed provinces had to export goods to earn coin back, driving trade (1980). Duncan-Jones (1990) found money taxation less general and taxation in kind more widespread than the model assumes.

  9. What does the Tungrian strength report show about the army in peacetime?
    Answer

    Of 752 men only 296 were at Vindolanda; 46 guarded the governor and 337 were at Coria (Tab. Vindol. II 154). A unit was a pool of manpower dispersed on guard, escort and administrative duties, not a garrison waiting for battle.

  10. How do Haverfield, Millett, Woolf and Mattingly differ on "Romanisation"?
    Answer

    Haverfield saw a civilisation spreading from Rome; Millett made native elites the agents, adopting Roman culture to keep status; Woolf saw Roman culture itself as a changing structure remade as provincials became Roman; Mattingly rejects the term for hiding power and the discrepant identities of different groups.

Carry forward

  1. The Roman state governed through others: an emperor who answered petitions, amateur governors on short terms, and self-governing cities that collected taxes and judged small cases. When the cities' elites failed or the levers bit too hard, there was little machinery behind them.
  2. The army was the empire's civil service as well as its defence: soldiers guarded, escorted, policed, built and kept records, and the frontier armies were the largest market for taxes and goods. Changes in the army are therefore changes in government.
  3. "Romanisation" is a modern word for many local bargains; ask of each piece of evidence who adopted what, for whose benefit, and under what pressure, and remember that the Greek East became Roman while staying Greek.

Maximinus and the soldier emperors

Module 7.4 ends with the recruits at Mainz proclaiming their trainer in 235. Maximinus was a Thracian of humble, half-barbarian origin, Herodian says (7.1.1–2); the Historia Augusta makes him a giant. He never entered Rome as emperor. He fought on the Rhine and Danube, and the Harzhorn battlefield in Lower Saxony, found in 2008 and dated by coins to the 230s, bears out the Historia Augusta's campaign deep in Germany (Maximini duo 12). To pay the troops he seized the property of the rich and the funds of cities and temples (Herodian 7.3).

In 238 landowners at Thysdrus in Africa killed a procurator and proclaimed the aged proconsul Gordian and his son (Herodian 7.4–5); within weeks the governor of Numidia had killed the son and the father had hanged himself (7.9). The Senate chose two of its own, Pupienus and Balbinus, and the crowd forced it to add the boy Gordian III (7.10). Maximinus stalled before Aquileia and was killed by his soldiers (8.5); the praetorians then murdered Pupienus and Balbinus (8.8). Herodian ends there, and no contemporary narrative of the next forty-six years survives. Gordian III died on the Persian front in 244; his prefect Philip, an Arab from the Hauran, celebrated Rome's thousandth birthday in 248 (Eutropius 9.3) before Decius overthrew him.

The pattern held: armies made emperors, the Senate ratified them, few died in bed. Many of these soldier emperors came from the Danubian provinces, as would Diocletian and Constantine. The table leaves out the Gallic and Palmyrene rulers and a swarm of usurpers.

Numerian; Carinus283–285found dead; killed by his own officers at the Margus

Shapur I, Valerian and the rock of Naqsh-e Rustam

Module 7.4 introduced Ardashir. His son Shapur I, crowned about 240, made the Sasanian claim good. The best witness is Shapur himself: a trilingual inscription in Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek on the Ka'ba-ye Zardosht at Naqsh-e Rustam, near Persepolis, known as the Res Gestae Divi Saporis. It narrates three campaigns. Gordian III fell in a great battle at Misiche in 244, and Philip bought peace for 500,000 denarii, by Shapur's figure. Most Roman writers blame Philip instead: Zosimus says he engineered a grain shortage and turned the troops against Gordian (1.18–19), Eutropius that his treachery killed him (9.2); the Byzantine chroniclers Zonaras and Malalas have Gordian die after a fall from his horse in battle. About 252–253 Shapur destroyed a Roman army of 60,000 at Barbalissos (his figure) and took Antioch; Dura-Europos fell about 256, its synagogue and house church preserved under the siege embankment. In 260 Valerian came with 70,000 men, again by Shapur's count, and beyond Carrhae and Edessa Shapur took him with his own hands, with his praetorian prefect and senators; the captives were settled in Persian lands.

On the cliff below the Achaemenid tombs at Naqsh-e Rustam Shapur carved himself on horseback, one Roman kneeling, another held by the wrist: usually read as Philip suing for peace and the captive Valerian. A relief at Bishapur adds a third Roman, dead beneath the horse, taken as Gordian. No emperor had been taken alive before.

Where sources disagree. Shapur claims a battle. Zosimus says plague had wasted the Roman army and that Valerian, hoping to buy peace, went to a parley with a small escort and was seized (1.36). Lactantius has Shapur use him as a mounting block and hang his flayed, dyed skin in a temple (On the Deaths of the Persecutors 5), the end a persecutor deserved; Eutropius says only that he grew old in shameful servitude (9.7).

Decius: the order to sacrifice and the death at Abritus

The order of 249–250

Decius, a senator from Budalia near Sirmium (Eutropius 9.4), was proclaimed by the Danube army and defeated Philip near Verona in 249 (Zosimus 1.21–22; the place from Eutropius 9.3). Late in 249 or early in 250 he ordered every inhabitant of the empire to sacrifice, pour a libation and taste the sacrificial meat before local commissioners, who signed a certificate (libellus). Some four dozen survive from Egypt, dated June to July 250, in one formula: the applicant has always sacrificed, has now done so in the commissioners' presence according to the order, and asks them to sign. Whole households applied, and one certificate comes from a priestess of the crocodile god Petesouchos.

For Christians this replaced Trajan's rule of not seeking them out (module 2.5) with a test all had to pass. Fabian, bishop of Rome, died in January 250 and Origen was tortured (Eusebius, Church History 6.39); Dionysius of Alexandria saw Christians come forward pale and trembling, some to sacrifice, some to refuse (6.41). Cyprian's On the Lapsed addresses the readmission of those who yielded or bought certificates, the issue behind Novatian's schism at Rome. Valerian struck at clergy and Christians of rank in 257–258 (Cyprian, Letters 80), and Cyprian was beheaded at Carthage on 14 September 258; Gallienus restored church property (Eusebius, Church History 7.13). Module 8.2 takes the persecution of 303.

Where sources disagree. Cyprian and Dionysius present the order as an assault on the church, and Lactantius leaves his naked corpse to the beasts and birds in punishment (On the Deaths of the Persecutors 4). J. B. Rives ("The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire", 1999) read it as a general religious act that for the first time treated the empire's inhabitants as one religious community; the priestess's certificate shows pagans were tested too. The order's text is lost, so its purpose is inferred.

The Goths and Abritus

In 250 the Gothic king Kniva crossed the Danube, surprised Decius at Beroe and took Philippopolis (Jordanes, Getica 101–103). In the summer of 251, at Abritus (Razgrad in Bulgaria), Decius and his son died with their army in a marsh, the first emperor killed by a foreign enemy. Zosimus blames Trebonianus Gallus for luring him into the fen (1.23), but the army proclaimed Gallus and he adopted Decius' surviving son, which tells against betrayal. Gallus let the Goths go home with plunder and captives and promised a yearly payment (Zosimus 1.24). Sea raids followed across the Black Sea and the Aegean, and Claudius II won the name Gothicus at Naissus in 268 or 269 against a host Zosimus puts at 320,000 men in 6,000 ships (1.42).

The plague of Cyprian

An epidemic reached Alexandria about 250 and lasted more than a decade. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, lists its symptoms: flux, fever, sores in the throat, vomiting, burning eyes, and in some the loss of limbs to putrefaction, or of hearing or sight (On Mortality 14). Dionysius wrote that Alexandrians aged fourteen to eighty on the grain register now numbered fewer than those aged forty to seventy once had, and praised Christians who nursed the sick (Eusebius, Church History 7.21–22). The Historia Augusta's 5,000 dead in a day at Rome (Gallienus 5.5) cannot be checked; Claudius II died of the disease in 270. Kyle Harper (The Fate of Rome, 2017) argues from the symptoms for a viral haemorrhagic fever like Ebola; smallpox and influenza have also been proposed. Turning such reports into mortality is the method dispute of module 7.3.

Gallienus and the Gallic empire

Valerian made his son Gallienus co-Augustus in 253 and left him the West. After 260 the empire split three ways. The Rhine army proclaimed Postumus, who forced Cologne to surrender Gallienus' son Saloninus and killed him (Zosimus 1.38). Postumus and successors such as Victorinus and Tetricus ruled Gaul, the Germanies and Britain, at first Spain and Raetia too, with their own consuls and mints. An altar found at Augsburg in 1992 records a victory of 24–25 April 260 over the Semnones or Iuthungi, returning from Italy with many thousands of Italian captives; it was dedicated in September under Postumus' consuls, so Raetia had already gone over. Postumus never marched on Rome, and his troops killed him in 269 for refusing them the sack of Mainz (Aurelius Victor 33.8).

The Latin tradition remembers Gallienus as a voluptuary (Eutropius 9.8). Yet he held Italy and the Balkans, ended the persecution, honoured Plotinus (Porphyry, Life of Plotinus 12) and built up mobile cavalry under Aureolus at Milan. Aurelius Victor says he barred senators from army commands by edict (33.34); inscriptions show a slower change over decades (module 9.2, and module 0.2 for the dispute over Luttwak's grand strategy). In 268, marching against the rebel Aureolus at Milan, he died in a plot devised by his prefect Heraclianus and known to Claudius (Zosimus 1.40).

Odaenathus and Zenobia of Palmyra

Palmyra, a caravan city between Roman Syria and the Euphrates, had long been Roman; its leading man, Septimius Odaenathus, held consular rank. After Valerian's capture he harried Shapur's retreating army, destroyed the usurper Quietus at Emesa in 261 and kept the East for Gallienus; Zosimus says he retook Nisibis and twice reached Ctesiphon (1.39). Palmyrene inscriptions after his death call him king of kings, turning the Persian title on Persia, but no coin makes him Augustus. He was murdered at Emesa in 267 or 268 (Zosimus 1.39).

His widow Zenobia ruled for their son Vaballathus. In 270 her general Zabdas took Egypt, with 70,000 men against 50,000 by Zosimus' figures (1.44). The mints of Antioch and Alexandria paired Aurelian on one face with Vaballathus, bearing Roman titles, on the other; in 272 mother and son became Augusta and Augustus. Aurelian beat Zabdas near Antioch and at Emesa, besieged Palmyra and caught Zenobia at the Euphrates, fleeing on a fast camel to seek Persian help (Zosimus 1.50–55); her adviser, the rhetorician Longinus, was executed (1.56). When Palmyra rose again in 273 it was sacked (1.60–61).

Where sources disagree. Zosimus says Zenobia died on the road to Europe, of illness or by refusing food (1.59). The Historia Augusta parades her in golden chains in Aurelian's triumph and retires her to an estate near Tibur (Tyranni triginta 30.24–27), with an invented descent from Cleopatra and a defiant letter to Aurelian (Aurelian 27). Her aims are read from the coins: the step from Vaballathus beside Aurelian to Vaballathus Augustus looks like a claim to share the Roman empire, not a separate kingdom.

Aurelian: reunification, the wall and the Sun

After Claudius and his brother Quintillus, the cavalry commander Aurelian took power in 270 and in five years reversed the division. Invaders of Italy were driven out after a near-disaster; Dacia beyond the Danube was given up and its name moved to a new province south of the river (Eutropius 9.15). Palmyra fell in 272; in 274 Tetricus, last of the Gallic emperors, deserted his army near Châlons and was made governor of Lucania (Eutropius 9.13). Aurelian's coins hailed him restorer of the world.

He began to wall Rome, unwalled for centuries, and Probus finished the work (Zosimus 1.49): about 19 km by modern measurement, some 8 m high at first, taking in the praetorian camp and the pyramid of Cestius. The Historia Augusta's nearly fifty miles (Aurelian 39.2) is fiction; much still stands.

In 274 he dedicated a temple of Sol in Rome, adorned with Palmyrene spoils, statues of Helios and Bel among them (Zosimus 1.61), with a new college of senatorial pontiffs and four-yearly games. The Sun was a god every army could share, the emperor's companion rather than his rival; Constantine's coins kept him into the 320s (module 8.3). The Calendar of 354 marks 25 December as the birthday of the Unconquered; that Aurelian fixed the date is a modern inference. In 275, outside Perinthus in Thrace, officers deceived by a secretary's forged order for their own execution killed him (Zosimus 1.62).

Where sources disagree. The Historia Augusta has Aurelian see the god of Emesa aid him against Zenobia (Aurelian 25), and Gaston Halsberghe (The Cult of Sol Invictus, 1972) took his Sol for the Syrian Elagabal; others prefer Palmyrene Malakbel. Steven Hijmans (Sol: The Sun in the Art and Religions of Rome, 2009) argued from coins and monuments that Sol had been a Roman god continuously since the Republic, and that Aurelian gave an old god a new priesthood.

The coin and the prices

Caracalla's antoninianus of 215 (module 7.4) weighed about one and a half denarii and was probably tariffed at two, a hidden debasement from the start. On the assays summarised by Kenneth Harl (Coinage in the Roman Economy, 300 B.C. to A.D. 700, 1996), it held about half silver at its launch and a few per cent by the late 260s: bronze with a silver wash. Mints multiplied near the armies, hoards of thousands of pieces fill museum stores, and in Britain and Gaul local copies circulated beside them.

Trust failed at the counter. In 260 the strategos of the Oxyrhynchite nome ordered bankers who had shut their exchanges rather than take the divine coin of the emperors to reopen and accept all but plain forgeries (P.Oxy. 12.1411). The state increasingly levied and paid in kind, the road to Diocletian's taxes (module 8.2). Rome's mint workers, who had adulterated the coin, rose about 271: Eutropius has them kill the finance officer Felicissimus (9.14), and the Historia Augusta counts 7,000 soldiers dead (Aurelian 38.2). Aurelian's reform of 274 struck a heavier coin marked XXI, read as twenty parts copper to one of silver or as a mark of value. Dominic Rathbone ("Monetisation, not price-inflation, in third-century AD Egypt?", 1996) found Egyptian prices broadly steady through most of the debasement, then a sudden multiplication after the reform.

Lost and garbled sources

No half-century of imperial history is worse documented. Herodian stops in 238. The best contemporary historian, Dexippus of Athens, wrote a Chronicle to 270 and a Scythica on the Gothic wars, and led the Athenians against the Heruli in 267 (Historia Augusta, Gallienus 13.8; Greek module 7.4 notes the damage to Athens). He was known only in fragments until a Vienna palimpsest, identified between 2007 and 2009 and published by Gunther Martin and Jana Grusková from 2014, yielded new pages on Kniva's war and the Herulian invasion.

The rest is late. Zosimus, a pagan writing at Constantinople about 500, follows Dexippus in book 1 of his New History and blames Rome's decline on neglect of the gods. The Latin breviaries of the 360s, Aurelius Victor and Eutropius, with the later Epitome de Caesaribus, compress a lost common source (module 0.1) into a few lines a reign; Byzantine chroniclers such as Zonaras keep Greek material otherwise lost. The Historia Augusta lacks its lives for 244–260 and fills the rest with forgery: the Thirty Tyrants, padded to echo the Thirty at Athens, and the letters of the Life of Aurelian (module 0.1 makes the case against it). The controls are contemporary: Cyprian's letters, Dionysius in Eusebius, the Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle, Shapur's inscription, papyri, the Augsburg altar and coins, which fix the order and length of reigns.

Was it a crisis?

The losses are plain: one emperor killed by the Goths and another a Persian prisoner, three regimes for a decade, Antioch sacked, Athens burned, Dacia given up, the silver coin turned to bronze. The curve of Latin inscriptions that Ramsay MacMullen traced ("The Epigraphic Habit in the Roman Empire", 1982) peaks under Severus and falls steeply after; Gallic towns shrank behind new walls. Cyprian told a pagan critic that the world had grown old (To Demetrianus 3). Yet Diocletian in 284 inherited the old frontiers, less Dacia and the angle between the upper Rhine and Danube, and the cities of Africa and much of the East kept building. What broke was how power worked: equestrian commanders, emperors from the camp, taxes in kind, a court that moved with the army. Module 8.2 shows Diocletian making a system of the century's improvisations.

Where sources disagree. Michael Rostovtzeff (The Social and Economic History of the Roman Empire, 1926) explained the century as a war of peasant soldiers against the urban classes; Géza Alföldy ("The Crisis of the Third Century as Seen by Contemporaries", 1974) argued that contemporaries themselves wrote of a world in crisis. Karl Strobel (Das Imperium Romanum im "3. Jahrhundert", 1993) and Christian Witschel (Krise, Rezession, Stagnation?, 1999) answered that the evidence shows regional variety and accelerated change, not one empire-wide collapse. Wolf Liebeschuetz ("Was there a crisis of the third century?", 2007) replied that a crisis need not be uniform, and that the convergence of usurpation, invasion, plague and monetary collapse in the 250s and 260s earns the word.

Self-test

  1. What did the events of 238 show about how emperors were made, and why does the narrative evidence thin out after that year?
    Answer

    An African tax revolt, the Senate's own candidates, the Roman crowd and finally the armies and praetorians each made or unmade emperors, and the army's choice proved decisive. Herodian, the last surviving contemporary narrative, ends with Gordian III's accession in 238.

  2. What does Shapur's inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam claim about Gordian III and Valerian, and how do Roman writers tell the same events?
    Answer

    It claims Gordian fell in battle at Misiche and that Shapur took Valerian with his own hands beyond Carrhae and Edessa. Zosimus and Eutropius blame Philip's intrigue for Gordian's death (Zosimus 1.18–19; Eutropius 9.2), and Zosimus has Valerian seized at a parley after plague had wasted his army (1.36).

  3. What exactly did Decius order, and what do the Egyptian certificates show about its scope?
    Answer

    That every inhabitant sacrifice, pour a libation and taste the offering before commissioners and obtain a signed libellus. Some four dozen survive, dated June to July 250; whole households and even a priestess of Petesouchos applied, which supports Rives' view that it was a general religious act, though Christians felt it as persecution.

  4. Why was Abritus a landmark, and why is Zosimus' charge against Trebonianus Gallus doubted?
    Answer

    Decius was the first emperor killed by a foreign enemy, dying with his son and army in a marsh in 251. Zosimus says Gallus lured him into the fen (1.23), but the army then proclaimed Gallus and he adopted Decius' surviving son, which a traitor would hardly have managed.

  5. What do Cyprian and Dionysius contribute to our knowledge of the plague, and what has Harper proposed?
    Answer

    Cyprian lists the symptoms, including flux, fever, throat sores and putrefying limbs (On Mortality 14); Dionysius gives the shrinking Alexandrian grain register and Christian nursing (Eusebius, Church History 7.21–22). Harper (2017) argued for a viral haemorrhagic fever; the diagnosis remains uncertain.

  6. What does the Augsburg altar reveal about the Gallic empire?
    Answer

    Dedicated in September 260 for a victory over the Semnones or Iuthungi returning from Italy with captives, it is dated by Postumus' consuls, so Raetia had joined him within months of his proclamation.

  7. How did Palmyra move from defending Gallienus' East to claiming imperial titles?
    Answer

    Odaenathus beat Shapur's retreating army, destroyed Quietus and reached Ctesiphon in Rome's name. After his murder Zenobia ruled for Vaballathus, took Egypt in 270, and the coins moved from pairing Vaballathus with Aurelian to naming mother and son Augusta and Augustus in 272, before Aurelian's reconquest.

  8. What did Aurelian do in Rome itself, and how does the Historia Augusta distort it?
    Answer

    He began a city wall of about 19 km, finished under Probus (Zosimus 1.49), and built a temple of Sol with senatorial pontiffs and games. The Historia Augusta gives the wall nearly fifty miles (Aurelian 39.2) and derives his Sol from a vision of the god of Emesa (25).

  9. What does P.Oxy. 12.1411 show, and how does Rathbone's price evidence complicate the link between debasement and inflation?
    Answer

    In 260 Oxyrhynchite bankers refused the emperors' coin until the strategos ordered them to accept it. Rathbone (1996) found Egyptian prices broadly steady during most of the debasement, with a sudden jump only after Aurelian's reform of 274.

  10. State the case for and against calling the years 235–284 a crisis, with a scholar on each side.
    Answer

    For: usurpation, defeat, plague and monetary collapse converged in the 250s and 260s, contemporaries spoke of a world in decline (Géza Alföldy, 1974), and Liebeschuetz (2007) defends the word. Against: Strobel (1993) and Witschel (1999) stress regional variety and accelerated change, with Africa and much of the East prospering.

Carry forward

  1. From 235 the emperor was whoever an army could make and keep; the men who survived were Danubian officers ruling from the camp with equestrian commanders, and the late Roman state of Diocletian and Constantine is their improvisation made permanent.
  2. The century is told by late, thin and partisan witnesses (the Historia Augusta, Zosimus, the breviaries, Christian writers judging persecutors), so the contemporary documents, Shapur's inscription, the libelli, papyri, altars and coins, are the controls on every story.
  3. Decius' universal sacrifice and Aurelian's Sol show emperors seeking one religion for the whole empire, a single test of loyalty or a single supreme god; the Great Persecution and Constantine's turn answer the same demand with opposite gods.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the crisis of the third century, AD 235 to 284. Cover: Maximinus Thrax and the soldier emperors; the Sasanian Persians, Shapur I, the capture of Valerian in 260 and the rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rustam; the Goths and the death of Decius at Abritus in 251, and Decius' order of universal sacrifice with its surviving certificates from Egypt; the plague of Cyprian; Gallienus and the breakaway Gallic empire; Odaenathus and Zenobia of Palmyra; Aurelian, the reunification, the wall of Rome and Sol Invictus; the debasement of the silver coinage and inflation; the lost and garbled sources (the Historia Augusta's fictions, Zosimus, the Latin breviaries, Dexippus); and the modern argument over whether 'crisis' is the right word. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

Diocletian and the Tetrarchy
