Adoration and the "Dominate"The ancestral gods defended: incest law and the ManichaeansThe Great PersecutionAbdication, Split and the collapse of the systemSelf-testCarry forward

Sources and the rise of Diocles

No narrative history of the reign survives. The Historia Augusta stops with Carus and his sons, Zosimus' account is lost in a gap in his text, and the Latin breviaries give a few pages (Aurelius Victor 39; Eutropius 9.19–28; Epitome de Caesaribus 39); module 8.1 weighs all three. The fullest witness is hostile. Lactantius, a teacher of rhetoric whom Diocletian had summoned to Nicomedia (Jerome, On Illustrious Men 80), wrote On the Deaths of the Persecutors about 314–315 to show that every persecutor died horribly; it is cited here by chapter alone. Beside it stand Eusebius, the Latin panegyrics, and an unusual wealth of documents: edicts on stone, papyri, and rescripts in the law codes.

Diocles was a Dalmatian of obscure birth, a scribe's son or the freedman of a senator Anullinus (Eutropius 9.19), who rose to command the household troops of the emperor Numerian (Aurelius Victor 39.1). In November 284 the army returning from Persia found Numerian dead in his closed litter. At Nicomedia on 20 November the officers chose Diocles, who swore he had no part in the death and killed the praetorian prefect Arrius Aper, Numerian's father-in-law, with his own hand before the troops (Eutropius 9.20). The Historia Augusta's druidess, who foretold that he would reign once he had killed a boar, aper (Carus 14–15), is the sort of tale module 8.1 warns against. In 285 Numerian's brother Carinus fought him at the river Margus and was killed by his own officers, men whose wives he had seduced on Victor's account (Aurelius Victor 39; Epitome 38.8), and Diocletian kept Carinus' prefect in office, a clemency Victor praises.

Two Augusti and two Caesars

Diocletian made Maximian, an old comrade born to labouring parents near Sirmium (Epitome 40.10), Caesar in 285 and Augustus in 286. Pressures multiplied: Carausius, commander of the Channel fleet, seized Britain and struck coins of himself with the two emperors as CARAVSIVS ET FRATRES SVI, "Carausius and his brothers", and wars on every frontier needed an emperor on several fronts at once (Eutropius 9.21–22). On 1 March 293 two Caesars were added, each adopted by an Augustus and married into his house. Lactantius saw greed: the world divided into four, each ruler wanting more soldiers than earlier emperors had had ruling alone (7.2).

RulerRankNameOriginMain residenceFamily tie
DiocletianAugustus 284JoviusDalmatiaNicomediafather of Valeria
MaximianCaesar 285, Augustus 286HerculiusPannoniaMilanfather or stepfather of Theodora
GaleriusCaesar 293JoviusDacia Ripensis (Epitome 40.16)Sirmium, later Thessalonicamarried Valeria
ConstantiusCaesar 293Herculiusthe Balkan provincesTriermarried Theodora, setting aside Helena, Constantine's mother

It was not a partition. Laws went out in all four names, and the Caesars fought where they were needed. Constantius recovered Britain in 296 and is hailed on a gold medallion found near Arras as REDDITOR LVCIS AETERNAE, "restorer of the eternal light". Galerius, beaten by the Persian king Narseh, was made to walk before Diocletian's carriage in his purple, for a mile in Ammianus (14.11.10), for several in Eutropius (9.24); in 298 he routed Narseh and won a peace that carried the frontier beyond the Tigris.

Diocletian took the name Jovius and Maximian Herculius, and each Caesar inherited his Augustus' name. The panegyric of 289 (Panegyric 10(2)) makes Maximian Hercules to Diocletian's Jupiter: the elder plans, the younger labours. The names claimed divine agency, not divinity, and fixed a hierarchy, Jovius above Herculius. Aurelius Victor says the other three looked up to Diocletian as to a father or a great god (39.29).

Two pairs of embracing rulers in porphyry, a stone quarried only at Mons Porphyrites in Egypt, are set into the corner of the Treasury of St Mark's in Venice, looted from Constantinople after 1204; a missing foot found in Istanbul in the 1960s suggests they stood at the Philadelphion. Each pair clasps shoulders, hands on sword hilts, one figure bearded and one not, usually read as Augustus and Caesar, though which college they show is debated. Module 10.3 reads them as art.

A rebuilt state: provinces, dioceses, army and court

Module 7.5 described government without bureaucracy: a few dozen governors and about a hundred procurators, with the cities doing the work. Diocletian built something of another order. The Verona List, a register of about 314, names some hundred provinces, roughly double the Severan number, grouped into twelve dioceses under vicarii, deputies of the praetorian prefects. Italy was divided into provinces and taxed, a great evil for part of Italy in Aurelius Victor's phrase (39.31). Governors became civil judges and assessors, while frontier troops passed to military commanders, the duces; Constantine completed the separation. Lactantius saw soldiers so multiplied that those who drew pay outnumbered those who paid, and provinces chopped into fragments with officials piled on every region (7.3–4).

Where sources disagree. Lactantius already mentions vicars of the prefects (7.4), and most accounts give the dioceses to Diocletian: William Seston dated them to 297, Timothy Barnes to 293. Constantin Zuckerman (Travaux et Mémoires, 2002) argued that the Verona List is the first evidence for the whole grid, that earlier evidence for diocesan vicars is thin, and that Constantine and Licinius created the dioceses in 314. The date of the dioceses is open.

John the Lydian, a sixth-century official, gives Diocletian's army as 389,704 men and his fleets as 45,562 (On the Months 1.27), a figure that does not suggest the fourfold increase Lactantius implies. New legions, apparently smaller than the old, and rebuilt forts, as on the Syrian desert road later called the Strata Diocletiana, held the frontiers; the formal division into field and frontier troops is usually credited to Constantine, and module 9.2 takes the late army as an institution.

The court travelled. Each ruler had his comitatus of guards, secretaries and treasury officials, and residences rose near the frontiers, at Nicomedia, Sirmium, Milan, Trier and Thessalonica. Rome received buildings instead of an emperor, among them the Curia still standing in the Forum, Diocletian's rebuilding after a fire of 283 (module 9.5). Yet the reactive government of module 7.5 survived inside the new machine. More rescripts survive from Diocletian than from any other emperor, collected by Gregorius about 292 and Hermogenianus about 295 in codes that module 9.1 follows to the Theodosian Code.

Taxes, coinage and the Edict on Maximum Prices

Module 8.1 told how the silver coinage collapsed. The state had come to feed its soldiers by requisition, and Diocletian made requisition a regular tax. Land was assessed in units called iuga and people in capita by census, and each year a rate per unit was announced to supply the army and court in kind, the annona. On 16 March 297 the prefect of Egypt, Aristius Optatus, proclaimed that the emperors had fixed what each aroura of land, by its quality, and each head of the rural population owed, so that everyone could know his burden (P.Cair.Isid. 1). The units varied: the fifth-century Syro-Roman Law Book counts as one iugum five iugera of vineyard, or twenty, forty or sixty of arable by grade. Reassessment produced the indiction of module 0.3.

The coinage was rebuilt about 294: gold at sixty to the pound, a silver argenteus at Nero's standard of ninety-six, some pieces marked XCVI, and a silvered bronze nummus struck across the empire. Prices kept rising, and late in 301 came the Edict on Maximum Prices. Its preamble, in all four names, denounces profiteers who in a single purchase strip a soldier of his donative and pay. It fixes ceilings, in denarii of account, on well over a thousand goods, wages and freight charges, with death for exceeding them or hoarding: an army modius of wheat 100 denarii, a farm labourer 25 a day with his keep, a teacher of rhetoric 250 a month for each pupil, a pound of purple silk 150,000. Copies come from Phrygia, Caria, mainland Greece, Crete and Cyrenaica, almost all in the eastern provinces. Lactantius gives the outcome: much blood shed over trifles, goods withdrawn from sale for fear, prices worse than before, and the law lapsing of necessity after many deaths (7.6–7).

Where sources disagree. The edict blames merchants' greed; Lactantius blames the emperor, whose armies, officials and buildings drove prices up (7.6–8). Simon Corcoran (The Empire of the Tetrarchs, 1996) judged that the edict was probably not widely published outside the East, so whether Maximian or Constantius enforced it is unknown.

Lord and god? Adoration and the "Dominate"

Eutropius says Diocletian ordered himself to be adored where earlier emperors had been saluted, put gems on his robes and shoes, and

regiae consuetudinis formam magis quam Romanae libertatis invexit

"brought in the form of royal custom rather than of Roman liberty" (9.26). Aurelius Victor makes him the first since Caligula and Domitian to be called lord in public and adored as a god (39.2–4). The visitor knelt and kissed the hem of the purple, a gesture Greeks had long associated with Persian kings (Greek module 11.4). At Rome for his twentieth anniversary in 303, Diocletian could not bear the people's free speech and left early (Lactantius 17.1–3). Theodor Mommsen made the change a divide, setting the Principate, a magistrate among citizens, against the Dominate, from dominus, a master of subjects; module 0.3 notes that most historians now say "late empire".

Where sources disagree. Victor and Eutropius make adoration Diocletian's innovation, yet Suetonius has Domitian styled "lord and god" (Domitian 13.2), Pliny addresses Trajan as domine throughout Letters 10, and the panegyric of 291 describes officials admitted to adore both emperors at Milan (Panegyric 11(3).11). Andreas Alföldi's studies of imperial ceremonial (1934–1935) traced its elements back through the Principate; Jochen Bleicken (Prinzipat und Dominat, 1978) argued that Mommsen's division rests on no genuine constitutional transformation; Frank Kolb (Herrscherideologie in der Spätantike, 2001) sees Diocletian formalising trends already present.

The ancestral gods defended: incest law and the Manichaeans

Diocletian's laws speak the old religion's language. An edict against incestuous marriages, issued at Damascus in 295, says that the immortal gods will stay favourable to the Roman name only if all its subjects live pious, religious, peaceful and chaste lives (Collatio 6.4). The same late antique compilation, which sets Roman law beside the law of Moses, preserves his rescript on the Manichaeans. Mani, a Babylonian prophet who died in prison under the Persian king Bahram I in the 270s, taught a dualism of light and darkness. Writing from Alexandria on 31 March to Julianus, proconsul of Africa, Diocletian called the sect a recent growth among the Persians, a nation hostile to Rome, that threatened to infect the modest and tranquil Roman people with Persian customs. Its leaders were to be burned with their books, obstinate followers executed and men of rank sent to the mines (Collatio 15.3), on the principle that it is the greatest crime to undo what the ancients once settled. The year is lost from the text: most scholars, Corcoran and Samuel Lieu among them, prefer 302; others have argued for 297.

The Great Persecution

Lactantius was at Nicomedia in 303; Eusebius, at Caesarea, wrote during and just after the events, from what he saw in Palestine and Egypt. The persecutions of Decius and Valerian are module 8.1's; Trajan's rule that Christians were not to be sought out is module 2.5's.

Lactantius makes Galerius the driving force. In the East, probably at Antioch, when the haruspices could not read the entrails because Christian attendants crossed themselves, Diocletian ordered the palace to sacrifice and soldiers to sacrifice or be discharged (10; Eusebius, Church History 8.4). In the winter of 302–303 at Nicomedia Galerius, urged on by his mother, pressed for more; a council and Apollo's oracle at Didyma were consulted, and the answer was hostile (11).

On 23 February 303, the Terminalia, the church at Nicomedia, in sight of the palace, was sacked and levelled (12). Next day the first edict ordered churches destroyed and scriptures burned, stripped Christians of rank and of the right to bring actions at law, and re-enslaved Christian imperial freedmen (13.1; Eusebius, Church History 8.2.4). A Christian who tore it down was roasted alive (13.2–3). Eusebius records three further edicts: the arrest of the clergy; their release if they sacrificed, torture if they refused (8.2.5, 8.6.8–10); and in 304 an order that the whole population sacrifice (Martyrs of Palestine 3.1).

Enforcement followed the map of the Tetrarchy. Lactantius says the whole world suffered except Gaul, where Constantius let church buildings be pulled down but spared the true temple of God, its people (15.7, 16.1). In Maximian's Africa the first edict bit. The minutes of the search at Cirta on 19 May 303, preserved in the record of a hearing of 320 (the Gesta apud Zenophilum), list the chalices, lamps and clothing for the poor surrendered by Bishop Paul's clergy; the martyrs of Abitina, arrested at a forbidden service, told the proconsul sine dominico non possumus, "we cannot live without the Lord's day" (Acts of the Abitinian Martyrs). Those who handed over scriptures were branded traditores, the seed of the Donatist schism of module 8.3. In the East persecution ran, with pauses, until 311.

The dead cannot be counted. Gibbon found ninety-two martyrs in the Martyrs of Palestine and, taking Palestine as a sixteenth of the East, put the empire's judicial executions at somewhat less than two thousand (Decline and Fall, chapter 16). Geoffrey de Ste. Croix ("Aspects of the 'Great' Persecution", Harvard Theological Review, 1954) showed how unevenly the edicts were applied from region to region.

Galerius ended it. Dying of a wasting disease that Lactantius describes with relish (33), he conceded in an edict posted at Nicomedia on 30 April 311 that, since many Christians persisted and now worshipped neither the gods nor their own god, they might be Christians again and rebuild their meeting places, provided they kept public order and prayed for the emperors (Lactantius 34–35; Eusebius, Church History 8.17). Maximinus Daia resumed in the East; the settlement of 313 is module 8.3's.

Where sources disagree. Lactantius makes Galerius and his mother the instigators and Diocletian a reluctant old man (10–11). Constantine, as Eusebius reports him, blamed Diocletian himself, moved by Apollo's complaint that the just on earth kept him from prophesying truly (Life of Constantine 2.50–51); Eusebius' own history explains the persecution as God's chastisement of a church grown lax in the long peace (Church History 8.1.7–8). Lactantius also names Sossianus Hierocles, governor of Bithynia and a writer against the Christians, as an author of the persecution (16.4); the incest edict and the Manichaean rescript suggest Diocletian needed little prompting.

Abdication, Split and the collapse of the system

On 1 May 305 Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan abdicated on the same day. Galerius and Constantius became Augusti, with Severus, a soldier close to Galerius, and Maximinus Daia, Galerius' nephew, as Caesars. Lactantius has the troops expecting Constantine, who stood on the platform, as Diocletian, weeping, put his purple on a man nobody knew (19). Constantine and Maxentius, Maximian's son, were passed over.

Where sources disagree. Lactantius says Galerius bullied Diocletian, weakened by a near-fatal illness in 304, into retiring and chose the Caesars himself (17–18). The panegyrist of 307 says Maximian had sworn in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter to retire with his colleague (Panegyric 7(6)), implying a plan agreed years before, and Eutropius has Maximian obey unwillingly (9.27). Whether the Tetrarchy was meant to renew itself by merit cannot be settled from witnesses this partisan.

Diocletian retired to his palace at Split, beside Salona: a fortified rectangle laid out like a legionary camp, enclosing his residence, a temple and an octagonal mausoleum, now the cathedral of St Domnius, a bishop of Salona martyred in the persecution. The medieval town grew inside the walls; Robert Adam's Ruins of the Palace of the Emperor Diocletian at Spalatro (1764) carried its forms into Georgian architecture. Asked in 308 to rule again, Diocletian replied that if they could see the cabbages he had planted with his own hands at Salona they would never suggest it (Epitome 39.6).

The system did not long survive him. Constantius died at York on 25 July 306 and his army proclaimed Constantine, where module 8.3 begins; Galerius made Severus Augustus and allowed Constantine only the rank of Caesar. On 28 October the praetorians and people of Rome, angered at being brought into the census (Lactantius 26), proclaimed Maxentius, and Maximian left retirement to join his son. Severus invaded Italy and died a prisoner. At Carnuntum on 11 November 308 a conference attended by Diocletian made Licinius Augustus, yet by 310 six men claimed the title. Maximian died in 310, Galerius in 311, Diocletian at Split on 3 December 311 or 312, his statues thrown down with Maximian's (Lactantius 42); he alone, Eutropius notes, was deified though he died a private man (9.28). The Milvian Bridge in 312 and the war of 313 left two Augusti and no Caesars.

Self-test

  1. Why does a historian of Diocletian lean on documents more than on narratives, and what is the bias of the fullest narrative?
    Answer

    No connected history survives: the Historia Augusta stops with Carus, Zosimus has a gap, and the breviaries are brief, so edicts, papyri, rescripts and panegyrics carry the weight. Lactantius' On the Deaths of the Persecutors (about 314–315) was written to show that persecutors died horribly and is hostile above all to Galerius.

  2. How was the college of 1 March 293 held together, and why was it not a partition of the empire?
    Answer

    By adoption, marriage (Galerius to Valeria, Constantius to Theodora) and the shared names Jovius and Herculius. Each ruler had a region and a residence, but laws went out in all four names and the Caesars campaigned where needed, as Constantius did in Britain and Galerius against Persia.

  3. What did the names Jovius and Herculius claim, and what did they not claim?
    Answer

    That the rulers acted for Jupiter and Hercules, the elder planning and the younger labouring (Panegyric 10(2)), and that Jovius ranked above Herculius. They did not claim that the emperors were themselves gods.

  4. How did Diocletian's administration differ from the "government without bureaucracy" of module 7.5, and what of the old system survived?
    Answer

    Some hundred provinces on the Verona List against about fifty, grouped in dioceses under vicars, civil governors separated from military duces, a larger army and travelling courts; Lactantius complains that those paid outnumbered those paying (7.3). Petition and response survived: more rescripts survive from Diocletian than from any other emperor.

  5. What did the edict of Aristius Optatus of 297 announce, and why did it matter to taxpayers?
    Answer

    Assessment by units of land graded by quality and by heads of the rural population, with published rates, so that everyone could know what he owed (P.Cair.Isid. 1). Requisition became a predictable annual tax in kind, and its reassessments gave rise to the indiction (module 0.3).

  6. What did the Edict on Maximum Prices attempt, and what is the evidence on its success?
    Answer

    To fix ceilings on well over a thousand goods, wages and freight charges, on pain of death, blaming profiteers who robbed soldiers. Lactantius says it caused bloodshed, emptied the markets, made prices worse and lapsed (7.6–7); its copies come almost all from the East, and Corcoran doubted it was widely published in the West.

  7. Why do many historians avoid the term "Dominate"?
    Answer

    Mommsen's opposition implies a constitutional break, yet the elements were older: Domitian as "lord and god" (Suetonius, Domitian 13.2), Pliny's domine, adoration already in the panegyric of 291. Alföldi traced the ceremonial's gradual growth, Bleicken denied a genuine constitutional transformation, and Kolb sees Diocletian formalising trends already present.

  8. Give the four edicts of the Great Persecution and explain why its severity varied by region.
    Answer

    February 303: churches destroyed, scriptures burned, rank and legal rights lost; then the arrest of clergy; then their release if they sacrificed; and in 304 universal sacrifice (Martyrs of Palestine 3.1). Each ruler enforced in his own territory: Constantius only pulled down buildings (Lactantius 15.7), Maximian applied the first edict in Africa (Cirta, Abitina), and Galerius and Maximinus persisted in the East until 311.

  9. How does the Manichaean rescript bear on the question of who drove the persecution?
    Answer

    It shows Diocletian himself holding that undoing what the ancients settled is the greatest crime and treating a new cult from hostile Persia as contagion (Collatio 15.3), as his incest edict ties the gods' favour to piety (6.4). That weakens Lactantius' picture of a reluctant Diocletian pushed by Galerius.

  10. What happened on 1 May 305, and why did the arrangement collapse?
    Answer

    Diocletian and Maximian abdicated together; Galerius and Constantius became Augusti, with Severus and Maximinus Daia as Caesars, passing over Constantine and Maxentius. Armies and the city of Rome backed the passed-over sons in 306, Maximian returned, Carnuntum (308) failed, and by 310 six men claimed the title of Augustus.

Carry forward

  1. The late Roman state was Diocletian's answer to the third-century crisis: more emperors, more provinces, more soldiers and officials, paid for by a census-based tax in kind. Its machinery of prefects, vicars, governors and indictions frames the West to 476 and the East long after.
  2. The Tetrarchy solved the problem of presence, an emperor on every front, but not of succession: armies were loyal to sons, and Constantine and Maxentius broke the system within eighteen months of the abdication. Watch heredity return as the principle of imperial legitimacy.
  3. The Great Persecution was the last and most systematic attempt to secure the gods' favour by compulsion; it was uneven because enforcement followed the map of the Tetrarchy, Galerius conceded its failure in 311, and its victims, Lactantius and Eusebius, wrote the story the Christian empire remembered.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Diocletian and the Tetrarchy, AD 284 to 305. Cover: Diocletian's rise; the Tetrarchy of two Augusti and two Caesars, Jovius and Herculius, and the porphyry group now in Venice; the reorganisation of the provinces into dioceses, the separation of civil and military commands, the enlarged army and court; the tax reform and the Edict on Maximum Prices of 301; the 'Dominate' and the ceremony of adoration, and the debate over whether the term should be dropped; the Great Persecution from 303 as Lactantius' On the Deaths of the Persecutors and Eusebius tell it; the Manichaeans; the abdication of 305, the palace at Split, and the collapse of the system in the following decade. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.

Constantine

The evidence: panegyrists, a bishop and a hostile historianFrom York to Rome, 306–312The sign: three versions of one visionThe "Edict of Milan" and what it actually wasThe Arch of Constantine as evidenceSole emperor: Licinius, Crispus and FaustaThe emperor and the bishops: Donatists, Arius, NicaeaA new Rome on the BosporusThe legislationBaptism, death and the debate over the conversionSelf-testCarry forward

The evidence: panegyrists, a bishop and a hostile historian

Constantine is the best-documented emperor since Augustus and the hardest to see, because nearly every witness wrote for or against a convert. The Latin panegyrics (Panegyrici Latini VII(6) of 307, VI(7) of 310, V(8) of 311 and XII(9) of 313, spoken before him in Gaul, and Nazarius' IV(10), spoken at Rome in his absence in 321) give the official line of each year, unrevised by hindsight. Lactantius, a rhetorician at Nicomedia who in old age tutored Constantine's son Crispus (Jerome, On Illustrious Men 80), wrote On the Deaths of the Persecutors about 314–315 to show that God destroys persecutors. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, revised his Church History into the 320s and left the Life of Constantine unfinished at his death in 339, quoting imperial letters in full inside a frame of encomium. Zosimus' New History (book 2, about 500), following Eunapius' lost history, blames Constantine for the empire's ruin. Beside these stand the Latin breviaries, the anonymous Origo Constantini, Optatus' dossier on the African schism, the laws in the Theodosian Code (module 9.1), coins and inscriptions.

Where sources disagree. Burckhardt (Die Zeit Constantins des Grossen, 1853) called Eusebius the first thoroughly dishonest historian of antiquity, and Henri Grégoire (1938) denied him the Life in its present form. A. H. M. Jones and T. C. Skeat (1954) then identified in a London papyrus (P. Lond. 878) a near-contemporary copy of part of the letter to the provincials of Palestine quoted at Life 2.26–29. The documents are now accepted as genuine; the frame Eusebius built round them is what remains in dispute.

From York to Rome, 306–312

Constantine was born at Naissus (Niš) on 27 February, probably in the early 270s, the son of Constantius and Helena, and served at the eastern courts as a pledge of his father's loyalty (Origo 2.2–3). At the abdications of 1 May 305 the new Caesars were Galerius' men, Severus and Maximinus Daia; Constantine and Maximian's son Maxentius were passed over (Lactantius, Deaths of the Persecutors 18–19; module 8.2). Constantine left Galerius' court by night, taking or killing the post-horses behind him to stop pursuit (Lactantius 24; Origo 2.4), and joined his father at Boulogne for a campaign against the Picts. Constantius died at York on 25 July 306 and the army proclaimed his son, urged on, the Epitome de Caesaribus says, by the Alamannic king Crocus (41.3). Lactantius says Constantine's first act was to restore the Christians to their worship (24.9). Galerius recognised him as Caesar, not Augustus (25).

In late October 306 Rome proclaimed Maxentius, and Maximian came out of retirement to back his son. Severus' invasion of 307 collapsed when his troops defected, and Galerius' own withdrew. Maximian bought Constantine's goodwill with his daughter Fausta and the title Augustus, both celebrated by the panegyric of 307; Minervina, mother of Constantine's eldest son Crispus, vanishes from the record, dead or divorced. The conference at Carnuntum in November 308 made Licinius Augustus of the West over the heads of both Caesars; Galerius then offered Constantine and Maximinus the invented title "sons of the Augusti", which neither accepted for long (Lactantius 32). In 310 Maximian, now at Constantine's court, seized the treasury at Arles; Constantine cornered him at Massilia, and he died, by his own hand in the official version (Lactantius 29–30). The panegyrist at Trier that summer announced a new claim to rule: descent from Claudius II Gothicus (VI(7).2). Constantine no longer owed his throne to the Tetrarchy.

Galerius' edict of toleration and his death in 311 (module 8.2) left two pairs: Constantine with Licinius, betrothed to Constantine's half-sister Constantia; Maxentius with Maximinus. In spring 312 Constantine crossed the Alps with barely a quarter of his army, says the panegyrist of 313 (XII(9).3.3); Zosimus gives him 90,000 foot and 8,000 horse against Maxentius' 170,000 and 18,000 (2.15.1–2), figures modern historians treat as inflated. He stormed Segusio, broke Maxentius' armoured cavalry near Turin and took Verona after a siege. Maxentius had provisioned Rome and cut the Milvian Bridge; then, Lactantius says, the Sibylline Books told him that the enemy of the Romans would perish that day (44.8). On 28 October 312 he crossed the Tiber on a bridge of boats and fought with the river behind him. His line broke, the pontoon gave way and he drowned, a new Pharaoh in the Red Sea for Eusebius (Church History 9.9.5–8). Constantine abolished the praetorian guard (Aurelius Victor, Caesares 40.25) and the imperial horse guard, over whose barracks the Lateran basilica rose. The battle is one of module 0.3's anchor dates and the hinge of the late empire.

The sign: three versions of one vision

SourceWrittenSettingWhat he sawWhat followed
Panegyric, Pan. Lat. VI(7).21.3–5310, at Trier, soon afterGaul, at "the most beautiful temple in the world", probably Grand in the VosgesApollo with Victory, offering laurel wreaths each carrying the omen of thirty yearsHe recognised himself in the god of the poets' prophecies
Lactantius, Deaths of the Persecutors 44.5–6c. 314–315Near Rome, the night before the battleA dream telling him to mark the heavenly sign of God on the shieldsA Christ monogram painted on the shields
Eusebius, Life of Constantine 1.27–32after 337, from Constantine's sworn accountOn the march, before the Italian campaign; place unstatedAt midday a cross of light above the sun with the words "by this conquer", seen by the whole army; then Christ in a dreamThe labarum, a cross-shaped standard crowned with the Chi-Rho

Lactantius describes the shield sign as "transversa X littera, summo capite circumflexo", the letter X turned with its top bent round: a Chi-Rho or a looped cross. Eusebius' own Church History, written nearer the event, mentions a statue in Rome of Constantine holding the saving sign (9.9.10–11) but no vision; the sky-sign appears only in the Life, told him by the emperor under oath long afterwards (1.28.1). In hoc signo vinces is a later Latin rendering. The panegyrist of 313 says only that Constantine shared some secret with the divine mind (XII(9).2.4–5). The coins hedge too: a Ticinum medallion of 315 shows the Chi-Rho on his helmet, while Sol Invictus, the emperor's "companion", stayed on the bronze into the 320s.

Where sources disagree. Lactantius' dream on the eve of battle and Eusebius' daylight sign, seen by an army months earlier somewhere on the march, cannot both be literally true, and neither writer knows the other's version. Peter Weiss (1993; in English 2003) argued that all three accounts go back to one experience, a solar halo with cross-like arcs seen in Gaul in 310: read first as Apollo's wreaths, then retold after 312 as the sign of Christ. Barnes (2011) adopted the thesis as explaining all the early evidence, but it moves Eusebius' story two years and a country away from Lactantius' battlefield.

The "Edict of Milan" and what it actually was

In February 313 Constantine and Licinius met at Milan, where Licinius married Constantia, and agreed a religious policy; no edict was issued there. Licinius defeated Maximinus near Adrianople at the end of April, his troops having recited a prayer to the highest god dictated, Lactantius says, by an angel (46), and on 13 June posted at Nicomedia a letter to the governor of Bithynia (Lactantius 48; Greek version in Eusebius, Church History 10.5.2–14). It grants Christians and everyone else free choice of religion, so that whatever divinity dwells in heaven may favour the emperors and their subjects, and orders Christian churches and corporate property restored without charge. The Christians are named; the god is not.

It was thus Licinius applying in the East a policy Constantine had followed in the West since the winter of 312, with restitution, money for Caecilian's clergy at Carthage and exemptions for clergy (Church History 10.5.15–17, 10.6, 10.7). It went beyond Galerius' edict of 311 by returning property and by stating free choice as a principle for all.

Where sources disagree. Otto Seeck ("Das sogenannte Edikt von Mailand", 1891) showed that the text is a rescript posted by Licinius, not an edict issued at Milan, and most historians now speak of the Milan agreement. Milton Anastos (1967) defended the traditional name, arguing that the policy was framed by Constantine and issued in both emperors' names. The unnamed "divinity" is read either as Licinius' pagan monotheism or as a formula both rulers could sign.

The Arch of Constantine as evidence

The Senate dedicated the arch beside the Colosseum for Constantine's tenth anniversary in 315. Its inscription (CIL VI 1139) says he avenged the state on the tyrant and his faction "instinctu divinitatis, mentis magnitudine", by the prompting of the divinity and the greatness of his mind: words a pagan senate could write and a Christian emperor accept. Much of the sculpture is reused: slabs of a Trajanic battle frieze, eight Hadrianic roundels of hunting and of sacrifice to Silvanus, Diana, Apollo and Hercules, eight panels from a monument of Marcus Aurelius and Trajanic statues of captive Dacians, with the earlier emperors' heads recut. The new frieze tells the campaign, from the departure from Milan through Verona and the bridge to the entry, a speech from the Rostra and a distribution of money. Sol and Luna fill the end roundels. There is no Christian symbol.

As evidence it says three things: the Senate's Constantine stands in the line of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus; his victory is owed to an unnamed divinity; and in 315 the city still showed its emperor at pagan sacrifice. Its style and the meaning of the reuse belong to module 10.3; module 9.5 puts it on the walk.

Sole emperor: Licinius, Crispus and Fausta

The partnership with Licinius broke twice. War in 316 (once dated 314) brought victories at Cibalae and in Thrace and gave Constantine the Balkans except Thrace; on 1 March 317 Crispus and the infant Constantine II became Caesars, alongside Licinius' infant son. In the 320s Licinius purged Christians from his court and army (Eusebius, Life 1.51–54). In 324 Constantine won at Adrianople, Crispus destroyed Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont, and Chrysopolis on 18 September decided it. Licinius surrendered on Constantia's plea and was promised his life; he was killed at Thessalonica in 325, against the oath, Eutropius says (10.6).

In 326 Constantine had Crispus executed at Pola (Ammianus 14.11.20); soon afterwards Fausta died in an overheated bath. No contemporary explains either death, and Eusebius dropped Crispus from the last edition of the Church History. Later accounts conflict: Zosimus says Crispus was suspected of an affair with his stepmother (2.29.2); the Epitome says Fausta accused him and was killed when Helena reproached her son (41.11–12); Philostorgius has Fausta caught in adultery (2.4).

Where sources disagree. Zosimus (2.29.3–4), after Eunapius, says Constantine turned Christian because pagan priests would not purify him of these murders and an Egyptian from Spain promised that the faith washed away every sin; Julian had already shown Constantine running to Jesus, who makes murderers clean (Caesars 336a–b). Sozomen replied that Constantine had favoured the Christians long before (Church History 1.5). The story is impossible in its chronology but shows what opponents made of a convert with blood on his hands.

The emperor and the bishops: Donatists, Arius, Nicaea

Africa: the Donatists

The first church quarrel reached Constantine within months of the Milvian Bridge. At Carthage the bishop Caecilian had been consecrated by Felix of Abthugni, whom rigorists accused of surrendering the scriptures in the persecution of 303 (module 8.2); the Numidian bishops set up a rival, Majorinus, soon succeeded by Donatus, and appealed to the emperor. Constantine referred the case to Miltiades of Rome (Eusebius, Church History 10.5.18–20), whose council upheld Caecilian in October 313; on a further appeal he summoned western bishops to Arles, who confirmed it in August 314 (10.5.21–24). Constantine told his vicar of Africa that he feared the highest divinity might be roused against the human race and against himself while such dissension lasted (Optatus, appendix 3). He heard the case himself in 316, tried coercion from 317 and gave up in 321. The pattern was set: bishops appealed to the emperor, the emperor convened bishops, and the losers called him a persecutor.

Arius and the Council of Nicaea, 325

About 318 Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, taught that the Son was created from nothing: "there was when he was not". His bishop, Alexander, excommunicated him; Eusebius of Nicomedia and others took his side. Fresh from Chrysopolis, Constantine sent a letter calling it an idle question that should never have been aired (Eusebius, Life 2.64–72), carried, Socrates says, by Ossius of Corduba (Church History 1.7), then summoned a general council to Nicaea.

The bishops came on the imperial post in early summer 325: more than 250 by Eusebius' count (Life 3.8), about 300 by Athanasius' (On the Decrees of Nicaea 3); the later 318 echoes Abraham's servants (Genesis 14:14). Nearly all were eastern; the West sent Ossius, two Roman presbyters and a few others. Constantine entered in purple and gold and joined the debate (3.10–13). The creed declared the Son homoousios, "of one substance", with the Father and anathematised those who said "there was when he was not". Arius and two Libyan bishops were exiled; Eusebius of Nicomedia, who signed the creed but not the anathemas, followed within months. The council also fixed a common Easter independent of the Jewish calendar (Life 3.18–20), issued twenty canons and ended at Constantine's twentieth-anniversary banquet, which Eusebius thought an image of Christ's kingdom (3.15).

The settlement did not hold. Constantine readmitted Arius about 327 and recalled Eusebius of Nicomedia; Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria from 328, refused to receive Arius, was condemned at Tyre in 335 and exiled to Trier. Arius died at Constantinople in 336. Constantine wanted unity, not a formula; the formula outlived him, and module 8.4 follows Constantius II's attempt to replace it. For how the Church's thinkers used Greek philosophy, see Greek module 7.4.

Where sources disagree. Eusebius of Caesarea, explaining his signature to his own church, says Constantine himself proposed homoousios and glossed it harmlessly (letter in Socrates, Church History 1.8); Philostorgius says Alexander and Ossius had agreed on the word beforehand at Nicomedia (1.7). Beneath lies a larger dispute: Rowan Williams (Arius: Heresy and Tradition, 1987) and R. P. C. Hanson (The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God, 1988) treat Arius as a conservative theologian and "Arianism" as a party created by Athanasius' polemic, which is also our main source for it.

A new Rome on the Bosporus

Within weeks of Chrysopolis Constantine chose Byzantium, on the strait between his Danube and Persian fronts, and in November 324 marked out a far larger city, its land wall some fifteen stades beyond the old (Zosimus 2.30). Philostorgius has him pacing the line with a spear, saying he would go on until the one walking ahead of him stopped (2.9). The city was dedicated on 11 May 330 (module 0.3) and given a senate, a grain dole, a hippodrome joined to the palace, a forum with a porphyry column for the founder's statue, and art stripped from the Greek world: Eusebius lists the Delphic tripods set up in the hippodrome (Life 3.54), and Jerome's Chronicle under 330 says "dedicatur Constantinopolis omnium paene urbium nuditate", by stripping almost every other city bare. The church of the Holy Apostles was to be Constantine's tomb, his sarcophagus among twelve cenotaphs of the apostles (Life 4.58–60).

Where sources disagree. Eusebius says the city never saw an idol or a sacrifice (Life 3.48); Zosimus says Constantine built it temples to Rhea and to the Fortune of Rome (2.31.2–3). Gilbert Dagron (Naissance d'une capitale, 1974) traced how Constantine's city became a "New Rome" only by stages: a senate of equal rank under Constantius II, and the title itself in the third canon of the council of 381.

The legislation

Constantine's laws survive as dated, addressed excerpts in the Theodosian and Justinianic codes (module 9.1), and their mixture shows his priorities. Some favour the Church: clergy freed from civic liturgies (Theodosian Code 16.2.2, 319), bequests to churches permitted (16.2.4, 321), manumission in church made valid (4.7.1, 321), bishops' arbitration made binding (1.27.1). Traditional cult was restrained only at the edges: private haruspicy was banned (9.16.1), while the haruspices were to be consulted by ancient custom when lightning struck the palace (16.10.1). Courts and workshops rested on "venerabili die solis", the venerable day of the Sun (Code of Justinian 3.12.2, 321). Many laws are harsh in the old manner, such as molten lead for nurses who abetted an abduction (Theodosian Code 9.24.1) and chains for fugitive tenants (5.17.1, 332); others reach for mercy, forbidding branding on the face, formed in the likeness of heavenly beauty (9.40.2), and sending criminals to the mines rather than the arena because "cruenta spectacula" displease in peacetime (15.12.1, 325). Yet the Hispellum rescript (CIL XI 5265, 333–337), cited in module 1.2 for the games at Volsinii, still allowed a gladiatorial show there, and let the Umbrians build a temple to the emperor's family provided it was not polluted by the deceits of contagious superstition, probably meaning sacrifice. The Augustan penalties on the unmarried were repealed (8.16.1, 320) and unilateral divorce confined to grave causes (3.16.1, 331). The split of the army into field and frontier troops belongs to module 9.2.

Where sources disagree. Eusebius presents the family laws as Christian reform (Life 4.26); Judith Evans Grubbs (Law and Family in Late Antiquity, 1995) found most of the marriage legislation rooted in Roman moral traditionalism, with Christian influence hard to prove. On sacrifice the witnesses collide: Eusebius says a law forbade it (Life 2.45), and a law of his sons in 341 cited their father's law against it (Theodosian Code 16.10.2), but Libanius says Constantine took the temples' money and changed nothing in the lawful worship (Oration 30.6). Barnes ("Constantine's prohibition of pagan sacrifice", 1984) accepts a general ban in 324.

Baptism, death and the debate over the conversion

In spring 337 Constantine was preparing war on Shapur II of Persia, with bishops in his suite (Life 4.56–57). He fell ill after Easter and at a villa near Nicomedia asked for baptism, saying he had hoped to receive it in the Jordan (4.61–62); he put off the purple, wore white, and died at Pentecost, 22 May 337 (4.62–64). Eusebius does not name the baptiser; Jerome's Chronicle does: Eusebius of Nicomedia, Arius' patron. Late baptism was normal for men whose office required killing, so it is no evidence of a late conversion. He was buried among his apostles in Constantinople, yet he was enrolled among the gods (Eutropius 10.8), and his consecration coins show him veiled in a chariot, reaching for a hand from heaven (Life 4.73). The killings of his relatives that summer open module 8.4; the legend of his baptism by Pope Silvester and the forged Donation of Constantine, exposed by Lorenzo Valla in 1440, belong to module 10.4.

When, how and how sincerely he became a Christian is the oldest question in the field, and the evidence above pulls both ways.

ScholarWorkVerdict
Jacob BurckhardtDie Zeit Constantins des Grossen (1853)A genius driven by ambition, essentially unreligious, who used the Church as an instrument of power
A. H. M. JonesConstantine and the Conversion of Europe (1948)A real conversion in 312, to a God of battles who gave victory, with little grasp of doctrine
T. D. BarnesConstantine and Eusebius (1981); Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power in the Later Roman Empire (2011)A committed Christian from 312 at the latest, who after 324 pursued a Christian reformation; Eusebius largely reliable
Noel LenskiConstantine and the Cities (2016)No single Constantine: a pragmatic, experimental policy negotiated with cities, rewarding Christian communities such as Orcistus and Maiuma and bargaining with pagan ones such as Hispellum
Where sources disagree. The timing is as contested as the sincerity. Barnes reads Lactantius' notice that Constantine began his reign by restoring the Christians (24.9) as evidence of favour before 312; the panegyrist of 310, who puts him in Apollo's temple, and the mints that called Sol his companion describe a ruler still courting the sun god. H. A. Drake (Constantine and the Bishops, 2000) treats the ambiguity as policy: a consensus under a Supreme God broad enough for pagans, from which bishops later pushed his successors towards coercion.

Self-test

  1. Why does the panegyric of 310 matter for the history of the vision, and what modern argument builds on it?
    Answer

    It is the only account written within weeks of an experience: Apollo with Victory offering wreaths of thirty years at a Gallic temple (Pan. Lat. VI(7).21.3–5), two years before the Christian sign of 312. Weiss argued that the same event, a solar halo, was later retold as the sign of Christ.

  2. How do Lactantius' and Eusebius' accounts of the Christian sign differ, and why is Eusebius' version suspect?
    Answer

    Lactantius has a dream the night before the battle and a monogram painted on shields (44.5–6); Eusebius a midday cross of light with "by this conquer", seen by the army on an earlier march, then a dream of Christ and the labarum (Life 1.27–32). Eusebius heard it from Constantine long afterwards, and his own Church History mentions no vision.

  3. What was the "Edict of Milan" in fact?
    Answer

    A letter of Licinius to the governor of Bithynia, posted at Nicomedia on 13 June 313 (Lactantius 48; Eusebius, Church History 10.5), applying in the East the policy agreed at Milan: free choice of religion for all and restitution of Christian property. Seeck (1891) showed that no edict was issued at Milan.

  4. What do the inscription and decoration of the Arch of Constantine tell us about Rome in 315?
    Answer

    The Senate credited the victory to "instinctu divinitatis", an unnamed divinity both sides could accept. Reused Trajanic, Hadrianic and Aurelian reliefs set Constantine among the good emperors, the Hadrianic roundels show sacrifice, Sol and Luna appear, and there is no Christian sign.

  5. Why did the Donatist dispute matter beyond Africa?
    Answer

    It made the emperor the arbiter of church quarrels: a council at Rome (313), then Arles (314), his own hearing (316), coercion from 317 and surrender in 321. It set the pattern of appeal, council and coercion, and showed its limits.

  6. What did the Council of Nicaea decide, and why did it not end the dispute?
    Answer

    It declared the Son homoousios with the Father, anathematised "there was when he was not", fixed a common Easter and issued twenty canons. Constantine wanted unity rather than a formula, so he readmitted Arius about 327, recalled Eusebius of Nicomedia and exiled Athanasius in 335.

  7. Why are the deaths of Crispus and Fausta a problem of sources, and what did pagans make of them?
    Answer

    No contemporary explains them; Eusebius erased Crispus, and Zosimus, the Epitome and Philostorgius give conflicting motives. Zosimus, after Eunapius, made the murders the reason Constantine turned to a faith that forgave everything; Sozomen (1.5) answered that the favour to Christians came first.

  8. What evidence complicates the picture of Constantinople as a Christian city from its foundation?
    Answer

    Zosimus reports temples to Rhea and the Fortune of Rome (2.31.2–3), against Eusebius' claim of a city without idols (Life 3.48); even Eusebius records the Delphic tripods in the hippodrome (3.54). Dagron traced how the "New Rome" of equal rank grew only under Constantine's successors.

  9. Show with two laws how Constantine's legislation combined favour to the Church with tolerance of traditional cult.
    Answer

    Bequests to churches were permitted (Theodosian Code 16.2.4) and episcopal arbitration made binding (1.27.1), yet the haruspices were to be consulted when lightning struck the palace (16.10.1), and the day of rest was "the venerable day of the Sun" (Code of Justinian 3.12.2). The Hispellum rescript allowed a temple to his family if it was kept free of contagious superstition.

  10. Contrast Burckhardt's and Barnes's verdicts, and say what the deathbed baptism does and does not show.
    Answer

    Burckhardt saw an ambitious, essentially unreligious ruler using the Church; Barnes a committed Christian from 312 who pursued a Christian reformation after 324. Deathbed baptism was normal for men whose office required killing, so it does not show a late conversion.

Carry forward

  1. Read every Constantinian source by its date and audience: the panegyrics of 310 and 313, Lactantius about 315 and Eusebius after 337 tell one story progressively rewritten, and the later the account, the more Christian and the more shaped it is.
  2. The Christian empire began as patronage and arbitration, not prohibition: money, exemptions, courts and councils for bishops, with the emperor as judge of their quarrels. The pattern of imperial councils and coercion set by the Donatists and Nicaea governs the rest of the late empire.
  3. Ambiguity was a method: an unnamed divinity on the arch and in the Milan letter, Sol beside the Chi-Rho, a Sunday named for the Sun, let pagans and Christians each read in their own god. Constantine's successors were forced to choose (module 8.4).

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Constantine, AD 306 to 337. Cover: his proclamation at York; the wars of the Tetrarchs; the Milvian Bridge in 312 and the vision, comparing Lactantius' dream, Eusebius' Life of Constantine with the sign in the sky, and the earlier pagan panegyric's vision of Apollo; the 'Edict of Milan' of 313 and what it actually was; the Arch of Constantine and its reused reliefs; Constantine and the bishops: the Donatist dispute, Arius and the Council of Nicaea in 325; the killing of Crispus and Fausta; the foundation of Constantinople in 330; the legislation; his deathbed baptism; and the long debate over the sincerity and timing of his conversion (Burckhardt, A. H. M. Jones, Barnes, Lenski). Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 8 · Crisis and the late empire, AD 235 to 476 · 8.4 · 2,870 words

Julian, Theodosius and the end of the old gods

The sons of Constantine, 337–361Julian's restoration of the godsPersia, 363: the death of JulianValens, the Goths and AdrianopleTheodosius: the Goths, Thessalonica and AmbroseThe altar of Victory, 384Law, the Serapeum and the FrigidusThe last Vestals and the last GamesThe slow conversion of the senatorial aristocracySelf-testCarry forward

The sons of Constantine, 337–361

Module 8.3 ends with Constantine's death near Nicomedia on 22 May 337. That summer the soldiers at Constantinople killed nearly every male descendant of his father's second marriage, including his half-brothers Julius Constantius and Dalmatius (Eutropius 10.9; Zosimus 2.40). Julius Constantius' sons Gallus and Julian were spared; Julian later blamed Constantius openly (Letter to the Athenians). On 9 September 337 Constantine's three sons took the title Augustus and divided the empire.

EmperorReignShareEnd
Constantine II337–340Gaul, Britain, Spainkilled invading Italy
Constans337–350Italy, Africa, Illyricum; all the West from 340killed by the usurper Magnentius' agents
Constantius II337–361the East; sole Augustus from 353died marching against Julian
JulianCaesar 355; Augustus 360–363Gaul, then alldied of wounds in Persia
Jovian363–364alldied on the road
Valentinian I / Valens364–375 / 364–378West / Eaststroke / killed at Adrianople
Gratian / Valentinian II367–383 / 375–392Westkilled by Magnus Maximus / found hanged
Theodosius I379–395East; all from 394died at Milan

Constantius II is the hinge of the period. A committed Christian of the homoian party, which called the Son "like" the Father and set aside the Nicene formula of module 8.3, he imposed that creed through councils in 359. Against the old cults he legislated more than he enforced: cesset superstitio, sacrificiorum aboleatur insania, "let superstition cease, let the madness of sacrifice be abolished" (Codex Theodosianus 16.10.2, of 341). Yet visiting Rome in 357 he admired its temples (Ammianus 16.10), and Symmachus recalled that he left the Vestals their privileges and filled the priesthoods with nobles (Relatio 3). He removed one object: the altar of Victory from the senate house (Ambrose, Letter 18). Gallus, Caesar from 351, was executed in 354 (Ammianus 14.11); Julian became Caesar in 355.

Julian's restoration of the gods

Julian, born at Constantinople in 331 or 332, was raised a Christian and kept for six years with Gallus on the imperial estate of Macellum in Cappadocia. As a student he found the Neoplatonists; Eunapius says Maximus of Ephesus drew him into theurgy (Lives of the Sophists 474–475). In Gaul the bookish Caesar proved a general, beating the Alamanni at Strasbourg in 357 (Ammianus 16.12). When Constantius demanded his best troops for Persia in 360, the army at Paris proclaimed him Augustus (20.4), and Constantius' death on 3 November 361 averted civil war.

Julian ordered the temples opened and the sacrifices restored (Ammianus 22.5.2). He recalled the bishops Constantius had exiled and summoned the quarrelling parties to the palace, knowing, Ammianus says, that no wild beasts are as dangerous to men as most Christians are to one another (22.5.3–4). His law of 17 June 362 made teachers subject to approval by their city councils and the emperor (Codex Theodosianus 13.3.5); a rescript explained that men who disbelieved in Homer's gods should not teach Homer but go to the churches of the Galileans and expound Matthew and Luke (Letter 36). Ammianus, an admirer, calls it harsh and fit to be buried in eternal silence (22.10.7; 25.4.20).

His most original project was a pagan church. He set high priests over provinces, with authority over city priests, and wrote them pastoral letters: priests were to keep out of theatres and taverns and give to strangers and the poor. To Arsacius, high priest of Galatia, he wrote that the Galileans had grown by kindness to strangers, and that it was a disgrace when they fed "not only their own poor but ours as well" (Letter 22).

Where sources disagree. The letter to Arsacius survives only because the Christian historian Sozomen copied it (5.16). Peter Van Nuffelen (2002) argued that it is a Christian forgery, citing anachronistic uses of "Hellenism"; Jean Bouffartigue (2005) and others defend it on philological grounds.

Antioch, a Christian city devoted to theatre and racing, met him with mockery. At Apollo's festival at Daphne he found one priest with a goose brought from his own house (Misopogon). In October 362 the temple there burned; Julian blamed the Christians and closed the city's great church (Ammianus 22.13.1–2). The Antiochenes jeered at his beard and his hecatombs, and early in 363 he answered with the Misopogon, "Beard-Hater": a satire on himself, the shaggy, ink-fingered emperor with lice in his beard, and through himself on a city that preferred pleasure to virtue and Christ to the gods.

Persia, 363: the death of Julian

Julian left Antioch on 5 March 363 to finish the Persian war (Ammianus 23.2.6), and Ammianus went with him. Module 0.1 introduced him in outline, a Greek of Antioch writing Latin at Rome around 390; here he is the eyewitness, a staff officer who had escaped from besieged Amida in 359 (book 19). Books 23–25 slip at times into the first person plural, and their detail is a participant's: the burning of the fleet (24.7.4), the retreat up the Tigris under attack. On 26 June, hurrying to a skirmish without his breastplate, Julian was struck by a cavalry spear that lodged in his liver (25.3.3–6). Ammianus gives him a philosopher's death, discussing the soul with Maximus and Priscus until about midnight (25.3.23). The army chose the officer Jovian, who bought its escape by ceding Nisibis and five regions beyond the Tigris (25.7.9–11).

The obituary (25.4) shows Ammianus' independence. He praises Julian's chastity, learning, courage and justice, then lists faults: garrulous, vain, superstitious rather than truly religious, slaughtering victims so freely that people said there would be no cattle left if he returned (25.4.17).

Where sources disagree. Ammianus says no one knew where the spear came from (25.3.6). Libanius, in his funeral speech, insists the killer was a Christian in Julian's own army (Oration 18.274–275); Sozomen thinks this probably true and the deed blameless (6.1–2). Theodoret has the dying emperor cry "You have won, Galilean" (Church History, book 3). Ammianus' uncertainty, from a man in the column, outweighs them.

Valens, the Goths and Adrianople

Jovian died in February 364. The officers chose Valentinian, who gave the East to his brother Valens (Ammianus 26.4.3); on Valentinian's death in 375 his sons Gratian and the four-year-old Valentinian II held the West.

In 376 Gothic refugees reached the lower Danube, driven by the Huns (31.2–3). The Tervingi under Fritigern asked to be received as settlers and soldiers, and Valens, wanting recruits, agreed. Ammianus will not give their number: whoever wants it might as well count the sands of the Libyan plain (31.4.6). The reception was a scandal. The commanders Lupicinus and Maximus let the refugees starve and traded them dogs, one for each slave (31.4.11). At Marcianople Lupicinus tried to kill the Gothic leaders at a banquet; Fritigern escaped and raised his people (31.5.5–7), and for two years they ravaged Thrace.

On 9 August 378, outside Adrianople, Valens attacked without waiting for Gratian's approaching army. His scouts had put the Goths at 10,000 (31.12.3); the general Victor urged delay, Sebastianus attack, and courtiers urged the emperor not to share the glory with his nephew (31.12.6–7). The army marched eight miles in the noon heat, and as Fritigern played for time with envoys his cavalry returned and struck (31.12.11–17). The Roman left collapsed. Valens died, of an arrow with his body never found, or burned in a farmhouse (31.13.12–16). Scarcely a third of the army escaped, and Ammianus knows no slaughter in the annals to match it save Cannae (31.13.18–19). There he ends, signing himself miles quondam et Graecus, a former soldier and a Greek (31.16.9). The late army as an institution is module 9.2's subject.

Where sources disagree. Ammianus explains the disaster by human failings: the greed of Lupicinus and Maximus and Valens' jealousy of Gratian (31.4.11; 31.12.1, 7). Orosius, a generation later, sees divine justice: Valens had sent Arian teachers to the Goths and was burned alive by the people he had condemned to burn forever (7.33).

Theodosius: the Goths, Thessalonica and Ambrose

On 19 January 379 Gratian made Theodosius, a Spanish officer, Augustus in the East. He could not destroy the Goths. On 3 October 382, by the date in the Constantinopolitan consular list, they were received by treaty, settled in the Balkans as a body and bound to send soldiers; the orator Themistius sold the peace as victory by clemency (Oration 16). Whether this was something new, an undefeated people inside the empire on its own terms, is debated: Peter Heather (Goths and Romans, 1991) thinks so, while Malcolm Errington (Chiron, 1996) sees a surrender followed by patronage; module 8.5 follows these Goths under Alaric.

His match was Ambrose, a former governor made bishop of Milan in 374. In 388 Ambrose preached at the emperor in church until he withdrew an order that Christians at Callinicum rebuild the synagogue they had burned (Letters 40–41). In 390 a crowd at Thessalonica lynched the general Butheric, who had jailed a popular charioteer (Sozomen 7.25), and imperial troops massacred the people in the circus; Theodoret gives 7,000 dead (5.17). Ambrose wrote privately that he could not offer the sacrifice in the emperor's presence until he had done penance (Letter 51). Theodosius laid aside his insignia and wept for his sin in church (Ambrose, On the Death of Theodosius 34).

Where sources disagree. Theodoret, writing some sixty years later, has Ambrose bar Theodosius at the church door and exclude him for eight months (5.17–18); Ambrose's own letter is private and tactful. Peter Brown (Power and Persuasion in Late Antiquity, 1992) finds no confrontation at the door, and Neil McLynn (Ambrose of Milan, 1994) reads the penance as a negotiated ceremony that served the emperor's image as much as the bishop's.

The altar of Victory, 384

The altar stood in the senate house before the statue of Victory from Tarentum that Octavian set up there in 29 BC (Dio 51.22.1–2), and senators swore their oaths on it (Symmachus, Relatio 3). Removed by Constantius, it was back by the 380s. In 382 Gratian removed it again and confiscated the endowments of the Vestals and the public priesthoods. A senatorial embassy under Quintus Aurelius Symmachus was turned away, and Pope Damasus forwarded a counter-petition from Christian senators (Ambrose, Letter 17).

In 384, after Gratian's murder, Symmachus was prefect of the city and tried again. His third Relatio, to the thirteen-year-old Valentinian II, is the finest defence of the old religion in Latin. It argues from custom: Rome herself asks to keep the rites that drove Hannibal from her walls and the Gauls from the Capitol (3.9). It argues from the limits of knowledge:

uno itinere non potest perveniri ad tam grande secretum (Relatio 3.10)

"Not by one road can one come to so great a mystery." And it argues from consequence: since the Vestals' revenues were seized the harvest had failed (3.11–15).

Ambrose answered in two letters (Letters 17 and 18; 72 and 73 in the CSEL edition), the second a reply to the Relatio point by point: Rome's victories were won by courage, not rites; a few paid Vestals compared poorly with the Church's unpaid virgins; and antiquity was no argument, because all things improve with time, as the day grows from darkness and the crop from seed. Valentinian refused, and the altar returned only under the usurper Eugenius (Paulinus, Life of Ambrose 26).

Law, the Serapeum and the Frigidus

Theodosius' laws against cult came late. In the East the prefect Maternus Cynegius had already let monks wreck temples, which Libanius protested in Oration 30 (Greek module 7.4). Then came three laws: on 24 February 391, to the prefect of Rome, no sacrifice, no visiting shrines (Codex Theodosianus 16.10.10); in June 391 the same for Egypt (16.10.11); and on 8 November 392 every form of cult forbidden, down to incense before household gods: sacrifice and reading entrails counted as treason, incense cost the house where it burned (16.10.12). Greek module 7.4 tabulates the two main laws; the Code that preserved them is module 9.1's subject.

At Alexandria the bishop Theophilus was turning a disused temple into a church. When cult objects found in it were paraded in mockery, pagans rioted, killed Christians and barricaded themselves in the Serapeum, the great temple of Serapis, led by the philosopher Olympius (Rufinus 11.22; Sozomen 7.15). An imperial letter pardoned them but ordered the cult destroyed. A soldier with an axe struck the colossal statue; it was broken up and burned, and Theodoret adds that mice ran out of the hollow head (Rufinus 11.23; Theodoret 5.22). Eunapius, the pagan, says the monks who took the site were men in appearance who lived like swine (Lives of the Sophists 472).

Where sources disagree. Gibbon (Decline and Fall, chapter 28) charged Theophilus with destroying the library of Alexandria, citing Orosius' empty book-chests in the temples (6.15.32). But Rufinus, who describes the precinct in detail, mentions no books, and Ammianus, writing shortly before, speaks of the Serapeum's libraries in the past tense (22.16.12–13). Roger Bagnall ("Alexandria: Library of Dreams", 2002) doubts that any great collection survived to be lost in 391.

In the West Valentinian II, dominated by his Frankish general Arbogast, was found hanged at Vienne on 15 May 392. Arbogast raised Eugenius, a Christian teacher of rhetoric. The pagan senator Virius Nicomachus Flavianus, prefect of Italy, rallied to him. The armies met on the river Frigidus below the Julian Alps on 5–6 September 394. Theodosius' Gothic allies, Alaric among them, bore the first day's losses, which Orosius counts as a second victory for Rome (7.35.19). On the second day a gale, the bora, blew into the faces of Eugenius' army. Ambrose saw God's hand (Explanation of Psalm 36.25); the pagan Claudian sang it for Theodosius' son:

o nimium dilecte deo … cui militat aether / et coniurati veniunt ad classica venti (On the Third Consulship of Honorius 96–98)

"O dearly loved of God, for whom the sky fights and the leagued winds come at your trumpet's call." Augustine quotes the lines and adds that Theodosius gave his runners the golden thunderbolts from the statues of Jupiter set up against him on the passes (City of God 5.26). Eugenius was beheaded; Flavianus and Arbogast killed themselves. Theodosius died at Milan on 17 January 395, and module 8.5 begins with his sons.

Where sources disagree. Rufinus (11.33) and, after him, Theodoret (5.24) tell the Frigidus as a war of gods, Jupiter and Hercules against the Cross. Herbert Bloch ("A New Document of the Last Pagan Revival in the West", 1945) built on them a pagan senatorial revival crushed in 394. Alan Cameron (The Last Pagans of Rome, 2011) answers that Eugenius was a Christian usurper, that the pagan colouring derives almost wholly from Rufinus, and that there was no organised pagan party to defeat.

The last Vestals and the last Games

Module 2.3 described the Vestals at their height; their end went unrecorded. In 384 or 385 the chief Vestal Coelia Concordia set up a statue to the dead Praetextatus, and his widow returned the honour (CIL VI 2145); Symmachus, their champion, thought it improper for Vestals to honour a man (Letters 2.36). The last story of a Vestal is Zosimus', a century later: an old woman, the last of the Vestals, cursing Stilicho's wife Serena for taking a necklace from the statue of the Mother of the Gods (5.38). No source records when the flame went out. The end of the Olympic Games belongs to the Greek East and to Greek module 7.4; at Rome the Lupercalia lasted into the 490s (module 2.3).

The slow conversion of the senatorial aristocracy

Laws closed temples; they did not convert senators. The Roman aristocracy was the last pagan stronghold in the West and changed family by family. The Calendar of 354, a luxury codex made for a Christian aristocrat named Valentinus, lists the festivals of the gods beside the burial days of Rome's bishops and martyrs (Michele Salzman, On Roman Time, 1990). Marius Victorinus, the rhetorician honoured with a statue in Trajan's forum (Jerome, Chronicle, s.a. 354), asked whether walls made Christians, then professed his faith in public (Augustine, Confessions 8.2.4–5). Praetextatus, priest of many cults (module 2.5), told Pope Damasus, Jerome says, that he would become a Christian at once if they made him bishop of Rome (Against John of Jerusalem 8). Ammianus shows why the joke stung: after Damasus' contested election of 366, 137 bodies lay in a basilica, and Rome's bishops, he adds, rode in carriages, enriched by matrons' gifts (27.3.13–14). By 402 Prudentius could name the great houses, the Anicii first, as Christian (Against Symmachus 1).

Where sources disagree. Peter Brown (Journal of Roman Studies 1961) described a quiet conversion carried by marriage and household, in which Christian wives and mothers did much of the work. Salzman (The Making of a Christian Aristocracy, 2002), studying several hundred known aristocrats, found men converting as readily as women, drawn by imperial service and by a Christianity that adapted itself to aristocratic ideals of status and honour.

Self-test

  1. Why does Ammianus' account of Julian carry special weight, and where does he part company with his hero?
    Answer

    He marched on the Persian campaign and writes parts of books 23–25 as a participant. Though a pagan admirer, he calls Julian superstitious rather than religious, repeats the joke about his endless sacrifices (25.4.17) and condemns the teaching law as fit to be buried in silence (22.10.7).

  2. What was Julian's "pagan church", and what did it borrow from Christianity?
    Answer

    Provincial high priests set over city priests, moral rules for priests and organised charity to strangers and the poor. Julian's letter to Arsacius names the Galileans' kindness to strangers as the model to imitate (Letter 22), though Van Nuffelen has argued the letter is forged.

  3. What did Julian's teaching law require, and why did even a pagan admirer object?
    Answer

    Teachers needed approval from their councils and the emperor (Codex Theodosianus 13.3.5), and the rescript (Letter 36) barred Christians who disbelieved in the gods from teaching the classics. Ammianus thought it harsh because it turned the shared education of the elite into a religious test.

  4. Why is the identity of Julian's killer uncertain, and how did the question become partisan?
    Answer

    Ammianus, who was with the army, says no one knew where the spear came from. Libanius blamed a Christian soldier and Sozomen accepted and excused the deed, while Theodoret's "You have won, Galilean" turned the death into a Christian legend.

  5. On Ammianus' account, what turned the Gothic crossing of 376 into the disaster of 378?
    Answer

    Roman officials starved and exploited the refugees, trading dogs for slaves (31.4.11); the attempted murder of the leaders at Marcianople started open war; and Valens attacked on a false estimate of 10,000 Goths without waiting for Gratian, unwilling to share the glory (31.12).

  6. What does the Thessalonica affair show about Ambrose and Theodosius, and which source exaggerates it?
    Answer

    That a bishop could make a Christian emperor do public penance: Theodosius laid aside his insignia and wept in church (Ambrose, On the Death of Theodosius 34). Theodoret's confrontation at the church door is a later dramatisation; Ambrose's own letter is private and tactful.

  7. Set out the three main arguments of Symmachus' third Relatio and how Ambrose answered the appeal to antiquity.
    Answer

    Custom (Rome's rites had saved her from Hannibal and the Gauls, 3.9), the limits of knowledge (not by one road to so great a mystery, 3.10) and consequence (the famine after the Vestals lost their revenues). Ambrose replied that all things improve with time, so age was no argument for keeping a rite.

  8. What did the laws of 391–392 forbid, and how did the Alexandrian riot lead to the fall of the Serapeum?
    Answer

    Sacrifice and visits to shrines, and then every form of cult down to household incense, with sacrifice and reading entrails treated as treason and incense punished by loss of the house (Codex Theodosianus 16.10.10–12). When cult objects from a temple being made into a church were paraded in mockery, pagans rioted and occupied the Serapeum; an imperial letter pardoned them but ordered the cult destroyed, and a soldier's axe began the destruction of the statue.

  9. Why does Alan Cameron deny that the Frigidus was a last stand of paganism?
    Answer

    Eugenius was a Christian, the war was a usurpation like any other, and the pagan colouring comes almost entirely from Rufinus and the writers who followed him; Cameron finds no organised pagan party, against Bloch's pagan revival.

  10. How do Brown and Salzman differ on how the Roman aristocracy became Christian?
    Answer

    Brown stressed a quiet process through marriage and household, with Christian women prominent. Salzman, studying several hundred aristocrats, found men converting as readily as women, drawn by imperial careers and by a Christianity that accommodated aristocratic ideals of status.

Carry forward

  1. Law ended public sacrifice; society ended paganism as an elite identity. The edicts of 391–392 forbade sacrifice and temple visits, but the old religion lost the senatorial families through marriage, career and fashion over two or three generations, not by decree.
  2. Almost every narrative of these years is Christian and reads events as judgement: Valens burned for heresy, the wind at the Frigidus, the penance at Thessalonica. Ammianus, a pagan officer who saw much of what he describes and still criticised his hero, is the control to test them against for the years he covers, to 378.
  3. After Adrianople and the treaty of 382 an undefeated Gothic people lived and fought inside the empire, and after Thessalonica a bishop could discipline an emperor. Both precedents shape the West of module 8.5 and the relations of emperors and popes long after.
