The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the fourth century after Constantine, AD 337 to 395, and the end of public paganism. Cover: the sons of Constantine and Constantius II; Julian's reign, his attempt to build a pagan church, his Misopogon and his death in Persia in 363, with Ammianus Marcellinus as an eyewitness; Valens, the Goths crossing the Danube and Adrianople in 378; Theodosius, the settlement of the Goths, Thessalonica and Ambrose; the dispute over the altar of Victory between Symmachus and Ambrose in 384; the laws against sacrifice and the temples in the 390s, the destruction of the Serapeum in 391 and the battle of the Frigidus in 394; the end of the Vestals and the Olympic Games (point back to Greek module 7.4 for the Greek East); and the slow Christianisation of the Roman aristocracy. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 8 · Crisis and the late empire, AD 235 to 476 · 8.5 · 3,362 words

The fall of the West, 395 to 476

Two courts and a general, 395–408Alaric and the sack of Rome, 408–410Augustine's reply: the City of GodThe Rhine crossing and the lost provincesAetius and Attila, 425–454Gaiseric: Africa and the sack of 455Ricimer and the last emperors, 455–476Gibbon and Pirenne: why and whenTransformation, and the return of fallSelf-testCarry forward

Two courts and a general, 395–408

Theodosius I died at Milan on 17 January 395, where module 8.4 ends. Arcadius, about seventeen, held Constantinople; Honorius, ten, took the West. Nobody announced a partition, and laws still went out in both names. But the empire was never again governed from one court, and each court had a chief minister with his own army and his own claim to the Balkan prefecture of Illyricum.

The West was run by Stilicho, magister militum, of Vandal descent (Orosius 7.38.1) and husband of Theodosius' niece Serena. He claimed that the dying emperor had entrusted both sons to him, as his poet Claudian repeated in poem after poem. The eastern prefect Rufinus was cut down by returning troops in November 395 (Zosimus 5.7); in 397 the eunuch Eutropius had Stilicho declared a public enemy at Constantinople (5.11), while Gildo, count of Africa, transferred his province and its grain to the East.

Between the courts stood Alaric, leader of the Goths settled in 382. He rebelled in 395 and ravaged Greece, burning Eleusis (Greek module 7.4); Stilicho cornered him twice and twice let him go. In 401 Alaric entered Italy; after Pollentia (402) and Verona he withdrew, and Honorius moved his court behind the marshes of Ravenna. In 405–406 Radagaisus brought another Gothic host into Italy, 400,000 by Zosimus' count (5.26.3), more than 200,000 by Orosius' (7.37); Stilicho destroyed it near Faesulae.

In 408 Stilicho made the Senate pay Alaric 4,000 pounds of gold, and the senator Lampadius called it "not peace but a pact of servitude" (Zosimus 5.29). Arcadius died in May. The official Olympius persuaded Honorius that Stilicho meant to put his son Eucherius on the eastern throne, and Stilicho was beheaded at Ravenna on 22 August (5.34). Roman soldiers then killed the families of barbarian troops in the Italian cities, and some 30,000 men went over to Alaric (5.35.5–6).

Where sources disagree. Orosius, writing in 417, makes Stilicho a traitor who nursed Alaric and set the peoples beyond the Rhine in motion to win the throne for Eucherius (7.38). Zosimus, following the contemporary Olympiodorus, calls him more moderate than almost anyone in power in his day (5.34). Alan Cameron (Claudian, 1970) showed that Claudian's poems, the fullest contemporary account, track Stilicho's policy of the moment.

Alaric and the sack of Rome, 408–410

Alaric besieged Rome in autumn 408. The prefect Pompeianus let Tuscan diviners offer to save it (Zosimus 5.41.1–3; module 1.2), and the Senate bought the Goths off with 5,000 pounds of gold, 30,000 of silver, 4,000 silk robes, 3,000 scarlet fleeces and 3,000 pounds of pepper (5.41.4). Alaric wanted not loot but a place: land, grain and a Roman command. Honorius refused every version, even Noricum and grain alone (5.48–50). In 409 Alaric had the Senate proclaim Priscus Attalus emperor, then deposed him (6.6–12).

On 24 August 410 the Goths entered by the Salarian Gate and plundered the city for three days, the first capture of Rome by a foreign enemy since the Gauls eight centuries before. Orosius tells it as a story of restraint: Alaric, an Arian Christian, had the basilicas of Peter and Paul respected as sanctuaries, and church vessels were carried to St Peter's in procession, Goths and Romans singing hymns (7.39). Jerome, in Bethlehem, wrote that "the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken" (Letter 127.12).

Alaric took Honorius' half-sister Galla Placidia south, failed to cross to Africa and died at Consentia; Jordanes says he was buried in the diverted bed of the Busentus (Getica 158). His brother-in-law Athaulf led the Goths into Gaul and married Placidia at Narbonne in 414. Orosius heard a man of Narbonne tell Jerome that Athaulf had once meant to turn Romania into Gothia but resolved instead to restore the Roman name with Gothic strength (7.43.4–6). His successor Wallia returned Placidia, fought the Vandals and Alans in Spain as Rome's ally, and in 418 his people were settled in Aquitaine, the core of the later kingdom of Toulouse.

Augustine's reply: the City of God

Refugees brought to Africa the charge that Rome had fallen for abandoning its gods. Augustine answered in the City of God, twenty-two books written between 413 and about 426 because, he says, pagans were blaspheming more bitterly than usual after the sack (Retractations 2.43). Books 1–5 show that Rome had suffered worse under the gods, from the Gauls to Cannae (book 3), and that in 410 Christ's name saved those who fled to the basilicas (1.1–7). Books 6–10 take on Varro's theology (module 2.1) and the Platonists. Books 11–22 trace two cities made by two loves, of self to the contempt of God and of God to the contempt of self (14.28). Rome is not the heavenly city, and "without justice, what are kingdoms but great robberies?" (4.4). Module 1.6 reads his chapter on Lucretia (1.19).

Augustine set the young Spanish priest Orosius to write the Seven Books of History against the Pagans (417–418), a catalogue of pre-Christian disasters beside which 410 looks mild. Pagans answered in kind. Rutilius Namatianus, sailing home to Gaul in 417, praised Rome for making one fatherland of different peoples (On His Return 1.63) and cursed Stilicho for burning the Sibylline Books (2.41–60). Zosimus set out to tell how Rome lost its empire as Polybius had told how it won it (1.57), and traced the loss to the end of public sacrifice (4.59).

Where sources disagree. Orosius makes the Christian empire providential and Roman history improve after Christ. Augustine ties God's purpose to no earthly state and treats Rome's glory as the earthly reward of its love of praise (5.12–15). R. A. Markus (Saeculum, 1970) argued that Augustine had shared the "Christian times" triumphalism of the 390s and then abandoned it, so that the City of God breaks with the optimism his protégé went on to publish.

The Rhine crossing and the lost provinces

On the last day of 406, by Prosper's chronicle, Vandals, Alans and Sueves crossed the Rhine; Jerome lists the Gallic cities they took, from Mainz and Worms to Reims and Tournai (Letter 123). The army of Britain raised a usurper, Constantine III, who crossed to Gaul in 407. When his general Gerontius rebelled in Spain, the invaders crossed the Pyrenees (409) and in 411 shared the Spanish provinces by lot: Gallaecia to the Hasding Vandals and the Sueves, Lusitania and Carthaginiensis to the Alans, Baetica to the Siling Vandals (Hydatius, Chronicle, s.a. 411). Honorius' general Constantius ended Constantine III in 411, and the Goths, as Rome's allies, destroyed the Silings and broke the Alans in 416–418. The Burgundians held the middle Rhine by 413 (Prosper); in 436 Huns, probably in Aetius' pay, destroyed them, killing 20,000 by Hydatius' figure, and the survivors were resettled in Sapaudia, around Lake Geneva, in 443 (Gallic Chronicle of 452). Each settlement was a treaty with an army already standing on Roman soil.

Where sources disagree. Prosper dates the crossing to 31 December 406. Michael Kulikowski ("Barbarians in Gaul, usurpers in Britain", Britannia, 2000) argued for 31 December 405, which makes the British usurpations a response to the invasion and spares Stilicho, then fighting Radagaisus, the charge of ignoring Gaul. Most accounts keep 406; the evidence allows either.

Britain went first. Zosimus says that in 409 the Britons took up arms, freed their cities and expelled the Roman officials (6.5.2–3), and that in 410 Honorius told the cities of Britain to look to their own defence (6.10.2). New coin had stopped arriving soon after 402; within a generation towns and villas were abandoned. Gildas, in the sixth century, preserves an appeal to "Agitius, thrice consul", Aetius in or after 446, headed "the groans of the Britons" (On the Ruin of Britain 20.1).

Where sources disagree. Zosimus has the Britons expel Rome; Gildas has Rome abandon them, and the Saxons they hire betray them (On the Ruin of Britain 18–23). The Gallic Chronicle of 452 puts Britain under Saxon control in 441, Bede the Saxons' arrival in 449 (Ecclesiastical History 1.15), and some refer Honorius' letter to Bruttium in Italy. The end cannot be dated more closely than 409 to about 440.

Aetius and Attila, 425–454

For a generation the West rested on Aetius, once a hostage with Alaric and then with the Huns (Gregory of Tours, History 2.8, quoting the lost Renatus Frigeridus). He brought a Hunnic army to the usurper John in 425 and was bought off with a command in Gaul by Placidia, regent for her six-year-old son Valentinian III. His rival Boniface beat him near Rimini in 432 but died of his wounds; Aetius returned with Hunnic backing in 433 and was master of the government thereafter, consul in 432, 437 and 446. With Hunnic auxiliaries he beat Goths, Burgundians and the Armorican rebels called Bagaudae.

Attila, sole king of the Huns from about 445, devastated the Balkans and, by Priscus' account, made the East pay 6,000 pounds of gold in arrears and 2,100 a year. In 450 Valentinian's sister Honoria sent Attila her ring, and he claimed her with a share of the empire (Priscus; Jordanes, Getica). In 451 he invaded Gaul; Aetius, with the Visigoths of Theoderic I, Alans, Franks and Burgundians, checked him on the Catalaunian Plains near Troyes, where Theoderic fell. Jordanes, writing a century later from Cassiodorus' lost Gothic history, puts the dead at 165,000 (Getica 217); Hydatius has almost 300,000. In 452 Attila sacked Aquileia, received Pope Leo I and two senators at the Mincio, and withdrew. He died in 453 on his wedding night (Getica 254, after Priscus), and his empire broke apart. The West had lost the army it hired against its other enemies.

Where sources disagree. Prosper of Aquitaine, of Leo's circle at Rome, credits the withdrawal of 452 to the pope's embassy (Chronicle, s.a. 452). Hydatius, writing in Gallaecia, has the Huns struck by famine and disease and attacked by troops of the eastern emperor Marcian (s.a. 452).

On 21 September 454 Valentinian killed Aetius with his own hand (Prosper, s.a. 454). In March 455 Aetius' guardsmen killed Valentinian, and the house of Theodosius ended in the West.

Gaiseric: Africa and the sack of 455

In 429 Gaiseric led the Vandals and Alans from Spain to Africa; Victor of Vita, writing in the 480s, says they were counted at 80,000, old men and infants included (History of the Vandal Persecution 1.2). Augustine died in 430 in the third month of their siege of Hippo (Possidius, Life of Augustine 28–31). On 19 October 439 Gaiseric took Carthage in time of peace (Prosper, s.a. 439). It was the decisive loss: Africa fed Rome and paid much of the western budget, the senators' African estates passed to Vandal owners, and a law of 444 confesses that the treasury cannot supply the army.

The sack of 455 followed a broken betrothal. Gaiseric's son Huneric was promised to Valentinian's daughter Eudocia; Petronius Maximus, emperor after the murder, married her mother Eudoxia and gave Eudocia to his own son. Gaiseric sailed, Maximus was killed as he fled, and the Vandals entered Rome unopposed. Prosper says Leo persuaded Gaiseric to refrain from fire, slaughter and torture, and that the city was stripped for fourteen days (s.a. 455). Procopius has the palace treasures and half the gilded bronze roof of the Capitoline temple loaded aboard (Wars 3.5.3–5), and the Jerusalem Temple spoils that Titus had brought to Rome went too; Belisarius recovered them at Carthage in 534 (4.9.5). Eudoxia and her daughters were carried off, and Eudocia married Huneric.

Where sources disagree. Prosper's orderly fortnight was written in the pope's circle and credits the pope. Victor of Vita describes crowds of captives shipped to Carthage, husbands parted from wives, and the bishop Deogratias selling church plate to ransom them (book 1).

Ricimer and the last emperors, 455–476

For two decades power lay with the general of the army of Italy. Ricimer, magister militum from 456, was the son of a Suevic father and a daughter of the Visigothic king Wallia (Sidonius, Poems 2). An Arian of barbarian royal blood could not wear the purple, so he made and unmade those who did.

EmperorReignRaised byEnd
Petronius Maximus455himselfkilled in flight as the Vandals came
Avitus455–456Theoderic II's Visigoths and Gallic noblesbeaten by Ricimer at Placentia; made a bishop
Majorian457–461Ricimerput to death on Ricimer's orders
Libius Severus461–465Ricimer; unrecognised in the Eastdied; no emperor until 467
Anthemius467–472the eastern emperor Leo Ikilled when Ricimer took Rome

Glycerius473–474Ricimer's nephew Gundobaddeposed; made bishop of Salona

Romulus Augustulus475–476his father Orestesdeposed by Odoacer and pensioned

Majorian, the last western emperor to govern as well as reign, legislated against extortionate tax collectors and the quarrying of Rome's public buildings; when his African fleet was destroyed on the Spanish coast in 460 (Hydatius), Ricimer had him put to death the next year. In 468 East and West tried once more: Basiliscus' armada, which Procopius says cost 1,300 centenaria of gold, 130,000 pounds (Wars 3.6.2), was burned by Vandal fireships off Cape Bon. The West never again had the revenues it needed.

The end was played out by men who had served Attila. Orestes, a Roman from Pannonia, had been Attila's secretary and in 449 went with one Edeco on a Hunnic embassy to Constantinople (Priscus). In 475 he drove out Nepos and made his young son Romulus emperor, called Augustulus, "little Augustus". The troops in Italy demanded a third of its land; Orestes refused, and they made Odoacer, probably Edeco's son, their ruler (Procopius, Wars 5.1.4–8). Odoacer killed Orestes at Placentia in August 476 and deposed Romulus, sparing him out of pity for his youth and, because he was handsome, sending him with an income of 6,000 solidi to live in Campania (Anonymus Valesianus 8.38). He sent the palace regalia to Constantinople, which returned them to Theoderic in 497 (12.64). The embassy to Zeno, and how 476 became a turning point only in retrospect, are in module 0.3; module 8.6 begins there.

Gibbon and Pirenne: why and when

Edward Gibbon finished the western story in 1781, in his third volume, and closed chapter 38 with "General Observations on the Fall of the Roman Empire in the West". His answer is structural: the decline was "the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness", and "instead of inquiring why the Roman empire was destroyed, we should rather be surprised that it had subsisted so long". He names the corrupted legions, Constantine's institutions and the division of East and West, and then religion: the clergy preached "patience and pusillanimity", and the soldiers' pay went to monks and nuns. Yet Constantine's "victorious religion broke the violence of the fall", softening the conquerors. He ends with reassurance: modern Europe was safe, since "before they can conquer, they must cease to be barbarous", and every age had added to the wealth, happiness and knowledge of mankind.

The phrase usually quoted for his thesis comes from the end of the work, in 1788, looking back from the ruins of the city: "I have described the triumph of barbarism and religion" (chapter 71). It summarises six volumes; the argument of 1781 made Christianity a cushion as much as a cause. The afterlife of Gibbon's verdict is module 10.4.

Henri Pirenne moved the ending. In Mohammed and Charlemagne, published in 1937 after his death (English 1939), he argued that the Germanic kings changed rulers, not civilisation: Merovingian Gaul still used gold coin, papyrus and eastern spices, and the Mediterranean remained one economy until the Arab conquests closed the sea and turned the Franks north. Without Muhammad, he concluded, Charlemagne would have been inconceivable. Archaeology has reversed his timing while keeping his question. Richard Hodges and David Whitehouse (Mohammed, Charlemagne and the Origins of Europe, 1983) showed from pottery and coin that long-distance exchange in the western Mediterranean had already shrunk in the sixth century, before the Arabs; Michael McCormick (Origins of the European Economy, 2001) traced its recovery from the late eighth.

Transformation, and the return of fall

Peter Brown's The World of Late Antiquity (1971) turned the question from why Rome fell to what the centuries from about 150 to 750 created. Seen from Antioch or Alexandria, where nothing fell in 476, the period was inventive: the holy man, the bishop, a new art and a new inner life. The European Science Foundation's programme "The Transformation of the Roman World" (1993–1998) gave the word institutional weight. Walter Goffart argued that barbarian armies were settled on shares of tax revenue rather than confiscated land; Herwig Wolfram's Vienna school described the Goths as armies of mixed origin that became a people inside the Roman world. Module 0.3 names the camps; here is the evidence.

In 2005 two books restored the fall. Peter Heather (The Fall of the Roman Empire) argued that a strong empire was brought down from outside: the Huns drove two waves of Goths, Vandals, Alans and others across the frontier, in 376–380 and 405–408, and the loss of Africa in 439 removed the revenues that paid the army. Bryan Ward-Perkins (The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization) turned to the material record. Fine tableware and amphorae from specialised workshops vanish from western sites; tiled roofs give way to thatch and stone to timber; coin drops out of everyday use; graffiti and stamped tiles, signs of ordinary literacy, disappear; cattle bones from Italian sites show smaller animals. Britain, on his account, fell below the economic complexity of the pre-Roman Iron Age.

Where sources disagree. Heather makes the Huns the external shock that started the chain. Guy Halsall (Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West, 376–568, 2007) reverses the causation: the western court's civil wars drew barbarian armies in as allies and recruits, and migration followed political collapse. Salvian of Marseille, in the 440s, already blamed the Romans, claiming that the poor fled the tax collectors to the barbarians or the Bagaudae (On the Governance of God 5).

The material evidence is not all one way. Nikola Koepke and Joerg Baten (European Review of Economic History, 2005), compiling skeletal heights, found that stature stagnated under the empire and rose in the fifth and sixth centuries. The Greenland lead curve that module 7.3 used for the Antonine plague had already fallen in the late second century, so it cannot date a fifth-century collapse by itself. And the collapse was regional: sudden in Britain, gradual in Gaul and Spain, heaviest in Italy during the wars of the sixth century, and absent in the East, where villages in the limestone hills of northern Syria went on building in stone.

Where sources disagree. Ward-Perkins reads the disappearance of goods as a fall in living standards for almost everyone. Chris Wickham (Framing the Early Middle Ages, 2005) traces the simplification chiefly to the end of the Roman tax system and the impoverishment of aristocracies; where landlords weakened, peasants may have kept more of what they grew, which would fit the heights. Both accept that specialised production and exchange collapsed in the post-Roman West; they disagree about who paid for it.

Weighed together, the camps answer different questions. The western state fell: by 476 western Roman government reached little beyond Italy, and the process, not the date, is what counts. The economy it sustained fell too, unevenly, mostly after 450 and for long after 476. Roman culture did not end: law, Latin, the Church, the senatorial families and the habit of calling oneself Roman passed to the successor kingdoms and the East (module 8.6). "Transformation" describes religion and culture; "fall" describes the state and the material life it paid for. The late army is module 9.2, and late antique art, the strongest case for transformation, module 10.3.

Self-test

  1. Why did the division of 395 matter more than its makers intended?
    Answer

    It created two courts with rival chief ministers, each with an army and a claim to Illyricum. Stilicho's feud with Constantinople, which declared him a public enemy in 397 (Zosimus 5.11), let Alaric play one court against the other.

  2. What did Alaric want, and why did he end by sacking Rome?
    Answer

    Land for his people, grain and a Roman command, not plunder. Honorius at Ravenna refused every version, even Noricum and grain alone (Zosimus 5.48–50), and after his puppet emperor Attalus failed, Alaric took the city in August 410.

  3. How does Augustine answer the charge that Rome fell because it abandoned its gods?
    Answer

    Rome had suffered worse under the gods (City of God book 3), and in 410 Christ's name saved those in the basilicas (1.1–7). More deeply, Rome is not the heavenly city: the two cities are made by two loves (14.28), and kingdoms without justice are great robberies (4.4).

  4. How do Orosius and Augustine differ in reading Roman history?
    Answer

    Orosius makes the Christian empire providential and history improve after Christ. Augustine ties God's purpose to no earthly state; Markus (1970) read this as his break with the "Christian times" optimism of the 390s.

  5. Which peoples took which western provinces between 406 and 443?
    Answer

    Vandals, Alans and Sueves crossed the Rhine and shared Spain by lot in 411 (Hydatius); the Goths, as Roman allies, broke the Silings and Alans and were settled in Aquitaine in 418; the Burgundians held the middle Rhine from about 413 and, after their destruction in 436, Sapaudia from 443.

  6. Why can the end of Roman Britain not be dated more closely than 409 to about 440?
    Answer

    Zosimus has the Britons expel Roman officials in 409 and Honorius write to the cities in 410 (6.5, 6.10), a letter some refer to Bruttium; Gildas has Rome abandon Britain and preserves an appeal to Aetius in or after 446; the Gallic Chronicle of 452 gives Saxon control in 441 and Bede the Saxon arrival in 449.

  7. How did Aetius depend on the Huns, and why did Attila's death hurt the West?
    Answer

    A former hostage among them, he used Hunnic armies to reach power and to beat Goths, Burgundians and Bagaudae. When Attila died in 453 and his empire broke up, the West lost the army it hired against its other enemies, and Aetius was murdered the next year.

  8. Why was the Vandal conquest of Africa decisive?
    Answer

    Africa supplied Rome's grain and much of the western revenue, and the senators' estates there were lost; a law of 444 admits the treasury could not supply the army. The attempt to recover it in 468, which Procopius says cost 130,000 pounds of gold (Wars 3.6.2), ended in flames off Cape Bon.

  9. What does Gibbon argue in 1781, and how does Pirenne change the question?
    Answer

    Gibbon calls the fall "the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness" and makes Christianity both a cause and a softener of it; "the triumph of barbarism and religion" is his chapter 71 summary of 1788. Pirenne moved the end of the ancient economy to the Arab conquests, a timing archaeology has since overturned (Hodges and Whitehouse, 1983).

  10. What does the archaeology show about living standards, and how is it disputed?
    Answer

    Ward-Perkins documents the disappearance of traded pottery, tiles, coin, everyday literacy and large cattle, worst in Britain. Koepke and Baten found heights rising in the fifth and sixth centuries, and Wickham ascribes the simplification to the end of the tax system and of aristocratic wealth, which may have left peasants better off.

Carry forward

  1. The West fell through its revenues: each lost province, above all Africa in 439, shrank the taxes that paid the army, until the government depended on barbarian armies and on generals who made and unmade emperors. Follow the money and the army, not the battles.
  2. The "invasions" were mostly settlements negotiated with armies already inside the empire, often drawn in by Roman civil wars; Alaric, Athaulf and Odoacer wanted a place in the Roman system, not its destruction, and the successor kingdoms inherited Roman land, law and taxpayers.
  3. "Fall" and "transformation" answer different questions: the western state and its economy did fall, unevenly and over generations, while religion, law and Roman identity carried on, and the eastern empire did not fall at all. Ask of any claim which region, which class and which evidence.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the end of Roman rule in the West, AD 395 to 476. Cover: the division between Arcadius and Honorius; Stilicho; Alaric and the sack of Rome in 410, and Augustine's City of God as the reply to pagan blame; the Rhine crossing of 406, the loss of Britain, and Spain and Gaul to Vandals, Sueves, Goths and Burgundians; Aetius, Attila, the Catalaunian Plains and Pope Leo; the Vandal conquest of Africa and the sack of 455; Ricimer and the puppet emperors; Odoacer's deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 and the imperial insignia sent to Constantinople; then the great debate: Gibbon's 'triumph of barbarism and religion', Pirenne, Peter Brown's late antiquity and 'transformation', and the return of decline and fall in Ward-Perkins and Heather, with the archaeological evidence for living standards. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 8 · Crisis and the late empire, AD 235 to 476 · 8.6 · 2,864 words

The Rome that did not fall

Why the East survived

Module 8.5 ends in 476 with the western regalia on their way to Zeno. Nobody at Constantinople thought the Roman empire had ended: its emperor still reigned in Constantine's New Rome (module 8.3) and legislated for the Roman people. The question is why the half that Theodosius left to Arcadius in 395 outlasted the other by nearly a thousand years.

Four reasons do most of the work. Money: Egypt, Syria and Asia Minor were the most urban and productive provinces, and their taxes never stopped; Anastasius (491–518) left 3,200 centenaria of gold in the treasury, 320,000 pounds (Procopius, Secret History 19.7). Geography: the Danube peoples could ravage the Balkans but could not cross the Bosporus or the Hellespont against the fleet, so Anatolia and the East beyond were safe. The capital sat on a peninsula with water on three sides, and the Theodosian land walls, built in 413 and rebuilt after the earthquake of 447, were not broken until 1453; the crusaders of 1204 came over the sea walls. The frontier: Persia was a state that made treaties and kept them for long stretches, not a stream of migrating armies. Politics: the eastern court kept its generals under control. The Gothic general Gainas was driven out in 400 and his men massacred in the city; Leo I had the Alan Aspar, who had made him emperor, killed in 471, and recruited Isaurian highlanders as a counterweight; and in 488 Zeno sent Theoderic's Ostrogoths, the most dangerous army in the Balkans, to take Italy from Odoacer. The East exported its problem to the West.

A. H. M. Jones drew the conclusion in The Later Roman Empire (1964): the East had the same institutions, taxes, Church and army, and survived, so internal weakness cannot by itself explain the western collapse. The West was poorer and more exposed.

Justinian: reconquest, plague, law and the Great Church

Justinian (527–565), nephew of the guardsman-emperor Justin I, had a programme: to restore the empire to the limits of the old Roman world, purge it of heresy and give it one law. His historian, Belisarius' secretary Procopius of Caesarea, wrote the Wars, the panegyric Buildings and the Secret History, an invective against Justinian and Theodora unpublished in his lifetime: one author praises and damns the same reign.

The reign nearly ended in January 532, when the circus factions joined in the Nika riot, burned the city centre and proclaimed a rival emperor. Procopius has Theodora shame the council out of flight (Wars 1.24.33–37); Belisarius and Mundus then trapped the crowd in the Hippodrome, where more than 30,000 died by Procopius' figure (1.24.54).

Belisarius took Vandal Africa in one campaign, 533–534. Italy took twenty years: Rome fell to Belisarius in 536 and Ravenna in 540, then Totila's Goths retook most of the peninsula until the eunuch Narses destroyed them at Busta Gallorum in 552. A foothold in south-eastern Spain followed. In 568, three years after Justinian's death, the Lombards entered Italy and most of it was lost again.

In 541 bubonic plague reached Pelusium in Egypt, and in 542 Constantinople, where Procopius says the dead reached 5,000 a day and then 10,000 and more (Wars 2.22–23). Ancient DNA from sixth-century Bavarian graves confirms the plague bacillus, Yersinia pestis. The disease returned for two centuries.

Where sources disagree. Kyle Harper (The Fate of Rome, 2017) treats the plague, with the cold decades after 536, as a demographic catastrophe that ended late antique prosperity. Lee Mordechai, Merle Eisenberg and colleagues ("The Justinianic Plague: an inconsequential pandemic?", PNAS, 2019) found no clear break in papyri, laws, coinage or pollen and judge the maximal toll unproven.

The law is outlined here and analysed in module 9.1. Commissions on which the jurist Tribonian sat, leading them from 530, issued a Code of imperial constitutions in 529, revised in 534; the Digest, fifty books of extracts from the classical jurists, in 533; and the Institutes, a students' textbook, the same year. Justinian's later laws, mostly in Greek, were collected as the Novels. The name Corpus iuris civilis was given to the whole only in the sixteenth century.

Hagia Sophia, the church of Holy Wisdom, replaced the basilica burned in the riot. Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, mathematicians and engineers, built it in under six years, and it was dedicated on 27 December 537. Procopius says the dome seemed to hang from heaven on a golden chain (Buildings 1.1). The dome fell in 558 and was rebuilt higher for a second dedication in 562, celebrated in verse by Paul the Silentiary. Justinian's boast that he had outdone Solomon comes from a legendary account of the building written centuries later. Late antique style, the frame for reading it as art, is module 10.3; the closing of the Athenian schools in 529 is in Greek module 7.4.

Persians and Arabs: the seventh-century amputation

In 602 the Danube army mutinied and the centurion Phocas killed the emperor Maurice and his sons. Khusro II, whom Maurice had restored to the Persian throne, went to war as his avenger. Heraclius, son of the exarch of Africa, overthrew Phocas in 610 and lost almost everything: Antioch in 613, Jerusalem in 614, where the relic of the True Cross was carried off, and Egypt by 619. In 626 Avars and Slavs besieged Constantinople while a Persian army waited across the Bosporus. The walls held. Heraclius, campaigning in the Persian heartland, won near Nineveh in December 627; Khusro was overthrown and killed in 628, and the Cross returned to Jerusalem about 630. George of Pisidia's court poems, the Chronicon Paschale and the ninth-century chronicle of Theophanes tell the story.

Victory lasted less than a decade. Arab armies united by Islam beat the Romans at the Yarmuk in 636; Jerusalem surrendered about 638, and Alexandria was given up in 641–642. Syria, Palestine and Egypt, the richest provinces, were gone for good; Carthage fell in 698. Constantinople survived two Arab attacks, the first in the 660s or 670s (its date is disputed), the second by land and sea in 717–718, broken by Leo III, the Bulgars and the winter. Theophanes credits a Syrian refugee, Kallinikos, with inventing Greek fire.

What survived was a smaller and different state: Anatolia, the capital, footholds in the Balkans, Sicily and parts of Italy. Cities shrank to fortified kernels, coin grew scarce outside the capital, and the field armies were settled in Anatolian districts, the themes, which became the units of government. Greek replaced Latin in administration; a law of 629 is the first to style Heraclius basileus.

Where sources disagree. George Ostrogorsky made the themes a deliberate reform of Heraclius. John Haldon (Byzantium in the Seventh Century, 1990) traced a gradual settlement of the retreating armies from the 640s, and most now follow him.

Rhomaioi: Romans who spoke Greek

The people of this state called themselves Rhomaioi, Romans, their country Romania and their ruler the emperor of the Romans. Their capital was New Rome: the council of Constantinople in 381 gave its bishop rank next after Rome's, "because it is New Rome" (canon 3). They spoke Greek, but in Christian usage "Hellene" meant a pagan. Latin held on in the army and the law into the sixth century; John Lydus, Justinian's official, lamented its retreat from his department (On the Magistracies). From the seventh century the state was Greek in language and Roman in name, law and self-understanding.

Westerners denied them the name. From the ninth century popes and Frankish writers called them Greeks and their ruler emperor of the Greeks; when Liudprand of Cremona came to Nikephoros II for Otto I in 968, a papal letter so addressing the emperor caused fury at court (Liudprand, Embassy). "Byzantine", from the city's old name, is an early modern coinage, popularised by Hieronymus Wolf in 1557 (module 0.3). Montesquieu and Gibbon added the verdict: for them the eastern empire was Rome's degenerate sequel.

Where sources disagree. George Ostrogorsky (History of the Byzantine State, English 1956) defined Byzantium as a fusion of the Roman state, Greek culture and the Christian faith: a new civilisation built on Rome. Anthony Kaldellis (Romanland, 2019) argues that its people were a nation in the ordinary sense, Romans by language, custom and Orthodoxy, and that "Byzantine" hides a Roman state that never stopped being one.

Dynasties and the Macedonian height

Palaiologan1259–1453recovery; Ottoman conquest

Basil I, a peasant from the theme of Macedonia who rose as groom and favourite of Michael III, murdered his patron in 867 and founded a dynasty that ruled for almost two centuries. It made legitimacy hereditary: Constantine VII was Porphyrogennetos, born in the palace's porphyry chamber, and the house outlasted regents and usurping generals until 1056. Leo VI issued the Basilika, a Greek recompilation of Justinian's law in sixty books. Constantine VII sponsored the Book of Ceremonies and On the Administration of the Empire, a handbook of foreign peoples for his son. The copying of classical texts in the new minuscule belongs to this age and is told in Greek modules 7.4 and 9.3.

The soldier emperors then attacked. Nikephoros Phokas took Crete in 961 and, as emperor, Antioch in 969, and John I Tzimiskes drove the Rus' out of Bulgaria. Basil II (976–1025) spent decades destroying Tsar Samuel's Bulgarian state and annexed it in 1018. About 988 he sent his sister Anna to marry Vladimir of Kiev, who was baptised; the Varangian Guard and the Christianity of Rus' both date from this alliance. At Basil's death the empire ran from the Danube to the Euphrates and into southern Italy.

Where sources disagree. John Skylitzes, writing late in the eleventh century, says that after Kleidion in 1014 Basil blinded 15,000 Bulgarian prisoners, leaving every hundredth man one eye to lead the rest home; Kekaumenos gives 14,000. Paul Stephenson (The Legend of Basil the Bulgar-Slayer, 2003) argued that the epithet "Bulgar-slayer" and the picture of a war of annihilation took shape only in the later twelfth century.

Charlemagne and a second Roman empire

In 797 the empress Irene blinded her son Constantine VI and ruled alone. In the West the throne could be called vacant: the Annals of Lorsch say the imperial name had lapsed among the Greeks because a woman held power. On Christmas Day 800, in St Peter's, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charles and the Romans acclaimed him emperor; Theophanes, at Constantinople, has the pope anoint him with oil from head to foot.

There were now two Roman emperors. Constantinople withheld recognition until 812, when Michael I's envoys at Aachen hailed Charles as basileus; thereafter the eastern rulers styled themselves more insistently basileus ton Rhomaion, emperor of the Romans, and allowed the western ruler an emperor's title without the Romans. The western title lapsed with the Carolingians and was revived for Otto I in 962. Frederick Barbarossa's chancery added "holy" in 1157, the full "Holy Roman Empire" appears from 1254, and the institution ended when Francis II laid down the crown on 6 August 1806, under pressure from Napoleon. The idea of Rome it carried is module 10.4.

Where sources disagree. Einhard says Charles would not have entered the church that day had he known the pope's plan (Life of Charles 28). The Royal Frankish Annals and the papal Liber Pontificalis describe a ceremony with set acclamations by the Romans, and Leo had met Charles at Paderborn in 799. Einhard's story is now usually read as a modesty topos, or as dislike of owing the crown to a pope.

Manzikert, the Crusades and 1204

On 26 August 1071, near Manzikert north of Lake Van, the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured Romanos IV Diogenes. Released on terms within days, Romanos found himself deposed and was blinded the next year. Michael Attaleiates, who was present, blames the withdrawal of the rearguard under Andronikos Doukas; Michael Psellos, a Doukas partisan, blames Romanos' rashness. In the civil wars that followed, rival generals hired Turkish bands, and by 1081 Turkmen held most of the Anatolian plateau, with a sultan at Nicaea.

Where sources disagree. Speros Vryonis (The Decline of Medieval Hellenism in Asia Minor, 1971) made the battle the opening of a Turkish conquest that broke Greek society in Anatolia. Jean-Claude Cheynet ("Mantzikert: un désastre militaire?", Byzantion, 1980) argued that the losses were modest and much of the army withdrew intact; the disaster was the decade of civil war after it.

Alexios I Komnenos (1081–1118) rebuilt the state as a family regime and asked the West for soldiers; what came, after Urban II's appeal at Clermont in 1095, was the First Crusade. Its leaders swore oaths to Alexios and returned Nicaea to him, but Bohemond kept Antioch; Anna Komnene's Alexiad records her father's distrust of the Latins (book 10). John II and Manuel I recovered the Anatolian coasts; Manuel's defeat at Myriokephalon in 1176 ended hopes of the plateau, and the massacre of the Latins in Constantinople in 1182 poisoned relations with the Italians.

The Fourth Crusade owed Venice for ships it could not pay for. It took Zara for the Venetians in 1202, then sailed to Constantinople to install the exiled prince Alexios IV, who promised money and Church union he could not deliver. After his murder the crusaders stormed the city on 12 April 1204 and sacked it for three days; Niketas Choniates, who escaped, wrote the lament. A Latin emperor was crowned in Hagia Sophia, Venice took three-eighths of the empire, and the bronze horses of the Hippodrome went to St Mark's, as did the porphyry Tetrarchs of module 8.2. Three Greek states claimed the succession: Nicaea, Epirus, and Trebizond, seized that April by two grandsons of Andronikos I with Georgian help.

The Palaiologan revival and the last fragments

Nicaea won the contest of the exiles. On 25 July 1261 its general Alexios Strategopoulos found Constantinople weakly held and walked in; Michael VIII Palaiologos entered in August and later blinded the boy Laskarid emperor. The restored empire was a regional power with an imperial capital. Michael kept Charles of Anjou at bay by accepting Church union at Lyons in 1274 and, by his own later claim, by financing the Sicilian Vespers of 1282. Civil wars in 1321–1328 and 1341–1347, the Black Death of 1347 and Stefan Dušan's Serbia reduced it to little more than the capital, Thessalonica and the Morea. The Ottomans crossed to Gallipoli in 1354; Bayezid I blockaded Constantinople until Timur destroyed his army at Ankara in 1402, while Manuel II toured the West for help as far as London. Union with Rome, proclaimed at Florence in 1439, was rejected at home.

The siege and fall of 1453, when Mehmed II took the city on 29 May, are told in module 0.3. The fragments outlasted the capital. Constantine XI's brothers Thomas and Demetrios, despots of the Morea, quarrelled until Mehmed II came in person: Demetrios surrendered Mistra in 1460 and Thomas fled to Italy. Trebizond surrendered in August 1461, and its last emperor, David, was executed in 1463; the Orthodox principality of Theodoro in the Crimea fell in 1475. Thomas' son Andreas sold his claim to the imperial title to Charles VIII of France in 1494 and left it in his will of 1502 to Ferdinand and Isabella.

The afterlives of the Roman title

Three powers claimed the inheritance. Mehmed II called himself Kayser-i Rum, Caesar of Rome; Kritoboulos of Imbros wrote the history of his reign in the manner of Thucydides, and George of Trebizond told him in a letter that whoever lawfully held Constantinople, the capital of the Roman empire, was emperor of the Romans. The Ottomans called their Balkan provinces Rumelia, the land of the Romans. Moscow claimed the faith and the blood. Ivan III married Thomas' daughter Zoe, renamed Sophia, in 1472 and took the double-headed eagle; Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547; Moscow received its own patriarch in 1589. Early in the sixteenth century the monk Philotheus of Pskov wrote to Vasily III that two Romes had fallen, that Moscow was the third, and that there would be no fourth. The Holy Roman Empire carried the western title to 1806. Kaiser and tsar both descend from Caesar: the last tsar fell in 1917, the last Kaisers in 1918, the last sultan in 1922.

Where sources disagree. The charter founding the Moscow patriarchate in 1589 repeats Philotheus' formula, and Hildegard Schaeder (Moskau das dritte Rom, 1929) made it the core of Muscovite political ideology. Marshall Poe ("Moscow, the Third Rome: the origins and transformations of a 'pivotal moment'", 2001) argued that it was a monk's eschatological warning, rare in Muscovite state documents, and became a national creed only in the nineteenth century.

Self-test

  1. Give four reasons the eastern empire survived the fifth century when the western did not.
    Answer

    A richer, more urban tax base (Anastasius left 320,000 pounds of gold, Procopius, Secret History 19.7); the straits, the fleet and the Theodosian Walls, which kept Danube invaders out of Asia Minor; a Persian neighbour that made treaties; and a court that controlled its generals (Gainas in 400, Aspar in 471) and sent Theoderic to Italy in 488. Jones (1964) concluded that the West's poverty and exposure, not shared institutions, made the difference.

  2. What did the people we call Byzantines call themselves, and where does "Byzantine" come from?
    Answer

    Rhomaioi, Romans, living in Romania under the emperor of the Romans, with New Rome as capital. "Byzantine", from the city's old name, was popularised by Hieronymus Wolf in 1557; Montesquieu and Gibbon then treated the empire as Rome's degenerate sequel.

  3. Why is Procopius both indispensable and treacherous as a witness to Justinian?
    Answer

    He was Belisarius' secretary and is the main narrative source for the wars, the Nika riot, the plague and the buildings. But the same man wrote the panegyric Buildings and the invective Secret History, so each portrait has to be tested against the others and against documents.

  4. What did the reconquest win, and how much of it lasted?
    Answer

    Vandal Africa in 533–534, held until Carthage fell in 698; Italy after twenty years of war, ending with Narses' victory in 552, mostly lost to the Lombards from 568; and a foothold in south-eastern Spain.

  5. What is the dispute over the Justinianic plague?
    Answer

    Procopius reports 5,000 and then 10,000 dead a day at Constantinople (Wars 2.22–23), and DNA confirms Yersinia pestis. Harper (2017) makes it a demographic catastrophe; Mordechai, Eisenberg and colleagues (2019) found no clear break in papyri, laws, coinage or pollen and call the maximal toll unproven.

  6. What are the parts of Justinian's law, and which module treats them?
    Answer

    The Code (529, revised 534), the Digest of the classical jurists (533), the Institutes (533) and the later Novels, compiled under Tribonian; the name Corpus iuris civilis is sixteenth-century. Module 9.1 analyses the law.

  7. How did the seventh century change the empire?
    Answer

    After the Persian war and Heraclius' victory of 627, the Arabs took Syria, Palestine and Egypt (Yarmuk 636, Alexandria 641–642) and later Africa. The state shrank to Anatolia, the capital and western footholds, its cities contracted, Greek became the language of government, and the armies settled in the themes, whether by Heraclius' reform (Ostrogorsky) or gradually from the 640s (Haldon).

  8. Why did Constantinople object to Charlemagne's coronation, and how was the quarrel settled?
    Answer

    There could be only one Roman emperor, and the East had one, even if Irene's rule let westerners call the throne vacant. In 812 eastern envoys hailed Charles as basileus at Aachen, while the eastern rulers kept "emperor of the Romans" for themselves.

  9. Was Manzikert the disaster that lost Anatolia?
    Answer

    It ended in Romanos IV's capture, which Attaleiates blames on Andronikos Doukas' withdrawal and Psellos on Romanos' rashness. Cheynet (1980) argued the losses were modest and that the decade of civil war, in which rival generals hired Turks, lost the plateau; Vryonis (1971) stressed the conquest the battle opened.

  10. Name three claimants to the Roman title after 1453 and the right each claimed.
    Answer

    The Ottoman sultans, by possession of Constantinople (Kayser-i Rum; George of Trebizond's letter to Mehmed II); Moscow, by Orthodoxy and Ivan III's marriage to Sophia Palaiologina, with Philotheus' Third Rome; and the Holy Roman Empire, by papal coronation since 800 and 962, until 1806.

Carry forward

  1. The Roman state did not end in 476: it continued at Constantinople with Roman law, the Roman name and an unbroken imperial succession until 1453. The East's survival is the control case for every explanation of the western fall.
  2. Medieval Rome survived by money, walls and diplomacy more than by conquest: a tax base, an impregnable capital and the habit of buying, dividing and redirecting enemies. Each time the tax base was lost (the seventh century, after Manzikert, after 1204), the empire shrank to what its capital could defend.
  3. From 800 the Roman title had rival claimants, each by a different right: papal coronation in the West, conquest of the capital for the Ottomans, Orthodox faith and dynastic marriage for Moscow. Ask of any later "Rome" which of these rights it claims.
