Roman law

Ius, fas and mosThe Twelve Tables and the pontiffsThe praetor's edict and the formulaThe juristsPersons, things and actionsPaternal power, slavery and manumissionCitizenship and its gradesCriminal law and its penaltiesFrom the jurists to the codesBologna and the civil-law worldSelf-testCarry forward

Ius, fas and mos

Romans sorted binding rules under three heads. Ius was what one person could claim against another and a magistrate would enforce; Celsus, quoted by Ulpian, called it "the art of the good and the fair" (Digest 1.1.1 pr.). Fas was what the gods allowed: fas lex divina, ius lex humana, says Isidore (Etymologies 5.2.2). Mos was ancestral custom, enforced by shame, the censor's mark and the family council; Cicero quotes Ennius' line that the Roman state stands on ancient customs and on men (On the Republic 5.1, preserved by Augustine, City of God 2.21).

The three overlapped. The calendar marked days fasti, on which the praetor might speak the three words of jurisdiction, do, dico, addico, and days nefasti, on which he might not (Varro, On the Latin Language 6.29–30). The oldest sanction declared the offender sacer, given to the gods and so killable. Custom made law: Julian holds that inveterate custom is rightly kept as statute and that statutes may lapse by disuse (Digest 1.3.32.1). A father who killed his son acted within ius, yet mos expected a council of kin first (module 9.3). Roman legal history is the growth of ius at the expense of the other two.

The Twelve Tables and the pontiffs

Module 3.1 tells how the decemvirs wrote the Tables in 451–450, how they survive and what they said; module 2.4 gives the funeral rules and the evil song. The Tables gave rules, not the means to use them. Pomponius, a jurist of the second century AD, says that interpretation and the forms of action stayed with the pontiffs, one of whom presided over private law each year (Digest 1.2.2.6).

The forms were the legis actiones, five in Gaius' list, from the wager (sacramentum) to the seizure of a pledge (Institutes 4.12), each with set words: a man who sued for his vines cut down lost, because the Tables spoke of trees (4.11). Interpretation also stretched old words to new uses. The clause freeing a son sold three times became emancipation (module 9.3), and the sale by bronze and scales (mancipatio, 1.119) was adapted to make wills (2.102–104).

The monopoly broke in stages. Gnaeus Flavius published the forms and the calendar in 304 (module 3.1); Pomponius says he stole the book (1.2.2.7). Tiberius Coruncanius, the first plebeian pontifex maximus, was the first to profess law in public (1.2.2.35). Sextus Aelius Paetus, consul in 198, wrote the Tripertita, the Tables, their interpretation and the actions, which Pomponius calls the cradle of the law (1.2.2.38).

The praetor's edict and the formula

From 367 a praetor administered justice in the city (Livy 6.42.11), and from 242 a second praetor heard cases involving foreigners. Each posted an edict at the start of his year, stating the claims he would grant a remedy for; some called it an annual law (Cicero, Verrines 2.1.109). He could not legislate, but he could refuse an action or invent one: praetorian law, Papinian says, was introduced "to aid, supplement or correct the civil law" (Digest 1.1.7.1). Praetors gave estates to blood kin whom the Tables' rules of male descent passed over, and Cicero's colleague Gaius Aquillius Gallus devised formulas against deceit (On Duties 3.60). A tribune's law of 67 bound praetors to their own edicts (Asconius on Pro Cornelio).

Trial under the formula had two stages. Before the praetor the parties settled a written instruction to a private judge, a citizen and not a lawyer; before the judge they proved their case. In Gaius' model the judge is told that if it appears that Numerius Negidius ought to pay Aulus Agerius ten thousand sesterces, he is to condemn him, and if not, to absolve him (4.39–43); every condemnation was in money (4.48). The old actions, Gaius says, fell from favour because the smallest slip lost the case, and the Aebutian law and two Julian laws abolished them (4.30).

Under Hadrian, Salvius Julianus fixed the edict's final text (Eutropius 8.17), and governors' edicts copied it (module 7.5). Meanwhile cognitio, in which an imperial official heard the whole case subject to appeal, displaced the formula, which a law of 342 abolished outright (Code of Justinian 2.57.1).

The jurists

The Republican jurist was usually a senator who advised for nothing, skilled, in Cicero's definition, in answering, pleading and drafting (On the Orator 1.212). Quintus Mucius Scaevola, pontifex and consul in 95, was the first to arrange the civil law by categories, in eighteen books (Pomponius, Digest 1.2.2.41). Under Augustus, Pomponius sets Antistius Labeo, an innovator, against Ateius Capito, who held to tradition (1.2.2.47), and Tacitus sets Labeo's freedom against Capito's compliance (Annals 3.75). Their followers formed the Proculian and Sabinian schools; Gaius calls the Sabinians "our teachers". Augustus first let chosen jurists give opinions by his authority (1.2.2.49), and under Hadrian their agreed opinions had the force of law (Gaius 1.7).

Where sources disagree. Gaius records the schools' quarrels. If you make wine from my grapes or a cup from my silver, Sabinus and Cassius held that the product belongs to the owner of the material, Nerva and Proculus that it belongs to the maker (2.79; Gaius, Digest 41.1.7.7). Justinian's Institutes chose a middle view: the owner's if the thing can be reduced to its material, the maker's if not (2.1.25).

Gaius is a first name and a book. He wrote about 161, no other classical jurist cites him, yet the Law of Citations of 426 ranked him with the great Severans. His Institutes, a four-book course for students, is the one classical textbook to survive. In 1816 Barthold Georg Niebuhr, travelling to Rome as Prussian envoy, found in the Chapter Library at Verona a manuscript of Jerome's letters written over an erased legal text; Savigny identified it as Gaius, and Johann Göschen published it in 1820. Before 1816 classical law was known almost only through Justinian's excerpts; Gaius showed it whole and unrevised, procedure included.

The Severan jurists, whose careers module 7.4 tells, closed the classical age: Papinian on cases, Paul and Ulpian in vast commentaries on the edict and the civil law. Ulpian defines justice as the constant and perpetual will to give each his right, and the law's precepts as to live honourably, harm no one and give each his own (Digest 1.1.10 pr.–1).

Persons, things and actions

Gaius' plan has outlived his book: all the law we use concerns persons, things or actions (1.8). Justinian's Institutes kept it, and through them the modern civil codes.

Persons. The free are divided from slaves, the freeborn from the freed (1.9–11), the independent (sui iuris) from those in another's power (1.48). Status rested on freedom, citizenship and family, and losing any of them was a "diminution of head" (1.159–162).

Things. Temples and tombs lay outside ownership (2.2–9). The archaic res mancipi, Italian land, slaves, oxen, horses, mules and asses, passed only by mancipation or a fictitious lawsuit (2.14a–22). Obligations arose from contract or delict (3.88). Contracts bound by delivery, words, writing or consent (3.89): the stipulation, spondesne? spondeo (3.92), bound whoever said the words; sale, hire, partnership and mandate bound by agreement alone. The delicts were theft, robbery, damage under the Aquilian law and insult (3.182). The Tables' fixed twenty-five asses for assault (Gaius 3.223) grew absurd as money lost value: Labeo, as Gellius reports, told of Lucius Veratius, who slapped passers-by while a slave paid out the coins (20.1.13), and the praetor substituted damages assessed case by case.

Actions. An action was in rem when it claimed a thing, in personam when it claimed that someone ought to give or do (4.2–3). Romans thought from remedies: a right was what the edict granted an action for, and the jurists' commentaries follow the edict's order.

Paternal power, slavery and manumission

Module 9.3 gives paternal power in life; here are its mechanics. Power came by birth in lawful marriage, by adoption through three sales and a cession in court (Gaius 1.134), or by adrogation of an independent man, voted by the curiate assembly after the pontiffs' inquiry (1.99; Gellius 5.19). A son in power could contract, but his acquisitions went to his father (2.87), and for a son's or slave's delict the father could pay or surrender the offender (4.75). After a son named Macedo killed his father to clear his debts, a decree of the Senate under Vespasian made loans to sons in power irrecoverable (Ulpian, Digest 14.6.1; Suetonius, Vespasian 11).

The slave was a thing and a person at once. Florentinus calls slavery an institution of the law of nations subjecting one man to another's ownership against nature (Digest 1.5.4.1); Ulpian, that by civil law slaves count for nothing, while by natural law all men are equal (50.17.32). Slaves ran shops and ships with a peculium, and creditors sued the master on their dealings (Gaius 4.69–74). Antoninus Pius punished masters who killed their own slaves without cause and forced cruel ones to sell (1.53); the Silanian decree of AD 10 exposed every slave under the roof to torture and death when a master was murdered (Digest 29.5), the rule behind the execution of Pedanius' household (module 9.3).

Formal manumission made a citizen: by the rod, a collusive claim of freedom before a magistrate; by enrolment in the census; or by will (Gaius 1.17). Slaves freed informally became, under a lex Junia, Junian Latins (1.22), who lived free and died as slaves, their goods returning to the patron (3.56). Augustus narrowed the gate (Suetonius, Augustus 40.4). The lex Fufia Caninia of 2 BC capped freedom by will on a sliding scale, never above a hundred slaves (1.42–46). The lex Aelia Sentia of AD 4 required an owner of twenty and a slave of thirty unless a council approved the cause (1.18, 1.38), voided manumissions that cheated creditors (1.37), and made slaves once chained, branded or sent to the arena dediticii, free but never citizens (1.13–15). A tax of a twentieth on manumissions dated from 357 (Livy 7.16.7). Constantine validated manumission in church (module 8.3); Justinian made every freedman a citizen (Institutes 1.5.3).

Where sources disagree. Justinian's Institutes call the law the lex Junia Norbana (1.5.3), which points to the consuls of AD 19. Gaius calls it simply the lex Junia, and the Aelian-Sentian law of AD 4 already makes slaves freed under thirty into Latins (1.29), which seems to presuppose it; hence the common date of 17 BC.

Citizenship and its grades

Citizenship was a bundle: the vote, office, marriage with Roman effect (conubium), trade and ownership under Roman law (commercium), and protection from summary flogging. Module 3.4 gives the Republican ladder. Under the emperors there were Romans, Latins and peregrines. Under the greater Latin right a town's councillors became citizens, under the lesser only its magistrates (Gaius 1.96; module 7.5); a child of a Roman and a peregrine without conubium took the lower status (1.78). Paul, about to be flogged at Jerusalem, asked whether a Roman might be scourged uncondemned, and later appealed to Caesar (Acts 22.25–29, 25.10–12). After the grant of 212 (module 7.4) the line that mattered was rank.

Criminal law and its penalties

Rome had no public prosecutor. In the Republic capital charges went to the assembly, subject to appeal (module 3.1), and the accused could leave before the last tribe voted (Polybius 6.14.7). From 149 standing jury courts took over offence by offence (module 4.4), and Sulla's courts for murder, forgery and treason punished with interdiction from water and fire, exile in effect. Under the emperors trial passed to the emperor, the Senate, the prefects and the governors, and penalties followed rank, honestiores against humiliores (module 7.4). Callistratus ranks the capital penalties: the fork, Justinian's word for the cross, then burning alive, then beheading; below them the mines and deportation (Digest 48.19.28 pr.).

The worst penalties were meant to be seen. The Tables burned the arsonist (Gaius, Digest 47.9.9) and threw the false witness from the Tarpeian Rock (Gellius 20.1.53). The parricide was flogged, sewn into a sack and thrown into water; the Livian epitome makes the matricide Publicius Malleolus the first, in 101 (Periochae 68). Cicero praised the ancestors for denying him sky, sea and earth (Pro Roscio Amerino 70–72). Modestinus adds a dog, a cock, a viper and an ape, and Hadrian's rule sending him to the beasts where there is no sea (Digest 48.9.9 pr.); Constantine revived the sack (Theodosian Code 9.15.1).

Where sources disagree. Cicero and the Rhetorica ad Herennium (1.23) know no animals; Juvenal has the ape and the snake (8.213–214), and Mommsen (Römisches Strafrecht, 1899) doubted that the ape was ancient. J. D. Cloud (1971) argued that Pompey's law on parricide (Marcian, Digest 48.9.1) replaced the sack with interdiction, so that the imperial sack was a revival; Richard Bauman (Crime and Punishment in Ancient Rome, 1996) warned against assuming that Pompey changed the penalty at all.

Crucifixion was the slave's penalty, servile supplicium in Tacitus' phrase (Histories 4.11), and the bandit's. Cicero calls it the cruellest and foulest (Verrines 2.5.165); module 5.3 has Verres' crucified citizen and Spartacus' men. A heel bone pierced by a nail, found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem in 1968, is the clearest physical trace. Aurelius Victor says Constantine abolished the old penalty of the gibbet and leg-breaking (Caesares 41.4). Condemnation to the beasts or to a gladiatorial school delivered the criminal to the games (module 9.4): at Carthage in 203 the procurator Hilarianus condemned Perpetua and her companions to the beasts (Passion of Perpetua 6).

From the jurists to the codes

After the Severans the emperor, whose pleasure had the force of law (modules 7.2, 7.4), made new law by rescript, and private compilers gathered the rescripts in the Gregorian and Hermogenian codes of the 290s (module 8.2). The Law of Citations of 426 settled juristic authority by count: Papinian, Paul, Gaius, Ulpian and Modestinus were authoritative, the majority prevailed, and in a tie Papinian (Theodosian Code 1.4.3).

Theodosius II ordered a code of general laws from Constantine onwards in 429 (1.1.5). The Theodosian Code was promulgated on 15 February 438, valid from 1 January 439, and adopted in the West; its sixteen books arrange dated excerpts by subject, which is why the laws of modules 8.3 and 8.4 can be dated. The West knew it chiefly through the Visigothic Breviary of Alaric (506), issued with an abridged Gaius.

Module 8.6 outlines Justinian's compilation; its method matters here. Deo auctore (530) empowered Tribonian to cut and alter. Tanta (533) reports nearly two thousand books and over three million lines reduced to some 150,000 (Tanta 1). By the modern count the Digest holds about 9,000 extracts from thirty-nine jurists, Ulpian supplying over a third; each names author, work and book, which let Lenel reassemble the lost works (Palingenesia iuris civilis, 1889). Friedrich Bluhme showed in 1820 that the extracts in each title fall into three blocks, Sabinian, edictal and Papinianist, as if three subcommittees had read in parallel. The Code's twelve books ran from Hadrian to Justinian himself, and the Novels kept changing the law: Novel 118 (543) based intestate succession on blood kinship and ended the agnates' priority.

Where sources disagree. Tribonian was licensed to alter, but how much did he change? Otto Gradenwitz (Interpolationen in den Pandekten, 1887) and Gerhard Beseler made the hunt for interpolations the main business of Romanists, catalogued in the Index interpolationum (1929–1935). Franz Wieacker (Textstufen klassischer Juristen, 1960) moved many changes to editions made before Justinian, and since Max Kaser most scholars judge the compilers' interventions fewer and lighter than once supposed.

Bologna and the civil-law world

The Digest nearly vanished in the West: it is not cited between Gregory the Great and a lawsuit at Marturi in Tuscany in 1076. At Bologna, early in the twelfth century, Irnerius taught it word by word with glosses; Accursius' Glossa ordinaria, of the first half of the thirteenth century, fixed the commentary, and Bartolus of Sassoferrato in the fourteenth fitted it to the statutes of Italian cities. With canon law it formed the ius commune taught in the universities of Latin Europe. The German imperial chamber court applied Roman law from 1495, and the Pandectists built it into the German Civil Code of 1900. The French Civil Code of 1804 follows the Institutes' order of persons, property and modes of acquiring. Through conquest and borrowing, from Chile in 1855 to Japan in the 1890s, these codes made the civil-law world; Scotland and South Africa mix Roman with common law.

Where sources disagree. Odofredus, teaching at Bologna in the thirteenth century, says a certain Pepo first lectured on the laws but won no name, and calls Irnerius the lamp of the law. Burchard of Ursperg's chronicle says Irnerius renewed the neglected law books at the request of Countess Matilda of Tuscany. Charles Radding (The Origins of Medieval Jurisprudence, 1988) traced the new method further back, to the Lombard lawyers of Pavia.

Self-test

  1. Distinguish ius, fas and mos, and give one example of their overlap.
    Answer

    Ius is enforceable human law, "the art of the good and the fair" (Celsus in Digest 1.1.1 pr.); fas is what the gods allow (Isidore, Etymologies 5.2.2); mos is ancestral custom. The dies fasti and nefasti decided when the praetor might speak the words of jurisdiction (Varro, On the Latin Language 6.29–30), and a father's lawful power to kill a son was hedged by the custom of a family council.

  2. Why did publishing the Twelve Tables not end the pontiffs' control of law?
    Answer

    The Tables gave rules, but interpretation and the set forms of action stayed with the pontiffs (Pomponius, Digest 1.2.2.6), and a wrong word lost the case, as with the vines and trees (Gaius 4.11). The monopoly broke with Flavius' publication in 304, Coruncanius' public teaching and Sextus Aelius' Tripertita.

  3. How could a praetor change the law without legislating?
    Answer

    Through his annual edict he granted or refused actions, creating praetorian law "to aid, supplement or correct" the civil law (Papinian, Digest 1.1.7.1): estates for blood kin, Aquillius Gallus' formulas against deceit, assessed damages for insult in place of the Tables' fixed fine.

  4. Describe the formulary procedure and say what replaced it.
    Answer

    Before the praetor the parties agreed a written formula instructing a private judge, who heard the proof and condemned in money or absolved (Gaius 4.39–43, 4.48). It replaced the legis actiones under the Aebutian and Julian laws (4.30) and gave way to cognitio by imperial officials; a law of 342 abolished it.

  5. Why is the Verona palimpsest so important?
    Answer

    It preserves Gaius' Institutes of about 161, the only classical textbook to survive, unrevised by Justinian's compilers and including procedure. Niebuhr found it under Jerome's letters in 1816, Savigny identified it, and Göschen published it in 1820.

  6. What is Gaius' scheme of the law, and why has it mattered beyond Rome?
    Answer

    All law concerns persons, things or actions (1.8). Justinian's Institutes adopted it, and through them it shaped modern codes: the French Civil Code of 1804 is arranged by persons, property and modes of acquiring.

  7. Name the formal modes of manumission and the Augustan limits on them.
    Answer

    By the rod, by the census and by will (Gaius 1.17). The lex Fufia Caninia of 2 BC scaled freedom by will, never above a hundred slaves (1.42–46); the lex Aelia Sentia of AD 4 required an owner of twenty and a slave of thirty without a council's approval, voided frauds on creditors and created the dediticii. The informally freed were Junian Latins, who died as slaves (3.56).

  8. How did status shape criminal punishment, and what were the aggravated death penalties?
    Answer

    Republican citizens could escape into exile (Polybius 6.14.7); under the emperors penalties followed rank, honestiores against humiliores. Callistratus ranks the cross, burning alive and beheading (Digest 48.19.28 pr.); the parricide was sewn into the sack (Modestinus, 48.9.9 pr.), slaves and bandits were crucified, and the condemned were given to the beasts.

  9. How did the Theodosian Code differ from Justinian's Digest, and how did each reach the medieval West?
    Answer

    The Theodosian Code (438) collected imperial laws from Constantine onwards in sixteen books and reached the West mainly through the Breviary of Alaric (506). The Digest (533) excerpted the classical jurists; it nearly vanished in the West, reappearing at Marturi in 1076 and in Irnerius' teaching at Bologna.

  10. Why must the Digest be read with care as evidence for classical law, and how has the view changed?
    Answer

    Deo auctore licensed Tribonian to cut and alter, so a text may be his rather than its named author's. Gradenwitz and Beseler found interpolations everywhere; Wieacker moved many changes to earlier editions, and since Kaser most scholars think the compilers changed less than once supposed.

Carry forward

  1. Roman law grew less by statute than by interpretation and remedy: pontiffs, praetors and jurists made new law out of old forms and annual edicts, so the first question about any rule is who had the power to interpret it.
  2. Law was the grammar of status: freedom, citizenship and family defined the person, and rank fixed the penalty. Devices such as adoption, the triple sale, the Junian Latins and the grades of Latin right were instruments of social policy.
  3. Roman law survived as text, not as institution: what reached later Europe was what Theodosius' and Justinian's commissioners chose and altered, read at Bologna and recast in the modern civil codes, so every "Roman" rule has passed through a compiler's hands.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Roman law from the Twelve Tables to Justinian. Cover: ius, fas and mos; the Twelve Tables and the pontiffs' interpretation; the praetor's edict and the formulary system; the classical jurists (Quintus Mucius Scaevola, Labeo, Gaius, Papinian, Ulpian, Paul), and Gaius' Institutes as the one classical textbook to survive, found in a Verona palimpsest in 1816; persons, things and actions; paternal power, slavery and manumission in law; citizenship and its grades; criminal law and its brutal penalties (the sack for parricide, crucifixion, condemnation to the arena); the Theodosian Code of 438 and Justinian's Corpus of Civil Law (Code, Digest, Institutes, Novels); and the revival at Bologna and the civil-law world that descends from it. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 9 · Law, army and daily life · 9.2 · 2,872 words

The army

The citizen militia: census, levy and oathThe manipular legion and its disciplineMarius, the cohort and the end of the militiaThe standing army of the emperorsThe soldier's life: tablets and tombstonesEquipment and engineeringThe triumphThe late army: field and frontierThe army as political actorSelf-testCarry forward

The citizen militia: census, levy and oath

For most of the Republic Rome had no standing army. Each year the consuls raised legions from citizens who could arm themselves and dismissed them after the campaign. The census was in origin a military register; how Livy's five classes (1.43) grew from a single hoplite classis is module 1.5's question. Pay began, Livy says nearly four centuries later, at the siege of Veii in 406, funded by the citizens' war tax, tributum (4.59.11–4.60).

Polybius describes the levy he knew in the mid second century (6.19–21). Citizens rated above 400 drachmas owed ten campaigns in the cavalry or sixteen in the infantry before the age of forty-six; poorer men rowed (6.19). On the Capitol the tribunes chose men four at a time, tribe by tribe, matched in age and build (6.20). One man swore to obey his officers and each of the rest swore the same (6.21.1–3); Livy dates the first oath imposed by the tribunes to 216, before which there had been only an oath to muster and a voluntary pledge not to flee (22.38.1–5). The youngest and poorest became light-armed velites, then came the hastati, the principes and the oldest, the triarii (6.21.7–8). A foot-soldier drew two obols a day, a centurion twice as much, a cavalryman a drachma, less food, clothing and arms (6.39.12–15), until Gaius Gracchus made clothing free in 123 (Plutarch, Gaius Gracchus 5.1). Allies raised on the formula of module 3.4 marched beside each legion. The army was the citizen body under arms, graded by age and property and paid little more than its keep.

The manipular legion and its discipline

Module 3.4 sets the manipular legion against the hoplite phalanx and asks where it came from; module 4.5 reads Polybius' camp, punishments and rewards as his case for Roman success. Polybius' legion had 4,200 infantry, 5,000 in a crisis, and 300 cavalry (6.20.8–9): 1,200 each of velites, hastati and principes, and 600 triarii (6.21.9). Each heavy line formed ten maniples with two centurions apiece (6.24). The velites carried a sword, javelins and a round shield (6.22); the hastati and principes the curved oblong scutum, the Spanish sword, two pila, a plumed bronze helmet and a breastplate a span square, or mail if rated above 10,000 drachmas (6.23); the triarii thrusting spears. Centurions were chosen for steadiness rather than daring, men who would hold their ground and die at their post (6.24.9).

Each night the watchword went round the camp on a wooden tablet (tessera) and returned to the tribune (6.34); the sentry who failed and the unit that fled met the cudgel and the decimation that module 4.5 records. Decimation was rarer than Polybius' manual implies. Livy, writing more than four centuries after the event, gives a first case to Appius Claudius in 471 (2.59.11); Crassus revived it (module 5.3); Octavian decimated a cohort that gave way in Dalmatia and fed the survivors barley (Appian, Illyrian Wars 26; Dio 49.38), as Suetonius says he did with any cohort that yielded (Augustus 24.2); and Tacitus calls Lucius Apronius' decimation of a fleeing cohort in AD 20 rare in that age and a thing of old memory (Annals 3.21.1).

Rewards became a graded system. Gellius lists the crowns (5.6): the civic crown of oak leaves for saving a citizen's life; the mural and camp crowns for the first over a wall or rampart; and the grass crown, given by a rescued army to its rescuer, which Pliny says very few ever won (Natural History 22.6–13). Under the emperors decorations followed rank, as Valerie Maxfield showed (The Military Decorations of the Roman Army, 1981): torques, armlets and discs (phalerae) for the lower ranks, crowns and spears for officers. The centurion Marcus Caelius wears crown, torques, armlets and phalerae on his cenotaph (module 6.4).

Marius, the cohort and the end of the militia

Module 5.2 unpacks the "Marian reforms" and the modern doubt that Marius changed recruitment much. Wars in Spain kept men under arms for years, the property threshold sank, and an annual militia turned by degrees into a long-service army. The cohort, three maniples (one from each heavy line) with their light troops, is already named by Polybius at Ilipa in 206 (11.23.1); by Caesar's day it was the tactical unit, ten to a legion, and under the empire it held six centuries of eighty (Pseudo-Hyginus, On the Fortification of Camps). The velites vanished, their work passing to non-citizen specialists: Numidian horse, Balearic slingers, Cretan archers. Hastatus, princeps and pilus survived as the titles of each cohort's six centurions, ranked up to the primus pilus, senior centurion of the first cohort. That cohort grew larger than the rest. Vegetius' figure of 1,105 infantry (2.6) stands alone, but discharge lists and the fortress at Inchtuthil in Scotland, where the first cohort had ten barracks against six for each of the others, show it at about double strength by the late first century AD (David Breeze, "The Organisation of the Legion: the First Cohort and the Equites Legionis", Journal of Roman Studies 1969).

Where sources disagree. Mommsen's picture, long the standard one, was of legions filled by volunteers from Marius onwards. P. A. Brunt ("Conscription and Volunteering in the Roman Imperial Army", 1974) answered from levies attested in Italy and the provinces that conscription stayed far more common in the early Principate, and that volunteering prevailed only once legions recruited locally in the second century. Tiberius himself complained that volunteers were few and mostly needy vagrants (Tacitus, Annals 4.4).

The standing army of the emperors

Module 6.4 sets out the Augustan terms: twenty-five legions in AD 23, sixteen and then twenty years' service, 225 denarii a year, 12,000 sesterces on discharge. Domitian added a fourth instalment to the three, taking pay to 300 denarii, and after Saturninus' revolt in Upper Germany, which the savings banked with two legions had encouraged, capped any soldier's deposit at the standards at 1,000 sesterces (Suetonius, Domitian 7.3); Severus and Caracalla raised pay again (module 7.4). A papyrus of AD 81 (P.Gen.Lat. 1) shows two legionaries in Egypt, one of them Quintus Julius Proculus of Damascus, charged against each instalment for hay, food, boots and straps, the camp Saturnalia, clothing and the standards, with the balance banked.

A senatorial legate commanded the legion, with a senatorial tribune, five equestrian tribunes and a camp prefect risen from the centurionate. Its sixty centurions were the professionals, and a primus pilus could reach equestrian rank. Giovanni Forni (Il reclutamento delle legioni da Augusto a Diocleziano, 1953) showed from tombstones and discharge lists that Italians dominated the legions under Augustus and were rare by the second century, when legions recruited in their own provinces and many recruits gave their birthplace as "the camp" (castris): soldiers' sons.

The auxiliaries were non-citizen provincials in cavalry alae, infantry cohorts and mixed cohorts, nominally 500 or 1,000 strong, under equestrian prefects, many raised as ethnic units, such as Batavians and Tungrians, that kept their names after recruiting locally. After twenty-five years' service, the term the diplomas name, the reward was regular from Claudius onwards: citizenship for the veteran and his children and lawful marriage (conubium) with one wife, granted by an imperial constitution posted at Rome. The veteran could obtain, probably at his own cost, a certified copy on two bronze tablets sealed by seven witnesses: the military diploma. The earliest surviving diploma dates from 52; around 140, on the usual reading, children born during service ceased to be covered; the last auxiliary diploma dates from 203, nine years before universal citizenship (module 7.4). After 212 the legal line between legion and auxiliary unit lost its meaning, though the units kept their old names.

The soldier's life: tablets and tombstones

Module 7.5 uses the Vindolanda tablets to show the army running a province. The same archive shows life inside the fort. Flavius Cerialis, prefect of the Ninth Cohort of Batavians about 100, kept his letters at the fort. Claudia Severa, wife of a neighbouring commander, invited his wife Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday and added a greeting in her own hand, among the earliest Latin known to be written by a woman (Tab. Vindol. II 291). The decurion Masclus asked Cerialis for the next day's orders and added that his fellow-soldiers had no beer (III 628); socks, sandals and underpants were sent to a soldier (II 346); men applied to the prefect for leave. Officers' families lived in the fort, but soldiers could not marry lawfully while serving: Dio says Claudius gave them the privileges of married men because the law denied them wives (60.24.3).

Tombstones follow a formula: name, voting tribe, home, unit, rank, age, years of service and heir. At Colchester the centurion Marcus Favonius Facilis stands in armour holding his vine stick (RIB 200), and Longinus Sdapeze, a double-pay trooper from Sardica, rides down a naked barbarian (RIB 201); at Hexham Flavinus, standard-bearer of the ala Petriana, died at twenty-five after seven years' service (RIB 1172). The vine stick was used: in the mutiny of AD 14 the soldiers killed a centurion nicknamed "Bring another" for the sticks he broke on their backs (Tacitus, Annals 1.23). Josephus, who had fought the legions in Galilee, called their drills bloodless battles and their battles bloody drills (Jewish War 3.75), and Hadrian's address to the army of Numidia at Lambaesis in 128, cut in stone, praises unit after unit (ILS 2487).

Equipment and engineering

Equipment is known mainly from finds, sorted by modern typologies named after find-spots: Montefortino and Coolus helmets in the Republic, Imperial Gallic and Italic types later, Mainz and Pompeii types of short sword. The segmented iron cuirass, a modern name (lorica segmentata), appears at Kalkriese, probably the Varian battlefield of AD 9 (module 6.4), and is best known from a chest found at Corbridge in 1964; mail and scale were worn throughout and outlasted it. Hobnailed boots (caligae) gave Gaius, dressed as a little soldier in the Rhine camps, his nickname Caligula (Suetonius, Gaius 9). By the later third century the long spatha and an oval shield had replaced the short sword and scutum.

Where sources disagree. Conrad Cichorius, who published the reliefs of Trajan's Column in 1896–1900, and many readers after him took the frieze literally, so its division of legionaries in segmented cuirasses from auxiliaries in mail shaped reconstructions for a century. J. C. Coulston ("The Value of Trajan's Column as a Source for Military Equipment", 1989) argued that the division is a sculptors' device for marking citizens off from auxiliaries, and that the Column is no independent source for equipment.

The army was also Rome's largest body of builders. A marching army ditched and ramparted its camp every night, a city of streets, gates and headquarters in Josephus' description (Jewish War 3.76–84). Caesar bridged the Rhine in ten days (Gallic War 4.17–18) and at Alesia ran lines of eleven and fourteen miles, by his own figures (7.69, 7.74); the ramp against Masada still stands (Josephus, Jewish War 7.304–307). In peace soldiers built roads, forts and walls (module 7.5), and Corbulo set his men to dig a canal from the Rhine to the Meuse against idleness (Tacitus, Annals 11.20).

The triumph

Module 1.2 holds the dispute over the triumph's origins, module 4.4 counts the cash it displayed, and module 6.4 shows Augustus confining it to his own house after 19 BC. A general with imperium asked the Senate for a triumph and waited outside the city boundary, since crossing it ended his command. He entered by the Triumphal Gate and went by the Circus Flaminius and the Circus Maximus, round the Palatine and along the Sacred Way to the Capitol, behind spoils, captives and sacrificial oxen. He rode a four-horse chariot in the gold-embroidered purple toga, painted red with cinnabar as the face of Jupiter's statue was on festivals (Pliny, Natural History 33.111–112, citing Verrius). A slave held a crown over his head (Zonaras 7.21, from Dio) and, in Tertullian's version, told him to look behind him and remember he was a man (Apology 33.4); an amulet under the chariot warded off envy (Pliny 28.39), and the soldiers sang abuse of their general (Suetonius, Julius 49.4, 51). On the Capitol he sacrificed to Jupiter Best and Greatest, while enemy leaders were put to death, as Simon bar Giora was in the triumph of Vespasian and Titus in 71, which Josephus watched (Jewish War 7.123–157) and the Arch of Titus records (modules 7.2 and 9.5). A lesser victory earned an ovation, with a myrtle crown and no chariot (Gellius 5.6.20–23; Plutarch, Marcellus 22).

Where sources disagree. Valerius Maximus says a law required at least 5,000 enemy killed in one battle before a triumph could be granted, and sets out further conditions in the same chapter (2.8.1). Mary Beard (The Roman Triumph, 2007) treats such rules as fragile and changing, arguments deployed in particular Senate debates rather than a code applied, and finds only the general's wait outside the city consistently observed.

The late army: field and frontier

Module 8.1 saw Gallienus build up mobile cavalry, and module 8.2 sets Lactantius' fourfold army against John the Lydian's 389,704 and notes that the formal division of troops is usually credited to Constantine. The division made two armies of different status. Field armies (comitatenses, from the emperor's comitatus), with an elite of palatini, marched with an emperor or a regional commander; frontier troops (limitanei or ripenses) served under the duces of frontier provinces, with lower pay and fewer privileges. Constantine disbanded the praetorians after the Milvian Bridge (Aurelius Victor 40.25; Zosimus 2.17), let guard regiments, the scholae palatinae, take their place, and gave military command to masters of infantry and cavalry (Zosimus 2.33). Zosimus accused him of stripping the frontiers to quarter soldiers in cities where theatres softened them (2.34).

Units shrank: legions far smaller than the old stood beside new infantry regiments (auxilia palatina) and armoured cataphracts, whom Ammianus took for polished statues (16.10.8). State factories (fabricae), listed in the Notitia Dignitatum of about 400, made the arms. Soldiers' sons were bound to serve and landowners supplied recruits or gold; some men cut off their thumbs to escape, which no Gaul, Ammianus says, ever did (15.12.3). Barbarians served as recruits, as settlers (laeti) and, after 382, as whole peoples under their own leaders (module 8.4). Vegetius, about 400, set a lost ancient legion against an infantry that had given up helmet and cuirass since Gratian (1.20). The picture of the limitanei as a hereditary peasant militia rests chiefly on the Historia Augusta's claim that Severus Alexander gave frontier soldiers land on condition that their heirs served (Severus Alexander 58.4); Benjamin Isaac ("The Meaning of the Terms Limes and Limitanei", Journal of Roman Studies 1988) argued that the word meant simply the troops under a frontier dux.

Where sources disagree. Agathias, writing in the 570s, says the army had once numbered 645,000 and in his own day had shrunk to 150,000 (5.13.7–8). A. H. M. Jones (The Later Roman Empire, 1964) reached a similar total of about 600,000 by giving each unit in the Notitia an estimated strength. Richard Duncan-Jones (Structure and Scale in the Roman Economy, 1990), working from pay orders sent to units in the Thebaid in 298–300, judged Jones's unit strengths too high, which would cut the total sharply.

The army as political actor

The army entered politics through its oath and its pay. The Republican oath bound soldiers to a consul for a campaign; once commands lasted years and land on discharge depended on the general, the tie became personal. Sulla's march of 88 set the precedent (module 5.2); deep dive module 11.2 follows generals and armies from Marius to Octavian. Augustus made himself the only general. Soldiers swore to the emperor, renewed the oath each 1 January (Tacitus, Histories 1.55) and on the anniversary of his accession (Pliny, Letters 10.52), and carried his image among the standards. In AD 41 the guard made Claudius emperor for a donative (module 7.1), and in 69 the provincial armies showed that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome (Tacitus, Histories 1.4; module 7.2). The great provincial armies were the electors; the praetorians could kill and sell (module 7.4) but not hold the throne against them.

The third century put soldiers in command as well. Severus gave his new Parthian legions equestrian prefects (module 7.4), and Aurelius Victor says Gallienus barred senators from military commands by edict (33.34). The inscriptions show a slower change: senatorial legates and tribunes of legions thin out through the century and are last attested in the 260s, replaced by equestrian prefects, many risen from the ranks, the Danubian officers who gave the empire its rulers from Claudius II to Diocletian (module 8.1). Constantine's masters of the soldiers separated military from civil careers, and in the fifth century those masters made and unmade western emperors (module 8.5).

Self-test

  1. How did Polybius' levy assign recruits to the four kinds of infantry, and what does the arrangement tell you about the Republican army?
    Answer

    By age and wealth: the youngest and poorest became velites, then hastati and principes, and the oldest triarii (6.21.7–8). It was a citizen militia graded like the census, armed largely at its own cost and paid little more than its keep (6.39.12–15).

  2. Why does Tacitus' comment on Apronius qualify Polybius' account of decimation?
    Answer

    Polybius describes decimation as a standing penalty for units that fled, but Tacitus calls Apronius' decimation of AD 20 rare in that age and a thing of old memory (Annals 3.21.1). The recorded cases (Appius Claudius in 471, Crassus, Octavian in Dalmatia) are few and scattered.

  3. What was a cohort, and why can it not be credited to Marius?
    Answer

    Three maniples, one from each heavy line, with their light troops; under the empire, six centuries of eighty. Polybius already names it at Ilipa in 206 (11.23.1), and it replaced the manipular order gradually as the militia became a long-service army; no ancient source credits Marius with it (module 5.2).

  4. On what grounds did Brunt challenge the picture of a volunteer army from Marius onwards?
    Answer

    He gathered levies in Italy and the provinces and Tiberius' complaint that volunteers were few and mostly needy vagrants (Tacitus, Annals 4.4), and argued that conscription stayed common in the early Principate, with volunteering prevailing only once legions recruited locally in the second century.

  5. What did a military diploma grant, to whom, and how did the grant change?
    Answer

    It was a veteran's certified bronze copy of an imperial constitution giving an auxiliary, after twenty-five years, citizenship for himself and his children and lawful marriage with one wife. The earliest dates from 52; around 140 children born in service ceased to be covered; the last auxiliary diploma dates from 203, nine years before the edict of 212.

  6. What do the Vindolanda tablets of Flavius Cerialis add to the picture module 7.5 draws from the same site?
    Answer

    Life inside the fort rather than the army as government: Claudia Severa's birthday invitation with its greeting in her own hand (Tab. Vindol. II 291), Masclus asking for orders and beer (III 628), a parcel of socks, sandals and underpants (II 346), and leave requests. Officers' families lived in the fort though soldiers could not marry lawfully (Dio 60.24.3).

  7. Why does Coulston refuse to use Trajan's Column as evidence for legionary and auxiliary equipment?
    Answer

    He argued that the split between legionaries in segmented armour and auxiliaries in mail is a sculptural device marking citizens off from auxiliaries, not a record of what was issued (1989). He thus rejected the literal reading that goes back to Cichorius.

  8. Describe the triumphator's appearance and the warnings built into the ritual, and say what Beard doubts about its rules.
    Answer

    He rode a four-horse chariot in the gold-embroidered purple toga, painted red like Jupiter's statue (Pliny, Natural History 33.111–112), with a slave holding a crown over him and reminding him he was mortal (Tertullian, Apology 33.4), an amulet against envy and soldiers singing abuse. Beard (2007) treats conditions such as Valerius Maximus' 5,000 dead (2.8.1) as changing arguments rather than a fixed code.

  9. How did comitatenses and limitanei differ, and why does Isaac reject the idea that limitanei were a peasant militia?
    Answer

    Comitatenses were field troops with an emperor or regional commander, with the palatini as their elite; limitanei served under frontier duces with lower pay and privileges. The peasant-militia idea rests chiefly on Historia Augusta, Severus Alexander 58.4; Isaac (1988) argued the word meant simply troops under a frontier dux.

  10. How did the soldiers' oath bind the army to the emperor, and how did the third century change who commanded the legions?
    Answer

    Soldiers swore to the emperor, renewed the oath each 1 January (Tacitus, Histories 1.55) and on his accession day (Pliny, Letters 10.52), and carried his image among the standards. In the third century equestrian prefects, many from the ranks, replaced senatorial legates, more gradually than Aurelius Victor's edict of Gallienus (33.34) implies, and Danubian officers became the emperors (module 8.1).

Carry forward

  1. Rome's army changed by degrees from an annual citizen militia graded by the census into a long-service professional force paid by the state; whoever paid, settled and commanded the soldiers held their loyalty, which is why the army became a political actor from Sulla to the soldier emperors.
  2. The army and citizenship were bound together: service was a citizen's duty under the Republic and auxiliary service the road to citizenship under the emperors; after 212 the late army drew on soldiers' sons, conscripted peasants and barbarians, so changes in who served are changes in who counted as Roman.
  3. Normative texts (Polybius' manual, Vegetius' lost ancient legion, Valerius Maximus' rules of the triumph, Trajan's Column) describe an ideal; documents and finds (Vindolanda, papyri, diplomas, tombstones, Inchtuthil, Corbridge) show practice, and each should be read against the other.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the Roman army from the manipular legion to the late empire. Cover: the citizen militia and the census classes; the manipular legion in Polybius book 6 (hastati, principes, triarii, velites), extending module 3.4's outline of it against the phalanx, the camp, decimation and the rewards for valour; the changes associated with Marius and the cohort legion; the Augustan professional army (module 6.4 gives its establishment: point back), pay, length of service, the auxiliaries and citizenship on discharge (the military diplomas); the soldier's life from the Vindolanda tablets and tombstones; equipment and engineering; the triumph as ritual; the late army of field and frontier troops; and the army as a political actor from Sulla to the soldier emperors. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 9 · Law, army and daily life · 9.3 · 2,848 words

Family, women and slaves

Familia and paterfamiliasMarriage, manus, dowry and divorceAge at marriage and the shape of the familyWomen: law, practice and the Laudatio TuriaeChildhood, nurses and schoolsSlavery: numbers, sources and workManumission and the freedmenHow the study of the Roman family changedSelf-testCarry forward

Familia and paterfamilias

The Latin familia is not the English family. Ulpian lists its senses (Digest 50.16.195): a man's property; his slaves; everyone in one man's power; and all agnates, kin through males. The people under one roof, kin and slaves together, were the domus. Richard Saller ("Pater familias, mater familias, and the gendered semantics of the Roman household", Classical Philology 1999) showed that paterfamilias usually meant a property owner, and Ulpian counts a childless man, even a boy, as one (50.16.195.2). Module 2.4 gives his household priesthood; this module gives his law.

On paper it was extreme. Gaius calls paternal power, patria potestas, peculiar to Romans (Institutes 1.55). It lasted until the father died, whatever the son's age or office. A son in power owned nothing beyond a peculium held at his father's pleasure, as a slave's was; the father made and unmade his marriage and held the power of life and death. The Twelve Tables, as Gaius reports them (1.132), freed a son sold three times, and lawyers turned the rule into emancipation by fictitious sale.

The limits were real. Fathers who killed grown sons were remembered because they were rare, and the famous cases mix paternal with public authority: Brutus and Manlius Torquatus acted as consuls (Livy 2.5, 8.7), while the senator Fulvius, who had his son killed for setting out to join Catiline, acted as father (Sallust, Catiline 39.5). Custom expected a council of kin: Tarius, finding his son plotting against him, called one that included Augustus, and the son was exiled (Seneca, On Mercy 1.15). Hadrian deported a man who killed his son on a hunt, since paternal power should rest on devotion, not cruelty (Marcian, Digest 48.9.5). Death limited it most: most men had lost their fathers before they married.

Where sources disagree. Dionysius (Roman Antiquities 2.26–27) has Romulus give fathers lifelong power harsher than any Greek law. Saller ("Patria potestas and the stereotype of the Roman family", Continuity and Change 1986; Patriarchy, Property and Death in the Roman Family, 1994) called this a stereotype: Romans saw pietas as owed by fathers too, the power of life and death was almost never used, and his simulations leave few adult sons with living fathers.

Marriage, manus, dowry and divorce

Marriage needed no priest or document: it was the cohabitation of two people with conubium, the capacity to marry each other, who meant to be married. Consent, not intercourse, makes a marriage (Ulpian, Digest 50.17.30). A bride had to be twelve (Digest 23.2.4); slave unions had no legal effect.

What mattered was manus. Module 2.4 gives its three forms (Gaius, Institutes 1.110–113). A wife in manus passed into her husband's power "in the place of a daughter" (1.111), and her property became his. A wife without manus stayed in her father's power or, after his death, was sui iuris under a guardian; her property stayed hers, and custom voided gifts between spouses (Digest 24.1.1). By the late Republic marriage without manus was normal. The paradox: a wife belonged to her father's family, not her husband's, and at her father's death became an owner of property in her own right.

The husband managed the dowry (dos) but owed it back when the marriage ended, and could not sell Italian dotal land without his wife's consent (Gaius 2.63); if a divorce was her fault he kept a sixth per child, up to half (Ulpian, Rules 6.10). Divorce needed only one party's will, or in the Republic her father's. It ended no careers: Sulla and Pompey each married five times. Yet epitaphs praised the univira, married once. The Augustan marriage laws are module 6.2; Constantine's curb on unilateral divorce is module 8.3.

Where sources disagree. Gellius, citing the jurist Servius Sulpicius, makes Spurius Carvilius Ruga's divorce of a barren wife, about 230 BC, Rome's first and the reason dowry contracts began (4.3.1–2); Dionysius (2.25.7) and Valerius Maximus (2.1.4) agree. Yet Valerius records a senator expelled by the censors of 307 for divorcing without consulting his friends (2.9.2). Carvilius' may have been the first divorce without fault by the wife.

Age at marriage and the shape of the family

Keith Hopkins ("The Age of Roman Girls at Marriage", Population Studies 1965), from literary cases and epitaphs giving a marriage's length, concluded that girls commonly married in their early teens; for senatorial daughters that holds. Brent Shaw ("The Age of Roman Girls at Marriage: Some Reconsiderations", Journal of Roman Studies 1987) and Saller ("Men's Age at Marriage and Its Consequences in the Roman Family", Classical Philology 1987) traced instead the age at which the commemorator on thousands of epitaphs changes from parent to spouse: the late teens for ordinary women in the western provinces, the late twenties or about thirty for men. Roger Bagnall and Bruce Frier found a similar gap in the census returns of Roman Egypt (The Demography of Roman Egypt, 1994).

Husbands were often ten years older than their wives and died first. Frier's model of the imperial population (Cambridge Ancient History XI, 2000) uses a life expectancy at birth of about twenty-five, pulled down by infant deaths. Many children lost a parent young; widows, stepmothers and half-siblings were common. The three-generation household under an aged patriarch was for most Romans brief or imaginary.

Where sources disagree. Hopkins' young brides rest largely on elite cases and on the few epitaphs that state a marriage's length; Shaw and Saller's later ages assume that a spouse took over commemoration from parents, and their stones come from families able to pay for them, mostly urban. How far ordinary practice differed from the elite's is still argued.

Women: law, practice and the Laudatio Turiae

A woman could not vote, hold office or sit on a jury, and after Gaia Afrania wearied the praetors the edict barred women from pleading for others (Valerius Maximus 8.3.2; Digest 3.1.1.5). A woman sui iuris needed a guardian's authority to make a will or sell land. The Voconian law of 169 BC, which the aged Cato spoke for (Cicero, On Old Age 14), stopped the richest citizens making a woman their heir (Gaius 2.274). Augustus freed freeborn mothers of three from guardianship (module 6.2); Claudius abolished agnates' guardianship of women (Gaius 1.157).

Practice ran ahead of law. Cicero mocks jurists for inventing guardians in women's power (Pro Murena 27), and Gaius found the usual ground, women's light-mindedness, more specious than true (1.190). Women married without manus held fortunes: at Pompeii Eumachia built a hall on the forum (CIL X 810), and Julia Felix advertised her baths and shops for rent (CIL IV 1136). In 195 BC women thronged the Forum until the Oppian law, a wartime limit on their gold and dress, was repealed against Cato's opposition (Livy 34.1–8). Cornelia (module 5.1) and Hortensia's speech of 42 BC (module 5.5) were remembered as exceptional; deep dive module 11.4 takes up the women of the late Republic.

The empire gave women a new power, nearness to the emperor. Livia (module 6.1) was adopted by Augustus' will as Julia Augusta (Tacitus, Annals 1.8); Agrippina the Younger listened behind a curtain when the Senate met in the palace (13.5; module 7.1); Julia Domna was mother of the camps (module 7.4). None held office; each was accused of ruling through men.

The so-called Laudatio Turiae (CIL VI 41062; ILS 8393) is a husband's speech for his dead wife, cut in marble at Rome late in the first century BC. She brought her murdered parents' killers to punishment and beat relatives who tried to break her father's will and take her and the estate into their guardianship. In the proscriptions she gave her husband her jewellery, hid him, and threw herself at Lepidus' feet to have his recall honoured, and was dragged away bruised. Childless, she offered to divorce him so that he could have children by another wife; he says the offer nearly drove him out of his mind. The marriage lasted some forty years, ended by death, not divorce, which he calls rare. She is praised for wool-work in the speech that shows her handling law, money and armed men.

Where sources disagree. The surviving text names neither partner. Valerius Maximus (6.7.2) tells how Turia hid her husband Quintus Lucretius Vespillo in the proscriptions, a story Appian tells without her name (4.44), and Mommsen made the identification standard. Nicholas Horsfall (1983) judged the speaker too remote from politics to be the consul of 19 BC, and Josiah Osgood (Turia: A Roman Woman's Civil War, 2014) treats the couple as unknown equestrians.

Childhood, nurses and schools

The naming day, bulla and toga of manhood are in module 2.4. Before them came the father's decision to rear. Exposure was lawful: Hilarion, working in Alexandria in 1 BC, tells his pregnant wife to keep a boy and expose a girl (P.Oxy. 4.744), and Pliny asked Trajan about the status of foundlings reared as slaves (Letters 10.65–66).

Where sources disagree. John Boswell (The Kindness of Strangers, 1988) argued that most exposed infants were taken up by others, so that exposure redistributed children more than it killed them. W. V. Harris ("Child-Exposure in the Roman Empire", Journal of Roman Studies 1994) held that it was common, that many foundlings died, and that survivors fed the slave supply.

Propertied children were suckled by slaves. Tacitus' Messalla complains that a newborn is handed to some Greek slave girl (Dialogue on Orators 29.1); Favorinus urges a mother to nurse her own child (Gellius 12.1). The bond could last: Pliny gave his nurse a farm worth 100,000 sesterces (Letters 6.3), and nurslings set up nurses' epitaphs. Keith Bradley ("Wet-nursing at Rome", 1986) saw childhoods spent among many carers.

Schooling was private and paid: letters from about seven with a ludi magister, a slave paedagogus as escort, then poetry and grammar with a grammaticus and, for the elite, declamation with a rhetor. Horace remembered his flogging master Orbilius (Epistles 2.1.70–71); Quintilian opposed beating (Institutio oratoria 1.3.14). Harris (Ancient Literacy, 1989) argued that most people never learned to read.

Slavery: numbers, sources and work

Moses Finley (Ancient Slavery and Modern Ideology, 1980) counted Roman Italy among the few genuine slave societies, with classical Athens, the Caribbean, Brazil and the American South. Numbers are guesswork: P. A. Brunt (Italian Manpower, 1971) put Augustan Italy's slaves at about three million of no more than seven and a half million people; Walter Scheidel ("Human Mobility in Roman Italy, II: The Slave Population", Journal of Roman Studies 2005) at no more than one and a half million, built by two to four million imports over the last two centuries BC.

War came first: the second-century captives are in module 4.4, and Plutarch has Caesar take a million prisoners in Gaul (Caesar 15). Children of slave mothers (vernae) were slaves; foundlings, pirates' victims, self-sellers and convicts added more; trade linked them all.

Where sources disagree. Scheidel ("Quantifying the Sources of Slaves in the Early Roman Empire", Journal of Roman Studies 1997) argued that under the empire most new slaves were born to slave mothers. Harris ("Demography, Geography and the Sources of Roman Slaves", Journal of Roman Studies 1999) doubted that slaves reproduced on that scale and gave more weight to exposed infants and imports across the frontiers.

Cato's slave estate is module 4.4. Varro classes slaves as speaking farm equipment, beside half-speaking oxen and mute carts (On Agriculture 1.17.1); Columella keeps chained gangs in the ergastulum, lit by windows too high to reach (1.6). Great houses kept hundreds: the burial chamber of Livia's household lists slaves and freedmen by job, from hairdressers to wardrobe keepers (Susan Treggiari, "Jobs in the Household of Livia", 1975). Slaves were also craftsmen, managers, secretaries and doctors, and imperial slaves kept the emperor's accounts (module 7.5). They were flogged, used sexually, sold apart from their children and tortured as witnesses. When a slave killed the city prefect Pedanius Secundus in AD 61, the Senate sent his whole household to execution, four hundred in the figure Tacitus gives the senator Cassius, over the plebs' protests (Annals 14.42–45). Seneca's plea that slaves are men and humble friends (Letters 47.1) asks for gentler mastery, not abolition.

The great revolts fell within seventy years. Eunus' Sicilian war from about 135 is in module 4.4. The second began in 104, when the Senate ruled that no free-born ally be a slave in a province: the governor freed some eight hundred, then stopped under the owners' pressure, and slaves under Salvius and Athenion fought until Manius Aquillius crushed them (Diodorus 36.3–10). Spartacus' war of 73–71 is module 5.3. Each drew on newly enslaved adults, often sharing a language and a past as fighters, working as armed herdsmen or trained as gladiators. Keith Bradley (Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World, 1989) tied the revolts to these conditions. Nothing on that scale followed: home-born slaves became a larger share, and manumission, which Bradley elsewhere read as an instrument of control (Slaves and Masters in the Roman Empire, 1984), offered the able a way out.

Manumission and the freedmen

A slave formally freed by a Roman citizen became a citizen. Philip V of Macedon, urging Larisa in 214 BC to enlarge its citizen body, cited the Romans, who enrolled freed slaves and admitted them to office (Syll.³ 543). The forms of manumission, the Junian Latins and Augustus' limits on manumission are module 9.1. Most of the freed were urban household slaves.

A freedman took his patron's first and family names: Cicero's secretary became Marcus Tullius Tiro. He owed respect (obsequium) and often agreed days of work (operae); he could not hold office at Rome, and Augustus forbade senators to marry freedwomen. His freeborn son was a full citizen: Horace, a freedman's son, became a military tribune and Maecenas' friend (Satires 1.6.45–48). In the towns rich freedmen joined the seviri Augustales, honour without office. They dominate the city's epitaphs, partly because, as Lily Ross Taylor showed ("Freedmen and Freeborn in the Epitaphs of Imperial Rome", 1961), they commemorated themselves more eagerly than the freeborn. Their reliefs show a couple's busts, the man togate, hands joined in the marriage slaves could not make; on the relief of the butcher Aurelius Hermia and his fellow freedwoman and wife Aurelia Philematium, she says he took her into his lap when she was seven (CIL VI 9499).

Petronius' Trimalchio is the type drawn by a probably senatorial pen. Brought from Asia as a boy and his master's favourite for fourteen years, he inherited, lost thirty million sesterces in shipwrecks in a day, won ten million in one voyage, then bought land and lent money (Satyricon 75–76); his planned epitaph boasts that he was a sevir, left thirty million and never heard a philosopher (71). Module 10.2 reads the novel as literature. Paul Veyne ("Vie de Trimalcion", 1961) and Finley (The Ancient Economy, 1973) took the career as typical: trade to make money, land to make it respectable, and no way into the elite.

Where sources disagree. John D'Arms (Commerce and Social Standing in Ancient Rome, 1981) answered Veyne and Finley that commerce carried less stigma, and senatorial money ran deeper in it through freedman agents, than the Trimalchio model allows. Whether Petronius drew a specimen or a snob's caricature cannot be settled from the novel.

How the study of the Roman family changed

For a century the Roman family was legal history, read from Gaius and the Digest. From the 1980s social historians turned to epitaphs, demography and letters; Beryl Rawson's The Family in Ancient Rome (1986) marked the shift. Susan Treggiari's Roman Marriage (1991) followed the institution from Cicero to Ulpian, law and sentiment together. Suzanne Dixon (The Roman Mother, 1988; The Roman Family, 1992) set ideals against practice. Bradley (Slaves and Masters in the Roman Empire, 1984; Discovering the Roman Family, 1991) put slaves, nurses and step-kin inside the household.

Where sources disagree. Saller and Shaw ("Tombstones and Roman Family Relations in the Principate", Journal of Roman Studies 1984) found that most epitaphs in the western provinces were set up within the nuclear family of parents, children and spouses, and concluded that it was the primary unit of obligation. Dale Martin ("The Construction of the Ancient Family", Journal of Roman Studies 1996) argued from the inscriptions of Asia Minor that their counting method inflated the nuclear share, and that the family is better seen as a continuum running out to wider kin, freedmen and slaves.

Against the Athenian household of Greek module 8.5, the Roman father's power outlasted his son's coming of age; a Roman woman without manus owned property under a guardianship grown formal, where the Athenian woman never left her kyrios; and the freed slave who at Athens became a metic became at Rome a citizen.

Self-test

  1. Why is paterfamilias not simply the Roman word for "father"?
    Answer

    It denotes a man in no one else's power, the owner of the estate and holder of power over its members; Ulpian counts a childless man, even a boy, as one (Digest 50.16.195.2), and Saller showed it usually meant an owner of property.

  2. What did patria potestas give a father in law, and what limited it in practice?
    Answer

    Lifelong power: a son in power owned nothing beyond a revocable peculium, and the father controlled his marriage and held power of life and death. Custom expected a council of kin (Seneca, On Mercy 1.15), emperors punished abuse (Hadrian, in Marcian, Digest 48.9.5), and mortality meant most men had lost their fathers by the time they married.

  3. How did marriage without manus differ from marriage with it, for the wife's property and family?
    Answer

    In manus she passed into her husband's power as if a daughter (Gaius 1.111) and her property became his. Without manus she stayed in her father's power or became sui iuris under a guardian, kept her property, and could not receive gifts from her husband (Digest 24.1.1).

  4. What happened to a dowry when a marriage ended, and why did it matter?
    Answer

    The husband had to return it, keeping a sixth for each child up to half if the divorce was the wife's fault (Ulpian, Rules 6.10); Augustus forbade him to sell Italian dotal land without her consent (Gaius 2.63). Return gave the wife's family leverage and made divorce costly.

  5. How did Shaw and Saller estimate age at marriage, and how did their results differ from Hopkins'?
    Answer

    They noted the age at which the commemorator on epitaphs changes from parent to spouse: late teens for women, late twenties or about thirty for men. Hopkins, from elite cases and epitaphs giving a marriage's length, had argued for brides in their early teens, which remains true of the senatorial class.

  6. Why does late male marriage matter for understanding paternal power?
    Answer

    With men marrying near thirty and life expectancy at birth around twenty-five in Frier's model, most men were free of paternal power by the time they married, so the lifelong patriarch of the law books governed few grown men; widows, stepmothers and half-siblings were common instead.

  7. What does the Laudatio Turiae show about women in law and practice?
    Answer

    A wife defends her inheritance in court against relatives claiming guardianship, protects and supplies her proscribed husband, pleads before Lepidus, and offers divorce so he can have children; she acts in law, property and politics while being praised for wool-work and modesty.

  8. What is the evidence for exposure of children, and what do Boswell and Harris disagree about?
    Answer

    Hilarion's letter telling his wife to expose a girl (P.Oxy. 4.744) and Pliny's query about foundlings raised as slaves (Letters 10.65–66). Boswell thought most exposed infants were taken up by others; Harris that exposure was common, many died, and survivors fed the slave supply.

  9. Why did the great slave revolts fall between about 135 and 71 BC and not recur?
    Answer

    They drew on masses of newly enslaved adults with shared language and fighting experience, working as armed herdsmen or gladiators. Later the slave population was more home-born and manumission offered the able a way out, as Bradley stressed.

  10. What made Roman manumission different from Greek, and what kind of freedman does Trimalchio represent?
    Answer

    A slave formally freed by a citizen became a citizen, as Philip V noted (Syll.³ 543), and his sons were freeborn. Trimalchio is the rich freedman who made money in trade, moved into land and lending, and held the Augustal priesthood, but could not enter the elite; D'Arms warned against taking the satire as typical.

Carry forward

  1. Roman family law describes powers, not lives: patria potestas, manus and guardianship were extreme on paper and limited by custom, by emperors and above all by death, so every legal rule must be read against who was alive to exercise it.
  2. Marriage without manus, easy divorce and the returnable dowry gave women of property a practical independence the law never declared, while office stayed closed to them; women's power ran through fathers, husbands and sons, and under the empire through nearness to the emperor.
  3. Slavery was a structure of the Roman household and economy, and manumission its outlet: it made freed slaves citizens and their sons freeborn, which kept the system stable after the war captives of the late Republic and made freedmen and their descendants a large, visible part of the urban population.
