Reading a site: Rome on foot

The CapitolineThe Forum, west endThe Forum, east end and the Sacred WayThe PalatineThe Imperial Fora, Trajan's Markets and the ColumnThe Colosseum and the Arch of ConstantineThe Circus Maximus, the Forum Boarium and Sant'OmobonoThe Campus MartiusThe Baths of Caracalla and the Palazzo MassimoWalking ordersSelf-testCarry forward

The Capitoline

Greek module 9.2 walks Athens from an Acropolis where everything standing belongs to one generation. Rome is stacked: archaic cult under republican paving under imperial marble under churches, and what stands is usually the last rebuilding. Each stop gives what is there, the module that owns it and one thing to look for; the story stays in the module.

The temple platform. The foundations of Jupiter Best and Greatest, shared with Juno and Minerva (module 2.2), lie inside the Capitoline Museums: cappellaccio tufa, about 54 by 62 metres (module 1.5). The temple burned in 69 and rose again from 70 (module 7.2); Procopius has Gaiseric ship off half its gilded roof in 455 (module 8.5). Look for the size of the blocks, then decide with module 1.5's dispute whether the whole platform carried the temple.

The Tabularium. The arcaded substructure of 78 BC under the Senator's Palace closes the Forum's west end; the museum's underground gallery runs through it to a view of the Forum. Look for the arch framed by engaged half-columns, a Greek order drawn on a structure of arches, which the Theatre of Marcellus and the Colosseum later stacked in storeys (module 10.3).

Where sources disagree. The name rests on a lost inscription in which Catulus, consul in 78, records building a substructure and a tabularium (CIL VI 1314), long read as the state record office. Nicholas Purcell (1993) argued that the inscriptions do not name the building; Pier Luigi Tucci (2005) took it for one record office among many, with the temple of Juno Moneta on top; Filippo Coarelli (2010) reads it as the foundations of a large Sullan temple. The arches are certain; the name is not.

The Capitoline Museums. In the Hall of the She-wolf the bronze wolf stands among the Fasti Capitolini set into the walls. The wolf is module 1.4's: cast in one pour, radiocarbon-dated to about 1021–1153, its twins added after 1471. The Fasti, the Augustan list of consuls and triumphs found in the Forum in 1546, are modules 0.1 and 0.3. Look for the head of the triumphal list, Romulus over the Caeninenses, a record no one could have kept: two objects in one room that dress legend as record. The original equestrian Marcus Aurelius stands in the glass hall over the temple foundations. It survived at the Lateran because it was taken for Constantine (module 10.4); the reign is module 7.3, and deep dive module 13.7 uses statue and column as sources for the man. Look for the extended right hand and the absence of any weapon.

The Forum, west end

The temple of Saturn. Eight columns on a high podium below the Capitol. It held the state treasury, and its image wore woollen bonds loosed at the Saturnalia (module 2.2, with the doubts over its foundation date); Caesar emptied the reserve treasury in 49 (module 5.4). Look for the frieze inscription, incendio consumptum restituit, "restored when consumed by fire": the columns are a late antique rebuilding.

The Rostra. The speakers' platform is named from the beaks of Antium's warships fixed to its predecessor in 338 (Livy 8.14.12; module 3.3). Before Caesar moved it here in 44 (Dio 43.49.1), the platform displayed Octavius' head in 87 (module 5.2); Cicero's head and hands followed in 43 (module 5.5). Look for the holes in its front where bronze beaks were fixed, and later compare its picture on the Arch of Constantine, where Constantine speaks from it (modules 8.3 and 10.3).

The Arch of Septimius Severus. Dedicated in 203 for restoring the state and extending the empire (module 7.4); its campaign panels are module 10.3's. Look for the fourth line of the inscription, recut after Geta's murder as "best and bravest princes", the dowel holes of the bronze letters still showing the lost name (module 7.4).

The Comitium and the Lapis Niger. Before the Curia a patch of black stone paving marks a spot the late Republic chose to keep. Beneath it Giacomo Boni found in 1899 an archaic altar, a column stump and the cippus of about 570–550 BC with a sacred law naming a rex (module 1.5). Module 0.1 weighs it as a source; module 1.4 gives the ancient guesses, Romulus' tomb or Faustulus', and Coarelli's Volcanal. Look for the paving itself: a marker laid some five centuries after the stone it covers, over a place Romans could no longer explain.

The Curia. The brick hall standing to its roof is Diocletian's rebuilding after a fire of 283 (module 8.2), saved by becoming a church in the seventh century. Its predecessor burned as Clodius' pyre in 52 (module 5.4; deep dive module 11.3), and it housed the altar of Victory that Symmachus defended in 384 (module 8.4). Look for the height: here you stand inside the Senate's room at full scale.

The basilicas. The Basilica Aemilia to the north and the Basilica Julia to the south are roofed halls of the type of Cato's Basilica Porcia of 184 (modules 4.5 and 10.3). Augustus lists the Julia, begun by Caesar, among the works he finished (Res Gestae 20.3). Look for the gaming boards scratched into the Julia's steps, and on the Aemilia's floor the stains of bronze coins melted in a fire usually laid to Alaric's sack of 410 (module 8.5).

The Forum, east end and the Sacred Way

The temple of the deified Julius. Octavian dedicated it in 29 where the crowd had burned Caesar's body, and decked its platform with prows from Actium (modules 5.5 and 6.2; the funeral is deep dive module 11.7's). Look for the curved niche in the podium's front, whose round core is usually taken for the altar on the site of the pyre.

The temple of Castor. Vowed at Lake Regillus and dedicated, Livy says nearly five centuries later, in 484 (module 1.6); the three standing columns belong to Tiberius' rebuilding (Suetonius, Tiberius 20). Look for Juturna's basin beside it, where the twins watered their horses after the battle (module 0.2): a myth kept by keeping a place.

The Regia. A small building traced by Frank Brown from the late seventh century to the later sixth, where a bucchero sherd reads rex (module 1.5); the spears of Mars and the October Horse are modules 2.1 and 2.3. Look for the irregular plan, kept through every rebuilding: a king's cult house, too small for a palace.

The temple of Vesta and the House of the Vestals. The round temple held the fire and no image. The Vestals and their living burial are module 2.3, Augustus' gift of the rex sacrorum's house to them module 6.2, their end module 8.4. Look, in the long court of their house, for the statue bases of the chief Vestals, among them the base of 364 whose Vestal's name has been chiselled out (CIL VI 32422); no source says why.

The Arch of Titus. Walk up the Sacred Way, the triumphal road (module 9.2), past the temple of Antoninus and Faustina (module 7.3), kept standing as a church. At the top stands the arch dedicated to the deified Titus (CIL VI 945): history in module 7.2, the triumph of 71 in module 9.2, the relief as art in module 10.3. Look for the spoils panel, the Temple's lampstand and table carried through a gate seen at an angle. Then read the masonry: Giuseppe Valadier rebuilt the missing parts in travertine in the early nineteenth century; the marble is ancient.

The Palatine

The Iron Age huts. On the Cermalus, the south-west corner, hut floors with post-holes and gutters are cut into the tufa beside the spot where Romans kept a hut of Romulus (Dionysius 1.79.11; module 1.4). Look for the ring of post-holes, and keep module 1.4's verdict: a village, not a founder. The Lupercal of 2007 is module 1.4's dispute.

The House of Augustus. Octavian lived in Hortensius' house, bought its neighbours and on ground struck by lightning vowed the temple of Apollo, dedicated in 28 beside them (module 6.2). The rooms Gianfilippo Carettoni excavated are painted in the Second style (module 10.3). Look at how small they are beside the temple platform, and test Suetonius' word "modest" (Augustus 72.1) against them.

Where sources disagree. Carettoni took the painted rooms for Augustus' house. Irene Iacopi and Giovanna Tedone argued that they were filled in after 36 BC for the Apollo complex, and Andrea Carandini reconstructed a grand residence wrapped round the temple. T. P. Wiseman (The House of Augustus, 2019) rejects the reconstruction, trusts the texts' modest house and places it under the later palace.

The House of Livia. A house of the same years, named from a lead pipe stamped with Julia Augusta, the name Livia took under Augustus' will (module 9.3; her politics, module 6.1). Look for the Second-style panel of Io guarded by Argus, with Mercury coming to free her.

The Flavian palace. Domitian's palace covers the hill's centre (module 7.2); its concrete halls lead towards the Pantheon (module 10.3), and Palatium gave the word palace (module 6.2). Look for the scale of the state rooms, with Statius' poem of thanks for a dinner there in mind (Silvae 4.2; module 10.2).

The Imperial Fora, Trajan's Markets and the Column

The Via dei Fori Imperiali follows Mussolini's Via dell'Impero, opened in 1932 over a demolished quarter (module 10.4).

The Forum of Caesar. Dedicated in 46 with the temple of Venus Genetrix, ancestress of the Julii (module 5.4). Look for the three re-erected columns of the temple at the head of the square.

The Forum of Augustus. The temple of Mars the Avenger, vowed at Philippi and dedicated in 2 BC, closed a square whose exedrae set Aeneas and the Julii opposite Romulus and the republican great men (module 6.2). The Temple of Peace nearby received the vessels of Jerusalem (module 7.2). Look for the exedrae and their tiers of statue niches: module 6.2's argument in stone.

Trajan's Column. Dedicated in 113, it carries both Dacian wars in its spiral frieze, and its base later received Trajan's ashes (module 7.3); module 9.2 weighs the frieze as evidence for the army, module 10.3 reads it as art. Look for the inscription over the door, which says the column shows how high the hill stood that was cut away for the forum (module 7.3). St Peter has stood on top since 1587.

Trajan's Markets. A brick hemicycle and terraces cut into the Quirinal slope behind the forum's north-eastern exedra, built with it: streets, a vaulted hall and rooms with shop-like doors. No written module describes it; the reign is module 7.3, the city's supply module 9.4. Look for the vaulted hall, and ask what the rooms were for.

Where sources disagree. Corrado Ricci, who cleared the complex in 1924–34, published it as Trajan's market ("Il mercato di Traiano", 1929), and the name stuck. The Museo dei Fori Imperiali there reads the rooms as offices and record stores of a multi-functional centre tied to the forum, perhaps used by the procurator of Trajan's forum. No ancient text names the building.

The Colosseum and the Arch of Constantine

The Colosseum. Begun by Vespasian on the drained lake of Nero's Golden House and dedicated by Titus in 80 (module 7.2, with Alföldy's reading of its lost bronze letters). The games and the flooding question are module 9.4's; the radial vaults and the Tuscan, Ionic and Corinthian storeys module 10.3's. Look for the hypogeum, the cages and lift shafts under the arena, usually dated to Domitian, that made it, in module 9.4's word, a machine.

The Arch of Constantine. Dedicated by the Senate in 315 for Constantine's tenth anniversary (module 8.3); the reused Trajanic, Hadrianic and Aurelian sculpture, the new frieze and the argument over decline are modules 8.3 and 10.3. Look for instinctu divinitatis in the attic inscription (CIL VI 1139): an unnamed divinity a pagan Senate could write and a Christian emperor accept.

Where sources disagree. A. L. Frothingham (1912) dated the arch's core as early as Domitian, and Maria Letizia Conforto (Adriano e Costantino, 2001) argued that at least its lower part is a Hadrianic arch remodelled for Constantine. Patrizio Pensabene and Clementina Panella (Arco di Costantino tra archeologia e archeometria, 1999) and Mark Wilson Jones (Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians, 2000) defend a single Constantinian design.

The Circus Maximus, the Forum Boarium and Sant'Omobono

The Circus Maximus. The valley between Palatine and Aventine, laid out in legend by Tarquinius Priscus (module 1.5); the races, the colours and the dispute over its seating are module 9.4's, and every triumph passed through it (module 9.2). Look, at the curved south-eastern end, for the footings found in 2015 of the arch of 80–81 that claimed Titus took a Jerusalem never taken before (CIL VI 944; module 7.2): Pompey had taken it in 63 BC.

The Forum Boarium. The cattle market and harbour at the Tiber Island crossing (module 0.2), where the Ara Maxima served Hercules with a Greek rite (module 1.3) and Gauls and Greeks were buried alive after Cannae (module 4.3). Two temples stand: the round marble temple, Hercules Victor in module 2.2, and the temple of Portunus of about 100 BC (module 10.3). Look at Portunus for Ionic columns free in the porch and engaged round the cella: Greek orders on an Etruscan podium.

Sant'Omobono. Beside the church lie the twin temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta that tradition gives to Servius Tullius (module 1.5); the site gave eighth-century Greek pottery (module 1.1) and a terracotta Hercules and Minerva of about 530 (module 1.3). Look down: the republican podia stand on the fill that buried the archaic temple about 500 BC (module 1.5).

The Campus Martius

Largo Argentina. Four republican temples, lettered A to D because their gods are disputed; the round temple B is usually taken for the Fortune of This Day that Catulus vowed at Vercellae in 101 (Plutarch, Marius 26; module 5.2). Behind them lie remains of the hall of Pompey's theatre complex where the Senate met on 15 March 44 (module 5.4; the murder source by source, deep dive module 11.7). Look for that hall's foundation, and recall that the room was afterwards walled up (Suetonius, Julius 88).

The Pantheon. Hadrian's rebuilding under the original builder's name, probably begun under Trajan (module 7.3), its dome module 10.3's; Agrippa's building had held Caesar's statue inside and Augustus' in the porch (Dio 53.27.3; module 6.2). Look for the porch inscription, M AGRIPPA L F COS TERTIVM FECIT, and on the block behind it a second pediment above the first (module 10.3).

The column of Marcus Aurelius. In the Piazza Colonna, finished by 193 (module 7.3), its harsher frieze read against Trajan's in module 10.3. Look for the rain miracle, a winged storm god pouring rain over the army, which deep dive module 13.7 sets against the Christian versions. St Paul has stood on top since 1589.

The Ara Pacis and the Mausoleum. The altar dedicated in 9 BC and the tomb begun in 28 BC are module 6.2's, with the disputes over the sacrificer, the goddess and the sundial; the altar was reassembled away from its site in 1938, beside a Mausoleum isolated in a new square (module 10.4). Look on the long sides for the depth of carving, front figures deep and those behind shallow (module 10.3), then at the museum wall carved with the Res Gestae that once stood in bronze before the tomb (Suetonius, Augustus 101.4; module 6.2).

The Baths of Caracalla and the Palazzo Massimo

The Baths of Caracalla. Inaugurated in 216, with 1,600 marble seats by Olympiodorus' count (module 7.4); bathing as an institution is module 9.4's, the bath plan module 10.3's, and the Farnese Hercules and Bull found here in the 1540s are now in Naples. Look for the symmetry: the same suite of rooms on either side of the axis through the great hall. Beneath lies a Mithraeum (module 2.5).

The Palazzo Massimo. The National Museum's palace faces the Baths of Diocletian, whose cold hall is Michelangelo's Santa Maria degli Angeli (module 10.3). It holds the garden room from Livia's villa at Prima Porta, where the Prima Porta statue was found (module 6.2): a painted orchard full of birds round all four walls of an underground room, the Second style dissolving the wall (module 10.3). Look for the double fence, a light lattice in front and a stone balustrade behind, that holds you at the edge of a garden you cannot enter. Here too is the bronze Boxer, a Hellenistic original found on the Quirinal (module 10.3; Greek module 9.1). Look for the cuts picked out in inlaid copper. Then find the Fasti Antiates, the one surviving pre-Julian calendar (module 2.3), to set beside the Capitoline Fasti where the walk began.

Walking orders

One day: Capitoline, Forum, Palatine, Colosseum and arch, the fora from the street, the Pantheon. Two days: first the Capitol, Forum and Palatine, then down to the river quarter and along the Circus to the Baths of Caracalla; next the emperors' city, from the Colosseum through the fora to the Campus Martius, ending by Metro at the Palazzo Massimo.

Self-test

  1. What do the wolf and the Fasti in the Hall of the She-wolf have in common as evidence?
    Answer

    Both dress legend as record. The wolf, long thought Etruscan, is a medieval casting of about 1021–1153 with fifteenth-century twins (module 1.4); the Augustan Fasti open their triumphs with Romulus over the Caeninenses, a record no one could have kept (modules 0.1 and 0.3).

  2. Why is the name Tabularium insecure, and what about the building is certain?
    Answer

    It rests on Catulus' lost inscription recording a substructure and a tabularium (CIL VI 1314); Purcell argues that the inscriptions do not name the building, Tucci sets the temple of Juno Moneta on it, and Coarelli makes it a temple platform. Catulus' date of 78 BC and the arches framed by half-columns (module 10.3) are not in doubt.

  3. Name three inscriptions in the Forum that change what you are looking at, and say how.
    Answer

    The temple of Saturn's incendio consumptum restituit makes its columns a late antique rebuilding; the fourth line of the Severan arch, recut after Geta's murder, shows his name in the dowel holes (module 7.4); the Vestal base of 364 (CIL VI 32422) has had its honorand's name chiselled out.

  4. What does the Lapis Niger show about how Romans treated their own archaic past?
    Answer

    The late Republic covered an archaic altar, column stump and inscribed cippus of about 570–550 BC with black paving instead of removing them. The spot was kept, though ancient writers could only guess its meaning, Romulus' tomb or Faustulus' (modules 1.4 and 1.5).

  5. Which three modules own the Arch of Titus, and what does each take from it?
    Answer

    Module 7.2 the Jewish War and the dedication to the deified Titus (CIL VI 945); module 9.2 the triumph of 71 that the spoils panel records; module 10.3 the relief's procession swinging into and out of the plane. Valadier's travertine marks what is restoration.

  6. What is disputed about the House of Augustus?
    Answer

    Carettoni identified the painted rooms as Augustus' house; Iacopi and Tedone argue they were filled in after 36 BC for the Apollo complex; Carandini reconstructs a grand residence round the temple. Wiseman (2019) rejects the reconstruction and puts the modest house of the texts under the later palace.

  7. What does Trajan's Column say about itself, and why is "Trajan's Markets" a hypothesis rather than a fact?
    Answer

    Its inscription says it shows the height of the hill cut away for the forum (module 7.3). The name comes from Corrado Ricci's clearance and his publication of 1929; the museum now reads the rooms as offices and stores of a multi-functional centre, and no ancient text names the building.

  8. What does the attic inscription of the Arch of Constantine claim, and what is argued about the arch itself?
    Answer

    That Constantine won by the prompting of the divinity, instinctu divinitatis, a formula pagan senators and a Christian emperor could share (CIL VI 1139; module 8.3). Conforto argued that at least the lower part is a Hadrianic arch remodelled; Pensabene and Panella and Wilson Jones defend a single Constantinian design.

  9. What does the temple of Portunus show, and what lies beneath the visible temples at Sant'Omobono?
    Answer

    Portunus shows the Roman synthesis: Ionic columns free in the porch and engaged round the cella, on a high Etruscan podium (module 10.3). At Sant'Omobono the republican podia stand on the fill that buried the archaic temple about 500 BC (module 1.5).

  10. What links Largo Argentina to Caesar and to the war against the Cimbri?
    Answer

    Behind the temples lies the hall of Pompey's complex where Caesar was killed on 15 March 44, afterwards walled up (Suetonius, Julius 88; module 5.4, deep dive module 11.7). The round temple B is usually identified with the Fortune of This Day that Catulus vowed at Vercellae in 101 (Plutarch, Marius 26).

Carry forward

  1. Rome is a stack, not a set: on almost every site what stands is the last rebuilding (Diocletian's Curia, a late antique Saturn, Tiberius' Castor, Hadrian's Pantheon, Valadier's arch), so the first question at any ruin is which layer you are looking at.
  2. Monuments are claims before they are evidence: the Fasti's Romulus, the column's hill, Titus' Jerusalem, Agrippa's name and Constantine's divinity say what someone wanted said, and erasures such as Geta's line or the Vestal of 364 are part of the message.
  3. Names on the ground are hypotheses with histories: Tabularium, House of Augustus, House of Livia, Trajan's Markets, Lupercal and tomb of Romulus rest on an inscription, a pipe or an excavator's reading, and the city you walk was arranged by Michelangelo, Ricci and Mussolini as much as by emperors.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report that turns the city of Rome into a walkable exam on the course. Build it as a route: the Capitoline (the temple platform, the Tabularium, the Capitoline Museums with the wolf, the equestrian Marcus Aurelius and the Fasti); the Forum (the Lapis Niger, the Regia, the temple of Vesta and the House of the Vestals, the Curia, the Rostra, the temples of Saturn, Castor and the deified Julius, the basilicas, the arches of Septimius Severus and Titus); the Palatine (the Iron Age huts, the houses of Augustus and Livia, the Flavian palace); the Imperial Fora, Trajan's Markets and Column; the Colosseum and the Arch of Constantine; the Circus Maximus, the Forum Boarium and Sant'Omobono; the Campus Martius (Pantheon, Ara Pacis, Mausoleum of Augustus, Largo Argentina); the Baths of Caracalla; and the National Museum at Palazzo Massimo for the garden room from Livia's villa and the bronze Boxer. For each stop: what is there, which module it belongs to, and the one thing to look for. Point back to Greek module 9.2, which does the same for Athens. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 10 · Literature, myth-making and reception · 10.1 · 2,842 words

Ovid and the Roman remaking of Greek myth

A Roman poem that taught Europe Greek mythFrom Chaos to Caesar's starThe Roman frame: a heavenly Senate and a new starInvented and transformed: five storiesThe lost Hellenistic shelfThe Roman names, and why they stuckThe Fasti: the Roman year as a poemThe Heroides: myth in the heroine's voiceAfterlives: from the Ovide moralisé to BerniniSelf-testCarry forward

A Roman poem that taught Europe Greek myth

For a thousand years the Latin West met the Greek gods mainly in one book, written in Rome by a poet who never pretended to be Greek. Greek module 0.1 treats the Metamorphoses as a trap for anyone recovering Greek myth, and Greek module 3.7 sets its best-known stories against the Greek evidence; module 6.3 gives Ovid's career, the bare plan of the poem, its closing claim and the exile. This module reads the poem as a Roman artefact, with the Fasti and the Heroides beside it.

The proem states the paradox. The gods are asked to "spin down" (deducite) a "continuous song" (perpetuum carmen) from the world's first origin to the poet's own times (1.3–4). Callimachus had refused to write one continuous song (Aetia fr. 1.3 Pfeiffer), and deductum carmen was Virgil's phrase for the slender Callimachean poem (Eclogue 6.5): Ovid promises an epic's span built from a miniaturist's episodes. If the minority reading illa is right in line 2, the gods have changed the poet's own undertakings too, from elegy to epic.

From Chaos to Caesar's star

The poem runs to nearly 12,000 hexameters in fifteen books, ordered by time and drifting towards history. Books 1–2 run from Chaos and the flood to the loves of the gods; books 3–4 follow the house of Cadmus at Thebes; the middle books move through the heroes to Orpheus in books 10–11; book 12 reaches Troy. Ovid then compresses Virgil's epic into a "little Aeneid" (13.623–14.608) in which Dido gets four lines (14.78–81) and the space goes to Scylla, Glaucus, Circe and Polyphemus. Book 14 ends with the Alban kings, Vertumnus and Pomona, and Romulus; book 15 gives Numa, Pythagoras' long speech, the arrival of Aesculapius at Rome (15.622–744) and the death and deification of Julius Caesar (15.745–870).

The Roman books change what metamorphosis means. Early in the poem change is usually loss: a girl becomes a tree, a boy a flower. In the last books it becomes ascent. Aeneas is purged of his mortal part in the river Numicius and made the god Indiges (14.581–608); Romulus becomes Quirinus and his wife Hersilia the goddess Hora (14.805–851); Caesar becomes a star. Roman metamorphosis is apotheosis, and Pythagoras' doctrine, omnia mutantur, nihil interit, "everything changes, nothing perishes" (15.165), underwrites it. The same speech lists cities that rose and fell, Troy, Sparta, Mycenae, Thebes, Athens, and adds that Rome is now rising (15.420–435). The reader is left to finish the thought.

Where sources disagree. Brooks Otis (Ovid as an Epic Poet, 1966) divided the poem into four blocks: a divine comedy (1.1–2.875), the avenging gods (3.1–6.400), the pathos of love (6.401–11.795), and Rome and the deified ruler (books 12–15). Stephen Wheeler (Narrative Dynamics in Ovid's Metamorphoses, 2000) called such block schemes too reductive and found the design in repeated patterns and continuous linking that keep deferring closure.

The Roman frame: a heavenly Senate and a new star

The first council of the gods is drawn as a meeting of the Senate. Jupiter summons the gods along the Milky Way to his house; the halls of the noble gods stand open on either side, the plebs live elsewhere, and the narrator would not fear, if boldness were allowed, to call the place the Palatine of the great sky (1.168–176). When the gods clamour for punishment, the narrator compares the outcry to the world's horror when an impious band raged to blot out the Roman name in Caesar's blood: Augustus' people are as loyal to him as the gods to Jupiter (1.199–205). Whether the blood is the dictator's in 44 BC or that of a plot against Augustus is unsettled, and Greek module 3.7 weighs what the parallel implies about Jupiter's power. Greek gods are given a Roman constitution, with the princeps as the term of comparison.

The ending answers the opening. Told by Jupiter that the Fates' decrees are fixed, Venus stands unseen in the middle of the Senate house, snatches Caesar's soul and carries it up, where it catches fire and becomes a star trailing its hair (15.761–850). Pliny quotes Augustus' memoirs on the real comet of July 44 BC, taken for Caesar's soul received among the gods (Natural History 2.93–94). Ovid supplies the logic with a straight face: none of Caesar's deeds was greater than fathering this man, and he had to be made a god so that Augustus would not be born of mortal seed (15.746–761). After Jupiter and Augustus are paired as rulers and fathers (15.858–860), the epilogue sets the poet above both. His work will outlast Jupiter's anger, fire, sword and time (15.871–872); his better part will be borne above the stars, higher than Caesar's new one (15.875–876); he will be read wherever Roman power reaches, and the last word is vivam, "I shall live" (15.877–879). The exile poems call Augustus Jupiter and his sentence the thunderbolt, and after AD 8 these lines read as defiance. Ovid says he burned his own copy on leaving Rome and that friends' copies lacked his final revision (Tristia 1.7).

Invented and transformed: five stories

Greek module 3.7 gives the Greek evidence for Narcissus and Echo, Pygmalion and Arachne, and Greek module 0.1 for Medusa; the question here is what each owes to Rome.

Pyramus and Thisbe (4.55–166) is the clearest case of a story made Roman in texture. It is told by one of the daughters of Minyas, who refuse Bacchus' festival and work wool while they trade stories, and she chooses it because it is not a common tale (4.53). Two young Babylonians, forbidden to marry, whisper through a crack in a party wall and curse it as the lover of Latin elegy curses his mistress's locked door (4.73). They agree to meet at Ninus' tomb under a white mulberry; Thisbe, early, flees a lioness and drops her veil; Pyramus finds it bloodied and falls on his sword. His blood leaps up as water hisses from a split lead pipe (4.121–124), a simile from the city's plumbing, and darkens the fruit. Thisbe dies on the same blade, and their ashes rest in one urn (4.166).

Where sources disagree. No Greek text tells Ovid's story. Nicolaus' Progymnasmata, a rhetorical handbook of the fifth century AD, preserves a version in which Pyramus becomes the Cilician river of that name and Thisbe a spring, and a Roman-period mosaic in the House of Dionysus at Nea Paphos shows the river-god Pyramus with Thisbe. Many see here the Greek aetiology Ovid moved to Babylon; but both witnesses are later than Ovid, and his narrator's claim that the tale was not common (4.53) cuts either way.

Narcissus and Echo (3.339–510): the boy is Greek, the pairing Ovid's, and its stamp is the declaimer's trick of words returned with their meaning changed, as when Narcissus calls "let us meet here" and Echo returns coeamus as an offer of love. Arachne (6.1–145) is a contest between two arts. Minerva weaves the twelve gods enthroned on the Areopagus augusta gravitate, "with august dignity" (6.73), centred and hierarchical, with punished mortals in the corners, like a state relief; Arachne weaves a crowded, unframed sequence of the gods' rapes and disguises (6.103–128), which is to say the Metamorphoses, and neither Pallas nor Envy could fault it (6.129–130). After AD 8 a mortal artist destroyed by a goddess for telling the truth about the gods was hard not to read as autobiography. Pygmalion (10.243–297) courts his ivory girl with the gifts of elegy, shells, flowers and amber, so that the living statue is the elegiac lover's fantasy granted. Medusa's rape in Minerva's temple and the punishment of the victim (4.790–803) are told at Perseus' wedding feast, in answer to a guest's question, by the man who killed her: the most retold version of her story is her killer's after-dinner aetiology.

The lost Hellenistic shelf

Ovid's quarry is listed in Greek module 3.7: Nicander's Heteroioumena, Boios' Ornithogonia, Parthenius, Callimachus. Two points add the Roman side. The genre already had a Latin voice: Aemilius Macer, an older friend, read the young Ovid his poem on birds, after Boios, and his poem on snakes and healing herbs (Tristia 4.10.43–44). And where Antoninus Liberalis' summaries of Nicander allow a test, Ovid changes the frame more than the plot. Antoninus 10, citing Nicander's fourth book and Corinna, has the daughters of Minyas, maddened by Dionysus, tear Leucippe's son Hippasus apart and become a bat, an owl and an eagle-owl. Ovid keeps the defiance and makes all three bats (4.389–415), but drops the murder and turns the sisters into storytellers, so that Pyramus and Thisbe, the Sun's loves and Salmacis and Hermaphroditus enter the poem through them. Antoninus also gives Nicander's versions of the Pierides' contest with the Muses (9; Ovid's book 5), Battus (23; book 2), Byblis (30; book 9) and a girl turned boy, Leucippus where Ovid has Iphis (17; book 9). The Hellenistic catalogues supplied changes; Ovid supplied voices.

The Roman names, and why they stuck

Ovid's gods are Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Venus, Mercury, Diana, Neptune, Ceres, Vulcan and Bacchus; his heroes include Ulixes and Hercules; Persephone is Proserpina. The equations were centuries older than Ovid, and module 2.2 traces how they were made and how imperfectly they fit. Where Latin had no equivalent he kept the Greek, Phoebus and Apollo, and he dressed the Latin names in Greek epithets, Saturnia for Juno, Tritonia for Minerva, Cytherea for Venus, so that a Roman name carried a whole Greek story.

Three things made the names permanent. Ovid became a school author: the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, when he was taught, glossed, imitated and moralised more than any other ancient poet, are Ludwig Traube's aetas Ovidiana. Greek was almost unread in the Latin West, so there was no rival vocabulary (Greek module 9.3, with Bulfinch's Latin-named handbook of 1855). And the vernaculars translated Ovid long before Homer: Arthur Golding's English Metamorphoses (1567) gave Shakespeare his Jove and Juno. Only in the nineteenth century, with a new Hellenism and Greek central again in the schools, did English begin to prefer Zeus to Jove.

The Fasti: the Roman year as a poem

Modules 2.3 and 2.4 use the Fasti as a source for festivals, and module 6.3 reads its Augustan days; here it is a poem, the Metamorphoses' companion, written in the same years and in deliberate contrast. The Metamorphoses is hexameter, Greek in matter and ordered by time from the world's beginning; the Fasti is elegiac, Roman in matter and ordered by the civic calendar, a book to a month, a day at a time, with star-risings, festivals and anniversaries. The poet admits the metre is slight for it: now for the first time, elegiacs, you sail with larger sails (2.3). His voice is the antiquarian's and his method interrogation. Mars is asked why matrons keep his festival (3.167–258); Flora expounds her own cult (5.183–378); the Muses disagree over the name of May (5.1–110) and three goddesses over June (6.1–100), and the poet declines to judge. It is a poem of rival explanations, which is why module 2.3 warns against trusting its reasons.

Its Roman stories are those the Metamorphoses squeezes into its last books or leaves out: Carmenta, Evander, and Hercules and Cacus (1.461–586); the Fabii at the Cremera (2.193–242); Lucretia (2.685–852; module 1.6); Numa coaxing Jupiter into giving the charm against lightning (3.259–392); and Anna Perenna, Dido's sister, who flees to Italy, drowns in the Numicius and becomes a nymph honoured on the Ides of March (3.523–696). Some stories are told in both poems, and the doubles show the difference of key: Callisto (Metamorphoses 2.401–530; Fasti book 2), Romulus' apotheosis (Metamorphoses 14.805–828; Fasti 2.475–512) and above all the rape of Proserpina (Metamorphoses 5.341–661; Fasti 4.417–620).

Where sources disagree. Richard Heinze ("Ovids elegische Erzählung", 1919) compared the paired stories and found two consistent manners: the epic Metamorphoses grand, its gods majestic; the elegiac Fasti tender, intimate and sentimental. Stephen Hinds (The Metamorphosis of Persephone, 1987) showed Ovid playing with exactly those markers, putting elegiac matter into the epic and epic gestures into the elegy, so that genre becomes a subject of the poems rather than a rule they obey. Heinze's categories remain the starting point; his rigidity does not survive.

The poem stops at the end of June. From exile Ovid says he wrote "six and as many" books, each ending with its month, dedicated to Augustus, and that his fate broke the work off (Tristia 2.549–552); most read that as six books written and six planned, since no ancient author quotes July to December. What survives was retouched after Augustus' death: Carmenta foretells Livia's deification as Julia Augusta, a name she took only in AD 14 (1.536). The opening now addresses Germanicus (1.3), Tiberius' adopted son and himself translator of Aratus' poem on the stars, the right reader for a calendar of risings and settings. The end was not designed as one: on 30 June Clio points to the monument of Philippus and praises Marcia, Augustus' cousin and wife of Ovid's friend Paullus Fabius Maximus (6.797–812), and the poem stops. A calendar meant to fill a year fills half of one, revised by a poet writing to the dynasty that had banished him.

The Heroides: myth in the heroine's voice

The Heroides are fifteen verse letters from women of myth to absent husbands and lovers, most of whom have left them, among them Penelope to Ulixes, Phaedra to Hippolytus, Dido to Aeneas, Ariadne to Theseus, Medea to Jason and Sappho to Phaon, with three pairs of letters and replies (16–21) added later. Ovid claimed the form as a work unknown to others (Ars Amatoria 3.345–346), though Propertius' letter of Arethusa to her soldier husband (4.3) is a Roman precedent, and novavit can mean "renewed" as well as "invented". Each letter freezes a known story at one moment and lets the abandoned woman argue it, as Ariadne does from the empty shore. Dido's letter (7) is the most Roman, Virgil's fourth book reread by its victim, in which pious Aeneas is a deserter and the Roman mission a pretext. The collection's contribution is myth told from inside, and the heroic epistle from Drayton to Pope's Eloisa to Abelard descends from it.

Where sources disagree. Sappho's letter stands outside the main manuscript tradition of the collection. Karl Lachmann (1848) and R. J. Tarrant ("The Authenticity of the Letter of Sappho to Phaon", 1981) judged it an imitation; Edward Courtney (1997) and Thea Thorsen (Ovid's Early Poetry, 2014) defended it, pointing to the Sappho letter in Ovid's own list (Amores 2.18). E. J. Kenney's commentary on 16–21 (1996) accepts the double letters as late Ovid against doubts based on their metre.

Afterlives: from the Ovide moralisé to Bernini

Module 10.4 takes the reception of Rome at large; this is Ovid's own line. The Middle Ages kept him by moralising him. Arnulf of Orléans in the twelfth century and John of Garland in the thirteenth explained the fables as veiled truths; the anonymous Old French Ovide moralisé of the early fourteenth century turned some 12,000 Latin lines into about 72,000 French ones, following each story with expositions that read it as history, as moral warning and as a figure of Christ, the Virgin or the soul. It absorbed older French poems, among them the Philomena attributed to Chrétien de Troyes, which survives only there.

Chaucer used the Ovide moralisé beside the Latin but left its morals behind. The Book of the Duchess begins with its narrator reading Ceyx and Alcyone; Thisbe, Dido, Medea, Ariadne and Philomela are among the heroines of the Legend of Good Women; and the Wife of Bath retells Midas with his wife, not his barber, betraying the ass's ears, then sends her hearers to Ovid for the rest. Shakespeare had Golding and the Latin. The mechanicals stage Pyramus and Thisbe in A Midsummer Night's Dream, Wall included; Lavinia in Titus Andronicus turns the pages of the Metamorphoses to Philomela to name her own rape (4.1); Prospero's farewell to magic in The Tempest (5.1) reworks Medea's invocation from book 7 through Golding's words. Francis Meres wrote in 1598 that the sweet, witty soul of Ovid lived in Shakespeare.

Painters and sculptors read for the instant of change. Titian's poesie for Philip II, listed in Greek module 9.3, stage Ovid's moments: Actaeon as he sees Diana, Callisto's pregnancy exposed at the bath. Bernini's Apollo and Daphne (1622–25), carved for Cardinal Scipione Borghese, shows bark closing over Daphne's body and leaves sprouting from her fingers as Apollo reaches her, Metamorphoses 1.548–552 made marble. Its base carried a couplet by Cardinal Maffeo Barberini, the future Urban VIII, warning that whoever chases fleeting beauty fills his hands with leaves or plucks bitter berries: the method of the Ovide moralisé, three centuries on, attached to a statue that needs no moral.

Self-test

  1. How does the proem of the Metamorphoses combine two poetic programmes that had been set against each other?
    Answer

    It asks the gods to "spin down" (deducite, Virgil's word for the slender Callimachean poem, Eclogue 6.5) a "continuous song" (perpetuum carmen, the kind Callimachus refused, Aetia fr. 1.3) from creation to Ovid's own day (1.3–4): an epic's span made of miniatures.

  2. What happens to the meaning of metamorphosis in the Roman books? Give two examples.
    Answer

    Change becomes ascent rather than loss: Aeneas is made Indiges (14.581–608), Romulus Quirinus and Hersilia Hora (14.805–851), Caesar a star (15.843–850). Pythagoras' "everything changes, nothing perishes" (15.165) gives it a doctrine.

  3. How do the first council of the gods and the deification of Caesar frame the poem as Roman?
    Answer

    The council is a Senate meeting on the "Palatine of the great sky", with noble gods and plebs, and the gods' outcry is likened to the world's horror at an attempt on Caesar (1.168–205). At the end Venus takes Caesar's soul from the middle of the Senate house and makes it a star (15.761–850), and Jupiter and Augustus are paired as rulers (15.858–860).

  4. Why is the logic of Caesar's deification double-edged, and how does the epilogue answer it?
    Answer

    Ovid says Caesar's greatest deed was fathering Augustus and that he had to be made a god so that Augustus would not be born of mortal seed (15.746–761), so the apotheosis serves the heir. The epilogue then sets the poet's fame beyond Jupiter's anger and above the stars, ending on vivam (15.871–879).

  5. What makes Pyramus and Thisbe Roman in texture, and why is its Greek background uncertain?
    Answer

    The lovers curse the wall like the elegiac lover at a locked door (4.73), the blood spurts like water from a split lead pipe (4.121–124), and their ashes share one urn (4.166). The Cilician version with river and spring survives only in Nicolaus' fifth-century handbook and a Roman-period mosaic at Nea Paphos, both later than Ovid.

  6. What does comparison with Antoninus Liberalis 10 show about Ovid's use of Nicander?
    Answer

    Antoninus' daughters of Minyas kill Hippasus and become a bat and two kinds of owl; Ovid drops the murder, makes all three bats (4.389–415) and turns them into narrators of three tales. He changed frame and voice more than plot.

  7. Why did Ovid's Latin names for the gods become Europe's names?
    Answer

    He was the central school author of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries (Traube's aetas Ovidiana), Greek was almost unread in the Latin West (Greek module 9.3), and the vernaculars translated Ovid first, as Golding did in 1567. English began to prefer Greek forms only in the nineteenth century.

  8. How do the Fasti and the Metamorphoses differ, and what did Heinze and Hinds argue about the stories they share?
    Answer

    Elegiac against hexameter, Roman against Greek, the calendar day by day against chronology from creation. Heinze (1919) found consistent elegiac and epic manners in doubles such as Proserpina; Hinds (1987) showed Ovid deliberately crossing those markers.

  9. What evidence shows that the Fasti was left unfinished and revised in exile?
    Answer

    Ovid says his fate broke off the work (Tristia 2.549–552) and no ancient author quotes July to December; Carmenta's prophecy names Livia Julia Augusta, a name from AD 14 (1.536); the opening addresses Germanicus (1.3); and the poem stops on 30 June without a designed close (6.797–812).

  10. What links Bernini's Apollo and Daphne to the Ovide moralisé?
    Answer

    Maffeo Barberini's couplet for the base turns Ovid's scene into a warning that pursuing fleeting beauty yields only leaves and bitter berries. That is the medieval habit of attaching a Christian moral to an Ovidian story, as the Ovide moralisé did for every tale.

Carry forward

  1. Read the Metamorphoses as a Roman universal history: Greek in matter, its frame runs to Rome, and in the Roman books metamorphosis becomes apotheosis, ending with Caesar's star and the poet's own claim to outlast Jupiter's anger.
  2. Ovid changed frames, voices and textures more than plots, and his Latin names carried the result into Europe's schools; where Antoninus Liberalis allows a test, the plot is Hellenistic and the frame, voice and texture are Ovid's.
  3. The Fasti and the Metamorphoses are a pair, Roman myth in elegiac couplets by the calendar and Greek myth in hexameter by time; the Fasti is half a year, retouched in exile for the dynasty that banished its author, and its explanations are poetry before they are evidence.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Ovid's Metamorphoses as the book through which later Europe learned Greek myth, read as the Roman poem it is. Cover: its structure from Chaos to the apotheosis of Caesar; the Roman frame (the council of the gods as the Senate, Jupiter and Augustus, the ending on Caesar's star); which stories Ovid invented or transformed (Echo and Narcissus, Pyramus and Thisbe, Arachne, Pygmalion, Medusa) and which he took from lost Hellenistic poets; the Roman names and why they stuck; the Fasti as its counterpart for Roman myth; the Heroides; and the poem's later life in the Ovide moralisé, Chaucer, Shakespeare, Titian and Bernini. Point back to Greek modules 0.1 and 3.7, which treat Ovid as a trap for the Greek material, and concentrate on what he did as a Roman. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 10 · Literature, myth-making and reception · 10.2 · 2,865 words

Imperial literature, Seneca to Apuleius

Why drop "Silver Latin"Seneca's tragediesLucan: the anti-epic of civil warPetronius' Satyricon and Trimalchio's dinnerSatire and epigram: Persius, Juvenal, MartialThe Flavian epic: Valerius, Statius, SiliusThe Plinys and QuintilianTacitus and Suetonius as writersApuleius: the one complete Latin novelCoda: late Latin and the bridge to the Middle AgesSelf-testCarry forward

Why drop "Silver Latin"

Latin literature after Augustus has long been filed as a Silver Age, second to a Golden Age from Cicero to Ovid. The metals come from the myth of declining races (Hesiod, Works and Days 109–201; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.89–150), applied to Latin by early modern philologists; for English readers J. Wight Duff fixed the scheme in A Literary History of Rome in the Silver Age (1927), from Tiberius to Hadrian. The label turns a period into a verdict, so that point and paradox, which Ovid used freely, become symptoms. It misreads poets who wrote with the Aeneid open, answering it rather than failing to equal it. And it stops in the second century, leaving Apuleius and Augustine outside literature. Scholars now speak of Neronian, Flavian and Trajanic writing, by reign, the work of men for whom praise, silence and indirection were the conditions of writing under a princeps. The story of decline is also ancient: first-century Romans told it about eloquence.

Where sources disagree. Seneca made style a symptom of morals: as men live, so they speak (Letters 114.1). Petronius' Encolpius blames the declamation schools (Satyricon 1–2), and Quintilian wrote a lost book on the causes of corrupted eloquence. In Tacitus' Dialogue on Orators Messalla blames upbringing and the schools (28–35); Maternus answers that great oratory fed on the disorder of the free Republic, which peace under one man has ended (36–41).

Seneca's tragedies

Seneca's life and philosophy are deep dive module 13.5, his satire on Claudius module 7.1; here he is the one Roman tragedian whose plays survive whole. Eight of the ten under his name are accepted: Hercules Furens, Trojan Women, Phoenician Women (unfinished, without a chorus), Medea, Phaedra, Oedipus, Agamemnon and Thyestes; Hercules Oetaeus is doubted. Octavia, a historical play on Nero's divorce and killing of his wife, puts Seneca on stage and foretells Nero's end, so it postdates 68; the eleventh-century Etruscus manuscript omits it. None of the plays is securely dated.

The plots are Greek (the Theban saga is Greek module 3.5), the treatment Roman. Seneca compressed his models and moved the interest from action to passion: each play studies furor, anger, lust or grief swelling past every limit in self-exhorting monologues. Medea talks herself into her own name, "Medea nunc sum" (Medea 910), and kills her children in the audience's sight; in Thyestes a Fury drives Tantalus' ghost to infect his house, and Atreus feeds Thyestes his sons. Ghosts, messengers' anatomical horror, five acts and the pointed sententia are what the Renaissance took. Thomas Newton's collection, Seneca His Tenne Tragedies (1581), put all ten into English, and Kyd's Spanish Tragedy and Shakespeare's Hamlet owe their ghosts and revenge to Seneca more than to any Greek play.

Where sources disagree. Otto Zwierlein (Die Rezitationsdramen Senecas, 1966) argued that the plays were written for recitation, since scenes such as the reading of entrails in Oedipus are hard to stage. Dana Sutton (Seneca on the Stage, 1986) answered that every scene can be performed. No ancient source records a performance.

Lucan: the anti-epic of civil war

Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, Seneca's nephew, born at Corduba in 39, was dead at twenty-five. His ten books on the war of Caesar and Pompey, transmitted as Civil War, are often called Pharsalia from his boast that "our Pharsalia" will live (9.985–986); the poem breaks off with Caesar besieged at Alexandria (10.546).

It is written against the Aeneid. The first line promises wars "more than civil" (1.1). No Olympian intervenes; Fortune and Fate drive events. Virgil's hero founds; Lucan's leaders destroy or fail. Pompey, "the shadow of a great name", is an old oak standing by its own weight, Caesar the lightning that rejoices to make its way by ruin (1.135–157); Cato, the third, belongs to deep dive module 13.4. The winning cause pleased the gods, the losing one Cato (1.128). Book 6 inverts Aeneid 6: instead of a Sibyl showing Rome's future heroes, the witch Erictho reanimates a corpse to prophesy ruin to Pompey's son (6.507–830). Quintilian thought Lucan fiery, famous for his sententiae, and "more to be imitated by orators than by poets" (10.1.90). Nero forbade him to recite (Tacitus, Annals 15.49.3); a Pisonian conspirator, ordered to die, he recited his own lines on a soldier dying the same death (15.70.1; module 7.1). Statius wrote a birthday poem for him at his widow's request (Silvae 2.7).

Where sources disagree. The proem calls the civil wars worth their cost if they led to Nero, and asks him not to tilt heaven by his weight when he takes his place among the stars (1.33–66). Frederick Ahl (Lucan: An Introduction, 1976) read the praise as double-edged; Michael Dewar ("Laying It On with a Trowel", Classical Quarterly 1994) set it among conventional panegyrics and denied that its excess was meant to amuse.

Petronius' Satyricon and Trimalchio's dinner

The Satyricon survives in fragments, probably of books 14 to 16, in prose with verse inset, the mixed form of Menippean satire. The narrator Encolpius drifts through southern Italy with his rival Ascyltos, the boy Giton and later the poet Eumolpus, pursued, he says, by Priapus' wrath as Ulysses was by Neptune's (139.2). Epic and Greek romance are parodied, the romance's faithful couple becoming a fickle threesome. So is criticism: the text opens on the decline of eloquence, and Eumolpus' Civil War (119–124), 295 hexameters restoring the gods Lucan removed, is usually read as an answer to Lucan. Eumolpus also tells the Widow of Ephesus (111–112), seduced in her husband's tomb by a soldier guarding crucified men.

Trimalchio's dinner (26.7–78) survives in a single manuscript found at Trogir in Dalmatia about 1650. Module 9.3 reads the host as a social type; as literature the dinner parodies the philosophical banquet, a symposium whose talk is money, funerals and the weather. Every course is theatre: a zodiac dish (35), a boar that releases live thrushes (40), a pig cut open to spill sausages (49). The freedmen's talk (41–46) is the fullest record of colloquial Latin. Trimalchio ends by reading his will and rehearsing his funeral until the watch, thinking the house on fire, breaks in (71–78). F. Scott Fitzgerald considered calling The Great Gatsby "Trimalchio in West Egg".

Where sources disagree. The manuscripts name the author Petronius Arbiter, and Tacitus describes Petronius, Nero's arbiter elegantiae, who died in 66 after sending Nero a sealed list of his debauches (Annals 16.18–19). K. F. C. Rose (The Date and Author of the Satyricon, 1971) argued from names, prices and the quarrels with Lucan and Seneca for a Neronian date and that identification; Enzo Marmorale (La questione petroniana, 1948) had argued from the language for a much later date. Most accept the courtier, though Tacitus mentions no novel.

Satire and epigram: Persius, Juvenal, Martial

Quintilian claimed satire as wholly Roman (10.1.93). Persius (34–62), a rich young man from Volaterrae taught by the Stoic Cornutus, left six short satires, published after his death: compressed to obscurity, full of Horace turned inside out, Stoic in doctrine. The first mocks fashionable recitations ("who will read this?", 1.2); the fifth argues that only the philosopher is free.

Juvenal is almost unknown outside his sixteen satires, written from about 110 into the late 120s: Satire 1 alludes to Marius Priscus' conviction in 100 (1.49–50), Satire 15 to the consulship of Iuncus, 127 (15.27). It is hard not to write satire (1.30), and where talent fails, indignation makes the verse (1.79); yet he attacks only the dead (1.170–171), Domitian's Rome assailed under Hadrian. Satire 3 drives Umbricius from a city of Greeks and fires (module 9.4); Satire 6 rails against marriage; Satire 10, on the vanity of prayer, ends with a sound mind in a sound body (10.356) and became Johnson's The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749). The last books are cooler.

Where sources disagree. Gilbert Highet (Juvenal the Satirist, 1954) read the satires as autobiography, a life of poverty and disappointment. William Anderson's essays of the 1960s and Susanna Braund (Beyond Anger, 1988) treat the angry speaker as a persona the poet constructs and changes, which explains why rage gives way to irony. The persona reading prevails, and it leaves Juvenal's own views unknown.

Martial (about 40 to about 104), from Bilbilis in Spain, wrote On the Spectacles for Titus' amphitheatre in 80, Saturnalia gift-tags (books 13–14) and twelve books of Epigrams from 86 to about 101; his flattery of Domitian is module 7.2's. His programme is anti-mythological: readers of Oedipus, Thyestes and Medea read only monsters, while "my page tastes of man" (10.4.10). That page is the city, its patrons, clients, legacy-hunters and dinners, its obscenity defended as a playful page from a decent life (1.4.8). He fixed the closing sting that Lessing analysed in 1771 as expectation and resolution. Pliny, who paid his fare home, doubted the poems would last (Letters 3.21).

The Flavian epic: Valerius, Statius, Silius

Module 7.2 places these poets at court; as poems, all three answer Virgil with myth or the distant past. Valerius Flaccus' unfinished Argonautica retells Apollonius (Greek module 3.4) and Romanises him: in book 1 Jupiter makes the Argo the start of a passing of power from Asia to Greece and onward, and Medea's love is modelled on Dido's.

Statius of Naples (about 45 to about 96) spent twelve years, he says, on the Thebaid (12.811–812), the Seven against Thebes (Greek module 3.5): civil war displaced into myth, with brothers' hatred, Furies who start the action, helpless gods, and atrocity at its height when the dying Tydeus gnaws his killer's skull and Minerva, bringing him immortality, turns away (book 8). Theseus comes from Athens, city of an altar to Clemency, to enforce burial of the dead (book 12). The unfinished Achilleid hides Achilles on Scyros (Greek module 10.1). The thirty-two Silvae, occasional poems on villas, roads, a dead father and Sleep (5.4), show another Statius. Dante made him a secret Christian converted by Virgil's fourth Eclogue (Purgatorio 21–22).

Silius Italicus' Punica, seventeen books on the Hannibalic war, takes events from Livy and machinery from Virgil: Juno drives Hannibal to avenge Dido, and young Scipio chooses Virtue over Pleasure (book 15), the Choice of Hercules made Roman. Pliny judged that Silius wrote with more care than talent (Letters 3.7.5).

The Plinys and Quintilian

The elder Pliny (23/24–79) dedicated the Natural History to Titus in 77: thirty-seven books from the cosmos through geography, man, animals, plants and their medicines to metals and stones, where the history of Greek art survives as a digression (books 33–37). He claims 20,000 facts from about 2,000 volumes by a hundred authors (preface 17), and book 1 lists his sources. His nephew describes notes taken while he ate, bathed and travelled, 160 notebooks, and his saying that no book is so bad that no part of it is useful (Letters 3.5); his death is module 7.2's. Nature provides, and luxury, digging into her body for gold, abuses her (33.1–3). The Middle Ages used the work as their encyclopaedia.

The younger Pliny (about 61 to about 112) published nine books of letters, each letter on one subject, arranged, he says, without regard to date (1.1). Cicero's were written to be sent (module 5.6); Pliny's were written to be read, a self-portrait of the good senator: his villa (2.17), his wife Calpurnia (4.19), a ghost story (7.27). Book 10 is module 7.5's.

Quintilian of Calagurris was the first rhetorician paid from the treasury: Suetonius gives Vespasian's salaries as 100,000 sesterces (Vespasian 18), and Jerome's Chronicle names Quintilian first. His Institutio oratoria (mid-90s) trains the orator from the cradle and defines him, after Cato, as a good man skilled in speaking (12.1.1). Book 10 gives a reading list with verdicts (10.1.46–131), the first canon of Latin literature, Cicero its model (10.1.112). Poggio's discovery of a complete manuscript at St Gall in 1416 made him the humanists' schoolmaster.

Tacitus and Suetonius as writers

Module 0.1 introduces both as sources, and modules 7.1 and 7.2 use them. Tacitus (about 56 to about 120), praetor in 88 (Annals 11.11.1) and consul in 97, wrote the Agricola and Germania (98), the Dialogue on Orators, the Histories (69–96) and the Annals (14–68), thirty books for the two histories by Jerome's count (Commentary on Zechariah 3.14). What survives of the two histories rests on two manuscripts, one for Annals 1–6 and one from Monte Cassino for the rest.

His style is built against Cicero's: brevity, asymmetry, archaic and poetic words, Sallust the model (module 5.6). He promises to write without anger or partiality (1.1.3) and judges by arrangement. At Augustus' funeral the prudent men give two verdicts (1.9–10): the favourable one short, the hostile one longer and last. Rumour is reported and disowned, motives are offered as alternatives, and an epigram closes the paragraph. The Ciceronian Dialogue shows the manner was chosen. Nerva, he wrote, had joined principate and liberty, things once irreconcilable (Agricola 3.1); the Annals show senators learning servility.

Suetonius (about 70 to after 122), Pliny's protégé (Letters 10.94), ran the palace libraries and correspondence, as an inscription from Hippo Regius shows, and the late Historia Augusta has him dismissed under Hadrian (Hadrian 11.3). The Lives of the Caesars, Julius to Domitian, treat each life by categories rather than time (Augustus 9): family, career, public acts, private habits, appearance, death. He quotes documents, above all Augustus' letters, and lets the sorting of virtues and vices do the judging. Nepos had written Latin lives (module 5.6), Plutarch moral portraits in Greek; Suetonius set the form of imperial biography, continued by Marius Maximus, imitated by the Historia Augusta (module 0.1) and followed in Einhard's Life of Charlemagne.

Apuleius: the one complete Latin novel

Apuleius of Madauros, Platonist and orator, answered a charge of magic in the Apology (module 2.4). Augustine already called his eleven-book Metamorphoses the Golden Ass (City of God 18.18). The prologue promises Milesian tales to please the ear (1.1). Lucius, curious about magic, lodges at Hypata in Thessaly, gets the wrong ointment through the maid Photis and becomes an ass with a man's mind (3.24–25). Owned by robbers, begging priests of the Syrian goddess, a miller and a soldier, he sees the hidden life of the provinces and its adulteries (book 9), until he flees the arena at Corinth and is restored by Isis (book 11; module 2.5 has the dispute over its sincerity).

At the centre an old woman tells a captive bride the tale of Cupid and Psyche (4.28–6.24), a fifth of the whole. Psyche looks by lamplight at her forbidden husband, loses him, and wins him back through Venus' labours; her curiosity mirrors Lucius', and a goddess saves both. A Greek Ass among Lucian's works tells Lucius' story without Psyche or Isis, and Photius judged that it and a Greek Metamorphoses by Lucius of Patrae copied one from the other (Bibliotheca codex 129): Apuleius added the inset tales, the tone and the ending. Boccaccio took the lover in the tub (9.5–7) for the Decameron (7.2), Raphael's workshop painted Psyche in the Villa Farnesina, and C. S. Lewis retold her story in Till We Have Faces (1956).

Where sources disagree. Fulgentius (Mythologies 3.6) read the tale as allegory, Psyche the soul and Cupid desire, and Platonist readings still have defenders. Jan-Öjvind Swahn (The Tale of Cupid and Psyche, 1955) treated it as the oldest written version of an international folktale of the search for a lost husband. Detlev Fehling (Amor und Psyche, 1977) reversed the direction: Apuleius built the story from literary motifs, and the folktales descend from his book.

Coda: late Latin and the bridge to the Middle Ages

Pagan Latin literature thins in the third century and returns changed. Ausonius of Bordeaux (about 310 to about 395), Gratian's tutor and consul in 379, wrote the Mosella, a poem on the river, and a wedding cento of Virgil's half-lines rearranged into obscenity. Claudian, an Alexandrian Greek writing Latin hexameters, turned Stilicho's politics into panegyric and invective (module 8.5) and left an unfinished Rape of Proserpina. Ammianus Marcellinus, module 8.4's main source, began his history in 96, where Tacitus' Histories ended; his digressions on the Roman nobles and plebs (14.6, 28.4) are satire inside history.

The decisive works were Christian. Jerome (about 347–420), asked by Pope Damasus to revise the Latin Gospels in 383, went on to translate the Old Testament from the Hebrew; his version, the Vulgate, became the Bible of the Latin Middle Ages. He dreamt that he was flogged as "a Ciceronian, not a Christian" (Letters 22.30), and went on writing like one. Augustine's Confessions (about 397–400), addressed to God, make a life into an argument: Cicero's Hortensius turned him to philosophy (3.4.7), his tears for Dido (1.13; deep dive module 12.4) became a charge against his schooling, and a child's "take up and read" sent him to Paul (8.12.29). Virgil and Cicero survived inside the Christian books that renounced them.

Self-test

  1. Why is "Silver Latin" a misleading label, and what shows that the idea of decline is also ancient?
    Answer

    It borrows the myth of declining metals to turn a period into a verdict, reads deliberate answers to Virgil as failures, and stops before Apuleius and late Latin. Romans themselves argued about the decline of eloquence: Seneca blamed morals (Letters 114.1), Tacitus' Messalla the schools and Maternus the end of free politics (Dialogue 28–41).

  2. What makes Seneca's tragedies Roman rather than Greek, and why is the Octavia not his?
    Answer

    He compresses Greek plots and shifts the interest to the passion, furor, voiced in self-exhorting monologues, with ghosts, horror in anatomical detail and sententiae; Medea kills her children in sight. The Octavia puts Seneca on stage and foretells Nero's end, so it postdates 68, three years after Seneca's death.

  3. In what ways is Lucan's Civil War an anti-Aeneid?
    Answer

    It removes the gods as actors in favour of Fortune and Fate, tells civil war instead of a founding, gives it leaders who destroy or fail (Caesar the lightning, Pompey the shadow of a name, 1.135–157), and inverts the underworld book with Erictho's necromancy (6.507–830). The gods backed the winning cause, Cato the losing one (1.128).

  4. Which literary targets does the Satyricon mock, and what kind of scene is Trimalchio's dinner?
    Answer

    Epic (Encolpius pursued by Priapus as Ulysses by Neptune, 139.2), Greek romance, the declamation schools (1–2) and Lucan, through Eumolpus' Civil War with its restored gods (119–124). The dinner (26.7–78) parodies the philosophical banquet: staged courses, talk of money and funerals, and a rehearsed funeral at the end.

  5. What is Juvenal's stated programme, and how have Highet and Braund read the speaker?
    Answer

    Indignation makes his verse (1.79), but he attacks only the dead (1.170–171). Highet (1954) read the satires as autobiography; Braund (1988), after Anderson, as a constructed persona that moves from anger to irony across the books.

  6. How does Martial define his poetry against mythological verse?
    Answer

    Readers of Oedipus, Thyestes and Medea read only monsters, while his page "tastes of man" (10.4.10): the city's patrons, clients, legacy-hunters and dinners, ending on a sting. He defended his obscenity as a playful page from a decent life (1.4.8).

  7. How does each Flavian epic poet answer Virgil?
    Answer

    Valerius makes the Argo the start of a passage of empire that leads towards Rome and models Medea's love on Dido's. Statius displaces civil war into the Theban myth, with Furies and helpless gods, and ends with Theseus enforcing burial (books 8 and 12). Silius puts Virgil's divine machinery into Livy's war: Juno avenges Dido through Hannibal.

  8. How do Tacitus and Suetonius pass judgement differently?
    Answer

    Tacitus judges by arrangement and innuendo, giving the hostile verdict on Augustus more length and the last word (Annals 1.9–10) and closing on an epigram. Suetonius sorts each life by categories rather than time (Augustus 9) and lets the classification of virtues and vices, backed by quoted documents, carry the verdict.

  9. How is Cupid and Psyche connected to the rest of the Golden Ass, and what do Swahn and Fehling disagree about?
    Answer

    Psyche's forbidden curiosity mirrors Lucius', and a goddess saves both; the tale, absent from the Greek Ass, is one of Apuleius' additions. Swahn (1955) took it as the earliest written version of an international folktale; Fehling (1977) argued that Apuleius made it up and the folktales derive from him.

  10. How did Jerome and Augustine carry classical Latin into the Middle Ages?
    Answer

    Jerome's Gospel revision and Old Testament translation from the Hebrew became the Vulgate, the work of a man who dreamt he was condemned as a Ciceronian (Letters 22.30). Augustine's Confessions show a convert formed by Cicero's Hortensius and Virgil's Dido, so the classical schoolroom survived inside the books that renounced it.

Carry forward

  1. Imperial literature is a conversation with the Augustan classics, not a decline from them: Lucan, Valerius, Statius and Silius answer the Aeneid, the satirists rework Lucilius and Horace, and Petronius parodies epic and the critics of his own day.
  2. Under a princeps writing works by indirection: praise that may be irony, attacks kept for the dead, civil war displaced into myth, and history that judges by arrangement. Ask of each text what its author could safely say, and how he said the rest.
  3. The forms this period made, the comic novel, the epigram with a sting, biography by categories, the encyclopaedia and Quintilian's canon, together with the Christian Latin of Jerome and Augustine, are what the Middle Ages and the Renaissance inherited alongside Virgil.

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on Latin literature under the emperors, AD 14 to c. 200, with a coda on late antiquity. Cover: the 'Silver Latin' label and why to drop it; Seneca's tragedies (deep dive module 13.5 takes his life and philosophy); Lucan's anti-epic on the civil war; Petronius' Satyricon and Trimalchio's dinner; Persius and Juvenal; Martial; the Flavian epic poets (Statius' Thebaid and Silvae, Silius Italicus' Punica, Valerius Flaccus' Argonautica), whom module 7.2 places at court; the elder and younger Pliny; Quintilian on the orator; Tacitus as historian and stylist; Suetonius and the biographical tradition; Apuleius' Golden Ass as the one complete Latin novel; and a short coda on late Latin (Ausonius, Claudian, Ammianus, Jerome's Vulgate, Augustine's Confessions) as the bridge to the Middle Ages. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 10 · Literature, myth-making and reception · 10.3 · 2,844 words

Reading Roman art and architecture

The inheritance: an Etruscan plan and a Greek grammarThe republican portrait: verism and the ancestorsGreek statues in Roman settings: what "Roman copy" meansReading historical reliefPainted walls and mosaic floorsConcrete, arch and domeThe imperial portrait and its erasureSarcophagi: myth for the deadLate antique style: change, not declineSelf-testCarry forward

The inheritance: an Etruscan plan and a Greek grammar

Roman art was assembled from borrowed parts. Etruria gave the temple (module 1.2): a high podium, a frontal stair and a deep porch with columns only at the front, the form Vitruvius calls Tuscan (4.7). Pliny reports Varro's claim that the Greek modellers and painters Damophilus and Gorgasus decorated the temple of Ceres, dedicated by tradition in 493 BC, and that before it everything in Roman temples was Tuscan (Natural History 35.154): an antiquarian's claim, made some four and a half centuries later. Greece gave the orders, sculpture and painting, whose grammar Greek module 9.1 sets out.

The Roman synthesis put Greek columns on the Etruscan podium. The temple of Portunus in the Forum Boarium, of about 100 BC, is raised and frontal, its Ionic columns free only in the porch and engaged round the cella; beside it a round temple in Pentelic marble is a Greek building on Roman ground. Velleius makes Metellus Macedonicus' temple of Jupiter Stator, built after 146 BC, the first of marble in Rome (1.11.5). Rome added the plain Tuscan column and the Composite capital, Ionic volutes over Corinthian acanthus, whose earliest prominent surviving use is on the Arch of Titus.

The bronze Capitoline Wolf, long the textbook Etruscan casting, warns against dating on style alone: module 1.4 gives the case for the eleventh or twelfth century AD.

The republican portrait: verism and the ancestors

The portrait that looks most Roman is the head of an old man, bald, furrowed and hollow-cheeked, which modern scholars call veristic. It is a claim more than a likeness: age, toil and severity, the virtues of a man who has held office. Most such heads date to the first century BC, and freedmen soon borrowed the manner for the grave reliefs of husband and wife described in module 9.3.

The ancestors explain why a face mattered. The funeral masks, and Flower's argument that they were made in life, are module 2.4's. The Barberini Togatus in the Centrale Montemartini, of the last decade BC, shows the custom in marble: a man in a toga holds the portrait busts of two ancestors. His own head is ancient but not the statue's. He claims descent as the funeral did, by displaying faces.

Where sources disagree. A. N. Zadoks-Josephus Jitta (1932) and H. Drerup (1980) derived verism from the ancestral masks. Gisela Richter (Journal of Roman Studies, 1955) credited Greek sculptors working for Roman patrons, and R. R. R. Smith (Journal of Roman Studies, 1981) read the style as a Greek artistic response to a new kind of foreign patron. Chronology is the difficulty: the masks were displayed for generations before the style appears, so they cannot by themselves explain why it arose in the first century BC.

Greek statues in Roman settings: what "Roman copy" means

Rome met Greek art first as plunder: Marcellus, Paullus and Verres are modules 4.3, 4.4 and 5.3. Velleius' Mummius warned the contractors shipping the masterpieces of Corinth that if they lost any they would have to supply new ones (1.13.4): a Roman who could not tell an original from a replacement. A market followed. Cicero had Atticus buy statues suited to a gymnasium for his villa at Tusculum (Letters to Atticus 1.8–1.10), and scolded Fadius Gallus for buying him Bacchants and a Mars, useless to a man of peace (Letters to Friends 7.23).

Greek module 9.1 explains how Roman marbles preserve lost bronzes; the bronze Boxer in the Palazzo Massimo, a Hellenistic original found on the Quirinal, shows what the marbles lost. The Roman side adds four points. Versions changed scale, material and setting, chosen for the room. Greek bodies took Roman heads. Workshops made new works in old styles: Pasiteles wrote five books on famous works (Pliny 36.39–40), and his pupil Stephanus signed an athlete in the manner of four centuries before. And colossal versions furnished imperial buildings. The Farnese Hercules from the Baths of Caracalla (module 7.4) is signed by Glykon of Athens after a Lysippan type; the Farnese Bull is usually taken as a version of the group of Zethus, Amphion and Dirce by Apollonius and Tauriscus that Pliny saw in Asinius Pollio's collection (36.34). For a Roman patron a type was a word in a vocabulary, used in a sentence of his own.

Reading historical relief

Greek public sculpture told myths; Roman relief told what Romans had done. Its ancestor was the triumphal painting: Manius Valerius Messalla showed his Sicilian victory of 263 BC on the side of the Curia, and Lucius Hostilius Mancinus won a consulship by explaining his painting of Carthage under siege to the crowd (Pliny, Natural History 35.22–23).

The Ara Pacis (module 6.2 for its figures) takes the procession of the Parthenon frieze (Greek module 9.1) and makes the marchers a living family. Figures in front are cut deep and those behind shallow, so that a crowd stands in a few centimetres of marble; inside, the walls carve the wooden fence of the ritual enclosure hung with garlands and ox skulls, a rite turned to stone. The Arch of Titus (module 7.2) shows in its passage the spoils of Jerusalem carried through a gate seen at an angle, and Titus in his chariot crowned by Victory. The procession swings into and out of the plane, and Franz Wickhoff (Die Wiener Genesis, 1895) made this illusionism his proof that Roman art was not decadent Greek art. In the vault an eagle carries Titus to heaven.

The columns. Trajan's spiral frieze unrolls both Dacian wars up a column of a hundred Roman feet, in 155 scenes by Conrad Cichorius' numbering. Marching, building, sacrifice and speeches outnumber battles, and the emperor is the hinge of each episode (modules 7.3 and 9.2 for its value as evidence). The column of Marcus, finished by 193, keeps the form and changes the tone: deeper cutting and drilled shadows that carry further, an emperor more often frontal, villages burned and prisoners beheaded. The Arch of Septimius Severus (module 7.4) maps the Parthian campaigns on four panels in stacked registers seen from above, like the battle paintings Herodian says Severus sent to Rome (3.9.12). On his arch at Lepcis Magna he and his sons ride in a chariot facing straight out: the frontal ruler of late antiquity has arrived.

Read any such relief in four steps. Find the emperor: he is largest, central or frontal, and the action turns on him. Name the ritual, since most scenes belong to a small repertory. Separate persons from personifications: Victory, Roma, Virtus or the Genius of the Senate turn an event into a statement of value. Then look for recut heads.
