The shape was a pyramid: of six praetors a year, at most two could reach the consulship. The extension of commands beyond the year, which turned the pyramid into a base for generals, is deep dive module 11.2.

Voting by centuries and by tribes

Consuls, praetors and censors were elected by the centuriate assembly on the Campus Martius; its 193 centuries and their Servian legend are module 1.5. At some date after 241, when the thirty-fifth tribe was created, it was reformed: Livy notes that the centuries of his day, doubled with the tribes into juniors and seniors, no longer matched Servius' figures (1.43.12). The first class now had seventy centuries, a senior and a junior for each tribe. With the eighteen equestrian centuries it held 88 of 193, nine short of the 97 that made a majority.

The order was fixed. A century of the first class chosen by lot, the praerogativa, voted first and its result was announced. Romans treated it as an omen (Cicero, On Divination 1.103; Pro Murena 38), and Cicero claims that no candidate who carried it had failed to become consul at that election or the next (Pro Plancio 49). Then came the rest of the first class, then the six old equestrian centuries, then the second class; Cicero describes the sequence for an election of 44 (Philippics 2.82). Each century voted for as many candidates as there were places; a candidate was declared elected on reaching 97 centuries, and voting stopped once every place was filled. Cicero praised the design for ensuring that the greatest number did not have the greatest power (On the Republic 2.39).

The tribal assembly, under a consul or praetor, elected quaestors, curule aediles and some military tribunes; the plebs alone, under a tribune, elected tribunes and plebeian aediles. The thirty-five tribes counted equally, and thirty-one were rural. A rural tribe's vote was cast by whichever members came to Rome, chiefly men who could afford the journey, while freedmen were kept to the four urban tribes. In legislation the tribes voted in turn until eighteen made a majority, as at Octavius' deposition in 133 (module 5.1); in elections they probably voted together, results being read out in an order drawn by lot (Lily Ross Taylor, Roman Voting Assemblies, 1966). Voting was oral until the ballot laws, the Gabinian of 139 for elections and the Cassian of 137 for most trials (Cicero, On the Laws 3.35–37).

Where sources disagree. Livy says the vote hardly ever descended to the lowest classes (1.43.11), and Cicero treats the weighting as decisive (On the Republic 2.39). Alexander Yakobson ("Petitio et largitio", 1992; Elections and Electioneering in Rome, 1999) argued that in contested elections the first class split among several candidates for several places, so the count often ran into the middle classes, which is why candidates courted humbler voters.

The Senate: authority without legal power

The Senate of about three hundred was enrolled by the censors, in practice from former magistrates (module 3.1). It met only when a consul, praetor or tribune summoned it; it could not legislate, elect or judge, and its decrees bound no one in law. A senatus consultum was advice, typically that the consuls act if it seemed good to them. The presiding magistrate asked opinions in order of rank, the leader of the Senate first, then the former consuls and on down; Varro wrote a handbook of this procedure for Pompey (Gellius 14.7). A tribune's veto reduced a decree to an auctoritas, recorded but without force (Caelius in Cicero, Letters to Friends 8.8).

The leader, princeps senatus, was the man the censors placed first on the roll. Custom gave the place to the earliest surviving ex-censor. In 209 the censor Sempronius Tuditanus, who had drawn the lot to choose, set custom aside for Fabius Maximus, the first man of the state, he said, as even Hannibal would admit (Livy 27.11.9–12). Scipio Africanus followed; Marcus Aemilius Lepidus was chosen by six successive pairs of censors (Periochae 48); Appius Claudius Pulcher held the place in 133 (module 5.1). The leader had only the first word, but in a house that decided by moving to one side or the other, the first word framed the question.

Practice gave the Senate what law did not. It assigned provinces and armies, extended commands, controlled the treasury, received embassies and handled prodigies; Polybius' account of its powers is module 4.5. Its decree on the Bacchanalia in 186 reached into allied communities across Italy (module 2.5). Mommsen called its auctoritas more than advice and less than command, advice one could not ignore (Römisches Staatsrecht, 1871–88). Magistrates complied because they held office for a year and sat in the Senate for life, because it voted the money, supplies, extensions and honours they needed, and because their peers' judgement was the tribunal that counted.

Nobles, new men and the pursuit of glory

The nobiles were families with a consul among their ancestors (Gelzer's definition; module 3.1), a matter of repute, not law. A man with no senatorial forebears who entered the Senate was a novus homo, a new man; one who reached the consulship was rare. Cato, consul in 195, called himself new to office but old in ancestral deeds of courage (Plutarch, Cato Maior 1). Sallust, writing in the 40s, has the nobility pass the consulship from hand to hand, a new man however distinguished being thought unworthy and almost polluted (Jugurtha 63.6–7); Marius' reply is in module 5.2.

The counts are less closed than the rhetoric. Keith Hopkins and Graham Burton (Death and Renewal, 1983) found that over the last two centuries of the Republic only about 40 per cent of consuls had consular fathers and only a third had consular sons. The nobility dominated the top office without reproducing itself in it: families dropped out as others rose, and each generation competed afresh.

The currency was glory (gloria, laus), office (honos) and standing (dignitas), won in the state's service and displayed before the people. In 221 Quintus Metellus said in his father's eulogy that his father had achieved the ten greatest goods that wise men seek: to be foremost warrior, best orator and bravest general, to win great victories under his own auspices, hold the highest office, show the greatest wisdom, be the leading senator, gain wealth honourably, leave many children and be the most famous man in the state (Pliny, Natural History 7.139–140). The epitaph of Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Hispanus, praetor in 139, says he added to his family's virtues, strove to match his father's deeds and kept his ancestors' praise, and ends stirpem nobilitavit honor, "office ennobled my stock" (CIL I² 15). The funeral with masks and eulogies is modules 2.4 and 4.5. The ethic also demanded restraint. Annual office, colleagues, ages and intervals spread the honours, and sumptuary laws on banquets, the Orchian of 182 and the Fannian of 161, limited display (Macrobius, Saturnalia 3.17). The nobility rationed glory so that no member could monopolise it.

Patrons and clients

Tradition made patronage as old as the city: Dionysius has Romulus give the plebeians to patricians as clients (2.9–10; module 3.1), and the Twelve Tables cursed a patron who cheated his client. By the second century the bond took many forms. Freedmen owed duties to their former owners by law; conquered cities and provinces had patrons in the Senate; humbler men sought a great man's help in court and attended his morning greeting (salutatio). Plutarch says Gaius Herennius refused to testify against Marius in 116 because custom excused patrons from witnessing against clients (Marius 5). The canvassing handbook ascribed to Quintus Cicero, of 64 BC, tells the candidate to mobilise friends, clients, freedmen and tribes.

The older modern model built politics on these ties. Matthias Gelzer (Die Nobilität der römischen Republik, 1912) explained noble power by networks of personal obligation; Friedrich Münzer (Römische Adelsparteien und Adelsfamilien, 1920) and H. H. Scullard (Roman Politics 220–150 BC, 1951) turned them into family alliances that delivered blocs of votes. Three doubts weigh against it. Clients had several patrons, and patrons competed for them; after 139 a written ballot could not be checked; and great men with great followings lost elections often enough for Valerius Maximus to give such defeats a chapter (7.5).

Where sources disagree. Gelzer and Scullard read clientship as the machinery of the vote. P. A. Brunt ("Clientela", in The Fall of the Roman Republic and Related Essays, 1988) found little evidence that clients voted to order, the word covering loose and overlapping attachments; Millar and Henrik Mouritsen (Plebs and Politics in the Late Roman Republic, 2001) both rejected the clientela model, from opposite directions, Millar for a sovereign people, Mouritsen for an electorate too small and propertied to need herding.

Canvassing, bribery and the laws against it

Ambitus, "going round", meant canvassing before it meant a crime. The candidate (candidatus) whitened his toga, toured the Forum with escorts, greeted voters by name with a slave name-caller (nomenclator) at his ear and courted the tribes. Livy, writing three to four centuries later, records a law of 432 against whitening clothes for candidacy (4.25.13) and the Poetelian law of 358 against new men touring markets and country gatherings (7.15.12–13). Gifts were the danger. In 181 the consuls, on the Senate's authority, carried a law on bribery (Livy 40.19.11), and another followed in 159 (Periochae 47). The ballot cut both ways: it freed the voter from his patron's eye and from the briber's. Later laws, the Calpurnian of 67 and Cicero's own of 63, mark an escalation that the Pro Murena shows at its height.

Where sources disagree. Polybius, writing about 150, says that at Rome bribery for office carried the death penalty, unlike Carthage (6.56.4); yet laws of 181 (Livy 40.19.11) and 159 (Periochae 47) show the problem already real, and no execution for it is recorded. Yakobson (1999) reads the growth of bribery as proof that ordinary votes were worth buying; Mouritsen (2001) as proof that poorer citizens had little other reason to come and vote.

The contio

A contio was a meeting called by a magistrate to address the people, with no vote. The augural writer Messalla, quoted by Gellius, distinguishes holding a contio, speaking to the people without a proposal, from dealing with the people, asking them to order or forbid by vote (13.16). The convening magistrate decided who spoke; a private citizen addressed the crowd only if brought forward by him. Every bill was posted for three market days and argued in contiones before the vote, so argument happened in the contio and the assembly, once divided into its units, only voted. Magistrates also used it to report news, publish decrees and deliver funeral eulogies.

The setting was the Rostra. Cicero and Varro credit the tribune Gaius Licinius Crassus, in 145, with first turning from the Comitium to face the open Forum (On Friendship 96; On Agriculture 1.2.9); Plutarch gives the gesture to Gaius Gracchus (Gaius Gracchus 5). The contio could change outcomes: in 200 the centuries rejected war with Philip V almost unanimously, and the consul Sulpicius Galba carried the second vote after addressing a contio (Livy 31.6–8; module 4.4 tells the episode). Its late-Republican uses, Clodius included, are deep dive module 11.3.

Where sources disagree. Francisco Pina Polo (Contra arma verbis, 1996) and Robert Morstein-Marx (Mass Oratory and Political Power in the Late Roman Republic, 2004) treat the contio as the arena where opinion formed and the elite had to persuade. Mouritsen (2001) argues that audiences were small and, until the late Republic, largely propertied; Karl-Joachim Hölkeskamp (Reconstructing the Roman Republic, 2010) reads the meeting as a ritual that displayed the hierarchy of speaker above hearers.

Was Rome a democracy?

Fergus Millar attacked the orthodoxy of Gelzer, Münzer and Syme, an oligarchy managing its assemblies through clientship and family alliance, in "The Political Character of the Classical Roman Republic, 200–151 B.C." (1984), a sequel on 150–90 (1986) and The Crowd in Rome in the Late Republic (1998). Only the people could pass laws, and every law was passed by them; office came only by popular election, competitive and uncertain; the Senate had no legislative power; and politicians spent their lives addressing crowds. Rome, he concluded, belonged among ancient democracies, a direct democracy of its own kind. The second century supplies his cases: the war vote of 200; tribunes jailing the consuls of 151 over a harsh levy (Periochae 48); the people's insistence on electing Scipio Aemilianus consul for 147 when he stood, under age, for the aedileship, which made the Senate have the Villian law suspended for a year (Appian, Punica 112; Periochae 50); and the ballot laws of 139 and 137.

John North ("Democratic Politics in Republican Rome", 1990) welcomed the attack on what he called the "frozen waste" theory of an inert electorate, but argued that popular choice became decisive only when the elite divided and offered alternatives, as the united nobility of the early second century seldom did. Mouritsen (2001) separated the people as an ideal from the crowds who came. He estimated that the Comitium held some 3,600 to 3,800 people and the Forum perhaps 10,000, and that electoral assemblies seldom exceeded 10,000, against a census of 337,022 citizens in 164 (Periochae 46): sovereignty exercised by a self-selected few, mostly propertied, was no democracy. Hölkeskamp (2010; German 2004) judged the question unfruitful and studied instead a political culture of consensus, in which the people's votes, applause and presence at rituals confirmed a hierarchy of merit embodied by the nobility. Morstein-Marx (2004) took up Millar's oratory: the people were arbiters the elite had to persuade, but since every speaker claimed to serve them, they heard no real alternative and judged whose claim was credible. Most historians now stand between the poles: the people held real powers, used them seldom and on terms the elite set, and the system held while the nobility agreed. What changed after 133 is deep dive modules 11.3 and 11.8.

Where sources disagree. Polybius found a democratic element in the people's control of honours, punishments, laws and war (6.14). Sallust, writing a century later of the years after 146, has affairs at home and abroad run at the will of a few, who held the treasury, provinces, offices and triumphs (Jugurtha 41.7). Syme sided with Sallust, holding that an oligarchy lurks behind the façade of every government (The Roman Revolution, 1939); Millar wrote against Syme, his own teacher, and for Polybius (module 4.5).

Self-test

  1. What did the lex Villia annalis of 180 do, and what about it is inferred rather than attested?
    Answer

    It fixed the ages at which each magistracy could be sought and held (Livy 40.44.1). The figures, usually given as a two-year interval between curule offices and minimum ages of about 39 for the praetorship and 42 for the consulship, are reconstructed from known careers, and are best attested only for Sulla's law of 81.

  2. Why did the voting order of the reformed centuriate assembly matter beyond its arithmetic?
    Answer

    The first class and the equites held 88 centuries, nine short of the 97 needed, so the second class decided close contests and the poorest rarely voted. The praerogativa, voting first by lot, was announced and read as an omen, so it swayed those who followed (Pro Plancio 49; On Divination 1.103).

  3. How did the tribal assembly favour the propertied when every tribe counted equally?
    Answer

    Thirty-one of the thirty-five tribes were rural, and their votes were cast by members present in Rome, chiefly men who could afford to travel; freedmen were confined to the four urban tribes.

  4. On what did the Senate's authority rest, if not on law, and what did its leader contribute?
    Answer

    On practice and interest: magistrates were senators for life, and the Senate controlled provinces, money, extensions of command and honours, so its advice could not safely be ignored; Mommsen called it more than advice and less than command. The princeps senatus spoke first and so framed the debate; in 209 Fabius was chosen by merit over custom (Livy 27.11.9–12).

  5. How do Sallust's picture of the nobility and Hopkins and Burton's counts differ?
    Answer

    Sallust has the nobles hand the consulship among themselves and treat new men as polluted (Jugurtha 63.6–7). Hopkins and Burton found only about 40 per cent of consuls with consular fathers and a third with consular sons: a dominant but self-renewing elite, in constant competition.

  6. What do the Metellus eulogy and the Hispanus epitaph show about aristocratic values, and how was competition kept within bounds?
    Answer

    Both measure a life by office, military glory, fame and the matching of ancestors (Pliny, Natural History 7.139–140; CIL I² 15). Annual and collegiate office, the age and interval rules of 180, and sumptuary and bribery laws rationed glory among the nobility.

  7. Why do modern historians doubt that clientship decided elections?
    Answer

    Clients had several patrons who competed for them; the ballot after 139 hid the vote; and great men often lost (Valerius Maximus 7.5). Brunt (1988) found little evidence of clients voting to order, and Millar and Mouritsen rejected the model from opposite sides.

  8. What does the sequence of bribery laws suggest, and why is Polybius 6.56.4 hard to square with it?
    Answer

    Laws in 181 and 159 show electoral gifts were already a problem, and the later laws of 67 and 63 an escalation. Polybius claims bribery for office was a capital crime at Rome, yet no execution is recorded and the repeated legislation implies the practice persisted.

  9. What was a contio, and what does the war vote of 200 show about it?
    Answer

    A meeting summoned by a magistrate to address the people without a vote (Gellius 13.16), where every bill was argued and only invited citizens spoke. In 200 the centuries rejected war with Philip, but after Galba's speech in a contio a second vote carried it (Livy 31.6–8): persuasion before the vote could reverse a result.

  10. State Millar's case and the replies of North and Mouritsen.
    Answer

    Millar: the people alone passed laws and elected magistrates, the Senate had no legislative power, and oratory to crowds was central, so Rome was a kind of direct democracy. North: popular choice mattered only when the elite divided. Mouritsen: assemblies of seldom more than 10,000, mostly propertied, against a census of over 300,000, made formal sovereignty no democracy.

Carry forward

  1. The Republic gave formal power to the people and structured its use: weighted units, a fixed voting order, and a presiding magistrate who controlled proposals and speakers. Ask of every later crisis not who held the powers but who could use them.
  2. The Senate ruled by authority and the nobility by competition policed among peers: age rules, collegiality, sumptuary and bribery laws were the aristocracy's self-discipline. When individuals escaped it through long commands, armies or popular tribunates, the informal restraints failed, which is the story of this deep dive.
  3. The democracy debate turns on which evidence counts: formal rules (Millar), numbers present (Mouritsen), elite unity (North), ritual and consensus (Hölkeskamp), persuasion (Morstein-Marx). Test each later episode, from the Gracchi to Caesar, against all five.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1 (sampled)

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on how the Roman Republic actually worked at its height, c. 200 to 133 BC, extending modules 3.1 and 4.5. Cover: the magistracies and the cursus honorum after the lex Villia annalis of 180 BC; elections in the centuriate and tribal assemblies, the voting order and what it did to the result; the Senate's authority without legal power, its decrees and the leader of the Senate; nobles and new men, and the competitive aristocratic ethic of glory and standing; patronage and clientship and the modern doubts about how far they decided votes; electoral bribery and the laws against it; the role of the contio; and the debate begun by Fergus Millar in the 1980s over whether Rome was a kind of democracy, with the replies of North, Mouritsen, Hölkeskamp and Morstein-Marx. Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 11 · Deep dive I: the fall of the Republic · 11.2 · 2,874 words

Generals and their armies

Volunteers, levies and the poorLong commands, rich provincesVeterans and the landThe oath, the donative and the general's nameFour marches on RomeCaesar and his legionsImperator: acclamation and victoryWas it a client army?Self-testCarry forward

Volunteers, levies and the poor

Module 5.2 sets out what Marius did in 107 (Sallust, Jugurtha 86) and why historians doubt it was a reform; module 9.2 follows the levy into the Principate. The question here is political. A soldier who owned nothing had nothing to go back to, so he depended on whoever could give him land or money at discharge, and a general who could give it held him. Appian put it most sharply, explaining the indiscipline of the armies of 41: their generals were not regularly chosen, their men were not raised by the ancestral levy, and they served the individuals who had gathered them rather than the public; desertion, once unpardonable, was now rewarded, and the generals knew that their authority rested on donatives, not on law (Civil Wars 5.17).

That chain, from proletarian recruits to personal armies, is Emilio Gabba's (articles of 1949 and 1951, in English as Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies, 1976). Its first link is weaker than it looks. Magistrates went on levying citizens throughout the century: Caesar enrolled two new legions in Cisalpine Gaul in 57 (Gallic War 2.2), Pompey swore in men there as consul in 55 (6.1), and in January 49 the Senate decreed a levy throughout Italy (Civil War 1.6). The recruits were mostly countrymen, not the urban plebs of deep dive module 11.3.

Where sources disagree. Sallust's volunteers of 107 and Appian's armies "not drawn from the enrolment" of 41 underlie Gabba's proletarian army of volunteers. P. A. Brunt (Italian Manpower, 1971) answered that the levy remained the normal way of raising legions throughout the first century, now falling mostly on the poor. Arthur Keaveney (The Army in the Roman Revolution, 2007) warns against overestimating the soldiers below the property qualification, whose lowering he treats as a long process, not a Marian break.

Long commands, rich provinces

An army raised for a season belonged to the Republic; an army kept together for years by one man became his. Sulla spent 87–83 in the East, outlawed by the government at Rome (module 5.2), and bought his men while he waited. Wintering in Asia after Dardanus, he billeted them on the cities, each host paying his soldier sixteen drachmas a day and feeding him and his friends, a military tribune fifty drachmas and two suits of clothes (Plutarch, Sulla 25.2). Sallust says that Sulla, to bind the army of Asia to himself, indulged it against ancestral custom, and that there it first learned to make love and drink and to covet statues, paintings and plate (Catiline 11.5–6).

The young Pompey's army in Africa formed the same bond within months. Ordered by Sulla to send it home, his soldiers refused to forsake their general and told him not to trust the tyrant (Plutarch, Pompey 13). Lucullus, harsh with his men, lost his army to mutiny (Plutarch, Lucullus 33.2, 34; module 5.3). From 67 the great commands ran for years: three for Pompey against the pirates, five for Caesar in Gaul and five more after Luca, five for Pompey's Spains, which he held through legates while staying outside Rome (modules 5.3 and 5.4). A province with legions was a base where a proconsul recruited, paid and rewarded beyond the reach of the courts. Caesar raised legions at his own expense beyond those the state gave him, one of them, the Alauda, from Transalpine Gauls, whom he later made citizens (Suetonius, Julius 24.2), and he doubled the legionary's pay for good (26.3).

Legions were also counters between dynasts. In 50 the Senate ordered each to give up a legion for a Parthian war; Pompey reclaimed the one he had lent, so Caesar lost two, and both were kept in Italy (Gallic War 8.54–55, by Hirtius). Appius, who brought them back, told Pompey that Caesar's army would come over to him (Plutarch, Pompey 57); nine years together had made it Caesar's.

Veterans and the land

The Republic paid its soldiers by the campaign and owed them nothing at discharge. Land came, when it came, from a measure forced through each time by a tribune, a consul or a dictator, usually against senatorial resistance: Saturninus' allotments for Marius' men and Sulla's colonies on confiscated land (module 5.2); Pompey's veterans, dismissed at Brundisium in 62 and kept waiting until Caesar's law of 59 (modules 5.3 and 5.4); Caesar's colonies and the triumvirs' eighteen towns (Appian 4.3; modules 5.4 and 5.5). Appian states the consequence for 41: the leaders needed the soldiers to keep their power, and the soldiers needed the leaders' rule to keep their land (Civil Wars 5.13). Brunt ("The Army and the Land in the Roman Revolution", Journal of Roman Studies 1962) made this the thread of the whole century: the veterans, like the Gracchan settlers of module 5.1, were countrymen who wanted land of their own, and men of that class, "with arms in their hands", brought the Republic down.

Settlement bred its own trouble. At Pompeii Sulla's colonists were still quarrelling with the old citizens over walks and votes when Cicero defended the colony's founder, Publius Sulla, in 62 (Pro Sulla 60–62). In Etruria some had spent the last of their plunder and joined Manlius in 63 (Sallust, Catiline 28.4); Cicero said they would need Sulla raised from the dead to clear their debts (Against Catiline 2.20). Caesar gave his veterans land in scattered plots so that no owner was dispossessed (Suetonius, Julius 38.1); the triumvirs dispossessed whole towns. Augustus' boast that he was the first and only founder of soldiers' colonies within living memory to pay for the land (Res Gestae 16.1) names what the Republic had seldom done: Caesar's law of 59 bought from willing sellers at the census value (Dio 38.1.4); his cash discharge and military treasury are module 6.4.

Where sources disagree. Cicero (Against Catiline 2.20) and Sallust (Catiline 28.4) show Sullan veterans ruined within twenty years, and Gabba read the soldiers' demand for land as a demand for capital they could turn into money. Cicero's picture is a consul's invective, and Brunt (1962) rejected Gabba's reading: the veterans were countrymen seeking a secure living from land they owned. Keaveney (2007) doubts again that most veterans wanted farms, noting how many re-enlisted.

The oath, the donative and the general's name

The sacramentum was sworn to the commander in person, not to his office, and had to be sworn again when commanders changed (module 9.2 gives its Republican form). Because it bound men to a man, it went where he sent it: Pompey lent Caesar the men he had sworn in Cisalpine Gaul as consul and ordered them to report (Gallic War 6.1). In civil war it changed hands with the army. At Corfinium Caesar had Domitius' captured soldiers swear to him (Civil War 1.23); at Ilerda, as his men fraternised with Caesar's, Petreius made them swear afresh not to desert or betray the army and its commanders (1.76), an oath renewed because the first no longer held. Sulla's veterans in 83 swore of their own accord to stand by him and to harm Italy only on his orders, and offered him their savings, which he refused (Plutarch, Sulla 27.3).

Money spoke more plainly. Caesar paid his men 2,000 sesterces each at the start of the civil war and, at the triumphs of 46, 24,000 more praedae nomine, as booty (Suetonius, Julius 38.1): nearly twenty-seven years of a legionary's pay at his doubled rate of 225 denarii (module 6.4). In 44 the dynasts bid against each other. Octavian paid Caesar's veterans 500 denarii a man (Cicero, Letters to Atticus 16.8; module 5.5); Antony offered the Macedonian legions at Brundisium 100 drachmas, was laughed at, and executed men chosen by lot from the tribunes' lists of troublemakers (Appian, Civil Wars 3.43), and two of those legions went over to his rival. Caesar called his men commilitones, fellow-soldiers (Julius 67.2), a courtesy Augustus dropped (module 6.4). In 32 the oath of all Italy to Octavian (module 5.5) made the soldier's bond a political one; Anton von Premerstein (Vom Werden und Wesen des Prinzipats, 1937) derived the Principate itself from that oath, read as clientship and military allegiance extended to the whole citizen body.

Four marches on Rome

YearCommander and armyWhat moved the soldiersSources
88Sulla, consul; six legions at Nolathe eastern war and its plunder about to pass to Marius and other soldiers; Rome to be freed from tyrantsAppian 1.57; module 5.2
83–82Sulla, declared a public enemy; five Italian legions and 6,000 horse, about 40,000 in all (Appian 1.79)eastern wealth; a voluntary oath; vengeance promised on the guilty onlyPlutarch, Sulla 27; Appian 1.77
49Caesar, proconsul; the Thirteenth at Ravenna, then the Gallic armythe tribunes' veto overridden; the general's standing; rewards rumouredCaesar, Civil War 1.7; Suetonius, Julius 33
43Octavian, propraetor; eight legions (Appian 3.88)the Senate's slights and unpaid bounties; the consulship for their generalAppian 3.86–94; Dio 46.42–46; Suetonius, Augustus 26

Each army was given two reasons, one material and one constitutional. Sulla's officers in 88, all but one quaestor, refused to follow (module 5.2). His letter to the Senate from the East, in 85 or 84, promised vengeance on the guilty and no complaint against other citizens, old or new (Appian 1.77); he crossed in 83 and took Rome in November 82. At Ravenna in 49 Caesar told the Thirteenth that the tribunes' veto, which even Sulla had left free, had been crushed by arms, and asked them to defend the reputation and standing of the commander under whom they had served for nine years; they shouted that they were ready to avenge the wrongs of their general and of the tribunes (Civil War 1.7). Suetonius adds that when Caesar, in tears, pointed to his ring, men at the back thought he had promised each of them a knight's ring and 400,000 sesterces (Julius 33). His chief legate, Labienus, went over to Pompey (Dio 41.4.3–4); no other senior officer is recorded as leaving him.

In 43 the order looked reversed. After Mutina the Senate rewarded only two legions and sent its envoys to the troops past their commander; Octavian's centurions went to the Senate to demand the consulship for him, and when rebuffed the soldiers demanded to be led on Rome (Appian 3.86–88). Dio says Octavian had his soldiers take an oath, seemingly of their own motion, and then sent four hundred of them to the Senate (46.42); refused, one fetched his sword and said it would win the consulship if the senators would not (46.43). Suetonius makes him the centurion Cornelius, leader of the men sent to ask in the army's name (Augustus 26.1). The three legions in Rome went over against their commanders, one of whom, Cornutus, killed himself (Appian 3.92). Consul at nineteen, Octavian paid each man 2,500 drachmas from public funds and promised the rest (3.94). All three writers make the soldiers' voice his instrument.

Caesar and his legions

Caesar built the bond deliberately. At Vesontio in 58, with the army panicking before Ariovistus, he said he would march with the Tenth alone if no one else followed and make it his bodyguard, and when he mounted the Tenth on Gallic horses for a parley a soldier joked that he was making them knights (Gallic War 1.40–42). Suetonius says there was no mutiny in the ten years of the Gallic war (Julius 69), and in 49 every centurion offered to equip a horseman from his savings and the soldiers to serve without pay or rations (68.1).

Civil war, with its clemency and little plunder, tested the bond twice. At Placentia in 49 the Ninth mutinied, complaining that the war was being dragged out and that the five minae promised at Brundisium were unpaid; Caesar threatened to decimate it, reduced the threat to 120 ringleaders and executed twelve chosen by lot (Appian, Civil Wars 2.47). Suetonius has him discharge the legion in disgrace and take it back only after pleas and punishment (Julius 69); Dio (41.26–35) and Lucan (Civil War 5.237–373) give him a speech. In 47 the legions in Campania, owed rewards promised after Pharsalus and kept beyond their term, refused to sail for Africa. They nearly killed Sallust, the future historian, sent to treat with them (Appian 2.92; Dio 42.52), killed two ex-praetors, Cosconius and Galba (Plutarch, Caesar 51), and marched on Rome. On the Campus Martius Caesar granted the discharge they demanded and addressed them as Quirites, citizens, not soldiers; they begged to follow him to Africa (Appian 2.93–94; Suetonius, Julius 70). Suetonius adds that he docked the most insubordinate a third of their booty and land.

Where sources disagree. Caesar's own narrative passes over Placentia, and Suetonius credits every recovery to his authority, not his indulgence (Julius 69–70); Appian (2.93–94) and Tacitus' Germanicus (Annals 1.42) make one word end the mutiny of 47. Dio has the mutineers kill two senators and enter Rome carrying their swords, and Caesar later rid himself of the boldest by spending them in Africa (42.52–55). Stefan Chrissanthos ("Caesar and the Mutiny of 47 B.C.", Journal of Roman Studies 2001) argued that Caesar, without loyal troops enough to crush so large a mutiny, gave way rather than prevailed.

Imperator: acclamation and victory

The army also conferred standing. After a victory soldiers hailed their commander imperator, and he kept the title until he triumphed or laid down his command. Tacitus calls it an old honour, the army's joy acclaiming a successful general, with several imperatores at once, and says that Junius Blaesus in AD 22 was the last outside the emperor's family to receive it (Annals 3.74). Acclamation opened the road to a triumph, whose rules and ritual are module 9.2. The soldiers marched in it and expected their share, and they could withhold their part: Pompey's army, paid less than it hoped, threatened to disrupt his African triumph until he said he would rather give it up than truckle to them (Plutarch, Pompey 14).

Victory became a title of rule. Sulla called himself Felix (module 5.2), and his coins of 84–83 showed two trophies with IMPER ITERVM, imperator for the second time (RRC 359). Caesar after Munda took Imperator as a permanent title (Dio 43.44.2; Suetonius, Julius 76.1), and Octavian made it his first name, Imperator Caesar (Ronald Syme, "Imperator Caesar: A Study in Nomenclature", Historia 1958). What soldiers shouted on the battlefield became the ruler's name, and the acclamation of armies, not the vote of the people, would make emperors (module 9.2). Augustus confined the triumph to his own house (module 6.4): a victorious general with an army was what he had been.

Was it a client army?

The modern argument turns on what bound soldiers to generals. Gabba's answer was need: proletarian volunteers whose only prospect was land became a military clientele, attached to their commander by economic interest alone. Brunt (1962, revised in The Fall of the Roman Republic and Related Essays, 1988) denied that the soldiers were clients. Their loyalty was conditional; the expectation of future rewards counted for more than gratitude for past ones, and the hope of plunder made them readier to follow generals into civil war. Erich Gruen (The Last Generation of the Roman Republic, 1974) added that service did not alienate soldiers from the Republic, since they followed a consul or proconsul as the state's lawful officer; his wider case is deep dive module 11.8.

Keaveney (2007) moved the turning point from Marius to Sulla, who first made the army a political instrument. Regular armies, he argued, saw their commander as a magistrate, and patron and client fit only the private armies of the mid-first century. Soldiers were reluctant to fight fellow citizens, and their leverage lasted only while a rival commander existed to desert to; after Actium none did. Lukas de Blois (The Roman Army and Politics in the First Century before Christ, 1987, and an essay of 2000 on the military "middle cadre") looked to the officers, the centurions, tribunes and prefects through whom generals reached the ranks, and insisted that soldiers did not follow automatically: a commander had to keep his promises and justify himself to his men.

Where sources disagree. Appian's armies that served individuals rather than the public (5.17) support Gabba's clientele; the same Appian shows soldiers sending deputies to force Antony and Octavian to terms at Brundisium in 40 (5.64), the independent actors of Keaveney's account. Brunt's bargain and de Blois's officers explain the defections of 83, 49 and 43 better than gratitude does. Yet Pompey's veterans, dismissed in 62, went home quietly (Velleius 2.40.3) and waited three years for land, which no model of a client army predicts.

What survives of the client army is narrower than Gabba's model. The Republic never made discharge its own business, the oath bound men to a man, commands lasted years, and in civil war each side bid for the other's soldiers. The soldiers' price, more than their dependence, was what the Principate had to meet.

Self-test

  1. What did Appian say about the armies of 41, and why does it not prove that the legions after Marius were volunteers?
    Answer

    That their generals were not regularly chosen, their men were not raised by the ancestral levy, they served individuals rather than the public, and their generals' authority rested on donatives (Civil Wars 5.17). It describes the triumviral armies; levies continued throughout the century (Gallic War 2.2, 6.1; Civil War 1.6), and Brunt took the levy to be the normal method.

  2. How did Sulla bind the army of Asia to himself, and what does Pompey's African army show about the same bond?
    Answer

    He billeted it on the cities at sixteen drachmas a day per soldier and indulged it against ancestral custom (Plutarch, Sulla 25.2; Sallust, Catiline 11.5–6). Pompey's soldiers, ordered by Sulla to disband, refused to forsake their general (Pompey 13): a commander who rewarded his men could hold them against the government.

  3. Why was the veteran problem never solved under the Republic, and what does Augustus' claim in Res Gestae 16.1 reveal?
    Answer

    The state paid by the campaign and owed nothing at discharge, so each settlement had to be forced through by a tribune, a consul or a dictator, usually against senatorial resistance. Augustus' claim to be the first within living memory to pay for soldiers' land names what the Republic had seldom done: Caesar's law of 59 bought from willing sellers (Dio 38.1.4), but Sulla's and the triumvirs' colonies were made on confiscated land.

  4. Did veterans want farms or money? Give the ancient evidence and two modern positions.
    Answer

    Cicero (Against Catiline 2.20) and Sallust (Catiline 28.4) show Sullan colonists who spent their plunder and fell into debt, and Gabba read the demand for land as a demand for convertible capital. Brunt held that they were countrymen seeking a living from land of their own; Keaveney doubts that most wanted farms, given how many re-enlisted.

  5. Why did the soldier's oath fail to tie armies to the state?
    Answer

    It bound men to their commander, not his office, so it went with him: Pompey lent Caesar men sworn to himself (Gallic War 6.1). In civil war it changed hands with the army (Civil War 1.23) or had to be renewed to stop desertion (1.76), and Appian says desertion came to be rewarded (5.17).

  6. Compare how the armies of 88 and 49 were persuaded, and how their officers reacted.
    Answer

    Both were given a material motive and a legal cause: in 88 the threat to the eastern plunder and the claim to free Rome from tyrants; in 49 the overridden veto of the tribunes and the general's standing (Civil War 1.7), with rumoured rewards (Julius 33). In 88 all Sulla's officers but one quaestor refused to follow; in 49 Labienus is the only senior officer recorded as leaving Caesar.

  7. Who drove the march of 43, the soldiers or Octavian?
    Answer

    The soldiers appeared to: their centurions and envoys demanded the consulship, one threatening the Senate with his sword (Dio 46.43; Suetonius, Augustus 26.1). But Appian (3.87), Dio (46.42) and Suetonius all make Octavian the director, using the army's voice; the soldiers' reward was 2,500 drachmas a man from public funds (Appian 3.94).

  8. How did the mutinies of 49 and 47 end, and why is the record open to doubt?
    Answer

    At Placentia Caesar executed twelve of 120 ringleaders, chosen by lot (Appian 2.47); in 47 he granted the discharge and called the men Quirites, and they begged to follow him (Appian 2.93–94; Suetonius, Julius 70). Caesar's own narrative omits Placentia, Dio records two senators killed and the boldest later spent in Africa (42.52–55), and Chrissanthos argued that Caesar gave way rather than prevailed.

  9. What did salutation as imperator mean, and how did it become a title of rule?
    Answer

    An army hailed a victorious commander imperator, the first step towards a triumph, and several men could hold the title at once (Tacitus, Annals 3.74). Caesar made it a permanent title (Dio 43.44.2) and Octavian his first name, Imperator Caesar (Syme 1958); the acclamation of armies would make emperors.

  10. Set out the positions of Gabba, Brunt, Keaveney and de Blois on the client army.
    Answer

    Gabba: a proletarian clientele bound to its general by economic need. Brunt: not clients but countrymen whose loyalty was conditional on land and plunder. Keaveney: Sulla, not Marius, made the army a political instrument, and regular armies saw their general as a magistrate. De Blois: the officers were the link, and a general had to keep his promises and justify himself to his men.

Carry forward

  1. The Republic never made the soldier's future its own business: pay by the campaign, nothing at discharge, land only by a contested law. Whoever could provide land and money held the army, which is why Augustus' military treasury (module 6.4) was a constitutional act.
  2. Armies were persuaded, not owned: oath, donative, officers and a legal cause all mattered, and soldiers deserted, mutinied or forced their generals to terms when the bargain failed. Test every claim about a "client army" against what the soldiers were offered.
  3. Victory became a title of rule: acclamation as imperator, the triumph and names such as Felix, Magnus and Imperator set a military source of legitimacy beside election, and the Principate made that source a monopoly.

Written with Opus 5.5, reviewed with Fable 5.1

The prompt this answers
Give me an in-depth report on the relationship between Roman generals and their armies from Marius to Octavian, extending modules 5.2 to 5.5 and 9.2. Cover: the property qualification and the recruitment of the poorest citizens, and the modern doubt over whether Marius changed recruitment as much as the textbooks say; long commands and provinces as bases of power; the veteran problem and land settlement; the soldiers' oath, donatives and loyalty to the general rather than the state; the marches on Rome of 88, 83 to 82, 49 and 43 BC and how each army was persuaded; Caesar and his legions (the Tenth, the mutinies of 49 and 47); triumphs, salutations as imperator, and the ideology of victory; and the argument over whether the 'client army' explains the fall of the Republic (Gabba, Brunt, Keaveney, de Blois). Format: about 2500 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
ROME · UNIT 13 · Deep dive III: Roman philosophy, the Stoics and Marcus Aurelius · 13.1 · 2,831 words

Philosophy comes to Rome

Edicts and expulsions, 181–92 BCPanaetius and the Romans who heard himPosidonius at RhodesThe philosopher in the houseAthens and Rhodes: the finishing schoolCicero's Latin philosophy, in outlineWhy the Romans took the ethicsWhat the suspicion was aboutSelf-testCarry forward

Edicts and expulsions, 181–92 BC

Module 4.5 tells the first three episodes, and each needs only a sentence here. In 181 a praetor had Greek books of philosophy, found in a chest at the supposed tomb of Numa, burned as dangerous to religion (Livy 40.29). In 161 the Senate authorised the praetor Marcus Pomponius to see that philosophers and rhetors did not remain in Rome (Gellius 15.11.1). In 155 Carneades argued for justice one day and against it the next (Lactantius, Divine Institutes 5.14), and Cato urged the Senate to send the embassy home (Plutarch, Cato Maior 22).

Two further measures complete the series. Athenaeus records that the Romans expelled two Epicureans, Alcaeus and Philiscus, in the consulship of a Lucius Postumius, because of the pleasures they introduced (12.547a); Aelian repeats the story and makes the young their victims (Historical Miscellany 9.12). The likely consuls of that name held office in 173 and 154, so the date is uncertain.

In 92 the censors Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Lucius Licinius Crassus, the orator, issued an edict that Suetonius (On Grammarians and Rhetoricians 25) and Gellius (15.11.2) preserve. Men had set up a new kind of teaching and called themselves Latin rhetors, and young men idled whole days in their schools; the ancestors had laid down what their children should learn and which schools they should attend; these novelties, against custom and ancestral usage, neither pleased the censors nor seemed right. The edict declared that displeasure to teachers and pupils alike and expelled no one. In Cicero's dialogue Crassus explains that the new masters could teach nothing but boldness, a school of impudence (On the Orator 3.93–94); Tacitus remembered the phrase (Dialogue on Orators 35.1).

None of these measures names a doctrine. Each targets teachers and their hold on the young, asserts that the ancestors decide what a Roman boy learns, and works by declaration with little enforcement: within a generation of 161 a Stoic lived in Scipio Aemilianus' house. Erich Gruen (Studies in Greek Culture and Roman Policy, 1990) reads the series as gestures by which the governing class displayed its authority over Hellenism rather than attempts to stop it. The edict of 92 was not even aimed at Greeks, but at Romans teaching Romans in Latin.

Where sources disagree. The edict speaks only of custom and Cicero gives Crassus only a teacher's reason. Friedrich Marx, in his edition of the Rhetorica ad Herennium (1894), saw a political act against Latin rhetoric under Lucius Plotius Gallus, which would open oratory to men outside the Greek-educated nobility and to Marius' friends. Matthias Gelzer rejected the thesis, and Jürgen von Ungern-Sternberg (Chiron, 1973) found nothing certain about Plotius' politics. Suetonius' one witness is a letter of Cicero recalling that learned men kept him as a boy from Plotius' school, because Greek exercises trained the mind better (On Grammarians and Rhetoricians 26).

Panaetius and the Romans who heard him

Module 4.5 places Panaetius in Scipio Aemilianus' household, at home and on campaign (Velleius Paterculus 1.13.3), and weighs the modern "Scipionic circle"; Greek module 12.7 gives the doctrines he softened or dropped. What matters here is what he taught Romans. Cicero's Laelius recalls Scipio discussing the state with Panaetius in Polybius' presence, two Greeks the most expert in public affairs (On the Republic 1.34). The teaching was practical: Panaetius wrote to Quintus Aelius Tubero on enduring pain (On Ends 4.23), and Cicero praises him for avoiding the gloom and harshness of the other Stoics (4.79). Laelius heard Diogenes of Babylon as a young man and Panaetius later (2.24).

His pupils show what the school meant in a Roman career. Publius Rutilius Rufus, who had heard Panaetius (On Duties 3.10), was condemned for extortion by an equestrian jury in 92 (module 5.2); he refused to let his advocates plead for pity and preferred conviction to a defence beneath the truth (On the Orator 1.229–230), and spent his exile at Smyrna (Tacitus, Annals 4.43). When Quintus Fabius Maximus gave the funeral feast for his uncle Scipio, Tubero, another nephew, spread the couches with goatskins and set out Samian crockery, and the voters, Cicero says, punished the austerity by rejecting him for the praetorship (Pro Murena 75–76). Athenaeus, probably following Posidonius, names Rutilius, Tubero and Mucius Scaevola as the only Romans who kept Fannius' sumptuary law (6.274c–e). The lessons were endurance, frugality and clean hands in office. Panaetius' On Proper Functions, the model of Cicero's On Duties, and its four personae are deep dive module 13.2's.

Posidonius at Rhodes

Greek module 12.7 gives Posidonius' doctrine, his travels and his embassy to Rome in 87/86, when he saw Marius in his last illness (Plutarch, Marius 45). At Rhodes he became a fixed point for Romans going east. Cicero names him with Diodotus, Philo and Antiochus as the men who formed him (On the Nature of the Gods 1.6), and Plutarch says that at Rhodes Cicero studied oratory with Apollonius Molon and philosophy with Posidonius (Cicero 4). The tie outlasted the student years: in 60 Cicero sent him a Greek memoir of his consulship to be worked up in style, and Posidonius replied that reading it had not encouraged him to write but frightened him off (Letters to Atticus 2.1.2).

Pompey came as a conqueror. Returning from the Mithridatic war in 62, he heard the Rhodian teachers and gave each a talent, and Posidonius wrote up the lecture he gave before him (Plutarch, Pompey 42). Pliny says Pompey, about to enter Posidonius' house, forbade his lictor to knock as custom required and lowered his fasces to the door of learning, the man to whom East and West had submitted (Natural History 7.112). Pompey himself told the story Cicero repeats: he found the philosopher crippled by gout, and Posidonius lectured from his bed that nothing is good but the honourable, telling the pain at each spasm that it would never make him admit it was an evil (Tusculan Disputations 2.61). Strabo calls him Pompey's friend and says he wrote Pompey's history (11.1.6).

Both sides gained: the general showed reverence for Greek wisdom before the Greek world he was reordering, and the philosopher gained a patron and a subject. Rhodes, a free ally on the road to Asia, offered what Athens after Sulla's siege could not.

Where sources disagree. Cicero's own account of his travels names at Rhodes only Molon, the rhetor he had already heard at Rome (Brutus 316); Plutarch adds Posidonius (Cicero 4). Cicero's list of his teachers (On the Nature of the Gods 1.6) supports Plutarch, though the Brutus, which names Philo, Diodotus and Antiochus, is silent. Whether Cicero followed a course or paid calls cannot be settled.

The philosopher in the house

Most Greek philosophers entered Roman life through a household. Deep dive module 13.3 takes Philodemus with Piso and Antiochus with Lucullus. The type was well established: Marcus Pupius Piso kept the Peripatetic Staseas of Naples with him for years (On Ends 5.8), and Crassus' companion Alexander the Peripatetic was lent a cloak for each journey and asked for it back on return (Plutarch, Crassus 3). The philosopher taught the sons, followed his patron to provinces and camps, and lent the house a name for learning.

Diodotus

Cicero worked with the Stoic Diodotus, above all at dialectic, and says that he lived in his house and had lately died there (Brutus 309). Blind in old age, Diodotus went on studying, had books read to him day and night, played the lyre in the Pythagorean manner and, what seemed impossible without sight, taught geometry (Tusculan Disputations 5.113). He died in 59 and left Cicero his property (Letters to Atticus 2.20.6). A resident of more than twenty-five years who made his patron his heir was a companion, not a hired tutor.

The two Athenodori

Strabo, listing the philosophers of Tarsus, keeps two Stoics of the name apart (14.5.14). Athenodorus Cordylion lived with Marcus Cato and died in his house. Plutarch tells how Cato, a military tribune in Macedonia about 67, used his leave to sail to Pergamum and persuade the old man, who had refused the friendship of kings and governors, to join him, and came back prouder of this capture than Pompey and Lucullus of their kingdoms (Cato Minor 10). He is probably the Athenodorus who, as keeper of the library at Pergamum, cut the embarrassing passages from Zeno's Republic (Diogenes Laertius 7.34; Greek module 12.7). Deep dive module 13.4 follows him into Cato's Stoicism.

Athenodorus son of Sandon taught the young Octavian and was greatly honoured by him; in old age he went home to Tarsus and, with the authority Augustus gave him, drove out Boethus, who had risen by flattering Antony, and reformed the city's government (Strabo 14.5.14). A saying in Plutarch's collection shows the courtier: taking leave because of his age, he advised Augustus, when angry, to say or do nothing until he had recited the twenty-four letters of the alphabet, and Augustus took his hand and kept him another year (Sayings of Kings and Commanders 207c).

Arius

Arius of Alexandria was the court philosopher in the full sense: Suetonius says Augustus' learning came from living with Arius and his sons Dionysius and Nicanor (Augustus 89.1). Entering Alexandria in 30, Octavian walked hand in hand with Arius and told the citizens he spared them for Alexander's sake, for the city's beauty and as a favour to his friend (Plutarch, Antony 80; Dio 51.16). Plutarch adds that Arius helped seal Caesarion's death with a pun on Homer: too many Caesars are not a good thing (Antony 81). Seneca gives the consolation Arius offered Livia after Drusus died in 9 BC (Consolation to Marcia 4–5). That he is the Arius Didymus whose epitome of Stoic ethics Stobaeus keeps (Greek module 12.7) is usually assumed; Tryggve Göransson (Albinus, Alcinous, Arius Didymus, 1995) challenged the traditional picture of Arius as that doxographer.

Athens and Rhodes: the finishing school

Greek module 7.3 states the pattern in a sentence: the senatorial boy finished his education at Athens or Rhodes. Cicero's Brutus gives the fullest case (306–316). At Rome he heard Philo of Larissa, head of the Academy, who had fled the Mithridatic war in 88 (Greek module 12.8 takes his doctrine), Molon on a visit, and Diodotus at home. In 79 he left for two years: six months at Athens with Antiochus, the rhetors of Asia, then Molon again at Rhodes, returning in 77, he says, almost changed. At Athens he and Atticus heard the Epicureans Phaedrus and Zeno (On Ends 1.16), and Atticus stayed in the city for some twenty years (Nepos, Atticus 2–4). Caesar was captured by pirates on his way to study under Molon at Rhodes (Suetonius, Julius 4).

The next generation followed. Horace says Athens added a little more art, so that he might wish to tell straight from crooked and seek the truth among the groves of Academus (Epistles 2.2.43–45), until civil war swept him away. In 44 Brutus at Athens attended the Academic Theomnestus and the Peripatetic Cratippus and drew the young Romans studying there into his army (Plutarch, Brutus 24); Cicero's son, Cratippus' pupil, was among them (deep dive module 13.3). The tour mixed rhetoric, philosophy and pilgrimage to the places of Plato and Demosthenes (On Ends 5.1–5); nobody expected a Roman to stay.

Where sources disagree. Cicero says he went abroad in 79 because his thin frame and strained voice needed rest and a gentler delivery (Brutus 313–314). Plutarch says he feared Sulla after defending Sextus Roscius and gave out his health as a pretext, and that he meant, if shut out of public life, to move to Athens and live as a philosopher (Cicero 3–4). Cicero's version is his own, but written in 46 to justify a career.

Cicero's Latin philosophy, in outline

Module 5.6 lists the works of 45–44, gives Cicero's reason (with the state ruled by one man, teaching Romans philosophy was the service left to him) and his new Latin words. Two things matter here. First, he made Roman nobles the speakers: Cato expounds the Stoics, Torquatus the Epicureans, Lucullus Antiochus, Varro the Old Academy. He knew the objection and met it: some thought it unbecoming to show men of such rank discussing philosophy, others doubted they had the learning (Academica 2.5–7). The dialogues naturalise Greek argument by setting it in consulars' villas.

Second, his prefaces catalogue the Roman objections. Some disapprove of philosophising at all; some allow it if pursued lightly; some would rather read the Greeks; some think it beneath his rank (On Ends 1.1–3). His answers became the standard Roman defence. The lost Hortensius turned the nineteen-year-old Augustine to philosophy (Confessions 3.4.7).

Why the Romans took the ethics

Greek module 12.7 hands on the question why Romans kept Stoic ethics and left the physics and logic that held it up; Greek module 7.2 outlines the systems they chose from. Four reasons can be read from the sources.

  1. The goal was action. Virtue, unlike an art, cannot be held without being used, and its greatest use is governing the state (On the Republic 1.2); all the praise of virtue lies in action, so to be drawn from affairs by study is against duty (On Duties 1.19). Knowledge that did not serve the community ranked below the duties of fellowship (1.153–158).
  2. Philosophy came through rhetoric. Romans met it in an orator's training, and Cicero's Crassus wants the orator to master philosophy's matter because speeches turn on justice, duty and the good (On the Orator 3). Logic became the art of argument.
  3. Religion was public business. Stoic theology and Epicurean indifference both bore on a cult run by magistrates, and Romans kept school and cult apart, as the three theologies of Scaevola and Varro and the pontiff Cotta's trust in the ancestors show (module 2.1).
  4. Latin lacked the terms. Lucretius lamented it and Cicero coined words (module 5.6), but ethics could be argued in the language of virtus, officium and honestum that Romans already used of their own conduct.

The teachers pointed the same way. The Stoicism Romans met in Scipio's house and at Rhodes was the revised school of Panaetius and Posidonius (Greek module 12.7), spoken to men of affairs. A century on, Seneca mocked the logic that proves a syllable gnaws cheese because a mouse is a syllable (Letters 48.6), as a waste of a short life.

Where sources disagree. The picture is partly a modern inheritance. Eduard Zeller's history of Greek philosophy classed the period as eclecticism, a mixing of doctrines for use, and the label coloured judgements of Cicero for a century. Elizabeth Rawson (Intellectual Life in the Late Roman Republic, 1985) and Katharina Volk (The Roman Republic of Letters, 2021) show senators arguing physics, astronomy, grammar and theology in earnest, and John Dillon and A. A. Long (eds.), The Question of "Eclecticism" (1988), took the label apart. Lucretius' six books of physics and Cicero's On Fate tell against the thesis; Cicero's own ranking of action above knowledge tells for it.

What the suspicion was about

Roman objections to philosophy were rarely objections to doctrines. Cato wanted the envoys of 155 gone so that the youth would listen to laws and magistrates as before (module 4.5). Four fears recur. Time: the edict of 92 complains of young men idling whole days, and philosophy was otium, leisure a Roman had to justify against business. Authority: the ancestors decided what children learned, and a man who could argue both sides of justice, as Carneades did, claimed a court above custom. Politics: Tiberius Gracchus had a Stoic adviser, Blossius of Cumae, who said he would have burned the Capitol at Tiberius' bidding (module 5.1), and the imperial charge that Stoicism made men restless and meddling (Tacitus, Annals 14.57) is deep dive module 13.4's. Manners: philosophy was Greek, and Athenaeus' Epicureans were expelled for the pleasures they brought.

The Roman answer was not rejection but measure. Ennius' Neoptolemus said he must philosophise, but in few words, since to do it wholly did not please him (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 2.1; On the Orator 2.156); Tacitus gives the classic case. Agricola used to say that in early youth, studying at Massilia, he drank in philosophy more keenly than was allowed to a Roman and a senator, ultra quam concessum Romano ac senatori, had not his mother's prudence restrained his burning spirit; reason and age tempered him, and he kept from wisdom what is hardest, a sense of measure (Agricola 4). Suetonius says Agrippina turned the young Nero from philosophy as unsuited to a future ruler (Nero 52). Two centuries after the decree of 161, governing families still treated philosophy as a drug to be dosed.

Self-test

  1. What did the censors' edict of 92 BC object to, and what penalty did it impose?
    Answer

    New schools of Latin rhetors where young men idled whole days, against the ancestral rule on what children should learn. It declared them displeasing to teachers and pupils and expelled no one (Suetonius, On Grammarians and Rhetoricians 25; Gellius 15.11.2).

  2. Why is the date of the expulsion of Alcaeus and Philiscus uncertain?
    Answer

    Athenaeus (12.547a) dates it only by the consulship of a Lucius Postumius, and the likely consuls of that name held office in 173 and 154; no other source fixes the year.

  3. How did Crassus justify the edict, and what political reading has been offered?
    Answer

    In On the Orator 3.93–94 he says the Latin rhetors could teach only boldness, a school of impudence. Marx (1894) saw a blow at Latin oratory open to Marius' friends; Gelzer rejected the thesis, and von Ungern-Sternberg found nothing certain about Plotius' politics.

  4. Name two Roman pupils of Panaetius and say how each lived the teaching.
    Answer

    Rutilius Rufus refused to plead for pity at his trial in 92 and accepted conviction (On the Orator 1.229–230). Tubero's austere funeral feast for Scipio cost him the praetorship (Pro Murena 75–76).

  5. What did Pompey do at Posidonius' door, and what did it show?
    Answer

    He forbade his lictor to knock and lowered his fasces (Pliny, Natural History 7.112). The conqueror of the East deferred in public to Greek learning, which advertised his own standing as well as the philosopher's.

  6. Who was Diodotus, and what does his case show about house philosophers?
    Answer

    A Stoic, blind in old age, who lived in Cicero's house, trained him in dialectic and died there in 59, leaving him his property (Brutus 309; Tusculan Disputations 5.113; Letters to Atticus 2.20.6). The relation was lifelong companionship, not hired tuition.

  7. How does Strabo keep the two Athenodori apart?
    Answer

    Cordylion lived with Cato and died in his house; the son of Sandon taught Octavian, was honoured by him and in old age reformed the government of Tarsus (14.5.14).

  8. What roles does Arius play in the sources for Augustus?
    Answer

    Teacher and companion (Suetonius, Augustus 89.1); counsellor at Alexandria in 30, where the city was spared partly for his sake and Caesarion's death was sealed with his pun (Plutarch, Antony 80–81); and consoler of Livia (Seneca, Consolation to Marcia 4–5).

  9. Give two passages in which Cicero ranks action above knowledge.
    Answer

    Virtue exists only in use, and its greatest use is governing the state (On the Republic 1.2). All praise of virtue lies in action, so study that draws a man from affairs is against duty (On Duties 1.19).

  10. What does Tacitus, Agricola 4, show about Roman attitudes to philosophy in the first century AD?
    Answer

    That philosophy was respected but rationed: Agricola's mother curbed a zeal beyond what was allowed a Roman and a senator, and he kept from wisdom a sense of measure, the same limit Ennius' Neoptolemus set two centuries earlier.

Carry forward

  1. Rome never banned philosophy as doctrine. It regulated teachers, the young and the use of time, and its measures asserted that the ancestors, not foreign masters, decided what a Roman learned, usually without force behind the words.
  2. Greek philosophy entered Rome through persons: house philosophers, teachers at Athens and Rhodes, and the patrons who kept them. Its Roman form was shaped by that client relation and by teachers who addressed men of affairs rather than sages.
  3. Romans took philosophy in measure and for use, ethics for conduct and office and the rest as equipment for argument. How much philosophy a Roman in public life may allow himself is the question every later Roman Stoic faces, from Cato to Marcus Aurelius.
